en: Oṃ tat sat. Salutations to Brahman.
*The Garland of Jewels of Saṃskāras*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita.
In this regard, the first section:
The Benediction.
Seeing her parents come to kiss the pair of her cheeks out of affection, she quickly closed her stainless lotus-face, which was slightly smiling.
Then, O fair-faced one, as those two Śivas were thus engaged with one another, may that blessed Lord, the elephant-faced child by whom they were so entertained, protect you. || 1 ||
I bow to that elephant-faced one, praised by the gods, peaceful, endowed with knowledge,
encompassed by the three tantras and yantras, and bestowing welfare upon the worlds.
This is the arrangement of a six-petaled lotus. [I praise] Vināyaka, who has a beautiful neck, who is praised by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu,
who has destroyed the infinite asuras, and who holds a tusk and a noose in his hands.
I worship and ever honor the Lord, who shines with a forehead radiant like the sun, who is the supreme illuminator, the divine one, the all-pervading master who possesses a vast staff-like elephant.
This is the arrangement of an eight-petaled lotus.
Homage to that Gaṇeśa, the bestower of theoretical and practical knowledge,
whose name acts like fire for the total burning away of the forest of obstacles.
I shall praise the god Vidyāmahāgaṇapati, as well as Vyāḍīśvara,
Yogeśvarī, the goddess of speech (Sarasvatī), Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and the gurus.
Having paid homage to Satyāṣāḍha, the best of sages, whose hair was like refined gold,
as well as to his parents and likewise to Mātṛdatta.
Having examined the Sūtra-bhāṣya, various manuals (paddhati), and the Smṛtis, the learned Gopīnātha, known by the surname Okopa, has [composed this] out of curiosity. 7.
For the pleasure of Viśveśa and to bring satisfaction to the wise and the virtuous,
this manual entitled the *Saṃskāraratnamālā* (The Garland of Jewels of Sacraments) is being composed.
Since the two manuals (paddhati) composed by Mahādeva and Maheśa did not include the root text (mūla), [I have composed this] in order to collect that as well.
In some places, having abandoned the commentary composed by those two which lacked the natural elegance of the Sūtra,
he likewise proceeded to compose another one there.
In some sūtras, no commentary whatsoever was provided by the author of the Bhāṣya;
therefore, in order to explain even those sūtras, another commentary [is composed] in certain places.
Therefore, I am making this effort to compose [this work] in accordance with the natural intent of the Sūtras;
[I address] those wise ones who are worthy of respect, free from envy, and endowed with virtuous conduct.
Bowing down again and again with palms joined in reverence, I pray:
whatever has been left unsaid here, or poorly expressed, due to the dullness of my intellect or my lack of learning; [may that be forgiven].
That which is to be filled and that which is to be purified must be discerned by the wise. || 13 ||

The formative forces (*saṃskāra*). Now, regarding the formative forces, Gautama says of them: "The rites of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), and the initiation (*upanayana*); the four Vedic vows (*vedavrata*); the ceremonial bath (*snāna*); union with the partner in dharma (*sahadharmacāriṇī-saṃyoga*); the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahāyajña*); and the seven forms of domestic sacrifice (*pākayajña-saṃsthā*)—namely, the *aṣṭakā*, the *pārvaṇa*, the *śrāddha*, the *śrāvaṇī*, the *āgrahāyaṇī*, the *caitrī*, and the *āśvayujī*; and [the seven forms of the fire sacrifice]: the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the daily fire offering (*agnihotra*), the new and full moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, the bound animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*), and the *sautrāmaṇī*."

"The forms of the *havis*-sacrifices are seven; the forms of the *soma*-sacrifices are seven—namely, the *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśī*, *vājapeya*, *atirātra*, and *aptoryāma*. These constitute the forty sacraments (*saṃskāras*). Furthermore, there are eight qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇas*): compassion toward all beings, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of weariness, auspiciousness, generosity, and lack of possessiveness. He who possesses these forty sacraments and the eight qualities of the self attains union with Brahman."

The *snāna* is the ritual of returning home from one's teacher. Marriage is the union with a partner who shares religious duties (*sahadharmacāriṇī*). The *pārvaṇa* is the *sthālīpāka* offering performed on the new and full moon days; it is called *śrāddha* because it is a specific instance (*saṃsthā*) of that rite. We shall establish this in the section on *śrāddha*. The *śrāvaṇī* is the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa; the *śravaṇākarma* is to be performed there. The *āgrahāyaṇī* is the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa; the *pratyavarohaṇa* is to be performed there. The *caitrī* is the full moon day of Caitra; the *śūlagava* sacrifice is to be performed there.

The full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja (Āśvinī) is the occasion for which the Āśvayujī rite is to be performed. Compassion (*dayā*) is the protection of one who is distressed, even if that person is an enemy. Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is the absence of anger toward another, whether external or internal, even when suffering is inflicted upon oneself; it is the same as patience (*kṣānti*). Envy (*asūyā*) is the failure to acknowledge the virtues of those possessed of them; its opposite is non-envy (*anasūyā*). Purity (*śauca*) is the firm adherence to one's own duty (*svadharma*), preceded by the avoidance of association with the censurable and the consumption of forbidden food.

*Āyāsa* is the performance of minor actions that cause physical pain; *anāyāsa* is the opposite of that. *Maṅgala* is the performance of commendable actions preceded by the avoidance of uncommendable ones; its state is *māṅgalya*. *Akārpaṇya* is daily giving to a worthy recipient with devotion and according to one’s capacity, characterized by a lack of wretchedness. *Spṛhā* is the longing for another’s property; *aspṛhā* is the opposite of that. Since the author of the Sūtra does not prescribe [the *Aupāsanahoma*] specifically for the month of Āśvayuja, the *Aupāsanahoma* should be understood as the concluding rite (*saṃsthā*) therein.
And it has been stated by Vaikhānasa:

"The Sthālīpāka, the Aṣṭakā, the Amāśrāddha, the Aupāsana-homa, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrahāyaṇī, and the Caitrī—these are the seven forms of the Pākayajña; some, however, prescribe the Vaiśvadeva in place of the Caitrī."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that there are seven forms of the *pākayajña* sacrifices. With reference to the *pākayajña* sacrifices, the property of being seven is enjoined. And this "being seven" is, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) on the final word, the state of being one of the seven. In a context involving the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that the predicate is understood as being co-extensive with (*vyāpaka*) the subject, in terms of the defining characteristic (*avacchedaka-rūpa*) of the predicate. The defining characteristic of the subject is the state of being a *pākayajña* sacrifice; the defining characteristic of the predicate is the state of being one of the seven.

And that [quality] consists in the absence of the sevenfold division beginning with the *aṣṭaka*. Thus, when the meaning is established as "any one of the seven forms of the *pākayajña*," the exclusion of any addition is also established. By this, the contradiction between proof and non-proof is refuted. Furthermore, the exclusion of deficiency is obtained simply from the connection with the number seven. However, Baudhāyana, in the *Karmāntasūtra*, has stated the view that the forms of the *pākayajña* are even unlimited:
"Some indeed say they are unlimited; whatever else is performed apart from the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), all those are forms of the *pākayajña*."
Regarding this, there is the commentary of Bhavasvāmin: "Whatever is offered without distinction other than in the *tretāgni* fire, all those are forms of the *pākayajña*.
By this, its unlimited nature is demonstrated. In this view, the state of being one of seven is not to be indicated by the word "seven" (*sapta*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Aṅgiras:
Garbhādhāna, puṃsavana, sīmantonnayana, and also bali; "bali" here refers to the viṣṇubali.
The birth-rites, the naming ceremony, the departure from the house, the first feeding of solid food,
the tonsure ceremony, the initiation (upanayana), the four sets of vows (vrata) associated with it,
the ritual bath, the marriage, the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, and the Aṣṭakā rites— each according to its proper time.
The *pārvaṇa* rites of the months of Śrāvaṇa, Āśvayuja, and Mārgaśīrṣa;
the ritual of the formal commencement of Vedic study (*upākarma*); the ritual of its conclusion (*utsarga*); and the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*s) are "obligatory" (*nityaka*).
They are indeed obligatory (*nitya*); the suffix *ka* is used here in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*).
"These sacraments are mandatory, especially for the Brāhmaṇa.
Those twice-born ones who have been consecrated by the twenty-five sacraments are pure and worthy [to participate] in rites such as the Śrāddha, provided they are well-restrained."

In the phrase "of those vows" (*tadvratānām*), the word *tat* (that), which denotes what is well-known, refers to the Veda. Since the venerable teacher Satyāṣāḍha has prescribed the *kāṇḍavratas* (subject-specific vows), the *kāṇḍavratas* are to be understood in place of the [general] Vedic vows. These [vows] will be specified further on as being nine, six, five, or four. [The term] *śrāvaṇyam* refers to the rite performed in the month of Śrāvaṇa; *āśvayujyam* refers to that performed in Āśvayuja; and *mārgaśīrṣyam* refers to that performed in Mārgaśīrṣa.

The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule beginning with "dig-ādi. The meaning is that the *Śravaṇākarma*, the *Āśvayujī*, and the *Pratyavarohaṇa* are to be performed respectively on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa, Āśvayuja, and Mārgaśīrṣa. Regarding the term *pārvaṇa*, it is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) of both "pārvaṇa" and "pārvaṇam," followed by the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*. By this, the *sthālīpāka* of the *pārvaṇa* is also included. *Utsarga* refers to the ritual conclusion (*vedotsarjana*) of Vedic study. In the phrase "in the *śrāddhas*, etc.," the word "etc. includes sacrifices and other such rites. Here, the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *kṣatriya* and *vaiśya* as well.
"From hereafter, the sacraments (saṃskāra) of the twice-born (dvijāti) are stated as being fixed;

for those who are devoid of sacraments, their birth is useless"—since Āśvalāyana employs the term *dvijāti* [here], [the sacraments] are *niyata*, meaning obligatory (*nitya*). In the cited statement of Aṅgiras, the mention of "twenty-five" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaka*) of the sacraments prescribed in their respective Gṛhya-sūtras.

And there is a traditional authority (smṛti) on this point: "All consecratory rites (saṃskāras) must be performed exactly as prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra by one desiring prosperity; otherwise, one does not attain success."
Therefore, there is no fault even if certain sacraments (*saṃskāra*) are not mentioned in our own *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
Āśvalāyana also states their specific designations:
"Sixteen occasional rites (*naimittika*) have been declared, ending with marriage."
The seven sacraments beginning with the Āgrayaṇa are considered to be performed annually.

"The monthly *pārvaṇa* is prescribed for those who are capable, whereas for those who are incapable, it is annual (*vārṣika*). The great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) are obligatory, like the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*).

The meaning is that the sixteen occasional rites (*naimittika*), beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and ending with marriage (*samudvāha*), are mentioned in the words of Aṅgiras. The seven sacraments (*saṃskāra*) other than the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, such as the *āgrayaṇa* and others, are considered annual (*vārṣika*). The *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must be performed every month; however, for those who are incapable, it is annual. For the incapable, it means it should be performed once a year on any new moon day (*amā*).
From this very statement—that "the monthly rite is declared to be the *pārvaṇa*"—it is understood that it must be performed on every new moon (*pratidarśam*).
This is clearly stated in another *smṛti*:
"The *pārvaṇa* should be performed on every new moon; in case of inability, it may be performed annually."
The *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, however, is performed on every single festival day (*parvan*).
Yājñavalkya states:
"The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are the social classes (*varṇas*); the first three are the twice-born (*dvijas*)."
"The rites for them, beginning with conception (*niṣeka*) and ending with the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), are indeed performed with mantras.

Here, *niṣeka* refers to the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). By the word "cremation ground," the funeral rites (*antyakarma*) are indicated. "For them" means for those twice-born (*dvija*). From the statement "for them with mantras," it is understood that for a *śūdra*, the rites are without mantras.
Having stated the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), Yama says:
"A Śūdra of this same description should also be consecrated by means of the rites, but without mantras.

In that regard, because a Śūdra lacks the study of the Vedas and so forth, there is an exclusion of the initiatory section (upanayana-kāṇḍa), the vows, and other such requirements for those purposes. Rites such as the birth-ceremony (jātakarma) and others are performed for women without mantras;
for the Smṛti states: "These rites for women are to be done silently (tūṣṇīm), but the marriage ceremony is accompanied by mantras."
These [rites] begin with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) and end with the tonsure (cūḍā). The fire-oblation (homa), too, is for the twice-born alone:
"By the oblations pertaining to pregnancy, by the birth-ceremony, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle, the sin of the seed and the sin of the womb are wiped away from the twice-born."

In this statement of Manu, because of the mention of the *dvija* (twice-born), Kullūkabhaṭṭa explains that *bīja* refers to the semen and blood; the *baijika* (pertaining to the seed) is that which is produced by intercourse at forbidden times and so forth, while the *gārbhika* (pertaining to the womb) is that which arises from staying within the impure embryonic sac. He states that these two depart [from the child]. Medhātithi, however, holds that since the seed and the womb are not themselves causes of sin, the meaning of the word *enas* (sin/impurity) is merely impurity resulting from the union of both, and not actual moral guilt.
Vijñāneśvara, on the other hand, says:
"In this way, the sin arising from the seed and the womb goes to pacification."
In explaining this, he states that the sin is caused by the transmission of disease and so forth, and not by being born of an outcaste (patita) or similar reasons;
these are the fruits of the purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Now, regarding the fruits of the purificatory rites, in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*:
"Through the *niṣeka* rite, the impurity pertaining to the seed and that pertaining to the womb are wiped away;
the perfection of the purification of the field (*kṣetra*) is recorded as the fruit of the *garbhādhāna*."
And the establishment of masculinity occurs in the womb prior to birth as a male;
"puṃsūti" means the rite of male-production (puṃsavana).
The fruit of the parting-of-the-hair ceremony (sīmantonnayana) should be understood to be like the fruit of the rite of impregnation (niṣeka).
*Niṣeka* is the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*).
Every defect arising from drinking the fluids of the womb is destroyed by the *jāta* [rite];
that is, by the performance of the birth-rites (*jātakarma*) following birth. The word "api" (even/also) is to be construed with the word "doṣa" (defect).
There is an increase in lifespan and luster, as well as success in worldly affairs;
"worldly affairs" (vyavahṛti) means conduct, and "success" refers to its accomplishment. This, indeed, has been declared by the wise to be the fruit of the name-karma (nāmakarma).
From beholding the sun, the increase of lifespan will certainly occur.
The wise have declared that from the time of departure [from the womb], there is an increase in lifespan and prosperity;
furthermore, by eating food, one is purified even from the impurities of the mother's womb.
The increase of strength, longevity, and luster is recorded as the fruit of the *cūḍākarma*;
however, the fruit of the *upanayana* is the prior attainment of the status of a twice-born (*dvijatva*).
"The accomplishment of the qualification for Vedic study has been declared by the seers;
the discharge of the debts to the gods and the ancestors is recorded as the fruit of marriage.

Wherever the word "api" (also) is heard [in this context], it should be understood that the destruction of the impurities pertaining to seed, womb, and mind is also a fruit. Other purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) such as ear-piercing and so forth, mentioned in other scriptures, will be described in their respective places.

Thus [end] the formative suffixes (*saṃskāra*). [Now follow] the mnemonic verses on technical definitions (*paribhāṣā-kārikā*). Since the rituals to be described hereafter depend upon technical definitions, the meaning of those definitions is first set forth in brief by means of these mnemonic verses.
Having bathed, wearing the sacred thread, and possessing purificatory grass, one should perform all rites;
having sipped water, one should sip water again, wearing the *tilaka* mark and with the topknot tied.
One should perform the rite with faith, wearing clean garments;
being composed, adorned, observing silence, and free from hypocrisy, envy, and the like. || 2 ||
Even when engaged in a calamity, one who is pure should perform his ritual duties;
he should not touch another person without cause during the performance of recitations, fire-offerings, and other rites. (3)
If the contact was unintentional, one should touch water;
if the contact was intentional, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Upon contact with one of the three [higher] castes, one should become pure by sipping water (ācamana);
however, upon contact with those of the inverse order (pratiloma), bathing alone is prescribed.
If a man should be without a crest due to defects such as baldness,
he should then wear a lock of hair on the right side, provided with the Brahma-knot.
This rite is to be performed while holding seven blades of darbha grass in the right ear;
one must never do so while wearing only a single garment, nor on an island, nor in the middle of a body of water.
One who is impure should never perform any rite prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
A region that is surrounded on all sides by water is called a dvīpa (island).
That region which is unobstructed is proclaimed as the "intermediate space" (antarāla);
there, one may perform giving, receiving gifts, burnt offerings, eating, and even the offering of oblations (bali).
It should always be performed with the thumb; otherwise, it would belong to the Asuras.
One should perform it with feet not crossed and having already completed the āyāma.
The *praṇava* consisting of three measures (*trimātra*) should always be uttered at the commencement of a ritual act;
one should perform the rite while fasting, except when authorized by the injunctions.
As long as sound proceeds from grinding-machines and the like, and as long as there is the sound of outcasts, Caṇḍālas, and others who have fallen [from their caste]. (12)
One should not perform [any other] ritual action during that time, nor likewise during the two twilights;
having announced the month, fortnight, and so forth, as well as the specific occasions.
One should form the resolve, "I shall perform this action";
and for as many stars as there are connected with that action, [one should recite the corresponding mantras]. (14)
In the same manner, the mention of the days of the week and so forth is appropriate everywhere;
however, this has been stated by some modern author on the basis of reasoning. (15)

In this ritual manual (kalpaka), since the rite is accomplished by days whose [astrological] influence is not fixed, the mention of the weekdays and so forth must be carried out according to the general rule.
The Prāyaugikas, however, perform the recitation starting from the first [deity] alone;
one should perform the ritual action without transgressing the procedure prescribed in one's own scripture. (17)
Having realized that an action was performed incorrectly, one should perform it again at that very moment;
however, if the principal rite itself was not performed, one should perform it again along with all its constituent parts.
If that limb is not performed, there is only expiation and no ritual act;
if the eastern direction is not mentioned, then the northeastern direction is prescribed.
If humility and the like are not specified, the posture of the agent shall be sitting;
however, if the limbs of the agent are not specified, it is proclaimed that the right limb [is to be used]. (20)
The wise Nārāyaṇa thought, "This [distinction] would not apply to the eyes and other sense organs;
for when touching one limb, it is the left hand, and when touching another, it is the other. (21)
The limbs below the navel should not exist, while those above the navel should indeed exist;
it should be understood by the wise that one hand is located at the navel.
If there is disease in the hand, then both [hands] are traditionally recognized as such;
one should not perform the improper touching of the navel or lower body during the time of ritual action.
Bathing is prescribed upon contact with blood, pus, semen, and the like.
For the rites of the gods, the orientation is toward the east, with the conclusion in the northern direction. (24)
It should be situated facing north, or ending toward the east;
or indeed, it may end toward the south, facing westward.
The ancestral rite (pitrya-karma) should be performed clearly if there is explicit instruction;
likewise in the case of touching a limb or touching the hem of a garment.
In acts of cutting, splitting, casting away, and likewise digging;
and in rites pertaining to the ancestors (paitṛka), the Rākṣasas, the Raudra, the Nairṛta, and those of malevolent magic (abhicārika).
Indeed, on these occasions, there should be contact with water:
upon the emission of downward wind (flatus), at laughter, and when speaking untruths. || 28 ||
Upon touching a cat or a mouse, during a cry of distress, when anger arises,
or upon any such other omens, one performing a ritual act should touch water.
"Regarding the bath for dogs and donkeys that has been mentioned, some wise men say that it refers to wild animals; others, however, have declared as follows. (30)
If there is contact with another part of the tail, it shall be the mere touching of water;
however, if the tail itself is touched during the time of a ritual act or while eating, it shall be a formal bath.

Some wise scholars have said that if one touches water in a place where there is no contact with impurity, it is merely a ritual sipping (upasparśana); however, if it is done intentionally, it constitutes a full bath (snāna).
In rites for the gods, the Nirāsa should be performed in the direction known as Saumya (the north);
in rites for the ancestors, it is proclaimed that this should be done in the direction known as Yāmya (the south). || 33 ||

In rites for the gods and in the presence of a neighbor, circumambulation from left to right is prescribed; this should be understood by the wise to apply likewise in rites for the ancestors, but it does not apply during the ritual sprinkling (pariṣecana).
In that case, according to the statement of the author of the Sūtra, there would indeed be no circumambulation;
the *nivīti* position is for rites pertaining to humans, while the *yajñopavīta* position is for rites pertaining to the gods.
However, the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta) should occur in rites for the ancestors (pitrya), provided there is a clear scriptural statement;
both [the methods] should be understood according to the manner prescribed in the Smṛtis regarding the ancillaries mentioned in those Smṛtis. (36)
In cases where the movement is counter-clockwise or with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), there may be an option here regarding the rules prescribed in the Sūtras;
this applies to the fire-oblation, eating, giving gifts, ancestral rites (śrāddha), worship of the gods, and so forth.
One should not perform the sipping of water (ācamana) with the knees extended outward; likewise, one should never walk behind a teacher.
The vessels, the clarified butter, the oblation, and the fire—within these, in sequence, is the Supreme;
whereas the agents are external to them, the performer of the oblation is within them. (39)
Therefore, Brahmā is said to be external compared to others, yet internal to them;
within all these is the wife, and within her, moreover, is the husband.
This should be understood to apply everywhere, except where a specific rule exists;
mantras whose accents are unknown should be employed by practitioners [with the default accent]. (41)

Since Jayantasvāmin has stated everywhere that [the mantra] should be recited with a single accent (ekaśruti) alone, one should likewise [know] the seer, the deity, the meter, the application, and the mental visualization. 42.

Actions must be performed only after having understood [the mantras], according to the Smṛti of the sage Yājñavalkya; [one should know] the seer, the meter, and the deity, as well as the meter, the seer, and the deity. (43)
The sequence should be threefold, consisting of the seer (ṛṣi), the deity (devatā), and the meter (chandas).
According to those learned in the Vedas, the seers of the Sūtra-mantras are remembered as Vāmadeva.
The deity is indicated by the gender; when the deity is not clearly specified, Agni is traditionally understood [as the deity].
Regarding the Sūtra, it is stated in the Pārijātaka that there is no requirement for the knowledge of the Ṛṣi and other such details.

The ancients maintain that there is no requirement for the knowledge of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth in the Vedic sacrifice (*vaitānika makha*), the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*), or likewise in the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*).
Even the syllable *praṇava* is not desired at the beginning of the mantras in the *śrauta* Śrāddha;
others, however, [reject it] here as well because this statement lacks a foundation.

They indeed say that there should be the recollection of the ṛṣi and so forth, as well as the utterance of the *tāra* (Om), at the time of reciting the final syllable of the mantra during the ritual action. (48)
In every case, the preliminary rite (upakrama) must be performed according to the words of the Sūtra-author;
for it is proclaimed that the utterance of "svāhā" at the end of a mantra is obligatory in domestic rites (gārhye). || 49 ||
"Even in a mantra dedicated to the ancestors, where there is no indication of the word 'svadhā', it should end with 'svāhā'; thus it has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya. (50)
If the word *svāhā* occurs at the beginning or in the middle of a mantra,
Āśvalāyana has declared that it should not be employed at the end.
If the recitation of the word *svāhā* occurs immediately before the name of the deity, then this [word *namaḥ*] shall not occur at the end.
If the recitation were not thus, then it would be so even at the end;
for there is indeed an illustration of this meaning in the mantra "svāhādhim". (53)
Therefore, this alone should be followed by the wise:
that which is the wife of Fire (Svāhā) at the end of a mantra is indeed the very form of the mantra itself.
At the end of that, one should employ another [mantra], which is considered to be an integral part of the oblation (homa), according to this statement from the Śaktisaṃgama Tantra: || 55 ||
One should employ the word "svāhā" because of the predominance of the ritual system (tantra);
this is the specific distinction in a Vedic fire-offering (homakarma) when it is joined with the tantric system.
This rule is prescribed for those mantras connected with the injunction for oblation (juhoti);
in the case of offerings made without mantras, the mantra should consist of the name [of the deity] ending in "svāhā."
Upon the completion of the ritual, one should discard the water remaining from the rite.
But one should not employ it for any other purpose, such as for sipping water (ācamana) or washing. || 58 ||
One should recite the mantra while praising the object to be accomplished by that mantra, which is the primary subject; being single-mindedly focused on it, this constitutes *anumantraṇa*.

Because of the excellence of facing and gazing [at the deity], this itself constitutes the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*). Standing properly nearby, one should perform the contemplation of the principal object of worship (*śeṣin*).
Accompanied by the *nati-mudrā*, one should recite the mantra; this is "attendance" (*upasthiti*).
If the listening occurs while standing, then that [attendance] is certain in this case. (61)
Abhimarśa is the recitation of mantras simultaneous with physical contact;
in the ritual injunction, "he mutters," japa consists of the utterance of the four vowels.

Since the nature of recitation (japa) has already been established by the authors of commentaries regarding the rites of touching, consecration, mental visualization, and the presence [of the deity], this [topic] is therefore not further explained here.
The property of having four tones is prescribed for these mantras as well;
however, elsewhere, the mantras shall have a fixed single tone.
According to the opinion of Kātyāyana, here too they may be joined with their own inherent vowels;
however, in all cases, four fixed vowels belong to the *nyūṅkha* and the *sāman*.
The muttering of mantras that are distinct from the calls for response (*saṃvāda*) and the *praisha* formulas should be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*),
as should the *āśrāvaṇa*, the *pravaraṇa*, and the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*.
These [rites] should also be known by the wise as being performed with the Śrauta fires;
however, one should perform the rites beginning with initiation (upanayana) and ending with marriage (vivāha) using the Laukika fire.

Rites known as expiations (prāyaścitta) as well as rites performed for specific desires (kāmya-karma) should always be performed by the wise either in the domestic fire (aupāsana) or in the common secular fire (laukika). || 68 ||

If he performs the *upākarma* and *utsarjana* rites accompanied by his disciples, then he should perform them for the worldly [deities]; however, if he is without disciples, he should do so in his own fire.
The fire-oblation pertaining to the complete recitation (pārāyaṇīyaka) should be performed in the domestic fire;
however, if the performer of the complete recitation is the officiating priest (ṛtvij), then it should be performed in the "world-fire" (lokānala).
The remaining domestic rites should be performed in the *aupāsana* fire;
likewise, those rites for the purification of offspring which are to be accomplished by the *aupāsana* fire [should be done there]. (71)
If, due to the absence of the primary performer, another person should act as the performer,
then that rite may be performed in a common fire, but never in the domestic (gṛhya) fire.
O Brahmin, if one were to perform all the fire-installations [at once], then in that case, the *sthālīpāka*, the rite known as *pārvaṇa*, and likewise the *aupāsana* oblation would be omitted. (73)
Some wise ones have declared that the monthly *śrāddha* and other rites are performed in the *laukikāgni* (worldly fire);
however, the monthly *śrāddha* is performed in the *dakṣiṇāgni*, while the *aṣṭakā* and other such rites are performed in the worldly fire.
Some others also say that Vaijayantī said this:
"The rites for the purification of subjects should indeed take place in the fire of the world. (75)
The mental oblations (citta-homa) taught in other scriptures are causes for reconnection; since they serve to restore lost ritual action, they should indeed be adopted.

Because it is independent, the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña) and other such rites prescribed in other scriptures should be performed in the ordinary fire alone; one should not perform them in the domestic fire (gṛhyānala). || 77 ||
One should perform [the rite] either in the *laukika* fire as prescribed in other *Gṛhya* texts, or in the *gṛhya* fire;
for those who have performed the *sarvādhāna*, it is done in the fire produced by friction (*mathita-anala*).
When the fire has been brought from the house of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), the preparation of the *brahmaudana* rice is performed;
however, if the fire for the marriage is produced by friction (*nirmanthya*), then the churning must take place at this point.
If the second alternative were to be accepted here, that alone should be adopted;
for such a systematic arrangement has been demonstrated by the authors of the commentaries. (80)
When the fire has abundant dry fuel, is well-kindled and smokeless, and when it is glowing with embers and licking [the offerings], one should offer the oblation; never otherwise.

Since the author of the Sūtra has prescribed that in an oblation of clarified butter (ājya-homa) the ladle (darvī) alone is to be used, therefore in that case only that [ladle] should be employed; the offering should not be made with the small spoon (sruva).
In a homa involving milk, curd, and so forth, the implement is a ladle (darvī) or a small spoon (sruva);
however, in a homa prescribed by the Sūtrakāra for solid substances, [the implement is a large ladle].

Alternatively, it should be known that a ladle (darvī) is used for rites such as pacification (śānti), but for the fire-oblation (homa), only the hand is respected by the learned; therefore, in this case, the hand alone is indeed employed.
According to the teacher’s instruction, the offering in the *aupāsana* fire should be made with the hand alone;
however, when no specific substance for the oblation is prescribed, clarified butter (*ājya*) is declared to be used in all cases. (85)
If the measurement of one span (prādeśa) for the fuel-sticks (samidh) is explicitly stated by a direct scriptural injunction, it should apply only in that specific case;
elsewhere, however, this measurement is said to be optional.
Herbs, flour, flowers, wood, roots, fruits, and grass—these may be offered with the hand; nothing else, unless specifically enjoined by a scriptural injunction.
When no specific instruction is given, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall be a cow, gold, or a full vessel;
however, silver must never be given in rites for the gods, for it is born of tears.
A vessel touched by the feet must be washed in every way by the wise;
for the deities do not consume that which has been offered with a vessel cleansed by meat.
The cleansing of vessels should not be performed with the bare hands alone; rather, it should be done with *darbha* grass, or even with blades of grass, leaves, or cloth. (90)
In all religious rites, the wife should be on the right side;
however, during the consecration and the washing of the Brahmins' feet, she is prescribed to be on the left.
"He who, though capable of following the primary rule, conducts himself according to a secondary rule, does not obtain the fruit thereof in the hereafter; so say the Śruti and the Smṛti. (92)

Whether it be much or little, whatever has been prescribed for anyone by their own Gṛhya-sūtra, when that much of the meaning of the scripture has been performed, everything is considered performed. || 93 ||

That which is not prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, provided it is from another branch, is non-contradictory, required by the context, and serves as a necessary supplement—this should be performed by the wise. (94)
When those [rites] are performed, there is excellence of the fruit; however, when they are not performed, there would be no fault.
The duties pertaining to conventional conduct arise from place, caste, and family. (95)
The customs of the villages are to be adopted, provided they do not contradict the scriptures; likewise, the duties of the age (yuga-dharma) are to be adopted everywhere as is appropriate. 96.
Thus, in brief, are the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*).
[Next follow] the determination of the quantity of the materials for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and the characteristics of the creditor (*dhanika*) and others.
Now, the determination of the quantity of the materials for the sacrificial fee to be given by the creditor and others.
Regarding that, first the definition of a moneylender (*dhanika*) and others is given in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
"He who, having increased his wealth, does not consume even a portion of it from that [increase] here, but remains intent on accumulation— he is declared to be a moneylender."
One should obtain only that much annual income by which the maintenance of the family to be supported can be accomplished with ease.

He who has no debt at all is declared to be of middle status. He whose wealth, both ancestral and acquired, exists in great abundance, and who is the acquirer of even more, is called one of great wealth.
A Brahmin who delights in virtuous conduct and turns his back on the acquisition of wealth.
He who is excessively intent on household efforts is known as "poor. Indeed, he who is devoted to right conduct but lacks food is truly poor;
he is a "greatly poor" man if he is destitute of both clothing and grain.
That man who, having increased his wealth, earns only a single meal's worth for the duration of a year,
is indeed declared to be truly blessed for accomplishing this in one year.
He who eats a mouthful for the duration of two years is indeed considered most blessed.
He who earns more than that is declared to be most blessed;
yet he who, without wealth at all, should earn enough for a year's sustenance is likewise praised.

"He is indeed called wise (dhīra), and the gradation [of his status] is as before. Now, regarding the inquiry as to which of these [officiants] should receive how much, the *Vārāha-purāṇa*, introducing the oblation accompanied by a hundred thousand salutations (*lakṣa-namaskāra-homa*), states: "In the case of a homa of a thousand *vyāhṛtis*, one should offer a fee (*śulka*) to the twice-born."
It is said: "In the case of a *lakṣahoma*, [the fee] is one *māṣa* of gold or one hundred barley grains.
Furthermore: "A wealthy person should give two-fold, while one of great wealth should give three-fold;
however, by a poor person, half a barley grain should be given for the sake of attaining merit."
"But one who is very poor should give half of that as the fee (*śulka*).

By this, it follows by implication that for those of middling means and so forth, the amount to be given should be proportionally determined—slightly less than that of the wealthy and slightly more than that of the poor. However, for one who is steadfast (*dhīra*), even less than what is required of the poor, or an equal amount, may be determined according to their profit. This rule applies specifically to items such as gold, and not to items such as cattle, because doubling and other rates have been stated specifically with reference to gold. All of this should be understood to apply to obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and to cases where the quantity has not been explicitly prescribed.

In the case of optional rites (*kāmya*) performed according to the prescribed measurements, however, the fee must be given exactly as ordained. But one who, being wealthy, proclaims himself to be poor and does not give accordingly, does not obtain the fruit of the rite at all.
And so Manu says:
"He who, though capable of following the primary rule (*prathamakalpa*), proceeds by way of the secondary rule (*anukalpa*)."
"He does not obtain the fruit thereof in the hereafter," so says the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Also in another Purāṇa: "That man who indeed practices stinginess regarding wealth when he possesses it..."
"He does not obtain the fruit therein; he is proclaimed as nothing but a thief.

In this manner, for rites that can be accomplished in a short time or those requiring a long time, the amount of material to be used should be determined in accordance with the effort involved. This refers to the injunction regarding the fetching of *kuśa* grass and other such items.
Now, the procedure for fetching *kuśa* grass and so forth in brief: Regarding this, Śātātapa states—"A Brāhmaṇa should fetch fuel-sticks, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and the like himself;
by performing ritual acts with items brought by a Śūdra or purchased, he falls downward."

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *dūrvā* grass and others are included. From the latter half [of the verse], this is also understood: that when one is unable to fetch [the materials] oneself, there is no fault in performing the rite with those fetched by a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya. Regarding the worship with a hundred thousand flowers (*lakṣapuṣpa*) and the like, however, the prohibition against purchasing them does not apply, because the author of the *Mantrakośa* states: "In the case of worship with a hundred thousand flowers and the like, even what is purchased is permitted. By the word "and so forth," the worship with a hundred thousand *dūrvā* blades and other items is intended. Aṅgiras states the time for gathering *kuśa* grass:
"Every day, the cutting of *kuśa* grass for the sake of ritual action is recommended;

however, those *kuśa* blades that were held during a previous rite would not be suitable for the subsequent rites. The meaning is that those *kuśa* blades which were held during a prior ritual are not fit for the rituals being performed immediately thereafter.
Jābāli says:
"On the day of the new moon, a twice-born man may take kuśa grass, kāśa grass, flowers, and fodder such as grass for the sake of cows, even if it is otherwise prohibited."

Regarding the impossibility of cutting *darbha* grass day by day, another *smṛti* text specifies an alternative time: "The *darbha* grass gathered month by month is prescribed for that very same month. In the event that even this is impossible, Viṣṇu states:
"On the new moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, kuśa grass that has been plucked with the appropriate mantra is *ayātayāma*;
such *darbha* grass may be employed again and again.
Here, *ayātayāma* means not stale. *Niyojyāḥ* means that even when already used, they may be employed elsewhere provided there is no prohibition. As for the one who—
On the new moon day, one must not harm even *kuśa* grass or sacrificial fuel;
for since Soma is present everywhere, one who commits violence on that day becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
"If one should injure a tree while the Soma has entered the trees, he is joined with the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this."

Thus, the prohibition refers to that three-muhūrta period during which Soma dwells in the trees, and not to the entire afternoon. It should be understood that this prohibition against cutting during the time when Soma resides in the trees pertains to ordinary (secular) cutting, and not to the cutting of sacrificial fuel (idhma) and the like, because such cutting is prescribed by rule. Regarding the duration of Soma’s residence, it is stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*: "Soma dwells for three muhūrtas in the sun, likewise for three muhūrtas in water, for three muhūrtas in cows, and for three muhūrtas in a tree."
This should be understood as beginning with me. Kauśika states the procedure for cutting the *kuśa* grass:
"Having become pure and standing in a clean place facing the northeast, the best of the twice-born, having touched the *kuśa* blades with the mantra consisting of the syllable *Oṃ*..."
Born together with Viriñci, produced from the creation of Parameṣṭhin—
O Kuśa, dispel all evils and be a bringer of well-being.
Having recited this mantra, then facing the northeast,
one should cut the *darbha* grass once with the syllables *huṃ phaṭ* and extract it.

Since facing east or west is already established by the suffix *ktvā* itself even in the case of cutting, the repetition is for the purpose of excluding (*parisaṃkhyā*) other properties prescribed by specific injunctions. Therefore, because the act of "standing" is what is specifically enjoined, it is excluded from the act of cutting; however, it should be understood that the requirement "having become pure in a clean place" is not excluded, as it is not prescribed by a specific injunction [in this context]. A specific rule regarding certain types of cutting has been stated by Bharadvāja:
"For the sake of rites for the deceased, for the sake of ancestors, and likewise for malevolent magic (*abhicāra*)."
"A twice-born man, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), should cut [the kuśa grass] facing south.
Aṅgiras specifies the kuśa grass to be cut:
"[The kuśas should be] with uncut tips, pure, without holes, tender, and auspicious."
"And a twice-born man should take kuśa grass for the sake of rites for the ancestors and the gods.
Regarding the kuśa grass that must be discarded, Hārīta says: "The kuśas on the road, the kuśas on a funeral pyre, and those kuśas which are on sacrificial grounds..."
"Their abandonment is prescribed in the case of the grass-mat, the seat, and the alms-food.
Āpastamba says:
"Those *darbha* blades used in the *brahmayajña* and those used in the libation to the ancestors..."
"They are defiled by urine and feces; their discarding is prescribed.
Devala says:
"Darbha grass that is impure, contains seeds, or has had its tips cut with the fingernails [is unfit for use]."

"Kuśa grass that is boiled or burnt by fire must be carefully avoided. "Garbhitā" means those joined with internal sheaths. In reality, however, it should be understood that the requirement is mandatory only where the author of the Sūtra has explicitly stated the necessity of being "without internal sheaths" (anantargarbha), whereas in other cases it is not mandatory. Jābāli says:

"One should know that the darbha grasses situated at the middle of the waist-knot and those worn upon the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) are purifiers; as is the body, so too are the kuśa blades. Thus it is stated in another Smṛti.
"In rites for the gods they are rootless; in rites for the ancestors they have roots. Kauśika says:
"Darbha grasses are traditionally said to be with flowers; kuśa grasses are traditionally said to be without flowers."
"It is said that *kutapa* grasses with their roots intact are [called] *kutapas*, while those with their tips cut off are designated as *tṛṇa*.
*Prasūna* means a flower.
Atri says: "The twice-born should [hold] the *darbha* purifiers with both hands..."
"With effort, [it should be] worn together with the Brahma-knot.
The construction is: "with effort, it should be worn together with the Brahma-knot.
He himself says:
"In the *brahmayajña* and in silent recitation (*japa*), the *brahmagranthi* is prescribed; at the time of eating, it is said to be circular. Thus, dharma is not lost.
The definition of the *brahmagranthi* was stated by Hemādri:

"When a loop made of double-folded tips of *darbha* grass is formed by wrapping them clockwise around half [the length] and then inserted from the rear, it is a circular knot (*vartula-granthi*). When the same [grass] is wrapped completely clockwise and then inserted from the front, it is a *brahmagranthi*. Thus says Hārīta:
"The twice-born man who, having placed *kuśa* grass in his left hand, sips water [for *ācamana*]," etc.

"It would become defiled by that blood or impurity"—this refers specifically to the left hand alone. Nor can it be said that this [verse] prohibits the holding of *kuśa* grass in the left hand during ritual sipping (*ācamana*), for it says:
"The twice-born who sips water while holding *darbha* grass in both hands..."
Having enjoyed the fruit of drinking Soma, he too shall obtain the fruit of the sacrifice.

This is because it would result in a contradiction with the statement of Devala: Mārkaṇḍeya says—“One should never sip water while holding the *brahmagranthi*, nor ever with *dūrvā* grass; one should never sip water while holding *kāśa* grass, even out of apprehension regarding the ritual rule.”

Kātyāyana states the characteristics of the *pavitra*: "The *pavitra* should be known as being without a central core, with a tip, made of *kuśa* grass, consisting of two strands, and measuring one span (*prādeśa*) in length, wherever it may be used."

Specifically, the characteristics of the *pavitra* are stated in another Smṛti: "One should make it two finger-breadths at the base, the knot likewise one finger-breadth, and the tip four finger-breadths; such is the characteristic of the *pavitra*."
The method for making the knots of the *pavitra* with the *praṇava* is stated in that very same [text]:
"The wise one should make the knot of the *pavitra* with the *tāra*.
*Tāra* is the *praṇava*.

Mārkaṇḍeya states the number of *darbha* blades for the purifier (*pavitra*): "The purifier for a Brāhmaṇa consists of four *darbha* stalks; it is prescribed that there is a reduction of one by one, respectively, for each social class (*varṇa*)."
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa, however, it is said:
"The purificatory ring (pavitraka) for a Brāhmaṇa consists of seven blades of Darbha grass;
for a Kṣatriya, five; and likewise for a Vaiśya, four."
"For a Śūdra, it is prescribed by two [strands]; likewise for those who are ill.
Or for all [castes], it may be purified by two [strands], whether knotted or not. Thus it is stated in another Smṛti.

"A purifier (pavitraka) should be made with four blades of *darbha* grass, or with two; it is prescribed that for rites pertaining to the gods (*daiva*), it should be performed [with two], while for those pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*), it is said to be with three. Thus, in the *Ratnāvalī*:
"A wise person should wear the *pavitra* between two festival days (*parvan*).
Regarding the expiation for the falling of the *pavitra*, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"When the *pavitra* is known to have fallen, as well as when the rosary (*japamaṇi*) [has fallen]," and so forth.
"A Brahmin, having bathed, should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and the Aghamarṣaṇa [rite]. The word "should recite" (japet) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding the discarding of the purificatory grass (pavitra), a specific rule is stated in another Smṛti:
"In both obligatory and occasional rites, the twice-born should wear the *pavitra* during the performance of the ritual;
at the conclusion of the rite, he should release the knot and discard it. Regarding the absence of *kuśa* grass, another *smṛti* states:
"In the absence of *kuśa* grass, however, *kāśa* grass may be used; *kuśa* and *kāśa* are remembered as equal.
In the absence of *kāśa*, other *darbha* grasses should be taken as appropriate. Thus says Hārīta.
In the absence of kuśa grass, one may use kāśa, dūrvā, rice, or barley; likewise, wheat, wild rice (nīvāra), śyāmāka, uśīra, and valvaja grasses.
"Or rather, muñja grasses are certainly to be used for all rites.
Here, the words *vrīhi*, *yava*, *godhūma*, *nīvāra*, and *śyāmāka* refer to specific types of grass. The details will be explained in the *Ācāraratnamālā*.
[This concludes the section on] the trees for sacrificial vessels and the characteristics of sacrificial vessels.
Regarding the vessels for collection, the *Pātravṛkṣa* states: "The vessels should be made of wood according to one's capacity and suitability;
full vessels and others should be taken, preferably those produced from sacrificial trees."
"In a praiseworthy sacrifice, for the purpose of the *pūrṇapātra*, [the vessels] should be made of wood or bronze"—
here, "vessels" (*pātra*) is the understood term.
"The *sruva* ladle should be made of *khadira* wood, while the *juhū* ladle should be made of *palāśa* wood."
There should be a hole in a section of bark, or else in other trees suitable for sacrifice.
"In the absence of that, the oblation is offered with two leaves of the *palāśa* tree;

but in the absence of *palāśa* leaves, it may be offered with leaves produced from the *pippala* tree. Regarding all *ājya*-offerings in domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*), Mātṛdatta states that a ladle (*darvī*) is prescribed by the Teacher (Ācārya). Because it is seen in another scripture, Mātṛdatta maintains that a ladle made of *khadira* wood may also be accepted; by the use of the word "also," one made of *palāśa* is likewise permitted. This is stated in the *Baudhāyanagṛhya*.

"A ladle made of *khadira* wood is for one desiring splendor; one of *udumbara* wood is for one desiring food; one of *palāśa* wood is for one desiring spiritual luster. Regarding the *sruva* spoon, the same author states the distinction:

"With a *palāśa* spoon, says Ātreya; with a *khadira* one, says Āṅgirasa; with a copper or iron one, says the Ātharvaṇa; and with a black-iron one when performing malevolent magic—this is the universal rule."

The shape of the *darvī* (ladle) is well-known in the world and is called *apalī* in common speech. In the absence of that, whether a *sruva* (small spoon) or a *darvī* is unavailable, a leaf (*parṇa*) should be taken here in place of the middle [leaf], for the Śruti states: "He offers with the middle leaf; this is indeed a *sruc*. A pestle should be made of *khadira* wood, and the mortar should be of *pālāśa* wood.
Alternatively, both elephants should be made; if those are unavailable, they may be made from other trees.
"The vessel for the *praṇītā* waters should be a *camasa* or else a bronze (*kāṃsya*) bowl.
Regarding the characteristics of the clarified butter pot (*ājyasthālī*), the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* states:
"The clarified butter pot should be made from a metallic substance."
Or it may be made of clay, and this applies to all offerings of clarified butter.
"As for the measure of the *ājyasthālī* (ghee-pot), one should have it made according to one's desire; they declare that a ghee-pot which is very firm, without flaws, and auspicious is excellent.

Regarding this, Mātṛdatta and the author of the *Vaijayantī* state that the *ājyasthālī* is made of clay; some, however, say it is made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*). Its size is determined by practical necessity, as no specific measurement has been mentioned, and because of the aforementioned statement from the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: "one should have it made according to one's desire. According to the view that it is made of clay, it must be hand-fashioned and not produced on a potter’s wheel, because the Sūtra author states in the section on the *agnihotra* oblation: "without the turning of a wheel."
Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Karmapradīpa*: "That which is produced on a potter’s wheel is known as *āsura* (demonic), being made of clay;

that very same [clay object], such as a cooking vessel (*sthālī*) and so forth, when fashioned by hand, becomes *daivika* (divine). Regarding the term *acakrāvartām*: that which has a turning or whirling (*āvarta*, *bhrama*) by means of a wheel (*cakra*) is *cakrāvartā*; that which is not so is *acakrāvartā*. This is an adjective qualifying the *agnihotra-sthālī* (the sacrificial vessel for the *agnihotra*). Due to the great abundance of clarified butter (*ājya*) offerings, if a single *ājya-sthālī* is insufficient, several large *ājya-sthālīs* should be employed.
And this has been demonstrated by the Teacher with the sūtra: "Or, due to impossibility, as in the case of the animal rites in the Aśvamedha.

Alternatively, another pouring out (nirvāpa) should be performed. This same rule applies even if there is a spilling of the clarified butter (ājya) contained in the vessel (sthālī). However, those who follow the practical tradition (prāyaugika), having brought ordinary (laukika) clarified butter into the consecrated (saṃskṛta) butter already in the vessel, perform the ritual with that. The vessel for carrying the *praṇītā* water is a cup (*camasa*). It should be made of *nyagrodha* or *rauhītaka* wood, with a handle four finger-breadths long, square in shape, six finger-breadths in length, three finger-breadths deep, and with a square cavity; or it may be without a handle.

In this view, leaving a space of two finger-breadths on all sides, the entire area is the pit itself. Commentators explain in the section on sacrificial animals that the *rauhītaka* is a sub-species of the *vaṭa*. Although Amara states that the word *rauhītaka* applies to a variety of the *karañja*, nevertheless, in the commentary on Amara it is said:
"The word *rohī* or *rauhītaka* is masculine when referring to the *caitya-vaṭa* tree."

Thus, according to another lexicon cited by Rāmāśrama, the word *vaṭa* also denotes [the *rohitaka*]. Although the synonymy between the words *nyagrodha* and *rohitaka* is understood from another lexicon, nevertheless, because they are mentioned separately in the sūtra, "The *naiyagrodha* and *rauhītaka* [vessels]," the word *rohitaka* refers to a specific type of *vaṭa*. The words *rohītaka* and *rohitaka* are synonyms. Alternatively, the cup may be made of *vāraṇa* wood, according to the statement: "But those not intended for the *āhuti* [oblation] are made of *vāraṇa*."

Furthermore, it will be made known in the commentary on the *Somasūtra* that this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is not mandatory for domestic rites (*gārhyakarman*). Accordingly, [the vessel] may also be made from any of the sacrificial woods such as *vikaṅkata*. Mātṛdatta, however, states that the vessel for carrying the *praṇītā* water is made of clay. Some say it may be a bronze vessel when there is a desire for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). The *prokṣaṇī* vessel is shaped like a ladle (*sruk*) and is made from the *vāraṇa* tree, because it is not used for making oblations (*ahomārthatvāt*).
Regarding this, the ritualists (*yājñika*) teach the characteristics of the ladle (*sruk*) as follows:
"Having divided the length into five parts or four, [one part] at the front of two [parts]..."
The penultimate [syllable] is called the "vessel" (pātra) because it serves as the locus for the oblation.
At its uppermost portion, the width should be equal to its own length;
it is described as having the shape of a hollowed palm (añjali),
with a circular cavity therein measuring six finger-breadths in breadth and half that in depth.
A pit is prescribed to be one aratni in measure and the size of the palm of the hand.
The depth at the final portion should be half the width; now follows the determination:
in the last part, there should be a neck, wide by half its length.
Her mouth is like the beak of a swan or like the trunk of an elephant;
the channel from the opening extends as far as is appropriate for its purpose.
The two ears should have apertures, and likewise, they should be directed toward the sides of the neck;
at the base of the opening there should be a lotus, and now follows the description of the staff.
The remaining three or two parts are said to be the shaft (daṇḍa);
at its base, the circumference should be thick, measuring nine finger-breadths.
The circumference is its width;
at the end, it should be five finger-breadths wide, smooth, and circular due to the lathe.
Thus, the state of having a crow’s tail [at the end] of the *daṇḍas* and the *sruks* has been declared.
Baudhāyana stated that the *sruks* should be fashioned according to what is aesthetically pleasing;
however, other specific details should be understood from other scriptural authorities.
According to the opinion of Baudhāyana and others, it may also be one span (prādeśa) in length;
the staff should consist of two parts, the vessel of two parts,
and the neck above that of one part, according to the actual requirements.

"The *sruva* ladles, together with the *sruva* spoon, should be made from the prescribed woods, or otherwise. Since the *khadira* wood was introduced previously in these verses, this constitutes an option alongside it. Regarding the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*): because of the statement "in the domestic rite, [the measure is] a span," the *sruk* ladle for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇī*) should be one span in length. The same applies to the *darvī* spoon and other implements. A span (*vitasti*) is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); some say it is thirteen finger-breadths. The winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is well known in the world; and regarding that, Bharadvāja says it should be made of bamboo (*vaiṇava*) or reed (*nala*). The mortar (*ulūkhalam*) should be made of *pālāśa* or *vāraṇa* wood.

The *muśala* (pestle) is made of *khadira* or *vāraṇa* wood; its dimensions are established by practical necessity. The *dṛṣad* and *upalā* (upper and lower grinding stones), made of stone for the purpose of grinding, have dimensions established by practical necessity. The *pātrī* (pot) is made of metal or clay. As for the *kapālas* (potsherds), they are four fragments obtained by breaking a new earthen jar, suitable for baking the *puroḍāśa* cake; their size is such that when joined together, they result in a width equal to a horse's hoof. However, according to the *Yajñapārśva*: "They should be level, square, and two finger-breadths on all sides."
One should fashion the sacrificial potsherd for offerings made on a single potsherd so that it is the size of the palm of the hand.
"One should fashion [the vessels] with two, three, or more potsherds according to that [rule];
one should always perform such instructions as these as the general rule.
Maṇḍana also says:

The shape is like that of a chariot wheel, measuring six finger-breadths on all sides; each individual skull-fragment should be joined so as to form a complete shell, with a height of two finger-breadths for each; one should thus fashion them separately from clay.

Or else, one should take the parts here from broken jars and the like. Having fashioned a circular pedestal with clay prepared by a potter—measuring six *aṅgulas* on all sides, shaped like a chariot wheel, two *aṅgulas* high, and level with the ground—one should leave a small portion remaining at the bottom and then divide it both lengthwise and crosswise. By this, four *kapālas* (potsherds) are produced. Then, having baked them, one should divide them according to the remaining spaces; for it is precisely here that the word *kapāla* is conventionally established. He himself also describes the measure of the *śamyā*: "The *śamyā* should be three *prādeśas* long, with a rounded tip, and exceedingly beautiful."
"Or it may be one *prādeśa* in measure, according to the view of Laugākṣi.
The grinding stones (*dṛṣad*) and other implements are to be used on the previous day for the *śrāddha*.
Maṇḍana describes the characteristics of the *sruva* ladle as follows:
"The *sruva* ladle has a hole measuring half a finger-breadth and a base of one finger-breadth;
alternatively, its bowl is as large as the circumference of a thumb-joint.
Thus it is stated in the *Āśvalāyana-smṛti*.
"The vessel (*sthālī*) is measured at eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the *prokṣaṇī* at six finger-breadths;
the *camasa* and the butter-vessel (*ājyapātra*) are also recorded as being six finger-breadths.

The height is established by implication. The *sthālī* is the vessel for the *caru* offering; the *ājyapātra* is the vessel for the clarified butter (*ājya*). Some maintain that the measurement of six finger-breadths is an optional alternative to the measurement of a *vitasti* (span) for the *prokṣaṇī*, as established by the rule stating that "in domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*), [the vessels] are one *vitasti* long."

Kātyāyana has described the characteristics of the *caru*-vessel differently: "A firm vessel made of clay or of *udumbara* wood, one span high, with a horizontal opening that is not too large, is praised as a *caru*-vessel."

And this measurement of one span (prādeśamātra) is optional with the measure of eight finger-breadths (aṣṭāṅgula) mentioned in the Āśvalāyana-smṛti. The Audumbarī ladle is made of copper. The definition of the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa) has also been stated by Kātyāyana:

"The stirring-spoon should be of the same wood as the fuel-sticks (idhma), half the size of the fuel-sticks; it should be round, made of wood, broad-tipped, and capable of performing the act of taking portions (avadāna)."

By the phrase "of the kind of fuel-wood" (*idhmajātīya*), once a tree has already been obtained, the specific mention of "made of wood" (*vārkṣa*) is for the purpose of including, as an alternative, a tree other than those used for fuel.
In the *Saṃgraha*: "Having divided the length into five parts, one should take three parts for the staff."
"The lotus-shaped [ladle] is said to have two parts; this is the excellent characteristic of the *darvī*.

Furthermore, this *darvī* should be fashioned according to the requirements of the oblation (*homa*) in rites such as the *pūrṇāhuti*. Where there is an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) taken twice or thrice, as in expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and the like, it should be made accordingly. Where such an oblation of clarified butter does not exist, a *karṣa*-measure of clarified butter should be used, and the *darvī* should be taken with a cavity of such a size that it can hold that amount.
This is the method for the purification of vessels.

Now, briefly, the method for purifying vessels and materials: Among those made of wood, stone, or bamboo, if they are free of stains and have been touched by a person who has not washed after eating (ucchiṣṭa) or similar impurities, purification is achieved by washing them with water. If these same items are stained or have been touched by a person who has not washed after eating, purification is achieved by planing and then washing. If these same items are stained but have been touched by a person who has not washed after eating without leaving a stain, purification is achieved by washing them with hot water.

However, because it is impossible to plane a winnowing basket, it must simply be discarded. Wooden and stone vessels that have been smeared with food residue and licked by the mouths of crows and similar animals are purified by planing; those free from such residue are purified by washing with warm water. The same applies to those licked by the mouths of beasts of prey, excluding the cat. In cases of contact with outcastes (caṇḍāla) and so forth, or defilement by feces, urine, and the like, however, there is always only the option of discarding the object.

The purification of vessels made of gold, silver, bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), and copper that have been smeared with impurities is by means of hot water, cow-dung, ashes, and acid, respectively. For vessels other than those of gold and silver that have been smeared with impurities, defiled by the touch of crows and the like, or touched by a *śūdra*, purification occurs through scraping and washing. The same applies even to unsmeared vessels used by a *śūdra*. However, for vessels of gold and silver, purification is achieved through heating and washing with hot water.

In the case of these [earthenware vessels], if they are touched by Caṇḍālas and others, or if they are defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, they must be remade. Alternatively, purification occurs by immersing them in cow’s urine for seven nights, by burning, and by washing with warm water. For new earthenware vessels that have not been smeared [with oil], if they are touched by a person who has eaten leftovers (ucchiṣṭa) and the like, they are purified by washing with water. Those smeared with clarified butter (ājya), if touched by a person who has eaten leftovers and the like, are purified by burning again. However, those that have been smeared [with oil] and touched by a person who has eaten leftovers and the like, or those defiled by urine, feces, and so forth, must simply be discarded. This is the method of purifying substances.

If one touches the remains of food while handling a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) without its coating, it should be washed with cow-dung water. If one touches the remains of food while the skin still has its coating, purification is achieved by rubbing it with ground white mustard seeds, cow-dung, earth, and warm water. The same applies even when it is defiled by feces, urine, and the like. If solid ground is defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, it should be smeared with cow-dung. If the ground is porous, it should be plowed. If it is moist, it should be covered with pure earth. Objects placed upon impure ground should be washed.

Wood, stone, and bricks carried by men that have been touched by *caṇḍālas* and others must be washed and thoroughly dried. Darbha grass, wood, and other materials brought for sacrifices and similar purposes by Śūdras and others are purified by sprinkling with water while reciting the *Pavamāna-anuvāka*. Rice, barley, wheat, and other grains sufficient for one person's meal must be discarded if they are defiled by feces, urine, or similar impurities. However, if the quantity is greater, one should discard only as much as has been defiled; for the remainder, one should perform sprinkling, threshing, and washing.

For husked rice, there should be cleaning with the hands, sprinkling, and washing. If the sacrificial materials, such as the *caru* (cooked rice) intended for the oblation, are defiled by hair, insects, moths, or the like, they must be discarded entirely. If clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) or oil is touched by food remnants, one should place that vessel in water, remove the contents, and then use them again. Honey, milk, curd, and similar substances should be transferred from that vessel into another vessel before being used. If these substances come into contact with a smear of impurity, they must be discarded entirely.

In all cases other than those involving total abandonment [of the substance], there is a combination of the *pavamāna-anuvāka* recitation and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). When clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and the like come into contact with small insects, hair, and so forth, one should remove that portion, perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), strain it through cloth or similar materials, and silently purify it with two strainers (*pavitra*). The same applies when these substances are smelled by crows and other such creatures. However, in the event of contamination by feces, urine, and the like, there must be total abandonment. The scriptural authorities upon which this is based should be consulted in the works of Hemādri, Vijñāneśvara, Madanapārijāta, and others. This concludes the method for the purification of vessels and substances.

**The Determination of Substitutes** Now, a brief determination of substitutes (*pratinidhi*). In that regard, rice or barley are the primary materials; in their absence, *nīvāra* grain or wheat, as appropriate; in their absence, bamboo seeds (*veṇuyava*); and in their absence, any substance other than prohibited items such as black gram (*māṣa*), chickpea (*caṇaka*), and *kodrava*. Cow’s clarified butter (*gavyājya*) is the primary [offering]; in its absence, buffalo butter; in its absence, goat’s butter; in its absence, oil; and in its absence, the oils of wild sesame (*jartila*), linseed (*atasī*), safflower (*kusumbha*), mustard (*sarṣapa*), madhūka seeds, coconut, and so forth—these are to be accepted in the absence of each preceding one.

If even these are unavailable, one should mix the flour of barley, rice, or *śyāmāka*—whichever is available—with water and employ it for the purpose of clarified butter (*ājya*). The same applies to the application as an ointment (*añjana*). For the purpose of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), *darbha* is primary; in its absence, *kāśa*; in its absence, *śara*, fragrant grass, horse-tail grass (*aśvabāla*), *muñja*, *dūrvā*, barley grass, *śyāmāka* grass, sugarcane leaves, or leaves of milk-exuding trees (*kṣīradruma*)—these are to be taken in the order of preference when each preceding one is unavailable. For the purpose of fuel-sticks (*samit*), the *palāśa* tree is primary; for the purpose of firewood (*idhma*), the *khadira* tree is also acceptable.

In the absence of that [cow’s milk], one may use the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *śamī*, *arka*, *apāmārga*, and so forth; or else, having avoided the prohibited trees—such as the *kapittha*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *kadamba*, *nimba*, *karañja*, *śālmali*, *tilaka*, *cañcāra*, *śleṣmātaka*, *vibhītaka*, and *śākadruma*—one should employ the remaining pure forest trees. Cow’s milk is primary; in its absence, buffalo milk; in its absence, goat’s milk; in its absence, the curd of cows and other animals; and in its absence, water mixed with flour derived from any one of barley, rice, or *śyāmāka*.

According to the opinion of certain teachers, the sequence is as follows: in the absence of cow’s milk, [one uses] curd; in its absence, buffalo milk; in its absence, goat milk; in its absence, the curd of buffaloes and so forth; and in its absence, water mixed with flour derived from any one of barley, rice, or śyāmāka grain. This same order applies to curd as well. Regarding the vessels: in the absence of the aforementioned trees, one should take any sacrificial tree suitable for a vessel, excluding the previously mentioned wood-apple (kapittha) and others. This is the measure of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

Regarding the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the bride-price (*vara*), if the prescribed substances cannot be obtained, one should give wealth according to one's means, measured by the standard set forth in the chapter on Valuation (*mūlyādhyāya*). In that regard, the measure is fivefold, distinguished as cowries (*varāṭaka*), copper, silver, gold, and silver coins (*rajata*). Among these, the value of a single cow, measured by cowries, is two thousand five hundred and sixty cowries. By the copper standard, the value of a single cow is one hundred and forty-four *guñjās* of a copper *paṇa*, since a copper *paṇa* is marked with the "honey-seal" (*madhumudrā*) and consists of one hundred and forty-four *guñjās*.

Since it consists of eighty *guñjās*, it amounts to eighteen *ḍhabbūkās* less a small fraction. According to the silver standard (*raupyaka*), however, the price of one cow is gold measuring two *guñjās* plus a little more than one *yava*. According to the gold standard (*suvarṇa*), the price of one cow is gold measuring forty *māṣakas*. According to the silver standard (*rājata*), the price of one cow is silver measuring forty silver *māṣakas*.

The price of the bridegroom is five thousand and one hundred twenty *varāṭakas* according to the measure of *varāṭakas*; however, by the measure of copper, it amounts to slightly less than thirty-six *ḍhabbukas*; by the measure of silver, it is gold weighing slightly more than four *guñjās* and two *yavas*; by the measure of gold, it is five *suvarṇas* consisting of sixteen *māṣas* each; and by the measure of silver, it is silver weighing eighty *māṣakas*.

In terms of cowrie shells (*varāṭaka*), the price of a bull amounts to seven thousand one hundred and fifty-six; in terms of copper, it is slightly less than fifty-four *ḍhabbūkas*; in terms of silver, it is gold measuring slightly less than seven *guñjās*; in terms of gold, it is seven and a half *suvarṇas*; and in terms of silver, it is one hundred and twenty *rajata-māṣas* of silver.

In the case of an ox, it should be understood that the value is double that of a cow. According to the measurement of cowries (*varāṭaka*), the price of a cow is twelve thousand one hundred and eight cowries. By the measure of copper, this amounts to slightly less than ninety *ḍhabbukās*. By the measure of silver, it is two *māṣakas* plus two *yavas*. By the measure of gold, it is twelve and a half *suvarṇas*. By the measure of silver, it is two hundred *māṣakas*.

By the measure of cowries (*varāṭaka*), the price of a horse is nineteen thousand two hundred cowries. By the measure of copper, it is one hundred twenty-five *ḍhabbūkas*. By the measure of silver, it is three *māṣakas* plus three *yavas* of gold. By the measure of gold, it is nineteen *suvarṇas* less a quarter. By the measure of silver, it is three hundred *māṣakas* of silver.

In terms of the *varāṭaka* measure, the value of the gold is two thousand *varāṭakas*. In terms of the copper measure, it is fourteen *ḍhabbukas*, less eight *guñjās*. In terms of the silver measure, the gold amounts to slightly less than five and a half *māṣas*. In terms of the gold measure, it is thirty-one and a quarter *māṣas*. In terms of the silver measure, it is thirty-one and a quarter silver *māṣas*.

The price of the cloth, measured in cowries (*varāṭaka*), is one thousand two hundred and eighty cowries. Measured in copper, it amounts to slightly less than nine *ḍhabbukas*. Measured in silver, it is slightly less than three *sarṣapa* seeds and more than one *guñjā*. Measured in gold, it is twenty *māṣas* of gold. Measured in silver, it is twenty *māṣas* of silver. Compared to a cow, the price of a goat is one-quarter.

In comparison with the *avāva* (cow), the price of a female slave (*dāsī*) should be understood as five times more, and the price of a male slave (*dāsa*) is equal to that of a female slave. According to the measure of *varāṭaka*, the price of an elephant is six hundred and forty thousand *varāṭakas*. By the measure of copper, according to a rough calculation, it amounts to four thousand five hundred *ḍhabbūkas*. By the measure of silver, according to a rough calculation, it is gold weighing five hundred and eighty *guñjās*.

By the gold standard, the amount is five hundred *māṣas* of gold; by the silver standard, it is five hundred *rājatamāṣas* of silver. The value of a human-carryable vehicle is half that of a milch cow, and the value of a house is equal to that of a bull. This fundamental principle should be consulted in the commentary on the chapter concerning the fees paid to cowherds. In the case of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), even in the absence of a fee, one should offer ground flour, cooked rice, bulbs, roots, fruits, and so forth, in order of preference from the first mentioned to the last.

In the case of optional rites (*kāmyakarma*), however, there is no substitute for the materials exactly as prescribed. But once these rites have been commenced, if the prescribed materials are unavailable, a substitute is indeed permitted.
This concludes the brief exposition on substitutes.
