Now, the necessity of worshipping Gaṇeśa at the beginning of a rite.

Now follows the worship of Gaṇapati. This should be performed at the beginning of all rites for the sake of removing obstacles, according to the indicative power of the mantra: "Nothing is done without you. And from the Padma Purāṇa: "O best of gods, because the Lord of the Gaṇas was not worshipped at the beginning of the sacrifice, this obstacle has indeed arisen from his anger."

In this context, worship is of two kinds: with sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) or with five services (*pañcopacāra*). Among these, in the case of an installed image, because there is no invocation (*āvāhana*) or dismissal (*visarjana*), the worship consists of fourteen services. Alternatively, in place of invocation and dismissal, there is the offering of a handful of flowers (*mantrapuṣpāñjali*); by that means, it becomes a worship of sixteen services. However, in the case of a newly consecrated image, it must indeed be with sixteen services, because worship is impossible for an image and so forth in the absence of invocation. In some instances, however, the dismissal is postponed due to a specific scriptural injunction, just as in the rule: "They perform the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) after the *Āgnimāruta* [section]. This occurs, for example, in the *Grahayajña* and other such rites.
Having thus completed everything in its entirety, one should dismiss all the deities.

Thus, according to the *Mātsya Purāṇa*, the dismissal (*visarjana*) occurs at the end. This very same form of worship—even when it is independent, like a *śrāddha* for a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) performed without rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), yet with certain items omitted by virtue of a specific scriptural injunction—is of this nature. However, the five-fold worship (*pañcopacāra-pūjā*) refers to those cases where the worship of installed deities is prescribed prior to their dismissal.
[Next is] the recitation of auspiciousness (*svastivācana*). Now, regarding the recitation of auspiciousness, Vyāsa says:

"Having honored the Brahmins with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, one should have them recite benedictions during a religious rite, an auspicious occasion, in battle, or upon witnessing a marvel."

The expression "with perfumes, garlands, and so forth" (*gandhamālyādyaiḥ*) is intended to indicate that the preliminary services such as washing the feet, which precede the offering of perfumes, are not mandatory. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), betel-leaf and other items are included. In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "Now, the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*); [rites] for prosperity and for public works; prosperity consists of the sacraments for offspring ending with marriage."
"In the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), the concluding rite (udyāpana), and the act of charity (pūrta).
Here, the mention of *pratiṣṭhā* is indicative of *utsarga* (the ritual release or dedication). Baudhāyana states:

"The construction of bridges, river channels, tanks (*taḍāga*), lotus ponds (*puṣkariṇī*), large wells (*vāpī*), small wells (*kūpa*), temples (*devagṛha*), palaces (*prāsāda*), and dwellings (*vasati*), as well as [the planting of] medicinal herbs and trees, constitutes *pūrta*."

A *setubandha* is a causeway for crossing over water. A river-bank (*nadīkhāta*) refers to a raised ground and steps on the banks of rivers such as the Godāvarī for the purpose of sitting down to perform rites like ritual bathing and the *saṃdhyā* prayers; "river" here is used figuratively, so by the term *khāta*, the area surrounding the roots of trees such as the *aśvattha* is also included. A *taḍāga* is a pond that is closed off [on one side] and possesses steps on its four sides. A *puṣkariṇī* is either a small *taḍāga* or one that is enclosed on all sides with doors and steps on its four sides. A *vāpī* is an open tank that has steps on only one side.

A *kūpa* (well) is well known. A *devagṛha* is a temple. A *prāsāda* is a lofty hall for the purpose of providing food through a perpetual charity (*anna-satra*) and so forth on riverbanks and similar locations. A *vasati* is a place constructed for the lodging of travelers. *Oṣadhivanaspati* refers to flower gardens, groves, and the like. The meaning is that the dedication (*utsarga*) of these objects constitutes *pūrta*, which is designated as *pūrta*. The specific application of this will be explained in the *Utsargaratnamālā*. Āśvalāyana states:
"In both Vedic and Tantric rites, the recitation of the *svasti-vācana* is required at the beginning."
In the *Prayogapārijāta*, another Smṛti states:

"In the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*, as well as in sacrifices for desired results (*iṣṭa*) and those for public welfare (*pūrta*), the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* must first be performed; at the commencement of the rite, the recitation of the *svasti-vācana* [should follow]."

The *iṣṭas* are the rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and the cooked offerings (*sthālīpāka*) associated with them. The *pūrtas* are rites such as the consecration of temples (*pratiṣṭhā*). The *kratavas* are the Soma sacrifices such as the *agniṣṭoma*. Following the literal meaning of the statement that "the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* should be performed first," some practitioners perform the rite in this specific sequence: first the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and then the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*).

Others, however, maintain that in the statement beginning with "garbhādhānādi" (starting from conception), although the matter is already established by the sequence "first the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, then the *svastivācana*," the further mention of "at the beginning of the rite" (*karmādau*) is intended to ensure that the *svastivācana* occurs at the beginning of the rite together with the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Consequently, they say that the actual order of performance is: first the *svastivācana*, followed immediately by the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Baudhāyana, on the other hand, has prescribed that in all cases the *nāndī-śrāddha* is to be performed on the day preceding the day of the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*).

In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*, however, the following rule is stated: "On the day before [the rite] for great [ceremonies], and on that very day for small ones. Here, "great" refers to those rites to be accomplished over many days; "small" refers to those other than these. Other occasions for the recitation of the *svasti* formula are also mentioned in the *Saṃgraha*: "When an auspicious day has arrived, such as at a marriage or likewise at a *caulaka* (tonsure ceremony)—[note:
*caulaka* is the same as *caula*; the suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*)]."
At the binding of the sacred vows, at sacrifices and the like, as well as at birth ceremonies,
at the commencement of a house, upon the acquisition of wealth, at visiting sacred pilgrimage sites,
at the entry into a new home, and at the settling into a village.
"In the sacrifice to the nine planets (navagraha), as well as for the pacification of portents,
in the tethering of elephants and horses, in the gathering of servants and others,
and in all religious rites, the recitation of the Svastivācana should be performed at the commencement."
In the Viśvaprakāśa: "At the commencement and conclusion of Vedic rites (upākarma and utsarjana), as well as for Śrauta rituals,
the recitation of the Svasti-vācana is desired only when they are performed for the first time."

The mention of the *upākarma*, *utsarjana*, and *grahaṇa* rites is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the obligatory rites such as the *śravaṇākarma*, the *āgrahāyaṇī-sthālīpāka*, and others. Regarding this, Yama states the specific rule according to the social classes (*varṇa*):
"The entire procedure for pronouncing the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa;
that same procedure, however, should be performed by the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya without the syllable *oṃ*."
Everything is accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*; some say that it may be without *oṃ*, meaning devoid of the syllable *oṃ*, or even without the syllable *oṃ* uttered aloud.
In the *Saṃgraha*:
"In an auspicious rite, during the recitation for a 'day of merit' (*puṇyāha*), there should be two water-pots."
"One should place one [kalaśa] for the inauspicious," so the knowers of sacrifice understand.

Here, because of the word "should place" (*sthāpayet*), the connection with the inauspicious pertains specifically to the act of placement. Therefore, in the recitation of the *puṇyāha* (declaration of auspiciousness) connected to an auspicious rite, there is no harm even if there is only a single water-pot (*kalaśa*) according to the method stated by Baudhāyana, since there is no placement in that case. Regarding what must be done previously, Hārīta says:
"Having smeared the ground with cow-dung, one should worship it with a *raṅgavalli* (colored powder design)."
One should establish two full jars containing a *prastha* of grain;

regarding the term "to be established" (*pratiṣṭhāpyam*), the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs here due to the prefix [pra-] according to the rule *sunoti* [Pāṇini 8.3.65]. "Full" means filled with water.
One should place them on the right and the left; however, one should cause the northern one to be placed specifically on the north.
Having properly placed betel-leaf, unbroken grains, ritual substances, dūrvā grass, flowers, sandalwood,
vessels smeared with saffron, unbroken grains mixed with saffron,
and auspicious water from sacred fords (tīrtha) into a beautiful pitcher;
"One should place substances such as gold, fruits, and flowers there; and one should set down a vessel filled with unbroken grains (akṣata) upon the water-pot."

This is the meaning: where one is about to perform the *svastivācana* (rite for auspiciousness), one should first smear the ground with cow-dung and decorate it with a multi-colored floral design (*raṅgavallikā*). Then, to the north of that decorated area, one should place a measure of grain (*prastha*) sufficient to form two heaps beneath the two jars that are to be placed there. To the north of that, one should set down two jars filled with pure water, arranged facing north, for the purpose of filling the two jars that are to be placed.

To the north of that, one should place the materials for worship, such as betel and other items. The vessels for the betel, unbroken rice grains, and so forth, should be colored with saffron. Likewise, there should be two water-pots and unbroken rice grains suitable for worship.

Having placed a third pitcher filled with water from sacred fords (puṇyatīrtha) for the purpose of worshipping Gaṇapati and others, and having set down gold, fruit, incense, and other ritual substances near the third pitcher; and having placed two vessels nearby for the purpose of covering the mouths of the two pitchers that are to be installed, and having placed a vessel of unbroken rice (akṣata) upon the pitcher for the purpose of filling those vessels, one should commence the formal resolve (saṃkalpa). Regarding the measurements of a *prastha* and a *pala*, the *Smṛtisaṃgraha* states the measure of a *prastha* as follows:
"A *pala*, a *kuḍava*, a *prastha*, an *āḍhaka*, and a *droṇa*—
these should be understood as increasing fourfold in sequence for the measurement of grain.
Regarding the measure of a *pala*, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"Two *palas* are a *prasṛta*, and one *muṣṭi* is recorded as one *pala*.
However, in the *Skānda Purāṇa*, it is stated otherwise:
"Five *kṛṣṇalas* make a *māṣa*; sixty-four of those [make] a *pala*."
A *kṛṣṇala* is a *guñjā* seed; [the measurement] is by those *māṣas*. Regarding the prohibition against moving the southern pitcher, another *smṛti* states:

"In the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), he who performs the worship of the pitchers should remain steady while stationed on the south, whereas the one stationed on the north may move."

The stability [of the vessel] prior to the pouring of the stream is performed with the mantra "vāstoṣpate. The materials for the pitcher and the five gems are described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* as follows: [the materials for] the pitchers and the five gems.
"They may be made of gold, silver, or copper, or even of clay, provided they possess the proper characteristics.
Excluding gold, silver, ruby, and coral,
these are known as the 'five jewels' (pañcaratna), which are beloved by all the gods."
In the absence of the five jewels, gold [is used], according to the *Ādityapurāṇa*: "In the absence of all jewels, one should employ gold everywhere.
There are also five sprouts and five barks.
Regarding the five shoots and the barks, the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa* states:
"The five shoots are to be known as those originating from the *nyagrodha*, *pippala*, *plakṣa*, *jambū*, and *cūta* trees; their barks are likewise desired."

*Nyagrodha* is the banyan tree (*vaṭa*). *Pippala* is the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*). *Plakṣa* is well known by the vernacular name *pāyarī*. *Jambū* is well known. *Cūta* is the mango tree (*āmravṛkṣa*). These are the trees [mentioned]. However, in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, the *udumbara* is mentioned in place of the *jambū*.
[Now for] the group of all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhigaṇa*).
All the medicinal herbs are listed in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"Kuṣṭha, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, candana, saṭī, campaka, and mustā are known as the group of all medicinal herbs.

*Kuṣṭha* is well-known in the vernacular as *koṣṭha*. *Māṃsī* is *jaṭāmāṃsī*. One *haridrā* is well-known; the second is well-known in the vernacular as *dāruharidra*. *Murā* is well-known in Paraśurāmakṣetra as *moravela*. *Śaileya* is *śilārasa*. *Candana* is white sandalwood (*śvetacandana*). *Saṭī* is *kacora*. *Campaka* is well-known; [the term refers to] its bark. *Mustā* is *bhadramothā*.

The names of the deities of the rites. Regarding the deities of the rites, Baudhāyana says: "Now we shall explain the deities of the auspicious days (*puṇyāha*): for the marriage rite, the deity is Agni; for the *aupāsana* fire, the deities are Agni, Sūrya, and Prajāpati; for the *sthālīpāka*, Agni; for the *garbhādhāna*, Brahmā; for the *puṃsavana*, Prajāpati; for the *sīmanta*, Dhātṛ; for the *viṣṇubali*, Viṣṇu; for the *jātakarman*, Mṛtyu; for the *nāmakarman*, Savitṛ; at its conclusion, Prajāpati; for the *upaniṣkramaṇa*, Savitṛ; at its conclusion, Citriya; for the *annaprāśana*, Savitṛ; for the *caula*, Keśin; at its conclusion, Prajāpati; for the *upanayana*, Indra."

Śraddhā is at the end of the *medha* sacrifice; Suśravas is at the end of the *visarga*, as well as for the re-initiation (*punarupanayana*), Agni for the *avapāya-homa*, Savitṛ for the *samāvartana*, Śrī or Indra for the *śūlagava*, Īśāna for the *pratyavarohaṇa*, Savitṛ for the *upākarma* and for the *vrata*s, Vāstoṣpati for the *vāstu-homa* with Prajāpati at the end, Indra for the *ahuta-homa* with Prajāpati at the end, Agni Āyuṣmat for the *āyuṣya-homa*, and for the *nakṣatra-homa*, the eighth [deity] is the one mentioned in the *nakṣatreṣṭi*s.

Īśāna is the deity for the *pradoṣa* [rite]; the deities of the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice are the deities of the *āgrayaṇa*; the serpents are the deities for the *sarpabali*; Prajāpati is at the end of the *ekoddiṣṭa*; Varuṇa is the deity for tanks and the like; the *yakṣas* are the deities for the *yakṣabali*; the nine planets beginning with Āditya are the deities for the *grahaśāntihoma*; Brahmā and the others are the deities for the *nāgāritantrahoma*. In this same manner, for other *homas*, one should say, "May that deity who is the object of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* be pleased. At the end of a period of impurity (*sūtaka*), and at the conclusion of the primary water-offering (*pradhāmodaka*), Prajāpati is the deity.

"The Ādityas and others [are the deities] for the *kūṣmāṇḍa* oblation; Agni and others for the *cāndrāyaṇa*; Agni and others for the *agnyādheya*; Indra for the *agniṣṭoma*; and likewise, Prajāpati for rites where no deity is specifically prescribed—thus says the venerable Baudhāyana.
This is the rule for the recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*). He also states the rule for the recitation of the auspicious day:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the recitation for the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*). In a pure and level place, four praiseworthy Brāhmaṇas, holding *dūrvā* and *darbha* grass and with their hands not empty, stand facing the east. To their south, the officiant (*vācayitṛ*), facing north and holding a covered water-pot, stands. The wives stand leaning against his right arm. Then, he should pour water into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas, which hold sacred grass (*pavitra*), saying, "Om, waters! They respond, "May the waters be auspicious. Then [he says], "Fragrances!"

He offers fragrance with the words, "May those who possess good scent protect [you]," and they accept it. Then he offers flowers with the words, "May there be joy of mind," and they accept them with the words, "May there be joy of mind. Then he offers unbroken grains (*akṣatān*) with the words, "The unbroken ones. By the word *akṣata*, rice-grains mixed with husked rice (*taṇḍula*) are meant.

They accept [the gift] saying, "May it be uninjured and free from misfortune. Then, regarding the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives the fee saying, "May the sacrificial fees protect [us] with well-being; may there be much to give. They accept it saying, "May there be much to give. Then the one who causes [the sacrificer] to recite, having placed his right knee on the ground and raised his left, facing north, mutters the mantra, "The *iḍā* is the invoker of the gods," and taking a water-pot, he stands up.

Then the officiant says, "May your minds be concentrated," to which the Brahmins reply, "Our minds are concentrated. Then the officiant says, "May you be gracious," to which the Brahmins reply, "We are gracious. Then the officiant says, "May there be peace, may there be nourishment, may there be contentment, may there be growth, may there be freedom from obstacles, may there be longevity, may there be health, and may the rite be auspicious," to which the Brahmins reply, "So be it. He then utters the name of whichever deity the rite is dedicated to.

"May [the deity] be pleased. Then, "Sirs, declare it an auspicious day (puṇyāha)," to which the Brahmins reply, "Om, an auspicious day! Then, "Sirs, declare it well-being (svasti)," to which the Brahmins reply, "Om, well-being! Then, "Sirs, declare it success (ṛddhi)," to which the Brahmins reply, "Om, may it succeed! He causes all these to be recited three times each.

"Then the Brahmins, having sat down, should sprinkle the one being addressed with the *surabhimatī*, *ābliṅga*, *vāruṇī*, *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and *pāvamānī* verses; then the one being addressed mutters 'bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om'—thus says the venerable Baudhāyana."

"Praiseworthy" means those [verses] free from the acceptance of gifts at a *śrāddha* feast and so forth. *Surabhimatī* refers to the single verse beginning with "I have performed the act for Dadhikrāvan. *Abliṅgāḥ* refers to those beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed... (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*). *Vāruṇyaḥ* refers to those beginning with "Whatever [sin] of yours... (*yacciddhi te*). *Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ* refers to those beginning with "Golden-hued, pure, purifying... (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*). *Pāvamānyaḥ* refers to those contained in the section beginning with "The purifying one, born of heaven... (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*). The rest is clear. Now follows the ritual procedure for the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), as accepted by all learned authorities (*śiṣṭas*).

The performer, accompanied by his wife, having performed his daily obligatory rites, having bathed for auspicious purposes, and being well-adorned with his topknot tied, should prepare a certain area on the ground smeared with cow-dung, decorated with *raṅgavalli* patterns for the purpose of placing the jar for the *puṇyāhavācana*. To the north of that, having arranged all the necessary materials according to the prescribed method, he should sit facing east upon a seat covered with cloth behind the area decorated with *raṅgavalli*, and cause his wife to sit to his right, also facing east.

To the south of that [fire], he should seat an even number of Brāhmaṇas facing north, and to his own north, others facing east. However, in rites such as the recitation of the *puṇyāha* (declaration of auspiciousness) which are ancillary to sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) for a son or others, the person undergoing the rite (*saṃskārya*) should also be seated to the south of the wife. Then, with the *pavitra* grass in hand, having sipped water (*ācamana*), performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and offered salutations to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and others, he should recite auspicious verses beginning with "sumukhaśca," announce the place and time, and declare: "I shall perform such-and-such a rite."

One should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "As an integral part of this [rite], I shall perform the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*), and the *nāndīśrāddha*. However, when the declaration of an auspicious day and so forth are performed outside the actual ritual procedure, then one should first perform the declaration of an auspicious day and so forth—preceded by the resolve: "In order to perform such-and-such rite, I shall first perform the declaration of an auspicious day, the worship of the Mothers, and the *nāndīśrāddha*"—and thereafter make the primary resolve (*pradhānasaṃkalpa*).

In reality, however, it appears more reasonable to consider that the *saṃkalpa* (formal resolve) regarding the *puṇyāhavācana* and other such rites belongs exclusively to the external category and not to the internal one. Alternatively, the *saṃkalpa* for the *puṇyāhavācana* and other rites may be performed at the time of their respective commencement.

Just as one says, "I shall perform the *puṇyāhavācana*" at the commencement of the *puṇyāhavācana*, "I shall perform the *mātṛkāpūjana*" at the commencement of the *mātṛkāpūjana*, and "I shall perform the *nāndīśrāddha*" at the commencement of the *nāndīśrāddha*—in the view of those who accept that the *mātṛkāpūjana* is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the *nāndīśrāddha*, there is no separate formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for it, since its accomplishment is achieved by the very resolve for the *nāndīśrāddha*.

Regarding those actions prescribed as to be performed in the future but not the immediate present—such as "he does," "he offers oblations," "he sacrifices," and so forth—in place of words such as "I shall do," "I shall offer," or "I shall sacrifice," one should use "I am the doer" (*kartāhe*), "I am the offerer" (*hotāhe*), or "I am the sacrificer" (*yaṣṭāhe*), according to the specific case. However, when there is no fruit of the action accruing to the agent, the usage is "I will be the doer" (*kartāsmi*) or "I shall do" (*kariṣyāmi*). This applies everywhere in the same manner.

The period beginning from the latter half of the past night until the former half of the coming night is the "future today" (*bhaviṣyad-adyatana*); beyond that is the "future non-today" (*bhaviṣyad-anadyatana*). Therefore, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati for the sake of achieving freedom from obstacles at the commencement of that [rite]"—[one recites]: "Oṃ *gaṇānāṃ tvā*... (Ṛgveda 2.23.1). The seers are the Viśvedevas; the deity is Gaṇapati; the meter is Jagatī; the application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Gaṇapati: "Oṃ *gaṇānāṃ tvā gaṇapatiṃ havāmahe...* sit on thy seat."

"Obeisance to Gaṇapati, who is endowed with supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and perfection (*siddhi*); I invoke Gaṇapati, who is endowed with supernatural power and perfection. Having thus invoked him, [one recites] "narya prajām"; here Agni is the deity, Narya is the meter, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the installation (*pratiṣṭhāpana*). Having installed him with the mantra "narya prajāṃ... pratiṣṭhitām," and having worshipped him with the services beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and ending with the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one offers a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and says:
"O Elephant-faced One, whatever has been worshipped by me—whether deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion—may that, O God, be complete for me."
"O Vakratuṇḍa of great body, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
O God, always grant me freedom from obstacles in all my undertakings.
Having thus prayed:

"Obeisance, obeisance to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, son of Gaurī! To Vighneśvara, the bestower of boons, beloved of the gods, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Gajānana, Vināyaka, adorned by the Vedas and sacrifices—to you, I bow.
Thus one should offer salutation. The learned hold that the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*) occurs at the conclusion of the rite; this applies everywhere.
Then follows the installation of the water-jar (*kalaśasthāpana*).

For the verse beginning with *mahī dyauḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the metre is Gāyatrī, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for touching the ground. Reciting *oṃ mahī dyauḥ pṛthivī ca na imaṃ yajñaṃ mimikṣatām* and *pīpayatāṃ dhiyo juṣāṇe imāṃ barhirūrṇamradāṃ svāsasthāṃ dhiṣaṇāṃ vītam*, one touches the ground on the south and the north. For the verse beginning with *oṣadhayaḥ saṃvadante*, the deity is Agni, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and its application is for forming heaps of herbs upon the two touched spots. Reciting *oṃ oṣadhayaḥ saṃvadante somena saha rājñā yasmai kṛṇoti brāhmaṇastaṃ rājan pārayāmasi*, one forms two heaps of the prepared grain (*prasthadhānya*) on the two touched locations.

The mantra *ājighra* belongs to the Viśvedevas; it is in the Mahī Śakvarī meter, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the installation of the pitcher (*kalaśa*). [One recites: *oṃ ājighra kalaśaṃ... śatādrayiḥ*. Upon those two heaps, one should place two new pitchers with unbroken mouths, made of gold, silver, or copper—or in their absence, of clay—having their necks wrapped with thread.

For the verse *imaṃ me gaṅge*, the deities are the sacrificial ones, the Upaniṣads, and the rivers such as the Gaṅgā; the meter is Jagatī; the application (*viniyoga*) is for filling the water-jar (*kalaśa*). Oṃ *imaṃ me gaṅge yamune... suṣomayā*. Having filled those two [jars] with the waters prepared for the jar, [one recites]: For the verse *gandhadvārām*, the deities are the sacrificial ones, the Upaniṣads, and Śrī; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; the application is for the scattering of perfume. Oṃ *gandhadvārāṃ... śriyam*. Having scattered perfume into those two [jars].

Regarding the verse *yā jātā oṣadhayaḥ*, Agni is the deity, the plants (*oṣadhayaḥ*) are the subject, and the *anuṣṭubh* is the metre; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the scattering of medicinal herbs. *Oṃ yā jātā oṣadhayaḥ... sapta ca*. Having scattered all the medicinal herbs with these two [verses], [one proceeds]. Regarding the verse *kāṇḍātkāṇḍāt*, Agni, the sacrificial deities, the Upaniṣads, and the plants are the subjects, and the *anuṣṭubh* is the metre; its application is for the scattering of *dūrvā* grass. *Oṃ kāṇḍātkāṇḍātpraroha... śatena ca*. Having scattered the *dūrvā* grass with these two [verses], [the rite is completed].

For the verse beginning with *aśvatthe vaḥ*, Agni and the plants are the deities, the Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the throwing of the five barks and five sprouts. Reciting *oṃ aśvatthe vaḥ... pūruṣam*, one should throw the barks and sprouts of those two aforementioned trees, repeating the mantra for each. For the verse beginning with *yāḥ phalinīḥ*, Agni and the plants are the deities, the Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application is for the throwing of fruit. Reciting *oṃ yāḥ phalinīḥ... tva hasaḥ*, one should throw the fruit into those two [fires].

For the verse *agneretaś candram*, Agni is the deity, gold is the substance, and the Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the casting of gold. *Oṃ agneretaś ca... tareyam*. Having cast gold into those two [fires], [he recites] *bṛhaspate juṣasva naḥ*. For this [verse], the Viśvedevas are the deities, Bṛhaspati is the deity, and the Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is in the casting of the five jewels (*pañcaratna*). *Oṃ bṛhaspate juṣa... dāśuṣe*. Into those two [fires] he should cast the five jewels, or, in their absence, gold. This same mantra is also used for the casting of gold.

For the verse beginning with *yuvā suvāsāḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for wrapping the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). [Recitation: *oṃ yuvā suvāsāḥ... devayantaḥ*. Having wrapped those two with two garments, [one proceeds]. For the verse beginning with *pūrṇā darvī*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its application is for covering the mouth of the pitcher (*kalaśa*). [Recitation: *oṃ pūrṇā darvī... śatakrato*.

Having filled a vessel prepared upon the previously arranged water-jar with rice placed in a new vessel, one should cover the openings of the two jars with those two vessels containing rice. In all cases, it should be understood that the mantra is repeated for each jar and that the placement follows the sequence from north to south. Then, for the mantra *tattvā yāmi*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Varuṇa, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Varuṇa: *Oṃ tattvā yāmi brahmaṇā vandamānas tad āśāste yajamāno havirbhiḥ | aheḷamāno varuṇeha bodhy uruśaṃsa mā na āyuḥ pra moṣīḥ ||* (Oṃ, I approach you, being honored with a sacred prayer; this the sacrificer desires through oblations. O Varuṇa, be present here without anger; O you of wide renown, do not steal away our life.)

Having invoked Varuṇa into the northern jar and established him with the mantra "narya prajām," one should worship him. Regarding this, the *Prayogadarpaṇa* states: "Some maintain that the invocation of Varuṇa should be performed in both jars. Then, one should invoke the deities into that very [northern] jar with the verses: "Viṣṇu is at the mouth of the jar... all the oceans... the destroyers of misfortune. Having thus invoked and worshipped them, one should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) into the northern jar while reciting: "Be one for whom the mother is a god; be one for whom the father is a god; be one for whom the teacher is a god; be one for whom the guest is a god."

If the invocation of Varuṇa is performed for both pitchers, the mantra "viṣṇor-mukham" (Viṣṇu’s face) is to be repeated for each pitcher. Then, having knelt with the circles of his knees upon the ground, placed his hands in the form of a lotus bud joined at the head, and holding the gold-filled pitcher with his right hand, he should pray for blessings: "May these blessings be true! May the Nāgas, the rivers, the mountains, and the three steps of Viṣṇu exist; by that measure of longevity, may this auspicious day and long life be granted. The Brahmins should give the appropriate responses: "May they be so," or "May it be so."

Then the performer [says]: "May the waters be auspicious. May there be mental well-being. May there be security and freedom from misfortune. May the scents protect us; may there be auspiciousness. May the unbroken grains protect us; may there be longevity. May the flowers protect us; may there be prosperity. May the betel leaves protect us; may there be sovereignty. May the sacrificial fees protect us; may there be much to give. May there be long life, welfare, peace, nourishment, and contentment. May there be fortune, fame, knowledge, discipline, wealth, many sons, and longevity."

One should recite these sentences. Regarding this, the traditional practice (*saṃpradāya*) is as follows: having poured water into the hands of the Brahmins at the end of the first three sentences, and having offered the respective articles of worship (*upacāra*) at the end of each pair of sentences according to their specific characteristics, one should pray to the Brahmins with the two sentences beginning "May there be long life" (*dīrgham āyuḥ*). The Brahmins should give the appropriate responses, such as "May they protect" (*pāntu astu*). Alternatively: "May the waters be auspicious" (*śivā āpaḥ santu*); "May the perfumes protect" (*gandhāḥ pāntu*); "May the unbroken rice grains protect" (*akṣatāḥ pāntu*); "May the flowers protect" (*puṣpāṇi pāntu*); "May the betel leaves protect" (*tāmbūlāni pāntu*)."

With these sentences beginning with "May the sacrificial fees protect," one should worship the Brahmins in sequence with water, scents, rice, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), flowers, betel leaves, and sacrificial fees. In the absence of rice, one may use only the unbroken grains. Then, the Brahmins should respond in sequence with the remaining sentences immediately following each respective one.

Then the performer should say: "Having made that which, when performed, causes all auspicious and beautiful undertakings of Vedic sacrifices and ritual actions to proceed—I shall, with that *oṃkāra* as my beginning, and being authorized by you, cause the recitation of the meritorious *puṇyāha* (day of merit), consisting of the benedictory words of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, according to the tradition of many sages and well-known [to us]. The Brahmins should reply: "Let it be recited."

Then the performer [recites]: "May we hear with our ears what is auspicious... long life. May the Giver of Wealth... long life. May Savitṛ from behind... long life. New and new he becomes... long life. High in heaven... may they extend our lives. May the waters moisten us... for splendor. He whom I love with my heart... may I attain immortality. For which well-doer you grant a hundredfold well-being. With a *yajus* mantra I sprinkle you: progeny, long life, and wealth."

Having recited these mantras, he should request the Brahmins, who are distinguished by their observances of vows, restraints, austerity, self-study, sacrifices, self-control, and charity, saying: "May your minds be composed. The Brahmins respond: "Our minds are composed. The performer says: "May you be gracious. The Brahmins respond: "We are gracious."

Then the performer [recites]: "May there be peace (śānti) 1; may there be nourishment (puṣṭi) 2; may there be contentment (tuṣṭi) 3; may there be growth (vṛddhi) 4; may there be freedom from obstacles (avighna) 5; may there be long life (āyuṣya) 6; may there be health (ārogya) 7; may the rite be auspicious (śivaṃ karma) 8; may there be success in the rite (karmasamṛddhi) 9; may there be success in dharma (dharmasamṛddhi) 10; may there be success in the Vedas (vedasamṛddhi) 11; may there be success in the scriptures (śāstrasamṛddhi) 12; may there be success in progeny (putrasamṛddhi) 13; may there be success in wealth and grain (dhanadhānyasamṛddhi) 14; may there be the attainment of desired goals (iṣṭasaṃpat) 15; may there be the removal of misfortunes (ariṣṭanirasana) 16; and may whatever sin exists be destroyed (yatpāpaṃ tatpratihataṃ bhavatu) 17."

May that which is most auspicious be so. (18) May there be no obstacle to future actions. (19) May there be daily increase in excellence, higher and higher. (20) May subsequent rites be auspicious and splendid. (21) May there be the perfection of the lunar day, the *karaṇa*, the *muhūrta*, and the asterism. (22) May the presiding deities of the lunar day, the *karaṇa*, the *muhūrta*, the asterism, the planets, and the ascendant be pleased. (23) May the lunar day and the *karaṇa*, along with the *muhūrta* and the asterism, together with the planets and their presiding deities, be pleased. (24) May Durgā and Pāñcālī be pleased. (25) May the Viśvedevas, headed by Agni, [be pleased].

May the hosts of Maruts, led by Indra, be pleased. (26) May all the Vedas, led by Brahman, be pleased. (27) May all the gods, led by Viṣṇu, be pleased. (28) May the Mothers, headed by Umā and led by Māheśvarī, be pleased. (29) May the hosts of sages, led by Vasiṣṭha, be pleased. (30) May the wives devoted to a single husband, led by Arundhatī, be pleased. (31) May the sages, the meters, the teachers, the gods, the Vedas, and the sacrifices be pleased. (32) May the Absolute (Brahman) and the Brāhmaṇas be pleased. (33) [And] may Śrī and Sarasvatī be pleased. (34)

May Faith and Intelligence be pleased (35); may the Blessed Kātyāyanī be pleased (36); may the Blessed Māheśvarī be pleased (37); may the Blessed Puṣṭikarī be pleased (38); may the Blessed Tuṣṭikarī be pleased (39); may the Blessed Ṛddhikarī be pleased (40); may the Blessed Vṛddhikarī be pleased (41); may the two Blessed Lords, Vighna and Vināyaka, be pleased (42); may the Blessed Lord Mahādeva Mahāsena, together with his wife, his sons, his retinue, and present in all places, be pleased (43).

May Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha be pleased (44). May all the village deities be pleased (45). May all the family deities be pleased (46). May all the chosen deities be pleased (47). May those who hate the Veda be slain (48). May the adversaries be slain (49). May the obstructors of this rite be slain (50). May the enemies meet with defeat (51). May the terrible things be pacified (52). May sins be pacified (53). May calamities be pacified (54). May auspicious things increase (55). May the waters be auspicious (56).

May the seasons be auspicious; may the fires be auspicious; may the oblations be auspicious; may the herbs be auspicious; may the trees be auspicious; may the guests be auspicious; may day and night be auspicious. May Parjanya rain for us according to our desire; may our herbs ripen with fruit; may our acquisition and security be well-ordered; may all the planets, led by Āditya, be pleased; may the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa be pleased.

"May the Blessed Lord Parjanya be pleased" (70); "May the Blessed Lord Mahāsena, the Master, be pleased" (71). One should recite these seventy-one statements. While reciting these statements, one should pour water into the vessel with each statement. Regarding this, the traditional practice (*saṃpradāya*) is that water should be poured outside the vessel to the north with the two statements, "May there be the removal of misfortune; may whatever sin exists be struck down," and with the seven statements beginning with "Slain are the haters of Brahman."

The Brahmins should give their responses in accordance with the speaker's sentence, saying: "May it be," "may they be accomplished," "may they be pleased," "may they both be pleased," "may he be pleased," "may those who have been struck go away," "may they be pacified," "may they increase," "may they be," "may they two be," "may it rain," "may they ripen," and "may it be fit."

Then the performer should say: "I shall cause the auspicious day and time to be proclaimed. The Brahmins reply: "Let it be proclaimed. Then the performer says: "Like the Udgātṛ, O bird, proclaim what is auspicious. He sacrifices with the *yājyā* verse; the *yājyā* is indeed a gift (*pratti*), and the gift is auspicious fortune. Thus he brings about auspicious fortune and consecrates auspicious fortune. Whatever auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) there may be, at that time he should perform whatever rite he intends to do. He performs it on an auspicious day itself. These, indeed, are the lunar mansions of restraint (*yama-nakṣatrāṇi*). He performs them as the very lunar mansions of the gods (*deva-nakṣatrāṇi*).

He should say three times: "For me, together with my family, who am being saluted by the great assembly and who am awaiting a word of blessing, may you, sirs, declare the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) for such-and-such a rite. The Brahmins [should respond] three times: "Oṃ, it is an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). "May Vāyu be for our well-being (*svasti*); the rising Āditya is the leader of the path. By the very path of well-being they set out from here; they ascend toward the path of well-being. Verily, by well-being they set out from here, and by well-being they ascend. May Indra, of increased glory, grant us well-being. The eight gods, the Vasus, are well-being."

"May you, sirs, pronounce a blessing for the well-being of such-and-such a rite, for me and my family, as we, a great multitude, bow down and await your words of benediction. Thus the performer should say three times. "Om, Svasti! the Brahmins should reply three times. "May we prosper; may he fulfill our desire. "He who knows thus shall attain all prosperity. "May we prosper through our offerings, together with our heroes. "Three by three, indeed... "He becomes firmly established."

The performer (the *kartṛ*) should say three times: "For me and my family, for the great multitude who are bowing down and awaiting words of blessing, may you all declare the success (*ṛddhi*) of this rite. The Brahmins should reply three times: "Om, may it succeed! [Then the following mantras are recited: "Born for glory, for glory... [Śrīsūkta] "...in the measured wood. Verily, he brings him glory through cattle, he who knows thus. "In whom Brahmā conquered all this; and that which is being offered... "O Ahi Budhnya, protect my mantra; that which the seers [discovered] among the immortals..."

The performer should say three times: "To me, along with my family, who am being saluted by the great multitude and who am awaiting words of blessing, may you all say, 'May there be prosperity (śrī) for such-and-such an act. The Brahmins should reply three times: "Om, may there be prosperity."

In this rite, according to custom, women whose husbands are living should perform the *nīrājana* (lustration) ceremony. Then the performer (the *kartṛ*) should utter these formulas: "May there be a full hundred years; may there be auspiciousness; may the rite be auspicious; may there be prosperity for the lineage. When the Brahmins have given their appropriate responses, he should pronounce the name of the specific deity of the rite mentioned by Baudhāyana in the nominative case, followed by "may [he/they] be pleased"—using the singular, dual, or plural as required by the number of deities—and then pour water into the vessel.
In cases where no instruction is given or when there is doubt regarding the deity, Prajāpati should be understood as the deity.

Then—having recited: "With white-limbed bodies, O Aja, spreading out the full *bṛhatī* verses; regarding this, this verse is also sung: 'The Maruts were the attendants in the house of Marutta, the son of Avikṣita, the fulfiller of desires; all the gods were the members of his assembly,'" one should take the northern jar in the right hand and the southern jar in the left hand, and with those two, pour two continuous streams into the vessel. The mantras for that are: "O Vāstoṣpati... and "...for the four-footed."

"O Lord of the Dwelling, grant us further [protection]... O Lord of the Dwelling, with your auspicious [presence], be ever with us... be the dispeller of our ailments. Then one should say "Śivam" (Auspicious) three times. According to the statement of Āpastamba, "In the base and in the stream, there is a connection from the beginning," the commencement of the ritual action occurs simultaneously with the commencement of the mantra.

Then the Brahmins, having seated the wife to the left of the performer, while standing or sitting facing north, should sprinkle the performer together with his wife using water poured into a vessel along with sprouts and *dūrvā* grass.

Therein are the mantras: "Those whose chief is the ocean... (RV 7.49.2); "May they protect us here... (RV 10.9.4); "These waters are most auspicious... (RV 10.9.5); "The mother has given birth to the auspicious one... (RV 10.9.6). "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the splendor of Agni. "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I sprinkle you with the sovereignty of Agni. "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I sprinkle you with the sovereignty of Indra."

With the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the sovereign power of Bṛhaspati. With the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the hands of the Aśvins, I sprinkle you with the healing medicine of the Aśvins for the sake of splendor. With the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the [hands] of the Aśvins, I sprinkle you with the healing medicine of Sarasvatī. With the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the [hands] of the Aśvins, I sprinkle you with the sensory power of Indra. O Surā, I sprinkle you for the sake of accomplishing all desires and purposes.

"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May that [favor] of Śaṃyu [be for us]... for the four-footed. Having thus sprinkled [the water], they should say, "May there be the sprinkling of nectar (amṛtābhiṣeka). The performer should reply, "So be it. Then he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice. The wife, having sipped water once, should sit down to the south. Then, according to custom, well-dressed women should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the recitation of benedictions (āśīḥ-prayoga), the giving of new garments, and so forth. According to the elders, when the husband is putting on the garment, the wife should be on his left side. Thus concludes the procedure for the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) as accepted by the learned. [Now follows] the rule for the Nāndī-śrāddha.

Now follows the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* (prosperity-śrāddha). It is performed on occasions such as: the *saṃskāras* for the fetus beginning with *garbhādhāna*; the *saṃskāras* for the child beginning with *jātakarma*; the *śravaṇākarma* and other rites; the consecration (*utsarga*) of tanks, wells, ponds, gardens, and the like; the installation of deities; the conclusion of a vow (*vratodyāpana*); the formal adoption of a stage of life (*āśrama*) such as that of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); great gifts (*mahādāna*) such as the *tulāpuruṣa*; the entry into a new house; the *vrata* ceremonies for the various Vedic sections (*kāṇḍa*); the coronation of a king; rites for peace (*śāntika*) and prosperity (*pauṣṭika*); the *ādhāna* of the sacred fires and other Śrauta rituals; and the commencement (*upākarma*) and conclusion (*utsarjana*) of the Vedic term.

The *nāndīśrāddha* should be performed at the first performance of rites such as the *pārvaṇasthālīpāka*, the *śravaṇākarma*, and others, as well as at festivals and similar occasions. However, the *nāndīśrāddha* is not to be performed during the conclusion of a vow (*vratodyāpana*), nor for propitiatory rites intended to remove afflictions from malefic planets and the like; some maintain this because such a prohibition is stated in the *Śākalakārikās*. Others, however, hold that this view should not be respected, as it contradicts many authoritative Smṛti texts and established treatises.

This *śrāddha* and the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*) should be performed only once at the very beginning when several consecratory rites (*saṃskāras*) performed by the same agent are to be undertaken simultaneously; there is no need to repeat them for each individual rite.

For example, it is like the case where, by fate, the *jātakarma* and other rites were not performed for a child; then, at the time of his initiation (*upanayana*), the *jātakarma* and other rites are performed. Or, when someone who has gone to another country is presumed dead and his funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) are performed, he returns, and the prescribed purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the *jātakarma* must be performed all at once. Or again, it is like the simultaneous performance of the purificatory rites prescribed as expiations (*prāyaścitta*) for those who have touched a corpse or similar impurities, such as the water from the *karmanāśā* river. Thus, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"When the worship of the Mothers is being performed in groups, it is done only once."
"The śrāddha should be performed only once at the beginning; it is not to be repeated separately for each [subsequent] occasion."
Bopadeva states that this statement concerns the performance of the sacramental rites for many children simultaneously.

Because of the separate injunction that "the worship of the Mothers is performed once," it is understood that the worship of the Mothers is not an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *nāndī-śrāddha* itself. Therefore, in this ritual procedure, there must be a distinct formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the worship of the Mothers.
And wherever there may be a *śrāddha*, there the Mothers [should be worshipped].

Thus, its status as an ancillary rite (*aṅga*) is established by the statement of another Purāṇa. In this ritual cycle (*kalpa*), there is no separate formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Now, regarding the timing: the *mātṛ-pārvaṇa* is performed on the day immediately preceding the commencement of the rite; the *pitṛ-pārvaṇa* on the day of the commencement of the rite; and the *mātāmaha-pārvaṇa* on the day following the completion of the rite. If one is unable to perform it in this manner, the three *pārvaṇas* should be performed in sequence over the three days immediately preceding the commencement of the rite: the *mātṛ-pārvaṇa* on the first day, the *pitṛ-pārvaṇa* on the second day, and the *mātāmaha-pārvaṇa* on the third day.

If one is unable to do it in this manner, then on the day prior to the commencement of the rite, during the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa), one should perform the *pārvaṇa* for the mothers; at midday, the *pārvaṇa* for the fathers; and in the afternoon (aparāhṇa), the *pārvaṇa* for the maternal grandfathers. If there is still an inability to do even this, then on the preceding day, during the forenoon itself, all three *pārvaṇas* should be performed together (*tantra*)—or else on the very day of the commencement. However, in the case of the birth of a son, even if one has already eaten, the rite must be performed immediately after the birth, even if it occurs at night.

When the *nāndī-śrāddha* is being performed at the commencement of a sacrifice (*yajña*) and similar rites, rootless *darbha* grass should be held in both hands. In auspicious ceremonies such as marriage and others, *dūrvā* grass alone is used in place of *darbha*. Regarding the *nāndī-śrāddha* performed at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), the *Soma* sacrifice, and so forth, some authorities maintain that the deities are Dakṣa and Kratu; elsewhere, they are Satya and Vasu. Others hold that Dakṣa and Kratu are the deities even for the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, and *sīmantonnayana* rites. Still others maintain that Dakṣa and Kratu are the deities only for the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, and *Soma* sacrifices, and not elsewhere. [The following concerns] those entitled to perform the *nāndī-śrāddha*.

Now, regarding the qualified persons: at the conclusion of the first marriage and during the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) for a son, the father should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. However, in the case of a second or subsequent marriage, the bridegroom alone should perform it. Even if, in the first marriage, there is an absence of all the aforementioned qualified persons such as the father and others, he himself should perform it. In the event that the father is absent due to travel abroad or other reasons, the elder brother, performing the rite, should offer the oblations to his own father’s ancestors.

If, however, the father is not living but the grandfather is residing abroad, then one should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite dedicated to the father’s father (*pitṛ-prapitāmaha*) and the father’s great-grandfather (*vṛddha-prapitāmaha*). The same should be understood regarding the *pārvaṇa* rites for the mother and the maternal grandfather. When all [ancestors] are living, there is indeed an omission of the *nāndī-śrāddha*; for it is established by the scriptural injunction of omission that one should not perform it even according to the rule for the obligatory *nāndī-śrāddha*.

In the *Prayogapārijāta*, it is stated that if, due to the absence of all the aforementioned qualified persons, a mother should perform the marriage of her daughter, she should then personally make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) alone and have all other rites—such as the recitation of the *svasti* formula and the *nāndī-śrāddha*—performed through a Brahmin. Regarding the *samāvartana* (the student's return home), some hold that the father alone should perform the *nāndī-śrāddha*; however, others maintain that if the father is absent due to travel or other reasons, the son himself should perform it. Still others maintain that in this case, even when the father is present, the son himself should perform it.

Regarding the *saṃskāras* for which one has heard the injunctions, if the father’s mother, father, or maternal grandfather is living, he should perform three *pārvaṇa* rites dedicated respectively to his own mother and the others. If the mother is living, there is an omission of her *pārvaṇa*. If the maternal grandfather is living, there is an omission of his *pārvaṇa*. In that case, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is accomplished by means of two *pārvaṇas* alone. When both the mother and the maternal grandfather are living, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is accomplished by the *pārvaṇa* of the father alone. When the father and mother are living, it is accomplished by the *pārvaṇa* of the maternal grandfather alone. When the father and maternal grandfather are living, it is accomplished by the *pārvaṇa* of the mother alone, excluding the deity [of the paternal grandfather].

If the great-grandfather is living, one should perform the *pitṛ-pārvaṇa* rite intended for the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather. If the grandfather and great-grandfather are living, one should perform the *pitṛ-pārvaṇa* rite intended for the father, the great-grandfather, and the great-great-grandfather. The same principle should be understood to apply to the *pārvaṇa* rites for the mother and the maternal grandfather. When a stepmother has died, the *mātṛ-pārvaṇa* rite must be performed together with her.

Some maintain that even while one’s own mother is living, the *mātṛ-pārvaṇa* (the ancestral rite for the mother) can be accomplished through the stepmother, together with one’s paternal grandmother and great-grandmother. This is not correct; for she is the deity of the *ekoddiṣṭa* (single-offering rite), and thus there is no inclusion of her in the *pārvaṇa*. Furthermore, there is no scriptural injunction prescribing such a practice, as there is for the *āparapakṣika*, *ānvaṣṭakya*, and other types of *śrāddha*.

Regarding the *pārvaṇa* rite for the maternal grandfather, some hold that when the principal maternal grandmother and others are living, their status as being "accompanied by a wife" (*sapatnīka*) should be understood through their co-wives. When the first members of the three groups [of ancestors] are living, there is simply an omission of the *nāndī-śrāddha* during the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) of a son. Likewise, one whose father is living, performing the *nāndī-śrāddha* as an ancillary part of his second or subsequent marriage, should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite directed toward his father’s father and so forth. One whose father and paternal grandfather are living should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite directed toward his paternal grandfather’s father and so forth.

In this context, the term "grandfather" (pitāmaha) is to be substituted in place of "father" (pitṛ); the same applies to the *pārvaṇa* rites for the mother and maternal grandfather. Regarding the *nāndīśrāddha* performed for the sake of the individual (*puruṣārtha*) on the occasion of the *jātakarman*, one opinion holds that it should be performed in exactly the same manner as the *nāndīśrāddha* performed as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *jātakarman*. However, regarding the *nāndīśrāddha* that is a subsidiary to the second *nāndīśrāddha* or the *nāndīśrāddha* that is a subsidiary to a son’s first marriage, it should be performed in the same way as the *nāndīśrāddha* that is a subsidiary to a rite of passage (*saṃskāra*) for a son. The phrase "in the rites of passage for a son" (*sutasaṃskāreṣu*) refers specifically to rites of passage for a son other than marriage and birth.

Furthermore, there is another opinion that even in the case of the first marriage and the birth of a son, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed solely in accordance with the scriptural injunction, "to whomsoever the father would give. Some say that for one whose father is living, in rites other than the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) of a son, one should perform two *pārvaṇa* rites directed toward the father’s paternal grandfather and others, as well as directed toward one's own mother and maternal grandfather if they are deceased, based on the scriptural rule "to whomsoever [the father] would give. That is not correct.

Because it is impossible for two mutually contradictory texts—the *Itiśāstra* and the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*—to apply simultaneously in one instance. However, when paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others perform the marriage of a girl, the initiation (*upanayana*) of a boy, or the first marriage of one who has already been initiated, they should perform three *pārvaṇa* rites directed toward the father and other ancestors of the person being consecrated, provided that his father, mother, and maternal grandfather are deceased.

In the case of a biological elder brother, there is no special distinction [in the formula], because his father and other ancestors are non-different from the father and other ancestors of the person for whom the rite is being performed (*saṃskārya*). Regarding a step-elder brother, some say that he should perform the *mātṛ-pārvaṇa* (offering to the mother) by addressing the mother and other ancestors of the *saṃskārya*. Others maintain that in this case, there is simply an omission of the *mātṛ-pārvaṇa*. However, in the case of an uncle (*pitṛvya*) and others, one should employ a formula with a qualifying attribute, namely "of the *saṃskārya*," in all *pārvaṇa* rites.

If the person undergoing the sacramental rite (*saṃskārya*) has his father, mother, or maternal grandfather living, he should perform three *pārvaṇa* rites directed toward his father’s father and the others. Likewise, even in the case of the first marriage, if the bridegroom himself performs the *nāndī-śrāddha* due to the absence of another officiant while his own father is living, he should perform a *pārvaṇa* directed toward his father’s father and the others; some say this applies similarly to the *pārvaṇas* for the mother and the maternal grandfather as well. Others, however, maintain that in this matter, if the head of each respective group is living, the corresponding *pārvaṇa* is simply omitted. [As it is said: "Having taken possession of another's daughter with gold..."
"Even one who is not of the same lineage (asagotra) is fit to give [the bride] according to the righteous rite," so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
"By giving away a maiden who is without a protector to a suitable or even superior groom,
one obtains double the fruit that is proclaimed for the gift of a daughter."

Thus, based on the statement from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, or because of some reason preventing the person authorized to give the gift from doing so, or due to a request such as "you must perform the giving of the girl," he who desires to give away another's daughter should—addressing the father and other elders of the girl to be consecrated—perform, as far as possible, the *pārvaṇa* rite directed toward her mother and others, provided that her father is still living.

If, however, the adopted son has received both the seed (the biological father's lineage) and the inheritance, he should perform the rite in honor of both sets of parents, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers. This same principle should be understood to apply to the other two types of *pārvaṇa* rites. But if, because there exists another eligible heir for the inheritance of the seed, he does not receive that inheritance—according to the scriptural injunction, "The adopted son shall not share in the lineage or the estate of his biological father"—then he should perform the rite solely in honor of the ancestors belonging to the family of the adoptive father.

The Procedure for the Worship of the Mothers (Mātṛkā-pūjanaprayoga). Now, the procedure: If the performer has not made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the worship of the mothers at the time of the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), he should then make the resolve: "I shall perform the worship of the mothers as an ancillary part of such-and-such rite. Having done so, he should worship with saffron and other offerings, as appropriate, those among his mother, paternal grandmother, paternal great-grandmother, maternal grandfather, maternal grandmother, maternal great-grandmother, paternal aunt, and maternal aunt who are still living. This is to be done in a place smeared with cow-dung and decorated with colored powders and festive designs.

Once the rites of fire-transference (*agnyuttāraṇa*) and the infusion of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) have been performed and the images have been consecrated, one should invoke the deities such as Gaurī and others into them; in their absence, one may invoke them into paintings on cloth or heaps of unbroken rice grains.

Namely: Homage to Gaurī; I invoke Gaurī. Homage to Padmā; I invoke Padmā. Homage to Śacī; I invoke Śacī. Homage to Medhā; I invoke Medhā. Homage to Sāvitrī; I invoke Sāvitrī. Homage to Vijayā; I invoke Vijayā. Homage to Jayā; I invoke Jayā. Homage to Devasenā; I invoke Devasenā. Homage to Svadhā; I invoke Svadhā. Homage to Svāhā; I invoke Svāhā.

Salutation to the Mothers; I invoke the Mothers. Salutation to the World-Mothers; I invoke the World-Mothers. Salutation to Dhṛti; I invoke Dhṛti. Salutation to Puṣṭi; I invoke Puṣṭi. Salutation to Tuṣṭi; I invoke Tuṣṭi. Salutation to the family deity named so-and-so; I invoke the family deity named so-and-so. Salutation to Brāhmī; I invoke Brāhmī. Salutation to Māheśvarī; I invoke Māheśvarī. Salutation to Kaumārī; I invoke Kaumārī.

"Salutation to Vaiṣṇavī; I invoke Vaiṣṇavī. Salutation to Vārāhī; I invoke Vārāhī. Salutation to Indrāṇī; I invoke Indrāṇī. Salutation to Cāmuṇḍā; I invoke Cāmuṇḍā. Salutation to Gaṇādhipa; I invoke Gaṇādhipa. Salutation to Durgā; I invoke Durgā. Salutation to Kṣetrapāla; I invoke Kṣetrapāla. Salutation to Vāstoṣpati; I invoke Vāstoṣpati. Thus one should invoke them. Alternatively, the invocation of Gaṇādhipa may take place before that of Gaurī.

Then, one should worship with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) using the respective name-mantras, either according to the sequence of sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) or the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*). Alternatively, the worship may be performed using the collective formula: "Obeisance to the deities invoked, beginning with Gaurī. If the invocation of Gaṇādhipa precedes that of Gaurī, the formula is: "Obeisance to the deities invoked, beginning with Gaṇādhipa. If the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed as a separate rite by making a distinct formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), then after the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjana*), one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* offering with a different portion of cooked food, and then carry out that [śrāddha] rite.

If this *saṃkalpa* is performed together with the *puṇyāhavācana-saṃkalpa*, then the *vaiśvadeva* rite must be performed with a separate cooking of food prior to the *puṇyāhavācana*. In reality, however, it is more appropriate to perform the *saṃkalpa* separately.
[Now follows] the procedure for the *nāndīśrāddha*.

The performer, taking water along with *durvā* sprouts and unbroken rice grains, should pour it into the vessel, saying: "O Viśvedevas named Satya and Vasu, who are *nāndīmukha*, *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*, this *pādya* is for you, *svāhā*; it is not mine; and this is a *vṛddhi* [ceremony]. He should do the same for those who follow. "O *nāndīmukha* mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother, *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*, this *pādya* is for you, *svāhā*; it is not mine; and this is a *vṛddhi*. Some say, "O *nāndīmukhīs* [plural feminine]."

O Nāndīmukha fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers—bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ—this water for washing the feet is for you, svāhā; it is not mine, and this is a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi). O Nāndīmukha maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers, together with your wives—bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ—this water for washing the feet is for you, svāhā; it is not mine, and this is a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi).

Then, taking water with all the sprouts (*sarvāṅkura*), along with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), fragrance, and flowers, one should pour it into the vessel, saying: "O Viśvedevas named Satya and Vasu, who are *nāndīmukha*, *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*! This preparation of offerings, beginning with the seat and fragrance, is for you; *svāhā*. And this is my *vṛddhi* [festival], not mine. The same applies hereafter. "O Mothers, Grandmothers, and Great-grandmothers, who are *nāndīmukha*, *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*! This preparation of offerings, beginning with the seat and fragrance, is for you; *svāhā*. And this is my *vṛddhi*."

O Nāndīmukha fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers—bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ—this preparation of offerings, including the seat, scents, and so forth, is for you; svāhā! This is a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi), not mine. O Nāndīmukha maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers, together with your wives—bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ—this preparation of offerings, including the seat, scents, and so forth, is for you; svāhā! This is a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi), not mine.

Then one should give, according to one's means, [the following]: "O Gaurī and the other sixteen Mothers, the seven Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, Gaṇādhipa, Durgā, Kṣetrapāla, and Vāstoṣpati—*bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, this gold, fourfold, twofold, or equal in measure, which serves as the price for food sufficient for the feeding of these pairs of Brahmins, is offered in the form of nectar, *svāhā*; may this prosperity be not mine. Thus he should give.

According to the view that the worship of Gaṇādhipa precedes that of Gaurī, one should understand the ritual application beginning with "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ" to include Gaṇādhipa, Gaurī, and the sixteen Mothers (starting with Brāhmī), the seven Mothers (starting with Brāhmī), Durgā, Kṣetrapāla, and Vāstoṣpati. Then: "The Viśvedevas named Satya and Vasu, who are Nāndīmukhas—bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ—this [gift], consisting of four times the value sufficient for the feeding of a pair of Brahmins, is for you."

"O Nāndīmukha maternal grandmother, great-grandmother, and great-great-grandmother! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! This [is] for you, O pairs of Brāhmaṇas! "O Nāndīmukha paternal father, grandfather, and great-grandfather! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! This [is] for you, O pairs of Brāhmaṇas! "O Nāndīmukha maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather, together with your wives! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! This [is] for you, O pairs [of Brāhmaṇas]! Thus one should give [the offerings] in this order.

Then—having caused [the Brahmins] to recite, "Sing forth to him, O men! ... the honey... they have eaten the two bay steeds," and for the sake of accomplishing the completion of the performed *nāndī-śrāddha*, having given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to each Brahmin grapes, *āmalaka* fruits, roots, and barley, or their equivalent value in money, according to availability or measured by a *kuḍava* or a *prastha*, and having recited, "O Prajāpati, not these... and "of riches...", and having paid homage to the family deity (*kuladevatā*), [one honors] the mother, the grandmother, and likewise the great-grandmother.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
May the maternal grandfather, his father, the great-grandfather on the mother’s side, and the others—
may these be well-pleased and grant us auspiciousness.

One should recite these two verses. (Here, by the word "etcetera," the maternal grandmothers and others who have entered as secondary participants are to be understood. If the maternal grandmother is present, one should recite "and likewise for the great-grandfather of the maternal grandfather" [pramātāmahakastathā], but not "for the great-grandfather of the maternal grandfather and others" [pramātāmahakādayaḥ]). However, if due to the death or absence of any particular person required for a specific *pārvaṇa* rite, that *pārvaṇa* is omitted, then even a portion of the verse pertaining to that *pārvaṇa* must be omitted. This is because the recitation of the verse serves the purpose of consecrating the intended deities, just like the *sūktavāka*.
In the case of a pārvaṇa rite for the mother alone, the modification is: "May these [deities] be well-pleased. In a pārvaṇa rite for the mother alone, there is an omission of the gods (devalopa).

Then, reciting the mantra "iḍāmagne... bhūtvasme," he should stir a small amount of the substance with another vessel. Thereafter, he should say: "May the Nāndīmukha deities be pleased by this Nāndīśrāddha; may there be prosperity. At the conclusion of the rite, he should dismiss the deities beginning with Varuṇa. However, in rites other than marriage and initiation that require several days to complete, the dismissal takes place on that very day. This should be understood as a secondary procedure (anukalpa) to be followed when the primary procedure (mukhyakalpa) is impossible;
that primary procedure will be explained in the section on Śrāddha.

Thus concludes the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*. Now follows the procedure for the sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurāropaṇa-prayoga*). Next, the procedure for the sowing of sprouts: The performer, having sipped water (*ācamana*) and performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), shall announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of ensuring the success of such-and-such rite and the attainment of uninterrupted auspiciousness, I shall perform the sowing of sprouts. Having worshipped Gaṇapati and honored an even number of Brāhmaṇas beginning with four, and having served them food, he should say: "May you, sirs, declare the day to be auspicious (*puṇyāha*) for the rite of sowing sprouts; may you, sirs, declare it to be a blessing (*svasti*) for the rite of sowing sprouts."

"May you, sirs, declare the success (*ṛddhi*) of the rite of planting the sprouts. Thus he should cause the Brahmins to recite this three times each. [The Brahmins] should respond three times each, saying: "Oṃ, it is an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*); Oṃ, may there be well-being (*svasti*); Oṃ, may there be success, may it succeed! (*oṃ puṇyāham*, *oṃ svasti*, *oṃ ṛddhiḥ oṃ ṛdhyatām*).

Then the performer, having poured water into the vessel with the words, "May Brahmā and the other deities be pleased," should prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide (*gocarma*) on a clean spot by smearing it with cow-dung. Having adorned it with colored lines and patterns, scattered white unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and sprinkled it with water, he should place there five small bowls (*pālikā*) made of gold, silver, or copper—or, in their absence, of clay. In this context, the word *gocarma* is to be understood in its etymological sense alone, and not as referring to the area where "one hundred and one bulls stand together surrounded by cows."
"The wise know *gocarma* to be [an area] containing a hundred cows with their calves"—this is the technical definition.

Since this refers to the subject of giving [as a gift], it is not applicable in the present context. Thus, in this case, the preparation of the square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) is according to the exact measurement of a cow's hide. Then, having combined anthill earth, riverbank mud, and dried cow-dung powder, and having placed them in the central *pālikā*, he deposits them in order starting from the east.

Then, having placed *dūrvā* sprouts and leaves of the *aśvattha*, *śirīṣa*, and *bilva* at the lower parts of those vessels, and having wound white thread around the *pālikās*, one should invoke the deities into them in sequence. For the *praṇava*, the seer is Parabrahman, the deity is either Paramātman or Agni, and the metre is Gāyatrī. For the individual *vyāhṛtis*, Agni is the seer. For the collective *vyāhṛtis*, Prajāpati is the seer; the deities are Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati, respectively.

The meters are, in order, Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, and Bṛhatī. This is the application for the invocation. "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke Brahmā. "Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke the four-faced Brahmā. "Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke Prajāpati Brahmā. "Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I invoke Hiraṇyagarbha Brahmā. Having thus invoked Brahmā into the central *pālikā* (earthen vessel), [one proceeds with]: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra). "Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke the Lord of Śacī (Indra)."

*Oṃ suvar indram āvāhayāmi | Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ śatakratum āvāhayāmi |* Thus, one invokes Vajrin in the eastern *pālikā*. *Oṃ bhūr yamam āvāhayāmi | Oṃ bhuvo vaivasvatam āvāhayāmi | Oṃ suvaḥ pitṛpatim āvāhayāmi | Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ pretapatim āvāhayāmi |* Thus, one invokes Yama in the southern *pālikā*. *Oṃ bhūr varuṇam āvāhayāmi | Oṃ bhuvaḥ pracetasam āvāhayāmi |*

Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke Surūpin. Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I invoke Apāmpati. Thus, Varuṇa is in the western vessel. Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke Śaśin. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke Indu. Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke Niśākara. Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I invoke Soma. Thus, Soma is in the northern vessel.

Then one should worship with the respective mantras or the name-mantras, either by the method of sequential sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) or by the method of sequential items (*padārthānusamaya*). For the three mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the deities are Agni and the Viśvedevas, and the metre is Gāyatrī. For the four mantras beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, the deity is Agni, the substance is water, and the metre is Triṣṭubh. For the mantras of the *pavamāna-anuvāka*, the seer is Prajāpati; the deities are Pavamāna, Suvarjana, Vicarṣaṇi, and Potṛ; and the subjects are the divine folk (*devajanāḥ*), the Manus, and all living beings (*āyavaḥ*).

Jātavedas Agni, Agni the god, Savitṛ, and Punatī Vaiśvadevī; Vaiśvānara, Vāta, iṣira, Mayobhū, and the two, Dyāvāpṛthivī and Ṛtāvarī; the god Savitṛ, Agni, Brahmā, and the Pāvamānyas—these are the deities for the first sixteen verses. Then, for the seventeenth verse, the deities are respectively: Brahmā accompanied by Indra with Sunīti; Soma accompanied by Svasti; Varuṇa accompanied by Samīcī; King Yama accompanied by Pramṛṇās; and Jātavedas accompanied by Ūrjayantī. Thus are the deities of the seventeen verses in their sequence.

The *gāyatrī* metre is for the first, second, fourth, fifth, and eighth [verses]; the *anuṣṭubh* for the third, ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth; and the *triṣṭubh* for the sixth, seventh, and seventeenth. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the installation ceremony. With these verses—*oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ* (3 times), *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*, *pavitreṇa vicarṣaṇiḥ*, and *mārjayantyā punātu*—one should bathe Brahmā and the other deities at the conclusion of all [the mantras]. Some say this should be done verse by verse. At the end of the offering of the handful of flowers:

"I bow to the lords of the directions, who bestow the fruits of all desires; may they make my actions fruitful and may they constantly perform what is auspicious. This is the specific procedure for worship while standing behind the *pālikās* facing east.

Then, having sat down and mixed rice, barley, sesame, mung beans, and mustard seeds together, he washes them with milk and pours them out according to the sequence beginning with the middle *pālikā*. With the two verses beginning "Brahma jajñānam," Agni and Brahmā are the seers, Triṣṭubh is the metre, and their application (*viniyoga*) is in the pouring of the herbs. Reciting "Oṃ brahma jajñānaṃ prathamaṃ... and "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartata... vidhema," he pours [the mixture] into the middle *pālikā*. With the two verses beginning "Yata indra," the Viśvedevas are the seers; Indra is the deity.

The first [verse] is in the *bṛhatī* meter and the last is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the scattering of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*). With the two verses beginning, “O Indra, from where... slay” (*yata indra... jahi*) and “Bestower of well-being, protector of the people, maker of fearlessness” (*svastidā viśaspa... abhayamkaraḥ*), he scatters [the herbs] into the eastern bowl (*pālikā*). For the two verses beginning, “He who is his... of the belly” (*yo'sya kauṣṭhyeti*), Prajāpati and Yama are the seers, the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter; the application is for the scattering of medicinal herbs. With the two verses beginning, “He who is his... of the belly” (*yo'sya kauṣṭhyena...*) and “The earth is firm” (*pṛthivī dṛḍhā*), he scatters [the herbs] into the southern bowl.

Regarding the two verses beginning with *imaṃ me*: the seers are the Viśvedevas; Varuṇa is the deity; the first is in the Gāyatrī meter and the last is in the Triṣṭubh meter; their application (*viniyoga*) is in the scattering of medicinal herbs. With the two verses, *oṃ imaṃ me varuṇa...* and *mā mā...* (VS 6.22–23), he scatters [the herbs] into the western cup. Regarding the two verses beginning with *somo dhenum*: the seers are the Viśvedevas; Soma is the deity; the meter is Triṣṭubh; their application is in the scattering of medicinal herbs. With the two verses, *oṃ somo dhenuṃ...* and *aṣāḍhaṃ yutsu...* (VS 6.24–25), he scatters [the herbs] into the northern cup.
In the event that rice, barley, and other grains are unavailable, one should sow only one of these substances into the earthen mounds (*pālikās*).

Then, having covered the mounds in due order with pure sand and sprinkled them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should perform the following: the Supreme Brahman is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the *praṇava*; the deity is either the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or Agni; the meter is the divine *gāyatrī*; and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the covering of the mounds. Having covered [the mounds] with the syllable *oṃ* using a large vessel, one should keep them well-protected until the completion of the rite. Alternatively, the formula may be used thus: "The deity is the Supreme Self, denoted by the word Agni."
