When the rite is completed, having worshipped the deities with the previously mentioned mantras beginning with "Oṃ bhūr Brahmāṇam," one should dismiss the deities in their proper order by substituting the word "I dismiss" (*udvāsayāmi*) in place of "I invoke" (*āvāhayāmi*); then, one should dedicate the work to the Lord of Karma.

And this [rite] should be performed for seven days, five days, three days, or one day prior to the commencement of the work—excluding the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with *nāmakarma*, as well as other auspicious acts such as the consecration of offspring (from *annaprāśana* to *vivāha*), the entry into a new house, and so forth. Furthermore, this must be done during the first *muhūrta* of the night, which is designated as *kalyāṇa*.
Thus says Śaunaka:
"The planting of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) is to be performed at night during the first *muhūrta*, which is auspicious (*kalyāṇa*)."
The word "should do" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He himself also states the reason for sowing sprouts at night: "For the Moon is declared to be the presiding deity (adhidaivata) of all medicinal herbs."

"Therefore, with every effort, the planting of sprouts should be done at night. The particle *hi* indicates a reason. According to some, in cases of extreme urgency, it may be done immediately, even during the day; for as Bṛhaspati has stated: "In matters of the utmost urgency, the planting of sprouts on another day is [permitted] immediately during the day.
By that same authority, the non-performance of the planting of sprouts in specific types of rites has been declared:
"Excluding the *niṣeka*, the *garbhasaṃskāra*, the *jātakarma*, and the naming ceremony, there shall be the planting of the sprout in other auspicious rites. Here,
*niṣeka* refers to the *garbhādhāna* (the rite of conception).
Thus concludes the procedure for the planting of sprouts according to the Baudhāyana-sūtra.
Now follows the rite of the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha). Regarding that, the location for the fire-altar is stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra:

"In a place sloping toward the east, or sloping toward the north, or sloping toward the northeast, or on level ground, having dug up [the site] and sprinkled [it with water]"—this is the meaning: having prepared the sacrificial ground (*āyatana*) in any one of these locations, such as one sloping toward the east, one should dig it up with a spade or another digging tool and sprinkle it with water. *Pravaṇa* means gradually descending. By the use of the locative case in the phrase "or on level ground," it is shown that something other than the location itself is the object of the actions of digging and so forth; and when the question arises as to what that thing is, the term "sacrificial ground" (*āyatana*) is understood.
(By this, the view that only the site [of the altar] is to be leveled and sprinkled, and that the preparation of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) occurs therein, is refuted.
Its measurement is stated in the *Śulbasūtra*: "It is known that the hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*) are to be the size of a *piśīla*."

The *piśīla* is of six kinds: the first is eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the second is twenty finger-breadths, the third is the distance between the two arms, the fourth is a *ratni* with the fist closed, the fifth is twenty-four finger-breadths, and the sixth is thirty-six finger-breadths. The *ghiṣṇiya*s are the fire-places. Regarding the phrase "it is known," the word "scriptural authority" (*śruti*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The measurement of a finger-breadth has been stated by Baudhāyana:
"Now, the measurement of a finger-breadth consists of fourteen atoms (*aṇu*) and thirty-four sesame seeds (*tila*)."

"Another [view] is that they are 'broadly joined' (*pṛthusaṃśliṣṭāḥ*). The remainder of the explanation is that the measure of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) is stated because it is the basis for all other measures. An *aṇu* is a specific type of grain. The meaning is that the measure of a finger-breadth is as much as the extent occupied by fourteen *aṇus* joined together with one another. Another opinion is that thirty-four sesame seeds (*tila*) joined together over a broad area, like the shape of a sheath (*kośa*), constitute the measure of a finger-breadth; this has been explained by Dvārakānātha. The sheath (*kośa*) states the ground for the application of the word *aṇu*: [Sheath: "An *aṇu* is the smallest visible form (*mūrti*). It is the size of a grain of rice (*taṇḍula*) when it is not split and is joined with its husk (*tuṣa*). [Commentary: The word *aṇu* refers to the smallest visible form. Its measure is the size of a grain of rice when it is unbroken and joined with its husk. This is the primary definition. "The *aṇu* is a variety of rice, a male [deity]. Some, however, say it is the measure of a finger, or merely the size of a thumb-joint, or merely the middle joint of the middle finger. And this measurement should be taken from either the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*). This is because of the *Śulbasūtra*: "For he (the *aṇu*) is the performer of the movements of either the sacrificer or the *adhvaryu*. Since the *adhvaryu* is absent here, the measurement is that of oneself alone. Furthermore, in the case of a rite performed by a teacher (*ācārya*), the measurement of the teacher may also be taken as an alternative, since he is equal to the *adhvaryu*. The entire sacrificial ground (*āyatana*) with its constituent parts is described in the *Smṛti*:
The auspicious site for the fire-altar should be known to measure one *aratni* in length;
it should be free from a throat-like depression or a cavity at the base, whether for the *śrauta* or *aupāsana* rites.
Two girdles should be made, joined to the lines on the exterior.
"The outer [ring] is two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in width and the inner is four finger-breadths;
the outer is six finger-breadths in height and the inner is twelve finger-breadths.
Here, the mention of the *aupāsana* fire is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those rites performed with the ordinary fire as prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*.
Now, the method for constructing the fire-altar (*agnyāyatana*) is demonstrated by means of verses:
The cord should be the measure of a *piśīla*, and it should be both fine and firm; the cord should be as long as required by the measurement, and that much should be added. (1)
The mark of the guest-line (āgantukī) is at the midpoint; it should extend halfway across the hips and shoulders.
At the midpoint between the marks, there are two loops on either side in all the cords.
Having laid out the spine-line extending eastward, one should fix pegs according to the measurement;
one should then attach the loop situated in the long section to the eastern peg.
One should cast the noose situated at the short portion toward the western gnomon;
this is the mark for the purpose of pulling, and then, having pulled it, [one proceeds] to the south.
Then, one should fashion the right hip according to the established measurement;
likewise, having drawn it on the left side, one should fashion the left hip.
Then, having crossed the two nooses, one should fashion them over her shoulders in front. Thus it is said.

Viśvakarman also says: "Having drawn a single straight line from east to west, and having placed a thread between the two 'fish' at the south and north, one then forms a square marked by the corners."

The meaning is as follows: having first established an east-west line (prāgapara-sūtra) of the desired measurement, such as one cubit, and having determined the south and north directions by means of a "fish" (matsya) figure, one should take a cord of that same length and mark its two ends with equal divisions. Then, by pulling the center of that cord to those marks—either by means of a "fish" figure or by marking four corners—a square is produced. If one is unable to construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as a fire-sanctuary, it should be performed on a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), according to the statement in the *Smṛtisāra*: "One should perform the rite of oblation (homa) either in a pit or on a leveled mound. This measurement is found in the *Gṛhyakārikās*.
"A sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) for all rites should be one cubit square, or even one arm-span [square], and four finger-breadths in height. Regarding this,
it should be understood that the determination between these two stated measurements depends upon the specific fire-oblation (*homa*) being performed.
Also in the *Saṃgraha*:
"One should construct with a thread a square that is very smooth and symmetrical; it should be level, four finger-breadths in height, and sloping toward the east and north."
"One should make it either an arrow's length longer or according to the homa," it is said.

It should be understood that this measurement of an arrow's length (*iṣumātra*) is from the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), and not on all sides. The intended meaning is that four strings, each consisting of eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), should be made.
An arrow (*iṣu*) consists of three *aratni*s, according to the statement of Āpastamba: "An arrow is traditionally held to be three *aratni*s long."
The measurement of an *aratni* is given in the *Śulbasūtra*: "Twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) make an *aratni*, and half of that makes a *prādeśa*; such is the established rule.

In his commentary on this sūtra, both Sundara and Karavinda explained that this is the universal convention. Furthermore, according to another Smṛti, an *aratni* is the length from the elbow to the tip of the little finger.

In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, the measure of the arrow (iṣu) is stated differently: "The arrow consists of five spans (prādeśa). According to this ritual manual (kalpa), it consists of four strings, each measuring fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgula). Regarding the measure of the sand (sikatā) and its specific color and form, [the details are found] in the Baudhāyana Sūtra.

"One prepares a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) five *prastha*s in measure of pure, white, and dry sand, square and equal on all sides with a span (*aratni*) for a Brāhmaṇa; red-colored and triangular for a Kṣatriya; yellow-colored and shaped like a chariot wheel for a Vaiśya; sloping toward the east or toward the north. Here, "sand" refers to fine particles of earth. The measurement of "five *prastha*s of sand" is intended to mean a span in length. He [the author] also states the method of preparation:

"One raises the sand four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) towards the east, five finger-breadths towards the west, a specific excess of finger-breadths on the south, and a measure of one finger-breadth on the north. The portion ending with "towards the west" refers to the case where the altar slopes toward the east; the portion beginning with "a specific excess of finger-breadths" refers to the case where it slopes toward the north. The meaning is that the height on the south is measured by whatever specific excess there may be from the measure of one finger-breadth, while the height on the north is exactly one finger-breadth. The definition of this "specific excess" is found in the Śulba-sūtra:
"One should increase the measurement by one-third, and that [increase] by one-fourth, minus its own thirty-fourth part.

The intended meaning is as follows: having divided the measurement of the index finger or the upper portion of the middle finger into three parts, one should increase it by the measure of one such part; then, having added to that [increase] a fourth part of that part, minus its own thirty-fourth part, an elevation of that much should be made on the right side. On the left side, however, the elevation should be the full measure of the upper portion of the finger. This is the essential meaning. In another scripture, however—

"He prepares a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) sloping toward the east or toward the north, five finger-breadths high at the back and four finger-breadths high at the front; it is exactly the same elsewhere.

"Elsewhere" refers to the case where it slopes toward the north. Although the option of sloping toward both the east and the north is not mentioned here, it is nevertheless applicable because such a slope is observed in [other] locations.
Baudhāyana has also stated that these options are for the sake of specific desires (*kāmya*).

"One inclined toward the east is for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); one inclined toward the north is for one desiring food; one inclined toward the northeast is for one desiring offspring; and one that is level is for one desiring stability.
He also mentions the defects regarding sand: He [the same author] says:

"Now, therefore, we shall explain the defects of sand. One should avoid sand that contains ashes, hair, husks, potsherds, gravel, grass, bones, or ants, or which is moist. [The Lord Baudhāyana said: 'By ashes there is the ruin of the sacrificer; by hair, the death of a wife; by husks, the loss of sons; by potsherds, the loss of wealth; by gravel, separation from kinsmen; by grass, the failure of the ritual; by bones, the destruction of the village; by ants, the destruction of the kingdom; and by moist sand, fear arises.'"

The word "one should avoid" implies that the preparation of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) follows immediately thereafter. The mention of ants is intended as an illustration for all living creatures. A specific rule regarding the height of the sacrificial mound is stated in the *Vidhānapārijāta*:
"For a sacrifice of fifty oblations, the height should be measured at five finger-breadths; for a hundred oblations, the height should be measured at two finger-breadths;
for a thousand oblations, the height is four finger-breadths; and for ten thousand oblations, the height should be eight finger-breadths."

"The height for a *lakṣa* [sacrifice] shall be one hundred thousand finger-breadths (*nṛpāṅgula*), while the height for a *prayuta* [sacrifice] shall be one hundred twenty thousand finger-breadths (*viśāṅgula*).
For a *koṭi* sacrifice, the height shall be two hundred fifty-six thousand finger-breadths (*tattvāṅgula*); one should not prescribe a measurement greater than that."

Now, as an incidental discussion, the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the altar-ground (*sthaṇḍila*), which are required for rites such as pacification (*śānti*) involving many oblations, are described. Among these, up to forty-nine oblations, one uses only the altar-ground (*sthaṇḍila*). That should measure eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) on all sides and be raised by the height of a thumb. Regarding the subsequent [number of oblations], there is an option with the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) depending on whether one is incapable or capable [of performing the rite]. From fifty up to ninety-nine oblations, the size is that of a closed fist (*muṣṭi*); a *muṣṭi* is equivalent to a *ratni*.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for offerings from one hundred up to nine hundred and ninety-nine is measured by an *aratni*. An *aratni* is the distance from the tip of the little finger to the tip of the thumb when the hand is closed in a fist. For offerings of one thousand (*sahasra*) and above, it is one cubit (*hasta*). For ten thousand (*ayuta*) and above, it is two cubits. For one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) and above, it is four cubits. For one million (*daśalakṣa*) and above, it is six cubits. For ten million (*koṭi*) homas and above, it is eight or ten cubits. A cubit consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). A finger-breadth should be understood as the measure of eight barley grains placed side-by-side, or the length of the middle joint of one's own middle finger.

Or, by the fist-measure, [the length is] four *aṅgulas*. With thirty-four *aṅgulas* less half a barley-corn (*yava*), it is two cubits (*dvihasta*); with forty-one and a half *aṅgulas*, three cubits; with forty-eight *aṅgulas*, four cubits; with fifty-three and three-quarters *aṅgulas*, five cubits; with fifty-nine and three-quarters *aṅgulas*, six cubits; with sixty-three and a half *aṅgulas*, seven cubits; with sixty-eight minus one barley-corn *aṅgulas*, eight cubits; with seventy-two *aṅgulas*, nine cubits; and with seventy-six *aṅgulas*, ten cubits.

A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila) measuring ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgula) becomes sixteen cubits (hasta) in size. Only when there is a correct knowledge of the dimensions of the pit’s components—the diameter, the excavation, the navel, the neck, the girdle, and the womb—is the pit considered properly prepared. The method for constructing it will be explained in the section on pacification rites (śāntiprakaraṇa). As for the leveled altar, it is square and should be one or four finger-breadths in height. In the case of equal proportions, if the prescribed measurement is insufficient for the homa of coarse substances, a larger measurement may also be adopted. As for that which was stated by the author of the Kārikā:
Regarding the statement, "From the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the rice-grain lines should be two finger-breadths [apart], or two finger-breadths more;
one should have it made with either a single line or a double line as the Agnibhadra," the source for that must be investigated.

Regarding the preparation of the sacrificial site (*āyatana*), such as its smearing with cow dung, it is stated in the *Saṃgraha* concerning the consecration of the site: "One should smear that with cow dung. "That" refers to the fire-altar (*agni-āyatana*).
The reason for this is stated in the *Smṛtiratnākara*, citing a Purāṇa:
"Everywhere the earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, is pure;
so then, why is this [spot] smeared with the dust from Viṣṇu’s foot?"
"In ancient times, indeed, Śakra slew the great asura Vṛtra with his thunderbolt;
this plastering was performed for the purpose of being smeared with his fat."
If, after the ground has been leveled for the altar, a dog stands upon it or elsewhere, then a specific expiation has been stated by Baudhāyana:

"If a cow, a horse, or some other beast of prey should scatter [the earth] on the leveled ground or stand upon it, one sprinkles its footprint and mutters: 'O Earth, place of sacrifice to the gods, I have not harmed your root with plants. Then one proceeds with the ritual from where it was interrupted."

"One should scatter" means one should make it strewn with urine and so forth; or else, the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. In this view, "one should scatter" means one should perform the discharge of semen, urine, and excrement. In the word *adhitiṣṭhet* ("one should step upon"), the words ending in the accusative—*sthaṇḍila* and *uddhata*—are to be supplied. The mention of *sthaṇḍila* (a leveled mound) is indicative of a *kuṇḍa* (sacrificial pit). The mention of a dog is indicative of forbidden two-footed or four-footed animals. The method of drawing lines and the sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) and so forth are described in the *Dharma-sūtra*:

"In whatever place one is about to establish the sacred fire, having drawn three lines each toward the east and the north, having sprinkled water and poured it out, one should set aside the remainder of that water either to the north or to the east."

Whenever one intends to kindle or establish the fire for any domestic rite (*gārhya*) or customary rite (*sāmayācārika*), whether at home or in the forest, one should first draw three lines directed eastward with their tips pointing east and ending toward the north. Having drawn three lines directed northward with their tips pointing north and ending toward the east, one should sprinkle them with water. Having sprinkled them, one should pour out this sprinkling-water either to the north or to the east of the fire’s hearth. After pouring it out, one should place another vessel of water nearby.

However, in the case of cooking, [the rule] does not apply to women, because the gender is intended to be significant in the phrase "about to kindle the fire. But regarding the phrase "the noble ones being purified," Ujjvalākāra has explained that [the rule] does apply. Having set aside water sufficient for the rite—other than the water used for sprinkling—from the vessel used for sprinkling, one should place it near oneself.

Alternatively, having taken water from a jar filled with pure water into another vessel for the purpose of sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) and pouring out (*utsecanā*), and having performed the sprinkling and pouring out with that water, one should place the remaining water still in the jar near oneself for the sake of the ritual action. Since the placement of the water near oneself is established by the very fact of the matter, the explicit statement here is for the purpose of ensuring that the jar from which the water was taken for sprinkling and pouring out is itself placed near oneself immediately after those acts.

Thus, it is established that the water-pitcher (kalaśa) should remain in the very middle of the house until the point of overflowing. Alternatively, this statement is intended to prohibit placing that pitcher on the ground for that duration. Nor should it be argued that this has only an invisible (transcendental) purpose; for when a visible purpose—namely, the accomplishment of the functions of the *praṇītā* water and so forth—is possible, it is improper to assume an invisible one. Even in the absence of overflowing, this [placement] must indeed take place because it is necessary.

The prescription for drawing lines, sprinkling, pouring out, and placing [the water] in the *Dharmasūtra* serves to exclude the ritual procedures (*tantra*) prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras*—other than the sprinkling and so forth—in rites such as the fire-oblation (*agnikārya*), by virtue of the force of that specific enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*). Consequently, since those [procedures] are not prescribed there, the drawing of lines, sprinkling, pouring out, and placing would also be excluded; it is for this purpose [that they are mentioned]. Alternatively, it is to indicate that these are not mandatory in the rite stated in the *Gṛhyasūtra*. However, the placing of water (*udakanidhāna*) certainly takes place because it is mandatory. But in the *Vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, even this does not occur.

Because of the contradiction caused by the specific injunction, "Perform according to the instruction," the sequence beginning with the drawing of lines and ending with the placing of water must be performed prior to the *uddhanana* (sweeping/scraping), and not between the *uddhanana* and the *avokṣaṇa* (sprinkling). Otherwise, there would result a contradiction of the immediate succession (*avyavadhāna*) between the sweeping and the sprinkling, which is indicated by the suffix *-lyap* in the expression "having swept, one should sprinkle" (*uddhatyāvokṣyet*).

The necessity of performing [the rites] in the middle, setting aside the lack of interval between the sweeping (*uddhanana*) and the sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*), should only be asserted when a basis for their performance in the middle is found among the acts such as scraping (*ullekhana*) mentioned in the *Dharmasūtras*. Such a basis does not exist here. On the contrary, the lack of interval between the sweeping and the sprinkling is observed in many instances.

Nor can it be argued that, according to the principle of "not contradicting the learned" (*śiṣṭākopa*), just as the interruption by sneezing between the making of the altar-ground (*vedakaraṇa*) and the making of the sacrificial altar (*vedikaraṇa*) sets aside the lack of interval between both, the same should apply here as well.

In this regard, when the question arises as to which of these two—the sequence [of ritual acts] or the [act of] hunger—is to be sublated, since both reside within the same defect, it is argued that the sequence, being a property of the ritual act (*padārtha-dharma*), is weaker than the *ācamana* (sipping of water) caused by hunger, which is the nature of the act itself; for Jaimini accepted the sublation of non-intervention [only] in such cases where there is a basis for it. However, in the present case, because there is no evidence for such a meaning—that the *ullekhana* (scraping) must be performed immediately after the *uddhanana* (throwing up)—one cannot assume a sublation of the non-intervention between these two.

Nor should it be argued that because Mātṛdatta demonstrates the acts of smearing and so forth immediately after the act of stirring the fire, they must be performed at that very moment. For the passage from the Bhāṣya beginning with "again" (*punar*) indicates that smearing, sprinkling, pouring out, and placing water are also to be performed because they are prescribed in the *Dharmaśāstras*; thus, since this [Bhāṣya] intends merely to include them, one must assume that the immediate sequence implied by the gerund suffix (*lyap*) is set aside.

Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction regarding immediate succession, and that the passage beginning with "punar" (again) is intended merely to indicate a sequence; for when a matter can be resolved through consistency with immediate succession itself, it is improper to assume anything else. The statement "having lifted up" is merely an utterance intended to show the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) and the means (*sādhana*) of that refinement; it is not intended to exclude the act of sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*). Otherwise, the Bhāṣya text would lose its authority due to being in conflict with the Sūtra.

The non-mention of sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) is because it is self-evident. Furthermore, its existence is indicated by the word "again" (*punaḥ*) in the phrase "because it is seen again in the Dharmaśāstra. How so? Since the word "again" indicates repetition, and since there can be no connection of "again" with either the digging out (*uddhanana*)—as there is no repetition of that—or with the scraping and other acts mentioned in the Dharma-sūtras (as there is no repetition of those), it follows that sprinkling occurs twice; thus, the word "again" must be construed with the sprinkling mentioned in the Dharma-sūtra, occurring prior [to the second instance].

Since there is no other sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) subsequent to the removal of the soil (*uddhanana*), by this [argument] even the suspicion that scratching (*ullekhana*) and the other rites occur after the removal of soil and the sprinkling is dispelled. If one were to say that the single sprinkling and the pouring out (*utsecanādi*) are not performed now and are not mentioned in other manuals (*paddhati*), that is based solely on error.

If it is argued that these [rites] are not mentioned in other manuals because they are considered non-obligatory due to the force of their prescription in the *Dharmasūtra*, then even the mention [of them] should not have been written down. We see that the very basis for the claim that "the scratching was written down while the sprinkling and pouring out were not," despite both being prescribed by the same sūtra and being dependent on whether or not the scratching is performed, is nothing but error.
The implements for drawing lines are [described] in the *Baudhāyanagṛhya*—

"Not with a clod of earth, nor with wood, nor with a pebble, nor with a fingernail. Indeed, by means of wood one becomes diseased; by a clod of earth, there is the destruction of the family; by a pebble, the loss of sons; and by a fingernail, the destruction of kinsmen. Therefore, having taken up a fragment of gold, silver, or copper, or rice, barley, or *darbha* grass, with the thumb and the ring finger (*mahānāmni*), he should draw a straight line from the middle [of the hair] towards the east. And so forth.

The *mahānāmī* [finger] is the ring finger (*upakaniṣṭhikā*). It is employed here precisely because it serves for the act of grasping, as there is no contradiction; however, the method of drawing lines—namely, "having drawn three lines toward the east and three toward the north"—is not employed here, as it would contradict that [act of grasping].
In the *Gobhilapariśiṣṭa*:
"Neither with a fingernail, nor with wood, nor with stone, nor with anything made of clay..."
A Brahmin who desires spiritual accomplishment should draw a sacrificial altar.
If one uses a fingernail, one becomes afflicted with bad nails; by using a wooden stick, one contracts disease;
by using a stone, there will be loss of wealth; and by using an earthen vessel, discord is certain.
If it is richly laden with fruit, one shall be prosperous; if with flowers, one attains glory;
if with leaves, there will be gain of wealth; and by means of *kuśa* grass, long life is attained.
"Therefore, one should first draw an excellent *sthaṇḍila* with fruit, a flower, a leaf, or even *kuśa* grass combined with copper filings.
Regarding the characteristics of sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*), the *Saṃgraha* states:
"The sprinkling should be performed with the hand turned downwards.
In the Gṛhya-sūtra: "Having churned the fire, or having brought a common [fire], he scatters it and adds fuel."

The meaning is that, having produced fire by churning wood from a sacrificial tree, or having brought ordinary fire from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), one establishes it in the middle of the sacrificial ground (*āyatana*), adds fuel-wood, and causes it to blaze.
As stated in the *Saṃgraha*: "In a pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should properly [invoke] the Fire-god by his respective name."
"One should place [the fire] in the central region," it is said.
Also, in the *Smṛtisāra*:
"In either a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should [invoke] the eater of oblations by his respective name."

"With the *vyāhṛtis*, one should cast [the fire] into the center, facing oneself, so that it is fit"—this refers to the sacrificial fire (*havirbhujam agnim*). "Fit" (*alam*) means sufficient; here, the word "for the oblation" (*homāya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis for *alam*. Fitness is twofold: being born from the *araṇi* wood, and consisting of many well-kindled embers.
Of these, the first is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"The fire produced from friction is the best; that produced from a sun-crystal is the next best;
that from the house of a Vedic scholar is middling; and that produced from one's own home and so forth is inferior. Thus it is stated. The second [source] is in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:

"In either a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the wise man should establish the consumer of oblations (Agni) in the central region— consisting of brightly glowing embers and free from smoke. Regarding the vessels for the bringing forth of the fire, Atri says:
"Gold, silver, or copper; in the absence of these, however, one made of clay—this is prescribed for the bringing forward of the fire when covered by another vessel. Gobhila also says:
"When a beautiful copper vessel or the like is covered with another vessel, one should perform the bringing of the fire; or even in such a case, in a shallow earthen bowl (*śarāva*).
Here, "in such a case" means when it is covered. A *śarāva* is a specific type of earthenware vessel.
As for the statement: "One should not perform the bringing forward of the fire in a shallow dish, a broken vessel, a potsherd, or even an iron pan; it brings about the fear of loss of health."

The prohibition stated in the *Smṛtisāra* refers to old earthenware bowls (*śarāva*), because the *Nāradapañcarātra* states that a new bowl is to be accepted: "In a metallic vessel, or a copper vessel, or indeed in a new earthenware bowl. In this context, the term "metallic" (*taijasa*) refers to vessels other than copper, according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*).

(From the *Gobhilīyapariśiṣṭa*: "The bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) should not be performed with potsherds or broken vessels, nor with dry cow-dung; [if done so], it brings fear to the sacrificer.")

"With broken vessels, whether made of clay or metal. Regarding the term *āmair* (unbaked), by virtue of contextual appropriateness, it should be understood as referring specifically to those made of clay. "With cow-dung" means with a piece of cow-dung.
Furthermore, in that very same [text]:
"Small, poorly prepared, interrupted, not well-kindled, and unadorned..."
He was brought back again in haste, bringing fear to the sacrificer.

Therefore, with an auspicious vessel, one should perform the bringing forth of the fire (agnipraṇayana) in a manner that is uninterrupted, not meager, and abundant, which brings prosperity to the sacrificer. Indeed, an auspicious vessel should be prepared, which brings happiness to the sacrificer.
"A wise person should lead the fire using a beautiful vessel made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*);

in its absence, with a new earthenware dish (*śarāva*) facing it. [Commentary: "Small" means insufficient for the ritual; "disconnected" means sufficient for the ritual but loose and having many parts even when led forward; "unignited" means not flaming; "unrefined" means not consecrated by the rites such as covering with another vessel; "because of smallness" means brought again and again; in the compound *avicchinnākṛśam*, there is a *karmadhāraya*; "much" is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*); in the absence of gold and so forth, [one uses] bell-metal.
The installation of the fire must be performed by one who has restrained his speech—
“One should perform the installation of the fire while restraining one's speech and controlling the senses,” as stated in the *Saṃgraha* within the *Prayogadarpaṇa*.
Likewise, silence must be maintained even at the time of the fire-oblation (homa):

"Varuṇa takes away the luster of one who bathes; Agni takes away the fortune of one who offers oblations; and Death takes away the lifespan of one who eats. Therefore, silence is prescribed for these three occasions."

Thus it is stated in the *Prayogapārijāta* based on another Smṛti text: "One should establish the Fire-eater (Agni) by means of their respective names. When there arises the inquiry as to what those names are, the *Pārijāta* states:
"The first is proclaimed as the common fire, Pāvaka."
The fire named Māruta is prescribed for the rite of conception (garbhādhāna);
thereafter, at the rite for male progeny (puṃsavana), it is to be known as Pavamāna; at the parting of the hair (sīmanta), it is named Maṅgala; and at the birth-rite (jātakarman), it is Prabala.
Indeed, the fire named Pārthiva is for the naming ceremony; Śuci is prescribed for the first feeding of solid food.

The fire named Sabhya is for the tonsure ceremony (caula), and Samudbhava is for the instruction in vows (vratādeśa). At the gift of a cow (godāna), the fire is named Sūrya, and at the marriage, he is known as Yojaka.
On the fourth day, Śikhin is proclaimed, or alternatively Dhṛti-Agni;
he is to be known as Dvija in the Āvasathya rite, and Rukmaka in the Vaiśvadeva;
Viṭ is indeed in the Prāyaścitta, and Pāvaka in the Pākayajñas.
He is the carrier of oblations for the gods and the bearer of funeral offerings for the ancestors;
he is declared the bestower of boons in rites of pacification (śāntika) and the increaser of strength in rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika);
in the rite of final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) he is named Iḍa, and in rites of sorcery (ābhicārika) he is the fire of wrath.
For the purpose of subjugation, he is named Kāmada; in forest fires, he is Dūṣaka;
in the stomach, he is known as Jāṭhara; in the cremation of the dead, he is Kravyāda;
in the Lakṣahoma, he is Vahni; and in the Koṭihoma, he is Hutāśana.
In the ocean is indeed the Vāḍava fire, and likewise the Saṃvartaka fire in the dissolution;
Brahmā is the Gārhapatya fire, and Īśvara is the Dakṣiṇa fire;
Viṣṇu is the Āhavanīya fire—these are the three fires in the Agnihotra.
"Having thus known the names of the fires, one should commence the domestic rites."

Although this statement appears to concern merely the knowledge of the names, nevertheless— because the requirement to fulfill the expectancy for a name is necessary in such summary statements as, "One should establish the Fire-god by means of each respective name," and because there is no other scripture to fulfill that expectancy— it should be understood that this [text] also has that purpose. Furthermore, the installation should be performed with the *vyāhṛtis* ending in the *praṇava*.

Regarding the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*): because of the observation [in scripture], "Having established the fire with *bhūrbhuvaḥ suvarom*," and because of Bharadvāja’s statement, "He establishes the fire with *bhūrbhuvaḥ suvarom*. And this ending with the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*) is made optional by the injunction of the mere *vyāhṛtis* found in the cited essence of the Smṛti and the forthcoming statement of Baudhāyana. This applies wherever the author of the Sūtra says, "Having kindled the fire," from the digging up of the ground until the establishment of the fire.

Where [the text] does not state [a specific action], there, while remaining in one's own place, the rite should be performed according to the procedure for strewing grass (*paristaraṇa*) and so forth. Some consider the kindling of the fire (*agniprajvalana*) and its settling (*upasamādhāna*) to be a restatement of what is already established; for them, it should be understood that the actions such as adding fuel (*samindhana*) and so forth are to be performed at the *aupāsana* fire, whereas digging out the ground (*uddhanana*) and so forth are to be done elsewhere. This very view is the correct one, because of the scriptural observation: "Having settled the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire."

[Objection: "Is it not the case that in the passage 'having kindled the Dakṣiṇāgni,' since fetching [the fire] is impossible, the meaning of the word *upasamādhāna* must be 'kindling'? But here, since fetching is possible, the meaning of the word *upasamādhāna* is indeed 'fetching. Once fetching from another place is established, the placing [of the fire] is also established, and consequently, the actions connected with it, such as digging up [the ground], are also established. [Reply: No, because this would result in a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*). [Objection: "In that case, the restatements (*anuvāda*) found here and there would be useless, since the kindling is already established by the very nature of the situation. [Reply: True.

In this regard, because the repetition serves the purpose of restricting the location, it is not redundant. Where there is the injunction, "Having kindled the fire," the rite must be performed at that very location specified; elsewhere, however, there is no restriction. It should be understood that if it is not performed at the specified location, the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) applies, and not otherwise.

The kindling of the fire must not be performed with wood that has not been sprinkled [with water]. This is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*: "One should not place un-sprinkled fuel into the fire. One should not place un-sprinkled fuel into the *śrauta*, *smārta*, or worldly (*laukika*) fire. Regarding this, Ujjvalākāra explained that some do not permit it for the worldly fire.

Regarding the specific rules for kindling the fire, the *Dharmasūtra* states: "And one should not blow upon it. This implies "while impure" (*aprayata*). One who is impure should not blow upon this fire; however, some say there is no fault for one who is pure. Others say one should not blow upon it with the mouth, based on the observation in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "One should not blow upon the fire with the mouth. Yet, in another *Smṛti*, it says: "One may blow upon the fire with the mouth, for fire was born from the mouth."

There is an option between the two. Another says that because it is seen in the *Vājasaneyaka* within the context of the Śrauta rites—"From the mouth fire was born; therefore it is kindled by means of the mouth"—blowing with the mouth applies to the Śrauta rite, while elsewhere there is a Smṛti prohibition. Others, however, desire blowing by means of a hollow tube made of bamboo or iron. Thus, through the connection of the mouth’s function with the fire, the Śruti is also upheld. And because of the fear of the danger of spitting drops from the mouth, the Smṛti prohibition is also maintained; so it has been explained by the author of the *Ujjvalā*. In the *Saṃgraha*:
"Placing a blade of grass or even a piece of wood between them, one should blow upon the fire with the mouth;
for fire was born from the mouth.
Since fire was produced from the bamboo, the bamboo is purifying to the fire."
"Therefore, the wise man should kindle the fire of dharma with a bamboo flute alone.
The Śruti also says:
"The bamboo is indeed brilliance; the Pravargya is brilliance. By means of brilliance, he thus perfects brilliance."

The prohibition against touching fire with bamboo is stated in another text: "One should not touch fire with bamboo. Regarding this, Devala states the materials that should be used: "One should not blow on the fire with cloth, nor with a leaf, nor with the hand, a winnowing basket, the mouth, or wood; nor should one do so with a fan or similar objects."
In the *Saṃgraha*:
"Blowing [the bellows] with a leaf causes disease; with a winnowing basket, the destruction of wealth;
with the hand, one meets death; and with a harsh [material], the destruction of beauty."
"By [blowing] with a cloth there would be the destruction of one's wife; by [blowing] with the mouth, there would be the loss of life.

As for the prohibition of blowing with the mouth during the *kali* age, as stated in the rule "blowing with the mouth," this should be understood to apply only to direct blowing with the mouth, and not even to that which is prescribed by the rule "having placed a tube (*dhamanī*) in between.

Thereafter, the worship (*upasthāna*) of the consecrated fire must be performed. This is because of the statement of Baudhāyana: "Having scattered [the grass] with the *vyāhṛtis* and having added fuel, he worships [the fire] with the mantra: 'The beloved domestic guest in the house... etc.
Then, meditation upon the fire should be performed:
"One who is about to offer oblations should know the nature of the fire as enjoined by the Śruti;
a rite performed by one who does not know it is held to yield meager fruit."

This is according to the statement of Gobhila. "Enjoined by the Śruti" refers to that which is enjoined by the Śruti verse beginning with *catvāri śṛṅgā*. This is also an illustration for that which is enjoined by Smṛti, namely: "seven-handed and four-horned. Regarding the specific visualization, the *Śāradātilaka* states:
"The preceptor should meditate upon Vaiśvānara standing during the oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*)."
"He should lie down during the oblations of clarified butter and remain seated for the remaining rites"—
this rule is mandatory in Tantric ritual.

Then follows the *anvādhāna* (the preliminary placing of fuel). This is established by traditional practice (*ācāra*), and it is likewise stated in the *Prayogavaijayantī*: "In this case, the *anvādhāna* is performed according to traditional practice. And that consists of the placing of three large fuel-sticks (*samidh*), as it is observed in the Śrauta ritual. Regarding this, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) also perform the mention of the deities, which will be explained in the practical manual (*prayoga*). As for the statement here, "as he says 'that'," which refers to the sweeping (*parisamūhana*) mentioned in another ritual procedure—that is trivial; for what is stated in the section on the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) has no application in the preceding context. Then follow the spreading of grass around the fire (*paristaraṇa*) and so forth. This is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:

"He strews darbha grass around the fire with the tips pointing eastward; or [he may have them] with the tips pointing northward, being behind and in front. He places those on the south above those on the north, and those on the north below those on the south, if they are pointed both eastward and northward."

He strews [the grass] with darbha blades whose tips point eastward, first in the front, then to the south, then to the west, and then to the north; those in the rear and in the front are short and end toward the north. Alternatively, those darbha blades which are in the rear and in the front have their tips pointing northward, while those to the south and to the north have their tips pointing eastward. In the expression "having tips pointing east and north," the word *agra* (tip) is completed with each [direction] individually, meaning "those with tips pointing east" and "those with tips pointing north."

The meaning is: "if" refers to this alternative view that the *darbha* grass used for the strewing has its tips pointing toward the northeast (*prāgudagagra*). In that case, one places the southern *darbha* blades so that they lie above the eastern and western *darbha* blades; and one places the northern *darbha* blades so that they lie below them. Regarding the mention of "with *darbhas*" here, according to custom there are four *darbha* blades in each section. However, according to logic, the plural number resolves into three, as stated in the *Vaijayantī*. Kaśyapa states the limits of the area for the strewing:
"One should spread the *kuśa* grasses in sequence according to a measurement of ten finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)," it is said.
However, in another *Smṛti*, the limit of the area for spreading is stated to be five finger-breadths:
"By three, four, five, or six finger-breadths..."
"The sprinkling, the enclosing sticks, the strewing, and likewise the worship.
Thus, there is an option here. In this context, the "fire-field" (agnikṣetra) or the outer girdle (bāhyamekhalā) should be understood as the limit from which the materials are taken.
Then follows the strewing of *kuśa* grass and so forth in the place of the Brahman priest. This is stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra:

"To the south of the fire, having strewn darbha grass in the place of the Brahman, he takes the fire into himself with the two verses, 'I take into myself that Agni who is ours,' and so forth; then, to the north of the fire, having strewn darbha grass, he arranges the ritual materials as required."

Having strewn abundant *darbha* grass correctly upon the seat for the Brahman priest to the south of the fire that has been encircled, and having taken his own fire into himself with the two verses beginning "May he who is our Agni... while forming the corresponding intention and reciting them, and likewise having strewn abundant *darbha* grass correctly to the north of the fire, he arranges the ritual materials according to their purpose and as required; this is the meaning.

The author of the *Gṛhyakārikā* has explained the meaning of the verse "mayi yo naḥ" as "having established the fire situated in the heart with two blades of darbha grass" and "having taken the fire into oneself"; however, this should be disregarded because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding the statement in another ritual manual (*prayoga*) that one should hold the right hand together with kuśa grass to the heart at the time of taking the fire into oneself, its source must be investigated. Although the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is not mentioned in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, it should nevertheless be accepted because it is seen in the *Śrauta-sūtra* and because it is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
There is a specific rule regarding its measurement in another *Smṛti*: [text follows].
"Having cut off from the tips of the sacrificial grass a span's length,
one should take up a handful of it for the *barhis*."

In rites involving a single oblation, such as the *sthālīpāka* and others, [the sacrificial grass] should be the size of a fist. However, in rites involving multiple oblations, one should take sufficient sacrificial grass (*barhis*) so that all the oblations can be placed upon it; this is because of Kātyāyana’s statement: "The measure is determined by the purpose. Regarding the number of fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and their binding, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* states: "One binds the fuel consisting of twenty-one pieces of wood, or a number equal to the quantity of oblations; upon it, one places the *śamyā* pegs and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and binds the fuel."

He binds together twenty-one pieces of wood as a sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) consisting of twenty-one logs; "having bound them" means having prepared them. Alternatively, the meaning is exactly as it is heard in the text. In this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), only the binding itself should be performed prior to the offering of the ladle (*darvī*). However, the placing (*āsādana*) [of the fuel] occurs only after the placing of the *upaveṣa*, according to the rule "by whatever means the purpose is served," because it is seen so in the Śrauta ritual. Furthermore, after the binding, they should also be placed not below [the altar]; for the binding of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) before the fuel is also seen in the Śrauta ritual.

The sacrificial grass (barhis) is to be placed down together with the fuel (idhma). Nor should it be argued that the placing of the fuel and the sacrificial grass must occur immediately after the placing of the vessel for the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī); for it is appropriate to place those items useful through their mere existence immediately after placing those items useful through their own consumption.

For objects of utility are of three kinds: some by their own existence, some by their transformation, and some by their destruction. Among these, the ladle (*darvī*), clarified butter (*ājya*), the pot (*sthālī*), the vessel for carrying forward the water (*praṇītāpraṇayana*), the sprinkling-vessel (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), and the fire-wood-rake (*upaveṣa*) are useful for the oblation (*homa*) by their own existence. The stone, the two garments, the upper cloth, the skin of an antelope (*ajina*), the girdle of muñja grass (*mauñjīmekhalā*), the staff, the loincloth (*kaupīna*), the thread for binding it, the sacred thread (*upavīta*), the alms-bowl (*bhikṣāpātra*), and the broom (*kūrca*) are useful for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) by their own existence.

Rice grains are useful for the cooking of the *sthālīpāka* through their transformation into something else (*svānyathābhāva*). They are useful for the common oblations (*sādhāraṇahoma*) through their own disappearance (*svalopa*), consisting as they do of the *saṃmārjana*-grass, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the fuel-wood (*idhma*), the kindling-grass (*avajvalanadarbha*), and the clarified butter (*ājya*). The seven *palāśa* fuel-sticks are useful through their own disappearance. Thus it should be understood in each respective case. "Its own existence" (*svasattā*) refers to the unchanging essential nature (*avikārisvarūpa*) of its own vessel and so forth. "Its transformation into something else" (*svānyathābhāva*) refers to the rice and so forth transforming into another state, such as the form of rice-grains (*taṇḍula*) or cooked porridge (*odana*).

"Svalopa" means the loss or destruction of one's own [substances], such as the sacrificial fuel (*samid*) and so forth. In this manner, the ritual implements (*yajñasādhana-padārtha*) are of three kinds.
As the Bhaṭṭācāryas have said:
"The means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) are [of three types] by way of their own transformation (*anyathābhāva*), their existence (*sattā*), and their loss (*svalopa*)."
"The threefold [factors] are conjoined with action as its directors."

"Parimāṇa" means the measure or number of oblations (*āhutis*). "Āhutiparimāṇa" refers to that which has a measure equal to the measure of the oblations; this is a *madhyamapadalopa* (middle-term-elided) compound, like the word *uṣṭramukha*. The meaning is that the fuel-wood (*dāruka*) should be as many [pieces] as there are oblations. According to some, the principal and subsidiary oblations (*aṅga-pradhāna-āhutis*) are to be counted, excluding the *jaya* and other secondary offerings (*upahoma*). According to others, even the *jaya* and others are to be counted. Upon that fuel-wood (*idhma*), he binds—that is, fastens—three enclosing sticks (*paridhis*) shaped like *śamyās*.

The word *śamyā* here denotes a specific shape. Since the fact that the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) have the shape of a *śamyā* is already established by the subsequent injunction, "He encloses with *śamyās*," the mention of *śamyā* here is for the purpose of ensuring that they are fashioned into the shape of a *śamyā* at the very time of binding [the sacrificial post], and not later. According to some, in the case of the twenty-one-wood fire, and in Vedic modifications (*vikṛti*) where twenty-four woods are observed, one should desire additional enclosing sticks.

Others, however, include the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) within the count [of the fuel-wood], because they are seen to be so included in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. But according to the view that [the fuel-wood] constitutes the measure of the oblations, since a kindling-stick (*samidh*) is seen for each oblation, it is logical that the enclosing-sticks must indeed be additional. When it is said, "He binds the *śamyā*-sticks to the enclosing-sticks," it would follow that there is a separate binding of those that are additional; so that this shall not happen, it is stated: "in that very faggot" (*tasminn idhme*).

Since that [number] was already established by the word *tasmin* (in that), the mention of *idhma* (fuel-wood) is for the purpose of including the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) within the count of the fuel-wood. Although it would have been sufficient to say simply *idhme*, the use of the word *tasmin* is intended to indicate that even when the fuel-wood serves as the measure for the oblations, these [enclosing sticks] are indeed additional; thus also says Mātṛdatta.
The type of wood for the fuel-wood is stated in the Śrautasūtra: "He binds together the fuel-wood of twenty-one pieces, made of Palāśa or Khadira wood."
The nature of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) is also stated in that very same place:

"The three enclosing sticks are made from unspecified trees; they are with their bark, moist, for it is known that 'they are succulent,' and they are dry, for it is known that 'this is for the sake of purity. The southern one is the thickest and the longest; the northern one is the thinnest and the shortest."

"Aniyatavṛkṣāḥ" refers to those for which various kinds of trees are the material cause (*upādāna*). "With bark" (*satvakkāḥ*) means accompanied by their bark. This qualification, however, is not possible in the case of the *paridhi* enclosures, because the author of the Sūtra prescribes that the *paridhis* must have the shape of a *śamyā*, and that [shape] is impossible without carving. By logical reasoning, for the sake of achieving the shape of a *śamyā*, one must indeed perform carving so that the base part of the thick wood becomes thin and the tip part becomes thick.

And thus, there is a sublation of the *śamyā* shape prescribed in the *Śrautasūtra* by the rule regarding the *sattva-kṛtā* [wooden peg]. For it is known that "they are moist"—this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Regarding the sense "they are fresh," the sense "they are dry" is known as being for the sake of purity (*medhyatva*)—this is an explanatory passage. This demonstration of the two explanatory passages is for the purpose of knowing their status as auxiliary elements of the ritual (*karmāṅgatva*). And it has been stated by Baudhāyana: "By means of explanatory passages, [one attains] prosperity."

Thus, it should be understood that there are two options: the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) may be made either moist or dry. If one is unaware of the specific explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), one should perform the expiation for a lapse in the *yajus* formula by offering the oblation "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā" into the *aupāsana* fire itself, and then offer the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). "Thickestness" means being more massive; this refers to the middle enclosing stick. "Fineness" means being slender; this refers to the southern stick in comparison to the middle one. Likewise, "longer" means greater length.

*Aniṣṭhatva* means being more minute; *hrasiṣṭhatva* means being shorter. These [qualities] apply to the southern and northern [sacrificial posts] in relation to the middle one. The word *ardha* denotes a part. That which exists in the southern part is *dakṣiṇārdhya*; that which exists in the northern part is *uttarārdhya*.

Regarding the dimensions of the fuel (*idhma*) and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), Vailaṅkika and Ātreyāyana state: "The fuel is two *prādeśas* long, and the enclosing sticks are three *prādeśas* long."

In the *Baudhāyana-gṛhya*, however, the measure of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) is stated to be one cubit (*aratni*): "The enclosing sticks are one cubit long, either dry or fresh, and with their bark intact. This should be understood as being applicable here when the sacrificial altar (*āyatana*) is of small dimensions. Furthermore, the measure of the fuel-stick (*idhma*) as one span (*prādeśa*) is also stated by that same author: "There are twenty-one pieces of wood for the fuel-stick, each measuring one span; thus it is explained in the Brāhmaṇa."

From this sūtra, which enumerates twenty-one [items], it follows that the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are distinct. However, this applies only to the followers of Baudhāyana and not to us. This is because, in the passage "In that [fire-altar] he binds the sacrificial pegs (*śamyā*), the enclosing sticks, and the fuel (*idhma*) together," the author of the sūtra, by including the term *idhma*, has indicated the absence of any distinction [between the enclosing sticks and the fuel]; therefore, we do not accept a distinction that contradicts that. Furthermore, the fuel is either two *prādeśas* long or merely one *prādeśa*.

The fact that the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are arm-length is also stated by Bharadvāja: "The enclosing sticks are either the length of a *śamyā* or the length of an arm. A *śamyā* is thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), while an arm is forty-two finger-breadths.
In the *Saṃgraha*:
"The fuel-stick (*samit*), the purifier (*pavitra*), and the *veda*—these three are measured at one span (*prādeśa*)."

"The fuel-stick (idhma) should be made double [the length of the sacrificial grass], and the enclosing-stick (paridhi) is traditionally held to be triple; according to the Smṛti, the fuel-stick is a span (prādeśa), or the enclosing-stick is traditionally held to be double [that]."

*Prādeśa* means the measure of a *prādeśa*. *Dviguṇa* means double that, i.e., two *prādeśas*; this refers to the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). The singular number used for *paridhi* is employed in the sense of a class. From this statement, it should be understood that the *prādeśa* measurement of the fuel-stick (*idhma*) is optional, as is the double-*prādeśa* measurement of the enclosing sticks. And this option is to be understood as applicable when [the standard size] is impossible. Regarding the variation in the size of the enclosing sticks, it is stated in the Baudhāyana Gṛhya-sūtra: "He makes three enclosing sticks [of the lengths of] the middle finger, the ring finger, and the little finger."

The word "measures" (*pramāṇāni*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. [The *dakṣiṇa* measure] is measured from the base of the upper arm to the tip of the middle finger; [the *madhyama* measure] is measured from the base of the upper arm to the tip of the ring finger; [the *uttara* measure] is measured from the base of the upper arm to the tip of the little finger—this is the meaning. The rest is clear in its sense. In reality, however, just as the word *śamyā* denotes a specific shape, so too does it denote the measurement of thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). And thus, in this case, the lengthiness and shortness mentioned in the Vedic scripture (*śrauta*) do not apply.

Nor is there a difference in the measurement of the southern and northern enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) as stated by Baudhāyana—namely, that they are respectively the middle, ring, and little fingers; rather, it should be understood that for all of them, the measurement is exactly thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Furthermore, the binding of the fuel-wood (*idhma*) must be performed with a cord (*śulba*) alone, because this is seen in the *Śrauta* texts and is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
As for the making of the cord, it is described in the *Śrautasūtra*:

"Having made a cord (*śulba*) from *darbha* grass—either with roots or rootless—with an odd number of strands, he lays it down with its tip pointing eastward or northward. Here, "with an odd number of strands" (*ayugdhātu*) means having an uneven number of strands. *Dhātu* means a joint; some say it means a part. Since there is no specific qualification regarding "an odd number of strands" here, a cord with an uneven number of strands sufficient for binding the fuel-wood (*idhma*) should be prepared; however, unlike the cord used for binding the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), there is no restrictive rule that it must have three or five strands.
Then follows the setting out of the vessels and so forth. This is stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra:
"The ladle, the bunch of grass, the vessel for clarified butter, the vessel for carrying forward the Praṇītā water, and whatever else is required—all these at once, or as they become available."

The *kūrca* is a seat for the purpose of reciting the *Sāvitrī*. The phrase "that by which there is a purpose" (*yena cārthaḥ*) is intended to include even those items not explicitly mentioned that possess a functional purpose. "Only once" (*sakṛd eva*) means simultaneously. He prepares all the vessels and materials—both those mentioned and those unmentioned—that have a purpose, "as they arise" (*yathopapādam*), meaning according to their availability.

Because the scripture states, "If one were to bring them up one by one, they would belong to the ancestors," it is prescribed that for rites dedicated to the ancestors—such as the monthly *śrāddha*, the *aṣṭakā*, and others—only a single vessel at a time should be set down. Because the scripture states, "If all together, they belong to humans," it is prescribed that for rites dedicated to humans—such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and others—the vessels are to be set down simultaneously.

The meaning of the term *yathopapāda* is either the rule that, according to the scriptural statement “he prepares two by two,” the vessels for the remaining divine rites are to be set out in pairs; or it refers to the fact that the *kūrca* grass-bundle is used only at the initiation (*upanayana*). Since the subsequent injunction states, “having turned the vessels face upwards,” it is understood that they were placed with their openings facing downwards during the initial setting out.
Thereafter follows the seating of the Brahman priest and so forth. This has been stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:

"At this time, Brahmā, having placed the sacred thread over his left shoulder, having sipped water, having stepped around behind the fire toward the south, having cast away a blade of grass from the seat of the Brahman priest, and having touched water, sits down facing the fire."

At this time—specifically at the interval following the setting out of the sacrificial vessels—the Brahman priest, having placed his sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavīta), having sipped water, and having stepped past the fire from the west toward the south with his right foot, stands behind the Brahman’s seat facing east. Having cast away a blade of grass from his own seat and touched water, he sits down facing the fire. The statement "at this time" is intended to show that even in Vedic rites, the entry of the Brahman must occur immediately after the setting out of the vessels and not before.

The mention of the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread) is for the purpose of taking up either a woolen skin or a garment as a constituent part of the ritual; or else, it is for the purpose of precluding its being worn as the *prācīnāvīta* in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*); or rather, it is for the purpose of declaring the *yajñopavīta* itself to be the primary element. Consequently, in the absence of a Brahmin, the *yajñopavīta* may take his place, as it is said: "Now, according to some, [the substitutes] mentioned are an umbrella, a *yajñopavīta*, or a water-pot. Alternatively, the statement "at this time" is for the purpose of making known that while the person is non-eternal, time is eternal.

Therefore, one of the items beginning with the parasol must necessarily be placed in the position of the *brahmán*. By the phrase "having sipped water," a second sipping of water is prescribed as a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), even for one who is already pure. By the word "behind" (*apareṇa*), the status of the person performing the vessel-offering (*pātrahoma*) as an internal participant is set aside. "The seat of the *brahmán*" means his place of sitting; the meaning is that one should cast away a blade of grass from that spot. The explicit mention of the term "*brahmán*" implies that there are seats for others as well.

Therefore, all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must perform their respective rites while seated upon their own seats, and not merely while standing on the ground. According to the observation in the *Śrauta* tradition, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) must also perform the removal of grass from his seat; since it is observed that "having removed a blade of grass from the seat of the Brahman priest (*brahmasadana*)," it is understood that the seat is made of grass. Although touching water after the removal of the grass is already established by *Smṛti* alone, its repetition here is for the purpose of providing a *Śrauta* expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Furthermore, all these duties, such as the wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth, the sacrificer should perform only after having been chosen; for there is a prohibition against engaging in ritual action by one who has not been chosen, as expressed in the rule: "They should not officiate for one who has not been chosen. Moreover, the status of being a priest (*ṛtvij*) depends upon both being chosen and being remunerated, as has been explained in detail by the Mīmāṃsakas in the section concerning priests (*ṛtvig-adhikaraṇa*); that should be consulted there.

However, in the case of a *sattra* sacrifice according to the Śrauta tradition, even in the absence of choice and remuneration, the Mīmāṃsakas have accepted that a specific mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) also serves as the cause for establishing the designations of the *hotṛ* and other priests.
Then follows the preparation of the *pavitra* (strainers) and so forth. This is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:

"Having made two *pavitra* strainers from two *darbha* blades whose tips are not torn apart and which are a span (*prādeśa*) in length, having cut them with another [blade] away from the nails, having wiped them with water, having poured water into a vessel over which the *pavitra* are placed, having filled it up to the rim, having purified it three times with the two northward-pointed *pavitra*, having set it down on *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, he covers it with *darbha* grass."

They are equal in color and form; as for their equality in length, that is already established by the phrase "measuring a span" (*prādeśamātrau*). In the expression *pracchinnāgrau* ("with tips cut off"), the prefix *pra-* is intended to exclude the possibility of having barely perceptible tips. Being "measuring a span" means having the measure of a span; such two blades of *darbha* grass he prepares as *pavitra*s—meaning they are fit for purification through ritual consecrations. Although the word *pavitra* has masculine gender when used as a substantive, it is seen here in the neuter because it refers to the instrument of purification.

The dual number [dvivacanam] is used because the parts have become prominent. Having placed either grass or wood on the ground as an interposition, one leaves two *darbha* blades at the tips measuring a span (*prādeśa*) and holds them over that; then, having cut them with a knife or a piece of wood other than a fingernail, one makes them fit for purification. Having done so, one wipes them with water, rubbing from the base to the tip with a hand containing water. This is for the purpose of removing dust; some say that if there is no dust, it need not be done, while others maintain that it must certainly be performed for the sake of an invisible merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Then, having taken the vessel, once that *praṇītāpraṇayana* vessel has been covered by the two purifiers (*pavitra*), one should pour water into it and fill it up to the brim so that it does not spill during the purification and other rites. Then, having purified [the water] three times with the two purifiers whose tips point northward, and having placed it upon *darbha* grass in a spot very close to the north side of the fire, one covers it with *darbha* grass; this is the meaning. In the phrase "with the two purifiers whose tips point northward," the mention of "purifiers" is for the purpose of excluding the possibility of the hands themselves pointing northward.
[As stated: "One makes two purifiers out of two *darbha* blades of equal length, with unbroken tips, measuring a span (*prādeśa*)."

Regarding this *Kātyāyana-sūtra*, Devayājñika, Pitṛbhūti, and Harisvāmin state that because equality is mentioned specifically in relation to the two *pavitra*s, it is the two *pavitra*s alone that must be made equal by cutting; there is no insistence on cutting two *kuśa* blades of equal length. They explain the intended meaning (*tātparya*) as follows: even if they are of different lengths, once cut, they should be made equal. Following that is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *prokṣaṇī* water and so forth. This is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:
"Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters across the *pavitra*s, [he places] the vessels with their openings upward, as before..."
"Having spread [the grass] and placed the fuel, he sprinkles [the vessels] three times with all [the waters].

Having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters by placing the two strainers (*pavitra*) between them, as previously described in the case of the *praṇītā* waters; having turned the perforated vessels face upwards and having spread and loosened the fuel, he sprinkles the vessels three times with all the waters contained in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel using his hand together with the strainers. Although the result is already established by the phrase "having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters," the specific mention of "between the strainers" (*tiraḥpavitram*) is for the purpose of excluding other ritual procedures.

Therefore, the silent triple washing of the vessel, the bringing of water, and the filling—simultaneous with the meditation upon the Earth as the instrument—do not occur here as they do in the case of the *praṇītā* waters. The phrase "with all [the water]" is for the purpose of excluding any remainder.
Regarding the definition of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"Sprinkling should be performed with the hand turned upward."
Then follows the heating of the ladle and so forth. This is stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra:
"Having heated the ladle, wiped it, heated it again, and set it down, he sprinkles the wiping-brushes with water and places them in the fire."

Having heated the *darvī* (ladle) over the fire, wiped it, heated it again over the fire, he sets it down. They teach that the wiping is to be done as with the *juhū*. Since the *sruva* (small spoon) is also required for the purposes of under-layering (*upastaraṇa*) and pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) during the *caru* oblation, and since only one that has been consecrated is fit for performing the ritual acts consisting of under-layering, pouring over, and so forth, the consecrations consisting of placing, sprinkling, heating, wiping, and so on must be performed for the *sruva* just as they are for the *darvī*. And these [consecrations] are to be performed together with the *darvī*.

The cleansing (saṃmārjana), however, should be performed first, just like the cleansing of the *śrauta* *sruva* ladle. Some say that the placing [of the implements] is upon *darbha* grass; the meaning is that one sprinkles the *darbha* blades used for cleansing with water and then casts them into the fire. Regarding the definition of sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*), it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"Having formed a fist, the water [thus held] is known as 'sprinkling'. After that comes the melting of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth. This is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:

"Having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*), having poured the *ājya* into the *ājya-sthālī* which has been covered with a strainer (*pavitra*), having drawn out embers toward the north, having placed [the vessel] over them, having illuminated it, having thrown two young *darbha* blades [into it], having carried fire around it three times, having removed it from the fire toward the north, having pushed the embers back, and having purified the *ājya* three times by moving the strainers back and forth with their tips pointing north, one should place the two strainers into the fire."

Having melted the clarified butter (ājya) outside until it is liquefied, one should pour the clarified butter into the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī) which has been covered with a purifier (pavitra). The repetition of the term "clarified butter" is for the purpose of indicating its primary importance; therefore, it should be clarified butter derived from a cow. It is also for the purpose of prohibiting contact with other substances; thus, after purifying it, it should be taken up by means of a strainer placed above.

Then, having pushed out the embers situated in the northern part toward the north with a piece of wood, and once those embers have been pushed out, he places clarified butter over them, heats it until it bubbles, and kindles it from above with *darbha* grass whose flames point downward. Having cast two young *darbha* tips into it, he throws the [other] [substances] into that [butter], circumambulates it three times with a firebrand, carries it out to the north, pushes those embers back toward the fire with that same piece of wood, and throws them back into the fire. Then, with two purifiers (*pavitra*) whose points face north...

He brings it back and purifies it again. Such is the sequence here: having taken the two strainers (*pavitre*) from the rear part of the butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*) toward the front part, and having brought them back again to the rear part, he purifies [the butter]. He does this twice more in the same manner. The scriptural injunction itself, which prescribes the completion toward the west (*pratyagapavargatā*), overrides the general rule. In the Brāhmaṇa it is said: "In this very way, the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*) circulate," thus describing the circulation of the two strainers, which are of the nature of the out-breath and in-breath.

For the *prāṇa* moves toward the east as its culmination; its cessation occurs through the obstruction of the mouth and nostrils. The *apāna* culminates toward the west; its cessation is observed through the obstruction of the genital organ, which is the gateway of the *apāna*. Therefore, because the movements of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* are sequential, the state of culminating toward the west (*pratyag-apavarga*) during the subsequent inhalation (*punar-āhāra*) cannot be prevented. The term "subsequent inhalation" (*punar-āhāram*) ends with the suffix *ṇamul*; this subsequent inhalation is an auxiliary part of the purifying process (*utpavana*).

The repetition of the term "ghee" (ājya) is for the purpose that, even in the case of fresh butter (navanīta) used in the Pitṛyajña, the rule of "re-introduction" (punar-āhāra-dharma) regarding the purification (utpavana) should not apply. Others say that the previous mention of "ghee" was intended to show that this very same procedure of preparation applies to the ghee taken silently (tūṣṇīka), and not merely the procedure belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices with the exception of the mantras.

Regarding the phrase "having placed [the two] purifiers upon the fire," the repetition of the word *pavitra* is for the purpose of placing them together after they have been untied and separated. This is explicit in the Baudhāyanīya: "Having untied the two purifiers and touched them with water, he throws them into the fire. As for the combination of the two darbha-blades and the fire-brand (*ulmuka*) during the circumambulation (*paryagnikaraṇa*) mentioned by the author of the Gṛhyakārikā, that should be disregarded due to a lack of authoritative evidence.

Regarding the place for pouring the clarified butter (*ājya*), the Āpastamba-gṛhya states: "To the west of the fire, having poured the clarified butter into a butter-pot over which the two purifiers have been placed.
In the *Prayogapārijāta*:
Then, having taken the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī) and poured the clarified butter into it,
[he places it] upon embers that have been removed from the fire toward the north, together with their ashes.
"Having dissolved this [mixture], having placed it on the fire, and having kindled it with burning grass,
one should cast [the oblation] into the clarified butter using the tip of a *darbha* blade the size of a thumb-joint.
The meaning of the word *nirūḍha* mentioned here has been explained in the *Smṛtidīpikā*:

"The fire that is separated from the *paristaraṇa* grass is *nirūḍha*; indeed, that fire which remains within the *paristaraṇa* is *anirūḍha*. This [definition] refers to cases where there is an injunction for the shifting (*pratyūhana*) of the fire. However, where there is no injunction for shifting, the meaning of the word *nirūḍha* is the separation [of the fire] right in the middle of the sacrificial ground (*āyatana*), according to the statement of the venerable Vidya-aranya-pāda.
Regarding the specific procedure for the removal of grass during the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire), the author of the *Saṃgraha* states:

"If one should bring the fire for the *paryagnikaraṇa* before it has been fully established (*anirūḍha*), one should cast out the remainder outside; however, if one should employ it once it has been established (*nirūḍha*)," so it is said.
In the *Sudarśanabhāṣya* as well:

"Because of the injunction for the removal of the embers intended for the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), it does not follow that they become worldly (*laukika*) once the ritual action has concluded. However, in the case of the fire used for the sprinkling and the fire used for the circumambulation (*paryagnikaraṇa*), when they are taken from their place of origin, then—since the ritual action has concluded—they are abandoned because they have become worldly.
