But when they are taken from the established fire (*nirūḍha*), then they are to be cast back into that very same fire. After that follows the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and so forth. This is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:

"He encloses [the altar] with yoke-pins: he places the middle pin behind the fire with its notch facing north; to the south of the fire, he places one touching the middle pin with its notch facing east; to the north of the fire, he places one touching the middle pin with its notch facing east;
then he sits behind the fire, facing east."

He encloses [the fire] with *śamyās* as enclosing-sticks (*paridhis*). How? To the west of the fire, he places the middle *śamyā* with its thick end (*kumba*) pointing northward. "Thick end" refers to the broad part. To the south of the fire, he places the southern *śamyā*, touching the middle one, with its thick end pointing eastward. To the north of the fire, he places the northern *śamyā*, touching the middle one, with its thick end pointing eastward. The relative positioning of lower and upper should be understood here as it was in the case of the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*).

Since this is already established by the context (*adhikāra*), the three mentions of "fire" (*agni*) are for the purpose of ensuring that only the fire itself is understood, so that the *paristaraṇa* (the strewing of grass) is not included. Therefore, the encircling of the fire with the *paridhi* sticks must be performed only on top of the *paristaraṇa* grass, and not on the outside. Otherwise, as in the case of the placing of the vessels or the seat of the Brahman priest (*brahmasadana*), it would result in being placed on the outside.

The repetition of the words "south" and "north," as well as the word "joined" (*saṃspṛṣṭām*), is for the purpose of ensuring that they are placed to the south and north of the fire respectively, that they are properly joined together, and that there is a distinct upper-and-lower relationship between them. Otherwise, one might conclude that they should be placed only to the south and north of the middle [fire] and merely touch it. The sūtra "He sits behind the fire facing east" connects with the subsequent sūtra: "To the south, the boy, wearing the sacrificial cord over his left shoulder and having sipped water..."

By this, both the reason for the prince facing eastward and the avoidance of the redundancy of the sūtra stating "he sits facing east with [the fire] behind him" are established. Furthermore, this is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any person to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*). Therefore, wherever the wife is the one to be consecrated, she too must sit facing east to the right of the husband. The statement "he should sit in front" is intended to ensure there is no temporal interval between the act of sitting and the act of taking hold (*anvārambha*).

Alternatively, the two sūtras—"Then he sits down facing east in front of the fire"—and "The boy, having sat down to the south, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī) and having sipped water (ācāntaḥ), takes hold [of the teacher]"—are distinct. In that case, the former [sūtra] refers to the teacher by implication, while the latter refers to the boy because of the explicit mention of the "boy" and because no other person is possible [in that context]. On this view, the first sūtra should be understood as intended to indicate that this rule is determined by the nature of the ritual action. The mention of "fire" here is for the purpose of identifying the fire that has been strewn around (paristīrṇa).
As for what is stated in another Smṛti:
"With three, four, five, or six finger-breadths [in width],
there is the placing of the grass, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the spreading [of the grass], and likewise the worship"—
this is the statement defining the limit of the area for laying the enclosing sticks, which consist of four finger-breadths. And as for that which was stated by Kaśyapa:

The statement, "One should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) according to the rule by a measurement of nine finger-breadths," is a description of the extent of the area for placing the enclosing sticks as being nine finger-breadths in size; it pertains to other *śākhās* (Vedic schools) and does not apply to those following the *Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra*. This is because the author of the commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*) has stated that the placing of the enclosing sticks occurs precisely upon the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*). Furthermore, the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) must be performed only after the placing of the enclosing sticks; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the immediate succession established by the gerund suffix (*lyap*) in the sequence of "placing the purifiers (*pavitra*)" and "placing the enclosing sticks."
By this, it should be understood that the view expressed by some—that the spreading of the *barhis* grass should occur even before the purifying (*utpavana*)—is refuted.

After the spreading of the *barhis*, the placing of the clarified butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*) therein and the discarding of the *upaveṣa* stick should take place immediately after the removal of the consecrated water (*praṇītā*), but before the Brahman and the sacrificer exit, as this is seen in the Śrauta ritual. If the removal of the *praṇītā* water is not performed, then these acts occur at the end of the subsequent sprinkling (*uttarapariṣeka*).
Following that comes the sprinkling and so forth. This has been stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra:

Then he sprinkles water around [the fire]: to the south, eastward, with the words, "O Aditi, give your consent"; to the west, northward, with the words, "O Anumati, give your consent"; to the north, eastward, with the words, "O Sarasvatī, give your consent"; and all around clockwise, with the words, "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]. Having anointed the fuel, he places it on the fire with the mantra: "This fuel is your self, O Jātavedas; prosper it, svāhā!"

Immediately thereafter, the teacher sprinkles [water] all around; he sprinkles from all sides. How? With the words "O Aditi, give your consent," he sprinkles water toward the east from the south of the fire. Regarding the form "Sarasvate," the shortening of the vowel is Vedic, as is the elision of the vocative ending and the application of *guṇa*. With the words "O divine Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]," he sprinkles that fire clockwise from all sides. Some say that this is the inclusion of the beginning of the mantra for the *sāvitra* oblation, because it is seen so among the Chandogas; however, we shall demonstrate later that this is not the case.

The word *atha* (now) serves to terminate the section concerning the boy (*kumāra*). Everything previously stated is to be performed by the teacher (*ācārya*), because the boy is not yet subject to Vedic injunctions. The mention of "circumambulation" (*pradakṣiṇa*) is for the purpose that the sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) should be done only once everywhere, rather than being repeated at each instance. Having thus sprinkled the fire and having anointed the fuel-wood (*idhma*) with clarified butter using a ladle (*darvī*), he places it into the blazing fire with his hand while reciting the mantra: "This is your fuel."

Although the placing of the fuel (idhmābhyādhāna) is enjoined by the term *juhoti*, the utterance of *svāhā* occurs because of a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*). This should be understood to apply to the placing of all fuel-sticks as well. Regarding the statement "having sprinkled" (*pariṣicya*), even though it is a mantra-less act, the purpose of the mention of the sprinkling—from "to the south, towards the east" up to "circumambulating from left to right on all sides"—is to demonstrate that the sprinkling must be performed in this manner and not merely as a simple circumambulation from left to right; furthermore, it is intended to exclude any other intervening ritual action between the sprinkling and the anointing of the fuel. Consequently, in the case of the *caru* oblation within the *tantra* of the *sacrifice*, it is established that the removal of the *caru* vessel must take place precisely before the sprinkling.
Regarding the specific rules for the *samiddhoma* in the *saṃgraha*: "If [the fuel] is offered from the base, there will be the destruction of the ritual act; from the middle, the loss of sons;
if one releases it from the tip, disease occurs; and if held with only one hand, there is the loss of wealth."

"The characteristic of the *samidh*-oblation is by the middle of the root and the middle. "By the root" means with the root; "by the middle" means with the middle. In both cases—"by the root" and "by the middle"—the word "releasing" (*muñcati*) is to be construed. Having held [the fuel-sticks] in the middle portion between the root and the middle parts, the *samidhs* are to be offered. This alone is to be understood as the characteristic of the *samidh*-oblation, that is, the placing of the fuel-sticks. Here, by the prohibition of the *samidh*-oblation with a single hand, [it is implied that it should be done] with the right hand while being supported by the left hand.
"The procedure for the *homa* is understood," so it is said in the *Prayogapārijāta*.
Regarding the specific manner of holding the *sruva* ladle, the *Vidhānamālā* states:
"Held at the tip leads to destruction; held in the middle causes the decay of progeny."
If the *sruva* ladle is held at the base, it will certainly cause the death of the officiating priest (*hotṛ*).
"The wise should hold the *sruva* at the middle of the top, at the middle of the middle, and at the middle of the base, for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
This is the meaning: having divided the staff into five parts, the holding of the *sruva* should be performed at the second or the fourth part.
In the *Prayogārṇava*:
"In the case of an oblation of solid substances, the holding of the *sruk* ladle is with the fist;
however, in the case of an oblation of liquid substances, it is prescribed that [the fingers] be turned upward."

The *sruva* ladle should also be held with the fingers turned upwards. Furthermore, this holding of the *sruc* and *sruva* must be performed by means of the *saumya-tīrtha*. This is because of the statement of Baudhāyana: "One should perform the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*), the collecting of remnants (*saṃsravaṇa*), the offering of parched grains (*lājahoma*), and the daily offerings (*nityahoma*) by means of the *kāya-tīrtha*; rites for the gods (*daivika*) by the *daiva-tīrtha*; and rites for the ancestors (*paitṛka*) by the *pitrya-tīrtha*. One should touch the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), partake of the first-fruits of new grain (*navānna-prāśana*), and take up the *sruva* by means of the *daiva-tīrtha*; and one should perform the acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*) by the *saumya* or *āgneya-tīrtha. In this context, the taking up of the *sruva* is illustrative of the *sruc* as well. Here, because of the qualifying term "rites for the gods," the holding of the *sruva* for ancestral rites must indeed be done by the *pitrya-tīrtha*.

The characteristics of the *saumya* (northern) and *āgneya* (southern) sides of the sacrificial ladle (*darvī*) as stated by Baudhāyana are: "The root of the finger is *saumya*; the middle of the hand is *āgneya*.
The same applies to the *darvī* as well, because it occupies the position of the *sruva* ladle.
Then follows the *āghāra* oblations and so forth. This is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:

"Then, having brought the *darvī* spoon over the northern junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), while meditating mentally, 'To Prajāpati, to Manu, svāhā!', he pours a straight, long, continuous stream toward the south-east along the southern junction of the enclosing sticks. Then, having poured the two *āghāra* streams—one directed eastward and one northward—with the formula 'To Indra, svāhā!', he offers the two *ājyabhāga* portions: with 'To Agni, svāhā! in the eastern part of the northern half, and with 'To Soma, svāhā! in the eastern part of the southern half. Between these two, he offers the other [oblations] with the verse: 'Yoked, O Jātavedas, carry...'"

"O Agni, know the work being performed here before you; you are the physician, the maker of the remedy. Through you may we win cattle, horses, and men—*svāhā*! You who lie across as the supporter, 'I am the sustainer,' so I say—to you, the one who brings success, I sacrifice with a stream of clarified butter in the fire—*svāhā*! *Svāhā* to the goddess Sarādhani! *Svāhā* to the goddess Prasādhani!"

Now, immediately after the placing of the fuel (idhmādhāna), he offers the oblations (homān) that are about to be described with the wooden spoon (darvī). The word "atha" (now) serves to establish the connection between the placing of the fuel and the pouring of the clarified butter (āghāra). By this, it is established that the placing of the fuel occurs only where there is the pouring of the āghāra, and not elsewhere. Consequently, it is proven that there is no placing of the fuel in the Āpūrvika [offering], and likewise, the anointing of the fuel is also performed with the wooden spoon alone.

Having marked the northern junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he brings [the ladle] along that [line], having caused it to enter; then, while meditating mentally upon Prajāpati with the mantra "To Prajāpati," without uttering it aloud with his voice, he offers (*juhoti*)—meaning he pours the oblation (*āghārayati*)—along the southern and eastern directions, straight, continuous, and uninterrupted. The mention of the *darvī* (ladle) is for the purpose of prohibiting the offering after having brought it along together with the pot and subsequently taking it up.

Therefore, having first taken [the ladle] and entered [the altar], he should pour the libation. Having brought the spoon along the southern junction of the enclosing sticks as before, he offers—pours the libation—with the formula "To Indra, svāhā! in a manner that is straight, long, continuous, and ending toward the north-east. The instruction "meditating with the mind" is omitted; for it has been stated that this is indeed the *prājāpatya* libation by the Śruti text, "Therefore, they offer to Prajāpati with the mind. Consequently, he sprinkles [the butter] with speech alone.

The statement "having poured the two Āghāra-libations" is for the purpose of assigning the technical name *āghāra* to the two oblations just mentioned. By this, the oblation in the *jyotiṣmatī* fire and the touching of all the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) are established. The statement "toward the south and eastward" is for the purpose of excluding a transverse direction. The statement "straight" is for the purpose of excluding a crooked path. The statement "long" is for the purpose of excluding the assumption of a "short" measure for the one who is hated, as mentioned in other scriptures.

The term *saṃtatam* (continuous) is for the purpose of rejecting the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) that one who hates [the opponent] cuts [the stream] downwards; the inclusion of the word *ṛju* (straight) in the rule for the subsequent pouring (*uttarāghāra*) is intended to indicate that length and continuity are not mandatory. However, if one accepts the specific rule stated by Āpastamba—that "in the case of the pouring (*āghāra*) and the stream (*dhārā*), there is a connection with the beginning"—then the commencement of the two pourings occurs at the same time as the commencement of the mantra. The technical designation *ājyabhāgau* (the two butter-portions) is for the sake of conventional usage.

"Having performed [the rites] up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings"—here, the remainder of the sentence is that one offers in the eastern part of the northern half of the fire with the mantra "To Agni, svāhā!", and in the eastern part of the southern half with the mantra "To Soma, svāhā!". "Between those two, he offers the others"—that is, between those two *ājyabhāga* offerings, in the middle of those two offering-places, he offers the other oblations.

If only "he offers in the interval" (*tāvantareṇa juhoti*) were stated, it would follow that the connection with the location [of the offering] would apply only to the verses beginning with *yukto vaha*. To prevent this and ensure that it applies to all of them, the word "the others" (*itarāḥ*) is used. Regarding the mantra *yātiraścī*, the reading is *sa rādhanīm* according to some, because the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) requires an object. Others hold that the reading is *sa rādhanī yaja*, due to a change in case endings. Mātṛdatta maintains that the reading without the nasal (*niranunāsika*) is simply a corruption.

It is more appropriate, however, to consider this a Vedic (chāndasa) reading. [The text states: "He offers with the vyāhṛtis—bhūr, bhuvaḥ, suvar—both individually and collectively. He offers with these vyāhṛtis: bhūr, bhuvaḥ, suvar. "Individually" means with each one separately; for example: bhūḥ svāhā, bhuvaḥ svāhā, suvaḥ svāhā. The mention of "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar" is intended to include all the vyāhṛtis together, given their plurality.

Since the term "with the *vyāhṛtis*" is already established by the statement "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ," this specific mention is for the purpose of ensuring that these [three] alone are understood whenever the word "*vyāhṛti*" is used elsewhere. Consequently, in Vedic and Smṛti rites such as "He places the fuel with the *vyāhṛtis*" and "I invoke Rākā," it is established that these very three are intended. [Objection: But is this not already established by the rule "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ are the *vyāhṛtis*"? [Reply: It is not so established. For by that [rule], the inclusion of the desired [mantras] would have been restricted only to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) itself.

Based on the statement that "the clarified butter (ājya) should be one karṣa in measure," it should be understood that for all oblations, the clarified butter is merely the substance of the ritual act.
Now follows the subsequent procedure (tantra) which brings about the success of the rite. Regarding this, the Gṛhya-sūtra states:

"O Varuṇa, I implore you for this truth of mine... "O Agni, do thou [grant us]... "O Agni, do thou [grant us]... "O Agni Ayāsya, [grant us] health, Svāhā! This verse beginning with "O Prajāpati... follows. With the formula, "Whatever in this rite has been omitted... to the one who brings it to fulfillment, Svāhā," he offers [the oblation] in the eastern part of the northern half, without letting it touch the other oblations. At this point, some offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. He offers the *jayas* with the formulas: "Consciousness, Svāhā! Perception, Svāhā! and "To consciousness, Svāhā! To perception, Svāhā!"

"May Agni, the lord of beings, protect [us] equally"—with these words he joins the *Abhyātāna* formulas; "In this Brahman, in this Kṣatra"—with these words he joins the *Abhyātāna* formulas. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he offers oblations and worships with the formula, "The fathers, the grandfathers. Having recited the sequence of the *Rāṣṭrabhṛt* formulas beginning with "The conqueror of the earth, whose abode is truth," he offers the first oblation with "To him, svāhā! and the second oblation with "To them, svāhā! Thus it is said.

The statement "to Prajāpati" is intended to indicate that wherever a general offering to Prajāpati is prescribed, this very [offering] is to be understood as the one to be performed. Some, however, believe it is for the purpose of a mental oblation (*mānasa-homa*), based on the observation: "Therefore, they offer to Prajāpati mentally. That is not correct, because that observation refers specifically to the *āghāra* (libation). Therefore, the offering must be made with speech alone. With the formula "That of his," he offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation in the northeastern quarter of the fire.

Because of the statement, "unmixed with the other oblations," one should offer [this] after passing over the other oblations. "Unmixed" means unblended. In this ritual, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, some teachers say that one should offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*. The word "and" (*iti*) has the sense of conjunction; according to some, it has the sense of specification. Since they are taught as subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) immediately following the *jayas*, *abhyātānas*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, one offers the *jaya*-offerings and the others in the vicinity of the principal oblations.

The statement here is intended so that this [rite] may be understood as the primary *upanayana* for the purpose of Vedic study, and not the *upanayana* performed for the sake of penance (*prāyaścitta*). Now, one might object: should not the sūtra beginning with "And [the verse] 'O Prajāpati... and ending with "To them, Svāhā" (starting from *cittaṃ ca svāhā cittiśca svāhā* up to *tābhyaḥ svāhā*) be recited immediately after that, and only then should the subsequent sūtra beginning with "Whatever I have exceeded in this rite... and ending with "He offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations" follow?

Thus, by rejecting such simplicity—whereby one would not need to state "before the *sviṣṭakṛt*"—and instead accepting this complexity, it is intended to make known that there is no option regarding the location (such as "the subsidiary offerings are before the *sviṣṭakṛt*" or "after the *sviṣṭakṛt*"), but rather an option regarding the performance itself.

The statement "before the *sviṣṭakṛt*" is for the purpose of excluding [the performance of the *jayas*] at a time subsequent to the *sviṣṭakṛt*. Now, for what reason is there a separate compound for the *jayas* and *abhyātānas* alone, rather than including them with the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, [given that] the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* also have companions? It is for the sake of making known that they do; which are these? They are the oblations performed with the mantras recited in the *Acchidrakāṇḍa*, beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods... (*yad devā devaheḍanam*). Since they are not explicitly mentioned [in the compound], there is an option [regarding their inclusion].

And Baudhāyana prescribes that one should perform the fourth *homa* with the *anuvāka* beginning "Whatever offense we have committed against the gods" (*yad devā devaheḍanam*) according to option. The sequential enumeration of the *jaya*-offerings and the rest is for the sake of knowledge and for the purpose of specific injunctions. One offers the thirteen *jaya* oblations according to the recitation: "To thought, svāhā! To perception, svāhā! (*cittam ca svāhā cittiś ca svāhā*), and so forth. The passage beginning "The gods and the asuras... (*devāsurā...*) is the *brāhmaṇa* explanation. Alternatively, one may offer with twelve [formulas] ending in the dative case, such as "To thought, svāhā! To perception, svāhā! (*cittāya svāhā cittaye svāhā*). The thirteenth remains unchanged.

It should be understood that this reading also exists in another recension (*śākhā*). He offers eighteen *abhyātāna* oblations with the formula beginning "Agni" and ending with "devahūtyām" in the section on the *abhyātānas*. With the formula beginning "O Pitṛs," he offers this oblation while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), or he worships the ancestors with this mantra while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder. Some say [he offers] to Agni; that is not correct, because it contradicts the indicative mark (*liṅga*). He offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations with the formula beginning "Ṛtāṣāṭ."

These are twelve mantras; among them, the seventh and the last are without the *anuṣaṅga* (appendix) and consist of a single oblation (*ekāhuti*). The remaining ones are with the *anuṣaṅga*. Having recited those which have the *anuṣaṅga*, one offers the first oblation with the words "to him, svāhā" (*tasmai svāhā*), and the subsequent oblation with the words "to them, svāhā" (*tābhyaḥ svāhā*). This is the meaning. Here, in this threefold division of the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* mantras, there are ten cycles (*paryāya*); the seventh and the last are alone [without the appendix], thus making twenty-two mantras in total.

In this regard, one view is that the first oblation begins with "Ṛtāṣāṭ" according to the recited text and ends with "tasmai svāhā," while the second oblation consists solely of "tābhyaḥ svāhā. For example: "Ṛtāṣāṭ, Ṛtadhāmā, Agni the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the plants, named Ūrjas; may he protect this priesthood and nobility; may they protect this priesthood and nobility; to him svāhā! To them svāhā! The same applies to the subsequent [formulas].

The second alternative is as follows: beginning with "Ṛtāṣāṭ" according to the recension and ending with "tasmai svāhā," this is the first oblation; then, again beginning with "Ṛtāṣāṭ" according to the recension and ending with "tābhyaḥ svāhā," this is the subsequent oblation. For example: "Ṛtāṣāḍ ṛtadhāmā... kṣattraṃ pāntu tasmai svāhā"; and "Ṛtāṣāḍ ṛtadhāmā... kṣattraṃ pāntu tābhyaḥ svāhā. The same applies to the subsequent [mantras]. The third alternative will be explained in the section on the *agnimukha* procedure. Every oblation must be performed upon the very tongue of the Sacrificial Person (*yajñapuruṣa*), for it is heard in scripture that there is fault in performing it otherwise.
Thus says the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"If a man who causes disease offers oblations where there is wood, he should offer at the ears;
'he should offer' is the Vedic usage.
The place of smoke is said to be the head; here, mental suffering shall arise."
Where the sacrificial fire has little flame, it brings destruction to the sacrificer.
In the place of ashes, there will be affliction; in the place of embers, the wise know there is loss of position, depletion of wealth, injury to the nose, and mental suffering.
"Where there is a blazing, there the tongue is proclaimed;
and fire that sounds like an elephant or a horse bestows auspicious results.
He (the same author) states the names of the tongues as follows:
"Kālī, Karālī, Manojavā, Sulohinī, Sudhūmravarṇā, Sphulliṅginī, and Viśvaruci— the goddess Lelāyamānā— these are the seven tongues.
Thus it is said in another text.
Suvarṇā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā,
and Atiriktā— these are proclaimed as the seven tongues of fire.
The tongue in the west is golden; the middle one is known as Kanakā;
the northern tongue is red, and that in the southern direction is known to be black.
Suprabhā is in the eastern direction, while the tongue in the domain of Agni is exceedingly red;
in the northeast is Bahurūpā—these are the locations of the tongues in successive order.
In marriage rites, the tongue is turned westward;

in sacrificial acts, it is turned northward; in the initiation ceremony, it is turned southward; in rites for the ancestors, it is turned eastward; in all other activities, it is turned toward the southeast; and in rites for peace, it is turned toward the south-east.
"And the northeast [is used] for fierce rites; this indeed is the characteristic of the *homa*.

This should be understood to apply specifically to *ājya-homas* (oblations of clarified butter). In that case, because the *ājya* is instantly reduced to ashes, there is no fault in casting a second oblation into it. Nor does this rule apply to *homas* involving many oblations or hard substances, as such a practice would be impossible. These tongues are to be understood as existing within a single flame situated between the two *ājya-bhāgas*, distinguished by their respective locations.
Then follows the subsequent sprinkling (*uttara-pariṣeka*) and so forth. This is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:
"Then he sprinkles water around [the fire]; as before, he modifies the ends of the mantras, [reciting]: 'Thou hast assented,' 'Thou hast impelled.'"

Then he sprinkles water around the fire as previously described. The word "atha" (then) is intended to indicate that this is not identical to the previous [rite]. Therefore, this is an ancillary part of all *darvihoma* offerings, not merely of the initiation (*upanayana*). The phrase "as previously described" is for the purpose of extending the rules of the preceding [rite]. The end of each mantra, the end of each mantra, the end of each mantra—these are the "ends of mantras. He modifies them as follows: for those [mantras] ending with "anumanyasva," he uses "anvamasthāḥ"; for those ending with "prasuva," he uses "prāsāvīḥ. For those ending with "anumanyasva," he uses "anvamasthāḥ"; and for that which ends with "prasuva," he uses "prāsāvīḥ."

For example: *adite 'nvama sthāḥ*, *anumate 'nvama sthāḥ*, *sarasvate 'nvama sthāḥ*, *deva savitaḥ prāsāvīḥ*. Since it was already established that these are mantras, the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the purpose of making it known that the entire sequence—up to "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]" (*deva savitaḥ prasuva*)—is to be recited, and not merely the beginning.
Here, Mātṛdatta has described certain ritual duties (*dharmāḥ*) prior to the sprinkling around (*pariṣecana*).

Having anointed the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) with the *darvī* ladle, and having taken a small amount of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) from the strewn grass, he silently anoints its tip with the *darvī*, its middle with the butter-vessel, and its root [with the butter-vessel], just like the *prastara*. Then, having removed a blade of grass and set it aside, and having silently laid down [the grass] as for the *prastara*, he points toward [the fire] three times with his finger, touches his nose, his eye, and the earth, and having cast the enclosing-sticks into the fire in order, he makes an offering over them with the residue of the butter.

Then, having performed the sprinkling, having carried the *praṇītā* waters around the front of the fire, having placed them behind the fire, and having poured a little water [there], he should perform the purification silently (*tūṣṇīm*) as before. Then he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahman according to his faith; the Brahman, having accepted it, departs. Thus [it is said].
Following the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the *prayogavaijayantī* states that an expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittahoma*) must be performed as a constant rule:
"The three *anājñāta* verses, *tvaṃ no agne*, *sa tvaṃ no agne*, *yata indra bhayāmahe*, *svastidā*, *tryambakaṃ*, *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, and the seven *vyāhṛti*s."

The source for this must be investigated. However, the rites beginning with the anointing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and ending with the silent sprinkling (*mārjana*), excluding the final sprinkling (*pariṣeka*), are considered both performed and unperformed. The same applies to the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*). But the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahman priest is indeed mandatory. For it is said: "If one should sacrifice with a sacrifice lacking a fee, that sacrifice is wasted and does not lead to long life; a fertile field should be given as the fee—that is the expiation."

Thus, because the *Sūtrakāra* has stated the fault incurred by not giving a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), [the following applies]. "Prakṣāma" means burnt. Regarding the phrase "anāyuḥ," the word "the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) would become" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Urvarā" means land; it is prosperous and rich in crops. Since no specific sacrificial fee is mentioned here, gold or a cow should be given according to one's faith (*śraddhā*).
However, in the *Chāndogya-gobhila-gṛhya-sūtra*:
"One should give a full vessel as the sacrificial fee to the Brahman priest, having filled a bronze cup (*camasa*) or a wooden bowl with food."

"It is said: 'Whether it be prepared or unprepared, this is called a full vessel of fruits. Here, "prepared" means threshed, and "unprepared" means unthreshed. At the conclusion of the oblation, the worship of the fire is prescribed in another Smṛti:

"One should worship the fire with perfumes, flowers, and so forth at the conclusion of the *homa*. By the phrase "with perfumes, flowers, and so forth," the previously mentioned ritual offerings (*upacāra*) are set aside. One should worship, taking the external fire as the object. "With three, four, five, or six finger-breadths..."

For it is stated in another Smṛti: "The sprinkling, the enclosing sticks, the spreading [of grass], and likewise the worship"—thus, by specifying particular requirements for the location, the exclusion of worship [from that specific site] is also implied. The tradition of the learned (śiṣṭas) is also thus. In the Āgama scriptures, however, worship is prescribed as being performed in the fire itself. This method is not practiced by the Vaidikas nowadays. The experts maintain that in the worship of the fire, one should avoid red perfumes, flowers, and so forth. Since the prescription of red perfumes and flowers occurs in the context of fire-worship belonging to the section on divine rites (divyaprakaraṇa), the prohibition of red perfumes and flowers does not apply there.

By this it is understood that elsewhere there is a prohibition against flowers that are red in color or possess a red scent. This also serves as an illustration for [the prohibition of] uncolored rice-grains (*akṣata*) and so forth.
Regarding the application of ashes, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states:
"Having bathed, one should apply a sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*) with clay, and having applied it, one should indeed [apply another] with ashes."
"Having worshipped the gods with fragrant scents for the removal of all sins.
Herein, the expiation for when someone enters between the fire and the sacrificer is stated.
Regarding that, the *Parāśara-prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa* says:

"If one should pass between two Brahmins, or between a Brāhmaṇa and the sacred fire, or between a husband and wife, or between a cow and an excellent twice-born, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance."
This refers to occasions other than the time for ritual action (*karmakāla*).
However, regarding the specific rules for the time of ritual action, it is stated in that very same source:
"Likewise, during the time of the fire-oblation (*homa*), milking, Vedic study, and taking a wife..."
"If a twice-born man should pass between [the two women], he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
The Procedure for the Fire-mouth (Agnimukha) Rite.

Now, the procedure: Having sipped water and restrained his breaths, the performer should prepare a very smooth sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in a location that slopes toward the east, or toward the north, or toward the northeast, or is level—whichever of these orientations is appropriate—in a space measuring one cubit or more, such as half a cubit, using five *prasthas* of white sand that is free from pebbles, bones, and the like, and not moist; the sand should be measured according to the requirements of the fire-oblation (*homa*). The mound should be square and measure one cubit, or more up to the length of an arm.

In the case of a slope toward the east, the height at the back is five finger-breadths and the height at the front is four finger-breadths. In the case of a slope toward the north, one should divide the length of either the index or middle finger into three parts; having increased that by one part, one should add to it a quarter of that part diminished by its own thirty-fourth part. The height there [at the back] is measured by that amount, while the height at the north is the measure of a full upright finger-breadth.

In the case of sloping toward the north, the height is exactly as in the case of sloping toward the east. In the case of sloping toward the northeast, there is a height of four finger-breadths in the eastern half of the northern direction and in the northern half of the eastern direction; in the other region, the height is five finger-breadths, or otherwise as in the case of sloping toward the north.

Then, having decorated that sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on all sides with unbroken rice grains, sprouts, creepers, and so forth, having smeared it with cow-dung, and having sprinkled it with pure water, he should take a single fruit, flower, leaf, or blade of *kuśa* grass together with a fragment of copper; and with that, having drawn three lines one *prādeśa* long with intervals of six finger-breadths each, running eastward and ending toward the north, and likewise three lines running northward and ending toward the east in the middle of the mound, he should cast away the instrument used for drawing those lines to the north and touch water.

Having taken pure water in some large vessel, he sprinkles the entire sacrificial ground with half of it. Sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) is the act of pouring water with a loose fist held upside down. Then, having poured out the remaining water either to the north or in front of the fire-altar, he brings another pure water into that same vessel for the purpose of touching water, the *praṇītā* water, sprinkling, and other rites, and places that vessel to his own north.

Even in the absence of sprinkling, this [act] must indeed be performed because it is obligatory. There is no bringing of a vessel for sprinkling, as that very thing is absent. Therefore, having dug up [the ground] with any one of the digging tools, such as a spade, he sprinkles it. "Digging up" consists merely of striking once with the digging tool.

Then, having become silent, he should enclose [the fire] within a pair of vessels—either made of metal (if available), or smeared [with ghee], or new earthenware—and, having brought fire consisting of brightly glowing charcoal that is smokeless, fetched from the house of a *śrotriya* woman of good character (or, in her absence, from his own house), he should place it on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the south-eastern direction. [The mantra for this is: Prajāpati is the seer of all the *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the deity; the *bṛhatī* is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the installation of the fire.

Reciting "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," one should establish the fire facing oneself in the spot scratched by both hands, preceded by the utterance of the name of the specific object of the rite in the accusative case, saying: "I establish the fire. In the case of establishing [the fire] with the *vyāhṛtis* ending in the *praṇava*, after the verse "Prajāpati, Bṛhatī," one should add: "The ṛṣi of the *praṇava* is Para-Brahman; the deity is either Paramātman or Agni; the meter is Daivī Gāyatrī."

Then, having cast in sprinkled fuel-sticks and kindled the fire with a bamboo bellows, he should rise and worship the fire with the mantra beginning "juṣṭo damūnāḥ. For this verse, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Agni, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and its application is for the worship of the installed fire: "Oṃ juṣṭo damūnā... bhojanāni. Having thus worshipped the fire and sat down, he should meditate on the fire with the mantra "catvāri śṛṅgā. For this mantra, the deities are the sacrificial ones, the source is the Upaniṣads, the deity is Agni, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and its application is for the meditation on the fire: "Oṃ catvāri śṛṅgā... āviveśa | saptahastaścatuḥśṛṅgaḥ..."

"One should meditate on the Fire-god as being of such a form: holding a *tomara* (spear) and a fan with his left hands, and holding a vessel of clarified butter while seated facing oneself. Where the author of the Sūtra says "having established the fire," there the oblation (*homa*) should be performed after bringing the fire and placing it in a location consecrated by digging and other rites. Where he does not say so, it should be performed in its own place while remaining stationary, according to the rules for spreading the grass (*paristaraṇa*) and so forth. Some consider the kindling of the fire (*upasamādhāna*) to be a restatement of what is already established.

Among those rites to be performed at the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), it should be understood that while the kindling of fuel and so forth are done there, the sweeping (*uddhanana*) and other such acts are performed elsewhere. When a visible fire has been brought from another location for some reason and is to be established, the sweeping and other acts must certainly be performed during the rite of lowering the fire (*avaropaṇa*) and during the oblation-rite for the expiation of following the fire (*agnyanugamana-prāyaścitta*).
Next is the *anvādhāna* (adding fuel) as required by custom;
it is as follows: taking three large pieces of wood (*samidh*), one says: "O Faith, come! I summon you with Truth."

Having recited this three times, and having read: "Those [deities] who were in front... and "I begin the sacrifice with faith," and "For the sake of intention, thee... entered," and having performed the touching of the heart, the touching of water, and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [he says]: "In this *amuka* oblation, all those deities who are to be sacrificed to, I shall encompass; I shall sacrifice to Agni Jātavedas with fuel."

In the *ādhāra-homa* (foundation oblation): "I shall worship Prajāpati, Manu, and Indra with one offering of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) each. In the *ājyabhāga-homa* (butter-portion oblation): "I shall worship Agni and Soma with one offering of clarified butter each. In the general primary oblation (*sāmānya-pradhāna-homa*), having stated: "I shall worship Jātavedas Agni, the goddess Sarādhanī, the goddess Prasādhanī, Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati with one offering of clarified butter each," one should then mention the aforementioned principal deities using the second case ending (*dvitīyā-vibhakti*) and [the offerings] using the third case ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*).

Having mentioned the substances as previously stated, one should say: "I shall sacrifice. For the *aṅga-homa* (limb-offerings): "I shall sacrifice to Varuṇa with two oblations of clarified butter; I shall sacrifice to Agni and Varuṇa each with one oblation of clarified butter; I shall sacrifice to Agni Ayāsya and Prajāpati each with one oblation of clarified butter. For the *jayopahoma* (subsidiary victory-offerings): "I shall sacrifice to Citta, Cittī, Ākūta, Ākūtī, Vijñāta, Vijñāna, Manas, Śakvarīs, Darśa, Pūrṇamāsa, Bṛhat, Rathantara, and Prajāpati each with one oblation of clarified butter."

In the *abhyātāna* subsidiary oblations: Agni, the lord of beings; Indra, the lord of the eldest; Yama, the lord of the earth; Vāyu, the lord of the intermediate space; Sūrya, the lord of heaven; Candramas, the lord of the stars; Bṛhaspati, the lord of the sacred word (*brahman*); Mitra, the lord of truths; Varuṇa, the lord of the waters; Samudra, the lord of streams; Anna, the lord of sovereignties; Soma, the lord of plants; and Savitṛ.

"I shall worship Rudra, the lord of plants, and the lord of cattle; [having said this, there is the touching of water]. I shall worship Tvaṣṭṛ, the lord of forms, Viṣṇu, the lord of mountains, and the Maruts, the lords of the hosts—with one oblation of clarified butter for each. Having said this, he should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and say, "I shall worship the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, further ancestors, and still further ancestors with one oblation of clarified butter," and then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he should touch water. In the case of the ritual of standing in attendance (*upasthāna*), the sentence beginning with "the fathers, grandfathers" is not to be recited.

In the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* subsidiary offerings: Agni, the Gandharva of Truth, who possesses truth and whose abode is truth; the plants as his Apsarases; Ūrja, the Saṃhita, the Viśvasāman, and Sūrya, the Gandharva; the rays as his Apsarases; Āyu, Suparṇa, Sūryaraśmi, and Candramas, the Gandharva; the constellations as his Apsarases; the Bekurīs; Bhujyu, Suparṇa, Yajña, the Gandharva; the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) as his Apsarases; the praises (*stavāḥ*); Prajāpati, Viśvakarman, Manas, the Gandharva; the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* verses as his Apsarases; the Vahnis; and the Impetuous One (*iṣira*).

Vāta, the Gandharva of wide extent; the Waters, the Apsarases of joy; Bhuvanapati Parameṣṭhin, the overlord; Mṛtyu, the Gandharva; the Viśvas, the Apsarases of the earth; Sukṣiti, Subhūti, Bhadrakṛt, Suvarvat; Parjanya, the Gandharva; the Lightnings, the Apsarases of radiance; Dūreheti Amṛḍaya, the Gandharva; the Progeny, the Apsarases of fear; Cāru Kṛpaṇakāśin, the Gandharva; the Ādhis, the Apsarases who cause sorrow; Bhuvanapati.

One should specify: "I shall sacrifice with each individual oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*). Alternatively, the specification may be made in a collective form: "I shall sacrifice with each individual oblation of clarified butter to the deities of the *jaya* offerings; I shall sacrifice with each individual oblation of clarified butter to the deities of the *abhyātāna* offerings; I shall sacrifice with each individual oblation of clarified butter to the deities of the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings.
Regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* homa: "I shall sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with a single oblation of the remnants of what has been offered."

In the *prāyaścitta-homa*: "I shall worship Agni with three oblations of clarified butter; I shall worship Agni and Varuṇa each with one oblation of clarified butter; I shall worship Indra Maghavan, Indra Vṛtrahan, Tryambaka, Viṣṇu, Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Bṛhaspati, Varuṇa, Indra, and the Viśvedevas each with one oblation of clarified butter."

In the *saṃsrāva-homa*: "I shall sacrifice to the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas with the residual clarified butter (*saṃsrāvājya*). One should mention, "I shall sacrifice to these deities. In the case of an immediate performance (*sadyaḥpakṣa*), one says, "I shall sacrifice immediately. However, in a rite to be accomplished over many days, one should say, "I shall sacrifice to these deities from this day forward; I am the sacrificer. From tomorrow onwards, one simply says, "I am the sacrificer. If the principal rite is to take place on the very next day, then one should say only, "Tomorrow I am the sacrificer."

The formulation "I shall sacrifice" (*yakṣye*) and "I am the sacrificer" (*yaṣṭāha*) is used when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the agent. However, when the teacher (*ācārya*) is the agent, the formulation is "I will sacrifice" (*yakṣyāmi*) and "I am the sacrificer" (*yaṣṭāsmi*). Since these are not mentioned in the Sūtra, they are not to be recited in the case where the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) and the concluding pouring-out oblation (*saṃsrāva-homa*) are not performed.

Then, regarding all the *vyāhṛtis*, Prajāpati is the deity and the *bṛhatī* is the meter; their application (*viniyoga*) is in the placing of the fuel-sticks for the *anvādhāna*. One should place the *anvādhāna* fuel-sticks into the fire with the mantra: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. Some authorities also desire the utterance of *svāhā* here. In that case, the ritual renunciation (*tyāga*) is: "To Prajāpati, this [is mine], not mine. Beginning from "having taken three large fuel-sticks" up to the end of the placing of the fuel-sticks, the ritual action is recorded because it is established by tradition (*ācāra*) and accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭas*).

Then, having left a space measuring ten or five finger-breadths all around—either outside the fire-pit or outside its girdle—he spreads darbha grass with tips pointing eastward in the directions starting from the east. The shorter blades are placed with their ends toward the north, both behind and in front; alternatively, the darbhas in front and behind have their tips pointing north. To the south and to the north, the tips point eastward. The southern spreading of grass is placed over the roots of the darbhas used for the eastern and western spreadings.

The upper layering (*uttaraparistaraṇa*), however, is beneath the tips of those [blades]. In the layering, there are four or three *darbha* blades each. But in the case of layering with the tips pointing eastward, they are indeed unlimited. This relationship of lower and upper applies only to the case where the tips point toward the northeast.

Then, to the south of the fire, he spreads a profusion of *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward upon the seat of the *brahmán*. If the teacher is to perform the oblations, he also prepares a seat behind the *brahmán*'s station for the sacrificer to sit upon. Then, with the two verses beginning "I take Agni into myself" (*mayi gṛhṇāmi*) and "He who is our Agni" (*yo no agniḥ*), whose deity is Agni and meter is *triṣṭubh*, and which are employed for the internal appropriation of Agni—he takes Agni into himself with these two: "Oṃ, I take Agni first into myself... and so on, ending with "...has gone away. The meaning is that having meditated upon Agni as being taken into himself, he mutters [the mantra].

Then, having strewn *darbha* grass with its tips pointing north immediately to the north of the fire, he should place upon it the common and specific vessels and materials, either all at once as required or as they become available. Therein, having cut off a portion of a span's length from the tips of the sacrificial *darbha* grass for the purpose of the *barhis*, and having touched water and tied it with a cord of three or five strands, he should place it among the vessels.

Then, having made a cord with uneven or even knots and coiled it to the right, he should stretch it out with its tip pointing north; having tied a fuel-stick consisting of twenty-one pieces of wood from a *pālāśa* or *khadira* tree, he should place it down. Alternatively, prior to the placing of the ladle, he should perform the binding of the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*) and their placement below [the fire], and prior to the placing of the *avajvalana* (flaming) *darbha* grasses, he should perform the placing of these two within the vessels.

In this context, the *idhma* (sacrificial fuel) consists of twenty-one pieces of wood together with the three *paridhi* (enclosing sticks); it may have separate *paridhis*, or its pieces may be equal in number to the intended offerings. It is either one *aratni* or one *prādeśa* in length. The *paridhis* are shaped like *śamyās* (wooden pins), made from any sacrificial tree, and may be either dry or moist. Herein lies the requirement for the *paridhis* to be fashioned in the shape of *śamyās*. Among them, the middle *paridhi* measures from the base of the arm to the tip of the ring finger.

The right [pillar] should have a measurement from the base of the arm to the tip of the middle finger and be thinner than the middle one; the left [pillar] should have a measurement from the base of the arm to the tip of the little finger and be thinner than the right one. Alternatively, all may be made of equal measurement. However, contact between the two sides is necessary in either case. This measurement applies specifically to a shrine measuring one *aratni* in size.

In the case of an increase [in size], however, the western enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) should be of such a measure that its root lies upon the southern spreading-grass (*paristaraṇa*) and its tip lies upon the northern spreading-grass; the other two [enclosing-sticks] should follow accordingly. Then, to the northeast of the fire-altar (*agnyāyatana*), the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should choose a Brahmin who is skilled in ritual and most learned in the Veda (*brahmiṣṭha*), saying: "I choose you, [Name], born of the [Name] lineage (*gotra*), belonging to the [Name] *pravara*, a student of the [Name] Vedic branch (*śākhā*), [Name]-Śarman, as my *brahmā* for this [Name] rite."

Having said, "O Brahmā, I am chosen; I shall perform the rite," wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), having sipped water twice (*dvirācamya*), and having gone to the north of the vessels, he passes between the two performers of the fire-oblation (*agnihoma*) with his right foot, steps southward, and throws away a blade of grass to the north of the *darbha* grass spread for sitting. Having touched water, he sits facing the fire. From this point until the conclusion of the rite, he should remain silent and focused on the ritual.

If there is a lapse in the restraint of speech (*vāgyama*), then one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the Vaiṣṇava verse, "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and the recitation of the complete *vyāhṛtis*, "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ. In whatever rite another person has been chosen for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*), there the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), once the *brahmā* priest is seated, shall sit facing the fire behind that priest, having cast away a blade of grass from the seat prepared by the performer of the oblation and having touched water.

In the absence of a Brahmin, one should place upon his seat an umbrella, a *kūrca* grass mat, a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a staff, or a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). Then, having placed either a piece of wood or a blade of grass upon the ground, he takes two *darbha* blades that are equal, pointed, and free from internal knots; holding them so that their tips remain at the distance of a span (*prādeśa*), he cuts them with a piece of wood or a knife, but not with his fingernail. Having touched water, he rubs them with his hand, moistened with water, starting from the roots and proceeding to the tips.

Then, having taken the *praṇītā* vessel and washed it three times, having placed two blades of *pavitra* grass with their tips pointing eastward within it, and having poured a little water into it while meditating upon the earth as the instrument of action, he should again fill it with water until it reaches the rim. Holding the two *pavitra* blades with their tips pointing north and tied together with his thumb and ring finger, and using both hands turned upward with fingers pointing east, he should purify the water contained in the *praṇītā* vessel by pouring it back and forth. Then, holding the *praṇītā* vessel with his left hand and covering that vessel with his right, [he should hold it] level with his nose.

Holding them without letting them touch one another, having carried them across by the north, he places them upon the *darbha* grass to the north of the fire. He covers them with *darbha* blades whose tips point northward. Then, having placed those two strainers (*pavitre*)—without even washing them—with their tips pointing north into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, he fills that vessel with water. In this case, there is no fetching of water from the earth; rather, there is the mental visualization of the earth as the instrument, and the filling of the opening with water again, just as in the case of the *praṇītā* water.

Then, having purified that water as before, having turned the perforated vessels face upwards, and having loosened the fuel, he sprinkles all the vessels three times with all the water using his hand together with the *pavitra*, directed toward the east. Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is the pouring of water with the hand held open and turned upwards.

Then, taking the *sruva* ladle, the *darvī* spoon, and the prepared *saṃmārga* (cleansing) *darbha* blades with their tips intact, he heats them together over the fire using only his right hand; having placed the *darvī* on the *darbha* grass, he takes the *sruva* in his left hand and, with the tips of the *darbha* blades held in his right hand, cleans the interior of the bowl by moving from the inside toward the outside, and the handle with the roots of the *darbha* blades.

Then, having heated it again and placed it upon *darbha* grass, he takes hold of the *darvī* in the same manner; having wiped the upper part of the bowl (*puṣkara*) from east to west with the tips of the *darbha* blades, the lower part of the bowl from west to east with the middle parts of the *darbha* blades, and the handle with the roots of the *darbha* blades, he heats it again and places it on the *darbha* grass to the north of the *sruva*. Some maintain that there should be no mixing of cleaned and uncleaned vessels until the entire act of cleaning is completed.

Others say [the rule applies] up until the completion of the preparatory rite (*prayoga*). In that regard, if there is contact [with the vessel], then according to the statement of Bhāradvāja—"Having heated it again, one should wipe it with its own mantra"—if there is contact with a vessel that has not been wiped, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is indeed wiping it again. Then, having sprinkled the wiping-grass (*darbha*) with water, he throws it into the fire. Sprinkling water with the hand closed into a fist and turned downward is called *akṣyukṣaṇa*. In a ritual procedure involving only an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*), the *sruva* ladle is not used.

Then, having melted cow’s clarified butter outside [the fire], he pours a copious amount of strained butter into the butter-pot—which has been placed on *darbha* grass to the west of the fire-altar and covered with a strainer—and having removed embers from the north side of the outer layer of sacrificial grass using the *upaveṣa*, and having made them separate, he places [the pot] upon them; then, having ignited it over the fire in the altar with *darbha* blades whose flames point downward, and holding those [blades] in his left hand, he [takes] with his right hand [a portion] the size of a thumb-joint.

Having thrown two tips of *darbha* grass into the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagni-karaṇa*) three times using those same *darbha* blades or others that have been ignited; then, having cast even those *darbha* blades out to the north, one should touch water. However, when the kindling takes place in a permanently maintained fire (*nirūḍhāgni*), the disposal occurs right there and not outside.

Then, having poured out the clarified butter (ājya) while drawing it out as if with a ladle toward the north, and having brought the embers from the fire-drilling wood to their place in the hearth, he holds two strainers (pavitra) with their tips pointing north. Beginning from the western part of the clarified butter, he moves them toward the eastern part, then brings them back again to the western part; thus he purifies the butter three times. Having untied the knot of the two strainers and cast the strainers into the fire, he encircles the fire with enclosing sticks (paridhi) shaped like yoke-pins (śamyā).

To the west of the central fire, one should place the western fire with its water-jar facing north; to the south of the central fire, the southern fire with its water-jar facing east; and to the north of the southern fire, the northern fire with its water-jar facing east. In this arrangement, the root of the middle enclosing-stick of the southern fire should be placed over the root of the middle enclosing-stick of the central fire. The middle enclosing-stick of the northern fire should be placed beneath the tip of the middle enclosing-stick of the central fire, and the laying of the enclosing-sticks must be done directly upon the sacrificial grass strewn on the ground.

Then, having sprinkled the ground to the west of the fire, he spreads the cord used for binding the sacrificial grass (barhis) there with its ends pointing north. Upon that, he spreads the sacrificial grass with its tips pointing east and its ends toward the north. Therein, he places the dipping-spoon (sruva), the large ladle (darvī), and the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī) in sequence from left to right. If there is an oblation of cooked rice (caru), he pours clarified butter over the cooked rice, removes it from the fire toward the north, and places it on the sacrificial grass to the north of the vessel for clarified butter, behind the fire.

Then, having set aside a space measuring three finger-breadths all around the site of the fire-altar, he sprinkles water. For the four mantras beginning with "O Aditi, give your consent," Vāmadeva is the seer; Aditi, Anumati, Sarasvatī, and Deva Savitṛ are the deities respectively; they are *yajus* formulas; their application is for the ritual sprinkling (*pariṣeka*). With the mantra "O Aditi, give your consent," he sprinkles from the south toward the east. With "O Anumati, give your consent," he sprinkles from the west toward the north.

With the words, "O Sarasvatī, give your consent," he sprinkles water toward the north, facing east. With the words, "O God Savitṛ, impel," beginning from the northeast, he sprinkles all around in a clockwise direction.

Then, taking clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* with the sacrificial ladle (*darvī*) using the right hand, he anoints the fuel-stick (*idhma*) lying on the ground at its base, middle, and tip. Having placed the ladle back in its proper place and taken the fuel-stick with the right hand, holding it between the middle of the base and the middle of the stick, [he offers it] with the verse beginning "This fuel is for you," whose seer is Vāmadeva, the deity is Agni Jātavedas, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and the application is for the placing of the fuel-stick: "This fuel is your self... through wisdom, svāhā! while the left hand supports the right.

With his hand, he places [the fuel] with its tip pointing eastward into the blazing fire, [reciting]: "To Jātavedas, to Agni, this... In all acts of relinquishment (*tyāga*), one should maintain the sense: "I relinquish this substance standing before me to this deity; it is not mine. Even when the oblation (*homa*) and other rites are performed by another agent, all acts of relinquishment must be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) himself.

Then, having taken clarified butter with the *darvī* spoon and aiming toward the northern junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he inserts the spoon there—[the mantra] "To Prajāpati Manu, Svāhā! has Vāmadeva as its seer, Prajāpati-Manu as its deity, and the Yajus as its meter; its application is in the first pouring oblation (*pūrvāghāra-homa*)—"To Prajāpati Manu, Svāhā!"—meditating on Prajāpati with the mind and reciting the mantra with the mind alone, he offers it continuously, straight, and long from the northwest corner to the southeast corner. [The dedication is: "To Prajāpati Manu, this..."

Again, taking clarified butter with the ladle (*darvī*) and aiming toward the southern junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), one inserts the ladle through it. For the mantra "indrāya svāhā," Vāmadeva is the seer, the Viśvedevas or Indra is the deity, and the Yajus is the meter. Regarding the application in the northern *āghāra* oblation: while reciting the mantra "indrāya svāhā," one offers a continuous, straight, and long stream of oblation, starting from the southwest corner (*nairṛtakoṇa*) and ending at the northeast corner (*aiśānakoṇa*), while remaining seated. "To Indra, this [is offered]. In both cases, all the fuel-wood sticks (*idhmakāṣṭha*) must come into contact with the *āghāra* clarified butter.

If the clarified butter (*ājya*) becomes solid due to cold, then, for the sake of maintaining the continuity of the *āghāra* libation, one should melt it by placing it near the fire associated with the ritual at hand. However, practitioners nowadays melt it with a rod made of copper or other metals heated by that fire; this is improper, as it leads to defects such as the destruction of the external fire-altar or the loss of particles of the fire that have entered the rod. Thus, having poured the *āghāra* this morning—

Regarding the two [mantras] "Svāhā to Agni" and "Svāhā to Soma," Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi). Agni and Soma are the respective deities in order; they are Yajus formulas, and their application (viniyoga) is in the offering of the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga). "Svāhā to Agni. He offers into the fire in the eastern part of the northern half. "To Agni, this [is mine]. "Svāhā to Soma. He offers into the fire in the eastern part of the southern half. Having thus offered the two butter-portions, he offers the other oblations in between them, either upon the specific tongue prescribed for each respective rite or in the very center of the flame.

For the verse *yukto vaha*, Vāmadeva is the seer, Jātavedas Agni is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter; for *yā tiraścī*, Vāmadeva is the seer, Sā Rādhani is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter; for the two [verses] *sā rādhanyai devyai svāhā* and *prasādhanyai devyai svāhā*, Vāmadeva is the seer, and Sā Rādhani Devī and Prasādhanī Devī are the deities respectively; these are Yajus formulas, and their application is in the general principal oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*): "*yukto vaha jātavedaḥ... nema svāhā*"—this is for Jātavedas Agni.

"To her who goes crosswise, I sacrifice, svāhā!"—to Sa-rādhanī, this [offering]. "To the goddess Sa-rādhanī, svāhā!"—to the goddess Sa-rādhanī, this [offering]. "To the goddess Prasādhani, svāhā!"—to the goddess Prasādhani, this [offering].

For the Vyāhṛtis taken individually, Agni is the seer (ṛṣi); for the Vyāhṛtis taken collectively, Prajāpati is the seer. Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati are the deities (devatās) respectively; Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, and Bṛhatī are the meters (chandāṃsi); their application (viniyoga) is in the general principal oblation (pradhāna-homa): "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā"—to Agni, this [is offered]; "Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā"—to Vāyu, this [is offered]; "Oṃ suvaḥ svāhā"—to Sūrya, this [is offered]; "Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā"—to Prajāpati, this [is offered]. Thereafter, one should perform the specific principal oblation (vaiśeṣika-pradhāna-homa) for each respective rite.

Next are the subsequent ancillaries (*aṅga*). For these two verses beginning with *imaṃ me varuṇa*, the seers are the Viśvedevas; Varuṇa is the deity; the meter of the first is Gāyatrī, and that of the second is Triṣṭubh. For the two verses beginning with *tvaṃ no agne*, the seers are the Viśvedevas; Agni and Varuṇa are the deities; the meter is Triṣṭubh. For the verse *tvamagne ayāsi*, the seers are the Viśvedevas; Ayāgni is the deity; the meter is Anuṣṭubh. For the verse *prajāpate*, Prajāpati or the Viśvedevas are the seers; Prajāpati is the deity; the meter is Triṣṭubh.

The application (*viniyoga*) for the subsidiary oblations (*uttarāṅgahoma*): "Oṃ *imaṃ me varuṇa*... *cakre svāhā*" — to Varuṇa this [is offered]. "Oṃ *tattvā yāmi*... *moṣīḥ svāhā*" — to Varuṇa this [is offered]. "Oṃ *tvaṃ no agne*... *smat svāhā*" — to Agni and Varuṇa this [is offered]. "Oṃ *sa tvaṃ no*... *na edhi svāhā*" — to Agni and Varuṇa this [is offered]. "Oṃ *tvamagne a*... *ṣaja svāhā*" — to Agni the Unassailable (*ayase'gnaye*) this [is offered]. "Oṃ *prajāpate*... *yīṇā svāhā*" — to Prajāpati this [is offered]. Thus ends the subsidiary oblation.

For the mantras of the *jayopahoma* (subsidiary oblation for victory), the Viśvedevas are the deities as indicated by their names; they are in the *yajus* meter. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the subsidiary oblation for victory which constitutes a subsequent part [of the rite]: "Oṃ *cittaṃ ca svāhā*"—to *Citta*, this [oblation]. "Oṃ *cittiśca svāhā*"—to *Citti*, this [oblation]; or alternatively, "to *Citti* this. "Oṃ *ākūtaṃ ca svāhā*"—to *Ākūta*, this [oblation]. "Oṃ *ākṛtiśca svāhā*"—to *Ākūti*, this [oblation]; or alternatively, "to *Ākūti* this. "Oṃ *vijñātaṃ ca svāhā*"—to *Vijñāta*, this [oblation].

"Oṃ *vijñānaṃ* ca svāhā"—this is for *vijñāna*. "Oṃ *manaś* ca svāhā"—this is for *manas*. "Oṃ *śakvarīś* ca svāhā"—this is for the *śakvarīs*. "Oṃ *darśaś* ca svāhā"—this is for *darśa*. "Oṃ *pūrṇamāsaś* ca svāhā"—this is for *pūrṇamāsa*. "Oṃ *bṛhat* ca svāhā"—this is for *bṛhat*. "Oṃ *rathaṃtaraṃ* ca svāhā"—this is for *rathaṃtara*. "Oṃ *prajāpatiḥ* jayā0 *bhūva* svāhā"—this is for *Prajāpati*.

Alternatively, the oblation is performed with [mantras] ending in the dative case: "To thought, svāhā! To thinking, svāhā! To intention, svāhā! To intending, svāhā! To the knower, svāhā! To consciousness, svāhā! To the mind, svāhā! To the Śakvarī verses, svāhā! To the new moon, svāhā! To the full moon, svāhā! To the Bṛhat [sāman], svāhā! To the Rathantara [sāman], svāhā! The renunciation (tyāga) is according to the respective gender of the deity. The thirteenth mantra remains unchanged.

For the *abhyātāna* subsidiary oblation mantras, the deities are the Viśvedevas as specified by their respective indicative marks (*liṅga*); the meters are *yajus*; and the application (*viniyoga*) is in the subsidiary oblation of the *abhyātāna*, which constitutes a subsequent limb [of the rite]. "Oṃ, Agni is the lord of beings; may he protect me in this [rite]... svāhā! — for Agni, the lord of beings, this [offering]. "Oṃ, Indra is the lord of the eldest... — for Indra, the lord of the eldest, this [offering]. "Oṃ, Yama is the lord of the earth... — for Yama, the lord of the earth, this [offering].

"Oṃ, Vāyu is the lord of the intermediate space... [To Vāyu, the lord of the intermediate space, this...]. "Oṃ, Sūrya is the lord of heaven... [To Sūrya, the lord of heaven, this...]. "Oṃ, Candramas is the lord of the stars... [To Candramas, the lord of the stars, this...]. "Oṃ, Bṛhaspati is the lord of sacred knowledge (Brahman)... [To Bṛhaspati, the lord of sacred knowledge, this...]. "Oṃ, Mitra is the lord of truths... [To Mitra, the lord of truths, this...].

"Oṃ varuṇo'pām adhi... To Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, this [offering]. "Oṃ samudraḥ srotyānām adhi... To Samudra, the lord of the flowing streams, this [offering]. "Oṃ annaṃ sāmrājyānām adhi... To Anna, the lord of sovereign powers, this [offering]. "Oṃ soma oṣadhīnām adhi... To Soma, the lord of herbs, this [offering]. "Oṃ savitā prasavānām adhi... To Savitṛ, the lord of impelling forces, this [offering].

"Oṃ Rudra is the overlord of animals... [Offering: To Rudra, the overlord of animals, this... | Here, there is the touching of water. "Oṃ Tvaṣṭṛ is the overlord of forms... [Offering: To Tvaṣṭṛ, the overlord of forms, this... | "Oṃ Viṣṇu is the overlord of mountains... [Offering: To Viṣṇu, the overlord of mountains, this... | "Oṃ Maruts, you who are the overlords of the hosts, may you protect me... [Offering: To the Maruts, the overlords of the hosts, this... | Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī): "O fathers, grandfathers, further ancestors... [Offering: To the fathers, grandfathers, and further ancestors, this... | May you protect me.

"To the fathers, grandfathers, further ancestors, and more recent ancestors—to them [I offer] this... Then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he should touch water. Even in the case of the ritual of standing in attendance (*upasthāna*), the sacred thread remains worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*); there is neither the utterance of *svāhā* nor the formal abandonment of the offering. This [procedure] applies even to one whose father is living, without any modification of the formula. The person performing the act of holding on (*anvārambha*) must also wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder. In this rite, the wife does not hold on, because it is a rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkarman*). For the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* mantras, the deities are the Viśvedevas as indicated by their characteristic marks (*liṅga*); they are Yajus formulas. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the subsidiary oblation (*upahoma*) of the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, which constitutes a subsequent part of the rite.

"Oṃ, Agni, the Gandharva, who is the conqueror of truth and whose abode is truth—may he protect this spiritual power (brahman) and the ruling power (kṣatra). To him, svāhā! [This is] for Agni, the Gandharva, the conqueror of truth, whose abode is truth: to him, this [offering]. "His Apsarases are the plants, named Ūrj; may they protect this spiritual power and the ruling power. To them, svāhā! [This is] for the plants, the Apsarases, named Ūrj: to them, this [offering]. "He is the giver of health... may he protect you... [This is] for Sūrya, the Gandharva, the giver of health, whose essence is the All: to him, this [offering].

"May his rays, the Apsarases, and the Āyus protect us; this [is for] the Marīcis, the Apsarases, and the Āyus. *Oṃ suṣumnaḥ sūryaraśmiḥ...* "This [is for] Suṣumna, the sun-rayed Gandharva, and the Moon. *...tasya nakṣatrāṇi matāni...* "This [is for] the Nakṣatras, the Apsarases, and the Bekurīs. *Oṃ bhujyuḥ suparṇaḥ...* "This [is for] Bhujyu, Suparṇa, and the Yajña Gandharva. *...tasya dakṣiṇā matāḥ...* "This [is for] the Dakṣiṇās, the Apsarases, and the Stavās."

"Oṃ Prajāpatiḥ viśvakarmā manasā saṃkalpayatu. To Prajāpati Viśvakarman, to Manas, to the Gandharvas... "His Ṛk and Sāman... To the Ṛks and Sāmans, to the Apsarases, to the Vahnis... "Oṃ Iṣiraḥ viśvavyacāḥ saṃkalpayatu. To Iṣira Viśvavyacas, to Vāta, to the Gandharvas... "His waters and Apsarases... To the Waters, to the Apsarases, to the Mudās, this... "Oṃ Bhuvanasya patiḥ svāhā. To the Lord of the World, this...

"Oṃ parameṣṭhya... rvaḥ sa... [This is] for Parameṣṭhin, the overlord, for Mṛtyu (Death): perfume. "Tasya vi... ma tā... [This is] for Viśva, for the Apsarases, for the Bhūs (Earths), etc. "Oṃ sukṣitiḥ... rvaḥ sa... [This is] for Sukṣiti, for Subhūti, for Bhadrakṛt, for Suvarvat, for Parjanya: perfume. "Tasya vidyu... ma tā i... [This is] for the Vidyuts (Lightnings), for the Apsarases, for the Rugs (Shines), etc. "Oṃ dūre heti... rvaḥ sa... [This is] for Dūreheti, for Amṛḍaya, for Mṛtyu, for the Gandharva: this [perfume].

"tasya prajā0 ma tā i0"—to the *prajā* (progeny), to the *apsarases*, and to those who are fearful, [this offering]. "oṃ cāruḥ kṛpaṇa0 rvaḥ sa0"—to *cāru* (the beautiful), to *kṛpaṇakāśin* (the one appearing in distress), and to *kāma* (desire), to the *gandharvas*. "tasyā''dhayo0 ma tā i0"—to the *ādhis* (mental anxieties), to the *apsarases*, and to those who cause grief, [this offering]. "oṃ sa no bhuva0 yaccha svāhā"—to the Lord of the World (*bhuvanasya pati*), [this offering]. And these subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) beginning with *jaya* are optional.

Then, for the verse beginning with *yadasya*, Vāmadeva is the seer, Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the deity, and the metre is Atyaṣṭi; its application is in the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation: "yadasya ka0 yitre svāhā. He offers this into the eastern half of the northern half of the fire, in a quantity slightly greater than the previous offering, so that it does not touch the preceding oblations. [The formula is: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, this... If there is contact [between the offerings], one should perform the *sarvaprāyaścitta* expiation and the recitation of the *anājñāta* and other mantras.

Then, having untied the cord used for binding the fuel, sprinkled it with water, and thrown it into the fire, he anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the ladle (*darvī*) in the order they were placed. Having taken some *darbha* blades from the surrounding grass-strew, or all of them, or the entire sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that was spread out, he anoints the tips in the ladle and the middle and roots in the clarified butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*). He does this a second time. For the third time, however, he places the roots and the middles in the clarified butter vessel and the tips in the ladle.

Having thus smeared one blade of grass, taking it from among the smeared blades and setting it aside as a marker, he inserts the other blades through the junction of the northern enclosing-stick with his right and left hands; without letting them pass beyond the tips of the fire, and keeping their tips not pointing upwards, he roasts them over the embers while holding the hand slightly straight with its tips upward, then raising it upward and subsequently bringing it downward in a descending motion, finally turning them around within the hearth so that they lie one above the other.

Then, having taken three [stalks] upward with his joined palms (*añjali*) at the very place of the receptacle, he throws them into the fire. Then, having struck away the grass that was placed there, having pointed toward it three times with his fingers, having touched both nostrils simultaneously and sipped water, and likewise having touched both eyes and sipped water, he should touch the earth. Then, having thrown the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) into the fire, he throws the other two enclosing-sticks together with both hands. He pushes the tip of the northern [stick] downward onto the embers.
Then follows the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*).

For the three mantras beginning with *anājñātam*, the Viśvedevas are the seers (*ṛṣi*), Agni is the deity (*devatā*); for the first two the meter is *anuṣṭubh*, and for the last it is *triṣṭubh*. For the two mantras beginning with *tvaṃ no agne*, the Viśvedevas, Agni, and Varuṇa are the deities, and the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the two mantras beginning with *yata indra*, the Viśvedevas are the seers; Indra Maghavan is the deity of the first, and Vṛtra-han Indra is the deity of the second. The meter of the first is *bṛhatī*, and that of the second is *anuṣṭubh*. For the mantra *tryambakam*, the Viśvedevas and Tryambaka are the deities, and the meter is *anuṣṭubh*.

For the verse *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, Soma, Viṣṇu, and Gāyatrī are [the deities, ṛṣis, and meters]. For the seven *vyāhṛtis*, the seers are the Upaniṣads, and the deities are Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Bṛhaspati, Varuṇa, Indra, and the Viśvedevas, respectively. The meters are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī, respectively. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the expiatory *ājya* oblation: *Oṃ anājñātaṃ... tathā svāhā*; to Agni, this [offering]. *Puruṣasaṃmito... tathā svāhā*; to Agni, this [offering].

"Oṃ yatpākatrā ma...jāti svāhā"—to Agni, this [offering]. "Oṃ tvaṃ no agne...smat svāhā"—to Agni and Varuṇa, this [offering]. "Oṃ satvaṃ no a...edhi svāhā"—to Agni and Varuṇa, this [offering]. "Oṃ yata indra bha...jahi svāhā"—to Indra Maghavan, this [offering]. "Oṃ svastidā vi...karaḥ svāhā"—to Indra Vṛtrahan, this [offering]. "Oṃ tryambakaṃ yajā...tāt svāhā"—to Tryambaka, this [offering].

"Oṃ idaṃ viṣṇuḥ... sure svāhā"—this for Viṣṇu. "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā"—this for Agni. "Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā"—this for Vāyu. "Oṃ suvaḥ svāhā"—this for Sūrya. "Oṃ mahaḥ svāhā"—this for Bṛhaspati. "Oṃ janaḥ svāhā"—this for Varuṇa. "Oṃ tapaḥ svāhā"—this for Indra. "Oṃ satya svāhā"—this for the Viśvedevas.

If occasional expiations consisting solely of oblations (*kevalahoma*) should occur and remain unperformed immediately after their respective causes, they must be performed here. He offers the remnants of the clarified butter (*saṃsrāva-ājya*) upon the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the mantra: "Oṃ, svāhā to the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas. [The formula for the dedication is: "To the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas who partake of the remnants, this [is offered].

Then follows the subsequent sprinkling (*uttarapariṣeka*) as before: "O Aditi, you have consented; O Anumati, you have consented; O Sarasvatī, you have consented; O God Savitṛ, you have impelled [the sacrifice]."

Such is the distinction regarding the sprinkling mantras (*pariṣeka-mantra*). For these mantras, the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as before. In the case where the rite of lifting the fire (*praṇītoddhāsana*) is performed according to the rule, one should discard the *upaveṣa* (the fire-stirring stick) here.
