According to tradition, it should be broken; this breaking is appropriate to prevent the mistaken use of the *upaveṣa* for purposes such as kindling, which might arise from the confusion that it is actually a fuel-stick (*samit*). Thus, its breaking is justified.

If this [wood] is in the form of a thick piece of wood, however, since there is no purpose for breaking it, it should be cast into a common fire other than the one used for the ritual. Then, having carried the *praṇītā* waters around the front of the fire and placed them behind the fire, one should sprinkle water in the four directions starting from the east, as well as upwards and downwards; then, having poured the remaining water on the ground and sprinkled himself and his wife, he should wipe his face.

As for what the author of the *Gṛhyakārikā* stated—that water should be brought into the *praṇītā* vessel prior to the sprinkling (*utsecana*)—that is to be disregarded due to a lack of authoritative evidence. In a *homa* performed by the teacher (*ācārya*), the ritual purification (*mārjana*) belongs only to the sacrificer and his wife, not to the teacher.

Then he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahman priest consisting of gold, or a cow, or a full vessel; in its absence, grain that has been threshed once or not threshed at all, or fruit, or gold as a substitute for those items, filled in a bronze cup (*camasa*). The Brahman priest, having breathed upon it seventeen times, accepts the gold with the mantra: "Oṃ, by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I accept thee with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan; for Agni, thee, gold; may he accept it with that. For this mantra, Prajāpati is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity, Yajus is the meter, and its application is in the act of acceptance. He recites: "Oṃ devasya tvā... [etc. ...kṣiṇe'gnaye hiraṇyaṃ tenā0 hṇātu," and thus he accepts the gold.

In the case of accepting a cow—the specific modification in the mantra is: instead of "Oṃ, [I give] gold to Agni, by that... one says "To Rudra, the cow, by her..."; having offered grass, the acceptance is performed. The rest is the same.
However, in the case of accepting grain, he accepts the grain with the mantra: "Oṃ, by the impulse of the God... in the right hand; to the Viśvedevas, the grain, by that may the Immortal accept."

Regarding the acceptance of fruit, however: for the mantra *uttānas tvā* (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.3), Prajāpati Āṅgirasa is the seer, the Yajus is the meter, and its application is in the acceptance [of fruit]. One accepts the fruits with: *Oṃ uttānas tvāṅgīraso gṛhṇātu*. On this point as well, some say that the *sāvitrānvādhāna* (the preliminary rite of placing the firewood) should be performed. In all cases, the acceptance is done after turning away. The bending down of the lower wind is the *apānana*. "Turning away" (*vyāvṛtti*) is the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that the acceptance is for the deity of the substance mentioned in the mantra of acceptance, and not for oneself.

In the case of giving gold as a substitute (*pratinidhi*), however, the mantra belongs to that for whose sake the gift is given. In the alternative view regarding its redemption (*niṣkraya*), the acceptance is with the mantra "uttānastvā" (VS 18.52). Or rather, the acceptance of all [substitutes] may be performed silently; in this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), there is no exhaling (*apānana*). In the acceptance of a cow, there is neither the offering of grass to her nor the formula for turning away (*vyāvṛtyapratigrahaṇa*). Some say that it does occur. In every case, the acceptance is performed solely through the *āgneya* (southern) part of the hand.

"One should perform the acceptance [of the gift] with the *āgneya* [tīrtha]," according to the statement of Baudhāyana. The definition of the *āgneya* tīrtha was stated by that same author: "The *āgneya* is in the middle of the hand. The definition of the *pūrṇapātra* (the full vessel) is stated in the *Sudarśanabhāṣya*: "Eight handfuls make one *kiñcit*; four *kiñcit*s make one *puṣkala*."
"But four [of these] in abundance are declared to be a full vessel (pūrṇapātra)."
"A small amount (kiñcit) consists of eight handfuls (muṣṭi); eight of those constitute a *puṣkala*.
Eight *puṣkalas* are declared to be one full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*)."
Such is the reading in the *Ādhānavaijayantī*.
However, in the *Āgamasārasaṃgraha*, it says:
"A copper vessel fashioned from thirty-two palas of copper..."
Having filled it with rice, together with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
"The performer should give that to the chosen [priest]; the wise know this as the *pūrṇapātra*.
Thus has been stated the definition of the *pūrṇapātra*.

In the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*, however, it is stated that even a vessel filled with enough grain for one person's meal constitutes a *pūrṇapātra*. These [definitions] should be applied according to one's capacity. Some maintain that wherever a specific sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed, this gift of a *dakṣiṇā* must also be performed there. In reality, however, just as the offering of the ordinary *anvāhārya* rice is omitted in the case of Soma sacrifices, *Iṣṭis*, and *Paśubandhas*, the omission of this [gift] is likewise appropriate. In this context, the discarding of the *upaveṣa* (the fire-stick) takes place. Then the Brahman and the Sacrificer exit by the way they came.

These ritual rules (*dharma*) are observed in various *Gṛhya* texts as being either performed or not performed during *darvihoma* offerings made with hostile intent (*āghāra*). Some perform these rules immediately after the *vāstubali* rite. Then, for the mantra "O Sacrifice, homage to you" (*yajña namaste*), the Viśvedevas are the deity, the *Yajus* is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the worship of the fire (*agnyupasthāna*). With the words "Oṃ, O Sacrifice, homage to you... homage to you," both the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the *Brahman* priest perform the worship. The teachers (*ācārya*) and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) also perform this worship.

For the verse beginning with *agne naya*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), the meter is *triṣṭubh*, and the application (*viniyoga*) is in the worship of Agni: "O Agni, lead us... let us offer [oblations]. Having left a space of six finger-breadths from the hearth of Agni and having focused on the fire according to the ritual manual (*tantra*), one should worship it. According to tradition, this is in the north-western direction (*vāyavyā diś*). In the worship of Agni, one should avoid red perfumes, flowers, and consecrated rice (*akṣata*). Among red flowers, one should specifically avoid the *japā* flower. Some have written that one should avoid incense and lamps; however, we do not know the source for that.

For the verse beginning with *mā na stoke*, Agni is the deity, Rudra is the seer, and the Jagatī is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the wearing of the sacred ash (*vibhūti*). Having applied the ash of Agni to the forehead with the mantra: *oṃ mā na stoke tanaye...
mā te*, [one recites]: "O Havyavāhana (Bearer of Oblations), grant me faith, intelligence, fame, wisdom, learning, intellect, prosperity, strength, longevity, splendor, and health."

Having thus prayed to Agni, one should pay obeisance. At the conclusion of the rite, if there is water remaining that was used for the ritual, one should discard it; then, for the sake of ensuring the vessel is not empty, one should pour pure water into that vessel and set it down.
This concludes the procedure for the "Face of Agni" (agnimukha).
He extends the rules for the fire-oblation (homa) taught in the initiation (upanayana) to other contexts as well:
"The ritual procedure for all *darvihoma* offerings is this.

This is its meaning: *darvihomas* are those rites enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice); for all of them, this prescribed ritual (*kalpa*)—beginning with the digging [of the altar] and ending with the *prasādhanī-devī-homa*—is the rule (*vidhi*) that has been set forth. Alternatively, the meaning is that this prescribed ritual consists both of what has already been set forth, ending with the *prasādhanī-devī-homa*, and of what is yet to be set forth, such as the *vyāhṛti-homas*, the *vāruṇī-homas*, and so on.

In the first alternative (*kalpa*), the statement "having performed [the rites] up to the *vyāhṛti*s in each respective place at the beginning" and the injunction regarding the mantras beginning with "this for me, O Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa*) and "I go to thee" (*tatvā yāmi*) serve the purpose of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), as they were not otherwise established. In the second alternative, however, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*). The inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of extending the rule—ending with the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī—to those rites mentioned in the Sūtras or in other scriptures where the performance of the *vyāhṛti* oblations and the sequential recitation of the Vāruṇī verses have not been specifically prescribed.

In this explanation, there would be an over-extension to the *aupāsana* oblation; that [over-extension] is to be prevented by the inclusion of the term "oblations" (*āhutī*) in the rule: "He offers these two oblations with rice or barley using his hand. If it is asked how this is so, it is said: since the requirement is already established by the words "he offers these," the inclusion of the term "oblations" is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). It serves to ensure that only the two oblations themselves are performed, and not the rest of the ritual procedure (*tantra*). In this alternative, there is also the cessation of the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*) and the sprinkling of water (*pariṣeka*).

(And this is also for the purpose of making known that the oblation should never be made even with the tip of the hand; rather, the oblation must be made only with the upper side of the hand joined to the *juhū*. However, because of the force of the repeated mention of the sprinkling (*pariṣeka*)—which was already established by the rule "In the *vaiśvadeva*, however, there is sprinkling on both sides"—and because of the force of the injunction "perform [the rite] according to the instruction," there is an exclusion of the other ritual framework (*tantra*).

In the second ritual manual (*kalpa*), the prescription for the *vyāhṛti*-oblations and the enumeration of the *vāruṇī* offerings and so forth are intended as a restrictive definition (*parisaṃkhyā*). Consequently, in other cases, the entire procedure does not apply; rather, it extends only up to the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī. However, in the case of the *āgneya* cooked rice offering (*sthālīpāka*), because the gerund suffix (*lyap*) in the word "having taken out" (*udvāsya*) indicates that there is no interval between the taking out and the oblation, the ritual framework (*tantra*) beginning with the placing of the fuel sticks (*idhmābhyādhāna*) and ending with the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī is excluded.

Nor should it be said that everything from the placing of the fuel (idhmābhyādhāna) up to the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī should take place even before the cooking (śrapaṇa); for such a performance is not accepted because it contradicts other scriptural authorities. Furthermore, there is no cessation of the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* water, the taking of the fire into oneself (*ātmany agnigrahaṇa*), or the role of the Brahman priest; for by the rule, "This is the ritual procedure for all *darvihoma*s," there is no obstacle to the commencement of the ritual framework (*tantra*) prior to the placing of the fuel. Alternatively, in the case of those sacrifices belonging to the *āpūrvika* class, the preparation of materials (*dravyasaṃskāra*), the strewing around (*paristaraṇa*), and the sprinkling around (*pariṣeka*) are performed only as far as necessary.

Since it is stated, "up to the *āhutis* and other specific rites (*vaiśeṣika-karmāṇi*)," the status of being an *āpūrvika* (a rite performed for the first time) is established here by the statement of Baudhāyana. Consequently, there is a cessation even of the *praṇītā*-water carrying and other such preliminary acts. Because these [acts] are not applicable among the *āpūrvika* rites, the injunction for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is made; for if only "he offers the *sauviṣṭakṛtī*" were said, the oblation might be performed with the formula "that which belongs to this" (*yad asya*). To prevent that, the expression "he offers to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" is used. Due to the absence of the *āghāra* ritual framework, the offerings to Varuṇa and others are likewise excluded. The subsequent sprinkling (*uttara-pariṣeka*) is obtained precisely because of its connection to the preceding sprinkling (*pūrva-pariṣeka*).

The dismissal of the *paristaraṇa* grass, however, is implied by the sense of the context. Alternatively, the meaning of the sūtra is as follows: "Darvihomas" are those rites enjoined by the verb *juhoti*; in all of these, this ritual procedure (*kalpa*) and rule (*vidhi*) applies as appropriate. The inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose that, through this [sūtra], there may be an extension (*atideśa*) to all three types of Darvihomas—those with the *āghāra* libation, the *āpūrvika*, and the *āgnihotrika*—so that wherever there is a Darvihoma involving an *āghāra*, the entire appropriate procedure applies.

In a case where there is a *darvihoma* not preceded by another rite (*āpūrvika*), the preparation of the substance according to its requirements, as well as the strewing and sprinkling around, constitute the entire procedure, because these alone are appropriate for it.

If it is argued that, by the force of the term *āpūrvika* (pertaining to the first time), only the oblation as far as stated and the other specific (*vaiśeṣika*) rites are to be performed, and no other ancillaries (*aṅga*) are to be performed here—this is true. However, because another scriptural injunction prohibits offering with unconsecrated material, stating "one should not offer with unconsecrated material," the consecration of the material is necessary. Furthermore, because they are connected to the locus of the rite, the strewing (*paristaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) are also required.

Nor should it be argued that the placing of fuel (idhmābhyādhāna) would likewise occur because of its connection with the fire; for its absence is established precisely because Baudhāyana has not mentioned it. Furthermore, the absence of the placing of fuel follows from the absence of the *āghāra* libation. There is no dispute regarding the fact that when one related member ceases, the other related member also ceases, since the placing of fuel is connected to the *āghāra*. The evidence for the mutual connection between these two is demonstrated in the sūtra: "Then he offers with the *darvī* ladle. Baudhāyana states all of this as follows:
"In the *āpūrvika* [rites], there is the preparation of the substance according to the requirements, the strewing and the sprinkling, as far as stated, the oblations, and other specific rites.
The mention of "substance" (*dravya*) is an elliptical indication for the means of the *homa* sacrifice.

"One should not offer with an unrefined vessel," according to the corroboration of another scripture (*śāstra*). There are exactly these many auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) in the *Āgnihotrika* [section]: having taken four portions of consecrated clarified butter (*ājya*), and having recited all the mantras, the first oblation is offered. The second oblation is with the mantra: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! Then follows the threefold tasting as in the *Agnihotra*, the washing of the *sruva*-ladle with *darbha* grass, and the specific rites as previously described. And so says Baudhāyana:

"In the rites pertaining to the *āgnihotra*, having employed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having taken four portions, he recites all the mantras and offers the first oblation with the formula, 'To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! He offers the second oblation as in the *āgnihotra*. Having consumed [the remnants] three times, he washes the *sruk* with *darbha* grass. Then he performs the specific rites as they have been prescribed."

In the phrase "of the *darvihomas*," the plural number is appropriate because they involve various sacrificial materials (*havīṃṣi*). This is the same in both ritual systems (*kalpa*). While it could have been stated simply as "this is the procedure everywhere," the specific mention of "*darvihomas*" is for the purpose of ensuring that this procedure applies only to those rites enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), and not to those enjoined by *jap* (to mutter) and so forth. This point is also common to both systems. Where there is a reference to both or a reference to either one, the ritual framework (*tantra*) is exactly like that of the *āghāra* libation.

Elsewhere, there is an option between three or two [procedures], or in some cases a restriction. In that regard, regarding the *trivṛdanna-homa*, because of the force of the present scriptural statement which brings about the use of food prepared outside [the sacrificial ground], it is necessarily of the *āpūrvika* type. However, in the monthly *śrāddha*, even when the *homa* involves food prepared outside, since the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is observed to be like that of the *āghāra* offering, the *āghāra*-type procedure also applies optionally.

Regarding the *sthālīpāka*, however, both explanations maintain that it follows the *āpūrvika* ritual procedure. But the Commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*) has stated that, according to one view, the *tantra* (the main ritual framework) here is like that of the *āghāra* offering. Where there is no injunction using the term *sthālīpāka* for a mere oblation of cooked rice (*caru*), but rather an injunction such as "he offers from the cooked [rice] by means of the word *caru*," there the *tantra* is indeed the *āpūrvika*. However, where the oblation of cooked rice is accompanied by oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth, the oblation of cooked rice is performed with the *tantra* of the *āghāra* offering.

The evidence regarding this matter will be demonstrated in the following sūtra: "Then he causes her to sacrifice with a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni. In the case of single-oblation homas performed on account of specific occasions such as the spilling of the offering (*uddravaṇa*), there is an optional choice between the three or two methods. However, in the case of homas consisting of two, three, or more oblations, the rule for the *āgnihotrika* method does not apply, because it contradicts the injunction: "Having recited all [the verses], he offers the first oblation. In the *aupāsana* homa, however, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is indeed *āpūrvika*.

In this context, although there is neither a prescribed extension (*atideśa*) nor a specifically ordained preparation (*saṃskāra*) of the substance, nevertheless, because another scripture prohibits an oblation with an unprepared substance—stating that "one should not offer with an unprepared substance"—the preparation of the substance appropriate to the occasion must indeed be performed, excluding the mantra, as taught for Vedic (*śrauta*) oblations. The same applies to the preparation of the implements used for the oblation as taught for Vedic oblations; and that consists of heating (*niṣṭapana*) and wiping (*mārjana*). In the case of an oblation offered with the hand, the right hand is wiped by means of the left hand.

In the case of performing the *upāsana-homa* with clarified butter (*ājya*), the consecration of the *ājya* should be performed either according to the rules stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*—excluding the mantras—or according to the *Śrauta* ritual. The strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) and the sprinkling of water (*pariṣeka*) should also be performed. In this procedure, the purpose of taking up the oblation is simply to ensure the successful completion of the *homa* by means of the upper side of the finger. Regarding the *vaiśvadeva*, there is an exclusion of other ritual frameworks (*tantra*) as before; this applies here as well. However, in rites taught in other scriptures that are accomplished with substances other than cooked rice (*caru*), the framework (*tantra*) should be understood as being established according to local custom, whether it be the *āghāra-tantra* or the *āpūrvika-tantra*. This is the general direction. Thus concludes the application of the *agnimukha*.
Thus ends the first section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā* composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of the illustrious Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, whose surname is Oka. || 1 ||
Now begins the second section:
Verses Summarizing Expiatory Rites (*Prāyaścitta-saṃgraha-kārikā*).
Now, for the purpose of reconnecting ritual acts, there are expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) performed in brief. Regarding these, here are the summary verses composed by me:
In the case of the non-performance or the improper performance of what has been prescribed, the entire expiation characterized by Vedic injunction is ordained. (1)
The conjunction of that which is generally a process of destruction is called *citta*;
and that should be known as twofold, through the distinction between the perceptible and the supersensuous. (2)
Furthermore, there is the re-establishment of fire that has gone outside, and the re-taking of spilled sacrificial oblation (havis) once it has been placed in a pure location. (3)
For the wise have proclaimed that the mind, as described above, is perceptible;
however, the wise maintain that the mind involved in recitation, burnt offerings, and so forth, is beyond the reach of the senses.
If, on the occasion of a rite of expiation, any mention of a specific number or similar details is heard, that should be understood as being unintended (not to be taken literally).
Having consecrated the clarified butter (ājya), one should perform the strewing around the fire;
then, having sprinkled it with water, one should honor it with white flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth.
Having adorned himself and established the sacred fire, he should then offer the prescribed oblation with a fuel-stick of *pālāśa* wood, accompanied by the mantra ending in *svāhā*.

The procedure for the expiatory oblation (prāyaścittāhuti) should be understood as being performed with a consecrated ladle (darvī), or else according to the method prescribed in the Śrautasūtras. || 8 ||
Mental oblations (cittahoma) should be performed according to the rules by the wise;
however, all those mentioned in other scriptures must indeed follow the domestic (gārhya) ritual procedure.
We shall examine these points immediately hereafter;
however, in the case of the Śrauta rite, the oblation is to be made with the *sruva* ladle, and the placing of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) is mandatory.

In a homa involving many oblations, that many fuel-sticks (samidh) are prescribed. There may be an option regarding the spreading of the grass (paristṛti), but the sprinkling (pariṣeka) is to be done without a mantra.
Having circumambulated the fire from the front, he should stand to its south;
holding the *sruk* ladle toward the navel, he should offer the prescribed oblation.

In a homa involving many oblations, the homa is said to be performed with separate offerings; where the procedure for oblations with the *sruva* ladle is prescribed, one should not employ the *sruc* ladle.
Even in the Gṛhya rules regarding the procedure for oblations with a *sruva*, only the *darvī* is mentioned;
however, for oblations involving two or three scoops and so forth, the *sruva* may also be used in both cases.
In this rite, the placing (sādana) of the *sruva* ladle must also be performed for the purpose of taking [the oblation];
however, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) of the *darvī* or the *sruk* is prescribed as occurring prior to the cleansing [of the other implements]. (15)
The cleansing of the *śrauta* *sruva* ladle should be performed without mantras;
however, if the *cittahoma* should occur before the placement of the *darbha* blades used for cleansing, [the procedure must be adjusted]. 16.
Then, having consecrated the clarified butter (ājya) intended for the mental sacrifice, one should perform the oblation with it;
however, if the intention arises at the time of the formal pouring out (nirvāpa), then there should indeed be only a single portion of clarified butter.
Whether for the sake of the mind (meditation) or for the sake of ritual action, there is no separate origin here;
even in the case of the fire-oblation (homa), the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya) is exactly as prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, according to the method stated in the Śruti.
After the fire has been strewn around, no further strewing should be performed;
nor should the placing of fuel-sticks be done after the primary sacrificial wood (idhma) has already been placed. || 19 ||
The time for the expiation is traditionally taught to be immediately after the occasion [for it arises], or else prior to the principal oblation, according to the Smṛti of the sage Baudhāyana. (20)
Wherever a specific expiation has not been prescribed,
it is indeed declared that a single oblation with all the vyāhṛtis is to be offered.
This oblation should be made with a ladle or a large spoon, but not with a small dipping-spoon;
for this alone is remembered by the ritualists as the universal expiation.
If the oblation (homa) prescribed therein were not intended for an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), then one should perform that expiation which names all [the deities]. || 23 ||
Even in a case where a fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed for an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha),
one should nevertheless perform it with a mind that designates everything.
The first opinion is that of Ālekhana, while the latter is the opinion of Āśmarathya;
when no vessel is specified for the mental oblation, the means of offering in the Vedic rite is the *sruva* ladle.

In the domestic rite of the mental oblation (*cittahoma*), the ladle (*darvī*) is the instrument for the offering. When no number is specified, it should be understood as once; when no substance is specified, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is traditionally prescribed.
He who is the performer of the ritual fire-offering (karmahoma) is declared here to be the one [authorized];
in the case of a gift, the husband is said to be the performer, but in his absence, it shall be the wife.

The same should be understood regarding renunciation according to the Smṛti of the sage Kātyāyana; for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, the rites should take place by way of cooked offerings in the place where the Citestī is performed.
The wise should understand from other treatises that these ritual movements (cāravaḥ) apply everywhere;
however, the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is performed when one lacks the capacity [for the full rite], and its procedure is now described.
Having taken clarified butter four times, or even eight times, or twelve times in the *sruk* ladle, or likewise in the *darvikā* spoon; || 30 ||
But by means of the penultimate [vowel], or together with the inclusion of the final one.
Having filled it with clarified butter, one should offer it accompanied by the utterance of the word "svāhā. || 31 ||
Having pronounced the name of the deity in the dative case, an oblation should be offered by the wise at the end of the word "svāhā"; this is known as the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
If one is unable [to perform the full oblation], the *pūrṇāhuti* (final full-offering) is prescribed using a ladle filled to the brim (*pūrṇasruva*).
In all cases where [the ritual] is not known, the recitation of the *vaiṣṇavī-ṛc* is indeed enjoined.
And the recitation of all the vyāhṛtis should be performed by the wise man, provided there is an absence of the prescribed substance in its essential form. (34)
A substitute may be made for the woman, but there is no substitute for the expiation in this case;
when there is a conflict between the purpose and the material substance, the purpose is declared to be the more powerful.
In this regard, even though the action under discussion possesses its own essential existence, this principle is proclaimed to apply when it lacks the capacity for the primary effect. (36)

In a conflict between substance and quality, the substance is said to be stronger; it is not for the sake of accomplishing a quality that the substance's capacity for its primary function is set aside. (37)
In that case, this rule regarding substitution has been declared;
when there is an omission of vowels, syllables, and so forth, the offering is traditionally remembered as being made with the word "ābhiḥ."
In the event of an omission of the mantra, an omission of the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and other rites, or likewise in the case of a transposition,
one should offer two oblations with the two verses beginning "tvaṃ naḥ" and "sa tvaṃ naḥ."

If there were a recollection of that which was omitted prior to the principal sacrifice, then the performance of the subsidiary parts whose purpose remains unaccomplished would indeed follow the principal rite. (40)
If a limb [of the ritual] has its purpose already accomplished, it is the mind alone and not the action;
fuel such as wood and so forth should be known as an illustration of this.

If the Smṛti is prescribed after the *ājyabhāga* offerings but before the principal oblations (*mukhyāhuti*), then, having placed the fuel (*idhma*) into the fire, one should perform it with the intention of correcting the inversion.
"If the mind alone were to exist hereafter," as stated in the Nidāna Sūtra;
[yet] when the auxiliary parts such as the *ājyabhāga* offerings are omitted, you are not ours, nor are those *āhutis* ours. (43)
If an action is performed at the wrong time, it will not bear fruit at all;
however, for the sake of the proper sequence, there is a return [to the body], as stated in the Kaṭha-sūtra. (44)

And likewise, upon the burning or cutting of the darbha grass used for strewing, the enclosing sticks (paridhis), the sacrificial grass (barhis), the fuel (idhma), the fire-tongs (upaveṣa), and the cord (śulba). || 45 ||
And in the case of damage by urine and the like, or in the event of total destruction,
[one should provide] that which is of the same kind, of the same form, and likewise of the same size.
Having brought [the materials] back and having placed them in their respective positions as before, he should perform that ritual action; he must not include anything that has been damaged.
O Agni, you have indeed performed two offerings with the *prājāpatya* verse and the *sruva* ladle;
if there should be a deficiency in the fuel-wood (*idhma*) or the kindling-sticks (*samit*), then one should offer that as a *pākayajña* oblation.
Having offered [the oblations], one should rectify what is deficient, preceded by the prescribed purificatory rites (saṃskāra);
however, if there is an excess, that which is redundant should be discarded, and in this case as well, it is an oblation (āhuti).
If fuel or other materials fall outside during rituals such as the *sthālīpāka*,
one should silently place them back in their proper position and perform the entire offering (*sarvacittaka*) with the *svāhā* mantra.
But if the fire deposited [in the hearth] is damaged, a fuel-stick (samit) should be offered again with the mantra "punastvā";
by this very same [mantra], one oblation (āhuti) must be offered when the fire has been impaired.
Whenever the fire should spontaneously ignite,
then two fuel-sticks are to be placed into the fire with the two mantras beginning with "uddīpyasva."
In the event that the *praṇītā* or *prokṣaṇī* waters spill, one should fill the vessel again;
then, one should perform the oblation with the verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and the verse beginning with "tat savituḥ. (53)
In cases of drying up or leaking as well, the same expiation is proclaimed.
If the fire should happen to leap out from the sacrificial ground, [the following applies].
Having taken it up again with boldness when it is fit for being cast back,
he should then place it in its own position while reciting the Vyāhṛtis.
The universal expiation consists of the recitation of the three *anājñāta* verses and so forth;
likewise for the *adhvaryu*, *āgnīdhra*, and *hotṛ* priests, as well as for the *prayāja* offerings. (56)
"Because of its non-existence, let there be no fear for me"—such a thought would not arise here, if a glowing coal had fallen from its place onto the ground outside. (57)
It is not known from the proximity of either the Vedic fire or the worldly fire which fire this is; therefore, having disregarded that charcoal, [he proceeds]. (58)
It has been stated in the Dviśatī that one should offer all conceptual thought (sarvākhyacitta) as an oblation;
thus, the offering of all mental states should be performed in either the Vedic fire or the domestic fire. 59.
If the clarified butter should spill after the extinguishing [of the fire] but before the purification, one should give a boon to a Brāhmaṇa and say: "The gods have gone to the assembly. (60)
With these five mantras, one should consecrate whatever has been spilled.
If the clarified butter being purified should spill, then, having offered a boon, [one should perform the rite]. 61.

Having given away either a goat or a cow, and having performed the rites for the gods as before; if the clarified butter (ājya) that has been purified should spill, then whatever [substance] may be found in one's own house [should be used]. 62.

Having offered the principal substance, one proceeds as before with "tad devān" and so forth; however, if the clarified butter (ājya) is spilled while being taken up, there is the recitation for the granting of boons (varadāna-anumantraṇa).
Having first performed the rite with this mantra, "vidhāya bhūpataye," one should subsequently make a span-long mark upon the spilled clarified butter.
With the mantra "bhuvane," there should be [an offering] to its south;
with "bhūtānāṃ pataye," there should be [an offering] to its west. || 65 ||
After "to the Being" (bhūtāya), the subsequent [mantra] is prescribed with the Vyāhṛtis;
the Mantras are to be known by the wise as ending in "svāhā," even when devoid of the Vyāhṛtis.

Then, one should sprinkle water over what has been spilled with the mantra beginning with *saṃ tvā*, and if it is located in a pure place, one should cast it away with the mantra beginning with *ced yajñasya*.
If, after consecrating it, one should take [the oblation] from an impure place, this same rule for expiation is prescribed even when the sacrificial offering (havis) spills. || 68 ||
Whether it be the amount contained in the dipping-spoon or even more than that, if there is such overflowing, this is to be known by the wise as the "overflowing mind" (skandana-citta). || 69 ||
If the heap is less than the capacity of the *sruva* ladle, it shall be designated as "all."
In all liquid substances as well, it is proclaimed in exactly this same way.
Among all hard substances, the thumb-joint is superior;
if [the substance] has previously spilled, it is for the mind, but in the case of deficiency, it is for everything.
The mind would not exist in the sacrificial heap (skanda), nor outside, nor in the ashes, the fire, and so forth;
for if the sacrificial heap were to exist outside the enclosing sticks (paridhi) when an oblation has been cast into the fire. 72.
Having drawn that [libation] with his joined palms, he should offer it with the words "mā yaja" (sacrifice for me);
here, the agency belongs to himself alone, as the Āgnīdhra is not possible [in this context].
"Having drawn these together, offer them as oblations"—on this very basis, the omission [of the mantra] is established;
furthermore, the omission of the presentation of the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) is also proclaimed here.
If one should employ a deity not prescribed for the offering and so forth, then one should join that substance with the deity who is prescribed for it. (75)
If one should offer oblations with the mantra "yad vo devā atīta," and then remembers a deity who was not previously prescribed, that [deity] becomes the recipient of the sacrifice. || 76 ||
Having performed this expiation, one should repeat the sacrifice that was already performed;
this very same mental disposition should also apply to the *aupāsana* oblation.
If there should be an inversion in the utterance of "svāhā" or in the act of offering, then one should indeed offer the Manasvatī oblation with the mantra "manojyotiḥ."

If there is a discrepancy regarding the sacrificial portions, the substances, the sacrifice, the deity, or the mantra, then before the completion of the ritual procedure is known, you are ours and we are yours; [therefore, grant] us the oblations.
Then one should perform two oblations; thereafter, the performance of all expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) and so forth is prescribed.
Then, one should indeed give to a Brahmin whatever is the most precious substance in one's own home.
Furthermore, the winding of the thread must be performed; from this point onward, there shall be no offering.
This applies whether the principal substance is one or even many. (81)

If, in a sacrifice where many [offerings] are primary, there should be a failure in production due to the ritual act, then let there be remembrance of you first; O Agni, you are ours, you are our oblation.
Having offered the substance and produced that [result], one should perform the sacrifice as it stands;
once the sacrifice has been remembered, one should then complete the ritual action already commenced. || 83 ||

Thereafter, one should perform the mental offering consisting of the oblation just described; then follows the performance of the principal rite together with its ancillaries, which is indeed internalized. (84)
If one part of the fire is extinguished, there should be an oblation with the Manasvatī verse;
if the fire for the morning homa of the aupāsana rite has been offered, [the following applies].
If, however, the evening oblation has already been offered to Sūrya, the rite must be performed again once the [new] fortnight has been accepted. || 86 ||
At that very moment this mind would arise; it could not exist otherwise if, prior to the sacrifice, it were known that the single portion had not been taken. (87)
One should offer two oblations with the two mantras "tvaṃ naḥ" and "sa tvaṃ naḥ";
having taken the portion to be offered, one should perform that sacrifice as prescribed.
If, however, it is realized after the sacrifice that [an error occurred], then only two oblations should be offered;
in that case, the wise should not perform the sacrifice again.
Now I shall describe the defects of the oblation (havis) by which the oblation becomes defiled:
it is impure when blue flies are present upon the body of the horse. (90)
The *kuśātikā* dwells on the limbs of cattle, while the bedbug (*matkuṇa*) resides in beds and the like;
the louse (*yūkā*) is found on clothes and the head, and the *kīṭa* insect forms a mass of filth. (91)
A cat, a mongoose, a rat, excrement, a crow, a cock, a dog, a monkey, the hem of a garment, and cut-off hair and nails. (92)
Even the loathsome nail residing within the body is impure, as are substances with a putrid odor and the insect known as the wood-worm. (93)
Experts should know that *drapsa* refers to sweat, tears, blood, oiliness, coughing, sneezing, and likewise, the drops produced from the nose or the mouth. (94)
Sweat is the water born of the body, for tears are said to be born of the eyes.
Asṛj is to be known as blood; sneha is remembered as the impurity of the nose. || 95 ||
Cough is a disorder of phlegm that issues forth from the mouth and other parts;
it is called *kṣavathu* or *kṣuta*, according to the sage named Gopāla. (96)
If one is touched by urine, marrow, fat, semen, earwax, pus, or likewise by other such impurities as these; || 97 ||
A woman in her courses or one who has recently given birth, a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, and so forth—a child, a sacrificer, a pregnant Brāhmaṇa, and a king—these [are exempt from impurity]. 98.
Those who destroy this [knowledge] are considered by the wise to be slayers of an embryo (bhrūṇahan). Whatever may be touched or seen by these and other most sinful persons— || 99 ||
Where a woman gives birth, where one dies or is cremated, where a Caṇḍāla dwells, or wherever there is contact with excrement and the like. || 100 ||
Whatever is placed in that impure place also becomes defiled;
if the sacrificial offering (havis) should become defiled prior to the principal sacrifice, then [the following applies]. || 1 ||
Then, one should cast that oblation into pure water with the hand;
likewise, one should offer the two *minda* oblations and perform all the expiations and so forth.
Furthermore, having produced exactly that much sacrificial material again, the sacrifice should be performed in due order;
however, if one is utterly unable, one should perform the sacrifice with clarified butter alone.
If the offering is spoiled after the sacrifice has begun, one should complete the remainder with clarified butter alone;
if the sacrifice was performed with a spoiled oblation, then one should offer [an expiation]. || 4 ||
One should offer two oblations with the *sruva* ladle using the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*;
according to the tradition of the sage Kātyāyana, there is no need for a further sacrifice here.
When one recognizes the fault in taking up the sacrificial portion (avadāna), then one should cast all that defiled oblation into pure water. || 6 ||
Having again prepared the oblation, you— being that very person for us—
should offer the oblations to us and perform the sacrifice with it, as well as the recitation of mantras and other rites not previously known.
If that which was cut and taken from the middle or the eastern half has fallen into a defect,
one should discard it into pure water and then [cut] again from the middle or the eastern half.
Having cut off [the portion], one should perform the sacrifice; thereafter, the rites such as the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta) follow.
This refers to the destruction of the substance for the principal sacrifice occurring prior to the principal offering itself.
If it should be known that [the offering] has been lost at that very moment within that same tantra, one should produce a replacement oblation and perform the sacrifice with it. || 110 ||
If, in a sacrifice involving many oblations,
there should be the loss or the defilement by some fault of all the oblations, one should perform the rite again after enumerating the deities.
Having sacrificed with clarified butter alone, one should repeat the entire sacrifice again,
even if [the offering] has been defiled by unavoidable minor impurities such as flies, insects, and the like.
If the sacrificial oblation should come into contact with five or more living beings, such as ants and the like, then it should be known that the offering is defective.
If [the breaths] are deficient, one should extract the fallen vital airs (jīvas), sprinkle them with water, and purify them with the two common purifiers; by this, their fitness is restored.
Having completed that rite which was begun with the mind fixed upon food cooked with sacrificial offerings (haviṣya),
he should cook four śarāvas of well-boiled rice.
He should feed four virtuous and pure Brahmins with that;
among them, one should be a descendant of Bhṛgu (Bhārgava), and the boons should be given to them equally.
When that [offering] has been entirely burnt, one should produce the oblation again;
that very same sacrifice must be performed, for another sacrifice is not required. (17)
If the oblation is very small or if it is not burnt, then one should perform an expiation that names all [the deities], and thereafter complete the sacrifice with what remains.
One should complete [the rite] with clarified butter; no further sacrifice is required.
Now, the expiation for the spilling of the oblation will be explained. (19)
If there is an overflow in the eastern direction, there should be an oblation with "Svāhā to Agni";
in the southern direction, "to Yama," and in the western direction, "to Varuṇa."

The offering to Soma should be made in the northern direction; if it is for all [deities] in all directions, then if the oblation is in the intermediate directions, it should be performed with the Vyāhṛtis.
In all these [offerings], because they are *homās*, there should be the utterance of *svāhā* at the end;
and with the mantra "āpyāyasva" and the word "samit," one should cause the oblation to swell with clarified butter (*ājya*).
One should offer two *minda* oblations, as well as all the expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth,
if a solar eclipse should occur between the commencement of the sacrifice (*yāga*) and the ritual preparation (*anvādhāna*).
One should offer three principal oblations with the three verses "ud vayaṃ tamasaspari," "ud u tyam," and "citram," indeed prior to the main offering.
By some, even the ritual worship (upasthāna) here is proclaimed by means of three mantras.
If there is an eclipse of the moon in the middle [of the rite], two oblations are offered before the principal [offering].
At that time, one should offer oblations with these two [verses], "navo navo yaḥ" and "ādityāḥ";
by some, the ritual attendance (upasthāna) here is also proclaimed to be performed with this pair of mantras.
However, no expiation is required for the omission of the *anvādhāna* rite;
in the event of breaking a vessel made of wood, one should simply procure another.
Then, one should strike the broken staff, ignited in the domestic fire (gṛhyāgni), which was previously [prepared];
for a rite to be accomplished by the common fire (laukikānala), it should be done in the common fire.
If a vessel made of wood breaks, its disposal should be as previously described;
if one made of clay should break, [one should recite] "The earth has gone to the earth. (29)
If the vessel consecrated with the Brahma-mantra is broken, one should cast it into pure water after consecrating it with one's own mantra; for that purpose, one should employ another vessel.
Others, however, say that this rite should be performed at all times;
for whatever vessel-breakage occurs, there should be an oblation of clarified butter with the syllable *praṇava*.
Alternatively, one should offer oblations with all the vyāhṛtis at the side of the sacrificial altar;
prior to the placing of the clarified butter, there may be the destruction of the consecrated fire (nirūḍhāgni).
If [the enema] should remain, then one should again perform a nirūhaṇa from that position;
thereafter, an oblation with the Manasvatī verse should be made using four portions of ghee.

If the fire of one who has performed the *nirūḍha* sacrifice should go out after the removal of the clarified butter (*ājya*), the *manasvatī* verse alone must be offered; however, the *nirūhaṇa* rite is not to be performed there.

If the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation is offered together with the principal oblations, then the mental recitation (*citta*) called "all-encompassing" (*sarvābhidha*), as well as the recitation of the *anājñāta* verses and so forth, [should be performed]. 135.
If, after the anvādhāna, there should occur an emission of semen by the patron or the officiating priests in a dream,
then [they should offer] the two oblations with the mantras "imaṃ me" and "tattvā yāmi."
Having offered one oblation with the *vyāhṛtis*, he should then worship the Sun;
furthermore, he should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *māmanuvāka* three times or once.
If the emission [of semen] was intentional, then it is superior to the Vrātapata rite;
a Sthālīpāka sacrifice should be performed, or else a Pūrṇāhuti.
If there is an occasional cessation while some *prārabdha* karma remains, one should always offer the mind—which bears all names—into the fire and complete what is left over. (39)

If, during the performance of a ritual, there should occur [an obstacle] among quadrupeds or bipeds, or among the officiating priests, or between the sacrificial fire and the priests, or even between the master of the sacrifice and his wife; 140.
If, however, there should be sexual intercourse between the husband and the wife,
then one should offer the *gaṇa* sacrifice known as *mindādi* or *durgādi*.
Having taken clarified butter twelve times with a ladle or a sruk-spoon,
five oblations should be offered with it during the homa for the group of deities beginning with Durgā.
If one is unable to perform this, one should offer the *sarvacittaka* oblation,
as well as two *mindā* oblations, followed by the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the *praṇava*.
The Vāruṇīs, the Tantumatīs, the Ānūkhyā, and the Manasvatī;
the seven Mahāvyāhṛtis and that of Prajāpati. || 44 ||
This collection of mantras is known as the *mid-ādi* group;
the first is *jātavedase*, and the second is *manojyotiḥ*. (45)
The three Mahāvyāhṛtis and this group beginning with Durgā—these are the deities. If one who has maintained the sacred fires intends to depart, he should then offer oblations.
Having offered an oblation with the mantra "To you," he should then deposit the fire either into the two kindling woods or upon a fuel-stick;
then, wherever he intends to dwell, he should perform the churning of the fire there.
Having performed [the rite] with the *upāvaroha* mantra, one should complete the ritual.
If, due to negligence or other causes, the sacrifice is not performed after the *anvādhāna*, [one should proceed as follows].
There shall be four oblations, both individually and collectively;
the substance for the aupāsana oblation may be either solid or liquid.
Having consecrated it with these two [mantras],
"skandadaskāndyaudaskān" and "unnambhaya," one should then pour water over it.
Having performed the *anājñāta* recitation and having composed all his thoughts,
he should collect the spilled substance after going toward the northern direction.
One should open the clean opening of an anthill and, having touched pure water with the right hand, [proceed]. (52)
Having gathered all that has fallen, he should cast it into that hole with the ṛc verse beginning "prajāpate," and then he should stand over it with the word "bhūḥ" while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Due to the absence of an injunction for the *juhoti* offering, there should be no utterance of *svāhā* over the fire;
one should perform the oblation again, beginning with the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as before.
Whether the substance for the *aupāsana* oblation be solid or liquid,
if an impure insect should fall into it while one is preparing the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), [the following applies].
Then, in that case, one should perform the expiation as before;
for the taking [of the water] there may be done with either the last or the middle [finger]. (56)
With a leaf of the *palāśa* tree and the verse "The great heaven,
the earth," one should discard that purification of the vessel in the space inside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Thereafter, one should perform the appropriate rite; everything else, however, is as before.
If, during the oblation in the aupāsana fire with milk, there should be an overflow from the cooking pot (sthālī), [the following should be done].
One should consecrate [the medicine] with this mantra: "The embryo-dropping remedy.
Then, nine nāḍīs after sunset are declared to be the time for the fire-oblation (homa).
Upon transgressing that, one should offer an oblation with the mantra beginning "doṣe.
Varuṇa is proclaimed to be the deity of this oblation. (160)
One should perform the ritual actions as they were previously established, up until the placing of the fuel sticks;
one should restrain the breath according to one's strength and then offer the boon.
Having recited all the vyāhṛtis, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (homa);
having performed the worship with the vyāhṛtis and completed the remainder of the oblation.
An oblation (caru) for Varuṇa should be prepared, or alternatively, a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
the time for the morning homa is twelve or ten ghaṭīs.
The *saṃgava* period is declared by the wise to consist of exactly one *prahara*;
if this is exceeded, an oblation should be made with the mantra "prātar. (64)
The deity of this oblation is traditionally held to be either the god Mitra or Sūrya;
and prior to the placing of the fuel-sticks, one should restrain the breath according to one's strength. (165)
One should perform the granting of boons as well as the recitation of the *vyāhṛtis*;
likewise, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) and the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) with the *vyāhṛtis*.
Having completed the remainder of the *homa*, the *caru* offerings for Mitra and Sūrya are prescribed;
now I shall describe the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the interruption of the *homa*.
If the interruption occurs before three nights have passed, the *ayāścāgah* oblation should be performed;
if it occurs before seven nights have passed, there should be a second oblation with the *manasvatī* verse.
If [the fire] is extinguished before twelve days have passed, it should be rekindled by means of the *tantumatī* [verse];
even in that case, if there is an interruption of the *homa*, there must indeed be a re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*).
One should perform these oblations after careful consideration during a great calamity;
however, this rule is not applicable if such a calamity occurs after [the initial period]. || 170 ||

Even though the *khaṇḍa* (the prohibitory injunction) is sublated, because it is in fact more powerful, the mind would indeed be directed toward the Vedic [rite], and there would be no [need for] the *nāyī* and so forth. (71)
For that [method] is weak because it is taught in other scriptures; it is not appropriate here.
Now, the Śrauta-citta will be clearly explained. (72)
In the event of the omission of two, three, or even one oblation,
one should immediately thereafter offer the Saptahotṛ and Manasvatī oblations.
Others have declared that one should not perform the *homa* once it has been passed;
in the same manner, one should perform the morning *aupāsana-homa*. (74)
Some ancient wise men have said that there is indeed a transgression regarding one [of the days] from the fourth up to the sixth; however, others say it concerns those ending with the seventh. (175)
A caru offering for Tantumatī should be made for two, three, or all [the deceased];
even in the case of the eighth and subsequent [anniversary rites], it should be a caru for Tantumatī alone.
If one should pass beyond this time, there must be another offering;
according to the Śruti, it may be after one day, or indeed after two days.
It has been stated that in the event of a lapse in the fire-oblation (homa), no mental distress should arise;
for if one should offer the oblation at the wrong time due to the subsiding of confusion, [no fault occurs]. 78.
Then, the fire sacrifice (homa), complete with its constituent parts, must be performed again in that very same fire.
Since it has already been produced, there is no need for its manifestation here again.
After the oblation, there should be the ritual attendance upon the fire;
likewise, this very expiation is proclaimed for when such an error has arisen. (180)
After the fire has been produced but before the oblation is offered, the owner should perform [the rite];
if the consumption [of the remnant] is to occur before the offering, it should then be done in that very same fire.
One should perform the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice for the *Vrātapati*, or there may be two oblations;
"yatte vayam" and "yathā heti" are proclaimed as the two mantras for the *homa*.
Or he should place two fuel-sticks upon the fire, or otherwise recite these [mantras];
this very same expiation is proclaimed for the wife as well. (83)
If the morning oblation cannot be performed due to extreme difficulty,
then on that day the master shall not take his meal.
However, after the evening oblation, one should not take food during that night;
by this much alone the oblation is accomplished, and no expiation is required.
If Skanda should appear above the eastern oblation or the northern oblation,
then one should offer into the fire with the verse beginning "yatra" (RV 10.87.22), which is addressed to the Vanaspati.
One should subsequently place a fuel-stick with the remainder of what was spilled;
having offered an oblation silently, one should complete the entire remainder of the fire-sacrifice.

Then one should perform the homa again; this same rule applies even for the consecratory homa (abhihoma). However, it does not apply if there is sufficient material present for the subsequent oblation.
If a drop of rain should fall upon the substance for the *aupāsana* oblation,
one should set down the sacrificial offering (*havis*) on the grass-bundle (*kūrca*) and perform the offering of the original fuel-stick (*samid*).
Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should then mutter the vyāhṛtis with that very same oblation;
the first offering is made with the verse, "Mitra ordains the people. (190)
Then one should perform the remainder of the oblation, beginning with the northern oblation (uttarāhuti).
Thereafter, one should again perform the oblation starting from the formal resolve (saṃkalpa). || 91 ||

If the time for the manifestation [of the fire] is exceeded, it shall consist of all the mental offerings; this applies if there is a forgetfulness regarding the second oblation during the *aupāsana* sacrifice. (92)

If the lapse of the rite occurs before its completion, that omitted oblation (antaritā-āhuti) must be offered; however, if the lapse is remembered only after the completion, one should simply perform the entire rite again, and there is no need for an oblation.
If the first oblation is forgotten, one should perform the entire homa again;
likewise, if there is no commencement of the initial aupāsana oblation at its proper time.
Then, on the following day at evening, there should likewise be the oblation of the Saptahotr;
the second [oblation] should be with the Manasvatī mantra, and then one should commence the fire-offering (homa).
The Saptahotṛ-homa is prescribed to be performed at the conclusion of the Piṇḍayajña;
when proceeding to the Aupāsana fire, the rites beginning with the smearing [of the ground] are as before.

Having fetched fire from the house of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya) and established the consumer of oblations (havirbhuj), if it is for a marriage, then the fire should be produced by friction (nirmanthya). || 97 ||
From this point until the time of the oblation, neither the woman nor the householder shall eat;
however, another rule is now stated for those unable to observe the fast.
The rites beginning with the smearing [of the altar] and ending with the placement of the fire are as before;
having brought forth the vessels, one should perform the purification (pavitraka) as previously described.
Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he should then sprinkle the vessels;
then, having cleansed and consecrated the ladle (*darvī*), he should prepare the clarified butter (*ājya*) according to the previously stated procedure.
Having strewn [fuel] around the fire, one should thereafter perform the sprinkling;
likewise, one should provide ornaments, the placing of fuel, and the offering of sacrificial wood.
Having offered the oblation with the mantra "ayāścāgne" and having discarded the sacrificial grass mats,
he should then perform the final sprinkling and regularly carry out the daily fire sacrifice.
But if, while the [fire] has been set aside and the primary fire is moving, [the primary fire] goes to a portion of the set-aside fire within the location of the primary fire; || 3 ||

Having concentrated the entire mind, one should offer the oblation of the earth (bhuva-āhuti) in rites for pacification and nourishment, as well as in those domestic rituals not explicitly mentioned [in the scriptures].
If there should be a following of the fire, one should cast that ash outside;
immediately thereafter, the smearing, drawing of lines, and other rites for the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be performed.
Having prepared and established the fire there, one should perform the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya);
with that, once the fire has been established, one should offer oblations for the sake of the so-called "all-encompassing" mind (sarvākhyacitta).
Some wise ones have declared that "ayāśca" should also be offered as an oblation; others consider that "ayā" [is used] specifically when the *aupāsana* fire has gone out.
According to this view, this [attainment] would not occur during the stages such as *upanaya*;
rather, in these stages as well, it should be understood that it is indeed the mind alone that is designated by all these names. (8)
If the fire is extinguished after the instruction in the Gāyatrī mantra and before the homa facing east during the initiation ceremony, one should re-establish the fire as previously described.
Having offered the principal oblations there, one should offer the *sarvacittaka*;
according to the subsequent instruction, upon its destruction, it becomes merely the name of everything.
If the fire is extinguished before the taking of hands during the marriage ceremony, then one should simply perform the principal oblations (mukhyāhuti) and so forth; this is the settled rule.
Beyond this, however, this same [purification] applies to everything in both cases;
but in the case of contact with a corpse, a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, an outcast, and so forth, [the rule is as follows].
If there is contact with other fires, there should be a re-establishment of the sacred fires;
however, in reality, when there is contact with other fires, only the Vaiśvadeva caru offering is required.
However, because the *khaṇḍa* section is an insertion (*kṣepaka*), there is no re-establishment (*punarāhiti*) here;
rather, this [re-establishment] occurs only through contact with the pressing of the Soma and so forth, due to the scriptural extension (*śrautātideśa*). (14)
When two domestic fires come into contact,
both owners of the domestic fires should take fuel-sticks and together place the combined fire upon them.
Having superimposed that worldly fire [upon the conceptual fire] by means of the mantra,
he should then divide it into two within the fire with the mantra beginning "ācchā giraḥ."
Each person should offer their own respective fuel-stick according to the mantra;
he should then cast it [into the fire], for the cooking of both shall be performed by the Vaiśvadeva fire.
If a portion of the fire has gone out separately and then comes into contact with either a common (laukika) fire or a Vedic (śrauta) fire, then it would no longer be distinct.
However, setting aside that single portion, one should offer the entire *cittaka*;
thus it has been stated by the two, Śatadvayīkṛt and Varadarāja. (19)
If there is contact with the fire of a forest conflagration, the *caru* should be prepared on a bed of leaves;
if the contact is with the fire of a corpse, then the *caru* should be for the sake of purification.
In the event of contact with the fire of a woman who has recently given birth, there should be a *sāṃkusuka* oblation;
in the event of contact with lightning fire, there should be an *āpsumat* oblation. || 21 ||

In the case of the five cooked items, such as rice and so forth, even though there exists a sequence based on their causal factors, the sequence should be understood as that which is prescribed by the scriptural injunction. || 22 ||
Vivici, Śuci, then Vratavṛt, Āpsumat, and then Saṃkusuka;
such is the sequence there, indeed, in this very order.
In a combination [of causes], this [result] would indeed occur even for one who is emaciated;
however, in cases such as the fourfold [causes], there may be an impossibility of a particular causal factor.
Having omitted only that much, the other sequence should proceed as before;
however, in the event of the omission of the *sthālīpāka*, there should be a *caru* offering dedicated to Pāthikṛt.
Upon the lapse of two [periods], one should perform the Vaiśvānara and Pāthikṛt offerings as two *caru* oblations;
however, upon the lapse of the third and subsequent periods, there shall be a re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādhāna*) therein.
But if a fragment [of the offering] falls outside while being cast, the procedure shall be that of the Śrauta ritual; that will now be explained.
If the two *sthālīpākas* for the new and full moon sacrifices have been omitted,
then one should perform the *pāthikṛta* *sthālīpāka*.
If these two [fires] have not been established, or if they have both passed away,
then the wise man should indeed perform the Vaiśvānara sthālīpāka.
If there is a failure in the performance following the initial resolution of the first ritual application,
then three *caru* oblations must be performed as a remedy for that cause of deviation.
The procedure for the preparation of the *sthālīpāka* is now demonstrated;
if there is a secondary time for the rite, its performance should also take place then. (31)
Now I shall describe another alternative regarding this premature falling away:
if there should be a falling away from two rites that have already been commenced, then the *pāthikṛt* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) must be performed.
If there is a lapse even regarding the two subsequent [offerings], then a Vaiśvānara caru is required;
likewise, if there is a failure to commence both sthālīpākas at their proper time, [the same penance applies].
Then, for the sake of averting failure, the wise should perform three *sthālīpāka* offerings;
however, if there is a lapse of the vow on the festival day (*parvan*), one should offer a *caru* to Vātāpati.
If tears fall due to distress on a festival day (parvan), one should offer a caru-oblation for the maintenance of the host;
if the purifier (pavitra) is destroyed, there should be a caru-oblation for the vow of the purifier.
Upon the loss of gold, however, there should be an oblation of cooked rice (caru) to Hiraṇyavān;
but upon the burning of one's own house, one should perform an oblation of cooked rice to Kāmavān.

One should perform the domestic fire sacrifice (aupāsana), the new-moon oblation (darśasthālīpāka), and so forth; likewise, if one has not bathed in the morning, one should offer the Vāruṇa caru-oblation.
If the officiating priest should be well-bathed, or if he himself should be unbathed, even then the Vāruṇa rite must be performed; however, this [Vāruṇa] is not for one who is extremely ill.

This should be understood as being for the morning alone; at evening, it would pertain to all types of consciousness. Upon eating food from a birth-impurity (sūtaka), there shall be a sacrificial oblation (caru) according to the Tantramata.
If the wife gives birth to twins, or if it is a cow, then there should be an oblation of caru for Māruta;
this applies whether two males are born as twins, or even if only one among them is male. (240)
Some wise ones have declared that [the fire] is Vaiśvānara and Māruta;
such forms are described in the Sūtra, and thus the procedure for the Ādbhuta rite is also mentioned in the Gṛhya texts. (41)
In this context, that [fire] should indeed be included in the domestic (aupāsana) rite;
for Kātyāyana and others have indeed declared its marvelous nature as well.

This *sthālīpāka* is indeed for one who has accepted the injunction "for one who has established the sacred fires" (*ya āhitāgniḥ*); however, if this [injunction] is not accepted, this [rite] does not take place. (43)
In this ritual procedure, one should perform exactly the rite prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras;
when a cow that has calved an even number of times belongs to a Snātaka, [the offering] should be made in the common fire.
Then he should perform the *sthālīpāka* and the domestic (*gārhya*) rite;
or rather, the *sthālīpāka* may consist merely of the procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. || 45 ||
Such is the rule proclaimed for a student (varnī) even when his teacher has died;
some, however, have stated that the rule prescribed by Kātyāyana applies here as well.
Other wise men have declared that all [the sons] should perform this rite;
even if one of them has died, there too [the ritual is performed], for the vital breath (māruta) resides in him as well.

For one who has maintained the sacred fires, there shall be the *iṣṭi* sacrifice; thus, according to the rule stated by Kātyāyana, there may be an option regarding the performance of these sacrifices as appropriate.
Upon hearing the word "dead," one's own *saurabha* oblation becomes subject to the rule;
likewise, if one should eat fresh food without having first performed the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice. (49)
One should prepare a sacrificial oblation (caru) dedicated to the deity named Vaiśvānara;
however, even when accepting a gift from one who is not a Brahmin, gold is the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in this case.
If one should eat the food of an enemy, then this fire would also become possessed of those qualities; for these qualities are said to be distinguished according to the food consumed. || 51 ||
If the *sthālīpāka* has been missed and one performs the sacrifice oneself in another fire,
or if another person performs the sacrifice in one's own fire, there should be a *caru* offering to Agni and Viṣṇu.
This oblation (caru) is prescribed specifically for the primary subsequent consciousness;
furthermore, the wise man should perform the pot-cooking (sthālīpāka) on a day that is not prohibited.

If, having previously abandoned that [ordinary] mind consisting of all conceptual thought, one offers the oblation, then only this [transcendental] mind is to be offered as the sacrificial pap (caru), and not the [ordinary] caru.
Regarding this as well, the teachers state that there should be a repetition of the rite for the *sthālīpāka*;
or rather, in all these cases, a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) should be performed.
But when the cooking of the sacrificial pot has not yet begun, this [observance] is declared to be mandatory. || 56 ||
Thus, the expiations have been stated in brief.
Now, the statement of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details for the mantras of the expiations follows;
the mantras of the expiations as recorded in the *Kārikās*, together with their seers and so forth, are now being declared:

For the three mantras beginning with *anājñātam*, the Viśvedevas are the seers (*ṛṣi*), Agni is the deity (*devatā*); the first and second are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and the third is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation (*japa*) for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). "Oṃ *anājñātaṃ yad...* [omitted] ...*yajāmi*. For the mantra *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, Soma-Viṣṇu is the deity and the *gāyatrī* is the meter. Its application is for recitation for the purpose of expiation: "Oṃ *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ...* [omitted] ...*sure*."

Prajāpati is the deity of all the *vyāhṛtis*, and Prajāpati is the *bṛhatī* meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the recitation intended as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*): "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. For the verse beginning with "ābhir gīrbhiḥ," the deities are the Viśvedevas and Indra accompanied by the Haris; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. Its application is for the *ājya* oblation in expiation caused by the omission of vowels, syllables, and so forth: "Oṃ ābhir gīrbhir ya0 te syāma svāhā. [The offering is] for Indra accompanied by the Haris. This belongs to him.

In these two mantras, *tvaṃ no agne* and *sa tvaṃ no agne*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), Agni, and Varuṇa; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for the expiatory *ājya* oblation (*prāyaścittājyahoma*) occasioned by the omission of a mantra, the omission of a specific rite, or an inversion [of the ritual order]: *Oṃ tvaṃ no a0 smat svāhā*—to Agni and Varuṇa, this [oblation]. *Oṃ sa tvaṃ no0 edhi svāhā*—to Agni and Varuṇa, this [oblation]. In the mantra *tvamagne ayāsi*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), the deity is Ayāgni, and the meter is *anuṣṭubh*.

For the verse beginning with *prajāpate*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Prajāpati; the meter is Triṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the expiatory *ājya* oblation caused by the burning of the sacrificial grass strewn around the fire (*paristaraṇa*). *Oṃ tvamagne a0 ṣaja svāhā*. To Agni Ayasas, this [is offered]. *Oṃ prajāpate0 ṇā svāhā*. To Prajāpati, this [is offered]. However, in the case of the burning of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and so forth, there is a modification (*ūha*) of the words according to the specific object in the application formula. In cases such as cutting and so forth, there is a modification of the word "burning" (*dāha*) to the word "cutting" (*chedana*) and so forth. For the verse beginning with *yatpākatre*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Agni; the meter is Triṣṭubh.

The application (*viniyoga*) for the *ājya* oblation as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) caused by the deficiency of fuel-sticks (*idhma-samit*) is: "Oṃ yatpākatrā... jāti svāhā. [Dedication: "To Agni, this... The application for the *ājya* oblation as an expiation caused by the excess of fuel-sticks is: "Thus is the statement of application for the *ājya* oblation as an expiation for the excess of fuel-sticks. For all the *vyāhṛtis*, Prajāpati is the seer and Prajāpati is the meter (*bṛhatī*).

The application (*viniyoga*) for the *ājya* oblation as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) caused by the falling of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*): "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā. [This is] for Prajāpati. The same applies to the falling of the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and so forth. For the mantra "punastvā," the deities are Agni, Ādityas, Rudras, Vasus, and Brahmā; the metre is Triṣṭubh. Or, for the mantra "punastvā," the deities are Agni, Vasunītha, and Agni; the metre is Triṣṭubh. This is the application for placing the fuel-stick (*samidh*) as an expiation caused by damage to the fire.
This is the application for the *ājya* oblation as an expiation caused by damage to the fire; thus [ends] the section on oblations.

"Oṃ punastvādityāḥ... kāmāḥ svāhā. This is for the Ādityas, Rudras, Vasus, and Brahmas. Or alternatively: "This is for Agni, the leader of the Vasus. Regarding the two [mantras] beginning with "uddīpyasva" and "mā no hi sīḥ," the deities are those of the sacrificial tradition (*yājñikya*), the secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*), Jātavedas, and Agni; the meter is Anuṣṭubh. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of performing the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when the fire goes out by itself, during the placing of two fuel-sticks (*samidh*): "Oṃ uddīpyasva jātavedo... diśa" and "mā no hi sīḥ... pātaya."

For the three mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the deities are Agni and the Viśvedevas, and the metre is Gāyatrī. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for filling the *praṇītā* vessel when it has been spilled; their application is for filling the *prokṣaṇī* vessel when it has been spilled; their application is for filling a vessel that has become empty through evaporation—this refers to evaporation; and their application is for filling a vessel that has become empty through leakage—this refers to leakage.

"Oṃ āpo hi ṣṭha... and "tataṃ ma āpaḥ. For the verse "tataṃ ma āpaḥ," the deities are the Viśvedevas and the Ṛbhus; the meter is Jagatī; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the *ājya* oblation for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) caused by the spilling of the *praṇītā* water, and in the *ājya* oblation for the expiation caused by the spilling of the *prokṣaṇī* water. [It is also applied] in the expiation caused by the drying up of the *praṇītā*, in the expiation caused by the leaking of the *praṇītā*, in the expiation caused by the drying up of the *prokṣaṇī*, and in the *ājya* oblation for the expiation caused by the leaking of the *prokṣaṇī*. "Oṃ tataṃ ma āpaḥ... ṛbhūṇāṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā. This is for the Ṛbhus.

Prajāpati is the seer of all the *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the *bṛhatī* meter. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for the re-placement of the fire that has slipped outside its abode into its own proper place. Alternatively, their application is for the *ājya* oblation as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the fire being carried outside unknowingly; thus the statement of application is according to the specific case. For the five Vedic mantras beginning with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and "devān," Vāmadeva is the seer. The deities are, in order: the gods (*devāḥ*), the *gandharvas*, the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*), the waters (*āpaḥ*), and the plants and trees (*oṣadhayo vanaspatayaḥ*), known as the five peoples (*pañcajanāḥ*). They are *yajus* formulas. Their application is for the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of what has been spilled.

"The gods have eaten this oblation; may the blessing of the sacrifice come to me from that; may it increase! The Gandharvas have eaten this oblation... may it increase! The ancestors have eaten this oblation... may it increase! The waters, the plants, and the trees have eaten this oblation... may it increase! The five peoples have eaten this oblation... may it increase!"

The seer (*ṛṣi*) of these four mantras beginning with *bhūpataye* is Vāmadeva; for the first three, Agni is also an option. The deities (*devatā*) are, respectively: Bhūpati, Bhuvanapati, Bhūtānāṃ pati, and Bhūta. They are Yajus formulas. For the entire set of *vyāhṛtis*, Prajāpati is the seer and Prajāpati is the deity; the meter is Bṛhatī. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the rite of making the *prādeśa* gesture:
"Oṃ bhūpataye svāhā, bhuvanapataye svāhā, bhūtānāṃ pataye svāhā, bhūtāya svāhā, bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā."

For the mantra beginning with *saṃ tvā siñcāmi*, Prajāpati is the seer, the spilled oblation (*skanna-havis*) is the deity, and the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is for sprinkling water over what has been spilled. For the Sautra mantra beginning with *yajñasya tvā*, Vāmadeva is the seer, the spilled oblation is the deity, and the *yajus* is the meter; its application is for placing the spilled oblation back in its own place. However, according to the ritual procedure for consecration (*abhimantraṇa-kalpa*), the statement of application is: "its application is for the consecration of what has been spilled."

"Oṃ, with the *pramaya*, *abhimaya*, *vimaya*, and *unmaya* of the sacrifice, I enclose you. For this *sautra* mantra beginning with "mā yajamāna," Vāmadeva is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the *yajus* is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the re-offering into the fire of an oblation that has spilled outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). "Oṃ, may the sacrificer not [be harmed]... svāhā. [The formula is: "To Agni, this... Or, according to some, the meaning of the word *juhuyāt* (he should offer) is merely the act of throwing [the oblation]. In this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), there is no formal renunciation (*tyāga*). The satisfaction of the brothers of Agni occurs simply by the falling [of the oblation] outside the enclosing sticks.

For the verse *yad vo devāḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas; the meter is Triṣṭubh.
