Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the *ājya-homa* expiation for the occasion of failing to assign the deity [to the offering]. "Oṃ yad vo devā a... dhetana svāhā. To the Devas, this [offering]. For the verse *manojyotiḥ*, known as *Manasvatī*, Agni is the deity, the meter is Triṣṭubh. Its application is in the *ājya-homa* expiation for the occasion of the reversal of the *svāhā*-utterance during the offering. "Oṃ manojyotir ju... ghṛtena svāhā. To Manas and Jyotis, this [offering].

In these two [verses], *tvaṃ no agne* and *sa tvaṃ no agne*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), Agni, and Varuṇa; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the *ājya-homa* expiation (*prāyaścitta*) caused by the transposition of the portions cut off (*avadāna*). "Oṃ *tvaṃ no a0 smat svāhā*" — to Agni and Varuṇa, this [is offered]. "Oṃ *sa tvaṃ no 0 edhi svāhā*" — to Agni and Varuṇa, this [is offered]. The same applies by modification (*ūha*) in the case of transpositions involving the substance, the renunciation, the deity, or the mantra.

The phrase "the application [is] in the *ājya*-oblation for the expiation caused by the non-production of the primary substance" constitutes the statement regarding the application of the *ājya*-oblation for the expiation caused by the non-production of the primary substance. Regarding the two verses beginning with *yan ma ātmanaḥ* and *punar agnim*, Soma is the seer (*ṛṣi*). For the first verse, Agni Mindvit is the deity; for the second, Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and the Aśvins are the deities. For the first verse, the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī; for the second, it is Anuṣṭubh.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the *ājya* oblation as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) caused by defects in the sacrificial offering (*havirdoṣa*). "Oṃ yanma ācarṣaṇiḥ svāhā. This is for Agni Jātavedas accompanied by the Mind (*minda*); [the dedication is]: "This for Agni... "Oṃ punaragniḥ... makṣyoḥ svāhā. This is for Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and the two Aśvins; [the dedication is]: "This for... For the mantras beginning with "Agnaye svāhā," Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*). The deities (*devatā*) are, in order: Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma. They are in the form of *yajus* verses. For the collective *vyāhṛtis*, Prajāpati is the seer and Prajāpati is the meter (*bṛhatī*).

The application (*viniyoga*) for the *ājya* oblation as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) caused by the spilling of the sacrificial ladle (*carūtsēka*): "Oṃ agnaye svāhā"—to Agni this [is offered]. "Oṃ yamāya svāhā"—to Yama this [is offered]. "Oṃ varuṇāya svāhā"—to Varuṇa this [is offered]. "Oṃ somāya svāhā"—to Soma this [is offered]. "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā"—to Prajāpati this [is offered]. Regarding the two [verses] beginning with *āpyāyasva* and *saṃ te payāṃsi*: Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Soma is the deity (*devatā*). The meter (*chandas*) of the first is *gāyatrī*, and that of the second is *triṣṭubh*.

The application for the swelling of the overflowing oblation is: "Oṃ āpyāyasva... gathe" and "Oṃ saṃ te payāṃsi... dhiṣva. Regarding the two mantras beginning with "yanma ātmanaḥ" and "punaragniḥ," Soma is the seer (ṛṣi). For the first mantra, the deity is Agni accompanied by Mind; for the second, the deities are Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and the Aśvins. The meter of the first is Gāyatrī, and that of the second is Anuṣṭubh.

The application (*viniyoga*) for the *ājya* oblation as an expiation caused by the spilling of the sacrificial offering (*havirutseda*) is as follows: "Oṃ yanma ātma... svāhā. This is for Agni Jātavedas who possesses the *mindava* [offering]; [the dedication is]: "To this Agni... "Oṃ punara0 kṣyoḥ svāhā. This is for Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and the two Aśvins; [the dedication is]: "To these... Regarding the verse "udvayaṃ tamasaḥ": Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sūrya is the deity, and the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. Regarding the two verses "udu tyam" and "citram": Soma is the seer, Sūrya is the deity; the meter of the first is *gāyatrī*, and that of the second is *triṣṭubh*.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the *ājya* oblation of the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by a solar eclipse occurring during the preparation of the sacrificial materials (*yāgānvādhāna*). Regarding the application for the worship of the Sun (*sūryopasthāna*) for the sake of the expiatory rite occasioned by a solar eclipse occurring during the preparation of the sacrificial materials, the distinction lies in the statement of the application for the worship: "Oṃ *udvayaṃ tamasaspari...* [RV 1.50.10] ... *svāhā*. To the Sun, this [oblation]. "*Udu tyaṃ jātavedasaṃ...* [RV 1.50.1] ... *sūryaṃ svāhā*. To the Sun, this [oblation]. "Oṃ *citraṃ devānām...* [RV 1.115.1] ... *paśya svāhā*. To the Sun, this [oblation]."

(udvayaṃ0, udu tyaṃ0, citraṃ0), *navo navo*, and *yamādityāḥ*—in these [mantras], the Viśvedevas and Candra are the deities; the metre is Triṣṭubh. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the *ājya-homa* performed as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) caused by a lunar eclipse occurring during the *yāgānvādhāna*. The distinction in the statement regarding the application for the worship (*upasthāna*) is that their application is for the purpose of worshipping the Moon as an expiation caused by a lunar eclipse occurring during the *yāgānvādhāna*: "navo navo bha0 māyuḥ svāhā"—this is for Candra. "oṃ yamādityā a0 gopāḥ svāhā"—this is for Candra.

For the Sautra mantra *bhūmirbhūmim*, Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Bhūmi is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of a broken earthen vessel: "Oṃ, the earth has gone to the earth; the mother has gone to the mother. May we prosper with sons and cattle; may he who hates us be shattered. For the Praṇava (*oṃ*), the Supreme Brahman is the seer, the Supreme Self or Agni is the deity, and Daivī Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is in the *ājya* oblation for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) caused by the breaking of a vessel: "Oṃ Svāhā! This [is for] the Supreme Self," or "This is for Agni."

Regarding the verse *mano jyotiḥ*, which belongs to the deity known as Manasvatī Agni, the metre is Triṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the clarified butter oblation (*ājyahoma*) for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) caused by the destruction of the consecrated fire (*nirūḍhāgni*): "Oṃ *mano jyotir juṣatām̐... ghṛtena svāhā*. [The dedication is: "This [is] for the mind as light."

Prajāpati is the deity of all the *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the *bṛhatī* meter. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the *ājya-homa* expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by the mixing of the principal oblation (*pradhāna-āhuti*) and the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā"; [this is] for Prajāpati. For these two [verses], "imaṃ me" and "tattvā yāmi," the Viśvedevas and Varuṇa are the deities; the meter of the first is *gāyatrī*, and that of the second is *triṣṭubh*. Prajāpati is the deity of all the *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the *bṛhatī* meter.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the *ājya* oblation in the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) intended to remove the defects arising from the emission of semen during sleep: "Oṃ imaṃ me... ke svāhā"—to Varuṇa, this [oblation]. "Oṃ tattvā yāmi... ṣīḥ svāhā"—to Varuṇa, this [oblation]. "Bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā"—to Prajāpati, this [oblation].

Regarding the mantras of the *punarmām* section: the seers (*ṛṣi*) are Aruṇas; the deity (*devatā*) is Sūrya. The meter (*chandas*) of the first is *anuṣṭubh*, of the second is *dvipadā triṣṭubh*, of the third is *dvipadā gāyatrī*, and of the fourth is *anuṣṭubh*. Now follows the *grahamakhā* (sacrifice to the planets). It is of three kinds, distinguished as obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). The obligatory sacrifice is performed on auspicious days, the three lunar phases (*tithi*), one's birth star (*nakṣatra*), the solstices (*ayana*), the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), eclipses, and so forth. The occasional sacrifice is performed at the commencement of rites such as the initiation (*upanayana*) and others. The optional sacrifice is performed when there is a desire for the removal of calamities, the attainment of prosperity, and the like. Among these, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and other requirements are mandatory for the optional sacrifice, but not for the obligatory or occasional ones—according to the statement in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "Excluding the obligatory and occasional [rites], everything else, including the pavilion, is [required]."

When there is a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), it is indeed an altar (vedi) and not a pavilion (maṇḍapa), because such is seen in the practice of the learned; thus it is stated in the *Prayogapārijāta*. The definition of a pavilion is given in the *Mātsya Purāṇa* within the *Hemādri*:
"A wise man should have a pavilion constructed to the northeast of the house, or on the ground of a temple of Rudra, making it square and sloping toward the north."

"One should construct [the pavilion] according to the rules, measuring ten or eight cubits; its four doors should be made by the wise. Here, the third case ending in *uttarapūrveṇa* (northeast) is used in the sense of the seventh case (*saptamī*). *Udakplava* means sloping toward the north or low in the north. Regarding the phrase "one should make it eight cubits," the word "for the sake of the pavilion" (*maṇḍapārtham*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "One should make" (*kuryāt*) means "one should take possession of" or "one should prepare. The resulting meaning is that one should construct a pavilion of either ten or eight cubits. By the term "according to the rules" (*vidhānataḥ*), all the ritual actions such as the purification of the ground and the division into nine parts are included. "Of that" (*tasya*) refers to the maṇḍala.
Regarding the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), it is stated in the *Skānda*: "In the sacrifice to the nine planets, the pit should be one cubit (*hasta*) on all sides;
it should be square, with its base at one cubit, having a 'womb-mouth' (*yonivaktra*) and provided with a girdle (*mekhalā*)."

"The girdle (*mekhalā*) is four finger-breadths wide and likewise high. The "lower hand" refers to a pit one cubit deep in the lower part. The "vulva-face" (*yonivaktra*) is like the face of a vulva; "face" (*vaktra*) means the neck, and it is to be of that same width. Regarding this sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), Hemādri states that in the case of a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), it should be made in its northeast or northern portion. Some say it should be in the center. As for the vulva, it is described in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*:
The womb (yoni) should be one vitasti in length and six or seven aṅgulas in width;
it should be elevated like the back of a tortoise in the middle and raised by one aṅgula at the sides.
"It is like the lip of an elephant, likewise long and provided with a cavity;
it is everywhere above the girdle, resembling a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree."
It should be as high as a finger, meaning it is spread across the two sides; there is an option for it to be like an elephant's lip or like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
And that *yoni* should be made at the back, according to the statement of Garga: "One should fashion the *yoni* in the middle of the western part according to the prescribed rule."

In the absence of a fire-pit (kuṇḍa), the oblation (homa) should be performed on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila); for the *Śāradātilaka* states: "One should perform the daily or occasional oblation either [in a pit] or on a sacrificial mound. By mentioning these two [options] here, it is implied that a sacrificial mound is not used for optional (kāmya) rites. In the *Mātsya*:
And to its northeast, there should be a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit,
square in shape, with three tiers, and equal in height to a span (vitasti).
The first tier is declared to be two finger-breadths (aṅgula) in height.

"Furthermore, two embankments (*vapra*) joined with a height of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) [should be made] on top; the width of all of them is stated by the wise to be two finger-breadths. Regarding that *kuṇḍa*: a *sthaṇḍila* is an altar (*vedi*). A *vapra* is a girdle (*mekhalā*). A *vitasti* is twelve finger-breadths; the meaning is "joined with" or "measured by" a height determined by that [unit]. In the phrase *dviraṅgulocchritaḥ*, the use of the suffix *suC* is an archaic (Vedic) usage. "On top" means above the first embankment. "Of all" refers to all the embankments.
In rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*) is mandatory. This is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"The lunar day (*tithi*) plus one, joined with the weekday (*vāra*), divided by four; if the remainder is two, zero, or one, there is residence in fire (*vahni*).
For the sake of success in the fire-oblation (*homa*), [the remainder] should be two or four; otherwise, there is loss of life and wealth, whether in heaven or on earth."

The traditional astronomers maintain that the counting here begins from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*). "Accompanied by one" (*saikā*) means that when the lunar days (*tithi*) have been counted, one additional lunar day is to be reckoned. In this context, the singular number should be understood as referring to the class [of lunar days] in cases involving two, three, or more. The two terms "conjoined with the weekdays" (*vāraiḥ yutā*) and "divided by four" (*kṛtāptā*) are qualifiers of the lunar day. By the word *kṛta*, the number four is indicated, as it represents the four ages beginning with Kṛta; thus, the number four is obtained. *Āptā* means divided.
There are three qualities (*guṇas*). *Abhra* is zero. *Śaśi* is one. *Yugma* is two. The rest is clear.
The exception to this is stated in that very same place: "In obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*) does not exist."
The wheel of fire does not exist; the meaning is that there is no dependence upon the wheel of fire.
Now, regarding the descent of the oblation into the luminaries:
"The Sun, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Rāhu, and Ketu..."
"Starting from Sunday, one should count the days of the week in order; for each planet, one should assign three [days] each.
The Sun, Saturn, Rāhu, Mars, Ketu, and Venus are not auspicious, while the others are auspicious.
Let this 'Fire-Wheel' (Dahana-cakra) be observed for the sake of total success in the rite of fire-offerings."

*Taraṇi* is the Sun; *vidbudha* is Mercury; *bhṛgu* is Venus; *bhāskari* is Saturn; *candramas* is well known [as the Moon]; *kuja* is Mars; *surejya* is Jupiter; *vidhuntuda* is Rāhu; *ketu* is well known; *dinakara* is the Sun; *ārki* is Saturn; *tamas* is Rāhu; *kuja* is Maṅgala; and *ketu*—if these are fire-eaters (*hutabhuj*), they are not auspicious. The meaning is that the remaining ones—the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—if they are fire-eaters, are auspicious.

An exception to this is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "In daily rites, occasional rites, and in the fire-offerings (*homa*) to Durgā and the like, one need not deliberate [on the suitability of the planets]."

Based on the traditional injunction, "The *sarvatobhadrapīṭha* is proclaimed as the support for all," one should construct the *sarvatobhadrapīṭha* upon the altar in the manner to be described in the *Śāntiratnamālā*. Having invoked and worshipped the deities beginning with Brahmā therein, one should fashion the planetary seats (*grahapīṭha*) upon a smooth cloth—either silk or cotton—that measures the same size as the altar.

The procedure for that is as follows: having spread out a smooth cloth made of linen or cotton, measured according to the altar, one should draw a line on each of the four sides around the edge of the cloth to mark its limit; then, inside that, one should likewise draw three lines with an interval of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) between them. Having divided the remaining inner square into three parts both eastward and northward, nine compartments are thus produced. In the central compartment is the Sun; in the southeast compartment is the Moon.

In the southern square is that of Mars; in the northeast square, that of Mercury; in the northern square, that of Jupiter; in the eastern square, that of Venus; in the western square, that of Saturn; in the southwest square, that of Rāhu; and in the northwest square, that of Ketu. Having written them in this sequence according to the method to be described, one should fill each with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) of their respective colors.

Alternatively—having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp, the size of which is such that the planetary seats (grahapīṭha) may be arranged upon the petals—one places the Sun in the pericarp, the Moon on the southeast petal, Mars on the south petal, Mercury on the northeast petal, Jupiter on the north petal, Venus on the east petal, Saturn on the west petal, Rāhu on the southwest petal, and Ketu on the northwest petal.
Now follows the method for constructing the planetary seat (grahapīṭha).

In the center of the spread cloth, one should fashion the circular pedestal of the Sun using red-colored powder, with a radius of one finger-breadth (aṅgula) plus six barley-corns (yūkā) and seven barley-seeds (yava).

In the southeast, the square pedestal of the Moon should be made with white powder, having four sides each measuring four finger-breadths plus two barley-corns and two barley-seeds. In the south, the triangular pedestal of Mars should be made with red-colored powder; it has three sides each measuring three finger-breadths plus four barley-corns, and a perpendicular height of two finger-breadths plus one barley-corn and five barley-seeds, with its apex pointing southward.

In the northeast (īśānī), having drawn two lines named *bhuja*—four *yava*s apart, four *aṅgula*s long, oriented toward the north, and with their tips meeting—using yellow powder; and having drawn a single line between the northern tips of these two lines, measuring one *prādeśa* in length and joining their tips; and having likewise fashioned an eastern line measuring four *yava*s, attached at the tip and extending forward from the northern tip of the eastern *bhuja*; and in the same manner...

Having drawn a western line measuring four *yavas* that joins the rear end of the northern extremity of the western arm to the front [of the eastern arm], and having placed a straight horizontal thread to the north between the two arms, one should measure two *aṅgulas* plus five *yavas*, two *yūkas*, and five *likṣās* from the center of the two arms toward the north; having made a mark there, one should fashion the two arms—measuring two *aṅgulas* plus six *yavas*—starting from the outer ends of the east-west line consisting of four *yavas* and extending to the mark.
In this manner, the altar (*pīṭha*) for Mercury is shaped like an arrow.

In the north, with yellow powder, one should fashion for the Guru a long rectangular pedestal, two *aṅgulas* wide on each of the two eastern and western arms and one *aṅgula* wide on each of the two southern and northern arms.

In the east, with white powder, one should draw a circle using a compass with a radius of one *aṅgula*, seven *yavas*, and five *yūkas*; then, within that circle, starting from the eastern direction, one should mark five chords measuring two *aṅgulas* plus two *yavas* and three *yūkas*, and erase the remainder—thus is the five-cornered pedestal for Śukra.

Alternatively, having constructed a circle with a radius of two *aṅgulas* plus six *yūkas* and six *yavas*, one should mark a point on that circle starting from the eastern direction at a distance measured by three *aṅgulas* plus six *yūkas* and six *yavas*. Starting from that point, one should likewise mark points in the other directions; thus, having made five marks with a compass, one should [draw a line] from any one mark, skipping the immediately adjacent mark, so as to meet the third mark.

Having made each arm five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) plus two lice, three barley-corns, and one-third of a barley-corn, and having likewise prepared the other four arms, one should erase the arms situated below the corners as well as the circle; thus, the five-cornered pedestal of Śukra, known as *utkāra*, is described.

In the west, having drawn a circle with black powder using a radius of four *aṅgulas* plus four *likṣās*, four *yūkas*, and four *yavas*, one should fashion a chord attached to that circle measuring six *aṅgulas* plus five *yūkas* and three *yavas*; thus, the pedestal of Saturn has a western chord and an area of six *aṅgulas*.

Alternatively, having drawn a circle with a radius of two *aṅgulas* plus five *yavas* and six *likṣās*, one should draw a line known as a *jyā* (bowstring), measuring three *aṅgulas* plus five *yavas* and six *yūkas*, attached to the circumference of the circle; thus, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) of Saturn has an area of two *aṅgulas*.

In the southwest (nairṛtyāṃ), having fashioned a square measuring four fingers with blue powder and consisting of four arms, one should extend a straight line from the southeast corner (āgneyakoṇāt) toward the south by a distance of one finger plus six *yūkās* and one *yava*, and mark a point there; likewise, extending it toward the north and marking a point there, one should draw a line from the southern point to the southwest corner (nairṛtakoṇa) and a line from the northern point to the northwest corner (vāyavyakoṇa).

Having written [the measurements] and made marks at the ends of the two lower arms, each measuring two finger-breadths (aṅgula), one should draw two circles with a radius of one finger-breadth using a compass from those two marks; then, one should erase everything situated between them—thus is the winnowing-basket-shaped (śūrpākāra) pedestal of Rāhu.

In the northwestern direction, having drawn two lines of various colors, eight finger-breadths long from east to west and separated by four barley-corns, one should leave a space of one finger-breadth at the upper end starting from below—measuring five finger-breadths—and having wiped away the remaining line of two finger-breadths, one should form two arms measuring four finger-breadths plus one barley-corn each, joined to one another on the northern side; thus is the banner-shaped pedestal of Ketu.

In all cases, the central portion of the pedestal (pīṭha) is to be conceived in accordance with the central portion of the square cell (koṣṭha). According to the view that "all [deities] face the sun," for Soma, the corners of the square pedestal are to be conceived in the cardinal directions; for Bhauma, however, it remains as before. For Budha, the pedestal is in the shape of an arrow, such that the tip of the arrow faces the northeast corner and the southwest corner of the cell. For Bṛhaspati, it is as before. For the pedestal of Śukra, the five bowstrings (jyā) are to be conceived starting from the western direction.

The seat of Śani (Saturn) should be imagined in the eastern [section]; the seat of Rāhu should be imagined in the south-western cell, facing the northeast corner, with its tip like the point of a winnowing basket. Regarding the flagstaff, while its northern tip was mentioned previously, here it has a southern tip; this refers to the seat of Ketu. Such is the distinction. Since there is no statement that one should offer oblations into the seats of the Sarvatobhadra and others using the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), the *homa* is not performed with the root mantra;
rather: "In the *homa* for the deity of the seat, the mantra is declared to be the name itself, preceded by the *praṇava*, ending in the dative case, and joined with the word 'svāhā'."

According to the statement of the author of the *Tantraprakāśa*, it should be understood that the fire offering (*homa*) is to be performed with the name-mantra (*nāmamantra*) alone, even without the word *namaḥ*. As for the nature of the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), it is stated in the *Gāruḍatantra*:
"O best of beings, the deity's own name, preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), ending in the dative case, and concluding with *namaḥ*, is proclaimed as the root-mantra."

And thus, wherever there is an injunction stating "one should offer oblations with the root mantra" (mūlamantra) and no specific mantra is prescribed, this is the root mantra. Therefore, in the homa to be performed by means of it, the word *svāhā* follows after the word *namaḥ*.
This is the application for the *grahamakhayāga*.

Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): Having bathed and performed his daily duties (*nityakarman*), the performer, at the time indicated by an astrologer, should perform the ceremonial sipping of water (*ācamana*) and breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then, having announced the place and time, he makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the occasional planetary sacrifice (*naimittikagrahayajña*) at the commencement of rites such as the initiation (*upanayana*): "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*), through the attainment of favorability toward the planets in the performance of the [specific] rite about to be undertaken, I shall perform the planetary sacrifice. In the case of the three birth-asterisms (*trijanmanakṣatra*), the solstices (*ayana*), the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and eclipses, the resolve is: "I shall perform the planetary sacrifice on the [specific] birth-asterism."

The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the obligatory *grahayajña* is: "I shall perform the *grahayajña* on the solstice (*ayana*), the equinox (*viṣuva*), or during an eclipse. The formal resolve for the optional (*kāmya*) *grahayajña* follows the specific desire, such as: "for the removal of calamities," "for the attainment of prosperity," or "for the attainment of nourishment. Then, one should gather the necessary materials. In that regard, for the obligatory and occasional rites, one should procure the substances as prescribed; in their absence, one should provide substitutes according to availability.

In the case of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), however, because there is no substitute (*pratinidhi*), one must use only the materials exactly as prescribed; or else, the gathering of the requisites may take place prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

Then, having performed the rites beginning with the worship of Gaṇapati and ending with the *nāndī-śrāddha*, he should proceed to the formal selection (*varaṇa*) of the preceptor (*ācārya*). With his hand touching the hand [of the chosen one], he should select a Brāhmaṇa who knows the ritual rules, is skilled in the performance of rites, is learned in his own Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā*), and is of virtuous conduct, saying: "I, Amuka-śarmā, born in the lineage of such-and-such *pravara* and such-and-such *gotra*, and a student of such-and-such Vedic branch, choose you, Amuka-śarmā, born in the lineage of such-and-such *pravara* and such-and-such *gotra*, and a student of such-and-such Vedic branch, as my preceptor for this sacrifice to the planets (*graha-yajña*).
It is the established custom to place fruit and other offerings into his hand.
Then, having honored him, he should pray to him as follows:
"O you of noble vows, just as Bṛhaspati is the preceptor of Śakra and the other gods in heaven, so may you be the preceptor for me in this sacrifice.
Then, having chosen and fully honored the Brahman priest—
"One should entreat him thus: 'O best of the twice-born, just as the four-faced Brahmā, the Grandfather, is in the heavenly world, so may you be the Brahmā in this sacrifice of mine.
Then, having chosen and honored the Sadasya (the assistant priest):"
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, best among the upholders of all dharmas; O observer of noble vows, be a member of the assembly at this extensive sacrifice of mine. Thus one should entreat him.
Then, having selected and worshipped the officiating priests according to the requirements of the *homa*:
"Your honors have been requested by me for the successful completion of this sacrifice;
with well-pleased minds, you must perform this rite according to the prescribed rules. Thus he should entreat them.
Then the preceptor (ācārya), having sat down behind the fire-altar, having sipped water (ācamya), and having restrained his breath (prāṇāyāma)—
Whatever being is stationed here, always depending upon this place—
let all that, having abandoned the place, go wherever it belongs.
Let the spirits and piśācas depart in every direction.
"I shall commence the rite of Brahman without contradicting anyone.

Having thus scattered mustard seeds in all directions starting from the east, he sprinkles the sacrificial ground with *pañcagavya* using the following: for the verse beginning with *śucī vaḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and the Maruts, the metre is Triṣṭubh; for the two verses beginning with *agniḥ śucivratatamaḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and the pure Agni, the metre is Gāyatrī; this is the application (*viniyoga*) for sprinkling the ground with *pañcagavya*: "Oṃ *śucī vo havyā marutaḥ śu0 pāvakāḥ | agniḥ śucivrata0 hutaḥ | udagne śu0 pyarcayaḥ*. Having thus sprinkled the entire sacrificial ground with *pañcagavya*.

For the *ṛc*-trio beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," Agni, the Waters, and the Gāyatrī are the deities; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sprinkling of the ground with pure water: "Oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo... yathā ca naḥ. Having thus sprinkled the entire sacrificial ground with pure water, [one recites] "svasti naḥ": for this [verse], the Yājñikyas, the Devas, the Upaniṣads, Indra and others, and the Virāṭ-Ṭriṣṭubh are the deities.

The application for the recitation (*japa*) is as follows: having recited, "Oṃ, may Indra grant us well-being... (*svasti na indro vṛddha... dadhātu*), one should touch the ground behind the fire-altar (*agnyāyatana*) while saying, "May the gods come; may the sorcerers depart; O Viṣṇu, protect the sacrificial ground of the gods. In the case of a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), one should perform the purification of the ground intended for the pavilion and so forth, up to the worship of its presiding deities, according to the method described in my *Śāntiratnamālā-paddhati*.

When the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) possessing the previously described characteristics is present, one should sweep it with a handful of *kuśa* grass. Then, upon the upper girdle (*mekhalā*) of the pit, which is adorned with white color, one should invoke Viṣṇu with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ"; for this, Soma is the deity, Viṣṇu is the seer, and Gāyatrī is the meter. For the invocation of Viṣṇu: "Oṃ idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame tredhā nidadhe padam | samūḷhamasya pāṃsure | Viṣṇave namaḥ, I invoke Viṣṇu. Thus one should invoke Viṣṇu. Then, upon the middle girdle, which is adorned with red color, [one should invoke] Brahmā with the mantra "brahma jajñānam"; for this, Agni is the deity, Brahmā is the seer, and Triṣṭubh is the meter.

In the invocation of Brahmā (*brahmāvāhana*), one should invoke Brahmā with: "Oṃ *brahma jajñānaṃ prathamaṃ purastād viśvaśca vivah* | *brahmaṇe namo brahmāṇam āvāhayāmi*" (Om, Brahmā was born first in the east... salutations to Brahmā; I invoke Brahmā). Then, on the lower girdle (*mekhalā*) which is adorned with black color, one should invoke Rudra with: "Oṃ *mṛḍā no rudrota no mayaskṛdhi praṇītau* | *rudrāya namo rudram āvāhayāmi*" (Om, be gracious to us, O Rudra, and grant us happiness... salutations to Rudra; I invoke Rudra). [Then] touch water.

Then, in the womb [of the altar] adorned with the color red, one should invoke Gaurī with the mantra "gaurīrmimāya," for which the Viśvedevas are the seers, Gaurī is the deity, and Jagatī is the meter; its application is in the invocation of Gaurī: "Oṃ, Gaurī has fashioned the waters and the sky. Salutation to Gaurī; I invoke Gaurī. Thus, one should invoke Gaurī.

Then, having worshipped with those same mantras in sequence according to the *padārthānusamaya* method using the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), and having decorated the sacrificial ground on all sides with a *raṅgavalli* (colored powder designs), smeared it with cow dung, and performed the rites beginning with the *uddhanana* (smearing and leveling), one should establish the fire—either churned or brought from the house of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*)—known by the name Varada, and meditate upon it with the mantra: "Oṃ, four are its horns... If there is a desire for prosperity (*puṣṭi*), however, the fire is named Balavardhana. Thereafter, one should perform the installation of the deities of the planetary altar (*grahapīṭha*) and so forth.

For example: having constructed in the northeast corner of the pavilion, in the center, an altar (*vedi*) measuring one cubit square and twelve finger-breadths high; having made beneath it one embankment (*vapra*) one finger-breadth high and two finger-breadths wide; having likewise made another embankment beneath that; and having made beneath that one embankment two finger-breadths high and wide—one should color those three embankments, starting from the uppermost embankment, in sequence with white, red, and black powders.

These mounds (*vapra*) are indeed included within the dimensions of the altar (*vedi*). Therefore, if possible, one should construct a *sarvatobhadra* diagram there according to the method described in my work, the *Śāntiratnamālā*, and invoke the deities beginning with Brahmā therein.

It is as follows: for the verse "brahma jajñānam," Agni is the deity, Brahmā is the subject, Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Brahmā. "Oṃ brahma jajñānaṃ... vivaḥ. Homage to Brahmā; I invoke Brahmā. Thus, one invokes Brahmā in the center of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).

For the mantra *āpyāyasva*, Soma or Agni is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Soma: "Oṃ, swell up, O Soma... for the sake of union. Salutation to Soma; I invoke Soma"—thus [one invokes] Soma in the north. For the mantra *abhi tvā*, the Viśvedevas are the deities, Īśāna is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is in the invocation of Īśāna: "Oṃ, toward you... for the great [glory]. Salutation to Īśāna; I invoke Īśāna"—thus [one invokes] Īśāna in the northeast.

For the verse beginning with "indraṃ vo viśvataḥ," the deities are the Viśvedevas and Indra, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the application (viniyoga) is in the invocation of Indra: "Oṃ indraṃ vo viśva... valaḥ | Salutation to Indra; I invoke Indra"—thus first [invoking] Indra.

For the verse beginning with *agniṃ dūtam*, Prajāpati is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the Gāyatrī is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Agni: "Oṃ, I choose Agni as the messenger... the wise one. Obeisance to Agni; I invoke Agni. Thus, [one invokes] Agni in the southeast. For the verse beginning with *yamāya somam*, Prajāpati is the seer, Yama is the deity, and the Anuṣṭubh is the meter. Its application is in the invocation of Yama: "Oṃ, for Yama, the Soma... is prepared. Obeisance to Yama; I invoke Yama. Thus, [one invokes] Yama in the south.

For the verse beginning with *devīm aham*, Agni is the deity, Nirṛti is the meter (triṣṭubh), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Nirṛti: "Oṃ *devīm ahaṃ*... *caṣṭe*. Salutation to Nirṛti; I invoke Nirṛti. Thus, one invokes Nirṛti in the southwest. For the verse beginning with *tattvā yāmi*, the Viśvedevas are the deities, Varuṇa is the deity, and triṣṭubh is the meter. Its application is in the invocation of Varuṇa: "Oṃ *tattvā yāmi*... *pramoṣīḥ*. Salutation to Varuṇa; I invoke Varuṇa. Thus, one invokes Varuṇa in the west.

For the mantra *vāyo śatam*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Vāyu; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Vāyu: "Oṃ vāyo śataṃ... pājasā. Salutation to Vāyu, I invoke Vāyu"—thus [one invokes] Vāyu in the northwest. For the mantra *aṣṭau devāḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and the eight Vasus; the meter is Virāṭ-Triṣṭubh; its application is in the invocation of the eight Vasus: "Oṃ aṣṭau devāḥ... svasti. Salutation to the eight Vasus, I invoke the eight Vasus"—thus [one invokes] the eight Vasus between Vāyu and Soma.

Regarding the verse *nīlagrīvāḥ śitikaṇṭhāḥ*, Agni is the deity, the Rudras are eleven, and the metre is Anuṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of the eleven Rudras: "Oṃ nīlagrīvā... śritāḥ. We unbend our bows a thousand yojanas away from them. Homage to the eleven Rudras; I invoke the eleven Rudras. Thus, one invokes the eleven Rudras between Soma and Īśāna.

For the verse *tyān nu*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and the twelve Ādityas; the meter is Gāyatrī. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of the twelve Ādityas: "Oṃ *tyān nu kṣattri... ṣṭaye*. Salutation to the twelve Ādityas; I invoke the twelve Ādityas. Thus, one invokes the twelve Ādityas between Īśāna and Indra. For the verse *yā vāṃ kaśā*, the deity is Soma and the deities are the Aśvins; the meter is Gāyatrī. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of the Aśvins: "Oṃ *yā vā kaśā... kṣatam*. Salutation to the Aśvins; I invoke the Aśvins. Thus, one invokes the Aśvins between Indra and Agni.

For the verse beginning with *omāsaḥ*, Soma and the Viśvedevas are the deities; the metre is Gāyatrī. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of the Viśvedevas: "Oṃ, *omāsaśca*... [the pressed juice]. "Salutation to the Viśvedevas; I invoke the Viśvedevas. Thus, one invokes the Viśvedevas between Agni and Yama. For the verse beginning with *abhi tyam*, Soma and the seven Yakṣas are the deities; the metre is Prakṛti. Its application is in the invocation of the seven Yakṣas: "Oṃ, *abhi tyaṃ deva*... [the light]. "Salutation to the seven Yakṣas; I invoke the seven Yakṣas. Thus, one invokes the seven Yakṣas between Yama and Nirṛti.

For the mantra *ā'yaṃ gauḥ*, Agni, the serpents (*sarpa*), and the Gāyatrī are the deities. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of the serpents: *Oṃ ā'yaṃ gauḥ pṛ0 ntsuvaḥ*. "Salutation to the serpents; I invoke the serpents. Thus, one invokes the serpents between Nirṛti and Varuṇa. For the mantra beginning with *ṛtāṣāḍ* and ending with *pāntu*, the Viśvedevas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases are the deities, and the Yajus is the meter. Its application is in the invocation of the Gandharvas and Apsarases: *Oṃ ṛtāṣāḍṛtadhā0 pāntu*. "Salutation to the Gandharvas and Apsarases; I invoke the Gandharvas and Apsarases. Thus, one invokes the Gandharvas and Apsarases between Varuṇa and Vāyu.

For the verse beginning with *yadakranda*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), the seer is Skanda, and the meter is *triṣṭubh*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Skanda: *Oṃ "yadakrandaḥ prathamaṃ jātaṃ te avan,"* obeisance to Skanda; I invoke Skanda. Thus [one invokes] Skanda between Brahmā and Soma.

For the mantra "tatpuruṣāya vidmahe cakratuṇḍāya," the deities are the Yājñikyas, the Upaniṣads, and Nandīśvara; the meter is Gāyatrī. Its application (viniyoga) is in the invocation of Nandīśvara: "Oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe cakratuṇḍāya dhīmahi | tanno nandiḥ pracodayāt. "Salutation to Nandīśvara; I invoke Nandīśvara. Thus, one invokes Nandīśvara to the north of Skanda.

For the mantra *yatte gātrāt*, the deity is the Viśvedevas, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of the trident (*śūla*). "Oṃ yatte gātrā... mastu. *Namaḥ* to the trident; I invoke the trident. Thus, to the north of Nandīśvara, [he places] the trident. For the mantra *kārṣirasī*, the deity is Soma, the meter is Yajus, and the application is for the invocation of Mahākāla. "Oṃ kārṣira... ṣāṃ mṛdhram. *Namaḥ* to Mahākāla; I invoke Mahākāla. Thus, to the north of the trident, [he places] Mahākāla.

For the verse beginning with *dvāvimau vātau vātaḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Dakṣa. Reciting: *Oṃ dvāvimau... yadrūpaḥ; Dakṣāya namaḥ, I invoke Dakṣa*. Thus, one should invoke Dakṣa between Brahmā and Īśāna. For the verse beginning with *tāmagnivarṇām*, the deities are the Yājñikyas, the subject matter is the Upaniṣads, the deity is Durgā, and the metre is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Durgā. Reciting: *Oṃ tāmagnivarṇāṃ... tarase namaḥ; Durgāyai namaḥ, I invoke Durgā*. Thus, one should invoke Durgā between Brahmā and Indra.

For the mantra *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, Soma-Viṣṇu is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Viṣṇu. "Oṃ idaṃ viṣṇu... sure," [saying] "Salutation to Viṣṇu, I invoke Viṣṇu"—thus one invokes Viṣṇu in front of Durgā. For the mantra *udīratām*, the Viśvedevas are the deities, Svadhā is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application is for the invocation of Svadhā. "Oṃ udīratām... haveṣu," [saying] "Salutation to Svadhā, I invoke Svadhā"—thus one invokes Svadhā between Brahmā and Agni.

For the mantra *paraṃ mṛtyo*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the subject is Mṛtyuroga (the Disease of Death), and the meter is Triṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Mṛtyuroga. "Oṃ paraṃ mṛtyo... vīrān. [Reciting: "Salutation to the Diseases of Death; I invoke the Diseases of Death," one invokes the Diseases of Death between Brahmā and Yama. For the mantra *gaṇānāṃ tvā*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the subject is Gaṇapati, and the meter is Jagatī. Its application is in the invocation of Gaṇapati. "Oṃ gaṇānāṃ tvā... sādanam. [Reciting: "Salutation to Gaṇapati; I invoke Gaṇapati," one invokes Gaṇapati between Brahmā and Nirṛti.

For the verse beginning with *śaṃ no devīḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and the Waters (*āpaḥ*), the meter is Gāyatrī; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation (*āvāhana*). Reciting: *Oṃ śaṃ no devī... ntu naḥ*, [saying] "Salutation to the Waters (*adbhyo namaḥ*); I invoke the Waters," one places the Waters between Brahmā and Varuṇa. For the verse beginning with *maruto yasya*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and the Maruts, the meter is Gāyatrī; its application is in the invocation of the Maruts. Reciting: *Oṃ maruto yasya... janaḥ*, [saying] "Salutation to the Maruts (*marudbhyo namaḥ*); I invoke the Maruts," one places the Maruts between Brahmā and Vāyu.

For the verse "Syonā pṛthivi," the deities are the ritual goddesses (*yājñikya-devatā*), the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) is the Earth, and the meter is *gāyatrī*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of the Earth. "Oṃ syonā pṛthivi bhavā... prathāḥ. [Reciting this,] one says: "Salutation to the Earth; I invoke the Earth. Thus, one invokes the Earth at the base of the feet of Brahmā, below the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

For the verse *imaṃ me gaṅge*, the deities are the sacrificial goddesses, the Upaniṣads, and the rivers such as the Gaṅgā; the meter is Jagatī. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of the Gaṅgā and other rivers. "Oṃ imaṃ me gaṅge... suṣomayā. "Homage to the Gaṅgā and other rivers; I invoke the Gaṅgā and other rivers. Thus, there itself, [one invokes] the Gaṅgā and other rivers. For the verse *dhāmno dhāmnaḥ*, the deity is Soma, the objects are the seven oceans, and the meter is Paṅkti. Its application is in the invocation of the seven oceans. "Oṃ dhāmno dhāmno... no muñca. "Homage to the seven oceans; I invoke the seven oceans. Thus, there itself, [one invokes] the seven oceans.

"Oṃ, salutation to Meru; I invoke Meru. Thus, one places Meru upon that [seat]. Then, the weapons: "Oṃ, salutation to the mace (gadā); I invoke the mace. Thus, one places the mace to the north of Soma. "Oṃ, salutation to the trident (triśūla); I invoke the trident. Thus, one places the trident to the northeast of Īśāna. "Oṃ, salutation to the thunderbolt (vajra); I invoke the thunderbolt. Thus, one places the thunderbolt to the east of Indra. "Oṃ, salutation to the spear (śakti); I invoke the spear. Thus, one places the spear to the southeast of Agni. "Oṃ, salutation to the staff (daṇḍa); I invoke the staff. Thus, one places the staff to the south of Yama.

"Oṃ, obeisance to the sword; I invoke the sword"—with these words, [one places] the sword in the southwest, the direction of Nirṛti. "Oṃ, obeisance to the noose; I invoke the noose"—with these words, [one places] the noose in the west, the direction of Varuṇa. "Oṃ, obeisance to the goad; I invoke the goad"—with these words, [one places] the goad in the northwest, the direction of Vāyu. Thus are the weapons.

"Oṃ, obeisance to Gautama; I invoke Gautama"—thus, one invokes Gautama to the north of the mace (*gadā*). "Oṃ, obeisance to Bharadvāja; I invoke Bharadvāja"—thus, to the northeast of the trident (*triśūla*). "Oṃ, obeisance to Viśvāmitra; I invoke Viśvāmitra"—thus, to the east of the thunderbolt (*vajra*), one invokes Viśvāmitra. "Oṃ, obeisance to Kaśyapa; I invoke Kaśyapa"—thus, to the southeast of the spear (*śakti*), one invokes Kaśyapa.

"Oṃ, obeisance to Jamadagni; I invoke Jamadagni"—thus, Jamadagni to the south of the staff (daṇḍa). "Oṃ, obeisance to Vasiṣṭha; I invoke Vasiṣṭha"—thus, Vasiṣṭha to the southwest (nairṛti) of the sword (khaḍga). "Oṃ, obeisance to Atri; I invoke Atri"—thus, Atri to the west of the noose (pāśa). "Oṃ, obeisance to Arundhatī; I invoke Arundhatī"—thus, Arundhatī to the northwest (vāyavya) of the goad (aṅkuśa). Thus [are invoked] the sages (ṛṣis).

"Oṃ, obeisance to Aindrī; I invoke Aindrī"—thus, for Viśvāmitra, first [in the east] is Aindrī. "Oṃ, obeisance to Kaumārī; I invoke Kaumārī"—thus, for Kaśyapa, in the southeast (āgneyī) is Kaumārī. "Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmī; I invoke Brāhmī"—thus, for Jamadagni, in the south is Brāhmī. "Oṃ, obeisance to Vārāhī; I invoke Vārāhī"—thus, for Vasiṣṭha, in the southwest (nairṛtī) is Vārāhī.

"Oṃ, obeisance to Cāmuṇḍā; I invoke Cāmuṇḍā"—with these words, one should invoke Cāmuṇḍā to the west of Atri. "Oṃ, obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī; I invoke Vaiṣṇavī"—with these words, one should invoke Vaiṣṇavī to the northwest of Arundhatī. "Oṃ, obeisance to Māheśvarī; I invoke Māheśvarī"—with these words, one should invoke Māheśvarī to the north of Gautama. "Oṃ, obeisance to Vaināyakī; I invoke Vaināyakī"—with these words, one should invoke Vaināyakī to the northeast of Bharadvāja. These are the eight Śaktis.

Having invoked these deities, [one recites] "narya prajām," wherein Agni is the deity, Narya is the seer, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the installation of these deities. Having installed them with the mantra: "Oṃ, O Narya, protect my progeny; [establish it] in immortality... established," one should worship [them] according to the *padārthānusamaya* method. In the case of the *kāṇḍānusamaya* method, having performed the worship of one [deity] with the sixteen services beginning with invocation, one should then perform the worship of the next with the sixteen services beginning with invocation; in this manner, the worship of all the deities is performed.

Then follows the preparation of the sanctuaries (*āyatana*) and so forth. According to the procedure for the *āghāra* oblations, one should offer ten sesame oblations or ten oblations of clarified butter under each of these headings; it is the traditional teaching that there is one oblation for each [name]. The fire sacrifice (*homa*) for Meru and the others is performed with their respective name-mantras, which begin with the *praṇava* (OM), end in the dative case, are devoid of the word "namaḥ," and are accompanied by the word "svāhā. When the rite of the fire sacrifice is completed, one should spread the cloth of the planetary pedestal (*graha-pīṭha*) upon the *sarvatobhadra* pedestal such that the pedestal of Venus (*śukra-pīṭha*) is situated toward the east, and then perform the ritual of removing the images from the fire (*agnyuttāraṇa*).
Next follows the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), preceded by the removal from the fire.

For the mantras of the section beginning with "aśmann ūrjam," Agni is the seer (ṛṣi) and Agni is the deity; the meters are Triṣṭubh and others. Their application (viniyoga) is for the removal of fire from the images. Having performed the removal of fire from the images with the section beginning "Oṃ aśmann ūrjaṃ... svasti," and having washed them with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and pure water, one should install the images of the planets facing their respective directions. Then, touching the cheeks of the image of the Sun, one should perform the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).

Of this venerable *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra*, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (*ṛṣis*); the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas are the meters (*chandās*); the Supreme Vital Energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) whose form is consciousness (*cid-rūpā*) is the deity (*devatā*); *Āṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *Hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *Kroṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana*) in the image of the Sun. *Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Vaṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ Hoṃ (Oṃ Kṣaṃ Saṃ Haṃsaḥ Hrīṃ Oṃ)*. *Haṃsaḥ So’haṃ*. May the vital breaths of the image of the Sun be established here as its vital breaths.

Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ haṃsaḥ so’haṃ; may the life-force (jīva) of the image of the Sun remain here. Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ haṃsaḥ so’haṃ; may all the sense organs—speech, mind, eyes, ears, skin, tongue, nose, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—having come right here for the sake of well-being, remain happily for a long time, svāhā! Thus one should recite.

"May her vital breaths be established; may her vital breaths flow forth. To this divinity, the image, Svāhā! Having recited this mantra, one should meditate upon the image as being endowed with life. Having thus performed the rite of Prāṇapratiṣṭhā (the installation of the life-force), one should bathe the image with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then bathe it with pure water.

Next, for the mantra *ud u tyam*, Soma is the deity, Sūrya is the meter (Gāyatrī), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the opening of the eyes of the Sūrya image. With the mantra "Oṃ ud u tyam jātavedasaṃ sūryam," one takes cow’s ghee using either a golden needle or a blade of *darbha* grass, and having opened the right and left eyes of the image in sequence by repeating the mantra for each, [one proceeds]. For the mantra *añjanti tvām*, the Viśvedevas are the deities, Vanaspati is the meter (Triṣṭubh), and its application is for anointing the two eyes of the Sūrya image with honey.

Reciting the mantra, "Oṃ añjanti tvāmadhvare... pasthe," one should anoint the eyes with honey in sequence according to the ritual procedure and present the offering. From the commencement of the opening of the eyes, one should not stand in front of the image. In this manner, the rite of *agnyuttāraṇa* (removal from the fire) and so forth for the images of Soma and others should be performed by adaptation (*ūha*). If it is impossible to perform each individually, they may all be done together by adaptation.

In that case, after the formula "I am He, the Swan" (*haṃsaḥ so'ham*), when performing the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) for the images of Sūrya and others, the appropriate adaptation should be made, such as "the vital breaths of the images of Sūrya and others. Then, one should invoke the planets (*graha*).

Namely: for "ā satyena," the Viśvedevas are the deity, Sūrya is the divinity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. For the Vyāhṛtis taken as a whole, Prajāpati is the deity, Prajāpati is the divinity, and Bṛhatī is the meter. Their application (viniyoga) is in the invocation of Sūrya.

"Oṃ ā satyena... vipaśyan. Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ! O Lord, Sovereign of Planets, wearing a crown, composed of the three deities, seated upon a lotus, with two arms holding a lotus and the gesture of fearlessness, clad in red garlands and garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents, adorned with rubies as ornaments, possessing a luster like the *japā* flower, mounted on a chariot drawn by seven horses, born in the Kaliṅga country, of the Kāśyapa lineage: O Sūrya, come here! [Thus, he should invoke him] into the center of a twelve-fingered circular seat filled with reddish *akṣata* grains, facing eastward.

In a copper image, one should invoke the Sun with red unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and establish him with the words, "Come here, be present here. Having recited "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and so forth up to the name of the deity, one should say, "I invoke you for the sake of worship," and then establish him with "Come here, be present here. This is the procedure to be applied in all cases.

For the verse beginning with *āpyāyasva*, Soma is the deity, or alternatively, the Viśvedevas; Soma is the deity; the metre is Gāyatrī. For the *vyāhṛtis*, the seers and other details are as previously stated in all instances. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Soma. *Oṃ āpyāyasva sametu te... vājasya saṃgathe*. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. O Blessed One, Lord of the Constellations, wearer of a diadem, holding a mace made of nectar in your two hands, clad in white garlands and garments, anointed with white perfumes, adorned with ornaments of pearls, possessing a luster like cow’s milk, mounted upon a chariot drawn by ten horses.

One should invoke Soma—born on the banks of the Yamunā, of the Ātreya gotra—with the words, "O Soma, come here! and establish him, facing westward, upon a square pedestal twenty-four finger-breadths in size, filled with white unbroken rice (*akṣata*), located in the southeast; he should be placed either in a crystal image or a silver image, having invoked Soma with white *akṣatas* and saying, "Be seated here."

The seer of "Agnirmūrdhā" is Prajāpati or Agni Aṅgāraka; the meter is Gāyatrī. [The application is] for the invocation of Aṅgāraka in the entire Vyāhṛtis. "Oṃ agnirmūrdhā jinvati bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ. O Blessed One, whose form is Fire, wearing a crown, holding a spear, trident, mace, and shield in your four hands, clad in red garlands and garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents, adorned with ornaments of coral, possessing a splendor like a mass of blazing fire, mounted upon a chariot drawn by red rams, born of Avantikā—[I invoke you].

Saying, "O Aṅgāraka of the Bhāradvāja lineage, come here," one should invoke Aṅgāraka with red unbroken rice (*raktākṣata*) upon a south-facing pedestal (*pīṭha*) shaped like a triangle with three finger-breadths, filled with red unbroken rice, and containing either an image of red sandalwood or a golden image; then, saying "Be seated here," one should establish him. For the verse beginning with *udbudhyasva*, Agni is the deity, Budha is the seer, and Triṣṭubh is the meter.

The application (viniyoga) for the invocation of Mercury (Budha): "Oṃ udbudhyasvāgne... "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. O Blessed One, of gentle form, wearing a crown, consisting of all knowledge, holding a sword, shield, mace, and book in your four hands, wearing yellow garlands and garments, anointed with yellow perfumes and unguents, adorned with emerald ornaments, possessing a luster like saffron, mounted upon a yellow lion-chariot; O Mercury, born in the Magadha country, of the Ātreya lineage, come here! [Thus, one should invoke him] in the northeast, in a yellow-colored space measuring four finger-breadths, shaped like an arrow, and filled with yellow *akṣata* grains.
On a pedestal facing north, one should invoke Budha with yellow unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) into a golden image and establish him with the words, "Be seated here."

For the verse beginning with "bṛhaspate," the deities are the Viśvedevas, the seer is Bṛhaspati, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. [The application is] for the invocation of Bṛhaspati in its entirety. "Oṃ bṛhaspate ati yad arya ā citram. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Blessed One, Preceptor of all the gods, wearer of a crown, composed of all branches of knowledge, with four arms holding a staff, a rosary, a water-pot, and a book; wearing yellow garlands and garments, anointed with yellow perfumes, adorned with topaz ornaments, possessing a luster like gold, and mounted upon a chariot drawn by yellow horses.

One should invoke Bṛhaspati with the mantra, "O Bṛhaspati, born in the land of Sindhu, of the Āṅgirasa lineage, come here! and establish him upon a yellow-colored pedestal measuring six aṅgulas square, filled with yellow unbroken rice (akṣata), where a golden image is placed facing north; one should then install him with the words, "Bṛhaspati, be seated here."

For the verse beginning with *śukraṃ te*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Śukra, the meter is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Śukra in its entirety. *Oṃ śukraṃ te anya... rātirastu*. Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ! O Blessed One, Preceptor of all the Daityas, wearer of a crown, composed of all branches of knowledge, holding a staff, a rosary, a water-pot, and a lotus in your four hands; wearing white garlands and garments, anointed with white perfumes, adorned with diamond ornaments, possessing a luster like silver, mounted upon a chariot drawn by white horses, born in the land of Bhojakaṭa, of the Bhārgava lineage.

Saying "O Śukra, come here," one should invoke Śukra with white unbroken rice (*akṣata*) upon a five-cornered pedestal nine finger-breadths wide, filled with white *akṣata*, situated on the east; and having placed a silver image facing east, one should establish him with the words "Be seated here."

For the verse *śaṃ no devīḥ*, the deity is Agni or Prajāpati, the planet is Śanaiścara (Saturn), and the meter is Gāyatrī. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Śanaiścara in its entirety. *Oṃ śaṃ no devī... tu naḥ*. Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Blessed One, you of fierce form, wearing a crown, holding a trident, an arrow, and a bow in your four hands, clad in blue garlands and garments, anointed with blue perfumes and unguents, adorned with blue ornaments, possessing a luster like collyrium and a fish, mounted upon a chariot drawn by blue vultures, born in the land of Saurāṣṭra, of the Kāśyapa lineage—[I invoke you].

Saying, "O Śanaiścara, come here," one should invoke Śanaiścara with blue *akṣata* grains into a metal image facing west, which is placed upon a seat two *aṅgulas* wide, shaped like a bow, and filled with blue *akṣata*, and then establish it with the words, "Be seated here."

For the verse beginning with *kayā na*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the metre is Gāyatrī, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Rāhu. *Oṃ kayā naści... vṛtā*. Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Blessed One, of fierce form, wearing a crown, with a formidable face, son of Siṃhikā, holding a sword, shield, and excellent trident in your four hands, wearing black garlands and garments, anointed with black perfumes, adorned with ornaments of *gomeda* gems, possessing a luster like a dark cloud, mounted upon a chariot drawn by black lions, born in the city of Rāṭhināpa, of the Paiṭhīnasi *gotra*, O Rāhu!

Saying "Come here," one should invoke Rāhu with black *akṣata* grains upon a seat in the southwest that is twelve finger-breadths in size, shaped like a winnowing basket, and filled with black *akṣata*; then, having invoked him upon a lead image facing south, one should establish him with the words, "Be seated here."

For the verse beginning with *ketuṃ kṛṇvan*, the deities are the Viśve Devās, the meter is Gāyatrī. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Ketu as a whole. *Oṃ ketuṃ kṛṇvanna... yathāḥ*. Bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ! O Blessed One, of fierce form, wearing a crown and holding a mace and a shield in your two hands, adorned with variegated garlands and garments, anointed with various fragrances and unguents, decorated with Vaiḍūrya ornaments, possessing a smoke-like luster, mounted upon a variegated pigeon-chariot, born from the Inner Altar (*antarvedi*), of the Jaimini lineage—O Ketu, come here! [Invoke him] in the northwest at a distance of six finger-breadths.

Upon a pedestal shaped like a banner and filled with various grains and unbroken rice, one should invoke the Ketu deity into a bell-metal image facing south that is likewise filled with various grains and unbroken rice, and install him with the words, "Come here, take your seat. Alternatively, the word *ketu* may be used in the plural; in that case, in the formula for recollecting the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, one should substitute "the Ketus" (*ketavaḥ*).

"O Blessed Ones, of fierce appearance, wearing crowns, holding maces in your hands, two-armed, wearing variegated garlands and garments, anointed with variegated perfumes, adorned with ornaments of lapis lazuli, possessing a smoke-like luster, mounted upon variegated pigeon-chariots, born of the Antarvedi region, and belonging to the lineage of Jaimini—come here! This is the modification (*ūha*) for the invocation formula. "Dwell here! is the modification for the installation formula.

Alternatively, the specific place and lineage (*deśagotra*) should be recited in every instance; if these are impossible, one may merely contemplate them. As stated, if the prescribed images cannot be obtained, all [the deities] should be made of gold; in their absence, they may be represented by heaps of rice and so forth. If the prescribed unbroken grains (*akṣata*) are unavailable, all [the offerings] should be white. Or, all the planetary deities (*graha*) should be installed facing the sun alone. Even in this case, the Sun should face the well-known eastern direction. Next, the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*):

For the mantra *tryambakam*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the Lord (Īśvara) is the deity, Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application is for the invocation of Īśvara in the complete Vyāhṛtis. Reciting "Oṃ tryambakaṃ yajāmahe... tāta," and "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, obeisance to Īśvara, I invoke Īśvara," one should [visualize] Īśvara on the right side of the Sun, five-faced, with three eyes in each face, mounted upon a bull, moon-crested, and bearing a skull, a trident, and a khaṭvāṅga staff.

For the verse beginning with "gaurīrmimāya," the deities are the Viśvedevas, the meter is Jagatī. The application (viniyoga) is for the invocation of Umā in its entirety: "Oṃ gaurīrmimāya... vyoman. Bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ; salutation to Umā, I invoke Umā. Thus, on the right side of Soma, one should visualize Umā, who is worshipped by the thirty gods, seated upon a white throne, preceded by a lion, and holding a rosary, a lotus, a mirror, and a water-pot.

For the verse *yadakrandaḥ*, Agni is the deity, Skanda is the subject, and the metre is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Skanda using the entire mantra. "Oṃ yadakrandaḥ... jātaṃ te arvan; bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; obeisance to Skanda; I invoke Skanda. Thus, on the right side of Aṅgāraka, one should visualize Skanda: six-faced, wearing red garments, adorned with a tuft of hair (*śikhaṇḍaka*), having a peacock as his vehicle, and four-armed. With his two right hands he holds a cock and a bell; with his two left hands he holds the Vaijayantī banner and a spear (*śakti*). This is Skanda.

For the mantra *viṣṇorarāṭam*, Soma is the deity, Viṣṇu is the seer, and the meter is Yajus; or it is a single-pada *nicṛd-gāyatrī* for the entire *vyāhṛti*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Viṣṇu: "Oṃ *viṣṇorarāṭam*... *tvā*. With the words "Salutation to Viṣṇu, I invoke Viṣṇu," one should invoke Viṣṇu on the right side of Budha—having the luster of a dark cloud, marked with the *śrīvatsa*, the *kaustubha* gem upon his chest, mounted upon Garuḍa, four-armed, and bearing the *kaumodakī* mace, lotus, conch, and discus. Alternatively, Nārāyaṇa is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*).

In this rite, for the verse beginning with *sahasraśīrṣā*, Prajāpati Nārāyaṇa is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Nārāyaṇa in his entirety. Reciting: *Oṃ sahasraśīrṣā... daśāṅgulam*, *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ*, "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa; I invoke Nārāyaṇa. Thus, on the right side of Budha, one should visualize Nārāyaṇa, who has the luster of a dark cloud, is marked with the Śrīvatsa, has the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, is mounted upon Garuḍa, possesses four arms, and holds the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus.

For the verse beginning with *brahmā devānām*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the seer is Brahmā, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Brahmā in its entirety. "Oṃ *brahmā devānāṃ*... *rebhan*. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. "Salutation to Brahmā; I invoke Brahmā. Thus, one should visualize Brahmā on the right side of Bṛhaspati: wearing a sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*), seated upon a lotus throne (*padmāsana*), with matted hair (*jaṭila*), four-faced, holding a rosary, a book, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), with a yellow garment and a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) placed at his side, and with a swan standing by his side.

For the verse beginning with *sajoṣā indra*, the deity is Soma, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Indra using the entire [mantra]. *Oṃ sajoṣā indra... to naḥ*. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. Salutation to Indra; I invoke Indra. Thus, on the right side of the Śukra [cup], one should visualize Indra, the Lord of Śacī, mounted upon a four-tusked elephant, holding a thunderbolt and a goad in his hands, and adorned with various ornaments.

For the verse beginning with *imaṃ yama*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Yama; the meter is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Yama (*yamāvāhana*). *Oṃ imaṃ yama prastaraṃ āsādayasva.* Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. "I invoke Yama, salutations to Yama. [One should meditate upon] Yama, who is slightly yellow at his side, two-armed, holding a staff and a noose, black in color, with red eyes, adorned with various ornaments, and mounted upon a buffalo. For the mantra beginning with *kārṣir asi*, the deity is Soma; the deity is Kāla; the meter is Yajus or Ekapadā Gāyatrī. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Kāla.

Reciting "Kārṣirasya... mṛdhram," "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ," and "Obeisance to Kāla; I invoke Kāla," one should [visualize] Kāla on the right side of Rāhu—having a terrifying face, ever-moving, with hair consisting of snakes and scorpions, and holding a noose and a staff in his hands.

For the verse beginning with *citrāvaso*, the seer is Prajāpati Citragupta; the metre is Yajus, or alternatively Ekapadā Jagatī. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Citragupta in its entirety. Reciting: "Oṃ citrāvaso svaśīya," and "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, obeisance to Citragupta; I invoke Citragupta"—one should invoke Citragupta on the right side of the banner (the *ketu*). He is to be visualized as having a northern (northerly) appearance, two arms, a pen in his right hand, and a leaf in his left hand, and possessing a gentle countenance. Thus one should invoke the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*) either upon golden images or upon heaps of unhusked rice (*akṣata*). Thus end the presiding deities.
Now, the secondary deities (*pratyadhidevatā*).

For the verse beginning with *agniṃ dūtam*, Prajāpati is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the Gāyatrī is the meter. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Agni in its entirety. *Oṃ agniṃ dūtaṃ vṛṇīmahe... sukratum*. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. "Salutation to Agni; I invoke Agni. [One should visualize] Agni on the northern side of the Sun: tawny-browed, bearded, with three tawny eyes, seated upon a goat, ruddy, possessing seven flames, holding a rosary and a spear, and granting boons.

For the verse beginning with *apsu me*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), the deity is Water (*āpaḥ*), the meter is Anuṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the complete invocation. "Oṃ *apsu me somo'vasthitaḥ*... *ṣajīḥ*. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. "Salutation to the Waters; I invoke the Waters. Thus, on the northern side of Soma, one should visualize the Waters in female form—white, riding upon sea-monsters (*makara*), adorned with pearl ornaments, and holding nooses and water-pots.

For the verse beginning with *syonā pṛthivī*, the deities are those of the sacrificial tradition (*yājñikya*), the Upaniṣads, the Earth, and the *Gāyatrī* meter. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of the Earth (*bhūmyāvāhane*). "Oṃ syonā pṛthivī... prathāḥ. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. "Salutation to the Earth; I invoke the Earth. [One should meditate upon] the Earth on the northern side of Mars: white in color, adorned with divine ornaments, four-armed, of gentle form, wearing garments resembling the fierce sun, holding a vessel of jewels, a vessel of grain, a vessel of medicinal herbs, and a lotus, seated upon the backs of elephants from the four directions.
Alternatively, one may utter the word *pṛthivī* instead of the word *bhūmi*.

For the mantra *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, Soma is the seer, Viṣṇu is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Viṣṇu as a whole: "O Viṣṇu, pervade this... and "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; salutations to Viṣṇu, I invoke Viṣṇu. Thus, on the northern side of the wise [image], one should visualize Viṣṇu, possessing the luster of a dark cloud, marked with the Śrīvatsa, bearing the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, mounted upon Garuḍa, four-armed, and holding the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus.

For the verse beginning with *indraṃ vaḥ*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) and Indra; the meter is *gāyatrī*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Indra as a whole. "Oṃ indraṃ vo viśvataḥ... kevalaḥ. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. "Salutation to Indra; I invoke Indra. Thus, on the northern side of Bṛhaspati, one should visualize Indra, the Lord of Śacī, mounted upon a four-tusked elephant, holding a thunderbolt and a goad in his hands, adorned with various ornaments.

For the verse beginning with "indrāṇīm," the deities are the Viśvedevas, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the application (viniyoga) is for the invocation of Indrāṇī: "Oṃ indrāṇī... patiḥ. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. Salutation to Indrāṇī; I invoke Indrāṇī. [One should meditate upon] Indrāṇī on the north-eastern side of Śukra, having two arms, adorned with various ornaments, wearing divine garments, anointed with white sandalwood paste, gentle in appearance, holding a cluster of *saṃtāna* flowers in her left hand, and granting boons.

For the verse beginning with "Prajāpate," the deities are the Viśvedevas and Prajāpati; the metre is Triṣṭubh. The application is for the invocation of Prajāpati in its entirety: "Oṃ Prajāpate na... rayīṇām. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Salutation to Prajāpati! I invoke Prajāpati. [Thus one should visualize] Prajāpati on the left side of Śanaiścara, wearing a sacred thread (yajñopavītin), seated upon a swan, having one face and four arms, holding a rosary, a sacrificial ladle (sruva), a book, and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).

For the mantra *ā'yaṃ gauḥ*, Agni, the serpents (*sarpas*), and the Gāyatrī are the deities. The application (*viniyoga*) for the complete [mantra] is in the invocation of the serpents: "Oṃ ā'yaṃ gauḥ pṛśniḥ... suvaḥ. Saying "Bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ, obeisance to the serpents (*sarpebhyaḥ*); I invoke the serpents," one should [visualize] the serpents on the northern side of Rāhu, holding rosaries, possessing tails shaped like water-pots (*kuṇḍikā*), and appearing fearsome with either a single coil or three coils.

For the verse beginning with *brahma jajñānam*, the deity is Agni, the Yājñikyas, or the Upaniṣads; the metre is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) for the invocation of Brahmā is as follows: "Oṃ *brahma jajñānaṃ*... *vivaḥ*. *Bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ*. "Salutation to Brahmā; I invoke Brahmā. [One should visualize] Brahmā on the north-eastern part of the sacrificial pole (*ketu*), wearing a sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*), seated upon a lotus throne, with matted hair (*jaṭila*), four-faced, holding a rosary, a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), a book, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), with a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) placed at his side.

[One should visualize] Brahmā with a swan situated at his side. Thus one should invoke the secondary deities (*pratyadhidevatās*) either into golden images or upon heaps of unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Alternatively, Agni and the others are the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*), while Īśvara and the others are the secondary deities. Or, the invocation of the respective presiding and secondary deities may take place immediately after the invocation of the respective planets. These are the secondary deities. Now, the deities who protect the sacrifice (*kratusaṃrakṣaṇadevatās*):

For the verse beginning with *gaṇānāṃ tvā*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the meter is Jagatī, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Gaṇapati: "Oṃ *gaṇānāṃ tvā gaṇapatiṃ...* sit down upon your seat. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. Salutation to Mahāgaṇapati, accompanied by Siddhi and Buddhi; I invoke Mahāgaṇapati, accompanied by Siddhi and Buddhi. To the north of Rāhu, one should [visualize] Gaṇeśa, who has the face of an elephant, rides a mouse, wears a sacred thread of serpents, has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, is joined by Siddhi and Buddhi, possesses four arms and three eyes, and holds a tusk, a rosary, an axe, and a sweetmeat (*modaka*).

For the verse beginning with *jātavedase*, the deities are those of the sacrificial tradition (*yājñikya*), the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) is Durgā, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) for the invocation of Durgā in its entirety is as follows: *Oṃ jātavedase sunavāma somam arātīyato ni dahāti vedaḥ | sa naḥ parṣad ati durgāṇi viśvā nāveva sindhuṃ duritāty agniḥ ||* *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.* "I bow to Durgā; I invoke Durgā. To the north of Śani [Saturn], one should invoke Durgā, the destroyer of the distress of Durgā, mounted upon a lion, possessing ten arms, and holding in her hands a spear, an arrow, a trident, a sword, a discus, the orb of the moon, a shield, a skull-bowl, a conch, and a battle-axe.

For the mantra *vāyo śatam*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Vāyu; the metre is Anuṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Vāyu in its entirety: "Oṃ vāyo śataṃ harīṇāṃ... pājatā. With *bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ*, [one says] "Salutation to Vāyu, I invoke Vāyu. Thus, to the north of Sūrya, one visualizes Vāyu, smoke-colored, with two arms, standing upon the back of a galloping deer, holding a banner in his hand and granting boons.

For the mantra *ghṛtaṃ ghṛtapāvānaḥ*, Soma is the deity, Ākāśa is the Yajus. The application (*viniyoga*) for the invocation of the totality [of the elements] is as follows: "Oṃ ghṛtaṃ ghṛtapā0 rikṣāya," *bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ*; "Salutation to Ākāśa, I invoke Ākāśa. Thus, to the right of Rāhu, one should invoke Ākāśa, who has the luster of a blue lotus, wears blue garments, is two-armed, gentle, beardless, and holds the moon and sun in his hands.

The verse *yā vāṃ kaśā*, addressed to the Aśvins, has Soma as its deity and Gāyatrī as its meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of the Aśvins in their entirety: "Oṃ yā vāṃ kaśā... kṣatam. Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! With the words "Salutation to the Aśvins; I invoke the Aśvins," one should visualize the two divine physicians, the Aśvins, to the right of the banner-post (*ketu*). They have two arms; their right hands hold divine medicinal herbs, and their left hands hold beautiful books. Their bodies are joined together, they are handsome and lovely to behold, and their sides are flanked by a pair of women with beautiful forms who hold jewel-ornaments and wear white garments like the moon. They are the physicians of the gods.

For the verse beginning with "vāstoṣpate," Prajāpati is the seer, Vāstoṣpati is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. The application (viniyoga) is for the invocation of Vāstoṣpati in its entirety: "Oṃ vāstoṣpate... catuṣpade. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Salutations to Vāstoṣpati; I invoke the venerable Vāstu-puruṣa to the north of Bṛhaspati—he who possesses great strength and prowess, whose body is the abode and refuge of all the gods, the son of Brahmā, the sustainer of the entire universe, and whose head bears the weight of the earth.

[One should meditate upon] Vāstoṣpati, who establishes the arrangement of cities, towns, palaces, pavilions, ponds, lakes, wells, and so forth; who bestows all perfections; who has a serene countenance; who is the sustainer of the universe; who is the supreme Puruṣa; who bears the discus and the Śārṅga bow; and whose hands grant boons and fearlessness.

For the verse beginning with *kṣetrasya patinā*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Kṣetrapāla, the meter is Anuṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Kṣetrapāla: "Oṃ kṣetrasya pati... tīdṛśe," *bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ*; "Salutation to Kṣetrapāla, I invoke Kṣetrapāla. To the north of Aṅgāraka (Mars), one should meditate upon [Kṣetrapāla] as dark-complexioned, three-eyed, with hair standing erect, possessing fine fangs, a face contorted by a frown, feet adorned with anklets, girt with a serpent-belt, having serpents for limbs, exceedingly fierce, and [wearing] a small bell.

One should visualize Kṣetrapāla, who holds a garland made of skulls reaching down to his ankles, bound with a serpent, possessing a beautiful face marked by a crescent moon, and having eight hands; his right hands hold a trident, a spear, a sword, and a drum, while his left hands hold a skull-cup, a bell, a shield, and a bow; he is terrifying, naked, and of immeasurable splendor.
Alternatively, one may install Gaṇapati and the other deities in the space between the Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, and Ketu, according to available space.
These are the deities who protect the sacrifice.
Now, for the World-Guardians (Lokapālas):

for the verse beginning with *trātāram indram*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, Indra is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Indra as a whole. "Oṃ trātāram indraṃ... tv indraḥ. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Salutation to Indra; I invoke Indra. [Thus one should visualize] from the sphere of light (*śukramaṇḍala*), Indra—the Lord of the Immortals, the protector of heaven—mounted upon Airāvata, holding a thunderbolt in his hand, golden-hued, thousand-eyed.

For the verse beginning with "agne naya," the deities are all the gods (Viśvedevas) and Agni; the metre is Triṣṭubh. Its application is in the invocation of Agni for the entire [rite]. Reciting: "Oṃ agne naya suvidatrebhiḥ... vidhema," and saying "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ, obeisance to Agni, I invoke Agni," one should visualize Agni coming from the lunar orb toward the southeast—golden-hued, possessing seven flames, seven hands, fond of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, having four horns, seven tongues, two heads, and three feet, mounted upon a ram, and holding a spear, food, a *sruc* ladle, a *sruva* spoon, a *tomara* lance, a fan, and a vessel of clarified butter.

For this [verse] beginning with *imaṃ yama*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Yama; the meter is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Yama in its entirety. "Oṃ imaṃ yama prastaraṃ āsadaḥ... mādayasva. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ!
