With the words "Salutation to Yama, I invoke Yama," one should invoke Yama from the orb of Aṅgāraka (Mars) to the south—one who holds a staff, is dear to Ilā, has a buffalo as his vehicle, is black in color, and bestows the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious actions.

For the verse beginning with *asunvantam*, Agni is the deity, Nirṛti is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of Nirṛti for the entire [rite]. "Oṃ *asunvantam*... *mastu*"; *bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ*, obeisance to Nirṛti, I invoke Nirṛti. From the orb of Rāhu, one should visualize Nirṛti in the southwest direction: blue in color, bearing a sword and a shield, mounted upon a man, with hair standing erect, deformed eyes, terrifying, and fond of Kālikā.

For the verse *tattvā yāmi*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Varuṇa; the metre is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Varuṇa in its entirety. *Oṃ tattvā yāmi... pramoṣīḥ*. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. Salutation to Varuṇa; I invoke Varuṇa. [One should visualize] Varuṇa, holding a serpent-noose, the Lord of Waters, adorned with white ornaments, beloved of the lotus-lake, mounted upon a crocodile, [seated] to the west of the orb of Śani.

For the verse beginning with *ā no niyudbhiḥ*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) and Vāyu; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Vāyu in its entirety: "Oṃ ā no niyudbhiḥ śati... sadā naḥ. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. "Salutation to Vāyu; I invoke Vāyu"—thus [one invokes] Vāyu from the circle of the banner (*ketumaṇḍala*), in the northwest direction, having the form of the world's measure, mounted upon a black deer, holding a golden staff, dark-complexioned, and beloved by Mohinī.

For the mantra *saṃ te payāṃsi*, the deity is Agni-Soma, the meter is Triṣṭubh. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Soma: "Oṃ *saṃ te payāṃsi... nidhiṣva*. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. Salutation to Soma; I invoke Soma. [Thus one invokes] Soma from the circle of Bṛhaspati—from the north—white in color, mounted upon a deer, holding a mace in his hand, and fond of Rohiṇī.

Regarding the side of Kubera: [one should meditate on] Kubera, mounted upon a horse, spear in hand, lord of treasures, golden-hued, the giver of wealth, handsome, the sovereign, and beloved of Citriṇī. According to the rule of Aindrī, the mantra is the same; or alternatively, the mantra is "rājādhirājāya. For this mantra, the seers are the Āruṇas, the deity is Kubera, and the meter is Jagatī; thus the seers and other details should be understood. This mantra should be seen as ending with "namaḥ."

For the verse beginning with *abhi tvā*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), the lord (*īśāna*), and the meter is *gāyatrī*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation of the entire [deity] Īśāna: "Oṃ *abhi tvā deva*... *mīmahe*. *Bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ*. I invoke Īśāna—Īśāna who is like pure crystal, mounted upon a bull, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a trident, and a rosary, five-faced, three-eyed, adorned with various ornaments, the beloved of Pārvatī—from the circle of the intellect (*budhamaṇḍala*) in the northeast.

Thus, one should invoke the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) into the images or into piles of unbroken rice. Alternatively, the ritual application may be as follows: having invoked them into [the icons of] Īśvara and the others with the words "Come here," one performs the installation with the words "Be seated here.
Then: "O protector of men, guard my progeny for the sake of immortality and life—those already born and those yet to be born, established in immortality and truth."

(Thus, having installed all the deities, one should worship them either by the method of *kāṇḍānusamaya* or by the method of *padārthānusamaya*. The *kāṇḍānusamaya* consists in completing the entire worship of one deity before proceeding to the next. The *padārthānusamaya*, however, consists in performing the invocation for all the deities and then offering each respective article of worship to each one in sequence. This is the specific procedure for the worship of the planets: garments of the colors of the planets; red sandalwood for the Sun; white sandalwood for the Moon.)

Red sandalwood for Mars; sandalwood mixed with saffron for Mercury; likewise sandalwood mixed with saffron for Jupiter; white sandalwood for Venus; agallochum for Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu; red *karavīra* for the Sun; white *karavīra* for the Moon; red lotus for Mars; *campaka* flower for Mercury; *agastya* flower for Jupiter; *atasī* flower for Venus; *kālāñjanī* flower for Saturn; mustard flower for Rāhu; and *śaṅkhinī* flower for Ketu.

One should offer the incense of *sallakī* resin to Rāhu; to Soma, the incense of unbroken rice grains mixed with clarified butter; to Bhauma, the incense of *sarjarasa*, commonly known as *sāraphalī*; to Budha, the incense of *agaru*; to Guru, the incense of the substance *sihlaka*, commonly known as *lohabāṇa*; to Śukra, the incense of *agaru* combined with the resin of the *bilva* fruit; to Śani, the incense of *guggulu*; and to Rāhu and Ketu, the incense of lac. A lamp fed with clarified butter is for all of them.

In the absence of the aforementioned sandalwood and flowers, one should use whatever sandalwood and so forth possesses those same colors. In the absence of garments, perfumes, and flowers of those respective colors, white ones are to be used. In the absence of the aforementioned incense, guggulu is to be used; in its absence as well, any fragrant substance whatsoever may be used.

One should offer jaggery-rice (*guḍaudana*) to Rāhu; milk-porridge mixed with ghee (*ghṛtayuktapāyasa*) to Soma; sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*) to Bhauma; milk-porridge of *ṣaṣṭika* rice to Budha; curd-rice (*dadhyodana*) to Guru; ghee-rice (*ghṛtaudana*) to Śukra; food mixed with sesame and black gram (*tilamāṣamiśrita*) to Śani; rice mixed with salt and milk (*lavaṇamiśrakṣīrayukta*) to Rāhu; and rice mixed with red flour, salt, goat’s milk, sesame, and rice (*āraktapiṣṭayutalavaṇamiśrajākṣīrayutatilataṇḍulamiśrita*) to Ketu.
In the absence of these, the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of rice colored according to each planet's respective color, or ghee-rice (*ghṛtaudana*).

[One should offer] grapes to Ravi; sugarcane to Soma; betel nuts (*pūga*) to Bhauma; oranges (*nāriṅga*) to Budha; citron fruits (*jambīra*) to Guru; *bījapūra* fruits to Śukra; dates (*kharjūra*) to Śani; coconuts (*nārikela*) to Rāhu; and pomegranates (*dāḍima*) to Ketu.
In the absence of the aforementioned fruits, one may offer coconut fruits or date fruits.
If available, a canopy (*vitāna*) adorned with fruits and flowers should also be offered.

These same ritual offerings apply to the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) and their secondary deities (*pratyadhidevatā*). However, for Gaṇapati and others, only white sandalwood paste is used; the flowers are exclusively *śatapatra* (hundred-petaled) lotuses; and the incense is exclusively *guggulu*. The lamp is of cow-ghee. The food offering (*naivedya*) consists of rice cooked with ghee. If *śatapatra* flowers are unavailable, any available flower may be used. As for the fruit, it should be understood that either coconut or dates (*kharjūra*) are appropriate.

Then, in the northeast or the north of the pedestal and so forth, having touched the earth with the mantra "mahī dyauḥ," and having fashioned a lotus-design with colored powders (*raṅgavallī*) there, and having placed a heap of grain measuring one *prastha* there with the mantra "oṣadhayaḥ saṃvadante," he should establish a water-pot (*kalaśa*)—new, without cracks, made of metal or clay, smeared with sandalwood paste, adorned with curd, unbroken rice, flowers, garlands, and so forth, its neck wrapped with three threads—with the mantra "tatrā'jighra. Having filled it with water using the mantra "imaṃ me," [he recites] "āpyāyasva"; its deity is Agni.

The Soma mantra, the Gāyatrī, is employed for the pouring of milk: "Oṃ āpyāyasva sametu te viśvataḥ somavṛṣṇiyam | bhavā vājasya saṃgathe. Having poured milk into the pitcher with this, [one uses] the Dadhikrāvan mantra; its deities are the Viśvedevas, its seer is Dadhikrāvan, and its meter is Anuṣṭubh. It is employed for the pouring of curd: "Oṃ dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣaṃ0 tāripat. Having poured curd into the pitcher with this, ...

The deity of the mantra *śukram asi* is Prajāpati; the meter is Yajus; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the pouring of clarified butter (*ājya*). Having poured clarified butter into the pitcher with the mantra: *oṃ śukram asi jyotir asi tejo 'si*, [one proceeds].

For the three mantras beginning with *madhu vātāḥ*, the deities are Agni and the Viśvedevas; the meter is Gāyatrī; their application is for the pouring of honey (*madhu*). Having poured honey into the pitcher with the mantra: *oṃ madhu vātā... bhavantu naḥ*.

For the verse *tve kratum*, Soma is the seer, Prajāpati is the deity, and the Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the casting of pebbles: having cast pebbles into the pitcher with "Oṃ tve kratum api... yodhi," [one proceeds].

For the Gāyatrī verse *tatsavitur*, Viśvāmitra is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity, and the Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is in the casting of cow-urine: having cast cow-urine into the pitcher with "Oṃ tatsavitur... yāt," [one proceeds].

For the mantra *gandhadvārām*, the deities are those of the sacrificial tradition (*yājñikya*), the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), the goddess Śrī, and the meter is Anuṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the scattering of cow-dung: having scattered cow-dung into the pitcher with "Oṃ *gandhadvārāṃ*... [grant] *śriyam*," and then having poured milk, curd, and ghee into the pitcher with the three mantras beginning with "*āpyāyasva*," one should silently scatter the minerals from a newly brought, variegated mountain. For the mantra *uddhṛtā'si varāheṇa*, the deities are those of the sacrificial tradition, the secret doctrine, the earth (*mṛttikā*), and the meter is Anuṣṭubh.

The application (*viniyoga*) for the casting of the seven types of earth is as follows: Reciting "Oṃ, you were lifted up by the black boar with a hundred [tusks]... one should cast into the pitcher seven types of earth brought from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, an anthill, a river-confluence, a lake, the gate of a royal palace, and a cow-pen. Then, for the casting of fragrance, reciting "Gandhadvārām..."—where the deities are the sacrificial ones, the *upaniṣads*, and Śrī; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*; the application is for the casting of fragrance—one should cast fragrance into the pitcher with "Gandhadvārā... śriyam. Then [reciting] "The medicinal herbs that were born... [the herbs are to be cast].

For this [verse], the deity is Agni, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the scattering of medicinal herbs: "Oṃ yā jātā o... sapta ca. One should simultaneously cast into the jar the ten medicinal herbs consisting of *kuṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, the two types of *haridrā*, *murā*, *śaileya*, *candana*, *saṭī*, *campaka*, and *mustā*.

Kuṣṭha is *koṣṭha*. Māṃsī is *jaṭāmāṃsī*. Haridrā is well known; the second is *dāruharidrā*, which is well known in Paraśurāma-kṣetra as *murā* or *moravela*. Śaileya is *śilārasa*. Candana is well known. Saṭī is *kacorā*. Campaka is the bark of the *campaka* tree. Mustā is *bhadramothā*. In the absence of these, [one may use] *śatāvarī*. As for the mantra, it is the very same one used for the five jewels (*pañcaratna*).

For the verse *kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt*, Agni is the deity, the plants (*oṣadhayaḥ*) are the subject, and the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter; its application (*vi.*) is in the casting of *dūrvā* grass into the jar. Reciting *oṃ kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt... śatena ca*, one should cast *dūrvā* grass into the jar. For the verse *aśvatthe vaḥ*, Agni is the deity, the plants (*oṣadhayaḥ*) are the subject, and the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter; its application (*vi.*) is in the casting of the five barks (*pañcatvak*). Reciting *oṃ aśvatthe vaḥ... pūruṣam*, one should simultaneously cast the barks of the *nyagrodha*, *pippala*, *plakṣa*, *jambū*, and *cūta* trees into the jar. Alternatively, the *udumbara* may be used in place of the *jambū*.

For the verse *aśvatthe vo* (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.2.6.5), Agni is the deity, the plants are the subject, and the Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*vi*) is in the casting of five twigs (*pañcapallava*). One should cast the twigs of these very trees together into the pitcher with the mantra: *oṃ aśvatthe... pūruṣam*. For the verse *yāḥ phalinīḥ* (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.2.6.5), Agni is the deity, the plants are the subject, and the Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application is in the casting of five twigs. Having cast fruit into the pitcher with the mantra: *oṃ yāḥ phalinīḥ... hasaḥ*, for the verse *agne retaścandram* (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.2.6.5), Agni is the deity, gold (*hiraṇya*) is the subject, and the Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application is in the casting of gold. Having cast gold into the pitcher with the mantra: *oṃ agne retaḥ... reyam*,

For the verse *bṛhaspate juṣasva naḥ*, Agni and Bṛhaspati are the deities and Gāyatrī is the meter. For the rite of casting the five jewels (*pañcaratna-prakṣepa*), one should recite: "Oṃ bṛhaspate juṣasva naḥ... dāśuṣe" and cast the five jewels consisting of gold, silver, pearl, ruby, and coral. In the absence of these, one should cast gold into the pitcher.

Then, having covered the mouth of the jar with *dūrvā* grass and mango sprouts, one should perform the following: for the verse "yuvaṃ vastrāṇi," the deities are the Viśvedevas and Mitra-Varuṇa, the meter is Triṣṭubh; its application (*viniyoga*) is in wrapping the jar with a pair of cloths: "Oṃ yuvaṃ vastrāṇi sacethe. Having thus wrapped the jar with a pair of white cloths, one should place a vessel full of rice on the mouth of the jar: for the verse "pūrṇā darvi parāpata," the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Śatakratu (Indra), and the meter is Anuṣṭubh; its application is in placing the vessel full of rice upon the mouth of the jar: "pūrṇā darvi... śatakrato. Thus one should place the vessel full of rice on the mouth of the jar.

Then—having invoked the deities into the pitcher with: "O you who dwell at the mouth of the pitcher... all the oceans... the Rakas; O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and so forth, take up your residence in this water," and having worshipped them, one should invoke Varuṇa with the mantra "tattvā yāmi" and worship him. Then:
"When the great ocean was being churned during the conflict between the gods and the Dānavas..."
Then, O Kumbha, you were born, personally sustained by Viṣṇu himself.
In you reside all sacred fords; all the gods are established in you.
In you abide all beings; in you are the vital breaths firmly rooted.
You alone are Śiva himself; you are Viṣṇu and Prajāpati;
you are the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Viśvedevas, and the Pitṛs.
Since all [the gods] abide in you, bestowing the fruits of their desires,
I desire to perform this sacrifice through your grace, O Lotus-born One.
"O Lord of Devas, grant your presence; be forever gracious"—thus one should pray.

Then—of the three mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the deities are Agni and the Viśvedevas or the Waters; the metre is Gāyatrī. Of the four mantras beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, the deity is Agni and the Waters; the metre is Triṣṭubh. For the mantras of the *Pavamāna-anuvāka*, Soma is the seer (*ṛṣi*). The deities are Pavamāna, Suvarjana, and others. The metres are Anuṣṭubh and so forth. The application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation (*japa*): "Oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā... (3), "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ... (4), and "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ... (17). One should recite these while touching the established water-pot (*kalaśa*).

In the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), this recitation (*japa*) must be performed by the preceptor himself. In the case of obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rites, if he is unable to do so himself, he should appoint another Brāhmaṇa learned in the mantras, honor him, and have the recitation performed by him. For the purpose of reciting the mantras of the nine planets (*navagraha*) upon the planetary pedestal (*grahapīṭha*), one should appoint three Brāhmaṇas or a single Brāhmaṇa, honor them, and have the recitation performed. The number of recitations related to the water-pot (*kalaśa*) is either one hundred and eight or twenty-eight. The recitation of the planetary mantras is likewise performed for each individual mantra. Now follows the ritual preparation of the fire (*anvādhāna*).

The teacher, having taken up the three types of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), performed the rites beginning with "Come, O Faith" (*śraddha ehi*) and ending with the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then, having recited the formula beginning with "The deities who are to be sacrificed to in the *grahayajña* homa-rite... and ending either with the goddess Prasādhanī or with the *vyāhṛtis*, he should say: "I shall sacrifice to Gaṇapati with one oblation of a *palāśa* fuel-stick, an oblation of cooked rice (*caru*), and an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*). Alternatively, he may say: "I shall sacrifice with an oblation of cooked rice alone, or with an oblation of clarified butter alone. This applies when the reading is "the first is the excellent oblation" (*prathamā tu varāhutiḥ*).

However, in the reading "the first is the excellent oblation" (*prathamā tu varāhutiḥ*), at the conclusion of the enumeration of the *anvādhāna* for the secondary deities of the *ketu*, one should say: "I shall worship Gaṇapati with the first excellent oblation of fuel-sticks (*samit*), parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*"; or, "I shall worship him with a single abundant oblation consisting either of boiled rice alone or of clarified butter alone. The quality of being "excellent" (*vara*) means having a measure double the standard or a measure increased by half. Regarding the fuel-stick, this doubling or increase by half refers specifically to its length;
for there is a scriptural prohibition against the fault of placing two fuel-sticks at once without an explicit statement to that effect.

In the principal Vaiśeṣika oblation: to Sūrya, Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu—with this number [of items] each, respectively, using fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of arka and so forth, that many oblations of cooked rice (*caru*), and that many oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). In place of the word "this" (*etat*), one should recite one thousand and eight, one hundred and eight, or twenty-eight.

Īśvara, Umā, Skanda, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Indra, Yama, Kāla, and Citragupta—these are the presiding deities (adhidevatās). Agni, Apas, Bhūmi, Viṣṇu, Indra, Indrāṇī, Prajāpati, Sarpas, and Brahmā—these are the secondary presiding deities (pratyadhidevatās). With these respective numbers of sacrificial woods such as *arka* and others, with that same number of oblations of ground rice (*caru*), and with that same number of oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*).
In place of the word "this" (etad), one should recite for each principal deity a number less than that which was previously mentioned—either one hundred and eight, twenty-eight, or eight.

One should [worship] Gaṇapati, Durgā, Vāyu, Ākāśa, the two Aśvins, Vāstoṣpati, Kṣetrapāla, Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna with these respective numbers of *palāśa* fuel-sticks (*samidh*), that many oblations of cooked rice (*caru*), and that many oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). In place of the word "this" (*etat*), one should mention the number of the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) and the counter-presiding deities (*pratyadhidevatā*) as it was proclaimed; however, one may mention a number lower than that—namely twenty-eight, eight, or four.

The oblation for the presiding and secondary deities (*adhipratyadhidevatā*) shall be one-tenth of the number of primary oblations (*pradhānāhuti*). Alternatively, for the deities who protect the ritual action (*karmasaṃrakṣaṇadevatā*), it shall be one-twentieth for each deity. According to this alternative method, there are two specific numbers—either one thousand or one hundred—for each of the primary deities; however, these numbers are not increased by eight (i.e., they are not *aṣṭottara*), nor is there any possibility here of applying the one-tenth or one-twentieth portions of the number twenty-eight.

If the number of principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) is one thousand, then there shall be one hundred for each of the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) and sub-presiding deities (*pratyadhidevatā*), and ten for each of the deities who protect the ritual action (*karmasaṃrakṣaṇadevatā*). If the number of principal oblations is one hundred, then there shall be ten for each of the presiding and sub-presiding deities, and five for each of the deities who protect the ritual action; such is the distinction.

Regarding the deities of the *sarvatobhadra* pedestal, since the oblation must be performed immediately after the principal offerings in the case where the worship is not followed by a subsequent homa, the *anvādhāna* (the formal preparation of the fire) should be performed here as previously described.
Then, in the *aṅga-homa*, one offers to Varuṇa with two oblations, and so forth, according to the view that ends with the *vyāhṛti* offerings;
however, according to the view that ends with the *prasādhanī-devī*, one says, "I shall sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with one oblation of the remnants," and so forth.

At the time of setting out the vessels (*pātrāsādana*), the following must be set out and sprinkled with water: the sacrificial ladles (*darvī*) together with the right hands of those who will perform the *caru* oblations; the *sruva* spoons equal in number to those performing the *ājya* oblations; the vessel for taking up the *caru*; and the *ājya*-pots equal in number to those performing the *ājya* oblations. The cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) of the hands and the *sruvas* must also be performed. The hands that have been set out should remain in that very place until their cleansing; after the cleansing, they should be placed upon the sacred grass (*barhis*). Alternatively, these ritual requirements may be observed without the act of setting them out at all.

In place of the *sruva* ladle, there may be as many *darvī* spoons as required. Having cooked each *caru* or the *caru* collectively according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* to be described below, one must perform the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) of all the hands and *sruvas*—and of the *darvīs* if the *darvī* option is adopted—in order to facilitate the simultaneous performance of the *caru* and *ājya* oblations by multiple officiants.

Alternatively, at the very time of the *homa*, those performing the *caru* and *samidh* oblations should sprinkle their own right hands with water using their left hands, heat them over the fire, wipe them with a portion of the *saṃmārjana* grass placed to the side using the left hand, heat them again, set them down upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and then discard the *saṃmārjana* grass from their respective hands using the right hands alone. In the case of offering *caru* to each deity individually, there should be as many *caru*-pots and as many stirring-spoons (*mekṣaṇa*) as there are deities.

In the case of cooking them together in one vessel, one should draw out each portion separately and perform the *homa* for each respective deity. At the time of the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire), the clarified butter (*ājya*) is to be circumambulated along with all the sacrificial materials. Then, having poured clarified butter over the cooked rice-porridge (*caru*), having removed it to the north, and having placed it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), one should pour it into the vessels used for drawing out the porridge that were already placed there; if only one *caru* is used, one should pour it into a single drawing-vessel.

In the case of a single *caru*, one should divide it into rows according to each deity; the oblation (*homa*) is performed in that very order. Thereafter, one should perform the rites from the sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) up to the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī, or up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, in accordance with the specific option mentioned during the preliminary assignment (*anvādhāna*). Since it is currently impossible to cook the *caru* in this fire, the learned now perform the oblation using food prepared at home, which has been consecrated by the *devapavitra* purification.

Then, for the verse beginning with *gaṇānāṃ tvā*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Gaṇapati, and the meter is Jagatī. For the oblation (*homa*), [the procedure is]: "Oṃ *gaṇānāṃ tvā gaṇapatiṃ...* [svāhā]"—with this, he offers one *palāśa* fuel-stick (*samidh*). The renunciation (*tyāga*) is: "To Gaṇapati, not to me. In the same way, he offers one oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) and one oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*). The renunciation is as before.

According to the statement, "One should offer fuel-sticks, food, and clarified butter separately one hundred and eight times each," since it is stated that one should "offer" even in the case of fuel-sticks, the utterance of *svāhā* here follows the Smṛti tradition.

There, the officiating priests (ṛtvij), having sat down facing either north or east, having sipped water twice (dvirācamya), with their hair unbound, their knees bent, their minds attentive, and their speech restrained, should perform the oblation (homa). Before the commencement of the oblation, the traditional teachers (sāṃpradāyikāḥ) maintain that the sacrificer (yajamāna) should perform the renunciation of the materials (dravyatyāga), thinking: "These sacrificial materials (havanīyadravya) prepared here, sufficient for the number of oblations specified in the anvādhāna, are relinquished by me to whichever deities are to be worshipped; they are not mine."

If the fire-kindling (anvādhāna) for the oblations to the deities of the mandala was performed prior to the fire-kindling for the principal oblations, the preceptor himself should perform the oblation here in this manner.

Then the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) shall perform the oblation (*homa*) with the substances specified in the *anvādhāna* ritual, according to the number mentioned in that *anvādhāna*, preceded by the recollection of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes using the respective mantras prescribed for the invocation (*āvāhana*). (In this context, it should be noted as a distinction that in the statement of application (*viniyoga-vākya*), the phrase "application to the oblation" [*home viniyogaḥ*] is to be understood. The sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) for the planets are, in order: *arka*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *apāmārga*, *pippala*, *udumbara*, *śamī*, *dūrvā*, and *kuśa*. In the absence of these, *palāśa* fuel-sticks are to be used.

Therein, fuel-sticks (*samidh*) smeared with clarified butter, honey, and curd—measuring one span (*prādeśa*) in length, devoid of intermediate branches, and leaving a space of two finger-breadths from the base—should be offered after grasping them with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb. In this regard, there is one fuel-stick for *dūrvā* grasses and three blades each for *darbha* grasses. *Dūrvā* blades should be taken as unbroken, possessing either seven or five leaflets. *Darbha* blades should have their tips intact. The clarified butter (*ājya*) is to be offered using the sacrificial ladle (*darvī*) alone.

The traditionalists maintain that one should take a mouthful of the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the tip of the thumb, press it down with the thumb, and offer it while the right hand has its fingers joined and is turned palm-upward.

When the principal *homa* is completed, if the *anvādhāna* for the *pīṭha-devatā-homa* was performed here, then having performed its *homa* at this point and having conducted the subsequent worship (*uttara-pūjana*) of the installed deities, he should pray to them, saying, "May you be gracious," and then perform the *vāruṇī-homa* and so forth, or the *sviṣṭakṛt-homa* and so forth, prior to the *saṃsrāva-homa*, according to the method specified during the *anvādhāna*. There is no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for the *samidhs*.

Then the sacrificer, together with his wife, having sat down either behind the fire or in whichever place the offering of the *bali* is to be performed, should present *bali* offerings of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) along with lamps to the guardians of the quarters (*dikpāla*) in the directions surrounding the fire-altar. With each presentation of a *bali*, he should pour water mixed with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) into a vessel.

For the hymn beginning with *trātāram indram*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Indra, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Indra: *Oṃ trātāram indram avitāram indraṃ have-have suhavaṃ śūram indram / hvayāmi śakraṃ puruhūtam indraṃ svasti no maghavā dhātv indraḥ //* "I offer this oblation of black gram and rice flour (*māṣabhakta-bali*) together with a lamp, accompanied by grains of rice and water poured into the vessel, to Indra, along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*). O Indra, eat the oblation! Protect the quarter! Be the bestower of long life, the bestower of security, the bestower of peace, the bestower of nourishment, and the bestower of contentment to me and my family."
One should pray: "O Giver of Boons, be the remover of obstacles. Then one should say: "May Indra be pleased by this offering of the *bali*. For the mantra "O Agni, lead us...

(*agne naya*), the deities are the Viśvedevas, the meter is *triṣṭubh*, and its application is in the offering of the *bali* for the sake of pleasing Agni. "Oṃ agne naya supathā rāye asmān viśvāni deva vayunāni vidvān | yuyodhy asmad juhurāṇam eno bhūyiṣṭhāṃ te namaktiṃ vidhema ||" "I offer this *bali* of black gram and rice flour, together with a lamp, to Agni, along with his limbs, his retinue, his weapons, and his powers. "O Agni, [be present]. May Agni be pleased."

For this [verse] beginning with *imaṃ yama*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), the metre is *triṣṭubh*, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Yama: *Oṃ imaṃ yama ya*. To Yama, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*), I offer this oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) accompanied by a lamp. May [the deity] be pleased; may Yama be gratified.

For the verse beginning with *asunvantam*, Agni is the deity, Nirṛti is the seer, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Nirṛti: *Oṃ asunvantamaya0 mastu*. Having offered water along with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), saying: "I offer this oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣa-bhakta*) together with a lamp to Nirṛti, along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*)," one should say: "O Nirṛti, may you be pleased; may Nirṛti be gratified."

For the verse beginning with *tattvā yāmi*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Varuṇa; the metre is Triṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Varuṇa: *Oṃ tattvā yāmi brahmaṇā vandamānas tad āśāste yajamāno havirbhiḥ | aheḍamāno varuṇeha bodhy uruśaṃsa mā na āyuḥ pra moṣīḥ ||* "I offer this oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) together with a lamp to Varuṇa, along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*). Having cast water with unbroken rice grains (*sākṣata*), [one says]: 'O Varuṇa! O Bhava! May Varuṇa be pleased.'"

For the verse beginning with *ā no niyudbhiḥ*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) and Vāyu; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the oblation (*balidāna*) for the purpose of pleasing Vāyu: *Oṃ ā no niyudbhiḥ...* [recite the verse] ...*dānaḥ*. "I offer this oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) together with a lamp to Vāyu, along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*). Having thus offered water with unbroken rice grains (*sākṣata*), say: "O Vāyu! O Bhava! May Vāyu be pleased."

For the verse *saṃ te payāṃsi*, the deity is Agni, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the purpose of pleasing Soma: "Oṃ *saṃ te payāṃsi...* [dhiṣva]. I offer this oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣa-bhakta*) together with a lamp to Soma, along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*). Having thus cast water with unbroken rice grains (*sākṣata*), one says: 'O Soma! Be pleased! May Soma be gratified!'"

For the verse beginning with *abhi tvā*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), the lord is Īśāna, and the meter is Gāyatrī. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of a sacrificial oblation (*balidāna*) for the propitiation of Īśāna: *Oṃ abhi tvā deva... mīmahe.* "I offer this oblation of black gram and rice flour (*māṣabhakta*) together with a lamp to Īśāna, along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*). Having thus cast water with unbroken grains (*sākṣata*), one says: "O Īśāna! O Bhava! May Īśāna be pleased. Then follow the oblations for the planets (*graha*) and others near the planetary pedestal (*grahapīṭha*).

For the verse beginning with *ā satyena*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Savitṛ; the meter is Triṣṭubh; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the purpose of pleasing Sūrya: *Oṃ ā satyena rajasā paśyan*. To Sūrya, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and the counter-presiding deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) in the form of Īśvara and Agni, I offer this oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) along with a lamp.

"O Sūrya, accept this offering; be the bestower of long life, the provider of security, the bringer of peace, the provider of nourishment, the bringer of contentment, the remover of obstacles, and the granter of boons to me and my family"—thus one should pray. By this, may Sūrya be pleased.

For the verse beginning with *āpyāyasva*, Soma is the deity, Soma is the seer, and Gāyatrī is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of a bali-oblation for the propitiation of Soma: *Āpyāyasva same saṃgathe*. To Soma, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and the secondary deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) Umā, I offer this bali-oblation of black gram flour and rice with a lamp. O Soma! O Bhava! May Soma be pleased. For the verse beginning with *agnimūrddhā*, Prajāpati is the seer, Aṅgāraka (Mars) is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter.

The application for the offering of the *bali* for the propitiation of Aṅgāraka: "Oṃ agnirmūrdhā... jinvati. To Aṅgāraka, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and the secondary deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) in the forms of Skanda and Bhūmi, I offer this *bali* of black gram flour and lamps. O Aṅgāraka, accept this! May Aṅgāraka be pleased! May Aṅgāraka be pleased!

For the mantra *udbudhyasva*, Agni Budha is the deity and Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Budha: *Udbudhyasva... etam*. To Budha, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and the counter-deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) who are the forms of Nārāyaṇa-Viṣṇu, I offer this oblation of black gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) along with a lamp. O Budha, accept this [oblation]! May Budha be pleased!

For the verse beginning with *bṛhaspate atīti*, the deities are all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), the seer is Bṛhaspati, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Bṛhaspati: *Oṃ bṛhaspate citram.* I offer this oblation of black gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) together with a lamp to Bṛhaspati, who is accompanied by his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*), and who is joined by the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and the counter-presiding deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) in the form of Brahmā and Indra. O Bṛhaspati, accept this [oblation]... [may it be] auspicious. May Bṛhaspati be pleased.

For the mantra *śukraṃ ta*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Śukra, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Śukra: *Oṃ śukra te anya0 rastu*. To Śukra, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and the secondary deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) in the form of Indra and Indrāṇī, I offer this oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) along with a lamp. O Śukra, accept this [oblation]! May Śukra be pleased!

For the mantra *śaṃ no devīḥ*, the seer is Prajāpati, the deity is Śanaiścara, and the meter is Gāyatrī. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Śanaiścara: *Oṃ śaṃ no devīrabhiṣṭaya āpo bhavantu pītaye, śaṃ yorabhi sravantu naḥ.* I offer this oblation of black gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) together with a lamp to Śanaiścara, along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and the secondary deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) who are Yama and Prajāpati. O Śanaiścara! O Bhava! May Śani be pleased.

For the verse beginning with *kayā na*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Rāhu. *Oṃ kayā naścitra ā bhuvad ūtī sadāvṛdhaḥ sakhā | kayā śaciṣṭhayā vṛtā ||* To Rāhu, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and the secondary deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) in the form of the Black Serpent (*kālasarpa*), I offer this oblation of black gram and rice flour along with a lamp. O Rāhu! O Bhava! May Rāhu be pleased.

For the mantra *ketuṃ kṛṇvan*, Prajāpati is the seer, Ketu is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Ketu. *Oṃ ketuṃ kṛṇvannaketave0 jāyathāḥ*. To Ketu, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by his presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) Citragupta in the form of Brahmā and his sub-deity (*pratyadhidevatā*), I offer this oblation of black gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) along with a lamp. O Ketu, accept this oblation; may Ketu be pleased.

In the view that the word *ketu* takes the plural ending, [one says]: "To the *Ketus*, together with their limbs (*sāṅga*), retinues (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) and sub-deities (*pratyadhidevatā*) in the form of Brahmā—unto you I offer this *bali* of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) along with a lamp. O *Ketus*, accept this *bali*; be the bestowers of long life, security, peace, nourishment, contentment, and freedom from obstacles for me and my family; be granters of boons. The modification (*ūha*) is: "By this offering of *bali*, may the *Ketus* be gratified."

For the verse beginning with *gaṇānāṃ tvā*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the meter is Jagatī, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Gaṇapati. *Oṃ gaṇānāṃ tvā... sādanam*. To Gaṇapati, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by Siddhi and Buddhi, I offer this oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) along with a lamp. O Gaṇapati, accompanied by Siddhi and Buddhi, accept this [offering]. May Gaṇapati be pleased.

For the verse beginning with *jātavedase*, the deities are those of the sacrificial tradition (*yājñikya*), the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) is Durgā, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the offering of a sacrifice (*balidāna*) for the propitiation of Durgā. "Oṃ jātavedase sunavāma... [The deity is] Agni. To Durgā, together with her limbs (*sāṅgāyai*), together with her retinue (*saparivārāyai*), together with her weapons (*sāyudhāyai*), and together with her powers (*saśaktikāyai*), I offer this oblation of black gram and rice flour accompanied by a lamp. O Durgā, accept this oblation; be the bestower of long life, prosperity, peace, nourishment, contentment, and the removal of obstacles to my family, and be the granter of boons. May Durgā be pleased.

For the verse beginning with "vāyo śatam," the deities are the Viśvedevas and Vāyu, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the application is for the offering of the *bali* (oblation) for the propitiation of Vāyu. "Oṃ vāyo śataṃ... pājasā. I offer this *māṣa-bhakta* oblation along with a lamp to Vāyu, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*). O Vāyu, accept this oblation! May Vāyu be pleased.

For the mantra *ghṛtaṃ ghṛtapāvānaḥ*, Soma is the deity, Ākāśa (Space) is the *yajuḥ*, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the purpose of pleasing Ākāśa. *Oṃ ghṛtaṃ ghṛtapā0 kṣāya*. I offer this oblation of black-gram flour with a lamp to Ākāśa, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*). O Ākāśa, accept this oblation; may Ākāśa be pleased.

The verse *yā vāṃ kaśā* is addressed to the Aśvins; its meter is Gāyatrī. It is employed for the offering of the oblation (*balidāna*) for the purpose of pleasing the Aśvins. "Oṃ *yā vāṃ kaśā... bhikṣatam*. To the two Aśvins, together with their limbs (*sāṅga*), their retinues (*saparivāra*), their weapons (*sāyudha*), and their powers (*saśaktika*), I offer this oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta-bali*). O Aśvins, accept this oblation! Be the bestowers of long life, security, peace, nourishment, contentment, and freedom from obstacles upon me and my family; be granters of boons. By this offering of the oblation, may the two Aśvins be pleased."

The mantra beginning with *vāstoṣpate* has Prajāpati as its seer (*ṛṣi*), Vāstoṣpati as its deity, and the Triṣṭubh as its meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Vāstoṣpati. Recite: *Oṃ vāstoṣpate... catuṣpade*. "I offer this oblation of black gram and rice flour (*māṣabhakta-bali*) together with a lamp to Vāstoṣpati, along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), retinue (*saparivāra*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and powers (*saśaktika*). O Vāstoṣpati, accept this oblation! May Vāstoṣpati be pleased. If the oblation is placed at a distance, substitute the word *amum* (this one) for *imam* (this) in all instances.
In this ritual procedure, one should offer oblations (bali) while seated at each respective location; however, in all cases, one should say "this" (*imam*) and not "that" (*amum*).

Then, one should present to the Kṣetrapāla an oblation of black-gram flour (*māṣabhakta*) accompanied by saffron, red flowers, and the like, along with a lamp, betel, and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Some authorities also perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites of worship here.

For the verse beginning with *kṣetrasya patinā*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Kṣetrapāla, the meter is Anuṣṭubh; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the oblation (*bali*) for the propitiation of Kṣetrapāla. "Oṃ *kṣetrasya patinā*... *tīdṛśe*. To Kṣetrapāla, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his retinue (*saparivāra*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), and his powers (*saśaktika*), accompanied by his entourage of Bhūtas, Pretas, Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, Brahmarākṣasas, Vetālas, and others—I offer this oblation of black-gram porridge (*māṣabhakta-bali*) along with saffron, red flowers, and other offerings, together with a lamp, betel, and a monetary gift (*dakṣiṇā*). O Kṣetrapāla, together with your retinue, accept this oblation! May Kṣetrapāla be pleased!

Then, one should have the offering (*bali*) presented by a *śūdra* or an unworthy *brāhmaṇa* carried outside the house. Following behind it, preceded by the recitation of peace-mantras (*śāntipāṭha*), the teacher himself, accompanied by his wife, goes outside the house. Having returned, washed his hands and feet, sipped water (*ācamana*), approached the fire, sipped water again, and sat down in his own seat; the wife does likewise.

Then the preceptor, having likewise washed his hands and feet and sipped water (ācamana), takes twelve portions, eight portions, or four portions of clarified butter (ājya) with the large ladle (darvī) using the small spoon (sruva). Having placed upon it a fruit adorned with sandalwood paste and the like, together with a cloth, and identifying this fire as "Iḍā-nāma," he should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) while standing, supported by the touch of the sacrificer, his wife, and his attendants.

For the three mantras beginning with *samudrād ūrmiḥ*, the deities are the Yājñikyas, the Upaniṣads, and Agni; the meter is Triṣṭubh. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*): "Oṃ *samudrād ūrmiḥ... nābhiḥ*," "*vayaṃ nāma... etat*," and "*catvāri śṛṅgā... āviveśa*. For the mantra *mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ*, the deities are Soma, Agni Vaiśvānara, and [the Viśvedevas]; the meter is Triṣṭubh. Its application is in the offering of the final oblation: "Oṃ *mūrdhānaṃ... devāḥ*. For the mantra *punastvā*, the deities are Agni, the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas; the meter is Triṣṭubh. Its application is in the offering of the final oblation.

"Oṃ punasvā ādityāḥ kāmāḥ. For the verse beginning with "pūrṇā darvi," the deities are the Viśvedevas, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its application is in the offering of the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). "Oṃ pūrṇā darvi... to. For the verse beginning with "sapta te," the seer is Prajāpati, the deity is Agni Saptavān, and the meter is Jagatī; its application is in the offering of the full-oblation. "Oṃ sapta te agne... ghṛtena svāhā. The sacrificer should renounce [the offering], saying: "This is for Agni Vaiśvānara, for the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, for Śatakratu, and for Agni Saptavān; not mine."
Then the preceptor and the others should recite, according to custom, "The supreme *pūrṇāhuti* for the sake of stability," and so forth.

Then the preceptor should perform the ritual actions beginning with the *sa-srāva-homa* and ending with the *saṃsthā-japa*. The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) also perform the worship by means of the *saṃsthā-japa*.
Thereafter, the patron (*yajamāna*) may or may not receive from the preceptor and the others the fruit of the *japa* and the *homa*.

Then the preceptor (ācārya), accompanied by the members of the Brahma-council and the officiating priests (ṛtvij), standing facing either east or north, places a four-legged, long rectangular seat with a cover in a pure spot—either to the northeast of the planetary altar or to the west of the fire—which has been swept, smeared with cow dung, and decorated with colored lines and other ornaments. Upon this, having spread three green darbha grass blades with their tips pointing north and roots toward the ground—or not spreading them—he sits down there together with his wife, who wears a new tunic and garment, and his attendants, facing the east.

One should sprinkle the sacrificer, who is dressed in unwashed garments, with water taken from the consecrated jar into another vessel, together with the five types of sprouts along with *kuśa* and *dūrvā* grasses contained therein.

Regarding the mantras there: [they are] with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, with the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and with the section (*anuvāka*) beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*. The seers (*ṛṣis*) and other details for these have been stated in the exposition of the recitation (*japa*) to be performed after the placement of the water-pot (*kalaśa*). The specific application (*viniyoga*) here is in the statement of application: "May the Suras—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—consecrate you. [The consecration is performed] with these mantras: *oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā... 3*; *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ... 4*; *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ | pavitreṇa vi...* 17; and: "May the Suras—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—consecrate you."
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the omnipresent Saṃkarṣaṇa.
May Pradyumna and Aniruddha bring you victory!
May Ākhaṇḍala, the lord Agni, Yama, and likewise Nirṛti [grant you success].
May Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and likewise Śiva—
may all these guardians of the directions, together with Brahmā, protect you always.
Fame, Fortune, Fortitude, Intelligence, Nourishment, Faith, Action,
Intellect, Modesty, Body, Peace, Beauty, and Contentment are the Mothers.
May these wives of the gods, having assembled together, consecrate you:
Āditya, Candramas, Bhauma, Budha, Jīva, Śita, and Arkaja.
May the planets, including the honored Rāhu and Ketu, as well as the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas, consecrate you.
The seers, the sages, the cows, and the mothers of the gods;
the wives of the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the daityas, and the hosts of apsarases.
Missiles, all weapons, kings, vehicles,
medicinal herbs, jewels, and whatever are the constituent parts of time;
May rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds,
and streams consecrate you for the attainment of all desires and goals.
With these mantras spoken in the *Agnipurāṇa*:
"The Sun, the first of the planets, the protector of the world—
may that Ravi burn away the suffering born of adverse positions."
May the Moon— the lord of Rohiṇī, whose form is nectar, whose body is nectar, and who feeds on nectar—
burn away the pain born from unfavorable positions.
May Mars, the son of the Earth, possessed of great splendor, who constantly causes fear to the worlds,
both the bringer of rain and the withdrawer of rain, burn away your affliction.
May the wise Budha, the son of Candra, who possesses great luster, who brings prosperity to the worlds, and who acts for the pleasure of the Sun, burn away your affliction.
May your preceptor— the minister of the gods, Viśālākṣa, who is ever devoted to the welfare of the world and surrounded by many disciples— burn away your suffering.
May Bhṛgu— the minister of the Daityas, the preceptor and giver of life to them, and the lord of the planets Tārā— burn away your affliction.
May Śani— the son of the Sun, long-bodied, large-eyed, beloved of Śiva, slow-moving, and serene in soul— burn away your suffering.
May Mahāśiras, Mahāvaktro, Dīrghadaṃṣṭra, and Mahābala—
along with Atanu and Ūrdhvakeśa— burn away the affliction of your darkness.
With hundreds and thousands of various forms and colors,
may this fire, appearing as a portent, burn away the affliction of the world for you.

Thus, one should sprinkle [them] with the mantras beginning with *devasya tvā* and so forth. Then, having first performed an oil massage (*tailābhyaṅga*), an application of all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*), and anointment, the couple, well-bathed with the water from the jar and other water, discard their ceremonial bathing garments and put on new, unwashed clothes. Having applied white sandalwood paste, flowers, and ornaments, they sit behind the fire, the wife to the south. The discarded garments belong to the preceptor (*ācārya*).

Then, together with the preceptor (ācārya), the sacrificer (yajamāna) should perform the application of the *vibhūti* ashes with the mantra "mā na stoke," worship the preceptor and the others by washing their feet and offering *arghya*, perfumes, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and flowers, and give them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). In this regard, a cow is for the preceptor; an ox for the Brahman priest; a horse for the Sadasya priest; a tawny cow for the propitiation of the Sun; a conch shell for the propitiation of the Moon; a red ox for the propitiation of Mars; and gold for the propitiation of Mercury.

5. Yellow cloth for the propitiation of Bṛhaspati; 6. A white horse for the propitiation of Śukra; 7. A black cow for the propitiation of Śani; 8. Black iron for the propitiation of Rāhu; 9. An elephant or a goat for the propitiation of Ketu—one should give these respective sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the performer of each respective *homa* according to the established rule. If there are more than nine officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), then one cow should be given to each of them. If there are fewer, then the nine sacrificial fees—such as a cow, a conch-shell, and so forth—should be given to those same priests as far as possible. Now, the mantras for the nine items beginning with the cow, in their respective order, are as follows:
O Kāpili, you are always worthy of worship by all the gods;
since you consist of all the gods, therefore grant me peace.
In ancient times you were born from the ocean and were held in the hand by Viṣṇu;
O Pāñcajanya, I shall offer you to you, so grant me peace.
O Dharma, you who bring joy to the world in the form of a bull,
and who are the abode of the eightfold form— therefore, grant me peace.
O Fire-god, you who reside within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha and are the golden seed of the sun;
since you bestow the fruit of infinite merit, grant me peace.
Since this yellow garment is dear to Vāsudeva,
may Viṣṇu grant me eternal peace through its gift.
Since you are Viṣṇu in the form of a horse, born from the nectar of immortality,
and are the eternal vehicle of the Sun, therefore grant me peace.
Since you are the entire earth, O cow resembling a black antelope,
and the eternal remover of all sins, therefore grant me peace.
Since all iron implements, such as the plow and other weapons, are always under your control, therefore grant me peace.
O lordly elephant with beautiful tusks, you are the vehicle of the Lord of Gods;
by this gift being bestowed, grant me perpetual peace.
In the case of the goat:
"O goat, since you are established as an integral part of sacrifices and are the eternal vehicle of Agni, therefore grant me peace."

Even though these items have unequal values, one should achieve equality of profit by giving gold to those who receive a smaller share. In the absence of the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should give gold alone, which brings satisfaction to all. Therefore, the payment of the value as stated in the chapter on prices does not apply here. In all cases, however, one should give double to the teacher (*ācārya*). For the sake of the excellence of the rite, one should give more to other Brahmins.

Then, the patron, having performed the secondary worship (*uttara-pūjanā*) with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) for the deities of the planetary seats (*graha-pīṭha-devatā*) and, if there is a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), for the deities of that pavilion as well, should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) either with the specific name-mantras preceded by the *praṇava* (e.g., *oṃ Ādityāya namaḥ*) or in the collective form "Salutation to the deities beginning with Āditya.

Thereafter, the preceptor (*ācārya*) should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the deities of the planetary seats—and if there is a pavilion, of the deities of that pavilion—by means of the mantra "Arise" (*uttiṣṭha*).

Then the patron (yajamāna) should offer [the vessel] to the preceptor (ācārya), saying: "I give this pedestal of the planets (grahapīṭha), together with the image, the water-pot, and the ritual accessories, to you, O Preceptor. If it is a pavilion (maṇḍapa), he should say: "This pedestal of the planets, together with the pavilion and its accessories.
Then the preceptor, having worshipped the fire, [should recite]:
"Go, go, O best of gods, to your own abode, O Supreme Lord."
"O Consumer of Oblations, go to where the gods, beginning with Brahmā, reside"—with these words, he should dismiss [the fire].
Then the sacrificer, together with his family, should look at his own reflection in the clarified butter (*ājya*) contained in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), reciting:
"Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is remembered as the remover of sin."
Clarified butter is the food of the gods; in clarified butter all worlds are established.
"O clarified butter, destroy all misfortune and whatever wickedness resides within my limbs; increase my prosperity and nourishment."

Having recited this, he should give that clarified butter along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brāhmaṇa. Then, he should feed as many Brāhmaṇas as there were principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*), or as many as there were hundreds of those oblations, or as many as there were thousands, or as many as possible. Then, he should remember Viṣṇu with the verse beginning "yasya smṛtyā".

Then, having given sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to those who have eaten according to his means, having asked for their forgiveness, and having received their blessings, he should dedicate the rite known as the *grahayajña* (sacrifice to the planets) to the Lord with the prayer: "May the planets, beginning with the Sun, be pleased by this ritual; may it not be for me. Then, with a joyful mind and accompanied by friends, he should eat.
Thus ends the procedure for the *grahayajña* in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.
Thus ends the third section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā* composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of the venerable Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, whose surname is Okopa.
Now begins the fourth section:
Those Eligible for Initiation (*upanayana*).

Now, initiation (*upanayana*) is stated first, in accordance with the sequence of the Sūtras; for it is primary because it is prescribed by Śruti, because its purpose is the study of the Vedas, and because it establishes eligibility for performing ritual acts (*karma*). Furthermore, the Teacher has placed that very rite at the beginning in order to make it known that this [initiation] cannot be rendered effective merely through expiation (*prāyaścitta*), since it results in the acquisition of many constituent parts (*aṅga*). Initiation is the act by which, or the rite during which, the preceptor leads the boy near himself at an auspicious moment for the sake of learning.

And that [initiation] consists of a collection of rites beginning with the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and ending with the conclusion of the *Sāvitrī* vow. Among these, the principal element is the bringing of the boy into the presence of the teacher by means of the *vyāhṛtis*, the *Sāvitrī*, and the *Sāvitra* [oblation]. The others are subsidiary (*aṅga*) elements. Aparārka maintains that the instruction of the *Gāyatrī* is also a principal element. Furthermore, this is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) with a visible purpose, according to the scriptural statement: "The initiation of one seeking knowledge is a purificatory rite. And this applies only to those of the three higher castes, not to Śūdras.
"Initiation, Vedic study, the establishment of the sacred fires, and fruit-bearing rituals are for those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not corrupt"—
so says the *Dharmasūtra*.
Yājñavalkya declares that this alone is the second birth:
"The first birth is from the mother; the second is from the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are traditionally known as the twice-born."
Manu states that this alone is the birth of a Brahmin: "In that regard, the period of studentship (brahmacarya) marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass—
Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, and the teacher is called his father."

This applies only to men and not to women, because of the prohibition against women studying, as stated in the rule: "It should not be studied by women. Furthermore, there is a prohibition against women hearing [the Veda], as in: "One should not cause the Brahman to be heard in the presence of a woman or a Śūdra. Moreover, since marriage itself constitutes their initiation (*upanayana*), as expressed in the verse: "For women, the rite of taking the hand in marriage is the supreme substitute for initiation."

As for that which was stated by Hārīta—"Women are of two kinds: those who discourse on Brahman and newly-wed brides; among them, for those who discourse on Brahman, there is the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the kindling of the sacred fires (*agnīndhana*), the study of the Vedas, and the practice of begging for alms in their own home; while for newly-wed brides, having performed the initiation ceremony, marriage follows"—that refers to a different age-cycle (*yugāntara*).
"In a former kalpa, indeed, the binding of the girdle of muñja grass for women was prescribed,
as well as the teaching of the Vedas and the recitation of the Sāvitrī."
Thus it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
Regarding the time for the initiation ceremony (upanayana): now follows its timing. On this point, there is this Vedic revelation (śruti):

"One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn. Regarding this, the ancients hold that the act enjoined is the boy's approaching the teacher (*gurusamīpagamana*). The moderns, however, maintain that since there is no evidence for disregarding the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), what is enjoined is the initiation (*upanayana*) itself performed by the teacher with the boy as the qualified subject, and not the act of approaching. This is analogous to the cases in the texts "he makes the sacrificer recite the *klṛpti* formulas" and "he purifies him with five [verses]," where the recitation and purification are performed by the Adhvaryu priest with the sacrificer as the qualified subject.

For this very reason, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the agency of the one who approaches (the teacher) is described as being conducive to the activity of initiation performed by the teacher: "Jābāla, having taken leave of his mother, went to Gautama to have himself initiated. Likewise, in the words of Budha cited in Hemādri: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception."

Regarding the statement, "One should cause one who desires food to sacrifice with this [rite]," they say that since there is no evidence for the sacrificer being the instigator (*prayojya*) while the Adhvaryu and others are the agents (*kartṛ*), the verbal root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is uttered as having a transitive sense—qualifying the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—and thus the injunction would pertain to the act of causing another to sacrifice. Therefore, disregarding the literal meaning of the causative suffix, it is the act of sacrificing itself that is enjoined. However, some have stated that by the word *upanāyana*, the act of initiation (*upanayana*) itself is denoted; this is incorrect. Hemādri maintains that the word *upanayana* denotes the instigating activity directed toward the initiation, and there is no evidence for resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here.

Others, however, maintain that the instruction of the *gāyatrī*—which includes the act of leading the student into the presence of the teacher—is the primary rite. This is because the Vedic scripture, "By means of the *gāyatrī* he created the Brāhmaṇa," and the *smṛti* of Kātyāyana, "One should initiate the Brāhmaṇa with the *gāyatrī*," both show that initiation (*upanayana*) is actually a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of the instruction of the *gāyatrī*. Thus, they say, the term *upanayana* is both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*). For just as the word *samidh* (sacrificial fuel) and others denote their own parts, the term *upanayana*, though denoting a subordinate part, can appropriately function as the name for the primary rite through its connection to it.

Others, however, maintain that while a word like *paṅkaja* (lotus) possesses both etymological (*yogika*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) meanings and is therefore denotable as a *yogarūḍha* term, the word *upanayana* does not possess the status of a *yogarūḍha* because its etymological meaning—leading near (*nayana*)—and its conventional meaning—the instruction in the *gāyatrī*—do not coexist in a single referent. Consequently, they assert that the act of leading near itself is the primary sense.

The Gṛhya-sūtra states: "We shall explain the initiation ceremony (upanayana). One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at seven years of age, a Kṣatriya at eleven years, and a Vaiśya at twelve years. A Brāhmaṇa should be initiated in spring, a Kṣatriya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn; during the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, and especially under one with a masculine name."

One whose measure from birth is seven years is a "seven-year-old"; such a Brāhmaṇa one should initiate. The same etymological derivation should be understood for the terms "eleven-year-old" and "twelve-year-old. That fortnight in which the moon is filled by its digits is the "waxing fortnight," the "first fortnight," that is to say, the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa). Under an auspicious asterism (nakṣatra), a favorable constellation prescribed by the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra), [one should initiate] a boy who has a masculine name, i.e., one designated by a male word.

Because of the use of the word "especially" (*viśeṣeṇa*), the initiation (*upanayana*) for those denoted by masculine terms is distinguished [from the general rule]. This applies even to others, provided they are auspicious and not censurable.
Regarding the asterisms denoted by masculine terms, Mātṛdatța has stated them as follows:
"Aśvayuj, Punarvasū, Tiṣya, Hasta, Śatabhiṣaj, and the Proṣṭhapadas."
In the *Garga-smṛti*, however, Śravaṇa, Abhijit, and Anurādhā are also mentioned:
"Male names [should be given] under Śravaṇa, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Hasta, Punarvasu, Abhijit, Proṣṭhapadā, as well as Anurādhā and Aśvayuk."

The time for initiation is also stated in the *Dharmasūtra*: "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa; in summer, a Rājanya; in autumn, a Vaiśya; specifically, a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception, a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception."

The year coexisting with the conception (*garbha*) is also designated by the word "conception" through figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*). Those years, such as the sixth and so forth, for which the eighth is [the first] are called "those whose eighth is the conception" (*garbhāṣṭama*); the meaning is that the initiation (*upanayana*) occurs in those [years]. This is because of the scriptural statement: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from the beginning of the conception," where the number refers to the years starting from the conception. Regarding this year, some say it is according to the lunar measure (*cāndramāna*), beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra; others, however, state that the commencement of the year begins either from the start of the eighth month or from the time of the ritual impregnation (*garbhādhāna*).

Regarding the phrase "in the eighth [month] from conception," Sudarśana maintains that the plural number is intended to include the sixth and seventh months as well. Mahādeva Dīkṣita, the author of the *Ujjvalā*, holds that it is for the purpose of including the optional rites (*kāmya*) within those [periods]. Furthermore, the re-enactment of the spring season and so forth is intended to set aside the northern solstice (*udagayana*) mentioned by Āśvalāyana in the rule: "The tonsure ceremony (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), the cutting of the beard (*godāna*), and marriage are to be performed during the northern solstice in the waxing fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion," thereby excluding the northern solstice when it falls outside the spring season.

Regarding the statement, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring at seven years, a Kṣatriya in summer at eleven years, and a Vaiśya in autumn at twelve years," although it could have been stated simply thus, the separate mention of both time and age is for the purpose of indicating that these are not mandatory; rather, initiation may take place at any other age or at any time during the northern course of the sun (udagayana), provided there is either incapacity or a specific desire [to do so]. Yājñavalkya says:
"The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa occurs in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [from birth]."
"In the eleventh year for kings, and in the twelfth for Vaiśyas, according to their respective families."

Vijñāneśvara states that the eighth year is calculated either from conception (*garbhādhāna*) as the starting point or from birth. He further notes that the term "conception" (*garbha*) applies throughout these contexts, citing another *smṛti*: "For a king, [initiation] is in the eleventh year from conception; for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth year from conception. He explains that this means "in the twelfth year including the year of conception" (*saika-dvādaśe*). It should be understood that in the aforementioned statements, the status of being "eight years old" is determined by the connection to the eighth year itself, and not by having already passed through eight years.

Now follows the time for optional rites (*kāmyakāla*). This is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*: "Now, regarding the optional rites: in the seventh year [one should initiate] one desiring long life; in the eighth, one desiring Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*); in the ninth, one desiring splendor (*tejas*); in the tenth, one desiring food; in the eleventh, one desiring sensory power (*indriya*); and in the twelfth, one desiring cattle. For a Brāhmaṇa, this should be before the sixteenth year, provided there is no emergency; for a Kṣatriya, before the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, before the twenty-fourth."

These are the occasions for bringing [the boy] forward (*upanayana*) that are motivated by desire. The phrase "one should bring him forward" (*upanayet*) is to be supplied everywhere. Here too, the term "from conception" (*garbhataḥ*) is understood to follow. In this context, the prefix *ā-* denotes inclusion (*abhividhi*); some hold it denotes a limit (*maryādā*). *Atyaya* means transgression; its absence is *anātyaya*. The long vowel *ā-* is either used arbitrarily or as a variant form of the prefix. From the context, it is understood that *anātyaya* refers to the non-transgression regarding the *upanayana*. The essential meaning is that, in the event of an occurrence [of such a motive], the time for *upanayana* extends even until the sixteenth year.

From this point forward, however, the expiation (prāyaścitta) prescribed in the Dharmasūtras must be performed. And that is as follows: "When the time for the Sāvitrī has passed, one should practice the student's life (brahmacarya) according to the three Vedas for one season; then follows the initiation (upanayana), then the ritual touching of water (udakopasparśana), and then he is to be taught [the Veda]."

For whomever there is a specific time for the *sāvitrī*, if that is exceeded, one must perform the *traividyaka* penance. "Threefold knowledge" (*trividyā*) refers to the knowledge consisting of three branches; those who study that are called *traividyas*, and this [penance] belongs to them, hence it is *traividyaka*. The suffix *vuñ* is applied here according to the rule: "The suffix *vuñ* is used after a word denoting a branch of learning (*caraṇa*) when referring to its religious duty (*dharma*) or its traditional scripture (*āmnāya*). Having thus omitted the [specific duties of] fire-tending, Vedic study, and service to the teacher—namely, the entire duty of studenthood (*brahmacarya*)—one should perform [the penance]. For how long a time? "For a season" (*ṛtum*). The accusative case is used here according to the rule: "The accusative is used to denote the uninterrupted connection of time or distance."

Because of the statement "at the [proper] season," the commencement of the penance occurs at the beginning of the season; after that, the initiation (*upanayana*). Thus, one who has performed the vow is to be initiated.
Then follows the touching of water (*udakopasparśana*).

Starting from the initiation, the touching of water—that is, bathing—must be performed for one year. For one who is capable, it is three times a day; for one who is incapable, according to his ability. "For one year," says Āpastamba.
Now, regarding the one to be initiated: Ujjvalākāra has explained that one who has thus observed his vows is to be initiated afterwards.

Regarding the case where one's own father and grandfather have not been initiated, their status is equal to that of a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), and the avoidance of visiting them and so forth is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*: "Now, if one's father and grandfather should be uninitiated, they are declared to be equal to slayers of a Brahmin; one should avoid visiting them, eating with them, and marrying them."

If there be a young student whose father and grandfather were *anupeta*—that is, uninitiated—and if he himself is likewise such, then these young students are designated as *brahmahā*, meaning they are proclaimed as "slayers of Brahmins" by those who discourse on the Veda (*brahmavādibhiḥ*). The word "by those who discourse on the Veda" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Therefore, the application of that term (*brahmahā*) to him is for the purpose of attributing his specific characteristics. It will be stated later that Śūdras and outcasts are like the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), which implies a prohibition against studying in their presence. Consequently, just as one must not study in the vicinity of a slayer of Brahmins, so too must one not study in the presence of these [uninitiated persons].

One should avoid going toward them—that is, approaching them—even for the sake of protecting one's mother, father, children, wife, or one's own body, even though it will be stated later that protection must be maintained in all circumstances. One should also avoid food, even when it is being served, despite the statement that this applies even to those who have committed evil deeds. One should avoid marriage, even though there is the Mānava injunction that "a jewel of a woman may be taken even from a low family"; however, this has been explained by Ujjvalākṛt as referring to other cases. Regarding those who desire to associate with these [outcastes], the penance is stated in the Dharmasūtra:

"For those who desire [to perform it], the penance is as follows: just as there is one *ṛtu* for the first transgression, so for each person, having calculated the number of years, there shall be as many years as there were [persons] who remained uninitiated."

Because of the expression "of those who desire," the penance is not performed by force. Just as the time for the first [period] of celibacy is the season (*ṛtu*), so in this case, upon transgression, the time is one year. Then follows initiation (*upanayana*), and thereafter the touching of water; the remainder is as previously stated, according to the observation in the *Āpastamba* [Dharmasūtra]: "If the father himself has not been initiated, [the penance lasts] one year; if the grandfather also [has not been initiated], then two [years]."

Now, if he himself has not been initiated at the proper time, then [the rule] "for three years" has been explained by Ujjvalākāra. Immediately following this, it is stated in the Dharmasūtra that one should teach him: "Then he is to be taught.
The mantras for the ritual touching of water are found in the Dharmasūtra:

"With the seven *pāvamānī* verses beginning with 'That which is near and that which is far' (RV IX.67.21–27), with the *yajus*-purifier, with the *sāman*-purifier, with the *āṅgirasa*, and also with the *vyāhṛtis*. Those whose deity is the purifying Soma are the *pāvamānīs*. And those are the seven beginning with 'That which is near and that which is far. With the *yajus*-purifier: with the verse beginning 'May the waters, our mothers, cleanse us' (VS IV.2) and ending with 'I go purified. With the *sāman*-purifier: with the *Vāmadevya* *sāman* sung upon the triplet beginning 'With what [splendor] has he come to us? (SV I.169).

According to Āṅgirasa, one should pour water over the head with the palms joined using the mantra beginning with *śuciṣat*. Alternatively, the author of the Ujjvalā has explained that the pouring may be done with all the *vyāhṛtis* together. Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "Now, he whose father or grandfather... the singular form "whose" (*yasya*) is used at the start and also at the end in "then he may be taught. However, in the middle, in the phrases "those are declared to be slayers of Brahmins," "their arrival," and "the penance for those who desire [it]," the plural form is used.

In that regard, according to the beginning and conclusion [of the relevant texts], both the initiation (*upanayana*) and the instruction (*adhyāpana*) constitute an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the student alone; however, he also states that the plural number is used with reference to the multiplicity of such students. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Dharmasūtra* that if one's own father, grandfather, and great-grandfather have not been initiated, all three become equivalent to a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), and as before, there is an avoidance of guests and so forth, as well as an expiation.

"Now, those whose initiation (*upanayana*) is not remembered from their grandfather onwards are said to belong to the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*); one should avoid their approach and marriage. For those who desire [to be purified], the penance (*prāyaścitta*) is that they should practice the student-life (*brahmacarya*) according to the *Traividya* for twelve years; thereafter follows initiation, and then the ritual touching of water (*udakopasparśana*) with the *Pāvamānī* verses and others."

Those young students for whom the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—starting from the grandfather and including the great-grandfather—and their own father have not been initiated, and who themselves have not been initiated at the proper time, such young students are considered as the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
