Therefore, the prohibition of study "within the distance of a throw of a *śamyā* on all sides of the cremation ground" applies even in the presence of these individuals. The phrase "of them," etc., is clear in its meaning.
Regarding the expression "with the *pāvamānī* verses, etc.," the author of the *Ujjvalā* has explained that this should also be understood as "counting the years for each individual."
Furthermore, in the Dharmasūtra:

"Now, regarding the instruction on domestic duties, there is no [prohibition against] teaching; therefore, for one who desists from it, the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) is as prescribed for the first transgression; beyond that, it is according to the original rule."

The instruction given is that of the *Gṛhya* (domestic) scriptures, or the instruction on the duties of a householder; it is not the teaching of the entire Veda, but rather only of the *Gṛhya-mantras*. Therefore, for one who has performed the penance and become a householder, the sacrament known as *upanayana* must be performed. How so? Just as in the case of the first transgression, [the rule is] "having practiced the *brahmacarya* pertaining to the three Vedas for a season," and so on until the end.

Therefore, for one who returns [from the lineage], the initiation (*upanayana*) should be performed according to his natural status as it has occurred. Regarding one whose initiation is not remembered starting from his father, no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been stated there; however, it should be inferred from the *Dharmaśāstras*, as explained by Ujjvalākṛt. Now, a brief determination of the solstice (*ayana*) and other factors: regarding this, Āśvalāyana says—"The tonsure ceremony (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), the Godāna rite, and marriage should take place during the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), in the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*), under an auspicious asterism (*nakṣatra*).
The commentator on that text explains that "auspicious" means not contrary to the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
Garga says: "One should appoint a Brahmin in the spring, a Kṣatriya in the summer, and a Vaiśya who has taken the vow at the end of the rains.
Here, "nidāgha" refers to the summer season, and "ghanānta" refers to the autumn season.

But surely, because of this restriction regarding spring for a Brahmin, it is said: "If one is initiated during a non-season, during the month of Vasantaka, in the dark fortnight, during the seizure of the neck (galagraha),
or during a period of suspension from study (anadhyāya), he deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (punaḥsaṃskāra) again."

If it is argued that because Bṛhaspati has thus stated the fault in the absence of spring, the injunction would be redundant since the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) is already obligatory for a Brahmin, we say no; for its purpose is to prescribe another northern solstice in the event that spring cannot be obtained due to some cause. Thus says Garga:
"The five months beginning with Māgha and ending with Śukra (Jyeṣṭha) are common to all twice-born (*dvija*)."

*Śukra* is the month of Jyeṣṭha; those for whom it is at the end (*anta*) or conclusion (*prānta*) are *śukrāntakas*. The suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). They are also five months, forming a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Vṛddhagārgya says: "The six-month period beginning with Māgha is considered [appropriate] for the tying of the girdle (*mekhalābandhana*)."
In the *Maitreya-sūtra* as well, it is said:
"Spring, summer, and autumn—the seasons—or the six months beginning with Māgha, belong to all castes in their respective order."

"Succession" (*ānupūrvyam*) means sequence. This is intended to exclude the period from the beginning of Māgha to the end of Āṣāḍha, which is devoid of the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*). Since the injunction for the northern transit is mandatory, there is no tautology with these two scriptural passages. This scripture serves a purpose by prohibiting the month of Pauṣa when the sun is in Capricorn (*makarārkaviśiṣṭa*), and the injunction regarding the number five serves a purpose by excluding Āṣāḍha when the sun is in Gemini (*mithunārkaviśiṣṭa*); thus, even though the scriptural injunctions prescribing the months starting with Māgha would already be established by the injunction for the northern transit, they are not rendered redundant.

However, because the injunction regarding the number six is intended to prohibit [the initiation] for a Vaiśya during the month of Śrāvaṇa and so forth, and because it serves to prescribe the portion of Āṣāḍha within the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) when the autumn [months] cannot be obtained due to some cause, it is not purposeless.

For there exists an injunction for him regarding the southern solstice as stated by Bṛhaspati and Vṛddhavasiṣṭha: "The Mauñjī [initiation] for a Brāhmaṇa and also for a Kṣatriya should take place during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa)."
"But one should perform [the initiation] for Vaiśyas in the south, neither during a period of non-study (*anadhyāya*) nor at a solar transit (*saṃkrama*).

Thus, a Brāhmaṇa should not perform the initiation during the sun's southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), nor even during the months of Pauṣa or Āṣāḍha, despite it being the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*). It should be performed during the five months beginning with Māgha, which are characterized by the northern course. Even there, the recommended time is from when the Sun enters Pisces (*mīna*) until its entry into Gemini (*mithuna*), because of the attainment of spring according to either the lunar or solar reckoning. However, Pisces and Aries are even more highly recommended, according to Baudhāyana’s statement: "Spring occurs in Pisces or Aries."

"When the sun is situated in Capricorn or Aquarius, the initiation is middling; when the sun is in Pisces or Aries, it is excellent; and when the sun is in Taurus or Gemini, the initiation is indeed inferior."
And because of this statement by Bṛhaspati:
"Mṛga" is Capricorn; "Go" is Taurus; "Yuga" is Gemini; and the month of Caitra, when the sun is in Pisces, is most excellent, as it serves as an exception to many prohibitions.
"For when the sun is situated in Pisces during the month of Caitra, the binding of the muñja-grass girdle for a Brāhmaṇa is indeed auspicious"—
since this is the meaning of that statement by Bṛhaspati,
it has been stated by that very same [author]:
If the purity of Jupiter cannot be obtained through both the *gocara* and the *aṣṭakavarga*,
then the initiation (*upanayana*) should be performed in the month of Caitra when the Sun has entered Pisces.
"When Venus and Jupiter are lost [in retrogression] and the Moon and Sun are weak,
the vow and initiation (vratopanayana) should be performed in Caitra when the Sun has entered Pisces. Thus it is stated in the Mauñjīpaṭala.
"If Jupiter is in a sign of birth, or in Leo, or in its sign of debilitation, or in an enemy's sign,
the tying of the sacred thread (mauñjībandha) is declared auspicious when the Sun has entered Pisces in the month of Caitra. Thus says Śaunaka.
"If the preceptor of the gods (Jupiter) is situated in Leo and the thousand-rayed one (the Sun) is in Aries, one may perform auspicious rites; so say Nārada and Parāśara."
This should be understood as applying specifically to times of extreme distress.
Garga states in the Jyotiḥśāstra:
"In the month of Jyeṣṭha, there is certainly no [auspicious time] for an eldest son."
"One should perform the Mauñjī-bandha ceremony; if it has already been performed, it will bring about death."
In another Smṛti:
"One should avoid the month of one's birth during marriage and the initiation ceremony. In the Vṛttaśata:

"One should not perform auspicious rites on the natal asterism, nor in the natal month, nor on the day of the natal time; likewise, one should not perform auspicious rites for an eldest son or even a daughter during the month of Jyeṣṭha."
*Janmadhiṣṇya* means the birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*).
As stated in the *Muhūrtacintāmaṇi*:
"In a vow performed on the day of one's birth asterism, month, or ascendant, the practitioner of the vow becomes preeminent in learning."
Even for Brahmins, it is beginningless; for Kshatriyas and the others as well, it is without beginning.
Thus, the specific distinction regarding the initiation ceremony for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others has been stated.
Regarding the birth month, Garga said:
"Indeed, from the day of birth for thirty days..."
"That month of birth is to be known as censured for all ritual acts."

Based on this statement, some maintain that even the year (*varṣa*) in this context should be understood according to the *sāvana* measurement alone. Others hold that only the birth-month (*janmamāsa*) is to be taken here according to this statement, and not the year in accordance with the birth-month. Of these views, that which is correct should be accepted. And this [initiation] takes place at a time other than spring: "One should give [it] in the spring season, or in the eighth year from conception, or in the eighth [year]."
For it is stated in the Rājamārtaṇḍa: "One may wear the girdle even during the month of birth, under the birth asterism, or on the lunar day of birth."
Now, regarding the lunar days (tithis).
In the *Jyotirnibandha*, Nṛsiṃha states: "The third, fifth, sixth, second, or even the seventh [lunar day]..."
And they were especially well-honored on both sides.

Those who desire merit [should observe it] during the bright fortnight; likewise, the first day of the dark fortnight is also suitable. Furthermore, some sages maintain that the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight is likewise acceptable.

"The twelfth and the eleventh are indeed declared to be in the middle. Here, *dharma* (virtue) refers to the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*), and *kāma* (desire) refers to the thirteenth (*trayodaśī*). In the bright fortnight (*site pakṣe*), both virtue and desire are to be accepted. In the phrase "and in the dark [fortnight]," the word "and" (*ca*) serves to draw back the reference to the bright fortnight; by this, the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) is also included. Some teachers accept even the thirteenth day occurring at the end of the dark fortnight for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). In the phrase "and in the middle," it should be understood that this refers to both fortnights. Vasiṣṭha states in the *Ṭoḍarānanda*:
"One should observe an occasional suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) on the first day of the dark fortnight."
"It is recommended for the tying of the girdle, for the tonsure ceremony, and for the Vedic vows."

This rule for the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and the rule regarding occasional non-study (*anadhyāya*) concern the initiation (*upanayana*) of a distressed boy whose time has passed. [As it is said: "The first lunar day is auspicious in the dark fortnight when the moon is in a favorable asterism;
when the moon is endowed with strength, even if the [proper] years have been exceeded, [the initiation may take place] at a favorable *lagna*."
Thus it is stated by Vyāsa.

Likewise: "When the Moon is endowed with strength, situated in an auspicious house from the ascendant, and aspected by benefics, they praise the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], provided one is advanced in age like a youth."
Thus is the rule for the fourteenth day as well: "The days beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight are devoid of sacred study;
however, they are considered suitable for the tying of the girdle when performed as a rite of atonement."

Thus, according to the statement of Vṛddhagārgya cited in the *Kālādarśa* and other works, all occasional (*naimittika*) non-study days as well as the regular (*nitya*) non-study days beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*) apply specifically to the initiatory rite for expiation (*prāyaścittopanayana*), and not to a primary (*apūrva*) initiation. "Viyujaḥ" means odd; "ghasrāḥ" means days. The meaning is that in the initiatory rite for expiation, the days of the self-study [non-study period]—ending with the third, fifth, seventh, ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth—are employed.
However, the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is prohibited here as well, because of the statement: "The new moon day is censured everywhere in auspicious rites."
In the Aparārka: "When the moon has set, when Venus is in its eighth house, when the sun is without digits (niraṃśa),
during a period of non-study (anadhyāya), or during the 'throat-grasp' (galagraha) conjunctions, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) must not be performed."
Regarding the nature of the partless (*niraṃśa*) light, it is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*: "The Sun situated in the first portion of a zodiac sign is called 'partless' (*niraṃśa*). Thus says Atri.

"If one should initiate a student into a vow when Venus is defeated, extremely debilitated, or similarly situated in its sign of debilitation, and likewise when Jupiter is so situated, that person shall be deprived of the Vedas."
The *Rājamārtaṇḍa* states: "If Venus or Jupiter has disappeared, or if the Sun is devoid of its digits (niraṃśa),
the initiated disciple will suffer either dullness of intellect or even death."
Bharadvāja also provides a counter-exception regarding those days of non-study (anadhyāya) caused by the beginning of the Yugas and so forth,

stating: "The third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the seventh of Vaiśākha, the seventh of Māgha, and the second of the dark fortnight of Phālguna— these are declared as auspicious for the initiation ceremony by the preeminent sages, headed by Bharadvāja."

In this context, there is an exception for the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra and the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, as these are the beginnings of Manvantaras; for they are listed among the Manvantara-beginnings in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*. There is also an exception for the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, which is the beginning of a Yuga. As stated in the *Muhūrtatattva*:
"The four days beginning with the thirteenth, the three beginning with the seventh, and the fourth."
"Likewise, in the opinion of Garga, the eight *galagrahas* (obstructing periods) should be avoided, as well as the sixth [tithi].

Here too, an exception is shown by the presentation of the application of the sixth, seventh, and thirteenth [tithis]. Some maintain that this exception regarding the *galagrahas* pertains specifically to the initiation (*upanayana*) of those who are mute and so forth.
In another Smṛti:
"One should avoid the commencement and conclusion of a vow, as well as the commencement of study, on the day preceding a non-study period (*anadhyāya*) and on the day following a non-study period.
An exception to this is shown by the presentation of the application of the second, seventh, and thirteenth lunar days in the *Smṛtisāra*:
"One who has been initiated with a prefix (name) deserves to undergo the rite again.

And this prohibition does not apply to those who follow the Yajurveda: "In the case of the Vedic vows, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), as well as the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*)," and so forth.
"And there is no fault even in teaching the Yajus-mantras along with their accompanying words."

Some say this is because it is stated in another Smṛti in the *Smṛtidarpaṇa*. Others maintain that since this is not seen in the great compendia (*mahānibandha*), it is baseless; therefore, the prohibition applies to those [days] as well.
And they are mentioned in that very same work:
"The second day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, and the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina..."
"The fourth, the twelfth, and the month of Māgha—these are remembered as being accompanied by specific epithets.
In the phrase "the fourth, the twelfth, and Māgha," the word "bright" (sitā) is to be supplied. Regarding the days of the week, Nārada says:
"The days of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury are remembered as the most excellent."
Monday is the lowest, while Sunday is middling.
"The days of Mars and Saturn are to be avoided; on the dark fortnight, the day of the Moon (the Lord of Night) is to be avoided;
and for the twice-born, the day of Mercury when it has set is to be avoided."
Manda is Saturn (Śani). Āra is Mars (Bhauma). Niśāpati is the Moon (Candra). Saumya is Mercury (Budha).
Likewise:
"For all [vows], the days of Jupiter (Jīva), Venus (Śukra), and Mercury (Jña) are declared auspicious for a religious observance (vrata)."
The Moon and the Sun are to be known as the middling [planets] for the Sāmas and the Bāhuja [castes], while Mars is [the middling one] for the Kṣatriyas.

"The day of the lord of the branch (śākhādhipativāra), the strength of the lord of the branch (śākhādhipabala), and the ascendant of the lord of the branch (śākhādhipatilagna)—this triad is difficult to obtain during a vow.

This applies to all [castes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. Jīva is Bṛhaspati; Jña is Budha; Bāhuja is the Kṣatriya; and bala refers to [planetary] movement (gocara), the eightfold division (aṣṭavarga), and so forth.
Regarding the fault that arises when the strength of the presiding branch (*śākhādhipabala*) is absent, Vṛddhagārgya states in the *Madanaratna*:
"If the presiding branch is strong and situated in a quadrant (*kendraga*), the tying of the sacred thread (*mauñjībandha*) performed on its days leads to auspiciousness;
however, if it is devoid of strength, those who know the truth declare that for the twice-born there will be a confusion of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*)."

"In his days" means on the days of the lord of his Vedic branch (*śākhādhipa*). By this, the necessity of the strength of the branch-lord is expressed. Likewise, the strength of the caste-lord (*varṇādhipa*) is also required, according to the statement of Parāśara: "When one lord of the caste is always favorable and endowed with strength, one should initiate a boy of the Brāhmaṇa or other classes into the observance of vows. And: "Venus and Jupiter are the lords of Brāhmaṇas; Mars and the Sun are the lords of Kṣatriyas; the Moon and Mercury are the lords of Vaiśyas—thus are the lords of the castes remembered."
For this very reason, he demonstrates the established rule [in the following verse]: In the *Madanaratna*, the *Rājamārtaṇḍa* states:
"The strength of the Sun is most excellent for the father; for the student (*baṭu*), it is the strength of the presiding deity of his Vedic branch (*śākhā*) and its presiding deity (*varṇeśa*)."
For all [planets], the strength of the preceptor (Jupiter), the Moon, and the asterism is proclaimed to be the most excellent.
"At the tying of the *mauñjī* (sacred thread), at marriage, and especially at the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

By the word "of all," it is implied that for those boys whose teacher is not the presiding deity of their own Vedic branch (*śākhādhipa*), as well as for their fathers, the strength of the teacher (*gurubala*) is essential. It is further suggested that in the absence of both [the teacher and the *śākhādhipa*], the strength of the teacher alone is necessary for the boy. Regarding the lack of authority due to difficulties such as the absence of the strength of the moon and the stars (*candratārābala*), a gift is prescribed in the *Jyotirnibandha* for the sake of eligibility:
"If the moon is unfavorable, give a conch; on the day of the weekday, salt; and if the day is adverse, then rice."

"One should give grain when [the aspect] is in the *karaṇa*, and likewise gold when it is in the *bha* or the *yoga* is adverse. Here, "day" refers to the lunar day (*tithi*). In this context, the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the gift of a cow.
"They say that grain situated in the field is called *sasya*, while grain with its husks is called *dhānya*."
Based on the statement, "Raw grain is said to be husked, while boiled rice is called *anna*," the word *dhānya* refers to rice and other grains still with their husks.

Regarding the obligatory time (*nityakāla*), if the strength of Jupiter (*vaṭu-guru*) is not obtained, it may be obtained through propitiatory rites (*śānti*). Nārada states that this is not the case for the non-obligatory time (*anityakāla*).
"Even if a child lacks strength, the soul bestows strength through propitiation;
however, the ceremony should be performed in the year prescribed, and not in one that is unmentioned.
Vasiṣṭha states that even through propitiation, there is no eligibility for the initiation (upanayana) if Jupiter is situated in certain malefic positions.

"The ancients maintain that when the Sun is in the fourth house (the house of kinsmen), the sixth house (the sign of enemies), the first house (the natal sign), or the twelfth house (the house of expenditure), there is no eligibility for the sacred thread ceremony even through the performance of propitiatory rites.
Here, "kinsman" refers to the fourth house; "sign of enemies" refers to the sixth house; "birth" refers to the natal sign; and "expenditure" refers to the twelfth house.

Even in these most restricted zodiacal signs (*rāśi*), the initiation (*upanayana*) must certainly be performed by calculating a doubling or other increase in the number of offerings, oblations, and so forth; one must not allow the aforementioned years to pass.
This is because of the statement: "Therefore, due to its nature as time, the year is considered more powerful than the planets.
Bharadvāja states that even when Jupiter is situated in a specific sign, there is no obstruction to one's eligibility [for initiation], even if it occupies the eighth house or other such positions.
"If Jupiter is situated in Sagittarius, Pisces, or Cancer, and is placed in the birth, twelfth, or eighth house, it brings great happiness to the child; such is the word of Vasiṣṭha.
Here, *kulīra* means Cancer (*karka*), and that is the exaltation sign (*uccasthāna*) of Jupiter. As the astrologers have said:
"Aries, Taurus, Capricorn, Virgo, Cancer, Pisces, and Libra are the exaltations (tuṅga) of the Sun and the other [planets] respectively.

Here, Aries (*aja*) is Meṣa; Taurus (*vṛṣabha*) is the well-known sign; Capricorn (*mṛga*) is Makara; Virgo (*aṅganā*) is Kanyā; Cancer (*kulīra*) is Karka; Pisces (*jhaṣa*) is Mīna; and Libra (*vaṇij*) is Tulā. The meaning is that these seven signs, beginning with Aries, are the respective exaltation positions for the seven planets beginning with the Sun. The *Rājamārtaṇḍa* states:
"Even Jupiter, when situated in the eighth house from the natal ascendant during an initiation (*vrata*), is desired [as auspicious] through worship performed once."
"A benefic planet situated in the fourth, eighth, or twelfth house at an improper time [becomes auspicious] through double worship."

Nārada states regarding the lunar mansions: "The three [mansions] beginning with Arka (Punarvasu), the last [of the three] (Aśleṣā), Jyeṣṭhā, Śaśin (Mṛgaśīrṣa), Āditya (Puṣya), the three Uttaras, the three Viṣṇus (Śravaṇa), Aśvinī, Maitra (Anurādhā), and the two born from the lotus (Puṣya and Rohiṇī) are excellent for the initiation ceremony."

The three *arka* constellations are Hasta, Citrā, and Svāti; the last is Revatī; *ijyā* is Tiṣya (Puṣya); *candra* is Mṛgaśiras; *aditi* is Punarvasū; by the word "northern" (*uttara*), the three northern constellations are meant; the three *viṣṇu* constellations are Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj; the two *aśvinau* are Aśvinī; *mitra* is Anurādhā; *abjayonibha* is the Rohiṇī nakṣatra. Bṛhaspati says:
"In the three northern constellations, in Rohiṇī, in Hasta, in Maitra (Anurādhā), and in Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā)..."
"The initiation ceremony is indeed most excellent under the asterisms of Tvaṣṭṛ, Soma, and the two Punarvasus."
Maitra is Anurādhā; Vāsava is Dhaniṣṭhā; Tvāṣṭra is Citrā; Saumya is Mṛgaśiras.
According to the Śārṅgadharīya: "In [the nakṣatras] beginning with Śravaṇa, Āditya (Pūrvā-phalgunī), and Pauṣṇa (Revatī)—that is, in two pairs—and in the three Hastas and Mṛga..."
"The binding of the girdle for all twice-born men is declared to be auspicious."
Regarding the specific injunctions for particular constellations according to the specific Veda, it is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"In Mūla, the three Hastas, Āśleṣā, Śiva (Ārdrā), and likewise the three Pūrvās,
the binding of the girdle is commended by the wise for those who study the Ṛgveda."
The binding of the girdle for those who follow the Yajurveda is highly recommended under the asterisms of Puṣya, Punarvasu, Revatī, Hasta, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, and the fixed stars.
Puṣya, Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā), Hastā, Aśvinī, Śiva (Ārdrā), Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa),
and the three Uttarās are recommended for the girdle-tying ceremony of students of the Sāmaveda.
"The lunar mansions Mṛgaśiras, Maitra (Anurādhā), Aśvinī, Hasta, Revatī, Aditi (Punarvasu), and Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā)—
this group of constellations is prescribed for the investiture of vows by those who follow the Atharvaveda."

Sarpa is Āśleṣā; Śaiva is Ārdrā; Pauṣṇa is Revatī; Maitra is Anurādhā; Śaśāṅka-bha is Mṛgaśiras; the Dhruva asterisms are the three Uttarās and Rohiṇī; Vāsava is Jyeṣṭhā; Aśvin is Aśvinī; Śiva is Ārdrā; Viṣṇu is Śravaṇa; Aditi is Punarvasū. In the absence of these, the *Sārasamuccaya* states: "Excluding Maghā, Kṛttikā (Āgneya), Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā (Aindra), Bharaṇī (Yāmya), and Śatabhiṣaj (Vāruṇa), [the remaining asterisms] are recommended for the vow for all, provided that what is prescribed in the Vedas cannot be obtained."

Kṛttikā belongs to Agni; Jyeṣṭhā belongs to Indra; Bharaṇī belongs to Yama; Śatatārakā belongs to Varuṇa. Among these, the masculine lunar mansions (puṃnakṣatra) are especially recommended, according to the Gṛhya-sūtra statement: "Especially [those] having masculine names."
These, however, have already been mentioned. As for that which says:
"When the stars, the moon, and the planets are favorable, and even when the year is auspicious..."
"One who has been initiated under the asterism Punarvasu deserves the performance of the purificatory rite again."

Thus, the prohibition of Punarvasu mentioned in the statement from the *Rājamārtaṇḍa* is baseless; for it is not seen in the *Saṃhitās* of Vasiṣṭha and others well-known among astrologers, and because in the great compendia (*mahānibandhas*) such as those by Hemādri, there is only the prescription of Punarvasu, and because one observes that all learned Dākṣiṇātyas practice the initiation ceremony during Punarvasu. Even if it were based on a root text, it does not concern followers of the Yajurveda or the Atharvaveda, since in the aforementioned statement from the *Jyotirnibandha*, it is prescribed for those of the Yajurveda and Atharvaveda.
Śrīpati states the specific arrangement regarding the yogas:
The *vaidhṛti* yoga, as well as that named *vyatīpāta*, and all of *parigha* up to its midpoint, are entirely inauspicious.
However, three *muhūrtas* of the first *yoga* (namely *viṣkambha*) along with *vajra*, nine *muhūrtas* of *vyāghāta*, and five *muhūrtas* of *śūla* [are auspicious].
"In Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa, exactly six nāḍīs must be avoided for auspicious undertakings.
The first yoga is Viṣkambha. Regarding other previously mentioned cases, Bṛhaspati says:
"In the eighteen remaining yogas, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) is praised.
The determination of the specific instruments (karaṇas) was also stated by that same author:
"The group of six beginning with *bava* is highly esteemed for the initiation ceremony."
"One should especially avoid Śakuni and the other [yogas], as well as Viṣṭi."
Manu states the regulation regarding the divisions of the day:
"In all regions, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) should primarily take place in the forenoon;
it is declared to be middling if performed at midday, and censurable if in the afternoon."

The phrase "in all regions" is also to be supplied in the latter half [of the verse]. Even though the matter is thus settled regarding auspicious times, Garga states a prohibition based on specific omens: "In the event of an eclipse of the sun or moon, an earthquake, or defects such as the appearance of comets and the falling of meteors, those who know the truth say that ten days [are forbidden] for a vow; some say thirteen days."
The word "to be avoided" (*vārjyāni*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
However, Caṇḍeśvara says regarding times of distress:
"In the case of the burning of the quarters, an earthquake, the falling of a thunderbolt, or a splitting [of the earth]..."
"Likewise, during the fall of a comet, a meteor, or a shower of firebrands, one should not perform vows or auspicious rites for three days."
In the *Dharmaprakāśa*, Garga states:
"During lunar and solar eclipses, three days prior [to the eclipse] will be inauspicious;
seven days after [the eclipse] are traditionally declared to be the period of impurity (*grahaṇasūtaka*) caused by the eclipse."
And this refers to the case of a partial eclipse (*ardhagrāsa*):
"In the case of a total eclipse (*sarvagrāsa*), [one should avoid] seven days; in the case of a partial eclipse, three days;
for an eclipse measuring two, three, or one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), one should avoid one day."

Thus, because Aṅgiras has stated this specific rule, we shall describe the various defective times in detail in the section on marriage (*vivāha-prakaraṇa*). Among these aforementioned times, that which is declared in the *Sūtra* is the primary time;
however, that which is declared in the *Smṛti* applies in times of distress, according to the statement:
"The primary rule is that which is declared in one's own *Śāstra*, while the other [secondary rule] applies in times of distress."

Lalla says: "If a rain-cloud thunders during the morning twilight on the day of the vow (*vratya*), there shall be a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) on that day; one should avoid the vow on that occasion. Here, "the day of the vow" refers to the day of the initiation (*upanayana*); "on that day" means on the day of the vow, that is, the day of the initiation; and "the vow" refers to the initiation ceremony itself. Since this statement would imply a prohibition of the entire ritual complex of the initiation, the *Jyotirnibandha* states that the entire initiation must be performed—excluding only the commencement of Vedic study—after the *nāndī-śrāddha*.

"If an untimely suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) should occur after the *nāndī-śrāddha* has been performed, one may then perform the *mauñjī-bandha* (the tying of the girdle), but one must not cause the commencement of the Veda (*vedārambha*) to take place. The meaning is as follows: depending on the location, that rain, thunder, and so forth which occurs in asterisms other than those from Ārdrā to Jyeṣṭhā, or in those other than those from Mṛgaśīrṣa to Viśākhā, is "untimely" (*akālika*). The suspension of study caused by such an event is called "untimely" (*akālika*). If this occurs after the *nāndī-śrāddha*, then one may perform the *mauñjī-bandha*—that is, the initiation (*upanayana*)—but one must certainly not cause the specific act of commencing the Veda prescribed therein to be performed.

According to the statement, "When the *nāndī-śrāddha* has been performed," even the *mauñjī-bandha* (the sacred thread ceremony) does not take place if there is thunder from a cloud prior to the *nāndī-śrāddha*. However, the prohibition stating that one should not cause the commencement of the Vedas (*vedārambha*) refers specifically to those whose *sūtra* prescribes the commencement of the Vedas on that very day. For followers of the *Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra*, the *mauñjī-bandha* must indeed be performed even during an *akālika-anadhyāya* (an occasional interruption of study), because of this specific injunction; yet the commencement of the Vedas does not occur at all, precisely because it is not prescribed for them.

If it is argued that since it has been stated in another ritual manual (*prayoga*) that by the mere commencement of the *Gāyatrī* the commencement of all the Vedas occurs, therefore the commencement consisting of the instruction of the *Gāyatrī* itself is the commencement of all the Vedas, and its prohibition is expressed by the rule "one should not cause [the student] to perform the commencement of the Vedas," we say no. This is because that rule is intended to inform [the student] of the cessation of the *punarupanayana* (re-initiation) which is for the purpose of studying other Vedas besides the *Atharvaveda*. Nor should it be asked what the authority for this is.

"Indeed, the *Sāvitrī* is recited from all the Vedas; so says the *Brāhmaṇa*. Since this rule in the *Dharma-sūtra* does not specify a particular distinction, the logical principle is that there is only one initiation (*upanayana*) for the purpose of all [Vedas]. Regarding this point, the *Śāṭyāyana-brāhmaṇa* itself has been cited. However, for the *Atharvaveda*, a separate initiation must be performed because of a specific scriptural injunction. And thus it is heard in that very same text: "One who has been consecrated elsewhere [for another Veda] should not study the *Bhṛgu-Aṅgiras* (i.e., the *Atharvaveda*). "Elsewhere" means for the sake of another Veda. This is because the explanation by Ujjvalākṛt—that "the *Bhṛgu-Aṅgiras* is the *Atharvaveda*"—is authoritative.
Now, regarding those who perform the initiation (*upanayana*):
on this matter, Vṛddhagarga says— "The father, the grandfather, a brother, kinsmen, or agnates born of the same lineage who are elder [than the candidate];"
"One who is qualified for the initiation should be brought forward; in the absence of the preceding one, each subsequent one [is eligible]."
The brother of the father:
"The father himself should initiate the son; in his absence, the father's father;
in his absence, the father's brother; and in his absence, a uterine brother."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Pitāmaha:

if the father is learned, he alone should perform the initiation (*upanayana*); otherwise, he should not. This is because the *Dharmasūtra* states that there is a fault in an initiation performed by one who is unlearned, and this will be demonstrated further below. In the absence of the father’s learning, someone characterized by the marks mentioned in the forthcoming statement of Vyāsa should perform the initiation. These two statements refer specifically to the Brāhmaṇa, not to the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya, because the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* constitutes formal teaching (*adhyāpana*), and those two castes lack authority in that regard.

It is for this very reason that the mention of the term *vipra* (Brahmin) should be understood in the forthcoming statement of Vyāsa, "one who is devoted solely to the Vedas and knows the Dharma. Therefore, it should be understood that only a family priest (*purohita*) may perform the initiation for these two. Regarding the second quarter of the verse: the meaning is those among the *jñātis*—that is, the *sapiṇḍas*—and those other than them who are born of the same lineage (*gotraja*), provided they are elder or older than the student (*baṭu*). This is because it is forbidden for one of lower status than the person being initiated to act as the teacher (*ācārya*). When "born of the same lineage" and "elder" are expected [in the compound], the elision of the vowel *a* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

As for the statement of the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya): "Those who have not been consecrated, however, are to be consecrated by brothers who have already been consecrated," the ancients hold that this refers to a case where there is no paternal uncle, in accordance with the words of Pitāmaha (Vasiṣṭha). The moderns hold that it refers to the marriage of a sister and so forth.

Śaunaka states who the performer is when the aforementioned authorities, such as the father, are absent: "The initiation of a boy [should be performed] by one who possesses learning, noble birth, and good conduct..."
"A supreme twice-born man, having shaken off all evil without exception through austerity, should act [thus]."

With reference to the injunction that one should appoint an *ācārya*, Vyāsa also says: "One should desire a Brahmin who is devoted solely to the Vedas, knows the Dharma, is of noble birth, learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), pure, enriched by his own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), free from laziness, and [is the] desired performer."

One whose fixed devotion (*niṣṭhā*) is to the Vedas, to two Vedas, or to one Veda; a *śrotriya*, that is, one who studies the *chandas* (Vedic hymns), according to the Smṛti of Pāṇini: "One who has studied the *chandas* is a *śrotriya*.
And from the Dharmasūtra: "Having studied even a single branch (*śākhā*) of the Vedas in accordance with the law (*dharma*), one becomes a *śrotriya*."

"Rich in his own branch" means rich in that branch which has come down through his own lineage. By this it is indicated that the teacher must belong to one's own Vedic branch (*śākhā*). The mention of a "Brahmin" (*vipra*) is for the purpose of excluding Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. The exclusion of Śūdras follows simply from their lack of entitlement to study the Vedas and so forth. The meaning of the word *ācārya* is given in the *Dharmasūtra*: "He from whom one gathers (*ācinoti*) duties is an *ācārya*. He gathers—that is, he teaches. Bṛhaspati says:
"He gathers the scriptures and establishes them in right conduct (*ācāra*)."
"He who practices it himself is therefore called an Ācārya.
Yājñavalkya says:
"He is a Guru who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him."
Having initiated him and imparting the Veda, he is designated as an Ācārya.

"One who performs a portion [of the rite] is called an *upādhyāya*; one who performs the sacrifice is called an *ṛtvij*. These are to be honored according to their precedence, yet among them, the mother is the most venerable."

He who, having performed all the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception), bestows—that is, teaches—the Veda to this young student (*māṇavaka*), is the *guru*. And thus, the father is also his *guru* because he is the performer of the rites beginning with the *niṣeka*.
Devala has also mentioned other types of *gurus*:
"The sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), the father, the elder brother, and the preceptor (*ācārya*)..."
The maternal uncle, the father-in-law, the protector, the maternal grandfather, and the paternal grandfather.
The eldest in caste and the paternal uncle are remembered as teachers among males;
likewise, the mother, the maternal grandmother, the teacher’s wife, and the siblings of one’s father and mother [are also teachers].
"The paternal grandmother, an elder sister, and a nurse are also women who are gurus.

In this context, the father possesses the status of a guru even in the absence of performing the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as *puṃsavana*. He who performs only the initiation (*upanayana*) and teaches the Veda is an *ācārya*. The role of the *ācārya* as the initiator should be understood to apply when a learned father is absent. He who teaches only a portion of the Veda but does not perform the rites of initiation and so forth is an *upādhyāya*. He who officiates at sacrifices is designated as an *ṛtvij*.

These aforementioned persons, according to their order—that is, without deviating from the sequence—each preceding one is more venerable and worthy of honor; this is the meaning. Among these, the mother, the progenitor, is the most weighty and excellent, because she endured the hardships of bearing the fetus and so forth.
Furthermore, in the *Dharmaprakāśa Purāṇa*:
"In this world, according to dharma, a man has two gurus: his father and his mother."
"Of these two, the father is superior because of the observed predominance of the seed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother.
Thus, the greater status of the father has been stated. Regarding this, the moderns hold that there is an option according to one's wish, or rather, that they are of equal status.

The fault regarding initiation performed by one who is ignorant is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*: "It is known that he who initiates an ignorant person, as well as the one who is ignorant himself, enters from darkness into darkness."

When one who does not know the Veda initiates a young boy (*māṇavaka*), that ignorant boy and the ignorant initiator both enter—that is, they attain—from the presence of darkness characterized by evil action, the fruit of sin known as suffering; for it is "darkness" because it produces delusion. Indeed, the boy requires refinement for the sake of knowledge in order to dispel ignorance; when this initiation is performed by one who is ignorant, he does not thereby obtain knowledge.

The author of the *Ujjvalā* has explained that the meaning of the scriptural passage is that both [the teacher and the student] incur suffering through an action censured by the world. Furthermore, it should not be argued on the basis of these statements that the status of being a teacher belongs only to one who has studied the entire Veda and not to one who has studied only a portion of the Veda.

Regarding the passage in the *Dharmasūtra* commentary stating, "One worthy of the *gomadhuparka* [cow-honey offering] is a teacher (*ācārya*), an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a graduate (*snātaka*), a father-in-law, or a righteous king," the author of the *Ujjvalā* explains: "From this very [text], it is known that even those who have studied only a portion of the Veda may become officiating priests or teachers. Furthermore, in the *Viśvaprakāśa*, another *Smṛti* states:

"Whether he belongs to a different lineage (*asagotra*) or the same lineage (*sagotra*), when one becomes a teacher upon the initiation ceremony (*upāyana*), one should perform an auspicious rite (*abhyudaya*) dedicated to the father and other relatives of the person being initiated."
"This same path has been proclaimed by the sages even for the marriage of a maiden.
Regarding the expiation for the attainment of authority for the one who initiates a boy (the *upanetṛ*), Bṛhad-Viṣṇu states in the *Prayogapārijāta*:
"The initiator shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances, and the boy shall likewise perform three *kṛcchra*s."

The expiation for a *vaṭu* (a young student) is performed only through easily accessible substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*), such as feeding Brāhmaṇas, because of his incapacity. Vedic substitutes such as the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* or the *Rudraikādaśinī* do not apply to him at all, due to his lack of qualification.

Alternatively, the preceptor (*upanetṛ*) must perform it according to the primary rule, based on the scriptural statement: "The father shall perform the expiation for one who is less than twelve years of age."
The term "father" (*pitṛ*) is an elliptical designation for the initiator (*upanetṛ*).
To establish the teacher’s (*ācārya*) authority to instruct in the *gāyatrī*, that same [text] states regarding his recitation as well:
"He should practice the *sāvitrī* while recollecting the fires and the purifiers."
"The Guru should then recite the Sāvitrī twelve thousand times; for that is traditionally taught for the purpose of bestowing it upon him, indeed for the sake of his own qualification."

In some places, there is also the reading: "this is remembered for the purpose of offering. The *agnipavitra* mantras are the six mantras beginning with *agna āyūṃṣi pavase*, which are included within the section starting with *devasya tvā*. By the use of the present tense substitute (*laṭ*) in the word "remembering" (*saṃsmaran*), it is indicated that one should first perform a mental recitation (*mānaso japa*) of these [mantras] after having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to recite the *gāyatrī* twelve thousand times—or twelve thousand plus twelve—in order to achieve the qualification for the recitation of the *gāyatrī*. The meaning of "one should practice" (*abhyaset*) is "one should recite" (*japet*).
The statement "one should recite the *sāvitrī*" is a restatement (anuvāda) used in the sense of the accusative case.

If the injunction "one should mutter the Sāvitrī" is taken as the prescriptive rule, then one [text] prescribes a single recitation, while the other prescribes a recitation of either twelve thousand or twelve thousand plus one thousand; thus, there is no fault of tautology. According to this view, the sequence is as follows: having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one should mutter the six mantras known as the *agnipavitra* once, utter the Sāvitrī once, and then mutter the Sāvitrī with a count of either twelve thousand or twelve thousand plus one thousand.

Regarding the reading *saṃsmaret* (one should remember/contemplate): the sequence is that after reciting the fire-purifying mantras (*agnipavitrāṇi*) and having uttered the *gāyatrī* once, one should recite the *gāyatrī* twelve thousand times or twelve thousand plus one thousand times, preceded by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Here, "Guru" refers to the Preceptor (*ācārya*). The construction of the final half-verse is: "This is remembered for the sake of that authority which belongs to oneself for the purpose of bestowing this *gāyatrī*. Thus concludes the section on the Initiator and the expiation performed by the Initiator and the candidate.
Now follows the determination of the items required for the initiation (*upanayana*).
Regarding that, Vasiṣṭha has described the pavilion:
"One should construct a pavilion sixteen *aratnis* in size, adorned with four doors and provided with archways; there, one should prepare an altar."

"One should construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa) of eight cubits or sixty-two cubits. Regarding that pavilion: "sixty-two cubits" means twelve cubits. Since this pavilion is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) of initiation (*upanayana*) and marriage (*vivāha*), and since these two are prescribed by the Sūtra, one must accept the *aratni* as consisting of exactly twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)—as defined in the Sūtra—when it serves as an ancillary to a pavilion prescribed by the Sūtra for those sacraments.
This applies elsewhere as well.

"In all auspicious rites, a pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed according to the measurement of the house; it should be sixteen cubits [in size], or less, down to a minimum of ten. Here, an altar (vedi) is established in the center with exactly four pillars."

Regarding the phrase "according to the measurement of the house," the meaning is that in a large house the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is large, and in a small one it is smaller. "Ten as the limit" refers to the lower limit of its size. Therefore, the eight-cubit dimension mentioned by Vasiṣṭha applies only to cases of extreme distress. In the expression "with four pillars," the word "is appropriate" (*yuktā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Furthermore, this is an adjective qualifying the altar (*vedi*). Because of the statement "the altar is established in the middle," the pavilion must be constructed in accordance with the altar itself, and not independently.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction between the two statements: "The altar (vedī) should be made four cubits on the left side of the house," and "The altar is established in the middle.

According to the statement, "The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed at the door of the house according to the measurement of the house," if the pavilion is indeed constructed, then it must be understood that the altar is situated entirely outside the pavilion.

The altar is described in the *Saṃgraha* according to the procedure following the *Mānavasūtra*: "The altar for the student (*vaṭu*) should be six or four steps in length and width, and one step in height."
The wall should be two cubits long and three finger-breadths high;
it should be made at the western altar, twelve finger-breadths in width.
Then, one should fashion eight steps on each side.
"In the middle of that, it should be shaped like a water-pot (kalaśa); such is the opinion of those who know the sacrifice.

The characteristics observed in the marriage altar—such as being elevated in the shape of a tortoise shell, sloping toward the northeast, being adorned with flower garlands, pillars, and so forth—are to be understood here as well, provided there is no contradiction.
However, nowadays, learned people construct the altar exactly like the marriage altar.
In that very same other text, there is a specific detail:
"If the door faces west or perhaps faces north,
then the altar (vedikā) should be constructed to the right of the exit from the house."

By the word *nirgama*, the door is meant. Since it is stated that the altar (*vedi*) is to be made to the south of the west-facing and north-facing doors, it follows by implication that the altar should be made on the left side of the south-facing and east-facing doors. Thus, the intended meaning is established that there is no altar in the southwest (*nairṛtya*). Furthermore, a purely south-facing door is prohibited in the treatises on architecture (*śilpaśāstra*). Consequently, the remaining option is that the door faces east, and the altar is located on its left side; this is the meaning established.

Śrīpati has stated that the orientation of the door toward the south is determined by the specific zodiac sign [occupied by the Sun]: "When the Sun is in Cancer, Capricorn, Leo, or Aquarius, houses should face east or west;
when it is in Libra, Aries, Taurus, or Scorpio, one should make them face south or north."
"Otherwise, if a foolish person builds [a house] at other times, he suffers the loss of health, happiness, and freedom from fear;
however, one should not have houses constructed when the Sun has entered Pisces, Sagittarius, Gemini, or Virgo.
Regarding the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the author of the *Saṃgraha* permits eating together with one's mother:

"In the initiation ceremony (upanayana) with one's mother, and in marriage with one's wife; otherwise, if there is eating together, a man incurs loss of caste. Since the prohibition "one should not eat with a woman" becomes applicable immediately after the performance of the three-fold *kṛcchra* penance—just as the prohibitions against acting according to whim (*kāmacāra*), speaking according to whim (*kāmavāda*), and eating according to whim (*kāmabhakṣaṇa*) become applicable—it is this [specific rule] that effects the supersession of that general prohibition. Nor should it be argued that, because of the statement "in the initiation ceremony with one's mother," she must be present at every single meal during the entire period of the initiation.

Because this statement is appropriately applied only to eating that consists of the types of food mentioned in the Sūtra according to the agreement on conduct (*ācāra-saṃvāda*), and because the phrase "together with the proper measure" (*mātrā saha*) does not apply to eating that occurs after the primary meal—which was not explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtra in his own words—as in the following passage:
"One should eat only together with the proper measure; thereafter, the mother becomes menstruating."
"The Lord Yama has stated that the binding of the sacred thread (*vratabandha*) is commendable.

Based on this statement, some maintain that if the mother is in her menses prior to the meal, the *vratabandha* ceremony should not take place. Others, however, argue that since this statement is not found in the great compendiums (*mahānibandhas*), it is rootless; therefore, they say the ceremony must indeed be performed. In this matter, one should follow established custom (*ācāra*).

A waist-thread (*kaṭisūtra*) and a loincloth (*kaupīna*) should be provided; although both of these are not mentioned here in the Sūtras, Smṛtis, and so forth, they are nonetheless prescribed in the section on the duties of a religious student (*brahmacāri-dharma*).
"A student (brahmacārī) should always carry a girdle, an antelope skin, a staff,
and a sacred thread, as well as a waist-string and a loincloth."

Thus, just as the injunction for the perpetual wearing of the girdle (*mekhalā*), deerskin (*ajina*), staff (*daṇḍa*), and sacred thread (*upavīta*) by the religious student (*brahmacārin*)—as found in the forthcoming words of Yama—is established through the mandatory nature of the initiation (*upanayana*), so too is the perpetual wearing of the waist-thread (*kaṭisūtra*) and the loincloth (*kaupīna*) established by implication during that initiation.

This is because Ujjvalākara, in his commentary on the *Dharmasūtra* passage, "The garments are linen, silk, or deerskin," states: "It is called 'garment' (*vāsaḥ*) because it is worn (*vasyate*) or used to cover the loincloth (*kaupīna*).
[Furthermore: "A householder performs Vedic or Tantric rites..."
All that, even when joined with a waistband, would be fruitless."

Thus, because another Smṛti text prohibits the binding of a waist-cloth for a householder specifically during ritual performance—thereby demonstrating that the binding of a waist-cloth is permitted for students (brahmacārin) and others—and because Ujjvalākṛt, by his mention of wearing a loincloth (kaupīna), has effectively indicated the binding of a waist-cloth as well, and because it is the practice of the learned (śiṣṭa);

[the text continues]: "Having taken the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta)—the youth, having sipped water and being seated with the sacrificial thread over his right shoulder, takes hold [of the teacher]."
The phrase "to the south" is connected with the word "having sat down. In the *Baudhāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*:

"Having bathed and wearing clean garments, with his topknot tied, [the teacher] makes him recite while putting on the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*): 'The sacrificial thread... may there be strength for you, splendor. Having made him who wears the sacrificial thread sip water, he leads him to the place of sacrifice. In the *Dharma-sūtra*: "Or else, the thread alone serves the purpose of the sacrificial thread. This has been explained by Ujjvalākāra as meaning that the thread alone serves the function of the sacrificial thread for all [students], and that there is no restrictive rule that it must be a garment.
And this [sacred thread] should be made of cotton, according to the statement of Manu: "The sacred thread of a Brahmin should be made of cotton, twisted upward, and triple-stranded.
In the absence of cotton, Devala says:

"Cotton, linen, cow-hair, hemp, bark, grass, and so forth—these should be worn as the *upavīta* by the twice-born according to their availability. Here, *kṣumā* means *atasī* (linseed). *Valka* means tree-bark. In the expression "according to their availability" (*yathāsaṃbhavataḥ*), the suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings; thus, the meaning is "according to what is available."
In the *Chāndogya-gṛhya*:
"One makes the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) out of a cord, or even a cloth, or indeed a rope of *kuśa* grass. Thus says Bhṛgu.
"One should make it threefold with the strands twisted upwards and threefold with the strands twisted downwards;
the sacred thread (upavīta) should be threefold, and for it, a single knot is prescribed.
Regarding the method of twisting upwards, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says:
"With the right hand raised upwards, the thread is tripled; when it is wound by the Brāhmaṇas, that which is turned upwards is known as *ūrdhvavṛta* in the scripture.
The meaning is: that which is tripled and then wound with the right hand held upwards—that is *ūrdhvavṛta*.

Devala says: "One should discard a sacred thread woven by a widow, one made during a period of study-interruption (anadhyāya), one that is broken, one that has gone below [the navel], or one worn while eating."
In the phrase "gone downwards," the word "from the waist" (*kaṭeḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Kātyāyana says:
"That which, not being held at the back or at the navel, reaches the waist..."

"That sacred thread (upavīta) should be worn neither too low nor too high. By the phrase "not too low," that which extends below the waist is prohibited; by "not too high," that which is above the waist is prohibited. Vasiṣṭha says:

"Above the navel it is detrimental to longevity; below the navel it causes the loss of merit from austerity. Therefore, a wise person should make the sacred thread level with the navel. Thus says Devala.

"One sacred thread is prescribed for a student (vaṭu), two for the other two [the householder and the forest-dweller], and for ascetics (yatis) there should be only one; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures. Here, "the other two" refers to the householder and the forest-dweller. An ascetic (yati) is one who carries three staffs (tridaṇḍī).
In another Smṛti: "Upon cutting or destruction [of the thread], one who has bathed should take up a pure thread made by a maiden, or else by widows and others."
The term "widow" refers to a contingency.

In the *Āhnikaprayogapārijāta*, the planting of a cotton tree according to the procedure for obtaining cotton seeds and the making of a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from those seeds is described; that should be understood from that very source. Regarding its wearing, there is a specific rule in the Śruti:
"He raises the right arm and wears the left; this is the *yajñopavīta*. The reverse of this is the *prācīnāvīta*; the *saṃvīta* is for human beings.
Manu says:
"When the right hand is raised, the twice-born is called *upavītī*."
"On the left [shoulder] he should wear the *prācīnāvīta* [cord]; when it is suspended around the neck, he is *nivītī*."
Regarding the rules for the manufacture and wearing of the *upavīta* in the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*:

"Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for making the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*). Having brought a thread made by a Brāhmaṇa or his daughter, he measures out the first ninety-six [threads] with 'bhūḥ', the second with 'bhuvaḥ', and the third with 'suvaḥ'. Having measured them and placed them upon a *palāśa* leaf, he sprinkles them with water using the three verses beginning with 'āpo hi ṣṭhā', the four verses beginning with 'hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ', the entire section beginning with 'pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ', and the *Sāvitrī*. Then, holding them in his left hand and striking them three times, [he recites] 'bhūr agnim...'"

Having encircled [the thread] with these three—*bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*—and having made a knot with *candramasaḥ*, one should place Oṃkāra, Agni, the Nāgas, Yama, the Pitṛs, Prajāpati, Vāyu, Sūrya, and the Viśvedevas in sequence upon the nine threads and worship them. Then, taking up the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with the mantra "devasya tvā," and showing it to the Sun with the mantra "ud vayaṃ tamasaspari," [one should recite: "The sacred thread is the supreme purifier, which was born together with Prajāpati in the beginning."
"Brahmin, put on this foremost, auspicious life-prolonging sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); may there be strength and splendor for you"—thus one should wear it; so said the venerable Baudhāyana.
For one unable to do even this much, Devala says:
"Having gone out from the village and counted it upon the ninety-six fingers..."
Then, having washed that thread tripled [in size] with the three *ābliṅgaka* mantras, [one should proceed].
In a temple, a cow-pen, by a river, or elsewhere in a pure place, one should perform the *trivṛt* rite with the *Sāvitrī*; that [performance] should indeed consist of nine repetitions.
One should place a smooth, triple-stranded cotton thread upon the left hand and sprinkle it ten times with water consecrated by the Sāvitrī mantra.
"And having bowed down to and fully worshipped Hari, Brahmā, and Īśvara,
one should wear [the sacred thread] either with the mantra 'yajñopavītam' or even with the vyāhṛtis."

The term "ukṣayet" contains the causative suffix (*ṇic*) used in its own sense. Having silently fashioned the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) characterized by being wound over the right shoulder and so forth, one should sprinkle it ten times with water consecrated either by the *Sāvitrī* or by mantras such as "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and then wear it with the mantra "The sacred thread is supreme" (*yajñopavītaṃ paramam*) or with the *Vyāhṛtis*; thus it is stated in the *Smṛtyarṇava*.
However, in the *Kauṣītaki-śākhā*, it says:

The mantra for wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is stated as follows: "I invest myself with the sacred thread for long life, for good progeny, for heroic vigor, for sovereignty over all the Vedas, for glory, and for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
The meaning of the term *yajñopavīta* is stated in the *Smṛtisāra*:
"That which is called 'sacrifice' (*yajña*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is indeed spoken of by the Hotṛ priests."
"Therefore, this [cord] of his is the *upavīta*; hence it is called the *yajñopavīta*."
In the *Smṛtiprakāśa*:
"O best of the twice-born, one who does not realize the identity of the knower and the object of knowledge should not abandon the Brahma-thread of the Self created by Brahmā."
In the beginning, Śiva himself, desiring to create while seated alone,
beheld Māyā composed of the Guṇas and made it like a thread.
Having created Viṣṇu, the protector of the gods, from that [power], she herself becomes Brahmā; and Rudra exists for his destruction.
Because that thread is worn as a sacred thread by Hari— who is of the nature of knowledge— within the immutable Śiva, who is the self of Brahman, it is remembered as the *brahmasūtra*.
The wise know it as the *yajñasūtra* because it is associated with sacrifice through its state of being the sacred thread (*upavīta*);
and it is called the *brahmasūtra* because it is enveloped by Brahmā at his command.
There are three worlds, three Vedas, three gods, and three fires;
there are three castes created by Śiva—one should take refuge in this triple-stranded thread.
Residing at that knot, the Tāra consists of three mātrās and is joined with Nāda;
and at the tip of that knot is Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Vedas, by the command of Śiva.
Thus, Brahmā first fashioned this unsurpassed *brahmasūtra*, dedicated to twelve deities, for the twice-born who are worthy of the Vedas.
By merely wearing that sacred thread upon their shoulders,
those twice-born ones here become known as Brāhmaṇas and are worthy of the three Vedas.
From the time that the preceptor, being self-restrained, duly places the sacred thread upon the left shoulder of the twice-born, [he becomes a student].
From that time forward, he alone is called his father and his teacher.
And his mother is Sāvitrī, who is said to be his second birth; its measurement should extend to the waist, and it should likewise be long and well-established.

An excessively short sacred thread takes away one's lifespan, while an excessively long one destroys the merit of one's asceticism; the sacred thread should be thick with a measurement equal to the size of a white mustard seed.

"The sacred thread (brahmasūtra) is thus declared to be fame-bestowing, not too thick nor too thin, a remover of wealth [from the unworthy], supremely purifying, pure, life-prolonging, auspicious, bestowing vigor, and bestowing spiritual luster."

"The sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is supremely purifying, an ornament, and the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa; it was produced by the Grandfather (*Pitāmaha*), seated upon the lotus throne, from the fiber of a lotus stalk. Thus ends the origin of the sacred thread.
"If a Brāhmaṇa does not know the origin of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta),
he indeed carries books as a burden, just like an ox."
Regarding clothing, the *Dharmasūtra* states: "Clothing consists of linen, flaxen, and skins.

That by which the private parts are covered is called "clothing" (*vāsaḥ*). Linen (*śāṇī*) is a cloth made from the product of the *śaṇa* plant. Flaxen (*kṣaumam*) is the product of *kṣumā*, which is the *atasī* plant; others say it is a specific type of white silk-like cloth. A skin (*ajinam*) is that of any sacrificially pure animal. Ujjvalākara has explained that the meaning is that one should wear one garment from among these three.
Vasiṣṭha, however, has prescribed cotton clothing for a Brāhmaṇa:
"The garment of a Brāhmaṇa should be of cotton. And this must be unwashed; as it is stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra:
"Now he causes him to put on an unwashed garment.
Regarding the characteristics of an unwashed garment, Pracetas says: "Slightly washed, new, white, with its fringes intact, and never before worn."
"One should know that to be unsoiled, which is purifying for all ritual acts.
Furthermore, it is observed in the *Baudhāyana-gṛhya-sūtra* that this garment should be prepared during the Puṣya constellation; this is not contradictory even for us.
Immediately following this, the twice-rinsing of the mouth (*dvirācamana*) should be performed.

"Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, walked along a road, or put on a different garment, one who has already performed *ācamana* should perform *ācamana* again," according to the statement of Yājñavalkya.
In this context, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) is purely according to the Purāṇas and not Vedic— for it is said:
"Indeed, no rite whatsoever is prescribed for him until the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
he is equal to a Śūdra in all respects, but is not yet joined with the Veda."

Thus, because Manu has stated that the entitlement to perform Vedic rites begins only after the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the upper garment is prescribed in the *Dharma-sūtra*: "The upper garment of a Brāhmaṇa should be the skin of a black antelope or a spotted deer; if it is black, he should sleep on a seat spread with that skin. That of a Kṣatriya should be the skin of a Ruru deer; that of a Vaiśya should be the skin of a goat or sheep; the woolen blanket is for all castes."

*Hariṇa* is a deer; its product is *hāriṇa* (deer-skin). *Eṇī* is a doe; its product is *aiṇeya*, and that is black. If one should wear it, provided it is black—not merely *hāriṇa*—then one should neither sit nor lie down upon it when it has been spread out. *Ruru* is a spotted deer; its product is *raurava*. *Vasta* is a goat; its skin is [the *vasta*]. *Avi* is a sheep (*ūrṇāyu*); its product is *āvika*, which belongs to all castes (*varṇas*). Regarding this, Ujjvalākāra has explained that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between these, beginning with the *hāriṇa*, and that even a woolen blanket (*kambala*) made of sheep's wool belongs to all [castes].
Regarding the impossibility of obtaining a deerskin sufficient for both an upper garment and a cloak, Śākala states:
"One should always wear a deerskin that is either unbroken or divided into three parts, measuring forty-eight finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width."

Regarding the measurement of the three sections, another Smṛti states: "A brahmin should wear a skin with hair on the outside measuring three or four finger-breadths, [divided] by twenty-four, eight, or sixteen [sections]."

The first [piece] is twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas); the second is eight finger-breadths; the third is sixteen finger-breadths. Thus, the meaning is that a deerskin (ajina) measuring forty-eight finger-breadths in circumference should be worn, consisting of these three sections. In this regard, a small amount more than that should be taken for the purpose of sewing it together; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the rule that "a deerskin measuring forty-eight finger-breadths should be worn. Here, the finger-breadths are to be understood as those of the person undergoing the sacrament (saṃskārya). Regarding the girdle (mekhalā), the Gṛhya-sūtra states: "The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa is made of Muñja grass and is triple-stranded; that of a Rājanya is a bowstring; that of a Vaiśya is a thread of wool (āvīsūtra)."
*Mauñjīm* means made of *muñja* grass. *Trivṛtām* means threefold (having three strands). *Jyā* is the string of a bow. *Āvīsūtram* is a cord made of sheep’s wool. Also in the *Dharmasūtra*:

"The girdle (*mekhalā*) of a Brāhmaṇa is threefold and made of *muñja* grass, provided he is capable; that of a Rājanya is a bowstring or a *muñja* cord mixed with iron; that of a Vaiśya is a cord of sheep’s wool, or according to some, one of *sairī* or *tāmalī* grass."

"Trivṛt" means threefold. "Mauñjī" is a derivative meaning "made of muñja grass. Such is the girdle (*mekhalā*) for a Brāhmaṇa. And that, when possible—that is, when one has the capacity—should be wound from left to right (*dakṣiṇāvṛt*). This qualification applies even to the muñja grass, which is subordinate to the sense of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). "Jyā" is the string of a bow. Alternatively, the *mauñjī* may be mixed with iron; in some cases, it is bound with black iron. "Āviḥ" means "sheep"; "āvīsūtra" is a cord made of sheep's wool—a rope consisting of sheep's hair.

The *sairī* is the rope used for pulling a plough; *tāmalī* is a tree, and that which is woven from its bark is called *tāmalī*. Thus, some teachers maintain that such [a girdle] is the girdle for a Vaiśya; this is how it was explained by Ujjvalākṛt.
Manu states the specific rule: "The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth."

"But for a Kṣatriya it is a bowstring made of *maurva* [grass], and for a Vaiśya one made of hemp fibers. It is even, being neither thin in some places nor thick in others; rather, it is even and smooth throughout, possessing the quality of fine thread-gauge, and well-polished. A bowstring may sometimes be made of leather and sometimes of grass; in that regard, the word "bowstring" (*jyā*) is used as a qualifier for the *maurva* string in order to exclude those made of leather. Medhātithi states that with such a string, once it has been unfastened from the bow, a waistband (*śroṇibandha*) should be made. There is no requirement for the string to have qualities such as being threefold (*trivṛt*), because that would result in the destruction of its essential nature.
It should be understood that [the girdle] made of hemp fibers certainly exists as well. Manu states the secondary alternative (anukalpa):
"In the absence of muñja grass, however, it should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja;
it should have three strands and one, three, or five knots."

In this context, the elision of the word "etc. (ādi) is to be understood. Thus, the sentence becomes: "the absence of muñja grass, etc. Furthermore, the knots [on the staff] correspond to the number of *pravara* ancestors; the elders maintain that for one who has one *pravara*, there is one knot; for one with three *pravara*s, three; and for one with five *pravara*s, five. Regarding the staff, it is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of *bilva* or *pālāśa* wood, or of *naiyagrodha*..."

"For a Kṣatriya, [it should be] made of Udumbara wood; for a Vaiśya, [it should be] made of Bilva or Palāśa wood for a Brāhmaṇa, a staff grown from a branch of the Nyagrodha tree with its tip pointing downward for a Rājanya, or of Badara or Udumbara wood for a Vaiśya; some teachers, however, prescribe a wooden staff regardless of caste. Thus it is stated in the Dharmasūtra as well.

*Naiyagrodha* means made of *vaṭa* (banyan) wood; it is produced from a specific branch (*skandha*) of that tree, and its tip (*agra*) points downward. *Bādara* means produced from the *badara* tree. *Vārkṣa* means produced from any tree in general, without restriction to a particular species. The meaning is that some teachers teach that such a staff is for all social classes (*varṇas*).
Manu also says: "For a Brāhmaṇa, [staffs] of *bilva* and *pālāśa*; for a Kṣatriya, of *vaṭa* and *khadira*."
"The *paippala* and *audumbara* [staffs] are prescribed by law for a Vaiśya.

Here, although there is a dual designation (*dvandvanirdeśa*), the conjunction (*sāhitya*) should be understood as unintended, because the *Dharmasūtra* states that the staff may be either *bailva* or *pālāśa* as an option (*vikalpa*).
In the *Baudhāyanadharmasūtra*:
"The staff of a tree suitable for sacrifice shall be measured by the height of the head, the forehead, or the tip of the nose.

This means that the measurements of the staffs for the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya are, respectively, according to their order. The phrase "in their order" follows from the introduction made previously. In this context, the measurements starting from the head and so forth are to be taken as those of the person undergoing the consecration.
Manu states the characteristics of the staffs:

"They should all be straight, without blemishes, pleasant to look at, not causing agitation, possessed of their bark, and not damaged by fire. Here, "straight" means not crooked; "without blemishes" means without holes; "pleasant to look at" means not prickly and so forth; and "not damaged by fire" means not scorched by fire. Thus it is stated in the *Gobhila-Gṛhya-Sūtra*.

"Their garments are made of linen, hemp, cotton, or wool; their skins are those of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, or the goat; their girdles are made of Muñja grass, Kāśa grass, or Tāmbala; and their staffs are of Pārṇa, Bilva, or Aśvattha wood. Linen or hemp is the garment for a Brāhmaṇa, cotton for a Kṣatriya, and wool for a Vaiśya; these are the prescribed materials, and no others. In the absence of these, however, any of the aforementioned materials may be used by all. Here, the words *tāmbalī* and *tāmalī* are synonyms. As for the *kūrca*, it consists of an indefinite number of *darbha* blades.
"Regarding the sacrificial materials, the handful [of grain], the stalk, the *darbha*-thicket,
as well as the *kūrca* and the spreading [of grass], the number of *darbha* blades is not prescribed.
Thus says the authoritative statement.
As for that which is stated in the *Prayogapārijāta*: "A *kūrca* made respectively with nine, seven, or five blades of *darbha* grass is declared to be excellent, middling, and inferior."
"The knot of that [grass] should be known as two finger-breadths [in length], and four finger-breadths above that.
Thus, it should be understood that this definition of the *kūrca* refers to a *kūrca* intended for sitting, excluding other types of *kūrca*.
In the *Smṛtisāra*:
"One should not perform the marriage of two sisters born of the same mother, nor likewise the initiation ceremony (*vratabandhana*) for two brothers.
Regarding the specific rule when a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs after the commencement of the initiation ceremony, it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"Having offered clarified butter with the *Kūśmāṇḍī* verses, one should give a milch cow; then one should perform the tonsure, initiation, marriage, consecration, and so forth.

Thus, the instruction of the mantras—such as "śaṃ no devīḥ"—which serve as the instruments of the rites performed by the religious student (*brahmacārin*), must be carried out even prior to the initiation ceremony, because this is permitted by the author of the commentary on the Sūtra, just as [the instruction] of the mantras for the wife's inspection and so forth [is done before the sacrifice].
Now follows the *annahoma* (oblation of food). Regarding this, the Sūtra states as follows:

"When food is available, having taken equal portions of boiled rice, cakes, and barley meal, he offers them mixed with clarified butter, saying: 'To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! To Agni, the eater of food, Svāhā! To Agni, the lord of food, Svāhā! To Prajāpati, Svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, Svāhā! To all the deities, Svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā! In every case where no deity is specifically prescribed, [one offers] with 'To such-and-such, Svāhā,' according to the respective deity; when a deity is specifically prescribed, one takes equal portions of these very same foods and [offers them] on blades of grass pointing eastward."

"On darbha grass he offers an oblation with the words, 'To the Lord of the Dwelling, svāhā! Having served the brahmins with threefold food and having caused them to recite, 'An auspicious day! Prosperity! Success!', he observes the vow for three days."

The meaning of this is as follows: when food has been presented—that is, brought or served—for the purpose of serving the Brahmins, one takes equal portions (*samavadāya*) of three items—boiled rice (*odana*), cakes (*apūpa*), and parched barley flour (*saktu*)—and having broken off as much as required and mixed them together, one then offers the mixture into the fire with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) while reciting these mantras: "To Agni, Svāhā! and so forth. The use of the word "presented" (*upasthita*) is for the purpose of including that which has already been prepared outside; for if only "of boiled rice, cakes, and parched barley flour" were stated, the preparation would logically apply only to those items at that specific point.

Since the purpose would have been accomplished merely by mentioning "of the rice, cakes, and parched grain" (*odanasyāpūpānāṃ saktūnām*) when these are present, the inclusion of the word *anna* (food) is for the sake of including side dishes (*vyañjana*). By this it is understood that these items are presented for the purpose of eating as well, and not solely for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*). From this it is also known that eating consists only of the remnants of the oblation, and not of anything else. The mention of rice and the other items using a copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*) might imply that they could sometimes be taken together in a single vessel; to prevent this, they are mentioned here without a compound.

Because of the plural number in the word *apūpānām* (of cakes), three or more cakes are to be taken. The word *saktu* (barley meal), like the word *piṣṭa* (flour), ends in the plural, as in the passage "he offers with barley meal" (*saktubhir juhoti*). Rice and other such foods are to be taken provided they are not alkaline or salty; for it is said: "There is no sacrifice involving alkaline or salty substances."

Because of this prohibition in the *Dharmasūtra*. The word "iti" is for the purpose of restriction, meaning: "one should take a portion only of the rice, the cakes, and the barley-meal. By this, there is an exclusion of side-dishes that have become sacrificial oblations (*haviṣya*). Having taken a portion from each of the rice and the others, one offers it with that [portion] mixed with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). It is not a mixing of all three together. From the word "clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ*), it follows that the butter used for mixing is simply unrefined ghee (*ājya*). The *Sviṣṭakṛt* oblation is to be offered in the eastern half of the northern half, so as not to be joined with the previous oblations.

He extends this *trivṛt* food-oblation to other cases as well: "In all cases where no deity has been specified, it is thus. This means: in every ritual action whatsoever, when no deity has been prescribed—where no deity is *ādiṣṭā* (prescribed), that is *anādiṣṭā*; that in which the deity is *anādiṣṭā* is *anādiṣṭadevatam*—when such food is present, the oblation must be performed in this manner.

The statement "in all cases" is intended to ensure that this oblation occurs whenever food is present during any ritual action, and not only when ordinary (laukika) food is present.
