The phrase "when no deity has been assigned" is for the purpose of excluding the food from the *sthālīpāka*, the monthly *śrāddha*, and so forth, because those involve deities that have already been assigned. This oblation does not take place during the *kāṇḍavrata* and similar rites, as there is no presence of food [in the sense required] at that time.

And this "presence of food" (*annopasthiti*) must be understood as that which is explicitly stated by the words themselves; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since the presence of food intended for feeding Brahmins established at another *śrāddha* exists in the *kāṇḍavrata* and other rites mentioned in the Sūtras, as well as in rituals such as ear-piercing mentioned in other scriptures. Nor is this an acceptable consequence, because such a practice does not exist. If this is so, then in the case of the rule "even-numbered Brahmins," since the presence [of food] explicitly stated here also exists, the *trivṛd-anna-homa* would follow. This is not a fault.

If this were intended, then [the text] would have prescribed this very rule there and extended it by analogy (*atideśa*). Therefore, it is established that this *homa* pertains only to cases other than those where the food is already present as previously described. Regarding the phrase "to such-and-such a one, svāhā" (*amuṣmai svāhā*): the meaning is that when the food has been assigned to a specific deity, the *homa* should be performed according to that deity, saying "to such-and-such a one, svāhā."

When the *sthālīpāka* has been prepared for the deity to whom it was assigned, some teachers have prescribed an oblation (*homa*) accompanied by *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses; the statement "to such-and-such [a deity] svāhā" is intended so that this [specific rite] shall not occur. The statement "according to the deity" (*yathādevatam*) is for the purpose that whatever Vedic grammatical feature is observed in the word for the deity within the mantra in a given ritual, that same feature should likewise apply to the name-mantra.

And because the mantra "dṛṣṭaśca kṣetrasya patiḥ" contains the word *kṣetrasya* with the genitive case ending, the rule "aṣaṣṭhīyuktaśchandasi vā" prescribes the optional application of the technical designation *ghisamjñā* in Vedic usage; by that very rule, the oblation (*homa*) is performed with the name-mantra according to its specific grammatical form. For example, when the *ghisamjñā* designation is absent, one says "kṣetrasya pataye svāhā," whereas in its presence, one says "kṣetrasya patye svāhā. The statement "the deity is specified" applies only to the name-mantra used for the oblation of food (*annahoma*), and not to the name-mantra used for the oblation of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*).

Therefore, at the commencement of the Veda-study (vedopākaraṇa) and other rites, the mantra is precisely "sadasaspataye svāhā," and not "sadasaspatye svāhā. Because the general rule (paribhāṣā) is established prior to the prescription of the Vāstu-bali offering, it is understood from this that the Vāstu-bali is to be performed only after completing the remainder of the ritual following the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation. Alternatively, the placement of the general rule in the middle is intended to indicate that the Vāstu-bali is not mandatory.

Alternatively, the phrase "as before" occurring later [in the text] is connected also with the words "having served food to the Brāhmaṇas," according to the maxim of the central gem (*madhyamaṇinyāya*). By this, the necessity of the *vāstubali* (the house-offering) is established in all cases, and traditional practice (*ācāra*) is upheld. The reason for providing this general rule (*paribhāṣā*) in the middle [of the section] is so that, because the *vāstubali* itself is not separated [from it], its extension (*atideśa*) may apply everywhere; whereas for the *homa*, since it is separated, there should be no such extension—this is for that purpose. The expression "of these" (*eteṣām*) indicates that those very same materials are to be used when performing the offering.

The particle *eva* is for the purpose of excluding even vegetable side-dishes (*vyañjana*). Because of the instruction "one should take portions equally" (*samavadāyet*), having taken [portions] separately from each, having broken them off, and having mixed them together, one offers the *bali* upon *darbha* grass blades with their tips pointing eastward. The specification "with tips pointing eastward" is for the purpose of excluding [the practice of using grass] with tips pointing northward. There is no mixing with clarified butter (*sarpis*) here, as there is no scriptural injunction for it. Because of the instruction "one offers the *bali*," having first sprinkled [water] around [the site], having placed the *bali* there, one sprinkles water around it.

The meaning is that, having served and fed the Brahmins with *trivṛt*—that is, food of three kinds accompanied by side dishes—and having caused them to pronounce the *puṇyāha* and other auspicious formulas, he observes the vow for three days. Although the purpose would have been accomplished by the word "food" (*anna*) alone, the inclusion of the term *trivṛt* is intended to ensure that when it says "having served the even-numbered Brahmins with food," one understands that the food consists of the threefold set: boiled rice, cakes, and barley meal (*saktu*). The procedure for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) follows.

Now follows the procedure for the initiation (*upanayana*). The preceptor, desiring to perform the initiation, should prepare one sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of cotton according to the prescribed method, a stone of the measure of a span (*prādeśa*), two unwashed garments (either linen or cotton), a loincloth (*kaupīna*) with a linen cord for binding it, an upper garment that is either saffron-colored cloth or an antelope skin (*ajina*), and a triple-stranded girdle (*mekhalā*) made of muñja grass with knots equal in number to the *pravara* ancestors, as well as a staff of the characteristics previously described, with its tip untrimmed.

One should prepare seven fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *palāśa* wood, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length; a seat-mat (*kūrca*) made from an indefinite number of *darbha* grasses; an alms-bowl other than one of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*); and a cow. One should also arrange the materials for the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth. Furthermore, the cow should be prepared by the father or the person initiating the boy (*upanetṛ*) to be given as a boon (*varadāna*) by the boy upon his request. Having performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), the teacher (*ācārya*) should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), restrain his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), and announce the place and time. He should then make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), saying: "For the sake of establishing my authority as the initiator, I shall perform the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of three *kṛcchra* penances through such-and-such a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*)," and he should then carry it out.

Thus, having first proclaimed the place and time, and having caused the student (vaṭu) to make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), saying, "I shall perform the penance consisting of three *kṛcchra*s as a substitute for the gift of a cow (*godāna-pratyāmnāya*) in order to accomplish the qualification for initiation," the teacher should cause that to be performed; or, in the event of his inability, the initiator himself may perform it.

Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the recitation (*japa*) of the Gāyatrī twelve thousand times, or twelve thousand plus one thousand, for the purpose of qualifying myself for the instruction in the Gāyatrī," [one should know the following]: for the six mantras beginning with *agna āyūṃṣi*, the Viśvedevas are the seers (*ṛṣis*). For the first two, Agni Pavamāna is the deity; for the middle two, Agni Pāvaka; and for the last two, Agni Śuci. The meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the recitation.

Having recited once the six mantras known as the *agni-pavitra*, beginning with "Oṃ agne āyuṣi... and ending with "...pyarcayaḥ," and having recited once the Gāyatrī mantra—"Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ... and ending with "...dayāt"—with Viśvāmitra as the seer (*ṛṣi*), Savitṛ as the deity (*devatā*), and Gāyatrī as the meter (*chandaḥ*), its application being for the purpose of recitation (*jape viniyogaḥ*)—one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī twelve thousand times, or twelve thousand plus one thousand more, according to the time available and in accordance with the previously made resolve, preceded by the remembrance of the seer and other elements.

Alternatively, having recited once the six mantras known as the *agnipavitra* and the *gāyatrī*, one should perform the recitation of the *gāyatrī* the prescribed number of times preceded by a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Or else, a single recitation of the *gāyatrī* need not be performed at all.

Then the teacher, having performed all the daily rites on the day preceding or on the very day of the initiation—having ascertained the date from astrologers and others—and having performed an auspicious bath and donned auspicious attire, sits facing east upon a seat covered with a cloth and decorated with *raṅgavalli* designs. To his right, he seats his wife, who has performed an auspicious bath and donned auspicious attire; to her right, he seats the person to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), who has likewise performed an auspicious bath and donned auspicious attire. Having done so, he performs the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Having restrained his breath and having proclaimed the place and time, he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord, I shall perform for this boy the sacrament called *upanayana*—which has the teacher as its father, the *Sāvitrī* as its mother, and is preceded by the attainment of the status of the twice-born—in order to achieve the qualification for the study of the Vedas."

Then, as part of that [rite], I shall perform the recitation for a "meritorious day" (*puṇyāha-vācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjana*), the *nāndī-śrāddha*, the sacrifice to the planets (*graha-yajña*), the sowing of seeds (*aṅkura-āropaṇa*), and the installation of the deities of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-devatā-pratiṣṭhāpana*). At the outset, one should perform the rites beginning with the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati for the sake of achieving freedom from obstacles, and the worship of the family deity (*kuladevatā*) and others according to custom"—up to the end of the sowing of seeds. Alternatively, the sequence may be such that the sowing of seeds comes first and the sacrifice to the planets afterwards.
The specific modification in the recitation for the "meritorious day" is: "May Indra be pleased."

Alternatively, the *grahayajña* (sacrifice to the planets) and the *aṅkurāropaṇa* (sowing of sprouts) should be performed even before the primary formal resolve (*pradhāna-saṃkalpa*). In this view, there is no mention of these two in that particular resolve.

Because the initiation (*upanayana*) is distinguished by its purpose of Vedic study and its function of establishing the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*), one should perform the propitiation of Vināyaka (*vināyaka-śānti*) separately—or by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*)—prior to the *grahayajña*, for the sake of ensuring freedom from obstacles therein. That propitiation is to be found in the *Ratnamālā*.
As for the *grahayajña*, it should be performed within seven days, or at the very latest within ten days, prior to the day of the primary formal resolve.
One should perform the sacrifice to the planets (grahamakhā) prior to the day of erecting the pavilion;
it may be done ten days or seven days before, but one should never perform it earlier than that.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Jyotiḥsāgara*: "Before the day of establishing the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*)—that is, prior to the day of the primary formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—one should perform the *grahamakhayajña* (the sacrifice to the planets). Regarding the rule for the timing therein, it says "ten days": the meaning is that one should not perform that *grahamakhayajña* earlier than ten days or seven days from that point. In this context, the Mothers such as Gaurī and others, as well as Gaṇapati and the rest, should be installed upon a cloth spread over a bamboo vessel (*vaṃśapātra*).

Then, according to custom, one should wrap *dūrvā* grass and branches of the *śamī* tree—which are covered with leaves from excellent trees such as the mango—with a thread in six places. Having inserted a pestle in one place and a knife-weapon in another, they should be wrapped around.

Then, having placed those branches in a bamboo vessel dedicated to the Mothers (*mātṛkā*), one should invoke Nandinī, Nalinī, Maitrī, and Umā by their respective name-mantras into those four [branches] in a clockwise direction. To the north of them, in the branch containing the pestle, one should invoke Paśuvardhinī by her name-mantra; and to the north of that, in the branch containing the knife-weapon, one should invoke the Goddess (Bhagavatī) by her very name.

Then, to the north of the vessel for the lineage of the Mothers (mātṛkāvaṃśapātra), having placed two small earthen jars—or one according to custom—filled with rice, provided with pieces of turmeric, sweetmeats (laḍḍuka), and betel nuts, covered with an inverted shallow dish (śarāva), colored with white powder, and wound with thread; having invoked Gaṇapati, the Lord of Obstacles, with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," and having established him with the mantra "narya prajām," and having offered the services beginning with the seat (āsana) and ending with the water for sipping (ācamanīya); and having placed a copper vessel near oneself, [one should place] those branches therein.

Having established [the image], and having caused the wife to perform the lustration (*nīrājana*), the anointing with fragrant oil, the rubbing with *yavāraka*, turmeric, and other substances, and the bath with warm water, he should bathe it with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. Having offered water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) and having placed those branches in a vessel belonging to the lineage of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-vaṃśa-pātra*) as before, he should present the services from clothing up to flowers. Then, having worshipped with curd using the verse *dadhi krāvṇo* and with *dūrvā* grass using the verse *kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt*, and having presented the services from incense onwards, [he should pray]:
"O deities, whatever is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion..."
May this worship that has been performed be complete for me.

Having thus prayed, he himself takes the bamboo vessel (*vaṃśapātra*) and causes his wife to hold the jar of Gaṇapati free from obstacles (*avighnagaṇapatikalaśa*). Accompanied by the sounding of bells and other musical instruments, and together with the Brahmins, he recites the mantras: "Oṃ, may Indra grant us well-being... may Bṛhaspati bestow it," "The eight gods, the Vasus... may there be immortality and well-being for me," and "May we prosper through oblations and reverence... with our heroes. Having entered the middle of the house, he smears the place of installation, adorns it with colored powders, creepers, and other decorations, and [proceeds] there.

Having poured rice grains into those [vessels] and placed that bamboo vessel upon them with the mantra "narya prajām," and having had his wife place a water-pot to the north of that very spot, he should worship it with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra). Then, for the sake of pleasing the deities installed there, he should feed Brāhmaṇas and married women according to his means, and give them clothing and other gifts according to his means.

Then, after the couple have been consecrated by the *nīrājana* rite, their friends should give them garments and other gifts. Thereafter, the performer should perform any other rites according to his family tradition (*kuladharma*). Until the dismantling of the pavilion (*maṇḍapodvāsana*), he should worship the deities installed each day.

As it has been stated, when it is convenient to construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa), it should be made—measuring sixteen or twelve cubits according to one of those numbers, or eight cubits if that is impossible, or according to the available space—with four doors, adorned with arches (toraṇas), and supported by four sturdy pillars. This pavilion should be constructed on the left side of the house or near the entrance. Here, the "hand" (hasta) to be used as a unit of measurement is that of the preceptor (ācārya), and not that of the person for whom the rite is being performed; otherwise, in the case of an eight-cubit pavilion, it would result in being excessively small. "When an auspicious pavilion is constructed according to the measurement of the preceptor’s hand..."
"In the center, an altar should be constructed, square on all sides."
This is also because of the statement in the *Jyotirnibandha*:

"The teacher (*ācārya*)" is an elliptical designation for the performer of the consecration (*saṃskāraka*); therefore, even in the case of marriage, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) must be [constructed] by the hand of the performer of the consecration, such as the father or others.
"The altar (*vedi*) should be made with five or seven hands of the maiden; it should be raised like the back of a tortoise."

By this statement, once it is established that the measurement of the girl’s hand pertains specifically to the altar (*vedi*), it follows by implication that the measurement of the officiant’s hand pertains to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). In that regard, there is a pillar made of mango wood or rose-apple wood in the southeast; one made of *khadira* wood or from the *dhātrī* tree in the southwest; one made of *udumbara* wood or *śamī* wood in the northwest; and one made of jujube wood or *aśmantaka* wood in the northeast.

Having constructed a firm pillar-pavilion (stambha-maṇḍapa) covered with mats and the like, and having adorned it with arches and other decorations, one should tie four branches as before. Having placed them in the hands of four Brāhmaṇas while reciting the two mantras, "I have performed the act for Dadhikrāvan" and "The herbs that were born," one should invoke Gaṅgā at the pillar in the southeast, saying, "Obeisance to Gaṅgā; I invoke Gaṅgā," worship her, and pray, "Be very firm and stable."

Thus, one should invoke Gaurī in the southwest (Nairṛtya), Dharaṇī in the northwest (Vāyavya), and Lakṣmī in the northeast (Īśāna). Then, having taken those branches from the hands of the Brahmins and tied them to the pillars starting from the southeast (Āgneya), one should invoke and install Nandinī on the southeastern branch, Nalinī on the southwestern branch, Maitrā on the northwestern branch, and Umā on the northeastern branch.

Then, having tied a branch containing a pestle—which is held in his own hand—to the central beam of the pavilion, he should invoke and install Paśuvardhinī there by name alone. Thereafter, he should worship them either according to the method of *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performing all rites for one object before moving to the next) or according to the method of *padārthānusamaya* (performing each rite for all objects in succession). In this regard, the four mantras beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhā" are, respectively, the bathing mantras for the four deities Nandinī and the others; all four [mantras] also apply to Paśuvardhinī.

In all cases, the three mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* are to be used together. The mantra *gandhadvārām* is for the fragrance; *dadhikrāvṇo* is for the curd; and *kāṇḍātkāṇḍāt* is for the *dūrvā* grass. The distinction is that after the offering of the *dūrvā*, one should offer the secondary services (*upacāra*) such as flowers and so forth.

Then, having placed four jars in the middle of the pavilion according to the rite for installing jars in the sequence starting from the southeast (āgneyī), and having encircled them with a triple-thread (*trisūtrī*), one should perform the installation of the deity within them. This is done as follows:

Having placed a bamboo vessel upon an undamaged seat, one should invoke and install the Goddess within a branch containing a small knife known as a *devaka*; after offering the services beginning with the seat and ending with water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), one should have four married women perform the lustration (*nīrājana*), anointing, rubbing with unguents, and bathing with warm water; then, having placed the *devaka* in the bamboo vessel and worshipped it with offerings such as garments, one should [place] those two jars—or one jar—upon that very same seat.

Having placed Gaṇapati, known as "the one whose name is free from obstacles," there, he should invoke him, install him, and worship him. Then, having placed the lineage-vessel (vaṃśapātra) of the Mātṛkās near that, he should perform everything else, such as the feeding of Brāhmaṇas, as previously described.

Then, in the center of that pavilion, an altar (*vedi*) should be constructed with a length and width of six cubits, or a length and width of four cubits, and a height of one cubit. There, having made a mark at a distance of one cubit to the south and one cubit to the north from the intersection of the central line of the altar and the western line, and having likewise made two marks in front of the southern and northern marks for the sake of straightness, one should lay an eastward line between the two southern marks at those intersections and make a mark every twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) along that line; the same should be done between the two northern marks.

Having thus prepared it, one should construct a wall there thirty finger-breadths high. On both sides of that wall, eight steps each should be made. Upon the wall, in the middle portion, one should place a lump of clay shaped like a water-pot (*kalaśa*). Regarding this as well, the measurement is according to the teacher's preference. Properties observed for the wedding altar (*vivāhavedi*), such as being raised like the back of a tortoise, should also be applied here since they are not in conflict. However, nowadays the learned perform the altar exactly as for the wedding altar.

Then, on the morning of the second day, the preceptor, having fed six or an even number of Brāhmaṇas starting from six and having had them pronounce the *puṇyāha*, *svastyayana*, and *ṛddhi* blessings, should say, "May Indra be pleased. Thereafter, he should feed the boy—who has performed the auspicious bath and is adorned—along with his mother; in the absence of the mother, with another woman who does not refuse; and in the absence of even her, he should feed him alone. It is also the custom to feed eight celibate students (*brahmacārins*).

Then, after the prince has eaten, the barber shall shave his hair; having bathed the prince and caused him to sip water twice, he shall bind his top-knot (*śikhā*), adorn him with perfumes and other ornaments, clothe him in a new garment silently, seat him, and cause him to perform the sipping of water twice. In this context, the sipping of water follows the *paurāṇa* (traditional) method as follows: one should drink water while reciting the three names beginning with Keśava; with the fourth and fifth [names], one should touch the palms of the hands; with the sixth and seventh, one should touch the lips.

With the eighth and ninth [grains], one should wipe the mouth; with the tenth, sprinkle the left hand; with the eleventh, sprinkle the feet; with the twelfth, touch the head; with the thirteenth, touch the upper lip with the tips of the fingers; with the fourteenth, touch the right nostril with the thumb and forefinger; with the fifteenth, touch the left nostril with those same two fingers; with the sixteenth and seventeenth, respectively, touch the right and left eyes with the thumb and ring finger; and with the eighteenth and nineteenth...

Respectively, one should touch the right and left ears with the thumb and ring finger; the navel with the twentieth [finger] using those same two; the heart with the palm of the hand using the twenty-first; the head with the hand using the twenty-second; and the right and left arms respectively with the fingertips of the twenty-third and twenty-fourth fingers. The names beginning with Keśava should end in *namaḥ*, or be in the nominative case, or in the vocative case.

In the view of those who hold that [the mantra] ends with *saṃbuddhi* (vocative), some pronounce *viṣṇupada* and *haripada* without case endings; however, this is trivial because of the rule that one should employ only correct forms (*sādhu*). All acts of sipping water (*ācamana*) prior to the instruction on the *gāyatrī* are likewise performed in this same manner.

Then, having seated [the student] upon the altar (vedī), and having prepared the sacrificial ground (āyatana) or the leveled mound (sthaṇḍila) on the altar according to the aforementioned method, and having performed its consecration as before; having established the fire—either one produced from common wood or brought from the house of a Vedic scholar—reciting "I establish the fire named Samudbhava," and having kindled it, meditated upon it, and taken three fuel-sticks; having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) ending with "O Faith, come" (śraddha ehi), and having recited from "In this Upanayana-homa rite, those deities which are to be worshipped... up to the Vyāhṛtis; then, for the specific principal oblation (vaiśeṣika-pradhāna-homa):

"I shall sacrifice with one oblation of clarified butter to Agni, the giver of life; I shall sacrifice with one oblation of clarified butter to the divine Agni, the giver of life. Regarding the *aṅga-homa* (limb-offerings), [the deities are] Varuṇa and so forth. At the setting out of the vessels, [one prepares]: a stone, two unwashed garments, a saffron-colored garment for an upper cloth or a skin, a girdle of muñja grass, a staff, a wooden ladle (*darvī*), a broom (*kūrca*), a vessel for clarified butter, the vessel for carrying forward the *praṇītā* water, the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessel, the *upaveṣa* fire-stirring stick, a vessel for removing embers, a loincloth, and a linen thread for binding it.

Having employed the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and the alms-bowl (*bhikṣāpātra*) according to the procedure prescribed by Baudhāyana, and having stationed a cow nearby, one should set down the *saṃmārga* (cleansing) *darbha* grasses, the *avajvalana* (ignition) *darbha* grasses, the outer fuel (*bahiridhma*), the clarified butter (*ājya*), and seven fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *palāśa* wood. Mātṛdatta has stated that the use of the *kūrca* grass-mat belongs only to the school of Pauṣkarasādi; this [view] is to be considered.

Then, having performed the rites beginning with the selection of the Brahman priest and ending with the encircling of the altar, he should tie the previously prepared cord around the waist of the boy standing to the north of the fire; having clothed him in the prepared loin-cloth and seated him upon Darbha grass, he should cause him to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.

Then the boy sits down right there: for the mantra "Of the god thee" (*devasya tvā*), Prajāpati is the seer, the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is the deity, the Yajus is the meter; its application is in the act of taking up [the thread]. Having taken up the placed sacred thread with the words, "Oṃ, of the god thee... with both hands I take," [he proceeds]: for the mantra "Upwards we two" (*udvayaṃ tam*), Soma and Sūrya are the seers, Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application is in showing the sacred thread to the Sun. Having shown the sacred thread to the Sun with the words, "Oṃ, upwards we two... the highest light," [he recites]: for the mantra "The sacrificial thread" (*yajñopavītam*), the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the meter.

The application [of the mantra] is for the wearing of the sacred thread (*upavīta*). One should lift the right arm and wear it [over the left shoulder], reciting: "Oṃ, the sacrificial thread is your luster.

Nowadays, however, since the manufacture of a sacrificial thread according to the procedure prescribed by Baudhāyana is often impossible, the learned simply perform the required rites with the respective mantras over a ready-made sacrificial thread and wear it.

If even this is unavailable, one should silently fashion a substitute sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and, having sprinkled it ten times with water consecrated either by the three mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* or by the *Gāyatrī* together with the *Vyāhṛtis*, one should wear it with either the mantra, "The sacred thread is the supreme purifier," or with all the *Vyāhṛtis* together, or with the mantra spoken in the *Koṣītakī*: "I invest thee with the sacred thread for long life, for good progeny, for great vigor, for sovereignty over all the Vedas, for glory, and for spiritual luster."

Then, having sipped water twice, and having sipped water twice again in the northeast direction from the fire-altar, he goes to the south of the teacher, passing between the fire and the *brahmā* priest, and having sat down there facing east, he takes hold of him. According to Mātṛdatta, [he sits] behind the fire. This is the initiation-oblation (*upanayana-homa*).
Then the teacher, with the boy taking hold of him, performs the rites beginning with the sprinkling and ending with the *vyāhṛti* oblations, and then performs the principal oblation.

For the mantra *āyurdā*, the deities are the Viśvedevas; the deity is Agni, the metre is Triṣṭubh. For the Sautra mantra *āyurdā deva*, the seer is Vāmadeva; the deity is the divine Agni, the metre is Triṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal *ājya* oblation of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). "Oṃ āyurdā agne... dima svāhā"—this is for Agni, the giver of life. "Oṃ āyurdā devaja... nayema svāhā"—this is for the divine Agni, the giver of life. Thus one should offer the two principal oblations.
Mantras whose accents (*svara*) are unknown should everywhere be recited with a single tone (*ekaśrutya*).

Then, having performed the rites beginning with "tata imaṃ me varuṇa" and ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he places the stone that was set aside in front of the junction of the northern enclosing sticks to the north of the fire. Having led the boy in front of the fire, he makes him stand upon the stone with his right foot, reciting: "Oṃ, step upon this stone; like a stone, be firm yourself. Crush those who wish you ill; overcome those who attack you in battle. The mention of "with the right foot" in the Sūtra is intended either to exclude the left foot or to indicate the proper sequence.

In the first case, only the right foot is to be placed upon the stone, not the left. In the second case, however, having first placed the boy’s right foot, the left one is then to be placed. In all instances, the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the Sūtra-mantras is Vāmadeva; the deities are those mentioned in the mantras; and the meters (*chandas*) are to be inferred. Since there is also the view that for Sūtra-mantras there is no requirement to know the seers and so forth, the seers and other details are not stated here.
However, if they were stated by adopting another view, there would be excessive prolixity due to the great number of Sūtra-mantras.
Then, having brought the boy down from the stone and having removed the stone from that spot, he set aside the previously worn garment in a known place.

"Oṃ! Those goddesses who cut [the wool], those who carded it, those who spun it, and those who bestowed the threads on all sides—may those goddesses clothe you with old age. Long-lived, put on this garment! Clothe him, dress him in a garment; make him live for a hundred years, grant him long life. Bṛhaspati gave this garment to King Soma to put on. Go to old age, put on the garment; become a protector against the curses of the people."

"May you live for a hundred autumns with great luster; may you clothe yourself in the increase of wealth"—with these words, he causes the boy to put on one of the two garments that have been placed there. "Oṃ! You have put this garment on for well-being, as a protector against the curses of rivals. May you live for a hundred long autumns; living, may you distribute riches among the worthy. He thus addresses the boy who has finished dressing. (Note: *vasūni cāyyo vibhajāsajīvan* is a reading resulting from a scribal error.)

Then, having seated him, he should cause him to perform the *ācamana* twice. With the mantra: "Oṃ, she who comes to us, warding off misfortunes, purifying our protection and refuge, bringing strength through the out-breath and in-breath—may this auspicious sister of the gods, the girdle, [be ours]," he wraps the prepared girdle three times around the boy’s waist from left to right at the level of the navel; some say it is twice, while the mantra is recited once. Then, having made a triple knot above the navel, he pulls the end down to the right side of the navel.

"Oṃ! The eye of Mitra, supporting, sustaining, brilliant, glorious, firm, kindled, unwearied, ageless, and clothing—put on this skin, O powerful one, as a conqueror. May Aditi bind this girdle for you, so that you may recite the Veda, for the sake of intelligence, faith, the non-rejection of what has been spoken, and for sacred knowledge and spiritual luster.
With these words, he places the black antelope skin over the boy, with the hair upward and the neck toward the north, as an upper garment.

The skin of the Ruru deer is for a Kṣatriya, and the skin of the goat for a Vaiśya. If a skin large enough to serve as an upper garment (*uttarīya*) cannot be obtained, one should take a skin measuring forty-eight *aṅgulas* in length and four or three *aṅgulas* in width; having taken a small amount more than that for the purpose of sewing the edges, one should sew it so as not to exceed the measurement of forty-eight *aṅgulas*, and thus have that circular skin made into an upper garment.

In that regard, the sections to be consecrated consist of eight finger-breadths for the first, sixteen finger-breadths for the second, and twenty-four finger-breadths for the third. When the lower garment itself serves as the upper garment, there is either an omission of the mantra or the elision of the word "ajina" (deerskin). In whatever mantra the word *asau* occurs, there the vocative form of the person to be consecrated—ending in *śarman* and being their common secular name—is to be inserted.

Then he should say to the boy, "Oṃ, I entrust you to Indra. The boy replies, "Entrust me. Then the teacher, [addressing] a Brāhmaṇa boy, entrusts him to Indra with the mantra: "Oṃ, we entrust this one to Indra for the sake of great Vedic learning; may he remain awake for a long time in his hearing until old age. This means that having touched the boy, he recites the mantra. According to the author of the Gṛhyakārikā, the act of entrusting consists in raising the boy, touching him, and reciting the mantra.
In place of the word "ear," the word "kingdom" is used; in the handing over of a Kṣatriya boy, the word "nourishment" is used; and in the handing over of a Vaiśya boy.

Then, having led the boy to the south of the fire and seated him to the west of the fire facing north, he makes him consume the remainder of the clarified butter—either all of it or half of it—once with each of these three mantras: "Oṃ! May Agni bestow wisdom upon you, may he bestow offspring upon you; may he bestow splendor upon you. May Indra bestow wisdom upon you, may he bestow offspring upon you; may he bestow sensory power upon you. May Sūrya bestow wisdom upon you, may he bestow offspring upon you; may he bestow radiance upon you. The consumption takes place at the end of the three [mantras].

When the entire portion is consumed, then for the purpose of placing seven palāśa fuel-sticks, one should anoint them with ordinary ghee (*laukikājya*). Since the anointing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) must be performed, one should prepare another portion of ghee as before and perform both rites with that. However, when only half is consumed, then the anointing, the anointing of the enclosing sticks, and the expiatory oblation are to be performed with that very remainder.

Alternatively, having brought all—or half—of the clarified butter remaining from the oblation into a small amount of worldly curd and, by stirring, having made it possess the quality of *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter), one should have him consume it with these very same mantras. It is not the case that *pṛṣadājya* is to be prepared by bringing a small amount of curd into the clarified butter remaining from the oblation; for it is more appropriate to adopt here the rule seen in the *Paśusūtra* regarding the purpose of the quality of *pṛṣadājya*, which prescribes bringing the clarified butter into the curd as "one-third of the clarified butter into the curd."

Then, for the verse "yoge yoge" (RV 4.2.1), the deities are Agni and Indra, the metre is Gāyatrī; for the verse "imamagna āyuṣe" (RV 3.16.19), the deities are the Viśvedevas—specifically Agni, Varuṇa, Soma, Aditi, and the Viśvedevas—and the metre is Bhūriṣṭup. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the beholding of the child: with the two verses, "oṃ yoge yoge tava... mūrtaye" and "imamagna āyuṣe... thāsat," he gazes at the child as he consumes [the food].

Alternatively, he causes [the child] to eat either the remains of the oblation (*hutoccheṣa*) or speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with these two mantras. In this case, however, there is an omission of the three mantras beginning with "In you, wisdom... (*tvayi medhām*) and of the act of looking. Then the boy should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*), which is an ancillary part of the eating. If the remains of the oblation butter are lost, there is no eating; and because there is no eating, there is also no sipping of water. Some say that another portion of butter should be taken in its place and eaten.

Then the teacher, having caused the boy who has sipped water to touch himself, consecrates the boy with the mantra: "Oṃ, a hundred autumns are before us, O gods, wherein you have ordained the aging of our bodies; wherein sons become fathers—do not harm our life-span in its course.

Then the boy, having moved outside the teacher and the Brahman priest, circumambulates the fire together with the vessel from left to right. The teacher says: "Oṃ, we have come together with those who have come; keep away the death that has arrived."

"May we move about unharmed; may we move about safely here; may we go safely from our homes. While remaining seated, he addresses the boy as he circumambulates the fire from left to right, making him recite: "Om! I have come to the life of a student; lead me near; become a student, impelled by the god Savitṛ. Thus he causes the boy to recite.

"Who are you by name?"—thus he asks the boy. Then the boy declares his own name, which ends in *śarman*, is used for common usage, and is derived from the lunar mansion (*nākṣatra*); for example: "I am Devadattaśarman Kārtika. Then the teacher takes up the two names of the boy, saying: "Oṃ, may it be well! O God Savitṛ, may I attain the highest through this Devadattaśarman Kārtika. Regarding the verse beginning with *śaṃ no devīḥ*: Prajāpati is the seer, the Waters are the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is for the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*). "Oṃ, may the divine [waters] be auspicious to us... Both [the teacher and the boy] sprinkle themselves with water; the mantra belongs to both.

Now follows the principal initiation (*pradhānopanayana*). Then the teacher, having honored an astrologer, sits facing east to the south of the fire. To the southeast of the fire, in front of himself and facing him, he seats the boy. Between the two, while an astrologer holds a curtain marked with a *svastika* and having its fringes toward the north, and while Brahmins recite auspicious hymns and verses, the teacher should sit reflecting upon the deities of his own lineage and so forth, and gazing at the *svastika* on the curtain. The boy should do likewise.
Alternatively, both [the teacher and the boy] remain in their respective places. In this view, the curtain (*antaḥpaṭa*) is at the end of the preliminary period (*prāg-daśa*).

Then, at the moment of an auspicious conjunction (*sulagna*) determined by the astrologers, once the curtain has been removed—either toward the north or the east—the teacher, remaining right there, should perform the initiation (*upanayana*) of the boy. It is done as follows: having silently touched the boy’s right shoulder with his own right hand and his left shoulder with his left hand, [he recites]: Prajāpati is the seer of the collective *vyāhṛtis*; the metre is *bṛhatī*. Viśvāmitra and Agni are the seers of the *gāyatrī*; Savitṛ is the deity; the metre is *gāyatrī*.

The seer of the mantra "devasya tvā" is Vāmadeva; the deity is Savitṛ; the metre is Yajus. Its application is in the initiation (upanayana) of the boy. Saying: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," "Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt," and "Oṃ devasya tvā savituḥ prasave'śvinorbāhubhyāṃ pūṣṇo hastābhyām upanaye'mukaśarman," he brings the boy's right arm toward himself while seated and initiates the boy—that is, he brings the boy into his own presence facing him.

The teacher should not forget this principal initiation (*pradhānopanayana*) during the course of the ritual. If it is forgotten, the entire rite must be repeated, according to the statement of Mātṛdatta; the implication is that it constitutes the core of the ceremony. Regarding the procedure where the initiation takes place to the south of the fire, both sit here in their respective places. Here, according to custom, they should bestow blessings such as: "Oṃ, those who have been consecrated by the sacrifice and the sacrificial fee, O Agni, may you be radiant... and so forth.

Then the teacher [takes] the boy’s right hand with [the mantra]: "Oṃ! Agni has taken your hand; Soma has taken your hand; Savitṛ has taken your hand; Sarasvatī has taken your hand; Pūṣan has taken your hand; Bṛhaspati has taken your hand; Mitra has taken your hand; Varuṇa has taken your hand; Tvaṣṭṛ has taken your hand; Dhātṛ has taken your hand; Viṣṇu has taken your hand; Prajāpati has taken your hand."

He takes [the boy] by the right hand, including the thumb, with the words: "Oṃ, may Savitṛ protect you; you are Mitra by virtue of dharma; Agni is your teacher. Impelled by the god Savitṛ, become a student of Bṛhaspati, O [Name], [Son of] Śarman! Drink water, place fuel on the fire, perform your duties, and do not sleep during the day. This is the instruction (*saṃśāsana*), which means teaching. "Drink water" is an elliptical expression for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) and so forth. It means: when there is a cause such as the voiding of urine and the like, perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth according to the rule at the conclusion of purification.

"Place fuel on the fire as long as you remain in the state of a student (*brahmacarya*); perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) in the evening and morning, or at least in the evening alone. Perform your duties, such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other rites, as well as service to the teacher and the study of the Vedas. Do not sleep during the day"—that is, do not take naps by day. The boy should respond, "So be it" (*bāḍham*), thereby accepting the instruction.

Then the teacher, with his right hand, silently inserts it near the boy's right shoulder from behind, and having stroked it downwards in sequence, touches the boy's heart, saying: "Oṃ! May your heart be in my heart; follow my mind with your mind; delight in my speech with a focused mind; may Bṛhaspati join you to me; cling to me alone; may your thoughts be in me; may your devotion be directed toward me; restrain your speech for me. Thus he touches the boy's heart.

Having touched water, he likewise touches the region of the navel with the mantra: "Oṃ, you are the knot of the vital breaths; do not loosen. Having touched water again, he consecrates the boy with the mantra: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May I be rich in offspring through my progeny, rich in heroes through my men, rich in luster through my splendor, rich in nourishment through my sustenance, rich in wisdom through my intellect, and rich in sacred knowledge through my students. Then, he says: "Oṃ bhūḥ! I give you, O Amukaśarman, to the Ṛg-verses, to Agni, to the Earth, to Speech, and to Brahman."

"Bhuvaḥ! I give you, O Vāyu, among the Yajus-formulas, in the intermediate space, in breath, in the Brahman—O Amukaśarman! Suvaḥ! I give you, O Sūrya, among the Sāmans, in heaven, in sight, in the Brahman—O Amukaśarman! May I be dear to you through sacrifice, O Amukaśarman! May I be dear to you through fire, O Amukaśarman! Here we two shall dwell; in breath and in life we two shall dwell; may we dwell, O Amukaśarman! With these words, he again consecrates the boy with mantras.

"Agni is long-lived"—these are the *yajus* mantras, including their appendages, addressed to Viśvedevas and others such as Agni Āyuṣmat. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for the seizing of the boy's right hand. With these five recitations—"Agni is long-lived, he [bestows] life upon you; Soma is long-lived, he [bestows] life upon you; Yajña is long-lived, he [bestows] life upon you; Brahmā is long-lived, he [bestows] life upon you; the Devas are long-lived, they [bestow] life upon you"—he seizes with his own right hand the boy's right hand, including the thumb.

For the verse beginning “*āyuṣṭe viśvato*,” the deities are the Viśvedevas, the giver of life is Agni, and the meter is Anuṣṭubh. For the formula beginning “*agnau pṛthivyām*,” the seer is Vāmadeva, the deities are Agni and others, and the meter is Yajus. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation into the right ear of the boy. “*Oṃ āyuṣṭe viśvato dadhat... amite*”; “*In Agni on earth, in Vāyu in the atmosphere, in Sūrya in heaven; whatever well-being Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, Candramas, and the Waters move toward, may we follow that well-being, O [Name], son of [Father’s Name]! Be a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) of the vital breath, O [Name], son of [Father’s Name]*!”—with these words he recites into the boy’s right ear.

For the verse beginning with *āyurdā agne*, the deities are the Viśvedevas; for *āyurdā agniḥ*, the deity is Agni; the meter is Triṣṭubh. For the mantra beginning with *agnau pṛthivyām*, the seer is Vāmadeva; the deities are Agni and others; the meter is Yajus. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation into the right ear of the boy. [He recites: "Oṃ āyurdā agne... and "...imam"; "agnau pṛthivyām... and "...bhūr amukaśarman. He recites these into the right ear of the boy. [Then he recites: "May Indra grant you wisdom, may the goddess Sarasvatī grant you wisdom; may both the Aśvins, adorned with lotus-garlands, bestow wisdom upon you. Placing his own mouth close to the boy’s mouth, he recites this.
"Hand you over to Kaśyapa and the other gods," he should say to the boy. "Hand me over," says the boy.
Then the teacher—

I entrust you to Kaśaka; I entrust you to Antaka; I entrust you to Aghora; I entrust you to Gada; I entrust you to Yama; I entrust you to Makha; I entrust you to Vaśinī; I entrust you to Pṛthivī together with Vaiśvānara; I entrust you to the Waters; I entrust you to the Herbs; I entrust you to the Forest Trees; I entrust you to Heaven and Earth; I entrust you to Subhūta.

"I entrust you to Brahma-splendor; I entrust you to all the gods; I entrust you to all beings; I entrust you to all deities"—with these words, he entrusts the boy to the teachers and others. If, however, it is a *punarupanayana* (re-initiation), then one should perform the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* here, followed by the ritual of offering oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from the seven *palāśa* trees and so forth; the vow of not eating pungent or salty food and the like need not be observed here, as it has already been performed. The procedure for *punarupanayana* will be explained later.

Regarding the first initiation (*upanayana*), however, one opinion holds that after the ritual entrustment (*paridāna*), one should perform the rites from the oblation of seven *palāśa* fuel-sticks up to the threefold food-oblation (*trivṛd-anna-homa*) according to the method to be described; then, having caused the boy to observe the three-day vow—consisting of eating food free from pungent and salty substances and so forth—preceded by the worship of the deities according to the method to be described, one should complete on the morning of the fourth day the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* and all subsequent rites, such as the threefold food-oblation of the fourth day, in their proper sequence.

According to the view of Pauṣkarasādi, the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra occurs immediately [after initiation]. Even in this view, the three-day vow (*tryahavrata*) certainly takes place; for Mātṛdatta states that in the sūtra "Pauṣkarasādi [holds it] immediate," the study of the *Śukriya* texts is observed prior to the completion of the performance of the vow, since the study of those texts is untenable unless the vow has been undertaken.

In this regard, the ritual procedure is stated according to the opinion of Pauṣkarasādi: immediately after the formal entrustment (*paridāna*), the preceptor causes the boy to anoint seven *palāśa* fuel-sticks with clarified butter and causes him to place them on the sacred fire of the initiation (*upanayana-agni*), while causing him to recite the mantras. The boy says: "Oṃ! To Agni, the great Jātavedas, I have brought a fuel-stick."

"Just as you, O Agni, are kindled by the fuel-stick, so may I be prospered with wisdom, insight, offspring, cattle, Vedic luster, and the enjoyment of food—*svāhā*. With this, he places one fuel-stick, anointed with clarified butter, into the fire. He should perform the ritual relinquishment (*tyāga*) with the formula: "This for Agni. In the same manner, he offers two second sticks. In the same manner, he offers the remaining four third sticks. The modification of the mantra for the second offering is: "I have brought two fuel-sticks for Agni. For the third offering, it is: "I have brought fuel-sticks for Agni."

The act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), however, remains as before in both cases. But there is no modification (*ūha*) regarding the word *samidh* (fuel-stick) occurring within the mantra, because that word denotes fuel in general and because there is no scriptural injunction for such modification. Some also perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) prior to the placing [of the sticks] upon the fire, but that is not correct.

Because it would lead to the over-extension [of the rule] to all constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the ritual acts, and because the Sūtra—"The sacrificer desires what is heard for the sake of the entire sacrifice; but those things which he desires, he causes to be heard"—states that the duty of forming a resolve (*saṃkalpa*) occurs only in direct association with the verbal root *kam* (to desire), whereas here the root *kam* is not heard; and so it is elsewhere as well.

Then, having completed the ritual actions beginning with the throwing of the sacrificial cord (*śulba*) and ending with the recitation (*japa*), he instructs the youth in the vows of the student stage (*brahmacarya-āśrama*): those prescribed in the *Dharma-sūtras*, such as "he shall not sing, nor weep, nor be a spectator of dancing, and he shall avoid eating honey, meat, and so forth"; and those prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, beginning from "from this time forward, in this very vow... up to "...he does not approach a woman."

Next, for the four mantras beginning with "O Agni, Lord of Vows," the seers are the Viśvedevas; the deities are Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Vratapati respectively; and the meters are Yajus. Their application is in the act of worship (upasthāna). [One worships] Agni with: "Oṃ, O Agni, Lord of Vows, may my vow be fulfilled... [and so on]. [One worships] Vāyu with: "Oṃ, O Vāyu, Lord of Vows... [One worships] Āditya with: "O Lord of the Vow of Āditya... [One worships] Vratapati with: "O Lord of Vows, Lord of Vows... In this context, by the word *vratapati*, Agni is to be understood.

"By means of the vow (*vrata*), Agni becomes worthy of sacrifice; he is the Lord of the Vow (*vratapati*)," according to the Śruti. This is the undertaking of the vow. Its relinquishment occurs at the *samāvartana* (the student's return home). Here, one gives a gift (*vara*) to the Guru, saying: "O Guru, I give you a gift. The Guru is the *ācārya*. Even if the father is the *ācārya*, a cow previously prepared and brought by another for the purpose of the gift must be given. A cow is the gift for a Brāhmaṇa, a village for a Rājanya, and a goat for a Vaiśya. In the absence of a cow, wealth should be given according to one’s capacity, measured by any one of the five types of measures. According to Paiṅgya, it is gold weighing one *guñjā*.

The preceptor, having drawn away [the breath] seventeen times, [recites] the mantra beginning with *devasya tvā savituḥ*. Prajāpati is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity, and Yajus is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the acceptance of the gift (*vara*). He accepts the gift [with the words]: "Oṃ, by the grace of the divine Savitṛ... for Rudra, the cow; through her may I attain immortality; may she grant me vitality... [and so on]. The offering of the blade of grass is done with the left hand, and the acceptance with the right hand. In the Sūtra, the phrase *bhūyān maya* is recited after *dātre*; he should likewise say that.

Even in the case where the gift of the substance is made as a substitute (*pratinidhi*), this same mantra is used. However, in the case where the gift of the substance is made as a price (*niṣkraya*), the following applies: for the verse beginning with "uttānastvā," Prajāpati Āṅgirasa is the seer and the *Yajus* is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the act of receiving. One receives it with the words: "Oṃ, may Utāna Āṅgirasa receive you. Regarding this, some say that the *Sāvitra-anvādhi* (the placing of fuel with the Sāvitra formula) should be performed; however, in reality, the reception is done silently and not with a mantra, because this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) lacks a direct connection to the sacrifice itself.

In the Śruti text, "The gods indeed caused Varuṇa to sacrifice," since the sacrifice itself is introduced at the outset, it is stated that the acceptance of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) associated with it is to be performed with mantras. This is also because the author of the Sūtra states, "He shows the Tantric sacrificial fees. In this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), there is neither the blowing away [of the grass] nor the offering of grass. Furthermore, the acceptance [of the fee] is not done by turning away; however, some say it does occur. Even regarding the mantra for acceptance, there is an option concerning the recollection of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details.

Then, with the verse beginning "udīyuṣā," Soma is the deity and Yajus is the meter; its application is for the raising up of the boy. Reciting "Oṃ udīyuṣā... anu," he raises the boy up. He should say to the boy, "Oṃ, I entrust you to Sūrya. The boy replies, "Entrust me. The teacher, saying "Oṃ, O Sūrya, this is your son; I entrust him to you," hands over the boy to Sūrya. Then the student or the teacher—[with the verse] "taccakṣuḥ," Soma is the deity, Sūrya is the subject, and Yajus is the meter.

The application is for the worship of the Sun (*sūryopasthāna*). With the mantra, "Oṃ *taccakṣur devahitaṃ purastāt*... *dṛśe*" (That divine eye... for seeing), he worships the Sun. Then the Teacher, having given to the youth the staff with its tip pointing upwards that was previously set aside, with the mantra, "Oṃ may Agni extend your life further; may Agni bestow prosperity upon you further; may Indra with the Maruts bestow it upon you here; may Āditya with the Vasus establish it for you," and having silently given the non-empty alms-bowl that was previously set aside, says, "Go forth on the practice of begging."

Then the religious student (brahmacārī), having said "Om," should first beg from his mother; in her absence, from another woman who occupies the position of a mother and will not refuse, saying, "Lady, give alms. Then he should beg from the families of friends, addressing a man there as, "May your honor give alms. Having brought back that begged substance, he should present it to the teacher, saying, "O Sir, here is this alms-food. The teacher accepts it, saying, "This is good alms. Regarding this, some maintain that there should be seventeen suppressions of breath (apāna).

Then—reciting, "Oṃ! That first garment of yours which we take away, may all the gods protect it; may many brothers and friends follow you, the well-born one, as you grow"—he takes the previously placed garment from the boy. Then follows the *trivṛdanna-homa* (the three-fold food oblation).

The teacher, with the student (*brahmacārin*) holding onto him, takes three pieces of fuel, performs the rites beginning with "Come, Faith" up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and says: "In this rite of the *trivṛdanna-homa*, I shall encompass all those deities who are to be worshipped."

Having recited the mantras beginning with "I shall kindle Agni Jātavedas" up to the end of the *prasādhanī* deities, [he proceeds] to the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*), saying: "I shall worship Agni with an oblation of threefold food; I shall worship Soma with an oblation of threefold food; I shall worship Agni, the eater of food, with an oblation of threefold food; I shall worship Agni, the lord of food, with an oblation of threefold food; I shall worship Prajāpati with an oblation of threefold food; I shall worship the Viśvedevas with an oblation of threefold food; I shall worship all the deities with an oblation of threefold food; [and I shall worship] Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an oblation of the remains of the offering."

Having said, "I shall sacrifice; I shall sacrifice immediately to these deities," he should place three pieces of fuel on the fire. Some say that after saying, "I shall sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the remnant of the oblation," one should then say, "I shall sacrifice to Vāstoṣpati with an offering of threefold food. Then, having strewn grass around the fire, he should take the fire into himself with the two verses, "I take [the fire] into myself" and "The fire which is ours.
Thereafter follows the preparation of the seat for the Brahman priest and so forth.

In the preparation of the vessels (pātrāsādana), one should set down the *sruva* ladle, the *darvī* spoon, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessel, the *upaveṣa* fire-stirring stick, the *saṃmārga* cleansing-grass, the fuel-wood (*idhma*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the *avajvalana* ignition-grass, the clarified butter, and the threefold food (*trivṛdanna*) consisting of boiled rice, cakes (*apūpa*), and parched barley-meal (*saktu*), which has been taken from the food prepared outside the area brought for serving the Brāhmaṇas. Among these, the cakes (*apūpa*) to be used must be more than three and sufficient for the oblation; by the word *apūpa*, perforated wheat preparations such as *pūrikā* are meant.
Some say they are *maṇḍakas*. *Saktavas* are roasted barley flour; in its absence, roasted wheat flour may be used. *Apūpas* (cakes) that are free from alkaline salt (*kṣāra-lavaṇa*) should be taken.
Then follows the preparation of the *pavitra* and so forth.

In this context, Brahmā is either that same person [who officiated previously] or someone else. In the first case, there is no selection (*varaṇa*) of him here, because he has already been chosen. Then, having performed the rites from the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* water up to the laying around of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), one places the prepared threefold food (*trivṛd-anna*) on the fire—since it was prepared outside—and after sprinkling it with clarified butter (*abhighārya*), removes it to the north and sprinkles it with water. According to the opinion of Mātṛdatta, this is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the "divine filter" (*devapavitra*); however, according to the opinion of Ujjvalākṛt, this is not a purificatory rite, because he states that it refers specifically to cooking performed by a Śūdra.

The same applies to the monthly *śrāddha* and other such rites. Then, having sprinkled that [mixture] with clarified butter, placed it on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) behind the fire, broken off pieces of the cakes (*apūpa*), added them to the boiled rice (*odana*), and having also added the parched barley flour (*saktu*), one should pour in common clarified butter, mix it, divide it into seven equal portions, and designate the deities for the final two portions as follows: "This for the Viśvedevas" and "This for all the deities. Alternatively, there may be neither division nor designation.

Then, having sprinkled water around the fire and performed the rites from the placing of the fuel-sticks up to the *prasādhanī* offering to the goddess, he takes portions of the threefold food mixed with clarified butter according to the rule for taking portions (*avadāna-dharma*) and offers them. The rule for taking portions is as follows: having spread a base of ghee in the ladle (*darvī*), he takes a portion from the middle and a portion from the eastern half, pours ghee over it, and then pours ghee over the oblation again. This is the rule for taking portions. In the case of dividing the food into parts, the portions are taken sequentially from each respective part. He offers: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! To Agni, the eater of food, svāhā! To Agni, the lord of food, svāhā!"

Having offered oblations in sequence with "To Prajāpati, svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, svāhā! To all the deities, svāhā!", he spreads a base of clarified butter in the *darvī* spoon. Then, taking portions from the northern halves of all the sacrificial offerings (*havir*)—once each, using either the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) or his hand—and having sprinkled clarified butter over them twice, he does not sprinkle clarified butter back over the sacrificial materials themselves. He offers the oblation in the northeastern part of the fire with the formula "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!", ensuring it does not touch the previous oblations; the renunciations (*tyāga*) are made according to the respective indicative marks of the mantras.

In the view that there is no division [of the offering], there is only a single portion (*avadāna*) because the oblation (*havis*) is a single entity; and this rule regarding the portions is according to the opinion of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*). However, it should be understood that according to the opinion of others, the rule regarding portions does not apply anywhere except in the case of the *lāja-homa* (oblation of parched grains).

Then, having performed the spreading of the grass-bundle (*paristaraṇa*), its dismissal (*visarga*), and the sprinkling (*pariṣeka*), and having offered the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation, he should perform the worship (*upasthāna*). The ritual rules regarding the throwing away of the cord (*śulba*) and so forth are optional. Then, having strewn some *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, poured some water thereon, and combined the three types of food previously set out as before, he offers an oblation (*bali*) with it, saying: "Svāhā to Vāstupati! [The formula is: "This to Vāstupati. Thereafter, he sprinkles water around the oblation. There is no mixing of ghee here, as it has not been prescribed.

Then, having fed the Brahmins with this food and other side dishes, he should have them pronounce the *puṇyāha* and other benedictions as before. In that context, the specific variation in the formulas is as follows: "May the venerable ones declare the *puṇyāha* for the rite of the threefold food-oblation (*trivṛd-annahoma*); may the venerable ones declare the *svastyayana* for the rite of the threefold food-oblation; may the venerable ones declare prosperity (*ṛddhi*) for the rite of the threefold food-oblation. The responses of the Brahmins are: "Om, let there be the *puṇyāha*; Om, let there be the *svastyayana*; Om, let there be prosperity."

Then he should say, "May Śraddhā and Medhā be pleased. And this *homa* is to be performed in those rites prescribed by the Sūtras—other than the *sthālīpāka*, the monthly *śrāddha*, and so forth—starting from the initiation (*upanayana*), except for the presentation of food prescribed by the author of the Sūtra itself.
Now follows the procedure for the *homa*, including the *vyāhṛti-homa*, the *vāruṇī-homa*, and others.

The teacher, having been touched by the student observing the vow of celibacy (*brahmacārin*), takes three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and performs the rites up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Having recited the formula beginning with "those which are about to be sacrificed" (*yā yakṣyamāṇāḥ*) up to the *vyāhṛtis* for the rite of the three-fold food-oblation (*trivṛd-annahoma*), he states for the principal oblation: "I shall sacrifice to Agni with an oblation of three-fold food," and so on, naming all the deities as before, ending with "I shall sacrifice to all the deities with an oblation of three-fold food. Then, having performed the rites from "to Varuṇa" up to the placing of the three fuel-sticks, he strews grass around the fire (*paristīrya*) and proceeds with the setting out of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*), etc.

Having performed the rites up to the *prasādhanī* deity-oblation as before, he should offer four oblations with the *vyasta* and *samasta* *vyāhṛtis*. Then, having offered the seven oblations beginning with "To Agni, svāhā! using the threefold food (*trivṛdanna*) as before, he should offer the six oblations beginning with "This [is my prayer], O Varuṇa... If the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations are to be performed, he should offer those as well; finally, he should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the formula "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! alone.

Then, having completed everything remaining from the fire-oblation beginning with the throwing of the cord (*śulba*), having offered the *vāstubali*, having fed the Brahmins, and having caused them to recite the *puṇyāha*, *svastyayana*, and *ṛddhi* formulas, one should say: "May Faith (*śraddhā*) and Intelligence (*medhā*) be pleased.
Thus concludes the procedure for the threefold food-oblation (*trivṛd-annahoma*) together with the *vyāhṛti-homa*, the *vāruṇī-homa*, and so forth.
Now follows the procedure according to the *āpūrvika* ritual system.

The teacher, having been grasped by the student who is observing the vow of celibacy (*brahmacārin*), takes three pieces of fuel and performs the rites up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the words "Come, O Faith" (*śraddha ehi*), etc. He then declares: "In the rite of the *Trivṛdanna* oblation, I shall encompass all those deities who are to be sacrificed to: I shall sacrifice to Agni with an oblation of *Trivṛdanna*; I shall sacrifice to Soma with an oblation of *Trivṛdanna*; I shall sacrifice to Agni, the eater of food, with an oblation of *Trivṛdanna*; I shall sacrifice to Agni, the lord of food, with an oblation of *Trivṛdanna*; I shall sacrifice to Prajāpati with an oblation of *Trivṛdanna*."

"I shall worship all the gods with an oblation of threefold food; I shall worship all the deities with an oblation of threefold food; I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an oblation of the remains of what has been offered. I shall worship these deities this very day. Having said this, he places three fuel-sticks into the fire, spreads grass around the fire, strews *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, and sets out the sacrificial vessels.

Having placed the *darvī* spoon, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessel, the *upaveṣa* fire-stick, *darbha* grass for placing the oblation, *darbha* blades for wiping, *darbha* blades for kindling, clarified butter, fuel-sticks, and the threefold food, and having prepared the two strainers (*pavitre*) and consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters; then, having turned the vessels face-upward and sprinkled them, he should perform the rites from the heating of the *darvī* up to the consecration of the clarified butter.
Then, having spread the *darbha* grass placed behind the fire and having set the clarified butter upon it, he should place the *darvī* to the north of that.

Then, having consecrated [the food] with the rite known as *devapavitra*, having sprinkled clarified butter over it, and having placed boiled rice, cakes, and groats upon the *darbha* grass spread behind the fire, he unites them into one mass, pours common clarified butter over them, and mixes them. Having sprinkled water around the fire and added one of the previously prepared fuel-sticks (*samidh*), he takes portions from the ladle repeatedly and offers eight oblations of the mixed threefold food (*trivṛdanna*) with the formulas: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Agni, the eater of food! Svāhā to Agni, the lord of food!"

"To Prajāpati, svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, svāhā! To all the deities, svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!"—with these [formulas], he offers [the oblation] in the eastern half of the northern half [of the fire], without letting it touch the previous offerings. The renunciations (tyāgas) are according to the respective marks [of the deities]. The final offering is to be offered in the eastern half of the northern half, without touching the previous offerings. Herein, the rule regarding the cutting of portions (avadāna-dharma) does not apply, because it belongs to the *āpūrvika* class.

Then, having performed the spreading of the grass (*paristaraṇa*), the dismissal (*visarga*), and the sprinkling around (*pariṣeka*), he should offer the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation and perform the worship (*upasthāna*). Or, he may omit the worship. Alternatively, the final sprinkling (*uttarapariṣeka*) occurs immediately after the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation.

Then, having strewn some *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, poured some water thereon, and combined the three types of food previously set out as before, he offers the *bali* with the formula, “To the Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstupati*), svāhā. [The formula is: “To the Lord of the Dwelling, this [is offered]. Thereafter, he sprinkles water around the *bali*. There is no mixing of clarified butter (*sarpis*) here, as it has not been prescribed.

Then, having fed the Brahmins with this food and other side dishes, he should cause them to pronounce the *puṇyāha* and other benedictions as before. Then he should say, "May Faith (*śraddhā*) and Intelligence (*medhā*) be pleased.
Thus concludes the *trivṛd-anna-homa* according to the *āpūrvika-tantra*.

This [rite] occurs only at the following occasions: the initiation (*upanayana*), the return home (*samāvartana*), the first suckling of the calf (*vatsātirikta*), the milking of the cow (*gokṛta*), the drinking by the cow (*gostana*), the preparation of the ritual pegs (*śālākaraṇa*), the pacification of the building site (*vāstuśamana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), and the cutting of the beard (*godāna*); it does not occur elsewhere. Furthermore, according to the method stated in the section beginning with "The fire [is established] at the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) and so forth," this also takes place in the case where the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) is performed. Regarding the *trivṛt-anna-homa* (the three-fold food-oblation) and the *vāstu-bali* (offering to the site), there is an option between them.

Then he instructs the boy in the three-day vow (*tryaha-vrata*): one must not consume products of sugarcane, salt, black gram, green gram, or other grains, nor honey or meat; one must not sleep on a bedstead or similar elevated furniture, drink water from an earthen vessel, eat from an earthen or bell-metal plate, give the remains of one's food to a *śūdra*, or sleep during the day. One must practice begging for alms at both times [of day and night], fetch a water-pot, and perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) every day at both times, or at least every evening.

Immediately after the completion of the three-day vow (*tryahavrata*), there is an option regarding the consumption of products of sugarcane, salt, and *śamī* grains. The fetching of the water-jar and the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) continue only until the completion of the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Having said "Certainly" (*bāḍham*), the student (*brahmacārī*) should perform the worship of the deities with the mantras beginning with "O Agni, Lord of Vows" (*agne vratapate*) and so forth, and then undertake the three-day vow.

Then the teacher, having performed the worship of Gāyatrī according to custom, and having placed a grass-bundle (kūrca) with its tips pointing north behind the fire for the purpose of instructing the Gāyatrī, should sit upon it facing east, reciting: "Thou art the throne of the preceptor, the sustainer of the kingdom; do not forsake me."

Then the religious student (brahmacārī), having silently made a gesture of salutation with joined palms toward the sun, should touch the teacher’s right foot from below and above with his right hand while his left hand grasps it from behind; then, crossing his hands, he should hold both of the teacher’s feet together with his knees. This is the ritual of clasping the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*). At this point, the teacher should whisper the secret name to the boy. The boy should then address the teacher with that name as it was whispered. However, if the secret name is unknown, he should address him by his common name, but still whispering it.

The manner of salutation therein is as follows: extending the right arm, grasped by the left hand at the level of the ear, and pronouncing in a low voice, "I, [Name], born of the [Gotra] lineage and belonging to the [Pravara] line, salute you, sir," one should pay homage to the teacher while standing with the head bowed. This is the salutation.

Then, having become seated and bowed with humility, desiring the instruction of the Sāvitrī for the purpose of commencing all Vedic study, he should recite the two mantras in the form of a request in a single tone (*ekaśruti*): "O Sir, please teach me" (*adhīhi bho*), and "O Sir, please recite the Sāvitrī to me" (*sāvitrīm bho anubrūhi*). This is done by the Preceptor pronouncing the name of the venerable student—such as "Bhavān-amaukaśarmā"—either with a long final vowel followed by the vowel *a* without a visarga, or by the pronunciation of the long final vowel alone, while the benediction is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

Then, having made firm the union of the fingers and thumb of the left hand turned upward with the fingers and thumb of the right hand turned downward, and having placed them on his right lap, he should sit.

Then the preceptor, with the verse "gaṇānāṃ tvā" (VS 23.19), for which the Viśvedevas are the seers, Gaṇapati is the deity, and Jagatī is the meter; its application is in the consecration of the boy. He consecrates the boy with the words: "Oṃ gaṇānāṃ tvā... sādanam. Then, taking that joined palms (añjali) with his own hands, and having recalled the Ṛṣi and other details of the Vyāhṛtis—both individual and collective—as well as of the Gāyatrī as before, he recalls the statement of application: "Its application is in the instruction of the Gāyatrī to the boy."

"Bhūr, tat savitur vareṇyam; bhuvaḥ, bhargo devasya dhīmahi; suvaḥ, dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. Bhūr-bhuvaḥ, tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi; suvaḥ, dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt."

In this manner, he causes the boy, facing eastward, to recite the Sāvitrī verse—verse by quarter (pāda), then by half-verse (ardharca), and finally without pause. Since the entire recitation here serves an invisible (transcendental) purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the recitation must be performed in such a way that it proceeds without pausing. In every case, if he is unable to pronounce it in this way, he causes him to recite according to his capacity. Regarding this, the *Kaustubha* states: "While reciting according to his capacity, he should not alter the phonetic modifications resulting from euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*). For the Taittirīyas, the very commencement of the Gāyatrī constitutes their qualification for the study of the three Vedas—the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma.

Then, for the sake of pleasing the deities associated with the ritual, one should feed two hundred, fifty, or—if unable—ten Brahmins and give them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Thereafter, for the sake of pleasing the deities associated with the ritual, having performed the worship of the Brahmins with perfumes, betel leaves, and other offerings, and having given them even more abundant sacrificial fees, blessings should be received with the mantras beginning with "Oṃ agne tejasvin. Then, for the sake of ensuring the perfection of the rite, one should remember Viṣṇu with the words "Through negligence... and so forth.

Then the religious student (brahmacārī), at his own time, should perform the midday twilight rite (madhyāhna-saṃdhyā) when its time has arrived. In this case, the commencement in the evening is not mandatory, as it is not specifically prescribed; for it is said: "One who is devoid of the twilight rites is eternally impure and unfit for all ritual acts. Furthermore: "As long as the instruction in the Veda (brahmopadeśa) has not occurred, there is no twilight rite or similar duty; but once the instruction in the Veda has taken place, one should perform the ritual acts such as the twilight rites."

Furthermore, because the midday *saṃdhyā* is established as the first duty even according to the statement of Jaimini; and because the word "likewise" (*tathā*) in the sūtra, "When three days have passed, having likewise served the Brahmins with food consisting of the *trivṛt* [oblation]," indicates that the fire of initiation (*upanayanāgni*) is obtained [for use]; and because the Baudhāyana school explicitly states that the initiation fire must be maintained until the completion of the ritual, the initiation fire is to be preserved until the conclusion of the rites on the fourth day.

Until the completion of that very rite, one should perform the fuel-wood offering known as *agnikārya* either morning and evening, or in the evening alone. Following that, [the offering is made] in the common (*laukika*) fire; its procedure will be explained later.
