By the statement of Jaimini, "But once instruction in the Veda has been received, one should perform the rites such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth," the obligation to perform the twilight worship after instruction was previously demonstrated. Now, in response to the inquiry as to how that worship is to be performed, it is described here preceded by a presentation of the nature of the three twilights.

Regarding that, the Śruti declares the nature of the *saṃdhyā*: "The Rākṣasas, indeed, stood firm against the *puronuvāka* with the *tapas*. Prajāpati invited them with a boon; they chose this boon: 'Let the Sun be our warrior. Prajāpati said to them, 'Fight! Therefore, those Rākṣasas rise up and fight the Sun until he has gone to his setting. Those very Rākṣasas are pacified by water consecrated with the *gāyatrī*. For this reason, these exponents of the Veda (*brahmavādinaḥ*), facing the east during the *saṃdhyā*..."

Water consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra is sprinkled upwards; these waters, having become thunderbolts, cast those Rakṣasas into the island of Mandehāruṇa. By circumambulating [the sun] from left to right, they shake off evil. A learned Brāhmaṇa who, while performing [this rite], meditates upon the sun as it rises and as it sets, attains all that is auspicious. "The sun is Brahman"—he who knows this, being Brahman itself, goes to Brahman.

Performing the practices such as *prāṇāyāma* in the manner that will be described, and meditating on the Sun—designated by the term *saṃdhyā* and endowed with the name, color, and form as stated below—as Brahman, one attains all auspiciousness pertaining to both this world and the next. He who, through the aforementioned meditation, purifies his inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and realizes Brahman directly, was previously Brahman itself but attained the state of a living soul (*jīva*) due to ignorance; now, upon the removal of that ignorance through the aforementioned knowledge, he attains Brahman itself—this is the meaning.
Here, "meditation" (*abhidhyāna*) refers to spiritual practice (*upāsana*).
Vyāsa also said this very thing with this intention:
"One should not treat the Gāyatrī as distinct from Brahman;
one should worship it with the thought 'I am He,' by whatever means prescribed."
In another Smṛti as well: "The Sandhyā is Brahman residing in the Sun, due to the performance of the rites of union and so forth;
it is the Saccidātman [the Being-Consciousness-Bliss] connected with all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass."
"The thought of the worshiper should be either 'I am his servant' or 'I am he';
thus indeed do those who know the Veda understand."

Parāśara describes the nature of the twilight (saṃdhyā): "That junction of day and night which is devoid of both the sun and the stars is declared to be the twilight by the sages who perceive the truth."

In this context, although the word *saṃdhyā* is understood as denoting a period of time, nevertheless, the deity to be worshipped during that time is indicated by the word *saṃdhyā*. Thus, in the statement of Parāśara, the word *saṃdhyā* is employed with reference to the ritual act (*karman*), having the worship of the deity as its implied object. Alternatively, *saṃdhyā* is the rite that occurs at the junction (*saṃdhi*).
For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"One worships at the juncture-time of night and day."
"Therefore, the wise call that very state 'Sandhyā' (the junction)."
Yājñavalkya prescribes that very same practice:
"One should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) at the junction [of day and night], neither when the sun has set nor when it has risen.
And that twilight is threefold.
Thus it was said by Atri:
"The three junctions (saṃdhyās) must always be performed by a twice-born who knows the Self.
Regarding that, Vyāsa states the differences in the name and other attributes of the deity according to the distinction of time:
She is known as Gāyatrī in the forenoon, Sāvitrī at midday, and Sarasvatī in the evening; she alone is remembered as the Saṃdhyā throughout the three periods.

Because it protects one from the sin of accepting gifts, from the sin of eating forbidden food, and from both major and minor transgressions, the Gāyatrī is so called; for it saves that which sings it.
"Because she is the illumination of Savitṛ, she is celebrated as Sāvitrī;
or because she is the progenitor of the world, or because her nature is speech, she is Sarasvatī."

A distinction of colors is prescribed in another Smṛti: "Gāyatrī should be red, Sāvitrī white in color, and Sarasvatī likewise black; they are to be worshipped according to this distinction of colors."
In that very same [text]:
"Gāyatrī is indeed the form of Brahmā, Sāvitrī is the form of Rudra, and Sarasvatī is the form of Viṣṇu; they are to be worshipped according to their distinct forms."
In another Smṛti: "One should meditate [on her] resembling the rising sun, holding a book and a rosary in her hands,
wearing a water-pot and a deerskin, richly adorned with red perfumes, and moving with the gait of a swan."
One should meditate in the morning upon the goddess Brāhmī, who wears red garlands and garments.
[He should meditate on] the goddess who is white, clad in white garments, anointed with white perfumes, three-eyed,
and holding a boon-granting gesture, a trident, an axe, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness.
At midday, one should meditate upon Rudra’s power, Vṛṣagā,
as a black goddess, dressed in black garments and anointed with black perfumes and unguents.
"One should always meditate at the time of sunset upon the Goddess, the power of Viṣṇu, who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and who is mounted upon Garuḍa."
The Determination of the Time for the Twilight Rites (Saṃdhyā). Now, regarding time: Dakṣa states the duration of the morning twilight as follows:
"The two nāḍīs at the end of the night are said to be the time for the commencement of the twilight rite."
"The end of that [period] is recorded by the sages as being from the appearance of the line of the sun."
In the *Agnismṛti*, however, the period of two muhūrtas prior to sunrise is stated:
"The time for the morning twilight (*saṃdhyākāla*) for a Brahmin is two muhūrtas before sunrise.
Maheśa and others maintain that this refers specifically to those who perform the *Bahvṛca* ritual.
In the *Dharmasāra*: "The morning twilight is considered to be of three kinds: the best is accompanied by stars, the middling has its stars obscured, and the lowest is joined with the sun."
Regarding the duration of the time for the midday sandhyā, it is stated in that very same work:
"The midday sandhyā is traditionally held to last until one and a half yāmas before sunset.
In the Smṛtisaṃgraha:
"The time immediately following the midday bath is the period for the midday *saṃdhyā*; that which follows after this is considered secondary (*gauṇa*) by the wise."

Regarding the duration of the time for the evening twilight (sāyaṃsaṃdhyā), the *Dharmasāra* states: "The best [evening twilight] is when the sun is still present; the middling is when the stars have disappeared; and the lowest is when the stars are visible. Thus, the evening twilight is considered to be of three kinds."
In another Smṛti: "One should perform the morning twilight worship while the stars are still visible, the midday [worship] during the act of bathing,
and the evening twilight worship with the sun present, according to the prescribed rule."
In the phrase "in the rite of bathing," the word "performed" (*nirvṛtta*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, the meaning is "after the midday bath.
Gobhila states the secondary time for the *saṃdhyā* (twilight prayer): "From sunrise until three *ghaṭikās* after sunset..."
"One should perform the twilight worship for that long; after that, [the period of] penance follows."
Now, regarding the location:
Vyāsa states— "The twilight prayer performed at home is said to have a single-fold merit; in a cow-pen, it is ten-fold."

"A hundred thousandfold [merit] is obtained at a river, and infinite in the presence of Viṣṇu; the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) performed outside is tenfold [more effective], as are those performed at pits and springs;
it is a hundredfold at a dug-out holy site (tīrtha), and indeed infinite in the waters of the Gaṅgā."
"Viṣṇu" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for Śiva and the other deities. "Khāte" means in a natural pond or a pond excavated by the gods.
Śātātapa says: "Falsehood, the smell of liquor, and sexual intercourse during the day..."
"For the twilight devotion performed outside indeed purifies the food of a Śūdra."
If there is a lapse in the auxiliary limbs such as wandering [for alms] and so forth, then the two twilights must be performed at home; thus says Atri:
"The knower of the Self who is a twice-born must always perform the three twilights;
however, the two twilights must always be performed at home by Brāhmaṇas and others."

Although the three *saṃdhyās* are prescribed to be performed exclusively outdoors because that is the commendable practice, nevertheless, since the act of moving about (*viharaṇa*) is more authoritative as it is based on Vedic injunction (*śrauta*), the evening and morning *saṃdhyās* are permitted to be performed at home in accordance with that rule.

However, the commentators on the *Bhāradvāja-sūtra* state a specific exception regarding the evening *saṃdhyā*: "One who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should perform the evening *saṃdhyā* behind the *gārhapatya* fire."
Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*):
Bṛhaspati says— "Then, standing upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, being well-composed..."
"Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas), one should meditate upon the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā); such is the Vedic revelation."

In the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*: "Having assumed a posture, having restrained the breaths, and likewise having remembered the *ṛṣi* and so forth, with eyes closed and observing silence, one should practice *prāṇāyāma*."
In the *Smṛtisāra*:

"Having performed breath control according to the rules, with speech restrained and senses controlled, one should then perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), thinking: 'Now I shall perform the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*')."
Prior to *prāṇāyāma*, the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) must also be performed.
This is stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:
"Having sipped water and restrained the vital breaths, one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*)."
"Asūn" means the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).

The method of sipping water (*ācamana*) is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*: "Sitting down, one should sip water three times with water reaching the heart; one should wipe the lips three times, though some say twice; one should touch [the lips] once, though some say twice; having sprinkled the left hand with the right hand, one should touch the feet, the head, and the sense organs—the eyes, the nostrils, and the ears."

Gautama also says: "Seated in a clean place, having placed his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacred thread, he should wash his hands up to the wrists; being silent, touching his heart, he should sip water three or four times, sprinkle his feet, and touch the cavities of his head.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Sitting with his knees together in a clean place, facing north or east,
a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha."
In this context, touching [the water] is followed by sipping (ācamana).
Yājñavalkya describes the nature of the Brāhma-tīrtha as follows:
"The base of the little finger, the index finger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand."
"The tirthas of Prajapati, the Pitrs, and Brahma [are used] in their respective order."
This very point has been clarified by Śaṅkha and Likhita:

"The *brāhma* *tīrtha* is on the line to the north of the base of the thumb, pointing eastward; between the forefinger and the thumb is the *pitrya*; between the little finger and the palm is the *prājāpatya*; and the joints of the fingers toward the front are the *daivata*.
Śaṅkha further specifies the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*):
"One should perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) with water that has been drawn up, which is free from foam and bubbles, not heated by fire, and free from salt."
Yājñavalkya also says: "The twice-born [should sip water] with water that is natural, free from foam and bubbles, reaching respectively the heart, the throat, and the palate."
"A woman and a Śūdra are purified by water that merely touches the extremities once.
Manu also says:
"A Brāhmaṇa is purified by water reaching the heart; a Kṣatriya, however, by water reaching the throat."
"A Vaiśya [is purified] by water reaching the palate, and a Śūdra by water merely touched at the extremity."
Pracetas also says:
"One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) three or four times with water that is not hot, free from foam, pure to the eye and cloth, reaching the heart, and silent."

In the *Gobhilagṛhya*, it is stated that in the rite of sipping water (*ācamana*), the water must invariably reach as far as the heart; otherwise, there is the fault of being defiled by remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*).
It says: "One should sip water only so that it touches the heart; otherwise, one indeed remains defiled.
This is an elliptical expression [that includes] reaching the throat and other such levels.

Bhāradvāja describes the manner of taking up water and its quantity: "Having formed his hand like a mountain in length and shaped like a cow's ear, the twice-born man should take up the water with his palm, the fingers being held close together."
"With the thumb and little finger released, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with the remaining fingers;
having taken up water in an amount sufficient to submerge a bean, one should drink it three times."
And that hand should be understood as the right one, according to the Purāṇic statement: "One should drink three times with the right [hand].
Regarding the specific mantra for sipping water (ācamana) and the touching of the sense organs, Bhāradvāja says:
"Having drunk [the water] with three parts of the goddess's feet, one should afterwards touch the cavities. Here, "of the goddess" refers to Gāyatrī. However, by Atri:

It has been stated: "One should perform the sipping [of water] three times with the three mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. Furthermore, this sipping (ācamana) must be performed twice. This is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"At home, during mealtime, and at both twilights,
as well as during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again."
In the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*, based on the *Devīpurāṇa* and the *Nandipurāṇa*:

"At the time of giving, receiving, performing oblations, the three-fold salutation of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), and the ritual offering of bali, a twice-born man should sip water (*ācamana*) at the beginning; he should not do so twice at the end."
Manu has stated the definition of *prāṇāyāma*:
"One who has restrained his breath should recite three times the *praṇava*, the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī* together with its head; that is called *prāṇāyāma*."
Yājñavalkya also says:
"One should mutter the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras), preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and joined with each Praṇava; this is the threefold restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama)."

In this context, by the words "recitation" (*pāṭha*) and "muttering" (*japa*), there is intended merely the mental contemplation of the phonemes, not their vocal utterance, because the latter is impossible [in this state].
As stated in another Smṛti:
"One should slowly release the breath through the nostrils, but not with force."
"One should not let the body tremble; that is considered the supreme yoga. Vyāsa says:
"One should practice the taking in, the retention, and the exhaling of the breath three times each."
"Meditating upon Brahmā, Keśava, and Śambhu, one should contemplate the deities in their proper order. Thus says the Yogayājñavalkya:
"Inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recya) constitute the threefold characteristic of prāṇāyāma."
"The breath held in the nose when meditated upon is called *pūraka*;
*kumbhaka* is the motionless breath; and that which is being emptied is *recaka*.
Thus says Yājñavalkya.
"One should perform exhalation through the right [nostril] after filling the abdomen with [air] through the left;
one should perform the recitation during the retention (kumbhaka)—this is the definition of prāṇāyāma. Thus says Dakṣa.

"One should perform exhalation through the left [nostril], fill the abdomen by inhaling through the right, and perform the recitation during retention; such is the definition of prāṇāyāma," so it is said. In the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*:

"One should press the tip of the nose with the five fingers while reciting the *praṇava*. This mudrā destroys all sins for forest-dwellers and householders; for ascetics and students, it is performed with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb."

It was previously stated that one should first form a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with the thought, "I shall perform the twilight worship. Regarding that, the manner of forming the resolve is threefold according to different philosophical views. First, in the system of the followers of Kumārila (the Bhaṭṭa school), although there is no fruit explicitly enjoined by the authoritative injunctions for obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) such as the twilight worship, a fruit is nevertheless postulated—namely, the destruction of accumulated sins—by reflecting upon various statements such as the indicative power of mantras (*mantra-liṅga*) and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). In accordance with this view, the resolve for all obligatory rites is made in the following manner: "For the sake of destroying accumulated sins, I shall perform the morning twilight worship," or "I shall sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth.

In the view of the Guru, however, the very accomplishment of the injunction (*vidhisiddhi*) is the fruit of the injunction; thus, even in the absence of an impelled fruit, there is a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding obligatory rites (*nitya*) in such a manner as, "I shall perform the morning twilight worship," or "I shall sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," for the sake of accomplishing the injunction itself.

In the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*, however, under the sūtra "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*), in the commentary on the subject passage beginning with "from which" (*yato vā*), it is stated that the entire collection of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has arisen from Brahman alone. Just as a pot produced from clay exists by not abandoning its own material cause, the clay, and even when being dissolved, is dissolved back into that very clay; so too the world, born from Brahman, exists by not abandoning Brahman, and when being dissolved, is dissolved back into Brahman alone.

Having spoken thus, and having established the concordance with Brahman (*samanvaya*) and other principles through the textual sequence of the subsequent scripture (*uttara-śāstra*), it was stated that actions must be performed with the very intention of offering them to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa-buddhi*). According to this view, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is made in such a manner as: "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrī-parameśvara*), I shall perform the morning twilight ritual (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*)," or "I shall sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth.
This is the method of the resolve.
Following that is the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*).
Thus it is stated in the *Prayogapārijāta*:
"Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the three verses beginning with 'āpo hi ṣṭhā'.
It is also stated in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*:
With the three mantras beginning with "āpo hi," he should sprinkle drops on the head and the shoulders;
then, having cast water below with the mantra "yasya kṣayāya," he should perform a circumambulatory sprinkling with water.
One should perform the sprinkling with kuśa-water using the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, [thereby removing] those born of passion,
ignorance, and delusion, as well as those arising from the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
"Through sprinkling, one should burn away these nine defects born of speech, mind, and body.
Prajāpati also says:
"With a concentrated mind, one should perform the sprinkling at the end of a Ṛg-verse or at the end of a quarter-verse."
"Or one may perform it at the end of the half-verse; such is the opinion of the Śiṣṭas.
Another method is summarized [in the Saṃgraha]: "The three syllables *sa-sa-tha* in the ether, and the three excellent syllables on the head."

"Three *natras* (the syllable *nam*) are prescribed on the ground; this is the definition of cleansing (*mārjana*). The reading "three excellent heads" (*varavatrayamastaka*) is indeed inconsistent. In some places, the reading for the second quarter is "in heaven there may be three excellent [worlds]" (*kvacid divi syād varavatrayam*). In the mantra "The earth was not, nor the intermediate space" (*nānyā āsīd antarikṣam*), since the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is born from the heart, the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*) is used here to denote the ether (*ākāśa*) by accepting the metaphorical identification of the produced and the producer. Here, the word "navel" (*nābhi*) indicates the "heart," and the word "intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*) denotes the "ether" (*ākāśa*), according to the lexicon which states: "Nabhas, antarikṣa, and gagana [are synonyms for the sky]."

Thus, just as in the verse "From the head the sky evolved," one accepts a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) even in the case of "from the feet the earth," whereby the words "head" and "feet" respectively denote the sky and the earth. These syllables are intended to indicate the end of the quarters (*pāda*). At the ends of the quarters in the phrases *cakṣase*, *rasaḥ*, and *jinvatha*, one should perform the purification (*mārjana*) in the space [of the heart]. At the ends of the quarters in the phrases *mayobhuvaḥ*, *mātaraḥ*, and *gamāma vaḥ*, one should do so on the head. At the ends of the quarters in the phrases *dadhātana*, *iha naḥ*, and *ca naḥ*, one should do so on the earth—that is, at the feet.
Hārīta states:
"One should perform the acts of sprinkling, worship, offering oblations, and eating with the *devatīrtha*.
Furthermore, that sprinkling (*mārjana*) should not be performed with water falling from a stream.
And so says Brahmā:
"The twilight worship performed with water that has fallen as a stream is censured;
neither the ancestors, nor the deities, nor the sages praise it."
To the question, "How then is the cleansing performed?", he himself says:
"In a river, at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), or in a lake; or even in a vessel made of clay, or one made of udumbara wood, or of gold, silver, or wood."
"Or, having [placed water] in the left hand, one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsti*).
Following the word "having," the word "water" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
However, when a vessel made of clay or other materials is available, the use of the left hand is prohibited.

For there is a traditional legal text (*smṛti*) stating: "Those who perform the *saṃdhyā* rite while holding water in their left hand—that *saṃdhyā* should be known as that of a *vṛṣalī*; by them, the Asuras are gratified.

The mention of "in a vessel" and so forth refers to the *saṃdhyā* performed at home, and not to the *saṃdhyā* to be performed in the vicinity of a river or similar location. After the initial sprinkling (*mārjana*), the learned (*śiṣṭas*) perform the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) with the section beginning "Water indeed is this" (*āpo vā idaṃ*). In reality, however, one should merely meditate upon [the water] through its nature as the Self of all (*sarvātmakatva*) by means of this [mantra].
Then one should perform the drinking of water with the mantra, and again the sprinkling (mārjana).
Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:

"Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Having gone to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), being pure, having bathed, and having washed his hands and feet, he should sip water (*ācamana*). In the evening, having drunk water with the mantra 'Agniśca mā manyuśca...', and in the morning with 'Sūryaśca mā manyuśca...', he becomes pure after sprinkling himself with water using his hand holding a *pavitra* (purifier) [made of kuśa grass], reciting the *Sāvitrī*, the *Surabhimatī*, the *Abliṅga*, the *Vāruṇī*, the *Hiraṇyavarṇā*, the *Pāvamānī*, the *Vyāhṛtis*, and other purificatory mantras.
Thus says Bhāradvāja: "Having said 'Agniśca mā... in the evening and 'Sūrya... in the morning, one should drink water."
"May the waters purify me at midday; thereafter, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana).
Here too, the word "having spoken" connects with "sūrya" [in the morning]. When "sūrya" is expected, the sandhi form "sūryeti" is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. Kātyāyana also says:

"One should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) of the head with kuśa grass and drops of water; the first three [sprinklings] are done respectively with the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Gāyatrī, and the fourth is with the verses addressed to the Waters (Ab-daivata)— this is the procedure for mārjana."
After the wiping, Prajāpati said: "Having taken water in the right hand, shaped like a cow's ear, one should,
while breathing out through the tip of the nose, contemplate the personified sin."
"One should recite the *Ṛtaṃ-ceti* hymn, or the three verses, or the *Drupadā* verse;
by means of the right nostril alone, one should expel the impurity (*pāpmāna*). Then, without looking at that water, one should cast it upon the ground to one's left side."
Now follows the offering of the *arghya*. One should perform it while practicing the worship of the Sun (*ādityopāsana*).
And so says the Śruti:

"Meditating upon the sun as it rises and as it sets, one should perform [the rite]. This very meditation is the primary element. "Those who constantly perform the *saṃdhyā* worship, firm in their vows..."
With their sins shaken off, they go to the eternal world of Brahman.

Because the connection with the fruit is understood in this very context. For this very reason, in battle, Arjuna and the others, being incapable [of performing the full ritual] regarding the ancillary parts (*aṅga*), performed only the primary worship of the Sun.
As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "O great king, they, having thus donned their armor at the front of the battle..."
"They worshipped the thousand-rayed Āditya as he had reached the twilight.
Some maintain that the offering of the *arghya* (water libation) is the principal act, while others consider it a subsidiary part (*aṅga*).
Vyāsa describes the manner of offering the *arghya*:
"Taking water with both hands and consecrating it with the *gāyatrī*, one should stand facing the sun and then throw it upwards three times.

In this context, the continuous (*saṃtata*) reading alone is to be accepted. Regarding the word "atha" in the phrase "atha saṃtatām," Mātṛdatta states that it is for the purpose of indicating predominance; therefore, in the performance of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other rites, the third reading (the continuous one) is to be accepted. The same applies to the *japa*. When there is continuity between the words "dhīmahi" and "dhiyaḥ," the sandhi is accompanied by its original accent (*sasvara*). Alternatively, in this reading, one should simply observe the absence of a pause (*anavānatva*). The syllable *hi* is unaccented (*anudātta*).
Āśvalāyana also says:
"Then, standing and holding water with his joined palms while facing east,
he should remember the light well-established within the maṇḍala, equal to the brilliance of crystal."
Having crossed that [ocean] and reached the southern path, one should offer the añjali;
having uttered the *vyāhṛtis* and other mantras, and while recollecting the sun in this manner all around,
one should cast the añjalis upon the cruel Mandehas who are fighting.
Having drawn [the essence] back again quickly with the sixteen-syllable mantra,
and having likewise taken up water once more while recollecting the *tejomantra*, [he should proceed].

Having thus repeated this three times and burned those asuras, the twice-born one should draw forth their splendor with the mantra and, while recollecting [the deity], establish it in the primary location and other places.
"As before, having remembered [the mantra] by way of the left path and established it within oneself,
one should turn clockwise and then, taking water, perform the ritual sipping (ācamana)."

The overall purport is as follows: one should contemplate that the light situated in the *ādhāra-maṇḍapa* at the starting point travels through the right nostril from the *ādhāra-maṇḍapa* to a distance of one *añjali* within, and having been cast along with water for the destruction of the Rākṣasa named Mandeha, it is brought back again through the left nostril by means of the *Gāyatrī-śiras* mantra and established once more in the *ādhāra-maṇḍapa*.
Vyāsa states the sixteen-syllable mantra:
"The sixteen-syllabled Brahman is known as the head (*śiras*) of the Gāyatrī."
"The mantra 'Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ' indeed [is found] in the Taittirīyaka."

The single syllable is [to be understood] as the *praṇava*; otherwise, this would contradict the statement that Brahman consists of sixteen syllables. Alternatively, the state of having sixteen syllables should be seen by contemplating the word *suvar* as consisting of a single syllable.
In the absence of water, the *arghya* offering should be given with dust:
"In the absence of water, on a great road, in captivity, or even in impurity..."
"One should offer the *arghya* with menstrual blood at the time of both twilights," according to the *Agni-smṛti*.
Regarding the specific details for the offering of the *arghya*, the *Saṃgraha* states:
"It should be given with an open hand; one should not employ a ritual mudrā therein."
When the index finger and the thumb are joined together, it is known as the Rākṣasī mudrā.
By means of the *rākṣasī* mudrā and the *arghya*, that water shall become blood.
The *arghya* should be offered in water; in the absence of water, on a pure spot.
Having thoroughly sprinkled [the area] with water, one should then properly offer the arghya;
indeed, being slightly bowed at dawn, one should stand upright at midday.
"One should offer handfuls of *arghya* water to the Sun, but in the evening, one should sit upon the ground.
Now follows the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*:
"One should remain seated reciting the *Sāvitrī* until the appearance of the stars."
"One should remain thus during the evening and morning *saṃdhyā* until the appearance of the sun.

This means that in the evening, one should sit facing west and recite [the mantra] until the rising of the stars; in the morning, one should stand facing east until the rising of the sun. Śaunaka says:
"In the morning, one should recite the mantra while standing; in the evening, while seated;
and at midday, having sat down, one should perform the recitation facing the east."
Manu states the procedure for that:
"Having sipped water, being pure and composed, one should constantly attend upon both twilights,
muttering the prayers prescribed in a clean place according to the rule."
In response to the question "How?", Śaṅkha says: "Seated upon a mat of kuśa grass, or with a kuśa mat as an upper garment, with kuśa blades as a purifier in hand,
facing the sun and meditating on the deity, one should perform the recitation."
Vyāsa describes the seats as follows:
"One should prepare a seat made of silk, woolen cloth, deerskin, or even fine cotton cloth; or one made of wood or palm leaves."
Success in knowledge is attained on a black antelope skin; liberation and prosperity on a tiger skin;
the destruction of disease on a seat of kuśa grass; and all desired objects on a multicolored woolen blanket.
On a bamboo seat there is poverty; on a stone seat, indeed, disease;
on the bare ground, suffering; and on a seat made of perforated wood, misfortune.
"In grass there is loss of wealth and fame; in a sprout, there is delusion of mind. Thus says Pracetas:
"A vessel made of cow-dung or clay, if broken, as well as one made of Palāśa or Pippala wood..."
"A wise man should always avoid a seat bound with iron or made of *arka* wood. Thus it is said.
In another Smṛti:
"A householder who has sons should carefully avoid a deer-skin seat."
In the Purāṇa:
"Having sipped water (ācamana) both evening and morning, one should offer a handful of water (añjali) to the Sun;
having offered it and performed circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa), one becomes pure by touching water."
The Śruti also says:
"In that they proceed clockwise, by that they shake off evil.
And in the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"One should sprinkle water while circumambulating clockwise, [saying] 'That sun is Brahman.
The mantra for sitting down is stated in the *Gāyatrīkalpa*:
"O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu."
"And you, O Goddess, support me; make the seat pure," said Vyāsa regarding the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the others:
"The back of Mount Meru on the earth is designated as the seer."
"The deity is the back of a tortoise, Sutala is declared to be the metre;
its application is proclaimed for ascending the seat."
In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:

"In a clean place sprinkled with water and *darbha* grass, having spread out *darbha* blades, sitting down with the *vyāhṛtis*, performing three *prāṇāyāmas*, and sprinkling oneself with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should recollect the seer, deity, and meter of the *Sāvitrī*. Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon oneself according to the respective limbs using the six limb-mantras, one should contemplate oneself as being of that [divine] form."

Having performed the placement [of mantras]—saying "Tat Savitur, to the heart, namaḥ" on the heart; "Vareṇyam, to the head, svāhā" on the head; "Bhargo devasya, to the tuft, vaṣaṭ" on the tuft; "Dhīmahi, to the armor, huṃ" on the chest; and "Dhiyo yo naḥ, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ" on the eyes and the forehead—one should place the weapon-mantra with "Pracodayāt, to the weapon, phaṭ" on the palms of the hands and in the ten directions beginning with the east. This is the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa); some do not accept this, for that procedure is non-Vedic.
Since the procedure for sitting on the seat is demonstrated here, it is understood that in the previous case, one sits silently upon a seat of *darbha* grass.
However, in the *Gāyatrī-kalpa*, it is stated: "Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the six limbs, one should then recollect the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [components]."

In the *Bṛhat-Parāśara-smṛti* and other texts, however, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities corresponding to the syllables of the *praṇava*, the seven *vyāhṛtis*, the *varga*, the *kukṣi*, and the *pāda*, as well as other rites, have also been described; these should be consulted in those very sources, and are not stated here for fear of prolixity.
Following that is the invocation:
"Then one should invoke the Goddess with the mantras beginning with 'āyātu'."
Thus, even according to the sequence of the recitation, the invocation (āvāhana) occurs right here.
In the case of the recitation (japa), the Gāyatrī should be understood as being joined with the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis. And so Vyāsa says:
"Then one should recite the Gāyatrī joined with the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis."
Regarding the number of recitations (*japa*), Yogayājñavalkya says:
"A student (*brahmacārin*) and one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should recite one hundred and eight times;
a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and an ascetic (*yati*) should recite more than a thousand times."

"In the evening, morning, and at midday, one who is restrained in speech should mutter the Sāvitrī. The wise man should recite the Gāyatrī— the goddess who destroys all sins— up to a maximum of a thousand times, a middle of a hundred, or a minimum of ten."
Baudhāyana also says:

"Seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, with his hand containing water, facing westward, one should repeat the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or an unlimited number of times, or by means of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) a hundred times; or, with the *praṇava* at both ends and the seven *vyāhṛtis*, one may repeat it ten times mentally.
A specific rule for the morning twilight (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*) has been stated by him as follows:

"In this very manner, rising early in the morning," it says. "By means of *prāṇāyāma*" means by way of the method of breath-control. He explains that very method with the words beginning "with the *praṇava* on both sides. And this method belongs only to the followers of Baudhāyana; for those who follow the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha, it is more appropriate to adopt the third recitation taught during the initiation (*upanayana*), which is established by an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). The meaning of the word "unlimited" (*aparimita*) is simply an excess over the stated number, and not even a deficiency from it.
For Kātyāyana has stated that the meaning of the word *aparimita* (immeasurable) is precisely "more than the measure," as in the phrase "immeasurable, exceeding the limit.
Vyāsa says:
"One hundred and eight [times] daily, or indeed twenty-eight."
Or, according to the prescribed rule, the wise man should mutter the ten [verses] at the three times of day.
Nārada says: "In all cases during the *pradoṣa* periods, one should recite the Gāyatrī eight times;
on the twenty-eight days when study is forbidden (*anadhyāya*), one should recite it one hundred and eight times."
Sumantu says: "On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, the wise man should recite half of the daily [quota]."
"One should recite a fourth part on the days of practice, and an even smaller amount on the festival days."
Regarding the rosary for recitation, it is stated in another Smṛti: "One should recite the Goddess using joints; the rosary is prescribed for recitation for specific desires.
Because the Gāyatrī is the root of the Vedas, the Veda itself is said to be sung upon the joints."
Beginning from the middle joint of the ring finger,
one should recite over the ten joints in successive order up to the base of the index finger;
specifically, at the two joints that form the base of the middle finger.
"One should indeed recognize that as Meru; one must not overstep it during the recitation.
Thus it is said in the Agastyasaṃhitā:
"The little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the fourth is considered the index finger."

The three fingers should have three joints each, while the middle finger has only one joint. Recitation should be performed by means of the joints, not by the lowering of the fingers. One should avoid using the first two joints of the middle finger during the time of recitation.
"The wise should understand this as Mount Meru in the recitation performed with a rosary."
But in another Smṛti it is said: "Beginning from the base of the ring finger and proceeding clockwise in sequence,
one should recite [the mantra] over the ten joints up to the base of the middle finger."
Recitation (*japa*) is of three kinds. As stated in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*: "The sacrifice of recitation is threefold; learn its divisions:
it is traditionally held to be of three types—vocal (*vācika*), whispered (*upāṃśu*), and mental (*mānasa*)."
"Among the three sacrifices consisting of recitation, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding."

The definition of the whispered (*vācika*) and the silent (*upāṃśu*) [recitations] is stated in the Purāṇa: "When one utters the mantra with speech using high, low, and circumflex tones, with words and syllables clearly articulated, this is remembered as *vācika* recitation."
"One should recite the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly;
when it is heard only faintly by others, that is remembered as *upāṃśu-japa*."
Viśvāmitra has stated the definition of mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*):
"The repeated contemplation of the meaning of words, proceeding from syllable to syllable and from word to word by means of the intellect through a series of phonemes, is called mental recitation."
And the relative gradation among these three was stated by that very same [author]:
"O twice-born one, among all mantras, mental recitation is said to be the best, whispered recitation is considered middling, and vocal recitation is declared to be the lowest."
"For the verbal [japa], each [syllable] shall be one; for the whispered, it is said to be a hundred;
and for the mental, it is declared to be a thousand by Manu, Atri, Bhṛgu, and Nārada."
The fruit of mental recitation (*mānasajapa*) is stated in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*, concerning mental recitation:
"By this, the deity, being constantly praised, becomes pleased;
being pleased, she bestows abundant enjoyments and eternal liberation."
In another Smṛti: "While reciting the twenty-four-syllable Gāyatrī within the heart, one should meditate upon all the phonemes, as well as the deity and the meaning itself."

The word *akṣara* (syllable) refers to vowels (*svara*). Although there are only twenty-three vowels present in the *gāyatrī* mantra, nevertheless, in the case of *ṇyam*, one should understand it as two vowels, *ṇi-y-am*, through mental visualization (*bhāvanā*).
And it has been stated by Piṅgala: "The vowel *i* and others serve to complete [the meter]."

The word *pāda* (foot) is understood from the previous context. *Iyādipūraṇaḥ* means that for which there is a filler beginning with *iyā* and so forth. By the word *ādi* (beginning), [the particles] *u*, *ā*, and others are included. In this regard, the meaning is as follows: where in a meter such as the *gāyatrī* the syllable count of a foot is not complete, it must be completed by means of *iyā* and so forth. Halāyudha has explained this with examples such as: *tatsaviturvareṇiyam*, *divaṃ gaccha suvaḥ pata*.

[He states]: "The word *ghṛṇi* consists of two syllables; *sūrya* consists of three; *āditya* consists of three. This indeed is the eight-syllabled foot of the *Sāvitra* [mantra], consecrated with glory."
Thus, it should be understood that the Śruti also provides authority for this matter.
Regarding the rules for recitation (*japa*), Śaunaka says:
"In the morning, one should hold both hands with palms facing upward; in the evening, they should be held with palms facing downward."
"In the middle [of the body], the recitation is declared to be performed with both hands facing each other.
In another Smṛti: "Holding the two hands level with the navel, one should perform the morning twilight recitation."
"The two hands should be level with the navel, but in the evening, the hands should be level with the face.
Vṛddha-Manu says: "He who always recites [mantras] while covering his right hand with a cloth..."
"His recitation is fruitful; that which is devoid of it is declared fruitless.
Regarding the prohibition of wearing wet clothing while covering oneself, another Smṛti states:
"If one should perform recitation while covering his hand with a wet cloth..."
"His recitation shall be fruitless, and the deity will not be pleased.
Vyāsa says: "Contentment of mind, purity, silence, and reflection on the meaning of the mantra..."
"Absence of distraction and lack of despondency are the causes for the perfection of *japa*.
The meaning of the mantra has been stated by Bṛhat-Parāśara:
"That is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self know."
"We meditate upon the splendor of the divine Savitṛ, which is worthy of choice;
may he impel our thoughts toward the state of Brahman."

Of that Savitṛ, the cause of the universe—the glorious Sun—*vareṇyaṃ* means worthy of being chosen (*varaṇīyam*). [The suffix] *eṇya* is applied to the root *vṛ*. *Bhargaḥ* is splendor (*tejaḥ*), so called because it consumes (*bharjana*) darkness. [The form is derived] from the root *bhṛj* with the suffix *asun* and the augment *ku*, according to the rule: "After the roots *vyañj*, *yuñj*, and *bhṛj*, [the suffix *asun* is added and *k* is the augment]. *Dhīmahi* means "we should meditate. [We meditate on] Him who would impel (*pracodayāt*) our thoughts—that is, He who impels our intellects toward His own essential nature; this is the meaning. In this way, one should perform the mental contemplation and recollection of the meaning of the Gāyatrī mantra. The same applies to the words themselves. For it has been stated by Viśvāmitra immediately prior [to this]: "The supreme form of recitation is mental. Baudhāyana says:
"One engaged in ritual action should avoid contact below the navel. Thus says Atri:
"Neither with desire, nor laughing, nor looking to the side..."
Neither leaning against anything, nor talking, nor likewise with his head covered.
"One should not recite while stepping with one foot upon the other, nor likewise with the hands;
nor with an unconcentrated mind, nor while causing others to hear."
Vyāsa says:
"One should not speak at the time of recitation, nor during vows, fire-offerings, and the like. Even while walking, O best of the twice-born, one should remain intent upon these very acts."
"Then, having saluted the Brahmin, one should inquire after his *yoga* and *kṣema*.

The meaning is that just as at the time of departure one proceeds with the mind fixed solely on that [destination], so too in the case of recitation (*japa*) and other such acts, one should remain with the mind fixed solely on that. Having saluted the Brahmin, one should inquire after his *yoga* and *kṣema*—that is the meaning. *Yoga* is the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained; *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been obtained. Yājñavalkya on Yoga states:
"If, at any time during recitation and other such acts, there should be a lapse in the restraint of speech..."
"One should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the immutable Viṣṇu. Saṃvarta says:
"Having heard worldly gossip and the like, or having heard harsh words..."

"And that which is recited without a count shall all be fruitless. "Without a count" means without calculation. Even in the case of the view that [the number] is unlimited, calculation must indeed be performed; otherwise, the recitation would result in being fruitless.
And so says Gautama:
"Whether walking or standing, or performing actions according to one's own will,
if one is impure, all that— beyond counting— shall be fruitless. Thus also says Bṛhat-Parāśara:
"Since it is an innumerable demonic [obstacle], one should therefore certainly count that [breath].
Gautama says:
"Anger, delusion, sneezing, sleep, spitting, and yawning..."
And one should avoid the sight of dogs and low-caste persons during the practice of recitation.
If these are unavailable, one should sip water, remember Viṣṇu who is worshipped by the gods,
praise the luminaries, or perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
"One should look upon fire, cows, Brahmins, or even ascetics for the sake of purification"— the word "should look upon" (paśyet) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In the *Saṃgraha*:
One should perform the pure recitation with clarity of tone, color, words, and sentences;
one should not shake the head or neck, nor should one show the teeth.
Initiated twice-born reciters should not touch one another;
having conversed with them, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Stretching out the feet, gossiping, scratching the ground, yawning,
sticking out the tongue, tearing clothes, and biting the nails [are all improper].
Spitting after eating, shaking the limbs, binding the hair,
loosening the topknot, and even combing the hair [are forbidden].
Crying out, wandering about, binding oneself with grass, threads, and so forth;
quivering of the lower lip, grinding of the teeth, and trembling of the body.
Slapping one's arms, laughing, lying down, looking around,
searching for lice with a finger, and filling the mouth with air.
Covering the head, performing crafts, and chewing the lips—
these actions occur if there is negligence of the mind.
Having washed his feet and hands and sipped water according to the rule,
he should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and gaze at the sun.
"Then, having paid homage, the wise one should complete the remainder of the recitation.
As for the rule regarding the location, it was stated by Yogayājñavalkya:
"One should recite either in a fire-sanctuary, at the edge of water, or even in a temple."
"At a holy pilgrimage site, in a cow-pen, in a sacred field, or in one's own home.
Śaṅkha also says: "Recitation performed at home is said to have one-fold merit, but at a river it is twice as effective."
In a cow-pen, the merit is tenfold; in a fire-sanctuary, it is more than a hundredfold.
"At the Siddha-tīrthas, in sacred fields (kṣetras), and in the presence of a deity, [the fruit is] a thousand times ten million; in the presence of Viṣṇu, it is infinite.

Here, the word "in the river" (*nadyām*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean "on the bank," just as in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the word "Ganges" refers to its bank. Alternatively, it may be a locative of proximity (*samīpa-saptamī*). Or, it may refer to the context of wearing wet clothes (*ārdravāsas*).
"If one should indeed have wet clothes, one should mutter the Gāyatrī in water;
otherwise, however, being composed, [one should do so] on pure ground upon Kuśa grass," according to the statement of Yama.
Also, in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Since Guhyakas, Rākṣasas, and Siddhas carry it off by force,
one should therefore always perform the recitation in a solitary and auspicious place.
Vyāsa praises the recitation of the Gāyatrī:
If that [mantra] is recited ten times, it quickly destroys whatever minor sin has been committed within three days; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
When that goddess is recited one hundred times, she is known as the pacifier of the flood of sins;
when she is recited one thousand times, that goddess is the destroyer of minor offenses.
"By reciting it one hundred thousand times, O King of Kings, it likewise destroys even the greatest sins; by reciting it ten million times, one shall obtain whatever one desires."
Yama also says:
"There is no recitation superior to the Gāyatrī; there is no austerity superior to the Gāyatrī;
there is no meditation superior to the Gāyatrī; there is no oblation superior to the Gāyatrī."
Manu also says:
"He who, transcending the senses, studies this [text] day after day for three years,
attains even the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind yet possessing a form."
Gautama also says:
"One should perform the recitation daily with diligence according to this rule;
being pleased, [the deity] grants vast enjoyments, and after having experienced them, one attains liberation."
Regarding the offering of the recitation (*japa*) at its conclusion, it is stated in the *Ācārapradīpa*:
"By this morning twilight prayer and the recitation of the Gāyatrī performed one hundred and eight times, may the Sun, who is the Self of Brahman, be pleased."

In this way, when performing the *japa* prescribed for the midday twilight (*madhyāhnasaṃdhyā*), one substitutes the word "Madhya-Rudra" in place of the two words "Prātar-Brahman"; however, when performing the *japa* prescribed for the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*), one substitutes the word "Sāyaṃ-Viṣṇu. Indeed, such mantras are shown in the *Jaṭamalla-grantha*.
Then, one should dismiss the *Gāyatrī*. As it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"Having recited the verse 'Uttame śikhare,' one should dismiss the Goddess."
Now, regarding the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*):

On this point, Baudhāyana says—"One attends upon the night with the *Brahmatṛhadaya* and the two verses addressed to Varuṇa, namely, 'This [oblation] for me, O Varuṇa' (*imaṃ me varuṇa*) and 'That I implore of thee' (*tattvā yāmi*); and in the morning, standing facing the east, one attends upon the day with the two verses addressed to Mitra, namely, 'Of Mitra, the upholder of the people' (*mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*) and 'Mitra, knowing all, directs the people' (*mitro janānyātayati prajānan*)."
The Praṇava is the heart of Brahman.
Regarding the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyopasthāna*), it is also stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Then, with a well-concentrated mind, one should worship the Sun at its rising."

"With various friendly mantras originating from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas"—here "friendly" (*maitra*) means those addressed to Mitra as their deity; that is to say, with such [mantras] as *mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ* and so forth.
The ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) for the midday *saṃdhyā* is described in the Brahmapurāṇa:

"And having properly cast the añjali [salutation], one should recite 'ud u tyam', 'citram', 'taccakṣur deva', and also 'haṃsaḥ śuciṣat'; with arms raised and mind concentrated, one should look at the sun while reciting these."
Baudhāyana, however, has prescribed that the worship (upasthāna) should take place immediately after the recitation of the Gāyatrī; he states:

"Having sipped water, seated on Darbha grass, holding Darbha blades, and facing east, one should repeat the Sāvitrī a thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number—at least ten times—and then one should worship the Sun with the verses: 'ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ parī,' 'ud u tyaṃ,' 'citraṃ,' 'tat cakṣur devahitaṃ,' and 'ya udagāt. This very procedure should be adopted by the followers of the Taittirīya school, because Baudhāyana’s teaching is more authoritative than other scriptures.

Regarding the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyopasthāna*), it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Likewise, with composed mind, one should worship the Sun with the Vāruṇī verses. The Vāruṇī verses are those beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa" and so forth. Although the worship of Varuṇa by means of the Vāruṇī verses is established by the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), nevertheless, because direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful, it overrides the indicative mark; thus, the mantras are employed for the worship of the Sun, just as in the case of the Aindrī verses. According to the view that the worship is performed with the two mantras mentioned in the *Baudhāyana Sūtra*, there is worship of the night in the evening and of the day in the morning. In reality, however, since the Sun is the essence of both night and day, one should worship him while meditating upon the Sun.
Thus, there is no contradiction between Baudhāyana and the Kūrma Purāṇa. Now follows the worship of the quarters and the two lords. Regarding this, Nārāyaṇa says:
"Having likewise worshipped the Sun with the Vāruṇī verses, [one should perform] a circumambulation."

"One performing [the rite] should pay homage to the directions and the lords of the directions individually. Although from this statement the status of the salutation to the directions and their lords as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*) is understood, nevertheless, this should also be observed for the morning twilight (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*), because that [salutation] is prescribed for the morning twilight as well in the *Bhagavad-smṛti*. And this is indicated by the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras beginning with "Salutation to the eastern direction and to those deities... and so forth.
The mantra "Namo Gaṅgā-Yamunayoḥ" is applied, by virtue of its indicative mark (*liṅga*), for the purpose of saluting the sages who dwell between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Alternatively, in this context, there is the dismissal of Gāyatrī:
"Having performed the worship (*upasthāna*) of the Sun, one should then dismiss Gāyatrī."
Thus, from a statement in another Smṛti in the *Ācāradarpaṇa*:
Yama praises the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*):
"Those who constantly perform the twilight worship, being firm in their vows..."
With their sins shaken off, they go to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Whatever sin one commits during the day by deed, thought, or speech, one destroys that by sitting for the evening twilight ritual and performing breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
Whatever sin one commits during the night by deed, thought, or speech,
one dispels it by sitting for the morning twilight (pūrva-saṃdhyā) and performing breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
"The sages, by virtue of their long observance [of this vow], obtain long life,
progeny, fame, renown, and spiritual luster.
Dakṣa has shown the transgression incurred by its non-performance:
"One who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever other rite he performs, he shall not partake in its fruit."
Gobhila also says:
"He by whom the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) is not known, and he by whom the twilight prayer is not performed,
shall remain a Śūdra while living and, after death, is reborn as a dog."
Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O King, those evil-minded ones who do not attend upon the morning or the evening twilight go to the Tāmisra hell."
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa* as well:
"O best of the twice-born, he who performs all other religious duties while omitting the salutation of the *saṃdhyā* goes to ten thousand hells."
All of this refers to one who is not in distress.
Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"That twice-born man who, being free from distress, should abandon [his duties], is equal to a Śūdra."
"He shall indeed be subject to penance and becomes censured in the world.
Atri also says:
"Those twice-born men who, while in a state of health, do not perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā)..."
"For the wicked always seek to harm the Blessed One, the Sun."
Jamadagni states that in some cases, even the omission of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) does not constitute a fault:

"In times of national upheaval, during a king's agitation, when afflicted by disease, or when fear has arrived; and when a great matter concerning the gods, fire, twice-born ones, or the king is at hand."
"There is no fault in the omission of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), since that [omission] is a means of attaining merit."
Now follows the expiation for the transgression of the time of twilight (*saṃdhyā*).
(In that regard, the *Smārtaprāyaścittakutūhala* quotes the *Skānda*:
"From after sunrise until three *ghaṭikās* have passed...")
"One should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana) for that long; beyond that, it is an expiation."
And this is intended for those who are extremely weary;
otherwise:
"He who, through negligence, does not perform the morning twilight worship while the stars are still visible..."
The recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times is his expiation for the sake of purification.

Otherwise, this would contradict the statement in the *Karmapradīpa*: "The morning twilight [should be performed] while the stars are still visible, but the evening twilight while the sun is still present. Pṛthvīcandra notes that this is merely an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding this, Yama states:
"One should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) in the morning; at the time of *saṅgava*, one should perform double that amount."
It is said to be threefold at midday and fourfold in the afternoon.
"In the evening it is fivefold, and it becomes so upon the passing of the twilight."
In the *Smārtaprāyaścittakutūhala*, however, regarding the ritual of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyākalpa*), it is stated:
"Three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) are prescribed for the morning; they are remembered as being double that at the time of *saṅgava*;
they are said to be triple at midday; and at the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), they are sixfold."
"It is said that in the evening [the fault] is twelvefold; from that, one incurs the sin of killing the sun.

Here, the rule is established according to whether one is capable or incapable [of performing the rite]. By failing to perform [the rite] at dawn and other times, one incurs the sin of killing the sun; the meaning is that one attains the state of having killed the sun.
As for the statement of Jamadagni—
"When the time for the twilight ritual has passed, having bathed and sipped water according to the rules,
one should recite the Goddess's mantra one hundred and eight times, and thereafter perform the twilight ritual."
Thus, that [text] refers to one who is incapable of *prāṇāyāma*. The statement in the *Karmapradīpa* is likewise:
"He who does not perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) nor the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) according to rule, shall, having bathed and being composed, mutter the *Gāyatrī* eight thousand times."
Thus, the statement of the *Smṛti* refers to the case of a single omission due to that [specific] intention.
As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha:
"And even when there is a lapse of time, at all three junctions of the day..."
"On the fourth day, one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun, [using] the *vyāpti-ṛti-sampuṭa*."
That refers to the transgression of a short period of time.
Regarding the transgression of one day or more, Jamadagni states:
"If the rite of the twilight prayer (*saṃdhyāvandana*) is omitted for even one day..."
"Having fasted for one day and night, one should recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times;
for two nights it is said to be double that, and for three nights it is traditionally held to be triple.
If it should exceed three nights, he becomes a Śūdra, without a doubt."
If, by chance, the midday rites have not been performed during the day, then a specific rule is recorded in the Smṛti:
"One may perform the daytime duties until one watch (prahara) of the night;
however, one must avoid immersion in water, the Brahmayajña, and the recitation dedicated to the Sun."

Also in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*: "The rites prescribed for the day should be performed at night as well, in their proper order, with the exception of immersion in water, the solar rites, the Brahma-yajña, and the libations (*tarpaṇa*)."
By the word *avagāha*, bathing in the form of immersion is prohibited.
As for the prohibition of the *brahmayajña*, it refers to those other than the Taittirīyas. [As stated:
"In the village, one should study the *svādhyāya* mentally, by day or by night."

Thus, because the *Taittirīya* Śruti establishes that this [Brahmayajña] must be performed even at night; or rather, this Smṛti prohibits the Brahmayajña only extensively. Therefore, the Brahmayajña, though brief, must indeed be performed by the Taittirīyas and others at night as well. This is because the Śruti, being universal and authoritative, applies without obstruction to all branches (*śākhā*) of the Veda. And this has been stated according to the opinion of Āhneya Ṛṣi regarding the purity [of the time]:
the midday *saṃdhyā* should be performed even at night, provided it is done without the ritual worship (*upasthāna*), since the latter is characterized by passion (*saura*).
"One should perform the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) even at night; it is not considered faulty.
However, one should offer the arghya with the Gāyatrī mantra, but should exclude that which is specifically addressed to the Sun."
This is also because of statements in the *Smṛtiratnāvalī* and other texts.
Regarding the performance of the *saṃdhyā* rites otherwise, Saṃvarta states in the *Smārtaprāyaścittakutūhala*:
"That which is devoid of proper accents and measures, and lacking the correct words and syllables..."
"But having made it either deficient or excessive, one should utter [the verse] beginning with 'ābhir gīrbhiḥ'."
Now, since it follows in sequence, first is the procedure for the midday twilight worship (*madhyāhna-saṃdhyopāsanā*).

Having spread *darbha* grass in a clean place, having sat down upon them facing east in silence, holding *kuśa* grass in his hand, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) three times—either with the three feet of the *Gāyatrī*, or with the three mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," or silently. Then, with his right hand containing water, he should wipe both lips three times or twice against the direction of their hair; he should touch the two lips twice or once, sprinkle his left hand, his feet, and his head, and touch his eyes, nostrils, and ears; after each such touching, he should sip water. Thus [is the procedure].

As before, having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) three times, having wiped both lips twice, having touched [the mouth] properly, having sprinkled water on the left hand and the two feet, and having touched the head, the eyes, the two nostrils, the two ears, and the heart, one should touch water after each such touching; or else, having performed the ritual sipping twice in this manner—

The *ṛṣi* of the *praṇava* is the Supreme Brahman; its *devatā* is Agni; its *chandas* is Gāyatrī. For the seven *vyāhṛtis*, the *devatās* are the sacrificial deities (*yājñikyaḥ*), and the *ṛṣis* are the Upaniṣads. Their respective *devatās* are, in order: Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Bṛhaspati, Varuṇa, Indra, and the Viśvedevas. Their respective *chandas* are, in order: Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī.

For the *gāyatrī*, Agni Viśvāmitra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Savitṛ is the deity, and *gāyatrī* is the meter. For the *śiras-mantra*, the Yājñikas are the deities, the Upaniṣads are the seers, the waters and so forth are the deities, and the *yajus* is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is for all breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*). Reciting "Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ suvaḥ, Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ," one should practice it three times according to the sequence of filling (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhaling (*recaka*), while meditating on Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva respectively. Alternatively, one may practice it three times by means of retention alone.

For the mantra beginning with *oṃ tadbrahma* and ending with *puronamaḥ*, the deities are the Yājñikīs, the meter is the Upaniṣad, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*). One should perform the regulation of breath either with this [mantra]: "Oṃ, that is Brahman; Oṃ, that is Vāyu; Oṃ, that is Puronamaḥ," or by means of this [formula]. Having performed the three regulations of breath in this manner, one should meditate upon the *saṃdhyā*.

Having meditated upon Sāvitrī as non-different from the Sun—visualizing her as the youthful Midday Sandhyā, white in complexion, clad in white garments, anointed with white perfumes, three-eyed, holding a boon-granting gesture, a trident, and an axe while displaying the gesture of fearlessness, riding upon a bull, and possessing the form of Rudra—and having declared the place and time, made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord, I shall perform the worship of the Midday Sandhyā."

For the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the deities are Agni or the Viśvedevas, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*). One should perform the sprinkling with water from *kuśa* grass using the middle finger, ring finger, and thumb—at the end of each *ṛc*, at the end of each half-verse, or at the end of each foot—with the mantra: *oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā... ca naḥ*. In the case of sprinkling at the end of each foot, one should sprinkle on the head and the two shoulders at the end of each foot, up to the verse ending with *tasmā araṃ gamāma vaḥ*. Then, with the two [remaining] verses, *oṃ yasya kṣayāya jinvatha* and *āpo janayathā ca naḥ*, one should sprinkle below the throat; this is the specific distinction.

Alternatively—the sequence for sprinkling (*mārjana*) is as follows: "Oṃ *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*" on the head; "*tā na ūrje dadhātana*" on the feet; "*mahe raṇāya cakṣase*" on the heart; "*yo vaḥ śivatamo rasaḥ*" on the heart; "*tasya bhājayateha naḥ*" on the feet; "*uśatīriva mātaraḥ*" on the head; "*tasmā araṃ gamāma vaḥ*" on the head; "*yasya kṣayāya jinvatha*" on the heart; and "*āpo janayathā ca naḥ*" on the feet. Thus is the sequence for sprinkling.

Next, regarding the section beginning with "The waters, indeed, this": the deities are those of the sacrificial tradition (*yājñikya*), the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) is the waters, and the meter is the *yajus*. Its application is for the meditative contemplation (*abhidhyāna*) [of the Self] as being identical with all things: "Oṃ, the waters, indeed, this; the waters, Oṃ"—thus one should meditate upon the waters as being identical with all things. Next, regarding the verse beginning with "May the waters purify": the deities are those of the sacrificial tradition, the secret doctrine is the seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*). The deities are the waters, the earth, Brahmaṇaspati, and Brahman; the meter is the eight-footed *aṣṭi*. Its application is for the drinking of water: "Oṃ, may the waters purify... [pṛthivī... graha svāhā]"—with these words, he drinks the water.

Then, having sipped water twice, one should perform the *mārjana* (sprinkling) again. For the *praṇava*: the Supreme Brahman is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Agni is the deity, and the *gāyatrī* is the meter. For the *vyāhṛtis*, both individually and collectively: Prajāpati is the seer; Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati are the deities; and the *gāyatrī*, *uṣṇih*, *anuṣṭubh*, and *bṛhatī* are the meters. For the *gāyatrī*: Viśvāmitra is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity, and the *gāyatrī* is the meter. For the verse beginning with "dadhikrāvṇo": the Viśvedevas are the deities, Dadhikrāvan is the deity, and the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter.

For the triad of mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the seers are Agni or the Viśvedevas, the deity is Water, and the metre is Gāyatrī. For the triad of mantras beginning with *yacciddhi te*, the seers are the Viśvedevas; Varuṇa is the deity; for the first [mantra], the metre is Gāyatrī, and for the second and third, it is Triṣṭubh. For the tetrad of mantras beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, the seer is Agni, the deity is Water, and the metre is Triṣṭubh. For the mantras of the *Pavamāna-anuvāka*, Prajāpati is the seer; the deities are Pavamāna, Suvarjana, and others as indicated by their respective characteristics (*liṅga*).

The meters are *gāyatrī*, *anuṣṭubh*, and *triṣṭubh*. Having stated the seers and other details for the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively as before, [one should state]: for the verse beginning with "drupadā," the seers are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Water, the meter is *anuṣṭubh*; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*). Having performed the first sprinkling at the end of the *praṇava* ("oṃ"), the second sprinkling at the end of the *vyāhṛtis*, the third at the end of the *gāyatrī*, and the fourth at the end of the remaining mantra, one should sprinkle. Some maintain that the sprinkling is to be performed with each individual mantra.

Then, having formed the *gokarṇa* mudrā with the right hand and taking water therein, while exhaling and visualizing the *pāpapuruṣa* (the personification of sin) at the tip of the nose, one should perform the *viniyoga* for the expulsion of the *pāpapuruṣa* with the verse beginning "drupadā," whose deities are the Viśvedevas, its meter is *anuṣṭubh*, and its application is for the expulsion of the *pāpapuruṣa*: "Oṃ drupadādiva... tu mainasaḥ. Having thus expelled the *pāpapuruṣa* with this mantra, one should cast that water onto the ground to one's left side without looking at it. Then, rising and facing the sun, while meditating on the non-difference between the Sun (*āditya*), who is of the nature of Rudra, and the *saṃdhyā* named Sāvitrī, one should take water in both hands.

Prajāpati is the seer of all the *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the deity of the *bṛhatī* meter. Viśvāmitra is the seer of the *gāyatrī*, and Savitṛ is its deity; the *gāyatrī* is its meter. This is the application for the consecration of water: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ."

Having consecrated that water with the mantra, "Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ... codayāt," and having visualized that the splendor residing in the solar orb has entered through the right nostril, one should—recalling the seers and other attributes of the *vyāhṛtis* and the *gāyatrī* as before, and recollecting the application (*viniyoga*) as being for the offering of the *arghya*—utter the *gāyatrī* together with all the *vyāhṛtis* in a continuous flow. Then, facing the sun and lifting the water upward with cupped hands, one should offer the *arghya* into the water, saying: "This *arghya* is for Savitṛ, by means of the Sāvitrī; it is not mine."

The deities of the sixteen-syllable *śiromantra* are the sacrificial verses (*yajñikyaḥ*), the Upaniṣads, and the *avādayaḥ*; its meter is the *Yajus*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of re-establishing the light that was cast out for the sake of destroying demons back into its own place: "Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ... suvaḥ oṃ. One should visualize drawing that light in through the left nostril and having it arrive at its own place. Having thus performed the sequence from the taking up of water again until the re-establishment of the light in its own place twice, while circumambulating oneself clockwise, one should sprinkle oneself with the formula "This sun is Brahman," and then, sitting down, touch water.

Then, having sat down, performed the ritual sipping of water twice (*dvir-ācamana*), and restrained the breath (*prāṇāyāma*), he touches water and expels the obstructive spirits (*bhūta*) with the mantra: "Oṃ, may the beings depart... I begin. Having sprinkled the area of the seat with water and *darbha* grass, he spreads out a seat made of *darbha* and other materials there.

Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of all the *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the *bṛhatī* meter; for this mantra beginning with "O Earth," Meru-peak is the seer, the back of the tortoise is the deity, and Sutala is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in sitting upon the seat. Having sat upon the seat with "Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ" and "Oṃ Earth, by you the worlds are supported... and you [are the support]... the seat," and having performed the three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) as before—Prajāpati is the seer of all the *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the *bṛhatī* meter. Its application is in sprinkling oneself. One should sprinkle oneself with "Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ."

Now follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): *Tatsavitur*—*namaḥ* to the heart, on the heart. *Vareṇyam*—*svāhā* to the head, on the head. *Bhargo devasya*—*vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), on the crest-lock. *Dhīmahi*—*hum* to the armor (*kavaca*), on the chest. *Dhiyo yo naḥ*—*vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes, on the eyes and between the eyebrows. *Pracodayāt*—*phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*), [performed] by clapping the palms of the hands as the weapon [is directed] toward the ten directions beginning with the East. This *nyāsa* may or may not be performed.

The deities of the mantras contained in the section beginning with *āyātu* are the sacrificial deities (*yājñikya-devatā*); their seers (*ṛṣi*) are the Upaniṣads. The deity is Sandhyā, who is non-different from the Sun, possessing the form of Rudra, and designated as Sāvitrī. The meters for the first and second [mantras] are *anuṣṭubh*. For the mantra *sarvavarṇa*, the meter is *dvipadā-gāyatrī*. From *ojo'si* until *śriyamāvāhayāmi*, the form is *yajus*. The application (*viniyoga*) is in the invocation: "May the boon-granting goddess come... and "I invoke Śrī. Having invoked her with these [mantras]—

For the *praṇava*, Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Agni is the deity, and the *gāyatrī* is the meter. For the *vyāhṛtis* taken as a whole, Prajāpati is the seer and the *bṛhatī* is the meter. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation (*japa*). Regarding the *gāyatrī*: the *gāyatrī* is the meter, Viśvāmitra is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity; Agni is the mouth, Brahmā is the head, Viṣṇu is the heart, Rudra is the tuft (*śikhā*), and the Earth is the belly. It has five heads and its application is for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Having thus remembered the seers and other attributes, one should remain silent, free from restlessness, not speaking, with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose and the body held erect.

With a one-pointed mind, contemplating that he is meditating upon the *bharga*—the adorable, desirable splendor (*tejas*)—of the Lord, the self-luminous Savitṛ, the glorious Sun; [he should think: "May we meditate upon that which shall impel our thoughts," meaning it impels our intellects toward its own true nature. While reflecting thus in his mind, he should perform the recitation (*japa*) either one thousand and eight times, one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times, according to his capacity, following the rule of the third reading prescribed for the initiation (*upanayana*), in a low voice.
Upon the completion of the recitation, he should again perform the sixfold ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
[The verse continues: "And by the recitation of the Gāyatrī employed during the midday twilight..."
"By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, may the Sun, whose essence is Rudra, be pleased"—with these words, he should offer the recitation.

In cases such as a thousand repetitions, the word "thousand" (sahasra) and so forth should replace the word "hundred" (śata). Then, having sipped water twice or once, and having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma)—

For *ud vayam*, the deities are Agni, the Viśvedevas, or Sūrya; the meter is Anuṣṭubh. For *ud tyam*, the deity is Soma or Sūrya; the meter is Gāyatrī. For *citraṃ devānām*, the deity is Soma, the Viśvedevas, or Sūrya; the meter is Triṣṭubh. For *tac cakṣur devahitam*, the deity is Soma or Sūrya; the meter is Gāyatrī. For *ya udagāt*, the deity is Soma or Sūrya; the meter is Triṣṭubh. For *saḥ śuciṣat*, the deities are the Viśvedevas or Agni or Sūrya; the meter is Jagatī.

The application (*viniyoga*) for the worship of the Sun (*sūryopasthāna*) is as follows: with these [mantras]—"Oṃ *ud vayaṃ tamaḥ*," "Oṃ *ut tyaṃ jātavedasam*," "*citraṃ devānām*," "*tac cakṣur devahitam*," "*ya udagād anīkaḥ*," and "*haṃsaḥ śuciṣat*"—one worships the Āditya with arms raised upward.

For the mantra and the *anuvāka* beginning with "uttame śikhare," the seers (*ṛṣis*) are the ritual deities and the *Upaniṣads*; the deity is Sandhyā, who is non-different from Sūrya, named Sāvitrī, and possessing the form of Rudra. The meter of the first is *anuṣṭubh*, and that of the second is *triṣṭubh*. For the mantra and the *anuvāka* beginning with "ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādityaḥ," the seers are the ritual deities and the *Upaniṣads*; the deity is Sūrya, who is non-different from Sandhyā, named Sāvitrī, and possessing the form of Rudra. The meter of the first is *gāyatrī*, and that of the second is *yajus*.

The application (*viniyoga*) for the dismissal of the twilight prayer (*saṃdhyāvisarjana*) is as follows: "On the highest peak... to the world of Brahmā" (*uttame śikhare... brahmalokam*); "The radiant Sun... from my hair" (*ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādi... rom*). With these [verses], one should dismiss the twilight prayer. For the two mantras beginning with "He moves within beings" (*antaścarati bhūteṣu*), the seers (*ṛṣis*) are the *Yājñiky-upaniṣads*.
