The deity (*devatā*) of the first is the Self (*ātman*); its meter is the two-footed *gāyatrī*, while that of the second is the *yajus*. The application is for the worship of the Self (*ātmopasthāna*): "Oṃ, He moves within... from my hair" (*oṃ antaścara... rom*); with this, one worships the Self.

Then, having offered salutations with "Salutation to Sandhyā; salutation to the Gurus; salutation to the mother and father," and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) once as before, and having restrained the breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), one should meditate upon Viṣṇu.
This is the midday *sandhyā*.
Now follows the evening *sandhyā*.

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) as before, one should meditate on Sarasvatī in the form of Viṣṇu, who is the elder [Sāyaṃsandhyā], dark-complexioned, dressed in black garments, anointed with black perfumes and unguents, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and having Garuḍa as her vehicle—meditating thus through non-difference from the Sun, one should perform the rites beginning with the proclamation of place and time and ending with the visualization. Then, for the mantras of the *Anuvāka* beginning with "Agniśca me," the seers (*ṛṣi*) are the Vedic deities and the Upaniṣads; the deities are Agni, Manyu, the lords of wrath, and Day.

The mantra ending with *rakṣantām* is a Gāyatrī; the one ending with *duritaṃ mayi* is a Paṅkti; the remaining mantra is a Virāṭ, or alternatively, a single Yajus. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for drinking water: having drunk water while reciting, "Oṃ agniśca mā... yadahnā... satye jyotiṣi juhomi svāhā," and having sipped water (*ācamana*), one should again purify oneself (*mārjana*) with the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, the Gāyatrī, and so forth. Having dispelled evil, sitting facing west and meditating upon the Twilight (*saṃdhyā*) named Sarasvatī as non-different from the Sun, one should offer three handfuls of water (*arghya*).

One should offer [the water] on the ground as before. In that regard, the specific difference lies in the formula for offering the *arghya*: "This *arghya* is for Savitṛ and Sarasvatī; it is not mine."

Then, having circumambulated as before and performed *ācamana* and *prāṇāyāma*, one should face west and perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī* according to the procedure beginning with "May [the Twilight] depart" (*apakrāmatu*). Then, as before, one should perform the *uttara-nyāsa*. In this regard, the specific difference in the statement concerning the deity (*devatā-vākya*) among the mantras of the *Āyātu* section is that the deity is the Twilight (*Sandhyā*), who is non-different from Sūrya, whose form is Viṣṇu, and who is designated by the name Sarasvatī. However, the statements regarding the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), and the application (*viniyoga*) remain exactly the same. This same deity should also be understood in the mantra of dismissal (*visarjana*). The remainder is as before. Then: "By means of the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* employed in the evening twilight..."
"By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, may the Sun, whose self is Viṣṇu, be pleased.
Having thus offered the recitation (*japa*) and performed the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*), one should perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*).

It is as follows: for the two verses beginning "imaṃ me varuṇa" and "tattvā yāmi," the seers (*ṛṣi*) are the Viśvedevas; Varuṇa is the deity (*devatā*); the meter of the first is *gāyatrī*, and that of the second is *triṣṭubh*. For the three mantras beginning "yacciddhi te," the seers are the Viśvedevas; Varuṇa is the deity; the meter of the first is *gāyatrī*, and that of the second and third is *triṣṭubh*.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*): reciting "Oṃ imaṃ me varuṇa...", "Tattvā yāmi...", "Yacciddhi te...", "Yat kiṃ cedaṃ...", and "Kitavāso...", one should worship the Sun while facing westward. Then, [one should say]: "May that Twilight (*saṃdhyā*), whom all beings, both stationary and moving, always salute in the evening and morning, protect me; Oṃ, obeisance!"
Having thus performed the *saṃdhyopasthāna* (the ritual worship of the twilight):

for the mantras beginning with "Obeisance to the eastern direction," the *ṛṣi* is Svayaṃbhū; the deities are the eastern and other directions, their respective guardians, and the deities residing in those directions. For the mantra "Obeisance to the Gaṅgā and Yamunā," the deities are the sages dwelling between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, and the *chandas* are *yajus*. The application (*viniyoga*) is in the ritual of worship: "Oṃ, obeisance to the eastern direction, and obeisance to the deities who [reside] therein."

Having thus worshipped the eastern direction, its presiding deity, and the gods dwelling therein, one should perform the worship of each respective direction with their corresponding mantras, beginning with: "Obeisance to the southern direction. The mantras for worshipping the intermediate directions and so forth may be repeated four times or just once. Facing east, one should worship the sages with the mantra: "Obeisance to the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. Some, however, say that the sequence here begins with the western direction. At this point, the dismissal of the *saṃdhyā* may take place.
Then, one should perform the rites from "Obeisance to the *Saṃdhyā*" up to the remembrance of Viṣṇu. This concludes the evening *saṃdhyā*.
Now, for the morning twilight (prātaḥsaṃdhyā):

having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and breath-control (prāṇāyāma) as before, one should meditate on Gāyatrī—the embodiment of Brahmā—as the morning twilight, red in color, wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and red unguents, holding a book, a rosary, a water-pot, and a deer-skin in her hands, and seated upon a swan; having meditated thus through identification with the Sun, and having performed the rites from the proclamation of place and time up to the visualization—

The deities of the sacrificial formulas in the *anuvāka* beginning with "sūryaśca" are the Upanishadic deities; the seers are Sūrya, Manyu, the Lords of Wrath (Manyupati), and Rātri. The meter for the portion ending with "rakṣantām" is Gāyatrī; for the portion ending with "duritaṃ mayi," it is Paṅkti; for the remaining mantras, it is Virāṭ—or alternatively, they are a single Yajus formula.

The application regarding the drinking of water is as follows: Having drunk water with the mantra, "Oṃ, may the Sun [protect me]... whatever sin was committed by night... that [sin], O Night, I offer into the light of the Sun, Svāhā," and having sipped water (ācamana), one should again purify oneself with the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī*. Then, having dispelled the personified sin (*pāpapuruṣa*), standing facing the east and meditating on the *saṃdhyā* named *Gāyatrī* as non-different from the Sun, one should offer three handfuls of water (*arghya*) with joined palms right there in the midst of the water. In this regard, the specific difference in the formula for offering the *arghya* is: "This *arghya* is for Savitṛ via the *Gāyatrī*; it is not mine."

Then one should perform the rites beginning with the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*) and ending with the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). In this regard, the specific distinction in the statement concerning the deity is that for the mantras of the *Āyātu* section, the deity is the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) named Gāyatrī, who is non-different from the Sun and has the nature of Brahman. However, the statements regarding the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), and the application (*viniyoga*) remain exactly the same.
Then:
"By the recitation of the Gāyatrī employed during the morning twilight..."
"By reciting this one hundred and eight times, may the Sun, the self of Brahman, be pleased."

Having thus offered the recitation (*japa*) and dismissed the twilight (*saṃdhyā*), he stands before the sun with palms joined in the *mukula* gesture, [reciting] the three mantras beginning with *mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*. For these, the *ṛṣis* are the Viśvedevas and the deity is Mitra. The meter of the first is *gāyatrī*, and that of the second and third is *triṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for the worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*). Having worshipped the Sun with "Oṃ mitrasya... (RV 3.59.6), "mitro janān... (RV 3.59.2), and "pra samitra... (RV 3.59.4), and having worshipped the Twilight with "yāṃ sadā... (RV 1.106.1), he should perform the rites from "namaḥ prācyai diśe... up to the remembrance of Viṣṇu, as in the evening twilight. This concludes the morning twilight ritual.

Now, as a supplementary topic, the rules for eating: one desiring long life should face east; one desiring fame, south; one desiring prosperity, west; and one free from specific desires, east—never facing north, except during ancestral rites (*paitrya*). One whose mother and father are both living, or either of them, should never face south. Having resolved thus and sat down, having stated the seers and other details for all the *vyāhṛtis* as before, and having stated the application (*viniyoga*) as "for the consecration of food (*annopasthāna*)," he should consecrate the food being brought with the words "Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Suvar Oṃ," and [consecrate] that which has been served.

Having sprinkled [the food] with the Gāyatrī mantra accompanied by the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis, and having removed the silver ring from the ring finger if it has been worn, one should hold the square-shaped eating vessel placed upon a maṇḍala with the left hand. Taking water in the right hand, one recites: "Oṃ *ṛtaṃ tvā*..."—for this verse, Agni is the deity, *anna* (food) is the subject, and the Yajus is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sprinkling of the food. With the words, "Oṃ *ṛtaṃ tvā saṃsiñcāmi*," one sprinkles the food in the evening.

The mantra *satyaṃ tvartena* has Agni as its deity, food as its subject, and the Yajus as its meter; its application is for the sprinkling around the food: "Oṃ, I sprinkle you with truth through the Real. With this, one sprinkles the food in the morning.
Then, leaving a space of ten or five finger-breadths to the right of the eating vessel, one silently sprinkles that spot, takes a small portion of food from the meal, and—

Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the individual *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the seer of the collective *vyāhṛtis*. Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati are, respectively, the deities (*devatās*) of the four [syllables]. Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, and Bṛhatī are, respectively, the meters (*chandāṃsi*) of the four. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the offering of the oblation (*balinivapana*): "Bhūḥ svāhā"—to Agni, this [is offered]. Again, taking from the food: "Bhuvaḥ svāhā"—to Vāyu, this [is offered]. Taking again: "Suvaḥ svāhā"—to Sūrya, this [is offered].

Taking it up again, he offers the oblations (*balis*) in a sprinkled area, facing either east or north, with the formula: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā; this for Prajāpati. There is no formal renunciation (*tyāga*) regarding the oblations. This applies to all oblations.

Then, having sprinkled the offerings and washed his hands, he consecrates the food with the mantra beginning "O Lord of Food," for which Agni is the deity, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, and its application is in the consecration of food: "Oṃ annapate 'nnasya no... catuṣpade. Then, taking water in the measure of a māṣa with his hand shaped like a cow's ear, [he recites] the mantras of the first section beginning with "In faith, O Prāṇa," for which the deities are the sacrificial ones, the Upaniṣads, and the meters are the Yajus formulas such as Prāṇa and the rest.

The application (*viniyoga*) is the contemplation of the union of the self with the Supreme Self: "Oṃ, [I unite] myself with faith in the *prāṇa*, [I unite] myself with faith in the *apāna*, for the sake of immortality. Having thus contemplated the self as united with the Supreme Self, regarding the mantra "Thou art the under-layer of nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇamasi*), the deities are those of the sacrificial formulas (*yājñikyaḥ*), the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), and the water is the *yajus* formula. The application is in the drinking of water: "Oṃ, thou art the under-layer of nectar"—with this, he drinks water first.

Then, for the mantras of the second section beginning with "In faith, in breath," the deities are those of the sacrificial ritual, the Upanishads are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and the *yajus* formula is as follows: its application is in the fire-offering (*ātma-homa*) performed within oneself—"Oṃ, in faith, in breath, [may Śiva establish me]; to the breath, Svāhā!"—with this, one offers a single oblation into the mouth from the food served on the ring finger, middle finger, and thumb, which has been soaked in ghee.

With the middle finger, ring finger, and thumb, one offers the second oblation with the mantra: *śraddhāyām apāne*. Likewise, with the little finger, ring finger, and thumb, one offers the third oblation with the mantra: *śraddhāyāṃ vyāne*. With the ring finger, middle finger, and thumb—excluding the index finger—or alternatively, with the little finger, index finger, and thumb, one offers the fourth oblation in the same manner with the mantra: *śraddhāyām udāne*. With all the fingers, one offers the fifth oblation with the mantra: *śraddhāyāṃ samāne*. Regarding the act of relinquishing [the offering], there is an option.
Alternatively, all oblations may be offered with the hand from which the little finger has been released.

Then, meditating upon Prajāpati in his mind, he should offer an oblation once more silently. This oblation must be performed in silence by one who does not perceive the taste of the food and does not touch it with his teeth. From this point onward, there is no restriction regarding silence. For one whose father is living, there is absolutely no silence after the offering to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*). In the event of a lapse in silence, one should remember Viṣṇu.

Then, having placed the food vessel upon a stand and having had someone remove the four offerings (*bali*) that were given, or, if that is impossible, having covered them; having placed his feet on the ground and holding the food vessel with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger of his left hand, he should eat with five parts moistened and with his hair loose. Having sprinkled a small portion of food with the *gāyatrī* mantra and set it aside separately in some place, he should not take any other food until he has eaten that. At the conclusion of the meal, he should eat that [set-aside portion].

One should not touch food with the left hand. One should not touch one's feet, head, or bladder. One should not touch the food vessel with the foot. One should not take up used clarified butter (*ājya*) or liquid substances. One should not eat with fingers spread apart.

One should not eat while making a hissing sound with the breath; nor when one has indigestion, nor when one is excessively hungry; nor in large quantities; nor while wearing wet clothes, nor with a wet head; nor in a temple; nor with legs outstretched, nor with the head wrapped; nor making noise; nor with the vessel placed on one's lap; nor with food remaining from a previous mouthful; nor while many people are eating; nor in haste; nor while reciting the Veda; nor together with one's wife; nor in a broken vessel; nor on the ground; nor on the palm of the hand; nor while the sounds of oil-presses, frying-pans, mortars, or grinding-machines are occurring.

If one should eat [forbidden food], one should perform three *prāṇāyāmas* and recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times. One must never drink water that has been drawn up, drunk from, and left over;

if one should drink it, then one must perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. After the *prāṇāhutis*, if the water vessel is not placed on the right side, there shall be three *prāṇāyāmas* and the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times.

One should not consume even a single mouthful of food while listening to the words of a Caṇḍāla, an outcaste, or a woman in her menses; if one should so eat, one must fast for one day. At the time of drinking water, if water should fall from the mouth into the eating vessel, one must not eat that food; if one should so eat, one must perform a thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī.
A *brahmacārī* (celibate student) should eat food—excluding beans, mung beans, alkali, salt, and the like—from a vessel other than one made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*).

Regarding the rule for eating from copper, lotus leaves, or *palāśa* leaves found in another *smṛti*, some maintain that it refers to persons other than householders; others say this rule pertains specifically to *śrāddha* rites; and still others hold that it concerns the *brahmacārī*.

In this context, the rule for eating from a *palāśa* leaf refers to leaves other than those from a creeper-vine (*vallī*), because another *smṛti* prohibits eating from a vine-leaf, stating: "One should not eat from a vine-leaf. The same determination applies to *pittala* (brass), which is similar to copper.

Eating from the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, or *arka* trees, from a leaf with a tip on it, from a *kadali* leaf, from the middle leaf of a *palāśa*, from the hand, from a bowl (*kharparaka*), or from a stone is forbidden for everyone. In cases other than times of distress (*anāpadi*), one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *gāyatrī* mantra one hundred times after eating; in times of distress (*āpadi*), ten times. During the three-day vow (*tryahavrata*) alone, there is the avoidance of *māṣa*, *mudga*, alkaline substances, salt, and so forth; beyond that, however, there is an option. For one whose father is living, the holding of the vessel lasts only until the offering of the breath-oblations (*prāṇāhuti*), but not thereafter. Some say this applies to everyone; many hold that for those whose fathers are deceased, the vessel must be held as long as the meal continues.

At the time of drinking water, holding the bowl with the right hand and taking up the vessel containing the water with the left hand, one should touch that bowl to the right wrist and drink from it using the left hand alone. Some, however, say that one should hold it with the left hand and drink from it with the right hand.
Then, taking all the food remaining from the meal:
"To those embodied beings submerged in Raurava and other hells who long for food..."
"May this food given for the sake of satisfaction remain inexhaustible."

Having thus given the leftover food to those entitled to receive the remnants, [one says]: "May this water, offered to the needy who dwell in the Raurava hell— the abode of pus— amidst millions of lotuses, become inexhaustible."
Thus, one should pour water over the food. Some say this applies even to one whose father is living; others say it does not.

Then, for the mantra "amṛtāpidhānam asi," there is the Yajurvedic formula consisting of six syllables. Its application is for drinking water: having drunk the water with "Oṃ amṛtāpidhānam asi," one should rise.

If, among those seated in a single row, anyone should rise first while others are still eating—whether out of atheism or negligence—the remaining food in the vessel should be discarded. In cases of difficulty, the row should be divided by means of fire, ashes, *darbha* grass, water, or by creating a physical barrier at the doorway.

If salt remains in the food vessel, one should rinse that vessel with water using the left hand without touching it. If one does not rinse it, then one must perform three *prāṇāyāmas* and the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times. After the *uttarāpośana* (the final sipping of water), if one touches the food vessel, there must be a bath and *prāṇāyāma*.

Then, having removed the food vessel and performed the washing of the hands—beginning first with a single mouthful of water—he should wash his hands and face with the fingers excluding the index finger until all traces of oil have disappeared; then, removing whatever remnants stuck to the teeth until they come out without any blood appearing, he should take sixteen mouthfuls of water, wash his face and feet, perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) twice, smear the ground (or, in its absence, smear it himself), wash his hands and feet again, sip water twice more, and touch the ground after performing the ritual sipping twice.

For the mantra *prāṇānāṃ granthiḥ*, the Yājñikas, the Ṣaḍas, the Ātman, and the Yajus are the authorities. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the touching of the heart: "Oṃ prāṇānāṃ granthiḥ... pyāyasva. With this, he touches his heart. Then, having sipped water again, for the mantra *aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣaḥ*, the Yājñika deities, the Upaniṣads, the Paramātman, and the Anuṣṭubh are the authorities. Its application is for pouring out the water from the right hand onto the big toe of the right foot: "Oṃ aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ pu... bhuk. With this, he pours out his right hand onto the big toe of his right foot.

The Upanishadic portion of the *yajus* for the mantras beginning with "Having entered into faith and breath" has the sacrifice as its essence. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the consecration of the oblation (*hutānumantraṇa*). With the mantra: "Oṃ! Having entered into faith and breath, the immortal oblation is offered; swell the breath with food. [Oṃ! Having entered into faith and breath,] swell equally with food," one should perform the consecration of the oblation with the hands raised upward.

The *ātman* of the mantra "brahmaṇi me" is the Yājñikya Upaniṣad; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of uniting the self with one's own [nature]: "Oṃ, may my self be in Brahman for the sake of immortality. Thus, one should unite the self within oneself. "Self" here refers to one's own heart.

If one is unable to perform this much, then having performed the consecration of the food (*annābhimantraṇa*), one should drink water while reciting: "Oṃ, you are the nectar... (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*).

"Oṃ, svāhā to Prāṇa! Oṃ, svāhā to Apāna! Oṃ, svāhā to Vyāna! Oṃ, svāhā to Udāna! Oṃ, svāhā to Samāna! Having offered oblations with these very mantras as before, all [rituals] such as the removal of the *bali* offering are performed as previously described. At the end of the meal, one should drink water alone with the mantra "Thou art the covering of immortality" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*), and no other collection of ritual acts accompanied by mantras. This is the rule for when one is unable [to perform the full rite].

Then, regarding the mantras beginning with *vāṅ ma āsan*, the Upaniṣads pertaining to the ritual (*yājñikya upaniṣadaḥ*)—namely, the *Yajus* formulas concerning speech and the other [senses]—are applied to the touching of speech and so forth. The application (*viniyoga*) is as follows: With the mantra "Oṃ, may speech be in my mouth," he touches the mouth. With "Oṃ, breath in the nostrils," he touches both nostrils simultaneously and only once, due to the indicative mark of the dual number in the mantra. With "Oṃ, sight in the eyes," he touches the two eyes in the same manner. With "Oṃ, hearing in the ears," he touches the ears. With "Oṃ, strength in the arms," he touches the two arms. With "Oṃ, vigor in the thighs," he touches the two thighs.

For the parts ending with the arms, [he should touch] them in order with the right hand; for the two thighs, with the left hand alone; and for the mouth and other parts, with the right and left hands as appropriate. Even in these cases, because of the dual number [in the mantras], the mantra is recited only once. With the mantra "ariṣṭā...," he touches all the limbs; the mantra is recited only once.

For the verse "vayaḥ suparṇā...," the Upaniṣads belonging to the sacrificial tradition state that the *suparṇā* verses are in the *triṣṭubh* meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for wiping the eyes. Reciting "Oṃ vayaḥ suparṇā... baddhān," he should wipe his eyes: with the thumb the right eye, and with the ring finger the left.

Regarding the mantra *namo rudrāya*: the seers are the Yājñikyas and the Devas; the deities are Rudra and Viṣṇu; the metre is Yajus. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of worship (*upasthāna*). With the words, "Oṃ namo ru... pāhi," one worships Rudra and Viṣṇu. Regarding the mantra *tvamagne dyubhiḥ*: the seers are the Yājñikyas and the Upaniṣads; the deity is Agni; the metre is Triṣṭubh. Its application is for the worship of the fire for the purpose of cooking food. With the words, "Oṃ tvamagne dyubhiḥ śuciḥ," one worships the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*). Regarding the mantra *śivena me*: the seers are the Yājñikyas and the Upaniṣads; the deity is Agni; the metre is Triṣṭubh. Its application is for making a prayer (*prārthana*). With the words, "Oṃ śivena...", one should pray.

Regarding the placement of vegetables and other items during the serving, Jātūkarṇya states in the *Smṛtiratnākara*: "Vegetables and the like should be placed in front; solid foods and soft foods on the left; rice should be placed in the middle, and ghee with milk-rice on the right."
"But one should place the soup on top of the latter half of the rice.
Here, *sūpaka* means *sūpa* (soup); the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the base word itself.
Jātūkarṇya states the expiation for the non-performance of the offering of the *bali*:
"A Brahmin who eats without having performed the *citrabali* when not in a state of distress shall perform three *prāṇāyāmas* and recite the *gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times. Thus,
at the beginning of a meal, one must set aside a portion of food for the *bali* before eating.

"But he who eats without having set aside [the portion], shall perform eight *prāṇāyāmas*. By the use of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the word "having set aside" (*samuddhārya*), it is understood that the setting aside is performed by another agent, not by oneself.
Saṃvarta states the expiation for failing to perform the *āpośāna*:
"If a twice-born man eats without having performed the *apośāna* rite when not in an emergency,
or if he should speak while eating, he should mutter the *gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times. Here, "one hundred and eight" means one hundred plus eight.
Regarding mutual touch during a meal, the *Smṛtisāra* states: "If a Brāhmaṇa should touch another Brāhmaṇa at the time of eating,
he must leave that food, rise, and perform three *prāṇāyāmas*."
In the *Prayogadarpaṇa*, however, another Smṛti states:
"If a Brāhmaṇa should touch another Brāhmaṇa at the time of eating,
he should eat that food without discarding it and recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times."
Regarding eating without the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), Laghuhārīta states: "If a Brāhmaṇa eats without the sacred thread,
he becomes pure by bathing, performing recitation (*japa*), and fasting."
The recitation of the Gāyatrī; and this [is required] when one knows [the rule]. But when one does not know it—"If a Brāhmaṇa eats without his sacred thread (brahmasūtra) out of ignorance..."

"One is purified by eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī and by breath control (prāṇāyāma)"—this statement of Saṃvarta should be observed. "Eight thousand" means one thousand and eight. (In another Smṛti:)
If one eats food and other items produced in a field of indigo, the penance is the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Regarding food and other items that are given after one has worn indigo, the penance for both the giver and the eater is the Sāntapana.
As for what Śaṅkha says:
"One who has put on indigo-dyed clothing should bathe after eating"— this refers to a case of ignorance. In another Smṛti:
"In the case of woolen cloth and silk thread, the defect caused by indigo does not exist. In another Smṛti:

"If one rises without having sipped water after eating, one must bathe immediately; if one eats food defiled by bone, one must consume clarified butter; likewise if a tooth falls out, or if the mouth is defiled by blood and such, for three nights; and having consumed oil that is the leavings of a lamp or the leavings of anointing oil, one should observe a fast during the night."
Regarding the discharge of semen, urine, or feces during the time of eating, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"If the discharge of semen, urine, or feces occurs through negligence,
then purification must first be performed with water and joy."

"Afterwards, having sipped water (ācamana), the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn should be recited while in the water. This refers to a case where the morsel has not been swallowed. However, regarding a case where it has been swallowed once, Āpastamba states: "If, while a Brahmin is eating, his anus should occasionally discharge [feces]..."
"How can there be atonement for impurity caused by being left-over food?
Having first performed purification, one should thereafter sip water;
having fasted for a day and night, one becomes pure through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
As for that which Śātātapa says: "If, out of delusion, one eats or drinks after having discharged urine or feces,
one should then perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for three nights."

Regarding the consumption of more than that [quantity]: after the phrase "for three nights," the word "fasting" (*upoṣaṇam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Discharge of feces" (*viḍutsargaḥ*) means the voiding of excrement.
Regarding impurity at the time of eating, Śātātapa says:
"Now, if a twice-born man becomes impure at the time of eating..."
"Having cast that morsel on the ground and bathed, a Brahmin becomes pure;
but having swallowed that morsel, he becomes pure after a day and night;
having eaten all the food, however, he becomes pure after three nights."
All of this is to be understood as occurring after the offering of the vital breath (*prāṇāhuti*).

Regarding the consumption of forbidden food, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states: "If one should give what is fit to be eaten under the pretext that it is unfit to be eaten, out of a sense of duty toward a guest..."
"One must not eat even from a guru if it is defiled by speech, except in a great emergency.
Regarding this expiation, Gautama says, beginning with the topic of food defiled by speech and so forth: "Vomiting and the consumption of clarified butter."
And this refers to cases where it is done unintentionally;
however, Śaṅkha states regarding intentional acts: "That which is corrupted by speech, that which is corrupted by intention, and that which is in a vessel corrupted by intention..."
"Having eaten food, a twice-born man should thereafter observe a vow for three nights. (In this context, the "vow" refers to subsisting on *yāvaka* [barley gruel]. Saṃvarta states:
"Food contaminated by hair or insects, or tainted by indigo or lac..."

"Having consumed [food] mixed with sinews, bones, and skin, one should fast for a day. This refers to an occasion of distress when done unintentionally. However, regarding intentional consumption when not in a state of distress, Śaṅkha says:

"If food is defiled by hair or insects, or likewise by cats, mice, flies, or sparrows, one should observe a vow for three nights. Regarding repeated intentional acts, Pracetas says, beginning with the discussion of "defiled insects": [text follows].
"If food should be defiled by these [birds] such as crows and others, having eaten that food intentionally, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance;
if unintentionally, half [of it]."
As for what Viṣṇu has said:
"Having eaten [food] that is untouchable, or likewise defiled by insects, hair, or the like,
one should [purify it] with kuśa grass, udumbara, bilva, and so forth, as well as with jackfruit and lotus leaves."

"Having drunk a decoction of *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *suvarcā*, and so forth, one becomes purified. This refers to cases of incapacity due to an emergency. Regarding the falling of hair, insects, and the like into prepared food, Pracetas says:
"If food at the time of eating is defiled by flies or hair, one should immediately touch it with water; that food should then be touched with ashes.
Thus it is stated in the Brāhma [Purāṇa] as well.

[Water] defiled by Caṇḍālas, outcasts, impure things, those with bad nails, lepers, as well as by those who have killed a Brahmin, women in childbirth, menstruating women, dog-keepers, and their families;
or [water] that has been left overnight, or contaminated by hair and insects— [should be purified] with earth, ashes, gold, and water.
"One should eat what is pure if it has been inspected by the virtuous, but that which is defiled is indeed impure.

*Kauleyaka* means a dog. *Kuṭumbī* is a specific type of insect. *Vyuṣṭa* means stale. "One should avoid even pure food that has been defiled by flies, worms, or small creatures, or even by hair, body hair, and nails.
Regarding this, Yama states an exception in certain cases:
"In a temple courtyard, at weddings, and during sacrifices that have been commenced,
one should not discard food touched by crows or dogs;
having removed only that portion of the food, the remainder deserves purification."
"Purification of liquids occurs through sprinkling with ghee;
purification of water and ghee occurs through intense heating and contact with fire;
and that which has been touched by the mouth of a goat indeed becomes pure."
Saṃvarta states: "Having eaten from the vessel of Śūdras, or from a broken vessel,
one becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow."
A broken vessel refers specifically to one made of bell-metal (kāṃsya)—
according to the traditional teaching of Devala: "The breaking or even the non-breaking of vessels made of copper, silver, gold, stone, conch, or crystal [is a cause for impurity]."

Furthermore, according to the statement of Baudhāyana: "But the twice-born who eats from a cracked bronze vessel should bathe in a river and recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times while eating only one meal; then he becomes pure.
This [penance] applies when the act is done intentionally, whereas that stated by Saṃvarta concerns cases of ignorance.
As for that which Parāśara states:
"If a preeminent twice-born man eats from a broken vessel out of ignorance,
he becomes pure by consuming ghee that has been touched by water containing gold."

Thus, it should be understood that this refers to the same subject matter as the statement of Saṃvarta. In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, it is stated that if dust is seen while food is being served, the food touched by it must be discarded; the same applies if it is touched by a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, or others. Regarding spitting while eating, the *Saṃgraha* states:
"If anyone should happen to sneeze while in the midst of a meal,
they should sprinkle their head with water and remember the Sun and their place of birth.
Thus ends the rule for eating.

Now, the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-abhyādhāna*), known as the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), is described. Regarding this, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* states: "At both times, or only in the evening, he places the fuel-sticks. Before the sprinkling of water, having wiped the fire clockwise with the mantra, 'As the Vasus [wiped] Gaurī,' he sprinkles water around it as before. He places the fuel-sticks with the *Vyāhṛtis*, both individually and collectively: 'This is thy fuel, O Agni; through it mayest thou increase and swell; and may we increase and swell, Svāhā! May Indra grant me wisdom... [and] two garlands, Svāhā! "

"And [he offers] with 'May the Apsarases be pleased with me, svāhā! and 'May wisdom be pleased with me, svāhā! Having wiped around in that same manner, he sprinkles water around as before, and worships with the verses beginning "That splendor of yours, O Agni... and also with "In me be wisdom, in me be progeny."

The meaning of this is as follows: one places fuel-sticks (*samidh*) on the fire at both times—morning and evening—or at evening alone, until the *samāvartana* ceremony. From the rule "every day a bundle of wood," the phrase "every day" (*aharahar*) must be understood as carrying over [from that context]. Otherwise, repetition would apply only to the option of placing fuel-sticks in the evening, because the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is heard [only] there. It would not apply in the case of "at both times," because the distributive repetition is not heard there. Nor should it be argued that the mention of the distributive repetition in the phrase "in the evening" (*sāyam*) is therefore redundant.

This is because it serves to establish the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "in all cases, whichever position was first commenced must be maintained until the end. Nor is the matter established by the statement "but [the order] is restricted by the commencement," for that statement refers specifically to the *anunirvāpya* offerings.

Alternatively, one might argue that the word "daily" (*aharahar*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], and that repetition should apply only to the phrase "in the evening" (*sāyam*), since repetition is explicitly heard there; thus, in the view that both times are prescribed, repetition would not occur because it is not explicitly heard for that case. This should not be said, because when repetition is established by the distributive particle (*vīpsā*) in the alternative case (*anukalpa*), its establishment in the primary case (*mukhyakalpa*) follows by the logic of *kaimutika* (how much more so). In this interpretation, the accepted position is established by the very statement: "But by the initial undertaking, the rule is restricted."

Prior to the sprinkling [of water], as previously described, he sprinkles around the fire-altar clockwise with his hand holding water, using the mantra "As the Vasus [did] for Gaurī"; this means according to the method of the initial sprinkling mentioned in the section on the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

Having placed eight fuel-sticks (samidh) upon the fire—four by placing them one by one with each of the *vyāhṛtis* individually and all together, and four more with the four verses beginning with "eṣā te"—he then wipes [the fire] in the same manner as described for the initiation ceremony, sprinkling water around it according to the procedure for the subsequent sprinkling (*uttara-pariṣeka*).
Then he worships that fire with the three mantras beginning with "yatte agne," and with these three: "mayi medhām, mayi prajām, mayyagniḥ."

The statement "prior to the sprinkling" (*purastāt pariṣecanāt*) is intended for the purpose of sprinkling in all Śrauta rites, in *darvihoma* offerings, in the internal initiation (*abhyantaradīkṣā*), in the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), and so forth. The statement "he sprinkles in front" (*agre pariṣiñcati*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the connection between the wiping (*parimārjana*) and the sprinkling (*pariṣeka*). By this, the wiping is also established in the rites mentioned immediately above.

Since the sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) is established as being accompanied by mantras simply through the restatement of what is already known in the phrase "prior to the sprinkling" (*purastāt pariṣecanāt*), the specific mention of "as before" (*yathā purastāt*) is for the purpose of indicating that the sprinkling here is with mantras, whereas elsewhere it is silent (*tūṣṇīm*), and also for the sake of restriction (*parisaṃkhyāna*). Consequently, the preparation of the fire-altar (*agnyāyatana-saṃskāra*) and the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) do not take place. Furthermore, since the subsequent sprinkling is already implied by its connection with the preceding sprinkling, the repetition of the rule indicates that this subsequent sprinkling is specifically one preceded by mantras.

But this is not the case even when there is no prior sprinkling (*pūrva-pariṣeka*) accompanied by mantras. Therefore, in rites other than the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*), there is no subsequent sprinkling (*uttara-pariṣeka*). Alternatively, the statement "from the sprinkling in front" (*purastāt pariṣecanāt*) is a restatement of what is already established, intended to introduce the *tantra* (the ritual framework) beginning with the digging out (*uddhanana*). Furthermore, the statement "he sprinkles again in front" is for the purpose of showing that the prior sprinkling itself serves as the limit for the preceding *tantra*. Later on, the statement "having wiped it around in the same way, he sprinkles as before" is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyāna*). By this, the other [ritual] *tantra* is excluded.

Alternatively, the statement "before the sprinkling" (purastāt pariṣecanāt) is intended to show that here only those preparatory acts for the locus which are similar to the sprinkling—namely, those consisting of the preparation of the fire-altar and the strewing of grass—are performed, and no others. The statement "he sprinkles in front" (agre pariṣiñcati) is intended to show that only those preparatory acts for the locus ending with the sprinkling are to be performed, and not the subsequent ones such as the placing of the fuel (idhmādhāna), even though they are of a similar nature. As for the purpose of the phrase "as before" (yathā purastāt), it is exactly as explained previously.

The mention of "clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇa*) in the context of wiping is for the purpose of indicating that the wiping is performed with a single effort, rather than by separating the action to wipe in various directions.

This is understood precisely from the dual expression "each individually and collectively"; when only the *vyāhṛtis* are mentioned, the *vyāhṛtis* should be understood as either separate or combined, but not as both separate and combined simultaneously.

Having wiped [the fire], one should place fuel sticks upon it in the evening and in the morning according to the instruction; "the worship of the fire is only in the evening," according to some—this statement in the *Dharmasūtra* is for the purpose of excluding the sprinkling [of water]. Therefore, because it is both prescribed and prohibited, there is an option.

And since the morning time has passed, this must be performed starting from the evening until the completion of the student's studies (*samāvartana*), either every day at both times or only in the evening.

Nor should it be argued that, in the case where both [rites] are treated as a single performance (*kriyāpakṣa*), the commencement must take place on the morning of the second day, just as in the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice; for there is no authority for abandoning the evening time that has already arrived, nor is there any authority supporting a morning commencement as in the *vaiśvadeva*. In the *vaiśvadeva*, however, the very fact that the word "day" (*divā*) is placed first within the pair of words "day and night" (*divānakta*)—which denote the morning and evening times respectively—in the mantra "Those beings who roam by day and by night," serves as the authority for a morning commencement.
But here, no such authority is found.
Yājñavalkya states that the period for the secondary performance of the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*)—which was not performed after the morning twilight (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*)—lasts until one has eaten:
"Having performed the fire-ritual, being restrained in speech, one should eat with the permission of the teacher.
Regarding the specific rules for gathering fuel-sticks (*samidh*) for the purpose of the fire-ritual, the *Dharmasūtra* says:
"One should always fetch fuel from the forest and place it below; one should not go out to fetch fuel after the sun has set.

This means that one should fetch wood—logs—for the purpose of adding fuel to one's own fire every day. Once fetched, they should be placed below. Ujjvalākāra explained that one should not go to fetch fuel when the sun has set because of the possibility of encountering thieves, tigers, and other dangers.
Another specific detail has been stated by Baijavāpa:

"Before sunset, having gone toward the north-eastern direction, one should fetch fuel-sticks from the forest without harming them—dry sticks for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), moist ones for one desiring food, and both kinds for one desiring both.
"Without harming" means without cutting; it should be understood that in the absence [of uncut wood], one may cut them as well.
The rule regarding fuel-sticks is stated in the *Vāyavīya*:
"The fuel-sticks should be made of *pālāśa* wood, or of *khadira* if those are unavailable; or of *śamī*, *rohitaka*, or *aśvattha*; and in the absence of these, of *arka* or *vetasa*."

The *rohitaka* is a sub-species of the banyan tree (*vaṭa*). The suffix *-ac* is added in the sense of possession because it has the color *rohita* (red), and the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the base itself; thus, *rohītaka*—even with a long vowel—is synonymous with this very meaning.
Kātyāyana states the definition of the fuel-stick (*samidh*): "The fuel-stick should never be made thicker than the thumb."
It was not stripped of its bark, nor infested with insects, nor torn asunder.
"A wise person should not, in the fire-oblations, use fuel-sticks that are longer than a span, nor shorter, nor having two branches, nor with leaves attached, nor lacking potency."

The rule "not more nor less than a span" (*prādeśāt*) does not apply to the matter of the fuel-sticks (*samit*) prescribed in the Sūtra, because otherwise the specification of "being exactly a span long" regarding the fuel-sticks mentioned in that very Sūtra would become redundant. However, it should be understood that with respect to fuel-sticks mentioned in other scriptures, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*):

Having performed the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*) according to the aforementioned method, having sipped water (*ācamana*), and having restrained the breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), one should announce the place and time, make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) saying, "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (*Śrīparameśvara*), I shall perform the evening fire-rite (*sāyamagnikārya*)," kindle the fire, set it ablaze, and meditate upon it.

The fire-rituals (*agnikārya*) that follow the collective conclusion of the initiation (*upanayana*) must be performed using only the ordinary worldly fire (*laukika-agni*) brought from the house of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).

However, according to the view that the initiation fire itself becomes the marriage fire (*vivāha-agni*), the fire-ritual is to be performed in that very same fire. The marriage oblation (*vivāha-homa*) is also performed there; the distinction is that the requirement for establishing the status of the fire as the *aupāsana* (domestic) fire is omitted. Regarding the fire-ritual therein, there is an option between performing the consecration of the fire-pit (*agnyāyatana-saṃskāra*) and the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*). In the case where the rites of scraping (*ullekhana*), sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*), and pouring water (*utsecanakaraṇa*) are performed, one should prepare the site, establish the ordinary fire upon it, and then perform the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) therein.

Then, for the verse beginning "yathā ha tad vasavaḥ," the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Agni, and the metre is Triṣṭubh. Its application is in the sweeping around [the fire]: "Oṃ yathā ha tad va... āyuḥ. With his hand moistened with water, he should sweep around the fire clockwise.

Then, having performed the sprinkling with the verses beginning with "adite," he himself goes toward the north before sunset—or, if that is impossible, toward any direction whatsoever—and having cut [the wood] himself, or, if unable, having had another cut it, he takes eight Palāśa fuel-sticks (samidh) brought [to him] and placed on the ground below; these he sprinkles with pure water. [The seers and deities are as follows: Agni is the seer (ṛṣi) of the individual Vyāhṛtis; Prajāpati is the seer of the collective Vyāhṛtis; and Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati are respectively the deities of the four [Vyāhṛtis].

The *gāyatrī*, *uṣṇih*, *anuṣṭubh*, and *bṛhatī* are, respectively, the four meters (*chandas*). Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samid-abhyādhāna*): with the four [verses]—"Oṃ bhūḥ," "Oṃ bhuvaḥ," "Oṃ suvaḥ," and "Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ"—one places four fuel-sticks. Since there is no injunction for an oblation (*juhoti-codanā*), the exclamation *svāhā* is not used;
however, some do desire the use of *svāhā*. In that case, the renunciations (*tyāga*) are: "To Agni, this... "To Vāyu, this... "To Sūrya, this... "To Prajāpati, this..."

‘Oṃ eṣā te agne... mahi svāhā’—to Agni, this [offering]. “Oṃ medhāṃ ma indro... srajau svāhā”—to Indra, Sarasvatī, and the two Aśvins, this [offering]. ‘Oṃ apsarāsu ca yā... daivīṃ... ṣatā svāhā’—to Medhā, this [offering]. For the mantra beginning with ‘ā māṃ medhā surabhiḥ’, the Yājñikya-Upaniṣads state that Medhā is the deity and Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application is in the placing of the fuel-stick (samid-abhyādhāna): “Oṃ ā māṃ medhā juṣantāṃ svāhā”—to Medhā, this [offering]. With these four mantras, he places four fuel-sticks. The utterance of ‘svāhā’ in these cases is because it has been prescribed by the author of the Sūtra.

Then, having swept around as before with the mantra "Adite 'nvamasthāḥ" and so forth, and having performed the subsequent sprinkling, he should discard the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa) if they were present.

The three mantras beginning with *yatte agne tejaḥ* have Agni as their deity, are in the *dvipadā gāyatrī* meter; the three mantras beginning with *mayi medhām* have Agni as their deity, are in the *dvipadā gāyatrī* meter. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for the ritual of worship (*upasthāna*). One worships Agni with these: *oṃ yatte agne tejaḥ... yāsam*, *yatte agne varcaste...*, *yatte agne haraste...*, *mayi me... yagnistejo...* (from *mayi medhām*), *mayi medhām... mayīndra indriyaṃ dadhātu*, and *mayi medhām... mayi sūryo bhrāja...*. The application of the final two mantras, *mayi medhām*, follows the principle of the *aindrī* [mantras].

Then, having taken up ashes and worshipped the fire, having prayed to the fire with the mantra "Śraddhām medhām," having remembered Viṣṇu with the mantra "Pramādāt," he should dedicate the rite to the Lord of Action (Karmeśvara).

In this manner, having performed the morning twilight ritual (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*) according to the procedure stated above, he should perform the morning fire-rite (*prātar-agnikārya*) just as the evening fire-rite was performed. In that regard, the specific difference lies in the formula of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), which should be: "I shall perform the morning fire-rite. Thus ends the fire-rite.

Then, in the manner previously described, one should perform the salutation and respectful greeting of those situated nearby, such as one's father, mother, and others. Among these, the formal greeting (*abhivādana*) should be performed only toward those who know how to return it; however, for those who do not know it, a mere salutation (*namaskriyā*) is sufficient. In an assembly hall, a sacrificial shed, or a temple, one should salute all [deities] simultaneously, rather than individually.

One should not salute, nor offer obeisance to, one who is insane, impure, running, yawning, vomiting, brushing his teeth, having oil applied to his head, performing a ritual bath, chanting, or engaged in sacrificial rites and the like; nor to one standing in water, carrying sacrificial fuel, flowers, or *kuśa* grass; nor to a heretic, a eunuch, a rogue, one guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*), an atheist, one who has lost caste (*vrātya*), an outcast, a gambler, or an ungrateful person. If, through negligence, one should nevertheless perform such acts, one must recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times and perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).

Upon greeting a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, one becomes pure by greeting ten or eight Brāhmaṇas. Upon greeting a Śūdra, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on and greeting one hundred Brāhmaṇas. In an assembly hall, a sacrificial shed, or a royal palace, one should merely offer a salutation (*namaskāra*); there is no formal greeting (*abhivādana*). Those who are menstruating, women recently delivered, a woman who has killed her husband, and a woman who has caused an abortion are not to be greeted. For greeting these women, one must observe a fast. If one is oneself young, then for young wives of elders, one should perform the greeting upon the ground.

Even among officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), only those who are older in age are to be saluted; the same applies to fathers-in-law, maternal uncles, paternal uncles, and others. However, for the sake of pleasing those who are younger, one should face them and address them. Furthermore, that address should be with the word "kuśala" (well-being) toward a Brāhmaṇa, with the word "anāmaya" (health) toward a Kṣatriya, with the word "kṣema" (prosperity) toward a Vaiśya, and with the word "ārogya" (freedom from disease) toward a Śūdra.

One should offer blessings such as "May it be well with you" to Brahmins younger than oneself, as well as to Kṣatriyas and others. The formal return-greeting (*pratyabhivādana*) must also be performed toward a Śūdra, because of the exclusion [of Śūdras] in Pāṇini’s sūtra: "In the case of a return-greeting, except for a Śūdra. If one does not perform a salutation upon seeing an image of a deity or a Tridaṇḍin ascetic, then there shall be a fast for one night. However, at the conclusion of the *saṃdhyā* prayers, one must indeed salute everyone who is younger than oneself—except for a disciple, a son, a daughter's son, and a daughter's husband.
The source of this is clear in the original treatises (*ākara*).
Now, as a related topic, the expiation for the loss of the *upanayana* fire is stated.

The teacher, having announced the place and time, makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the expiation for the following of the *upanayana* fire. Having performed the consecration of the site through tracing lines and other rites, he establishes there either a fire churned from wood or a common worldly fire brought from the house of a learned *śrotriya*. Having kindled it, strewn grass around it, silently wiped it, sprinkled water around it, and adorned it, he should fast until sunset if the fire was lost in the morning; if the fire was lost in the evening, he should fast until sunrise.

Then, having consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*), added fuel (*samidh*) to the fire, and performed the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation, one should mutter the *anājñāta* and other mantras. If the fire goes out before the addition of fuel, then at the conclusion of the fast, after performing the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation and the recitation of the *anājñāta* and other mantras, one should perform both the missed addition of fuel and the one required by the current time in a single ritual sequence (*tantra*). However, if the fire goes out after the addition of fuel, one should perform only the one required by the current time. In the event of being unable to observe the fast, one should offer a single oblation of clarified butter with the mantra "ayāścāgne."

In this matter, the procedure is according to the *Āpūrvika-tantra*. Having announced the place and time, and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) "I shall perform the expiation for following the fire," one should perform the rites from the drawing of lines (*ullekhana*) up to the installation of the fire (*agni-pratiṣṭhāpana*), and then meditate [on the fire] with the verse beginning "Four are the horns" (*catvāri śṛṅgā*). Here, the fire is named Viṣṇu.

Then, having taken up the sacrificial fuel (samidh) along with the fire-drill (mitra), and having performed the rites beginning with "Come, O Śraddhā" up to the end of the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), he should place the fuel-sticks for the *anvādhāna* into the fire, saying: "In this rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of following the fire of initiation (*upanayana*), I shall encompass those deities who are to be worshipped; I shall worship Agni Ayāsya with one oblation of clarified butter; I shall worship this deity immediately. Alternatively, there may be no *anvādhāna* at all.

Then, having strewn grass around the fire, and having placed the wooden ladle (*darvī*), the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), the *saṃmārga* blades of grass, the *avajvalana* blades of grass, the clarified butter, and a single fuel-stick (*samit*) nearby; having prepared the two strainers (*pavitre*), consecrated the sprinkling water, sprinkled the vessels, wiped the ladle, and consecrated the clarified butter; having placed the clarified butter and the ladle on the *darbha* grass behind the fire; having sprinkled water around the fire with mantras and adorned it; and having taken the clarified butter with the ladle, he should offer one oblation with the mantra: "Oṃ ayāścāgne'sya... bheṣaja svāhā. [The dedication is: "To Agni Ayāsya, this..."

Then, having removed the surrounding grass mats (*paristaraṇa*) and offered the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation, one should perform the final sprinkling (*uttarapariṣeka*). According to this view, even if the fire goes out before the placing of the fuel sticks (*samid-ādhāna*), the placing of the fuel sticks must be performed immediately after the *prāyaścitta* oblation. Alternatively, in this case, there is only the *sarvaprāyaścitta*; there is neither the fast nor the oblation "O Agni, come hither" (*āyāhyagne*); thus ends the expiation for the loss of the fire. Now follow the subsidiary rites for the initiation on the fourth day.

The teacher, having performed his daily morning rites, having performed the morning twilight devotion (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*), the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), and the formal greeting (*upasaṃgrahaṇa-abhivādana*) together with the student who has likewise performed these, shall sit facing the east. Having sipped water (*ācamya*) and restrained his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), he shall perform the *trivṛd-annahoma* and the offering of the oblation (*bali*) to the Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstupati*) as before. Then, having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce the *puṇyāha*, *svastyayana*, and *ṛddhi* blessings, he shall say: "May Faith (*śraddhā*) and Intelligence (*medhā*) be pleased."

Then the religious student (brahmacārin), having sipped water (ācamya) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), should perform the worship of the deity (devatopasthāna) as before for the purpose of concluding the vow (vratavisarga). In that rite, in place of the mantra "May I be able to do that; may it be successful for me," the modification of the mantra is: "I have been able to do that; it has been successful for me. Thereafter, he should release the three-day vow (tryahavrata).

Then the preceptor, having performed the worship of the installed deities at that very spot with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), should himself take the bamboo vessel and, accompanied by his wife—who holds the jar of Gaṇapati—and a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), approach the vicinity of the altar. Having sat upon the altar and worshipped Gaṇapati, he should worship the invoked deities with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). There, at the time of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the rites such as the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), the anointing with oil (*tailābhyaṅga*), the offering of fragrant substances, and the bath with warm water are to be performed as before.

Then, after the dismissal of the invited deities (*devatāvisarga*), one should perform the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) and so forth according to the procedure beginning with "The earth, the sky... as before. In that context, the formulaic utterance for this rite of the dismantling of the pavilion (*maṇḍapodvāsana*) is: "O sirs, declare the auspicious day for this rite. The designation of the deity is: "May Faith (*Śraddhā*) and Intelligence (*Medhā*) be pleased."

Then, at the conclusion of the consecration with the mantra "samudrajyeṣṭhā," a family priest or some other venerable person shall untie those branches and that thread; having anointed that thread which encircles the jar with milk and provided it with unbroken rice and betel nuts, he shall place it in the hand of the performer. He, in turn, having shown that thread to his wife, shall deposit it in a chest containing garments and other wealth.

Then, having extinguished the fire and placed those branches and the water used for that bath in a pure spot above the house, one should perform the release (vimocana) in the northeast corner of the canopy over the courtyard. However, if there is a primary pavilion (maṇḍapa), the worship of the deities must be performed by going to each respective location according to the sequence of invocation (āvāhana).

Then, having provided a meal for Brahmins as appropriate, and having given abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to Brahmins of various names and lineages after first honoring them with perfumes and other offerings, he should give a cow or its equivalent in wealth to one respected by the family or to another person worthy of honor, in order to accomplish the completeness of the *upanayana* rite. Then, having recollected Viṣṇu, he should dedicate the act to the Lord of Karma (*karmeśvara*).

Thereafter, the religious student (*brahmacārī*) shall reside in the teacher’s household and perform service agreeable to the teacher. He should observe, according to his ability, the vows previously mentioned, those prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, and those declared in the *Dharma-śāstras*. He should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) in the worldly fire until his formal return home (*samāvartana*).
If the practice of *moṭana* is followed, that too must be performed. That *moṭana* has been described in the *Meru-tantra*:
"Now I shall explain *moṭanaka*, which is the cause for the manifestation of the deity."
The act of cooking should be performed, provided with four kinds of food.
The wife of the lord of practitioners, endowed with conjugal fidelity and other virtues,
having summoned five women who have not yet borne children along with young girls—
One should seat those who are adorned and purified in a single row;
therein, first of all, is the station of Vighnapati, and then that of Baṭuka.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), [one includes] the family deity (*kuladevatā*).
Having worshipped them, one should offer them there into a great vessel (*mahāpātra*) that is pure,
in due order and with double the quantity of honey, clarified butter, sugar, and curd.
One should pour milk into it and place the food offering (naivedya) therein;
then the women should churn it with the hand of a young girl.
While it was being churned by the women, a divine possession occurred;
as that divine possession arose, a fragrant breeze blew.
The deity quickly reveals everything that is in one's mind and becomes propitious;
all undertakings are accomplished even with a hundred *moṭana* [hand-claps].
With twenty nails there shall be marriage, and likewise with fifty, a son; "with twenty nails" means this very thing, and "with fifty" means the attainment of a son.
With eighty one obtains a lost kingdom, and with twenty one obtains wealth.
"One should even mix [the substance] with one hundred and eight [repetitions], though it may be difficult to accomplish;
this is the procedure for Kaumārī, the beloved deity of Kaumārī, as proclaimed."

One should unite [the deity] even with an unattainable task by means of one hundred and eight "crushings" (*moṭana*). The meaning is that one should accomplish even an unattainable task. (Alternatively, the practitioner should unite the desired deity with one hundred and eight "crushings" numbering one hundred and eight; the meaning is that the desired deity of the practitioner shall become [his own]. Or, the maiden (*kaumārikā*) should perform one hundred and eight "crushings"—the remainder being that it is for the sake of obtaining an excellent husband. This rite belongs specifically to Kaumārī, the Mistress of Yoga; such is the meaning.)

Alternatively, "Kaumāryāḥ" means that this rite is proclaimed as being primarily for the maiden (*kaumārī*); the intended meaning is that this ritual does not take place without a maiden. A maiden (*kaumārikā*) should perform this rite directed toward her chosen deity for the sake of obtaining an excellent husband. This rite is proclaimed specifically for the maiden; the sense is that the ritual does not exist without a maiden. She is called *Kaumāry-Īśvarī* because she is described in exactly that manner within her own *Māhātmya*.

The meaning is also that this procedure is performed with reference to that [initiation]. In the same way, if there is a traditional custom (*ācāra*), it should be performed for other sacraments (*saṃskāra*) as well.
Thus ends the section on initiation (*upanayana*) in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.
This concludes the fourth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāraratnamālā* composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of the venerable Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, whose surname is Oko.
Now begins the fifth section.
Here, as an incidental topic, the expiation for eating food from a *saṃskāra* (consecrated offering) is stated.
Regarding this, Aṅgiras says in the *Prāyaścittaviveka*:
"From birth until the performance of the purificatory rites, and during the feeding of the child,
food must not be eaten by those who are not sapindas, especially at the edge of a cremation ground."
Vyāsa states: "O best of the twice-born, if one has eaten after the purificatory rite of the tonsure (caula) has been completed,
or likewise after the birth-rite (jātakarman), he should perform the Sāṃtapana penance."
"But after eating food at other [impure] rites, O best of the twice-born,
one is purified by a restricted diet and fasting when eating from a censurable source."
Niyoga is breath control (prāṇāyāma). Dhaumya said: "In the case of the brahmaudana, the soma sacrifice, and likewise the sīmantonnayana ceremony..."
"Having eaten at a birth-śrāddha or a new-śrāddha, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."

Āpastamba states: "A twice-born man who eats sacrificial food, food from a *navaśrāddha*, food at a social gathering (*saṃgraha*), or food during the first pregnancy of a woman, shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."

*Yajñiya-anna* refers to food connected with the sacrifice. The prohibition against consuming food connected with the sacrifice lasts until the completion of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, or until the offering of the *vapā* (omentum) of the *agnīṣomīya*, or until the purchase of the King Soma. There is no fault, however, if the sacrificer has already designated the substance for the sacrifice at the very time of the commencement. All of this is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*: "The initiated one may eat only upon the conclusion of the *agnīṣomīya*, or when the *vapā* has been offered, or when the King Soma has been purchased; or, as the Brāhmaṇa text says, they may eat from the remainder once it has been designated for the sake of the sacrifice."
*Saṃsthā* means completion. Or, according to the *rājanīti* position, it refers to the contingency when [the soma] has been purchased.
In the *Agniṣṭoma-yājamāna-sūtra*:
"Having assigned what belongs to him for the sake of the sacrifice, they eat from the remainder; they do not eat without having assigned it, prior to the *agnīṣomīya* [offering]."

Of this initiated [sacrificer]. Because of the introduction of that very person in the preceding [text]. Having assigned whatever substance has been prepared for the sake of the sacrifice—having assigned it for the sake of the sacrifice, saying "this much is for the sacrifice from among these"—the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is implied here. Thus, *nirādeśya* means having caused [the sacrificer] to assign, *nirādeśa*, *nirādeśana*, or *nirdeśana*; that is to say, having had the sacrificer designate [the portions]. The meaning is: having had the sacrificer do so, the Brahmins eat from the remainder (*śeṣa*). The rest is clear. *Saṃgraha* means marriage. As for the statement:
"If a twice-born man eats food at any of the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*s)..."

"One should perform the fast and the *niyoga* as an expiation. Thus, the prescription for *niyoga* and fasting in all sacraments beginning with the tonsure (*cūḍā*) should be understood as pertaining to times of distress (*āpad*). Now follows the procedure for the performance of the omitted sacraments.
In that regard, first is the expiation for its omission. On this point, the Smṛti states:
"When the time for the rites has passed, beginning from the laying of the fires (ādhāna) up to the tonsure ceremony (caula)..."
Having thoroughly consecrated the clarified butter with the vyāhṛtis and having offered it, one should perform the ritual actions in their proper sequence.

"If even one of these is omitted, one should perform a *pādakṛcchra* penance; for the *cūḍā* ceremony, it would be half a *kṛcchra*. This has been declared specifically for times of distress (*āpad*).
But in non-distress (*anāpad*), the penance shall be double, and double again, in every case."

Regarding the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires): when the time for any of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), beginning from *garbhādhāna* up to *caula*, has passed—whether all of them or some of them—and there is thus a lapse of the prescribed time, one should prepare clarified butter (*ājya*) and, having offered oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis* individually and then with the *vyāhṛtis* collectively according to the number of rites omitted, one should perform the penance (*prāyaścitta*). In times of distress (*āpad*), the penance is a quarter-*kṛcchra* for each; for the specific occasion of the omission of the *caula*, it is a half-*kṛcchra*. However, in the absence of distress (*anāpad*), the distinction is that the penance for the omission of the *caula* is a full *kṛcchra*, while for others it is a half-*kṛcchra*.

Then one should perform the past rite in due order. In the phrase "when time has passed," the word *tu* (but) has the sense of *api* (also); by this, omission (*lopa*) is also included. If, through negligence, one performs a subsequent consecration (*saṃskāra*) without having performed the omitted rite or its corresponding expiation for the omission, then there is an "omission" (*lopa*) of the former; otherwise, there is merely a "transgression" (*atikrama*). In that case, even regarding the omission, the expiation should be understood as being the same as for a transgressed rite. However, the performance of the past rite itself does not take place here [in the case of mere transgression]. [As stated: "Once the expiation has been performed, even a rite that was past..."
"One group of teachers says it is an effect, while other wise ones say it is not."

Because this statement establishes that only a transgressed rite is to be performed; although here the sequence appears to be the performance of the past rite after the oblation (homa), followed by the penance (prāyaścitta) such as the Kṛcchra thereafter, nevertheless—since the order of meaning (ārthakrama) is stronger than the order of textual recitation (pāṭhakrama)—the sequence here is actually that the penance such as the Kṛcchra follows the oblation, and the performance of the past rite occurs after that.

Regarding the reading "having offered oblations in due order" (*hutvā caiva yathākramam*), the meaning is that one should perform the *kṛcchra* and other penances after having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* mantras in their proper sequence and according to number. The word "afterwards" (*paścāt*) implies an option regarding the performance of the penance for past rites. The meaning of the phrase "even upon the omission of each one of these" is that when any single rite among those beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with *caula* is omitted, one should perform the *pādakṛcchra* penance. The particle "api" (even) serves to include the omission of two or more rites.

Therefore, when there is an omission of two rites, or even when there is an omission of all three or more rites, or of some of them, the penance is a *pādakṛcchra*. It should be understood that the statement that the omission of each individual rite is the cause for the *pādakṛcchra* implies that the status of the omission of each individual rite as a cause for the *homa* is merely optional (*pākṣikatā*). Alternatively, the construction may be as follows: the particle *api* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*), and it connects with the phrase "the *pādakṛcchra*. Thus, the meaning becomes this:

In the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with *caula*, if any one of the purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāra*) is omitted in the interim, one should perform only a *pādakṛcchra* penance, not a *homa*. Furthermore, this *homa* must be performed for each individual ceremony using all the *vyāhṛtis*, according to the aforementioned Smṛti passage. Kātyāyana, however, prescribes seven expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittāhuti*), stating:
"With the two [verses] 'tvaṃ naḥ' and 'sa tvaṃ naḥ', and with this verse 'imaṃ me'..."
Those hundred [sins] of yours which are within these two, drive them out with oblations.
"Having offered [the oblation] for each foot separately, one should perform the half-portion in the *caula*.
Even when the expiation has been performed, there is an option regarding the performance of the rites that were omitted:
"Once the expiation has been performed, even a rite that was previously passed over [may be performed]."

"One group of teachers says it must be performed, while other wise ones say it need not be," it is said. Among the learned, however, the view that it must be performed is generally accepted. If, however, all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) prior to the initiation (*upanayana*) have been omitted, then the initiation should be performed after first carrying out the appropriate expiation (*prāyaścitta*). According to the view that the purpose of the rites is fulfilled by the expiation alone, one should perform the initiation after merely performing the expiation.
Now follows its ritual procedure (*prayoga*).

On the day preceding the initiation ceremony (upanayana), having performed an auspicious bath together with his wife and son, sipped water (ācamana), and performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma), he shall announce the place and time and make this formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (Śrī Parameśvara), by means of removing the sin arising from the transgression of the proper time for the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), the rite of securing a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), birth-rites (jātakarma), naming (nāmakaraṇa), the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), and the tonsure (caulakarma), I shall perform a penance-oblation (prāyaścitta-homa). Having thus resolved, he prepares the hearth (agnyāyatana) according to the procedure beginning with the smearing of the ground (ullekhana).

Having consecrated the worldly fire (laukikāgni) brought from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) under the name *Viṇṇāman*, having established, kindled, and meditated upon it, having strewn grass around the fire, and having spread *darbha* grass to the north of the fire; having placed upon that grass the vessels—the ladle (*darvī*), the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the *upaveṣa*, the *darbha* blades for wiping, the *darbha* blades for igniting, a single fuel-stick (*samit*), and the clarified butter—and having prepared the two strainers (*pavitra*), consecrated the sprinkling water, sprinkled the vessels, performed the rites beginning with the heating of the ladle and ending with placing the strainers in the fire;
and having sprinkled the fire with the mantras beginning with "O Agni, protect us" (*agnim adite*) and having placed the fuel-stick that was set out, [he proceeds].

For the two mantras *tvaṃ naḥ* and *sa tvaṃ naḥ*, the seers are the Viśvedevas; the deities are Agni and Varuṇa; the metre is Triṣṭubh. For *imaṃ me varuṇa*, the seers are the Viśvedevas and Varuṇa; the deity is Varuṇa; the metre is Gāyatrī. For *ye te śatam*, the seers are Vāmadeva, Varuṇa, Indra, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, and the Maruts; the metre is Triṣṭubh. For *ayāścāgne*, the seer is Vāmadeva; the deity is Agni; the metre is Paṅkti. For *uduttamaṃ varuṇa* and *ava te heḍaḥ*, the seers are the Viśvedevas and Varuṇa; the metre is Triṣṭubh.

Prajāpati is the deity for all the *vyāhṛtis*; the *bṛhatī* metre; and their application (*viniyoga*) is in the *ājya-homa* expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by the omission of purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*). "Oṃ *tvaṃ no a...* *smat svāhā*. To Agni and Varuṇa, this [oblation]. "Oṃ *sa tvaṃ no a...* *edhi svāhā*. To Agni and Varuṇa, this [oblation]. "Oṃ *imaṃ me...* *ke svāhā*. To Varuṇa, this [oblation]. "Oṃ *ye te śataṃ varuṇa ye sahasraṃ yajñiyāḥ pāśā vitatāḥ purutrā*."

"From them may Indra, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts release us with well-being—Svāhā! To Varuṇa, Indra, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts, this [is offered]. "Oṃ, O Agni, [with] this [oblation]... release [us], Svāhā! To Ayas Agni, this [is offered]. "Oṃ, the highest [noose], may we be free from it, Svāhā! To Varuṇa, this [is offered]. "Oṃ, loosen those bonds of Varuṇa, Svāhā! To Varuṇa, this [is offered]. "Oṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, Svāhā! To Prajāpati, this [is offered]. Thus, for each rite, he offers eight oblations of clarified butter (ājya).

Then, having removed the sacrificial grass coverings (*paristaraṇa*) and performed the final sprinkling (*uttarapariṣeka*) with the mantras beginning with "O Aditi, you have consented," one should worship the fire. Alternatively, for each consecration (*saṃskāra*), one may offer a single oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) using all the *vyāhṛtis* together; the other seven oblations are not required.

Furthermore, if the sacraments other than the *caula* are omitted through negligence, the student (*baṭu*) should cause each one to be expiated by means of a *pādakṛcchra* penance, specifically through the substitution of feeding four Brahmins; however, in the case of omitting the *caula*, he himself should perform a half-*kṛcchra* penance, either through the substitution of feeding six Brahmins and students or according to the primary method. If the sacraments other than the *caula* are omitted due to laziness or similar reasons, there is a half-*kṛcchra* for each; for the omission of the *caula*, there is a full *kṛcchra*.

In the event that the primary rite (*mukhyakalpa*) is impossible, one must perform a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) consisting of any one of the following: a thousand *tila*-oblations, ten thousand recitations of the *Gāyatrī*, or feeding twelve Brahmins.
