Since substitutes such as the gift of a cow (*godāna*) or the recitation of the eleven *Rudra* hymns are not possible for the *pādakṛcchra* and *ardhakṛcchra*, only the *tila*-oblation and similar rites serve as substitutes. Furthermore, these should be calculated according to the *pādakṛcchra* and *ardhakṛcchra* respectively as being either a fourth part or a half [of the standard requirement]. As it is said: "For a *pādakṛcchra*, the gift of clothing; for an *ardhakṛcchra*, sesame oil and gold; for a *pādonakṛcchra*, the gift of a cow; and for a full *kṛcchra*, a pair of cattle is prescribed."

Or rather, an alternative expiation (*pratyāmnāya*) as stated by Viṣṇu should be prescribed. "Tailakāñcana" is a compound meaning gold mixed with oil. The oblation of sesame seeds numbering one thousand may be performed with the Gāyatrī accompanied by the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*, or with the entire set of *vyāhṛtis* accompanied by the *praṇava*, or with the *praṇava* alone. The recitation (*japa*) of ten thousand Gāyatrīs, however, should be performed according to the third recension taught at the initiation (*upanayana*).

I shall perform the formal resolve for expiation (*prāyaścittasaṃkalpa*) as follows: for the sake of removing the sin incurred by the failure to perform, at their proper times, the purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarmāṇi*) for my son—beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), birth (*jātakarman*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), and ending with the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*)—I will perform a *pādakṛcchra* penance; likewise, for the sake of removing the sin incurred by the failure to perform, at its proper time, the purificatory rite of tonsure (*caula*), I will perform an *ardhakṛcchra* penance, in due order.

One should perform this preceded by a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), by means of either feeding a Brahmin or performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) as a substitute. Since looking at the sun and going outside are mentioned in other scriptures as optional, there is no expiation for their non-performance.

If it is argued that this sacrament (*saṃskāra*) is indeed mandatory because the word "then" (*atha*) in the rule "Now, in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*)" indicates the *niṣkramaṇa* (the first outing), then the mention of this [first outing] follows from the term "first feeding of solid food," and the expiation for its omission certainly occurs. Having thus prescribed the expiation, one should perform the past sacraments either on the day of the initiation (*upanayana*) or on the day prior to it, by means of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). However, the tonsure (*caula*) should take place on the very day of the initiation.

Having sat down together with his wife and the person to be consecrated, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and having announced the place and time, [he shall perform] the rite called *garbhādhāna* for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*), by means of the excellence of the purificatory rites for each subsequent conception of this wife of mine, and through the perfection of the purification of the field (*kṣetra-saṃskāra*) which destroys the impurities arising from seed and womb for this child born and for the embryos yet to be born; and for this child who has been born, for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord, by means of destroying the impurities arising from seed and womb.

The rite called *puṃsavana*, for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord by means of destroying the taints pertaining to seed and womb of this born child and of future embryos; the rite called *sīmantonnayana*; the *jātakarma* for this boy, for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord by means of destroying the defects produced by drinking the water of the womb and the taints arising from seed and womb; [and] for this son...

The naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*) is performed for the purpose of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*) by means of the increase of life-span, radiance, and prosperity, and the removal of defects arising from the seed and the womb; the gazing at the sun (*sūryāvalokana*) is performed for the purpose of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord by means of the increase of this child’s life-span; the first exit from the home (*niṣkramaṇa*) is performed for the purpose of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord by means of the increase of this child’s life and fortune and the removal of defects arising from the seed and the womb; [and so on] for this son...

Today, for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, the rite known as *annaprāśana*—which, by way of purifying the consumption of the impurities of the mother’s womb and destroying the taints arising from the seed and the womb, increases food, Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*), splendor, the senses, and longevity—is performed; and likewise, for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, through the increase of strength, longevity, and luster by destroying the taints arising from the seed and the womb of this boy [named] Amukaśarman, the rite known as *caula* is performed today.

The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord, by means of establishing the qualification for Vedic study preceded by the attainment of the status of the twice-born, I shall perform tomorrow the rite known as the initiation (*upanayana*), which has the Ācārya, the Father, the Sāvitrī, and the Mother as its [respective] causes."

Just as the term "kumāra" (boy) is employed in the rites of birth (*jātakarman*) and tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇakarman*), so too, because it occupies an intermediate position between them, it is employed in the naming rite (*nāmakarman*) and others as well; thus, according to the ritual manual (*kalpa*), in the formal intention (*saṃkalpa*) for the naming rite and so forth, the word "kumāra" should be used in place of words such as "son" (*putra*). Alternatively, the dual usage of both "of the boy" (*kumārasya*) and "of the son" (*putrasya*) is prescribed by the *Dharmasūtras* and *Smṛtis* for the naming and first-feeding rites (*annaprāśana*). However, the conventional designations of "infancy" (*śiśutva*) and "childhood" (*bālatva*) are to be understood as pertaining to the specific stages of purification from those [impurities].

That arrangement will be explained further on. Because of the difference in timing between the *puṃsavana* and other purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*) and the *caula* and *upanayana*, their ancillary elements (*aṅga*) are performed separately; however, the *tantra* (the common procedure) extends only as far as the recitation for a propitious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) and so forth. Since it is mentioned in another scripture, there is no formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in the case where the "beholding of the sun" (*sūryāvalokana*) is not performed.

Then, as ancillary parts of that [ceremony], one should perform the worship of Gaṇapati, the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*), and the *nāndīśrāddha*. Following this, one should perform the sowing of seeds (*aṅkurāropaṇa*) as prescribed for the initiatory rites of the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), and the initiation (*upanayana*). Furthermore, as an ancillary part of the initiation, the sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajña*) and the installation of the deities of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), such as Nandin and others, must be performed. If possible, the sequence is as follows: immediately after the *nāndīśrāddha*, one should perform the intermediate sacraments (*saṃskāra*), and then carry out the sacrifice to the planets, the sowing of seeds, and the installation of the pavilion deities.

Alternatively, the intermediate sacraments (*antarita-saṃskāra*) should be performed after the *grahayajña*. However, if all of them are to be performed immediately, one should utter the formal declarations (*saṃkalpa-vākya*) for all the sacraments ending with the initiation (*upanayana*), saying simply, "I shall perform [them] today. In this view, the purpose of the *annaprāśana* sacrament is fulfilled by the expiation alone, and there is no need to perform it as well. If it were to be performed, it would be done after the performance of the *annaprāśana*, according to the rule:
"A man who has eaten, one who has anointed himself, or one under a vow, should not have his hair and so forth shaved."

Thus, because shaving is prohibited after a meal, the *caula* ceremony cannot take place [immediately]. In this case, all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) should be performed only once. Even a specific oblation (*vaiśeṣika-homa*), if it shares the same deity, should be performed only once; for example, the fourfold oblation to the *dhātrīs*.

Then, having performed the consecration of the sacrificial ground through tracing and other rites, one should establish the *aupāsana* fire there, kindle it, and meditate upon it. If another person is the performer, then whatever rite is due at its own time in the common (*laukika*) fire—whether that be the fire employed for that specific rite or all fires—should be understood as the "name" of the fire here.

Then, having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and performed the rites from "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) up to the end of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), he recites from "The deities who are to be worshipped in this *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *nāmakaraṇa*, *annaprāśana*, and *homa* ritual" up to the end of the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, regarding the specific principal oblations (*vaiśeṣika-pradhāna-homa*), he says: "I shall worship Dhātṛ with four oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*); I shall worship Anumati with four oblations of clarified butter; I shall worship Rākā with two oblations of clarified butter; I shall worship Sinīvālī with two oblations of clarified butter. In the case of thirteen oblations, the additional phrase is: "I shall worship Kuhū with one oblation of clarified butter."

Then, having performed the limb-oblations (*aṅgahoma*) beginning with "to Varuṇa with two verses" and ending with the *vyāhṛti* oblations, the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*) follows. Because they share the same deities, one should offer the four *dhātrī* offerings related to the *puṃsavana* and *sīmantonnayana*, and the four *dhātrī* offerings which constitute a portion of the principal rite related to the naming ceremony (*nāmakarman*), performing them by a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Then, one should offer eight or nine oblations beginning with "May Anumati favor us today."

Since, according to the view that all rites are to be performed immediately, the *caula* (tonsure ceremony) must also be performed together [with the others], the mention of the *caula* term should be made in the *anvādhāna* following the *annaprāśana* term. Then, having performed the subsidiary oblation (*aṅgahoma*) beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa," as well as the *jaya* and other subsidiary offerings, and having completed the rite from the *sviṣṭakṛt* up to the concluding *japa*, one should perform the threefold food-oblation (*trivṛdannahoma*) and the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*). Regarding the *vāstubali*, there is an option.

Regarding the rites of *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, *nāmakaraṇa*, and *annaprāśana*—beginning with the words "May you declare it an auspicious day for me"—the performer should say this three times. Likewise: "May you declare it a blessing (*svastyayana*); may you declare it a success (*ṛddhi*). If the *caula* (tonsure) is also to be performed together [with these], then the word *caula* should be inserted after the word *annaprāśana*. Thereafter follow the principal rites in their proper order.

In that regard, where an action is impossible, one should recite the respective mantra while touching the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), and at the end, one should visualize that particular action. However, where an action is possible, one should perform that specific action at the end of the respective mantra with the thought, "This very action is now being accomplished by me," or simply by the recitation of the mantra alone.

Therein, for the sake of accomplishing the *saṃskāra* of conception (*garbhādhāna*), one should touch the person to be consecrated, recite the mantras for the invocation of the deity, the descent of the seed, and so forth, and visualize each respective action at the conclusion of its corresponding mantra. Likewise, for the rites connected with the *puṃsavana* (the rite for ensuring a male child), such as the consumption of curd and *drapsa*, one should touch the person to be consecrated, recite the mantras, and visualize each respective action.

Then, touching the person to be consecrated according to the method of application to be described, and having performed the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), one should perform the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) according to the method to be described. In that rite, even though the son has already been born, one should consider him as being born at this very moment; looking upon his face and holding the boy over a stone, one should perform the entire ritual—from the fumigation to the touching of the breast—as far as possible. Alternatively, having touched the person to be consecrated and recited the mantras, one should mentally visualize each respective action at the conclusion.

The recitation of the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" alone [is required], because at this time, since she lacks the status of being in the state of childbirth (sūtikā), the ritual injunctions contingent upon that status are impossible. Nor should it be argued: "In that case, since fumigation (uddhūpana) must be accomplished with the *sūtakāgni* (the fire of childbirth), and that fire is currently absent, how can the performance of the rite associated with it take place? For the term *sūtakāgni* refers to a fire intended for a rite characterized by the state of childbirth; and since that rite—namely, fumigation—is possible even in another fire when intended for that purpose, the performance of the act of fumigation remains entirely unimpeded.
Alternatively, the recitation of the mantra may be performed exactly as it stands. However, when the boy has grown older, the recitation should be performed by all [the officiants].

Then, having performed the naming ceremony (*nāmadāna*) in the manner to be described, and having caused him to consume, with the appropriate mantra, the threefold mixture of curd, honey, and ghee along with seasoned food in the manner to be described, one should feed the Brahmins, cause them to pronounce blessings (*āśis*), and meditate upon Viṣṇu.

Then, on the very day of the initiation (*upanayana*), one should perform the tonsure (*caula*) according to the method to be described hereafter and commence the initiation. Because of the statement, "Or else together with the initiation," there is a rule that the tonsure must be performed on the day of the initiation. In this context, the word "together" (*saha*) refers to a time proximate to the initiation.

If, while the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) for the first-born child have been omitted, any sacramental rite whatsoever should accrue to a subsequent child, then that accrued rite must be performed only after having first performed the omitted sacramental rites for the first-born; for it is proper that the performance of the subsequent child's sacraments be preceded by the completion of the first-born's sacraments.

Because it is observed that the performance of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) for twins must follow the order of seniority, and because there is no obstacle to accepting the scriptural injunction regarding twins for the sake of establishing this rule; otherwise, if there were no great impediment, performing the rite for the younger brother before the elder brother would result in the elder brother becoming unworthy of receiving salutation (*abhivādana*). Custom (*ācāra*) is likewise the same.

Furthermore, there is the statement of Śātātapa: "If the elder brother has not yet had the sacraments performed for him through the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), the younger brother must by no means undergo them."

In reality, however, the underlying principle here must be considered. Because of the qualification "provided there is no great obstacle," there is no prohibition against the younger brother’s initiation (*upanayana*) for up to sixteen years if the elder brother is obstructed by imprisonment or similar circumstances for that duration. Nor does this render the scriptures that establish the fault of being a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother) meaningless; for those texts remain purposeful insofar as they aim to demonstrate the multiplicity of faults pertaining to various subjects, such as the elder and younger brothers, the giver of the girl in marriage, and so forth.

For those whose sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) have been interrupted, because the performance depends upon the continuity of the preceding rites, there is no restriction regarding the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) or the aforementioned time. The rites for the younger [brother] must be postponed in accordance with the time of the rites for the elder [brother]. Even then, they should be performed at the time prescribed for them. Alternatively, the rites for the younger [brother] may be performed at their own proper time, and the rites for the elder [brother] may be postponed accordingly. Regarding this matter, the wise should accept whatever is stated as correct.

If the *saṃskāras* have been omitted and another person performs them, there is only an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the *garbhādhāna*. When the *saṃskāras* beginning with *garbhādhāna* cannot be performed, their purpose is fulfilled by means of expiation alone. However, if the time for the *saṃskāras* beginning with *upanayana* has elapsed, one must perform the respective expiations for the lapse of those times and then necessarily carry out the *saṃskāras* such as *upanayana* in their proper sequence. For this very reason, the Teacher has prescribed [the study of the Veda] by way of *upanayana*. Marriage (*vivāha*), on the other hand, occurs when there is a desire [to do so].

When intense dispassion (*vairāgya*) has arisen, there is an omission of the *samāvartana* (return home) and subsequent rites; in that case, only the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsāśrama*) remains. Thus ends the section on the simultaneous performance (*tantra*) of omitted sacraments (*antarita-saṃskāra*) in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.
This concludes the fifth chapter in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāraratnamālā*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of the venerable Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, whose surname is Oko.
Now begins the sixth section:
the initiation of those with deficient limbs.
Regarding this, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"He who is born of a Brāhmaṇa father from a Brāhmaṇī mother is a Brāhmaṇa; such is the Vedic revelation.
Therefore, [this applies] even to those who are eunuchs, blind, deaf, hunchbacked, dwarfs, or lame."
[One should not give] to those afflicted by dullness, stammering, or disease; to those with white limbs or deformed limbs;
nor to the insane, the mute, those whose virility is destroyed, or those lacking sense organs.
In all these cases, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) should be performed as appropriate;
however, some declare that those who are mute or insane are not to be consecrated with such rites.
Furthermore, because they have no entitlement to perform ritual acts, there is no loss of caste for these two; their offspring, however, must undergo the sacramental rites. But others say otherwise.
The preceptor alone performs the ritual preparations, the mantras, the fire oblations, and so forth;
and the preceptor [initiates] those to be initiated according to the rules into his own presence.
"Or, having brought [the fire] near the fire, or having touched the Sāvitrī, he should mutter it;
everything other than the formal acceptance of the girl should be caused to be performed by a Brahmin."

*Gadgada* means one who speaks with a stammering voice. *Rogārta* means afflicted by diseases such as epilepsy (*apasmāra*) and the like. *Śuklāṅga* means one who has white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*) or similar conditions. *Vikalāṅga* refers to one whose limbs are weak or deficient. *Unmatta* means one who suffers from insanity. *Dhvastapuṃstva* refers to one whose virility is destroyed. *Nirgatendriya* refers to one whose sensory faculties have departed; that is to say, one whose organs have been severed by a blow.

By the phrase "as is appropriate" (*yathocitam*), it is indicated that whatever purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are prescribed as suitable for accomplishing the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*) must also be performed for these [deaf-mutes], even by omitting those parts that are impossible to execute. By providing the qualification "accomplishing the status of the twice-born," the exclusion of rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) and the *sthālīpāka* offerings is effected; for these merely serve to avert sin (*pratyavāya*) and do not accomplish the status of the twice-born. Some teachers state: "The mute and the insane are not to be consecrated."

The phrase "by means of initiation and so forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence]. Since study is impossible for them, there is no initiation (*upanayana*) for the purpose of study; and just like initiation, there is likewise an absence of the *kāṇḍavrata* and other such rites. "Unmatta" means one who is insane, that is to say, one whose mind is deranged. Because these two—the mute and the insane—lack eligibility (*anadhikāra*), that is, the absence of entitlement, for rituals such as initiation and the rest; the word "ca" (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The meaning is that precisely because they lack eligibility for rituals, there is no loss of caste (*pātitya*). The second "ca" has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

The synthesis is as follows: there are no rites such as the initiation (*upanayana*), nor is there any loss of caste (*pātitya*). Because those who are mute or insane lack eligibility for ritual acts, they do not incur loss of caste; however, according to the Vedic revelation stating, "He born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Brāhmaṇa," since it is established that even the mute and insane born of a Brāhmaṇa are worthy of sacraments such as initiation, others maintain that these two must also undergo the sacraments, and their offspring likewise must be consecrated.

Otherwise, this would contradict what has been stated by certain teachers: "He is not one to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*). Regarding the statement, "The teacher alone performs the consecrations, mantras, oblations, and so forth," the word "having touched the boy" is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus, the teacher alone should perform the recitation of the consecration-mantras—which are normally recited by the boy—as well as the rites such as the oblations (*homa*). Since there is no oblation performed by the boy during the initiation (*upanayana*), the term "oblation" here refers to the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-abhyādhāna*) into the fire.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the omission of the *kāṇḍavrata* rites—such as the ritual cleansing (*mārjana*) and the formal attendance (*upasthāna*)—is indeed intended, because these are auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of Vedic study (*adhyayana*). Nor should it be argued that, since the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) also serves the purpose of Vedic study, its omission should likewise apply in the case of those who are mute or mentally deranged. This is not so, because while the initiation ceremony serves the purpose of Vedic study by way of establishing one’s status as a twice-born (*dvijatva*), it must necessarily be performed even when Vedic study is impossible, for the sake of establishing that very status of being twice-born. In the same way, the *godāna* rite also takes place, precisely because it lacks the status of being an auxiliary element of Vedic study.

If marriage is possible, even the *samāvartana* (the student's return home) should be performed during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) after observing the vows for some time; since neither the *vidyā-snāna* nor the *ubhaya-snāna* applies to them, only the *vrata-snāna* pertains to those two. However, if marriage is not possible, his state is that of a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*). As for the prohibition of lifelong celibacy in the Kali age, it refers to men who are free from defects such as being mute or insane.

The meaning of the statement, "But the teacher should bring those who are to be initiated into his presence according to rule," is as follows: the teacher should bring those previously mentioned [persons], such as the eunuchs and others, into his presence—that is, facing toward him—in accordance with the rule, namely, the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Regarding the statement, "Or, having brought them near the fire, he should mutter the Sāvitrī while touching [them]," the meaning is: or he should place them near the fire, that is, facing toward the fire. In the previous case, it was stated that the teacher should make them face himself; this is an alternative option to that.

Regarding the phrase "or he should mutter the Sāvitrī while touching [him]," the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an option with the well-known recitation of the Sāvitrī. This option is to be understood as being determined according to the boy's capacity: if the boy is mute, there is the muttering of the Sāvitrī preceded by touching; if he is insane, there is recitation if he can read, otherwise there is muttering after touching. However, in cases such as impotence or blindness, the rule is that there is only recitation. This is the settled conclusion.

Regarding the statement, "Or, having touched [the boy], he should mutter the Sāvitrī," the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Or, having touched the Sāvitrī, he should mutter it. In the word *spṛśya*, the word "the boy" (*kumāram*) is to be supplied as the object. Although there is no compound here, the substitution of *lyap* for *ktvā* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) anomaly. Thus, it should be understood that two rules are established: one for the recitation of the consecration mantra performed by the boy himself, and the other for performing the *homa* and other rites on his behalf. The former rule is to be understood when the boy is mute; the latter rule applies when the boy has a physical deformity. In the case of insanity, it is as in the former case.

The procedure beginning with "those who are to be initiated according to rule" and ending with "near the fire" is common to all. In the case of the mute, the deaf, and others, there is no question regarding their name, such as "What is your name?", because they are incapable [of responding], and because Baudhāyana states, "he does not ask the name. Other constituent parts of the rite should be performed as far as possible. For the initiation of the mute or the insane, the formula for the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of establishing the status of the twice-born for this person, I shall perform the sacrament known as initiation, which has the Teacher, the Father, Sāvitrī, and the Mother as its components.
This concludes the initiation for those with deficient limbs. Now follows the re-initiation (*punarupanayana*).

And that [penance] is of three kinds: (1) that prescribed as a penance for the cause of transgression (*pratyavāya*); (2) that prescribed for the sake of the fruit [of the rite] when one who has already undergone initiation falls into a vain activity due to a specific occasion; and (3) that prescribed for the sake of that [fruit] when there is a desire to study another Veda. Regarding the first, Śātātapa states in the *Prayogapārijāta*:
"Having eaten garlic, leeks, onions, or likewise dog-flesh..."
Furthermore, one should perform the Upanāyanam and likewise the Taptakṛcchra penance."
Garlic (*laśuna*) is well known. Moreover, only the white variety is prohibited; thus says Parāśara:
"Fresh milk, white garlic, eggplant, and *gṛñjana* [are forbidden]."

The term *śvetapada* (white root) is connected with both garlic (*laśuna*) and eggplant (*vṛntāka*). Therefore, Mādhava maintains that there is no expiation for eating red garlic or black eggplant. Vijñāneśvara states that *gṛñjana* is a bulbous root similar to garlic. Mādhava further explains that it is a specific leaf used by singers for clearing the throat and by debauchees for intoxication; its powder is what they consume. However, in the *Śrāddhaprakaraṇa* of the *Mādhavīya*, it is stated:
"The white-rooted *gṛñjana* is a specific type of onion (*palāṇḍu*). Garlic has long leaves, a pungent smell, and is a great medicinal herb (*mahauṣadha*)."
For it has been stated by Suśruta: "Pharaṇya, palāṇḍu, latārka, parārikā, gṛñjana, and yavaneṣṭa— these are the ten species of onion (palāṇḍu)."
Mādhava has also stated that the *mūlaviśeṣa* is another synonym for *gājarā*:
"It is similar to the onion (*palāṇḍu*) in its smell, shape, and taste,
but it differs from the onion because its stalks are slender and its leaves grow from the tips of those slender stalks."

Thus, in the *Vāgbhaṭṭa-ṭīkā*, the statement of Bāṣpacandra found in the *Hemādri* should indeed be considered as the decisive authority here; however, its identification with the *gājara* (radish) must be seen as refuted by what will be stated later. Furthermore, even in the *Hemādri*, it is stated further on that this refers specifically to a particular type of onion (*palāṇḍu*).
In the *Rājanighaṇṭu*:
"The *rasebha* is indeed the *mahākanda*, the *gṛñjana*, and the *dīrghapatraka*."
It has broad leaves and a thick bulb; it is favored by the Yavanas and is beneficial for strength.
The wise declare that the root of the *gṛñjana* is sweet, its bulb pungent, and even its stalk astringent;
they hold it to be bitter when considered by its leaves, and say its seed-pod is salty.
Gājara, Piṇḍamūla, Pītakanda with its roots, Svādumūla, Supīta, Nāgara, and Pītamūlaka.
Carrot is sweet, appetizing, slightly pungent, and removes phlegm;
it destroys flatulence, worms, and colic, and alleviates burning sensations and bile.
In medical science:
"Gṛñjana, śikhimūla, yavaneṣṭa, vartula,
granthimūla, śikhākanda, kanda, ḍiṇḍīra, and modaka."
"Gṛñjana is pungent and hot; it removes disorders of phlegm and wind, stimulates the appetite, is digestive, pleasing to the heart, foul-smelling, and destroys abdominal tumors. (And:
"The deer that is struck by an arrow smeared with poison..."
"His meat is not to be eaten, for that is considered *gṛñjana*," so says Aparārka.
As for Hemādri’s statement that the root called *gājarā* is *gṛñjana*, and Mādhava’s statement that *gṛñjana* is a specific kind of root synonymous with *gājarā*—neither of these is correct.
[The authoritative definition is: "*Gṛñjana*, *cukrikā*, *cukra*, *gājara*, and likewise *potikā*..."

Thus, because a separate mention [of these items] in the *Brāhma* [Smṛti] would otherwise be untenable; *cukrikā* is well known in the vernacular as *cukkā*; *cukra* is curd that is extremely sour; *potikā* is well known as *poī*. Furthermore, this re-initiation (*punarupanayana*) applies to eating with intention (*buddhyā*); however, for eating without intention, there is merely the *taptakṛcchra* penance, according to the statement of Bṛhaspati:
"Having unknowingly eaten mushrooms, garlic, onion, and likewise *gṛñjana*, a twice-born man shall perform the *taptakṛcchra*."
However, there is no fault in this regard when the illness must be cured by the consumption of onions and such;
for thus Sumantu states in his *Palāṇḍvādy-anuvṛtti*:
"These very things are not prohibited for a sick person undergoing medical treatment."
Gautama states: "Upon consuming camel's milk or human milk, there shall be a second initiation (*punarupanayana*) and the *taptakṛcchra* penance.

Śūlapāṇi holds that this applies to the repeated consumption [of such milk]. (Regarding the consumption of the milk of sheep, goats, camels, and so forth, there shall be a second initiation and the *taptakṛcchra* penance.)

In another Smṛti: "Upon consuming semen, urine, or feces, as well as the liquor made from molasses (gauḍī) or honey (mādhvī), purification is held to be achieved through the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) prescribed for the consumption of the excrement of carnivorous animals."
Manu states:
"Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or that which is contaminated by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the rite of re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*)."

This refers to contact with liquor that has already been consumed. This procedure should be understood as being preceded by the *taptakṛcchra* penance; for, regarding the re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) preceded by the *taptakṛcchra*, Gautama states: "The same applies to the consumption of urine, feces, a corpse, or semen.
Bṛhaspati says: "For the purification of semen, urine, and feces, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."

The word "eating" (*prāśana*) is to be understood as the remainder of the phrase "of flesh, urine, and excrement. In this regard, the application of the *Cāndrāyaṇa* or *Taptakṛcchra* penances should be understood as determined by whether the act was committed intentionally or unintentionally. Śūlapāṇi maintains that the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), however, is identical in both cases.
In the *Padmapurāṇa*: "One who accepts the bed of a deceased person deserves to undergo the purificatory rite once again."
In another Smṛti: "Having gone to Sindhu, Sauvīra, and Saurāṣṭra, as well as those dwelling in the border regions, and to Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga, one deserves the rite of purification."

And this applies to traveling without going on a pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā), according to the statement of Baudhāyana: "Having traveled without going on a pilgrimage to sacred sites, one deserves the performance of the purificatory rite (punaḥsaṃskāra) again.
Mārkaṇḍeya says:
If a Brahmin travels one yojana mounted upon a donkey,
three *taptakṛcchra* penances are prescribed for the purification of his body.
"One should perform a rebirth according to the rite of the 'womb of ghee' (ghṛtagarbha);
consecrated by the purificatory rites beginning with the birth ceremony (jātakarma), he shall attain purity."
Śākala said: "If indeed a twice-born man should go [on a journey] having mounted a camel, a donkey, or a bull,
the rites for him must be performed again, including the shaving of the topknot."
"But first, one should perform the penance for three years according to the prescribed rule.
Thus says Vṛddha-Gautama in the Prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa of Hemādri:
"A donkey, a camel, a buffalo, an ox, and likewise a sheep..."
"Having mounted a goat, one should designate the lunar [day] at a distance of one krośa from the mouth."
A Brahmin is one born from the mouth. *Cāndra* refers to the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
Manu states:
"Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, a twice-born man should properly perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*."
"But if it was done intentionally, there shall be a year of *kṛcchra* penance and also the performance of the initiatory rite (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) again."
"This refers to the subject of repeated practice," according to the *Madanaratna*.
Parāśara states: "A Brahmin who has fallen away from his vows and has returned from the life of a wandering mendicant..."
And having desisted from fasting, if he desires to enter the life of a householder;
"He shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances and three *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts;
through all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*), he shall attain purity."
In the *Bhāradvājīya-pitṛmedha-sūtra*:

"If, after this [rite] has been performed, [the husband] returns, he should undergo the vow for twelve nights beginning with the birth-rites (*jātakarman*) of one who has emerged from a jar of ghee; then, together with that same wife, he should establish the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), or he should sacrifice with the *vrātya* animal or the *aindrāgna* animal. Having gone to a mountain, he should offer the *iṣṭi* to Agni Kāma, and he should sacrifice with whatever rites he desires. "In this having been performed" means when the subsequent rite has been completed. "With the *vrātya*" refers to the *vrātyastoma*. "With the animal" refers to the *aindrāgna* animal.
Vṛddha-Manu states: "If he should return alive, one should immerse him in a jar of ghee;
having lifted him out and bathed him, one should perform for him the birth-rite (jātakarman) and the other ceremonies."
Having observed the vow for twelve days or, alternatively, for three nights,
he should bathe and then marry a wife, or another woman in her absence.
Having established the sacred fires according to the rules, he should indeed perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifice;
then, having gone to a mountain, he should perform the Aindrāgna animal sacrifice there.
"One should perform long-life sacrifices as well as desired rites.
The meaning is that in the absence of that [the former], there is an absence of that [the latter].

The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*), through the means of successfully re-establishing the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) preceded by the removal of the undesirable defects arising from my funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*), I shall marry that same woman"—or, alternatively, "not through the means of successfully re-establishing the householder stage of life. However, if one has not yet discharged the debts to the gods and ancestors (*devapitrarṇa*), one should also say: "through the means of discharging the debts to the gods and ancestors. If there was no previous wife, then after the words "for the sake of [pleasing]...," one should say: "I shall perform my own marriage."

In this case, there is no gift performed by the father or others. The formula for the vow (*saṃkalpa*) of the marriage-oblation (*vivāha-homa*) is: "For the sake of establishing her fitness for my enjoyment in this previously married wife, and for the sake of establishing the status of the *aupāsana* fire in this fire. However, when marrying another woman, the vow for the marriage is exactly like the vow for the first marriage. Following the marriage-oblation, there is the entry into the house (*gṛhapraveśa*), the *sthālīpāka* offering, and the *caturthī-karma*. Regarding the consumption of honey and meat, Paiṭhīnasi states: "There shall be a fast for three nights and a re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*)."

And it is stated in the *Madanaratna* that this three-night fast is for one who is unable to perform the *prājāpatya* penance. Furthermore, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: "In the case of eating these two [garlic and onion] unintentionally, a *kṛcchra* penance is required; intentionally, a *parāka*; and in the case of repetition, double the penance and a re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) must be performed. Likewise, in that same work: "For a student (*brahmacārin*), a re-initiation must be performed when he performs the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*) for anyone other than his mother, father, guru, teacher (*ācārya*), or preceptor (*upādhyāya*). The same is stated in the *Aparārka*.

Likewise: "In the case of excessive repetition of consuming semen, feces, urine, curd churned with a finger, or sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) outside the altar, there shall be an Atikṛcchra penance and a second initiation. Regarding this, some hold that "consuming the sacrificial cake outside the altar" refers to the consumption of a worldly (non-sacrificial) sacrificial cake. Others maintain that "worldly sacrificial cake consumption" refers specifically to the consumption of a consecrated sacrificial cake when it is prepared by someone other than the officiating priests (ṛtvij). Furthermore, others argue that the compound here should be analyzed as "that which is both worldly and a sacrificial cake consumption."

Since the word *puroḍāśa* denotes a substance characterized by a specific form resulting from prescribed consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*), the latter ritual procedure alone is superior. Furthermore, this [penance] applies whether the act was committed knowingly or unknowingly; fasting is likewise required. Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The *śaṇa* flower, the silk-cotton tree (*śālmalī*), curd churned with a hand-whisk..."
"Having eaten the sacrificial cake outside the altar, one should not eat for a day and a night."
In another Smṛti it is said: "Due to contact with the waters of Karmanāśā, crossing the Karatoyā,
and swimming across the Gaṇḍakī, one deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) once again."
The Gauḍas, however, say: "By the touch of the waters of the Karatoyā, there is the destruction of karma through its transgression."
Thus they recite; but that is not correct, because the excellence of bathing in the Karatoyā is declared among the duties of giving (*dānadharmas*):
"O Karatoyā, always possessing pure water, most excellent of rivers, renowned far and wide, born from the hand of Hara, you wash away the sins of the citizens."
This is also evident from the bathing mantras written in the *Smṛtidarpaṇacandrikā*.
In the *Smṛtimañjarī*:
"If a twice-born man, out of delusion, should return home without having performed the *upākaraṇa* ceremony..."
"He, however, deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) preceded by that pertaining to Prajāpati."
When the rite of re-initiation (*punarupanayana*) for the purpose of expiation has been thus performed, a specific rule is stated by Kaśyapa in the *Pārijāta* and *Madanaratna*:

"Having completed the expiation, having gone toward the eastern or northern direction to a place where the sound of domestic animals is not heard, one should kindle a fire in that location, spread out the seat of Brahmā (*brahmāsana*), and perform the rite of consecration (*saṃskāra*) once again according to the previously prescribed procedure."

The statement "having spread the Brahmāsana" is for the purpose of establishing the rule of Brahman; therefore, the realization of Brahman is not achieved here by means of the staff and so forth. "By the previously prescribed method" means by the procedure stated earlier.
In another Smṛti: "The girdle, the antelope skin, the garment, the staff, alms-begging, and the vows."
"They cease [their duties] during the rites of re-consecration for the twice-born."

Now, as for the second occasion for re-initiation (*punarupanayana*): this has been stated by Mātṛdata in the sūtra prescribing the primary rite of initiation—which consists of bringing the boy near him after first touching his shoulders with both hands—as follows:
"The word *atha* here is intended to indicate that this is the principal rite, and that if it is forgotten, the entire ritual must be repeated.
Furthermore, in the *Samayodyota*, another Smṛti states:
"One who has been initiated during the rainy season, in the spring, during the dark fortnight, during a throat-seizure (galagraha),
or during a period when study is forbidden, deserves to undergo the consecration again."

"By the season being out of turn, namely by spring"—this is one further cause for re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). Likewise, there are three other causes: the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the seizing of a planet (*graha*), and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). Regarding "by the season being out of turn, namely by spring," this is the cause for re-consecration when spring has arrived and the rite is performed elsewhere; it does not apply at other times. Otherwise, the injunctions for the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Jyeṣṭha, and Āṣāḍha would be contradicted.

Alternatively, because of its proximity to the phrase "without the spring season," the word "dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is construed with it. Thus, the meaning becomes this: "In the initiation ceremony, if performed during the dark fortnight without the spring season, it is a re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*); otherwise it is not. Some maintain that both the words "dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) and "throat-seizure" (*galagraha*) are to be construed [with the preceding]; others hold that only the word "throat-seizure" is to be construed. Vasiṣṭha states in the *Smṛtidarpaṇa*:
"If the Moon is situated in a malefic division (*pāpāṃśaka*), or even if it is in an enemy or debilitated sign, one who has been initiated in the afternoon deserves a re-consecration."
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Madanaratna* that "afternoon" refers to the third part of the day divided into three portions.

Now, for the third occasion for re-initiation (*punarupanayana*): on the occasion of commenting on the *Dharmasūtra*, which states, "The *Sāvitrī* is indeed recited from all the Vedas; so says the Brāhmaṇa," Ujjvalākāra said: "The recitation of the *Sāvitrī* at the initiation ceremony serves as the means by which all the Vedas are recited. Therefore, since no distinction is perceived, there is only one initiation for all purposes."

On this point, the Śāṭyāyanabrāhmaṇa itself has been recited. However, for the sake of the Atharvaveda, a separate initiation (upanayana) must be performed because of a specific scriptural injunction. Thus it is heard in that very same text: "One who has been consecrated elsewhere [for another Veda] should not study the Bhṛgvaṅgirasaḥ. "Elsewhere" means for the purpose of another Veda; "Bhṛgvaṅgirasaḥ" refers to the Atharvaveda.

Regarding the threefold repetition of initiation, since no specific distinction is mentioned in any text concerning the second and third initiations, the repetition of initiation is to be performed in its unmodified form before sunrise, prior to the establishment of the Gārhapatya fire, just like the unmodified establishment of the fires.
The Procedure for Re-initiation as an Expiatory Rite (Prāyaścitta):

Regarding re-initiation performed as an expiatory rite, since numerous specific details are understood from the aforementioned scriptural statements, its procedure is now set forth. Furthermore, where it is prescribed together with an expiatory rite—as in the case of drinking camel’s milk and so forth—it must be performed after having first undergone the expiation according to the rules taught by the assembly (parṣad).

In cases where the performance of the sacraments (saṃskāra), beginning with the birth-rite (jātakarma), is prescribed, the option of performing them immediately after the occasion arises requires no consideration of the northern solstice (udagayana), spring, or other seasons; one should perform the sacraments up to the tonsure (caula) according to the instruction of the assembly (parṣad). Otherwise, the northern solstice, spring, and so forth, are mandatory. Or, at the very least, there must be consideration of the lunar day (tithi) and the asterism (nakṣatra). Even when the re-initiation (punarupanayana) is to be performed at a later time, the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana) must certainly continue until that point, because of the scriptural statement: "One who neglects the twilight worship is eternally impure and unfit for all ritual acts."

In the section concerning the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), since the Smṛti states, "One should properly perform the *saṃdhyā*," the obligation to perform the *saṃdhyā-vandana* is established even for one who has committed a great sin; what then need be said regarding others? However, the *brahmayajña* and other such rites do not apply [to him] because of his impurity and because there is no scriptural injunction to that effect. But for one who is eligible for re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), the rite is prescribed even at night out of fear of omitting obligatory duties, and not for anyone else—thus it is stated in the *Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa-ṭīkā*. Furthermore, if the father is alive, he alone is the performer [of the rite].

In his absence, a *sapiṇḍa* such as a paternal grandfather or paternal uncle [should perform it]; in their absence, any learned person well-versed in his own Vedic branch (*śākhā*). The birth rites (*jātakarma*) and other ceremonies are to be performed in the very same place where the re-initiation (*punarupanayana*) takes place. The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "For the sake of pleasing the Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of accomplishing the re-consecration of this deceased person whose funeral rites have been performed, I shall perform the sacramental acts beginning with the birth rites and ending with the initiation. In the same way, when there is another occasion for such a rite, the resolve should be made according to the specific cause.

Then, for the sake of all [the rites], the recitation of auspicious prayers (*svastivācana*) and so forth should be performed. Regarding the shaving of the hair, the specific distinction for one of advanced age is that the shaving of the head (*keśavāpana*) occurs after the shaving of the beard and side-locks (*śmaśrūpapakṣa*). However, the formal declaration of intent (*saṃkalpa*) for the marriage and the subsequent recitation of auspicious prayers for that purpose must be performed separately by the person undergoing the sacrament themselves. But where only the re-initiation (*punarupanayana*) is prescribed as an expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*), then only that should be performed according to the procedure instructed by the assembly (*parṣad*).

In that case, the teacher should perform three *kṛcchra* penances preceded by the recitation of the *agnipavitra* mantra, followed by the recitation of the *gāyatrī* twelve thousand times or twelve thousand plus one thousand times. Some maintain that if the initiation (*upanayana*) occurs immediately after the cause [of the impurity], the person to be consecrated need not perform this expiation.

Then, having performed his daily obligatory rites, the teacher—accompanied by his wife if she is present—should go from the village in an easterly or northerly direction to a place where the sound of domestic animals is not heard. Having purified such a spot as much as necessary by sweeping and smearing it with cow-dung, he should sit down there, seat the person to be initiated to his right, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), practice breath control (prāṇāyāma), and announce the place and time, [stating]: "For the sake of [so-and-so] Śarman, except for a pilgrimage to sacred fords..."

Having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) according to the specific occasion—thinking, "I shall perform the *punarupanayana* (re-initiation) for the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord, by means of accomplishing the re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) after first removing the defects arising from traveling to border regions and other such places"—one should perform the rites beginning with the worship of Gaṇapati and the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), up to the installation of the deities of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). However, in the proclamation of the auspicious day, the specific variation is that one should say, "May Agni be pleased."

Then, having served food to an even number of Brāhmaṇas and having caused them to recite the *puṇyāha*, *svastyayana*, and *ṛddhi* mantras, one should cause the person undergoing the sacrament—who has performed an auspicious bath—to eat, and then have him undergo shaving and bathing. For one of advanced age, the shaving of the hair follows immediately after the shaving of the beard and sideburns. Then follows the preparation of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and so forth.

In the rite of the *punarupanayana* (re-initiation) performed as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) during the *anvādhāna*, one should state from "with [the verse] beginning with *yāḥ*" up to "I shall sacrifice to Prajāpati with each individual oblation of clarified butter," and then continue with "to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the remainder of the offered clarified butter," and so forth. Regarding the placement of vessels (*pātrāsādana*), one should set out all vessels except for the new garment (*ahata-vāsa*), the girdle (*mekhalā*), the deerskin (*ajina*), the staff (*daṇḍa*), and the alms-bowl (*bhikṣā-pātra*).

Then, having seated Brahmā to the south, [the procedure] from the preparation of the *pavitra* grass down to the handing over of the *pakva* (cooked food) is performed; however, in this rite, the donning of new garments, the binding of the girdle (*mekhalā*), and the wearing of the deerskin as an upper garment (*ajinottarīya*) do not take place, because the absence of these specific acts is indicated by the word "atha" in the respective sūtras that prescribe them. Furthermore, there are no secondary oblations (*upahoma*) such as the *jaya* offerings here.

Then, having performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī according to the procedure beginning with "the fire, the grass-bundle" (*kūrca*) and so forth, [the student performs] the oblation of seven *palāśa* fuel-sticks and other rites. There is no vow here, because it has already been observed. Nor is there the practice of begging for alms; for the absence of that is indicated by the word "atha" in the sūtra prescribing it. This is because the giving of the staff and the giving of the mantra for begging are mutually connected; thus, when one related element ceases, the cessation of the other related element is also established.

The mutual relationship between these two [the staff and the garment] is established by the suffix *lyap* in the expression "having given the staff" (*daṇḍaṃ pradāya*). Furthermore, there is no giving of the first garment either, because it has already been worn. If there is a re-initiation (*punarupanayana*) for a student who has completed his Vedic studies, then the meaning of the word "rite" (*karma*) in the injunction "perform the rites consisting of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth" must be taught as referring only to that; however, the meanings consisting of service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*) and the study of the Vedas (*vedādhyayana*) need not be taught here.

If, however, there is a re-initiation for one who has not been a celibate student (*abrahmacārin*), then the sentence "Place the fuel-sticks" (*samidha ādhehi*) is omitted. The maintenance of the sacred fire for three days is as it was at the first initiation. If he is entitled to perform the fire-rituals (*agnikārya*), then the sentence "Place the fuel-sticks" is indeed present. In the initiation fire, both the fire-ritual and the three-fold food-oblation (*trivṛdanna-homa*) take place. The offering to the site-spirit (*vāstubali*) is mandatory. Whatever duties belong to the stage of life (*āśrama*) in which the re-initiation occurs, those duties must be performed.

However, where there is the undertaking of another stage of life (*āśrama*) immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*), one should discard the worn-out girdle and other items, don new ones, complete the observance of the student’s vows (*brahmacārivrata*) at the appropriate time, and then formally enter the next stage of life according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the procedure for the re-initiation (*punarupanayana*) when the original initiation was deficient in its constituent parts, in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.

Thus ends the sixth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was himself the performer of the Agnicit, Vājapeya, and Pauṇḍarīka sacrifices, and who bore the surname Okopāhva Śrīmatsāgnicit.
Now begins the seventh section.
Now, the duties of a religious student (brahmacārin) in brief. Regarding this, the Gṛhya-sūtra states as follows:

"From this point forward, remaining under this very vow, he dwells in the teacher's family and eats no pungent food, salt, or leguminous grains; he carries a staff, wears matted hair, a girdle, or has his hair matted in a top-knot; he wears ochre-colored robes or an antelope skin; he does not approach a woman; [he remains thus] for forty-eight years, twenty-four, twelve, or until he has mastered the Veda; but he must never be without his vow."

By the word "this" (*etad*), the Sāvitrī-vow under discussion—consisting of eating food free from pungent and salty substances and so forth—is referred to. He who has this vow is "one who has this vow" (*etadvrataḥ*). He should remain one who has this vow even after this point. The particle "eva" (only) is for the purpose of indicating that the vows to be mentioned hereafter also apply for three days. There are two types of religious students (*brahmacārin*): the one who dwells in the teacher’s house (*ācāryakulavāsī*) and the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). Of these two, he whose character is such that he dwells in the teacher’s house solely for the sake of knowledge is the "one who dwells in the teacher’s house."

He who, even after [the completion of] the duties of knowledge and ritual action, practices celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for the sake of the higher stages of life (*āśrama*) is a *naiṣṭhika*. Of these two, the one dwelling in the teacher’s family eats alkaline substances, salt, and *śamī* grains; the word "iti" here has the sense of inclusion. In the terms *daṇḍī* and *mekhalī*, the suffix *-in* expresses possession. In the term *jaṭī*, it expresses a constant connection. One whose matted locks (*jaṭā*) consist of nothing but the top-knot (*śikhā*) is called *śikhājaṭa*; the meaning is that he should maintain only the top-knot and have the rest of his hair shaved off.

He wears or puts on a garment or skin dyed with an astringent (kaṣāya) substance; the mention of "kāṣāya" is merely illustrative, as it may be of any color such as madder-red (māñjiṣṭha) or turmeric-yellow (hāridra). He does not approach a woman; that is to say, he does not engage in sexual intercourse. When there is an inquiry as to for how long he observes these vows, [the text states] "forty-eight years," and so forth; the practice of the vow lasts for forty-eight years, twenty-four years, twelve years, or for as long as his study [of the Veda] takes.

He who has no vow is "one without a vow" (*avrata*). But he should certainly not remain without a vow. The word "but" (*tu*) is used for this purpose: that even when the previously resolved period has elapsed and the Veda has not been mastered, one should not be without a vow before the *samāvartana* (the student's return home), but rather, possessing the vows, one should continue to study. Furthermore, as the author will state regarding the law (*dharma*), that one should study even after returning home until settling down [in marriage]; the particle "indeed" (*eva*) is used so that even while studying in the teacher's house, one should certainly not be without a vow.

Since the injunction "he should indeed be one who observes vows" (*vratī tveva syāt*) would suffice [to establish this], the statement of two prohibitions—"not one without vows" (*nāvrata*)—is for the following purpose: even when settled [in the teacher's house], should he encounter some hardship or distraction, he must not remain without vows for any length of time while living in the teacher’s family. In the *Dharmasūtra*: "He should not sing, nor weep, nor be a spectator of dancing. Singing refers to anything other than the *Sāman* chants. Weeping is the shedding of tears. He should not perform either of these two.

The meaning is that one should not be a spectator of dancing, nor have a habit of watching it. Likewise: "One should not look at a naked woman; having cut [parts from] herbs and trees, one should not sniff them; one should avoid shoes, an umbrella, and a vehicle. For one who gazes [upon such things], a transformation of the mind occurs. Therefore, one should not look at a naked woman. "Herbs" (oṣadhyaḥ) are those that perish at the ripening of their fruit. "Trees" (vanaspatayaḥ) are those that bear fruit without flowers. This is also an elliptical designation for creepers and shrubs.

One should not pluck their leaves or flowers and smell them. By the use of the word "plucking," there is no fault in incidentally catching a scent. *Upānahau* refers to sandals; *chatram* is well known; *yānam* refers to a cart and the like. The word *hi* is intended to indicate other such items. Yama says: "The girdle, the deer-skin, the staff, and the sacred thread—at all times..."
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), however, should wear a loincloth and a waist-string.

"A twice-born man who has undergone initiation (upanayana) shall perform the tending of the fire, the practice of begging for alms, sleeping on the ground, and what is beneficial for his teacher until his formal return (samāvartana).
Here, "tending of the fire" refers to the ritual of offering fuel to the fire, known as *samid-abhyādhāna*. —From the Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra.

A Brahmin, indeed, when undertaking the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*), enters into these four parts. The fire is one foot, death is one foot, the teacher is one foot; his fourth foot remains within himself. When he places fuel upon the fire, he thereby ransoms that foot of his which is in the fire; having consecrated it, he deposits it within himself, and it enters into him. Then, when he impoverishes himself, becomes a mendicant, and wanders for alms while practicing the life of a religious student, [he ransoms] that very foot of his which is in death.

"He purchases it; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him. Then, when he obeys the word of his teacher, he purchases with that very act the foot which is in the teacher; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him. Then, when he studies his private recitation (*svādhyāya*), he purchases with that very act the foot which is in himself; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him. And elsewhere in this same [text]:

"If he should not find anyone else from whom to beg, he may even beg from his own teacher’s wife, or even from his own mother; he should not go seven nights without begging, for there is a fault in the non-performance of begging. If he has failed to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he should perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of chastity). All the Vedas enter that man who knows this and practices it in this way. Just as a fire, when well-kindled, shines brightly, so indeed does he shine after his bath who, knowing this, practices the life of a student (*brahmacarya*)—so says the Brāhmaṇa, so says the Brāhmaṇa. Thus says Vyāsa.
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas should go for alms every day;
they should do so either only in the houses of their own caste or among all castes."
In the *Bhaviṣya*:

"Or indeed, one may wander through the entire village if those previously mentioned are unavailable, with the exception of the lowest castes, O mighty-armed one; thus said the Lord, the All-pervading One."

The last [of the four castes] is the Śūdra. In the Dharmasūtra: "In the evening and in the morning, he should practice the wandering for alms with the sacred formula (mantra); when begging, he should avoid those of low birth (apapātra) and those who are accused of crimes."

"By *amatra* means by a vessel. Those from whom vessels used for cooking and other purposes have been removed, along with members of the four castes, are *apapātras*; these include those of inverse castes (*pratiloma*), such as washermen, and the accused (*abhiśasta*) and the outcast (*patita*). The meaning is that one should practice the mendicant's round for alms (*bhikṣācaryā*) apart from these.

Even according to the views regarding all castes or all villages, cooked food must never be accepted from a Śūdra; thus says Aṅgiras: 'In the event of distress, one may take raw food from him for a single night.'"
The impurity of raw meat is purified by the ritual preparation for those who accept it from them in accordance with the Dharma.
"Therefore, those who are composed in mind may accept raw grain even from a Śūdra; however, they should not beg for even a tiny amount of raw grain from Caṇḍālas, outcasts, or the like."
It purifies (*pūyati*) and cleanses (*punāti*). In some places, the reading is exactly the same.
Vyāsa stated that one should wander for alms among those of the same class without distinction; regarding this, Manu specifies:
"Among those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, and who are praiseworthy in their own duties..."
"A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), being self-restrained, should fetch alms daily from the houses [of householders]."

Those who are not devoid of the Vedas—whether by means of all the Vedas, two Vedas, or even one—and who likewise are not lacking in sacrifices, and who moreover are praised for performing the duties prescribed for their own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*); from the houses of such persons, one who is purified and observant of rules, being a *brahmacārī* (one who practices a vow for the sake of the Veda, i.e., Brahman), should collect alms every day. In the word *bhaikṣam*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of a collection according to the rule *abhikṣādibhyo ’ṇ*.
Regarding this, that same author states an exception to begging in certain cases:
"One should not beg in the family of the guru, nor among the families of one's paternal or maternal kin."
"But if houses belonging to others are not available, one should resort to each preceding one."
"In the family of the Guru. Some say this means "in the house.
However, it has been stated by that very same author:
"Whether it be his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal sister..."
He should beg for alms first from her who would not treat him with contempt.

Thus, this [verse] refers specifically to the alms-round (*bhikṣā*) which is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the initiation (*upanayana*). The first word *vā* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The words *mātṛ* and so forth have their well-known meanings. *Nijā* means a uterine sister. The meaning is that he should beg even from her who does not refuse—that is, who does not show contempt (*avamāna*) or disregard (*avajñāna*) by saying "it is not given.
And so Āśvalāyana says:
"He should first beg from one who does not refuse, or from a woman who does not refuse."
Gautama states that if [alms] cannot be obtained elsewhere, one may beg even from one's teacher and others:
"In the absence of [alms] elsewhere, [one may beg] from the teacher, kinsmen, and gurus.
The meaning is that one should beg even from the teacher, kinsmen, and gurus when alms cannot be obtained elsewhere.
Yama says: "One should never collect alms in excess of what is required for food;
for he who collects more than that out of desire incurs a fault."

The meaning of the second half of the verse is that if one should take more than what is required for a meal—that is, more than the necessary amount—out of desire or willfully, then he would be joined with fault, that is, sin. By the use of the word "kāmataḥ" (out of desire), it follows that there is no fault in taking more unintentionally.
As stated in the *Dharmasūtra*:
"Having collected that [alms-food] and placed it before his teacher, he should announce: 'This is alms-food, O Sir...'"
"One should eat what has been thus prescribed by him.

Having brought that alms-food into the presence of the teacher and having placed it right there near the teacher, one should announce to him, "This is the alms-food, sir. Then, one should eat the food that has been prescribed—that is, authorized for consumption—by that teacher. This is how it was explained by the author of the *Ujjvalā*.
Likewise:

"When away from home, one should not act for one's own sake by begging from others—even from other *śrotriyas*—if one is away from the presence of one's guru or the teacher's family; having returned from his journey, he should offer the alms-food into the fire and then eat."

If the Guru is away on a journey and not present, then one should announce, "This is alms-food, sir," to the Guru’s family—that is, to his wife, sons, and so forth—and eat what is provided by them. In the absence of the Guru, one may also announce it to other Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) along with those kinsmen; the construction of the sentence follows this by adapting the verb to read, "one should eat what is provided by them.
Gautama also says:
"In his absence, [one should seek alms] from his wife, son, or fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*)."

"One whose purpose is the Self alone" (ātmaprayojana) means one for whom the Self is the sole objective. Such a person should not go out for alms; the meaning is that he should not go for alms solely for his own sake. The inclusion of the term "ātmaprayojana" is for the purpose of ensuring that the rule to be stated later—namely, "when even those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) are not available, then one who is away from home (*proṣita*) should eat after having offered [a portion] into the fire"—is applicable.

The meaning is that a student (*śiṣya*) who is away from home, whether his purpose is to serve his teacher or his own, should, in the absence of a teacher's family or a *śrotriya*, take a small portion of the food obtained by begging and, having cast it into the fire, then eat.
Likewise:

"Having eaten himself, he should wash his vessel and must not leave it soiled with remnants; if he is unable to do so, he should bury it in the ground, or cast it into water, or hand it over to a noble person, or to a servant, or to a Śūdra."

*Amatra* means a food vessel. Because of its proximity to the word "having eaten," one should wash the food vessel oneself. However, there is no fault in having the alms-bowl washed by another. Others maintain that the term refers to both vessels. One should eat only as much as one is able to consume, placing it in the food vessel. If, once engaged in eating, one is unable to continue, then one should bury that food in the ground or cast it into water.

An Ārya of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) should offer [the food] to one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*). Having placed everything in a single vessel, he should set it on the ground near him. *Antardhī* means one who possesses concealment (*antardhi*); the suffix *-in* is applied here according to the rule for words beginning with *vrīhi*. Thus, an *antardhī* is a slave (*dāsa*), for his Śūdra-status is indeed concealed. From the context, this refers to the teacher’s [slave]. The meaning is that he should offer or give [the food] to the teacher’s slave or to a Śūdra. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the prohibition against eating another’s leavings: “One established in the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*) shall not eat the food of a single person, except in times of distress.”
Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the renunciation of the eightfold sexual union.
Dakṣa describes them as follows:
"One should always protect celibacy, which has eight distinct characteristics."
Remembering, chanting, playing together, gazing, and speaking in secret;
Intention, determination, and the actual accomplishment of the act—
wise men declare this to be the eightfold sexual union.

Prajāpati has declared that celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is lost when there is the opposite [of its proper conduct]. Regarding the word "lost" (*naṣṭam*), the word "it becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. One should not meditate, one should not speak, and one should by no means listen [to improper things].

"One becomes a perfected ascetic (*yati*) through all of these, and not otherwise. Thus, longing, recollection, verbal praise, and gazing [upon women] are forbidden. *Keli* refers to external activities such as jesting and the like. *Guhyabhāṣaṇa* is secret consultation for the purpose of sexual union. *Saṃkalpa* is mental action. *Adhyavasāya* is the determination for sexual union. "One belonging to one master" means having a single owner. A specific rule regarding eating alms-food is stated in another Smṛti:
"One should always worship food and eat it without disparaging it.

Worship here consists of prostration; in some versions, the reading is simply "one should always bow to food. "Without disparaging" means without censuring. By the word "always," its universal applicability is indicated.
In the *Dharmasūtra*:
"A sage's meal consists of eight morsels, that of a forest-dweller sixteen,
that of a householder thirty-two, and that of a student is unlimited."

The sage who is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) has eight morsels for his food; the forest-dweller, the forest-hermit (vānaprastha), has sixteen; and the householder has thirty-two. The meaning is that there is no restriction on the number of morsels for the student (brahmacārī) seeking knowledge or for the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika).
Furthermore, it says in that same place:
"The one who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni), the ox, and the student—these three..."
"They succeed only while eating; there is no success for those who do not eat.

By this, it is understood that even for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), although the previous verse established a rule regarding the number of morsels due to his status as a householder, there is no restrictive rule regarding the times of eating. The meaning is that since the fetching of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and fuel-sticks (*samidh*) is mandatory for one who maintains the fires, and since service to the teacher is a necessary duty for a student (*brahmacārin*), optional vows (*kāmyavrata*) and the like—which would cause physical weakness and thus conflict with those duties—are not fit to be practiced. The mention of the ox (*anaḍut*) is for the sake of illustration.
Regarding this, Hārīta states the rule for the vessel:
"One should eat from a vessel made of iron or earthenware. Here, "iron" (loha) means gold, because the word *loha* is listed among the names for gold in the Nighaṇṭu lexicon.
Pracetas prohibits eating from a bell-metal vessel,
as well as the use of betel and ointments: "A mendicant, a student, and a widow should avoid betel, ointments, and eating from a bell-metal vessel."
Āhātri states regarding prohibited food:
"Alms-food given by hand, as well as salt and condiments— if these are eaten,
the eater indeed incurs impurity and the giver does not go to heaven."
Manu says:
"Whether in a vow dedicated to a deity or even in a rite for the ancestors, one may eat at will when invited; his vow is not thereby violated."
The grammatical connection is: "One who has been requested may eat according to his desire. "Requested" means entreated.
Āśvalāyana says:
"The one observing the vow [should avoid] collyrium, ointment, honey, perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains."
"One should avoid sandals, umbrellas, vehicles, turbans, chariots, and so forth."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"One should not look into a mirror, nor should one perform the cleaning of teeth;
one may use the remnants of the guru's food for medicinal purposes, but not out of desire."
Vasiṣṭha also says: "If one is ill, one may at will eat all the remnants of the guru's food for the sake of medicine."

The term *vyādhitaḥ* (afflicted) contains the suffix *-itac* in the sense of one who has acquired a condition. The inclusion of the word *sarva* (all) is for the purpose of encompassing all things that are unfit to be eaten, such as meat, garlic, and so forth. Having been freed from his affliction by eating those [forbidden things], he should worship the Sun. Accordingly, Baudhāyana, concerning the consumption of forbidden food, states: "When he has become free from disease, then, having risen, he worships the Sun with [the verse]: 'He indeed sits in purity... etc.
"He is the sick man. The word division is *agadaḥ*. "Ha saḥ śuciṣat" is one *ṛc*. In the *Dharmasūtra*:
"When there is a gathering of teachers and alms have arisen, the alms are dependent upon whichever teacher one is currently following.

When a student (*māṇavaka*) who is studying a second or third Veda encounters a gathering of teachers—that is, when several teachers are assembled—then, when alms have arisen, it has been explained by Ujjvalākāra that "the alms are dependent upon whichever teacher one is currently following, from whom one is studying at that time."
And furthermore: "Upon returning from his studies, he should give [the fee] to his mother; the mother shall send him to her husband; the husband shall send him to the teacher."

Having performed the *samāvartana* ceremony, he should give to his mother what was acquired prior to marriage. The mother should cause him to go to the husband—that is, she should lead him to her spouse. And he [should give it] to the teacher of the youth; this is the completion of the sense, as explained by that very same author.
Bṛhaspati says: "These eight do not destroy one's vows: water, roots, fruits, milk," and so forth.
"The sacrificial oblation, the desire for Brahman, and the word of the teacher are medicine."
*Brāhmaṇakāmyā* means the desire of a Brāhmaṇa.
Yājñavalkya states:
"Honey, meat, collyrium, leavings, white [garments], women, and injury to living beings..."
"One should avoid looking at the sun, vulgar speech, slander, and so forth."

*Madhu* refers to honey. As for the prohibition of intoxicants (*madya*), that is already established by the general prohibition [of *madhu*]. *Māṃsa* (meat) here includes even consecrated meat (*prokṣita*) and the like. *Añjana* refers to applying collyrium (*kajjala*) and so forth to the eyes; this is also indicative of anointing (*abhyañjana*). By extension, anointing the limbs with oil and such is also forbidden. This too applies except when prescribed by a physician, because medicine does not constitute a violation of the vow. In this context, the prohibition regarding leftovers (*ucchiṣṭa*) should be understood to apply when one is free from disease, based on the cited statement of Vasiṣṭha:
"One may use the leftovers of the teacher for medicinal purposes, but not out of desire."
This is also evident from the cited statement in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
"Harsh speech" (*śukla*) refers to cruel words, according to the dictum of Gautama: "One should avoid harsh words."
One must not look at the sun at either its rising or its setting; as it is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*:
"One should avoid looking at the sun when it is rising or setting.
This means that one should not look at the sun at the time of its rising or at the time of its setting.
Manu also says:
"One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting, nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky."
*Aslīla* is speaking of one's vital points (*marmabhāṣaṇa*). *Parivāda* is censure. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), joking and the like are included.
Yama says:
"One should avoid sleeping on a bed or seat, as well as cleaning the teeth."
"One should sleep alone on *kuśa* grass and should never spill one's semen.
Manu says:
"Gambling, idle gossip, jesting, and likewise falsehood..."
