"A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should avoid looking at or touching women, causing injury to others, and sleeping on beds or seats.
Gambling refers to playing with dice; public gossip refers to news of the country.

Gautama states: "In the presence of the guru, one should avoid covering the neck, using a waist-band (āvasakthikā), leaning on [the back], stretching out the feet, spitting, yawning, laughing, and cracking the knuckles. Covering the neck means concealing the neck with a cloth. An *āvasakthikā* is a yogic belt (*yogapaṭṭa*). Leaning on it means resting it against the hips or other parts of the body. Spitting is the discharge of saliva. Cracking the knuckles refers to slapping the arms and so forth. Hārīta says:
"One should avoid mounting horses, chariots, elephants, sacred trees, or bulls, as well as crossing great rivers and performing acts of great daring.
Gobhila says: "One should avoid scraping [the body], cleaning the teeth, washing the feet, and so forth.
Scraping refers to grooming the hair on the head with a comb or similar instrument. Washing the feet refers to rubbing them with an unguent or washing one foot with the other.

In the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra: "One should not look at urine or feces; having seen something impure, one mutters: 'The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights; O consecration, do not abandon me.'"
And this should be understood as common to householders and others alike.
In the Prāyaścittakāṇḍa of Parāśara:
"Having addressed a guru with 'huṃ' or 'tuṃ', or having defeated a Brahmin in debate..."
"In a waterless region in the forest, he becomes a brahmarākṣasa."
Regarding his expiation, Baudhāyana says:
"Having defeated a Brāhmaṇa in debate,
one who desires to perform the rite of expiation should fast for three nights, bathe, prostrate himself, and ask for forgiveness."
In this context, the mention of *vāda* (debate) is intended to include by implication the *huṃkāra*, *tuṃkāra*, and *chala*.
The definition of *chala* was stated by Akṣapāda Gautama in the first chapter of the *Nyāyasūtra*: "Chala is the subversion of a statement through the fabrication of an alternative meaning."

The statement of a refutation by imagining a different meaning for a word that was employed with a different intention. For example, regarding the sentence "This Devadatta has nine blankets," which was uttered with the intention of [the word *nava* meaning] "new," one imagines a different meaning and offers a refutation: "He does not possess nine blankets because he is poor; since even two are not possible for him, how could he have nine? There are three types of quibble (*chala*): quibble regarding words (*vākchala*), quibble regarding generalities (*sāmānyacchala*), and quibble regarding figurative usage (*upacāracchala*).

The characteristics of a *tallaka* (teacher) should be sought in that very same [text]. Devala and Baudhāyana state the fruit of service (*śuśrūṣā*): "Just as a man digging with a spade obtains water, even so does one who desires to serve obtain the knowledge residing in the teacher."
Yama speaks of the fault in failing to perform [service]:
"Just as food mixed with poison, or poison mixed with food, so too is the Veda studied by one who does not serve; of this there is no doubt."
Regarding this, Nārada states another means:
"Knowledge is acquired through service to the teacher, or by abundant wealth, or else by knowledge;
a fourth [means] is not found."
In another Smṛti:
"Having bathed daily and become pure, one should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors,
as well as the worship of the deities and the twilight prayers."
Jaimini states: "As long as there is no instruction in Brahman, there is no performance of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and so forth;
but once instruction in Brahman has occurred, one should perform the rituals such as the twilight prayers."

The *gāyatrī* is the *brahma*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the twilight rites, etc.," the *brahmayajña* (study of the Veda) is included. The essential meaning is that this [recitation] must be performed daily by means of the *gāyatrī* from that day forward, following the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsanā*), for as long as even a small portion has not been studied. A religious student (*brahmacārin*) must not perform any actions such as carrying a corpse. If he does so, the penance consists of a *kṛcchra* and a re-initiation (*punarupanayana*).
Thus says Devala: "A religious student shall not perform actions such as carrying a corpse."
"If one should do so, he must perform the Kṛcchra penance and undergo the rite of re-consecration once again."

The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes ornaments and the like, but not burning and the like, because the penance for those acts is more severe. Since the prohibition of actions motivated by greed is already established by the general statement, the specific prohibition directed at the *brahmacārin* is intended to prohibit even those actions performed for the sake of *dharma*. Otherwise, it would be redundant.
Manu also says:
"The teacher, one's own sub-teacher, mother, father, and guru..."
"But having carried out the deceased, the observer of the vow is not deprived of his vow."
In the *Mitākṣarā*, Gālava states:
"A disciple should perform the *pitṛmedha* (funeral rites) for his deceased preceptor;
he becomes pure there after ten nights together with those who partake of the funeral meals."

And this refers to cases other than those involving one's mother, father, preceptor (upādhyāya), teacher (ācārya), and maternal grandfather. Thus it is said in the Kālādarśa: "One who observes a vow should perform the funeral rites for his mother, father, preceptor, teacher, and maternal grandfathers; he does not fall from his vow."
Thus says Saṃvarta: for him there is no lapse of ritual duty (*karmalopa*). And likewise in the Candrikā:
"Even that man who is a student (*brahmacārī*) when his father, mother, or guru passes away..."
One who observes vows should also perform the rites for the funeral cakes and the water libations for the fire.
"Therefore, one should not observe impurity, nor should the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) be omitted;
the fire-ritual (agnikārya) must be performed daily, both evening and morning."

As long as one performs that person's funeral rites, for that long there is indeed impurity. As it is said: "If a student (brahmacārī) should perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) for his father, there shall be impurity for that duration; he becomes pure again by bathing."

Thus, from the words of Prajāpati. However, Aparārka, Mādhava, and others state that the impurity lasts for one day (*ekāha-āśauca*), and they cite this statement: "Whether it be the teacher (*ācārya*), the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), the preceptor (*guru*), or the father..."
Or having himself burned his mother, one established in the vow should take food there.
Having done so, one falls; therefore, one should not eat the food of the pretas there.
One should take food elsewhere and should not lie down with them.
The meaning is "on another day," beginning from the second day;
for it is stated in the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa]: "Having remained impure for one day, one becomes pure on the second day.
As for that which—
"A disciple, however, should perform the funeral rites for his deceased preceptor;
he becomes purified there by a period of ten nights together with those who partake of the food offered to the deceased."

This statement refers specifically to the consumption of those various funeral foods. By "the food of the deceased" (*pretāhāra*), one means the eating of those funeral meals. However, when there is another person present to perform the *aurdhvadehika* rites, there is indeed no impurity (*āśauca*) even upon the death of one's father or other ancestors. In the case of a religious student (*brahmacārī*), after his return home (*samāvartana*), he must offer water according to the order of seniority for deceased *sapiṇḍas*; this replaces all other grounds for impurity, and he must observe a three-night period of impurity. But prior to the *samāvartana*, there is neither the offering of water nor the observance of impurity.
Thus says Manu: "One who is under a formal vow (*ādiṣṭī*) shall not offer water until the completion of that vow."
"But when it is completed, having offered water, one shall remain impure for three nights."
The *Mitākṣarā* explains that one who has been initiated is a *brahmacārī*.
Yājñavalkya also states: "Those under a vow of celibacy (*brahmacārin*s) and likewise those who are outcasts (*patita*) shall not offer water [libations]."

Students (*brahmacārin*) shall not even perform the offering of water for the deceased; likewise, those who have fallen from their status (*patita*) shall also not perform it. "Fallen" refers to those who have lost their eligibility for the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*). Consequently, if a *sapiṇḍa* dies while one is in the state of studentship, marriage does not take place after the completion of the return ceremony (*samāvartana*), due to the three-night period of impurity, even if permission has been granted by one's parents. Because this is mentioned in conjunction with the offering of water, it pertains specifically to the occasion of death-impurity. Thus, in brief, are the duties of the student. Now, the vows pertaining to the Vedic sections (*kāṇḍavrata*).

There, having performed the *upākarma* (commencement) of the first book on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or even before that at an auspicious moment favorable for beginning one's studies as will be described, he should perform the *upākaraṇa* of the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍavrata* preceded by a fire-oblation (*homa*). Having studied that book (*kāṇḍa*), he should perform its *utsarga* (conclusion). This should be understood to apply likewise to the *saumya-kāṇḍavrata* and the others.

Alternatively, having performed all the *kāṇḍavratas* simultaneously (*tantra*), and practicing the vows according to his capacity, he should study all the books and then conclude those vows simultaneously.

If, however, the study is conducted according to the Sārasvata recension, then the *upākaraṇa* (commencement) must be performed by means of a single ritual application (*tantra*), and the *utsarjana* (conclusion) likewise. In this case, where the *upākaraṇa* and *utsarjana* take the form of the commencement and completion [of the entire cycle], the *upākaraṇa* and *utsarjana* for the *kāṇḍavrata* (vows for the sections) and the *kāṇḍādhyayana* (study of the sections) do not occur separately. This is because the *kāṇḍavratas* are ancillaries (*aṅga*) to the *kāṇḍādhyayana*, and thus their requirements are fulfilled by the very *upākaraṇa* and *utsarjana* intended for the study itself.

When a section (*kāṇḍa*) is not yet completed and the time for concluding a chapter (*adhyāya*) arrives, one should conclude that chapter, pause, and then, having performed the formal commencement (*upākaraṇa*) again, study the section according to its proper time; then, having studied the section, one should conclude it at the proper time and cease. Since it is currently impossible to study the sections according to their original sequence due to their being intermingled, and because the *Sārasvata* recension is also permitted by the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇikā*, study is now conducted according to the *Sārasvata* recension alone.

There is no *tantra* (common procedure) for the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and the conclusion (*utsarjana*), as these consist of the beginning and the completion [of the study]. This is because their essential natures are mutually contradictory. In this matter, everything is performed by the teacher (*ācārya*). As for the student (*brahmacārī*), he is only as far as has been specifically prescribed. Now, even though the study is conducted through the recitation of the *Sārasvata*, since a thorough knowledge of the *kāṇḍas* (sections) is necessary, the *kāṇḍas* are here enumerated according to the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇī*.
The necessity of knowing the *kāṇḍas* is as follows:

By the statement, "Even in the Sārasvata recension, mere knowledge is taught here," the intended meaning is that even in the Sārasvata recension, scholars accept that there is indeed mere knowledge concerning the sequence of the *kāṇḍas* for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). From this very statement, it is understood that the Sārasvata recension also exists.
Now, as for the sections (*kāṇḍas*).
These have been stated in the *Baudhāyana-gṛhya-kāṇḍānukramaṇa-sūtra*. Among them is the section dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatya-kāṇḍa*).

The section beginning with *iṣe tvā*, excluding the final *anuvāka*; for the third [section], the two sections beginning with *pratyuṣṭam*; the remainder of the *anuvāka* beginning with *mama nāma*, starting from *payasvatīroṣadhayaḥ*; the section beginning with *saṃ tvā siñcāmi*, excluding the final *anuvāka*; the five *anuvākas* beginning with *pākayajñam*, excluding the second *anuvāka*; and the thirteen *anuvākas* beginning with *cittiḥ sruc*, together with the *śāntis*.

"Prajāpati, the expounder of Brahman"—this refers to two questions contained within the Brāhmaṇa of the second book (*kāṇḍa*). The question beginning with "Having entered upon truth" (*satyaṃ prapadye*). The four sections (*anuvākas*) beginning with "The gods, indeed, [do not recite] the Ṛg-verse" (*devā vai na rcā*); the section beginning with "The *nivīta* [mode of wearing the sacred thread] belongs to men" (*nivītaṃ manuṣyāṇām*) and ending with "and he conquers the world of men" (*manuṣyalokaṃ cābhijayati*); the section beginning with "He who has fame" (*sa śravāḥ*); the four sections beginning with "Manu [is the lord] of the earth" (*manuḥ pṛthivyāḥ*); and the six sections beginning with "Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ" (*viśvarūpo vai tvāṣṭraḥ*).

The portion beginning with "The gods, indeed, having recited the *sāmidhenī* verses... is the remainder of the section ending with "the *nivīta*. The six sections beginning with "He sacrifices to the *samidhs*," the section beginning with "Indra, having slain Vṛtra," and the section containing the propitiatory verses (*saśāntika*) starting with "O you two, come hither" constitute the *Praśna*. This concludes the *Prājāpatya-kāṇḍa*. Now begins the *Saumya-kāṇḍa*.

The two sections beginning with *āpa undantu* and *devasya tvā*, excluding the final section; the section *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*; the section *brahma saṃdhattam*; the section beginning with *ādade grāvāṇam*, excluding the final section; the section *cittiḥ sruc* from within the [following] section, specifically the section *taraṇiḥ*; the six sections beginning with *prācīnavaśam*; the three sections beginning with *prajananaṃ*; and the four sections beginning with *devāsurāḥ* and *sa prajāpatirindram*.

The two sections beginning with "Both these [groups] indeed, the exponents of Brahman say, how many vessels? constitute the first part. The six sections beginning with "O God Savitṛ, impel" constitute the second part. The eight sections beginning with "The gods, indeed, according to their vision... constitute the third part. The section beginning with "The Trivṛt-stoma" constitutes one question. The two sections beginning with "They yoke the mind" and "The gods, indeed, performed a sacrificial session" constitute the final questions. Thus ends the Saumya-kāṇḍa. Now follows the Āgneya-kāṇḍa.

The two sections beginning with *gharmaḥ śira uddhanyamānam* [TS 5.1.1–2]; the five sections beginning with *kṛttikāsvagnimādadhīta* [TS 1.1.2–6]; the three sections beginning with *ime vā eta* [TS 1.5.9–11]; the section *bhūmirbhūmnā* [TS 4.2.8]; the three sections beginning with *devāsurāste devā vijayam* [TS 2.3.8], *parā vā eṣa bhūmirbhūmnā* [TS 4.2.9], and *dyaurvariṇā* [TS 4.2.10] ending with *ityāha*; the section *devāsurā agnīṣomayoḥ* [TS 2.2.10]; and the two sections *upa prayantaḥ* [TS 1.7.7] and *saṃpaśyāmi* [TS 1.7.8].

The section beginning with "mama nāma" and ending with "tāḥ saṃdadhāmi haviṣā ghṛtena"; the three sections beginning with "ayajñaḥ saṃpaśyāmi prajā aham" and ending with "agnihotraṃ juhoti"; and the seven questions beginning with "yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ"—in these, one should exclude the final sections of the first four questions, as well as the five sections beginning with "añjīmūtasyeva," "yadakrando," "mā no mitra," "ye vājinaṃ," and "agnermanve."

After the section beginning with *mā no hiṃsīj janitā*, there is the section *āpyāyasva madintama* together with its concluding peace-verse (*śānti*). After the section beginning with *iyam eṣā*, there is the section *īyuṣṭe ye* together with its concluding peace-verse. After the section beginning with *prajāpatir manasā*, there is the section *jyotiṣmatīm* together with its concluding peace-verse. Then follow the two sections *āyuṣaḥ prāṇam* and *indro dadhīcaḥ*. Finally, there are the seven chapters beginning with those dedicated to Sāvitrī.

In that regard, one should exclude the following: the *anuvākas* beginning with "tatra samiddhaḥ," "añjan gāyatrī," "triṣṭubjagatī," "kastvā chyati," "prajāpaterakṣi," and "pavasva vājasātaye"; the fourteen *anuvākas* beginning with "indrāya rājñe sūkaraḥ"; the thirteen *anuvākas* beginning with "rohito dhūmrarohitaḥ"; and the sixteen *anuvākas* beginning with "stegāndaṣṭābhyām. Also excluded are the section beginning with "aṅgiraso vai satramāsateti," the two *anuvākas* beginning with "udasthān" and "ni vā etasya," the two sections beginning with "saṃjñānam" and "loko'si," and the five *anuvākas* beginning with "brahma vai caturhotāraḥ. This concludes the Āgneya-kāṇḍa.
Now follows the Vaiśvadeva section (*kāṇḍa*).

It consists of the questions contained within the *Saṃhitā*, excluding the final *anuvāka* [of each], as well as the *anuvāka* beginning with "Truth indeed is Parameṣṭhin. It also includes the three questions from within the *Brāhmaṇa* beginning with "To Anumati a cake," and the two *anuvākas* beginning with "The creatures indeed performed a sacrificial session" and "Agni indeed is the year. Furthermore, it includes the four questions beginning with "One desiring [success] for Vāyu [should sacrifice] a white [animal]. Among these, one should exclude the final *anuvākas*.

Prajāpati desired, "May I create offspring. This constitutes the third book (*kāṇḍa*). In that [book], one should omit the final *anuvākas* of the five sections (*praśnas*). From the section beginning with "For the sake of food" (*iṣe tvā*) up to the end of the section ending with "Thou art a ray" (*aśmir asi*), the final *anuvākas* of each section are to be excluded, as well as the *anuvāka* beginning with "Yoke the two bay steeds" (*yukṣvā hi*) which precedes the section beginning with "They desire thee" (*uśantas tvā*). The ten *anuvākas* beginning with "Of the god" (*devasya tvā*) are the remainder of the section on procreation. The eleven *anuvākas* beginning with "To the one" (*ekasmai*). The ten *anuvākas* beginning with "Hitherward" (*arvāṅ*).

The eleven sections beginning with *meṣastvā pacatairavatu* (May the ram protect you with cooked offerings); the fourteen sections beginning with *pṛthivyai svāhā* (Svāhā to the earth); the five sections beginning with *jīmūtasya yadakrando* (When the cloud thundered), *mā no mitra* (May Mitra not [abandon us]), and *ye vājinam agnermanve* (I meditate upon the vigor of Agni); the fourteen sections beginning with *indrāya rājñe sūkaraḥ* (For King Indra, the boar); the thirteen sections beginning with *rohito dhūmrarohitaḥ* (The red one, the smoke-red one); the sixteen sections beginning with *stegān daṣṭābhyām*; and the three sections beginning with *samiddho añjan gāyatrī kaḥ tvā*.

"Prayāsāya svāhā cittasaṃtānena"—these are two *anuvākas*. "Prajāpaterakṣi," "pavasva vājasātaye"—these are two *anuvākas*. "Yo vā aśvasya medhyasya śiraḥ"—this is one *anuvāka*. The two sections beginning with "Sāṃgrahaṇyā prajāpatiraśvamedhamasṛjata" constitute two *praśnas*. The seven *anuvākas* beginning with "Aṅgiraso vai satramāsatā" are included within the *prajanana-praśna*. The ten *anuvākas* beginning with "Sādhyā vai... [constitute one *praśna*]. The ten *anuvākas* beginning with "Prajavaṃ vā... [constitute another *praśna*].

The eleven sections beginning with "Bṛhaspati desired: 'May the gods be mine,'" the ten sections beginning with "Cows indeed," the remainder of the section beginning with "These become nine days," the three sections beginning with "Whose morning pressing," the two sections beginning with "He who is beloved as the domestic lord," the section beginning with "Fat-nosed," the two sections beginning with "Being the supporter, he carries away the one who carries," and the section beginning with "May Agni protect us"—these constitute the three sections beginning with "Of Agni, the Kṛttikās. These are the three sets of three sections.

The question "svādvīṃ tvā" constitutes one section; the hymn "yuva surāmam" constitutes another; the question "sarvānvā" constitutes another; the question "añjanti" constitutes another; the question "brahmaṇe brāhmaṇam" constitutes another; and the four hymns beginning with "tubhyaṃ tāḥ" constitute others. This concludes the Vaiśvadeva Section.
The question "saśāntikaḥ saha vai devānām" constitutes the Svāyaṃbhū Section; and the question "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ" constitutes the Āruṇa Section.

The question beginning with "śaṃ no mitra" (May Mitra be auspicious to us), together with its preceding and following propitiatory verses (*śānti*), is "We shall explain the Śīkṣā"; its deities are the Sāhitī-devatās, and its secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*) are the same. The question beginning with "ambhasya pāre" (On the further shore of the waters), together with its propitiatory verses, is the "Yājñikya" section; its deities are the Yājñikya-devatās, and its secret doctrines are the same. The two questions beginning with "brahmavid bhṛgur vai vāruṇiḥ" (Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, was a knower of Brahman), together with their propitiatory verses, belong to the Vāruṇī-devatās, and their secret doctrines are the same. However, Mātṛdatta has included only the *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* as an optional supplement.

The sections beginning with the Āruṇī, however, are not included at all. In that ritual manual (*kalpa*), the Bhadra-praśna is included within the Āgneya-kāṇḍa because of its commonality as a *Kāṭhaka* text. The remaining five praśnas, due to being the final part of the Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa, are included therein. According to the view that the Svāyaṃbhuva-kāṇḍa is separate, it should be understood that they are included in that very section, as it is the final one. This is the study according to the division of *kāṇḍas*. Regarding the Rudra and the Āraṇyaka, there is a specific distinction mentioned in the Anukramaṇikā:
"The Hotṛ-pravargya-kāṇḍa and those which they know as the Upaniṣads..."
The Aruṇa-āmnāya and the Vidhi are indeed proclaimed in the Kāṭhaka.
"Rudra, Nārāyaṇa, Medha, and this Pitriya—
neither Rudra nor the Āraṇyaka may one who has not taken vows hear."

The *Hotṛcitti* and the *Sruk* constitute one question (*praśna*). The *Pravargyakāṇḍa* and the section beginning with "The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session" (*devā vai satram āsata*) constitute two questions. The Upaniṣads—the three beginning with *Śīkṣā*—constitute three questions. The *Aruṇaketuka* and the *Bhadra* constitute one question. The *Āmnāyavidhi* and the section beginning with "He indeed [performed]" (*sa ha vai*) constitute one question. The *Rudra* and the section beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra" (*namas te rudra*) constitute one question. The *Nārāyaṇa* and the section beginning with "From the waters" (*ambhasya*) constitute one question. The *Pitṛmedha* and the section beginning with "Beyond, O youth, together" (*pare yuva sam*) constitute one question.

One who is devoid of vows, such as eating only once a day (*ekabhakta*) and celibacy (*brahmacarya*), is not even worthy to hear all of this, much less to study it. *Aruṇa* and *Āmnāyavidhi* constitute the *aruṇāmnāyavidhī*; these two are proclaimed in the *Kāṭhaka*. The meaning is that they are designated by the name *Kāṭhaka*. The passage beginning with "the *Hotṛ-pravargya-kāṇḍa*" and ending with "the *pitriya*" is intended to illustrate the [specific] designations. It is called *āraṇyaka* because it is to be studied in the forest (*araṇya*). Now, regarding the *divākīrtyas*:
"The *Kārīryas*, the *Pitryas*, and wherever there is the term *divākīrtya*."
The two anuvākas beginning with "Rudraḥ" and "Saṃtatiḥ" are for the Sātrika [rite].
And at the conclusion of the Hotṛ-vidhi, there are four Anuvākas:
among the Sūktas, that which is addressed to Sūrya, and this one concerning Medha and the Pitṛs.
"All the Kāṭhaka texts and all the Āraṇyakas, as well as the Divākīrtis—this is the extent of the branches; such is the traditional teaching."

The four *anuvākas* beginning with "kārīryo mārutamasi marutām" [are for the *Kārīrī* sacrifice]; those for the *Pitrya* [rites] are "somāya pitṛmate," "uśantastvā havāmahe uśantaḥ," "indro vṛtraṃ hatvā," "vaiśvadevena vai prajāpatiḥ prajā asṛjata tā varuṇapraghāsaiḥ," "agnaye devebhyaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ," "surāvantaṃ barhiṣadaṃ suvīram," and "uśantastvā havāmahe ā no agne suketunā"—these are the *anuvākas*.

The phrase "divākīrtya" refers to that which is in the [specific] anuvāka, and [the compound] means "that [anuvāka] and this Āditya [hymn] are in this [section]. "Rudro namaste" is the [opening of the] praśna. In the four anuvākas of the Sātrika [section], there are two anuvākas called "divākīrtyas"; the meaning is that they are in the context (prakaraṇa) related to the Satra.

Since the requirement [of the *daśahotṛ* formulas] is already established by the rule "at the *divākīrtya*" and so forth, the statement beginning with "the continuity" (*saṃtati*) is intended to ensure that the doubt regarding the non-application of the rule "at the *divākīrtya*" does not arise, because the Brāhmaṇa section is dependent on other [texts]. The "Hotṛ-vidhi" (the injunction for the Hotṛ) consists of the seven sections of the question beginning with "Prajāpati desired: 'May I create offspring; he created this Daśahotṛ'. The "end" (*avasāna*) of that refers to its pause or completion.

The meaning is that when that [condition] exists, the four sections beginning with *prajāpatiḥ so'ntarvān* are the *divākīrtya*. As it is said: "A twice-born man should recite on that day those sections beginning with *garbha*. And: "That which is the third [section] in the Brāhmaṇa of the second book..."
On that day, one should indeed recite the four final sections of its [the Veda's] Anuvākas.

From the agreement between these two statements, this meaning is obtained: among the *sūktas*, that *sūkta* which is dedicated to Sūrya—that is, having Sūrya as its deity—beginning with "Sūrya [illuminated] the goddess Uṣas" and ending with "Sūrya is the soul of all that moves and stands"; and that which is the *pitriya medhaḥ* (the ancestral sacrifice) concerning the question "In the highest assembly," that is the *divākīrtya*. This is the meaning.

Although [the term] is already established by the statement "the Kārīrīs and those pertaining to the ancestors" (*pitrya*), the specific mention of "the Medha which pertains to the ancestors" (*pitriya*) is for the purpose of establishing the technical name (*saṃjñā*) "the Pitriya Medha" as the answer to the question "What is *pare yuvā sam*? The *Kāṭhakas* are so called because they were spoken by the sage who originated the Kaṭha branch of the Veda. These consist of eight sections: five layers (*citayaḥ*) known as the Sāvitra, Nāciketa, Cāturhotra, Vaiśvasṛja, and Āruṇaketuka; among these, the section beginning with "Saṃjñānam" is the Sāvitra layer.

The section beginning with "The world is yours" (*loko'si*) is the Nāciketa piling (*citi*). The section beginning with "Brahman indeed is the four *hotṛ*s" (*brahma vai caturhotāraḥ*) is the Cāturhotra piling. The four sections beginning with "That which is immortal" (*yaccāmṛtam*) constitute the Vaiśvasṛja piling. The section beginning with "Auspiciousness for our ears" (*bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ*) is the Āruṇaketuka piling. These are the five *citayaḥ*. The collection of sacrifices known as the Divaḥśyenī is one; the collection of sacrifices known as the Apādyā is another. Among these, the two sections beginning with "For you, for the gods" (*tubhyaṃ devebhyaḥ*) constitute the Divaḥśyenī collection of sacrifices.

The two sections beginning with "By austerity the gods [attained divinity] from among the gods" constitute the collection of sacrifices known as the *Apādyā*. Thus, there are two collections of sacrifices. The eighth is the *Svādhyāyabrāhmaṇa*, which is the injunction for the study of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). That consists of the section beginning with "Together indeed with the gods. It is the Brāhmaṇa that contains the injunction for the *āmnāya*—that is, for the study of the sacred tradition—which is found within this section; by this, the inclusion of the entire section is established.

These eight *kāṭhakas*, beginning with "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ" and ending with the *Nārāyaṇa* sections, as well as the *āraṇyakas*, are the *divākīrtyas*. The meaning is that they are to be recited only during the day (*divā*), not at night. In the Taittirīya branch, one must make this restriction, that these alone are the *divākīrtyas*; this is the meaning of the final half-verse.
One should perform the daily libation (*tarpaṇa*) for these *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis; it is stated in that very same place: "Then, being pure, [one should satisfy] these *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis with handfuls of water."
"One should always satisfy [the ancestors] with food without distraction, especially on the new moon, full moon, and eighth lunar days."

Now, immediately after the study of all the *kāṇḍas*, being undistracted and pure, he should daily—every day—satisfy these *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis with handfuls of water. The meaning is that on the *parvan* days—the new moon, the full moon, and the eighth days—he should satisfy them even with food. Since this is not mentioned in the [original] Sūtra, it is optional (*kṛtākṛta*). It should be understood that there is an abundance of merit in performing it, but no transgression in omitting it.

Even for the study [of the Veda] according to the *Sārasvata* recension, knowledge of the sequence of the *kāṇḍas* is indeed required; a statement to this effect has already been cited previously. In response to the inquiry as to who this person named Sārasvata was and what the *Sārasvata* recitation consists of, the following historical account (*itihāsa*) is presented: In the assembly of Brahmā, Durvāsas was singing a *sāman*. Seeing him to be fierce in his splendor, Sarasvatī smiled in the midst of the assembly. Thereupon, the enraged sage cursed Sarasvatī, saying, "Be born in a mortal womb."

Then the goddess propitiated him, saying, "O Blessed One, may I give birth in the house of a brahmin. Thereupon, that sage said, "So be it," and departed. Consequently, she was born in the house of Atri. Then, having obtained a husband who was a knower of the Vedas, Sarasvatī gave birth to a son who was a treasury of learning. Then, once the initiation ceremony had been performed for his son Vidyānidhi, his father taught him the Sārasvata Veda according to the traditional order of the elders.

Then, because he was a child of little intelligence, his father struck him on the back with a bamboo splinter. Thereupon he wept. Seeing this, she too embraced her son and became deeply distressed. Vāgīśā restrained him, who was filled with tears, again and again; then she reflected: "Whose son indeed is not [dear]?"
"Having obtained me, this child, my son who is dearer than life, is being beaten.

Then Sarasvatī taught all sixty-four arts, the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), and everything up to the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) to Sārasvata. She also taught him the restraint of breath (vāyudhāraṇā) which wards off hunger and thirst.
Thereafter, having completed his education, that sage lived in Kurukṣetra.
The highly fortunate one performed austerities that are extremely difficult even for the gods to perform.
Then, after a long time, it is said that a drought occurred.
In Kurukṣetra, all the sages beheld the sage Sārasvata, who was joyful and well-nourished, sustaining the internal wind within himself. All those munis said to him, "O Lord, give us some food."
Enough with vegetables, O brahmins, even if there were vegetables on this earth!
The sage Sārasvata said to them, "Give Caṇḍikā [this];
O son, I shall give you vegetables if you are indeed satisfied with those vegetables."
Then the Sage indeed made her propitious as Śākambharī;
consequently, all the sages sustained their lives by subsisting on vegetables.
Even when the famine had ceased, they did not then remember their Vedic studies.
They rushed at one another, shouting at the top of their voices,
so that the sages completely forgot the Vedas.

Then, while the sages were in extreme distress, Nārada said to them, "Go to Sārasvata, who has completed his study of all the Vedas, and perform your studies there. Thereupon, they entreated Sārasvata, saying, "O Blessed One, please grant us instruction. Thus requested, Sārasvata taught the sixty-four thousand Vedas to the sixty-four thousand groups of sages. Consequently, those followers of the various branches studied those Vedas in their entirety.

However, the followers of the Taittirīya branch, having completed their study in its entirety and seeing that the Taittirīya branch was distinct from all other Vedas, said to one another: "Oh, what a great wonder! He has taught us a branch that is unlike all others, as if he had created it by making us fools. Thereupon, all the followers of the Taittirīya branch gathered together and said to Sārasvata: "This is not the Veda taught by you, because it is distinct from all other Vedas.
Then Sārasvata spoke these words to all the eminent sages:
"If this Veda does not exist, I make this solemn vow:
I shall enter the fire; you have heard my word."
All the sages said to him:
"O Brahmin, regarding the words you have spoken, if it concerns the sequence of the Vedas, we make this solemn vow."

Then all the sages, accompanied by Sārasvata, went here and there to other sages and said, "We are not able to reach a definitive conclusion. Having been told this, they went to Brahmā and reported their respective pledges. Brahmā also spoke to the sage Sārasvata: "The pledge made by the venerable Sārasvata is true. The recitation of the Vedas must be studied according to the sequence prescribed by Sārasvata; otherwise, there is no fruit from the study. Thereupon, he spoke to the other sages.

It is true that the sequence for performing a ritual does not necessarily follow the sequence of the text. Therefore, according to tradition, one should not enter the fire [to die] when all [the Vedas] have been mastered. However, the study of the Veda must certainly be carried out according to the sequence of the *kāṇḍas* or by way of the *Sārasvata-pāṭha*.
Thus says the Śruti:
"Therefore, one's own portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) must be studied; whatever seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu*) one studies, by that very one his desired goal is accomplished."
One's own recitation (*svādhyāya*) is one's own branch (*śākhā*).
As stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda:
"In this context, by the word *svādhyāya*, only one's own branch is understood."
By this, the priority and necessity of the study of one's own Veda are stated, but not the cessation of the study of a second Veda.
And thus, [the rule]—"Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda, in due order"—is not contradicted.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"The Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good for the twice-born;
whatever season of study one may pursue, one shall obtain the fruit of that very one. Thus it is stated in the *Smṛtisāramuccaya*.
He in whose body the Veda resides is not smeared by sin;
he should be known as the very soul of the Veda—for what purpose are physical bodies?
As many syllables of the Vedas as have been recited by the twice-born, so many names of Hari have been proclaimed; of this there is no doubt.
He whose Veda and sacrificial altar are lost for three generations is indeed called a "bad Brāhmaṇa," excluded from all ritual acts.
The daily rites, the occasional rites, the rites performed for specific desires, and whatever other Vedic ritual there may be—
all these become fruitless for a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas.
A twice-born man who, though having studied many scriptures, does not study [the Veda],
shall fall into hell and suffer destruction until the end of the Brahmā-cycle.
That Brahmin who, though having studied the Vedas, does not proceed according to the rules of conduct, does not obtain the fruit of his conduct; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
The son of a Brahmin who has not studied [the Vedas], even if he is endowed with learning, should be known as a Śūdra’s son; he does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas.
"Endowed with Vedic study means being engaged in the study of the Vedas.
Due to the lack of practice regarding the Vedas, the transgression of proper conduct, laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins."
In the Bṛhannāradīya: "That twice-born man who studies the scriptures without having first studied the Vedas should be known as equal to a Śūdra; he falls into hell."
And furthermore:
"Viṣṇu, who consists of the Brahman of sound, is remembered as the Veda itself, which is Hari manifest;
indeed, the brahmin who studies the Veda shall attain all desires."
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa must necessarily study the Veda. In that regard, the practice of the Veda is fivefold. And so says the Smṛti:
"First, the acquisition of the Veda; then reflection, repeated recitation, and silent chanting."
"And that gift [of knowledge] to disciples, as well as the fivefold study of the Vedas. Even there, at the outset, the Veda transmitted through tradition must be recited. And so says Vasiṣṭha:
"Those whose Veda, along with its supplements, has come down through tradition..."
"First, one should study that [Veda] and perform the rituals belonging to its branch."

The meaning is that one should first study the Veda as it has been handed down in its traditional succession, together with its supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*) such as the *chandas* (metrics) and other [auxiliaries], as well as the secondary supplements (*upāṅga*) such as the *mīmāṃsā*. As stated in the *Vārāha*:
"If one, having first recited his own *śākhā*, should then recite another..."
"But for every syllable of the Gāyatrī, one obtains double the fruit."
Vyāsa says: "The entire Veda, along with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows prescribed by the Śruti."
The secret is the Upaniṣad.
Vasiṣṭha states the fault in abandoning one's own branch [of the Veda] to take refuge in another branch:
"He who, having abandoned his own branch, takes recourse in another branch..."
He should be excluded from all ritual acts by virtuous people, just like a Śūdra.
A wise person should never perform a ritual prescribed in another branch [of the Veda];
one who performs what is prescribed in another branch is called a "branch-thief" (śākhāraṇḍa).
"Having studied his own Vedic branch, he should then study another branch;
once consecrated by the sacraments belonging to that [other] branch, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa."

The word *jātu* means "at any time whatsoever. By those belonging to that branch (*tacchākhīyaiḥ*), meaning by those who have studied their own specific recension, one should recite even the eight *vikṛtis* (elaborations) if one has the capacity, because they are mentioned in the *Śāṅkhāyana-brāhmaṇa*. Their characteristics are to be understood from the *Taittirīya-prātiśākhya*, the *Bahvṛca-prātiśākhya*, the *Śikṣā*, and other such works. Since in the *Taittirīya-prātiśākhya* authority is found only regarding the *jaṭā* and subsequent *vikṛtis*, the study should extend only that far, even if one has the capacity. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Bahvṛca-araṇyaka* that the study of the *saṃhitā*, *pada*, and *krama* is optional (*kāmya*).
"One desiring food and drink should recite *nirbhuja*; one desiring heaven, *pratṛṇṇa*; and one desiring both, that which is between the two.

The uninterrupted recitation of the junction (*saṃdhi*) between two words or two syllables is called *nirbhuja*, which is the *saṃhitā-pārāyaṇa*. The pronunciation of two words without their junction is *pratṛṇṇa*, which is the *pada-pārāyaṇa*. The meaning of [the phrase] "between these two, *nirbhuja* and *pratṛṇṇa*" is that it is neither merely *nirbhuja* nor merely *pratṛṇṇa*, but rather such a thing as the *krama-pārāyaṇa*.

The division of the recensions (*śākhābheda*)—whether based on differences in study or differences in the Sūtras—has been elaborated upon by the author of the *Vaijayantī* in the introductory section (*upodghātagrantha*).
Furthermore, the lineage of sages who studied this particular recension, as well as the fact that this recension takes the form of a bird, a bull, and a tree, is stated in the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇikā*:
"Vaiśampāyana taught this recension to Yāska and to Paiṅgi."
Yāska, Paiṅgi, and Tittiri spoke it to Ukha; Tittiri [spoke it] to [his disciple].
Ukha taught this branch to the illustrious Ātreya;
because it was composed by him, this branch is called the Ātreyī.
In that [recension], Ātreya is the author of the word-list (padapāṭha) and Kuṇḍina is the author of the commentary;
the learned who master that great branch attain great prosperity.
One should contemplate the Bird, who is equal to Brahman, having three heads, shoulders like the sun, nine souls, eight tails, and thirty-two wings.

The two suns are the shoulders of this Supreme Upaniṣad, the Lord of the World; its trunk consists of the nine [Upaniṣads], while those prescribed by Kaṭha are known as the tail—the eight [Upaniṣads]—and whatever remains, those two constitute the wings.

The Bull is the essence of mantra, with Dharma as his horns, the Upaniṣads as his hump, the Vedas as his limbs, and the Caturhotṛ formulas as the mark upon his forehead; he is the knower of the musical scales.

The wise say that this path leading to heaven consists of the Śākhās and other branches, beginning with the *Ādi*, free from evil, comprising both ritual injunctions and mantras, and extending as far as the *Samā*.
The Veda is a tree whose roots are the secret teachings, whose leaves are the Ṛgveda, whose flowers and sprouts are the Yajurveda,
whose branches are the Sāmaveda and Atharvaveda, and which is frequented by the bees that are the Brahmins.
"This glorious Brāhma tree is the manifest fruit of sacrificial rites;
the wise Brahmin who knows it shall attain fame and, together with the Ṛṣis, go to heaven."

Formerly, the Vedas existed as one. Seeing that those who studied the various Vedas were unable to perform the study of the entire Veda, and for the sake of establishing the mastery of the whole Veda as well as for the benefit of the world, Vyāsa divided the Vedas and established them according to their respective branches (*śākhā*).

Thereafter, the Blessed One taught the Yajurveda to his disciple named Vaiśampāyana. Then Vaiśampāyana taught this Taittirīya branch to the sage named Yāska. And that Yāska [taught it] to Paiṅgi (though *Paliṅga* is also a reading; the latter is consistent with our Sūtra).
From him, the sage Paiṅgi [received it] from Tittiri; he [taught it] to Ukha; and he to Ātreya. *Yaśasvī* is an epithet of Ātreya.
He states his illustriousness itself by means of this [statement]: "Therefore, this branch is called the *Ātreyī*."

This branch was brought forth and taught by that Ātreya to others, and thus it acquired the name "Ātreyī. Such is the glory of Ātreya, whose Ṛṣi is the author of the *Padapāṭha* for this branch, while the commentator is the Ṛṣi Kuṇḍina. The learned who have studied such a great branch attain great prosperity and auspiciousness.

Now, he describes the nature of the bird that constitutes this Veda consisting of the branches—beginning with "three-headed" and ending with "possessing the *caturhotṛ* as its crest-mark. One should contemplate such a bird: three-headed, with the sun for its shoulder, nine-fold in essence, eight-tailed, and thirty-two-winged. The meaning is that whoever knows this shall go to the world of Brahman, which is esteemed by Brahman. In the reading *brahmasaṃmitam*, it serves as an adjective qualifying the bird.

The *Uttamā-upaniṣad* consists of the *Śīkṣā*, the *Brahmavid*, and the three questions of Bhṛgu. Their status as "supreme" (*uttama*) is due to their extensive utility for the knowledge of Brahman. He whose two "arcs"—meaning shoulders—are the *Pravargya-kāṇḍa*. The Lord of the World (*bhuvanasya patiḥ*) is Prajāpati, according to the Śruti: "Prajāpati, indeed, is the Lord of the World. Those nine sections of Prajāpati—beginning with the *Śākhādya*, the *Yājamāna*, and so forth, and ending with the words "of whom he is the knower"—are said to be his body.

The eight *Kāṭhakas* taught by the sage who founded the *Kaṭha* branch are known as the tail—that is, the part situated at the tail—by those who know the Veda (the remainder being understood). Furthermore, whatever remains of the section (*kāṇḍa*), namely the remaining thirty-two sections, constitute the two wings of that bird; such is the nature of the bird. Now, the nature of the bull:

He whose self is the mantra-portion—that is, whose very essence consists of the mantras—is the Mantrātman. He whose two horns are the two *gharma* sections in the *Pravargya-kāṇḍa*; he whose mouth consists of the eight *Kāṭhaka* sections is the "Eight-mouthed" (*aṣṭāsya*). The *Upaniṣads* are his hump; the remaining Brāhmaṇas are his limbs, thus he is "Limb-vidhi" (*vidhyaṅga*). The mantras beginning with "The four *Hotṛ*s are consciousness, the ladle... together with their Brāhmaṇas are his ornaments, thus he is "Ornamented" (*lalāma*). He who knows this bull in its true form becomes a knower of heaven (*svarvit*)—this is the meaning.

Those whose own branches and so forth are their "sva-śākhā-ādyāḥ," those other Vedas are the "ādiḥ"—the root—of which [tree]; one should understand this as a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound. It is "vipāpmānam," free from impurity; "vidhimantramayam," consisting of both Mantras and Brāhmaṇas; "sakam," accompanied by bliss; and "samāntam," having an end that is even and devoid of unevenness. The wise seers (*manīṣiṇa ṛṣayaḥ*) say that such is the path, the way to heaven (*divaḥ*). The essential meaning is that the study of the Vedas and the performance of the rites prescribed therein alone constitute the path to heaven. Now, the nature of the tree: The meaning is as follows: 1. *Svaśākhādyāḥ*: Those for whom their own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*) and others are the beginning. 2. *Ādiḥ*: That of which they are the origin or root (*mūlam*). 3. *Tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhiḥ*: This is to be understood as a possessive compound where the qualities mentioned are included in the reference. 4. *Vipāpmānam*: Free from stain (*vigata-kalmaṣam*). 5. *Vidhimantramayam*: Consisting of the nature of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. 6. *Sakam*: Endowed with happiness (*sukha-sahitam*). 7. *Samāntaḥ*: That which has an end (*antaḥ-prāntaḥ*) that is uniform and free from irregularity (*vaiṣamya-rahitah*). 8. *Divah panthānam*: The path or road to the celestial realm (*svargasya mārgam*). 9. *Manīṣiṇaḥ ṛṣayaḥ āhuḥ*: The wise seers declare. 10. *Tātparyāḥ*: The intended purport is that the study of the Vedas and the practice of the actions enjoined therein are indeed the path to heaven. 11. *Atha vṛkṣasvarūpam*: Now, the actual form of the tree.

The Upanishads are its secret root; the Rigvedic verses are its leaves; the Yajurvedic formulas are its flowers and its sprouts; the Samavedic chants and the Atharvavedic hymns are its trunks and branches; it is frequented by the Brahmins who are like bees; its fruits are the sacrificial rites; and this glorious, beautiful tree of Brahma manifests as the very form of Brahman itself.

He who would know—that is, understand—that tree, that brahmin, together with the seers (*ṛṣi*), having attained and reached holy fame in this world, shall go to *svaḥ*, meaning heaven; such is the meaning. In the reading *sa harṣirvipraḥ*, the meaning is that he is a seer, or a brahmin equal to a seer. The particle *ha* is used for emphasis. The fruit of knowing these seers is also stated in the *Anukramaṇikā*:
"The knower of the Vedas who, while reciting the Yajurveda, knows these seers..."
"He attains union with the sages as well as the same world as Brahmā."

The meaning is that he who, while reciting the Yajurveda, knows these aforementioned sages, attains union (*sāyujya*) with the sages and residence in the same world as Brahman (*sālokya*). The entire Veda, along with its meaning, must be studied.
As it was said by Parāśara:
"The meaning of all the Vedas should be known for the successful accomplishment of all rites."
"One who studies merely the recitation sinks like a cow in the mud"— here, "mud" (paṅka) means mire.
Yāska also says:
"That which is grasped but not understood, which is merely recited as a sound,
never blazes like dry fuel in a fire that is not lit. He who, having studied the Veda, does not know its meaning, is indeed a mere pillar, a bearer of burdens."
"He who knows the meaning attains all auspiciousness; with his sins shaken off by knowledge, he goes to the heavenly realm."

The Mīmāṃsakas also state, during the occasion of commenting on the opening sūtras of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā—namely, *athāto dharmajijñāsā* and *athāto brahmajijñāsā*—that the study of the Veda must be accompanied by its meaning.
Regarding the nature of the Yajurveda, it is said in the *Tribhāṣyaratna*:
"The Yajurveda has tawny eyes, a slender waist, and a broad neck."
"He has large cheeks, black feet, copper-colored [hands], and is born of the Kaśyapa lineage. Thus it is said.
In the *Caraṇavyūha*, his height of one span (*prādeśa*) is also mentioned.
Now, regarding the auspicious time for study (*adhyayanamuhūrta*), the *Saṃgraha* states:

"One should avoid the month of Kumbha when the sun is in its northern course, especially for the commencement of learning, the undertaking of vows, and the shaving of the head. Thus it is stated in the Smṛtisāra.
"The commencement of learning, the initiation vow (vrata), and the tonsure ceremony should not take place during a *galagraha*.

The *galagrahas* have been described in the determination of the time for the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*). Regarding the days of the week, Mārkaṇḍeya, in the context of the commencement of learning, says:

"On the days of the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter, this person becomes learned. Here, *dineśa* means the Sun; *bhṛgu* means Venus; and *sujña* means Mercury. Vasiṣṭha says: "The commencement of learning is ordained on a Sunday during the forenoon."
"On Monday, during the afternoon, the weighty Vidyā is prescribed."

Maheśvara spoke concerning the lunar mansions: "The commencement of the first [rite] is traditionally held to be auspicious in the triad beginning with Hasta, as well as in the mansion of Nirṛti, in the first and last of the Pūrvas, in Aśvinī, in the mansion of Mitra (Anurādhā), and in the five beginning with Mṛga."

"On a day of the three lunar days sacred to Hari (the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth), on a day of the Sun or Venus, and on a lunar date other than those known as *anadhyāya* (days unfit for study) and so forth, provided that the benefic planets are situated in the *kendras*."

The triad beginning with Hasta refers to the constellations Hasta, Citrā, and Svātī. Nirṛtibha is the constellation Mūla. Pūrvā refers to the triad of the Pūrvās (Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā). Antyabha is the constellation Revatī. Aśvibha is the constellation Aśvinī. Mitrarkṣa is the constellation Anurādhā. Haribhatraya consists of Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj. Sūri is Jupiter (Bṛhaspati). Bhṛgu is Venus (Śukra).

The meaning is that the commencement—the very first beginning—of the sciences should be performed on lunar days (tithis) that are conjoined with or occupied by benefic planets situated in the angles (kendras), excluding the days forbidden for study (anadhyāya-dinas) and the initial days following such prohibitions.
Furthermore, the *Rājamārtaṇḍa* states:
"The commencement of learning is auspicious when the Moon has attained its awakening during the month of Madhuripu (Jyeṣṭha)."
"When the auspicious and sharp-rayed Venus has risen, and Jupiter—the preceptor of the thirty gods—is also risen;
when one is engaged in Vedic study; having left behind the Sun-god who is situated in Leo and joined with the hot-rayed [Sun];
on the days of Venus, the Sun, or Mercury; and when Jupiter is situated in a quadrant (kendram) and no malefic planet is present."

Madhuripu is Viṣṇu; when he has attained awakening (bodha). When the moon (śaśāṅka) is auspicious, and when the sun (tīkṣṇadyuti) is also auspicious. When Jupiter (tridaśapatiguru), the preceptor of the gods, and Venus (śukra) have risen and not yet set. Having left behind Jupiter—who is honored by the gods and situated in Leo (siṃhastha)—along with the sun (kharakiraṇa), on the day of sacred study (svādhyāya).

The meaning is that the commencement of learning is auspicious when Jupiter—the preceptor of the gods—is conjoined with any one of Venus, the Sun, or Mercury, and is situated in a quadrant (kendrastha), provided it is not in an inauspicious [sign] nor located in a prohibited position. For it is said: "Non-study days, the evening twilights, the sixth lunar day, and likewise the Rikta days, must always be avoided with great effort during the commencement of learning."
The procedure for the worship of Gaṇapati, Hari, Lakṣmī, and the Guru, which will be described at the beginning of the section on syllables (*akṣarārambha*), should also be performed here.
Regarding specific days for specific scriptures, Nṛsiṃha says: "One should study all the Vedas and the Śāstras on Sunday."
The Kāmaśāstra, the Mahātantra, and likewise the Vaiṣṇava treatise which destroys disease.
On a Monday, one may constantly obtain the science of anatomy (aṅgaśāstra), the science of medicine (bhiṣakśāstra),
as well as the science of minor arts (kṣudraśāstra), the science that destroys one's lineage (kulaghna), and treatises on warfare, fire, and weaponry.
The employment of missiles and weapons occurs when Mars (Kuja) is rising in its own division;
likewise, the science of Yoga, the Great Tantra, and the non-dual path dedicated to Brahman [occur under similar conditions].
One should begin singing, dancing, and the science of erotics on a Monday;
one should commence all the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs on a Thursday.
One desiring prosperity should commence auspicious dance and instrumental music,
as well as the worship of Śrī and the study of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, on a Friday.
"On a Sunday, one should not recall either auspicious or inauspicious scriptures;
if the commencement of learning occurs on the day of Saturn or during its divisional period (vāra/daśā/aṃśa),
it leads to the destruction of even the Purāṇas for men— of this there is no doubt."

The *kāmaśāstra* is well known. The *mahātantra* refers to the science of mantras (*mantraśāstra*). The *rogaghna* is the science of medicine (*bhiṣakśāstra*). The *vaiṣṇava* is that which sets forth the mantras, worship, and so forth of Viṣṇu. By the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the term *mahātantra* here refers to those [tantras] other than the Vaiṣṇava. The word *tathā* (likewise) is for the purpose of connecting these with Sunday (*sūryavāsara*). [Thus it is said: "One should practice the *kāmaśāstra*, the *mantraśāstra*, and so forth on Sunday."

This is because of corroboration from other statements. *Aṅgaśāstra* refers to the science of physiognomy (*sāmudrika*). *Kṣudraśāstra* refers to the teachings of the Buddhists and others. *Kulaghna* refers to the science of malevolent magic (*ābhicārika*). Since it is a *mahātantra*, practice on Sunday would otherwise be obtained [by general rule], but that does not apply in this particular case; rather, its practice should be performed on Tuesday. By the word *raṇa*, the science of wrestling (*mallaśāstra*) is meant, since the employment of missiles and weapons is mentioned separately later on. *Vāda* refers to the science of legal procedure (*vyavahāraśāstra*).

The *Agniśāstra* is the science of constructing fire-engines and the like; by this, all arts (*śilpa*) are to be understood as implied. The *Yogaśāstra* is well known. The *Mahātantra* refers to the Sāṃkhya, Nyāya, Dharmaśāstra, and so forth. *Advaita* is the Vedāntaśāstra. *Brahmanaiṣṭhika* is that which expounds the duties of the ascetic stage (*yatyāśrama*). The *Gītakādi* refers to the science of music composed by Nārada and others. *Nṛtya* is that composed by Bharata. *Maṅgala* is the science of ornaments and the like. *Śrīkāma* is that which bestows prosperity.
It is stated in the *Pratāpamārtaṇḍa* and the *Jyotirnibandha* that a sneeze at the time of beginning one's studies does not cause harm:
"In the case of taking medicine, mounting a vehicle, sitting, lying down, eating,
the commencement of learning, and sowing seeds, a sneeze is not harmful."
Thus ends the time for commencing study. Now follow the duties of the teacher.
Regarding this, Yama says:
"Having always risen at dawn and performed his daily obligatory rites, the teacher should perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) and thereafter instruct the disciple."
Manu also says:
"One who is about to teach, being alert at the proper time, should say, 'Recite, sir! and should pause when saying, 'May there be a stop.'"

In the phrase *adhyāpayiṣyamāṇaḥ*, the word *guruḥ* (the teacher) is to be understood as the ellipsis. In the phrase *ārabhet*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is inherent; thus, the meaning obtained is "he should cause the student to begin. Alternatively, *ārabhet* may be taken exactly as it is heard [in the root text], meaning "he should desist from teaching. In the Smṛti:
"One listener should sit to the right, or two, or more, according to available space."

The meaning of this is as follows: one listener-student should sit to the south, or else two students; or else many students—there is no fixed rule regarding their seating according to the available space. In another Smṛti it is said:
"The Guru, having sipped water (ācamana) and being seated upon his seat, facing the east..."
"Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should always cause the disciple to study."
In that very [text] it is said:
"For the purpose of practice, one should employ a rapid tempo; for the purpose of performance, a medium tempo;
and for the purpose of instructing disciples, one should employ a slow tempo."

For the purpose of practice—that is, for the purpose of studying the Vedas—one should know that the recitation should be rapid or swift. For the purpose of performance—that is, for the purpose of ritual action during the recitation of mantras—one should know that the recitation should be moderate. For the purpose of instructing disciples—that is, for the purpose of teaching students—one should know that the recitation should be slow; such is the meaning.
Yājñavalkya says:
"Those who are grateful, free from malice, intelligent, pure, capable, and not envious..."
"One should properly teach according to the Dharma those who are capable and who bestow knowledge, wealth, and [other] acquisitions upon their preceptors."

"Grateful" (*kṛtajña*) means those who recognize a favor received. "Non-malicious" (*adrohin*) means free from malice. "Intelligent" (*medhāvin*) means possessing the faculty of retention (*dhāraṇā*). "Pure" (*śuci*) means clean. "Healthy" (*kalpa*) means free from disease. "Envious" (*anasūyaka*) refers to those whose nature is not to expose the faults of virtuous people. "Capable" (*śakta*) means capable of service. "Trustworthy" (*āpta*) means non-deceptive. "Givers of knowledge" (*jñānadāḥ*) means givers of learning. "Givers of wealth" (*vittadāḥ*) means givers of material goods preceded by a formal offering (*arpaṇa*). The mention of "dharma" (righteousness) is an indicator for "artha" (wealth). [Objection: But does this not contradict the rule that one may teach even for the sake of wealth? [Response: No, because there is a traditional legal injunction (*smaraṇa*) prescribing penance for both teaching for a fee (*bhṛtakādhyāpana*) and studying for a fee (*bhṛtādhyayana*).
And likewise, Viṣṇu states in the Prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa of Parāśara:
"Having studied for hire, or likewise having taught for hire,
one should drink barley-gruel for three fortnights by way of providing instruction [for such a person]."
Not so; for teaching preceded by a prior agreement regarding remuneration is prohibited, whereas [teaching] for the sake of one's livelihood is not contradictory. Therefore, Manu says:
"Where neither dharma nor artha exists, nor even service of that kind, there knowledge should not be imparted, like seed sown in barren soil."
The meaning is that there is an absence of merit (*dharma*) in the imparting of knowledge to one who does not perform what is enjoined or to an atheist.
Yama also says:
"Where neither merit nor wealth exists, nor even a desire to learn of that kind..."
"One must die with one's knowledge; one should not sow it in the mouth of the unlearned."

Regarding the meaning of the word *anuyoga* found in the sentence "having performed the teaching for hire" (*bhṛtakādhyāpana*) just cited, the *Mitākṣarā* states: "Anuyoga is the insulting of a Brāhmaṇa or other [student] who is studying. Manu further states that even one who imparts knowledge is to be taught: [Manu 2.141: "One should not teach a person who does not offer a seat, nor one who has not brought forward the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); nor one who acts with hostility, nor one who is devoid of faith. [Manu 2.143: "But one who imparts knowledge to those who are not wealthy, who are humble, and who have come from a distance, should be honored as a father by them. [Manu 2.145: "One should not teach a person who is ill-behaved, nor one who is without faith; nor one who is averse to the Vedas, nor one who is a thief; nor one who is a slanderer, nor one who is cruel; nor one who is a drunkard, nor one who is a glutton; nor one who is a liar, nor one who is a cheat; nor one who is a hater of Brahmins, nor one who is a womanizer; nor one who is a gambler, nor one who is a servant; nor one who is a physician, nor one who is a messenger; nor one who is a seller of soma, nor one who is a usurer; nor one who is a seller of meat, nor one who is a spy; nor one who is a seller of horses, nor one who is a bard; nor one who is a seller of poison, nor one who is a seller of weapons; nor one who is a seller of human beings, nor one who is a seller of liquids; nor one who is a seller of milk, nor one who is a seller of ghee; nor one who is a seller of sesame seeds, nor one who is a seller of salt; nor one who is a seller of fur, nor one who is a seller of skins; nor one who is a seller of wool, nor one who is a seller of cotton; nor one who is a seller of fruit, nor one who is a seller of roots; nor one who is a seller of flowers, nor one who is a seller of vegetables; nor one who is a seller of grass, nor one who is a seller of fire; nor one who is a seller of fuel, nor one who is a seller of charcoal; nor one who is a seller of stones, nor one who is a seller of earth; nor one who is a seller of lead, nor one who is a seller of tin; nor one who is a seller of lac, nor one who is a seller of silk; nor one who is a seller of wool, nor one who is a seller of cotton; nor one who is a seller of hemp, nor one who is a seller of flax; nor one who is a seller of grain, nor one who is a seller of oil; "The son of a teacher who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, of a reliable lineage, a provider of wealth, and virtuous— such a person may be taught according to the Dharma."
Knowledge itself declares that those who are envious and so forth are not to be taught:
"Knowledge indeed approached the Brahmin, saying: 'Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is envious, nor to one who is not upright, nor to one who lacks self-control; thus shall I become powerful.'"

In another Śruti text, however, there is a different reading: *asūyakāyānṛjave śaṭhāya*. In the phrase *asūyakāyānṛjave'yatāya*, the word division is *ayatāya*. Knowledge approached a Brāhmaṇa and subsequently entreated him: "O Brāhmaṇa, protect me; guard me from those who lack the qualification [to receive me]. I am your treasure (*śevadhi*), your storehouse. The meaning is that just as a treasure bestows what is desired, so am I. He who was being entreated spoke [of the recipients] with the words beginning with *asūyakāya*.

One who, having presented his conviction to the teacher, strives with single-minded intent solely to find fault with it, and is habituated to adducing fallacious reasons, is a malicious person (*duṣṭa*) and an envious one (*asūyaka*). Trust (*viśvāsa*) is the knowledge that every word of the teacher is indeed true; he who lacks this is untrustworthy and dishonest (*anṛju*). One who, although having reached a conviction immediately after the teacher’s speech, strives to show—as if previously known—that "this was already understood" or "even now it is not understood," is a deceitful person (*śaṭha*).

In the reading *ayatāya*, the meaning is "to the impure. Therefore, both readings should be accepted. The meaning of the Śruti is: "Do not speak of me to such a person; for if it were so, I would be potent and bestow the desired fruit, but not otherwise.
Nārada says:
"Knowledge [is acquired] through service to the guru, or by means of abundant wealth."
Or else, by means of knowledge, knowledge [itself] is not perceived as a fourth."
The fourth proof:

Viṣṇu states—"One should not officiate at a sacrifice for, nor teach, nor initiate one who has not been examined; for if either the one who speaks [the instruction] or the one who asks [the question] proceeds [with such a person], one of them perishes and incurs fault. The meaning of "perishes" (*praiti*) is that he goes to death.
In the Dharmasūtra: "One should avoid teaching while lying down; one should not teach on that bed upon which one sleeps."

There is a prohibition against teaching while lying down, both by day and by night. However, there is no fault for one who studies for the purpose of memorizing his own [Vedic] texts. Regarding this, Ujjvalākāra has explained that one should not teach even while sitting on that same bed upon which one lies with one's wife at night. Furthermore, in that very same work it says:
"One engaged in formal recitation (pravacana) should not engage in sexual intercourse from the rainy season until the end of autumn."
He himself has explained that "teaching" refers to instruction, and that one engaged in this should avoid sexual intercourse during the rainy season and autumn.
Likewise:

"There is no study at night, except for the instruction of disciples; or one may teach by oneself mentally after midnight. Having risen [for study], there is no study during the latter part of the night; thus one should go to sleep."

During the night there is a suspension of study; one should neither study nor teach. However, the instruction of dharma to disciples is permitted. There is an exception to this suspension of study during the night: "Or one may reflect upon it mentally by oneself. Furthermore, teaching after midnight is also an exception. Study begins starting from the sixteenth *nāḍikā* of the night. The third part of the night is the latter part of the night (*apararātra*). Having risen repeatedly after midnight, one should teach.

One should not go to sleep nor lie down during the latter part of the night; this applies even when a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) such as that on the eighth day occurs, let alone during formal recitation (*svādhyāya*). Thus says Manu:
"Exhausted from the day's work, one should not go to sleep after having recited the Veda."
(Explained by that very same [author]):
likewise—
"There is no substitution when [the vowel] has been replaced."

An injunction such as "this must not be done by you" should not be given by the teacher to a student who has completed his studies (*samāvṛtta*). This is because such an injunction was given during the period before completion, such as "fetch the water-jar. He himself explained that regarding occasional duties (*naimittika*), one is not to be forbidden from performing them at will. Likewise: "In that regard, the teacher’s conduct toward him should be like that toward a son; desiring his welfare, never concealing anything regarding all duties, he should, being well-disciplined, cause him to grasp the knowledge, and should not [divert him] from his own tasks with obstacles to his study."

"In times of non-distress, the pupil who has surrendered himself to the teacher becomes a non-pupil if he fails to attain proficiency while remaining under the teacher. Regarding that pupil, the manner of the teacher’s conduct will now be described. Desiring to treat this disciple like a son, the teacher—expecting him to be so—should, being well-prepared, thoroughly attentive, and devoted to the task, cause him to grasp the knowledge, not concealing or hiding anything regarding any of the duties. Furthermore, in times of non-distress, he should not obstruct this disciple with impediments to his studies for the sake of his own personal interests. "Obstruction" (uparodha) means making one dependent or lacking independence.

Because of the statement "in cases of non-transgression," there is no fault if an obstruction occurs due to an impediment to study during a time of distress (*āpad*). The term *āpadyamānaḥ* contains an implied causative sense (*ṇyartha*). That disciple who, having surrendered himself to two teachers, brings about a lack of proficiency in his teacher by saying, "This has not been taught correctly; he should not be given [instruction]," is not a true disciple; the meaning is that such a person is to be abandoned. This was explained by that very same author. Likewise:
"And in the case of offenses, one should constantly reprove him through intimidation, fasting, touching water, or by ceasing to look upon him."
"Punishment [should be applied] according to the measure [of the offense], until [the student] turns away from it.

When offenses have been committed, they should constantly reprimand this student, saying, "This which you have done is improper. *Abhitrasa* means the production of fear. *Upavāsa* means the non-attainment of food during a meal. *Udakopasparśana* means bathing in cold water. *Adarśana* means acting so that he does not see himself, namely, the prohibition against entering the house. In all these cases, the suffix is applied to a causative (*ṇic*) verb form.

These punishments for a disciple—whether applied individually or collectively—are to be administered according to the measure [of the person] and the nature of the offense, until desistance; that is, these punishments continue as long as the disciple does not turn away from his transgressions. This method of striking a disciple was stated by Manu himself:
"The wife, the son, the slave, the pupil, and the uterine brother..."
"Those who have committed an offense should be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane."
In this context, because of the qualification "uterine," striking a brother born of a different womb is prohibited.
Vṛddha-Gautama also says: "The correction of a disciple should be done without corporal punishment; if that is impossible, [it may be done] with a rope or a split bamboo cane."
"One who strikes [a student] with anything other than thin [rope or bamboo] should be punished by the king.

*Śiṣṭiḥ* means instruction. "Without striking" means without a blow. If instruction is impossible without a blow, then the instruction is indeed carried out by means of a blow. And that [blow] must be with thin (*tanu*), that is, fine, ropes or bamboo splinters, but not with thick ones. The meaning is that he who strikes or hits the student with anything other than those thin ropes or bamboo splinters—such as a piece of stone or the like—should be punished by the king. Furthermore, this [striking] must not be done on the head. Thus says Manu:
"But [one should strike] on the back of the body, and never on the head; for by striking otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of a thief. Here, *uttamāṅga* means the head.
Yama says:
"The wise declare that he who, seeking wealth, causes a twice-born man to recite the Vedic chapters according to the rules during times when study is forbidden, is a defiler of the Vedas."

The Vedas are the subjects of study. In the phrase "and on non-study days," the word "and" (ca) serves to carry forward [the injunction] from the preceding half-verse, namely, "a twice-born man should cause [them] to be recited.
Vasiṣṭha states:
"For he who, having studied knowledge, does not impart it to one who requests it, does not partake in dharma."
Saṃvarta states the fruit of the gift of knowledge:
"By the gift of knowledge, one is glorified in the great world of Brahmā.
Thus, in brief, are the duties of the teacher.
Now, briefly, the duties of the student (*adhyetṛdharma*).
Regarding this, Manu says:
"One who is about to study, having sipped water (*ācānta*) according to the scripture, facing north..."
"With palms joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, wearing light garments, and with senses subdued.
Here, the *Kūrma Purāṇa* mentions performing *ācamana* twice:
"At the conclusion of the bath, at the commencement of Vedic study, and likewise upon the onset of coughing or asthma."
"Having approached a crossroads or a cremation ground, the best of the twice-born should likewise perform ācamana again, even though he has already performed ācamana, during both twilights."
He himself stated the nature of the *brahmāñjali*:
"Having joined the two hands together, one should study; for that is remembered as the *brahmāñjali*.
The meaning of "having joined" (*saṃhatya*) is "having made them joined together" (*saṃhatau kṛtvā*).

Regarding this, the *Dharmasūtra* first mentions the clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*): "But when the sun has risen, having come together with the teacher for the purpose of study, there is the clasping of the feet. The manner of performing that is explained in the section on initiation (*upanayana*). This [act] must also be performed at the conclusion [of the study].
This is because of the statement of Manu: "At the beginning and at the end of the *brahman*, the feet of the teacher must always be grasped.
Here, *brahman* means the Veda; thus, the meaning is that at the commencement of the Veda [the teacher's feet are to be touched].

Furthermore, the syllable *Oṃ* must also be uttered at the start of study, according to the *Dharma-sūtra*: "The syllable *Oṃ* is the gate to heaven; therefore, one who is about to study the Veda begins with this."
*Oṃkāraḥ* is the *praṇava*. *Brahma* is the Veda. "Beginning with this" means beginning with the *oṃkāra*. The rest is clear; thus it has been explained by Ujjvalākṛt. In the *Bhāradvāja-śikṣā*:
"At the commencement of a question or an *anuvāka*, [the syllable] 'hari' is uttered with the visarga and in a high pitch."
"There is no *saṃdhi* (euphonic combination) in the *praṇava*; at a pause (*virāma*), there shall be the *svarita* accent.

The term "questions and sections" (*praśnānuvākāḥ*) refers to questions and sections [of the text]. The meaning is: "at the beginning of whichever question or section is first. If only "at the beginning of questions and sections" were stated, the rule about to be mentioned would apply to the beginning of every question and section; to prevent this, the word "first" (*ādya*) is included. "With the visarga and high-pitched" (*savisargoccakaḥ*) means: with the visarga and ending in the nominative singular. "High-pitched" (*uccakaḥ*) means simply *udātta* (acute).

The word *hari* should be uttered in this manner at the beginning of a question, a section (*anu-vāka*), or the start of a recitation. The meaning is that when the *praṇava* (Oṃ) precedes it, one must never apply sandhi (euphonic combination) to the word *hari*. However, at a pause (*virāma*), that is, at the end of a sentence or the conclusion of the study, the word *hari* is not high-pitched (*udātta*); rather, it is always circumflex (*svarita*), meaning it should possess only the final *svarita* accent. Furthermore, the absence of sandhi applies here as well. One should first utter the *praṇava*, then the *vyāhṛtis*, and after that, the *sāvitrī*. As it is said: "One should employ the *praṇava* first, and the *vyāhṛtis* immediately thereafter."
For it is stated by Saṃvarta: "After the recitation of the Sāvitrī, one should then begin the account [of the study].
Here, "account" (vṛttānta) refers to the act of study.

Manu describes that prior to the Praṇava, one should sit upon a seat of Darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, perform the purification with purifiers, and practice three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).

"One purified by purifiers and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should sit upon Darbha grass with the tips pointing eastward; only then is one worthy of the syllable Om. Here, "prākkūlāḥ" refers to Darbha grass with the points directed toward the east.

Gautama, regarding the purification of the purifier (*pavitrapāvana*), states: "The touching of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with *darbha* grass. Haradatta explains that the "vital breaths" are the sense organs located in the head, such as the eyes and so forth; their "touching" is the cleansing (*mārjana*) of them by means of *darbha* grass. Furthermore, the syllable *Oṃ* (the *praṇava*) should be uttered even at the conclusion of Vedic study, according to the statement of Manu: "A Brahmin should always utter the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end."
Of Brahman, that is, the Veda.
Having touched the ground, one should pause. This has been stated in another Smṛti:
"Having first uttered the syllable Om, one should then proceed with the Veda."
"And having again uttered the syllable *oṃ*, one should conclude by touching the ground"—the word "recitation" (*adhyayana*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].

Even at the conclusion of the recitation, the disciple must perform the clasping of the feet; for Viṣṇu has stated that the clasping of the teacher's feet must be performed at both the beginning and the end of the Veda-recitation (*brahma*).
(In the *Vyāsaśikṣā*: "At the end of a section (*kāṇḍa*), a question (*praśna*), or a lesson (*anuvāka*), there are ten, eight, or five morae (*mātrā*s);
however, at the conclusion of entire books (*grantha*s), it is said that the duration is three times that.")

At the conclusion of a *kāṇḍa* and so forth, the durations of the pauses shall be ten *mātrās* and so on, respectively. For example, at the end of a *kāṇḍa*: *janadusriyāsu*.
