At the end of a *praśna*: *kalpayāti*. At the end of an *anuvāka*: *paśūnpāhi*. At the conclusion of entire texts (*granthas*), the pause is three times the duration of the pause at the end of a *kāṇḍa*; the meaning is that it lasts for thirty *mātrās*. For example: *samudro bandhuḥ*, *yebhyaścainatprāhuḥ*, and *om*. This is also stated in the *Sarvasammatā Śikṣā*:
"At the conclusion of an *anuvāka*, five *mātrās* are prescribed."
It should be understood that "eight" and "ten" are applied respectively to the questions and the sections (kāṇḍa).
At the conclusion of the Tantras, however, that time is held to be tripled;
the learned man, remaining unwearied, [should likewise attend] at the commencement and the end of the Veda.
One should clearly utter the Praṇava, which is Brahman, for the protection of the Vedic meters;
if it is not uttered at the beginning, the mantra flows away, and if it is not at the end, it falls apart.
The introductory syllable, when situated at the beginning of a Vedic section, consists of four morae; that which follows it consists of two and a half morae;
and the final syllable of a recitation-section (anuvāka) as well as the first syllable of a ritual action consist of three morae.

"The sounds beginning with *prārambha* are, in sequence, *nāda*, *mātrā*, *aṇu*, and *dvyaṇumātrika*; however, the sound at the commencement of the Veda is the syllable *makāra*, which consists of one *mātrā*."
*Tantra* means a book (*grantha*). In the phrase "it flows," "it falls," or "it disintegrates," the word *veda* is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Regarding the specific vow for the study of the *Kārīrī* and other rites, it is stated in the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇikā*:
"The twice-born one [should eat] food that is neither pungent nor salty, on the ground, with his mouth like an animal."
One should observe this vow for four nights during the study of the Kārīrī hymns.
Furthermore, the vow of the *kalā* is said here to be like the *kārīrī* vow;
one should not eat there like a beast, nor should one eat on the ground—such is the established rule.
Now, that which is called the *kalā-vrata* is described in the *Agnikāṇḍa*:
"Starting from the *Sāvitra* sections up to the *Oṣadhi-anuvāka*,
they bring a bundle of fuel-sticks for three days during the *Mṛgāreṣṭi*."

The meaning is that during the study of the four *anuvākas* beginning with "kārīryo mārutamasi marutāmojaḥ," this specific vow (*vrata*) must be observed. Just like the *Kārīrī-vrata*, the *Kalā-vrata*—the vow known as *Kalā*—which has been described, is to be observed during the study of the *Agnikāṇḍa*. By the phrase "sāvitrebhyaḥ," he states a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding what applies to the entire *Agnikāṇḍa*, even though [the general vow] would otherwise apply to it.

Regarding the *Sāvitra* [section]: this vow applies during the study of the eight mantras beginning with *yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ* up to the end of the section beginning with *yā jātā oṣadhayaḥ*. Regarding the *Mṛgāreṣṭi*: the meaning is that it applies during the study of the section beginning with *agnermanve*. A specific rule for the vow during the study of the *Vaiśvadeva* mantras is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*:
"Upon their commencement, there shall be celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for twelve days, sleeping on the ground, and the avoidance of pungent food, salt, honey, and meat;
furthermore, there is a fast for one night for the final [mantra]."

Regarding the employment and the formal acquisition of the mantras for those *homa* offerings and *bali* oblations according to the prescribed rules, the practitioner must observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*)—which entails abstaining from sexual intercourse—for twelve days, sleep on the ground on a bare mat, and avoid pungent substances, salt, and the like; this vow applies specifically to the one who employs them.

Others, however, maintain that this applies to the wife as well; they argue that "employment" (*upayoga*) refers to the first performance [of the rite], and thus the wife also has a right to participate therein. Regarding the statement "with the best [fire] one should go to the sky," which will be mentioned later, Ujjvalākāra explained that a fast for one night must be observed for the verse beginning with "those beings who roam. In this interpretation, the phrase "starting from 'the vow belongs only to the employer'" (*upayoktureva vratam*) is presented as showing an alternative view.
"Acquisition preceded by rules" means the acquisition of knowledge from a teacher for the sake of that [rite].

Regarding the specific rule for the study of the Bhadraprapāṭhaka, it is stated in the Anuvāka: "One should observe this vow for a year. Regarding the specific rule for the study of the Pravargyaprapāṭhaka, it is stated in the Pravargya-sūtra:

We shall explain the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, in the afternoon, having had his hair and beard shaved, and having gone out toward the east or the north, he establishes the fire on a desolate spot where no roof is visible, spreads grass around it, and causes [the student] to place four moist *udumbara* fuel-sticks—unbroken at the tips, a span in length, and smeared with ghee—while reciting these mantras one by one: "The earth is the fuel-stick... and "O Agni, lord of vows, the vow..."

With these [formulas], "I shall wander," he worships the deities according to their respective forms; then he causes [the student] to recite the beginnings of all the Anuvākas, or those of the first and the last. Then, having closed his eyes, he restrains his speech. Having wrapped his head with a new garment from left to right while facing it, he causes him to enter the village at sunset. Remaining restrained in speech, he stays either standing or sitting for that night. On the following day, having gone out toward the east or the north to a desolate place where no roof is visible, he kindles the fire.

Having strewn [the grass] all around and wrapped his face with the verse, "The birds, the fair-winged," he worships the sun with the verse, "That which has risen upward is the eye. Then he shows him six things—some say seven: fire, the sun, a water-pot, a stone, gold, and a calf; the great fire-altar is the seventh. Having first shown three, he then shows the remaining ones. Now, regarding his student life (*brahmacarya*): he should never eat at night; if he should eat, he should eat only from a vessel that has been heated, and not from one made of clay.

He should not offer a counter-oblation; he should not converse with a woman or a Śūdra; he should not carry an umbrella nor wear sandals; he should not mount a vehicle with wheels; he should not look at a social assembly, nor at those of low character, nor at palaces; he should not view a corpse; he should not bathe, nor apply collyrium, nor anoint himself with oil. || 15 ||

He should fast on the eighth day and on the festival days (parvan), and he should not sleep [in the daytime] during that very year; he should study again as long as this vow lasts for the duration of his study. When the year has elapsed, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, having established the fire in a cleared spot where no roof is visible, having strewn grass around it, and having added fuel sticks with the verses beginning "dyauḥ samit," he worships the deities with the verses beginning "āditya vratapate. Having given a choice gift to his teacher, he has his hair and beard shaved. Then, for him—

One should constantly apply oneself to the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) of the Veda; one should not study when the recitation has not been formally concluded, nor at night, nor at twilight, nor having entered upon a vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), nor after giving [food], nor after washing [the hands], nor after eating beans (*māṣa*), nor after arranging the hair, nor after shaving the hair and beard, nor after bathing, nor after being anointed, nor wearing a garland, nor being smeared with oil, nor being wet, nor while it is raining, nor when there are no clouds, nor in the shade, nor when the sun has turned away [from its zenith], nor looking at green barley, nor near a domestic animal, nor a wild animal.

Not at the edge of water, nor upon raw meat, nor having seen something fallen, nor blood, nor an empty vessel, nor palaces, nor a corpse, nor corpses; having gone out toward the east or the north, having established the fire on a barren spot where no roof is visible, having strewn it around, sitting on *darbha* grass and holding *darbha* grass, he should recite [the Veda] facing away. Or, having given a gift, when about to study, he should not speak other words at the *aupāsana* fire; when about to study, having touched the *madantī* water, he should perform the pacification with the first *anuvāka*.

"Having performed [the rite], one should study; and having studied, one should likewise perform it whenever one perceives that any ritual act has been rendered inauspicious. Having again performed the propitiatory rite (śānti), one should study. One should not study anything else after departing for the Pravargya ceremony until one has re-entered the village. One should study nothing else."

Although the word *keśa* (hair) begins with a vowel, it would normally take the first position in a compound; however, because shaving hair first is condemned in the Śruti as being characteristic of the Asuras, one does not shave the hair first, but rather shaves the beard first. *Khila* means covered or enclosed; the meaning is that it is a place where the roofs of houses are not visible. Because of the prefix *sam-* in the expression *saṃparistīrya*, the spreading [of the grass] is done with an abundance of Darbha grass, and there is no fixed rule regarding the number of blades. *Yathārūpam* means according to the specific characteristics [of each].

The word *atha* (then) signifies the absence of any interval of time. *Prabhṛtīḥ* means "beginnings. *Abhivyāhārayati* means "he causes to recite. In the event of incapacity, he causes [the student] to recite the beginning of either the first or the last *anuvāka*. *Tataḥ* means "after that," i.e., after the recitation. In the phrase *saṃmīlya*, the word "eyes" (*netre*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The word *atha* signifies the absence of any interval of time. *Ahatam* is defined by the characteristic: "new, white, unwashed, with its fringes intact, and not yet worn."

Since the requirement for circumambulation (prādakṣiṇya) is already established by the technical rule (paribhāṣā) itself, its restatement is intended to prevent the suspicion that—because wrapping the head is established by common worldly practice—the technical rule might not apply, and thus circumambulation might occasionally be performed in the opposite direction (aprādakṣiṇya). Alternatively, the word *pradakṣiṇa* may signify "favorable" (*anukūla*). [The verb] *prapādayati* means "causes to reach. "This night" (*etām rātrim*) means the night belonging to the day on which the ritual action ending with this [verse] was performed.

By the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge*, the accusative case is used to express uninterrupted connection; thus, the meaning "he should remain standing for the entire night" is established. In the event of inability, he remains seated. Here too, the phrase "restraining his speech for this night" is understood from the previous context. Because of the statement "having wrapped his face," it is the face alone that is wrapped, not the head as well. In the term *ṣaṭtaya*, the suffix *tayap* denotes a part of a number; the same applies to *saptataya*. A *mahānagnī* is a young heifer or a maiden.

Since the matter is already established by the mere mention of "the calf" and "the *mahānagnī*," the specific statement "the *mahānagnī* [places] the seventh" is intended to demonstrate that, according to the view of six [steps], there is no *mahānagnī* at all. "From the beginning" means in sequence; "facing him" (*abhyabhimukham*) means directly facing him—this refers to him (the bridegroom), as is understood from the context. Although the sequence is established by implication, this explicit statement is intended to show that there is no fixed rule of sequence regarding the subsequent items, such as the stone and so forth.

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) consists in the renunciation of the eightfold sexual union; practicing this, one should observe the prescribed duties such as not eating at night. Because of the inclusion of the word "constantly" (*nityam*), it is understood that there is no fault in eating occasionally when one is unable [to refrain]. If one must eat at night, one should do so after having lit a firebrand of *darbha* grass above [the food]. One should not use an earthen vessel; that is, one should not drink water from an earthenware bowl. One should not converse with a woman or a Śūdra.

Regarding the rule "one should not converse with a woman or a Śūdra," since the purpose is accomplished by a single negative particle (*nañ*), the use of a second negative particle indicates that while there might occasionally be no great fault in conversing with a woman on other occasions, here one must never engage in conversation even with a woman. Furthermore, one should not mount a donkey or similar animal, such as a wheel-bearer (cart).

Since the prohibition is already established here by the general prohibition [of looking at such things], this specific statement is intended to show that these acts are auxiliary to the ritual (*karmāṅga*). Therefore, if one should mount a donkey or similar animal through error or otherwise, the penance for the loss of an auxiliary to the ritual must be performed here along with the penance occasioned by mounting a donkey or the like. The same applies elsewhere. *Samāja* means a crowd of people. *Apapātra*s are *caṇḍāla*s; one should not look even at them. One should not look at mansions or houses. Nor should one look at a corpse.

By the phrase "he shall not bathe," bathing in the form of immersion is prohibited. "Parvans" refers to the full moon, new moon, and other such days. "Saṃveśana" means sleep. "In this very year he should study" means that the study of sections (*anuvākas*) and so forth must be carried out in the very same year in which this vow was undertaken. This vow is to be observed for as long as the study continues.

By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), it is indicated that within this very year, at another time, this vow (*vrata*) must be observed for as long as the study lasts during this subsequent study. When the entire study has been completed, there is no vow during the interval [of rest] in the middle; rather, the vow is strictly co-temporal with the study. When the year has elapsed—meaning it has passed—the word "constant" (*nitya*) from the phrase "having studied his own Veda" (*svādhyāyam adhītya*) is understood to apply here as well. This refers to those who have returned [to study] after having turned back [from worldly life].

Regarding *svādhyāya* (Vedic study), the rules to be described for its acquisition, retention, and recitation apply at all times and constantly. The phrase "one should not study when the Veda has not been formally concluded" (*anutsṛṣṭādhyāya*) means that this study must be performed only after the *utsarjana* (concluding rite) and not before it, even if the *upākarma* (commencement rite) has already been performed. Furthermore, from the time of the *utsarjana* until the *upākarma*, study is permitted by specific injunction despite the existence of periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*). Alternatively, the term *anutsṛṣṭa* means "not concluded"; *adhyāya* refers to the Veda.

"One who has not recited" (*anutsṛṣṭādhyāya*) refers to one by whom a chapter—meaning a portion of the Veda other than this [specific section]—has not been recited according to the rule for recitation (*utsarjana-vidhi*). Being such a person, he "should not study. This implies that this particular study must be performed only when the recitation of the other portions of the Veda has already taken place. "At night" (*naktaṃ*) means during the night; "toward evening" (*abhi doṣam*) means toward the earlier two-hour period at the end of the day, which constitutes the night (*doṣā*). "Having groomed" (*pravidhya*) means having adorned himself with a comb or similar items. "Not smeared" (*nānuliptaḥ*) means not anointed with perfumes and the like.

One who wears a garland is "sragvī" (garlanded). "Not in the wet" and "not when it has not rained"—these two are qualifiers of the location. "In the cloud" (*abhre*) is in the locative absolute; the meaning is that one should not study when there is a cloud. "Not in the shade" means not in a place not connected with the sun. "When the day has turned back" means from the middle part of the day onwards. Because of the mention of "green," there is no prohibition against looking at other barley. In the rule "not near a domestic animal nor a wild one," the phrase "near a beast" (*paśor ante*) carries over from the previous context. The ellipsis to be supplied in both cases is "one should study."

The purpose of the second mention of the negative particle (*nañ*) should be understood here in the same way as it was explained regarding the rule "one should not converse with a Śūdra. In the phrase "not raw" (*nāśṛtam*), the word "meat" (*māṃsa*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Lohita" means blood. "Utpatitam" (risen up) is an adjective qualifying blood. The word "having seen" (*dṛṣṭvā*) carries over from the subsequent rule as well. The word "should study" (*adhīyīta*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By the word "body" (*śarīra*), the bone is meant; there is a suspension of study even upon seeing this. The result of these prohibitions is that one should perform this study in a great forest devoid of people.

The "subsequent" refers to the next section of study. Since it was previously established that [the student] has completed [the first year] in order starting from the first *anuvāka*, in the second year—after having performed the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the shaving of the beard, which serve as the subsequent subsidiaries (*uttarāṅga*) to the *anuvākas* and so forth studied during the first year—he, observing the prohibitions such as "one who has not suspended his studies shall not recite," should kindle the fire for the purpose of studying the subsequent section, strew it around, and sit upon *darbha* grass.

The meaning is that, holding *darbha* grass, one should study the subsequent section while remaining right near the fire. Because of the specific statement here—"sitting on *darbha* grass and holding *darbha* grass"—only these [two] apply, and not the other previously mentioned rules ending with the shaving of hair and beard. He states another ritual option: "or having given a boon, [he may study] at the *aupāsana* fire"; that is, having given a boon, he may study in the vicinity of the *aupāsana* fire. And this giving of a boon pertains specifically to the occasion of studying in the vicinity of the *aupāsana* fire.

The word *vā* (or) implies that the granting of the boon is optional in its connection [to the preceding], or else that the word *vā* is connected to the term *aupāsana*. This latter view applies to one who is unable to go far away; furthermore, that *aupāsana* fire belongs specifically to the Guru, as he himself lacks it. Alternatively, the word *aupāsana* here is for the purpose of making known that the maintenance of the fire continues even after the initiation (*upanayana*).
And it has been stated by Baudhāyana: "The fire beginning with the initiation is called *aupāsana*; some say it begins with the taking of the hand [in marriage]."

Beginning from the *upanayana*, the maintenance [of the fire] continues until the *vivāha-homa* (marriage oblation); therein, the phrase "by means of establishing the status of the *aupāsana* fire" is omitted from the formal declaration (*saṃkalpa-vākya*) of the *vivāha-homa*. The *upākarma* and *utsarjana* rites also take place in that same location. Alternatively, the word *aupāsana* may be indicative of the household. One who is about to study—that is, one who intends to perform Vedic study—shall not speak other words, i.e., words distinct from those related to study, for as long as the study lasts.

When about to study, having touched the heated water of the *madantī* and performed the peace-chant (*śānti*) with the first section (*anuvāka*), "Homage to Speech," one should study. Having studied, one should perform the peace-chant with the final section, "May the wind be auspicious to us. Even when pausing in the middle of a chapter (*prapāṭhaka*), the final peace-chant is used; at the commencement, the first. This performance of the peace-chant applies also to those rites performed using the mantras of this chapter.

Now, one might object: "In that case, the statement 'in the rites' (nanvevaṃ karmasu) is intended to bring about peace (*śānti*) in those rites performed with mantras taught in the *Pravargya-prapāṭhaka*—namely, the gathering (*saṃbharaṇa*), the performance (*pracāra*), the removal (*udvāsana*), the ritual duties (*dharma*), and the laying down of bricks (*iṣṭakā*) and the *kulāyinī* [nest-brick], etc. If it is argued that the re-enactment of the rule for the performance of the *pravargya* is thus redundant, we reply: true, but there is no redundancy because it serves to indicate whether or not the performance of the rite of peace has already been carried out in the cases of the gathering, the removal, and so forth."

Wherever one might see anything performed that is not peaceful—that is, devoid of peace—one should know that the recitation or the ritual act has been performed while lacking peace. Having performed a rite for peace (*śānti*) there, one should then recite again and perform the ritual act once more. Although the injunction "if one should see it as not peaceful" would suffice for the purpose, the inclusion of the words "wherever" (*yatra kva ca*) is for the sake of a general rule (*paribhāṣā*). By this, it is established that even in the case of studying the entire *Āraṇyaka* section, the repetition of the study must likewise be preceded by that rite of peace.

The meaning is that for the sake of the *Pravargya*—that is, for the purpose of studying the *Pravargya-prapāṭhaka*—one should go out from the village and, without re-entering the village, one should not study any other [portion] of the Veda. The repetition of the phrase "one should study another" is intended to indicate the conclusion of the *prapāṭhaka*.
This is the specific rule regarding the study of the *prapāṭhaka*.
Viṣṇu states: "Having studied during the latter part of the night, one should not go to sleep."
In another Smṛti:
"One should devote the first watch of the night and the last watch to the study of the Vedas;
by sleeping for two watches, one becomes fit for union with Brahman."
In this context, by the word *pradoṣa* (dusk), the first watch of the night is to be understood; by the word *paścima* (latter), the final watch, because two watches are mentioned later on.
Vyāsa states that one should study only with the permission of the guru, for otherwise there is a fault: "Whether it be a verse (*ṛc*), a half-verse, a quarter, or even a single word..."
The twice-born man who takes [the knowledge] from another who is reciting it without permission.
"That Brahmin who commits theft from a Brahmin falls into hell."
Manu says:
"One should not study indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras; having studied the Veda at the end of the night while fatigued, one should not sleep again."

If conversation with a menstruating woman should inevitably occur at the time of Vedic study, what should be done? In response to this inquiry, the *Dharmasūtra* states: "One who is about to study the Veda, wishing to converse with a menstruating woman, should first converse with a Brāhmaṇa and then converse with her;
but having conversed with her, he must again converse with a Brāhmaṇa before he may study."

Ujjvalākāra has explained that if one who is about to study the Veda wishes to converse with a woman in her menses (*malavadvāsas*), he should first converse with a Brāhmaṇa and only afterwards with her; having conversed with her, he must again converse with a Brāhmaṇa before he may study. Vyāsa states:
"By students (*brahmacārin*s) wearing the girdle, deerskin, and staff..."
"The entire Veda is to be mastered by the twice-born through the acquisition of all knowledge."
The ablative case in the word *sarvajñānāt* is used in the sense of the dative; thus, it means "for the sake of omniscience.
Nārada states the means for attaining this knowledge:
"As one is afraid of a snake merely at the sight of it, and as one fears hell even from the mere mention of satiety [with worldly pleasures]..."
"He acquires knowledge from women as if they were rākṣasīs."
Contentment is a sin.
He [the same author] also mentions the causes of obstacles:
"Gambling, devotion to books, and attachment to drama..."
"Women, sloth, and sleep—these six are the obstructors of knowledge."

Gambling refers to playing with dice and the like. Devotion to books means the desire to hear Purāṇas and other texts, or merely the habit of attending to books. Attachment to drama is an intense longing for the science of dramaturgy. Women refers to constant delight in women. Drowsiness is laziness. Sleep is well known. In this way, other factors that destroy knowledge should also be understood from common worldly experience.
In another Smṛti it is said: "That which is studied relying solely on a book, and not studied in the presence of a teacher..."
"He does not shine in the midst of the assembly, like the offspring of an adulterer in the womb of a woman."
(Furthermore:
"The great anthill that is built by insects with fine particles of dust—therein lies no power or capacity; therein, exertion is the cause.")
Knowledge, when proclaimed a hundred times with a thousandfold intensity,
will come to the tip of one's tongue like water flowing toward a low-lying place.
Just as with noble horses sleeping at midnight, sleep does not remain in the eyes of those seeking knowledge; this is no wonder.
"One should not delay over food and drink, nor be bound by attachment to women;
for the sake of knowledge, one should travel even to the farthest distance, like a garuḍa or a swan."
The fruitlessness of knowledge devoid of service is stated in the *Nāradīya-śikṣā*:
"Even if knowledge, though lacking service, arrives through the qualities of intelligence, that knowledge does not bear fruit for him; it is like a barren woman in her youth."

Parāśara states that one who is engaged in Vedic study must avoid the food of a Śūdra: "For one who constantly studies, recites prayers, or performs oblations while nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food, no higher destiny exists."
The upward path is the path to heaven.
Manu says that in times of distress, one may study even from a non-Brahmin:
"In times of distress, study from a non-Brahmin is ordained."
"Service such as following [the teacher] and so forth, for as long as the study of the guru lasts."

[This refers to] from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who is not a Brāhmaṇa. "Following and service" means that merely following [the teacher] must be performed, but not tasks such as washing his feet. And this emergency situation for the student consists in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa instructor. Gautama also states:
"In times of distress, the acquisition of knowledge by a Brāhmaṇa from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa involves following and service until its completion."
The word division should be understood as *abrāhmaṇāt* and *samāpteḥ* in both cases.
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa: "They say that among all branches of knowledge, the Vedic science is unsurpassed."
Therefore, for the giver of that [gift], there is indeed the attainment of both heaven and liberation."
In the Mahābhārata:
"He who imparts to his disciples the righteous, divine Sarasvatī [the Veda] enjoys a fruit equal to that of giving land and cows."
Having performed this *upākarma* rite, one should undertake the study; so says Kārṣṇājini:
"Having performed the *upākarma* according to the Sūtra in the month of Nabhas or Nabhasya, a twice-born man should study the Vedas for five and a half months."
"According to the Sūtra" means in the manner stated in the Sūtra.
Parāśara also permits the study of even a single portion for one who is unable to perform the study of the entire Veda:
"Those who have fallen away from the fire-ritual and are devoid of the twilight worship..."
And all those who do not study the Vedas are considered Śūdras.
"Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who is afraid of a *vṛṣala*—that is, one who fears becoming a *vṛṣala*—should especially study at least a portion [of the Veda], even if he is unable to master it all.
Thus [it is said]. "Afraid of a *vṛṣala*" means afraid of the state of being a *vṛṣala*.
Laghuvyāsa says: "One who knows the Dharma should study even a single quarter-verse of the Ṛgveda by the prescribed method;
but one should never, under any circumstances, study the four Vedas by an improper method."
The fault in forgetting the Vedas is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa: "Even when knowledge has been acquired, if one forgets the scripture that was studied,
or fails to study it due to negligence, one shall become a donkey after death."
"For as many syllables of the Vedas as he has forgotten after they were recited,
for that many years shall that best of the twice-born experience birth in the womb of a donkey."

Even when the knowledge of the Vedas has been acquired, if one should forget the Śruti—even though it was studied—due to the cause of non-study (an-adhyayana), then that best of the twice-born, despite being endowed with good conduct, enters the womb of a donkey for as many years as there are syllables in the Vedic text; this is the meaning.
Thus, in brief, are the duties of the student (adhyetṛ-dharma).
However, the rules regarding the act of study (adhyayana-dharma) are to be found in the Pāṇinīya-Śikṣā, the Prātiśākhyas, the Bhāradvāja-Śikṣā, and other such works.
Now, as an incidental matter, the procedure for removing dullness of intellect:
therein, the *Ṛgvidhāna* states— "One should recite the mantra *oṣṭhāpidhānā* every ten days."
The goddess of speech, Mātṛkā, is always present at the tip of his tongue.
"One should offer oblations with the Oṣṭha-mantra; then the glory of the Vidyā will remain firm in that family.
Furthermore, one should offer the 'Three Honey' [substances] eight thousand times every year during the month of Phālguna."

In the phrase *trimadhu*, the masculine gender is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). The "three sweets" (*madhutraya*) consist of clarified butter (*ājya*), milk (*kṣīra*), and honey (*madhu*); and these must be taken mixed together, not separately. These three substances should be taken having made them equal in measure by weighing. Regarding their availability, cow-derived clarified butter and milk are primary. "Eight thousand" (*aṣṭasāhasra*) means eight thousand, or one thousand plus eight. As for the phrase "every year," since no specific number of years is mentioned, it should be performed as long as possible. For this mantra, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*) is *anuṣṭubh*, and the deity (*devatā*) is Nakulī Sarasvatī. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
"I always remember Nakulī, who resides in the blossoming lotus of the heart, who bestows radiance, who eternally paralyzes the speech of others, and who is ever-present.
As for the mantra:
"Oṃ! The mongoose (nakulī) with its lips as a lid, surrounded by teeth like a thunderbolt (pavi), the mistress of all speech—may she make me speak beautifully here.
This very mantra should be joined with the Bālā-mantra. In that [combination], there is one seed-syllable at the beginning, the second after the word *pavi*, and the third at the end.

For the purpose of increasing retention (*dhāraṇā*), the *puraścaraṇa* for the mantra "Namo Brahmaṇe" is described in the *Tripurāsiddhānta*, within the section on the greatness of Śrutadharī, preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is Anirākaraṇa; the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Bṛhatī; and the deity (*devatā*) is Dhāraṇāsarasvatī. The visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows: "May Sarasvatī—the consort of Virañci, seated upon the lotus-throne, whose lotus-feet are served by gods and demons, and who holds a beautiful book in her hand—always dance within my speech."

This mantra also, when joined with the mantra of Bālā, should be recited; it quickly bestows the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*). In that regard, the first seed-syllable follows the initial *praṇava*; the second follows the word "bhūyāsam"; and the third follows the final *praṇava*. One should drink water consecrated with this [mantra], and the attainment of Sarasvatī will occur.

Regarding the mantra found in the *Śīkṣā-prapāṭhaka*, "gīrvāṇaindvyāṃ tu yaśchandasāmṛṣabhaḥ," a *puraścaraṇa* of one hundred thousand recitations is prescribed. According to the statement, "In the Kali age, it is said to be fourfold," the *puraścaraṇa* is four times that amount. Furthermore, according to the conventions established in the Tantras, this consists of five parts, three parts, or two parts. In the absence of a specific injunction, the same applies to rites performed for desired objects (*kāmya*) and so forth.

Since it is observed in another Tantra that the ritual application (*viniyoga*) is of the same nature as the preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*), and because there is no specific statement regarding the present case, the number of recitations for the *puraścaraṇa* alone is prescribed here. Although the worship of the diagram (*yantra-pūjā*), ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and so forth are required and ought to be stated clearly, they are not mentioned; this should be understood as being due to the injunction in the *Kubjikā-tantra* that "the science of mantras (*mantra-śāstra*) must be kept secret," and out of fear of endless elaboration.
Thus concludes the procedure for removing dullness of intellect.
Now, the non-study periods (*anadhyāya*) are briefly described.
Regarding this, Uśanas says:

"One should observe a suspension of study during the solstices, the equinoxes, as well as at the times of the Lord's lying down and awakening, on the anniversaries of Manu, and on the anniversaries of the Yugas."

The meaning is: "on that day," referring to whichever day there is the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*) or the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*). The singular number is used with reference to the class [of transits]. The same applies to the term *viṣuva* (equinox). At the equinoxes, these are the scales (*tulā*) and the ram (*meṣa*). The "sleeping" of Hari refers to the day of his sleep, the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha. The "awakening" of Hari refers to the day of his awakening, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika. Regarding the specific rules for the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) occasioned by the transits and equinoxes, another Smṛti states:

"In the case of a transit occurring during the day, one should observe non-study for two nights; if at night, for two days. Likewise, in the case of a transit during the solstices (*ayana*) and the equinoxes (*viṣuva*)."

The meaning is that when the solstice (*ayana*) or equinox (*viṣuva*) occurs during the day, there is a two-day period of non-study (*anadhyāya*); and when the solstice or equinox occurs at night, there is likewise a two-day period of non-study.

The beginnings of the Manvantaras (*manvādi*) are summarized in the Hemādri: "The [Manu] is [found] by [adding] the lunar days (*tithi*) and fires (*agni*); the lunar day is [found] by the remainder of the lunar days; in the dark fortnight, the [Yuga] is [found] by the earth (*kṛṣṇa*) and the fires (*agni*); and the planet (*graha*) is [found] by the [remainder]."
"The lunar day (tithi) and the sun (arka) are not auspicious; the horse (aśva) and the lunar days beginning with Amāvāsyā are the Manvantara-beginnings of the month of Madhu."
The words are: *tithyagnī*, *na*, *tithiḥ*, *tithyāśe*, *kṛṣṇebhaḥ*, *analaḥ*, *grahaḥ*, *tithyarkau*, *na*, *śivaḥ*, *aśvaḥ*, *amātithī*, *manvādayaḥ*, *madhoḥ*. Thus [are] the words.

The lunar day (*tithi*) is the full moon (*pūrṇimā*). "Fire" (*agni*) refers to the third day. The sequence begins from *Madhu*, which is Caitra; thus, the meaning is the full moon and the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra. No, there is no beginning of a Manu-era (*manvādi*) in Vaiśākha. For Jyeṣṭha, the lunar day is the full moon. For Āṣāḍha, the lunar days are the full moon and the tenth day of the bright fortnight. For Śrāvaṇa, "the elephant" (*ibha*) refers to the eighth day of the dark fortnight. In the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, "fire" (*anala*) is the third day. In the bright fortnight of Āśvina, "the planet" (*graha*) is the ninth day.

The lunar days and suns of Kārttika are the full moon (pūrṇimā) and the twelfth day of the bright fortnight (śukla-dvādaśī). No, there is no Manvantara-beginning (manvādi) in Mārgaśīrṣa. In the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, Śiva is the eleventh day (ekādaśī). In the bright fortnight of Māgha, Aśva is the seventh day (saptamī). In Phālguna, the new-moon day (amāvāsyā) and the full-moon day (darśapūrṇimā) [are the Manvantara-beginnings]. The meaning is that these Manvantara-beginnings, starting from Caitra which is Madhu, are to be known in this sequence. Also in the Padma Purāṇa: "The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika..."
The third day of the month of Caitra, as well as that of Bhādrapada;
the new moon of Phālguna; the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa;
the tenth day of Āṣāḍha; and the seventh day of the month of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the full moon of Āṣāḍha,
as well as the full moons of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha.
"And these [times], such as the beginning of a Manvantara, cause what has been given to be inexhaustible."

The term *aśvayuḥ* refers to the month of Āśvina. In the phrase "and of Bhādrapada," the word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of carrying forward the term "bright fortnight" (*sita*). The word "likewise" (*tathā*) is for the purpose of connecting the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) even with "of Bhādrapada. In the phrase "also of Āṣāḍha," the word "also" (*api*) is for the purpose of carrying forward the term "bright fortnight. This word "also" is likewise to be applied to "of the month of Māgha"; by that, the connection of the term "bright fortnight" is established here as well. The Yugādis are described in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "The third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, and this ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika..."
"And on the thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, and [the same] in Māgha.
Nabhasya is Bhādrapada. Manu, concerning the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*), states:
"On the new moon and the fourteenth days, and on the full moon and the Aṣṭakā days. Hārīta says:
"On the first days [of the lunar fortnights], on the fourteenth day, on the eighth day, and on both the Parvan days."
"One should never study on a night when there is a suspension of study for the following day.

The first half of the verse beginning with "on the *pratipad*s," which prescribes a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) on the *pratipad* and subsequent days, does not have the same meaning as the second half, "on a night when there is a suspension for the following day. Otherwise, if the second day (the *dvitīyā*) follows immediately after a certain *pratipad* after sunrise, then since a suspension would already apply to the preceding night, the prohibition contained in this [second half] would be rendered redundant. Therefore, the phrase "on a night when there is a suspension for the following day" refers specifically to the suspensions of study occasioned by the beginnings of the Yugas (*yugādi*) and the Manus (*manvādi*).

And thus, the meaning is that one should not study on such a non-study day (*anadhyāya*) during the first part of the night on the following day (*śvas*). "On the following day" (*śvas*) refers to when the non-study lunar day (*tithi*) exists immediately after sunrise. However, if the regular study day (*svādhyāyatithi*) follows that, the learned authorities (*śiṣṭas*) maintain that there is no non-study period during the preceding night.
Yama states: "The eighth day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the student."
"The fifteenth day destroys intelligence; therefore, one should avoid these [days],"—the word "study" (svādhyāya) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.
This is a statement by Hanumān to Rāma in the *Ārṣa Rāmāyaṇa*:
"O slender-limbed one, she, emaciated by separation from you,
has become thin like the knowledge of one who studies the *pratipad* [days] of the Veda.
Thus it is said in the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*.
When the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight is seen before the setting of the sun,
one who knows the Dharma should observe a suspension of study on the thirteenth day.
"If it [the lunar day] extends to both [sides of the day], there is no suspension of study; yet some maintain that even in such a case there is suspension.
For the best of the twice-born consider there to be a suspension of study even when there is doubt.
Regarding the measurement that determines the suspension of study for the aforementioned lunar days over a full day and night (ahorātra), the *Smṛtyarthasāra* states:
The learned know that a day and night during which [the sun] remains within three muhūrtas at either its rising or its setting constitutes a period unfit for study.
Some say: "In some cases, the suspension of study lasts only as long as ten nāḍikās of the day; it does not extend to other days."

A lunar day (*cāndra-dina*) means a *tithi*. If on a given day, whether at sunrise or sunset, the day of non-study (*anadhyāya*)—which lasts for three *muhūrtas*—should coincide with that *tithi*, then on that day, that entire day and night (*ahorātra*) is known as a day of non-study; this is what the wise (*vidaḥ*) understand. (On another day, or another *tithi*: "Even by a mere fragment of the first lunar day (*pratipad*), or by a mere digit of the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*), it defiles the entire day, just as wine defiles a jar of cow’s milk.")
This statement should be understood as being based on the customs of the eastern regions.
The Smṛti in the Kālādarśa states: "On the second days of the Cāturmāsya festivals, one should avoid the study of the Vedas."
Gārgya said:
"The wise declare those second days of the months of Śuci, Ūrja, and Tapasya when the moon has waned to be the Cāturmāsya-dvitīyās."

In the term *vidhukṣaya*, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is intended; *vidhukṣayaḥ* means the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣaḥ*). This refers to the days following the full moon of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Phālguna.
Regarding the meaning that one should not study during the evening (*pradoṣa*) from the thirteenth day onwards, there is a Puranic statement:
"One desiring intelligence [should not study] on the thirteenth day, and especially on the seventh."
"And on the fourth [lunar day], during the evening twilights, one should neither remember nor recite [the Veda].
By the phrase "one should not remember," it is implied that there is a greater degree of fault here than in other occasions of non-study (*anadhyāya*).
Regarding the two-fold classification of the thirteenth lunar day and others, the determination is found in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
If one should see the thirteenth lunar day before two watches of the night have passed,
that indeed should be known as *pradoṣa*, during which all Vedic study is prohibited.
"One should not study during the evening twilight on the sixth, the twelfth, or when there is less than one *nāḍikā* remaining until midnight; nor on the third, when nine *nāḍikās* remain.

The phrase "less than one *nāḍikā* until midnight" means that it is less than one *ghaṭikā* (twenty-four minutes) before midnight. By this, it is established that in such cases, the prohibition against study based on the evening twilight (*pradoṣa*) applies only to the preceding day, and not to the commencement of the following night, even if the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*) or others should occur then. Bṛhan-Manu has described the evening twilight (*pradoṣa*) in another manner:
"On the fourth, the thirteenth, and the seventh lunar days,
one should not study until midnight if one desires its retention.
A specific rule is given in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:

"If the fourth lunar day is seen during the nine *nāḍīs* of the first watch of the night, there should be no study in the first watch; likewise for the seventh and thirteenth days. If they occur before midnight, there should be no study during the first watch of the night."
In the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"On the days of twelve, fifteen, and thirty [tithis], preceded by those [respective numbers of] days;
with half a night and one and a half watches—this is known as *pradoṣa*."

The meaning is: "by the days preceding [the respective tithis]," namely, by the days preceding the twelfth (arka), the sixth (tarka), and the third (tri). *Arka* is the twelfth; *tarka* is the sixth; *tri* is the third. The meaning is that if there is a connection with the thirteenth tithi during the first half of the night of the twelfth—consisting of two watches (*yāma*)—then it is *pradoṣa*. Likewise, if there is a connection with the seventh tithi during the first and a half watch of the night of the sixth; and similarly, if there is a connection with the fourth tithi during the first watch of the night of the third. Nowadays, the learned accept only this [definition].
Bṛhaspati has also stated that there is no study during the *galagraha* (throat-grasping) periods: "If one desires the life of a son, one should not study during a *galagraha*.

Because of the statement "if one desires the life of a son," the prohibition of study during *galagraha* applies only to those who have sons, and not to others. The *galagraha* periods were described during the determination of the time for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
In the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"One should observe non-study on all *aṣṭakā* days, on the beginnings of the *yugas* and *manvantaras*, and likewise on those [lunar days] accompanied by secondary names (*sopapada*)."
And this prohibition regarding [teaching] with the addition of explanatory words (*sopapada*) does not apply to followers of the Yajurveda:
"In the case of Vedic vows, initiation, and likewise in the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*),
there is no fault for those of the Yajurveda even when teaching with explanatory words."

Some say this is because it is stated in another *smṛti*. Others say that this is baseless (*nirmūla*), as it is not seen in the great compendia (*mahānibandha*). However, in this *kalpa*, there is indeed a prohibition even of those [days]. They have been mentioned in the section on initiation (*upanayana*). In the *Dharmasūtra*:
"Having commenced the term of study (*adhyāya*) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, for one month..."

"One should not study during *pradoṣa*. Regarding this, Ujjvalākṛt states that *pradoṣa* here refers to the first part of the night; Mādhava holds it to be the early part of the night. This prohibition applies to both the initial acquisition (*grahaṇa*) and the subsequent retention (*dhāraṇa*) of the study. Ujjvalākṛt maintains that because of the specific mention of *pradoṣa*, there is no fault in studying after that time even during the night. Following the *upākarma* ceremony, a period of non-study (*anadhyāya*) of either three days or one day must be observed.
This is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:
"They say that one should study according to the [prescribed] chapters after having waited for three days or one day.

The meaning of "having waited" (*kṣamya*) is that one should desist from study. The evidence that this non-study period (*anadhyāya*) is not permanent will be stated in the section on the *utsarjana* (concluding rite).
In the *Dharmasūtra*:

There is an option according to what is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "Some say that one should cease [studying] during the month of Taiṣya under the asterism Rohiṇī for four and a half months. According to these two views, one studies for five months. Those for whom a fifth month is half are called "four and a half"; thus some maintain that one should study for four months plus an additional half. In this view, the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) takes place on the full moon of Proṣṭhapada, because it is seen in other scriptures, and there is no postponement of the formal conclusion (*utsarjana*).

Regarding the *utsarjana* (concluding rite) performed after the *Śrāvaṇī*, Ujjvalākāra has explained that during the bright fortnights prior to it, one should engage in the *dhāraṇādhyayana* (memorization study) of the Veda, while during the dark fortnights, one should study the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) such as grammar; furthermore, having performed the *upākarma* on the *Śrāvaṇī*, one should undertake the *grahaṇādhyayana* (acquisition study) of what has not yet been mastered.
Gautama states: "There are three *aṣṭakās* and three *abhi-vārṣikas*."

The meaning is that the study which occurs after the *upākaraṇa* and before the *utsarjana* is the "annual" (*vārṣika*) study; therefore, regarding the ritual performed at its beginning and end, one must observe a three-night suspension of study.
This meaning is explicit in the *Auśanasa*:
"There is a three-day suspension of study at both the *upākaraṇa* and the *utsarjana*."
And in the *Mānava*: "At the *upākarma* and at the *utsarga*, a three-night suspension [of study] is prescribed.
Suspension (*kṣapaṇa*) means the cessation of study (*anadhyāya*). The same is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
Regarding the *Aṣṭakās*, the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra* states: "The *Aṣṭakās* occur on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons.
Hārīta includes those eighth days occurring within the *Mahālaya* period under the category of *Aṣṭakā*.
"Likewise, the Mahālayā-aṣṭamī.

By the inclusion of the word "one" (*ekā*) in this sūtra—"the eighth day of the latter fortnight of the month of Mādhya [Māgha] is called the Ekāṣṭakā"—the Teacher has made known that [this is the case].
In the *Dharma-sūtra*:

"In the case of [the death of] a mother, a father, or a teacher, there are twelve days [of suspension]"—this means that when the mother and others have died, there is no study for twelve days. This rule applies even to householders (*gṛhasthas*). Some maintain that the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for that same duration; we, however, say "no," because this is explained by Ujjvalākṛt as belonging to the section concerning the suspension of study (*anadhyāya-prakaraṇa*). Yājñavalkya states:

There is a suspension of Vedic study for three days upon the death of a pupil, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a relative; likewise, at the commencement (upākarma) and conclusion (utsarga) of the term, and when a person learned in one's own Vedic branch dies.
In the event of thunder at twilight, a lightning strike, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor, one should complete the Veda study for a day and night;
likewise, having studied the Āraṇyaka, one should do so for a day and night.
"On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, and the eighth [lunar day], during an eclipse of Rāhu,
at the transitions of the seasons, after eating, and after receiving gifts related to a Śrāddha ceremony."
A *nirghāta* is a thunderous sound arising from the atmosphere. "Day and night" means throughout the day and night (*ahorātra*). As for the statement:
"One should not recite the Veda for three days during the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) of a king or of Rāhu."

Thus, the proclamation of a three-day suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) regarding the birth-impurity of Rāhu refers specifically to the case when he eclipses the sun or moon at their setting. Vijñāneśvara states that the phrase "during the junctions of the seasons (*ṛtusaṃdhi*) on the first lunar days (*pratipat*) occurring at those junctions" applies to this. Furthermore, the rule "having accepted [food] for a Śrāddha" refers to the *Pārvaṇa* Śrāddha, because Manu and others prescribe a three-day period for eating at an *Ekoddiṣṭa* Śrāddha and similar occasions.
Moreover, he (Vijñāneśvara) says:
"By a dog, a frog, a mongoose, a snake, a cat, or a rat..."
"In the Kṛta age, however, a day and night [of Brahmā] lasts for the fall and the rise of Śakra."
As for the duration of the Śakrapāta festival: "The raising of Indra’s banner occurs on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, and its lowering takes place on the Vijayā-daśamī.
Thus it is stated in the Dharmasūtra.
"The sounds of dogs and donkeys, the cries of jackals, hyenas, and owls, all sounds of musical instruments, and the sounds of weeping, singing, and the Sāman chants."

The plural designation indicates the sounds of many dogs and donkeys. A *salāvṛkī* is a specific sub-species of wolf; others say it is a hyena (*koṣṭrī*). Since the gender is not intended to be significant, males are also included, as seen in such passages as "Indra gave the Yatis over to the *sālāvṛkas*. *Ekasṛka* (singular) refers to the jackal. *Ulūka* is the owl, which fears the day. These are their respective sounds. There are also the sounds of musical instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*), flute (*veṇu*), and drum (*mṛdaṅga*). Furthermore, there are the sounds of weeping, the sounds of singing, and the sounds of the *Sāman* chants.
The author of the Ujjvalā has explained that these, when heard, are causes for temporary suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). Likewise:

"In the forest, upon seeing [a corpse], and in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) from every direction within the range of a *śamyā*-throw; [the same applies] as in a cremation ground regarding a Śūdra or an outcaste (*patita*)."

In a forest, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for as long as a corpse or a *caṇḍāla* is visible. One should avoid studying in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). "In all directions" means within the range of a *śamyā*-throw from every side; because of the use of the fifth case ending (*sarvataḥ*), it is understood that the distance is "within" [the limit]. He himself has explained that one must not study even in the presence of a *śūdra* or an outcaste (*patita*) within the range of a *śamyā*-throw. Likewise: "And when the two hands are wet with water. From the preceding sūtra, the word "having eaten" (*bhuktvā*) is carried over. He himself has explained that one should not study as long as both hands are wet with water.
Likewise:
"One who has mounted the backs of animals should not study for that long.
He himself explained this as meaning: being mounted on the backs—that is, sitting on the backs—of animals such as elephants, horses, and so forth, one should not study for that duration of time.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"When there is the sound of dogs, jackals, donkeys, owls, the *sāman* chants, or cries of distress;
or in the vicinity of impure substances, a corpse, a Śūdra, an outcaste, a cremation ground, or one who has fallen [from his caste]."
In an impure place, or when one is personally impure; during a thunderstorm with lightning and thunder;
after eating while the hands are still wet; while inside water; at midnight; or during an excessively strong wind.
When there is a rain of dust, a conflagration of the quarters, fear during the twilights or from mist,
when running, when there is a foul odor, or when a learned man has arrived at the house.

"When riding on a donkey, a camel, a carriage, an elephant, a horse, or a boat; or when climbing a tree or ascending a mountain—these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary suspensions of study."

The *sāmānyāraṇyaka-sāmans*. Vijñāneśvara [states] that the *vāṇa* is a flute; Haradatta [states] that the *vīṇā* has a hundred strings. "Afflicted" (*ārta*) means tormented. "Impure things" (*amedhya*) refers to women who have recently given birth and so forth. "Thundering" (*stanita*) means the roar of clouds.
Regarding thunder during the twilight and lightning, there is a specific rule in the *Dharmasūtra*:

"When there is thunder following a lightning flash during the night, the suspension of study lasts until the end of the sleep-period; or when it occurs at dawn, as long as the dark clouds [of Rohiṇī] are visible, one should know that the time is such that one can perceive them from the distance of a *śamyā*-throw. When it thunders at this time, there is no study for the rest of the day along with the evening; and also during the first part of the night. According to some, however, if it thunders after midnight, the suspension lasts until the next day."

"At the junction" means at twilight. When there is thunder, that is, when the clouds roar, one should not study for the entire night. When there is lightning at the junction, [one should not study] for the remainder of the night until sleep. And this refers to the evening twilight. "Upavyuṣam" means near dawn; when there is lightning then, there is no study for the following day until the onset of *pradoṣa* (the first part of the night). After *pradoṣa*, one may study.

The syntactical connection is as follows: at such a time—namely, the time required for one to recognize a black or red cow standing within the range of a throw of a wooden pin (śamyā)—or when it is dawn, or while it is lightning. The third part of the night is the "latter part of the night" (apararātra); of that which is divided into three parts, the first portion is the "great night" (mahārātra), and its final portion is the "small [night]" (dahra).

Regarding that small interval (*dahra*), some teachers maintain that when there is thunder—the cause being the rumbling of clouds—there is a suspension of Vedic study for the remainder of the day along with the preceding evening; furthermore, they hold that from midnight onwards until the following night constitutes the period of suspension. However, their own position is that it applies only to the small interval itself. And this is to be understood as occurring during the rainy season, as explained by Ujjvalākṛt.
Hārīta, however, says: "If there is thunder at the evening twilight, the night [is forbidden]; if there is thunder at the morning twilight, the day and night [are forbidden]."
Regarding lightning, Gautama states a specific rule:

"In the case of lightning, [the suspension of study lasts] for the night, provided it occurs during the latter part of the night or the first third of the night; otherwise, it lasts until the end of the entire night. During the first part of the night, the period of non-study (*anadhyāya*) lasts until the end of the latter part of the night. If lightning strikes after the third portion of the day, the suspension continues until the end of that night. Vijñāneśvara maintains that this refers to the two middle watches (*yāma*) of the night at midnight. The *Nirṇayāmṛta* holds that it refers to four central hours (*daṇḍa*). This rule applies to occasions other than the rainy season (*varṣā*); however, during the rains, the suspension is understood to be only for the duration of the event itself. Such is the settled conclusion (*vyavasthā*) to be understood.
In the Dharmasūtra:
"Having vomited, until one goes to sleep.
The author of the Ujjvalā has explained this as: "Having vomited—that is, having performed emesis—one should not study until one goes to sleep."

Regarding this, Āpastamba has stated a specific rule: "Having vomited, or having slept, or having consumed ghee. Viṣṇu says: "One should not study while there is the sound of musical instruments; nor in the vicinity of a Śūdra or an outcast (patita); nor in temples, cremation grounds, crossroads, or on highways; nor at the edge of water; nor with one's feet placed upon a seat; nor while traveling in vehicles drawn by elephants, horses, camels, boats, or oxen; nor when one has vomited, nor when one has purged, nor when one has indigestion, nor when passing between five-toed animals."

"Having placed his feet on a seat" means having the soles of his feet positioned upon a seat. Regarding the phrase "in vehicles," the word "seated" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Vomited" means one who has performed emesis. "Purged" means one who has performed purgation. "One with indigestion" refers to one until the digestion of what was eaten is complete. "Five-toed animals" refers to dogs and the like. Manu says:
"Nor while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having placed a cloth between the knees..."
"One should not study after eating meat, nor likewise after food from a birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Regarding "prauḍhapādaḥ," Haradatta explains it as having the soles of the feet placed upon the [upper] feet, or alternatively, having the feet placed upon a seat. In another Smṛti:
"Not during a dispute, not during a quarrel, not in an army, nor in battle."
Not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor during the period of birth-impurity.
"And when blood has flowed from the body due to being wounded by a weapon."
The word "should study" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In the Hemādri, the Smṛti states:
"In a sacrifice, [the recitation is suspended] until the end of the Anūbandhyā rite for the initiated person and for the officiating priests."
Manu states:
"One should not recite the Veda for three days during the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
This means that once the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed, there is a period of non-study (anadhyāya) for the subsequent three days.

In the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*: "When in water, at midnight, after voiding feces or urine, when impure from food remnants, or after eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony— one should not even contemplate [the deity] in one's mind."
In the *Smṛtisāra*:
"When there are all kinds of foul odors, during a feast, in assemblies,
at the time of anointing the body, at the time of bathing, during great perspiration, or when there is excessive trembling..."

When cows or Brahmins are obstructed, during all types of *śrāddha* ceremonies or within the rows of those performing them, in a cremation ground, upon contact with a *śūdra*, or when impurities and the like are displayed; [in these cases, one should not study].
"A wise person should avoid Vedic recitation in a place where there is weeping, in a disturbed region, in a place of prayer such as a Mahālaya, and likewise during great portents."

By the phrase "in all *śrāddhas*," the prohibition of study for the performer of the *śrāddha* is intended. By the phrase "in the rows of the *śrāddha*," the prohibition of study for the eater of the *śrāddha* is intended. Due to the use of the locative case, this applies to those specific times. As stated in the *Dharmodyota*:
"Fruits, water, sesame seeds, edible foods, and whatever else may be part of the *śrāddha*..."
"Baudhāyana said that even after accepting [a gift], it is a time when study is prohibited."
Yama states: "Upon seeing a guest who has arrived, a wise man should certainly not study;
once permission has been granted by him, one should study with diligence."

At that time of the guest's arrival, having been granted permission by the guest, the specific rules regarding the intervening passage of forest-dwelling animals and the like are stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:

"If a wild cat, a snake, a mongoose, a five-clawed animal, or the like passes between, there is a three-night fast; for a wild dog, jackal, monkey, or the like, twelve nights; for a donkey, boar, camel, outcaste (*caṇḍāla*), a woman who has recently given birth, or a menstruating woman, one month; for a hare, ram, dog-cooker (*śvapāka*), or the like, six months; and for an elephant, crane, lion, tiger, a great sinner (*mahāpātakin*), an ungrateful person (*kṛtaghna*), or the like, one year. Furthermore:

"On an auspicious day, there is a suspension of study (anadhyāya) for those of the same lineage (sagotra) from the commencement of the marriage, installation, or consecration rites until their completion.
Here, the term "marriage" is an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) for the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
Likewise: "On the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī, the Mahābharaṇī, the Preta-Dvitīyā, the Ratha-Saptamī, and upon seeing a corpse in the sky, [one must observe] a fast for a day and night."
Mahābharaṇī is included within Mahālayā. Pretadvitīyā is Yamadvitīyā.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "In the shade of the Śleṣmātaka, the Śālmali, and the Madhuka..."
"One should never study under a *kovidāra* or a *kapittha* tree."
*Śleṣmātaka* is well known in the vernacular as "bhoṅkarī. *Śālmali* is well known in the vernacular as "sāvarī. *Madhuka* is well known in the vernacular as "mohā. *Kovidāra* is *kañcanāra*.

When the installation of a manuscript is performed under the *Mūla* asterism during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, there shall be a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) from that time until the formal dismissal (*visarjana*) of the manuscript.
As it is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"A twice-born man desiring knowledge, O Goddess, when a book is placed [before him], should never teach, nor write, nor study."
In this manner, other occasions for the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) should also be observed in the *Dharma-sūtras* and other texts.
The fault incurred by studying on forbidden days is stated in the *Bṛhannāradīya*: "For those who have studied on forbidden days, [the study destroys] their offspring, wisdom, fame, and prosperity."
Yama himself cuts short one's lifespan, strength, and health.
"One who studies during a period when study is forbidden should be known as a slayer of Brahman;
one should not speak with him, nor should one dwell together with him."
On the fourteenth, the eighth, festival days, and the first day of the lunar fortnight,
there is always a suspension of study for those of dull intellect, as well as during the intervals between [the recitation of] the scriptures.
In that regard, for those whose character is forgetful yet who recite many Vedic texts,
[the study should be suspended] on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, on festival days, and on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
"And one should study the Vedāṅgas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras."

Thus, on the basis of these Smṛti passages found in the section on forbidden days for study (*anadhyāya*) as cited by Hemādri, the learned (*śiṣṭas*), considering men in the Kali age to be of dull intellect, invariably observe these very rules regarding the study of the Veda.
This concludes the section on forbidden days for study. Now, the exceptions (*apavāda*) to those forbidden days:

In this regard, the *Dharmasūtra* states: "A suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) is prescribed with respect to sacred knowledge (*vidyā*), but not for the application of mantras in ritual action (*karmayoga*).

The author of the *Ujjvalā* has explained this to mean that while a suspension of study is heard of in connection with the Vedic study of sacred knowledge, the suspension of study is not, however, a cause for the non-employment of mantras in ritual performance.
In the Āpastamba Paribhāṣā Sūtra:
"There is no prohibition of study for the mantras during the periods when Vedic study is forbidden, because they serve a different purpose in ritual action.
Manu says:

"And likewise, there is no prohibition regarding the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, nor in the daily private recitation (*svādhyāya*), nor in the offerings of oblations (*homa*), mantras, and silent recitations (*japa*).
Here, "auxiliary sciences of the Veda" refers to the *aṅgas*; the singular number is used in the sense of a class.
In the Rāṇāyaṇīya [Śikṣā]: "In the daily obligatory rites and in the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), there is no suspension of study;
likewise in the Upākarma ceremony, at the conclusion of a ritual, and indeed in the mantras for the fire-oblation (homa)."

However, there is no suspension of study regarding the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), nor for the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, nor for the other Dharmaśāstras; one should only avoid these [specific] festival days (parvan).
This dharma of the religious students (brahmacārins) has been proclaimed in brief;
it was formerly declared by Brahmā to the sages of purified souls. One should always study the entire Vedic knowledge with a concentrated mind.

"One should constantly practice the Sāvitrī, the Śatarudrīya, and especially the Vedāntas, being disciplined and devoted to the bath of ashes. By the word "constantly" (sadā), it is indicated that there is no prohibition against the study of the Brahma-vidyā even on the festival days (parvan) or the first days of the lunar fortnights (pratipad).
In the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*:
"One should mutter [the mantra] slightly less on days when study is prohibited, and even less on festival days;
likewise in the case of daily recitation, Tantric rites, sacrifices, and the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*)."
It is traditionally taught that there is no suspension of study for the learning or teaching of the Vedas;
likewise, no suspension of study is prescribed for the mantras used in the worship of deities.
"One should not recite the Vedas during improper times (anadhyāya), especially the Rudra-hymns, nor the Puruṣa-sūkta or the Pāvamāna hymns, except when one has undertaken a formal vow.
The meaning is that if one has taken a vow such as "I shall not eat without having recited this," then it must be studied.
In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:
"One should study the Vedāṅgas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras on days other than the fourteenth, the eighth, festival days, and the first day of the lunar fortnight."

In the *Dharmodyota*: "For the daily recitation and performance of rites such as *japa* and *homa* of solar mantras, Raudra mantras, and those pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛka*), there is no prohibition regarding the days unfit for study (*anadhyāya*), nor in the case of optional rites (*kāmika*)."

Thus ends the seventh section in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā* concerning the duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), the teacher and the student, the rules for removing dullness of intellect, the regulations regarding days when study is forbidden (*anadhyāya*), and the exceptions thereto.

This concludes the seventh chapter in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was himself the performer of the Agnicit, Vājapeya, Pauṇḍarīka, and Sarvatomukha sacrifices, and who bore the surname Okopa.

Now begins the eighth section: the commencement of the *kāṇḍavrata* (the vow for a Vedic book). Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "At the commencement of a *kāṇḍa* and at its conclusion, [one offers oblations with] the verse: 'I have sought Sadasaspati, the wonderful, the beloved of Indra, the desirable, the winner, the wisdom; Svāhā! The seer of the *kāṇḍa* is the second [offering]. Then: 'Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa'; 'To thee I go'; 'Thou, O Agni, art our...'; 'So thou, O Agni, art our...'; 'O Agni, thou art the messenger'; 'O Prajāpati, whatever of this rite I have done in excess'—here some also offer the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, as previously described."

The meaning of this is as follows: there are nine, six, five, or four sections (*kāṇḍas*). Among these, in the case of nine sections, they are: the Prājāpatya, Saumya, Āgneya, Vaiśvadeva, Svāyaṃbhuva, and Āruṇa; and the Upaniṣads consisting of the Sāṃhitī Devatās, the Vāruṇī Devatās, and the Yājñikī Devatās. In the case of six sections, there are six ending with the Āruṇa; in the case of five sections, five ending with the Svāyaṃbhuva; and in the case of four sections, four ending with the Vaiśvadeva.

Their sequence is to be seen in the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇikā*. The "commencement of the sections" (*kāṇḍopākaraṇa*) refers to the commencement of the vows for those sections; the "conclusion of the sections" (*kāṇḍavisarga*) means the conclusion of the vows for the sections. Having performed that [rite] up to the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī, and having offered to Sadasaspati, he offers to the Ṛṣis of the sections. This is because of the statement: "In the case of those [oblations] without mantras, one says 'Svāhā to such-and-such' according to the deity. [Thus: "Svāhā to Prajāpati, the Ṛṣi of the section."

"To Soma, the seer of the section, svāhā! To Agni, the seer of the section, svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, the seers of the sections, svāhā! To the Self-existent One, the seer of the section, svāhā!"—thus one should offer according to each respective section. Then follow the offerings beginning with those to Varuṇa and ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt*, as previously prescribed, as well as the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*). By the phrase "as before," both the precedence of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the rule for the oblation are obtained. Alternatively, the meaning is that Sadasaspati is the second seer of the section.

In this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), the oblation to Sadasaspati follows immediately after the oblations to the *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis. Here, the mention of the second [oblation] is for the purpose of establishing the priority of the well-known *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣi. In the previous ritual procedure, the mention of the second was intended to ensure that Sadasaspati himself does not become the *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣi. The sequential enumeration beginning with the oblation to Varuṇa is for the sake of restriction, just like the *āghāra* libations; in some cases, the injunction for the *vyāhṛti* oblations serves the same purpose.

The statement "as before" (*yathāpura-stāt*) is intended to indicate that since there are alternative views regarding the mantras for both the *jaya-homa* and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt-homa*, the very same procedure adopted here [in the initiation ceremony] is to be applied here as well; it also serves to establish that the rites must be performed prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. If it is objected: "In ceremonies such as the *samāvartana*, since the rule is established by mentioning either one of the two—as in the case of the *āghāra* libation—mentioning both is redundant," we reply: No, because its purpose is restrictive (*niyamārtha*). To explain: [The text continues: "As before" means that the procedure is exactly as described previously. The phrase "the same as before" is used to indicate that the specific method adopted in the initiation ceremony is to be followed here too, even though alternative methods exist for the *jaya-homa* and *rāṣṭrabhṛt-homa*. Furthermore, it ensures that these offerings are to be performed before the *sviṣṭakṛt*. One might argue that since the rule could be established by mentioning just one of the two (like the *āghāra*), mentioning both is superfluous; however, this is not so, for its function is indeed restrictive. Where there is a joint reference (*ubhayānuvāda*) to both [the *āghāra* and the *samit*], as in the case of the *samāvartana* and other such rites, there the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is necessarily fixed as being accompanied by both, just like the *āghāra*. Consequently, in instances other than those where there is a joint reference, whatever is not so referred to remains unrestricted. Since there is no joint reference to the *vyāhṛti-homa* in the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and conclusion (*utsarga*) of the *kāṇḍavrata*, the *vyāhṛti-homa* is not mandatory in those cases.

In the fourth oblation (*caturthī-homa*), in the performance of the *saṃvāda*, in the *śūlagava*, in the monthly *śrāddha*, the *aṣṭakā-śrāddha*, and so forth, as well as in the *āgrahāyaṇī* rite, there is no restriction regarding the *vāruṇī* and other offerings, because there is an absence of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *vāruṇī* and others. In the *trivṛt-anna-homa* and in rites mentioned in other scriptures, even under the view that the procedure (*tantra*) is the same as in the *āghāra* offering, there is no restriction regarding the *vyāhṛti* oblations or the *vāruṇī* and others, due to the absence of a restatement of both. Alternatively, wherever there is no restatement of the *vyāhṛti* oblations or the *vāruṇī* and other oblations, there is simply the exclusion of these two.

Therefore, it should be understood that the *pūrvatantra* (the preliminary ritual procedure) extends up to the *homānta* (concluding oblation) for the goddess Prasādhanī, while the *uttaratantra* (the subsequent ritual procedure) begins with the *sviṣṭakṛt* (oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt) and so forth.
Now follows the practical application (*prayoga*).

The teacher, accompanied by the student (*brahmacārin*), having performed his daily obligatory rites, seated facing the east, sipped water (*ācamana*), and regulated his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), shall announce the place and time and make the following formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (*Śrī Parameśvara*), through the attainment of the qualification for studying the *Prājāpatya-kāṇḍa* of this [student] named So-and-so Śarman, I shall perform the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) for the vow of the *Prājāpatya-kāṇḍa*. As its ancillary parts, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*), and the *Nāndī-śrāddha*. Having thus resolved, he should perform the rites according to the prescribed method.
In this case, the specific modification is: "May Savitṛ be pleased. This applies likewise to all vows.

Here, some authorities maintain that as part of the *upākaraṇa* ceremony for the religious student (*brahmacārin*), one should have him undergo shaving and bathing; then, having silently given him a new waist-thread, girdle, sacred thread, deerskin upper garment, and staff, one should cast the old ones into the water.

Then, having performed the consecration of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the ritual rules for scraping and so forth, he should establish the common fire named *Samudbhava*, which has been brought from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), kindle it, and meditate upon it. Taking three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), he should perform the rites up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) beginning with "O Faith, come" (*śraddha ehi*). Then, having stated "In this rite of the introductory oblation for the vow of the *Prājāpatya* section, those deities who are to be worshipped... and so on, ending with the *Vyāhṛtis* or the goddess *Prasādhanī*, he should declare: "In the principal oblation, I shall worship Sadasaspati with an offering of clarified butter."

He should say: "I shall worship Prajāpati, the seer of the section (kāṇḍarṣi), with an oblation of clarified butter. Or alternatively: "Prajāpati, the seer of the section, with an oblation of clarified butter; and Sadasaspati, with an oblation of clarified butter"—thus in reverse order.
