Then, having performed the *aṅgahoma* (limb-offering) beginning with "Varuṇam" and so forth, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering beginning with "Agnim sviṣṭakṛtam" and so forth—according to whichever option was announced during the *anvādhāna*—and having completed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti-homa* or up to the *prasādhanī-devī-homa*, one should perform the principal offering (*pradhāna-homa*). For the verse "sadasaspatimadbhutam," the deities are the sacrificial ones, the secret doctrines (*upaniṣadaḥ*), and Sadasaspati; the meter is *gāyatrī*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal *ājya-homa* for the commencement of the vow (*vratopākaraṇa*) belonging to the *Prājāpatya-kāṇḍa*: "Oṃ sadasaspati... siṣa svāhā."

"To Sadasaspati, this [is offered]. "Oṃ, svāhā to Prajāpati, the seer of the section (kāṇḍarṣi). "To Prajāpati, the seer of the section, this [is offered]. Or else, the reverse. Having thus offered two oblations according to the alternative mentioned during the *anvādhāna*, one should complete the remainder of the homa, beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa. The *jaya* and other homas are optional. The inclusion of the word "here" (*atra*) is for the purpose of indicating that if the subsidiary homas such as the *jaya* were performed during the *upākaraṇa*, they must certainly be performed at the *utsarjana*; whereas if they were absent there, they are likewise absent here.

Then, having performed the worship of the deities according to the procedure prescribed for the initiation ceremony with the mantras beginning with "atha brahmacārī agne vratapate," the student should give a gift to the teacher; the *trivṛdanna-homa* is not performed here.

Then the teacher, having fed the Brahmins and given abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), should remember Viṣṇu for the perfection of the rite and dedicate it to the Lord of Action (*Karmeśvara*). When a section (*kāṇḍa*) has been studied, its *utsarjana* (concluding ceremony) is performed. Everything else is like the *upākaraṇa* (opening ceremony). In this regard, however, there is this much difference: the formula for the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is, "I shall perform the *utsarjana* of the vow of the Prājāpatya-kāṇḍa, which was undertaken for the purpose of studying the Prājāpatya-kāṇḍa of this student named So-and-so Śarman."

In the *anvādhāna* (preliminary rite), [the formula is] "The rites of the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍavrata* and the *utsarjana-homa*"; in the *viniyoga-vākya* (statement of application), [it is] "The application for the principal *ājya-homa* of the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍavrata-utsarjana*. If the *jaya* and other *homas* have been performed during the *upākaraṇa*, they should be performed here as well. In the mantras for the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation), there is a modification (*ūha*) of the words: "We have performed [the vow]," "we were able," and "we have worshipped. The rest is the same. Thus ends the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍavrata*. Now follows the *saumya-kāṇḍavrata*.

The *saṃkalpa* (declaration of intent) formula is: "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord, by means of accomplishing the qualification for the study of the *Saumya-kāṇḍa*, I shall perform the *upākaraṇa* of the *Saumya-kāṇḍa-vrata*. Regarding the *anvādhāna* (preliminary rite), the *viniyoga* (application) formula is: "In the ritual of the *upākaraṇa-homa* of the *Saumya-kāṇḍa-vrata*, [the offerings are] 'to Sadasaspati with an oblation of clarified butter,' 'to Soma, the *kāṇḍarṣi*, with an oblation of clarified butter,' and 'to Soma, the *kāṇḍarṣi*, with an oblation of clarified butter,' or alternatively, 'to Sadasaspati with an oblation of clarified butter' [first]. This constitutes the statement of application (*viniyoga*).

Following the fortnight (pakṣa) announced at the time of the *anvādhāna*, after the *sadasaspati-homa* or prior to it, there is an oblation with the mantra: "To Soma, the Ṛṣi of the section (*kāṇḍarṣi*), svāhā! The renunciation (*tyāga*) is: "This is for Soma, the Ṛṣi of the section. The procedure up to the taking of the vow (*vratagrahaṇa*) is like the commencement of the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍavrata*. The conclusion (*utsarjana*) takes place when one has studied the *saumya-kāṇḍa*. In the formula of the resolve (*saṃkalpa-vākya*), one says: "I shall perform the conclusion of the *saumya-kāṇḍavrata* which was undertaken for the purpose of studying the *saumya-kāṇḍa*."

Regarding the *anvādhāna* (preparatory rite), it is stated: "The rites of the *saumya-kāṇḍavrata-utsarjana-homa*. Regarding the *viniyoga-vākya* (statement of application), it is stated: "The application is for the principal *ājya-homa* of the *saumya-kāṇḍavrata-utsarjana*. Regarding the mantras for the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation), they are: "*acāriṣam aśakam arādhi*. All else is like the *saumya-kāṇḍavrata-upākaraṇa*.
Thus ends the *saumya-kāṇḍavrata*. Now follows the *āgneya-kāṇḍavrata*.

In the *saṃkalpa* formula: "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord, by means of accomplishing the qualification for the study of the Āgneyakāṇḍa, I shall perform the *upākaraṇa* of the vow for the Āgneyakāṇḍa. In the *anvādhāna*: "In the ritual of the *upākaraṇa-homa* of the vow for the Āgneyakāṇḍa," [one offers] with an oblation of clarified butter to Sadasaspati, and with an oblation of clarified butter to Agni Kāṇḍarṣi; or alternatively, with an oblation of clarified butter to Agni Kāṇḍarṣi, and with an oblation of clarified butter to Sadasaspati. In the *viniyoga* formula: "The application is in the principal *ājya-homa* of the *upākaraṇa* of the vow for the Āgneyakāṇḍa."

In accordance with the enumeration of the *anvādhāna* (preparatory rite), after the *sadasaspati-homa* or before it, there is an oblation with the mantra: "To Agni, the *kāṇḍarṣi*, svāhā. The formal renunciation (*tyāga*) is: "This [is for] Agni, the *kāṇḍarṣi*. Everything else is like the commencement of the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍavrata*. The *utsarjana* (concluding rite) takes place when one has studied the *Āgneya-kāṇḍa*. In the formula of the resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one says: "I shall perform the *utsarjana* of the *Āgneya-kāṇḍavrata* which was undertaken for the purpose of studying the *Āgneya-kāṇḍa*."

Regarding the *anvādhāna* (preliminary rite), [the formula is]: "The rites of the fire-section (*āgneyakāṇḍa*) vow and its dismissal (*utsarjana*), and the *homa*-ceremony. Regarding the *viniyoga* (application) statement for the principal *ājya-homa* of the fire-section vow dismissal, [it is]: "The application is for the principal *ājya-homa* of the fire-section vow dismissal. Regarding the *upasthāna* (reverential standing) mantras, [the formula is]: "We have performed [it], we were able, we have succeeded. All else is like the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) of the fire-section vow.
Thus ends the fire-section vow. Now follows the Vaiśvadeva-section vow.

In the *saṃkalpa* formula, one says: "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord, by means of accomplishing the qualification for the study of the Vaiśvadeva section, I shall perform the *upākaraṇa* (commencement) of the vow for the Vaiśvadeva section. In the *anvādhāna* (preparation of the fire), it is said: "Regarding the two rites of the *upākaraṇa-homa* of the Vaiśvadeva section-vow: [one offers] to Sadasaspati with an oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*), and to the Viśvedevas and the Section-Sages (*kāṇḍarṣis*) with an oblation of clarified butter; or alternatively, to the Viśvedevas and the Section-Sages with an oblation of clarified butter, and to Sadasaspati with an oblation of clarified butter"—thus either in the stated order or in reverse.

"In the *viniyoga* statement [it is said]: 'The application [is] in the principal *ājya* oblation at the commencement of the vow for the *vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa*. Following the enumeration in the *anvādhāna*, the oblation is offered either after or before the *sadasaspati-homa* with the formula: 'To the Viśve Devas, the *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis, svāhā! The renunciation (*tyāga*) is: 'This [is for] the Viśve Devas, the *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis. Everything else is like the commencement of the vow for the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍa*. The conclusion (*utsarjana*) is performed when [the text] has been studied in the *vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa*."

In the *saṃkalpa* formula: "I shall perform the concluding rite (*utsarjana*) of the Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa vow, which was undertaken for the purpose of studying the Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa. In the *anvādhāna* formula: "The ritual acts of the fire-kindling and the oblation for the concluding rite of the Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa vow. In the *viniyoga* formula: "The application [is] in the principal *ājya*-oblation for the concluding rite of the Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa vow. In the *upasthāna* mantras: "We have performed it; we were able; we have worshipped. All else is like the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) of the Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa vow. Thus ends the Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa vow. Now follows the Svāyaṃbhuva-kāṇḍa vow.

In the *saṃkalpa* (declaration of intent) formula, one says: "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*), by means of accomplishing the qualification for the study of the *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa*, I shall perform the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) of the *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* vow. In the *anvādhāna* (preparation of the fires), one says: "In the ritual of the oblation (*homa*) for the introductory rite of the *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* vow," [one offers] with an oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) to Sadasaspati, and with an oblation of clarified butter to Svayaṃbhu, the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the section (*kāṇḍarṣi*). Or alternatively, one may offer first to Svayaṃbhu, the seer of the section, with an oblation of clarified butter, and then to Sadasaspati with an oblation of clarified butter; thus it is done in reverse order.

"In the *viniyoga* statement: 'The application [is] in the principal *ājya* oblation at the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) of the *svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍavrata*'. Following the enumeration in the *anvādhāna*, the oblation is offered either after or before the *sadasaspati* oblation with the formula: "To Svayaṃbhu, the *kāṇḍarṣi*, svāhā. The renunciation (*tyāga*) is: "This [is for] Svayaṃbhu, the *kāṇḍarṣi*. Everything else is like the commencement of the *prājāpatyakāṇḍavrata*. The conclusion (*utsarjana*) takes place when the *svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* has been studied.

In the *saṃkalpa* formula: "I shall perform the concluding rite (*utsarjana*) of the *svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa-vrata*, which was undertaken for the purpose of studying the *svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa*. In the *anvādhāna*: "[This is] the ritual of the *homa* for the concluding rite of the *svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa-vrata*. In the *viniyoga* formula: "The application [is] in the principal *ājya-homa* of the concluding rite of the *svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa-vrata*. In the *upasthāna* mantras: "We have performed it; we were able; we have succeeded. All else is like the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) of the *svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa-vrata*. That this *kāṇḍa* is optional has already been stated previously.
Mātṛdatta also says thus: "Some [consider] the Svāyaṃbhuva section as the fifth.

This means that according to some, the Svāyaṃbhuva section is a separate fifth [section], while according to others, it is not separate. In the view that it is not separate, its inclusion should be understood within the final Vaiśvadeva section.
Now follows the procedure for the Upākaraṇa ceremony performed collectively for these [sections].

The teacher, having performed his daily obligatory rites together with the *brahmacārin*, sits facing the east, sips water (*ācamana*), performs breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and after proclaiming the place and time, makes this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of securing the student's qualification for the study of the Veda, I shall perform, in a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), the commencement of the vows (*upākaraṇa*) for the four sections known as Prājāpatya, Saumya, Āgneya, and Vaiśvadeva. Having thus resolved, he should perform the rites beginning with the worship of Gaṇeśa and ending with the *Nāndī-śrāddha*.

In the view that the *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* is not included [within the five], the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "I shall perform the commencement of the vows for the five sections known as the Prājāpatya, Saumya, Āgneya, Vaiśvadeva, and Svāyaṃbhuva, collectively.

After the *Nāndīśrāddha*, some authorities maintain that the student should have his hair shaved and bathed; then, having given him a new waist-thread, lower garment, sacred thread, deerskin upper garment, and staff, he should cast the old ones into the water.

Then, having performed the consecration of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the ritual procedure beginning with the scraping, and having established, ignited, and meditated upon the common fire named *Samudbhava* brought from the house of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), he takes three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), performs the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) ending with the mantra "O Faith, come" (*śraddha ehi*), and—having recited the portion beginning with "those who are to be sacrificed to" (*yā yakṣyamāṇāḥ*) up to the *vyāhṛtis*, or up to the oblation to the goddess *Prasādhanī*—proceeds to the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*) in the rite of the introductory oblation (*upākaraṇahoma*) for the four sections of vows known as the Prājāpatya, Saumya, Āgneya, and Vaiśvadeva.

"I shall sacrifice with one oblation of clarified butter to Sadasaspati, Prajāpati Kāṇḍarṣi, Soma Kāṇḍarṣi, Agni Kāṇḍarṣi, and the Viśvedevas Kāṇḍarṣis"—or conversely, "I shall sacrifice with one oblation of clarified butter to Prajāpati Kāṇḍarṣi, Soma Kāṇḍarṣi, Agni Kāṇḍarṣi, the Viśvedevas Kāṇḍarṣis, and Sadasaspati. In the Aṅgahoma, [he sacrifices] to Varuṇa with two verses, and so forth.

In the case where the *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* is not included, during the ritual of the fire-oblation (*homakarma*) for the commencement of the vows (*vratopākaraṇa*) of the five sections known as the *Prājāpatya*, *Saumya*, *Āgneya*, *Vaiśvadeva*, and *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa*, one should recite from "those who are about to be sacrificed to" (*yā yakṣyamāṇāḥ*) up to the end of the *Vyāhṛtis*, or up to the goddess *Prasādhanī*. Then, regarding the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*), one should declare: "I shall sacrifice with a single offering of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) to Sadasaspati Prajāpati, the seer of the section (*kāṇḍarṣi*); to Soma, the seer of the section; to Agni, the seer of the section; to the Viśvedevas, the seers of the section; and to Svayaṃbhu, the seer of the section. [And likewise] to Prajāpati...

"I shall sacrifice with each individual oblation of clarified butter to Soma, the Ṛṣi of the section; to Agni, the Ṛṣi of the section; to the Viśvedevas, the Ṛṣis of the section; to Svayaṃbhū, the Ṛṣi of the section; and to Sadasaspati"—or conversely. In the Aṅgahoma, "to Varuṇa with two [verses]," and so forth. The principal oblation (pradhānahoma) occurs either at the end of the Vyāhṛti-homas or at the end of the Prasādhanī-devī homas.

It is as follows: for the verse beginning with *sadasaspatim*, the Upaniṣads of the ritualists state that Sadasaspati is the deity and Gāyatrī is the metre. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal *ājya* oblation during the commencement of the vows for the four sections (*kāṇḍas*). However, in the view that the *Svāyaṃbhuva-kāṇḍa* is not included, the application is in the principal *ājya* oblation during the commencement of the vows for the five sections; this is the distinction in the statement of application (*viniyoga-vākya*). "Oṃ sadasaspati... siṣa svāhā. To Sadasaspati, this [is offered]. Oṃ prajāpataye kāṇḍarṣaye svāhā."

To Prajāpati, the seer of the section (kāṇḍarṣi), this [is offered]. Om! To Soma, the seer of the section, Svāhā! To Soma, the seer of the section, this [is offered]. Om! To Agni, the seer of the section, Svāhā! To Agni, the seer of the section, this [is offered]. Om! To the Viśvedevas, the seers of the sections, Svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, the seers of the sections, this [is offered].

In the view that the *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* is not included, there is a sixth oblation: "To Svāyaṃbhuva, the seer of the section, Svāhā! The renunciation is: "This is for Svayaṃbhuva, the seer of the section; not mine."

Either immediately after the *kāṇḍarṣi* oblations or following the *sadasaspati* oblation, one should perform the principal oblations. Having performed the principal oblations, one should complete the entire remainder of the ritual, beginning with the oblation "imaṃ me varuṇa" and so forth. Regarding the *jaya* and subsequent oblations, there is an option; the threefold food-oblation (*trivṛdannahoma*) is not performed here.
Then the student (*brahmacārī*), having performed the worship (*upasthāna*) with the formulas beginning "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall observe the vow," should give a gift (*vara*) to the teacher.

Then, having arranged for the feeding of Brahmins and the giving of abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and having recollected Viṣṇu for the perfection of the rite, one should dedicate the action to the Lord of Karma.

Thus concludes the procedure for the *upākaraṇa* (commencement) according to the *tantra* method. Now follows the *utsarjana* (conclusion). The teacher, accompanied by the student (*brahmacārin*), having performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), sits facing east in a commendable location such as a riverbank. Having sipped water (*ācamana*) and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he announces the place and time and makes this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform, by the *tantra* method, the conclusion (*utsarjana*) of the four-part vow (*vrata*)—namely the *Prājāpatya*, *Saumya*, *Āgneya*, and *Vaiśvadeva*—which was undertaken by the student [named] Amukaśarman for the purpose of Vedic study. Having made this resolve, he should perform the rites beginning with the worship of Gaṇeśa and ending with the *Nāndī-śrāddha*.

In the case where the inclusion of the *svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* is not accepted, the modification (*ūha*) in the formula of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "I shall perform the concluding rite (*utsarjana*) of the five-fold vow consisting of the *prājāpatya*, *saumya*, *āgneya*, *vaiśvadeva*, and *svāyaṃbhuva* sections by means of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). In this case, there is no shaving of the hair and so forth.

Then, having performed the consecration of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the procedure beginning with the scraping (*ullekhana*), and having established, kindled, and meditated upon the common fire named *Samudbhava* brought from the house of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), he takes three fuel-sticks (*samidh*). Having performed the rites ending with *prāṇāyāma*—beginning with "O Faith, come" (*śraddha ehi*)—he recites the formula beginning with "Those who are to be sacrificed to" (*yā yakṣyamāṇāḥ*) up to the *vyāhṛtis*, or up to the goddess *Prasādhanī*. Then, for the primary oblation (*pradhānahoma*) in the rite of the fire-offering (*homakarma*) for the conclusion (*utsarjana*) of the four sections (*kāṇḍa*) known as the Prājāpatya, Saumya, Āgneya, and Vaiśvadeva, [he offers to] Sadasaspati...

"I shall sacrifice with one oblation of clarified butter to Prajāpati Kāṇḍarṣi, Soma Kāṇḍarṣi, Agni Kāṇḍarṣi, and the Viśvedevas Kāṇḍarṣis. Or alternatively: "I shall sacrifice with one oblation of clarified butter to Prajāpati Kāṇḍarṣi, Soma Kāṇḍarṣi, Agni Kāṇḍarṣi, the Viśvedevas Kāṇḍarṣis, and Sadasaspati. In the Aṅgahoma, [he sacrifices] to Varuṇa with two verses, and so forth.

In the case where the *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* is not included, during the ritual of the concluding oblation (*utsarjana-homa*) for the five sections known as the *Prājāpatya*, *Saumya*, *Āgneya*, *Vaiśvadeva*, and *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa*, one should recite from "those who are about to be sacrificed" (*yā yakṣyamāṇāḥ*) up to the end of the *vyāhṛtis*, or up to the *prasādhanī-devī*, and then state: "I shall sacrifice with a single oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) to Sadasaspati, Prajāpati, the seer of the section (*kāṇḍarṣi*), Soma, the seer of the section, Agni, the seer of the section, the Viśvedevas, the seers of the section, and Svāyaṃbhuva, the seer of the section, each with one oblation of clarified butter."

"I shall worship Prajāpati Kāṇḍarṣi, Soma Kāṇḍarṣi, Agni Kāṇḍarṣi, the Viśvedevas Kāṇḍarṣis, Svayaṃbhū Kāṇḍarṣi, and Sadasaspati, each with one oblation of clarified butter (ājyāhuti)," or conversely.

In the Aṅgahoma, "Varuṇa with two [verses]," and so forth. At the end of the Vyāhṛti-homas, or at the end of the Prasādhanī-devī-homas, follows the Pradhāna-homa. It is as follows: for the verse beginning "Sadasaspatim," the deities are the Yājñikyas and the Upaniṣads; Sadasaspati is the deity; the metre is Gāyatrī. Its application (viniyoga) is in the primary clarified-butter offering (pradhānājyahoma) for the concluding rite (utsarjana) of the vows of the four sections (kāṇḍa).

In the view that the *Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa* is not included [within the four], the specific modification in the statement of application (*viniyoga*) for the principal *ājya* oblation during the concluding rite (*utsarjana*) of the vows of the five sections (*kāṇḍa*) is as follows: "Oṃ sadasaspati... siṣa svāhā. To Sadasaspati, this [oblation]. Oṃ prajāpataye kāṇḍarṣaye svāhā. To Prajāpati, the seer of the section, this [oblation]. Oṃ somāya kāṇḍarṣaye svāhā. To Soma, the seer of the section, this [oblation]. Oṃ agnaye kāṇḍarṣaye svāhā. To Agni, the seer of the section, this [oblation]."

Oṃ viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ kāṇḍarṣibhyaḥ svāhā | [This is] for the Viśvedevas, the seers of the sections (kāṇḍarṣis): "This [is mine]. If one follows the view that the section of the Self-born (Svāyaṃbhuvakāṇḍa) is not included, there is a sixth oblation with: "To Svayaṃbhu, the seer of the section, svāhā.
The renunciation [of the offering] is: "This is for Svayaṃbhu, the seer of the section; it is not mine."

The Sadasaspati-homa may take place either immediately after the Kāṇḍarṣi-homas or [later]. Having thus performed the principal oblations, one should complete the entire remainder of the sacrifice, beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa" and so forth.
If the Jayā and other oblations were performed during the *upākaraṇa*, they should be performed here as well. The Trivṛd-anna-homa is not performed at this point.

Then the religious student (brahmacārī), having performed the worship of the deities with the formulas beginning with "agne vratapate vratamacāriṣam," should release his vow and present a gift (*vara*) to the teacher.

Then the preceptor, having arranged for the feeding of Brahmins and the distribution of abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and having recollected Viṣṇu for the perfection of the rite, should dedicate the work to the Lord of Karma.
Now follows the procedure according to the view that the Āruṇakāṇḍa is not included [within the main ritual].

One who is about to study the *Āruṇa-kāṇḍa* should bathe at the three periods of the day. Having fasted during the day on one day, he should eat at night on the second day; having fasted for a full day and night on the third day, he should eat during the day on the fourth day and eat at night on the fifth day. In this manner, he should subsist on food taken only every fourth meal-time. "Drink" refers to milk and similar liquids; "food" refers to grain. In case of inability, he may eat alms daily. Both of these [regimens] are adopted twice a day every day.

For it is traditionally taught: "Therefore, twice a day it is offered to human beings—in the morning and in the evening. If one is unable to do this, one should beg for food every day and eat that. Having drawn water from a river or similar source with a vessel and purified it with a cloth, one should perform all water-related duties with that water, but not directly at the river or other such places. Furthermore, one should not be a collector of water; the commentators explain that one should not be occupied with the collection of foodstuffs and the like in any place other than the alms-bowl.

"Saṃgraha" means accumulation. One should perform the service of the sacred fire (*agniparicaryā*) with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *Audumbara* wood. One should perform the oblation (*homa*) for the deities beginning with Agni and ending with Aruṇa. One should also observe the ritual rules (*dharma*) declared in the *Pravargya-kāṇḍa*. One should maintain such a vow for one year, or for two months, starting from the day of commencing the study of the *Bhadra-prapāṭhaka*.

Upon the completion of the study of the *Bhadra-prapāṭhaka*, during the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), under an auspicious constellation (*puṇye nakṣatre*) of the waxing fortnight, having approached and saluted the teacher, one should request him: "Sir, teach me the *Āruṇa-kāṇḍa*."

Then the teacher, having gone to the forest with him, should give him permission, saying: "Perform the Aruṇakāṇḍa vow. Thereupon, the student, having saluted that teacher, having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, having cleansed his teeth, having put on two unwashed garments, and having sipped water, should offer libations, saying: "I satiate the seers of the Aruṇakāṇḍa," or he may omit the libation.

Then the teacher, accompanied by the religious student (brahmacārin), shall sit facing the east, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and practice breath control (prāṇāyāma). Having announced the place and time, he shall make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, and by means of securing the qualification for the study of the Āruṇakaṇḍa for this [student] named So-and-so Śarman, I shall perform the commencement (upākaraṇa) of the Āruṇakaṇḍa vow; as its ancillary rites, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati, the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), the worship of the Mothers (mātṛkāpūjana), and the Nāndī-śrāddha. Having thus resolved, he should proceed according to the prescribed method.

In this case, there is also shaving, followed by the sequence beginning with cleaning the teeth and ending with the *tarpaṇa* libation. According to the view of some, after silently giving a new waist-thread (*kaṭisūtra*), lower garment (*kaccha*), sacred thread (*upavīta*), deerskin (*ajina*), upper garment (*uttarīya*), and staff (*daṇḍa*) to the student (*brahmacārin*), one should discard the old ones in water; thus, these acts also take place here.

Then, having performed the consecration of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the procedure beginning with the scraping, and having established, kindled, and meditated upon the common fire (*laukika-agni*) named Samudbhava brought from the house of a *śrotriya*, he takes three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), performs the rites ending with the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) beginning with "O Faith, come" (*śraddha ehi*), and recites the formulas beginning with "Those which are to be sacrificed" (*yā yakṣyamāṇāḥ*) up to the end of the *prasādhanī* goddess or the end of the *vyāhṛti*s, saying: "In the primary oblation of this rite of the introductory sacrifice for the *Āruṇakāṇḍavrata*, I shall sacrifice to Sadasaspati with an oblation of clarified butter."
One should announce: "I shall sacrifice to the seers Aruṇāṅkaṇḍa with an oblation of clarified butter," or the announcement may be made in the reverse order.

Then one should announce: "I shall sacrifice to Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Brahmā, Prajāpati, Candramas, the Nakṣatras, the Ṛtus, Saṃvatsara, Varuṇa, and Aruṇa, each with a single oblation of clarified butter. Regarding the subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*), following the alternative chosen during the *anvādhāna*, one should perform the rites up to the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī or up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, and then perform the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*). For the verse beginning with "sadasaspatim," the deities are the sacrificial ones and the Upaniṣads; Sadasaspati is the deity and Gāyatrī is the meter.
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the principal *ājya* oblation at the commencement of the *āruṇakāṇḍavrata*:

"Oṃ sadasaspatim... siṣa svāhā | To Sadasaspati, this [is offered]. Oṃ aruṇebhyaḥ kāṇḍarṣibhyaḥ svāhā | To the Aruṇa Kāṇḍa-sages, this [is offered]. Having offered according to the alternative sequence mentioned during the *anvādhāna*, one offers: to Agni svāhā, to Vāyu svāhā, to Sūrya svāhā, to Brahmā svāhā, to Prajāpati svāhā, to Candramas svāhā, to the Nakṣatras svāhā, to the Seasons svāhā, to the Year svāhā, to Varuṇa svāhā, and to Aruṇa svāhā.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter (*ājya*) for the eleven vows according to their respective indicative marks (*yathā-liṅga*); this is the renunciation (*tyāga*).

Regarding the mantras contained in the *anuvāka* beginning with "punar mām," Aruṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Sūrya is the deity (*devatā*). The meter of the first [mantra] is *anuṣṭubh*, of the second is *dvipadā triṣṭubh*, of the third is *dvipadā gāyatrī*, and of the fourth is *anuṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the placing of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *udumbara* wood.

He places one fuel-stick (*samidh*) with the mantra: *oṃ punarmāmaitvi0 maitu mā*. He places the second with: *oṃ yanme'dya retaḥ0 dyadāpaḥ*. He places the third with: *oṃ idaṃ tatpunarā0 rcase*. He places the fourth with: *oṃ yanme retaḥ pra0 jasaṃ kuru*.
Then he should complete the remainder of the oblation (*homa*), beginning with *imaṃ me*. The subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) such as the *jaya* mantras are optional. There is no *trivṛd-anna-homa*.

Now, for the student (*brahmacārī*), regarding the four mantras beginning with *agne vratapate*, Soma is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Agni and the others are the deities (*devatā*) in sequence. The meter is *yajus*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the act of worship (*upasthāna*): with these [mantras], "Oṃ agne vrata...," "Vāyo vratapate...," "Āditya vratānām...," he worships Agni and the others.
The duties of the *pravargya* rite, such as "he should not eat at night" and "not looking at green barley," should also apply here.

Then the preceptor, holding *dūrvā* and *darbha* grass, silently touches the *madantī* water, [reciting] these two peace-mantras (*śānti-mantra*): "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ... and so forth. For these two, the seers (*ṛṣis*) are Aruṇa; the deities (*devatās*) are the Gods, Indra of Vṛddhaśravas, Pūṣan Viśvavedas, Tārkṣya Ariṣṭanemi, and Bṛhaspati; the meter (*chandas*) is Triṣṭubh. For the mantra "Oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ," the seer is Aruṇa, the deity is Brahman, and the form is Yajus.

The application for the purpose of peace (*śāntyarthaṃ jape viniyogaḥ*) is as follows: having recited the peace mantra "Oṃ bhadraṃ karṇe... śāntiḥ," and having stated the seers and other details for the two mantras beginning with "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ" as before, and having recalled the application for the recitation, one should recite the two verses: "Oṃ bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ | Svasti na indro... Then, for the five verses known as the *Mahānāmnīs* beginning with "Āpamāpām," the seers are the Aruṇas; the deities are the Waters (*āpaḥ*), characterized by their respective specific attributes.

The meter is *anuṣṭubh*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the touching of the *madantī* water: with the five *mahānāmnikī* verses beginning with "Oṃ āpamāpāma... mudīṣata," one should touch the *madantī* water. The student (*antevāsī*) should also be made to perform everything from the holding of *dūrvā* grass and *darbha* blades up to the touching of the *madantī* water. Then, one should teach the entire section (*kāṇḍa*) beginning with "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ."

Then, having silently touched the boiling water (*madantī*) and again performed the peace-chant (*śānti*) with the verse, "May [the gods] hear us with their ears... (*bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ*), [he proceeds]. For the verse beginning "Auspicious to us, most peaceful... (*śivā naḥ śaṃtamā*), the deity is Aruṇā, the metre is Gāyatrī consisting of one foot; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the touching of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhyālambhana*). With the mantra, "Oṃ, be auspicious to us, most peaceful," he touches the medicinal herbs. For the verse beginning "Most merciful... (*sumṛḍīkā*), the deity is Aruṇā, the earth, the metre is Gāyatrī consisting of two feet; its application is in the touching of the earth. With the mantra, "Oṃ, most merciful... śi," he touches the earth. Up to this point, the student (*antevāsī*) may also perform the rite. At this juncture, the conclusion of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) following the limb-oblations (*aṅgahoma*) and so forth takes place.

Then, having returned home with his pupil, he should have a meal for a Brāhmaṇa prepared with that food obtained as alms. In the view that this section is included [within the preceding], the oblations to the *kāṇḍarṣi* and the *sadasaspati* do not exist separately. Nevertheless, the oblations beginning with "To Agni, svāhā! and the placing of fuel sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) and so forth must certainly take place because they are specific [to this rite].
In reality, however, non-inclusion is more appropriate, according to the natural sense of the Vedic text: "Oṃ, the *kāṇḍarṣis* are Aruṇas."

In this manner, every day, the ritual beginning with the *ullekhana* (drawing lines) and ending with the touching of the ground—excluding the oblation to the *kaṇḍarṣi*, the *sadasaspati*, and the *homa*—must be performed for either one year or two months. Even when the study of the *Bhadra-prapāṭhaka* has commenced, the vow (*vrata*) must certainly be observed for either a year or two months. Having completed the vow according to the chosen alternative, one should perform the *utsarjana* (concluding rite).

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: the formula for the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is, "I shall perform the concluding rite (*utsarjana*) of the Aruṇa-section vow (*āruṇakāṇḍavrata*) undertaken for the purpose of studying the Aruṇa-section. In the preparatory rite (*anvādhāna*), one says, "The two rites of the concluding oblation (*homakarma*) of the Aruṇa-section vow. In the formula for the application (*viniyoga*), one says, "The application is to the principal clarified-butter oblation (*pradhānājyahoma*) of the concluding rite of the Aruṇa-section vow. Following the oblations to the Seers of the Section (*kāṇḍarṣi*) and Sadasaspati, there is an oblation to the deities beginning with Agni. If the *jaya* and other oblations were performed during the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*), they must likewise be performed here.

"O Āditya, I have performed your vow... [with these words] he worships Āditya; "O Vāyu, lord of vows... [he worships] Vāyu; "O Agni, lord of vows... [he worships] Agni; "Of vows, O lord of vows... [he worships] Agni, the lord of vows. The *ṛṣi* and other details for these are the same as before. The disciple should give to the teacher a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*) and a garment made of linen or cotton, as well as a cow. If he is unable, he should give one of these; if he is even more unable, he may give something else, such as grain.

One should perform a rite of peace (*śānti*) at the beginning and the conclusion of the recitation (*svādhyāya*) and its ritual performance; if one should stop in the middle, one should stop after performing a rite of peace, and having performed a rite of peace again, one should commence once more. Regarding the instruction "it is like the *pravargya*," according to the view that this vow (*vrata*)—ending with that point—is an auxiliary part of the ritual action and not an auxiliary part of the study itself, the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and the conclusion (*utsarjana*) are to be performed just as they are for the vow of the *prājāpatyakāṇḍa*.

After shaving the hair of the head, beard, body hair, and nails, and performing the ritual bath, the formal declaration (*saṃkalpa*) for the commencement of the *āruṇakāṇḍavrata*—for the purpose of gaining the right to study the *āruṇakāṇḍa*—is as follows: "I shall perform the commencement of the *āruṇakāṇḍavrata*. In the ritual of the oblation for the commencement of the *āruṇakāṇḍavrata*, [the offerings are made] with an oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) to Sadasaspati and an oblation of clarified butter to the seers (*ṛṣi*) of the *āruṇakāṇḍa*. Alternatively, during the *anvādhāna* (preparation of the fire), one may offer an oblation of clarified butter to the seers of the *āruṇakāṇḍa* first and then an oblation of clarified butter to Sadasaspati, or vice versa.

"In the *viniyoga* statement [it is said]: 'The application [is] in the principal *ājya* oblation at the commencement of the *āruṇakāṇḍavrata*'. Following the fortnight (pakṣa) announced during the *anvādhāna*, the oblation "To the *aruṇa* *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis, *svāhā*" is performed either after the *sadasaspati* oblation or prior to it. The renunciation (*tyāga*) is: "This [is for] the *aruṇa* *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis. This is the specific detail regarding the oblation; everything else is the same.
Then, having performed the rites beginning with holding the *dūrvā* grass and *darbha* blades up to the touching of water according to the *Mahānāmnī* verses, he should teach the *Bhadra-prapāṭhaka*.

Then, silently, from the ritual touching of water (*upasparśana*) up to the touching of the ground, and from the holding of *dūrvā* grass and *darbha* blades up to the touching of the ground, this should be performed daily for as long as the study lasts. There is no daily fire-oblation (*homa*). When this section (*kāṇḍa*) has been studied, the concluding rite (*utsarjana*) takes place. In the formal declaration (*saṃkalpa*), the wording is: "I shall perform the conclusion of the *āruṇakāṇḍavrata* undertaken for the purpose of studying the *āruṇakāṇḍa*. In the preparatory rite (*anvādhāna*), it is: "The two rites of the conclusion of the *āruṇakāṇḍavrata* and the fire-oblation."

"In the *viniyoga* statement: 'The application [is] in the principal *ājya* oblation for the concluding rite (*utsarjana*) of the *āruṇakāṇḍavrata*. Among the mantras for the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), this very one, 'O Agni, Lord of Vows' (*agne vratapate*), is the first mantra; it is not 'O Āditya, Lord of Vows' (*āditya vratapate*). At the end, there is the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*) and so forth; such is the performance."

If, due to laziness, the vow was not performed at the time of study, then one should offer one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the *gāyatrī* mantra, perform the *kṛcchra* penance, observe the vow during the first meal of the *Āruṇaketuka* rite, and having studied one recitation (*prapāṭhaka*) once from the presence of the teacher according to the rules, one should employ the fire.

Even if the *Āruṇaketuka* rite itself is not to be performed, the study of one recitation once from the presence of the teacher according to the aforementioned rules and preceded by the penance is mandatory.
Thus ends the procedure for the *Āruṇakāṇḍavrata*.

Therefore, in the view that the *Sāṃhitī*, the deity-mantras (*devatā*), the secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*), and so forth are not included [within the main Vedic texts], one should likewise dedicate and then release these separately. Upon the study of these, following the peace-chant (*śānti*), one should perform the teaching by reciting—from "He who is the bull of the meters, omniform; from the meters, from the nectar..."—up to "Protect what has been heard by me," having first recited this oneself and then caused the student to recite it. At the conclusion, having again recited and caused the student to recite, there is the peace-chant.
Regarding these vows, the determination of the time should be understood as being like the determination of the time for the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) which will be described later.
"Regarding the consideration of planets, asterisms, days, divisions, vargas, and ascendants,
it is declared to be the same as for the *caula* ceremony, and likewise for the *godāna* and *vrata* ceremonies"— so says Śrīdhara.
The phrase "and in the *vratas*" means "also in the *vratas*."
Regarding the expiation for the violation of a vow at its proper time, Atri states, concerning the breach of a vow:
"The father, the brother, or even another person shall perform three *prājāpatya* penances.
This application by the father and others occurs when the student (*baṭu*) is incapable; however, when he is capable, it must be performed by him alone.
Thus ends the concluding rite of the *kāṇḍavrata*. Now follows the *godāna* ceremony.

Although this was mentioned earlier in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* for the sake of convenience in applying it by extension (*atideśa*) to the *caula*, it is discussed here precisely because it must be performed prior to the *samāvartana*. Nor should one raise the objection: "Why was the extension of the *godāna* not applied to the *caula* instead? For since the *godāna* sacrament occurs subsequent to the *caula*, it is impossible to extend a later sacrament to an earlier one, such as the *caula*.
And regarding that gift of a cow (*godāna*), it is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*:

"When the sixteenth year has arrived as prescribed, the rite of *godāna* is performed; he causes [the hair] to be shaved except for the topknot (*śikhā*), though according to some, he leaves only the topknot remaining; or it is called the *agnigodāna*; he gives a cow to the teacher."

Just as the *cūḍākarma* (tonsure ceremony) has been prescribed, so too for one who has been initiated (*upanīta*), the *godānakarma* (hair-cutting ceremony) should take place in the sixteenth year. In this regard, there is this distinction: he causes the hair on the head to be shaved together with the top-knots (*saśikham*), meaning that even the central top-knot is not left remaining. According to the opinion of some, however, he leaves the central top-knot here. He whose *godāna* consists of the fire-ritual itself is called an *agnigodāna*; or rather, the boy becomes an *agnigodāna*.

The meaning is that the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) itself occurs, beginning with the *upasamādhāna* (kindling) and ending with the *puṇyāhavācana* (declaration of an auspicious day). Regarding the statement, "In both ritual procedures (*kalpa*), the teachers give a cow to the preceptor (*ācārya*) at the end," it should not be argued that this gift belongs specifically to that [latter] procedure because it is prescribed in proximity to the rule "there is either the fire or the cow-gift" (*agnigodāna*). Since there is no obstacle to the cow-gift being performed in both procedures, the argument that the proximity of the injunction establishes a restrictive rule (*niyama*) making it an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of only that specific procedure is ineffective.

And it should not be read that "he becomes one for whom the fire-sacrifice and the *godāna* [hair-cutting] are performed," because it must be read as "he gives a cow to the teacher" even prior to this. It might be argued that in the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttarakalpa*), this is obtained simply through the rule of continuity (*anuvṛtti*). However, by the statement "or he becomes one for whom the fire-sacrifice and the *godāna* are performed," the very same prior sublation (*bādha*) of the *godāna*—just as with the shaving—is established, since continuity in the subsequent procedure is impossible. And this should be performed after the initiation (*upanayana*), in the sixteenth year; having commenced it at this very time, as in the case of the *caula*, it is to be carried out. Manu also says:
"The *keśānta* (the hair-cutting ceremony) is ordained for the Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year."
"For a kinsman of the royal class [the age is] twenty-two, and for a Vaiśya, two more than that."
*Rājanyabandhu* means a Kṣatriya. The meaning is that [the ceremony] occurs when two years have been added to twenty-four.
Yājñavalkya also states: "And the *keśānta* occurs in the sixteenth [year].

The *keśānta*—the rite known as *godāna*—occurs for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year from conception. This should be understood to apply to the twelve-year Vedic vow (*vedavrata*). In the other case (the eight-year vow), it should be observed according to what is possible. Vijñāneśvara holds that for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, it should be observed at the time of their initiation (*upanayana*), namely in the twenty-second or twenty-fourth year. *Godāna* is the name of the rite, according to the principle of naming after its characteristic feature (*tatprakhyanyāya*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that this [rite] must be performed according to one's capacity within the option of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), prior even to the *samāvartana* ceremony, and not by waiting for the sixteenth year.
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*).

The preceptor, accompanied by a celibate student (brahmacārin), having performed his daily obligatory rites, shall sit facing the east at the time prescribed for the *caula* ceremony—such as the lunar day and so forth—to be described hereafter. Having sipped water (*ācamana*) and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he shall announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "For the sake of increasing the longevity and luster of this [student] named So-and-so Śarman, and for the propitiation of the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, I shall perform the rite known as the *godāna-saṃskāra*. He should then proceed according to the established method beginning with the worship of Gaṇapati and ending with the *nāndī-śrāddha*.
In this case, the specific modification is that one should say, "May the Keśins be pleased," because this rite shares the same ritual rules as the *caula*.

Then, having performed the purification of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and other rites according to the procedure beginning with the scraping (*ullekhana*), and having established the common fire named Sūrya there, kindled it, and meditated upon it; having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and performed the rites from "Śraddhā, come! up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*); and having recited from "Those deities who are to be worshipped in the rite of the Godāna-homa" up to the *vyāhṛti*s; and [recited] "Varuṇa" and so forth for the limb-oblation (*aṅgahoma*); there is no specific oblation (*vaiśeṣika-homa*) here. The *jaya* and other oblations are optional. The *vyāhṛti*-oblations, the *vāruṇī*-oblations, and others are mandatory here. Thus, by the extension (*atideśa*) from the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), the ritual is the same up to the concluding recitation (*saṃsthājapa*).
Then, having performed the *trivṛd-anna-homa* ending with the recitation of the *puṇyāha* and other verses, he should say, "May Prajāpati be pleased.

Thereafter, having seated the religious student (*brahmacārin*) in his own place behind the fire, and having himself sat down to the south of him, he should seat either the mother of the student or any other person on the north side of the fire or the student—having placed a fresh cow-dung pad beneath them—and perform the rites from the sprinkling with warm and cold water up to the shaving, according to the procedure for the tonsure (*caula*) to be described hereafter.

In this regard, there is this distinction: at the *caula* ceremony, according to local custom, the middle tuft (*madhyama-śikhā*) is shaved along with the other tufts already worn; or else, one should leave the middle tuft remaining. The statement "he shaves [the head] together with the tuft" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to enjoin the wearing of a tuft for those such as the Bhṛgus who are otherwise without tufts; it is not, however, an injunction that all must shave while keeping a tuft. Thus, it should be understood that for all others except those belonging to the *gotras* of Bhṛgu and so forth, the shaving is performed by leaving the middle tuft intact. For those belonging to the *gotras* of Bhṛgu and so forth, however, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the shaving of the middle tuft.

Then, having performed the binding of the hair and other rites according to the procedure described for the *caula* ceremony, he should give ghee-rich rice to the barber and present a gift to the preceptor (*ācārya*).

Thereafter, having arranged for the feeding of Brahmins and the giving of abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and having recollected Viṣṇu for the perfection of the rite, he should dedicate the action to the Lord of Karma (*karmeśvara*).

In the alternative view that it is the *agnigodāna*, one should perform the rites beginning with the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as before—up to the *trivṛdanna-homa* and ending with the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*)—and then proceed only with the granting of boons and the feeding of Brahmins; however, the shaving of the head (*vapana*) is not to be performed. If this rite is delayed beyond its proper time, one must perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) similar to that for the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), but the purpose is not fulfilled merely by performing that specific *caula*-expiation, because this rite occurs subsequent to the initiation (*upanayana*).
Thus ends the procedure for the commencement and conclusion of the *kāṇḍavrata* and the *godāna* in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.

Thus ends the eighth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā* composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was himself the son of Śrīmat Sāgnicit Vājapeyayājin Pauṇḍarīkayājin, known by the surname Oka.
Now begins the ninth section:
the expiation for the violation of the vows of a religious student (*brahmacārin*) according to the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*.

On the day before or on that very day, the student, having announced the place and time, should make this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of removing the fault arising from the omission of begging for alms and the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), I shall perform the expiation consisting of three *kṛcchra* penances preceded by an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*) as prescribed by Baudhāyana."

If one is unable to perform the three *kṛcchra* penances, however, the formula for the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) should be modified as follows: "I shall perform [the penance] by means of the substitution (*pratyāmnāya*) of such-and-such. In this same manner, the resolve should be adapted according to the specific cause for any omission of vows, such as the neglect of purification (*śauca*), sipping water (*ācamana*), or the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā-vandana*); contact with a Śūdra or others; the abandonment of the loincloth (*kaupīna*), the waist-thread (*kaṭisūtra*), the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), the girdle (*mekhalā*), the deerskin (*ajina*), or the staff (*daṇḍa*); sleeping during the day; wearing an umbrella, a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), or similar items; stepping upon sandals (*pādukā*); the use of fragrant unguents (*udvartana*), ointments (*anulepana*), collyrium (*añjana*), or oil-massage (*abhyañjana*); sporting in water; devotion to gambling, singing, dancing, instrumental music, and the like; conversing with heretics (*pākhaṇḍin*) and others; or eating food that has been kept overnight. In each case, the resolve must be formulated in accordance with the particular occasion.

Then, having performed the consecration of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) by means of scraping and other rites, and having established there the common fire (*laukikāgni*) known as *Viṇ*—which has been brought from the house of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*)—and having kindled it and meditated upon it, he takes three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), performs the ritual beginning with "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and recites the formula beginning with "Those deities who are to be worshipped... (*yā yakṣyamāṇā...*) up to the goddess Prasādhanī or ending with the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, for the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*), he declares: "I shall worship Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati each with a single offering of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*)."

"I shall worship Agni, Agni, the Earth, and the Great One with one oblation of clarified butter; Vāyu, Vāyu, the Atmosphere, and the Great One with one oblation of clarified butter; Sūrya, Āditya, the Sky, and the Great One with one oblation of clarified butter; Prajāpati, the Moon, the Nakṣatras, the Quarters, and the Great One with one oblation of clarified butter"—in every instance, one may use "Mahat" (the Great) instead of "Mahāntam" (the Great One).

Having said, "I shall worship Agni Viśvavedas, Vibhāvasu, and Śatakratu with one oblation of clarified butter each; I shall worship Agni with two oblations of clarified butter; and I shall worship Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati with one oblation of clarified butter each," and having stated for the *sviṣṭakṛt* homa, "I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the remaining clarified butter oblation," and so forth, or for the *aṅga* homa, "Varuṇa with two [oblations]," and so forth—then, according to the specific procedure announced during the *anvādhāna*, having performed the rites up to the *prasādhanī-devī* homa or up to the *vyāhṛti* homa, he should perform the principal (*pradhāna*) homa.

Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the individual *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the seer of the collective *vyāhṛtis*. Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati are the deities (*devatās*) respectively. The *gāyatrī*, *uṣṇih*, *anuṣṭubh*, and *bṛhatī* are the meters (*chandāṃsi*) respectively. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the principal *ājya* oblation as an expiation for the breach of the vows of a religious student (*brahmacārī*):
"Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā! To Agni, this [oblation]. Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā! To Vāyu, this [oblation]. Oṃ suvaḥ svāhā! To Sūrya, this [oblation]. Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā! To Prajāpati, this [oblation]."

The deities of the four mantras beginning with "bhūr agnaye" are the Upaniṣads; the deities mentioned in the mantras are the Yajus formulas. Their application (viniyoga) is in the principal clarified butter oblation (ājyahoma) for the expiation of the transgression of a student's vows.

"Oṃ bhūr! To Agni and to Pṛthivī and to Mahat, Svāhā! To Agni, to Agni, to Pṛthivī, and to Mahat, this [is offered]. Oṃ bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu and to Antarikṣa and to Mahat, Svāhā! To Vāyu, to Vāyu, to Antarikṣa, and to Mahat, this [is offered]. Oṃ suvaḥ! To Āditya and to Div and to Mahat, Svāhā! To Sūrya, to Āditya, to Div, and to Mahat, this [is offered]. Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ! To Candramas and to the Nakṣatras and to the Diśas and to Mahat, Svāhā!
To Prajāpati, to Candramas, to the Nakṣatras, to the Diśas, and to Mahat, this [is offered]."

For the four mantras beginning with "pāhi no agne," the seers are the deities of the sacrificial formulas (yājñikya-upaniṣads). For the first, Agni; for the second, Viśvavedas; for the third, Vibhāvasu; and for the fourth, Śatakratu. The metre is the one-footed Gāyatrī. Their application is in the principal clarified-butter oblation (ājya-homa) for the expiation of the breach of the student's vows (brahmacārivrata).

"Oṃ, protect us from sin, Agni; svāhā! To Agni, this [offering]. Oṃ, protect us, O All-Knowing One; svāhā! To Viśvavedas, this [offering]. Oṃ, protect the sacrifice, O Radiant One; svāhā! To Vibhāvasu, this [offering]. Oṃ, protect everything, O Śatakratu; svāhā! To Śatakratu, this [offering].

Regarding the two verses beginning with *punarūrjā*, the deity is Agni, the meter is Gāyatrī. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal clarified-butter oblation (*ājyahoma*) for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) of the transgression of a student’s vows (*brahmacārivratalopa*).
"Oṃ punarūjā nivartasva... viśvataḥ svāhā | To Agni, this [is offered]. Oṃ saha rayyā niva... spari svāhā | To Agni, this [is offered].

Having again recollected the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details for the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively as before, one should offer four oblations with them and perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of three *kṛcchra* penances. In case of inability, this may be substituted by the gift of a cow or another such equivalent.

Then, following the enumeration of the *anvādhāna*, one should complete the remainder of the oblation, beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* or the *vāruṇī-homa*. Having completed the remainder of the oblation, one should perform three *kṛcchra* penances; there is no *trivṛd-anna-homa*.
Now follows the procedure according to the *āpūrvika-tantra*.

As before, having performed everything from the *saṃkalpa* up to the point "I shall take possession of all these," and having stated for the principal oblation—as before—up to "I shall sacrifice with each individual offering of clarified butter to Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and so forth," one should place the fuel-sticks for the preparatory rite (*anvādhāna*), spread the grass around the fire, arrange the vessels as required, perform the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers and so on, ending with "having placed the two *pavitra* strainers in the fire" (omitting the *praṇītā* vessel), sprinkle water around the fire with the mantras beginning with "Adite," and silently place one fuel-stick into the fire.

Having offered the principal oblations as before, having performed the expiation consisting of three *kṛcchra* penances, having removed the surrounding grass mats (*paristaraṇa*), and having sprinkled water with the mantras beginning with "O Aditi, you have assented," he should feed the Brahmins and meditate upon Viṣṇu. Alternatively, the three *kṛcchras* may be performed after the conclusion of the remainder of the *homa*.
This is the expiation for the breach of the vows of a religious student (*brahmacārin*) according to the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*.
As for Devala:
In the event of a lapse of time, one should perform expiation according to the prescribed rule:
namely, a *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, having offered one hundred oblations of clarified butter.
"One should indeed perform twenty-eight or eight vows respectively;
however, in case of transgression, one should recite the Veda again for as long as it was practiced," so he said.
And this oblation is performed with the Gāyatrī:
"Having performed each Kṛcchra penance one by one, and having offered a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Gāyatrī, one should bathe; thus said Śaunaka."
Thus it is stated by Āśvalāyana.

Since this expiation (prāyaścitta) is heard to have the same agent as the bath, the agency belongs to the student (baṭu) alone. According to the *Prayogapārijāta*, these [rites] are to be performed together with the return ceremony (samāvartana) at a time subsequent to the expiation; however, the source for that must be sought. Furthermore, this expiation pertains to cases where the act was intentional.
As for that which was stated by Manu—
Regarding the statement, "Upon the omission of obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas,
and upon the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting," this refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally.
Regarding the performance of fire-rituals (*agnikārya*) and the practice of subsisting on alms-food (*bhikṣālopa*), the *Smṛtyarthasāra* states:
"Having bathed, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the Gāyatrī mantra one thousand and eight times;
in the case of subsisting on alms-food, one hundred and eight times."
And this refers to the case of a single omission; however, that which was stated by Baudhāyana refers to the omission of two up to six [meals].
Beyond that:
"Having omitted the begging for alms and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill..."
Having offered two oblations of clarified butter with these two [verses] beginning with "kāmāvakīrṇa," [he should proceed].

"Then one should perform the attendance (upasthāna), [reciting] 'May they sprinkle me with this,'" as stated by Yājñavalkya; this is to be understood as applying when there is an abandonment of the fire due to being occupied with other duties and the like.
But in the absence of such [occupation]—
"Without having gone out for alms and without having kindled the sacred fire,
one who is not ill shall perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin* for seven nights"— so it is stated by Manu.
Regarding the expiation for a religious student (*brahmacārin*) eating honey or meat, Śātātapa says:
"But a religious student who should eat honey or likewise meat must perform the Prājāpatya penance; he is purified by the Mauñjī-homa."
The Mauñjī-homa is a re-initiation.
Devala says:
"If a religious student should eat honey or meat unintentionally..."
"Having fasted for three nights, he should dwell properly in the water for one night."
Furthermore:
"He who consumes the food of a servant without having gone on a round for alms,
and he who eats without having bathed, shall mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times."

"If a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should eat food from a house of birth-impurity (sūtaka), food from a recent funeral rite (navaśrāddha), or likewise food from a monthly ancestral rite (māsika), he becomes pure after three nights alone."
But Bṛhadyama states: "If a twice-born man who has not completed his vow should eat at monthly śrāddhas and other such occasions,
a three-night fast is prescribed here as the expiation."
"By performing a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and consuming clarified butter (ghṛta), one becomes purified.
This refers to cases involving ignorance.
However, regarding acts committed with prior knowledge, he himself says:
"When one observing a vow eats at a *śrāddha* or during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*),
he should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance and complete the remainder of his vow."
Garga states the penance for speaking untruth:
"If a twice-born man should speak untruth out of delusion when not in a time of distress,
he should observe the vow of celibacy for three nights or one night."
Āpastamba states the expiation for failing to perform purification after voiding urine or excrement: "If a twice-born man, having voided urine or excrement,
eats food out of delusion without performing his own purification, he becomes pure by drinking barley-gruel for three nights."
"If a twice-born man, having urinated on a path, drinks water through a lapse of memory,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
The term "urine" is an elliptical expression for feces and other such substances.
Regarding the time of voiding feces and urine, Bharadvāja says:
"If one should discharge excrement or urine without wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), [then he must perform penance]."
Having discarded that sacred thread, he should then take up another new one.
In the phrase "without wearing," the word "in the ear" is to be supplied as the ellipsis, because another Smṛti states:
"Having placed the purifier in the right ear, one should void feces and urine. After the word "then," the word "should wear" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In the *Smṛtisāra*:
"Having placed the sacred thread behind [the neck] hanging from the throat, a householder may void feces and urine; or else, being composed, he may do so with it over the ear."

And this placing [of the sacred thread] upon the ear pertains to the case of wearing a single garment, according to Mādhava, because of the statement of Śaṅkha: "If one who wears a single garment should void urine or feces after placing the *yajñopavīta* on the ear. Regarding the voiding of urine and feces without water, Sumantu says:
"In the case of voiding urine or feces without water, there must be immediate bathing, as well as the drinking of ghee, *kuśa*-grass water, and gold-infused water."
The meaning is that one should drink water filtered through *kuśa* grass mixed with ghee, and water filtered through gold mixed with ghee.
Since the drinking of water filtered through ghee, *kuśa*, and gold is for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), there is a cessation of eating. [As it is said:
"If one should void excrement or urine without water..."
Having observed a fast for one day, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.

This meaning is obtained through agreement with the statement of Jātūkarṇya: "Having performed a bath with one's clothes on (sacaila), one should observe a fast for one day (ekāha-kṣapaṇa). Here, *kṣapaṇa* means fasting (*upoṣaṇa*). Alternatively, the word *pāna* may be construed with both clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and water; by that, the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*) becomes a separate requirement. As for what was stated by Aṅgiras:
"In the case of voiding urine or excrement without water, there shall be a bath with one's clothes on and an oblation with the *vyāhṛti* mantras."
This should be understood as applying to unintentional acts.
Marīci states: "If one eats without the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), or otherwise voids excrement or urine..."
"One is purified by eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī together with breath control (prāṇāyāma)."
Manu prohibits the suppression of natural urges when water is entirely unavailable and the urge has already arisen:
"Having considered the place, the time, and one's own condition, one should practice purification according to the law; one must not suppress natural urges."
In the phrase "one should practice for the purification of dharma," the absence of the *prakṛtibhāva* sandhi is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
Now follows the expiation for an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy).
Regarding this, the following is the *Dharmasūtra*:
"One who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*) by having intercourse with a woman should sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey using a *pākayajña*;

a Śūdra should eat the remains of its offering. The author of the *Ujjvalā* commentary explains this as follows: a student (*brahmacārī*) who approaches a woman is an *avakīrṇin* and should sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey according to the *pākayajña*, that is, by the procedure for the *sthālīpāka*. A Śūdra should eat the remnants of the ghee-offering from that donkey. This is explained as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule that one should serve a learned Brāhmaṇa [with the leftovers].

The Vādhūla and Vaikhānasa [Sūtras] also state: "A celibate student who approaches a woman shall sacrifice a donkey as the animal victim; the baking of the animal-cake is to be performed on the ground.
Manu also says:
"But one who has spilled his seed shall, at night, sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*."
In the *Prāyaścitta-sūtra* as well, it is stated:

"If a religious student (*brahmacārī*) should have sexual intercourse with a woman, he shall sacrifice a donkey as an animal; having cooked a cake on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla-paśupuroḍāśa*) upon the ground, they perform the rite with portions [of the cake] in water. It is dedicated to Nirṛti or Prajāpati, according to some; it is dedicated to the Rakṣases, according to others; it is dedicated to Yama, according to others.

This rule applies to one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and should have sexual intercourse with a woman during his period of studentship, because of the context concerning the one who has established the fires. Alternatively, the term refers specifically to the ordinary religious student (*prasiddha-brahmacārī*), since conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) possesses greater force.
And it is stated among the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*): "One who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*) shall sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey using a *pākayajña*.

Nor is this [text] purposeless, for it serves to provide an option regarding the deity. Nor is there an inconsistency in the statement within the context of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), since its purpose is to prescribe a Vedic performance involving a different deity. Therefore, even if it pertains to the state of studentship, there is no fault.
This has been stated by Bharadvāja:
"Regarding the statement, 'If a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should approach a woman,' whose [offense] is this?
Some say it is that of one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni), while others say it is that of one who has not."
In that regard, however, the expiation beginning with the *vrātapatī* [offering] should be observed for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
As it is stated: "On the day of the vow (*vratya*), he does not eat meat nor approach a woman, even if the initiated one should spill [the consecrated water]," and so forth.

By the word "on the ground" (*bhūmau*), the natural cooking of the oblation within the fire-enclosure (*agnyāyatana*) is indicated; this being set aside, cooking outside the fire-enclosure is prescribed by this [text]. Therefore, having placed a single potsherd (*kapāla*) outside the fire-enclosure upon the embers and having laid an ember on top of it, one should cover the embers with the *veda* grass-bundle. Alternatively, [the purpose] is that [cooking] takes place on the ground specifically within the enclosure, and not in the ashes. Nor should it be said that the phrase "on the ground" is intended to exclude the potsherd.

Otherwise, the term *ekakapāla* (one-potsherd) would become redundant. A cake prepared on a single potsherd is called an *ekakapāla*; one should bake it on that very potsherd. Having baked it, they should perform the ritual with the *asvavadānas*—that is, with the portions of the omentum and the limbs of the cake. It should not be argued: "Since the scriptural injunction 'he cuts eleven portions' uses the word *avadāna* to denote only the [limbs of] the animal, how can these [limbs] serve as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) for the performance of the cake, which is distinct from them? [This is because the term here refers to the specific ritual procedure.]

Since the water serves as the locus for the offering even during the performance of the *puroḍāśa*—because it occurs subsequent to the cooking (*śrapaṇa*)—there is no obstacle [to this]. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the performance of the *puroḍāśa* itself would take place in the waters while the performance of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) would take place in the ordinary fire; for in that case, the plural number in the word "with the portions" (*avadānaiḥ*) would become meaningless. Nor should it be argued that, under such circumstances, only the performance of the *puroḍāśa* and its subsidiaries would occur in the waters, whereas the performance of the omentum (*vapā*), because it precedes the cooking, would occur only in the ordinary fire.

In the view prescribed by the scriptural injunction, "Having immolated the animal, he offers the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)," it is possible for the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) to occur immediately after the cooking of the animal-cake. However, in reality, since the omentum is not included under the term "portioning" (*avadāna*), its oblation must take place in the fire itself. There is indeed evidence for this: the separate mention of the omentum in the passage, "If the omentum or the portion of the oblation should be spilled," as well as the natural sense of the gerund suffix (*ktvā*). The statement "in the waters" (*apsu*) is intended to set aside the performance in the fire that would otherwise apply by virtue of the original archetype (*prakṛti*).

The performance of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth takes place in the water itself, because subordinate members (*aṅga*) must occupy the same location as the principal sacrifice (*pradhāna*). Nor is there a restriction regarding movement—as there is in the case of the *avabhṛtha*, where one goes "wherever there is water"—because no such injunction exists here. Therefore, even though the water is established at the site of the *uttaravedi*, the ritual action proceeds. In that regard, just as in the *avabhṛtha*, one should observe the omission of the altar, the fuel-sticks (*idhma*), and other items whose purpose is lost, as well as the modification (*ūha*) of the mantras according to the requirements of the situation.

Even in the case where the omentum (*vapā*) is offered into the fire, the *prayāja* and other offerings must take place in the water itself, according to the Jaimini-sūtra: "In a conflict between those possessing contradictory properties, the property of the majority shall prevail," and from the statement of the Teacher (Śabara): "The majority prevails because of its primacy. Thus, it is established that in the event of a conflict, it is logical to favor the many.

In the *pañcadaśarātra* sacrifice, the first day is the *agniṣṭut*. Because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules of the one-day (*ekāha*) *agniṣṭut* based on its name, the *subrahmaṇyā* formula belongs to Agni. Thereafter follows the three-day period beginning with *jyotis*; because of the injunction regarding the *jyotis* etc. in the one-day rite, the *subrahmaṇyā* belongs to Indra. That [Indra-formula] alone applies to the remaining eleven days due to the extension from the twelve-day (*dvādaśāha*) sacrifice. In that case, since the *subrahmaṇyā* at the time of the *upasad*s is a common ritual element (*tantra*), there would be no fixed rule. However, the author of the *Bhāṣya* maintains that, because of the primacy [of the first day], the rules of the *agniṣṭut* should prevail; yet, for the sake of favoring the majority [of the subsequent days], the Indra-formula should be used.

The author of the Vārttika, however, [states]: "Since the consecration of one deity by means of an offering intended for another deity is not established, it is proper that the invocation be performed separately; therefore, this is not the example. Rather, the example is: 'One desiring cattle should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dātṛ, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Pradātṛ, and curds, honey, ghee, water, and parched grains—this mixture is dedicated to Prajāpati. In that case, there is no contradiction because the offering to Agni and the parched grains are both modifications (vikāra) of the original Agni-offering."

Since the curd for Indra is a modification of the *sāṃnāyya* offering to Indra-Agni, it possesses the characteristics (*dharma*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*). However, since the honey and ghee are modifications of the *upāṃśuyāja*, they possess the characteristics of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*). In that case, when the two are performed together, one might argue that because the *ājyabhāga* offerings to Indra and Agni are primary, their respective mantras—the *vārtraghna* and *vṛdhanvat*—should be employed, thereby favoring the characteristics of the curd for Indra. To this, [the author] says: "On account of the majority of factors, such as the honey and so forth, those very two [mantras] should be used in order to favor the *vārtraghna*."

Nor should it be argued that the application of this section—namely, "And a superior quality [belongs] even to the non-primary [substitute], because there is no contradiction with the common [quality], as in the case of one who eats from a bronze vessel"—is valid here, such that, just as a single flowering *barhis* grass intended for the cake on a single potsherd dedicated to Heaven and Earth is taken for all purposes, the opposite might hold true in this instance. For this principle operates only when there is mutual non-contradiction; since in the present case there is indeed a contradiction, this principle cannot apply.

And the principle is as follows: there are the oblations for Āgrayaṇa, Indra-Agni, Viśvedevas, and Dyāvā-Pṛthivī. Among these, because the oblation for Dyāvā-Pṛthivī is a modification of the Dyāvā-Pṛthivī [oblation] belonging to the Vaiśvadeva section, "flowered" sacrificial grass (barhis) is obtained for it; however, for the others, there is merely sacrificial grass in general.

In this matter, since the flowering *barhis* (sacrificial grass) is both primary and more abundant, it follows that only the flowering grass should be taken. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: although other types of grass would not be defective even if flowering grass were used, the non-flowering grass would render the *dyāvāpṛthivya* offering defective; therefore, there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the flowering grass alone. This is analogous to how, when a teacher has a rule of eating from a bronze vessel while consuming the remnants of his guru's meal, there is no contradiction in the student’s rule of eating from a bronze vessel. Since the present case lacks such a correspondence, the "bronze-eating" maxim does not apply here.

There are two performances (*pracāra*) with the omentum (*avada*) as their locus, and one with the fire (*agni*) as its locus; thus, there is a plurality of performances with the omentum as their locus. Alternatively, there is no performance of the omentum at all here. And so says Bharadvāja: "If a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman, he should sacrifice a donkey to Rudra. They perform the ritual with its portions (*avadāna*) in water; they do not perform it with its omentum. There is no animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). It ends with the *iḍā* offering, or with the *śaṃyu* formula. [The animal] belongs either to Nirṛti or to Prajāpati."

Since the *Sūtrakāra* has prescribed [the offering] for one of the deities—namely Nirṛti, Prajāpati, Rakṣas, or Yama—a deity such as Rudra is not intended here. Likewise, there is no prohibition of the *paśupuroḍāśa* (animal-cake), because its performance is prescribed by the rule: "Having baked the *paśupuroḍāśa* on a single potsherd upon the ground. In this ritual, the deity is any one among these: Nirṛti, Prajāpati, Rakṣas, or Yama. Furthermore, from the usage of the word "one should sacrifice" (*ālabheta*) in the *Prāyaścitta-sūtra*, a formal sacrifice (*yāga*) is established.

According to the view that Nirṛti is the deity, there is the procedure for the *pākayajña* because it is prescribed in the *Dharmasūtra*, and there is also the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) because it is prescribed in the *Prāyaścittasūtra*. According to the view that Prajāpati and others are the deities, there is only the animal sacrifice. Furthermore, this procedure for the *pākayajña* takes place specifically in the common (*laukika*) fire, based on the Mānava [Smṛti] statement: "In the procedure for the *pākayajña*, the penance for one who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*) is performed in the common fire."

Even when performing the rite according to the method prescribed in the *Prāyaścitta-sūtra*, one should establish the three worldly fires (*laukikāgni*) and perform the sacrifice in those very fires, but not the formal establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), because the Teacher has not prescribed the *ādhāna* for this case—just as in the cases of the Niṣāda and the Rathakāra.
