This is supported by Jaimini’s sūtra: "And the animal sacrifice for the *avakīrṇin* [is performed] in that same way, because the time for the *ādhāna* has not yet arrived," and by Kātyāyana’s sūtra: "Or, for the *avakīrṇin*, the sacrifice with a donkey is performed in the worldly fire. Thus, the sacrifice—namely, "He who is a *brahmacārin* and has broken his vow of chastity shall immolate a donkey as an animal"—is also to be performed only in the worldly fire.

The singular number in the word *laukike* (in the common fire) is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*). Some maintain that all rites are to be performed in that very same fire. Marriage cannot take place without the expiation for the violation of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) through this sacrifice, because of the scriptural injunction: "One whose celibacy has not been violated should enter the householder stage of life. In the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*, the word *vā* (or) is intended to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Furthermore, this rite is to be performed at night at a crossroads, according to the cited statement of Manu: "But the *avakīrṇin* [the violator of celibacy] with a one-eyed man... and so forth.

The performance at night applies to the *pākayajña* (cooked-sacrifice) side, not to the *yāga* (soma-sacrifice) side, because the *Āśvalāyana Sūtra* prohibits sacrifice at night, stating: "The *divākīrtya* [stotra] is the *vaṣaṭkāra*. Nor should it be argued that this very rule serves as the authority for performing it at night; for that would result in a contradiction with the injunction regarding the *pākayajña*. Furthermore, this remains the same even if Nirṛti is the deity, since Nirṛti is the lord of the *rakṣases*. It is likewise so if the *rakṣases* themselves are the deities, because *rakṣases* roam about at night.

In the statement of Manu, the use of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) in the term *pākayajña* is figurative due to its association [with the word]. By saying "therein" (*tatra*) rather than "of that" (*tasya*), it is understood that even in the case of the ritual procedure for animal sacrifices (*paśudharma*), the consumption is to be performed by a Śūdra alone. If the intention were that the consumption by a Śūdra applies only to the ritual framework of the *pākayajña*, then the action would have been specified as "therein," referring specifically to the *pākayajña* framework. Therefore, even in the case of the animal-sacrifice framework, the consumption is to be performed by a Śūdra alone. A specific point regarding this has been stated by Hārīta:

"One who has spilled his seed with women shall sacrifice a donkey as the victim at a crossroads to Nirṛti according to the ritual rules of a *pākayajña*. He should cook the animal-cake on the ground; having performed the offering with the cuttings (*avadāna*) in water, he sacrifices, saying: 'O Desire, I am one who has spilled his seed; I am one who has spilled his seed, O Desire! To Desire, svāhā! O Desire, I have committed an offense against you; I have committed an offense against you, O Desire! To Desire, svāhā! [Thus it is said.]

The performance of the *avadāna* (cutting-off) is followed by the injunction for a fire-oblation (*homa*) with these two mantras. In this section concerning the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy), however, it is stated that on the night of the new moon, after bringing forward the fire and adding fuel to it, one should offer two oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the mantras: "I have spilled my seed through lust; I have been overcome by lust. Immediately thereafter, with palms joined and slightly tilted sideways, one should consecrate the water used for the ritual (*praṇītāgni*) three times with the mantra "May they sprinkle me," and the granting of the boon is also mentioned.
This concludes the expiation for the *avakīrṇin*.
Now follows the expiation for one bitten by a dog.
Regarding this, Parāśara states:
"A student (brahmacārī) bitten by a dog should drink milk for three days at evening;
a householder, however, for two nights; and one who maintains the sacred fires (agnihotravān), for one day."
"For one bitten above the navel, that same [penance] shall be doubled;
it shall be tripled for the face, but quadruple for the head."
This expiation must be performed in its entirety, doubled, by one who is a *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate).
And so says Hārīta:
"But he who, while being an *upakurvāṇa*, should perform [an act] either intentionally or even unintentionally..."
"A lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika brahmacārī), however, should perform twice that amount."
Śātātapa states: "For one who, having ascended to the lifelong vow (naiṣṭhika-dharma), falls away from it again,
there is no expiation by which he may become pure."
Furthermore, because the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is heard in this sentence, there is no expiation for repetition at all; rather, he remains perpetually impure.
Now follows the expiation for the omission of the *kāṇḍavrata* (vow pertaining to a Vedic section).

Having performed his daily obligatory rites, the student (*brahmacārī*), sitting facing the east, sipping water (*ācamana*), and restraining his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), shall mention the place and time, and say: "For the purpose of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of removing the sin (*pratyavāya*) produced by the omission of the *kāṇḍavrata*, I shall perform the expiation consisting of one *kṛcchra* penance for each *kāṇḍavrata*, preceded by a fire-oblation (*homa*)."

If, however, one is unable [to perform the vow], one should resolve: "I shall perform [the vow] through this specific substitute (*pratyāmnāya*). Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the procedure beginning with the smearing (*ullekhana*), having established the common fire named Viṣṇu there, kindled it, and meditated upon it; having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*); having performed the rites from "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*); and having recited the formula "In the rite of expiation for the omission of the *kāṇḍavrata*, those deities who are to be worshipped... up to the end of the *vyāhṛtis* or up to the goddess Prasādhanī; then, for the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*), for each *kāṇḍavrata*...

"I shall sacrifice to Savitṛ with *ājya* oblations, one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times, using the *Gāyatrī* [verse]. Having stated this, and having declared for the *Aṅga-homa* "Varuṇa," etc., or "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the remainder of the *ājya* oblation," etc., one should perform the principal oblation (*pradhāna-homa*) after completing either the rites up to the *Vyāhṛti-homa* or up to the *Prasādhanī-devī-homa*, according to the alternative specified during the *Anvādhāna*. For the *Gāyatrī*: Viśvāmitra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Savitṛ is the deity (*devatā*), and Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*).

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the principal *ājya* oblation in the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the omission of the *kāṇḍavrata*. One should offer oblations with the *gāyatrī* mantra according to the prescribed number for each *kāṇḍavrata*: "Oṃ, we meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects, svāhā! The ritual relinquishment (*tyāga*) is: "This is for Savitṛ."

Then, one should prescribe for each [offense] an expiation consisting of a *kṛcchra* penance; if unable to do so, by means of any substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) such as the gift of a cow. Then, one should complete the remainder of the fire-oblation (*homa*), beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa" and ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. There is no *trivṛd-anna-homa*. Then, having arranged for the feeding of Brahmins and having meditated upon Viṣṇu for the perfection of the rite, one should dedicate the action to the Lord of Action (*karmeśvara*). Alternatively, the performance may follow the *āpūrvika* method.

As before, having performed everything from the *saṃkalpa* up to the point "I shall undertake all these," and having stated at the principal oblation for each section-vow (*kāṇḍavrata*), "I shall sacrifice to Savitṛ with one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight, oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) using the Gāyatrī [verse]," he should place the fuel-sticks for the preparatory rite (*anvādhāna*) into the fire, surround the fire, arrange the vessels as required, and perform the rites beginning with the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers up to the point "having placed the two *pavitras* in the fire," and [worship] the fire with the formulas beginning with "O Aditi, give your consent."

Having sprinkled [water] silently, having placed one fuel-stick [on the fire], and having offered oblations with the Gāyatrī mantra according to the number mentioned in the *anvādhāna* rite, he should perform the expiation consisting of *kṛcchra* penances for each section-vow (*kāṇḍavrata*). Then, having removed the surrounding grass-coverings and sprinkled water with the mantras beginning with "O Aditi, you have assented," and having fed the Brāhmaṇas, he should meditate upon Viṣṇu.

Then, on an auspicious day, having performed the commencement of the section-vow (*kāṇḍavratopākaraṇa*), and once the study of that section is completed, having performed the conclusion of the section-vow (*kāṇḍavratotsarjana*), he should perform the ritual of returning home (*samāvartana*).
Thus ends the expiation for the omission of the section-vows.
Now, the expiation for the loss of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*):

when the sacred thread is broken; when it has gone below the waist; when it is removed from the neck even for the purpose of washing—except on occasions such as anointing the body, bathing in the ocean, or the anniversary of the death of one's father or mother; at the time of voiding urine or feces; when it is not worn on the ear; or when it is defiled by blood, phlegm, wine, meat, feces, urine, and so forth—one should discard it, perform the expiatory fire-oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*), and wear a new sacred thread.

And it proceeds as follows: the performer of the expiatory oblation (prāyaścitta-homa), having put on a triple-stranded thread or a cloth for the purpose of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), having bathed and performed the putting on of new garments and other rites, having sat down facing the east, having sipped water (ācamana) and restrained his breath (prāṇāyāma), and having announced the place and time, makes the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of removing the sin (pratyavāya) produced by the loss of the sacred thread, I shall perform the expiatory oblation. Having thus resolved, he smears the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with cow-dung and performs its consecration (saṃskāra) according to the procedure beginning with the drawing of lines (ullekhana).

Having established the worldly fire, known by the name Viṣṇu, with the words "I establish the fire," having kindled it and meditated upon it, and having taken three fuel-sticks, he performs the rites ending with *prāṇāyāma*, beginning with "O Faith, come! Then, in the ritual of the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) for the loss of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), he recites from "Those deities which are to be worshipped" up to the end of the *vyāhṛtis*, or up to the end of the *prasādhanī-devī* mantra. For the principal oblation (*pradhāna-homa*), he shall worship Savitṛ with the *gāyatrī* using one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight, oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.

Having said this, and having performed the *aṅga-homa* with the two verses beginning with "varuṇam," etc., and having declared, "I shall sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the remnant of the oblation," etc., according to the enumeration in the *anvādhāna*, one should perform the rites up to the *vyāhṛti-homa* or up to the *prasādhanī-devī-homa*. At the time of the *paryagnikaraṇa* of the clarified butter, the *paryagnikaraṇa* of the sesame seeds must also be performed.

Then, having remembered the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details of the *Gāyatrī* as before, and having remembered the application (*viniyoga*) as "for the *tila*-oblation expiation for the loss of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)," one should offer clarified butter-mixed *tilas* with either the *haṃsī-mudrā*—defined as "the little finger is the *haṃsī*"—or the *mṛgī-mudrā*, where the little finger and index finger are straight while the others are joined with the thumbs. Having offered one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight oblations with the *Gāyatrī*, one should complete the remainder of the sacrifice, including all the subsidiary oblations (*aṅga-homa*) and those beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt*.

In this case, there is no offering of the *trivṛdanna* oblation. For the sake of accomplishing the completion of the rite, one should give a cow to the preceptor, feed the Brahmins, and meditate upon Viṣṇu. Alternatively, the oblation may be performed according to the *Āpūrvika-tantra*.
Regarding the specific Vedic branch (*śākhā*), Devala states an exception to the prohibition against removing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from the neck for the purpose of washing it:
"He whose sacrificial thread remains on his body, purified by mantras..."
Therefore, a wise person who desires his own welfare should not extract [the tooth] from there.
By reciting it once, that twice-born man becomes purified;
this applies to the Taittirīyas, Kaṭhas, Kāṇvas, Carakas, and Vājasaneyins.
The twice-born— namely the Bahvṛcas, the Sāmagas, and those known as the Yājuṣas— should indeed remove the thread from their necks and perform its cleansing.
Having removed the thread from the neck, it deserves to be consecrated again on the occasion of anointing the body,
bathing in the ocean, and on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father.
"Having removed the thread from their necks, the twice-born should indeed perform its washing."

For the followers of the Atharvaveda, however, the rite of crossing over (*uttāraṇa*) may be performed or not as circumstances dictate; this rule should be understood to apply specifically to those matters enjoined by the statement regarding the consecration (*saṃskriyā*) with a mantra, the wearing of an inner sacred thread (*upavīta*), and the anointing (*abhyaṅga*). Thereafter, having put on a new sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and sipped water twice, one should perform the daily obligatory rites such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). This same expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed by householders and forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*).
The source for this is found in the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*:
"In the event of the destruction of the sacred thread (*upavīta*), one should offer sesame seeds with the *gāyatrī* mantra,
either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times."

Hārīta, however, states that one should offer four oblations of clarified butter with the *vrātapatī* verses and then take up [the new sacred thread] again. One oblation is offered with the verse: "Oṃ *mano jyotiḥ... yā iṣṭā upa... ghṛtena svāhā*. Three oblations are offered with the three *vrātapatī* verses: "Oṃ *tvam agne vrata...*," "*yad vo vayaṃ pra...*," and "*vratānubibhrad vratapā adābhyaḥ...*. Having offered these oblations, the meaning is that one should then wear a new *yajñopavīta* while reciting the appropriate mantra.

This should be understood as applying to one who is unable [to perform the full rite]. When the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) has slipped down from the left shoulder to the elbow, or to the wrist, one should place that sacred thread back in its original position and perform breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) three, six, or twelve times respectively. However, if it has passed under the left arm, one should discard that sacred thread as before and wear others as previously described. Some say that this expiation does not apply if another sacred thread is already present around the neck.

Others maintain that because destruction is a cause [for impurity], an expiation is indeed required. If one, out of anger or by force, cuts the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) he himself was wearing, he should—just as before—wear a new nine-threaded thread, bathe in a river or similar body of water, wear other sacred threads as previously described, and discard the cut one as before. For the purification of the sin of cutting, he should recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra one thousand and eight times.

In this regard, one who is guilty of a *mahāpātaka* (great sin) should discard his consecrated sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) until he has performed the expiation for that sin, and wear a common worldly string instead; however, those who are merely nominal Brahmins, those born of an unmarried woman (*kānīna*), those born from a woman during her husband’s lifetime (*kuṇḍa* or *golaka*), those who have not undergone initiation (*vrātya*), those afflicted with leprosy, and those who have broken their vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*) should wear an unconsecrated sacred thread—so it is stated in the *Āhnikapārijāta*. Regarding the disposal of a worn-out thread, the specific rule is given in that same work: "One should discard a worn-out thread in the water of a river, the ocean, a pond, or any such body of water, with the mantra 'Go to the ocean, svāhā,' or with the *praṇava* or the three *vyāhṛtis*."
Now follows the expiation for the breaking of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). Regarding this, here is the *Baudhāyana-dharmasūtra*:

"If the water-pot is broken, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, or recite them; or one should consecrate the broken pieces with the mantra: 'The earth has gone to the earth, the mother has gone to her mother; may we abound in sons and cattle; may he who hates us be shattered! Having thus addressed it, having gathered the shards and cast them into the water, and having recited the *Sāvitrī* ten times at least, one should take up another [pot] with the words: 'O Varuṇa, let this return to me again.'"

Now follows the *samāvartana* (the student's return home). Regarding this, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* states: "Having studied the Veda, one performs the *snāna* (bath). The Veda consists of the *mantras* and the *brāhmaṇas*. This is according to the rule: "The designation 'Veda' applies to both *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa*. The *brāhmaṇa* is the injunction for ritual action (*karmavidhāna*). Passages such as *arthavādas* (explanatory statements) are supplementary to the *brāhmaṇa*. This is according to the rule: "The *brāhmaṇa* is the injunction for ritual action; its supplements are the *arthavāda*, censure, praise, the deeds of others (*parakṛti*), and ancient legends (*purākalpa*")."

Because the ten auspicious questions (*bhadrādidaśapraśna*) are to be studied in the forest (*araṇya*), it bears the designation *Āraṇyaka*, yet this is not a separate portion of the Veda. By the word "bath" (*snāna*), the ritual of returning home (*samāvartana*) is meant. There is a specific rule in the *Dharmasūtra*: "Some say one 'bathes' by means of knowledge; likewise, [one bathes] by means of the vow (*vrata*) which has a duration of forty-eight years, [that is,] by both knowledge and the vow. According to this, some maintain that one who is perfected through Vedic knowledge—that is, *vidyā*—should perform the ceremonial bath.

The mention of "forty-eight" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the twenty-four [years] and other durations mentioned in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. One should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) when endowed with a vow (*vrata*) of forty-eight years or similar duration; however, even if not so endowed, one may bathe if endowed with sacred knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding the term "knowledge," it ends in the third case by the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Some maintain that one should bathe when endowed with both: sacred knowledge and the vow. Thus, in the passage "Having studied the Veda, the ceremonial bath [is prescribed]; we shall explain that," the word "Veda" is an elliptical expression for the vow as well. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having brought either the Veda or the vows, or indeed both, to completion,
and with his student-life (brahmacarya) unviolated, he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks."

Here, by the word *vrata*, the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*)—such as "he does not eat pungent food, salt, and so forth" while living in the teacher's house—are meant. For in those cases, a specific duration of time is prescribed in the scriptures, and the word *vrata* is indeed seen used for them; as in the passage: "He should be capable in the *vratas*, which we shall describe. However, it does not refer to the *vedavratas* (the Vedic observances). This is because those [Vedic observances] are supplementary to the study of their respective specific sections of the Veda, and thus they do not exist in the absence of that study. Consequently, the alternative formulation "either the Veda or the *vratas*" would be untenable.

Therefore, the author of the *Ujjvalā* has explained that the meaning is: "having brought both [the Veda and the vows] to completion," referring to vows delimited by specific periods of time. Furthermore, Mātṛdatta stated that some maintain the following arrangement: in order to avoid contradicting the scriptural injunction, "One who has fathered a son and whose hair is black should establish the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*)," the view that "forty-eight years" applies to those ineligible for the fire-establishment ceremony, while the other views apply to those who are eligible.
Manu says:
"Having studied the Vedas—either all three, two, or even one—with a concentrated mind..."
"Having remained inviolate in his celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder."

And thus, in the rule "having studied the Veda, [one performs] the bath" (*vedasnānam*), the singular number in the word "Veda" (*vedam*) is not intended to be restrictive. Furthermore, this bath should be performed after giving a gift (*vara*) to the teacher.
Accordingly, Yājñavalkya states:
"Having given a gift to the teacher, one should bathe with his permission."
"Having mastered either the Veda, or the vows, or indeed both,
and having remained unbroken in his student discipline (brahmacarya), he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks."
Here too, the singular number in the word *veda* is not intended to be restrictive.
Regarding the specific nature of the gift (*vara*), Manu has stated:
"When about to bathe, being commanded by his teacher, he should provide for the teacher’s sake according to his ability."
A field, gold, a cow, a horse, and finally an umbrella and sandals.

"Or grain, or garments, or vegetables, bringing pleasure to the Guru"—thus he is commanded and authorized for the *samāvartana* (the return ceremony). "A field" means one containing a crop. The mention of the umbrella and sandals as a pair (*dvaṃdva*) indicates they are to be taken together. "Garments" refers to three. The intention is that from among these, one should give whatever is dear to the Guru. By the phrase "bringing pleasure to the Guru," it is also indicated that even without a formal gift, one may perform the *samāvartana* solely by the Guru's permission when he is pleased. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
And having spoken thus, the teacher should say: "Having performed it accordingly, the disciple should perform the bath.
'Enough with wealth for me, my child; I am gratified by your virtues.
Go home,' he says, and being thus permitted, the disciple may then perform [the rite]."

He replied: "It was said by the Guru: 'This gift is for the sake of pleasing the Guru, not as a fee for the knowledge, because a price for that which is worthy of Vedic knowledge is impossible. And thus says the Chāndogya Śruti: 'Even if one were to give this earth, encompassed by the waters and filled with food, this [gift] is still more than that. Here, *ilā* means the earth. This refers to the acquisition of knowledge. The Tāpanīya Śruti also states: 'The earth, consisting of seven continents, is not sufficient as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*').'"
In the Mādhavīya, Hārīta also says:
"If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple,
there is no object on earth by giving which he could become free from his debt."

If the teacher is one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), he should perform the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for receiving a horse) as prescribed by the Śruti: "If he should receive a horse, then having given a sixth or a twelfth part of its value to a Brāhmaṇa, he should offer oblations on four potsherds to Varuṇa for as many horses as he receives.
However, one who maintains only the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) should, in that place, perform *sthālīpāka* offerings—[according to the rule]:
"Having received a horse, one should perform three *Cāndrāyaṇa* penances."
Or, being concentrated and wise, he should recite the Gāyatrī three hundred thousand times.

When there is the capacity [to perform both], there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the Veda recitation three times and the feeding of a hundred Brahmins, as stated in the *Aruṇasmṛti*: "One should cause the Veda to be recited threefold and feed a hundred Brahmins. However, the Mīmāṃsaka position—that this sacrifice belongs to the giver—is not accepted by those who follow the *Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra*. This is because, in the section on optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), that sacrifice is prescribed for the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) alone: "In the case of accepting a horse, there is the Vāruṇī sacrifice for the *ṛtvij*. Here, "*ṛtvijaḥ*" is a genitive singular. The singular number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) because it resides in the objective (*uddeśya*), just as in the case of "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*).
After the study of the Vedas, one must perform the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home) only after having understood their meaning.

This is because of the statement in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda with a concentrated mind, and having understood their meaning, the best of the twice-born should then perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)."

The first statement, "the Vedas," intends the number four; the second intends the number three. "Having understood the meaning" means having known the meaning. And it has been stated by Jaimini and others in the very first sūtra that there is no entitlement to the rite of returning home (*samāvartana*) through mere study without knowledge of the meaning. Thus, it is established that for both the *vidyā-snātaka* and the *vrata-snātaka*, knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas is necessary prior to the ceremonial bath (*snāna*).

In this regard, the *snātaka* is of three kinds: the *vidyā-snātaka*, the *vrata-snātaka*, and the *vidyā-vrata-snātaka*. Here, by the word *vrata*, the duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*)—such as abstaining from pungent and salty food—are intended. Regarding the duration of this [studentship], it is stated in the *Gṛhyasūtra*: "Forty-eight years, twenty-four, twelve, or until [the Veda] has been mastered."

In the aphorism "Having studied the Veda, the ceremonial bath (snāna)," although the intended meaning is established by the mere statement "we shall explain the snāna," the specific wording "having studied the Veda" is for the purpose of making it known that the bath has study as its primary condition, not time as its primary condition. Therefore, even when the period for the observances (*vrata*) has passed, if possible, one should bathe only after having completed the study. Only in the event of absolute incapacity should one bathe by means of the observances alone. Thus, the "bath of knowledge" (*vidyā-snāna*) and the "bath of the knowledge-observance" (*vidyā-vrata-snāna*) are praised, whereas the "bath consisting of observances alone" (*vratamātra-snāna*) is censured.

Mātṛdatta maintains that because celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is for the sake of knowledge and because of specific scriptural injunctions, there is a distinction in the fruit when [the teacher] is honored.
In the *Gobhilagṛhya*: "There are three types of *snātakas*: the *vidyā-snātaka*, the *vrata-snātaka*,..."

"The *vidyāvratasnātaka* is the highest and best among them. Regarding this, Karka, in his commentary on the sūtra "But for the *yājñika*, at will," states: "A *yājñika* is one who knows the sacrifice; for him, the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) may take place at will, even without having mastered the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in their meaning. Harihara also says: "One view is that one should bathe after having studied and understood the Veda along with its auxiliaries (*sāṅga*). A second [view] is that one should bathe after having studied and understood the Veda consisting of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. A third [view] is that one should bathe after having studied the text and practiced the science of sacrifice (*yajñavidyā*)."

If it is argued that there is a prohibition stating that one should not perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) if one has studied merely the texts without the knowledge of sacrifice (*yajñavidyā*), then this is the time for it. Regarding this, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* states: "One should bathe during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Tiṣya (Puṣya), the two Uttaraphalgunīs, Hasta, Citrā, or the two Viśākhās."

During the northern course of the sun, when the sun is situated in the six zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn, starting from the midpoint of Śraviṣṭhā across fourteen and a half lunar mansions, one should bathe during those [lunar days] that follow Rohiṇī and end with Viśākhā in the waxing fortnight, and not others. The word "or" (vā) indicates an option regarding bathing: one may bathe or one may not. Consequently, for one who lacks eligibility for ritual acts, there should be perpetual celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*) alone.

The statement "in these [asterisms]" is established by the mere sequence [of the preceding list]; however, Mātṛdatta has explained it as meaning that one should bathe in Rohiṇī and so forth, or even in other such auspicious [asterisms] if those are not available.
In the Baudhāyana-sūtra it says: "One should bathe under Rohiṇī, Tiṣya (Puṣya), the two Uttaraphalgunīs, Hasta, Citrā, Indrā (Jyeṣṭhā), or Viśākhā."

The *jyeṣṭhā* [nakṣatra] belongs to Indra. Even though marriage takes place during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), the *samāvartana* (the return home) must indeed take place only during the northern solstice (*udagayana*). This is because the author of the Sūtra himself has stated that the interval between marriage and the *samāvartana* is occupied by the permission of one's mother and father; thus, he has thereby prescribed that rite for the northern solstice.
"The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice should be commenced by the householder in the morning;
it should also be performed by the *snātaka*, provided that he maintains a separate kitchen."

For, in the section on the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the mention of the two stages of life—namely, the householder and the *snātaka*—in the statement of Śaunaka cited in the *Prayogapārijāta* would otherwise be rendered meaningless; furthermore, it would result in the redundancy of the many duties of a *snātaka* shown in the Smṛtis, as well as the injunctions regarding independent times such as specific lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). [As it is said: "A twice-born man should not remain without an āśrama even for a single day."

Thus, this prohibition is intended to forbid the cessation of marriage for one who is not dispassionate; when there is permission from one's mother and father and an absence of dispassion, marriage must indeed be performed, and one should not desist from marriage. And this has been stated by the Śruti in the passage: "Having brought wealth that is pleasing to the teacher, do not cut off the thread of progeny."

Having brought and given to the teacher wealth that is dear and desired for the sake of the teacher, and being permitted by the teacher, one should take a suitable wife; "do not let the lineage of progeny be cut off"—the meaning is that one must not cause the interruption of the succession of offspring. The venerable Vidyaaranya has explained that the intention is that even if a son is not born, one should make an effort to produce one through such rites as the *putrakāmyā*.

The permission of the mother and father, however, is stated by this sūtra: "Having returned from the teacher’s house, he should support his mother and father; being permitted by them, he should take a wife. Therefore, since an interval between these two sūtras is established, the absence of an interval between the *samāvartana* (return ceremony) and marriage is utterly discarded.

Śrīdhara, in the *Pārijāta*, says: "In the asterisms of Vāgīśā (Śravaṇa), Āditi (Punarvasu), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Dinakṛt (Hasta), Maitra (Anurādhā), the Uttarās, Rohiṇī, and Govinda (Śravaṇa); and during the portions (*aṃśa*) and periods (*horā*) of the Moon, Sun, Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury..."

"One should perform the *samāvartana* on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, avoiding the new moon, the full moon, the eighth lunar day, the first lunar day, Aries, Cancer, and Leo, provided that the day is pure and free from blemish."

Vāgīśa is the Puṣya asterism; Aditi is the two Punarvasus; Pauṣṇa is Revatī; Saumya is Mṛgaśiras; Dinakṛt is Hasta; Maitra is Anurādhā; Uttarā refers to the three Uttaras; Govinda is Śravaṇa; Śaśāṅka is the Moon; Vid is Budha (Mercury). The Aṃśas and Horās are those already mentioned. Riktās are the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth lunar days. Parva refers to the two junctions (the new and full moon). Kīṭa is Scorpio; Hari is Leo. "Endowed with purity" means free from the defects of planetary transits and the like. "On a clear day" means free from defects such as the heliacal setting of Jupiter and Venus. Nārada says in the Madanaratna:
Then, during the northern course of the sun, when Jupiter and Venus are visible,
for the twice-born who have returned from the teacher's house and are self-restrained;

In the asterisms beginning with Maitra (Anurādhā), Uttarā-phalgunī, Āditya (Pūrvā-phalgunī), Tījya (Jyeṣṭhā), Antya (Revatī), Hari (Śravaṇa), Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Arka (Pūrvā-bhādrapadā), Dhātṛ (Rohiṇī), and Ṛṣi (Ārdrā); and on the days of the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus; and when the signs and their degrees are those of the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus.

Alternatively, even regarding the seed-syllable, lunar mansion, weekday, ascendant, and its degrees, one should avoid the first lunar day, the full and new moon days, those called *rikta*, the eighth day, and the day of the loss of a lunar day (*dinakṣaya*).
"On another day, having abandoned other duties, one should perform the rite of returning home (samāvartana) and the decoration."
The seed-constellations are the constellations for sowing seeds.
Vasiṣṭha says:
"One should perform an auspicious bath at midday under the constellation Rohiṇī."
"In the forenoon, or in its absence, one should perform the bath according to the prescribed rule."

This [rite], however, has the religious student (*brahmacārin*) alone as its performer. Prior to the *samāvartana*, the rituals are performed by the teacher (*ācārya*), while the student performs only those actions specifically prescribed for him. The *samāvartana* itself, however, has the religious student as its performer alone; for in the sūtra "Having studied the Veda, the bath," the suffix *-ktvā* in the word "having studied" (*adhītya*) expresses that the study and the bathing have the same agent.
Now, the practical application (*prayoga*).

A *brahmacārī* is one who is endowed with the vow of studying the Veda along with its auxiliary branches (*aṅga*) and their meanings, or one who is endowed merely with the study of the Veda along with its auxiliary branches, or one who is endowed merely with the study of the Veda, or one who is endowed merely with the vow; one who has observed the rules of a *brahmacārī*, performed the *kāṇḍavrata*, the *upākaraṇa*, the *utsarjana*, and the *godāna* rites, and performed the *upākaraṇa* of the *adhyāya*; having gratified his teacher with sacrificial fees, food, and so forth, and being permitted by him during the northern course of the sun in the waxing fortnight.

On a lunar day other than the empty quarters (riktās), the eighth, or the first (pratipad)—that is, on any one of the days beginning with the second—on any weekday among the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, or Venus, during its respective division (aṃśa) or hour (horā); under a constellation prescribed by the Sūtras such as Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Tiṣya, Uttarāphalgunī, Hasta, Citrā, or Viśākhā; or, if those are unavailable, under a constellation mentioned in other treatises such as Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, Uttarābhādrapadā, or Revatī; and when the ascendant is one other than Aries, Scorpio, or Leo.

On a day free from defects such as the heliacal setting of Jupiter or Venus, childhood, old age, an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), retrograde motion (*vakra*), direct overspeed (*aticāra*), or the loss of a lunar day (*dinakṣaya*), and at an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*) declared by an astrologer, one should perform the rite called *samāvartana*—also known by the synonym "bathing"—either at the teacher’s house, near water, or in a cow-pen (*goṣṭha*).

When it is performed in a cow-pen, one should first cover the pen with grass, cloth, and so forth, and properly enclose it with mats and other materials so that not even the rays of the sun can be seen; having entered there before sunrise and completed the entire rite in that very place, one should go outside at night.

Having performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*) at both times [morning and evening], he should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*). On the day of the ceremony, having performed the morning fire-ritual, sitting facing the east, sipping water (*ācamana*), and practicing breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "Having proclaimed the place and time, for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (*Śrī Parameśvara*) by means of accomplishing my eligibility for the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*), I shall perform the rite named *samāvartana*.

Thereafter, the father should perform the rites beginning with the worship of Gaṇapati—which is an ancillary part of the son’s *samāvartana*—up to the *nāndī-śrāddha*, according to the prescribed method. In this case, the specific modification is that one should say, "May Śrī be pleased," or alternatively, "May Indra be pleased."

Alternatively, while the *nāndī-śrāddha* alone is to be performed by the father, the worship of Gaṇapati, the recitation of the *puṇyāha*, and the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjana*) should be performed by himself. However, according to the view that the worship of the Mothers is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the *nāndī-śrāddha*, even that is to be performed by the father. Some maintain that even when the father is present, one may perform everything from the worship of Gaṇapati up to the end of the *nāndī-śrāddha* oneself.

Then, the religious student (brahmacārin), having performed the consecration of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) according to the procedure beginning with the smoothing [of the earth], and having established there the common fire named Pāvaka—brought from the house of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya)—and having kindled and meditated upon it, he takes three fuel-sticks (samidh). Having performed the rites ending with breath-control (prāṇāyāma) beginning with "O Faith, come" (śraddha ehi), and having recited the section beginning with "Those deities which are to be worshipped" up to the Vyāhṛtis in the ritual of the Samāvartana-homa, he says for the principal oblation: "I shall worship the fire Jātavedas with a fuel-stick of Palāśa wood."

"I shall sacrifice to Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati with one oblation of clarified butter for each; I shall sacrifice to Agni with an oblation of clarified butter. [In the *aṅgahoma*,] "Varuṇa," and so forth. At the time of arranging the vessels, one should place in the common fire (*laukikāgni*) warm water, cold water, a razor, the dung of a bull, *kuśa* grass for shaving, a piece of *audumbara* wood a span long for cleaning the teeth, moist wood brought by some relative, and fragrant substances mixed together or sandalwood alone.

Having procured two unwashed garments brought by some kinsman and marked on their right and left sides by making a sign; two earrings strung on a thread; a mirror made of sandalwood or jujube wood, covered with gold and strung on a thread; an umbrella; a bamboo staff; sandals; a garland; collyrium produced from the mountain named Trikakud—or, in its absence, lampblack; and also a vehicle such as a chariot or other means for entering the village.

Having placed the vessels used for the *homa*—such as the *darvī* ladle and others—near the sacrificial vessels according to available space, he should set down a fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *palāśa* wood. Alternatively, prior to placing the *palāśa* fuel-stick, he may station one of the vehicles, such as a chariot, intended for entering the village, near the sacrificial vessels according to available space. Then follows the selection of the *brahmā* priest and other rites. At the time of sprinkling the vessels with water, the sprinkling of the prepared vehicle—whether it be a chariot or another type—must also be performed. Thereafter, the procedure from the heating of the *darvī* ladle until the end of the *vyāhṛti* oblations is the same.

Then follows the principal Vaiśeṣika oblation: "Oṃ, this hymn we fashion with our inspired thought for the worthy Jātavedas, as one fashions a chariot; for his providence toward us is auspicious. O Agni, may we not suffer harm in your friendship—Svāhā! With this, he places the palāśa fuel-stick that has been set aside. "To Jātavedas Agni, this [is offered]. Because it is recited by the author of the Sūtra, the word *svāhā* is used here. Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the individual *vyāhṛtis*; Prajāpati is the seer of the collective *vyāhṛtis*.

Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati are the deities in order; Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, and Bṛhatī are the meters in order. This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the principal *ājya* oblation specific to the *samāvartana*. Having thus recollected, one should offer four *ājya* oblations with those [verses].

Then, having offered the principal oblations with: "Oṃ, may I have the triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa, that which is the triple life-span of the gods—may that triple life-span be mine, Svāhā! To Agni, this [oblation]. Having performed the *trivṛdanna-homa* beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa" and ending with the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), he should say, "May Prajāpati be pleased. The explicit mention of "here" (*atra*) is for the purpose of indicating that the *jaya*-oblations and so forth are optional in the case of the *vidyāvratasnāna* and the *vidyāsnāna*, whereas they are mandatory only in the case of the *vratamātrasnāna*.

Next, for the four mantras beginning with "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow," the seers are the Viśvedevas. The deities are, respectively, Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Vratapati. The meters are Yajus. Their application is in the act of worship (upasthāna). With "Oṃ agne vratapate vratamacāriṣam... rādhi," he worships Agni. With "Oṃ vāyo vratapa... he worships Vāyu. With "Oṃ āditya vrata... he worships Āditya. With "Oṃ vratānāṃ vrata... he worships Vratapati.

Having thus worshipped the deities mentioned in the mantras with these four mantras, he should perform the formal relinquishment (*utsarga*) of the vows prescribed for the stage of the religious student (*brahmacarya-āśrama*) that were undertaken at the time of initiation (*upanayana*).

For the two verses beginning with *ud u tyaṃ citram*, Soma is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Āditya is the deity (*devatā*). The meter (*chandas*) of the first is *gāyatrī*, and that of the second is *triṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the worship of Āditya. With these two verses—*om ud u tyaṃ jātavedasaṃ... sūryam* and *om citraṃ devānām udagān anīkaṃ... tasthuṣaś ca*—one worships Āditya. For the mantra *ut tamam varuṇa pāśam asmad avādhaḥ śrathāya*, Vāmadeva is the seer; the Viśvedevas or Varuṇa are the deity; the meter is *ekapadā svarāḍ jagatī*.
The application is for placing the upper garment (*uttarīya*). With the mantra: "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us," he places the upper garment.

Then, having covered his body with another large, unwashed cloth and having sipped water twice (*dvir-ācamya*), [he recites]: "Avādhamaṃ... Here, Vāmadeva is the seer; the Viśvedevas or Varuṇa are the deities; the metre is *ekapadā svarāj jagatī*. The application is for placing the lower garment (*antarīya*). With the mantra: "O Varuṇa, loosen the lowest bond from us," he places the lower garment. The lower garment (*antarīya*) is that which is worn below, namely the cloth used to cover the private parts.

For the verse *vimadhyamam*, Vāmadeva is the seer; the Viśvedevas or Varuṇa are the deities; it is in the *ekapadā svarāḍ jagatī* meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the laying down of the girdle (*mekhalā*). Reciting: *Oṃ vimadhyamaṃ varuṇapāśam asmad dhrathāya*, he unties and lays down the girdle. Then, for the verse *athā vayam āditya*, Vāmadeva is the seer; the Viśvedevas or Varuṇa are the deities; it is in the *dvipadā triṣṭubh* meter. Its application is in the laying down of the staff (*daṇḍa*). Reciting: *Oṃ athā vayam āditya syāma*, he lays down the staff.

Then, having silently cast his antelope skin, girdle, and staff into the water, he should give his inner garment to a student (brahmacārin) who needs clothing. Then, sitting to the west of the fire facing east, he touches the razor with the mantra: "Oṃ, you are named Kṣura; the axe is your father; homage be to you; do not harm me. Having handed it silently to the barber, he pours the hot water into the cold water that has been set out and touches those waters with the mantra: "Oṃ, be auspicious to us for our touch!"

This mantra is for touching alone, not for mixing, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra: "He touches. For the mantra *āpa undantu*, Soma is the deity; the meter is the two-footed Gāyatrī. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for moistening the right side of the head. With the words *oṃ āpa undantu... varcase*, he moistens the right side of the head. For the mantra *oṣadhe*, Soma is the deity; the meter is the one-footed Gāyatrī. Its application is for placing a kuśa blade with its tip pointing upward on the right side of the head.

"Oṃ, O herb, protect him! With these words, he places a blade of *kuśa* grass with its tip pointing upward, which has been brought there, at the region of the right side of the head where the hair is to be shaved. "O axe!"—for this verse, Soma is the deity, the *svadhiti* (axe) is the meter, and it is a single-footed *gāyatrī*; its application is in the placing of the razor. "Oṃ, O axe, do not harm him! With these words, he places the razor that has been brought there upon that [grass]. "O God-hearing one!"—for this verse, Soma is the deity, the *devaśrū* (God-hearing one) is the meter, and it is a single-footed *gāyatrī*; its application is in the shaving of the hair along with the *kuśa* blades.

"Oṃ, O divine razor, I shave these. With these words, he shaves the hair along with the *kuśa* grass. The ritual actions from the moistening up to the shaving are performed by the barber due to his capability; however, this applies when either some Brāhmaṇa learned in the mantras or the *ācārya* acts as such. The barber’s entitlement to recite the mantra, however, arises from the force of the scriptural injunction, just as the milk-er possesses the authority for the milking of the *sāṃnāyya* and other rites.

Then he gazes at the barber with the mantra: "O barber, with the razor that shaves well and is beautifully shaped, as you shave the hair and beard, make my face radiant; do not steal away our life-span. Then the barber shaves the beard, the side-locks, the hair of the head, the body hair, and the nails in due order, leaving aside the top-knot (*śikhā*). The one performing the shaving should bathe here.

Then, some friend of the *snātaka*, having brought a ball of bull-dung and placed the hair from his beard and other parts that were buried there, digs a pit in a cow-pen, at the foot of an *udumbara* tree, or at a clump of *darbha* grass, saying: "Oṃ, here I bury the sin of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so. Having cast those hairs into the pit along with the ball of bull-dung, he fills the pit with earth.

In place of the word *amuṣya*, one should take the conventional name ending in the word *śarman* with the genitive case in the singular; however, in place of *āmuṣyāyaṇasya*, one should take the family name (*gotra*) in the genitive singular. For example: "Here I conceal the evil of Devadattaśarman, the descendant of Vasiṣṭha."

Then the *snātaka*, having removed the impurities of the body by rubbing it with the paste of *karañja* and other substances, should clean his teeth with a piece of *audumbara* wood that has been set aside, reciting: "Oṃ, arrange yourselves for the sake of food; arrange yourselves for the sake of long life; arrange yourselves for the sake of Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*). May I become long-lived, an eater of food, and possessed of Vedic splendor. Thereafter, he should perform twelve mouthfuls of rinsing (*gaṇḍūṣa*) silently.

Then the preceptor or another [priest] [performs the rite]. For the three mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the seers are Agni and the Viśvedevas; the deity is Water; the meter is Gāyatrī. For the four mantras beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, the seer is Agni; the deity is Water; the meter is Triṣṭubh. For the mantras of the *pavamāna* section, Prajāpati is the seer. The deities of those respective mantras are Pavamāna, Suvarjana, and others as indicated by their specific characteristics (*liṅga*). The meters are Gāyatrī and so forth. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the ritual of bathing.

He causes [the student] to bathe with lukewarm water using the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, and this entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*. The mere act of directing [the ritual] belongs to the teacher, while the bathing preceded by the recitation of the mantras belongs to the student alone. The bathing takes place either at the end of each respective collection of mantras or at the end of the *Pavamāna* section. Some, however, desire that the bathing be performed after every single mantra; that is not correct.

In the injunction for a ritual act associated with a specific number other than that of the *homa*, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "ritual acts consist of a single mantra" does not apply. Although the *pavamāna* section lacks a specific number, it should be understood that because the statement "by this [section], namely *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*" declares the entire section as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the instrumentality does not belong to each individual mantra.

Then, having sipped water twice and silently put on his ordinary garment, having sipped water twice again, having loosened his waist-string and loincloth and set them aside in a known place, and having sprinkled the prepared sandalwood paste with water and smeared his hands with it, he makes a salutation with joined palms toward the east for the gods, saying: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Seizer and to the Over-seizer; obeisance to Śāka and Jañjabha; obeisance to those deities who are the Over-seizers. [And: "The fragrance that is in the Apsarases, and the glory that is in the Gandharvas..."
"May that divine and human fragrance enter into me here."
With that handful [of water], he anoints himself in regular order, beginning from the face.

Then, having sprinkled with water two unwashed garments that have been set out, he discards the garment previously worn. Taking one of the two garments set out, wrapping it clockwise, and reciting: "Oṃ, thou art the body of Soma; protect my body; enter me as my own body; enter me as an auspicious body," he puts on the garment wrapped clockwise by way of tying a knot at the waist and so forth. Then, having sipped water twice, he puts on the garment known as the upper cloth (uttarīya) with that same mantra.

Then, having sipped water twice, he should cast into the water the waist-thread and the loincloth that were previously placed in a known spot. From this point forward, the wearing of a waist-thread or a loincloth is not to be performed.

Then, sitting to the west of the fire facing east, taking the sandalwood or jujube staff covered with gold, and the jewel and the two earrings that have been set out, and having tied them together with a blade of *darbha* grass while holding them over the fire—

Oṃ! May this gold—which bestows long life, splendor, increase of wealth, and prosperity—enter me for the sake of longevity, splendor, and victory; Svāhā! Oṃ! O gold, which is exalted, victorious in battle, triumphant in assemblies, and a winner of wealth—in this gold all complete prosperities have been gathered together; Svāhā! Oṃ! I have grasped the auspicious name of gold as one would that of a father. May it make me golden-hued and dear among men; may it make me possessed of the luster of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcas); Svāhā!

Oṃ, make me beloved among the gods; make me beloved among the Brahmins; make me beloved among the Vaiśyas and Śūdras; make me beloved among the kings, svāhā! Oṃ, this herb is the protector, the victorious Sarasvatī; may she make me golden-hued and beloved among men, and make me possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge, svāhā!

Thus, with the clarified butter remaining from the previous [offering], he makes five oblations over it with the ladle using the five mantras. The renunciation (*tyāga*) is "This for Hiraṇyāya. Or, for the last [mantra], the renunciation is "This for Auṣadhī. There is no sprinkling around the fire here, because this is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the jewel and the earring.

Then, with these same five mantras, omitting the word *svāhā*, he thoroughly washes the jewel and the earring three times clockwise in a vessel of water—once with the mantras and twice silently—at the very end of the ritual. With the mantra: "Oṃ, Virāj and Svarāj, and the prosperity that is in our home; with that Lakṣmī who is at the head of the kingdom, we unite thee," he places the right earring on the right ear.

"Oṃ, with the seasons, with the seasonal periods, for the sake of long life and luster, with the nourishment of the year—with that, being present, you favor him. Saying this, he covers the earring on the right ear so that it does not fall off. "Oṃ, Virāj and Svarāj, Abhiṣṭo and Yā in our home; Lakṣmī who is at the head of the kingdom—with her, we unite him. Saying this, he puts on the second earring on the left ear.

"Oṃ, with the seasons, with the seasonal periods, for the sake of life and luster, by the nourishment of the year—with that, being present, you favor him. With this, he covers the earring on his left ear as before. In this case, there is indeed sequential performance (kāṇḍānusamaya) according to the sūtra: "But those [actions] joined together have a single completion. "Oṃ, this herb is protecting, overcoming, Sarasvatī..."

"May she make me golden-hued, dear among men, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*); you are a deliverer from bonds"—with these words, he ties the amulet, consecrated by the *abhihoma* rite, around his neck. "O *Śubhikā*, ascend as auspiciousness, beautifying my face; beautify my face and grant me abundant fortune."

With the two verses, "That which Jamadagni brought for Śraddhā out of desire for her—this I now fasten upon you, together with fortune and luster," he puts on the garland that has been placed before him. With the verse, "Oṃ! That collyrium from Trikakud which was produced upon the Himavat, with that I anoint your eyes, together with fortune and luster; [may the] mountain-person [be] in me," he simultaneously anoints both eyes with the collyrium provided, using both hands at once, because of the dual number in the word *vām* ("of you two").

Some, however, say that one should apply collyrium to the left eye with the right hand while reciting the mantra "yad añjanam," and to the right eye with that same mantra; they claim that applying the collyrium to the left eye first is established by the Śruti text: "For men first anoint the left eye. For them, the contradiction regarding the dual number and the gender [of the mantra] is quite evident. The mantra "yan me manaḥ" has Soma as its deity, Ādarśa (the mirror) as its subject, and Anuṣṭubh as its meter; its application is for looking at one's self in a mirror: "Oṃ, my mind which has gone afar, or that which has not gone afar..."

"King Soma has placed that vigor within us"—with these words, he looks at himself in a mirror. Because this [act] is prescribed by rule (*vaidha*), the prohibition against looking in a mirror on Sundays does not apply, just like the looking in a mirror at the time of departure. For the mantra "devasya tvā," Vāmadeva or Prajāpati is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity, and the *yajus* is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the receiving of the bamboo staff.

With the mantra, "Oṃ, by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you," he receives the bamboo staff that has been placed there; this implies that someone other than himself is the giver of the staff. Having recited the mantra once, "Oṃ, you are the thunderbolt of Indra; O Aśvins, protect me," he wipes that upright staff three times with his hand holding water. Although the upward wiping is already established by the word *ut* (up), the explicit mention of *ūrdhvam* (upright) is for the purpose of qualifying the staff.

In this way, the meaning that "one holds the staff upwards and wipes upwards" becomes established. As for wiping with a hand containing water, the injunction "he wipes with water, saying: *oṃ viṣṇormanasā pūte sthaḥ*" in this Sūtra—specifically the mention of "with water"—indicates that in all cases the wiping is done with water; whereas the author of the *Vaijayantī* explains that actions such as *anumārjana* (subsequent wiping) are performed with the hand alone. However, the *anumārjana* of the two *pavitra*s is done with water because of a specific scriptural statement.

Then, having recited the mantra once—"Oṃ, O Vege! Vejayā! Protect us from our enemies, thieves, reptiles, beasts of prey, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and fears caused by non-human beings; protect us with thy staff, protect us from all fear, strike down thieves on every side; thou art born upon all trees as one who is not naked, a slayer of rivals; destroy all hosts of enemies on every side like Maghavan"—he whirls the staff three times clockwise above his head.

"Oṃ, you two are supports, O divine ones; do not cause me distress"—saying this, while still seated, he simultaneously takes off his two sandals. Because of the dual number in the mantra, the mantra is recited only once. If simultaneous removal is impossible, the mantra is repeated due to necessity. However, the dual number may be interpreted in some other way, as in the case of the plural *uparava* holes. Here too, the mantra is recited only once. "Oṃ, you are the refuge of Prajāpati, the covering of Brahman"—with these words, he receives the parasol.

In this case as well, there may be some other donor for the sake of the ritual purpose. If the staff should fall from his hand, he takes it up again with the mantra: "Oṃ! That staff of mine which has fallen from the sky onto the earth—this very one I take up again for long life and for strength. This holding of the staff is obligatory either for as long as one lives or until the conclusion of the *madhuparka* ceremony.
Then, having mounted a chariot, a horse, or an elephant prepared and brought by another, he enters the village.

Therein—the mantra for mounting the chariot is as follows: "Oṃ! You are the Rathantara; you are the Vāmadevya; you are the Bṛhat. The two Nyankus are on both sides of the chariot, which moves along the edge of the wind through the darkness. May those fires of yours, the far-shooting, the winged ones, the senses, carry us across to safety. O Aśvins, may this chariot of yours not be harmed by either sorrow or joy. May it go unhurt and in safety, warding off those who seek to harm us. Here is stability, here is support; may it find delight here. Thus [ends] the mantra for mounting the chariot.

"Oṃ, you are a horse; you are a steed; you are a courser; you are a racer; you are a man; you are a swift runner; you are a prize-winner; you are a stallion; you are one whose mind is directed toward men; you are named 'the Swift'.
With these eleven mantras consisting of the names of the horse, one mounts the horse.

"Oṃ, I mount you with the thunderbolt of Indra. Carry me; carry prosperity; bring prosperity to me. You are an elephant; you possess the glory of an elephant; you possess the luster of an elephant. May I become possessed of the glory of an elephant and the luster of an elephant. With this mantra, one mounts the elephant.

When the ritual is performed in the cow-pen (*goṣṭha*), one should remain right there until the end of the night, then mount any vehicle such as a chariot and enter the village. However, when the ritual is performed in the house (*gṛha*), one should mount any vehicle such as a chariot and proceed immediately to the place where they intend to perform the worship. If, however, the worship is to be performed in the house itself, then there is no mounting of a vehicle. The prohibition against looking at the sun applies only to the case of performing the ritual in the cow-pen. Then [one recites]: "Oṃ, may the quarters flow toward me; may pleasant truths (*sūnṛtāḥ*) come together in me; may all desires..."
Having recited the mantra once—"May our beloved ones come toward us; may our beloved ones flow toward us"—he worships the directions.

Then he goes to where he intends to perform worship. While going, or even without dismounting from his vehicle, he approaches the person who is about to perform worship, facing them, and gazes intently at them, whether he has already dismounted or not, saying: "Oṃ, you are glory; may I become glory in you, O [Name]! (e.g., Amukaśarman).
Now, the honey-mixture (madhuparka).

On the day of the return ceremony (samāvartana), the host, having prepared a lodging for the bath-graduate (snātaka) who has returned to his own home—providing a bed, seat, and other necessities—and having honored the guest who has descended from his vehicle, shall cause him to sit facing the east. He should then prepare a cushion (kūrca) made of darbha grass of a fixed number and, having collected water for the foot-washing (pādya) in a smaller vessel, he should cover it with a larger vessel. In this same manner, the collection and covering of the water for the respectful offering (arghya) and the water for sipping (ācamana) are performed separately in two vessels.
There is no requirement here that these vessels must be made of bell-metal (kāṃsya).

Then, having brought curd into a smaller bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), he pours honey into it; then ghee—having thus prepared the *madhuparka* consisting of these three ingredients—he covers it with a larger [vessel] and winds it around with a thread. Or, it may consist of five elements: curd, honey, ghee, water, and parched grain (*saktu*). In this latter case, there is no fixed order for mixing the curd and the other ingredients; however, the ghee must certainly be added last, as its function is that of a final sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).

Even in the case of the *pāṅkta* [fivefold] set, one should perform the wrapping with thread after bringing a shorter [vessel] and covering it with a longer one. In the absence of the *trivṛt* or *pāṅkta* [sets], or if honey is unavailable, one should prepare the *madhuparka* mixed with honey; or else, according to the method stated in the *Dharmasūtra*: "Or milk mixed with honey, or in its absence, water."

Then, one should prepare a cow, a garment, two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*), ornaments according to one's means, garlands, and so forth. If possible, for the purpose of seating the venerable guest, one prepares a seat made of *meraka* grass with its fringes pointing northward, having many strands and covered with a cloth whose fringe is directed toward the north. This preparation of the seat is performed by spreading *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward in the middle of the house or in the northeast part of the house; upon these, the ritual materials are placed. There should be as many seats and other items as there are persons to be honored.

For each vessel, there is one *kūrca* for the purpose of placing it down. At the time of handing over the vessels, there are two *kūrca*s for the purpose of grasping the vessel from below and above; these two serve the purpose of all the vessels. This is the specific detail mentioned by Baudhāyana. Furthermore, the giving of garments, earrings, garlands, and so forth, is also according to the tradition of Baudhāyana alone.

The worshipper, having sat down to the south of the one to be honored facing north, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma), shall announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall honor this Snātaka with the Madhuparka. The rule for the offering is that, having taken the collection of items such as the *kūrca* (grass mat) as prescribed, he should speak each item aloud in accordance with the intention of the receiver. The worshipper says three times or once, "Oṃ, Argha" (the guest-water) to the one to be honored; the one to be honored replies, "Do so."

The worshipper says, "Oṃ kūrca," three times or once. The one being worshipped, having said, "A good kūrca," receives it with both hands and, saying, "Oṃ, you are the sustainer of the kingdom; you are the teacher’s seat; may you not be shaken," sits down facing east upon the kūrca whose tips point north. Then the worshipper says, "Oṃ pādya," three times or once. The one being worshipped says, "A good pādya. Then a servant of the worshipper, or a female servant, or a Brāhmaṇa belonging to him, washes the feet of the one being worshipped.

In that regard, a Brāhmaṇa washes his right foot first and then his left; for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, however, there is no fixed rule. If it is a male or female slave, they wash the left foot first and then the right. Here, the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) is performed twice according to the Smṛti rules. By the phrase "he who washes his feet," it is shown that there is no restriction regarding the person performing the washing.

Thus, it is established that the washing may even be performed by a Brāhmaṇa, and that the agency of the two alone—namely, the Śūdra and the Śūdrī—is not restricted. Furthermore, by the injunction regarding the touching of the hands of the washer, it is understood that the washing itself is indeed to be performed by another agent. Thereafter, the worshipper touches the hands of the washer with the mantra: "Oṃ, you are the milking of Virāj; may the milking of the Padyā-Virāj be in me."
Saying, "Oṃ! May splendor, sensory power, vigor, longevity, renown, luster, fame, and strength abide in me," one should touch oneself and then sip water.

Then the worshipper (pūjaka), having taken water for the *arghya* offering along with perfumes, garlands, two garments, two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*), and ornaments, says three times or once, "Oṃ, the *arghya*. The one being worshipped (pūjya) replies, "May it be well-offered (*svarghyam*"), and then receives in his joined palms the *arghya* water—which is being poured out slightly by the worshipper together with the perfumes, garlands, two garments, two sacred threads, and ornaments—while reciting: "Oṃ, come to me; unite me with glory, with splendor, with luster, and with nourishment (*payas*); make me dear to all creatures and the sovereign lord of cattle."

Then, having adorned himself with perfumes, garlands, garments, earrings, wreaths, and so forth, and having given the remaining *arghya* water to the officiant (*pūjaka*), he consecrates that water as it is being poured out by the officiant with the mantra: "Oṃ, I send you to the ocean... my water. Regarding the offering of the perfumes and other items together with the *arghya* water, the statement of Mātṛdatta is based on the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*, and the statement of Rudraskanda, the commentator, is also the source. Then the officiant says: "Oṃ, the water for sipping," three times or once.

The worshipper says, "Svācamanīyam" (water for sipping). For the mantra "Amṛtopastaraṇam asi," the deities are the Yājñikyas, the Upaniṣads, the water, and the Yajus; its application is in the act of sipping. Reciting "Oṃ amṛtopastaraṇam asi," the worshipper sips from half of the water offered by the worshipper. There is no ordinary purification-sipping here. The worshipper says, "Oṃ Madhuparka," either three times or once. The worshipper replies, "Sumadhuparka. For the mantra "Devasya tvā," Prajāpati is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity, and the meter is Yajus.

The application is for the acceptance of the *madhuparka* (honey-mixture). Having accepted it with an añjali (cupped hands) open like the sky, reciting: "Oṃ, by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I accept thee," and having placed it on the ground, reciting: "Oṃ, I set thee on the navel of the earth, in the station of Iḍā," he then says: "Oṃ, by that which is the honeyed, supreme form of the honey, the essence of food, may I, through that honeyed, supreme form of the honey, become supreme, honeyed, and an eater of food."

He stirs the *madhuparka* with his thumb, ring finger, and little finger once with the mantra and twice silently. Reciting the mantra, "Oṃ, for the sake of splendor, prosperity, fame, strength, and the enjoyment of food, I partake of thee," he consumes the *madhuparka* three times with his thumb, ring finger, and little finger. Having washed his hand, he gives the remainder to the attendants (*rātayas*). In their absence, he should consume it all;
however, because it is now loathed by the world, he should consume only a portion.

Then, for the mantra "amṛtāpidhānam asi," the deities are the Yājñikyas, the Upaniṣads, and water is the meter; its application is in the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). Reciting "Oṃ amṛtāpidhānam asi," he sips with all the water remaining from the previous sipping. Then, having washed his face and hands, he performs the Smārta ācamana with ordinary water. Thereafter, the worshipper says "Oṃ gauḥ" three times or once.

Having honored her by saying "O, Gaurī!", he should release her while reciting: "Om! The cow is auspicious, the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality. I have declared this to the wise person: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi. Let her drink water and eat grass. Om! Release her! Based on the indicative mark of the mantra, the "Gauḥ" here refers specifically to a female cow.

In the case of killing her, one should recite: "Oṃ, O bull, you are free from evil; destroy the evil of myself and of so-and-so! May my enemies be struck down! May my enemies be struck down! Make them struck down! and then eat that meat prepared by the attendants. In the case of release, one should eat meat not prohibited by others. Since the killing of a cow is forbidden in the Kali age, only the rite of release (utsarga) should be performed. Even the eating of other meat does not occur, because that too is forbidden in the Kali age.

In place of meat, food mixed with *māṣa* beans should be offered. The worshipper, having prepared the food mixed with *māṣa* beans, says "Oṃ bhūtam" three times or once when the food is ready. The one to be worshipped replies, "Oṃ, that is well-prepared; may the Virāṭ-food not perish for me, may I eat it, may it bestow strength upon me; that is well-prepared," and then says, "Feed the Brāhmaṇas. In this regard, there should be four Brāhmaṇas of different lineages (*gotras*).

"One should say, 'Feed four Brahmins of different lineages,'" according to the statement of Baudhāyana. Thereafter, the attendant gives the food remaining from the Brahmins' meal to the *snātaka*. The recipient accepts the food given by the attendant with the mantra: "Oṃ! May Heaven give it to you; may Earth accept it. May Earth give it to you; may Prāṇa accept it. Let Prāṇa eat you; let Prāṇa drink you."

For the hymn beginning with "indrāgnī me," the deity is Indra, Agni, and others; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; its application is in the eating of food. Reciting: "Oṃ, may Indra and Agni bestow luster upon me; may Soma and Bṛhaspati bestow luster; may all the gods bestow luster upon me; O Aśvins, bestow luster upon me," one eats as much as desired. If a remnant remains in the vessel, then one should either give it to a servant (rāti) or bury it. In the Kali age, since giving the leavings to a servant is censured by the world, burying it alone is prescribed.

Then, having washed his face and other parts, he should sip water twice. At this point, one may offer perfumes and other articles. To those who have eaten, one should give pairs of garments, pairs of earrings, garlands, and ornaments; some say one should also give a single piece of wealth and a *ṣaṣṭhauhī* cow. Baudhāyana states that some authorities prescribe the giving of ornaments prior to the *madhuparka*. This is an elliptical expression for perfumes and other such items. "Single piece of wealth" (*ekadhana*) means principal wealth. A *ṣaṣṭhauhī* is a four-year-old cow that has calved for the first time.

Having previously stated the prohibition against giving perfumes, garlands, and so forth, Devatrāta also said: "These [gifts] should be given when the ritual action has ceased. This means when the ritual action known as the *madhuparka* has ceased—that is, when it is completed. For the *madhuparka* concludes with the meal. In this very manner, the offering of the *madhuparka* is to be made to officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), teachers (*ācārya*), fathers-in-law (*śvaśura*), those related by marriage (*vaivāhya*), and others.

If one should desire, "May he be dependent on me for whatever gift [he receives]," then, having himself eaten and sipped water (ācamana), he takes the right hand of that person—who has finished eating his *vratocchiṣṭa* and has sipped water—with the mantra: "Oṃ, by him in whom the past and the future, and all worlds are supported here; by him I receive you; I take you with the Brahman, O so-and-so. Here, in the word "so-and-so," the name of the giver is to be inserted. And this grasping of the hand is optional (*kāmya*), because of the statement "if one should desire."

Then, having stayed that night in the prepared residence, the *snātaka* should go to his own home. However, if the father is the instructor and the bath takes place outside the village—such as by a river or in a cow-pen located far from the house—then after the rites ending with the holding of the umbrella, he should ascend one of the vehicles, such as a chariot, and proceed to his father’s house. If the instructor is someone other than the father, then having performed the bath in that [other] person's house, he should ascend one of the vehicles, such as a chariot, and go to his father’s house.

The father also must perform the *madhuparka* worship upon the arrival of his son who has completed his studies (*snātaka*) at his own home, according to Manu’s statement: "The father should honor him with the *madhuparka*. Likewise, others as well must perform the *madhuparka* worship for the *snātaka*. As for these acts—the mounting of the vehicle, the salutation of the quarters, and the looking at the worshipper—which have been prescribed with their respective mantras, they belong to the *snātaka* alone because they are ancillary to the *samāvartana* ceremony, not to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others.
For this very reason, the teacher employed the word "atha" (now) after the looking at the worshipper to indicate the commencement of a different set of rites.

Then, having performed the feeding of Brahmins and the giving of abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the *snātaka* should, for the sake of the perfection of the rite, remember Viṣṇu and dedicate the action to the Lord of Karma (*karmeśvara*).
Now, something is said regarding the subject of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).

The *madhuparka* is of two kinds: that accompanied by a cow and that devoid of one. Among these, the one accompanied by a cow is for teachers (*ācārya*) and others who have studied the Vedas. Regarding this, the *Dharmasūtra* states: "One worthy of the cow and the *madhuparka* is a teacher who has studied the Vedas, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a graduate (*snātaka*), a father-in-law, or a righteous king. The meaning is that he is fit for—or entitled to—the cow and the *madhuparka*. In such a compound, an additional cow is to be given in comparison to the cow already included within the *madhuparka*.

The term "one who studies the Veda" (*vedādhyāyī*) is an epithet for the teacher (*ācārya*) and others. This means that if the teacher and the rest have studied the entire Veda, only then should a cow superior to the *madhuparka* be given, and not otherwise. By this it is understood that even teachers and others who have studied only a portion of the Veda are indeed worthy of worship with the simple *madhuparka* alone.

Alternatively, the compound may be analyzed as "the honey-mixture joined with a cow" (*gomadhaparka*). In this case, the term *madhaparka* refers primarily to the ritual ending with the offering of the honey-mixture; consequently, even the cow included within that ritual would be absent, let alone the gift of an additional cow. Furthermore, there is another specific rule in the *Dharmasūtra*: "A cow and a honey-mixture [are to be given] to the teacher, the officiating priest, a *snātaka*, a father-in-law, and a king, when they present themselves after a year has passed."

The meaning is that for these teachers and others, who possess the previously mentioned qualifications and have arrived after a year has passed, worship with the *madhuparka* accompanied by a cow must be performed. By this sūtra, the time limit is established. A cow is to be given only to one who is a *vidyā-snātaka* or a *vidyā-vrata-snātaka*, and not to one who is merely a *vrata-snātaka*. This is understood from the subsequent sūtra: in the preceding sūtra, the *madhuparka* is prescribed on account of the fulfillment of qualities such as being an instructor of dharma.
