In this regard, it should be understood that the *madhuparka* is for the teacher of Dharma after the initiation (*upanayana*), for the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) after his selection, for the *snātaka* at the conclusion of the return ceremony (*samāvartana*), for the father-in-law at the conclusion of the ritual for raising the deity-image (*devakotthāpana*), and for the king at the conclusion of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

According to the maxim that "the effect follows each individual cause," and based on the *Āśvalāyana Sūtra* stating "having chosen the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), one should bring the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*)," as well as the *Chandoga Sūtra* stating "again and again at the sacrifice," it is possible for the officiating priests who have become gods and ancestors to be present outside of their ritual duties after every year-long sacrifice; however, this does not apply to those who have become human beings, because it is impossible for them to serve as officiating priests outside of their ritual duties.
Jābāli also mentions others worthy of the honey-mixture:
"The bridegroom, the officiating priest, and a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) who has come to the house..."
"One should honor with the madhuparka offering both a snātaka and a beloved guest."

Baudhāyana also states: "Now, these are the recipients of the *arghya* (those worthy of the *arghya* offering): the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, the maternal uncle, the teacher (*ācārya*), the king, the accomplished student (*snātaka*), and a dear guest who has arrived. One should offer this to these very persons when they visit within the course of a year; at a wedding, it is offered to the bridegroom, and at each respective ritual act, it is given to the officiating priests. The term *arghyāḥ* means those worthy of the *arghya*, that is to say, those entitled to the *madhuparka* worship. It should be understood that the paternal uncle, the maternal uncle, the person to be married, and the dear guest are included by the word "etcetera" (*iti*) in the sūtra. However, for the one to be married, there is only the *madhuparka* and no additional cow.

The specific number of cows to be given to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is stated in the *Baudhāyana-gṛhya*: "He announces the cows to the various priests; one cow to the *hotraka*s, or one for all of them according to his means. Regarding the option of release (*utsarga*), a specific rule has been stated by that same author: "When that [cow] has been released, he should sacrifice a ram or a goat, or with the meat of wild animals; however, the guest-offering (*argha*) must not be meatless, though in case of inability, it may consist of beans and rice. Furthermore, it was stated by that same author: "One should honor the officiating priest and the teacher; indeed, he who honors his own officiating priest and teacher honors himself."
The meaning is that he magnifies or honors [it].
Now follows the alternative procedure for the return ceremony (*samāvartana*) for one who is extremely ill.
Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "Now, this other [procedure]: having bathed silently at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), he silently places a fuel-stick (*samidh*) upon the fire."

This has been explained by Sudarśana: "Now, the remainder [of the sentence] is 'then another procedure is stated. At a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), such as a holy river and so forth. A fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *pālāśa* wood. And because of the particle 'eva' (only), nothing else whatsoever is to be performed in this procedure."

The procedure, however, is as follows: having discarded the marks of a student, such as the girdle and so forth, and having silently bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), put on another garment and performed the other preliminary rites; then, having fetched fire from the house of a Śrotriya and having established the fire according to rule wherever it may be, he offers a fuel-stick silently while meditating mentally upon Prajāpati. Other acts, such as the shaving of hair and beard, which do not contradict the rite, should likewise be performed silently.

The sequence here is as follows: having resolved [upon the rite], one discards the girdle and other items, then undergoes shaving, and subsequently bathes at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). By the phrase "wearing [the garment] and so forth," the two-fold sipping of water (*dvir-ācamana*) and the application of the sectarian mark (*tilaka*) are included. By the phrase "shaving and so forth," the clipping of the nails is intended.

Āśvalāyana states the fruit of the *samāvartana*: "It is known that the *snātaka* becomes a great being (*mahābhūta*). For the *snātaka* is indeed heard of as a great being. But how is the greatness of the *snātaka* established? It is said:
"Because the householder is served by gods, humans, and even those of animal birth, therefore the one in the householder stage of life is the eldest," according to the Smṛti.
"There is also the Śruti: 'He who is a Snātaka becomes a Mahābhūta. And another Smṛti states:
'Because he performs services just like the pentad beginning with earth...'"
The gods, humans, and ancestors—all depend upon him.
Knowledge, as well as those seeking knowledge and disciples who are desirous of hearing,
indeed declare that the Vedic science was taught first by Anu and the others.
"The greatness of the *snātaka* alone consists of the great elements,
for just as all living beings live by depending upon their mother,
so too do all mendicants live by depending upon the householder."
Thus ends the procedure for the *samāvartana* sacrament in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.

Thus ends the ninth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita— who was himself the performer of the *Agni-cit*, *Vājapeya*, *Pauṇḍarīka*, and *Sarvatomukha* sacrifices, and who bore the surname Okopa.
Now begins the tenth chapter:
Next, the duties of a *snātaka* in brief.

In this regard, the *Dharmasūtra* states: "With his face adorned with garlands, his hair and beard anointed, wearing red [garments], smeared [with unguents], wearing a turban and a lower garment, and equipped with a bodice, sandals, and wooden shoes."

*Mālī* means wearing a garland. *Āliptamukhaḥ* means one whose face has been smeared with sandalwood paste and the like; the mention of "face" (*mukha*) is illustrative, as Āśvalāyana states: "A Brāhmaṇa should first smear [the face]. *Upaliptakeśaśmaśruḥ* refers to one whose hair and beard have been treated and refined with fragrant substances such as sandalwood. *Aktaḥ* means having the eyes anointed with collyrium. *Abhyaktaḥ* means having the limbs rubbed with oil. *Veṣṭinī* means one whose head is wrapped. *Apaveṣṭinī* refers to one whose waist region is wrapped with a second garment.

*Kāñcuka* means a bodice (*kañcuka*); one who possesses that is a *kāñcukī*. One who possesses sandals (*upānah*) is an *upānahī*. Wooden shoes for protecting the feet are *pāduke*; one who possesses them is a *pādukī*. The author of the *Ujjvalā* has explained that the meaning is that one should be such [as described].
Regarding this, the mounting of wooden shoes (*pādukārohaṇa*) mentioned here is forbidden for one whose father is living and for one who has an elder brother.
[As it is said: "Wooden shoes, an upper garment, and the wearing of silver on the index finger..."
"One whose father is living should not perform [the rite] while his eldest brother is living," according to the statement in another Smṛti.

Furthermore, in the Dharmasūtra: "One should avoid all dyed colors on one's garment; one should wear a garment that is naturally black or lacks luster, provided it is not of inferior quality, as long as one has the means."

One should avoid all dyestuffs such as safflower (*kusumbha*) for one's clothing. One should not wear a garment dyed by anyone else. Even woolen blankets (*kambala*) and the like that are naturally black by their very nature should not be worn. "Radiant" (*udbhāsi*) means having the quality of shining; the opposite of that is "non-radiant. The long vowel [in *udbhāsi*] is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). One should wear clothing that is of this latter kind—lowly, base, worn out, soiled, and coarse—and its opposite is "not excellent. Such clothing one should wear, provided one has the capacity [to obtain better], as explained by Ujjvalākṛt when there is the ability [to do so].
And furthermore, in that very same [text]: "One should not cross a river with one's arms.

From the preceding sūtra, the word "one should avoid" (varjayet) is understood to carry over. The meaning is that one should avoid crossing a river by means of one's arms—that is, crossing (*taraṃ*) or swimming (*taraṇaṃ*). By the specific mention of "with one's arms," it is explained by that same author that there is no fault in crossing by means of a raft or similar device.

Likewise: "One should not bathe at night, nor should one bathe naked"; and likewise: "One should not look upon a naked woman. And this [prohibition against looking] should be understood to apply except in the case of sexual intercourse.
This is because of the statement of Āśvalāyana: "Except for sexual intercourse, one should not look at a naked woman.
Likewise: "One who has been initiated (upetaḥ) should avoid the leavings (ucchiṣṭa) of women and of one who has been initiated.

He himself explained this as meaning that one who has been initiated—that is, one who has performed the *upanayana* ceremony and returned home—should not eat the leavings of women or of one who has been initiated. Regarding the Gautama Sūtra rule, "one should cross a river with the arms," Haradatta maintains that the mention of the "river" (*nadī*) is intended to include ponds and other bodies of water, whereas the mention of "arms" (*bāhu*) is intended to be strictly observed.
Āśvalāyana says: "One should not run while it is raining, nor climb a tree, nor descend into a well.

In the Dharmasūtra: "And one should not walk over a calf-rope (*vatsatantī*). *Vatsatantī* means the rope for binding a calf. The commentator Ujjvalākāra explains that the word "calf" (*vatsa*) is indicative of the bovine species in general. Haradatta likewise explains this during his commentary on Gautama’s text.

And furthermore: "One should not pass between the fire and a Brāhmaṇa, nor between Brāhmaṇas and the fire; one should not hold fire and water simultaneously; one should avoid placing fires together unless there is an explicit injunction; when fire is being brought toward oneself, one should not circumambulate it before it has been established on the ground; and one should not let one's hands touch from behind."

In the phrase *brāhmaṇāṃśca*, the word *ca* (and) serves to draw forward [the preceding rule] that one should not pass between [the Brahmins]. In the absence of a specific injunction, one should avoid the *saṃnivāpa*—that is, the pouring together—of another fire into a single fire. One should not circumambulate an Agni being brought toward oneself from the front, while it is still unsupported on the ground and has not been established. One should not join one's two hands (*pāṇī*) behind one’s own back—the word *ca* implying also not on the head. The meaning is that one should not bring them together simultaneously. Devala says:
"One should never throw fire into fire, nor should one ever extinguish it with water."
From the statement "it is permitted," it is understood that there is no fault in the case of such occasions as a house fire and the like.
In the *Dharmasūtra* it says:
"One should avoid washing one foot with the other."
Likewise:
"Nail-scratching, biting, slapping, and spitting without cause," as stated in the Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
one should say "Bhadraṃ bhadram" (May it be auspicious) or simply utter "Bhadram" (May it be auspicious).
"One should not engage in groundless enmity or dispute with anyone. "Groundless" means devoid of fruit. In this way, even dispute is to be avoided.
In another Smṛti:
One should not throw spittle, blood, feces, urine, or semen into water;
one should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one step over it.

"One should not drink water from one's cupped hands; one should not wake a sleeping person; one should not play with dice or with those who destroy dharma; nor should one lie down to sleep with those who are diseased."

Regarding this fire: some maintain that the mention of "water" is merely an illustration for all drinkable substances, because Gautama’s rule stating "one should not drink with cupped hands" does not specify a particular type of drink. That is incorrect; for even a general rule of Gautama can be restricted by a specific rule of Yājñavalkya. Therefore, it is water alone that should not be drunk with cupped hands, but not every kind of drink.
One should not wake a superior person who is lying down, according to Manu's statement: "One should not sleep alone in the house of a Śūdra, nor should one wake a superior."

And furthermore: "One should not say to another, 'It is Indra’s bow'; one should not look at things falling; one should not pass between the two poles of a swing; and one should avoid looking at the sun as it rises or sets."
While walking, one should not look at or speak of luminous bodies such as the stars to another person.
Furthermore:
"Bathing after sunset, a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, wooden sandals, and the cleaning of the teeth [are forbidden]."
"One should avoid [these]," it says. Furthermore: "One should avoid ascending or descending uneven places.

And furthermore: "One should avoid a doubtful boat, as well as the cutting of grass, the crushing of clods of earth, and spitting, unless there is a specific reason. A "doubtful boat" is one regarding which a doubt has arisen as to whether one will sink in it; such a boat one should avoid when boarding.
And furthermore: "One should not look at oneself in water. Aṅgiras says:
"He who should ever eat together with his wife, or eat her leavings..."
"The wise always desire no fault in him. This [statement] refers either to the subject of marriage or to the subject of the minor nature of a fault.
"One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor what has been prepared as an oblation."
"And one should not teach him the Dharma, nor should one prescribe a vow for him.

Here, *mati* refers to matters such as the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*) and the like, because the prohibition against teaching the Dharma and so forth is recorded separately. Regarding this, Haradatta states: "In the rule 'one should not give leavings to a Śūdra,' the intention is that one should not give leavings to a Śūdra who is a householder (*gṛhastha*). [For it is said:
'Food that is a leaving should be given to a Śūdra who is a householder.'"
"But one should give to the householder every day what is not leftover."
Thus he says, "from the words of Vyāghra.
Furthermore, the prohibition regarding instruction for a Śūdra refers specifically to direct instruction:
"One should cause the four castes to hear [the scripture], having placed a Brāhmaṇa at the forefront."
For it is thus ordained that instruction is to be given through the medium of a Brāhmaṇa.
Vasiṣṭha states:
"For those who have completed their studentship (snātakas), there should be a second lower garment as well as an upper one."
This wearing [of the sacred thread] is obligatory. According to the statement of Devala, "And many for one desiring long life," even several upavītas may be worn.
Kaśyapa states the limit for this plurality: "A householder may have three, four, five, eight, or even ten."
In this regard, when holding more than three up to ten [rosaries], an abundance of fruit should be inferred.
As stated in the *Mādhavīya* based on the *Kaurma Purāṇa*:
"A pair of sacred threads, water, and a water-pot..."
An umbrella, a stainless turban, and also two pairs of sandals and shoes.
Wearing golden earrings and having his hair and nails clipped, he should remain pure and constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda; he should not wear garlands on the outside.
He should always wear white garments and be fond of pleasant fragrances;
when he has the means, he should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes.
"One should not wear clothing that is dyed red, ostentatious, worn by another, or patched."

*Pāduke* refers to wooden sandals for protecting the feet. *Raukme* refers to two earrings of gold, circular in shape. *Veda* means a handful of *darbha* grass; following the word "veda," the verb "should carry" (*vibhṛyāt*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Cut" (*kṛta*) means brought to shortness by clipping, but not by shaving, because of the prohibition: "Those who have returned [from studentship] shall not shave. The mention of hair includes the beard, according to Manu's statement: "With hair, nails, and beard clipped. He should be constantly engaged in his own study, that is, the study of the Veda.

Regarding the phrase *bahirmālyam*: *mālya* refers to *nirmālya*—sandalwood, flowers, and so forth, which have been removed from one's own body; one should not wear these again, but rather discard them outside. *Ulbaṇa* means that which causes bodily pain or is of great value. *Anyadhṛtam* means worn by another. *Kanthiskā* refers to a patched garment (*kanthā*); the meaning is that one should not wear it either. In the absence of a specific prohibition, these rules should be understood as common to students (*brahmacārins*), householders, and others. Even a *snātaka* must perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice: "The *vaiśvadeva* for a householder should begin in the morning."
Even by a Snātaka, that must be done, if there is separate cooking in the house.

Thus, according to the statement of Śaunaka in the *Prayogapārijāta*. Likewise, other duties (*dharmas*) mentioned in the *Dharmasūtras*, the *Gautamasūtra*, and the *Smṛtis* should be understood from those sources.
In the *Purāṇa*: "By that path by which his fathers have gone, and by which his grandfathers have gone..."
By that means, one should travel the path of the virtuous; proceeding in this way, one will cross over [the world].
"This eternal mode of life for a Brahmin householder has been declared.
If these rules are transgressed, whether intentionally or unintentionally, the penance to be known is the fasting for three days or one day as prescribed by Gautama and others.
Regarding the optional recitation (*kāmyajapa*) for the sake of marriage, it is stated in the *Ṛgvidhāna*:
"One should recite this hymn properly in a temple of Śiva;
by reciting it ten thousand times, a man shall obtain a wife within six months."

For the purpose of marriage, one should mutter twenty-three formulas beginning with *prajāpatiḥ striyām yaśaḥ* and ending with *asau me kāmaḥ samṛdhyatām*. If one performs twenty-three thousand recitations, marriage occurs within six months. Alternatively, one may mutter the mantra of Viśvāvasu, the king of the Gandharvas; the method for its concise recitation is as follows.

Of this mantra of the illustrious Gandharva king Viśvāvasu, Saṃmohana is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda), and the illustrious Gandharva king Viśvāvasu is the deity (devatā). Its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of obtaining a wife through recitation (japa). For this mantra of the illustrious Gandharva king Viśvāvasu: "Obeisance to the seer Saṃmohana" on the head; "Obeisance to the meter Gāyatrī" on the mouth; "Obeisance to the deity, the illustrious Gandharva king Viśvāvasu" on the heart.

For the purpose of recitation for the sake of obtaining a wife, [one should say] "Salutation to the application (*viniyoga*)"; this is for all limbs. Then, with the *kāma* mantra accompanied by the *praṇava* and the six long vowels, one performs the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) on the hands.
Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):
[He is seated] upon an excellent chariot fashioned from *puṇḍra* sugarcane, adorned with a golden lotus.

That man who recites the mantra of Viśvāvasu—the lord of the Gandharvas, whose heart is gracious, and who is served by maidens with lotus-hands red with saffron—will certainly obtain the maiden he desires. After the word "Viśvāvasu," the word "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. This is the visualization (*dhyāna*).
One should utter Tāra (Oṃ), Kāma (Klīm), Gaṇeśa (Gaṃ), and Dharaṇī (Lm) with its head (the nasal bindu),
followed by the seed-syllable of the Lord of Waters (Vaṃ) joined with fire (Ra) and its own head (the nasal bindu).
"The seed-syllable of fire (RA) joined with the mouth (A), then JA VI ŚVE, likewise VASO;
then the seed-syllable of the supporting earth (LA) joined with the head (M), and likewise ṢITĀM;
[then] 'grant me a maiden as a wife'—thus it is proclaimed at the end, followed by the two *ṭha* syllables (SVĀHĀ)."

Then one should mutter the mantra established by this statement. Furthermore, if it is encased between the *kāmabīja* and the *praṇava*, it bestows results quickly. Standing in the shade of a banyan tree near a body of water and facing west, one should mutter it forty thousand times. Having first performed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of five or three parts, one should thereafter perform the ritual application (*prayoga*) in that same manner. For this purpose, the application of mantras such as those of Vivāhagaurī should also be observed. In the *Āgneya-purāṇa*, in the *Yajurvidhāna*:
"With the mantra 'O Viśvakarman, the oblation...', [one should fashion] a ten-finger-long iron needle."
"One should bury a maiden at the door; she is not to be given to another."

"O Viśvakarman, increasing through the oblation, sacrifice yourself"—this is one *ṛc*. Agni is its seer (*ṛṣi*); Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*); Viśvakarman is the deity (*devatā*). The recitation (*japa*) consists of forty-four thousand [repetitions].
Thus concludes the summary of the duties of a *snātaka* in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.
This [work] was composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was a descendant of Śrīmat Sāgnicid Vājapeyin Pauṇḍarīkayājin Sarvatomukhayājin of the Okopāhva family.
The tenth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā*.
Now begins the eleventh section:
furthermore, certain optional injunctions for one who has returned home from his teacher's house.

If one should desire that a minister, a pupil, or a servant remain constantly by his side and not depart, he—having bathed in the forenoon, wearing clean garments, fasting for the entire day, and conversing only with a Brāhmaṇa—should sit facing the east at the eighth muhūrta of the night or at the end of the evening twilight. Having sipped water (ācamana), performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and announced the place and time, he should resolve: "For the sake of accomplishing the non-departure of my minister, pupil, or servant, I shall perform the rite prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras."

Having resolved upon that which is intended as the purpose for which he must not depart, he goes to the dwelling of the living animal; taking water in its horn, he circumambulates the residence three times to the right, while pouring water through the hole in the horn with the two mantras: "Oṃ, may you go around me; from this brother, from the kinsman, from all relatives, from those who sit around, you shall suffer; forever with the turbulent, the unbroken, the agitated stepping-over; you are sprinkled around; you are sprinkled around with the thick."

He walks around [the site]. He does so once with the two mantras and twice silently. He causes that living horn to be deposited securely outside the house in a place not occupied by anyone else, or he deposits it himself.

He for whom the ministers and others might go out for the sake of the remnants [of the offering] should call them from all sides with this mantra: "O you who turn back, who have increased the source; may Indra’s proclamation resound for you forever. If you think of me as 'this' or 'that,' O gods, do not deceive me further. May Indra, having bound the new noose, drive it back toward me again. Thus he should summon them from every direction.

Then, having entered his own house and performed the consecration of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the ritual procedure beginning with the smearing [of the ground], he should install the common fire named Pāvaka there, kindle it, and meditate upon it. Taking three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and having performed the rites beginning with "O Faith, come! up to the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*), he should say: "For the sake of ensuring that my minister, pupil, or servant does not depart, I shall take possession of those deities who are to be worshipped in this act of oblation. I shall worship Indra with an offering of clarified butter (*ājya*)."

Having said, "I shall sacrifice to this deity immediately," he should place fuel sticks into the fire, strew grass around the fire, spread *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, and set the vessels there.

Having set down the *darvī* ladle, or a wooden board (*phalaka*) as an alternative, the clarified-butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*), the *prokṣaṇī* water-vessel, the *upaveṣa* fire-stirring stick, the *saṃmārga* cleansing-grass, the *avajvalana* ignition-grass, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the clarified butter, a piece of *sīdhraka* wood fuel-stick one span (*prādeśa*) long, and having prepared the two strainers (*pavitre*) and consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he heats the *darvī*, cleanses it, heats it again, and sets it down. However, if a wooden board has been set down instead of a *darvī*, then the heating and subsequent rites must also be performed for that board.

Then, having sprinkled the *saṃmārjana*-darbhas and cast them into the fire, and having performed the rites beginning with the melting of the clarified butter (*ājya*) up to the placing of the two strainers (*pavitre*) in the fire, he should sprinkle water around the fire with the formulas beginning with "O Aditi, give your consent" (*adite 'numanyasva*). Having silently placed the fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *śīdhraka* wood that was set aside into the fire, [he recites] "O Āvartana, cause him to turn back," for which Soma is the deity, Indra is the seer, and the *paṅkti* is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the oblation for the purpose of achieving the state of not being able to depart. "Om! O Āvartana, cause him to turn back; O Nivartana, cause him to turn back; O Indra, O Nartabuda..."

With the mantra, "bhūmyāścatasraḥ pratiśastābhirāvartayā punaḥ svāhā," he offers one oblation of clarified butter using either the ladle or the wooden board that has been set down. The dedication is: "This is for Indra. Then, having removed the surrounding grass-coverings (paristaraṇa), and having offered the Sarvaprāyaścitta oblation for the sake of accomplishing the integrity of the rite, he sprinkles water around the fire with the mantras beginning with "adite 'nvama sthāḥ. Having worshipped the fire while performing the Saṃsthājapa prayer, he should remember Viṣṇu. Now follows the procedure according to the Āghāra-tantra.

Having performed the rites beginning with the *ullekhana* (marking) and ending with *prāṇāyāma* (breath control), and for the purpose of achieving the state of being non-departable (*anapakramaṇīyatva*), one should recite the formula beginning with "the deity who is about to be sacrificed" (*yā yakṣyamāṇā*) and ending either with the oblation to the goddess *Prasādhanī* or with the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, regarding the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*), having stated, "I shall sacrifice to Indra with an oblation of clarified butter," and [if applicable] "I shall sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an oblation of the remaining clarified butter," and so forth; and regarding the subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*), having performed the rites beginning with Varuṇa and ending either with the oblation to the goddess *Prasādhanī* or with the *vyāhṛti* oblations, according to the specific enumeration made during the *anvādhāna* (preparation).

At the conclusion of adding fuel-sticks of *saidhrakī* wood, having offered the principal oblation as before, one should complete the remainder of the rite—beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the verse "imaṃ me varuṇa" and so forth. There is no offering of the three-fold food (*trivṛdannahoma*), nor is there a ritual procedure (*tantra*) here such as that of the *āghāra* libation. Alternatively, the performance may be conducted according to the *agnihotra* ritual procedure.

Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) either by the method of scratching and so forth, or by the procedure alone as stated in the *Dharmasūtras*, having established the common fire (*laukikāgni*) there, kindled it, meditated upon it, and strewn grass around it; then, having spread *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, he places upon it the large and small ladles (*sruc-sruva*), or a wooden board and a small ladle, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), the *darbha* blades for wiping, the *darbha* blades for igniting, the clarified butter, a piece of *Saidhraka* wood fuel-stick one span long, and performs the preparation of the strainers (*pavitra*) and so forth.

Having performed the rites up to the end of "having placed [the ladle] in the purifier fire," and having silently sprinkled water around the fire, one takes clarified butter four times into the *sruc* or the *darvī* or upon a wooden board using the thread, places a fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *saidhraka* wood into the fire, and offers the oblation with the mantra "āvartana vartaya," in which Soma and Indra are the deities and the metre is *paṅkti*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of achieving the state of not being able to depart. He offers it, saying: "Oṃ āvartana vartaya... rāvartaya punaḥ svāhā. Again, taking [clarified butter] once more, he offers it, saying: "Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā. [This is] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

Then, having taken the clarified butter from the vessel into another vessel and consumed it three times as in the Agnihotra rite, he washes the implements of the oblation with *darbha* grass. Then, having removed the surrounding coverings (*paristaraṇa*), he should meditate upon Viṣṇu. Now follows the protection of the wife.

Having made the resolve, "I shall perform the act of guarding the husband," the *jārī* (the paramour) should have the thick and firm parts ground into powder. Taking these, he should sprinkle them into the womb of the unfaithful woman while she is asleep, using the mantra: "Oṃ, to Indra belongs the phallus of this woman; it is for her alone, not for other men. This should be performed by one intending to travel to another country. Upon returning from that foreign land, he should wash her womb with the urine of a brown cow (*babhru*). The teachers teach that her womb will then become capable of sexual intercourse.

A *jārī* is one who has a lover (*jāra*). "Guarding of the wife" (*dāragupti*) means protection regarding one's own wife, consisting of ensuring that no semen from another man enters her; for that purpose [the following is used]. *Dṛḍhā* is the name of a specific kind of reptile known as a *gaulikā*, which is called the *śatacaraṇā*. Regarding the term *sthūlādṛḍhā*, the reading in the *Āpastamba* tradition is *sthūlāḍhārikā*, which conveys the same meaning. This *śatacaraṇā* is of two kinds: domestic (*grāmyā*) and wild (*āraṇyā*). Of these two, the wild variety is thick (*sthūlā*), while the domestic variety is thin (*tanvī*).

The qualification "thick" (*sthūlā*) is for the purpose of excluding the "slender" (*tanvī*). Because of the plural number in the word "powders" (*cūrṇāni*), there are many [of them]. Having caused the powders of those [plants]—which are being crushed by a heavy blow from a stone or similar object—to be made, one should scatter them into the vagina of a sleeping woman. When this is done, the vagina of another man does not become fit for enjoyment. Then, for the sake of making it fit again for her own enjoyment, she should wash it with the urine of a brown cow (*babhru*). By this means, it becomes fit for enjoyment. And this has been clearly stated by Āpastamba:

"One desiring the non-existence [of others] should have coarse *laḍhārikā* seeds made into powder and, for the sake of success, scatter it into the vulva of a sleeping woman with the following verse; one should wash it with the urine of a brown cow."

One desiring non-conception—that is, one desiring the absence of another man’s semen—should have pills made from the powder of living *sthūlaḍhārikā* plants (by another person) and insert them into the vulva of his sleeping wife with the mantra, "As the bowstring [is drawn] upon the bow. It is explained in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) that she should wash [her organ] with the urine of a brown cow (*babhru*)—that is, the urine of a tawny cow—in order to ensure the production of her own semen. The phrase "as the bowstring" (*avajyām*) belongs specifically to the Āpastambas, because that mantra exists in their own *sūtra*. Now, the success of trade:

The sale at a high price and the prompt sale constitute the success of the merchandise (*paṇyasiddhi*). Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), "I shall perform the rite for the sake of the success of the merchandise," one should prepare the consecration of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the procedure beginning with the drawing of lines (*ullekhana*), and then establish the common fire (*laukikāgni*) thereon. In the case where the oblation (*homa*) is performed in the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), the ritual actions from the drawing of lines up to the establishment [of the fire] are not required.

Then, having taken three fuel-sticks and performed the rites from "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), he declares: "In this sacrificial rite for the success of trade (*paṇyasiddhi*), I shall encompass those deities who are to be worshipped. With the mantra 'Whatever bargaining (*prapaṇa*) you gods [have]...', I shall worship the gods—Soma, Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Īśāna—with oblations consisting of a portion of the merchandise suitable for all sacrifices."

Having said, "I shall sacrifice to these deities immediately," he should place fuel-sticks on the fire, spread grass around it, and strew *darbha* grass to the north of the fire. Upon that grass, he should set down the *darvī* spoon, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the *upaveṣa* stick, the *darbha* blades for wiping, the *darbha* blades for kindling, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood, the clarified butter, and the materials for the oblation. He should then perform the rites beginning with the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers and ending with the consecration of the clarified butter. At the time of the circumambulation of the clarified butter (*ājyaparyagnikaraṇa*), there is also a circumambulation of the oblation material.
There is no placing of a fuel-stick made of *sīdhraka* wood here, as it is not prescribed.

Then, having sprinkled the sacrificial materials with clarified butter (*abhighāra*), having spread sacred grass (*barhis*) behind the fire, and having placed the sacrificial materials upon it, he sprinkles water around the fire with the verses beginning "From the beginning... (*āditaḥ*). Then, using a ladle (*darvī*), he takes a portion of the goods intended for sale that are fit for sacrifice and offers one oblation with the mantra: "O gods, whatever bargaining we practice, O gods, desiring wealth through wealth—may Soma, Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Īśāna bestow radiance upon that; *svāhā*! Thus he offers a single oblation with that portion.

"To the gods, to Soma, to Agni, to Indra, to Bṛhaspati, and to Īśāna, [I offer] this. Then, having removed the surrounding grass mats (paristaraṇa), having offered the Sarvaprāyaścitta oblations, and having sprinkled water around the fire with the mantras beginning with "O Aditi, you have consented," he should worship the fire, perform the ritual attendance (upasthāna) with the Saṃsthājapa mantra, and dedicate the rite to the Lord of Action (Karmeśvara).

Alternatively, one who intends to go for the purpose of selling whatever must be sold should take that much and, having offered this oblation with clarified butter (*ājya*), depart. In this case, regarding the *anvādhāna* (preparation of the fires), one should say "with an oblation of clarified butter" in place of the phrase "with an oblation of a portion of the merchandise intended for all the offerings. It should be understood that in the case of the clarified butter oblation, there is no placing down (*āsādana*) or circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) of the portion of the merchandise. Or, the performance here may follow the procedure of the *āpūrvika* (the full-moon sacrifice). This is the duty of a Vaiśya;
however, it also applies to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas who live by merchandise in times of distress.
Now follows the subduing of anger.

And that [rite] consists of the pacification of the anger of one who is powerful and angry. Having formed the intention, "I shall perform the rite called 'the subduing of anger' (*krodhavinayana*)," he addresses the powerful, angry man with the following mantra: "Oṃ! That form of yours which is on the forehead, the mild form of wrath that destroys [it], may the wise, divine students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) subdue it. Since you pierce through this forehead of mine as if splitting open the sky, I stretch out your wrath from your heart like an archer draws his bow. As day and night, as heaven and earth, so do we lead away your anger, like the fetus of a she-mule. Thus he consecrates the powerful, angry person.
Now, the ritual for overcoming through debate (*saṃvādābhijayana*).

A dispute concerning either material objects or knowledge is a "debate" (*saṃvāda*); the "overcoming" (*abhijayana*) of that is as follows. One who desires to achieve victory for himself by surpassing his opponent should perform this rite.

A defeated man, when the time of his defeat is imminent, should sit in the middle of his house at some night, perform *ācamana*, practice *prāṇāyāma*, and make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), saying: "I shall perform the rite named *saṃvādābhijayana*. Having prepared the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the procedure beginning with the ritual scratching (*ullekhana*), he should establish the common fire (*laukikāgni*) there. In the case where the oblation is performed in the *aupāsana* fire, the rites from the scratching up to the establishment [of the fire] are omitted.

Then, having kindled the fire and meditated upon it, and having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should perform the rites from "Śraddha ehi" up to the end of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Having recited from "In this rite of oblation for the conquest of debate, those deities who are to be worshipped... up to the *vyāhṛtis*, one should state regarding the principal oblation (*pradhāna-homa*): "I shall worship with an oblation consisting of three *karavīra* seeds smeared with clarified butter, using the mantra 'Agnim avajihva'. Then, regarding the subsidiary oblations (*aṅga-homa*), one should state: "Varuṇa... and so forth, ending with: "I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an oblation of the remaining clarified butter," and so on.

Having performed the rites up to the placing of the fuel-sticks for the *anvādhāna* and the adding of the fuel to the fire, having strewn grass around the fire, having prepared the seat for the *brahmā*, and having internalized the fire within himself, he should spread *darbha* grass to the north of the fire. Upon that grass, he should place the *darvī* ladle, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājya*), the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *upaveṣa* rake, the *saṃmārga* *darbhas*, the *darbhas* for kindling, the clarified butter, the sacrificial fuel (*idhma*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the three seeds. Having seated the *brahmā* to the south, he should perform the rites beginning with the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers and ending with the *vyāhṛti* oblations.
The specific detail here is that at the time of the circumambulation of the clarified butter (*ājyaparyagnikaraṇa*), there must also be a circumambulation of the three seeds.

Then, at the conclusion of the *vyāhṛti* oblations, one should take the three *karavīra* seeds that have been set aside, smear them with consecrated clarified butter (*ājya*), and offer a single oblation with the hand using those three seeds while reciting: "Oṃ, bend down, O tongue, bend down! With this oblation I worship thee, so that I may speak superiorly and [so that] such-and-such may speak inferiorly; speak, svāhā! In place of the word "such-and-such," the name of the disputant is to be taken in the nominative case. "To Agni, this, not mine. Then one should complete the remainder of the sacrifice, beginning with the *aṅga-homa* and ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; here, the *sviṣṭakṛt* is performed with clarified butter alone.

Then: "Oṃ! From your mouth I take the speech, from the mind, from the heart; from every limb of yours I take the speech. Wherever speech is deposited, that I take from you. O Rudra, blue-crested one, performer of heroic deeds, deed by deed, strike down this person who opposes me, as a tree is struck by a thunderbolt. Strike him down, strike him low, speak against him from beneath the earth! Like a base opponent with a deceptive trap, he has been struck down by me. That which I speak is the truth: O [Name], may you fall lower than I!"
Looking at the disputant who speaks thus, he mutters: "In this case also, the word *asau* (that one) is replaced by the name of the disputant himself.

*Oṃ, Hiraṇyabāhu, Subhagā, jitākṣi, Alaṃkṛtā, seated in the midst of the gods, has declared the matter for my sake; svāhā!* Thus, touching a person of standing who is seated in some part of the assembly, he mutters."
"Oṃ! Mine is the other, mine is the next, and this great earth is mine; as if Agni and Indra were accomplishing a divine purpose for me.
With these words, he gazes at the members of the assembly. Acting in this manner, he certainly triumphs over his opponent.
Now, the incidental rites.
In this regard, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* states: "Having seen the moon on the new-moon day (*darśa*)," and so forth.

On the new-moon day known as *sinīvālī*, or on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) immediately following the new moon, having seen the moon, even one who is already pure should sip water for the sake of the ritual and hold water in his joined palms (*añjali*). For the two verses beginning with "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*) and "Being good" (*santa*), Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Soma is the deity, the meter of the first is *gāyatrī*, and that of the second is *triṣṭubh*. For the two verses beginning with "Ever new, O Ādityas" (*navo navaḥ*), the Viśvedevas and the Ādityas are the deities, and the meter is *triṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the worship (*upasthāna*) of the moon.

With the four verses: "Oṃ, swell up; let [the waters] come together for thee... for union," "Oṃ, may the milks be peaceful... bestow them," "Oṃ, new and ever-new he becomes... long life," and "Oṃ, he whom the Ādityas protect as their guardian," one worships the moon. Regarding the mantra "In me, skill and wisdom": Prajāpati is the seer, the ten-fold wisdom (daśakratu) is the meter, and the Yajus is the deity; its application is in recitation. One who is yawning recites: "Oṃ, in me, skill and wisdom. This is for the sake of human welfare and for the sake of ritual action; it applies to all. This should also be performed in the Śrauta rites.

Reciting, “*sigasinasi vajro namaste astu mā mā hiṃsīḥ*,” he murmurs while being struck by the edge of another’s upper garment. The instruction that he murmurs “again and again” is for the purpose of indicating a distinction between ritual acts.
Then, having torn a thread from that garment, he should silently blow it away with his breath.
"Oṃ! Those birds that cry out in fear along with the spirits of destruction—may they satisfy me with auspiciousness, peace, splendor, and luster.
Having been sprinkled above by the bird's excrement or its urine, he recites this mantra. Then, having wiped it clean with a cloth or similar item, he should wash that spot with water.

"Oṃ! From the great heaven, from the mid-air, a drop of water has fallen upon me for my welfare. Protected by the sacred word (*brahman*), by good deeds, and by what has been done, I have come with power and a peaceful mind. With this, he mutters [this mantra] when he is sprinkled by an unknown drop of water. "Oṃ! Whether a fruit fell from the top of a tree or from the mid-air, that is indeed the wind. Wherever the tree stands, or wherever its garment [the fruit] was, may the waters drive away Destruction (*nirṛti*) far away. With this, he mutters if an unknown fruit should fall upon him.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra who dwells on the path, whose arrow is the wind; obeisance to Rudra who dwells on the path.
Having approached a crossroads, he mutters this.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra who dwells among cattle, whose arrow is the wind; obeisance to Rudra who dwells among cattle."
Having stepped down once, he mutters:
"Homage to Rudra who moves among serpents, whose arrow is the wind; homage to Rudra who moves among serpents.
He mutters this at every crossing over a foundation.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra who dwells in the intermediate space, who is the impeller of the wind; obeisance to Rudra who dwells in the intermediate space.
If the wind should come swirling in a circle, then he mutters this.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra who dwells in the waters, who is the impeller of the wind; obeisance to Rudra who dwells in the waters."
Having thus entered the river Udakavatī, he mutters:
"Oṃ, obeisance to that which is Being, to Vāta, to the Arrow, to Rudra; obeisance to Rudra, to that which is Being.
Having approached a place worthy of worship containing a resident deity, or a sacrificial ground, or a tree, or an ancient site as his mark, he mutters this.

If one should sleep at the time of sunrise, then he shall remain for that entire day without eating and restrained in speech; this alone is the expiation. This does not apply to one who is exhausted or diseased.

If he should sleep at the time of sunset, then he should remain standing, silent and fasting for that entire night. For one who is unable [to do so], there is merely fasting in both cases, or alternatively, breath-control (prāṇāyāma). When the sacrifice is completed, he must not touch the sacrificial post (yūpa). If the Anūbandhyā offering is not performed, he must not touch it starting from the Avabhṛtha bath. If he should touch it, he should recite: "This is for you, O Vāyu. This applies when touching a single post. But when touching two posts, he should recite: "These two are for you, O Vāyus. When touching many posts, however, he should recite: "These are for you, O Vāyus."

According to the statement of Parāśara: "Having touched a *caitya*-tree, a corpse, a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a *caṇḍāla*, or a seller of *soma*, a Brāhmaṇa shall enter the water with his clothes on.
Having first performed the bath, the recitation should be carried out thereafter. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for Kṣatriyas and others as well.
That which is uninvoked, that which is invoked from all sides, that which is praised, and that which has been uttered by birds—
the hundredfold [power] of the deer moving crosswise— that we turn into fear for our enemies.
Thus, as he begins to travel along the road toward his desired destination, he recites:
"O Śakuna, like a Udgātṛ priest you sing the Sāman; like a son of Brahman you chant at the libations.
May there be well-being for us, O Śakuna; be auspicious and well-disposed toward us."

Having perceived such an undesirable omen, he mutters [the following] for the purpose of pacifying its evil influence: "Sing the *sāman*," because of this indicative mark (*liṅga*), some say this [muttering] applies only when there is the hearing of speech; others say it applies in all cases because it serves as a praise of this [act]. Regarding the verse beginning with "When you, O Soma," the *Ṛṣi* is Ekasṛka, the *Chandas* is Bhūri-gāyatrī-Anuṣṭubh, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the act of muttering. "Oṃ! When you, having entered into these beings, speak the divine word, speak away our enemies; O Death, lead them unto death. He mutters this while facing a howling jackal. A jackal making the sound of a deer is called an *ekasṛk*.

Then, for the verse beginning with *agne agninā saṃvadasva*, Soma is the deity; it consists of one-footed *bhūri* Gāyatrī or *bhūri* Anuṣṭubh, or it is a Yajus. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the casting away of the firebrand (*ulmuka*). [The mantra is]: "Oṃ, O Agni, converse with Agni; O Death, converse with Death. Having cast the blazing firebrand toward that direction where it makes a sound—both below and above—and having touched water, [he recites] the mantras of the section beginning with *vibhūrasi*. Soma is the deity of these mantras; they are Yajus formulas addressed to the deities mentioned therein. Their application is in the worship (*upasthāna*) of the single path.

"Oṃ, you are Vibhū, the carrier; with your fierce host, protect me, O Agni, nourish me, do not harm me! 1. Oṃ, you are Vahni, the bearer of oblations; with your fierce host... 2. Oṃ, you are Śvātra, the wise; with your fierce host... 3. Oṃ, you are Tutha, the all-knowing; with your fierce host... 4. Oṃ, you are Uśij, the sage; with your fierce host... 5. Oṃ, you are Aṅghāri, the supporter; with your fierce host... 6. Oṃ, you are Avasyu, the devoted; with your fierce host... 7. Oṃ, you are Śundhyu, the purifier; with your fierce host... 8. Oṃ, you are Samrāj, the radiant; with your fierce host... 9."

"Oṃ, you are the one who sits around; you are the purifier, O Raurava! 10. Oṃ, you are the swift mover; you are the wind-possessor, O Raurava! 11. Oṃ, you are the unsmeared; you are the preparer of the oblation, O Raurava! 12. Oṃ, you are the abode of Truth; you are the light of heaven, O Raurava! 13. Oṃ, you are the light of Brahman; you are the abode of heaven, O Raurava! 14. Oṃ, you are the unborn; you are the one-footed, O Raurava! 15. Oṃ, you are the serpent; you are the one dwelling in the depths, O Raurava! 16. With these sixteen mantras, he worships the single fire-brand (*ekasṛk*). In the absence of the fire-brand, this [rite] is omitted.

Regarding the verse beginning with *yadīṣitaḥ*: the deity is Soma, the meters are Indra and Agni, and the meter is the *nicṛt-triṣṭubh*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation (*japa*). The mantra is: *"Oṃ, whether impelled by another or acting out of his own desire, if the jackal utters a single cry, may Indra and Agni, in harmony with the sacred word (*brahman*), make that night auspicious for us in our homes."* One recites this facing a female jackal (*sālāvṛkī*) while she is making a sound.
A wild female dog is a *sālāvṛkī*. According to some, only the genus is intended here, not specifically the female gender.

For the mantra beginning with *prasārya sakthyau*, Soma is the deity, Śakuni is the seer, and Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is in recitation (*japa*). One recites: "Oṃ, spreading your legs you fly, you peck at my left eye; do not [peck] at anyone else’s name. Thus one recites this when hearing an undesirable word from a bird (*śakuni*). A bird is a crow (*vāṅkṣa*). One recites: "Oṃ, the golden-winged bird, who goes to the dwelling of the gods, having circumambulated the village to the right, speak auspiciousness to us, O Kauśika! Thus one recites this when hearing an undesirable word from a yellow bird (*piṅgala*).
Now follows the fire-oblation (*homa*) caused by the sight of an inauspicious dream.

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform a fire-oblation (homa) for the purpose of counteracting the sight of an inauspicious dream," one should prepare the consecration of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) according to the ritual procedure beginning with the marking out (ullekhana) and so forth, and then establish there the worldly fire named Pāvaka. In the case where the oblation is performed in the domestic fire (aupāsana), the rites from the marking out up to the establishment [of the fire] are not required.

Then, having kindled the fire and meditated upon it, and having taken three pieces of fuel (samidh), he performs the rites from "Śraddha ehi" up to the end of the breath-control (prāṇāyāma). He then declares: "In this rite of oblation performed for the purpose of [counteracting] the sight of an inauspicious dream, I shall encompass all those deities who are to be worshipped. I shall worship Agni, the Agnis, Vaiśvānara, and Heaven, each with a single oblation of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter."

Having said, "I shall sacrifice to these deities immediately," he should place fuel sticks on the fire, strew grass around the fire, and having spread *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, he should set down upon it the wooden ladle (*darvī*), the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), the *darbha* blades for wiping, the *darbha* blades for kindling, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), a single fuel stick, clarified butter, and sesame seeds. In the case of an offering made with the hand, there is no setting down of the ladle.

Then one should perform the rites beginning with the preparation of the *pavitra* and ending with "having placed the *pavitra* in the fire. At the time of the circumambulation (*paryagnikaraṇa*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*), there should also be a circumambulation of the sesame seeds (*tila*). In the case of offering by hand, one should place the right hand in the position of the ladle (*darvī*), and together with the left hand, set down the vessel of clarified butter; then, with the right hand alone, one should arrange the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *upaveṣa*, the *saṃmārga* darbha grass, the *avajvalana* darbha grass, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), a single fuel-stick (*samit*), the clarified butter, and the sesame seeds. This is because it is impossible to perform these actions with the left hand alone.

The rites beginning with the purification of the self (*pavitrakaraṇa*) and ending with the sprinkling of the vessels (*pātraprokṣaṇa*) are performed with the right hand alone. Therein, first, having placed the right hand palm-upward upon the spot for the *darvī* ladle, one should sprinkle the right hand three times with water taken from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel by the left hand holding the *pavitra* blades; then, with the right hand still holding the *pavitra*, one performs the sprinkling of the clarified butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*) and the other implements.

Then, taking the *saṃmārjana* grass-blades in his left hand and having heated the right hand together with the *saṃmārjana* blades, he wipes the right hand with the *saṃmārjana* blades held in the left hand as if they were a *juhū* ladle; then, having heated it again and placed the right hand behind the fire, he throws those very *saṃmārjana* blades into the fire.

Then, having performed all the rites from the melting of the clarified butter (*ājya*) up to the placing of the purifiers (*pavitra*) in the fire with the right hand alone, he should anoint the sesame seeds with the consecrated clarified butter, spread sacrificial grass (*barhis*) behind the fire, place the sesame seeds upon it, sprinkle water around the fire, silently add one fuel-stick (*samidh*), and then, using a ladle (*darvī*), take up the clarified-butter-anointed sesame seeds once.

For the verse beginning with *punarmāmaitvindriyam*, the deity is Agni, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the oblation performed upon seeing an inauspicious dream. *Oṃ punarmāmaitvindriyaṃ punarāyuḥ punarbhagaḥ | punarbrāhmaṇamaitu mā punardraviṇamaitu mā svāhā* || To Agni, this [is offered], not to me. *Oṃ athaite dhiṣṇiyāso agnayo yathāsthānaṃ kalpantāmihaiva svāhā* || To the Fires, this [is offered], not to me.

"Oṃ! May my self return to me; may life return; may breath return; may intention return. May Vaiśvānara, increasing with his rays, abide within me—my mind, the banner of immortality. Svāhā! This is for Vaiśvānara, not for me. "Oṃ! Whatever food is eaten in the evening that does not ward off hunger in the morning—may all that not harm us; for that is not seen by day. Svāhā! This is for Dyaus, not for me. With these mantras, one should offer four oblations of sesame seeds. Or the oblation may be performed with the hand.

Then, having removed the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa) and performed the final sprinkling (uttarapariṣeka), one should meditate upon Viṣṇu. This oblation may be performed according to the *tantra* procedure of the *āghāra* offering; here, the *vyāhṛti-homa*, the *vāruṇī-homa*, and so forth are optional. The *trivṛd-anna-homa* is not performed. The rest is the same.

According to the statement of Baudhāyana, the worship of Sūrya (*sūryopasthāna*) should also be performed with the two verses beginning "Adyā no deva Savitar" and "Viśvāni deva Savitar. For these two [verses], the seers (*ṛṣi*) are the Viśvedevas; the deity (*devatā*) is Sūrya; the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī; and their application (*viniyoga*) is in the worship of Sūrya. Thus the seers and other details are to be understood.
Now follow the expiations for portents (*adbhutaprāyaścittāni*).
Regarding this, the Sūtra states:
"When a pigeon has settled [on the house], when honey has settled in the house, when a cow licks another cow, when a pillar has cracked, or when an anthill has risen—[these are] of such a nature."

"Having become angry" means having manifested anger. "A pigeon" refers to a wild dove (*pārāvata*). "He sat down" (*upāvikṣat*)—the word "house" (*agāra*) is to be supplied as the object he occupied. "Honey being made by bees" (*madhukarībhiḥ*) means honey produced by flies; "it sat down" (*upāvikṣat*) means it settled there in the house. "A cow other than her calf" means another cow; "she drank" (*adhaiṣīt*) means she suckled. "A pillar" (*sthūṇā*) "grew" (*vyaraukṣīt*) means it sprouted upon the house. "An anthill" (*valmīka*) "rose up" (*udaikṣīt*) means it emerged within the house. "Of such a kind" (*ityevaṃrūpāṇi*) means of this sort;
"these and others" means that he for whose house these and other such portents occur should perform the rite that is about to be described. This is the meaning.

The performer, having bathed in the forenoon, wearing clean garments, being self-restrained, and conversing only with a Brāhmaṇa, should sit in the middle of the house, perform *ācamana*, practice *prāṇāyāma*, and announce the place and time. Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "For the propitiation of the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of averting the misfortune indicated by the entry of a pigeon into my house, I shall perform the rite prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras," he should then prepare the consecration of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the very middle of the house according to the procedure beginning with the drawing of lines (*ullekhana*), and there install the common fire named Varada.
In the case of performing the *homa* offering in the *aupāsana* fire, the ritual begins from the sweeping (*ullekhana*) up to the consecration (*pratiṣṭhāpana*).

Then, having kindled the fire and meditated upon it, and having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should perform the rites beginning with "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Having uttered the formula beginning with "Those who are to be sacrificed to in this rite of *homa* for the purpose of averting the misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) indicated by the entry of the pigeon," up to the *vyāhṛti* mantras; and having performed the subsidiary offerings (*aṅgahoma*) beginning with "Varuṇa" up to the *vyāhṛti* offerings; one should then perform the offerings to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī-homa*) and so forth, ending with the gift of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*).

Regarding this, some explain the inclusion of the word "here" (*atra*) in the sūtra "the *jayābhyātāna* [mantras] here" for the purpose that these [rites] should occur only upon such great portents (*adbhuta*), and not upon minor ones.

Thereafter, one should perform the *tridanna-homa* up to the conclusion of the *puṇyāhavācana*. "I shall perform the rite prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras for the propitiation of the venerable Supreme Lord, by means of averting the misfortune indicated by the appearance of bees entering my house. "I shall perform the rite prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras for the propitiation of the venerable Supreme Lord, by means of averting the misfortune indicated by a cow other than my calf sucking at her udder."

One should perform the ritual intentions (*saṃkalpa*) according to each specific occasion, thinking: "In my house, for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord by means of averting misfortune indicated by the emergence of an anthill, I shall perform the rite prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras. Regarding the portent of a cow licking another cow, there is this special procedure: as the cows are setting out, he consecrates them with the mantra: "Oṃ! May Indra and Agni send you forth; may the Aśvins protect you; Bṛhaspati is your herdsman; may Pūṣan drive you back again."

For the verse beginning with *pūṣā gāḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the meter is Gāyatrī, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the cows. With this mantra, "Oṃ, may Pūṣan follow our cows... may he lead them back to us," one consecrates the cows as they set out. One awaits the approaching cows with the mantra: "Oṃ, may these cows that have come here be free from disease and prolific; may they flow like rivers and pour forth like the ocean."
Having arrived and standing together in one place, he consecrates the cows with the mantra: *oṃ sa sthāḥ stha saṃsthā vo bhūyāsthācyutāḥ stha mā mā cyoḍhvaṃ mā'haṃ bhagavatībhyaścayauṣīḥ*.

With the two [mantras], *ūrjā vaḥ paśyāmi* and *sahasrapoṣam*, Agni is the deity and the Yajus is the meter; their application (*viniyoga*) is for looking toward the cows situated in the cow-pen. He looks toward the cows in the cow-pen with these two: *oṃ ūrjā vaḥ paśyāmyū0 rāmadaḥ* and *oṃ sahasrapoṣaṃ0 yaḥ śrayantām*.
Alternatively, the mantra is simply "May I nourish you for a thousandfold," and does not end with "may they rest.

Then, having established and kindled the common fire named Pāvaka in a consecrated site prepared by the ritual of delimitation (*ullekhana*) and other procedures in the midst of the cows, one should meditate upon it. In the case of performing the oblation (*homa*) in the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), the rites from delimitation up to the establishment [of the fire] are omitted.

Then, having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and performed the rites from "O Faith, come" (*śraddha ehi*) up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should recite from "Those deities who are to be sacrificed to" (*yā yakṣyamāṇāḥ*) up to the *vyāhṛtis*, saying: "In this rite of homa for the purpose of averting the misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) of cattle—indicated by the drinking of milk from the udders of cows other than the calf—I shall sacrifice to Jātavedas with two oblations of milk; I shall sacrifice to Pāvaka with two oblations of milk. He should then perform the subsidiary rites (*aṅgahoma*) beginning with "Varuṇa" and ending with the placing of the purifiers (*pavitra*).
In this regard, the specific distinction is that at the time of the circumambulation with clarified butter (*ājyaparyagnikaraṇa*), there is also a circumambulation of the milk.
Then one should perform the ritual actions beginning with the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and ending with the *vyāhṛti* oblations. Then follows the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*).

For the two verses beginning "Blaze forth" (*uddīpyasva*) and "Do not harm us" (*mā no hiṃsīḥ*), the deities are the Yājñikas, the Upaniṣads, and Jātavedas; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal milk-oblation for the rite intended to ward off cattle-misfortune, as indicated by the milking of the cow and the drinking from her teat. "Oṃ, blaze forth, O Jātavedas... [filling] the quarters, Svāhā!"—this is for Jātavedas, not for me. "Oṃ, do not harm us, O Jātavedas... protect us, Svāhā!"—this is for Jātavedas, not for me.

For the two [verses] beginning with *apām idaṃ nyayanam* and *namas te harase*, the deity is Agni Pāvaka and the meter is Bṛhatī. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the milk-oblation (*payohoma*), which is the principal rite for the purpose of averting cattle-misfortune as indicated by the drinking from a cow's udder by a calf. *Oṃ apām idaṃ nya0 vo bhava svāhā*—this is for Pāvaka, not for me. *Oṃ namas te ha0 bhava svāhā*—this is for Pāvaka, not for me. Then follows *imaṃ me varuṇa* and so forth. The *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering is made with clarified butter (*ājya*) alone. Some authorities maintain that because the word "butter" (*ājya*) is absent [in the formulas], it should be performed with milk.
The procedure is the same up to the giving of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*). There is no *Trivṛdanna-homa* in this rite.

Then, having worshipped the fire, provided a feast for the Brahmins, and given abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should remember Viṣṇu for the perfection of the rite and dedicate it to the Lord of Action (*karmeśvara*). The previous rite—"A cow shall suckle a cow"—was prescribed for the prevention of misfortune to the owner of the cow indicated by the portent; this rite, however, is ordained for the prevention of the calamity to the cows indicated by that same portent.

If there are only two cows, then there is modification (*ūha*) in the mantras: "O Indra and Agni, may Bṛhaspati, or Pūṣan, the cowherd, drive you both back. [The mantra becomes: "Pūṣan [drives] the two cows. "These two cows have arrived, free from disease, prolific; you two are steady, you two are steady; may you be steady; you two are immovable; do not move away from me; may I not be separated from you two, the blessed ones. We see you with vigor; look upon me with vigor. May I thrive through your thousandfold prosperity"—thus is the modification.

Alternatively, the mantras themselves may end in the plural, since they are intended for worship. The repetition of the word "atra" (here) is for the purpose of ensuring that the *jayā* and other oblations are performed only when there are many cows for the sake of averting misfortune, and not when there are only two cows for the same purpose. Thus ends the section on optional rites (*kāmyavidhi*) and so forth in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was himself the performer of the *Vājapeya*, *Pauṇḍarīka*, and *Sarvatomukha* sacrifices, and who bore the surname Okopa.
The eleventh section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā*.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Now, concerning marriage. In this regard, the following is the Gṛhya-sūtra:

"Having returned from the teacher's family, he should support his mother and father; authorized by them, he should marry a wife who is of the same caste (*sajātā*), a maiden (*nagnikā*), one who has been chaste (*brahmacāriṇī*), and not of the same lineage (*asagotrā*).

The meaning is this: having been a student (*brahmacārī*) dependent on the teacher since the initiation (*upanayana*), and having completed his studies, he has "returned" (*samāvṛtta*) from the teacher's family as a *snātaka*. He should support—that is, nourish—his mother and father by serving them through such means as bringing grain. The sense is that he remains dependent upon his parents.

Although it would have been sufficient to say simply "one who has bathed" (*snāta*), the expression "returned from the teacher's house" (*samāvṛtta ācāryakulāt*) is intended to show that even for one who has bathed, there may be a need for further study of the sciences; thus, he should reside once again in the teacher's house, rather than [immediately] supporting his mother and father. Having been permitted by those two, his mother and father, he should take a wife, that is, accept her. Of what sort? One of the same caste (*sajātāṃ*), meaning of equal varna and of the same lineage. A *nagnikā*, meaning fit for sexual intercourse. A *brahmacāriṇī*, meaning one who has not yet engaged in sexual intercourse.

One who has the same lineage (*gotra*) as her husband is *sagotrā*; one who does not have the same lineage is *asagotrā*. We shall explain both *sagotratva* and *asagotratva* in the section on the *pravara* (ancestral sages). The phrase "authorized by those two" is intended to prohibit the taking of a wife by one who has not been so authorized. Mātṛdatta has explained that even for one who has already taken a wife, there is no engagement in the prescribed rites without the father’s authorization.
In the *Mādhavīya*, Manu states: "Having bathed and returned home according to rule with the permission of his guru..."
"A twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks."

The fruit of marriage is the discharge of the debts owed to the gods and the ancestors. Thus says the Śruti: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts: to the Ṛṣis by means of Vedic study, to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of progeny; he alone is free from debt who has a son, who is a sacrificer, and who has lived as a student. Baudhāyana also states:
"The instruction for one desiring offspring is that the name [of the wife] is established through the completion of procreation; thus spoke the Aśvins."
Endowed with long life and austerity, devoted to Vedic study and sacrifice,
and having conquered his senses, he should diligently procreate offspring within his own respective caste.
From birth, a Brāhmaṇa becomes bound by three debts.
Having abandoned these, one becomes self-possessed and liberated from the accumulation of unrighteousness;
by means of Vedic study one honors the sages, and by means of the Soma sacrifice, Indra.
By means of offspring, one becomes free from debt to all the ancestors and rejoices in heaven;
through a son one conquers the worlds, and through a grandson one enjoys bliss.
"Then, by means of his son's grandson, he should cause him to ascend to heaven. It is also known from scripture:

"A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts—to the Ṛṣis through studentship, to the gods through sacrifice, and to the ancestors through progeny. Thus the Veda shows the connection to freedom from debt; it shows that bondage is the lack of liberation from debt, and that [liberation] depends upon progeny. Furthermore, the word "drawing after" (*anukarṣa*) indicates progeny, for one becomes possessed of undying progeny as long as his offspring supports him; he conquers an imperishable world and saves himself by procreating a virtuous son.

"Seven descendants, seven ancestors, and six others with oneself as the seventh—we desire these seven sons," so it is said. Because one obtains the fruit by producing the continuity of progeny, therefore a man of self-control should produce offspring for the sake of obtaining the fruit for himself. Therefore, having produced a virtuous son, he produces himself; and it is known from scripture: "The self indeed bears the name 'son'. Thus, the second self should be seen as living by him who produces a son; he becomes such [a second self]. Therefore, the self is never [lost] in the absence of a field (womb).

"One should abandon [the idea of] despising oneself; for as one conceives of oneself, so does one become. Therefore, from the very beginning, one should seek a field that is of the same caste and prepared through instruction. In that [field], through union with a wife and by means of the application of medicinal herbs and mantras according to his instruction, he should procreate offspring. Thus the Śruti is generally indicated for all castes, because it is fruitful for everyone."

The designation "progeny" (*prajā*) is a name established by procreation; it is brought about and accomplished solely through the act of procreating. The word "of progeny" (*prajāyāḥ*), ending in the genitive case, is to be supplied [as the subject]. This is a qualifying term for progeny itself, containing a causal implication: since progeny—in the form of sons and so forth—is produced solely by means of procreation, it is therefore called "progeny."

The established meaning is that marriage must necessarily be performed, because there can be no birth for progeny without the relationship of procreation, and that [procreation] is in every way impossible without a field (a wife). This is appropriate through approaching her at the prescribed time. By the term "one who has conquered his senses," approaching her on multiple occasions every night during the nights of her fertile period (*ṛtu*) is excluded, as is sexual intercourse with another's wife. Having liberated—that is, having cast far away—those debts from birth, starting from the very moment of origin.

Regarding the phrase "vimukto 'dharmasaṃcayāt," the word division is *adharmasaṃcayāt*. When the repayment of debts has been performed, one becomes liberated from the accumulation of demerit (*adharma*). Consequently, the meaning is that one becomes "possessed of self" (*ātmavān*), which is to say, one attains the true nature of the Self. In the word "pūjya," although there is no compound, the substitution of *lyap* for *ktvā* is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). "By means of *svādhyāya*" means by means of the study of the Vedas; the sense is "by means of the student life (*brahmacarya*) which is the instrument for that study. "By means of *soma*" means by means of a sacrifice characterized by the substance *soma*.

The word *puraṃdara* is an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) of the deity associated with each respective rite; *puraṃdara* refers to Indra. He is mentioned because of his preeminence, both as the recipient of the largest share and as the sovereign of the deities. In the phrase "all the ancestors" (*pitṝn sarvān*), the inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of including the divine ancestors (*devapitṛs*) as well. By worshipping these and by satisfying them through these rites, one becomes free from debt and rejoices—filled with joy—in heaven (*divi*). "Worlds" (*lokān*) refers to the worlds of the gods; "Nāka" is heaven.

He shows the scriptural authority for the fact that by these three duties, the discharge of the three debts occurs, in the passage beginning with "It is known: 'Indeed, one being born... and so forth. In this very manner, the Veda—through such passages as "This one indeed is free from debt"—shows and makes known the state of being joined with freedom from debt (*anṛṇasaṃyoga*), indicating that there is no other means for the discharge of the three debts. Regarding the phrase "bondage is the non-release from debt," the word "one's own" is to be supplied as the remainder. Non-discharge of debt is bondage; the release from debt is the discharge of debt.

These two are dependent upon offspring, subject to offspring; the meaning is that when offspring exists there is liberation from debt, and when it does not exist there is bondage—thus they are dependent upon offspring. The word *ca* (and), which follows immediately after "offspring," serves for emphasis. "And of the ancestors" (*pitṝṇāṃ ca*) means that for the ancestors as well, even those whose debts have not been discharged, both bondage and liberation are dependent upon offspring. By the phrase "dependent upon offspring," the subordination of the procreation of offspring is demonstrated.

The word *anukarṣa* (drawing after) is a term that constitutes one part [of the offspring], and the word *prajā* (progeny), which constitutes another part, refers to progeny in the form of a son; it does not denote the son alone, but rather, by means of a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), it denotes progeny even in the form of a daughter. When the production of progeny is accomplished, one becomes possessed of progeny that is not cut off. The intended meaning is that the fault of the extinction of the lineage does not occur.

For as long as one favors this progenitor of offspring—that is, for as long as one bestows grace upon him—for that long he conquers an imperishable world. If many offspring are born, there is the conquest of an imperishable world for a long time; if few, then the conquest of an imperishable world is for a short time—this is the meaning. The word *sat* (the good/true) indicates that the soul's own salvation occurs only through the son’s excellence and not otherwise.

It is not merely for one’s own salvation, but also for the salvation of others; in this regard, he shows the consensus of the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādins*) with the passage beginning "seven generations below" and ending with "we desire [it] from you. Since salvation depends upon a virtuous son, the *brahmavādins* say, "Therefore, we desire that very thing from you"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. He concludes with the passage beginning "because the continuity of progeny... and so forth.

Since one obtains the aforementioned fruit by producing offspring—that is, a lineage—one must certainly produce offspring. The word *saṃtāna* denotes a lineage (*saṃtati*). The term *saṃtāna* is used here to demonstrate its synonymy [with *prajā*]. Alternatively, the word *saṃtāna* is intended to indicate the necessity of having a large number of progeny; for there is also a traditional law (*smṛti*) stating, "Many sons are to be desired. "The aforementioned fruit" means: one becomes self-possessed and powerful.

"For the sake of attaining the fruit" means for the sake of attaining the fruit as previously described. Since it is known from the Śruti: "The self, indeed, is named 'son' (putra)," the logical connection is that by procreating a virtuous son, one should procreate the self itself. In this very way, a living man should regard his son as his own second self. Just as one procreates a son, so does one become; by procreating a virtuous son, one becomes truly existent (sat), whereas by procreating an unworthy son, one becomes non-existent (asat).

Regarding "in a non-field" (*akṣetre*): this refers to a field other than one's own, or a forbidden field, or a field where [intercourse] has been enjoyed through force. A son who is procreated in a non-field is indeed a self-degradation; therefore, one should procreate oneself only in one's own field at the prescribed time. It is not merely a matter of degradation, but the meaning is that by procreating a son in a forbidden field, one also assumes the very nature of that field.
