From the beginning—that is, at the very outset—one should desire to procreate offspring only with reference to the field, namely the wife.

By this, "examination" (*parīkṣā*) is included. *Savarṇām* means "of the same class. The word *āditaḥ* means "first"; the suffix *-tas* is used here in place of all case-endings. By this, the inclusion of daughters belonging to the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya classes as wives is established. "Field" (*kṣetra*) refers to that which has been consecrated by instruction—that is, by the ritual procedure of marriage. The word *dāra* is masculine; the singular number is Vedic.

In that case, with a wife of the same caste who has been consecrated through marriage and union—that is, through sexual intercourse according to the prescribed rites—if the procreation of offspring does not occur despite such union, then the application of medicinal substances and mantras must also be performed. "Union" means application. Through instruction regarding that application of medicinal substances and mantras—meaning through instruction in the medical and mantra sciences—the knowledge [of these matters] is obtained; this is the remainder of the sense.

The Śruti passage beginning with "Whether being born... and so forth, refers generally to the state of being equal (*sāmānya*), which is similarity (*sādharmya*) consisting in the quality of studying the Veda; by that reason, [the duty] is seen to be for the sake of all castes from among all castes. The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "in such Smṛti texts as 'A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya may discharge the three debts.'"

Although the scriptural text "being born" (*jāyamāna*) appears to refer specifically to the status of being a Brāhmaṇa, nevertheless, by taking the common characteristic of possessing the study of the Veda, it applies to all castes (*varṇas*), because all [castes] possess the fruit [of such study] and all possess the desire for that fruit. Alternatively, the scriptural text "being born" does not apply merely in a general sense—that is, to the mere generality of the caste of Brāhmaṇa—but rather refers to the three [castes] who possess the study of that which is *brahman*, namely the Veda. Why? Because all castes possess the desire for the fruit [of Vedic study].
In response to the inquiry as to who is eligible to be married, Yājñavalkya says:
"One whose student life has been unbroken should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks—
one who has not belonged to another before, who is pleasing, who is not a sapinda, and who is younger."

"One who is healthy, has brothers, and is not born of the same *ṛṣi* or *gotra*. "Endowed with auspicious marks" (*lakṣaṇyā*) means one possessed of both external and internal characteristics; these will be described later. "One who has not belonged to another" (*ananyapūrvikā*) means she who has not been previously taken by another through gift or enjoyment; that is to say, one who has not been remarried (*apunarbhūḥ*). There are seven types of remarried women (*punarbhūḥ*): one whose consent has been given mentally, one whose consent has been given verbally, one who has circumambulated the fire, one who has been led to the seventh step, one who has been enjoyed, one who has conceived, and one who has given birth. Among these, it will be explained later that marriage with the first three is permissible for another.

A bride who brings delight to the eyes and mind of the groom, and who is not a *sapiṇḍa*—that is, devoid of *sāpiṇḍya*. Regarding this, Candrikā, Parārkā, Medhātithi, Mādhava, and others state: "Sāpiṇḍya is the connection through one of the following relations within a single act of offering the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*): being the giver, being a recipient of the cake, or being a recipient of the smearings (*lepa*).
On this point, the Matsya Purāṇa says: "The fourth [ancestor] and those beyond are the recipients of the smearings; the father and those preceding him are the recipients of the cakes."
"The giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is the seventh among these; thus, the sapinda relationship extends for seven generations."
The words of Mārkaṇḍeya are also as follows: "The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
these three persons are to be known as those connected by the rice-ball (piṇḍa)."
The other relatives by marriage (lepasaṃbandhin) are said to begin from the great-grandfather’s grandfather;
these three, with the sacrificer as the seventh, [constitute the group].
"Thus has this seven-generation kinship been declared by the sages.

This is the meaning: the cause of *sāpiṇḍya* (the state of being a sapinda) is the inclusion within a single ancestral offering (*ekapiṇḍakriyā*) for seven persons. Accordingly, there is *sāpiṇḍya* between one person, Devadatta, and his own six ancestors beginning with the father, as well as with his six descendants beginning with the son.

If it is objected that, in this case, there would be no *sāpiṇḍya* (ancestral connection) with brothers, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, sisters’ sons, and so forth, nor with their wives and others, we reply: no. This is because what is intended here is the unity of the ritual act (*kriyaikya*) through the identity of the deity to whom it is offered (*uddeśyadevatāikyena*). Thus, among those who enter as deities into the piṇḍa-rite performed by Devadatta, any one of them also enters into the piṇḍa-rite performed by a brother, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, or others; therefore, *sāpiṇḍya* exists with them.
Furthermore, since wives also possess joint entitlement (*sahādhikāritva*) in the ritual of offering the piṇḍa performed by their husbands, the establishment of *sāpiṇḍya* with them is secured.

If it is asked, "Surely this [right] would exist once the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is established; what then is the proof for that very point?"—we reply: No. By the statement of the *Dharmasūtra*, "The state of partnership (*sahatva*) in rites, as well as in the fruits of merit, begins with the taking of the hand," and by the statement of Manu, "Therefore, every duty (*dharma*) is declared in the Śruti as common to both," the commonality of property between these two is established at the very time of marriage by these words: "In matters of duty, wealth, and pleasure, she must not be transgressed against. For it is not possible for one person alone to renounce that which is common to both.

Therefore, because of the common ownership of the property, one should not divide [the estate] with the husband; since this prohibits partition, there is no joint agency for two separate individuals—so says the *Tatparatna*. The inclusion of the word "together" (*saha*) in the phrase "jointness in ritual acts" is intended to demonstrate that it does not imply a grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) like that of "oxen."

Furthermore, she must be told by her husband: "I am performing the giving [of the Śrāddha] and so forth; you too should make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa). She too must act accordingly, for otherwise there is a fault, since Aparārka, Smṛticandrikā, Hemādri, Mādhava, and others have established the principle that the entitlement [to perform the rite] is joint. Nor should it be feared that, even so, the sisters, paternal aunts, and others would be excluded;

for, just as among undivided brothers the eldest alone is the performer while the younger ones possess a fitness for the purpose of establishing *sāpiṇḍya*, the same principle of fitness must be adopted here as well.

Now, one might object: [Is this not contradicted by] the fact that friends and others— who have attained the status of deities for the *śrāddha* at Gayā as established by the scriptural statement, "By uttering whose name one should cast the rice-ball, him one leads to eternal Brahman"—
as well as the king, who, in the absence of all [heirs], should cause the rite to be performed from the deceased's estate?

If it is argued that, according to the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, even a king incurs *sapiṇḍya* by virtue of being a performer of the *śrāddha* rite, this is true; however, there is no such contingency because the term *sapiṇḍa* is accepted as having both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) meanings only with respect to certain specific relatives of the father and others, in accordance with such scriptural injunctions as: "Beyond the seventh and fifth [generations] from the father's side, and likewise from the mother's side. Vijñāneśvara, Madanapārijātakāra, and others, however, state that *sapiṇḍya* consists in the connection through the integration of parts of a single body.

For indeed, the limbs of a single father’s or a single mother’s body persist—either directly or through a lineage—in their sons, grandsons, and so forth, in the form of semen, blood, and the like. However, the avoidance of the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) resulting from such a persistence of the Creator's limbs must be handled as previously described.

The essential meaning of the statement, "Beyond the seventh and the fifth [generations] on the father's side and likewise on the mother's side," is to be understood from the declarations of other scriptures.
"If the father of either the bride or the groom is the seventh from the *kūṭastha* (the common ancestor),
or if their mother is the fifth, then the *sāpiṇḍya* relationship ceases."

Since that which constitutes the distinction of the lineage is the immutable primordial person (*kūṭastha-mūlapuruṣa*), counting from him, if the father (the paternal grandfather) of either the bride or the groom should be the seventh, and if the mother of those two—the bride and the groom—should be the fifth from the *kūṭastha*, then the *sāpiṇḍya* relationship ceases. The distilled meaning is this: in the consideration of *sāpiṇḍya* through the paternal line, the cessation of *sāpiṇḍya* occurs beyond the seventh degree; however, in the consideration of *sāpiṇḍya* through the maternal line, it occurs beyond the fifth degree. This point is summarized in the *Viśvarūpa-nibandha*: [The text continues with the verse: "Beyond the seventh on the father's side, and beyond the fifth on the mother's side, the *sāpiṇḍya* relationship ceases. Thus, the *sāpiṇḍya* ends at the seventh generation for the father’s lineage and at the fifth for the mother’s lineage. This is the established rule.
"In the manner thus described, marriage is permissible with one who is beyond the seventh generation from the father's side,
and likewise beyond the fifth generation from the mother's side."
"Because the lineage is divided from the common ancestor in both cases,
one should count the best [male] starting from him up to the girl."

An illustration here is as follows: 1. Devadatta, the immutable progenitor; 2. his son, Brahmadatta; 3. his son, Viṣṇudatta; 4. his son, Śivadatta; 5. his son, Mitradatta; 6. his son, Haradatta; 7. his son, Yajñadatta; and 8. his son, Śrīdatta. This constitutes the *sāpiṇḍya* (lineage connection) through the father with respect to the bridegroom.

The progenitor (mūlapuruṣa) is Devadatta himself (1). His son (tatpuruṣa) is Mātṛdatta (2); his son is Rudradatta (3); his son is Bhānudatta (4). His daughter is Śrīdevī (5); her daughter is Śrīdattabhaktā (6). Thus is the sapinda relationship through the mother (mātṛdvāraka-sāpiṇḍya) regarding the bride. Here, the eighth descendant, Śrīdatta, may marry the sixth descendant, Śrīdattabhaktā. This same rule applies even if there is a succession of daughters in the intervening line, starting from the progenitor. It is the same even in the reverse order. As for that which Vasiṣṭha states: "The fifth and the seventh [degrees] on the mother's side, and likewise on the father's side."
The word "should marry" (*udvahet*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. And as for the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"O King, a householder should marry a maiden from the mother's side on the fifth [generation] and from the father's side on the seventh, according to the lawful rite."

This should be explained as meaning "having passed beyond the fifth and the seventh [generations]. This refers to the period beyond the fifth and the seventh, in accordance with such statements as "the father of the bride or the groom," and so forth:
"Those whose marriage rite takes place in the fifth or the seventh generation—even if they are devoted to sacred rites, they should be known as having fallen to the status of Śūdras."
Thus, according to the statement of Marīci in the Aparārka;
and as for that which is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "A girl who is third from the mother's side, and likewise third from the father's side..."
"Manu, Pārāśarya, Aṅgiras, and Yama have declared that one should cause [the girl] to be married."
As for what Paiṭhīnasi stated:
"Having passed over three on the mother's side and five on the father's side"; and as for the statement in the Smṛtyarṇava:
"The fourth [generation] girl and the fifth [generation] bridegroom, or the fourth [generation] bridegroom, but not the fifth [generation] bride;
for the ancestral rite (pitrya), one may marry a fifth or sixth [generation] girl, and likewise a third or even a fourth [generation] girl."
As for the statement of Parāśara: "A fourth son may marry a fourth daughter, or even a fifth; according to the opinion of Parāśara, a fifth son may marry a sixth daughter, but never a fifth."
There are also the words of Śākala:
"A fourth [brother] may marry a fourth [sister], or a fourth [brother] a fifth;
he may marry a sixth who is a relative, but a fifth [brother] shall not marry a fifth [sister]."
If there were two sons born previously, and they too have offspring—
if among them a fifth [son] does not choose a fifth daughter as his bride, O twice-born one, he should not marry her.
Two daughters may be born from an earlier marriage; there may also be offspring from those two.
In that case, a man may marry a fifth daughter as his fifth wife.
"If a daughter and a son are born [to them], and from those two a lineage is produced,
then the fifth [descendant] may choose even the fifth [as a bride]."

One should marry a girl from a renowned and great family of Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) at least seven generations beyond [one's own maternal lineage]. In the absence of such, one may marry a seventh-generation girl; in her absence, a fifth-generation girl. This rule applies specifically to the paternal side.
Likewise the seventh, the sixth, and the fifth;
Śākaṭāyana says there is no fault in marrying a girl in this manner.
Or [one may marry] the third or the fourth [from the mother's side] on either of the two sides.
Manu, Pārāśarya, Aṅgiras, and Yama have declared that one should cause [the girl] to be wedded.

Thus, since the *Caturviṃśatimata* states that even for the seventh and subsequent degrees, marriage is permitted specifically regarding those belonging to families of Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) renowned for ten generations, it should be understood that these statements refer either to such cases or to situations of extreme distress (*atyantāpad*).
Śūlapāṇi, in the *Saṃbandhaviveka*, says:
"Even within five or seven degrees, one may marry provided there is an intervention of three lineages (*gotra*)."
"She would be unrelated to the mother's funeral cake (piṇḍa) or even the water libation;
she is fit to be married by the twice-born, as well as she who is separated by three *gotras*," according to the statement of Bṛhan-Manu.
And because of the statement of Devala: "Even when there is proximity [of kinship], [the marriage] must be performed if [the girl] is beyond three generations [on the father's side].

An example of this is as follows regarding the bride: Mūlapuruṣa Yajñadatta (1), his son Viṣṇudatta (2), his son Rudradatta (3), his son Brahmadatta (4), his son Haradatta (5), his son Mitradatta (6), his son Śivadatta (7), and his son Śrīdatta (8). Thus it is with respect to the groom.

Regarding the lineage of the bride: the original ancestor is Yajñadatta (1); his daughter is Lakṣmī, belonging to the Vāsiṣṭha gotra (2); her daughter is Sarasvatī, of the Nitunda gotra (3); her daughter is Gaurī, of the Kauṇḍinya gotra (4); her daughter is Śrīdattabhaktā (5). This [girl] is to be married by Śrīdatta. Moderns claim that southerners do not accept this;
however, in reality—“For those whose marriage rite takes place in the fifth or seventh generation... [the prohibition applies].
For it is stated [in the Smṛti]: "Even those who are intent on ritual acts should be known as having fallen to the status of Śūdras.
Because this contradicts such prohibitory statements, it is logical that this [rule] also refers exclusively to times of distress (*āpad*).
In the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"She who is not a sapinda of the mother and not of the same gotra as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the matrimonial rite for sexual union."
A specific detail is found in another Smṛti: "One should avoid the sister and the daughter of a stepmother;
one should avoid the sister and the daughter of a paternal uncle's wife."
"A twice-born man should never marry the daughter of one who has taught him the Gāyatrī,
nor should a disciple ever marry the daughter of his preceptor.
There is also another specific rule:

"One should not marry the daughter of a nurse, the sister of a nurse, a beloved daughter, a beloved sister, the daughter of a beloved maternal uncle, the wife of an elder brother, the sister of one's own wife, a beloved paternal aunt, a beloved maternal aunt, the sister of a paternal uncle’s wife, the sister of a daughter-in-law, or the sister of a stepmother. Thus it is stated. Also, in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*, beginning with the section on marriage, after stating that "one should marry a woman whose relationship is not prohibited," it defines a prohibited relationship as one where there is a mutual equality of father and mother between the couple, such as: "the daughter of the wife’s sister, and the sister of a paternal uncle’s wife."

The meaning of this is as follows: A marriage in which there is a parity of father and mother between the couple—the bride and groom—such that the groom stands in the place of the father to the bride, or the bride stands in the place of the mother to the groom, is a prohibited relationship (*viruddhasambandha*). Regarding this, two examples are given in order: the daughter of the wife’s sister (*śālikāputrī*) and the sister of the paternal uncle’s wife (*pitṛvyapatnībhaginī*). Other examples concerning prohibited relationships should also be observed. Nārada says:
"A reciprocal marriage (*pratyudvāha*) must never be performed, nor should two daughters be given to one man."
"And it is not the case that two persons born of one [father] are [the same], but rather two daughters born of one [father]."
*Pratyudvāha* is the marriage of one's own daughter to the son of that man to whom one's daughter was previously given.
Sumantu states: "All the wives of one's father are mothers; their brothers are maternal uncles (*mātula*s); their sisters..."
"The maternal aunts, their daughters, [their] sisters, and their offspring—[that is,] the nephews—otherwise would become creators of social confusion.

Regarding this, some hold that according to the maxim "as far as the words go, so far the rule applies," sapinda-relationship exists only among those specifically enumerated, and not extending up to the seventh degree.

Others, however, maintain that because there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the difference between the qualifiers of the intended objects—such as "being the wife of the father" and "being his brother"—the text prescribes, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a four-generation *sāpiṇḍya* extended to the family of the step-grandfather (*sapatna-mātāmaha*) in order to avoid that split. Consequently, they say that just as with the daughters of maternal uncles and others, there can be no marriage for a girl with the son of her step-mother’s brother due to *sāpiṇḍya*.
As for the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter, it is only those among whom such a custom exists who incur fault if someone else performs it.

And so Baudhāyana says: "There are five points of divergence between the South and the North. We shall explain those that belong to the South: namely, eating with one who has not been initiated (*anūpeta*), eating with a woman, eating food that has stood overnight, and sexual intercourse with the daughter of a maternal uncle or a paternal aunt. Now, as for the North: the sale of wool, the drinking of *sīdhu* liquor, trade with people from both [coasts], military service, and sea-voyage."
"In this regard, one commits an offense by performing [a certain act] in another region, because of the authority of that specific region.

One person—a Southerner—commits an offense by entering into a marriage with his maternal uncle's daughter (*mātula-sambandha*) in another region—the North—but not in his own country. Likewise, another person—a Northerner—commits an offense by selling woolen cloth, drinking *sīdhu* liquor, and so forth, in another region—the South—but not in his own country. Why? Because of the authority of the region; the meaning is that the authority of custom is dependent upon the region.
Bṛhaspati also says:
The twice-born of the South marry the daughters of their maternal uncles;
the men of the East are eaters of fish, and the women are devoted to adultery;
those of the North are drinkers of liquor, and menstruating women are touched by men.
Even kinsmen seize the wife of a brother who is without a husband.
"In all countries, it is improper conduct to chew betel-leaf on the street."
Devala also says:
"In whatever region a custom is observed according to justice and is well-established, it should be practiced in that very place; it is not declared to be applicable in another region."
"In whatever country, city, village, or even town—
whatever dharma is prescribed for that place, one should not question that dharma."

[Objection: But if the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) were authoritative, then even marriage with one’s own daughter would follow as a consequence, since Prajāpati practiced it. For thus says the Śruti: "Prajāpati indeed lusted after his own daughter. [Reply: Not so. This is because of the maxim: "One should not imitate the conduct of the gods.
For this very reason, Baudhāyana states:
"That which has been performed by the gods and that which has been performed by the sages should not be performed by humans; rather, one should practice the dharma as it has been declared."
On the contrary, Śātātapa has stated a fault:
"Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, or likewise one of the mother’s lineage,
or even one of the same *pravara*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance after abandoning her."
Regarding the expiation for marrying within the same *gotra*, the *Smṛtyarthasāra* states:
"Thus, when the matter of marriage with one related by *gotra* has been established, if someone, through ignorance, marries and approaches such a girl..."
One is purified by performing the penance for violating the Guru’s bed; however, the child born from such an act shall become an outcaste.
Having abandoned that [child] on account of its [future] experience, one should protect it as if it were one's own mother.
"But through ignorance, Kaśyapa says that the embryo is purified by three [days] of the moon."

The *aindavāni* are the *cāndrāyaṇa* observances; because of the plural number, there are three or more. Regarding the name *Kāśyapa*, that embryo belongs to Kaśyapa—that is, it has the *gotra* of Kaśyapa—based on the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "All progeny are *kāśyapyas*.
For this very reason, it was stated by that same [author] that knowledge of the *pravara* is necessary:
"The *pravaras* must be known, for according to the Vedic revelation, one attains union with Brahman [only] through them; otherwise [it is not so]."
"Out of fear of being born as a Caṇḍāla due to the great sin of violating the teacher's bed."
Baudhāyana, in the *Tithitattva*, states:
"If one should marry a woman of the same gotra, he should maintain her as he would his mother."
Regarding the expiation for producing offspring in that [marriage], the same author states:

"If offspring has been born, one should perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance for a year and offer oblations with these two [mantras]: 'Whatever defect has occurred in my self,' and 'Agni has given sight back again.'"

Since this was undertaken previously out of ignorance and without intention, one should abandon that [course of action] after gaining knowledge. The application of the quarter-year *kṛcchra* penance and the *aindava* (lunar) fasts should be understood according to whether one is capable or incapable. However, if it was done intentionally, purification comes through the vow prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*).
Regarding the procreation of offspring with a *sapiṇḍa* woman, Bṛhad-Yama states: "In the case of the children or wives of a *sapiṇḍa*, the abandonment of life is ordained."
"Offspring and wife" refers to offspring together with the wife; "sapindas and those [wives]" means those [sapindas] and those [wives], or [if masculine] those [sapindas and husbands]—in them.
Maṇḍana also says:
"One should cast offspring born of a woman of the same lineage among the Caṇḍālas."
Having performed the vow for violating the Guru’s bed, he should protect her as if she were his own mother.
Having married a woman of the same gotra through ignorance, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise for a son begotten through ignorance upon a wife of the same gotra who has been married.
"Kāśyapa, however, is not a Caṇḍāla; at the end of his year-long penance for his father's sake, he should offer two Mindā oblations into a blazing fire."

Since the phrase "through ignorance" (*ajñānataḥ*) is heard in the subsequent sentence, it follows by implication that in the preceding context, "through knowledge" (*jñānataḥ*) is established. Furthermore, in the statement regarding a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*) who has been married, the mention of "through ignorance" indicates that if it is through knowledge, the offspring is indeed a *Caṇḍāla*; for the father, there is no expiation at all, but rather he is as good as dead. [The term] *yavīyasīm* means one who is inferior in age and physique. We shall explain that inferiority when discussing the proper time for marriage.

"Healthy" means free from incurable diseases. "Having a brother" means one who has either an elder or a younger brother; by this, the suspicion that she might be intended as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is dispelled.
For this very reason, Manu says:
"But she who has no brother, or whose father is not known..."
"A wise man should not marry her, for fear of violating the law regarding an appointed daughter."

One should not marry a girl whose father’s intention to make her an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is unknown; however, where no such suspicion exists, one may even marry a girl who has no brother—this is the intended meaning. From the statement "it would not be known [if] the father [intended it]," it is understood that a girl becomes an appointed daughter through the mere resolve of the father, even without a formal agreement with the groom.
For this very reason, Gautama says:
"According to some, she is an appointed daughter by mere intention; because of the doubt regarding that, one should not marry a girl who has no brother."
His intention was concealed by a hidden purpose.
Manu also says:
"A sonless man may, according to this rule, make his daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*)."
"Whatever offspring may be born of her, that shall be for my funeral offerings."
It is clearly understood that the practice of making her a *putrikā* occurs upon agreement with the bridegroom; and that agreement was demonstrated by Vasiṣṭha:
"I shall give you this daughter, adorned, who has no brother."
"The son who is born of her shall be my son. Thus [he spoke].
And this is the mantra for that gift: "In this manner, there is the cessation of *sapiṇḍya* and *sagotra* status for this daughter together with her father and the others.
For this very reason, Laugākṣi says: "The rites of the *piṇḍa* and water for the mother are performed according to the *gotra* of the maternal grandfather."
"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra) should perform [the rites]; thus spoke Prajāpati."

Thus, the intended meaning is this: one desiring a son, fearing [the birth of] a daughter, should marry only a woman who has brothers; and this is prohibited in the Kali age because it is listed among the practices to be avoided in that age.

Regarding the phrase "born of a different *ṛṣi* and *gotra*": she who is not born of one whose *ṛṣi* and *gotra* are the same is "born of a different *ṛṣi* and *gotra*" (*asamānārṣagotrajā*); such a woman [is intended]. That which belongs to an *ṛṣi* is *ārṣa*, namely the *pravara*. Thus, the meaning is: "born of a different *pravara* and born of a different *gotra*. A bride for whom there is no identity of *pravara* or identity of *gotra* with her groom is eligible to marry him. In some cases, even when there is a difference in *gotra*, there may still be identity of *pravara*.

For example: although the *vādhūla*, *mauna*, *mauka*, and others belong to different *gotras*, they share the same *pravara*—namely, Bhārgava, Vaitahavya, and Sāvedasa. Since a marriage might otherwise be proposed there, the phrase "born of a different *ṛṣi*" (*asamānārṣejām*) was stated to exclude such cases. In some instances, even when the *pravara* differs, the *gotra* remains the same. For example, in the case of "Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, Yauvanāśva" and "Māndhātṛ, Ambarīṣa, Yauvanāśva," although there is a difference in the *pravara* (Āṅgirasa versus Māndhātṛ), the *Yauvanāśva gotra* is one and the same.
Therefore, so that a marriage does not take place in those cases, the phrase "born of a different *gotra*" (*asamānagotrajām*) was stated. Now follows the determination of *gotra* and *pravara*.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana states: "Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa— these are the seven sages (ṛṣis)."
"The offspring of the seven sages, with Agastya as the eighth, is called a *gotra*.

Here, the term "offspring" (*apatya*) does not refer exclusively to sons, but includes grandsons and further descendants as well. For this very reason, Pāṇini states: "The lineage beginning with the grandson is a *gotra*. Now, one might object: "In the case of the Yaskas and others within the exclusive *Bhṛgu* group, and the Haritas and others within the exclusive *Aṅgiras* group, since they are not the offspring of the [seven] sages, they would not possess the status of a *gotra*. This is not so.
"As long as a single sage recurs among the *pravara* ancestors, so long does the state of having a common *gotra* persist, except in the case of the groups of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras."

This is because that [prohibition] is established through the untenability of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) stated by Baudhāyana; for an exclusion occurs only when there is a possibility of application. Just as, based on the general statement "one performs the *ye yajāmahe* at sacrifices," there is a possibility of the *ye yajāmahe* being applied to the *anūyāja* offerings, and thus the exclusion "not in the *anūyājas*" is made to mean "in those other than the *anūyājas*," so it is here as well.

As for the rule stating that "the offspring of the seven ṛṣis, with Agastya as the eighth, constitutes a *gotra*," this does not provide a formal definition; rather, it merely excludes what is not applicable (*ayogavyāvṛtti*). Thus, there is no contradiction with the preceding and following rules. For this very reason, Vijñāneśvara, Mādhava, Madanapārijāta, and others have stated that a *gotra* is that which is well-known through the lineage of one's ancestors.

And it has been stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda as well: "Even though Brāhmaṇahood is common [to all], the lineage (*gotra*) is characterized by the traditional recollection of such names as Kuṇḍina or Atri. Thus, wherever there is a well-known status as a lineage among those who are learned, that indeed is the faultless definition of a *gotra*; it is established just like the nature of being a mantra (*mantratva*) and so forth. By this, both the untenability of Vasiṣṭha and others being lineages, as well as the contingency of people like us being lineages by virtue of being their descendants through tradition, are avoided. There are forty-nine such groups with respect to whom the *pravara* (ancestral sages) have been recorded. And so says Baudhāyana:
"There are thousands, millions, and billions of lineages;
however, there are forty-nine among them that are preeminent, according to the vision of the sages."
Now, concerning the *pravaras* (ancestral sages).

Since no ancient commentary on the *Pravarasūtra* has been found, the *Pravarasūtra* itself is presented here along with its commentary. In this regard, the introductory sūtra is as follows: "We shall explain the *pravaras*. This declaration is for the purpose of establishing the technical designation "*pravara*" for those [sages] mentioned hereafter, such as Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jāmadagnya. They are called *pravaras* because they are proclaimed (*pravriyante*) as the qualifying attributes of the sacrificial fire.

We shall explain them by summarizing them together. The mention of Agni as a qualification is established in sacrificial mantras (iṣṭimantra) such as "O Agni, you are great, O Brāhmaṇa Bhārata. However, in the context of marriage, the mention is solely as his own qualification, because no other [qualification] is possible. Regarding the recitation of the Ārṣa lineage in marriage, it is based on scriptural injunction (vācanika); it serves both to dispel doubts regarding the presence of common *pravara*s or common *gotra*s and for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). In rites such as propitiatory ceremonies (*śānti*), however, it is based on scriptural injunction in some cases, and in others, it is obtained through custom (*ācāra*).

He demonstrates the scriptural authority for the meaning that "the *pravaraṇa* (selection of ancestors) must be performed," stating: "It is known from scripture: 'He chooses the *ārṣeya*; he does not depart from his kin; furthermore, it is for the sake of continuity. *Ārṣeya* refers to the descendant of a seer (*ṛṣi*), namely the Āhavanīya fire, because the sacrificer has produced it and thus belongs to the lineage of the seers. He chooses it—that is, he requests it—on account of its belonging to that lineage. This being so, "he does not depart from his kin" means he does not fall away from the connection with the former seers. Furthermore, "it is for the sake of continuity" means for the sake of the lineage of the ancestors, the forefathers, and of oneself; this is what is understood from the scripture, the word "scripture" being the ellipsis to be supplied.
He shows the scriptural authority for the point that the selection of ancestral seers (*ārṣeya-varaṇa*) should not be performed by gods or humans, but rather by the sages (*ṛṣis*) themselves:
"It is known from scripture: 'One should not choose the ancestral lineage through gods or humans; one should choose the ancestral lineage through the sages alone.

One does not choose the ancestral lineage through gods such as Prajāpati, nor through learned humans such as Devadatta; rather, it is known—that is, so says the scripture—that one should choose the ancestral lineage through the sages such as Vasiṣṭha, who are the seers of the mantras.
He shows the scriptural authority regarding the necessity of pronouncing the lineage of sages (ārṣeya):
"He recites the lineage of sages; for it is known that 'the gods recognize a person by means of his sage-lineage.'"

He recites the *ārṣeya* (the lineage of seers). Why? Because by means of the seer—his ancestor, who is renowned and celebrated among the gods—the gods recognize that person as his offspring; they know, "This man is fit to be fed because he is the offspring of such a one. This is the meaning. To show the scriptural authority for the fact that there is a fault in abandoning the selection of one's own *ārṣeya* and selecting another's, the Śruti says:
"Whosoever, being one [person], chooses the *ārṣeya* of another, he indeed..."
"It is known from scripture: 'The seer of that [yajamāna] takes away his desired and obtained [fruit].

This means that if a yajamāna, being of one gotra, chooses the *ārṣeya* (ancestral seers) of another gotra, that very seer of the other gotra takes away—that is, seizes—the *iṣṭa*, which is the fruit of the sacrifice, and the *vīta*, which is the fruit such as the satisfaction of Brahmins.
[The author] now shows the scriptural passage intended to restrict the number of *ārṣeyas* and to prohibit choosing more than four or five *pravara*s:"
"One chooses one, one chooses two, one chooses three; one does not choose four, nor does one choose more than five"—so it is known.

One chooses a single *ārṣeya*; having proclaimed one *ṛṣi*, one chooses his descendant as the *agni*. The same applies to the cases "he chooses two" and "he chooses three. "He does not choose four"—the meaning is that he does not choose beyond five, starting with six. Since there would otherwise be the possibility of choosing an unrestricted number of one's own ancestral *ṛṣis*, the rules regarding the restriction of number, such as "he chooses one," are prescribed. The prohibitions "he does not choose four" and "he does not choose more than five" pertain specifically to the case of a *vyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (one who belongs to two lineages).

In the case of a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (one belonging to two lineages), there would be the contingency of choosing from four *ṛṣis*, since he belongs to two lineages and each has its own three *ṛṣis*. If he were to have three *ṛṣis* for each lineage, there would be six; if five, or if there were a combination of those with two *ṛṣis* and so forth, there would even be the contingency of choosing from seven or more.

To preclude that [unrestricted choice], it is stated: "He does not choose four; he does not choose more than five. Following the Vedic text, "He chooses three; he chooses the composers of the mantras; he chooses the composers of the mantras according to the ṛṣis," the Mīmāṃsakas maintain in this section (*adhikaraṇa*)—namely, "There would be the exclusion of one who has no ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*), because of the qualification"—that the injunction is precisely "he chooses three. The two cases, "he chooses one" and "he chooses two," are both partial restatements (*avayutyānuvāda*). Otherwise, there would be the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of "one does not choose three," the injunction is impossible because the fault of *vākya-bheda* (splitting the sentence) remains; for when there is an injunction of a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa-vidhāna*), no such split occurs, and thus the status of an injunction is possible. This passage beginning with "one chooses one" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). It is a praise meaning: "If even choosing one or choosing two—which are not praiseworthy—are to be performed, then what need is there to mention that the praiseworthy choice of three must be performed?"

By means of both the prohibition of four and the prohibition of exceeding five, only the number three is praised; nor is there any need to enjoin a prohibition for those two [numbers], because they do not apply at all due to the absence of any occasion for their occurrence. Numbers such as four and so on are unpraiseworthy because they involve excessive delay, whereas the number three is praiseworthy because it is not like that. Therefore, they say the intended meaning is this: the sacrificer, when qualified for the ritual act, should utter exactly three [names], neither fewer nor more.

In the *Tantraratna*, it is stated that even those who have only one *ṛṣi* (ekārṣeya) and so forth are entitled [to perform sacrifices] by resorting to the position of Manu. Regarding the prohibition of marriage as stated by Yājñavalkya—"one should not marry a woman born of the same *ṛṣi* or *gotra*"—the factor that renders marriage impermissible is "sameness of *ṛṣi*" (*samānārṣatva*), which is synonymous with "sameness of *pravara*. This is of two kinds: similarity in one *pravara* and similarity in two or three *pravaras*. Among these, the first applies to those outside the *Bhṛgu* and *Aṅgiras* groups, while the second applies to the *Bhṛgu* and *Aṅgiras* groups.

In this regard, it should be understood that for those with five *pravaras*, similarity in three *pravaras* constitutes the cause for prohibiting marriage; for those with three *pravaras*, similarity in two *pravaras* is the cause.

This is because of the scriptural statement: "Among the five [classes], there is no intermarriage due to commonality among three; among the three [classes], it is forbidden with two; likewise among the groups of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras; and among the remaining [groups], even a single [common ancestor] prohibits it."
The meaning is that even if there is only one common *pravara* among the remaining [lineages], it shall prohibit marriage between them. Now, the enumeration of the *pravara*s:
first, the Bhṛgus.

Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "We shall first explain the Bhṛgus; the Vatsas are descendants of Jamadagni. Their *pañcārṣeya* [lineage] is Bhārgava-Cyāvāna-Āpnavāna-Aurva-Jāmadagna—[the invocation being] 'like Jamadagni, like Urva, like Āpnavāna, like Cyavana, like Bhṛgu. Some, however, use a *tryārṣeya*: Bhārgava-Aurva-Jāmadagna—'like Jamadagni, like Urva, like Bhṛgu. This same [lineage], unmodified, applies to the Jāmāli, Aitiśāyani, Virohita, Māṇḍavya, Vaṭa, Maṇḍu, Baida, Retavāha, and Prācīnayogya. Now, for the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, there is a *pañcārṣeya*..."

"Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Anūpa"—that is, like Anūpa, like Ṛṣiṣeṇa, like Āpnavāna, like Cyāvāna, and like Bhṛgu; thus it is a *tryārṣeya* (three-lineage) formula. Some, however, [recite] "Bhārgava, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Anūpa"—that is, like Anūpa, like Ṛṣiṣeṇa, and like Bhṛgu. Now, as for the Vītahavyas—Yāska, Vādhūla, Mauna, Mauka, Rajatavāha—their...

"One who has three *ṛṣis* [should recite]: Bhārgava, Vaitahavya, Sāvedasa—[meaning] like Saveda, like Vitahavya, and like Bhṛgu. Or alternatively, for the Vainya-Pārthas, their *tryārṣeya* is Bhārgava, Vainya, Pārtha—[meaning] like Pṛthu, like Vena, and like Bhṛgu. Then for the Gārtsamadas, the Śunakas: their *ekārṣeya* is Gārtsamada;

the Hotṛ [recites] 'like Gṛtsamada' and the Adhvaryu [recites] 'like Vaghyraśva. Or alternatively, for the Vāghryaśvas, the Mitrayus: their *ekārṣeya* is Vāghryaśva; the Hotṛ [recites] 'like Vaghyraśva' and the Adhvaryu [recites] 'like Vaghyraśva.'"

The particle *eva* (only) serves to exclude others. We shall explain—that is, we shall speak—of [Bhṛgu] first, at the beginning, because of his preeminence; this is the ellipsis. Bhṛgu’s preeminence is established by the Lord’s own statement in the *Mokṣadharma* sections, "Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu," by the scriptural hearing (*śruti*) that Bhṛgu is a portion (*aṃśa*) of Vāsudeva, and because in the *Ādhāna-mantras*, the mantras for the Bhṛgus alone are recited separately at the very beginning.

Alternatively, the particle *eva* connects with the word *agra*. We shall speak of those Bhṛgus who attained the status of Bhṛgu at the very beginning (*agre*), and not those who later attained the status of Bhṛgu by virtue of being *dvaimātura* (descendants of two lineages). This is because the *dvaimāturas* will be discussed later on.

In the phrase "the Vatsas are Jāmadagnyas," the qualification "Jāmadagnyas" is for the purpose of excluding the non-Jāmadagnya Vatsas, for the purpose of obtaining the five-fold portioning (*pañcāvattitva*), and for the purpose of obtaining the *jāmadagnyāprī* verses. For those Jāmadagnya Vatsas, the ancestral invocation (*pravara*) consists of five seers: Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jāmadagnya. This is because of the statement: "The Hotṛ invokes from that [ancestor] downwards. Starting from the root-seer (*mūlabhūtā ṛṣiḥ*), "downwards" refers to those mantra-seers born subsequently.

The meaning is that he requests that Agni by means of his connection with those ancestors in due order. According to the injunction, "The Adhvaryu chooses [the ancestors] beginning from Jamadagni, Aurva, Apnavāna, Cyavana, and Bhṛgu," the Adhvaryu chooses [the ancestors] starting from above that [yajamāna]. Therefore, having recited the names of those who are the original sources—uninterrupted by other seers of mantras (mantradṛś)—in the order they were seen, he chooses and requests Agni through a relationship of similarity, using the formula "like so-and-so, like so-and-so. This is the meaning.

This very specific sequence of the *pravara* (ancestral invocation) for both the *hotṛ* and the *adhvaryu* is to be taught everywhere until the completion of the study of this chapter. The phrase "some indeed say it consists of three *ṛṣis*" is the remainder [of the sentence]. The meaning is that some teachers state that the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*. The particle *u* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) or serves as a rhetorical ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*). He shows that *pravara*: "Bhārgava-aurva-jāmadagna"—that is, "like Jamadagni, like Urva, like Bhṛgu."

He extends this very same preeminent [lineage] to others by means of the sūtra beginning with "This very same unmodified [lineage belongs to] Jāmāli, Aitiśāyana," and ending with "up to Prācīnayogya. The meaning is that this aforementioned lineage—whether consisting of five ṛṣis or three ṛṣis—belongs to the nine [groups] beginning with Jāmāli.

Now, in the phrase "athā’’rṣṭiṣeṇānām," the word *atha* is for the purpose of indicating that this is a separate group; this applies everywhere. The rest has its meaning already explained. Furthermore, the sūtra beginning with "atha vītahavyāḥ" and ending with "pṛthuvad venavad bhṛguvat" is clear in its meaning. For the Śunakas are of four kinds: some are born from Śunaka himself; some are born from Gṛtsamada; and some are born from Gṛtsamada, who is the offspring of Bhṛgu.

Some hold that [the lineage] is the offspring of Bhṛgu, whose gotra is Śuna; his offspring is Gṛtsamada, and from him they were born. Among them, this *pravara* belongs only to those born from Gṛtsamada himself and not to others. For this reason, and for the purpose of obtaining the *ṛṣi-prīti* (propitiation) seen by Gṛtsamada, the qualification "Gārtsamadas" is used. However, for the others, the *pravaras* mentioned in other Sūtras should be understood. Among those, for the first group, the *pravara* is monarchical (*ekārṣeya*), consisting of Śaunaka alone. For the third group, it is dual-ancestral (*dvayārṣeya*), consisting of Bhārgava and Gārtsamada.

Regarding the fourth [class], there is the rule: "For the Bhārgavas, Śaunahotras, and Gārtsamadas, there are three ancestors. Since there is no regulating authority for these two rules—namely, that "in the case of one ancestor, the Hotṛ chooses those who are more recent than him, and the Adhvaryu chooses those who are more remote than him"—and because a lack of regulation would otherwise result, the mention of the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu is intended to demonstrate the following distinction: the *pravara* of the Hotṛ ends in a *taddhita* suffix, while that of the Adhvaryu ends in the suffix *vat*.

The qualification "mitrayuvāṃ vāghryaśvā" is for the purpose of obtaining the *aprī* verses seen by Vāghryaśva. The mention of the Hotṛ and Adhvaryu in the passage "vāghryaśveti hotā vāghryaśvavadityadhvaryuḥ" is for the purpose of dispelling any doubt regarding the application of that specific rule [of distribution] to them. Thus, these Bhṛgus have been explained.

The purpose of this restatement of what was previously said is so that even those who do not possess the *bhṛgu* word [in their lineage] may attain the status of *bhṛgu*, such as in the case of the *śunaka* and *mitrayu*. By means of this, there is established the inclusion [of these lineages] in the formula "of the Bhṛgus" (*bhṛgūṇāṃ tvā*) and in the *yatharṣi-ādhāna* (fire-consecration according to the seers), as in the passage "the Hotṛ priest is a descendant of Bhṛgu" (*bhārgavo hotā bhavati*), and so forth. Furthermore, there is no intermarriage between the *jāmadagnya-vatsas* and the *jāmālis*, etc., because they share the same *pravara* and the same *gotra*. The same applies to the *ārṣṭiṣeṇas*, due to the similarity of their three *pravaras*.

Although there is no similarity of two *pravara*s between the three-*pravara* Ārṣṭiṣeṇas and others, nevertheless, even a similarity of *pravara*s involving five *ṛṣis* serves as a cause for prohibiting marriage among these. This is because Baudhāyana states: "There is no marriage between the Vatsas, the Vidas, and the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas. Due to having a common *pravara* with the Ajāmadagnya-Vatsa and Ārṣṭiṣeṇa groups, there is no marriage.

However, for the Vītahavyas and others, once they have left their respective sub-groups, marriage indeed occurs both mutually among themselves and with those mentioned previously, as there is no similarity of two or three *pravara*s.
Thus ends the section on the *gotra* and *pravara* of the Bhṛgus.
Now begins the section on the *pravara* (ancestral lineage) of the Gautama *gotra*.

Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "Now, therefore, [concerning] the Āṅgirasa-Ayāsya-Gautamas; their *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis: Āṅgirasa, Ayāsya, and Gautama—[invoking them] as 'Gautama-like,' 'Ayāsya-like,' and 'Āṅgiras-like. Next, the Autathya-Gautamas; their *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis: Āṅgirasa, Autathya, and Gautama—[invoking them] as 'Gautama-like,' 'Utathya-like,' and 'Āṅgiras-like. Next, the Auśija-Gautamas; their *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis: Āṅgirasa, Auśija, and Kākṣīvata."
"As Kakṣīvat, as Vaduśija, as Aṅgiras; or [as] the Vāmadevas and Gautamas—of these, the three-lineage (tryārṣeya) is Āṅgirasa-Vāmadeva-Bārhaduktha: as Bṛhaduktha, as Vāmadeva, and as Aṅgiras."

Here, the word *ataḥ* (therefore) signifies a reason (*hetu*). For the Śruti states: "Since [it is said], 'O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases,' one should perform the establishment for those of the Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras lineages"—thus, within a single sentence, the mantra for the establishment of those belonging to the Bhṛgu lineage is stated first, and immediately thereafter, the mantra for the establishment of those belonging to the Gautama and other lineages is stated. Therefore, the meaning is "for this reason. In the term *aṅgirasām*, the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

The meaning is that among the groups of Aṅgirases, those who are Ayāsya-Gautamas and Aṅgirases have a *pravara* consisting of three ṛṣis. The qualification "Ayāsya" is intended to include only those listed in the group of Ayāsya-Udgātṛs. Terms such as "Utathya," "Auśija," and "Vāmadeva" are qualifiers of Gautama for the purpose of preventing confusion. The rest is clear. There is no intermarriage among all these Gautama-Aṅgirases with one another.
Because [the lineage] continues through Gautama by virtue of being chosen or by his very existence, there is a commonality of *gotra*, and generally also a similarity of two or three *pravara*s;
thus ends the section on the *gotra* and *pravara* of Gautama.
Now begins the section on the *gotra* and *pravara* of Bharadvāja.

Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "Now, for the Bharadvājas, there is a three-ṛṣi lineage: Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja—meaning 'like Bharadvāja,' 'like Bṛhaspati,' and 'like Aṅgiras. This very [lineage] remains unaltered for the Tuthyas, Agniveśyas, and Aurjayānas, and for all those whose names contain the words *stambha* or *stamba*. For the Ṛkṣas, there is a five-ṛṣi lineage: Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja, Vāndana, Mātavacasa—meaning 'like Matavacas,' 'like Vandana,' 'like Bharadvāja,' 'like Bṛhaspati,' and 'like Aṅgiras. However, some maintain that it is a three-ṛṣi [lineage]."

"Āṅgirasa-vāndana-mātavacasa"—that is, like Mātavacasa, like Vāndana, and like Āṅgirasa. Now, regarding families of *dvimūṣyāyaṇas* (those belonging to two lineages), such as the Śauṅga-Śaiśirayas who are Bharadvājas: the Śuṅgas are Kātas and the Śaiśirayas are [Bharadvājas]. For them, there is a fivefold *ṛṣi* lineage: *Āṅgirasa-bārhaspatya-bhāradvāja-kātya-ākṣila*—that is, like Akṣila, like Kata, like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, and like Āṅgirasa. However, some maintain a threefold *ṛṣi* lineage: *Āṅgirasa-kātya-ākṣila*—that is, like Akṣila, like Kata, and like Āṅgirasa. Now, for the Gargas, there is a threefold *ṛṣi* lineage.

"Āṅgirasagārgyaśainya—meaning like Śini, like Garga, and like Aṅgiras. Some, however, [recite] Bhāradvāja in place of Āṅgirasa, as 'Bhāradvājagārgyaśainya,' meaning like Bharadvāja, like Garga, and like Śini. Now, for the Kapis, there is a tri-ārṣeya: Āṅgirasamāhāyyavaurukṣayya—meaning like Urukṣaya, like Mahāyyu, and like Aṅgiras. Tarasvā, Tila, Vidu, Śālu, Patañjali, and Bhūyasī are the Dandvakīs; Jalandva is the Kapi; thus the offspring of Kapi are of eight kinds."

Tutthya, Āgniveśya, and Aurjayāna—among these, those whose names contain the word *stambha* are called *stambha-śabda*s; those whose names contain the word *stamba* are called *stamba-śabda*s. The meaning is that for these [lineages], this aforementioned three-lineage (*tryārṣeya*) *pravara* alone should be used. Families designated by two *gotra*s are *vyāmuṣyāyaṇa* families; for example, the "Śauṅgaśaiśirayas" is an ancient *vyāmuṣyāyaṇa* family.

In order to state that for those of the present day who belong to two *gotras*, there is no marriage between the two *gotras*, the following is cited by way of illustration: the Śuṅgas are Bharadvājas, and the Katas are Śaiśiras; they are Viśvāmitras. Those born from the seed of a Bharadvāja Śuṅga in the field of a Viśvāmitra Śaiśira are called Śauṅgaśaiśiras. For those born in their lineage, a *pravara* of five ṛṣis is to be observed: Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja, Kātya, and Ākṣila—this is the *pravara* for the Hotṛ.

"Like Akṣila, like Kata, like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, like Aṅgiras"—this is for the Adhvaryu. According to some, there is a three-ṛṣi lineage: "Āṅgirasa, Kātya, Akṣila"—this is for the Hotṛ; "like Akṣila, like Kata, like Aṅgiras"—this is for the Adhvaryu. In this *pravara*, the first belongs to the progenitor and the second to the recipient, as has been stated; likewise, in the case of others such as the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the adopted son (*dattaka*), the purchased son (*krīta*), the made son (*kṛtrima*), and so forth, the *pravara* of both lineages should be understood.
Because the Śauṅgas and Śaiśiris are cited as examples, Āśvalāyana states the rule for all Dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas when there is the possibility of choosing from two lineages:

"Of these, one should choose [the pravaras] from both sides—one from the one side and two from the other, or two from the one side and three from the other; for there is no *pravara* beyond four, nor is there a selection of more than five."

In the case of three *ṛṣis*, one is from one side and two from the other; in the case of five *ṛṣis*, two are from one side and three from the other. Regarding the question of whose *pravara* comes first in that instance, Kātyāyana and Laugākṣi state:
"The former *pravara* belongs to the progenitor, the latter to the recipient.

This should be understood to apply likewise to the Saṃkṛtis and others who will be mentioned hereafter. The fact that the Gargas belong to the Bharadvāja lineage is established precisely by the optional inclusion of the Bharadvāja *pravara*.

Although the recitation of the Kapis is seen in all Sūtra manuscripts within the midst of the *kevalāṅgiras* group, it should nevertheless not be accepted. This is because it contradicts many works such as the *Gotrapravaramañjarī*, the *Prayogapārijāta*, and the *Smṛtyarthasāra*; because it contradicts numerous Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Sūtras; and because it would result in a reversal of the conduct approved by the learned, namely that marriage with the Bhāradvājas is distinct from marriage with the *kevalāṅgiras*s. Alternatively, two groups of Kapis should be understood: one belonging to the Bharadvāja group and the other belonging to the *kevalāṅgiras* group.
And thus Maṇḍana says:
"In the enumeration of the Bhāradvāja pravara, some say that the Kapis are separate.
Now follows the section on the pravara of the Atri gotra.

Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "Now, for the Atris, there is a tri-ārṣeya [pravara]: Ātreya, Arcanānasa, Śyāvāśva—as in the case of Śyāvāśva, Arcanānasa, and Atri. Then, for the Gaviṣṭhiras, there is a tri-ārṣeya: Ātreya, Arcanānasa, Gaviṣṭhira—as in the case of Gaviṣṭhira, Arcanānasa, and Atri. This same [pravara], unmodified, applies to the Vāmarathya, Sumaṅgala, and Bījavāpa [sub-lineages]. The meaning is clear. There is no marriage among all those belonging to the Atri lineage because they share the same *gotra* and the same *pravara*.
Thus ends the section on the *pravara* of the Atri *gotra*.

Now follows the section on the *pravara* (ancestral seers) of the Viśvāmitra *gotra*. Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "Now, among the Viśvāmitras are the Devarātas, Cikitakas, Ālabavas, Mantantus, Babhrus, Yajñavalkas, Kaulontyas, Māris, Bṛhadagnis, Sāṃśityas, Vārakis, Tārakis, Tārakāyaṇas, and Śālāvatas; for them, the *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis: Vaiśvāmitra, Daivarāta, and Audala—[meaning] like Audala, like Devarāta, and like Viśvāmitra. Then there are the Śraumata-Kāmakāyanas; for them, the *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis: Vaiśvāmitra, Mādhucchandasa, and Dhānañjaya."

Like Dhanañjaya, like Madhucchandas, and like Viśvāmitra—thus [is the lineage]. Now, the Aṣṭakas are Lohitas; their *dvārṣeya* (two-lineage) formula is "Vaiśvāmitrāṣṭaka," [meaning] like Aṣṭaka and like Viśvāmitra. Then there are the Pūraṇas, known as the Pāridhāpayantins; their *dvārṣeya* formula is "Vaiśvāmitrapauraṇa," [meaning] like Pūraṇa and like Viśvāmitra. Then there are the Katas; their *tryārṣeya* (three-lineage) formula is "Vaiśvāmitrakātyākṣila," [meaning] like Akṣila, like Kata, and like Viśvāmitra. Then there are the Aghamarṣaṇas, who are the Kuśikas; their *tryārṣeya* [formula is...].

"Vaiśvāmitra-āghamarṣaṇa-kauśika," meaning "like Kuśika, like Aghamarṣaṇa, and like Viśvāmitra. The meaning is clear. There is no intermarriage among the various groups within the Viśvāmitra lineage because they share the same *gotra* and the same *pravara*.
Thus ends the section on the *gotras* and *pravaras* of the Viśvāmitras.

Now follows the section on the eminent lineages (*pravara*) of the Kaśyapa clan. Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "Now, for the Kaśyapas, there is a *tryārṣeya* [pravara]: Kāśyapa-Avatsāra-Naidhruva; that is, 'like Nidhruva, like Avatsāra, like Kaśyapa'—this very same [formula] applies without modification to the Dhaumyas, Abhiṣeṇyas, and Māṭharas. Now, for the Rebhas, there is a *tryārṣeya*: Kāśyapa-Avatsāra-Rebhya; that is, 'like Rebha, like Avatsāra, like Kaśyapa'. Now, for the Śaṇḍilas, there is a *dvyārṣeya*: Daivala-Asita; that is, 'like Asita, like Devala'. However, some maintain that it is *tryārṣeya*."

"Kāśyapadaivalāsita" means "like Asita, like Devala, and like Kaśyapa"; thus, according to this logic, all those with two *ṛṣis* (dvyārṣeya) ought to become those with three *ṛṣis* (tryārṣeya) in this manner, and not only the Śaṇḍilas. Therefore, it should be understood that even for the Aṣṭakas and the Lohitas who have two *ṛṣis*, there is indeed a state of having three *ṛṣis*. Some explain that all Śaṇḍilas ought to have only two *ṛṣis* and not three; however, that is untenable.

This is because it would contradict the Jaiminiya principle: "There would be the exclusion of one who lacks a Ṛṣi lineage, due to the [textual] qualification. The rest has already been explained. Among the Kaśyapas, there is no intermarriage among themselves, because they continue to be associated with Kaśyapa either by being chosen as their lineage-founder (*vṛyamāṇatayā*) or by his mere existence (*sattayā*), and thus they share the same *gotra* and the same *pravara*.
Thus ends the section on the *gotra* and *pravara* of the Kaśyapas.
Now begins the section on the *gotra* and *pravara* of the Vasiṣṭhas.

Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "The Vāsiṣṭhas have a single *ṛṣi* lineage; except for the Upamanyus, Parāśaras, and Kuṇḍinas, the Hotṛ says 'Vāsiṣṭha' and the Adhvaryu says 'like Vasiṣṭha. Now, for the Upamanyus, there is a threefold *ṛṣi* lineage: 'Vāsiṣṭha, Aindrāpramada, Ābharadvasu'; [the Hotṛ says] 'like Ābharadvasu, like Indrapramada, like Vasiṣṭha,' and the Adhvaryu likewise. Now, for the Parāśaras, there is a threefold *ṛṣi* lineage: 'Vāsiṣṭha, Śāktya, Pārāśarya'; [the Hotṛ says] 'like Parāśara, like Śakti, like Vasiṣṭha,' and the Adhvaryu likewise. Now, for the Kuṇḍinas, there is a threefold *ṛṣi* lineage..."

[Vasiṣṭha, Maitrāvaruṇa, and Kauṇḍinya—meaning like Kuṇḍina, like Mitra and Varuṇa, and like Vasiṣṭha]; and for the Saṃkṛtis, Pūtimāpas, and Taṇḍins, there is a tri-ārṣeya [lineage]: Śāktya, Sāṃkṛtya, and Gaurivīta—meaning like Gaurivīta, like Saṃkṛti, and like Śukti."

Since the three-lineage (tryārṣeya) status of Upamanyu and others is already established by their prescription later on, the statement "except for Upamanyu, Parāśara, and Kauṇḍinya" is solely for the purpose of demonstrating that those other than the Vasiṣṭhas—such as the Saṃkṛtis and so forth—are not included, because they are *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas* (belonging to two lineages). In the *pravara* "Vāsiṣṭha-maitrāvaruṇa-kauṇḍinya," one should understand Mitrāvaruṇa to refer to two specific seers (*ṛṣi*) who were the seers of mantras, and not to the well-known deities.

This is because of the prohibition: "One should not choose a lineage of seers [from among] gods or humans. Furthermore, in this context, the status of being a seer (ṛṣi) should be understood as belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa only when they are joined together, not individually; for there is a prohibition against choosing four, stating, "One should not choose four."

In the *Matsya Purāṇa*, it is observed that while Mitra and Varuṇa were performing austerities at the hermitage of Badarī, Urvaśī arrived; upon seeing her, their semen was discharged and caught in a water-filled jar, from which Vasiṣṭha was born, and from Vasiṣṭha, Kuṇḍina was born. Therefore, it should be understood that both together constitute the status of seer (*ṛṣi*) and father (*pitṛ*). Among these descendants of Vasiṣṭha (*Vāsiṣṭhas*), there is no intermarriage because they share the same *gotra* and the same *pravara*. As for the status of Vasiṣṭha-hood among the *Dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas* such as the Saṃkṛtis and others, it is due to their inclusion within the Vasiṣṭha group and because they were chosen by Śakti, who was himself a Vasiṣṭha.

Thus ends the section on the *pravara* of the Vasiṣṭha *gotra*. Now follows the section on the *pravara* of the Agastya *gotra*. [Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "Now, for the Agastis, the Hotṛ recites 'Āgastya' as the single *ṛṣi*, and the Adhvaryu says 'Agastivat. However, some prescribe a three-*ṛṣi* *pravara*: 'Āgastya-dārḍhacyuta-idhmavāha,' meaning 'Idhmavāhavat, Dṛḍhacyutavat, and Agastivat.'"
There is no intermarriage among all the Agastis with one another, because they share the same *gotra* and the same *pravara*.
Thus ends the section on the *gotras* and *pravaras* of the Agastis. Now begins the section on the *pravaras* of the Kṣatriyas.

[In this regard, the Sūtra states: "Now, for Kṣatriyas, there is a three-ṛṣi lineage: Mānava, Aiḍa, Paurūravasa—that is, like Purūravas, like Iḍā, and like Manu. Now, if they should choose their own ancestral seers (*sārṣa*), they have only one single *pravara*. But if they should choose separately, those whose [ancestors] are not the authors of the mantras would have the *pravara* of their domestic chaplain (*purohita*), whereas those who do have such [mantra-authors] would have the *pravara* of those [authors] rather than that of the chaplain. According to this rule, the Vaiśyas have a single-ṛṣi lineage: 'Vātsapra' for the Hotṛ, and 'Vatsapravat' for the Adhvaryu."

Kṣatriyas are of two kinds: those who follow the *ṛṣis* (*ārṣas*) and those who do not (*anārṣas*). In that regard, if kings who follow the *ṛṣis*—that is, those who possess ancestral *ṛṣi*-lineages (*ārṣeyas*)—should choose their own *pravara*, then for them there is said to be only one [such] *pravara*. If these [kings] should choose separately, they must choose the *pravara* of their domestic priest (*purohita*). Those kings for whom there are no ancestral *ṛṣis*—meaning no *ṛṣis* who are the authors of the mantras—should be known as having the *pravara* of their domestic priest. Conversely, those kings for whom there are authors of mantras [as their ancestral *ṛṣis*] should be known as having no *pravara* of a domestic priest.

Kings who are performers of mantras, together with their preeminent family priests (*purohita*), exist in this manner according to *nyāya* (logical principle), and not otherwise. What is this intended *nyāya*? It is said: because a family priest exists for all [of them], and because there is no entitlement to perform rituals without him—given the etymological derivation of the word *purohita* as "one who leads (*nayati*) all this that is beneficial (*hitam*) before (*puraḥ*) him"—there would follow the consequence of non-marriage among them, since they would all share the same ancestral lineage (*pravaras*) under the view that the *pravara* belongs to one's own [lineage]. This is the *nyāya*.

This same principle should be understood to apply to Vaiśyas as well. (The resulting meaning is that for all kings who are authors of mantras, even those whose ancestral lineages (*pravara*) do not include a domestic priest (*purohita*), there is *purohita-pravara* status in marriage alone. For Brāhmaṇas bestowed upon or given to kings, their *pravara* is that of the kings; likewise, for kings bestowed upon or given to Brāhmaṇas, their *pravara* is that of the Brāhmaṇas. And so says the Sūtra:
"Likewise for Brāhmaṇas bestowed by kings, or for kings bestowed by Brāhmaṇas."
Now follows the section on the *gotra* and *pravara* for those whose lineage is unknown.

Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "Now, for one whose lineage is unknown, [the pravara is determined] by the *pravara* of the family priest (*purohita*) or by the *pravara* of the teacher (*ācārya*)."

"No; he by whom a kinsman (*bandhu*) has not been correctly known is one whose kinsman is unknown (*anājñātabandhu*); [the reading] for such a person whose kinsman is unknown is *asaṃprajñātabandhoḥ*. This is the reading of the sūtra prescribing the *pravara* (ancestral invocation) found within the section on the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. Its grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) is: 'he by whom a kinsman has not been correctly cognized (*saṃprajñāta*) is one whose kinsman is uncognized (*asaṃprajñātabandhu*)'; the meaning, however, is the same. For that aforementioned domestic priest (*purohita*), the *pravaraṇa* (the act of choosing) is by means of the *pravara* of the teacher who is the instructor of dharma, or by means of the *pravara* of that [teacher].
Now, [it is objected]: 'He who, being one [person], chooses the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*) of another...'"

If it is objected: "Since the prohibition—'He indeed appropriates for himself that seer’s [portion], whether it be the desired or the discarded'—is still in force, how can there be the selection (*pravaraṇa*) of the *pravara* of the domestic priest (*purohita*) or the teacher (*ācārya*)? We reply: No, because this [prohibition] operates only when there is actual knowledge of the *pravara*.
It shows that the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*) belongs to all castes (*sārvavarṇika*).

"Now, the Tāṇḍins prescribe a single ancestral seer for all castes: 'Mānava' as the Hotṛ, and 'Manuvad' as the Adhvaryu; for [the people] are descendants of Manu—so says the Brāhmaṇa, so says the Brāhmaṇa."

The Tāṇḍin teachers prescribe a single *ṛṣi* lineage (*ekārṣeya*) consisting of the form "Mānava" as a *pravara* common to all castes—namely, all classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—and they cite the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) that serves as the reason for this: "For offspring are of Manu, so says the Brāhmaṇa. The meaning is: because such a Brāhmaṇa is explicitly recited in the Taittirīya branch (*śākhā*) within the section on the fire-pan (*ukhā*) in the context of the fire-altar piling (*agnicayana*), stating, "For offspring are of Manu," therefore [this is the case].

The repetition is for the purpose of indicating the conclusion of the inquiry. This sūtra does not intend to prohibit the *pravara* of the most eminent Vaiśeṣikas; rather, it is intended as a praise of the *pravara* common to all castes (*sārvavarṇika*).

If it is argued that this contradicts the sūtra which states, "Having thus prohibited the entire [list] for some, Manu enjoins [the following]," we say no. For here, by the word "prohibition" (pratiṣedha), only lack of excellence (aprāśastya) is expressed. Thus, when the lack of excellence of all the specific *pravara* lineages has been stated, the excellence of the *sārvavarṇika* [lineage] is established by implication: "The specific *pravara* lineages are difficult to discern and are obtained only with great effort; therefore, they should not be performed."

However, because this [latter] is obtained with less effort, it should be performed; thus is the excellence of the *pravara* common to all castes established. If it is asked, "How is this intention understood?"—it is because otherwise there would be the consequence of not commencing the chapter on *pravara*, yet this chapter is indeed commenced. Furthermore, this *pravara* applies only to Vedic rites such as the selection of priests (*varaṇa*) and salutation (*abhivāda*), and not to marriage; for otherwise, there would be the consequence of the impossibility of marriage due to having a common *pravara*.
Regarding the ignorance of the *gotra* and *pravara* of one's domestic priest (*purohita*) or the *gotra* and *pravara* of one's teacher (*ācārya*), however, another *Smṛti* states:

"But a twice-born man who is ignorant of his teacher’s lineage and *pravara* may, having offered himself to someone, come to have that person's lineage and *pravara*. Here, the mention of the "teacher" (*ācārya*) is an elliptical reference to the family priest (*purohita*). Since it is heard in scripture that the word "teacher" refers to the twice-born who performs rites such as the *niṣeka*, this rule applies to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.

As for the statement— "But when one's lineage (gotra) is unknown, the Kāśyapa lineage is prescribed"— this refers to matters other than marriage, provided that the lineages of both the family priest and the preceptor are indeed unknown.
This concludes the determination of the *pravara* as stated in the Sūtra.
Now, according to the Smṛti, the Pravaras and their respective groups are as follows.

Among them, the Bhṛgus are of two kinds: the Jāmadagnyas and the Kevalas. The Jāmadagnyas are of two types: the Vatsas and the Bidās. The Kevalas are six: the Vatsas, the Vainyas, the Vītahavyas, the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, the Vāghryaśvas, and the Gārtsamadās. Therein, both types of Vatsas are mentioned by means of the same [pravaras].

The Mārkaṇḍeyas, the Māṇḍūkeyas, the Māṇḍavyas, the Kāṃseyas, the Ālekhanas, the Dārbhāyaṇas, the Śārkarākṣyas, the Daivatāyanas, the Śaunakāyanas, the Mādhukeyas, the Pārṣikas, the Sākās, the Prāttāyanas, the Pailas, the Paiṅgalāyanas, the Dārdhvepakas, the Bāhyakas, the Vaiśvānarayas, the Vaihīnarayas, the Vairohitās, the Bāhyas, the Brādhras, the Goṣṭhāyanas, the Aṣṭīkayas, the Kāśakṛtsnas, the Vādbhutakas, the Kṛtabhāgas, the Aitiśāyanas, the Jñānāyanas, the Pāṇinayas, Vālmīki, the Sthaulapiṇḍāyanas, and the Saivātavas.

The Jihītayas, Sāvarṇikāyanas, Vālāyanas, Saukṛtayas, Maṇḍavas, Sauvipvayas, Hastāgrahas, Śauddhakayas, Śaurdvakayas, Vaikarṇas, Droṇakajihvayas, Aurasayas, Kambalodarayas, Vākārakṛtas, Vaihalayas, Sāṅkavas, Kāstambaras, Kāravāstāmasas, Virūpākṣas, Vṛkāśvas, Uccairmanyus, Dvaimatyas, Āryāyaṇas, Pākāyaṇas, Kāhvāyanas, Vānayas, Cāyaninas, Śārṅgaravas, Cāndramasas, Gāṅgeyas, Naudheyas, and Yājñiyas.
The Jābālis, Bāhumitrāyaṇas, Āpiśalayas, Vaiśvapurayas, Lohitāyanas, Uṣṭrākṣas, Mālāyanas, Śāradvatāyanas, Rajatavāhas, Vatsas, and Vātsāyanas—
these many are mentioned by Baudhāyana. Now follow those mentioned by Kātyāyana and Laugākṣi.

The Nālāyanas, Vāgāyanas, Anumātakayas, Jaihmatayas, Jīvantayas, Kāmbalodarayas, Vaihāyanas, Rekhāyanayas, Pārṣatayas, Pārṇilayas, Uccayamānas, Sātyakarṇayas, Kālākayas, Tālakeśins, Ṛtabhāgas, Ārtabhāgas, Ājīhitās, Ātithayas, Sthaumāṅgirayas, Sthaulās, Sauravas, Barhiṣas, Devamatayas, Gārgyāyaṇas, Gehyāyanas, Goṣṭhāyanas, Vaiśampāyanas, Gālavas, Sāṃkṛtayas, Vāṇakeyas, Aitikāyanas, Bhrāṣṭreyas, and Bhāstreyas.

The Lākṣeyas, the Lākucayas, the Lālāṭayas, the Āvayas, the Āṅgāvayas, the Saiṣpikayas, the Sātyakāyanas, the Naikarṣayas, the Śākalyas, the Pākānumatayas, the Kaniṣṇayas, the Jaihmāśinayas, the Āśmakramas, the Kaucahastayas, the Ānulomins, the Krauñcas, the Ikṣas, the Krauñcākṣayas, the Sauradhvajayas, the Vādhyātkeyas, the Nirīṇayas, the Vāsayas, the Sādanās, the Syoyas, the Syandanayas, the Kaṭeraṇayas, the Laveraṇayas, the Yaugolayas, the Mādhyodās, the Mātsyas, the Nāḍāyanas, the Vairāyaṇas, the Vainyas, and the Rauhityāyani.

Kṛpānīlu, Sāvarṇi, Pikasvara, Viṣṇu, Taulakeśi, Jahini, Vītina, Phenayāstalin, Śikhāpati, Jaladhi, Senājit, Kṛtsna, Paiṅgalāyani, Divaḥpati, Ṛṣabha, Suta, Palata, Palava, Kopiyajña, Mitrayajña, Āmilāyana, Hāpati, Vaikarṇini, Bhāllakāyani, Lākṣmaṇa, Śālyāyani, Mālyāyani, Kauṭali, Saukti, Koṭara, Sākṣin, Sāndramaṇi, Naikajihva, Jihvāśūnya, Kelaleṭi, and Hikaśvari.

Sāradhvaji, Naimiśya, Loṣṭākṣi, Garaveṇi, Paurṇasaigandhi, Kāśakṛdvilabhṛt, Saumadāyana, Svānumati, Maṇḍacitra, Śaukrāyaṇa, Tvāṣṭreya, Kovahuṇḍya, Śaunāyana, Śākapauṇi, Vrīhimati, Māyāmati, Rādhrevaki, Kośana, Maudgalya, Kāravaca, Sāṃtapanāyana, Gehri, Bhehri, Kiruṣa, Stanvata, Aulandhi, Vāyargirāyaṇi, Śyenayāgati, N aikaṭyi, Śaukakarṇi, and Niḍāyana— these are the Vatsas.
Among them, those Vatsas who are Jāmadagnyas have five *pravaras*: Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jāmadagnya; or three: Bhārgava, Aurva, and Jāmadagnya.
Those Vatsas, however, who are not Jāmadagnyas have three: Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, and Āpnavāna.
Now, the Bidas who are Jāmadagnyas...

The Bidās: Śailas, Avaṭas, Prācīnayogyas, Abhayadānas, Kāṇḍarathas, Vainabhṛtas, Pulastya, Ārkāyaṇa, Nāṣṭrāyaṇa, Tāmrāyaṇa, Krauñcāyaṇa, Kāmala, Paulastya, Vedabhṛt, Abhayajāta, Atrikāyanas, Bhrājas, Bhrādantyas, Ṣṭaikāyanas, and Bhṛñjāyanas. These are the Bidās. Their five *pravaras* are: Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Vaideti. Or there are three: Bhārgava, Aurva, and Jāmadagnya.

Kātyāyana states that for those who do not know the lineage of Jamadagni, there are three: Bhārgava, Aurva, and Jāmadagnya. He has also stated that for the Vatsas, there are likewise three: Bhārgava, Cyāvana, and Āpnavāna. Among the five-lineage Bides, the name of Jamadagni continues by virtue of his existence.
Now, as for the Vainyas: the Vainyas, Pārthas, Bāṣkalas, and Śaitas.
Thus [are] the Vainya lineages;
some say they are the Śyaitas. Among them, there are three: Bhārgava, Vainya, and Pārtha.
Now, the Vītahavyas.

The Vītahavyas, the Yāskas, the Maunas, the Maukas, the Vādhulas, the Varṣapuṣpas, the Bhāgalepas, the Bhāgavijñeyas, the Durdinas, the Bhāskaras, the Daivajāyanas, the Vārkaleyas, the Mādhyameyas, the Vāsayas, the Kauśāmbeyas, the Krovilyas, the Satyakayas, the Citrasenas, the Bhāguris, the Chapas, the Mādhūlas, the Mausalas, the Jīvantāyanas, the Ardhalekhas, the Vṛkāśmakas, the Madokadhvas, the Vāreyas, the Gairikṣitas, the Dairghacittas, the Pañcālavas, the Pauṣpāvatas, the Godāyanas, the Caṇḍamodanas, the Bhāgalis, the Bhāgavittis, and the Pilis.

Khali, Kāśyapi, Samada, Gapi, Sauri, Jvaribhāgāntapa, Sānusvaya, Mādāyanas, Śālaṅkāyanas, Tārkas, Prāvareyas, Śārkarākṣi, Kauṭilya, Vilebhi, Vāhviya, Hāleya, and Dīrghacittas—these are the Vītahavyas;
some say they are the Yaskas. For these, the three [gotras] are Bhārgava, Vaitahavya, and Sāvedasa.
Now, the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas:

the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, the Nairṛthayas, the Grāmyāyaṇas, the Kārṇāyanas, the Cāndrāyaṇas, the Pauṭakalāyanas, the Siddhas, the Sumanāyanas, the Gaurābhis, the Mṛṭvaṅgīyas, the Mārgapathas, the Naikarṣis, the Āṣastambis, the Vālmais, the Kārdamāyanis, the Gārlabhis, the Anūpas, the Vadāyanis, the Kavins, and the Āśvabhins.
These are the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas.

Their five *pravara*s are Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnavāna, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and Anūpa; or three: Bhārgava, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and Anūpa. Some, relying on the continued presence of Jamadagni within these [lineages], claim they possess the status of *Jāmadagnya*; however, this contradicts the *Smṛtyarthasāra* and other authorities. Furthermore, their practice of the five-fold portioning (*pañcāvattitā*) is based on scriptural injunction even though they are not *Jāmadagnya*. This is because Baudhāyana, after stating, "The Vatsas, the Bidās, and the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas," says, "These are those who take five portions.
There is no marriage between the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas and the Vatsas or Bidās due to the partial identity of their three *pravara*s.

For the Vātsyas, there are three: Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, and Āpnavāna. For the Vatsas and Purodhasas, there are five: Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Vātsa, and Paurodhasa. For the Vaijavanas and Mathitas, there are five: Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Vaijavana, and Māthita. These also [occur] in some cases. Among these, there is no marriage between one another or with those previously mentioned, due to the identity of their *pravara* lineages. Now, the Vādhryaśvas:

The Vāghryaśvas, Reiṣṭhyānas, Sāpiṇḍinas, Surabhineyas, Mālyas, Mahāvālyas, Tārkṣyāyaṇas, Kaitavāyanas, Khālāyanas, Śākaṭāyanas, Maitreyas, Sācaryas, Drauṇāyanas, Raukthāyanas, Apiśalas, Āṭikāyanas, Haṃsajihvas, Raupyāyaṇas, Sātyaṇḍinas, Piṇḍikākṣas, Maudāyanas, Kāpiśāyanas, Śāḍeyas, Sākṣitas, Mitrayatas, Āpiśāyanas, Pāṭikāyanas, Mitrayus, and Divodāsas— these are the Vāghryaśvas.
Some say [the lineage] is *mitrayu*; others say *divodāsa*. One of these is *vāghryaśva*. Or there are three: *bhārgava-vāghryaśva-daivodāsa*.

For the Gārtsamadas, *gārtsamada* is the single *pravara*. Among the Vainya, Vītahavya, Vāghryaśva, and Gārtsamadas, marriage occurs with one another and with those mentioned previously, even while setting aside their own respective groups, because there is no identity in two or three *pravaras*.
Thus it is stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:
"The Yaskas, the Mitrayus, the Vainyas, and the Śunakas— because they share a single *pravara*— should all,
having set aside their respective groups, marry one another."

In this context, the statement that the Yaskas, Mitrayus, and Śunakas constitute a single group is intended to refer to one specific branch. The connection is that they abandon their own sub-group due to the identity of their *pravara* (ancestral lineage).
