This is the group of five. Regarding strength, however, the *Laghujātaka* states: "A sign that is joined with or aspected by its own lord, and also observed by Mercury and Jupiter, becomes strong when it is likewise joined with or aspected by the remaining planets."
Now, the purification regarding the eclipses of the moon and sun, as well as the purification pertaining to earthquakes and other portents, is examined in detail.

In that regard, when [the sun or moon] is eclipsed at sunset, three days prior to the eclipse must be avoided; however, when it is eclipsed at sunrise, three days after the eclipse must be avoided. Even in the absence of an eclipse at sunset or sunrise, if there is a partial eclipse (khaṇḍagrāsa) of the moon or sun, six days in total must be avoided—three days before and three days after—at each respective location.
Regarding this very subject, in the case of a total eclipse (saṃpūrṇagrāsa), fourteen days in total are to be avoided—seven days prior and seven days after.
Thus, Bṛhaspati states in the Jyotiḥsaṃgraha: "In the case of a solar eclipse, three days before [the eclipse] and likewise three days after a total eclipse."
"In the case of a partial eclipse, it lasts for three days; when it is total, for seven days each.
Thus, "three days" is the meaning.
Likewise, Kaśyapa says:
"In the case of a solar eclipse (grasta-udaya), the fault is greater; in the case of a lunar eclipse (grasta-asta), it occurs before [midnight].
But during the halves of day and night, both occur according to the distinction between the partial and total phases.

By the phrase "during the halves of day and night," it is indicated that because a solar or lunar eclipse cannot possibly occur as either a "total setting" (grasta-asta) or a "total rising" (grasta-udaya) within the daytime or nighttime segments respectively, those two cases are excluded. Regarding the phrase "both of those," etc.:

The meaning to be understood is as follows: in the case of a partial eclipse (*khaṇḍagrāsa*), there is a defect for three days before and three days after at each location; however, in the case of a total eclipse (*sampūrṇagrāsa*), there is a defect for seven days before and seven days after. Both of these cases are indicated here, because this is consistent with the statement of Bṛhaspati: "During lunar and solar eclipses, one should avoid auspicious activities for three days prior [to the eclipse]."

Regarding the statement, "The impurity (*sūtaka*) resulting from an eclipse is remembered as inauspicious for seven days thereafter," it should be understood that the previously mentioned avoidance of auspicious acts for three days applies to cases of distress (*saṃkaṭa*) and to total eclipses (*sarvagrāsa*), because seven nights are specified in the subsequent portion. Regarding the capacity [of the performer], the first half [of the verse] concerns partial eclipses (*khaṇḍagrāsa*), while the latter half concerns full eclipses (*pūrṇagrāsa*) within that same context. In the reading "one should abandon the inauspiciousness for three days prior," it means that there is inauspiciousness for three days beforehand, and one should avoid performing rites during those three inauspicious days.

When there is an expectancy as to what [should be avoided], the word "auspicious" (*śubham*) is to be understood as the remainder by virtue of contextual fitness (*yogyatā*). However, in the reading "one should abandon the auspicious for three days beforehand" (*tryahaṃ prāktu śubhaṃ tyajet*), it should be understood that the subsequent word "inauspicious" (*aśubha*) also connects with "for three days," while the word "auspicious" remains [as it was].
And in this regard, King Bhoja states the limit of the days according to the difference in rites and the difference in capacities:
"In the case of an undesirable omen, a threefold portent, or at the sight of Rāhu (the son of Siṃhikā)..."
For seven nights, one should not perform auspicious ceremonies such as journeys or marriages.
"One should avoid marriage during an eclipse for one night;
however, during a journey for seven nights, and during the tying of the sacred thread (vratibandhana) for three nights."
"Threefold" means celestial, terrestrial, and atmospheric. Furthermore, this prohibition of seven nights regarding portents and the like pertains specifically to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
Thus says Bhṛgu:

"Bhṛgu has declared that for all undertakings, [the period of impurity] is seven days for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, three days for a Brāhmaṇa, and half a day for a Śūdra, beginning with [an event such as] a tremor."

Because of the mention of "the undesirable," [the restriction] applies for seven nights in the case of an auspicious portent, but only for one night there, according to the statement: "The day marred by an auspicious portent [is to be avoided]. In that regard, an auspicious portent is as described in the *Varāhasaṃhitā*:
"Fierce thunderbolts, earthquakes, twilight portents, atmospheric roars, halos, dust, smoke, and the rising or setting of the sun appearing blood-red."

"In the month of Madhu-Mādhava (Vaiśākha), the emergence of sap, oil, honey, flowers, and fruits from the trees, as well as the increase of intoxication in cows and birds, portends auspiciousness," and so forth.

Regarding *graha*, it refers to an eclipse of the moon or sun. In this context, it should be understood that for a total eclipse (*sarvagrāsa*), the period of avoidance is seven nights, as this pertains to times of great difficulty.
Furthermore, Aṅgiras states the days to be avoided according to the type of eclipse:
"In the case of a total eclipse, however, [avoid] seven days; in the case of a partial eclipse (*ardhagrāsa*), three days."
"One should avoid [eating] for one day when the eclipse is three, two, or one digit.
Vasiṣṭha, however, says:
"In all matters, one should avoid [the period] for eight days during a total eclipse."
In the case of a half-eclipse with one-third subtracted, it lasts for six days; in the case of a half-eclipse, it lasts for four days.

"In the fourth quarter [of the eclipse], it shall be for three nights during an eclipse of the moon or the sun. However, when a task is mandatory, the days and muhūrtas to be avoided in places defiled by Rāhu are stated in the *Jyotirnibandha* according to various opinions of the sages: "Vasiṣṭha says five days, Garga says three days, and Kauśika says one day."
"Rāhu vitiates five *muhūrtas* of the *muhūrta* belonging to the Yavana teacher.
Regarding this, King Bhoja states that when there is a conjunction of planetary phenomena such as earthquakes and the like, additional days are to be avoided:
"During a planetary conjunction of the sun and moon, an earthquake, or defects such as the rising of a comet (*ketu*) or the falling of a meteor (*ulkā*)," etc.
"Those who know the subject say ten days for a vow; some say thirteen days.

Here, "vow" is an elliptical expression for marriage and other such rites. In this context, it should be understood that when many portents such as earthquakes occur at the time of a planetary eclipse, the period of impurity is thirteen days, whereas when there is a small number of such occurrences, it is ten days.
Garga says:
One should avoid [the use of] fire for one day during a lightning strike, for seven days during a planetary eclipse,
and for three days when an earthquake has occurred.
"In the case of a falling meteor, one should avoid all activities for three days; in the case of smoke [from a comet], for five days;
and in the case of a thunderbolt strike, for one day."

In this context, by the statement "there is a threefold portent in an undesirable [situation]," seven days have been prescribed. However, Garga has stated that for the portents of a burning horizon and a thunderbolt strike, only one day is to be avoided. Where there is a discrepancy due to differing opinions regarding what is less or more [in duration], that contradiction should be resolved by considering whether those respective rites are dependent or independent [of other factors]. Thus says the *Rājamārtaṇḍa*:
"Those things which are prescribed, prohibited, and then again permitted—whether they are dependent or independent—should be investigated here by the learned."

The meaning of this is as follows: those very rites which were stated according to the general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*) as being to be performed at that specific time, are prohibited by a particular prohibitive rule (*niṣedhavidhi*) with respect to the determination of the time and so forth. Yet, once again, those same rites are presented as being to be performed when they are possible within a time duration shorter than that specific time. Regarding the phrase "dependent" (*sāpekṣa*) and so on: the meaning is that they are either dependent or independent—that is, characterized by a dependence on another time or devoid of such dependence on another time.

And here, "expectancy" (*apekṣā*) consists in the determination of the fitness for performance at another time. That [determination] too is dependent upon its own capacity (*sāmarthya*). Furthermore, in this context, capacity is ultimately reduced to one of two forms: either the presence of a collection of causal factors (*sāmagrī*) suitable for the employment of those respective actions at another time, or the absence of the occurrence of a powerful obstacle.

The term *mīmāṃsyāni* means "to be deliberated upon," that is to say, they are to be investigated by way of determining whether they possess the fitness for performance at a later time—which constitutes dependence—or whether they lack such dependence, being of the nature of an absence [of that fitness]. Thus, if the knowledge of the duties to be performed is understood as dependent, then their performance should take place on another day that is not prohibited, provided it has a wider scope; if, however, they are known to be independent, then the performance should take place on another day that is not prohibited, provided it has a narrower scope. Furthermore, the intended meaning is that the performance must be carried out even within the midst of what is prohibited for the more extensive period. To illustrate:

"In the northern solstice (udagayana), during the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion (nakṣatra), the rites of tonsure (caula), initiation (upanayana), the cutting of the beard (godāna), and marriage [should be performed].

Regarding such rites as initiation prescribed in the *Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* and other texts, which are ordained according to rule for any day within the northern solstice—even if one of the three types of portents occurs on that day—once such a general prohibition has been established by the previously cited statement, "In the case of an undesirable portent of the three kinds, or at the sight of Rāhu (Siṃhikāsūnu)... which prescribes a seven-day suspension from those respective rites, the Sage [Garga] further states in another verse, "Having omitted one night... and so forth.

By means of the prohibition of one or three nights for marriage and the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), permission is granted for days exceeding one night—even those occurring within a seven-day period—precisely through the consideration of whether the two events are dependent upon or independent of one another. This principle should be inferred in other cases as well; such is the direction.
Regarding this exception, the *Adbhutasāgara* states:
"Now, if the water becomes clear within three days..."
"The teachers declare that the pacification of the fault of portents brings auspiciousness at that very moment.
And in the *Saṃbandhatattva*: "There is no fault in earthquakes and the like once the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* has been performed."
Regarding the avoidance of the eight days of Holikā during marriages and other ceremonies due to regional differences, it is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"In the lands along the banks of the Irāvatī, the Vipāśā, and the Śatadru,
as well as in the region of Tripuṣkara, one should avoid [these days] for marriages and other such rites."
"A wise person, for the sake of auspiciousness, [should avoid] the eight days prior to Holikā.

The rivers such as the Irāvatī and others are well-known in the western region. Holikā refers to the full moon day of the month of Phālguna; the meaning is that one should avoid the eight days preceding it.
Likewise, there is also a verse found in a modern work:
"On the banks of the Vipāśā, Irāvatī, and Śatadrū, as well as at Tripuṣkara,
auspicious rites such as marriage are not desired during the eight days preceding Holi," according to the *Jyotirnibandha*.
"One should by no means perform the tonsure ceremony, the vows, marriage, and so forth, nor the commencement or entry into a new house, while Janārdana is asleep."
(From the *Kālāmṛtasaṃgraha*:

"Among years, the year of depletion (*kṣayavatsara*) does not bring auspiciousness; likewise, at the junction of years, the lunar fortnight, five days at the junction of two months, two days at the junction of two [lunar] days, and the junctions of two asterisms or two yogas [are inauspicious]."

Half a *yāma* is two *ghaṭikās*; for the two *karaṇas*, it is two *nāḍikās* in two *lagnas*; at the twilight (*saṃdhyā*), it is three *ghaṭikās*; however, two *ghaṭikās* are to be avoided at the junction of night.
Regarding the acceptability of the *Amṛtasiddhi-yoga* in all cases such as marriages and so forth, a certain prohibition is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"In marriage, Jupiter and Puṣya [are auspicious]; in departure, Saturn and Rohiṇī;
and in entry, Mars and Aśvinī; death is certain within six months."
In the *Jyotiṣprakāśa*:
"The sixteen nāḍīs preceding the saṃkrānti are merit-bestowing;
those following it should be avoided for such rites as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), vows (*vrata*), journeys (*yātrā*), and marriages."
Here, by the word *vrata* (vow), the Vedic vow (*vedavrata*) is meant; by the word *ādi* (and so forth), all auspicious actions are included. Nārada says:
"One, five, nine, two, six, ten, three, and seven."
The Vedas (4), Vasus (8), Śivas (11), Ādityas (12), and the Moon (1) [are the measures] in their respective order.
One should avoid the *ghātacandra* (the moon in its period of destruction) during journeys, military operations, marriages, all auspicious ceremonies, tonsure rites, and the initiation of vows.
"Pārāśara has declared that a *ghātacandra* (a moon in its waning phase) is not to be considered at all.
Now, the various types of marriage are described in detail. Regarding this, here is the *Dharmasūtra*:

"Having ascertained the kinship, character, learning, and health [of the groom], one should bestow the daughter upon him for the sake of shared duties in the *brāhma* marriage; in the *ārṣa* marriage, one should give her after adorning her according to one's ability; in the *daiva* marriage, one should present her to the officiating priest during the course of a sacrifice; in the *gāndharva* marriage, she should unite with him through mutual desire; in the *āsura* marriage, they should take her away after giving goods according to their means; in the *rākṣasa* marriage, they should take her away after overpowering the father. Thus it is said.

The *brāhma* [form of marriage] is that which is created by Brahmā. In that marriage, having learned of and examined the bridegroom’s relatives and others, one should bestow the daughter—the *prajā*—upon him for the sake of *sahatvakarmāṇi*, that is, for those duties (*karmāṇi*) which are to be performed together. The word *śaktivipayeṇa* is a particle resembling a case ending; it should be understood as having the meaning of "according to one's ability" (*yathāśakti*). Having adorned her according to one's ability, one should give her away: this is the *brāhma* marriage.
In the reading *prajāsahatvakarmabhyaḥ*, the meaning is "for the sake of offspring (*prajā*) and for the sake of duties to be performed together (*sahatvakarma*)."
In the marriage seen by the sages (*ārṣa*), a pair of cattle—a cow and a bull—should be given to the one who receives the daughter; this is the *ārṣa* marriage.

In the marriage seen by the gods (*daiva*), when the sacrificial ritual has been spread out, one should give the maiden to the officiating priest as he performs his duties; this is the *daiva* marriage.

In that case where the maiden and the groom unite with each other in secret out of desire and passion, becoming a couple, that is the *gāndharva* marriage (the word *sāṃvarteta* contains a long vowel for metrical reasons). In this instance, after their union, the sacramental rite of marriage must be performed.

In a marriage where one carries off a maiden after giving away wealth according to one's ability, that is the Āsura marriage. A marriage through the gift of a house, field, or similar property to the maiden is not Āsura. Where they carry her off by force, that is the Rākṣasa marriage;
as Āśvalāyana states: "Having killed and split open heads, he should take her while she is weeping from those who are weeping—that is the Rākṣasa."
Here too, there is the marriage sacrament (*vivāha-saṃskāra*). Furthermore, two other types of marriage are mentioned in other scriptures.
Regarding this, Āśvalāyana states:
"‘Practice dharma together’—this is the Prājāpatya [marriage] among those who have fallen asleep."
"Or that *piśāca* [form of marriage] might carry off those who are negligent.

Regarding this, the author of the *Ujjvalā* commentary has explained that these two are not mentioned separately here because they are included within the *brāhma* and *rākṣasa* forms. From the words "bandhuśīla" up to "pratipādayet," [the procedure] is mandatory for the *brāhma*, *ārṣa*, and *daiva* marriages, but it is not mandatory for the *āsura* marriage, as that depends upon the will of the bridegroom. However, this does not apply to the other [remaining] forms, because in their absence of formal bestowal (*pratipādana*), there is also an absence of examination. In the phrase "having adorned her, he should give (*dadyāt*)," the verb *dadāti* (to give) has the sense of "bestowing" alone, since the term "pratipādayet" (he should bestow) was introduced previously.
For one who has a daughter, the gift of a pair of cattle occurs immediately after the marriage *homa*.
Thus says Baudhāyana:
"Having first offered the oblation of parched grain, one should give a pair of cattle to the one who possesses the girl."

Since the requirement is already established by the mere statement that "one should present [the fee] to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in a sacrifice for the gods," the inclusion of the term *tantra* implies—by its very natural force—that only the great *saumika* (Soma-related) ritual is intended here, and not the *naiṣṭhika* or *pāśuka* rites. Because of the expression "one should present" and because the presentation is made to "the officiating priest" as a single individual, this is not a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) connected to the *tantra*. Regarding the term "officiating priest," any person who is not of the same lineage (*asagotra*) or sapinda relation should be understood as the recipient.
Furthermore, this presentation occurs after the giving of the primary sacrificial fees.
Thus says Baudhāyana:
"When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are being led forth, one should give [them] to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) within the altar (*antarvedi*).
Regarding the acceptance [of these gifts], a specific mantra is stated by Baudhāyana:

"Now, if it has been given together with the sacrificial fees, one should accept it with the six verses beginning 'Prajāpati [bestowed her] upon the woman,' in accordance with their respective meters."

The statement that [the bride] is "given along with the sacrificial fees" (*dakṣiṇābhiḥ saha dattā*) is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the bestowal of the maiden does not constitute a sacrificial fee (*yāgadakṣiṇā*) for the sacrifice. Furthermore, this specific mantra for acceptance (*pratigrahamantra*) is not contradictory even for us [Smārtas]. Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the sūtra stating, "it shows [the giving of] Tantric sacrificial fees."

Since this specific mantra for acceptance—which was not recited by the Sūtrakāra in the section on the acceptance of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā)—cannot possibly be the subject of the sūtra stating "it shows the [acceptance] of Tantric fees," there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the prohibition "one who is initiated does not give" does not apply to the giving away of a maiden within the framework of a sacrifice, due to the force of the specific injunction. However, the formal bestowal must be performed according to the entire procedure prescribed for the gift of a maiden.

However, there is indeed a prohibition regarding the gift of gold and other items that constitute part of the formal giving away (*pratipādana*) of the girl, because such gifts are enjoined by the verb *dadāti* [to give]. (The recitation for the auspicious day, the choosing of the bridegroom, the verbal betrothal, and the honey-mixture offering are omitted. Regarding these six mantras, the seers (*ṛṣis*) are the Viśvedevas; the deities (*devatās*) are Prajāpati and others; the first five are *anuṣṭubh* meters; and "āpastatsatyamābharan" is in the *gāyatrī* meter. This is to be understood as their application (*viniyoga*) in the acceptance of the girl, along with their respective seers and so forth. Āśvalāyana, however, has mentioned eight varieties, and has also stated the specific fruits resulting from the first four.

Having adorned the maiden, he should give her away preceded by a water-libation; this is the Brāhma marriage. A son born of her purifies twelve descendants on both sides—twelve on the lower side and twelve on the upper. When the sacrificial rite has been spread out, he should give the maiden, having adorned her, to the officiating priest; that is the Daiva marriage. He purifies ten descendants on both sides—ten on the lower side and ten on the upper. "May you two perform your duty together"—this is the Prājāpatya marriage. He purifies eight descendants on both sides—eight on the lower side and eight on the upper. Having given a pair of cattle, he should marry her; that is the Ārṣa marriage. He purifies seven descendants on both sides—seven on the lower side and seven on the upper. [The form of marriage] based on a mutual agreement...

"Having performed [the rites], one should marry her; that is the Gāndharva form. Having gratified [the groom] with wealth, one should marry her; that is the Āsura form. One should carry her off while she is asleep or intoxicated; that is the Paiśāca form. Having killed and having shattered heads, one should carry off a weeping woman from those who are weeping; that is the Rākṣasa form. Among these, the first three are commendable. And it is said in the Dharmasūtra: "Of these, the first three are commendable as they are prescribed..."
"In this way, offspring born of such marriages become endowed with excellence.
Among these, each preceding one is superior, while each succeeding one is more inferior.
Āpastamba also says: "Each preceding one is more highly praised than the next."
The rule regarding marriage according to the sequence of castes is stated in another Smṛti:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, the first four [forms] are recommended; for a Kṣatriya, the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa; likewise for a Vaiśya, the Āsura; but for a Śūdra, the last one is censured."
The last is the Paiśāca [form of marriage]. It is censured; the meaning is that it is not praised by anyone.
Baudhāyana also states all of this:

There are eight forms of marriage: when one gives a girl to a student who has been tested for his learning and character, that is the *brāhma* form; when one says, "Let him perform his duty with her," after clothing and adorning her, that is the *prājāpatya* form; when one has first offered the oblation of parched grain and gives a pair of cattle to the groom, that is the *ārṣa* form; when she is led away as a fee within the sacrificial altar to the officiating priest, that is the *daiva* form; when there is a union between two who desire each other, that is the *gāndharva* form; when she is won over by wealth, that is the *āsura* form; and when she is carried off by force, that is the *rākṣasa* form; [and when she is taken] while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged...

Or he may marry her; such is the Paiśāca rite. Of these, four are for the Brāhmaṇa, and among those, each preceding one is better than the following. For the others, each succeeding one is worse. Here too, the sixth and seventh follow the duties of a Kṣatriya, because they depend upon him; for the fifth and eighth belong to the Vaiśya and Śūdra, since the Vaiśya and Śūdra are by nature unrestrained regarding their wives, being occupied with agriculture and service respectively. Some praise even the Gāndharva rite, because it follows from affection;
for it is known that "as the marriage is conducted, so do the offspring become."

"Because it depends on that" means because it is subject to that. "Those with unrestrained wives" means those whose wives are not restricted, that is to say, those who have taken wives in violation of the prescribed rules. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used in the sense of a reason. Vaiśyas are those authorized for cultivation; Śūdras are those authorized for service. That the Paiśāca form is the last [of the eight] is established by the statement of Manu.
Vatsa permits even the Paiśāca form for Brāhmaṇas and others when other forms of marriage are impossible:
"If a maiden cannot be won by any other means by a man..."
"She is to be wedded even by stealthy marriage, remaining in secret."
As for the statement: "The *ārṣa* [form] is also inferior to the *āsura*, because there is no difference in the fact that she has been purchased by means of a transaction.
For this very reason, Kaśyapa says: 'A woman who has been purchased by means of a transaction is not designated as a wife (*patnī*')."
"She is fit neither for rites to the gods nor for rites to the ancestors; the wise know her to be a slave."
Yama also says: "The fools who sell their daughters and those who commit sins in secret fall into a terrible hell, burning their lineage down to the seventh generation."
And this [prohibition] applies to the taking of wealth for one's own sake; however, there is no fault when it is for the sake of the girl. As Manu said:
"That among whom the kinsmen do not take a bride-price (*śulka*), that is not a sale."
"That is merely a fitting honor for young maidens, and nothing but an act of compassion."
Compassion is the state of being free from malice.
Manu says:
"The Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, and likewise the Āsura [forms of marriage]..."
The Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest."

Having thus stated the eight types [of marriage] and described their characteristics, he says— intending that among them the Ārṣa form is unrighteous because it involves being purchased through a bride-price—
"Of these five, however, three are declared here to be righteous and two unrighteous;
namely, the Paiśāca and the Āsura, which should never be performed."

"Among those beginning with the Brāhma and ending with the Āsura, three—the Brāhma, Daiva, and Prājāpatya—are righteous because they lack the purchase-price (*kraya*); the two, the Ārṣa and Āsura, are unrighteous because of the purchase-price involved in them; and even among these, the Āsura, like the Paiśāca, must not be performed even in times of distress.

This is not so, because the statement "of the five" is intended as an introduction of an alternative opinion. Why is this? Because later on, he himself restates the view of another school regarding the pair of cattle being the purchase-price for the Ārṣa rite and then refutes it:
"Some say that in the Ārṣa rite a pair of cattle is the purchase-price; that is indeed false."
"Whether small or great, it is accomplished by that very amount.

As for what some say—that a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*) is the *śulka* (bride-price)—that is indeed false. For it is not possible for that [pair] to be a *śulka*. *Śulka* and *mūlya* (price) are synonyms. Price is indeed the means of purchase, which may be small or great depending on place, time, and other factors. In the present case, however, the quantity is fixed. Therefore, that [rite] is accomplished by that very pair of cattle alone and not otherwise; thus, because there is an absence of buying and selling, the *ārṣa* rite is indeed righteous (*dharmya*). For this very reason, Devala says:
"The first four types of marriage, which involve the offering of water, are righteous;
they are free of bride-price, are worthy of Brahmins, and deliver both families."
Āpastamba states the lunar mansion for the Ārṣa marriage:

"Cows are taken under the Maghās. Because of the injunction that in the Ārṣa rite a pair of cattle must be given to the father of the daughter, the two cows being given by the bridegroom in the Ārṣa marriage are received by the father of the daughter under the Maghās. This is what is meant: one should perform the Ārṣa marriage only under the Maghās, and not under other lunar mansions as in the case of the Brāhma and other forms of marriage.

Regarding the statement, "She is led away under the two Phalgunīs," Sudarśana has explained that the bride is led away from her own home specifically under the two Phalgunīs, and not immediately at that moment as in the case of the *brāhma* and other forms of marriage, because of the specific scriptural injunction.
Regarding the prohibition against eating and so forth during an improper marriage (*durvivāha*), as well as the expiation for it, it is stated in the *Pārijāta*:
"Eating [food] at unrighteous marriages and giving approval [for them]..."
A twice-born man should avoid betel-leaf and riding vehicles by all means.
"In the case of the Āsura [form], there shall be a fast; in the Gāndharva, a three-night fast;
and likewise in the Rākṣasa and Paiśāca forms, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
The Determination of Adverse Conditions.

Now, regarding the determination of adverse conditions, it is stated in another Smṛti: "When the matter has been arranged and firmly settled for the sake of the bride and groom, even if [the preparations] have reached the house of the groom or the girl..."
"If some man or woman were to die, then indeed you would not perform such adornment."

"Formed" means the relationship is well-ascertained; "ascertained by speech" means it is finalized through the rite of the giving of the bride's word (*vāgdāna*). This is obtained from the excellent word [in the source]. In the *Jyotiḥsāgara*:
"If, after the verbal agreement has been made, both parents subsequently pass away..."
"For those two, it would be contrary [to their nature], but never for others."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states: "The father, mother, paternal uncle, or uterine brother of either the bridegroom or the bride—
if these should become adverse, it will bring about great obstacles."
The father, the paternal grandfather, the mother, the maternal grandmother,
the paternal uncle, the wife, the son, the brother, and the unmarried sister.
"When these very [factors] fail, it is considered adverse by the wise;
however, others have said that even when other [factors] fail, that [adversity] may not occur."
(From the use of the word *ca*, the great-grandfather [is included]; the second *ca* is for the purpose of including the great-grandmother.
Māṇḍavya says:
"If, after the betrothal, the mother, father, or brother passes away..."
"A marriage must not be performed at all by one who desires the welfare of his own lineage."

The phrase "with him" or "with her" is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. If the groom's side is unfavorable, one should not accept her for the sake of the groom; if the bride's side is unfavorable, one should not give her to that groom. The meaning is that the marriage should simply not be performed, and not that marriage itself should never be performed.
Regarding the course of action in such a crisis, Medhātithi says: "When, after the verbal betrothal, the death of someone in either family occurs..."
Then, after one year has passed, the marriage will bring auspicious results.
This remains unfavorable for one's own kinsmen up to the third generation;
likewise applies the entry and exit [of a bridegroom], as well as shaving and adorning.
"One should not perform rites for prosperity until the funeral rites have been completed;
thereafter, it becomes auspicious for a male in the fourth [generation], and in the fifth."
In the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*:
"In this world, the period of impurity for a father is one year, and half of that for a mother;
for a wife it is three months, and half of that for a brother and a son."
"But for other sapinda relatives, the period of impurity lasts for one month;
having performed a propitiatory rite (śāntika) at its conclusion, the auspicious moment (lagna) is then prescribed."

Regarding the reading "pitrorabdam ihāśaucam" (here, the impurity for both parents lasts one year), some maintain that the word *mātṛ* refers to the stepmother. According to this view, it is understood that the reading "pitrorabdam" is intended. Others hold that it applies to both; the intention here is that there is no distinction between them. In this latter view, the reading is simply "piturabdam" (one year for the father). Thus, the distinction is as follows: if the reading is "pitrorabdam," the mother’s [natural] impurity lasts one year and the stepmother’s half a year; if the reading is "piturabdam," both [the natural and stepmothers] have an impurity of only half a year.
In the *Jyotiṣprakāśa*: "Even when unfavorable conditions exist, the marriage must be performed with a month's interval."
"Having performed the rite of peace (śānti) and given a cow, one should again perform the verbal betrothal (vāgdāna) and so forth.
In another Smṛti:
"An auspicious moment (lagna) should not be fixed for three menstrual cycles while [the bride] is in a state of opposition."
"Some say that [the marriage] should be performed even during an adverse period when there is a great abundance [of auspicious factors].
However, one should avoid the marriage for one month following an adverse period involving a sapinda; only after that time is it prescribed for those two."

The essential meaning is that when the bride and groom have been definitively chosen, and a crisis arises—either because the bride cannot find a groom or the groom cannot find a bride—one should not look for another bride or another groom.
As stated in the *Jyotiḥsāgara*:
"In times of famine, during the collapse of a kingdom, or when the lives of one's parents are in danger..."
"Even in the case of a mature maiden, one does not wait for favorable circumstances.
Also elsewhere:
"For one overcome by a long illness, or for one residing in a distant land..."
Even for one who remains indifferent, no adversity exists;
yet when a crisis has arrived, the yogi Yājñavalkya declared this peace-mantra of Gaṇeśa— having performed it, one should engage in what is auspicious.
"He who, when a terrible obstacle has arisen, performs an auspicious rite without first performing a *śāntika* (pacification rite), meets with obstacles at every step.

Regarding this statement, some maintain that because "auspicious rite" is mentioned in general terms, even the initiation (*upanayana*) must be performed preceded by the pacification of Vināyaka. Others, however, argue that the term "auspicious rite" is restricted specifically to marriage; therefore, only marriage is to be preceded by the pacification rite, while the initiation is not so required. Still others hold that the initiation may indeed take place even without the pacification rite.
Vasiṣṭha says: "But when an adverse [planetary configuration] has arrived, one should by no means perform the marriage;
at the end, for the destruction of the defect, one should perform this auspicious pacification ritual."
In the *Smṛticandrikā*:
"If death occurs for a kinsman of the same lineage after a verbal betrothal has been made, then no auspicious rite should be performed; it will certainly bring widowhood upon the woman."
Elsewhere it is also said: "If the death of anyone in either family occurs after the giving of the word [of betrothal],
then the marriage must not be performed at all, because it brings about the destruction of one's own lineage."

In this context, although it is stated without qualification that "if anyone dies" or "someone dies," nevertheless—because the death of maternal grandmothers and others is not mentioned in some places as being a cause for the defect of inauspiciousness (as it is for paternal grandmothers and others), because the death of a married sister is not described as being of such a nature [as the death of an unmarried one], because Medhātithi’s statement mentions "one's own *gotra*-relatives" and the *Candrikā*’s statement mentions "the *gotra*-relative of the deceased"—this applies to the *sagotra-sapiṇḍas* of either the bride or the groom.

When a mortal within the three generations (tripuruṣa) has died, it should be understood as the fault of adverse relationship (*pratikūladoṣa*). A woman previously married by the groom refers to his first wife; her son is one born from her previously. This is an elliptical expression for her grandson as well. Likewise, the mention of the paternal uncle includes his son. Thus, starting from the groom, the three generations on the father’s side and the three generations on the bride’s side must be understood here, even when there is a division in the lineage starting from the common ancestor (*kūṭastha*).

The phrase "having waited for some time" implies that the marriage should not be performed at that time if the death of both the bride and bridegroom occurs in the same house; this is understood through such words as "it would be adverse for those two. The intention is that the defect arising from the simultaneous death of both is incurable, except by waiting for the proper time and performing propitiatory rites (*śānti*). For this very reason it is said, "but never for others. The intention is that for other *sapiṇḍas*, as well as for each of those two individually, the defect is indeed curable.

In the statement of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha, the declaration that the death of these four brings about great obstacles is intended to show that, in such cases, one must perform the propitiation of Vināyaka (Vināyaka-śānti), either accompanied by waiting for the auspicious time or alone. For this very reason, in the supplementary portion of that injunction, it is demonstrated that if the propitiation is not performed, there will be a great obstacle at every step. The intention behind the phrase "by these very ones who have met with disaster" is that this very death serves as the occasion for performing propitiatory rites such as the worship of Śrī, provided they are accompanied by waiting for the proper time.

For this very reason, the statement of Māṇḍavya—"it must not be performed immediately after the cause [of impurity]"—should be explained accordingly. The same applies to the statement of Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha.

Furthermore, the three alternatives regarding the period of waiting—namely, one year, three seasons, or merely a month—should be understood from other Smṛti texts in conjunction with the statement of Medhātithi. In the statement of Ratnāvalī, the word "impurity" (āśauca) should be understood as intending the mere disqualification from marriage caused by adverse circumstances.

In the absence of any adverse event caused by the death of anyone other than a *mahāguru*, one may perform the marriage even during the first year after death, provided that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and the monthly *śrāddhas* have been brought forward (*apakarṣa*). However, it should be understood that in the absence of an adverse event caused by the death of a *mahāguru*, if the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is brought forward for the sake of an auspicious occasion (*vṛddhi*), there is indeed no eligibility to perform rites for the gods or the ancestors (*daiva-pitrya*) until the end of the period.

In that regard, upon the death of the father, there are three options mentioned immediately above according to the degree of distress. Upon the death of the mother, there are two options: waiting for half a year or merely one month. Upon the death of a wife, there are [two] options: three months or merely one month. Upon the death of a brother or a son, there are likewise two options: half a month or merely one month. However, the settled rule is that upon the death of other *sapiṇḍas* such as the paternal grandmother, one must wait for exactly one month. If, however, there is no satisfaction with waiting for three seasons (*ṛtu*) following the death of a particularly virtuous mother, then one should also wait for a full year.

Thus, with the intention that even in the case of the death of a wife or others who possess superior qualities, one must wait for three menstrual periods (*ṛtu*), the general rule is applicable to those two positions as well.

Upon the death of four—father, mother, paternal uncle, and uterine brother—one should perform the *vināyaka-śānti* at the conclusion of the aforementioned waiting period. In the event of the death of anyone else, another *śānti* is performed at the end of that period. These two types of *śānti* will be explained in the *Śāntiratnamālā*.

However, when due to extreme urgency it is impossible to wait for a month or more for any astrological sign (*nimitta*), then even in the interim, one may wait for a short time, perform the prescribed rites for pacification (*śānti*) to a lesser extent, give a cow, and then proceed again with the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*) and so forth; this is the specific distinction made by the author of the *Jyotiṣprakāśa*. But under no circumstances is it proper to proceed with an immediate marriage for one whose impurity has ceased due to a prior period of impurity (*āśauca*) or other such causes, even if there is an unfavorable [sign].

Just as, in the case of a sapinda of the same lineage (*sagotra*), the status of being an obstacle for a prohibited act exists only up to the third generation, so too the prohibition of the *praveśa-muṇḍana* (entry-shaving) and *nirgama-maṇḍana* (exit-adorning) applies to them only up to that same limit. This is the meaning of Medhātithi’s statement regarding "up to three generations. For the purpose of establishing the sense obtained through syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*)—namely, "up to the fourth [generation] for those of one's own lineage"—the text is placed immediately after the sentence "without having completed the funeral rites" (*pretakarmāṇyanirvartya*), even though that sentence has a different meaning.

The meaning is that as long as the rites prescribed for the sake of the deceased (*preta*)—extending up to four generations within the family—have not been performed and completed, one should not perform the *ābhyudayika* (prosperity) rite. However, the interpretation that these are rites specifically characterized by being designated for the deceased has been rejected, because it would result in the exclusion of the monthly rites (*māsika*) performed after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Regarding these rites, although they are prescribed for the sake of the deceased at the time of their initial performance, the *Śāṭyāyanins* state that they are to be repeated without the designation by that word (*preta*): "But those which were performed by drawing them back prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*..."
Furthermore, they are drawn back again because of the prohibition of further increase.

Although the reason given is "because of the prohibition of subsequent *vṛddhi* [funeral rites]," the modern scholars maintain that this must be construed as an injunction (*vidhi*), because—just as in the case of the statement "men first anoint the left hand"—it prescribes what was previously unestablished.
Kātyāyana states:
"Having completed the *vṛddhi* ritual procedure, one should not perform the monthly (*māsika*) rites according to that same procedure."
"His death shall not be untimely, nor shall he die again."

The moderns hold that if the monthly *māsika* rite is performed after a *vṛddhi-karman* (an auspicious rite), the death of the deceased would become "unworn" (*ayātayāma*), as if it were new again. Their view is that it is improper for the death of one who died prior to an auspicious rite to occur subsequent to that auspicious rite.
Some others say: "A brother, or a brother’s son, a sapinda, or even a disciple... [etc.]

Regarding the statement of Laghu-Hārīta, "Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should then perform the *abhyudaya* [rite]," since it mentions brothers, disciples, and others, the postponement does not refer merely to the deities of the *nāndī-śrāddha*. According to this view, upon the death of a brother or similar relative, the *nāndī-śrāddha* cannot be performed without first postponing their *sapiṇḍana* and monthly (*māsika*) rites.

Other modern scholars, however, maintain that this statement prescribes *sapiṇḍana* only for one whose *sapiṇḍana* cannot otherwise be accomplished because he is included among the deities of the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*; this is because it provides what is required by the context (*ākāṅkṣita-vidhāna*). Otherwise, they argue, even a teacher of a different caste would have to perform *sapiṇḍana* for his disciple. In this view, the distinction is that [the rite] occurs even without that [specific condition].

However, the second opinion alone is correct, as it accords with the practice of many learned authorities, beginning with all those from the South, who hold that the postponement (*apakarṣa*) applies only to the deities of the *nāndī-śrāddha*.

Regarding the phrase "without having completed the rites for the deceased" (*pretakarmāṇyanirvartya*), although it appears that the *ābhyudayika* rite—also known as an auspicious (*maṅgala*) rite—shares a common agent with the rites for the deceased, this must nevertheless be explained by taking the latter to have an instrumental agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*), since a primary agent [for the auspicious rite] exists while one for the rites for the deceased does not.

For it is exactly thus: in the Āśvalāyana-sūtra, it is stated, "Having spread [ghee] in the bride's joined palms, the brother or one standing in the place of a brother pours the parched grains (lāja) twice"; however, the commentators on that sūtra and others explain this by asserting that in the marriage oblation (*vivāhahoma*), while the spreading of the ghee is performed by the groom, the pouring of the grains is performed by the brother or his substitute, but for the purpose of reconnecting what was interrupted, even the grain-oblation in that context is performed by the groom.

Thus, even in the statement favored by the opponent—which aims at the postponement of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the sake of establishing the status of the deities of the *nāndīśrāddha*—the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) must be accepted in this very manner. For instance, Śāṭyāyani says:
"A twice-born man, in order to perform the *nāndīmukha* [rite], may even postpone all the *pretaśrāddhas* as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
Laghuhārīta also says: "A brother, or a brother's son, a sapinda, or even a disciple,
having performed the sapinda-rite, should thereafter perform the prosperity rite (abhyudaya)."

Indeed, regarding the giving away of a daughter by one who has died, his elder and younger brothers are the authorized persons, since her father, paternal grandfather, and brothers are no longer extant.

This is according to the statement of Yājñavalkya: "The father, the paternal grandfather, the brother, a sapinda relative, and likewise the mother—each subsequent one is the giver of the daughter in the absence of each preceding one, provided he is of sound mind."
Regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for him, however, the entitlement belongs only to the younger brother, not to the elder.
As it is said: "The father should not perform [the rite] for his son, nor should the elder brother for his younger brother;
even out of affection, they may perform it only excluding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."

Thus, because there is a specific prohibition against him [the younger brother] regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the common agency (*samānakartṛkatva*) of the two aforementioned statements must be established by accepting that the eldest brother is the *prayojaka-kartṛ* (indirect agent) for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, while the younger brother is the *mukhya-kartṛ* (primary agent). Furthermore, since these two statements do not mention a purpose for establishing the status of the deceased as a deity (*devatātva*), and since they share a single enjoined object, it is appropriate—following the principle of parsimony regarding the unity of the source—to accept that their purpose lies in the meaning of the statement cited in the *Kṛṣṇabhaṭṭī-prayoga*, namely: "without having completed the rites for the deceased. This is stated in the *Kaustubha*.

Furthermore, in that very same work: "When the grandfather or great-grandfather has not yet had the *sapiṇḍana* performed, and the father dies, it follows by propriety that after performing their *sapiṇḍana*, the *sapiṇḍana* of the father must be performed. However, when through such performance there occurs a lapse of the prescribed time for the father’s *sapiṇḍana*, then, although by rule the duty to perform it would arise only after the lapse of time, it is ordained by a specific scriptural statement that the *sapiṇḍana* of the father must be performed even with those two [ancestors] whose *sapiṇḍana* has not been performed.
As Kātyāyana says:"
"The two ancestors who have not yet been consecrated should not be consecrated by the grandson or great-grandson;
rather, one should consecrate the father in that case—so said Śātātapa."
"It is the settled rule that one should consecrate the father with the grandfather— even if the grandfather is most wicked or himself a doer of evil— provided he is pure."

The two ancestors, the grandfather and the great-grandfather, are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed. The meaning is that one should make the most sinful father—whose *sapiṇḍana* has not been performed—pure (*śuddha*), having brought him back from the state of a deceased spirit (*nivṛttapretāvastha*), by joining him with the grandfather, whether that grandfather is pure and for whom the *sapiṇḍana* has been performed, or is a wrongdoer for whom it has not been performed. When this has been done, it is stated by that same author that even the *darśa-śrāddha* must be performed together with those two such ancestors:
"Having performed the *sapiṇḍatā* of the father, one should perform the monthly rites."

And thus, since the *nāndī-śrāddha* is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *darśa-śrāddha*, even though those two [the father and grandfather] could theoretically serve as deities there, auspicious rites such as marriage must be performed only after first performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for them, because they have not yet passed beyond the four generations.
For this very reason, the *Kālādarśa* recites that the arrival of an auspicious occasion is itself the cause for the postponement of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*:
"On the eleventh or twelfth day, or in the third fortnight, or in the third month..."
In the sixth or eleventh year, or when the [twelfth] year is complete and auspicious conditions have arisen.
Thus, eight times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* have been proclaimed:
when the performer possesses the sacred fires (*sāgni*), the first two [times] apply; when the deceased possesses the sacred fires, the next [time applies].
"For one who has not yet kindled the sacred fires, seven times beginning with the second [day] are proclaimed as the [proper] times."

Having explained the phrase "the category of the immediate woman" (*anantarastripakṣaḥ*) and the phrase "when the arrival of an auspicious event such as a marriage is imminent" in that very same work, the following example from the root text is provided:

"In the *Mahābhārata*, beginning with: 'The sacrificer who lacks the sacred fires should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,' it continues: 'Or even in the eleventh month, when an auspicious occasion has arrived. [Thus.]

Regarding this, it is stated in that very same source: "Since the terms *śubha* (auspicious) and *maṅgala* (mangala) here are understood to refer specifically to the marriage ceremony and the like, there is no implication of the *nāndī-śrāddha*, and much less of its presiding deities. Furthermore, when the *sapiṇḍana* rite is performed prematurely, there is the cessation of the remaining monthly (*māsika*) rites preceding it; it should be understood that the cessation of the remaining monthly rites following it also occurs by virtue of scriptural injunction. This is based on the statement: "Without having completed the funeral rites (*pretakarman*)."
"A brother, or a brother's son, or a sapinda relative, or even a disciple,
having performed the sapindikarana rite, should thereafter perform the auspicious ceremony."

From this statement, the meaning is that for anyone within the four generations—whether a *sagotra* or a *sapiṇḍa*—even if their son is away abroad or otherwise distant, one must perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the monthly *śrāddhas*, and the *preta-śrāddhas* for the deceased before performing the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. As it is said: "A twice-born man, in order to perform the *nāndīmukha* rite, should even bring forward and perform all the *preta-śrāddhas* as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."

Thus, the statement of Śāṭyāyani recorded by Hemādri also has this very same meaning; for even in the rule regarding the postponement [of rites], the verbal consistency applies specifically to those rites for the deceased (preta-karmāṇi) which are ordained as necessarily to be performed for as many ancestors as required in accordance with the *nāndīmukha* ceremony. Although the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is indeed a *preta-śrāddha*, it is mentioned separately so that its postponement may be established even by overriding the three-fortnightly period and other times fixed for the case of those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), etc. As it is said: "But those [rites] performed by postponing [them] before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* are postponed once again, because of the prohibition against performing them after a *vṛddhi* (auspicious) occasion."

Thus, even the statement of Śāṭyāyani refers only to human beings, because it occurs again with the word "again" (punarapi), and thus its application is possible only with respect to them; so it is stated in the Kaustubha.
Furthermore, auspicious rites should not be performed for one suffering from fever until they have recovered their health.
And so says Garga:
"One should not cause the production of fever for one for whom it would be auspicious;
once the humors have been expelled and he has become healthy, he should practice the Dharma."
One should not even entertain the certainty that a severe fever has arisen in the body of someone born of a noble family.
And so it is said by that same [author]: "Some said that a certain householder suffered from a terrible fever."
"Therefore, the wise should not make a firm decision regarding an auspicious undertaking.
Thus concludes the section on unfavorable rules. Now follows the determination regarding the defect of menstrual flow (rajo-doṣa).
In the Mādhavīya:
"If the mother is in her menses prior to the commencement of the marriage,
the ceremony must be postponed, because of the scriptural injunction regarding [the bride's] companionship."

The meaning is that the cessation of that menstrual impurity must be brought about; for the sake of the ritual, purity is to be awaited. The intended sense is that if the mother should become menstruating prior to the commencement of the marriage, the wedding must be performed only when she has become pure, and she is not to be abandoned. He states the reason for this: "Because of the scriptural injunction regarding joint performance.
Although it might follow from the general statement that its cessation must be effected that the marriage could take place on the fourth day once the flow has ceased, nevertheless—

By the statement, "In rites for the gods and for the ancestors, one becomes pure on the fifth day," it is understood that since the eligibility for all rituals is declared specifically on the fifth day, the eligibility for marriage begins from that very day and not even from the fourth day. The meaning of the word *prārambha* (commencement) has been stated by Viṣṇu:
"In a sacrifice, the commencement is the choosing [of priests]; in vows and long-duration sacrifices (*satra*), it is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)."
"In the Nāndīmukha rite at marriages and other ceremonies, the preparation of the cooked food takes place during the Śrāddha."

*Nāndīmukha* refers to the *nāndī-śrāddha*. By the phrase "at marriages and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes ceremonies such as the initiation (*upanayana*). *Pākaparikriyā* means the commencement of cooking; some say it refers to the sprinkling of water over the food (*pākaprokṣaṇa*).
In the statement, "Once [the rite] has commenced, there shall be no impurity (*sūtaka*)," the term *sūtaka* is also indicative of *mṛtaka* (impurity due to death).
— Medhātithi.
If a wife is in her menses during the tying of the sacred thread, during the marriage ceremony, or during a sacrificial rite,
it is generally not auspicious for that man.
If the mother of either the bride or the groom should happen to be in her courses,
Manu has declared that the auspicious ceremony should be performed after she has become pure.
"If the mother is in her menses during the marriage, the vow, or the tonsure ceremony, then no auspicious rite should be performed; those desiring welfare should perform it once she has become pure."
Garga also says: "If, during an auspicious occasion such as a wedding, the mother is menstruating,
then that [ceremony] should not be performed, because it causes the destruction of longevity."
Since there is no distinction made in these statements, they include the stepmother as well.
Bṛhaspati says:
"If [the marriage] occurs during widowhood, there will be barrenness; if during the tying of the sacred thread [initiation], there will be dull-wittedness."
"And for a child, death occurs at the tonsure ceremony; there is an obstacle during journeys and upon entering [a new home]."

If menstruation occurs after the commencement of the marriage ceremony and so forth, or if menstruation occurs even before the commencement such that an alternative auspicious moment (muhūrta) can by no means be obtained, then one must perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) and proceed with the ritual immediately thereafter.
As it is stated in the *Kapardikārikā*:
"For the purification of a woman who has recently given birth or one who is menstruating, one should give a cow, preceded by a fire-oblation (*homa*)."
When the [prescribed] time has arrived, she becomes pure; in any other case, she is not purified.
If an auspicious moment (sumuhūrta) is not available and the defect of menstruation (rajodoṣa) has arisen,
one should worship Śrī and perform the auspicious ceremony of taking the hand in marriage.
"One should worship a golden lotus weighing one māṣa according to the ritual of the Śrīsūkta;
having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) with each verse and performed the consecration, one should perform auspicious rites."

In the *Kaustubha*, it is stated that because the commencement of the rite is prescribed by one verse and the attainment of a different auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) by another, and because these are heard as distinct, they are not mutually dependent. Regarding the purification for a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*) or one who is menstruating (*udakyā*), the purification established by the injunction "one should give a cow preceded by a fire-oblation" should be understood as pertaining to the fourth day. Here, the word "purification" (*śuddhi*) denotes eligibility (*adhikāra*). Thus, the meaning becomes: "One should give a cow preceded by a fire-oblation for the sake of eligibility."

Regarding the phrase "preceded by a *homa*," the *homa* prescribed is performed with the *Kuṣmāṇḍa* mantras alone, because in the *Kapardikārikās*, that very [rite] is introduced previously. Concerning the subject of a menstruating woman:
"In rites for the gods and for the ancestors, she becomes pure on the fifth day."
By this, the disqualification established by the aforementioned statement for the fourth day is set aside.

Regarding the case of childbirth, however, the disqualification set forth by the rule, "one who has given birth to a son is [impure] for twenty nights, and one who has given birth to a daughter for a month," is here set aside.
This scriptural purification is to be understood as applying in cases of distress.
Regarding the rule for performing the *nāndī-śrāddha* by postponing it when there is the possibility of menstruation occurring [during the scheduled time], another Smṛti states:
"In the case of a sacrifice, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is prescribed twenty-one days prior; for a marriage, ten days prior; and for the *caula*, the *upanayana*, and other rites, six days prior."
The meaning is that there are three days [of impurity] for the *caula* ceremony and six days for the *upanayana*.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the defect of menstrual flow (*rajodoṣa*).
Now follows the determination regarding the occurrence of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) during a marriage.
Yājñavalkya states:
"In giving, in marriage, in sacrifice, in battle, during a national calamity,
and even in times of dire distress, immediate purification is ordained."
Viṣṇu states:

"In the case of vows, sacrifices, marriages, ancestral rites (śrāddha), fire offerings (homa), worship, and recitation (japa), there is no birth-impurity (sūtaka) once they have commenced; however, where they have not commenced, there is indeed impurity."
The meaning of the word *prārambha* (commencement) has already been explained.
Regarding the question of for whom there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) in the case of a marriage, the *Brahma Purāṇa*, introducing the topic of immediate purification, states:
"In the giving of a daughter, there shall be no [impurity] for either the giver or the receiver."
"In the rite of the offering of parched grain (lājāhoma) and so forth for a maiden who is about to be married."

In this context, the mention of the giver and the receiver is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the person to be consecrated and the one who performs the consecration; by the word "and" (ca), the wife of the giver and the bride are also included. Regarding the means of eligibility even for one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), when there is no commencement [of the rite] and no other auspicious moment (muhūrta) is available later on, even after the Sāmāya [rite] has been performed, Viṣṇu states in the Pārijāta:
"To achieve purification before the rite has begun, one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras;
the one in a state of impurity should give a cow and consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); thereafter he becomes pure."

The moderns (*navīnāḥ*) maintain that since the purpose of performing [cooking] for the sake of purification when there has been no prior commencement is already established by the phrase itself, the repeated statement "thereby it becomes pure" is intended to indicate purity even in extremely difficult circumstances, such as when cooking and serving food used for marriage ceremonies and the like. Furthermore, some moderns hold that this rule applies only to one who is *sūtakī* (impure due to birth-impurity).
In the *Saṃgraha*:
"When a crisis has arrived and birth-impurity has set in..."
Having offered clarified butter into the fire with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses, one should give a milch cow as a gift.

"One should perform the tonsure, initiation, marriage, consecration, and so forth; for at the very moment that the birth-impurity (sūtaka) occurs, one may perform the rites for prosperity (abhyudayakriyā)."
Thus, Bṛhaspati states that there is no fault in eating food intended as an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the performance of marriage and other rites preceded by purification:
"In the case of marriage, festivals, and sacrifices, however, if a death or birth-impurity (*mṛtasūtake*) occurs in the interval,
no fault is proclaimed regarding food previously intended for the rite."

The meaning of the first half [of the verse] is that when rites such as marriage are performed during a period of impurity due to death or birth, they may be commenced provided the previously mentioned purification has been effected.
Regarding the specific rule concerning food intended for the purpose after the *nāndī-śrāddha*, even when a marriage or similar rite begins during a period of impurity (*sūtaka*),
the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states:
"But during marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, even if an impurity due to death or birth occurs in the interval,
food should be provided by others and may be eaten by the best of the twice-born."
By others who are not of the same lineage (*asagotra*).
Also, in the *Smṛtikaumudī*:
"If birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) should occur when a marriage, festival, or sacrifice has already commenced..."
"That ritual act, such as the giving of food and so forth, must be performed by others along with its constituent parts."
Regarding the specific rule for when a period of impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs at the time of eating food previously intended, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states:
"But while the Brahmins are eating, if a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interval,
they are all considered pure once they have rinsed their mouths with water from another house."

The intention is that the remainder of what has been eaten by the eaters—the leftover of the cooked food—should be discarded, while the remainder of the cooked food itself may be eaten by those who are in a state of ritual impurity (*sūtakin*).
As it is said: "If someone should die while half of the meal has been consumed, then, being composed, they should discard all that remains of the food left over from eating."

"Having sipped water with the water of another, the twice-born become pure," according to the *Brahmapurāṇa*. Regarding those who have prepared and gathered large quantities of food but lack the capacity to carry it, Viṣṇu says: "Not [is there a prohibition] during the installation of a deity or a marriage, provided the materials were previously gathered."

The meaning is that for one who is about to undertake the installation of a deity or a marriage where the materials have been previously gathered, there is no impurity (āśauca) even prior to the commencement. This is what is intended: this absence of impurity prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) applies only to those cases where, within the time available to hold the many gathered materials, no other interval can be found for the specific rites constituting the installation or the marriage.
Baudhāyana states in the Siṅgābhaṭṭīya:

"If the bride should die before the *sthālīpāka* rite, one should perform the *sthālīpāka* while holding her [hand] and cremate her with the *aupāsana* fire. If the death of the groom’s mother or father should occur, one should complete the remaining portion of the subsequent rites and thereafter perform the *paitṛmedhika* (funeral) rites. If that very person is the eldest [brother], one should tie the marriage bracelet on the hand of the girl and perform the opposite [of the usual procedure]. Thus ends the determination of impurity (*āśauca*) regarding marriage.
Now follows the consideration of simultaneous rites (*samānakriyā*).
In the *Sārāvalī*:
"Those born from the same womb never perform a marriage ceremony in the same year; however, they may do so otherwise."
In the *Jyotirvivaraṇa*:
"The marriage of two suitors born from the same womb on the same day leads to ruin;
some say it is auspicious if they are separated by a river, or in times of distress."
In the *Śārṅgadharīya* it is also said: "Even between rivers, [a marriage] is auspicious when there is a separation by distinct mountains.
In another Smṛti: "Marriage among those born of the same lineage occurs within a single family at a single [astrological] rising."
"In one year, destruction shall occur; of those two, one shall become a widow.
Here, *udaya* refers to the ascendant (*lagna*).
Garga says in the *Pārijāta*:
"In the case of a pair of brothers, a pair of sisters, or a pair of a brother and a sister, an auspicious rite should never be performed in a single pavilion on the same day.

The meaning is that one should not perform the decoration (the marriage ceremony) for a pair of brothers, a pair of sisters, or a pair consisting of a brother and a sister on the same day in a single pavilion. Furthermore, since this statement serves as a prohibition regarding siblings born of the same womb—such a prohibition already being established by the *Sārāvalī*—this [present] text pertains to cases other than those.

In the *Madaratna*, Nārada states: "One should not perform the same rite for a male and a female born of the same mother in the same year; it is ordained that [the rite may be performed] when the mothers are different."

By the phrase "not the same rite," it is understood that one should not perform two *caula* ceremonies, two *vratabandha* initiations, or two marriages for two [brothers] simultaneously. By the statement "it is prescribed when there is a difference of mothers," it is indicated that even two marriages for a single man on the same day are prohibited due to the absence of a difference of mothers.
Furthermore, in a treatise on astrology (*jyotirgrantha*):
"In no way should the house-warming and the marriage be performed in a single year."
By the word *geha*, both the commencement of a house and its entry are understood. He states this specific detail:
"After the marriage of a son, the marriage of a daughter should not take place within three menstrual periods."
"One should not perform a vow, nor a marriage, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
for if the marriage of maidens takes place within six months [of another],
without a doubt, one among them will become a widow within three years."
Auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) include marriage and the like; inauspicious rites (*amaṅgala*) include ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) and the like.
As stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"Having first performed the sacrifice to the Mothers (*mātṛyajña*), one should then perform the auspicious rite, making the eldest [brother] the presiding authority."
"One should not perform a minor auspicious rite (*laghumaṅgala*) for three *ṛtu*s [after a major one].

Here, "major auspicious rites" (*jyeṣṭhamaṅgala*) refer to marriage and the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), while "minor auspicious rites" (*laghumaṅgala*) refer to the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) and others. According to some, by this statement even the return home from studentship (*samāvartana*) is prohibited, because it too is a minor auspicious rite. Others, however, maintain that this refers to sacraments (*saṃskāra*) for a son and so forth performed by the father and others, but not to sacraments performed by oneself; they argue that since the *samāvartana* is performed by oneself, this prohibition does not apply to it. This view is to be considered doubtful, as there is no authoritative evidence for it.
Thus, it is stated that after marriage or after the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the tonsure (*caula*) should not be performed before the completion of three menstrual periods (*ṛtu*).
Accordingly, Atri states in the *Madanaratna*:
"In a family, the decoration [of the head] may take place before three periods have passed, but the tonsure must not."
"One should not perform the three auspicious rites (of entry, departure,
and marriage) one after another; however, after the marriage of a daughter,
the performance of the marriage rite for a son is not defective, even if there is a difference in mothers or a separation of households."
In this context, the family extends only as far as three generations.
Thus says Medhātithi:
"Within each family, for those of one's own lineage, [the relationship] extends up to three generations."
"Likewise, there are entry and exit, as well as shaving and adornment.
The meaning of the terms *maṇḍana* (adornment) and *muṇḍana* (shaving) was stated by Kātyāyana:
"Shaving is said to be the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), while the initiation vow (*vrata*) and marriage (*udvāha*) are adornment."
"Caula is said to be 'shaving' (muṇḍana); one should avoid it after the formal selection [of the bridegroom].
The Mauñjī ceremony, however, should be performed on both occasions, because the Mauñjī is not a shaving.

This is the intended meaning: since Caula has shaving as its primary element, that is his point. Since shaving is merely a subsidiary part of the Mauñjī and not its primary element, that is the purport of the statement "the Mauñjī is not a shaving. "After the selection" means after the selection of the bride and the groom; that is to say, from the time of the bride and groom's selection onwards.
The meaning of the terms *praveśa* (entry) and *nirgama* (exit) was stated by Kātyāyana: "The marriage of a son is called *praveśa*, while the marriage of a daughter is *nirgama*.
This is also stated in the *Saṃhitāsārāvalī*:
"Shaving the head is not desired after the decoration [of the first birthday]; nor should the decoration of two sons be performed in a single year.
Nor, even within three menstrual periods after a son's marriage, should one perform the marriage ceremony of a daughter.
Thus says Vasiṣṭha in the Madanaratna.
One should not perform the marriage ceremony for a daughter within three menstrual periods after the marriage of a son;
nor, if there is no difference in the year, should one perform the tonsure (initiation) after the decoration (marriage), when the lineage is the same.
Furthermore, the marriage of a sister should not be performed by a brother from the same womb who has already completed his own marriage rites.
The sages declared: "Within the interval of six months, shaving should not be performed even for the sake of ornamentation.
Mihira states: "Likewise, within six months following the initiation (*upanayana*) of a son..."
"One should not perform a son's marriage followed by the initiation ceremony (*vratabandhana*) immediately after the marriage. An exception to this is stated in that very same work:
"If the entry into another year occurs within the middle of three *ṛtu*s..."
"For then, even for those born of the same womb, marriage is indeed commended.

Here, by the word *tu* ("but/only"), it is indicated that regarding those born of the same womb, two auspicious rites other than marriage do not take place even when there is a difference of years. In the *Sārāvalī*:
"In the month of Phālguna or Caitra, [one may perform] the marriage of a son or his initiation..."
"One should observe the three seasons by dividing the year.
Regarding this difficulty, Garga says: "For four days following the marriage of a daughter..."
"The wise say that one should not perform the marriage of a daughter with one who is within the prohibited degree.
Here, *pariṇaya* means marriage. Also, the *Kapardikārikā* states:
"A father, having married off his daughter, should never perform the marriage of another daughter;
rather, he should complete everything here up to the fourth day and then perform the other marriage.
Regarding this fourth day, Kaśyapa says:

"The tying of the girdle (mauñjībandha) as well as marriage—even if within six months—one should not perform the marriage of a daughter; however, for those who are separated [in property], this does not cause any fault."

Since it is heard here and later that one should not perform the marriage of a daughter [immediately] after [the marriage of a son], it should be understood that the marriage of the son occurs first in the preceding case. The meaning here is as follows: the tying of the girdle (*mauñjībandha*) and likewise the marriage may be performed even within six months; however, within those six months, one should not perform the marriage of a daughter after the marriage of a son. But if the brothers are divided, there is no fault in performing the marriage of a daughter after the marriage of a son within six months. This should be understood to apply only in cases of extreme distress. As for what Medhātithi says in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
The marriages of two sisters born of different mothers should be performed on the same day,
in the same pavilion, yet upon separate altars;
furthermore, they should see one another through flower-patterned screens, but not with their heads visible.

The statement, "And by both these sisters, until the seven steps have been taken," intends to refer to a difference in the agents (of the action). This is because, when the suffix *kṛtya* (expressing the object) is used in the word *kārya*, it is possible for the construction to be "by two" or "by three. In the cited statements of Garga and in the statement of Kapardin, a prohibition is understood with respect to a single agent; this is perceived in exactly that way through such words as "one should perform," "one should do," and "the father should not arrange [it]. Consequently, even when there is a single auspicious moment (*lagna*) and a single house, the marriage of two uterine sisters may be performed by two different agents.

The distinction between the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-pratiṣṭhā*) and other rites is based solely on the difference in the officiating agent (*kartṛ-bheda*). If there is a single agent, he should first complete the marriage ceremony over the course of four days and then perform the subsequent rites. However, in an extreme emergency, even on a single day, one should understand that the arrangement may be made either by not differentiating the consecration of the pavilion deities and so forth, or by means of a division of households. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "A double auspicious rite (*dviśobhana*) is not desired even in a single house; however, an auspicious rite [performed] later is acceptable within nine days. Alternatively, a necessary auspicious rite or a festival may be performed [separately] through a division at the door or a division among the preceptors (*ācārya*)."

In this context, the latter half [of the verse] should be understood as applying to the common case of a divided abdomen (*bhinnodara*). Regarding the matter of [death occurring] before the fourth day, Vasiṣṭha states: "Where two auspicious houses are situated in one or two signs..."
"One of those two would perish; it does not flourish as it stands.

Regarding this, the *Cintāmaṇi* states that "in a house where there are two auspicious [days], it means two marriages.
