In the *Jyotirvivaraṇa*, it is stated that even for two siblings born of the same womb, the performance [of the rites] on a single day is prescribed in cases of extreme difficulty: [The text continues: "In a very narrow [circumstance], even for those of one womb, it is said they should be performed on one day..."
"A prohibited time for the auspicious moment (lagna) is not forbidden when a great emergency has arisen;
this applies when two [children] born from the same womb are to be initiated on the same day in separate pavilions at the proper time.
Regarding twins, however, there is a specific rule in another Smṛti:
"In the same year, on the same day, and likewise in the same pavilion,
an auspicious rite should be performed for sisters and brothers born as twins. Thus says Gārgya.
"When a single day arrives, one may perform the tonsure, the marriage, and the investiture with the sacred thread for twins.
This should be understood as a permissive injunction (*abhyanujñā*), and not as a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*).
Thus concludes the investigation into identical actions.
Now follows, in brief, the determination of those who give a daughter in marriage.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, and likewise the mother—
each subsequent one among these becomes the giver of the maiden in the absence of the preceding, provided he is of sound mind.
By not giving her away during each menstrual period, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo.
"But in the absence of givers, a maiden may choose a husband for herself.
This refers to the brother of the maiden, and he is one who has been consecrated.
For it has been stated by that same [author]: "But those who have not yet undergone the sacraments (asaṃskṛta) should be consecrated by brothers who have already been consecrated;

and the sisters, having given a fourth part from their own shares. The meaning is this: whatever share belongs to a son of a particular caste, a fourth part of that share should be given to each of the sisters, and they are to be consecrated. In the phrase "and the sisters," the word "and" (ca) serves to carry forward the qualification "by brothers who have already been consecrated. By the term "already consecrated," the eligibility of a brother who has not yet been initiated (anupanīta) is excluded.

On this point, Śūlapāṇi states: "The unmarried brothers should be consecrated with the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) and other sacraments from the paternal wealth itself by the brothers and others who have already been consecrated for the sake of their father; likewise, the sisters should also be consecrated with the sacrament known as marriage by giving them a fourth part from their own share, using that very wealth. However, Bṛhaspati says:
"Their mothers shall have equal shares, and the daughters shall have a fourth part."

By this, the entitlement to receive a fourth part of the paternal estate is stated; however, even that is solely for the purpose of performing the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). If marriage cannot be accomplished with a fourth part, then as much wealth as is necessary to accomplish it should be given.
As Devala says:
"To the daughters, from the paternal property, the wealth required for marriage should be given."
"A daughter of one who has no son, or one born according to the Dharma, shall inherit like a son.

Viṣṇu states that this is "according to one's own wealth": "For unmarried daughters, one should perform the sacraments according to one's own wealth. A *sakulya* is an heir. Among heirs as well, only one who is present is entitled [to the inheritance]. "In his natural state" (*prakṛtistha*) means free from defects such as loss of caste, insanity, and so forth. By the inclusion of the term "in his natural state" here, even an act performed by a father or other relative who is not in his natural state is considered as if it were not done at all. As it is said: "If one who is independent performs that act while having fallen into an unnatural state..."
"That too would remain unaccomplished, because of the lack of independence [of the agent]."

Thus, according to the statement of Nārada in the *Aparārka*: even though he is independent by virtue of being the father and so forth, if he becomes dependent due to the reason of not being in his natural state (*aprakṛtistha*), then the act performed by him—such as the formal betrothal (*vāgdāna*)—must be understood as unperformed, provided that the groom has incurable diseases or defects involving a fall from caste (*patanīya-doṣa*). However, in the absence of such defects of a fall from caste and the like in the groom, one who is in his natural state should perform the subsequent rites in the same manner.

However, when the marriage sacrament of a girl given by one who is not in their natural state has been completed, then—since the principal rite has been accomplished and there is merely a deficiency in the qualified person—the maiden must not be returned in its entirety even in that case.

If it is argued that this contradicts the principle that "even what is performed by one who lacks authority is as if not performed," that is true. However, that contradiction is resolved by the following analogy: just as in the case of a younger brother marrying before his elder (parivettṛ-vivāha), the wife is taken back from him and given again to the elder brother who is the rightful authority, so too here; and in that regard, the remarriage should be understood to be exactly like the marriage of the younger brother marrying before the elder, as stated in the Madanapārijāta.

However, if the rite has been completed up to the taking of the seven steps (*saptapadī*), then even in the event of a deficiency in the qualifications or the status of the giver, there is no repetition of the marriage; for some maintain that it is improper to repeat the principal act (*pradhāna*) merely for the sake of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*). Nārada also speaks of the givers:
"The father himself should give the girl, or the brother with the father's consent."
The paternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, kinsmen, and likewise relatives;
"In the absence of a mother for all [the brothers], if she remains in her natural state, then while she is not in that state, their own kinsmen should give away the maiden."

In this context, the mention of the "father" (*pitṛ*) is indicative of the grandfather (*pitāmaha*). Here, the sequence should be understood as follows: in the absence of the father, the grandfather; in his absence, the brother, and so forth, in accordance with the cited statement of Yājñavalkya. "Sakulyas" are kinsmen who are heirs; "bāndhavās" are those on the mother’s side; and "svajātayaḥ" refers to Brāhmaṇas and others of one's own caste—the meaning is that those of the same caste as the girl herself are the entitled parties. Kātyāyana states in the *Madanapārijāta*: "One should give the daughter in marriage oneself; in the absence of the father, her own kinsmen."

"The maternal grandfather, or the mother, or [the maternal uncle] shall give another daughter born of dharma. "Another" means one different from the legitimate (aurasī) daughter. "Born of dharma" means one born of a field (kṣetraja) through the practice of *niyoga*; such a girl the maternal grandfather, the mother, or the maternal uncle may give. Therefore, when the giver of the legitimate daughter is present among the paternal kinsmen, the maternal grandfather and others have no authority.
An exception to this is stated in that very same work:
"When kinsmen are engaged in a long journey or are in their childhood,
a mother may, at the proper time, give away even her own biological daughter."
*Paugaṇḍa* refers to one who is incapable of legal transactions and the like. *Samaya* refers to the period prior to the time suitable for the appearance of menses.
Manu states:
"But when there is no [eligible suitor] at all, the maiden shall approach the king."
In the absence of all the aforementioned eligible suitors, she should choose for herself, according to the scriptural injunction:
"In the absence of givers, a maiden may herself choose a husband. [She might say:
"O daughter, the time for your giving has arrived, yet no one chooses me."
Seek for yourself a husband who is equal to you in virtues."

Thus, in the *Sāvitrī-upākhyāna* of the *Mahābhārata*, although self-choice (*svayaṃvara*) is mentioned even with the father's permission, that refers specifically to the Kṣatriyas, as it is their prerogative. "Fit to be approached" (*gamya*) means one who is worthy of being married, that is, one endowed with qualities such as being of the same lineage (*sāvarṇya*). Regarding the performance of a marriage for the sake of dharma or worldly benefit by one who arranges the union for a girl who is without a protector, and its fruit, it is stated in another Purāṇa: "Having made a daughter belonging to another one's own through [the payment of] gold, even one who is not of the same lineage (*asagotra*) is fit to give her away according to the righteous rite."
"Having seen a maiden who is without a protector, he who gives her away to a suitable bridegroom obtains double the fruit that is proclaimed for the gift of a maiden."
Therefore, the daughter of another may be given by anyone else for the sake of dharma.
Regarding the fault in giving her away after she has reached puberty, Śāṭyāyani says:
"The mother, the father, and likewise the elder brother..."
"These three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses."
Marīci also says:
"That Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by pride, marries such a woman, is declared to be the husband of a *vṛṣalī*; he is unfit for conversation and excluded from the ritual row."
Hārīta also states: "A maiden who sees her menses while still in her father's house and remains unconsecrated by marriage is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; her husband is a *vṛṣalīpati*."
An unmarried girl is one who has not been wedded.

Regarding her, Śaunaka states that marriage should be performed after first undertaking an expiation: "Having purified herself by performing an expiation for herself, she may marry even if she has reached puberty."
The wise father should count the seasons from the very beginning of his daughter's life.
Until the marriage is completed, the father of the girl should diligently protect her who is menstruating in the house;
if he is able, he should give cows equal in number to the number of menstrual periods that have passed.
Even a single gift should be given with effort according to the prescribed rule;
or, being extremely poor, one should give food along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas.
When the number of past seasons [of her life] has reached that count,
the girl, having fasted for three days and drunk cow's milk at night, should present herself to the bridegroom.
"One should give jeweled ornaments to a maiden whose menses have not yet been seen;
and the groom, when marrying her, should also offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras."

The syntactical connection is as follows: having performed expiation for himself and having made his daughter pure after she has reached puberty, he should bestow her upon a bridegroom. Regarding his own daughter—that is, his own girl—when the giving of that girl is to be performed according to rule, a capable man should give as many cows as there have been menstrual periods by means of the *godāna* rite; however, the meaning is that one who is incapable must, at the very least, give even a single cow according to the *godāna* rite.

By the verse beginning with *upoṣya*, the gift of a cow (*godāna*) preceded by the drinking of cow's milk is prescribed for a girl who has seen her menses at the conclusion of three days of fasting. For a maiden who has not yet seen her menses, fitness for marriage is indicated by the giving of ornaments along with jewels. By the phrase *tām udvahan* ("marrying her"), the bridegroom’s fitness for that marriage is established through the *kuśmāṇḍa* oblation.
Furthermore, after the gift of the cow, the girl must also perform a quarter-penance (*pādakṛcchra*).
As it is said: "If a girl is overwhelmed by menses prior to her marriage..."
She shall become pure for the rite of taking the hand through a quarter-penance."

Thus it is stated in the *Smṛtyantara* cited by Hemādri. Baudhāyana, however, says: "Now, if a girl, while being seated [for the marriage ceremony] or being carried away, should become menstruating, he addresses her with the mantra: 'May Mitra and Varuṇa be males; may both Aśvins be males; may Indra and Sūrya be males; may she increase this male. Then, having adorned her for twelve nights, he should have her consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); thereafter she becomes pure. So he says.

"Being brought near" means being presented by the giver; "being carried away" means being led away by the groom for the purpose of taking her hand. The two uses of the word *vā* (or) are intended to indicate that both [the giver and the groom] are equally primary. Regarding her falling while being brought near or being carried away, he himself has said: "Now, if the maiden should fall while being brought near or being carried away, one should raise her up with [the mantra]: 'The goddess Aditi, of all forms, has risen; she has placed long life in the patron of the sacrifice, preparing a portion for Indra and for Mitra.'"
And [the offering] to Varuṇa.
Regarding the onset of menstruation at the time of the *homa*, Yajñapārśva states:
"When the marriage ceremony has been commenced and the time for the *homa* has arrived..."
Having seen a maiden who has reached her menses, how do the performers of sacrifices act?
"Having bathed that maiden and worshipped her according to the rule,
and having offered the oblation while engaged in yoga, one should then proceed with the ritual manual."
The meaning is: having offered that oblation called the *yuñjānā-huti*, which is to be accomplished with the single Ṛg-verse beginning "yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ.
However, Baudhāyana states a special rule for when menstruation occurs due to the absence of a donor (husband):
"A woman who has reached puberty should wait for her father’s command for three years."
Then, in the fourth year, she shall find a suitable husband.
"When a suitable [husband] is not available, she may resort even to one who is deficient in qualities.
Manu also says:
"A woman who has reached puberty should wait for three years."
But after this time has passed, she may obtain a husband of equal status.

"If she should obtain a husband by herself when not being given away, she incurs no sin whatsoever, nor does he whom she obtains. Mādhava has explained this as follows: "Not being given away" means due to the absence of a giver or the neglect of a giver; and he whom she obtains as a husband also incurs no sin.
As for the statement of Viṣṇu— "Having passed three seasons, a maiden may choose her own husband"—
that should be understood as applying when a bridegroom endowed with good qualities is available.
Manu states a specific rule regarding the *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage): "A woman who chooses her own husband shall not take the ornaments given by her father;
if she should take those given by her mother or her brothers, it would constitute theft."
He (the same author) states the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage:

"That fruit which a man obtains by giving a daughter according to the prescribed rite does not arise from the Agnihotra and other such rites, nor from protection, nor from [the service of] a Brahmin."
"From protection" means by means of guarding [them].
Saṃvarta states the specific fruit resulting from giving a daughter adorned with ornaments:
"The father-in-law, the performer of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, the giver of life, and the one who provides protection in times of fear..."

"Their three chariots indeed proceed evenly; of this there is no doubt. Regarding the word *kukuda*: according to the lexicon, "He who gives away a daughter after having honored and adorned her is a *kūkuda*"; thus, it is conventionally used for the giver of a daughter accompanied by honors and ornaments. Even when the reading is *kūpada*, the meaning is the same.
The ritual giving at marriage is described in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"For he who, being compassionate, gives the gift of marriage,
goes to the abode of Mahendra in a celestial chariot the color of the sun, garlanded with networks of tinkling bells, and is served by hosts of apsarases."

"Vaivāhika" refers to the goods, clothing, ornaments, and so forth, required for marriage. Nor should it be argued that this [act] is merely optional (kāmya) because of the mention of its fruit; for it is said: "That lowest of men who does not perform the giving of what is required for marriage shall become most sinful and is censured by all the world."
Thus, because the fault of not giving [the bride] is heard [in the scriptures], marriage is both obligatory and optional, like the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

Regarding another’s performance of marriage for the sake of dharma, the fruit is stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "Having assessed one's own financial capacity, one should marry off at least one twice-born man."
"By that [merit], a man who is a devotee of Śiva certainly attains that state. Dakṣa also says in the *Aparārka*:
"One who is deprived of mother and father [should be provided for] by means of sacraments, marriage, and so forth."

"For one who establishes [this], there is no measure of merit to be found here. Regarding the prohibition against eating in the house of an unmarried girl, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states: "One should never eat in the house of an unmarried girl who has no offspring."
"Having seen the face of his daughter's son, why does he grieve? Regarding the phrase "he should not eat," the words "in the house of the daughter" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Aparārka also quotes this in the Āditya Purāṇa:
"One should not eat in the house of a maiden who has no brothers;
nor indeed should one ever eat after giving away a maiden in the Brāhma form of marriage.
If, however, one should eat out of delusion, he certainly goes to hell."

The meaning is that after giving a daughter worthy of being given according to the *brāhma* marriage rite, one should never eat in her house; here too, the phrase "as long as she is childless" (*aprajāyām*) should be supplied. In the *Śākalakārikās* it is also said: "One should not eat the food of a daughter until a son is born to her."

"Otherwise, for one who eats [at such a time], that gift becomes futile. If one eats the food of an unmarried girl who has not yet borne a child, he consumes only sin; he is purified by the Prājāpatya penance."
Now, the rescission of what has been given.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"One may take back even what has been given if a more excellent suitor arrives first."

If a suitor who is superior in qualities and more excellent than the previous suitor should arrive—that is, come—if he should take away the maiden even though she has been given by word of mouth to the previous suitor, the meaning is that one should not give her to him. For this very reason, it is recorded by the learned at the time of the formal promise: "To one who is free from physical defects, not fallen [from caste], not impotent, and devoid of the ten faults, I shall give this maiden in the presence of the gods, the fire, and the twice-born."
Ten defects have been stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"Those who are insane, those devoid of proper conduct, as well as those afflicted by epilepsy;
those who live far away, lepers, fools, and those who follow the path of liberation."
"Brave men who are ignorant, those who have renounced the world, and those possessed of the ten defects;
likewise eunuchs, outcasts, and those deprived of sight or hearing—these must be avoided with great effort by the giver of a daughter; of this there is no doubt."
"She has desisted from marriage. As for that statement of Manu:
"But this [practice] neither those before nor those after have ever done, even though they were virtuous..."
As it is said: "That which, having been promised to one man, is given to another";
and as is the statement of Nārada: "The inheritance portion falls [to its owner] once; a maiden is given in marriage once."

It concerns a bridegroom who is free from defects and possesses excellent qualities. Regarding the abduction of a girl who is free from defects and of excellent quality, a punishment has been declared by Yājñavalkya:
"A maiden is given only once; he who abducts her shall incur the punishment of a thief.
The meaning is that the punishment for one who abducts that girl is exactly like the punishment for a thief.
Nārada also says:
"If a man does not give a daughter who has been rightfully given to a suitor,
and that suitor is not at fault, he shall be punished by the king like a thief."

By the phrase "if he is not wicked," it is understood that one should not give to a wicked person; and it has been stated by Gautama: "Even after having made a promise, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness."
Even if a marriage has been performed by a wicked man up to the completion of the seven steps, she must not be accepted thereafter.
For this very reason, Nārada says: "In the case of a man and a woman, the formal betrothal (*varaṇa*) is prescribed to take place prior to their union."
The taking of the hand from the act of choosing is this threefold relationship.
It is said that between these two, [the choice] is not fixed because of the perception of defects;
however, the mantras recited at the time of taking the hand are the fixed characteristic of a wife.

"And their completion should be understood by the wise at the seventh step. This is its meaning: the relationship between a woman and a man consists of sexual union; prior to that comes the formal betrothal (*varaṇa*), and immediately after that, the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). Thus, the relationship has three characteristics. That relationship which possesses the three characteristics—betrothal, taking of the hand, and sexual enjoyment—is called "three-characterized" (*trilakṣaṇa*). In the expression "of the woman and the man," the feminine form ending in *-ā* is used according to the rule *ācatura-*. This sequence does not apply in the case of the *gāndharva* marriage and others. "Of those two, the woman and the man" means, in other words, of the bride and the groom.

"Indeterminacy" (*aniyama*) refers to the lack of certainty, such as when one who has been chosen is not married, or one whose hand has been verbally given is not bestowed. The reason for this is stated as: "because of seeing faults after the choosing. This means that after the formal choosing (*varaṇa*), faults may be perceived in either the bride or the groom. By this, it is implied that there is no such indeterminacy once the marriage has taken place. Regarding the reason for the certainty (*niyama*) in that case, he says: "The mantras of the taking of the hand. The meaning is that there is no abandonment of those two who have had the sacramental refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by those mantras. He states the limit of the sacramental refinement produced by the mantras of the taking of the hand: "Of these, the conclusion (*niṣṭhā*) is the settled state."

"In the reading: 'The grasping of the hand is the consecration characterized by fire; between those two, betrothal is said to be non-binding because of the perception of defects,' the meaning is as follows: that which is the grasping of the hand is the consecration characterized by fire—that is, the consecration marked by fire and accomplished through rites such as the *homa*. Between those two—betrothal and the grasping of the hand—it is betrothal alone that is non-binding due to the perception of defects, not the grasping of the hand; for it is impossible for one to become an outcast (*patita*) prior to that [grasping of the hand]."
Yama says: "A girl's husband is not designated by water alone, nor by word alone;
he becomes her husband through the sacramental rite of taking the hand at the seventh step."
By this, it is understood that if the groom dies before the seven steps have been taken, widowhood does not occur.
And it has been stated by Vasiṣṭha: "If the groom indeed dies after she has been given [in marriage] with water and word..."
"And a maiden who has been offered by means of a mantra does not belong to anyone other than her father."

The meaning is that she does not belong to her father as one who has accepted her [as a bride]. She is to be given to the husband’s brother (devara); in his absence, to one of his lineage; and in his absence, to another. All of this occurs according to local custom.
Regarding a maiden who has been abducted by force, Yama and Vasiṣṭha state the following distinction: "If a maiden has been forcibly abducted and has not been consecrated with the sacred mantras..."
"She should be given to another according to the prescribed rule; she is exactly like a maiden."
Devala states: "In the case of marriages such as the Gāndharva and others, the formal rite of marriage must again be performed by members of the three castes who are capable, with fire as witness."

The meaning is that even in the case of *gāndharva* and other forms of marriage, having performed again the rites preceding the *vivāha-homa*, one must perform the *vivāha-homa* and subsequent rituals to be accomplished with fire. By this, the mantras beginning with the *homa* and ending with the *saptapadī* are intended; for it is precisely there that the status of wife (*bhāryātva*) arises—so says Mādhava.
Regarding the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*) to many suitors, the specific rule stated by Kātyāyana should be observed: "When [a girl] has been betrothed to many, but remains unmarried..."
"And may she obtain that first boon from all those who have come as suitors."

The meaning is that if all the excellent suitors possessing [required] qualities arrive, the very first one shall obtain that maiden. For those other than the first suitor, if all have arrived, he who has come from the furthest distance shall obtain her.
And so it is said in the *Candrikā*: "He who arrives later from a distant place shall indeed obtain her."

The meaning is that after the determination that the first suitor is unfit, the suitor who is far away shall obtain that maiden. If the first is possessed of defects and the other is possessed of virtues, she should be given to the latter alone—[as it is said]:

"To one devoid of family and character, to one who has subsequently fallen [from his status], to one afflicted by epilepsy, to those of unrighteous conduct, to the diseased, and to those wearing disguises..."
For it is stated by Vasiṣṭha: "One may take back even a girl who has been given in marriage, and likewise one wedded to a man of the same *gotra*";

and by Yājñavalkya: "One may take back even a girl who has been given [in marriage] if a more excellent groom should arrive. The meaning is: after the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*), if the [first] groom has become an outcast (*patita*). "Wedded to a man of the same *gotra*" means wedded to one who shares the same *pravara*.
Regarding the groom's departure for another country after the acceptance [of the bride], Nārada states: "But if the groom, having accepted the maiden, should depart for another country,
then after three seasons have passed, she may choose another groom."
"Having accepted" means having chosen [the bridegroom].
Regarding the departure of the giver of the nuptial fee (*śulka*) to another country, Kātyāyana states:
"He who, having given the nuptial fee and likewise the woman’s property (*strīdhana*) to the girl..."
"She should be worn for one year, after which she must be given to another according to the prescribed rule."

*Śulka* is the price for a maiden. *Strīdhana* refers to ornaments, wealth, and so forth, given for the pleasure of the maiden. Regarding the death of the one who paid the *śulka*, Manu and Vasiṣṭha state:
"If the giver of the *śulka* should die after the *śulka* has been paid for the maiden, she should be given to the brother-in-law (the husband's younger brother), provided the maiden consents."
Yājñavalkya says:
"But when a great defect is discovered before the rite of the seven steps (saptapadī), she may either die or give birth; she should be given to another man, and [the former husband] incurs no fault."
"A maiden who has been married by force must be given to another suitor."

The great defects [of a bridegroom] are stated in the *Kārikānibandha*: "One who is blind, mute, devoid of ritual action, epileptic, a eunuch, living far away, fallen, leprous, or chronically ill— such a person is not a fit groom."
If one is recognized by many for their virtuous qualities even while staying at a distance, then being far away is not a defect.
As it is said in another Smṛti:
"One who is known as virtuous is indeed a refuge, even if he resides afar."

Vasiṣṭha states that even after the taking of the hand in marriage, a girl may be given to another, saying: "If, after the taking of the hand has been performed, a maiden is merely consecrated by mantras, and she remains one whose virginity is intact, she deserves to undergo the sacramental rite again."
And this is forbidden in the Kali age:
"Begetting a son through the husband's brother, the slaughter of an animal at the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka),
and the remarriage of a girl who has not yet been deflowered to another man."

Thus, from the *Bṛhannāradīya* in the section on things to be avoided in the Kali age (*kalivarjya-prakaraṇa*). The meaning of "another's" is "from another. Regarding the abandonment of even a betrothed girl if a defect is discovered after the verbal promise (*vāgdāna*), Manu has stated:
"Even after accepting a girl according to the prescribed rite, one may abandon her if she is censurable"; "censurable" means defective.
Nārada says:
"One should not defile an unblemished maiden, nor should one defile an unblemished groom;
if a fault exists, there is no offense for the two who mutually abandon one another."

The defects of a maiden have been shown by that very same [authority]: "A maiden who is afflicted by long-lasting or loathsome diseases, one who is deformed, one who has already experienced sexual intercourse, one who is impudent, and one whose affection is directed elsewhere— such a maiden is declared to be defective."
She is one by whom affection—that is, desire—has been placed or directed toward another man.

Regarding the fault in abandoning a woman who is not at fault, Yājñavalkya says: "One who abandons a woman who is not at fault shall be fined; but he who falsely accuses her of being at fault shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]."
Nārada states that he who gives away a girl without disclosing her defects should be punished by the king:
"But for him who gives away a defective girl without having declared [the defect],
the king shall impose the punishment prescribed for the first degree of violence (pūrvasāhasa)."
Two hundred and seventy paṇas constitute the middle amercement (*pūrvasāhasa*).
As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"One who gives [a gift] without disclosing a defect shall be punished with the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*)."
This refers to the intention of the preponderance of those faults. The highest amercement (*uttama-sāhasa*) consists of one thousand and eighty *paṇas*.
And it has been stated by that same author in the section on penances (*prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa*):
"The fine of one thousand and eighty *paṇas* is the highest amercement."
Thus concludes the determination regarding the misappropriation of what has been given.
Now follows the examination of the family (*kulaparīkṣā*).
Regarding this, Āśvalāyana says:
"One should first examine the family, both on the mother's side and the father's side," as was stated previously.

This means that one should first examine the family in accordance with what was said in this sūtra: "Those who, on both sides—on the mother's and the father's side—for ten generations have been established in learning and austerity, and by meritorious deeds, such that their non-Brahminhood (*abrāhmaṇya*) has not descended from either side.
Manu says:
"In this world, one should always cultivate relationships with the superior through the superior;
they shall lead the family to excellence, while one should abandon those who are contemptuous."

The supreme characteristic was stated by him as follows: "Those who are purified by their actions, well-versed in the Śruti and Smṛti, whose celibacy has not been violated, and who belong to noble lineages."
The virtuous are contented, intent on the welfare of good people, and seers of reality;
they are entirely free from passion, hatred, resentment, greed, pride, and delusion.
"Relatives should always be made free from anger and well-disposed.
Devala has stated the families to be avoided:
"Those lineages in which there are elder brothers [who are neglected], as well as those in whom women give birth to offspring..."
"And one should carefully avoid those places where women are prone to hostility."
"Born of elder sisters" (*agrajā*) is a qualification for the offspring born of women; it refers to those families in which such [daughters] are born. Manu also says:
"Even if they are great and prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain—one should avoid these ten types of families in forming alliances with women."

"Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic desire, those with hairy anal regions, those afflicted by consumption, epilepsy, or white leprosy, and families suffering from skin diseases."

"Of deficient rites" means devoid of prescribed rituals; this is an elliptical expression implying the avoidance of prohibited acts as well. "Without males" means lacking male offspring. "Without Vedic study" means devoid of the recitation of the Vedas. "Hairy" means having hair grown over all its limbs. By such terms as "afflicted with hemorrhoids," families suffering from those respective diseases are indicated.
As stated in another Smṛti: "By bad marriages, by the omission of rites, and by the non-study of the Vedas..."
Families fall into the state of being non-noble by the transgression against Brāhmaṇas.
[One becomes a Śūdra] through craftsmanship, trade, and solely by having children from a Śūdra wife;
or by [keeping] cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king.
"By officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, and by the act of atheism,
families that are deficient in sacred mantras fall from their noble status to ignobility."

This examination of the family is for the purpose of avoiding the persistence of defects in the progeny that results from taking a wife; for there is a saying of Hārīta: "Offspring are born according to the nature of the family. Thus ends the examination of the family.
Now, the characteristics of a maiden.

Regarding this, Āpastamba and Baudhāyana state: "One should marry a girl who is endowed with [good] kinship, character, and auspicious marks, and who is free from disease. Here, the word "endowed" (*saṃpannā*) is to be connected with each of the preceding terms. "Endowed with kinship" means having a praiseworthy lineage. "Endowed with character" means possessed of virtues such as faith (*āstikya*). "Endowed with auspicious marks" means possessing characteristics such as hidden ankles (*gūḍhagulpha*). "Free from disease" means being devoid of incurable diseases such as consumption (*kṣaya*), epilepsy (*apasmāra*), and leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). Sudarśana has explained that one should marry—that is, take as a wife—a maiden of this description.

In the *Prayogapārijāta*, Śaunaka also says: "A twice-born man, having obtained permission from his guru, [should marry] a maiden who possesses the auspicious marks, is endowed with intelligence, good character, and virtues, and belongs to a different lineage."
"And one should marry a girl of younger age according to the prescribed rule.
Here, the word division is *avaravarṣām*. *Avaravarṣā* means "of younger age" (*nyūnavarṣā*). In this regard, there are two kinds of characteristics: external and internal.
Manu states the external characteristics:

"One should marry a woman whose limbs are free from defects, who has an auspicious name, who walks with the gait of a swan or an elephant, whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft."
She whose body hairs on the chest are fine and subtle, and whose hair and teeth are delicate, is called *tanulomakeśadatī*.
Śātātapa says:
"One who has the gait of a swan, the color of a cloud, and eyes tawny like honey..."
"A householder should choose such a maiden for the increase of his happiness."

Nārada also said: "A woman with the eyes of a deer, the secret parts of a deer, the neck of a deer, and the belly of a deer, and who possesses the gait of a swan or an elephant, shall become the wife of a king."
"The woman whose speech is gentle and whose soles of the feet are likewise soft,
and who has the complexion of a white lotus, shall become the wife of a king."
In this manner, many other characteristics are also to be found in the treatises on *sāmudrika* (physiognomy), such as the *Sāmudrika-tilaka*, the *Hasta-sañjīvana*, and others.
Regarding girls who are to be avoided, Āpastamba says:

"One should avoid for marriage a girl who is asleep, weeping, naked, or one who has been previously betrothed; likewise, one should avoid those who are guarded, radiant, like a bull, like a *śarabha*, hunchbacked, deformed, shaven-headed, suffering from a swelling on the neck, afflicted with scrofula, devoted to another, a guardian, a friend, a sister, or one who menstruates at the time of marriage. Furthermore, those named after constellations, rivers, or trees are censured; all those whose names end in the letters *ra* or *la* should be avoided in marriage. Baudhāyana states further:
"Those named after constellations, rivers, trees, mountains, birds, beasts of prey, or goblins are censured."

One should avoid—that is, strictly avoid—a woman who is asleep, one who is weeping, one who has gone out, or one who is soiled. One should avoid one who has been given to another—whether by word of mouth or formally bestowed with water. One should avoid one who is guarded, being covered by a veil or the like for the sake of concealment, or one who is being protected due to suspicion of immoral conduct and the like. One should avoid one who is radiant, or one with tawny eyes, or one with brown hair, or one with a squint.

One who has a body, gait, hump, or character like that of a bull (*ṛṣabha*), or one who is preeminent among bulls (*ṛṣabhapradhāna*). One who is "śarabhā"—meaning her radiance is withered, or she has dark hair on her limbs, or is misshapen, lusterless, or devoid of light. One who is "vinatā"—meaning she has bent limbs. One who is "vikaṭā"—meaning she has deformed shanks. One who is "muṇḍā"—meaning she has had her hair removed. One who is "maṇḍūṣikā"—meaning she is small-statured, or has reddish teeth, or has the skin of a frog. Some, however, say she is "vāmanā" (dwarf) or has burnt limbs.

A *sāṃkārikā* is one who, while still in the womb, her mother performs the collection of her husband’s bones; or one who has become the daughter of another family. "Delighting" (*ratā*) means being of a playful nature, fond of games such as with a ball, and so forth—some say it refers to one who has bathed after her menstrual period. A *pālī* is one who protects cattle, fields, and so on. A *mitrā* is one who has many friends. A *svanujā* is one whose younger sisters are beautiful; some, however, say she is one born later in the very same year as the groom's birth.

"One should avoid her who rains excessively" means either one who is superior to others by virtue of her rain-giving power, or one who flows [with menses] excessively. Although the word "avoid" (*varjayet*) is already understood from the preceding context, its repetition here is intended either to prohibit all these [types of women] starting with the *brāhmī*, or to indicate that the others are not prohibited. Those whose names are identical to the names of constellations (*nakṣatra*) are called *nakṣatranāmāḥ*. The elision of one instance of the word "name" (*nāma*) is like the compound *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced"). The analysis of the compound for the following two terms is likewise. *Rohiṇī*, *Citrā*, and so forth, are examples of *nakṣatranāmāḥ*.

Names such as Gaṅgā and others are names of rivers; names such as Śiṃśupā and others are names of trees. "Despised" means they are to be avoided. This refers to those whose penultimate letter (the *upāntya*) is either the letter *r* or the letter *l*—that is, the *upadha*. Examples include Gaurī, Śālā, and so forth. The rest is clear. Here, since it is already established that these are to be avoided by the word "despised" being drawn over (*anukarṣaṇa*) by the particle *ca*, the repeated statement "one should avoid them in choosing" might seem redundant; however, this is not so, for it is intended to facilitate easy comprehension.

Alternatively, Sudarśana has explained that this is for the purpose of making it known that one should avoid at the time of selection all those women whose names end in *repha* (r) or *lakāra* (l)—such as Gaurī, Śālā, and so forth—as well as those who, though not ending in *repha* or *lakāra*, are described in other Smṛtis as having the same *gotra* or the same *pravara*, or being unchaste (*puṃścalī*).

Although the author of the Bhāṣya has generally demonstrated that the meaning of the word *svanujā* in its analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is "one whose younger sisters are beautiful," nevertheless, in this context, the word *svanujā* must be understood as feminine and restrictive. Consequently, the resulting meaning is "one whose younger sisters are indeed beautiful. Thus, there is no contradiction with the rule: "One should not marry her who has no brother. Manu also says:
"One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with extra limbs, nor one who is diseased..."

"One should not [marry] a woman who is hairless, nor one with excessive body hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one with reddish-brown eyes; nor one whose name is that of a constellation, a tree, or a river; nor one whose name is that of a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one whose name is that of a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one whose name is terrifying."

The word "should marry" (*udvahet*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. *Kapilā* means reddish-brown, like the color of red rice grains; *piṅgalā* means tawny, like the color of fire; and *antyā* means one with a Mleccha name. Internal characteristics have also been stated by Āpastamba: "If [the bridegroom] has the capacity, he should place various concealed objects before her and say, 'Touch them. These are seeds mixed together, dust from the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), a clod of earth from a field, dung, and a clod of earth from a cemetery. By touching the former ones, there is success according to their respective signs; they declare the last one to be the worst."

*Śakti* means capacity; *viṣaya* means scope. In this examination of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-parīkṣā*), the meaning is that if there is the possibility of scope for the capacity of those belonging to the opposing side, then their daughters and [their] people may undergo this examination. Precisely because it is here called the "scope of capacity" (*śakti-viṣaya*), this examination of supernatural power is optional (*vaikalpikī*) according to astrology and so forth, and not mandatory (*nityā*).

Having placed the substances to be mentioned—concealed within lumps of clay—each in a separate vessel, and having set them near the girl, he should say to her: "Touch one of these lumps of clay. He states what those are: various seeds, such as seeds of rice, barley, and so forth; mixed together, meaning cast into a single lump; earth brought from the altar of the Soma sacrifice; and a clod of earth brought from a field rich in crops. The remaining two are well known.

In the case of touching the four preceding substances, there is prosperity according to their respective suitability: by touching various seeds, there is prosperity of offspring; by touching the dust of the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), there is prosperity of the sacrifice; by touching a clod of earth from a field, there is prosperity of crops; and by touching dung, there is prosperity of cattle. The meaning is that from the certainty of such prosperity follows the certainty that the marriage must be performed. Regarding the last item, the learned condemn the clod of earth from a cemetery; Sudarśana explains this as being because it is a sign of the death of either the wife or the husband.
Āpastamba and Baudhāyana state regarding one who is unable to do this much:

"In her upon whom the binding of the mind and the eyes [rests], there is success; one should not heed anything else—so say some. The meaning is: in whichever maiden the binding—that is, the intense attachment—of the bridegroom’s mind and eyes occurs, such that his mind and eyes remain as if bound due to an excess of passion for her; when such a wife exists, there is success in matters such as dharma, and one should not heed anything else, namely, the observation of other virtues or faults. Thus it has been explained by Sudarśana.

This prohibition—"one should not respect another"—applies only to those [women] whose names end in *repha* (r), *kāra* (k), or the penultimate letter, and not even to those of the same lineage (*sagotra*), the same ancestral rite (*sapravara*), or within the sapinda relationship as mentioned in the *Dharmasūtras*. It is precisely for this reason that the prohibition against marrying those of the same lineage and so forth is established in the *Dharmasūtra*, but not in the *Gṛhyasūtra*. Thus, the prohibition against marrying those of the same lineage and so forth certainly exists.

And thus, this prohibition is not capable of subverting the prohibition of marriage with one of the same *gotra* and so forth as stated in its own *sūtra*; it is not even capable of looking toward the prohibition of marriage with one of the same *gotra* and so forth stated in another *sūtra*, much less subvert it. Therefore, there is no suspicion whatsoever of subverting the prohibition of marriage with one of the same *gotra* and so forth as stated in the *sūtras* of Satyāṣāḍha and others. Furthermore, in the *sūtras* of Satyāṣāḍha and Āpastamba, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and from those related by birth to the mother" (*mātuśca yonisaṃbandhebhyaḥ*) serves to include both those who share the same *pravara* as the father and those who are *sapinda* to him.
Consequently, the prohibition applies to these two cases as well.
Baudhāyana has stated that the physical characteristics must necessarily be examined, for otherwise there is a fault:
"One should avoid by all means those girls who possess inauspicious characteristics;
if they are not examined due to negligence, they take away the life-span of the husband."
Thus end the characteristics of the bride.
Now, the characteristics of the groom.
Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "One who is learned in the Vedas."

He is endowed with learning (*śruta*) and study (*adhyayana*), because only one who is learned is entitled to perform the prescribed rites; such is the excellence of the groom (*vara-saṃpat*). Sudarśana explains that the meaning is: "one should give [the bride] to a groom who is thus qualified. Baudhāyana states: "One who is endowed with kinship, good character, auspicious marks, learning, and freedom from disease.
Āśvalāyana says: "One should bestow the maiden upon an intelligent man."
Yama says:

"Having examined these seven qualities—lineage, character, age, appearance, learning, wealth, and the presence of a protector—a daughter should be given away by the wise; everything else is not to be considered."
By the word *nātha* (protector), those who nourish one, such as fathers and others, are meant.
As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*:
"The lineage of a Brāhmaṇa is to be accepted, not his Vedas along with the *pada* and *krama* recitations."
"In the giving of a daughter in marriage as well as in the *śrāddha* rite, learning (*vidyā*) is not the determining factor there.

This statement is intended to establish the primacy of the family lineage (*kula*) for a Brāhmaṇa in matters such as the giving of a daughter in marriage, rather than being aimed at prohibiting other qualifications. As stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"It should be given only to a *śrotriya* Brāhmaṇa who is an ascetic, who has directly studied the Vedas, and who is a celibate (*brahmacārin*) according to the prescribed rule.

Here, the meaning of the term "celibate" (*brahmacārin*) is as follows: one should perform the first marriage only after having maintained unbroken celibacy. If a celibate student should violate his vow of celibacy and approach a woman, he should marry a maiden only after performing the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) ordained by such rules as, "He shall sacrifice a *gardabha* (ass) as an animal offering," and so forth.
Kātyāyana states:
"Those who are insane, those who are outcastes, lepers, eunuchs, and those born of one's own lineage; those deprived of sight or hearing, as well as those afflicted by epilepsy."
"A wise man should not give his daughter to those who are unlearned, those who live far away, those who follow the path to liberation, or those who are warriors who have renounced worldly life.
Thus also says Parāśara:
"He who gives his daughter to an old man, to one of low status, to one who is ugly, or to one of evil character out of a desire for wealth—that man is born as a *preta*.
(Also in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*: [as follows])
"To one who is excellent yet devoid of virtue, to one who is aged yet wise,
to one who is poor yet foolish, to one who is diseased and contemptible,
and to one who is extremely prone to anger and exceedingly foul-mouthed."
He who gives away his own daughter to one who is lame, physically deformed, blind, deaf, dull-witted, mute, impotent, or an extreme sinner,
incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.

By giving one's daughter to a Vaiṣṇava who is peaceful, virtuous, young, and even a learned scholar, one obtains the merit of ten large ponds. He who, having taken charge of a maiden, sells her, [incurs great sin].
Through greed for wealth, he undergoes misfortune and goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell;
there, that sinner eats the urine and excrement of a maiden,
bitten by worms and crows for as long as fourteen Indras endure.

"At the end of that [life], he will certainly take birth in the womb of a disease-bearing creature, selling loads of meat and carrying them indeed day and night. The term *vṛddha* (old man) indicates one who is extremely weak. The term *jñānin* (wise man) indicates one who is indifferent to marriage. *Paṅgulaḥ* means one deprived of feet. "To an extremely sinful person" means to one possessed of a great sin (*mahāpātaka*). By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that there is fault for the recipient as well. "To a Vaiṣṇava" means to a devotee of Viṣṇu. The word "Viṣṇu" is indicative of Śiva and others as well. "By misfortune" means by the cause that is misfortune, namely, greed for wealth.
Yājñavalkya states:
"A bridegroom of the same caste who possesses these very qualities, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*),
who has been carefully examined for virility, who is young, wise, and beloved by the people [is recommended]."

In this context, all qualities—distinguished from the three specific qualities of having a brother, not having been previously married to another, and being younger—are extended by analogy. A *savarṇa* is one of the same caste (*samānavarṇa*). By the extension of qualities such as not being a *sapiṇḍa*, the cessation of *sapiṇḍya* on both sides is intended. Therefore, the moderns hold that *sapiṇḍya* in the bride, as defined by the groom, and *sapiṇḍya* in the groom, as defined by the bride, exist separately; it is not a single, co-occurring (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) relationship defined by both together. The examination of virility was stated by Nārada: "He whose seed floats in water, and whose urine is clear and frothy..."

"A man shall be characterized by these marks; one who is the opposite is a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍhaka*). Here, "seed" (*bīja*) refers to semen. "Resonant" (*hrādi*) means possessing sound. "Foamy" (*phenila*) means like foam.
The cause for examination has also been stated by that same [author]:
"Women were created for the sake of offspring; the woman is the field, which requires seed.
Indeed, the field should be given to the one who possesses the seed; one without seed does not deserve the field.
Thus it is said in the *Sāmudrika-śāstra*.
"One should first examine the lifespan and afterwards indicate the physical marks;
for what is the use of physical marks for men whose lifespan has already expired?
Thus, other marks as well should be consulted in works such as the *Sāmudrika* and *Tilaka*.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of an excellent bridegroom.
Now follows the nature of being superseded in marriage (*parivitti*) and so forth, along with their respective expiations.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him,
she whom he marries, the giver [of the girl], and the officiating priest as the fifth— all these go to hell."

The meaning is that the girl with whom a man marries while she is still a maiden (parivindati) also goes to hell. Regarding the compound *dātṛyājakapañcamāḥ*: the analysis of the compound is that the giver (*dātṛ*) and the officiating priest (*yājaka*) are the "giver and priest" (*dātṛyājakau*); those for whom the bridegroom (*parivettṛ*), the one whose younger brother married first (*parivitti*), and the maiden (*kanyā*) have these two as the fifth—that is, completing the number five—are called *dātṛyājakapañcamāḥ*. Alternatively, the analysis is: the giver and the priests are the "giver and priests" (*dātṛyājakāḥ*); those for whom these are the ones completing the number five. The term *yājaka* refers to a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*).

Alternatively, the term *yājakapañcama* means one for whom a sacrificer (*yājaka*) is the fifth. The term *dātṛyājakapañcama* refers to those for whom both a donor (*dātṛ*) and a sacrificer (*yājaka*) are the fifth; all such persons, as well as those previously mentioned, go—that is, enter—hell.
The nature of the *parivitti* (the younger brother who marries before his elder) and others has been described by that same author:
"He who enters into the union of marriage and the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried]..."
"He is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother), while the elder brother is a *parivitti*."
For this very reason, Garga says:

"While the elder uterine brother remains [unmarried], one should not take a wife, nor establish the domestic fire (āvasathya), nor perform the formal consecration of the fires (ādhāna); otherwise, he becomes an outcast."
The meaning is: while the elder uterine brother remains unmarried.
And so Manu says:
"If the elder brother remains in the state of celibacy, the younger brother who takes a wife..."
"He who marries before his elder brother is a *parivettṛ*, while the elder brother is a *parivitti*."
Śātātapa states that there is no fault [in marrying] the sons of a paternal uncle, those born of a different womb, and so forth:
"Even when the sons of a paternal uncle, the son of a co-wife, the sons of another's wife,
and even elder brothers are present, [the marriage] of younger brothers [is permitted]."

"There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] when there is union with a wife and the *agnihotra*. Those born of a co-wife are *sāpatnāḥ*, meaning those born of a stepmother. Sons of another's wife are those born from adultery, or those such as adopted sons (*dattaka*) and so forth.
Gautama also says:

"There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] in the case of one whose womb is different, an adopted son, or the son of a paternal uncle, provided he is the eldest, when there is union with a wife and the sacred fire."
This also applies to the first marriage, the installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), and so forth.
And thus says Maṇḍana:
"The New Moon sacrifice (*darśeṣṭi*), the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāseṣṭi*), the Soma sacrifice (*somejyā*), and the collection of the fires (*agnisaṃgraha*)."
The Agnihotra and marriage are established as being performed at the first ritual application.

"One should not perform [the rite] if the father, the eldest brother, or even a uterine brother does not do so. Sumantu states that the kindling of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) may take place with permission: "If the eldest brother remains [inactive] and does not undertake the kindling of the fires at all..."
"But having been permitted, one should act according to the word of Śaṅkha."
By her command, only the formal assumption of the sacred fires and so forth takes place, but not the marriage itself.
Thus Hārīta says: "How can one among all uterine brothers become a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder)?"
"They are distinguished by their wives, not by the Agnihotra nor by sacrifice."
In the phrase "dārais tu," the word *tu* (but) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Regarding the matter of maidens, Garga states:
"In the case of marrying a woman who has already married when there are sisters born of the same mother, [there is a fault] in superseding one who has sons."
"There would be a fault among all castes, but there is no fault when they have different mothers."
Regarding uterine brothers, Kātyāyana states:
"Those residing in another country, eunuchs, those equal to Śūdras, uterine brothers addicted to prostitutes, those with testicular disease, outcasts, and those who are chronically ill— "
Those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, hunchbacked, dwarfs, or crippled; those who are very old, those without wives, those devoted to agriculture, and those belonging to the king.
"One who marries a younger sister does not incur fault if [the elder sister] is addicted to the increase of wealth, or likewise acts out of lust, or is a deceiver, insane, or diseased."

The impotent (*klība*) are those who lack virility regarding sexual intercourse with women. Those equal to Śūdras (*śūdratulya*) are those who follow the duties of Śūdras. Those attached to courtesans (*veśyāsakta*) are those who take delight in courtesans. Those with deformed testicles (*kuvṛṣaṇa*) have contemptible testicles. The fallen (*patita*) are those who have fallen away from Brahminhood. Those with excessive diseases (*atiroga*) are those afflicted by consumption, epilepsy, leprosy, and so forth. Those beginning with the dull-witted (*jaḍa*) and ending with the dwarfs (*vāmana*) are well known. The lame (*khelaka*) are those with broken feet. The very old (*ativṛddha*) are well known. The wifeless (*abhārya*) are perpetual celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*). Those who do not act out of desire (*kāmato'kārin*) are those who have desisted from marriage and other such acts through their own will.

*Kuhakas* are those intent on vain efforts for the sake of deceiving others. In some places, the reading *kuṭila* (crooked) appears in place of *kuhaka*. In this context, when there exist those such as eunuchs (*klība*) who are entirely disqualified from marriage, there is no fault in superseding [the elder brother] even without a specific time restriction.

Hemādri states that there is no fault for those who perform *parivedana* (marrying before an elder brother) after waiting for the time specified below, provided that the elder brothers are eligible for marriage at some future time due to being in another country, being excessively attached to a detached courtesan, being like a Śūdra, being addicted to agriculture, being dependent on a king, being obsessed with the increase of wealth, being prone to lust, being a liar, or being deceitful and a thief.
Regarding the case of an elder uterine brother who has gone to another country, Vasiṣṭha states the limit of the waiting period:
"If one does not wait for an elder brother who has not married for twelve or eight years..."
"He becomes liable for penance.
Regarding this, Hemādri states: For an elder brother who has gone to another country for the sake of dharma or for the sake of wealth, one must wait twelve years.
And so says the Smṛti:
"But for twelve years, it is proper for the elder brother to wait, being heard from again and again, on account of the pursuit of dharma and artha."

The phrase "through connection with dharma and artha" is intended as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *vidyā* (sacred learning) as well. For this very reason, Gautama, having introduced the topic with "when the husband has disappeared," and having stated the period for a wife’s waiting upon her husband as "twelve years for a Brāhmaṇa in connection with [the pursuit of] sacred learning," further declared: "In the same way, when an elder brother has disappeared, the younger brother [waits] regarding the marriage of a maiden and the rites of establishing the sacred fires. "When the husband has disappeared" means when it is unknown where he has gone; that is to say, when he has gone to an extremely distant land.

When a husband has gone to another country for the purpose of acquiring knowledge due to a connection with learning, his Brāhmaṇa wife should wait for twelve years and then perform the rites pertaining thereto. Likewise, if a younger Brāhmaṇa brother has gone to another country for the purpose of acquiring knowledge while the elder brother remains, the younger brother should wait for twelve years and then perform the marriage, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), and the *iṣṭi* sacrifices. However, if he has gone to another country for the sake of some other business, there are two options: ten or eight years. This is what is intended here.

When one who has gone to another country has accomplished his intended purpose and the possibility of his return has ceased, if the younger brother subsequently enters into union with the wife and the *agnihotra* fire, the fault consisting of being a "supplanter" (*parivettṛ*) does not occur.

In exactly the same way, even in the case of those excessively attached to courtesans and the like, if they remain in that state for some time and their inherent disposition is ascertained such that the possibility of marriage has ceased, there is no fault if the younger brother subsequently performs the marriage and so forth.
With this very intention, Sumantu also stated:
"If the elder brother is either addicted to vices, an atheist,
or otherwise unfit, while the younger brother desires to practice dharma, he may then perform the fire-consecration (ādhāna)."

The mention of *ādhāna* (the formal establishment of the sacred fires) is intended as an elliptical indicator for *vivāha* (marriage) as well. However, those who are impotent (*klība*) and so forth, being by their very nature entirely unfit for marriage, should not be waited for even for a limited period of time. Twelve years is the primary rule; eight years is the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*).
On this point, Garga states a specific qualification:
"One should wait for a man who has gone abroad for three years, even if one is in a hurry."
If she has not heard that he is away on a journey, she may perform [the rite] at the end of three years.
"But when he has returned, one should perform a quarter-penance for the sake of purification."
A quarter [of the penance] is the *pādakṛcchra*.
Kārṣṇājini says: "One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, an outcast, or even a eunuch..."
"And one suffering from the disease of consumption (rājayakṣmā) ought not to be waited for."
Now follows this expiation.
Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "The one who marries before his elder brother and the giver [of the girl] shall perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances."

"Having given her to him, he should enter [the house] again and marry her. Regarding this, Aparārka states: "The elder brother should marry her who was married by the younger brother; for since the status of being a wife as defined by the younger brother does not arise through an unscriptural marriage, she is fit to be married by the elder. The younger brother, however, should marry another woman. Hārīta, after describing the year-long vow (*abdavrata*) for the elder brother, has stated that the elder must indeed marry another: "When the year of the elder brother is completed, they should present that girl to the elder brother."
"Having obtained her permission, he may enter [another marriage] with another woman; thus the Dharma is not violated.

Therefore, the meaning of Vasiṣṭha’s rule is that the younger brother who has married before his elder (the *parivettṛ*) should perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, and then, having informed his elder—who is like a teacher—of his wife (just as one offers alms to a teacher), and having received the elder's permission, he should marry that very same woman in order to avoid the reproach of having superseded his elder. In this regard, the following settlement of the law applies: if the elder is present and the act was committed unintentionally, the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, as well as the fourfold vow prescribed by Yājñavalkya, should be applied according to the caste, capacity, and other relevant factors.

However, in the case of a marriage performed out of desire in the presence [of the family] with the permission of the girl’s father and others, the penance is that prescribed by Manu for three months.

As for what Sumantu says—"For the elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (parivitti), the younger brother who so marries (parivettṛ), the giver of the girl, and the officiating priest, the penance is eating of barley-meal (saktu) for twelve nights and the satiation of Brahmins; they call her a 'remarried woman' (punarbhū), and one should not approach her again"—that refers specifically to Śūdras.
As for that which Yama says:
"In the case of marrying a younger brother before the elder, there are two *kṛcchra* penances for the two [brothers] and one *kṛcchra* for the maiden;
the giver should perform an *atikṛcchra*, and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*."

Thus, due to ignorance of this, it pertains to the *kṣatriya* subject. For both the *parivettṛ* (the younger brother who marries before the elder) and the *parivitti* (the elder brother whose wife is married by the younger), there are two *kṛcchra* penances each.
The nature of the *agredidhiṣū* has been stated by Devala:
"If the younger sister is married while the elder sister remains unmarried..."
"She who is known as the *agredidhiṣū* is the one previously designated as the *didhiṣū*."
Vasiṣṭha states this expiation:

"The husband of an *agredidhiṣū* should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, and then marry her; the husband of a *didhiṣū*, having performed a *kṛcchra* and an *atikṛcchra*, should give her back to him and then marry again. According to the *Mitākṣarā* and the *Kalpataru*, the husband of an *agredidhiṣū* should perform a *prājāpatya* penance and then marry that same elder sister who was previously married by another; whereas the husband of a *didhiṣū*, having performed a *kṛcchra* and an *atikṛcchra*, should give his own married elder sister to the man who previously married the younger one and then marry another woman.
There is also another explanation in the *Smṛtyasāra*:
"The husband of the younger sister, having performed the penance for twelve nights, may marry that same woman he previously wedded once the marriage of the elder sister has taken place.

The husband of the elder sister, however, having performed the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, should offer his own wedded wife to the husband of the younger sister like alms received by a celibate student; then, with her permission, he may marry that very elder sister. In the *Aparārka*, however, the term "husband of the *didhiṣū*" (*didhiṣūpati*) is read in the place of "husband of the *agredidhiṣū*" (*agredidhiṣūpati*), and the term "husband of the *agredidhiṣū*" is read in the place of "husband of the *didhiṣū*"; thus, there is an option regarding the penance.
Thus ends the nature of the *parivitti* (the younger brother who marries before the elder) and others, as well as their penance.
Now, regarding the *kūṭas* (frauds):
thereon are the verses composed by me—

Only after examining the *kūṭas* (astrological configurations) should a marriage be performed so that it brings auspicious results; otherwise, it will cause misfortune. Therefore, I shall now describe them. ||1||
Although the sages have described as many peaks as there are cases of consumption (yakṣman), even among those, eight essential peaks have been proclaimed by them. || 2 ||

Caste, subjugation, lunar mansion, birth-source, the two groups of birds, as well as the zodiac sign and the nāḍī—these are the eight kūṭas; among them, each subsequent one is stronger than the preceding. (3)

O Brahmins, after Capricorn, there is a single quality; the auspicious ones follow in ascending order: Pisces and Cancer are the abodes of the Brahmins, while Aries, Capricorn, and Sagittarius belong to the Kṣatriyas.
The Vaiśya [signs] are Taurus, Leo, and Scorpio; the Śūdra [signs] are Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius.
If the groom belongs to a superior caste in this case, it will likewise be auspicious.
If a maiden of superior caste should be obtained through a boon, that will then bring inauspicious results;
for human beings, those born of water are to be eaten, and all others are to be brought under control, except for Hari.
All zodiac signs except Scorpio are favorable to Leo;
for the human sign [Aquarius], Cancer, Capricorn, Pisces, and Leo are its enemies.
All matters concerning subjugation, food, and so forth are to be understood according to worldly convention.
One should count the asterism of the bride from the asterism of the groom, and the asterism of the maiden from the asterism of the groom. (8)
When both results are divided by nine, the remainders are three, five, and seven;
these have been proclaimed as undesirable by Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and others.

The horse-eater, elephant-eater, ram-eater, snake-eater, and serpent-eater; the dog-eater, goat-eater, rat-eater, and *bhugundura*; the rat-eater, cow-eater, buffalo-eater, and likewise the buffalo-eater. (10)

The tiger, the deer, the antelope, the dog, the monkey, the snake, the enemy of snakes (the peacock), the ape, the lion, the horse, the lion, the cow, and the elephant are recorded as the origins of the Aśvinīs and the other [nakṣatras].
They are numbered in sequence by one, two, and so on; now, their state of enmity is described.
A lion and an elephant, a buffalo and a horse, a cat and a mouse, and likewise a dog and a deer. || 12 ||
The monkey and the ram, the cow and the tiger, and the mongoose and the snake are natural enemies;
this enmity between the bridegroom and the bride must be considered in every way by the wise. (13)
Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, the Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn, and Jupiter are remembered as the lords of the signs beginning with Aries. (14)
Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are enemies; Venus and Mercury are neutral;
and for the Moon, the Sun and Mercury are friends, while the remaining planets are neutral. (15)
The Moon, the Sun, and Jupiter are to be known as the friends of Mars;
Mercury is his enemy; and Venus and Saturn are proclaimed to be neutral. (16)
For Mercury, Venus and the Sun are friends; the Moon is indeed its enemy;
and Jupiter, Saturn, and Mars are proclaimed to be neutral. (17)
The friends of Jupiter are known to be the Sun, the Moon, and Mars;
Mercury and Venus are his enemies, while Saturn is considered neutral. (18)
For Kavi (Venus), Mercury and Saturn are friends; the Moon and the Sun are considered enemies;
and Mars and Jupiter are declared to be neutral. (19)
For Saturn, Venus and Mercury are friends; the Sun, Moon, and Mars are enemies;
and Jupiter is declared to be neutral. (20)
Aśvinī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Svātī, Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, and Revatī—these are remembered as the groups of deities (devagaṇas). || 21 ||
Bharaṇī, Rohiṇī, Ārdrā (Raudra), the three Pūrvās, and the three known as the Uttarās—these asterisms are proclaimed to belong to human beings. || 22 ||
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Maghā, Āśleṣā, Viśākhā, Citrā, Śatabhiṣaj, Kṛttikā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are proclaimed to be the Rākṣasa constellations. (23)
One should know that [a battle] within one's own group is excellent, while one between gods and humans is middling;
a conflict between gods and asuras leads to strife, whereas one between humans and rākṣasas results in death.
In the second and twelfth houses there will be poverty; in the sixth and eighth, there will be poison.
In the ninth house there will be childlessness; however, in the remaining houses, it will be auspicious. (25)
There is also a distinction regarding the remainder; that is now declared in its entirety.
The divisions of the Vedas for each [lunar day] have been proclaimed by the astronomers. (26)

When the asterisms are different but the zodiacal sign is the same, it is "different asterisms, same sign"; when the zodiacal sign is different but the asterism is the same, it is "same sign, different asterisms"; and when both the zodiacal sign and the quarter of the asterism are the same, it is "same sign, same quarter of the asterism. (27)
The last [sign] should be known as censurable; in the remaining cases, it would be auspicious.
If the signs are equal, such as Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, and so forth, they correspond to the true seasons and the elephants.
If it should be joined with the sixth [house], then this is remembered as auspicious;
for Taurus is an even sign, and therefore the sixth [from it] is indeed Libra.
However, that [aspect] should be understood as being associated with her [the wife] due to the state of friendship between the two spouses;
whereas in the eighth house, it is associated with the state of enmity between the two spouses. (30)
If, however, in the twelfth house there are two even signs together with a second [even sign], then it bestows auspicious results; the opposite is considered inauspicious. || 31 ||
Even a lion that is fierce is proclaimed to be excellent when accompanied by a female;
[the asterisms] Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Hasta, Ārdrā, Śatabhiṣaj, and Punarvasu. (32)
Pūrvā Bhādrapadā, Uttarā Phalgunī, and Aśvinī have the first nāḍikā [as their auspicious period];
likewise Puṣya, Mṛgaśiras, Citrā, Anurādhā, and Bharaṇī. (33)
Dhaniṣṭhā and the others, as well as Āṣāḍhā, Pūrvaphālgunī, and Uttarabhādrapadā, are known as the middle nāḍikās. || 34 ||

Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Maghā, Āśleṣā, Viśākhā, the last Āṣāḍhā, Śravaṇa (Vaiṣṇava), and Revatī— these are the constellations with terminal nāḍīs. If a marriage occurs within a single nāḍī of these, death is declared to follow.
If there should be a lack of a bride for the castes beginning with the Brahmins, then [this shall apply]. || 36 ||
It should be performed in the Pārśva-nāḍī in the region south of the Godāvarī;
in every respect, the Madhyamā nāḍī must be avoided by the wise.
The "Bāṇānanda" yoga, consisting of two divine [units], is considered auspicious due to the friendship of the planets;
the "Ṣaḍaṣṭaka," declared through the six [operations] beginning with subjugation (vaśya), bestows auspicious results. (38)
When the bride belongs to the class of men and the groom to the class of Rākṣasas, that union of two who possess true and excellent friendship bestows auspiciousness. || 39 ||
When the group of Rākṣasas is female and the human group is male, then,
by means of the six [operations] beginning with auspicious subjugation (vaśya), the "man-far" (nṛdūra) is now described.

If a male asterism should be near a female asterism, then it is not auspicious; however, this very same configuration is proclaimed to be beneficial when there is friendship between the planets and the asterisms. (41)

If the [sum] is two times ten (twenty), there is copper and gold; if it is six or eight, a cow and a bull; if it is five times ten (fifty), silver and bell-metal; and if the [remaining] nadīs are one, there is a cow and so forth.
When there is superiority for us and equality between the two castes, one quality is said to exist therein;
when the person is inferior, the absence of qualities is declared. (43)
In the case of a subjugating food, however, the quality is half; the edibility of a creature should be understood according to its species.
There is a mutual twofold quality in friendship, but there is no such quality in the case of an enemy's food.
In the subjugation of enemies, there is one quality that is the enemy of men: deceit.
Due to its universal renown, this is declared to be the enemy of even the lion. (45)
If there is an auspicious conjunction on both sides, then three qualities are to be known;
if it is on only one side, then it is half of three [one and a half]; in the absence of a star, there is no quality at all.
In the *yonikūṭa* of two very friendly planets, four qualities are declared;
for two friendly planets, three are proclaimed; and in the case of their own nature (*svabhāva*), two qualities are traditionally taught. (47)
There may be a single virtue between two equals, but there is no virtue in great enmity; such is the case with the lion and the elephant, as well as with the mongoose and the serpent. (48)
The natural qualities of the cow and the tiger, the deer and the dog, the owl and the mouse, as well as the goat and the monkey, and the horse and the mare, have thus been declared.
Sometimes, even among those born of the same species, there may be mutual enmity—between two elephants, two lions, two horses, two dogs, or even between a dog and a mouse. (50)
In this manner, wise men should also infer the case of friendship according to worldly convention;
for here, when two parties share a common overlordship or are friends, there are five mutual advantages. (51)

If there is equality in both friendliness and enmity, there are four units; if there is equality in the two [friendliness and neutrality], there are three units; in the case of friendship and enmity, there is one unit; and in the case of equality in enmity, there is half a unit. (52)
One should point out mutual enmity between planets and the absence of virtues; among these, six qualities are to be accepted, whether they belong to a god, a human, or a woman. (53)

In the case of the opposite [gender], there are five qualities; but when the genders are equal, there are six qualities. If the Daitya is male and the deity is female, then one quality is said to exist therein.

Vasiṣṭha and others have proclaimed that when the remaining [lunar day] lacks the [necessary] qualities, if there is a difficult conjunction (duṣkūṭa) and the friendship of the birth-signs (yonimaitra) is absent from the woman, then it is four [days]. (55)
