If these two are not present there, the absence of quality is proclaimed; if one of these two should exist, then a single quality is accepted. (56)

The absence of auspicious qualities in the *bhaikapāda* (the single-footed) has been declared here by the astrologers; however, when there is a favorable conjunction of constellations (*nakṣatra-kūṭa*), even that which is born of a base species is far superior.
In that case, there will be enmity; the wise should know the points (guṇas) to be equal to the [number of] syllables in the name.
When the asterisms are the same but the zodiacal signs differ, five points are proclaimed. || 58 ||
In the remaining *sukūṭa*, seven qualities are to be grasped by the wise;
in the division of the *nāḍīs*, there are eight qualities, but where none are mentioned, there is no quality.
In brief, I have described these eight types of deceptive speech according to my understanding. (59)
Thus end the *kūṭas*. Now follows the determination of the birth-ascendant (*janmarāśi*) and the name-ascendant (*nāmarāśi*).
In the *Jyotirnibandha*:

"In marriage, all auspicious ceremonies, journeys, and so forth, as well as in the transit of the planets, the birth ascendant (janmarāśi) is primary; one should not consider the name ascendant (nāmarāśi). In matters concerning a country, a village, a house, war, service, or legal affairs [the birth ascendant is likewise primary]."
"The predominance of the name-ascendant (nāmarāśi) applies when considering the birth-ascendant;
however, in matters of a kākīṇī coin, the purification of the vargas, giving, gambling, the onset of fever, mantras, and the marriage of a remarried woman, the name-ascendant holds primacy."

If, between the bride and the groom, the birth asterism (*janmarkṣa*) of one is known but that of the other is not known, then how should the examination of purity, conjunctions, and so forth be conducted? In response to this inquiry, the *Śārṅgadharīya* states: "In the arrangement of a marriage, one should consider the strength derived from the ascendant (*lagna*) and the planets;
if the birth [asterism] is not known, one should consider everything relative to the [bride's] natal asterism."

The meaning is: "from that lunar mansion (nakṣatra) which is established by the first letter of one's name. It should be understood that the determination of the lunar mansion by means of the first letter of the name is to be known from the *avakahaḍācakra* which will be described later.
Now, regarding the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and so forth;
concerning this, Vasiṣṭha says:

"One should construct a pavilion sixteen *aratnis* in size, adorned with four doors and provided with arches; there, one should prepare an altar. Alternatively, one may construct a pavilion measuring eight cubits or twelve cubits."
"Two-six-fold" means twelve-fold.
Also elsewhere:
"In all auspicious rites, the pavilion [should be] according to the measurement of the house."
"It should be sixteen cubits [in length], or less by one cubit down to ten; here, an altar is established in the center with exactly four pillars."

Regarding the phrase "according to the size of the house," the meaning is that in a large house the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be large, and in a small one, it should be smaller. The limit of "ten [cubits]" is the lower boundary for its size. Therefore, the eight-cubit pavilion mentioned by Vasiṣṭha pertains to cases of extreme distress. Furthermore, there is a reading in some places stating, "one should construct it as ten cubits," in which case the absence of contradiction with the proximate statement is quite evident. In the phrase "with four pillars," the word "is appropriate" (yuktā) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. And this is an adjective qualifying the altar (vedi). This altar is intended for the installation of the deity. Nārada says in the Pārijāta:
Raising it one cubit high and four cubits square on all sides,
with four very smooth pillars in the left part of the house,
level in the four directions, and beautifully adorned with staircases.

Sloping toward the northeast, it was adorned with pillars of plantain trees, with elephants, parrots, and other creatures marked by various ornaments, with diverse pitchers, with various arches and sprouts,
and with heaps of flowers and pigments that evoked the sentiment of love.
"With the auspicious words of blessing from the Brahmins, with three sacred lamps,
and with instrumental music, song, dance, and other such delights that gladden the heart— [the couple] should thus ascend that beautiful and auspicious altar containing the sacred fire."
On this matter, the authority is the girl who is to be consecrated:

"The altar should be made with five or seven cubits measured by the hands of the girl; it should be as high as the back of a tortoise. In a beautiful mansion, on the left side of the entrance, it should be provided with pillars and accompanied by the blessings of the bride and groom."

The term *āśiṣaiḥ* is a Vedic usage (*chāndasam*). By this, the view held by some that the measure of the boons (*vara*) should be accepted here is to be seen as refuted. "Sloping toward the east and north" means inclined toward the northeast. All the words ending in the instrumental case are to be construed with the word *samalaṃkṛtām* ("well-adorned"). The meaning is that it is adorned by elephants, parrots, and so forth, made of metal, wood, or clay, which are placed symmetrically on all sides. The meaning is that it is adorned by jars marked or inscribed with various colors.

It was adorned with clusters—meaning multitudes—of fragrant flowers such as *mālatī* and others that produce the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra*). It was beautified by pigments of various colors. By the phrase "with meritorious blessings of the Brahmins," it is indicated that at the time of the couple's ascending the altar, blessings must be bestowed by the Brahmins. It was delightful due to three lamps placed in front of the altar.

By the phrase "giving joy to the heart through instrumental music, song, dance, and so forth," it is indicated that instrumental music, song, dance, and the like should be performed at the time of the couple's ascent onto the altar (*vedi*). By the phrase "together with the fire on the altar" (*sāgnivedikām*), it is indicated that prior to the couple's ascent onto the altar, the preparation of the fire and other materials required for the *homa* sacrifice should be carried out upon the altar. This is under the interpretation where "with the fire" (*sāgni*) is an adjective qualifying the altar. If, however, "with the fire" is a separate word qualifying the couple and not part of the compound with "altar," [the meaning remains as described above].

In this view, it should be understood that at the time of ascending, the fire-altar (vedi) is to be prepared. A couple should ascend such an altar, characterized by the aforementioned qualities; the meaning is that the bridegroom should perform the ascent together with his bride. Keśavārka also says:
"One should construct the altar in such a way that it may be to the right of those entering."
"Public pavilions, barley sowing, and decorations should not take place on the first, ninth, or third days.

Here, "barley sowing" refers to the rite known as *aṅkurāropaṇa* (the planting of sprouts). "Public pavilion" (*janāśraya*) refers to a *maṇḍapa*. As Amarasimha states: "A *maṇḍapa* is a public pavilion, not feminine.
Regarding the number of days required for the construction of the pavilion and other structures, Nārada says:

"The ninth, third, and sixth days are unfavorable for the *navavāraka* [the sowing of seeds]; nor is the construction of the marriage pavilion (*vivāhamaṇḍapa*) auspicious even by way of a secondary alternative (*varṇaka*).

On the ninth, third, and sixth days, the *navavāraka*—which refers to the sowing of sprouts—is not auspicious. Nor is the construction of the marriage pavilion, even as a secondary alternative, auspicious on these days, such as the ninth. The intention is that if it were constructed according to the primary rule (*mukhyakalpa*), it should certainly not be done on these days. Some hold the view that a pavilion intended for the marriage itself is inauspicious if built even as a secondary alternative, whereas one intended for another purpose remains auspicious even when built as a secondary alternative.

*Daivajñamanohara*: "Excluding Citrā, Viśākhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Aśvinī, Jyeṣṭhā, and the four stars beginning with Ārdrā (Śivabhā), it is recommended for the offering of fruit, oil, and platforms, as well as for the threshing-floor pavilion and so forth."
The meaning is that one should exclude the four lunar mansions beginning with Śiva-bha (Ārdrā) and ending with Āśleṣā. Vyāsa states in the Hemādri:

"One should perform the threshing, pounding, preparation of barley-gruel, the construction of the pavilion, the clay for the altar, the painting of the colors, and all other related activities involving coming and going during the lunar mansion of the wedding."
*Yavāraka* is called *acikasa* in the vernacular.
Nārada, in the *Jyotirnibandha*, states: "It should be performed..."
At the outset, for the sake of auspiciousness, the planting of the seed-syllable (aṅkura-nyāsa) should be performed on the ninth,
seventh, fifth, or even the third day,
under a seed-constellation (bīja-nakṣatra), on an auspicious weekday, and during a favorable planetary rising.
Having properly decorated the houses with canopies, banners, and arches,
and having gone toward the northeast direction accompanied by musical instruments, dancing, and other festivities,
he returns after taking fine clay and sand from that place.
"Sands and clay-dust;
one should pour [the water] into vessels made of clay or else of bamboo,
combined with many kinds of seeds and adorned with water-flowers."

A specific rule in the *Jyotirnibandha* states: "Whatever limb [of the body] corresponds to whichever sign of the zodiac for a given person, one should apply the strength of the Moon there; however, this should not be considered in marriage, nor should it be performed before the third, sixth, ninth, or twelfth day."

The meaning of this is as follows: whatever limb (subsidiary rite) belongs to a particular primary action, one should perform that limb under the constellation prescribed for that primary action (*mukhya*). In this context, regarding such subsidiary actions, the strength of the Moon (*indu*) need not be observed or considered. However, there is a specific rule regarding marriage: one should not perform these marriage-related limbs on the third, sixth, or ninth day prior to the wedding day.
In that regard, the marriage-limbs are of nine kinds. As it is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*: "Crushing, husking, seasoning, and sweetmeats..."
"The barley-grain, the pavilion, the altar, the saffron, and likewise the cosmetic paste"—thus it is said.
"This [preparation] is a constituent part of the marriage; the wise employ these marriage-ornaments here, and do not consider the strength or weakness of the moon.
On the sixth, third, or ninth day from the auspicious moment (lagna), there is no requirement for the [specific] color, nor for the barley-grain, the pavilion, or the altar."
In the *Śārṅgadharīya*:
"The threshing, pounding, decorating, the altar, the sweeping of the house, the turn for the water-vessel, and the pavilion;
the grasping of the hand, and the coming and going—all these should be performed under the asterism of marriage."
"One should examine the entire marriage ceremony in the lunar mansion of the wedding; here, the strength of the moon is not required.
On the ninth, third, or sixth day prior to the wedding, there should be no application of unguents, nor the auspicious rites for the pavilion or the oil."

*Dalana* is the grinding of wheat and other grains into flour. *Kaṇḍana* is the cleaning of rice and other grains by striking them with a pestle and so forth. *Vyañjana* refers to items such as *parpaṭa*. *Modakas* are foods cooked in ghee. *Yavāra* (or *yavāraka*) is "chikasā"; the reading *vāraka* also exists. A *vāraka* is an auspicious water-pot (*maṅgalakalaśa*). A *maṇḍapa* is a pavilion for people to take shelter in. A *vedi* is a square altar for the bride and groom to sit upon. *Kuṅkuma* refers to fragrant substances and the like. *Varṇaka* refers to powders, red ochre, painting, and so forth.
By this, sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, and so forth are also included. "The entirety" refers to what was just mentioned.
Now, regarding the means for avoiding widowhood as indicated by the planets and other factors at the time of a girl's birth, it is stated in the *Karmavipāka*:
"Having invited a virtuous Brāhmaṇa and honored him with various offerings..."
To him, one should give an image of Viṣṇu with four arms according to the prescribed rite.
One should fashion an image of pure color, either made of gold or according to one's financial capacity,
beautiful and constructed with the conch, mace, discus, and lotus.
One should give her, who wears two yellow garments and a garland of white water-lilies and blue lotuses,
along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), while reciting this mantra:
In a previous birth, while I was killing [my husband] to prevent his reunion with his wife,
or else out of extreme aversion, I killed him with poison, potent herbs, weapons, and the like.
[They] encounter a most terrible [state] that robs one of fame, happiness, and wealth;
[this is done] for the destruction of the flood of great miseries such as widowhood and for the attainment of happiness.
O twice-born one, for the sake of attaining great good fortune, I bestow upon you this image of Mahāviṣṇu, fashioned from gold according to my ability.
Then, one should recite three times, "O sinless one, I am now [pure]";
having accepted his words with "So be it," one should enter one's own home.

In this context, the word "suvarṇa" denotes the species [of gold]. As for the quantity, it should be understood according to one's capacity as being either a *pala*, half a *pala*, or a quarter of a *pala*.
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*).

The maiden, having performed her ritual bath and sipping of water (ācamana), should announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall perform the gift of the image of Mahāviṣṇu, which removes widowhood. Having worshipped Gaṇeśa and invited a virtuous, humble, and learned Brāhmaṇa, she should appoint him as the officiating priest (ācārya). After worshipping him with various offerings according to her means, she should, through his hands, have the rite of removing the image from the fire (agnyuttāraṇa) performed, followed by the consecration of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and worship with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra). At the time of offering the garments, two yellow cloths should be given; at the time of offering flowers, a garland of white water-lilies and blue lotuses should also be given.
At the conclusion of the worship, having prostrated before the deity:
"Whatever [sin] was committed by me in a previous birth— by obstructing the union with my husband,
or by killing him with poison, potent herbs, weapons, and the like, out of extreme aversion— "
[They] encounter a most terrible [state] that robs one of fame, happiness, and wealth;
[this rite is performed] for the destruction of the flood of great miseries such as widowhood and for the attainment of happiness.
O twice-born one, for the sake of attaining great good fortune, I bestow upon you this image of Mahāviṣṇu, fashioned from gold according to my ability.
Having recited this, she should give it to the Brahmin.
Then, having given gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), she should say three times, "I am now sinless. The preceptor (*ācārya*) should reply three times, "So be it.
Then, having fed the Brahmins according to her means, she should dedicate the rite to the Lord of Action (*karmeśvara*). When this has been done, she becomes fit for marriage.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the image that removes widowhood. Now, the marriage of the water-jar (kumbhavivāha).
Alternatively, for the sake of avoiding widowhood, the marriage of the water-jar should be performed. That has been described in that very same [text]:
On the day prior to the wedding, when the moon and stars are in a favorable position and at the auspicious time prescribed for the marriage,
one should marry the maiden with a water-pot.
Thereafter, one should wrap [the vessel] with a thread according to the rule of ten strands;
the jar, adorned like a body, [should be placed] in a secluded chamber for those two.
Then, having removed the jar and broken it in the reservoir of water,
one should perform the consecration with the waters of the five sprouts.

The syntactical connection is as follows: one should wrap both the jar, which is adorned all around with sandalwood paste, flowers, and other offerings, and the body of the girl. Then, in the temple associated with those two, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) is as follows: the performer of the girl’s marriage, having sipped water (*ācamana*), restrained his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), and proclaimed the place and time, makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the jar-marriage (*kumbhavivāha*) for this girl, which removes widowhood. Having performed the rites beginning with the worship of Gaṇeśa up to the *nāndī-śrāddha*, he performs the rite of bringing down the fire (*agnyuttāraṇa*) upon the images of Varuṇa and Viṣṇu, and then establishes the jar according to the procedure beginning with the mantra "Mahī dyauḥ" (Earth and Heaven).

Having performed the worship of Varuṇa in that pitcher containing the image of Varuṇa upon which the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* has been established, and having worshipped Viṣṇu in the image of Viṣṇu placed in the water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon which the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* has likewise been established, one should pray as follows: "O refuge of all living beings, whose very nature is the limb of Varuṇa, revive the husband of this maiden; grant her the wonderful joy of sons."
"O Lord Viṣṇu, grant me a boon; protect this maiden from her suffering."

Then, having offered [the girl] with the words, "I offer this maiden, who is Śrī in form, to the jar which is Viṣṇu in form," and having wrapped both the jar and the maiden—repeating the mantras both below and above—with the wrapping mantras to be recited hereafter beginning with *pari tvā*, he should remove the jar, break it (or sprinkle it) in a body of water, and bathe the maiden with pure water and the five sprouts while reciting the mantras beginning with *samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ*. Then he should feed the Brāhmaṇas. This is the ritual for the Jar-Marriage (*kumbhavivāha*). Now follows the ritual for the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*).
In the Kaśyapa-saṃhitā: "Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the excellent selection of a bride,
as well as her proper bestowal, which increases one's sons and grandsons."
On a day when the five limbs are pure, endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars,
under the constellations prescribed for marriage, and on a day excluding Tuesday.
Having avoided the first day of the month, as well as the Riktā days, the eighth, and the ninth,
on any other day one should [worship] with perfumes, garlands, rice, fruits, and so forth.
Accompanied by a group of elderly brahmins, he should choose a virtuous maiden;
"So be it," says her father on a day when the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) prescribed for choosing a bride is in effect.
One should perform the giving away of the daughter, preceded by the recitation of auspicious prayers,
to a bridegroom who is handsome and endowed with noble lineage, good character, and virtue.
Then he should give him a maiden adorned with white garments and ornaments,
accompanied by auspicious sounds and the benedictory words of the Brahmins.
Having first performed the worship of Śacī, one should afterwards perform everything else;
[she] who is golden-hued, lotus-petal-eyed, and adorned with divine garlands and garments.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
she illuminated the quarters of the sky with her priceless garlands of jewels.
Having meditated upon that goddess Kumārī, who is served day and night by throngs of thousands of playful women, and having prostrated before her, one should then offer this prayer:
"O Queen of the Gods, salutations to you, O beloved wife of the Lord of the Gods!
Grant me marriage, fortune, health, and the birth of a son."
The asterisms have been stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*: "With Viśvā, the three beginning with Pūrvā, Karṇa, the pair [of Aśleṣā], Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, and Anurādhā—these are the asterisms for marriage.
Facing west, he should choose that maiden who faces east, is well-attired, and is offered fruits and other gifts."

Viśvarkṣa refers to Uttarāṣāḍhā. The three Pūrvas refer to Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā. Karṇayugma refers to Śravaṇa and Dhaniṣṭhā. Agni refers to Kṛttikā; Maitra refers to Anurādhā. In another Smṛti:
"The best of the twice-born should perform the formal betrothal (vāgdāna) during the month of marriage."
"One should perform the construction of the pavilion and other such rites in either the sacrificial fire-chamber or the wedding hall."
The *dhiṣṇya* is a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
Caṇḍeśvara also states regarding the choosing of a bridegroom: "The sacred thread, fruit, flowers, and various garments..."
"The father of the girl, or the twice-born [husband], should give her to the suitor at the time of the formal choosing."
Now, the procedure for that [rite]:

At an auspicious moment indicated by an astrologer, the father of the groom or another relative, accompanied by beloved kinsmen, elders, respectable persons, and women, and preceded by the sounds of auspicious musical instruments and the observation of favorable omens, shall go to the girl’s house and sit in the courtyard.

Then, a certain elder shall say to the father of the girl: "This son of yours is a groom; for his sake, I have come with friends to request your daughter. After you have deliberated with your own people, please grant permission for these men to worship the girl."

Then the father of the girl, having obtained the permission of those worthy of honor, as well as his beloved kinsmen and others, should grant them leave, saying, "I have given her; this is my permission for the sake of worship.

Thereafter, the family priest or another officiant should seat the girl—facing east, dressed in white garments, adorned with ornaments, and elegantly attired—upon a four-legged throne covered with a bright cloth, while reciting the two mantras: "Oṃ anṛkṣarā ṛjavaḥ santu panthāḥ... and "Oṃ devīṃ vācamajanayanta devāḥ...".

Then, the father of the groom, sitting facing west in front of the bride and near the father of the bride and others, having first performed the remembrance of Gaṇapati and other deities, should say to the father of the bride: "For this groom named Amuka Śarmā, born of the [Amuka] gotra and endowed with the [Amuka] pravara, the great-grandson of [Amuka], the grandson of [Amuka], and the son of [Amuka]; we choose this girl named Amukā, born of the [Amuka] gotra and endowed with the [Amuka] pravara, the great-granddaughter of [Amuka], the granddaughter of [Amuka], and the daughter of [Amuka], for the sake of her becoming his wife."

The giver, having obtained the consent of his wife, beloved ones, kinsmen, and others, should say, "Choose [me]," either after reciting the previously mentioned formula or without reciting it; this should be repeated twice. Then the giver should say loudly three times, "I shall give.

Thereafter, the father of the bride, having smeared the bride's joined palms with saffron and fragrant paste, should request her from his beloved kinsmen and others. They should reply, "She is Mahālakṣmī.
Then the father of the bride, having smeared the bride's forehead with sandalwood paste, should have the *nīrājana* ceremony performed by the auspicious women (*suvāsinī*) of his own party.

Then, having applied rice grains and unbroken *akṣata* seeds to her forehead and given her garments with the mantra "yuvam vastrāṇi," one should give her ornaments with the mantra "agne retaścandra hiraṇyam.

Then, having worshipped her with fruits using the mantra "yāḥ phalinīḥ," and having placed fruit, betel leaves, and other offerings into her hand, the learned authorities maintain that one should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) at the conclusion of the proclamation of place and time, saying: "I shall perform the worship of the maiden (*kanyā-pūjana*). However, it is more appropriate that there be no such formal resolve at all.

The father of the girl, however, should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the betrothal (*vāgdāna*) of my daughter. It is more appropriate to say that this too is a formal resolve. Then both [the bridegroom’s and the bride’s fathers] should perform the worship of Gaṇapati according to custom, as well as the worship of Varuṇa in the water-pot (*kalaśa*), and the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). If local custom permits, the recitation for auspiciousness (*svastivācana*) should also be performed here. Then the bridegroom’s father, sitting to the south of the girl facing north, or to her left facing east, should honor the girl with perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, garments, and other offerings.

Then the giver of the girl, having seated the father of the bridegroom facing east and sitting himself facing west before him, should honor him with perfumes, betel, and other offerings; and he [the bridegroom's father] should likewise honor the giver.

Then the giver, according to custom, taking a piece of turmeric, five firm betel nuts along with scents and unbroken rice, and saying: "To the bridegroom named [Name], son of [Name], grandson of [Name], great-grandson of [Name], born in the [Name] lineage and possessing the [Name] pravaras; I give this maiden named [Name], my daughter, born in the [Name] lineage and possessing the [Name] pravaras, the great-granddaughter of [Name], granddaughter of [Name], and daughter of myself, [Name], at the auspicious moment indicated by the astrologer," and thus having formally surrendered her by word—[he adds]: "O you who are free from physical defects, not fallen from caste, not impotent, and devoid of the ten blemishes..."

"I shall give this girl in the presence of the gods, the fire, and the twice-born. Having spoken thus, the father of the bridegroom should cast [the ring] into the hem of the garment; then, having tied a knot in the hem of the garment with the consecration mantra "narya prajāṃ," it should be smeared with sandalwood paste—this is the practice established by tradition. In the case of a verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*) performed by the grandfather, one should say "mine" (*mama*) even before the word "granddaughter" (*pautrīm*). Similarly, in the case of a betrothal performed by the great-grandfather due to family lineage, one should say "mine" before "great-granddaughter" (*prapautrīm*). However, when the betrothal is performed by a brother or others, the word "mine" is never used at all.

Then, having likewise taken a piece of turmeric, five fragrant unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and five firm betel nuts (*pūgīphala*), the father of the bride or others should say: "In the matter of the bridegroom named *amuka-śarman*, born of the *gotra* named *amuka* and belonging to the *pravara* named *amuka*, may you all be of one mind. Having thus cast these into the hem of the garment of the bride’s father or others as before, he should tie a knot and mark it with sandalwood paste. Then the giver of the girl should say to the father of the bridegroom: "The girl has been given by me through word; she has been accepted by you for the sake of your son. You have become the one decided upon in the rite of viewing the bride; may you be happy."
"The maiden has been given by you in word; she has been accepted by me for the sake of my son. You have been chosen in the rite of selecting the bridegroom; may you be happy.

Thus should the father of the bridegroom speak to the father of the maiden. In the case of a marriage for a grandson and so forth, the appropriate modification should be made in both instances as follows: "for the sake of my grandson," "for the sake of my brother," "for the sake of my friend," or "for the sake of my kinsman. Alternatively, one may simply say everywhere: "she has been accepted for the sake of the bridegroom."

Then the Brahmins should say: "May the waters be auspicious; may there be goodwill; may there be well-being and freedom from misfortune; may there be long life, prosperity, peace, nourishment, and contentment; may this be true for you.

Then the donor should have the worship of Śacī performed for the sake of increasing the prosperity of the marriage, good fortune, and so forth. Some authorities also desire that a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) be made here:
[one should worship her] "who is golden-hued, lotus-petal-eyed, and adorned with divine garlands and garments."
Endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
she illuminated the quarters of the sky with her priceless strings of jewels,
while being attended day and night by throngs of thousands of graceful women.
Having thus meditated upon Indrāṇī, the bride should perform the worship with offerings such as the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth upon a heap of white rice.
Then:
"O Indrāṇī, goddess, salutations to you, O beloved wife of the lord of gods!"

One should cause [the bridegroom] to offer this prayer: "Grant me marriage, fortune, health, and the birth of a son. Thereafter, the matrons should perform auspicious rites such as the *nīrājana* (waving of lights). The Brahmins, having been honored with perfumes, betel, and other offerings, should recite the benedictory mantras. They are as follows: 1. *Oṃ samiddhasya śraya... for great good fortune.* 2. *Oṃ vanaspate śatavalśo... for great good fortune.* 3. *Oṃ saṃdivye nadī... for great good fortune.* 4. *Oṃ narya prajāṃ me... established.* 5. *Oṃ tadastu mitrā... for the sake of the seat.*
One should also recite: "Oṃ, houses are indeed the foundation; may that hymn be the foundation.
This concludes the procedure for the giving of the bride's hand (*vāgdāna*). Now follows the groom’s journey to the bride’s house.
The procedure for that has been stated by Śaunaka: "At an auspicious moment, a twice-born man should perform the marriage according to the rules;
there he should perform the *ābhyudayika* śrāddha and cause the benediction (*svasti*) to be recited."
On the following day, having bathed,
wearing clean garments, adorned with perfumes, garlands, and other ornaments, and accompanied by an auspicious omen,
the bridegroom, after feeding the Brahmins, performed the rite of declaring the "Puṇyāha" (the auspicious day).
Having performed the tying of the marriage thread and being accompanied by friends, kinsmen, and others,
he should mount a suitable vehicle and proceed to the bride's house;
standing outside its door, facing eastward, he is met by those coming toward him.
"Having been welcomed by the women of the bride's house with full water-jars and other vessels held in their hands,
he should enter the home together with his kinsmen."

One should perform the *ābhyudayika* śrāddha. In the phrase "one should cause the *svasti* to be recited," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is understood as being included within the meaning; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the rule that "the father shall perform the *nāndī* śrāddha."

Regarding the statement "the father should perform the *nāndīśrāddha*," the mention of the *nāndīśrāddha* is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the recitation of the *svastivācana* and other rites, as such is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). According to the view that only the *nāndīśrāddha* is performed by the father while the *svastivācana* is performed by the groom, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the phrase "he should cause the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* to be performed" must be understood in one instance [referring to the *svastivācana*]. Some maintain that because of the rule "having performed the *puṇyāhavācana*," the groom must perform the *puṇyāhavācana* with five formulas at the time of going to the bride's house;
others hold that this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Thus concludes the groom’s journey toward the bride’s house.
Now, the procedure for the worship of Gaurī and Hara.
In the *Saṃgraha*: "On the day of the wedding, the Mothers are to be worshipped; Gaurī, accompanied by Hara, is to be worshipped."
On a pedestal, or in its absence, on a very smooth surface strewn with rice,
one should have a lotus fashioned and there worship Gaurī and Hara;
the rows of vessels should be made with water-pots, topped with lids.
One should place [the vessels] upon rice at the four corners of the directions;
then, one should fashion images of Gaurī and Hara from a pala of gold.
In that regard—
one should fashion Nandin in front with two *pala*s of silver;
however, one who is incapable may do so with half of that, or a quarter, or according to his ability.
If these are unavailable, one should write [the names] with saffron and other substances and worship them;
having meditated upon the two deities with the mantra, the wise person should worship them with devotion.
The Goddess of gods, seated upon a lion-throne and adorned with all ornaments;
and the God, wearing yellow garments and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
With his lower right hand he holds a jar filled with nectar,
while with his left he displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, embracing his slender beloved.
"Having meditated thus and worshipped Gaurī, those women who possess merit may thereafter certainly marry a maiden according to the prescribed injunctions."
The mantra for worship is found in that very same place: "O Gaurī and Hara, the Great Lords, bestowers of all auspiciousness!
O Sovereign Deities, accept this worship and grant us perpetual auspiciousness."
Likewise:
"One should then light a wick made of twenty-seven threads, with a size equal to that of a maiden's body, for the sake of the successful completion of the vow."
"Brahmins who are worthy of food and well-dressed women should be well-honored;
one should satisfy ten, eight, five, or a pair of them with gold."
Regarding the joint meal of the bride and groom at the wedding, the author of the Saṃgraha states: "One who has been initiated by his mother should eat with his wife during the wedding;
if he eats with her on any other occasion, that man incurs loss of caste."

In the Prāyaścittakāṇḍa of Hemādri, Gālava also states: "A Brāhmaṇa incurs no fault by traveling in the same vehicle, eating from the same vessel, or [sharing] a marriage, a journey, or a pilgrimage."
"Otherwise, one incurs a fault and should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the Smṛtiratnākara, Śākala states: "Protecting one's celibacy by [avoiding] sharing a bed, seat, or meal..."
"He should dwell there together with his bride for four days."
In the *Saṃgraha*: "Sitting on the same seat, sleeping on the same bed, eating from the same vessel,
performing auspicious rites together, bathing in the same place, and mounting the same vehicle."
"Performing these [rites] during marriage, a Brahmin incurs no fault.
The mention of the "Brahmin" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
Regarding this, Kaśyapa states a specific rule concerning unwashed cloth:
"The Self-Existent One has declared that a garment released from the loom is 'unbeaten' (ahata);
it is recommended for auspicious ceremonies, but only for that duration, not at all times."
Now, the installation of the ghaṭīs for the ascendant:
"In a place sloping toward the east or north, smeared with cow dung,
one should place a pair of auspicious, flawless earthen jars."
Having wound them around each other with a thread smeared with saffron,
[place them] upon rice that is filled with clear water.
"Afterwards, one should place the water-clock (ghaṭikā-yantra) upon a small pot filled with still water, by means of observing the reflection of the solar disc."
Vāmana states the definition of the *ghaṭikā*:
"A *ghaṭikā* is a vessel made of ten *palas* of gold, with a very fine opening,
six finger-breadths in height, and twelve finger-breadths in circumference, which is filled in sixty *palas* [of water]."
"One should fashion a circular ring of four-finger-width sticks with a golden base; by measuring that [ring] against a hole situated at the bottom, an auspicious water-clock (ghaṭikā) is produced."
That whose end is extremely subtle; gold weighing sixteen *māṣas*, a quarter of that being four *māṣas* in weight. Nārada also says:
"Six finger-breadths in height and twelve finger-breadths in length."
One should fashion a copper vessel shaped like a lotus from ten palas [of copper].
"Pierced very clearly by that golden circular rod, measuring four finger-breadths in length and joined with three *māṣas* and a third part [of a *māṣa*]."
"In a copper vessel filled with water, or else in an auspicious earthen vessel, one should pour [the water] there upon seeing the half-rising of the sun's mandala. Regarding that water:
"You are the foremost of all vessels, fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times."
"The cause for the existence or non-existence of a husband and wife depends upon time and the means."
Thus ends the mantra for placing the water-clock vessel.
Thus ends the installation of the water-clock.
Now, the result of the rotation of the water-clock mechanism.
In the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"The form which the first *ghaṭikā* assumes in the directions starting from the East, in due order, brings respectively good fortune, death, infamy, or affliction by diseases;
but that which is always steady and unchanging certainly attains the state of being beloved by women."
"She shall be virtuous, endowed with sons, wealth, and kinsmen, and she will rejoice greatly upon the earth."
In another treatise:
"That hour (ghaṭī) requested in the water, whichever direction it moves toward, shall produce results beginning with the East; if situated in the center, it bestows wealth."
"A woman [born under this yoga] possesses good fortune and wealth, yet suffers untimely death and disease;
she is beloved by her husband, obedient, honored, and endowed with riches and happiness."
"Requested" means requested by means of the mantra: "You are the foremost of all yantras.
Furthermore:
"A jar full [of water] placed in the north, northeast, or east brings auspiciousness."
"In the remaining directions, the maiden is submerged, bestowing widowhood."

In the *Vivāhapaṭala* according to the opinion of the Seven Sages (*Saptarṣimatam*): "One should worship the astrologer (*daivavit*) according to one's ability with perfumes, flowers, garments, and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
When the astrologer is fully honored and well-pleased, all the planetary deities (*grahadevatā*) are likewise satisfied."
The giver of the *daivavila* lagna;
Saṃvarta states its definition by way of exclusion:
"One who is blind, afflicted with leprosy, has deformed nails, is deficient in limbs, or is indeed lame."
Wherever there is one who bestows the ascendant, that indeed brings about the destruction of the family."
Regarding the granting of that *lagna*:
the characteristics of the time for the *lagna* have been stated by Nārada:
"While a man is healthy and sitting comfortably, as long as his eye blinks..."
A thirtieth part of that is proclaimed as the *tatpara*.
A hundredth part of that [moment] is called a *truṭi*;
a thousandth part of a *truṭi* is said to be the duration of a *lagna*.
Even a god does not know that, much less an ordinary person;
whether it be that time or another time, it occurs through the power of past karma.
"The astrologer considers it merely an omen, and based on that [omen], he determines the auspicious or inauspicious.
Bṛhaspati, however, states: "Either the rising of an auspicious planet and asterism, or indeed an auspicious *ṣaḍvarga*..."
And the words of Vedic knowledge, as well as great and auspicious qualities."

The phrase "the statement of the Vedavijñānas" has been explained in two ways in the *Pārijāta*: (1) those who possess knowledge (*vijñāna*) of the Veda are the *vedavijñānas*; they are knowers of the truth of the Veda and its auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), and their statement [is meant]. Alternatively, (2) they are called *vijñānas* because they discern (*vijānanti*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the causal agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Thus, *vedavijñānas* means "those who discern the Veda," which conveys the same meaning. Their statement, however, is of the form "let there be an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*)"—this is the sense.

Moreover—"He who is known through the Vedas" refers to the Lord of Lakṣmī (Viṣṇu), who is to be known by the Vedas (*vedavijñāna*) and is the one to be known through the Vedas (*vedavedya*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule regarding the frequentative form (*bahulagrahaṇāt*). The sentence consisting of the remembrance of the feet of that Lord of Lakṣmī is itself the *lagna* (auspicious moment), and so forth. This is what is meant:
may there be a good moment at this time of the *muhūrta*.
"That alone is the *lagna*, that alone is the auspicious day, that alone is the strength of the stars, and that alone is the strength of the moon."

Having said, "I remember that pair of feet of You, O Lord of Lakṣmī, which possess the power of knowledge and the power of destiny," one should offer [the gift] for a moment. Regarding the phrase "perfumes and so forth" (gandhādi), the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes ornaments.
The practice of commencing the *godhūli* lagna during times of distress is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"When no *ghaṭī-lagna* exists, then the *godhūlika* [time] is auspicious;
the wise have declared this for Śūdras and others, but never for the twice-born."
"When an auspicious lagna is not available as youth has arrived,
then for all castes, the Godhūlika lagna is indeed auspicious."
In the first marriage, the *nāndīśrāddha* is to be performed by the father alone—according to the rule:
"The father shall perform the *nāndīśrāddha* at the first taking of the hand;
from that point onward, however, he himself shall perform the *nāndika*."
In the absence of the father, any one of the grandfather or others [should perform it]; in the absence of all these, the person himself, according to the authors of the *Nibandhas*.
There is a specific rule in the *Reṇukārikās*:
"At the time prescribed, the father should perform the *Nāndīmukha* rite as an ancillary part of the marriage."
"If the marriage is to take place in another country, this should happen after going there."

In some places, there is also the reading: "if the marriage takes place in another village. The term *nāndīmukha* is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*), the installation of the deities of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-devatā-sthāpana*), and so forth. As for the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice and other rites upon entering one's own home, these should be performed only after returning to one's own house; however, nowadays people perform them right there [in the bride's house], which is a lax practice. Now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) for the marriage.

At an auspicious moment, the giver of the girl, having constructed a pavilion (maṇḍapa) in the courtyard of his house according to the prescribed characteristics and provided with arches (toraṇa) and other ornaments, should prepare an altar (vedi) there. This altar should measure four cubits on each side, or seven or five cubits in length, be perfectly square, one cubit in height, provided with steps, very smooth, and conforming to the stated characteristics. However, the father of the groom should construct only a pavilion in his own house according to the prescribed characteristics, and not an altar.

Then, at the appropriate time, during an auspicious moment (muhūrta) indicated by the astrologer for the wedding, the matrons on the bride's side, having first performed anointment with fragrant oils, barley-meal, turmeric, and other auspicious substances, shall bathe the bride with warm water according to custom; they should likewise bathe the groom, first performing anointment with the same residual substances—such is the tradition.

Then, on the day of the wedding or the day preceding it, during the forenoon, the giver of the girl—having performed the auspicious bath and donned auspicious attire—sits facing east upon a seat covered with a white cloth in a courtyard that has been smeared and decorated with *raṅgavallī* designs. Having seated his wife, who has likewise performed the auspicious bath and donned auspicious attire, to his right, and having seated the girl, who has also performed the auspicious bath and donned auspicious attire, to her right, he performs the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and paid homage to one’s chosen deity, teacher, and others, and having declared the place and time, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "I shall perform the marriage sacrament (*vivāhasaṃskāra*) for this girl named so-and-so according to the Brāhma marriage rite. Alternatively, the resolve may be formulated thus: "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (*Śrī Parameśvara*), by means of establishing my right—along with that of this girl—to perform religious duties, procreate offspring, and acquire property, I shall perform the marriage sacrament according to the Brāhma marriage rite."

The grandfather, however, should say, "of my granddaughter named so-and-so"; the great-grandfather, "of my great-granddaughter. But brothers, paternal uncles, and others should speak according to their respective relationship, such as "of [my] sister" or "of [my] nephew's daughter," and so forth.

Alternatively: "I, [Name] Śarmā, born of the [Name] Gotra and endowed with the [Name] Pravara, for the sake of attaining the fruit described in the Kalpas for the bestowal of a daughter—such as the attainment of the unsurpassed, blissful world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka) and so forth—for all my ancestors; and in order to purify twelve descendants and twelve ancestors through the progeny to be begotten upon this girl by means of the groom designated by me; and for the sake of pleasing Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa myself, perform the marriage in the form of the bestowal of this girl named [Name]."

The resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is "I shall perform [the rite]. In this view, no resolve need be made regarding the giving away of the girl. However, the father of the groom should make the resolve: "I shall perform the marriage sacrament (*vivāha-saṃskāra*) for my son, so-and-so Śarmā. The resolve should be: "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (*Śrī-Parameśvara*), by means of accomplishing the discharge of the debts to the gods and ancestors (*daiva-pitrya-ṛṇa-apākaraṇa*), I shall perform the marriage sacrament for my son, so-and-so Śarmā. The grandfather, however, should say "for my grandson."

The great-grandfather [performs the rite] for the great-grandson; as for the brother, paternal uncle, and so forth, they act according to their respective relationships, such as for the brother or the brother’s son. In reality, however, it is logical that the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) belongs solely to the groom, in the form: "I shall perform the marriage sacrament for myself. Nor should it be argued that because the father acts as the performer of the ancillary parts such as the recitation of the *svasti-vācana*, the resolve must also belong to him; for it is appropriate that the primary resolve belongs to the groom himself, who is the actual performer of the principal rite.
For the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) is the primary rite, and that is performed by the groom; therefore, this [rite] is indeed performed by the groom alone.

According to the statement, "The father shall perform the *nāndī-śrāddha* at the first taking of the hand," only the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed by the father. Some maintain that by the term *nāndī-śrāddha*, the recitation of blessings (*svastivācana*) is also implied. On the view that the recitation of blessings and so forth are external to the main rite, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the principal act must be made either before the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*) or before the giving away of the girl (*kanyādāna*) by the giver of the girl; or it must be made by the groom before his arrival at the bride's house.

In the view that the *svastivācana* and other rites are external to the core ceremony, the giver of the girl (*kanyādātṛ*) must first perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) beginning with "I shall perform the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) for the marriage of my daughter. The father of the groom (*varapitṛ*), however, should perform the resolve beginning with "I shall perform the declaration of the auspicious day for the sake of the marriage of my son. Regarding the marriage of the girl—which is a ritual act consisting of the provision of the wedding requisites by the groom's side—the distinction in the resolve is: "I shall perform the marriage sacrament (*vivāhasaṃskāra*) together with the provision of the wedding requisites by the groom's side."

Then one should perform the worship of Gaṇapati, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*), the *nāndīśrāddha*, the sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurāropaṇa*), the sacrifice to the planets (*grahamakhā*), and the installation of the deities of the pavilion (*maṇḍapadevatāpratiṣṭhāpana*). The father of the bridegroom should also perform the worship of Gaṇapati and the other rites. In this case, the specific modification is that "May Agni be pleased" (*agniḥ prīyatām*) should be used. Alternatively, the sowing of sprouts and the sacrifice to the planets may be performed separately beforehand, as space permits; there is no rule that they must necessarily follow the *nāndīśrāddha*.

Then, both [the bridegroom and the bride], immediately after the installation of the deities of the pavilion, should, according to custom, feed at the appropriate times the twice-born, married women, boys, and others with whatever food is available, for the sake of pleasing the deities associated with the marriage rite and the family deities. Likewise, other various local, village, and family customs handed down through the lineage of elders should be observed here. And this has been indicated by the author of the Sūtras with the rule: "At this point they place the seeds upon the fire."

Āśvalāyana has stated quite explicitly: "Now, indeed, there are various local customs and village customs; one should observe these at the time of marriage. Āpastamba also says: "And the rites should be observed from women. Here, "rites" (*āvṛta*) refers to wedding ceremonies. Since no distinction is made, they include both those with mantras and those without. All of these, having learned them from women of the same caste (*savarṇā*), the bridegrooms should observe and perform them. Those with mantras include the worship of the *grahas* (the celestial spheres) and so forth.

Worship of Indrāṇī and other such rites are performed without mantras. Regarding these, Sudarśana has explained that they are established according to region, caste, village, family, and gender—whether female or male—and are not to be combined from all sources indiscriminately. Śāṅkhāyana states: "When the bridegroom has bathed and performed auspicious rites, fortunate young women who are not widows lead the maiden to her dwelling; he should not oppose them, except in the case of forbidden foods or mortal sins."

The term "non-widows" is illustrative; learned twice-born men also bring the bridegroom to the girl's house preceded by the chanting of the Veda (*brahmaghoṣa*). The bridegroom should be agreeable and not antagonistic to those women; whatever family custom they enjoin that is not contrary to the sacred law (*dharma*), he should perform that. He should not do everything that has been mentioned; except for forbidden foods and sinful acts, he should not perform that which involves eating what is unfit to eat or that through which sin arises.
The commentary on this states that at this time, certain women perform rites such as *kārmaṇa* (magical spells), and whatever else they cause to be done is to be carried out.

Furthermore, Āpastamba says: "Likewise, auspicious ceremonies (*maṅgalāni*). Sudarśana explains that in the context of a wedding, the following auspicious acts—well-known through the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*)—should be performed: the sounding of conchs, drums, lutes, and other musical instruments; songs by women of the family; the grooming of hair and beards; the wearing of variegated garments; the application of perfumes and ointments; the wearing of garlands; the movement of foot-soldiers; and various banners and the like.

Then the giver of the girl, accompanied by horses and other vehicles, amidst the auspicious sounds of musical instruments, well-adorned, and joined by his own beloved relatives, elders, respectable persons, and women, arrives at the bridegroom's house with his wife. Having seated the bridegroom facing east and sitting himself to the south facing north, he likewise seats his wife on his own right side. Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and restrained his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), he worships Gaṇapati according to the aforementioned method, establishes the water-pot (*kalaśa*) according to custom, and worships Varuṇa therein.

One should perform the dismissal of the two [the bridegroom and the officiant]. They form the following *saṃkalpa*: "I shall perform the worship of the bridegroom (*vara-pūjana*) which is a constituent part of the maiden’s marriage; as a part of that, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati and the worship of Varuṇa. This [practice] has already been refuted in the section on the initiation (*upanayana*). Now follows the selection of the bridegroom (*vara-varaṇa*).

Therein, during the northern solstice (*udagayana*), in the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇapak� an*), under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the father of the maiden sends forth an even number of Brāhmaṇas as suitors (*vara*) for the purpose of determining the bridegroom.

With this mantra: "Oṃ! May the two who move forward, the companions of the one who meditates, sit down well with their choice gifts toward our choice gifts; may Indra enjoy both of us, when he takes notice of the Soma juice."

Then, as they depart, he addresses them with the mantra: "Oṃ, may the paths be thornless and straight, by which, O gods, my friends may go. Once the decision regarding the groom has been made and they have arrived, at some auspicious moment—either before or immediately after the formal selection of the bride—a certain elderly man from the bride's side should speak to the father of the groom.

"This man has a daughter who is a bride; he has come to you with his friends for assistance so that your son may accept her as his wife. After deliberating with your own people, please grant permission to these men for the sake of honoring the groom. Then the father of the groom, with the consent of the father of the bride and others, says, "I have granted my permission. Thereafter, the priest and others should seat the groom—facing east, dressed in white garments, adorned with ornaments, and well-attired—upon a four-legged seat covered with a bright cloth, while reciting the two mantras: "Oṃ anṛkṣarā... and "Oṃ svasti na indro...".
Then, one should worship him according to one's means with sacred threads, fruits, flowers, ornaments, perfumes, and garments.

Then, the father of the girl, sitting facing west in front of the groom and near the father of the groom and others, should first perform the remembrance of Gaṇapati and other deities, and then choose [the groom] with the sacred thread and other items, saying: "We choose the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so, and the great-grandson of so-and-so, born in the lineage of such-and-such gotra and possessing such-and-such pravara, named so-and-so Śarman, as the husband for this girl named so-and-so, who is the daughter of so-and-so, the granddaughter of so-and-so, and the great-granddaughter of so-and-so, born in the lineage of such-and-such gotra and possessing such-and-such pravara."

The father of the groom, having obtained the consent of all [the bride's relatives] and having either repeated or not repeated what was previously stated, should say, "Do you choose [her]? This should be done twice. With the words "So be it," the father of the groom should accept [the proposal], preceded by the consent of all. Once permission has been granted by the father and others that "this girl is to be chosen as a bride," the groom should say, "I accept. That which they now perform at the boundary (sīmānta) as the worship of the groom is precisely this. In that very place, the choosing of the groom (varavaraṇa) should be performed in this manner.

Then, having washed the feet of the bridegroom and worshipped him according to one's means with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, the waving of lights (nīrājana), garments, and so forth, and having caused him to consume milk and other substances according to custom, one should place a coconut fruit in his hand; this is what is obtained by established tradition.

Then the groom, having performed his daily rites, well-adorned, wearing a garland, and decorated with garments and ornaments given by the bride’s father, should pay homage to his chosen deity, family deity, preceptor, and others. He should then perform the *puṇyāhavācana* (declaration of an auspicious day) by saying, "May you all declare it an auspicious day for my journey to the bride's house," and so forth; or he may do so according to his means. Then, mounting any vehicle such as a horse, under a white umbrella, and accompanied by well-honored and well-adorned kinsmen and relatives, as well as Brahmins reciting mantras such as "This very one she is," he proceeds.

Accompanied by matrons with water-pitchers, mirrors, maidens, flowers, unbroken rice, rows of lamps, banners, parched grain, and the sounds of auspicious musical instruments, as well as by dancing girls and others who are performing, he should go to the bride's house. Standing at the doorway facing the east, he should be honored with the *nīrājana* rite by the matrons who have come forward with full pitchers in their hands. Having entered the inner house, he should sit facing the east upon a four-legged *bhadrapīṭha* (auspicious seat) covered with a cloth, which has been placed upon green *darbha* grass in the center of the pavilion.
In this regard, the learned perform the choosing of the bride, the worship of the bride, and the formal betrothal (*vāgdāna*).
Next is the *madhuparka* offering.
It is stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* that this should be performed according to the specific Vedic school (*śākhā*) of the groom:

"The *madhuparka* should be offered according to the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of the branch (*śākhā*) to which the bridegroom belongs, even if the giver belongs to a different branch. Here, the term "bridegroom" (*vara*) is an elliptical designation for the person being honored. However, Jayanta has stated that the *madhuparka* should follow the branch of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) alone. In reality, it appears more appropriate that those who follow the *Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra* should perform the *madhuparka* exactly as prescribed in that *sūtra*. The procedure for the *madhuparka* is explained in the context of the *Samāvartana* (the return home after Vedic study). The specific modification lies in the formula of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall honor this bridegroom who has arrived seeking a maiden with the *madhuparka*."

If, however, the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* itself is accepted by the learned in accordance with established custom, then, because the procedure for the *madhuparka* prescribed in that specific branch (*śākhā*) is required when the bridegroom belongs to the Āśvalāyana school, its practical application is now stated. Herein is the sequence:

Having prepared four vessels for water for washing the feet (*pādya*), for the respectful offering (*arghya*), for the three-fold sipping of water according to mantra (*mantravat-trir-ācamana*), and for pure sipping water (*śuddhyarthācamanīya*); and having prepared a bell-metal vessel containing the honey-mixture known as *madhuparka* (consisting of honey and curd), along with a seat (*viṣṭara*) made of twenty-five *darbha* grasses whose tips point downward and are tied together at the front in a counter-clockwise direction so that they form a braid, with a knot at the front; [he should think: "I shall honor the arrived bride-seeker, the *snātaka* groom, with the *madhuparka*."

Having mentally prepared a seat (*viṣṭara*)—having offered it three times, saying "The seat, the seat, the seat"—he should place it in the hand of the groom for the purpose of a seat, saying, "May it be accepted. The groom accepts it, saying, "I accept. [Then follows: For the mantra "I am the height," Vāmadeva is the seer, *viṣṭara* is the deity, and *anuṣṭubh* is the meter; its application is in sitting upon the seat. With the mantra, "Oṃ, I am the height of my kinsmen... may he not seek to harm me," he should sit upon the seat with its tips pointing north. Alternatively, having stepped onto the seat with his feet while reciting the mantra, he may sit down silently.

Then the officiant (arcaka) should offer the water for the feet (pādya) three times, saying, "The water for the feet, the water for the feet, the water for the feet. The bridegroom (vara) should accept it. In all instances, after the offering has been made, the officiant should say, "May it be accepted. Except in the case of accepting the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the bridegroom should say, "I accept it."

Then the officiant shall wash the right and left feet of the bridegroom in succession with that water. Thereafter, the bridegroom, having sipped water (ācamana) with ordinary water, shall receive the arghya—which has been offered three times with the words "Arghya! Arghya! Arghya! and is accompanied by perfumes, garlands, fruits, and so forth—into his joined palms and pour it out silently.

Then, having been offered water for sipping three times by the officiating priest (arcaka) with the words, "Water for sipping! Water for sipping! Water for sipping!", he should accept the water for sipping, take a portion of it, and drink it while reciting: "Oṃ, you are the underlayer of immortality. For this mantra, Vāmadeva is the seer, water is the deity, and the Yajus is the meter; its application is in the drinking of water. Having drunk thus, he should sip water with ordinary water. Then, the officiating priest, having presented the honey-mixture (madhuparka) with the words, "Honey-mixture! Honey-mixture! Honey-mixture!", should say, "May it be accepted."

Then the worship: for the mantra "Oṃ *mitrasya tvā*," Vāmadeva is the seer, the *madhuparka* is the deity, and the *virāṭ-yajus* is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the inspection of the *madhuparka*. Having inspected the *madhuparka* being brought while reciting, "Oṃ *mitrasya tvā cakṣuṣā pratīkṣe*," [one proceeds]. For the mantra "Oṃ *devasya tvā*," Vāmadeva is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity, and the *yajus* is the meter. Its application is in the acceptance of the *madhuparka*.
With the mantra, "Oṃ *devasya tvā savituḥ prasave'śvinorbāhubhyāṃ pūṣṇo hastābhyāṃ pratigṛhṇāmi*," one should accept with cupped hands the *madhuparka* offered by the worshipper.

Then—with the triplet beginning "madhu vātā" (The winds are honey for the one who follows the Truth), by Rāhūgaṇa Gautama, addressed to the Viśvedevas, in the Gāyatrī meter; its application is in the inspection of the Madhuparka: "Oṃ madhu vātā ṛtāyate... bhavantu naḥ"—he should inspect the Madhuparka contained in the vessel held in his joined palms.

Then, holding that vessel in the left hand and stirring the *madhuparka* three times clockwise with the thumb and ring finger, one recites: "The *vasus* are yours," etc. Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*). The *vasus*, *rudras*, *ādityas*, and *viśvedevas* are the deities (*devatās*) respectively; the *yajus* verses are the meters. The application (*viniyoga*) is for wiping. "Oṃ, may the *vasus* consume you with the *gāyatrī* meter"—with this, he wipes it on the front side. "Oṃ, may the *rudras* consume you with the *triṣṭubh* meter"—with this, he wipes it on the right side.

In this matter, there is an option regarding the touching of water. [One says: "Oṃ, may the Ādityas consume you with the Jāgata metre," and [this is done] from behind. "Oṃ, may the Viśvedevas consume you with the Ānuṣṭubh metre," and [this is done] from the north. Then—of the mantra "bhūtebhyastvā" (for the beings, you), Vāmadeva is the seer, Madhuparka is the deity, and the Yajus is the metre; its application is in the taking of the Madhuparka. Having taken a little from the middle [of the mixture] with the words "Oṃ, for the beings, you," one should silently throw it upward three times.

The reception [of the guest] involves the repetition of the mantra; alternatively, the taking [of the vessel] is silent while the pouring [into the mouth] is with the mantra. In this view, the distinction lies in the statement of application (*viniyoga*), which specifies that the mantra is applied to the act of pouring.

Then, having placed the vessel of *madhuparka* on the ground and taken a portion of the *madhuparka*, [one recites] the three mantras beginning with "Thou art the milking of Virāj. Vāmadeva is the seer, the *madhuparka* is the deity, and the *yajus* is the meter. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the consumption of the *madhuparka*.

Having first consumed [the portion] with the mantra "Oṃ, thou art the milking of Virāj," and having sipped water from the common supply (laukika-jala), he should take it up again in the same manner and consume the second portion with "Oṃ, may I partake of the milking of Virāj," and having sipped water from the common supply, he should take it up again in the same manner and consume the third portion with "Oṃ, may the milking of the Padyā Virāj be in me," and having sipped water from the common supply, he should give the remainder of the Madhuparka to a Brāhmaṇa facing north; however, because it is now loathed by the world, he should simply cast it into the water.

Then: for the mantra "amṛtāpidhānam asi," Vāmadeva is the seer, water is the deity, and the Yajus is the meter; its application is in the drinking of water. Reciting "Oṃ amṛtāpidhānam asi," one drinks a small amount of the water remaining from the previous sipping (ācamana), rinses the mouth with ordinary water, and takes up all the remainder of the sipping-water. For the mantra "satyaṃ yaśaḥ," Vāmadeva is the seer, water is the deity, and the Yajus is the meter; its application is in the drinking of water. Reciting "Oṃ satyaṃ yaśaḥ śrīrmayi śrīḥ śrayatām," one drinks it all and should perform the sipping of the mouth twice with ordinary water.

Then the worshipper should offer the cow three times, saying, "Gauḥ, Gauḥ, Gauḥ. Thereafter, he is to be honored: for the verse beginning with "mātā rudrāṇām," Bhārgava Jamadagni is the seer, the cow is the deity, and the Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application (viniyoga) is in the recitation that forms part of the ritual release of the cow. Having recited, "Oṃ mātā rudrāṇāṃ duhitā... pra nu vocaṃ... dhiṣṭa," and having said, "Oṃ utsṛjata" (Release her!), he should let her go.

Then the donor, having honored her according to his means with perfumes, garlands, a pair of garments, a pair of sacred threads, ornaments, and so forth, should feed her with food consisting of rice mixed with various side-dishes made from black gram (māṣa).
The characteristics of the *viṣṭara* are given in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"Brahmā is made with fifty [strands], while the *viṣṭara* is with half that number.
Brahmā has upward-pointing hair, whereas the *viṣṭara* has hanging hair."

"Brahmā has a clockwise coil, while the *viṣṭara* has a counter-clockwise coil; it consists of twenty-five *darbha* grasses, adorned with a knot at its tip. Twenty-five is half of fifty; the meaning is that the *viṣṭara* is made from that many *darbha* blades. "Whose tips (*keśāḥ*)—meaning the ends—are upward-pointing at the time of preparation"; and "whose tips are hanging down"—meaning suspended or downward-pointing—at the time of preparation. It should be understood that if curd is unavailable for the *madhuparka*, milk is used; if honey is unavailable, clarified butter or jaggery; and if nothing is available, water.
Thus concludes the *madhuparka* according to Āśvalāyana.

Now follows the worship of Gaurī and Hara. Then the bride, having bathed and put on new, unwashed garments, enters the house. In a consecrated place within the house, she arranges rows of three earthen jars each, covered with lids, at the intermediate quarters (vidiś), surrounding them by encircling them with a thread. In the center of that, she places a stone slab together with pebbles encircled by thread. Upon that, having fashioned a lotus upon a heap of white rice-grains (*akṣata*), she places there a golden [image] weighing one *pala* or more, which has been consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa through the rites of fire-purification (*agnyuttāraṇa*) and the infusion of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

Having installed an image of Gaurī and Hara, and having placed before it Nandin—crafted from silver weighing two *pala*s, one *pala*, or half a *pala* respectively, consecrated by a Brahmin through the rites of fire-transference (*agnyuttāraṇa*) and the infusion of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*)—one should have Gaurī and Hara painted on a wall or similar surface with saffron and other pigments, [reciting]:
"The Goddess of the Gods, seated upon a lion-throne and adorned with all ornaments;
the God, wearing yellow garments and having the crescent moon as his crest."
Having meditated thus: "In his lower right hand he holds a jar filled with nectar,
while with his left hand he grants boons and fearlessness, embracing his slender beloved," [one should worship] Gaurī and Hara, the Great Lords, the bestowers of all auspiciousness.

"O Lords of the Gods, accept this worship; grant us constant auspiciousness"—with this mantra, having worshipped [the deities] with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), one should worship Nandin with the desire for good fortune and other blessings. As for the dismissal (*visarjana*), it occurs at the end of the marriage ceremony according to custom. Then, having worshipped Devendrāṇī in that very same place—either in the image or upon a heap of unbroken rice (*akṣata*)—[one recites]: "O Devendrāṇī, salutations to you, O beloved wife of Devendra."
Having thus prayed, "Grant me marriage, fortune, health, and the birth of a son," she should remain right there, entreating for good fortune and other blessings.
Then, the father of the girl, having lit a lamp with the girl, should worship the Brahmins and the married women (suvāsinīs) and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Thus concludes the worship of Gaurī and Hara.

Then, while auspicious songs, dances, instrumental music, and the like are being performed according to custom in a well-decorated pavilion or house, the Brahmins—leaving a space of one cubit between the eastern and western sections—should form two heaps of white rice measuring one *prastha* each. In the middle, they should hold an inner-curtain (*antaḥ-paṭa*) marked with a *svastika* made of saffron by an astrologer, with its fringe facing north, positioned between the two heaps.

Then the kinsmen should place the bride, facing west, upon a stone in the eastern heap with her hands joined containing rice and cumin; and they should place the groom, facing east, upon a seat in the western heap with his hands joined containing rice and cumin. According to Āśvalāyana, if the groom is from that lineage, the bride faces east and the groom faces west. From this point until the end—the removal of the curtain—the twice-born should recite the mantras, while the matrons should perform auspicious songs. Regarding the quantity of rice, Yama has stated that it should be one *prastha*: [The text continues with the verses of Yama. ...the wise say that the bridegroom should give a gift according to his means. Then the bridegroom should give a pair of garments, a pair of earrings, and a pair of bracelets to the bride’s father. Having given these, he should circumambulate the fire three times, keeping it to his right. Then, having placed the bride’s hand upon his own, he should offer oblations of clarified butter with the [mantras] beginning with "Svāhā to Agni" and ending with "Svāhā to the Viśve-devās. Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should cause the bride to step forward seven steps with the [mantras] beginning with "One step for sap. Then, having led her out of the house, he should have her look at the sun with the mantra "Bhaga, Dhātṛ, Aryaman... and so forth. Then, having seated her on a stone with the mantra "I seat you upon the stone...", he should have her look at the pole star (*dhruva*) with the mantra "O Pole Star, thou art firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the polar mountain (*parvatam dhruvam*) with the mantra "May the mountain be firm...", he should have her gaze at the moon with the mantra "May the moon be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the sun with the mantra "May the sun be firm...", he should have her gaze at the fire with the mantra "May the fire be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the water with the mantra "May the waters be firm...", he should have her gaze at the earth with the mantra "May the earth be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the sky with the mantra "May the sky be firm...", he should have her gaze at the quarters with the mantra "May the quarters be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the self with the mantra "May the self be firm...", he should have her gaze at the progeny with the mantra "May progeny be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the cattle with the mantra "May cattle be firm...", he should have her gaze at the herbs with the mantra "May the herbs be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the trees with the mantra "May the trees be firm...", he should have her gaze at the ancestors with the mantra "May the ancestors be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the gods with the mantra "May the gods be firm...", he should have her gaze at the brahmins with the mantra "May the brahmins be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the guests with the mantra "May the guests be firm...", he should have her gaze at the world with the mantra "May the world be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the universe with the mantra "May the universe be firm...", he should have her gaze at the truth with the mantra "May the truth be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the dharma with the mantra "May the dharma be firm...", he should have her gaze at the auspicious with the mantra "May the auspicious be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the prosperity with the mantra "May the prosperity be firm...", he should have her gaze at the welfare with the mantra "May the welfare be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the well-being with the mantra "May the well-being be firm...", he should have her gaze at the peace with the mantra "May the peace be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the bliss with the mantra "May the bliss be firm...", he should have her gaze at the liberation with the mantra "May the liberation be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the ultimate reality with the mantra "May the ultimate reality be firm...", he should have her gaze at the supreme goal with the mantra "May the supreme goal be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the eternal with the mantra "May the eternal be firm...", he should have her gaze at the imperishable with the mantra "May the imperishable be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the undecaying with the mantra "May the undecaying be firm...", he should have her gaze at the immortal with the mantra "May the immortal be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the fearless with the mantra "May the fearless be firm...", he should have her gaze at the secure with the mantra "May the secure be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the invincible with the mantra "May the invincible be firm...", he should have her gaze at the unconquerable with the mantra "May the unconquerable be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the unassailable with the mantra "May the unassailable be firm...", he should have her gaze at the unshakeable with the mantra "May the unshakeable be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the steadfast with the mantra "May the steadfast be firm...", he should have her gaze at the unwavering with the mantra "May the unwavering be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the immovable with the mantra "May the immovable be firm...", he should have her gaze at the stable with the mantra "May the stable be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the constant with the mantra "May the constant be firm...", he should have her gaze at the perpetual with the mantra "May the perpetual be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the continuous with the mantra "May the continuous be firm...", he should have her gaze at the uninterrupted with the mantra "May the uninterrupted be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the unbroken with the mantra "May the unbroken be firm...", he should have her gaze at the whole with the mantra "May the whole be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the complete with the mantra "May the complete be firm...", he should have her gaze at the perfect with the mantra "May the perfect be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the flawless with the mantra "May the flawless be firm...", he should have her gaze at the pure with the mantra "May the pure be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the stainless with the mantra "May the stainless be firm...", he should have her gaze at the bright with the mantra "May the bright be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the radiant with the mantra "May the radiant be firm...", he should have her gaze at the luminous with the mantra "May the luminous be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the effulgent with the mantra "May the effulgent be firm...", he should have her gaze at the splendorous with the mantra "May the splendorous be firm... and so forth.
