Then, having caused her to gaze at the glorious with the mantra "May the glorious be firm...", he should have her gaze at the majestic with the mantra "May the majestic be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the venerable with the mantra "May the venerable be firm...", he should have her gaze at the worshipful with the mantra "May the worshipful be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the adorable with the mantra "May the adorable be firm...", he should have her gaze at the praiseworthy with the mantra "May the praiseworthy be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the laudable with the mantra "May the laudable be firm...", he should have her gaze at the excellent with the mantra "May the excellent be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the sublime with the mantra "May the sublime be firm...", he should have her gaze at the supreme with the mantra "May the supreme be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the highest with the mantra "May the highest be firm...", he should have her gaze at the unsurpassed with the mantra "May the unsurpassed be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the peerless with the mantra "May the peerless be firm...", he should have her gaze at the incomparable with the mantra "May the incomparable be firm... and so forth. Then, having caused her to gaze at the matchless with the
"Having ascended [the stool], one should gaze at the bride who is facing west.
Then the bride and groom should remain composed, meditating in their minds upon their chosen deity. At this juncture, according to the available time, astrologers may recite auspicious verses.
Among those, here are six verses composed by me:
The god Gaṇapati, the destroyer of obstacles, was meditated upon; and even the gods, such as Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others, became free from obstacles by means of the thought-removing [mantra].
He who has been installed here in the pavilion within the pitcher under the name "Free from Obstacles" (Avighna), delighted by the embrace of success—may he always bestow auspiciousness upon both.

Seeing their parents come to kiss the pair of their cheeks out of affection, the two with beautiful faces quickly contracted their pure lower lips with a slight smile; may that Blessed One, by whom Śiva and Pārvatī were thus delighted as they gazed at one another, always bestow auspiciousness.

Requested by the gods, sages, and the lords of the hosts who were terrified of the afflictions caused by the sons of Diti, the Lord Vighneśa, though the Supreme Sovereign, assumed a youthful body out of curiosity;
performing most exuberant childhood antics in the abode of Pārvatī, may that Blessed Lord, who delights the two Īśvaras, ever grant auspiciousness. (3)
The infant Lord Vighnarāja, who dwells upon the lap of Aparṇā’s son (Gaṇeśa), quickly drinks from both breasts simultaneously— either with the tip of his trunk or with his mouth—
at which time he smiles with curiosity as he moves from the lap of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain (Pārvatī) onto the lap of Hara (Śiva).
Moving swiftly and captivating the minds of Śiva and Śivā, may he always bestow auspiciousness. || 4 ||
The Lord, the Sovereign, while shaking his own lotus-hand— which is filled with humming bees that have come out of joy during the dance of the auspicious God Śiva—
produces charming speech and then spreads laughter with faltering words.
May that Blessed One always perform auspicious drama that brings great joy. || 5 ||

When the daughter of the Mountain had bestowed her consent for the rite known as initiation (*upanayana*), and when Brahmā, the Sun, the Moon, and other deities had brought various offerings to be accepted as alms in that auspicious vessel, the King of the Gods cast aside his pride and gradually began to practice the duties of a religious student day after day; may he always grant auspiciousness.
The Sun is illustrious, born of the Kāśyapa lineage, possessing the luster of dawn, and is the lord of the Leo zodiac sign.
Situated beautifully in the sixth, third, and tenth houses, he is the friend of Jupiter, Mars, and the Moon;
he is the enemy of Rāhu and Saturn, the progenitor of the Kaliṅgas, and has Agni and Īśvara as his presiding deities.
In the center, with a face like a round moon, he shall always bring about auspiciousness. || 1 ||

The Moon is the lord of Cancer, possesses white luster, is born of the Ātreya lineage, occupies a square in the southeast, faces the intermediate direction of water (the west), and has Varuṇa as its presiding deity.

It yields auspicious results when situated in the sixth, seventh, third, or first house; it is an enemy to Mercury and is dear to Mars and the Sun. Born in the region on the banks of the Yamunā, this maker of cold rays shall always bestow auspiciousness. || 2 ||
Mars faces the south; the lord of Avanti (Saturn) is situated in the south-eastern triangle;
he is dear to Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon; he is the enemy of Mercury;
he bestows six, three, and one fruit respectively; and Earth and Skanda are his presiding deities in order.
May the son of the Earth, born of the lineage of Bhāradvāja, always grant auspiciousness. || 3 ||

Jupiter is yellow in color, the lord of Magadha, facing north, born of the Ātreya lineage, situated in the northern part of Sagittarius (Bāṇastha), and has the Sun and Venus as his friends; he is indeed the enemy of the Moon.
As the lord of Virgo and Gemini, he is auspicious when located in the tenth, eighth, fourth, sixth, and second houses.
And when two Viṣṇus are in the deities above, the son of the Moon (Mercury) shall always bring auspiciousness.
Jīva, Sindhupati, Vidhi, and Surapati are the lords of the signs Dhanu and Mīna;
likewise, the lord of the Āṅgirasa [Gotra] faces north and resides in the northern region.
Mercury and Venus are dear to the Sun, Moon, and Mars, while they are enemies to Jupiter and Saturn, who are their lords.
In the [years] two, five, seven, nine, one, and six, it always brings auspiciousness and bestows blessings. || 5 ||
Śukra, born of the Bhārgava lineage, possessing white luster, facing the east, situated in the east;

he has five faces, is the lord of Vaṇija and Vṛṣa, originates from the land called Bhoja, has Indrāṇī and Indra as his deities, and is the enemy of Jña and Ravija; Rātri is his wife, and Śaśī is his enemy.
And the Sun in the seventeenth asterism during its season bestows auspiciousness and always brings about well-being.
Manda (Saturn) is dark-hued, has Varuṇa as his presiding deity, is born in Saurāṣṭra, and belongs to the Kaśyapa lineage; he is the lord of Capricorn and Aquarius.
Venus and Mercury are friends, while the Sun and Moon are enemies.
His position is in the western direction, and the two deities Prajāpati and Yama reside in Sagittarius.
Saturn, situated in the sixth, third, or twelfth house, always brings about auspiciousness for one who performs meritorious deeds. || 7 ||
Rāhu was born in Rāṭhinapura; he is a son of Diti, has Kṛṣṇa as his deity, and sits upon a winnowing basket (śūrpa).

He is presided over by the serpent Kālāhi, has a face toward the direction of Yama (the south), and possesses a blue luster. His fierce and crooked heart is situated in the direction of the Rakṣasas (the southwest), and he is born of the lineage of Paiṭhīnasi.
Situated in the sixth or third house, the auspicious Barbarapati will always bring about prosperity.

The Ketu born of the Jaimini lineage, situated in the direction of the Wind (Northwest), beloved of Mars and the Moon, possessing variegated luster, seated upon a throne marked by a banner, with a face turned toward the direction of Yama (South) and a terrifying countenance;
whose presiding deity is Brahmā accompanied by Citragupta; who is of the Kada clan, stationed in the sixth and third houses, and born in the region of Suvedi—may he always bestow auspiciousness. (9)
In this manner, they may also recite other auspicious verses (maṅgalaśloka) as space permits. Then:
"That alone is the auspicious moment (lagna), that alone is the good day; that alone is the strength of the stars, that alone is the strength of the moon."

"The power of knowledge, the power of destiny—that indeed is the pair of feet of You, O Lord of Lakṣmī; I remember them. When the astrologer has thus recited "Oṃ Pratiṣṭhā," the Brahmins shall immediately remove the inner curtain to the north and cause the bride and groom to gaze at each other during an auspicious moment.
Then, according to custom, they shall cause the bride and groom to scatter rice and cumin held in their joined palms at one another, with the girl acting first.

Then the twice-born should recite the *khaṇḍas* beginning with "ṛk ca ve," the *anuvāka* beginning with "prajāpatiḥ somam rājānam asṛjata," the *anuvāka* beginning with "siṃhe vyāghre," and the four mantras beginning with "asme devāsaḥ. At the conclusion of each, the offering of unbroken rice grains (*akṣata-āropaṇa*) should be performed according to custom.
Now follows the giving away of the bride (*kanyādāna*).
Regarding this, Vṛddhayājñavalkya states that the ceremonial bath may take place even at night: [The text continues with the verse of Vṛddhayājñavalkya.]

"Bathing on occasions such as eclipses, weddings, the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), journeys, times of distress, and childbirth is to be known as occasional (naimittika); it is indeed prescribed even at night."
Vyāsa says: "The 'great night' (mahāniśā) should be understood as the two middle watches of the night;
one should not perform a bath during that time, except for those baths performed for specific desires or occasional rites."
"At dusk, during the final watch of the night, one should perform a bath as if it were daytime."
Regarding the specific rule for the two middle watches of the night, Atri says:
"If a bath should take place at night, a Brahmin who sees fire should perform it; or, wearing a golden ring on his finger, he may perform it even without fire."
In another Smṛti, the *Prayogadarpaṇa*, it is stated:
"If the gift of the maiden takes place at midnight, eating is desired during the day;
one should perform the ritual bath at the proper time and then give the maiden to the groom."

In marriage, there are two principal acts: the giving away of the girl (*kanyādāna*) and the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). The former pertains to the father of the girl. As for the preeminence of the giving away of the girl, it is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*: "In the *Brāhma* form of marriage, one should give [the girl] after having adorned her according to one's ability," and: "Having adorned the girl, one should give her with a libation of water; this is the *Brāhma* marriage."
This is because the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra* indicates the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two terms "giving" (*dāna*) and "marriage" (*vivāha*);
furthermore, regarding the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), there is the sūtra: "The fire beginning with the taking of the hand is called the *aupāsana*."

From the *Dharmasūtra*—“The vow of the two householders begins from the taking of the hand”—their primacy is to be understood. Furthermore, the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*, which states that after mentioning the times for the *caula*, *upanayana*, *godāna*, and *vivāha* rites, one should offer four oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) before them, is also an authority here. Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency regarding the oblation mentioned prior to the *vivāha* as referred to by the word “those” (*teṣām*). For those oblations do not exist prior to the giving away of the girl (*kanyādāna*). In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
“In the *nāndīmukha* rite and in the *vivāha*, [the invocation] begins with the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*).”
"A wise man should recite the name [of the deceased], except in the case of the ancestors (where it is done starting with the father)."

The rule regarding the precedence of the *prapitāmaha* (great-grandfather) in the *nāndīmukha* rite, which is prescribed in certain Vedic branches (*śākhā*), pertains to those specific branches and is not the subject of our own Sūtra; for that [rule] is not enjoined in our Sūtra, and because teachers such as Cauṇḍapācārya, Rāmāṇḍāra, and others have stated that the order should follow the natural sequence (*ānulomya*) alone.

Some, however, say that "in the *nāndīmukha*" is an adjective qualifying the marriage (*vivāha*), and its meaning is "that which produces joy by means of the father and other ancestors"; they further state that the particle *ca* has the sense of "but" (*tvartha*).

In this manner, the precedence of the *prapitāmaha* (great-grandfather) in the *nāndīmukha* rite is simply not established. According to this view, since the *rākṣasa* and other such forms of marriage do not produce joy (*harṣa*), the precedence of the *prapitāmaha* does not apply there.
Vyāsa states: "One may marry a maiden after having eaten [the *nāndīśrāddha*], and likewise perform the *sāvitrī-grahaṇa* (initiation)."
"Having fasted, one should give one's daughter to a twice-born man who has been duly honored."
The phrase "having eaten" refers specifically to the meal that is a constituent part of the *madhuparka* offering. In the *Madanaratna*, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga states:
"Having pronounced the bridegroom’s lineage, beginning with the great-grandfather..."
The learned man should likewise proclaim the name of the maiden in this very same manner.
The giver should stand facing the east, while the bridegroom should face the west;
he should then give her, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to him who has been honored with the madhuparka offering.
Then, taking a vessel of water, he should cause him to give her with this mantra:
"O Brahmin, here is this maiden Gaurī, adorned according to his means."
O Brahmin, take refuge in you, Gotraśarman;
[I have] given you land, a cow, a female slave, and garments according to my ability.
One should give a buffalo, horses, as well as gold and jewels;
thereafter, one should have the rites beginning with the fire-oblation (homa) performed according to the rules of one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.
"According to custom, auspicious items and water-pots should be presented."

Since it is observed everywhere that [the lineage] begins with the father, the rule is established that it begins with the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*). By the phrase "in this very manner," the recitation of the *gotra* and so forth is extended to the bride as well. The statements such as "the giver should stand facing east" and "the receiver facing north" are intended to override the general rules of giving (*dānaparibhāṣā*) which dictate that the giver faces east and the receiver faces north. In the word *gṛhya*, although there is no compound, the substitution of *lyap* for *ktvā* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage. In the word *dāpayet*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in its own sense (without implying an agent). *Maṅgala* refers to the auspicious thread (*maṅgalasūtra*).
*Karakāṇi* means earthen vessels. By the use of the word *ca* (and), it is meant that articles of auspiciousness (*saubhāgyadravyāṇi*) should also be given to the married women.
In the *Prayogadarpaṇa*, another Smṛti states:
"Having proclaimed one's own lineage and gotra, and likewise that of the bridegroom..."
The wise man should proclaim the names, beginning with the great-grandfather.
Having spoken thus regarding the maiden, he himself, facing east, stands before the bridegroom who faces west, after the latter has been honored with the madhuparka offering.
"One should give a maiden along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), land, garments, horses,
a buffalo-cow, a cow, a female slave, and even gold and jewels."
In another Smṛti, however, it is stated: "The giver should stand facing north, while the recipient should face east.

There is no mantra for the acceptance [of the gift] here, because this is not connected with a sacrifice (*yajña*). The Sūtrakāra has demonstrated that the acceptance of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) connected with Tantric rites alone is accompanied by mantras, and not that of others.

By the phrase "he shows [the sacrificial fee] to the female practitioners (tāntrī) who receive the dakṣiṇā," the word *tantra* refers to the sacrifice (*yāga*), because that very [meaning] is introduced in the Vedic scripture: "The gods, indeed, caused Varuṇa to sacrifice."

The acceptance mantra, "manave talpam," is employed for the acceptance of a female slave during the Vājapeya sacrifice because of its connection to the ritual procedure (*tantra*). It is not, however, employed even in a divine marriage (*daiva-vivāha*), as it lacks such a connection to the ritual procedure. Furthermore, although the injunction "one should bestow" exists here [in the case of the *daiva* marriage], what Mātṛdatta stated—that there is an acceptance with the mantra "manave talpam" when she is given along with the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in a divine rite—appears to contradict the subsequent text. Moreover, the formula "not mine" (*na mama*) is also not used.
Because of the statement in the *Dharmasūtra*, "one should bestow [the bride]," she should accept her by saying either "Oṃ, may it be well! or "Oṃ, so be it.
Now, the ritual procedure:

the giver of the girl shall give the girl to the groom, having removed the garments, ornaments, and other items given by the groom's party, and having adorned her with the garments, ornaments, and other items to be given by himself, and having caused her to put on yellow garments.

Having removed the stone and seated the girl on the pedestal, he sits facing north to the south of the space between the bride and groom; having seated his wife to his right and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), with *pavitra* grass in hand and having restrained his breath, he announces the place and time: "I, [Name] Śarmā, born of the [Name] Gotra and endowed with the [Name] Pravara, for the attainment by all my ancestors of the unsurpassed blissful world of Brahmā and other fruits mentioned in the ritual manual for the bestowal of a daughter, shall procreate through this groom upon this girl..."

One should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "For the sake of purifying twelve ancestors and twelve descendants through this continuous lineage, and for the pleasure of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, I shall perform the bestowal of the girl according to the Brāhma marriage rite. If this resolve was already made at the commencement of the wedding ceremony, then it need not be performed here.
Then, the groom, together with his wife, stands up and, facing north, takes the hand of the girl—who stands facing south—in his right hand, [reciting]:
"The girl, endowed with gold and adorned with golden ornaments..."
I shall give it to you, O Viṣṇu, with the desire to conquer the world of Brahmā.
"O Viśvambhara, O all beings, O witnesses, O all deities:
I shall bestow this maiden for the sake of the liberation of my ancestors."

Having recited this, while the bridegroom stands facing east holding a vessel made of bell-metal or some other metal, he should recite thirteen statements while pouring water—mixed with *akṣata* grains, *tulasī* leaves, and *kuśa* grass—into the right hand (or both hands) of the bride, who stands facing west. Regarding the relative positions of the hands: if the bridegroom follows the *Āśvalāyana* tradition, his hand is below and the bride’s hand is above; if he follows the *Yājuṣa* tradition, the order is reversed, such that the bride’s hand is below and the bridegroom’s hand is above. This upper-lower arrangement should be understood accordingly.

Then: "May the maiden cross over; may merit increase; may the waters be auspicious; may there be goodwill; may there be well-being and freedom from misfortune; may there be long life, prosperity, peace, nourishment, and contentment; may there be the excellence of the lunar day, the *karaṇa*, the *muhūrta*, and the asterism; may that which is auspicious be so; may whatever is evil be averted; may you, sirs, declare it a holy day (*puṇyāha*); may you, sirs, declare well-being (*svasti*); may you, sirs, declare success (*ṛddhi*); may you, sirs, declare 'May there be prosperity' (*śrīrastu*). Thus [he says].

Then, having recited as before from "I, [Name] Śarmā, born of the [Name] Gotra and endowed with the [Name] Pravaras, for the sake of the gratification of all my ancestors... up to "...for the sake of [Name] Śarmā," he should say: "To the bridegroom [Name] Śarmā, born of the [Name] Gotra and endowed with the [Name] Pravaras, the great-grandson of [Name], the grandson of [Name], the son of [Name], who possesses the form of Śrīdhara and seeks a maiden; [I give] this daughter [Name], born of the [Name] Gotra and endowed with the [Name] Pravaras, the great-granddaughter of [Name], the granddaughter of [Name], the daughter of myself, [Name], who seeks a bridegroom and possesses the form of Śrī."

Having said, "I bestow upon you this girl, adorned according to your means, whose presiding deity is Prajāpati, for the sake of procreation and shared duties," he should pour water mixed with barley, unbroken rice, *tulasī* leaves, and *kuśa* grass into the hand of the bridegroom. In the Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca forms of marriage, there is no such formal bestowal, because these do not depend upon the ritual act of a donor.

Then the groom should accept [the gift] by saying "Oṃ, may it be well" (*svasti*) or "Oṃ, so be it" (*tathā*). In this case, the donor no longer has the sense of "mine. Likewise, there is no such mantra of acceptance for the groom. In this manner, the formula beginning with "May the maiden deliver [us]" (*kanyā tārayatu*) and ending with "Oṃ, may it be well" (*svasti*) should be performed twice again. However, when the grandfather performs the gift, he should say "mine" (*mama*) before the word "granddaughter" (*pautrīm*). When the great-grandfather performs it on account of kinship, he should say "mine" before the word "great-granddaughter" (*prapautrīm*).

When a brother or similar relative performs a gift, he should only mention three generations [of his lineage]; he must never say "mine. If it is the mother who performs the gift, then the modification is as follows: she should say, "I, of such-and-such a lineage, named so-and-so," using her husband's lineage in this manner; she should not say "born of such-and-such a lineage," nor should she ever mention her father's lineage.

Whether it be the maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, or any other relative, or any other Brāhmaṇa belonging to a different lineage (*gotra*) who performs the gift of the maiden, he should proclaim his own lineage as a qualifying attribute and say: "For the sake of the father of the maiden, N.N.-Śarmā, and for all [his] ancestors, for the sake of unsurpassed [merit]," and so forth. In the phrase "and for myself," one should say "and for the father of the maiden. If the mother is the giver, then one should say: "For the sake of my husband’s father and all [his] ancestors, for the sake of unsurpassed [merit]," and so forth. In the phrase "and for myself," one should say "and for my husband."

Regarding the phrase "and of myself" (*ātmanaśca*), if it is interpreted as being in the accusative plural, then [the reading] would be *kanyāpitṝn* or *kanyāpitaram*. In this context, since it serves as an adjective for the daughter, one must specifically mention the lineage (*gotra*) of the daughter's father. In phrases such as "the great-granddaughter of so-and-so," the names of the daughter's father and others should be uttered. Furthermore, in the verse to be recited later—"born in the family of my own lineage"—one should say the name of the daughter's father in the genitive case in place of the word "my" (*mama*).

If the adopted son (dattaka) performs the giving away of the girl, then he should state that the lineage (gotra) of the one by whom he was received belongs to both himself and the girl as their specific qualification. He should recite the names of the adoptive father, his father, and his grandfather. Even in the giving away of an adopted girl, the mention of one's own lineage must be made as the qualification of the girl. In the verse [beginning with] *jātā*, one should say *dattā* (given) instead. Likewise, in the giving away of the girl to the adopted groom, the lineage and other details belong only to the one by whom he was received.
Then: "O Brahmin, this girl Gaurī, adorned according to my ability..."
O Brahmin, take refuge in you, who are the source of protection for the lineage;
may my two daughters be before me, may my two daughters, O Goddess, be at my sides,
and may my two daughters be behind me— through this gift of yours, may I attain liberation.

"Brahmin, born into my family lineage and nurtured by me for eight years, this girl—who increases sons and grandsons—is given by me to you. Thus he should announce the girl. However, if she is less than eight years of age, the word *gaurīm* (the "fair-complexioned one") is omitted. Alternatively, the formula may be: "Brahmin, this girl, adorned according to my ability... The modifications *pālitā varṣasaptakam* ("nurtured for seven years") and *pāliteyaṃ ṣaḍabdakam* ("this one has been nurtured for six years") should be applied accordingly. But if she is nine years of age, one should substitute *rohiṇīm* for the word *gaurīm*, as in: "Brahmin, this girl Rohiṇī... and "she has been nurtured for nine years."

In the case of a ten-year-old girl, however, one should substitute the word "kanyā" (maiden) for the positions of the words "gaurī" and "rohiṇī," [reciting]: "O Brahmin, protect this maiden for ten years. As before, the word "gaurī" is omitted here as well. In this context, "year" refers to the year since her birth. Then, he should cause her to hear: "She must not be transgressed by you in matters of dharma, artha, or kāma. Thereupon, the groom should accept the meaning of the statement, saying: "I shall not transgress."

Then the giver, for the sake of accomplishing the completeness of the performed rite of giving the daughter in marriage, shall place this gold—intended for the deity Agni and prepared according to his means—into the hand of the bridegroom, saying, "I give this to you as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*"), and he should say, "It is not mine. The bridegroom, however, should shake it off seventeen times.

For the mantra "devasya tvā," Prajāpati is the seer, Savitṛ is the deity, and the Yajus is the metre; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the acceptance of gold. One should accept it with the words: "Oṃ devasya tvā savituḥ... agnaye hiraṇyaṃ te... tu. According to this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), the Sāvitra mantra is used only for the acceptance of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and not elsewhere; in that case, there is no seventeen-fold inhalation (*apānana*), and the acceptance is performed simply with the words "I accept" (*pratigṛhṇāmi*).

Thereafter, the donor, preceded by a formal declaration (*saṃkalpa*), should give to the bridegroom according to his means water-vessels, food-vessels, cows, buffaloes, horses, elephants, female and male slaves, land, beds, ornaments, and so forth.
In that regard, the mantras for giving are as follows:
"May the sin produced from slandering others, from backbiting, and from eating what is unfit to be eaten,
be destroyed by this gift of a copper vessel."
Thus [is the formula] for a copper vessel intended for drinking water:
"Whatever sins have been committed arising from desire,
may they always perish for me through the gift of this bell-metal vessel."
Thus [is the rite] for a bronze vessel used for eating and other purposes:
"May my transgression of approaching those who should not be approached and my violation of another's wife always perish through the gift of a silver vessel."
Thus for a silver vessel used for drinking water or for eating:
"Whatever sin has been committed by me throughout thousands of other births, may it always perish through the gift of this golden vessel. Thus for a golden vessel.

"For this cow, which is the means for accomplishing sacrifice and the destroyer of the multitude of sins of the universe, may the God who assumes the universal form be pleased. This is the mantra for the cow.
"She who is the beloved queen of the sovereignty of Indra and the other guardians of the world..."
"May she, the mother of Mahiṣāsura, be the granter of all my desires"— thus [the mantra] for the buffalo.
"O Uccaiḥśravas, born from the great ocean, son of [the Sea],
you who are given along with your trappings to this Brahmin, grant me peace."
Thus [is the mantra] for the horse equipped with its trappings, such as the bit.
"O noble elephant of auspicious form, you who have been consecrated by Sarasvatī,
the eternal vehicle of Indra, and highly honored by all the gods."
"O Brahmin, I give this elephant to you; with it, grant me peace," [is the formula] for the elephant.
"O Śrīvatsa, this dear maidservant has been offered by me to you; she shall always be your servant. May it be well with me according to your wish," [is the formula] for the maidservant.
"For this servant has been bestowed upon you by me, O Śrīvatsa;
may he, ever performing his duties and dear to my heart, grant me peace. Thus for the servant.
"The earth, the support of all crops, was lifted up by the Boar."
"O Earth, who bestows infinite crops and fruits, grant me peace. Thus [is the prayer] to the Earth.
"O Keśava, by the gift of this bed, grant me eternally an undiminished bed, undiminished prosperity and exaltation, and constant good fortune."
Thus for the bed together with its furnishings:
"I shall offer this golden bracelet, which bestows beauty, luster, and happiness; may it always adorn me."
Thus for the ornaments such as bracelets and the like.
For the ring: "I give this golden ring, produced from the Golden Womb (Hiraṇyagarbha), which bestows all things; may the Lord of Kamalā be pleased. Thus for the ring.
"The two auspicious earrings produced from the churning of the Ocean of Milk, which arose together with Śrī—may Śrī be pleased with me as I give them. Thus [he spoke] regarding the two earrings.
"May the golden seed of the Fire-god, residing within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha and bestowing the fruit of infinite merit, grant me peace"— thus for gold.
"Silver, which originated among the Asuras and is dear to the Pitṛs—may Rudra be well-pleased with me by the gift of this. This is for silver.
Now follow the mantras for their acceptance.

"Oṃ, by the grace of the God, I accept you, the cow, for Rudra; may she protect me. Thus for the cow. Having offered a blade of grass, the acceptance [is performed]. "Oṃ, by the grace of the God, I accept you, the buffalo-cow, for Prajāpati; may she protect me. Thus for the buffalo-cow; or alternatively, "for Yama, the buffalo-cow. "Oṃ, by the grace of the God, I accept you, the horse, for Varuṇa; may he protect me. Thus for the horse. Having offered a blade of grass, the acceptance [is performed]. "Oṃ, by the grace of the God, I accept you, the elephant, for Himavat; may he protect me. Thus for the elephant.

"Oṃ, to Prajāpati, the female slave; with her... for the female slave. "Oṃ, to Prajāpati, the male slave; with him... for the male slave. "Oṃ, to Manu, the bed; with it... for the bed. "To the Apsarases in the south, the ornament; with it... for the ornaments. The mantra is repeated for each individual ornament. "To Agni in the northeast, gold; with it... for the gold. In all cases, there is the addition of the Sāvitrī verse. For all [these offerings], Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi), Savitṛ is the deity, and Yajus is the meter.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the acceptance [of gifts]; this refers to the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details. For the mantras used in accepting a queen, female slaves, and male slaves, Vāmadeva is to be known as the seer. The mantra beginning with *uttānas tvā* is for the acceptance of remaining inanimate objects. Regarding this, some say that the *Sāvitrānvādhī* [formula] is also applied. For this [mantra], Prajāpati is the seer; Āṅgirasa is the deity; the *Yajus* is the meter; and the application is for acceptance—thus the seer and other details are to be understood. After the acceptance of each object, one must exhale seventeen times.

Or rather, the acceptance of all [gifts] is simply by saying "I accept. In this view, there is no [recitation of] *āpohiṣṭhā* or the offering of grass. Some maintain that [the recitation of *āpohiṣṭhā*] occurs here as well.

Then, the giver of the girl, for the sake of accomplishing the completeness of the rite of giving the girl, should feed the Brahmins and married women with food as available according to his means; having given them abundant gifts to the Brahmins preceded by worship with perfumes and other offerings, he should remember Viṣṇu for the perfection of the ritual.
Thus ends the procedure for the giving of the girl.
Regarding what must be done after this, it is stated in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*:

"A twice-born man, seated, should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for the couple by sprinkling water mixed with gold over them while reciting those *ṛc* verses that contain the word 'water' (*abliṅga*)."
Then, with these four verses beginning with "ā naḥ prajām," and likewise with the four beginning with "samudra" and the three beginning with "āpo hi."
Having prepared a white thread soaked in milk and doubled in length,
[he should place it] around the neck and likewise around the waist of both the bridegroom and the bride.
Then, starting from the northeast direction, one should circumambulate five times or even four times, moving clockwise without interruption.
One should draw out that sūtra which is located at the region of the throat;
having dyed it with saffron and joined it with a tuft of black wool.
Having firmly tied a piece of cloth with that thread,
the bridegroom should bind it very securely upon the bride’s left wrist.
This [thread] is traditionally prescribed for the purpose of protection by means of the *nīlalohita* mantra;
one should draw out that thread which is located at the waist region.
Having dyed it with saffron and joined it with a tuft of black wool,
one should firmly tie a piece of turmeric with that same thread.
The bride should bind [the bracelet] very firmly on the forearm of the right hand;
the same mantra mentioned previously is to be used here, or binding in silence is prescribed.
When the vessel made of refined gold has been brought, one should pour a small amount of cow's ghee into the milk;
then, having poured it into another vessel, one should scatter white, unhusked, moist grains (akṣata) into it.
Then the bride should pour rice produced from the *śāli* variety twice into the milk held in her joined palms;
thereafter, the groom should likewise pour it twice with his own joined palms into the milk.
Having spread [the base], one should place therein twice unbroken grains smeared with milk;
then, having sprinkled [them] with ghee as before, one should likewise offer them with the verse beginning "payasā" (with milk).
Either the donor or another person should place [the gold] in the joined palms of the bridegroom;
then the twice-born [priest] should place gold in the joined palms of both the bridegroom and the bride.
Then, joining his palms in *añjali*, he should utter four statements;
he should recite them in sequence as "Kanyā," "Puṇya," "Śānti," and "Tithi."
Then, with the mantras "Bhaga," "Yajña," "Śrī," "Dharma," "Prajā," and "Yaśas" respectively,
the two [the bridegroom and the officiant] should perform the rite of scattering unbroken rice grains (akṣatāropaṇa) upon the head.
The first [initiation] belongs to the bride; the next to the husband; the third should belong to the bride;
the fourth to the husband; the fifth to the bride; and the last belongs to the man alone.
One should perform this three times; then, one should do the reverse again.
The seventh is to be known as silent; this is remembered as being preceded by the granting of a boon.
Some have declared that this rite should be performed four times;
others do not accept the mantras beginning with "bhago me kāmaḥ."
Then the bridegroom, taking the flower from his own head and having soaked it in milk and clarified butter, [applies] that [mixture] to the forehead of the bride.
The groom should apply a *tilaka* on the bride's forehead; then the bride should do likewise. They both should then place flower garlands around each other's necks.
The well-dressed women should present two garments, a bodice, and a thread called "auspicious" (maṅgala) to the bride; and the groom [should present them] to that bride.
Having donned the garment and recollected his chosen deity,
he should adorn the region of his neck with a thread called *maṅgala*.
"This mantra, 'māṅgalyatantunā,' has been declared here by the wise;
afterwards, one should adorn the various limbs with other ornaments."
The bride and groom should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa,
as well as that of Mahālakṣmī, for the sake of increasing good fortune and other blessings.
One should likewise perform the worship of Pārvatī and Śacī;
for the sake of good fortune, one should, with a well-concentrated mind, offer gifts of barley-meal (vāyana).
"Then they should perform the observance of the vow for three days.

Now follows the ritual procedure for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth. The family priest [recites]: For the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the deities are Agni, the Viśvedevas, or the Waters; the meter is Gāyatrī. Their application is in the act of consecrating [the water]. Having consecrated the water contained in the well-adorned pitcher—mixed with gold—with the mantra: *oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ... canaḥ*, he should sprinkle [the recipient] with that water together with gold, *kuśa* grass, and sprouts of *dūrvā*.

For the four verses beginning with *ā naḥ prajām*, Sūryāsāvitrī is the seer; Sūryāsāvitrī is the deity. The first two are in the Jagatī meter; the last two are in the Anuṣṭubh meter. For the four verses beginning with *samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ*, Vasiṣṭha is the seer; the Waters (Āpaḥ) are the deity; they are in the Triṣṭubh meter. For the triad of mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, Agni or the Viśvedevas are the deities; the Waters are the deity; they are in the Gāyatrī meter. The application (*viniyoga*) of all these is for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the bridegroom and the bride. One should perform the consecration with: *oṃ ā naḥ prajāṃ janayatu... vṛṣu*; *oṃ samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ*; and *oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā*. According to some, the bridegroom alone should perform the consecration.

Then the priest, having wound a white thread doubled and soaked in milk five or four times clockwise around the necks of the bride and bridegroom starting from the northeast (īśānī), should likewise wind it around their waists. In this regard, these mantras accepted by the learned should be recited: "Oṃ pari tvā girvaṇo gira i0 dhvamadhvaram," and the Yajurvedic mantra "Oṃ mahīnāṃ payo'si vi0 yai dugdham" should also be recited.

Then, having removed the thread from the neck region, having smeared it with saffron and attached a tuft of black wool, and having firmly tied a piece of turmeric to it, the groom should bind it on the bride’s left wrist with the mantra: "Oṃ nīlalohitaṃ bha... badhyate. For this [mantra] "nīlalohitam," Sūryāsāvitrī is the seer, Sūryāsāvitrī is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application (viniyoga) is for binding the bracelet on the hand. (Note: The mantra fragment provided is incomplete; the full mantra is typically: *oṃ nīlalohitaṃ bhavati kumāraḥ pramukhaḥ śitiḥ / atho babhruḥ piṅgalo 'tha śyāvo 'tho bhavati sarvavṛṣaḥ //*)

Then, having drawn out the thread situated at the waist, having smeared it with saffron and attached a tuft of black wool, and having firmly tied a piece of turmeric to it, the bride should bind it on the right forearm of the groom, either with that same mantra or silently.

Then the bride and groom should perform the rite of scattering unbroken rice (*akṣatāropaṇa*), which increases their mutual longevity. It is as follows: when a metallic vessel has been brought, having poured a little ghee into cow's milk and placed it in another vessel, the groom—having washed his joined palms and having placed moist, unbroken white *śāli* rice grains into the washed palms of the bride—should, with the fingers of both his hands, spread the milk mixed with ghee twice; then, having likewise poured the rice grains twice in the same manner, he should sprinkle it twice over with the milk in the same way.

Then, even when the bridegroom’s joined palms are empty, the giver or another person may act in this manner. Then the giver himself, having placed gold within those two palms and having joined the bridegroom’s palms with the bride’s palms, should recite these words: "May the maiden cross over [to a better state]; may merit increase; may there be peace, nourishment, and contentment; may there be the excellence of the lunar day, the *karaṇa*, the hour, and the asterism."

Then the bride, with the mantra "Oṃ, may my desire for fortune (*bhaga*) be fulfilled," should place the parched grains (*akṣata*) held in her joined palms upon the head of the groom. With the mantra "Oṃ, may my desire for sacrifice (*yajña*) be fulfilled," the groom should place the parched grains held in his own joined palms upon the head of the bride. This is done a second and a third time as well. Therein, for the second time, the mantra of the bride is "Oṃ, may my desire for prosperity (*śrī*) be fulfilled," and that of the groom is "Oṃ, may my desire for dharma be fulfilled."

In the third [offering], however, the mantra for the bride is: "Oṃ, may my desire for progeny be fulfilled. For the groom, the specific mantra is: "Oṃ, may my desire for glory be fulfilled. Then the bride, having spread [rice] twice into the joined palms of the groom and having filled them twice with rice grains, should pour clarified butter over them twice.

Then the giver or another person should fill the bride's joined palms as before. Then the giver himself, having placed gold as before and having placed the bride's joined palms into the groom's joined palms, should recite the formulas as before.

Then the bridegroom—saying, "Oṃ, may my desire for sacrifice (*yajña*) be fulfilled"—should place the *akṣata* grains held in his joined palms upon the head of the bride. Then the bride—saying, "Oṃ, may my desire for fortune (*bhaga*) be fulfilled"—should place the *akṣata* grains held in her joined palms upon the head of the bridegroom. This is done a second and a third time as well. In that regard, the specific difference is that for the second [round], the bridegroom's mantra is "May my desire for dharma (*dharma*) be fulfilled," and the bride's is "May my desire for prosperity (*śrī*) be fulfilled. For the third [round], the bridegroom's is "May my desire for fame (*yaśas*) be fulfilled," and the bride's is "May my desire for offspring (*prajā*) be fulfilled."

Then the bridegroom, having filled the bride's joined palms as before, and having had them filled by the giver or another person into his own joined palms, should silently place the *akṣata* grains from the bride's palms onto her head. The bride should likewise silently place [the grains] onto the bridegroom's head. In this manner, the offering of *akṣata* should be performed seven times or four times. Some do not accept the mantras beginning with "bhago me"; according to that view, the offering of *akṣata* is done silently seven or four times.

Then the groom, having taken the flower from his own head and soaked it in milk mixed with ghee, should apply a *tilaka* mark on the forehead of the bride with it. Likewise, the bride should also apply a *tilaka* mark on the groom’s forehead with the flower from her own head.
Then the bride should place the flower garland from her own neck around the groom’s neck; the groom [should place] the one from his own neck around the bride’s neck.

Then, the auspicious women from the groom’s side, having seated the bride and groom facing east, shall perform the *nīrājana* ceremony and present the bride with the two garments known as the *aṣṭaputrī*, along with a bodice and the auspicious thread (*maṅgalasūtra*), as required by custom. Having caused her to put on one of these garments, they shall have the other serve as her upper garment (*uttarīya*). Then, they shall cause her to put on the bodice.
Thereafter, the groom [recites]: "By this auspicious thread, which is the cause of the husband's long life..."
"I bind this upon your neck, O fortunate one; may you live for a hundred autumns."
With this mantra, he should fasten that thread around the bride’s neck while recollecting his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). He should also adorn her with mantras beginning with *āyuṣyaṃ varcasyam*.

Then, having placed five firm betel nuts along with pieces of turmeric and sweets (*laḍḍuka*) in a vessel according to custom, the bride and groom should perform the worship of Gaṇapati for the sake of protecting the marriage vow, using the ritual services from the invocation up to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and reciting the two mantras *gaṇānāṃ tvā* and *ā tū na indra*. Here, a sacrificial fee should be given to the Brahmins according to one's means for the pleasure of Gaṇapati.

Then the priest, having called to mind Gaṇapati, the protector of the marriage vow, should tie two laddūkas—each containing a piece of turmeric and a piece of raw cotton—to the ends of the garments of the bride and groom respectively. The bride and groom must not untie those two knots until the completion of the marriage vow. Then the priest, with the mantra "Oṃ nīlalohitaṃ bhavati kṛtyāsaktiryajyate | edhante asyā jñātayaḥ patirbandheṣu badhyate" and the mantra "Bṛhatsāma," should tie the ends of their upper garments together.

Then the groom, together with his wife, and the elderly matrons, kinsmen, and relatives, should in due order perform the rite of offering moist *akṣata* grains along with blessings according to custom.

Then the bride, having invoked Mahālakṣmī, Pārvatī, and Śacī in sequence by their respective names and mantras upon three heaps of white rice placed in a vessel from left to right, should worship them with the ritual services ending with the gift of a priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Some authorities maintain that the groom should also perform the worship.

Then, for the sake of increasing the bride's good fortune and so forth, and for the pleasure of Mahālakṣmī, Pārvatī, and Śacī, she should honor the married women (suvāsinīs) and give them gifts of bamboo baskets (*vaṃśapātra*) filled with turmeric, cumin, and auspicious substances (*saubhāgyadravya*), along with *vāyana* offerings.
The mantras for this occasion are:
"Lakṣmī’s beloved, the giver of Lakṣmī, who like Lakṣmī herself is dear to virtuous people..."
"May the two turmeric plants, which bestow good fortune upon excellent women, be my constant prosperity.
This is the mantra for the gift of turmeric.
"Since from them old age does not arise, they are an ornament for auspicious rites."
"Therefore, may Girijā be pleased with me through this gift of cumin"— this is the mantra for the gift of cumin.
"May the daughter of Nimi be pleased by means of bodices, pairs of garments, as well as ear-ornaments, necklaces, and other decorations."

This is the mantra for the gift of a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) filled with auspicious substances (*saubhāgyadravya*). These items, along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), should be given. Then, blessings (*āśis*) should be bestowed by the twice-born: "Oṃ *navo navo bhavati*... "Oṃ *yathā ha tadva*... "Mā no arātira*... "Oṃ *bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ*... [And] "Oṃ *abhrātṛghnīṃ varuṇāpatighnīṃ bṛhaspata indrāputraghnīṃ lakṣmyantāmasyai savituḥ save*"—with these words, the groom gazes at the bride.

"Oṃ, may you have eyes that are not terrible; do not be a slayer of your husband; be auspicious to our cattle, well-disposed, and full of luster; be a mother of heroes, desirous of the gods, and pleasant; be a source of welfare to us, to our bipeds, and to our quadrupeds. Reciting this while looking at the bride, the groom mutters it. "Oṃ, this ill-fortune of yours which makes you a slayer of your husband—here I designate it. With these words, he wipes the bride's face with a blade of *darbha* grass. Having cast away the *darbha* and touched water, he takes the bride by her right hand, saying, "Oṃ, you are Mitra."

With the mantra, "Oṃ, may Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of food; may Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of strength; may Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of the priestly offices," he leads the bride to the sacrificial ground in the form of the altar. Having grasped her seventh step with the mantra, "Oṃ, you are my friend; we have become seven-stepped companions; may I attain your friendship; may your friendship not fail me; may your friendship not fail me," he recites this.

(Then, accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, the bridegroom, together with the bride, shall sit upon the altar facing the east. Thereafter, the bride shall go to the vicinity of Gaurī and Hara and sit down. From the ceremony of mutual gazing (*nirīkṣaṇa*) until the distribution of betel nuts (*vāyana*), learned authorities perform this in some regions within the inner chamber (*madhyagṛha*), while in others it is done in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Mutual gazing between the couple does not take place in the inner chamber on Sundays, Tuesdays, Thursdays, or Saturdays; nor does it take place in the pavilion on Mondays, Wednesdays, or Fridays.
Regarding the statement in the *Jyotirnibandha* that "because Time (Kāla) resides there [in the pavilion]," we do not know the reason why the learned nowadays do not accept it.

Let there be a distinction in the observation [of the stars] based on a specific location or a specific day; nevertheless, the giving of the bride (*kanyādāna*) must be performed in the pavilion itself, because it is logical that the primary act of giving the bride should take place in the pavilion. Otherwise, the construction of that [pavilion] would have no connection whatsoever to the primary rite performed by the agent himself. This should be accepted if it is indeed reasonable.
Now follows the marriage oblation (*vivāhahoma*).

Having sipped water (*ācamana*) and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), having announced the place and time, and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "For the propitiation of the glorious Supreme Lord (*Śrī Parameśvara*), by means of establishing the status of the *aupāsana* fire in the fire, preceded by the establishment of the state of wifehood directed toward the bride accepted by me, I shall perform the marriage oblation (*vivāhahoma*)," and having performed the drawing of lines on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and other rites, he should install the fire named Yojaka with the formula: "I establish the fire named Yojaka. [The fire] should have been produced by friction and brought from the house of a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*) by a well-dressed woman (*suvāsinī*) before the bride and groom ascend the altar (*vedi*). On the altar...

Having established and kindled the common (laukika) fire placed on the lower part to the north, and having meditated upon it, he takes three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and performs the rites from "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) up to the end of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then, having recited from "In this marriage-homa-rite, those deities who are to be worshipped... up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he declares for the principal oblation: "I shall worship Agni and Varuṇa with one offering of clarified butter (*ājya*); I shall worship Agni Gārhapatya with one offering of clarified butter; I shall worship Agni with one offering of clarified butter."

I shall worship Heaven, Vāyu, the Aśvins, Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati, and all the Gods with one oblation of clarified butter each; I shall worship Agni with two oblations of clarified butter; in the Aṅgahoma, I shall worship Varuṇa with two oblations of clarified butter; I shall worship Agni and Varuṇa with one oblation of clarified butter each; I shall worship Agni and Varuṇa with one oblation of clarified butter each; I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with one oblation of clarified butter; I shall worship Prajāpati with one oblation of clarified butter.

In the *lājahoma*: "I shall worship Agni with three oblations of parched grain (*lāja*); I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with one oblation of the remaining clarified butter (*ājya*) from the offering"—thus he should say. Wherever the author of the *Sūtra* employs the word "then" (*atha*) in the phrase "then he offers the *sauviṣṭakṛtī*" [oblation], there the *Sviṣṭakṛt* is performed with that specific substance; elsewhere, however, it is with clarified butter (*ājya*). For the word "then" (*atha*) has not been used by the author of the *Sūtra* here; therefore, in this case, the *Sviṣṭakṛt* oblation is indeed with clarified butter alone.

Then, having stated for the *jayopahoma* (the oblation for victory) the sequence beginning with "cittaṃ cittim" and ending with "I shall sacrifice to Kāma, Gandharva, the Ādhis, the Apsarases, and the Lord of the World (*bhuvanasya pati*), each with a single offering of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*)," and for the *prāyaścittahoma* (the expiatory oblation) the sequence beginning with "Agni with three [verses]," etc., one should simultaneously set out the following at the time of arranging the vessels (*pātrāsādane*): a stone of the measure of a span (*prādeśa*), seeds such as rice (*vrīhi*) and others, a well-adorned water-pot (*kalaśa*) filled with water and containing sprouts, a large wooden ladle (*darvī*), a vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for carrying forward the *praṇītā* water, the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessel, the *upaveṣa* fire-stirring stick, *saṃmārga* cleansing-grass, fuel-wood (*idhma*), sacrificial grass (*barhis*), *avajvalana* kindling-grass, clarified butter, and parched grains (*lāja*).

Then follows the seating of Brahmā and the subsequent rites. At the time of wiping the vessels, one should set aside some *saṃmārga* blades of darbha grass for the purpose of wiping the bride’s joined palms (*añjali*). At the time of the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) of the clarified butter, the fried grains (*lāja*) are also to be circumambulated together with it. At the conclusion of laying the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), one should pour clarified butter over the fried grains with the *darvī* ladle, bring them between the clarified butter and the fire, and place them on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the north of the clarified butter.

Then, at an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*), he gazes upon the bride as she is being led from the northeast direction by her kinsmen, while reciting: "Oṃ, this bride is most auspicious; come together and behold her! Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart for your homes. From this point until the end of the rite of grasping the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), the ceremony must be performed strictly during an auspicious moment, because it constitutes the principal part of the ritual.

Then the bride, having sat down in the northeast direction of the fire and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) as a part of the rite, goes to the south of the fire along its front, sits down to the south of her husband facing east, and takes hold of her husband with her right hand alone. According to some, she goes to the south of the fire by way of the rear.

Then the bridegroom, having taken hold of her, shall perform the rites beginning with the sprinkling of water and ending with the *vyāhṛti* oblations, and then perform the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*), reciting: "Oṃ! May Agni come first among the deities; may he release her offspring from the noose of death. May King Varuṇa grant his consent so that this woman may not incur the sin of losing a grandson, svāhā! This is for Agni and Varuṇa, not for me. "Oṃ! May Agni Gārhapatya protect her; may he lead her offspring to a long life."

"May the mother of the living be non-empty in her womb; may she awaken to the joy of a grandson, Svāhā!"—to Agni Gārhapatya, this [is mine], not mine. "Oṃ! Let no cry arise in your house at night; let other weeping women settle elsewhere. O Mother, may the hero not strike you down; as a wife with a living husband, shine in the world of your lord, beholding your offspring with a joyful mind, Svāhā!"—to Agni, this [is mine], not mine.

"Oṃ! May Dyaus protect your back; may Vāyu and the Aśvins protect your thighs; may Savitṛ protect your suckling sons. From the time of putting on the garment until it is worn, may Bṛhaspati and the Viśvedevas protect you from behind. Svāhā! To Dyaus, to Vāyu, to the Aśvins, to Savitṛ, to Bṛhaspati, and to the Viśvedevas—this [offering] is mine, not yours. "Oṃ! Childlessness, the death of a son, evil, or even the lowest state..."

"O Evil One, having unloosed it from my head like a garland, I cast it upon my enemies; Svāhā! To Agni, not to me. "Oṃ! By means of the divine-ordained, perfected *Brāhmaṇa* [mantra], I slay the Piśācas dwelling in the womb. I cast down the flesh-eating deaths; may your sons live a long life; Svāhā! To Agni, not to me."

Having thus offered the six principal oblations either on the tongue of Varuṇa or in the very midst of the flames, and having offered the six oblations beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa," he places the stone that was set aside in front of the junction of the northern enclosing-stick. Then, with the mantra: "Oṃ, step upon this stone; like a stone, be thou firm. Crush those who seek to harm thee; overcome those who attack thee," he causes the bride to step onto it, facing eastward, beginning with her right foot. Thereafter, he should remove the stone. Now follows the taking of the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa).

On an auspicious moment indicated by an astrologer, the bridegroom, having spread two heaps of *darbha* grass behind the fire—one to the east and one to the west—with their tips pointing north, [recites]: "O Sarasvatī, come hither, O blessed one, rich in food! I take your hand for the sake of good offspring, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband, being the foremost among all created beings."

With the two verses, "Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given thee to me for the householdership," the groom, standing on the eastern heap of darbha grass and facing west, should take the hand of the bride who is standing on the western heap of darbha grass and facing east; or alternatively, the groom, standing on the western heap of darbha grass and facing east, should take the hand of the bride who is standing on the eastern heap of darbha grass and facing west.
Now follow three optional alternatives.

If he should desire, "May I procreate a male," he should grasp the hand together with the thumb, but not by grasping the other fingers. If he should desire, "May I procreate females only," he should grasp the hand together with the fingers, but not by grasping the thumb. If he should desire, "May I procreate both," he should grasp the thumb along with the fingers as if covering the hair [of the palm]. These are the three optional alternatives; the third alternative is also obligatory.

Then, having grasped the right shoulder of his wife who was standing before him with her face toward him, he turned her back around so that she stood to his right facing westward, moving counter-clockwise.

"Oṃ! Be not of fierce aspect, nor a slayer of thy husband; be auspicious to our cattle, well-disposed, and full of luster. Mayest thou be a mother of living sons, a mother of heroes, pleasant; be a source of blessing to us—blessing to our bipeds and blessing to our quadrupeds. O Pūṣan, send her to us who is most auspicious, she in whom men sow their seed. She who, longing for us, shall part her thighs, so that we, longing for her, may pour forth our seed. Soma first obtained her; Gandharva obtained her next. Agni was thy third husband; I, born of man, am the fourth."

Soma gave [her] to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave [her] to Agni. And Agni gives me cattle and sons, and then you. I am this [earth], you are that [heaven]; I am the sky, you are the earth. I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛk; come, let us two unite; let us both deposit seed for the sake of a male son, for the increase of wealth, for good offspring, and for great heroism. O bountiful Indra, make her one who has many sons and is fortunate. Bestow ten sons upon her, and make her husband the eleventh.

Thus, he consecrates her with these six mantras. Alternatively, having gone around her to the north and turning clockwise so that her right shoulder is near his own, he stands behind her facing east; then, turning her back toward him so that she faces west while he remains to her south, he should consecrate her with the six mantras beginning with "aghora-cakṣuḥ. If she is already facing west, she should be made to face east.
In this case, there is no going around her to the north or behind her.

Then, having seated his wife in her proper place and washed her joined palms (*añjali*), he takes the remaining *saṃmārjana* blades of *darbha* grass. Having heated the bride’s joined palms over the fire with those *darbha* blades, he wipes them as one would a ladle; then, heating them again and placing the joined palms upon the *darbha* grass, he sprinkles the *saṃmārjana* blades with water and casts them into the fire. Holding the wiped joined palms of the bride with his left hand, he spreads a base of clarified butter (*ājya*) in that joined palm with a ladle using his right hand, [saying] "Oṃ..."

"I cast these parched grains (*lāja*) here, which bring prosperity to me; may this Agni grant his approval for this union (*saṃvanana*) for you as well"—reciting this mantra twice, the bridegroom alone pours the *lāja*s; thrice, if he follows the five-portion (*pañcāvattin*) ritual.

Then, having silently sprinkled [clarified butter] over them and poured them back into the winnowing basket, he—while remaining seated—offers them into the fire with his joined palms (añjali) acting as a ladle (darvī), using the *kāya-tīrtha*, while she is seated and recites: "Oṃ, this noble woman, scattering parched grains (*lāja*) into the fire, prays: 'May my husband have a long life; may my kinsmen prosper! Svāhā! This is for Agni, not for me. The offering is made using the *kāya-tīrtha*, according to Baudhāyana’s statement: "One should perform the pouring out, the remnants, the offering of parched grains, and the daily offerings by means of the *kāya-tīrtha*."
The region at the base of the two little fingers is the *kāya* tīrtha, according to the lexicon which states: "The *kāya* is at the base of the smallest fingers.
Also, in the *Maitrāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa*:
"One should not offer oblations with the tips of the fingers, nor likewise by breaking the hollow of the joined palms."
The offering of parched grain is prescribed with the left side of the joined palms.
"The left side of women, however, is remembered as the portion belonging to the gods.

And this [act] has the groom as its agent—according to the explanation: "Now, the mention of 'atha' (now) is for the purpose of a general rule (*paribhāṣā*); in the *tantra* system involving a substratum, this rule regarding the portions (*avadāna*) applies everywhere. [And further:

"The mention of 'atha' is for the purpose of indicating that in the act of pouring (*āvapana*), another person is the agent; and that person is either the brother or one who stands in the place of a brother."

According to this commentary, however, the brother or others should be understood as the agent here; yet, due to the contradiction with the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra, it applies only to the bridegroom and not to the brother or others. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the word "I pour" (*āvapāmi*); for there is no contradiction, since the causative sense is intended to be implied therein.

Then, having raised his wife with the mantra: "Oṃ, with long life, with good life, with the essence of the herbs, and with the vigor of Parjanya, I have risen up, following the immortals," and having himself recited the mantra: "Oṃ, with you we shall indeed cross over all enemies, as if crossing streams of water," he, together with his wife, circumambulates the fire along with the vessel clockwise. According to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, it is the groom who recites the mantra.

Then follows a second and a third [offering] in the same manner, beginning with the spreading of the underlayer (*upastaraṇa*) and the scattering of parched grains (*lāja*), and ending with the circumambulation (*parikramaṇa*). The distinction in the third [offering] is that there is no re-anointing (*pratyañjana*) of the grains remaining in the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*).

Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with clarified butter alone, one should offer the *jaya* and subsequent oblations. The statement "as before" is intended to make known that the very procedure adopted for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is to be followed here as well, since alternative options regarding the mantras exist for both the *jaya-homa* and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt-homa*.

Regarding the *jayahoma* mantras in the context of the *upanayana*, the meaning is simply that just as in the two preceding cases the procedure was stated exactly as before, so too should it be performed here; however, this does not imply the application of the rule "prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt*. This is because, by the use of the suffix *-lyap* in the phrase "having circumambulated for the third time" (*tṛtīyaṃ parikramya*), the absence of an interval between the third circumambulation and the *sviṣṭakṛt* is expressed, thereby precluding the priority of the *sviṣṭakṛt*.

This explicit statement is for the purpose of ensuring that [the offering] occurs only during the irreproachable forms of marriage for a Brahmin. By this, the sequence stated by the author of the *Kārikā*—that one should circumambulate three times, offer the *jaya* oblations and so forth, and then perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation—is refuted.

Thereafter, one should complete the ritual from the casting away of the cord (*śulba*) up to the concluding recitation (*saṃsthājapa*). In this case, there is no offering of the three-fold food (*trivṛdannahoma*).

Then, to the west of the fire, according to custom, having made seven heaps of unbroken rice-grains (*akṣata*) arranged either facing east or facing north, he instructs his wife: "Having stepped forward with the right foot, follow with the left; do not overstep the right foot with the left. Having grasped her right foot—either holding it firmly or not—he causes her to take the *Viṣṇukrama* steps across the seven heaps of rice-grains in due order; some say that he himself also takes the steps. According to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, the one who recites the mantra is the bridegroom alone.

"Oṃ, one for food—may Viṣṇu follow you!"—with this he performs the first Viṣṇu-step. "Oṃ, two for strength—may Viṣṇu follow you!"—with this the second. "Oṃ, three for the vow—may Viṣṇu follow you!"—with this the third. "Oṃ, four for well-being—may Viṣṇu follow you!"—with this the fourth. "Oṃ, five for cattle—may Viṣṇu follow you!"—with this the fifth. "Oṃ, six for the increase of wealth—may Viṣṇu follow you!"—with this the sixth.
"Oṃ, seven for the seven priestly offices (hotrās)—may Viṣṇu follow you!"—with this the seventh.

Then, while the bride stands with her feet placed exactly as before, the groom mutters: "Oṃ! We two have become companions through the seven steps; may I attain friendship with you; may I not be separated from your friendship; may you not be separated from my friendship."

Then, having stepped upon her right foot with his own right foot and having passed his right hand over her right shoulder from above, he touches the region of her heart while reciting: "Oṃ! May your heart be in my heart; follow my mind with your mind; enjoy my speech with a focused mind; may Bṛhaspati join you to me; cleave unto me alone; may your thoughts be in me; may your devotion be toward me; restrain your speech for me. Thus he touches her heart.

With the mantra, "Oṃ, you are the knot of the vital breaths; do not loosen," he likewise touches the region of her navel. Then, having seated her to the west of the fire facing eastward, he stands before her facing westward and recites the three mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. For these, Agni, the Viśvedevas, or the Waters are the deities, and Gāyatrī is the meter. For the four mantras beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," Agni and the Waters are the deities, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. For the Pavamāna-anuvāka, Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi). The deities are Pavamāna, Suvarjana, and others as indicated by their respective characteristics.

The *gāyatrī* and other meters are used for the sprinkling (*mārjana*) of all [the participants]. With the water from the prepared jar, using *kuśa* sprouts, he sprinkles his wife at the end of all [the mantras], or at the end of each respective collection of mantras, reciting: "Oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā... (RV X.9.1), "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā V.6.1), and "pavamānaḥ suvarjan... (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa II.6.6.2) ending with "...punātu. Some authorities maintain that this should be done with each individual mantra.

Then the elderly Brahmins, kinsmen, relatives, and auspiciously dressed women place seeds such as rice upon the head of the bride with blessings, reciting according to custom the mantras beginning with "Oṃ yā jātā oṣadhayaḥ" (Oṃ, those herbs which have been born...).

Then, having sat down behind the fire, applied sacred ash (*vibhūti*), and worshipped the fire, she should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor and others after first honoring them, for the sake of accomplishing the integrity of the performed marriage-homa rite; thereafter, she should feed the Brahmins and auspiciously dressed women according to her means.
Then the twice-born should offer benedictions beginning with "tato 'sme devāsaḥ. Thereafter, the groom should meditate upon Viṣṇu for the successful completion of the rite.
This concludes the *vivāhahoma* (wedding fire-rite).

Thereafter, the bride and groom, abstaining from eating sugarcane products and salt, adorn themselves according to their means with garments, ornaments, and the like; avoiding sexual intercourse and sleeping on the ground, they dwell together. This vow is to be understood as commencing from the day of the marriage ceremony.
Now, the entry of the bride.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
"Starting from the day of the wedding, on the sixth or alternatively the eighth [day]..."
"The entry of the bride on the tenth day leads to prosperity; likewise on the tenth day of the month and the year. Beyond that, it is not auspicious.
Thus says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha as well.
"The entry of the bride (vadhūpraveśa) should take place on the sixth, eighth, or tenth day from the wedding;
it may be performed even without a day that is pure in its five-fold constituents (pañcāṅga), provided there is an auspicious transit of the planets.
However, in another Smṛti:
"It is said: 'The entry of the bride on the first, third, or fifth day brings auspiciousness;
however, on the second, fourth, or sixth day, it shall cause separation, disease, and suffering. Thus it is stated in the Smṛtisāgara."
"The entry of the bride is not recommended during the day; the entry into a new house is not recommended at night.
However, the entry into a house may occur by night or by day; that entry is said to be of three kinds.

The phrase "by night or by day" refers to the entry into a house that is either dilapidated or newly prepared. Following the statement "the entry into a house may occur by night or by day," the word "should be performed" (*kartavya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
This has been clearly stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"The entry of the bride is auspicious at night, while the entry into a new house is auspicious by day;
the entry into an existing home is prescribed for both night and day by the eminent sages, headed by the lord of seers, Bharadvāja."
In the *Ratnamālā*:

"The constellations Hasta, Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Maitra (Anurādhā), Śravaṇa, Aśvinī, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Śraviṣṭhā, and Punarvasu are the most excellent asterisms for one who has set out on a journey; one should avoid the three, five, first, and seventh stars [of the others]."

"Citrā, Viśākhā, Anila (Svātī), Āśleṣā, Yāmya (Bharaṇī), Vāyavya (Vāyu), Pitrya (Maghā), and Īśvara (Ārdrā)—these are unfavorable for journeys; the other lunar mansions are said to be neither desired nor censured.
Here, *indu* refers to Mṛgaśiras. *Dhiṣṇyāni* means the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*).
In the *Muhūrtasaṃgraha*: "Revatī, Hasta, Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras,
the three Uttarās, Mūla, Śravaṇa, and Śatabhiṣaj."
Likewise, the paternal asterism is excellent for the rite of entry;
furthermore, the Riktās, the Parvas, the eighth lunar day, and Viṣṭi are to be avoided, while the remaining ones bring auspiciousness.
"In a benefic degree, on benefic days, when aspected by benefics, and in a benefic division;
whether at night or during the day, it will be auspicious if there is no obstacle to the entry."
In the *Vyavahāratattva*:

"The entry of the bride is auspicious during the asterisms of Revatī, Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, the pair [of Aśleṣā and Maghā], the three Hastas, Mūla, Maghā, the Uttarās, Puṣya, and Anurādhā; provided the lunar day is not one of the 'empty' (riktā) days, and the Moon and Mars are absent."
The Rohiṇī asterism is auspicious. "On days other than Sunday and Tuesday" means on days excluding the Sun and Mars.

In another Smṛti it is said: "During defects such as the loss of a day (dinakṣaya), the bride's entry into the house is not auspicious. "Veśaḥ" means entry. The definition of the loss of a day and other such defects has been stated by Śrīpati:
The sages have declared that when a single weekday touches three lunar days, it is called an *avamadin* (an omitted day) by astrologers; likewise,
that which occurs through the contact of three days with a lunar day [is also so designated].
Furthermore, this [object] that touches the three times and this duality are not accepted."
The entry [of the bride] on an even day must occur within the sixteen days [following the wedding].
As it is stated in that very same work:
"Starting from the wedding, the entry of the bride should take place on an even lunar day (tithi) within the limit of sixteen days."
"And thereafter, in the months up to the end of the fifth [month], there is no further restriction beyond that."
Regarding this, Nārada states a specific distinction:
"If a woman goes to her husband's house during an even year and an even month,
she takes away the life-span of her husband and that woman shall meet with death."
Regarding this, the months to be avoided have been stated by Bṛhaspati: "O King, when the Sun is in Cancer, Virgo, or Aquarius, one should not enter a house, nor a village, a city, or even a town."
In the *Jyotiṣprakāśa*:
"One should always enter [the city] having placed Venus either behind or to the right;
one must certainly not enter when Venus is in front or to the left."
In the ninth month from the departure, and likewise on the ninth day, during the Riktā lunar days,
in censurable yogas, and on the days of the Sun and Saturn.
"If the moon is situated in the front right portion [of the house], entering is not recommended.

Regarding the prohibition against the ninth day and the ninth month, the *Kālapradīpa* states the regional restriction: "If one has traveled less than two gavyūtis, however, one should not enter again on the ninth day or the ninth month from the time of departure."
A *gavyūti* is two *krośas*.
Lalla states an exception regarding Venus:
"In one's own residence, city, or region, during a regional upheaval, or likewise at a wedding..."
"There is no need for consideration regarding Venus (Pratiśukra) when a newlywed bride goes to her husband's home."
There is no defect of an adverse Venus (pratiśukra) regarding going with one's husband.
As it is said in the Bhīmaparākrama:
"For a woman being led away by her master, an adverse Venus does not exist."
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"A house with four wings, four doors, and verandas on all sides is called *sarvatobhadra*; there, the inauspiciousness of Venus does not apply."
"Among the Kāśyapas, the Vasiṣṭhas, the Bhṛgus, Atris, and Aṅgirasas,
and among the Bhāradvājas and Vātsyas, no one equal to Śukra is to be found."
In the *Jyotiḥsāgara*:
"As long as the moon remains in the quarters of the fire [starting] from Revatī, Venus shall be blind; traveling face-to-face with it is auspicious."
In that very context, there is another statement:
"As long as the moon remains among the constellations beginning with Revatī and ending with Mṛgaśiras, Venus shall be blind; facing it for travel is auspicious."
In this regard, an exception to the censure of [the period of] Bhṛgu and Guru was stated by Māṇḍavya:
"In the case of daily travel, a dilapidated house, the seven occasions ending with the first feeding of a child,
the entry of a bride, and auspicious ceremonies, there is no 'dullness' (inauspiciousness) of Venus and Jupiter."
Bhṛgu is Śukra; Jīva is Guru. There is no practice superior to this.
As stated in the *Jyotiṣprakāśa*: "If Venus is on the left, there is happiness for the newlywed bride; if on the right, there is loss."
Wealth and grain are found when it is situated behind; when it is situated in front, there is total destruction.
As for the widowhood of a newlywed bride that has been declared when Venus is in conjunction with the Sun,
that should be understood by the wise as applying only to her second marriage.
"When Venus has risen in the east, one should march toward the south and west;
and when it has risen in the west, one should march toward the east and north."

Likewise, beginning from the month of Bhādrapada, one should know that for three months in each direction starting from the East, the door is closed. Beginning from Caitra, one should know that the thorns are placed in sequence: for two months in the primary directions starting from the East and for one month in the intermediate directions (vidiś). Both of these [periods] are to be avoided when a newly married bride travels to another village. As stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"The departure of a beloved from her own home under a fixed asterism (*dhruvarkṣa*) on a Saturday (*kavivāra*) should never take place;
there would be loss of wealth on a Saturday, and loss of a son on a Thursday (*dhruvasaumyavāsara*)."
And another [source] says: "In the first Pauṣa or Āṣāḍha following the marriage, or during an intercalary month,
she should not stay at her husband's house, nor likewise at her father's house in Caitra."

In the *Jyotirnibandha*: "If a maiden should reside in her husband's house during the first month after marriage, she will kill her mother if it be the month of Kṣaya (Kārttika); her own body if it be Jyeṣṭha; and her husband’s elder brother if it be [the month of] Jyeṣṭha."
