"If she stays with her father-in-law in Pauṣa, with her husband in Māgha, and with her father's house in the month of Caitra, she destroys her father; there shall be no fear for them in his absence.
Jayanta said:
"Likewise, in the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Māgha, Mādhava, and that known as Jyeṣṭha,
the entry of new wives into the house is highly auspicious."
Now, regarding the second arrival:
in the *Ṛkṣoccaya*—
“In the months of Māgha, Phālguna, or Vaiśākha, during the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day.”
"In the purification of Guru and Āditya, there should always be a second arrival of the wife."

Bādarāyaṇa says: "When the sun is in Aquarius or Sagittarius, when Venus has risen auspiciously, and on a favorable lunar day among those presided over by the Moon, Uttarā-phalgunī, Uttarā-bhādrapadā, Jupiter, Rohiṇī, Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Jyeṣṭhā, Puṣya, Svāti, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, Vāyu (Svāti), Śatabhiṣaj, Śravaṇa, and Citrā."
"On the day of the deity Indra, for those who know [the rules], the entry of a new bride into her husband's house is auspicious."
The preceptor is the lord of the gods; *ina* is the sun; *vid* is Mercury.
Now follows the ritual procedure for entering a house:

after the marriage fire-sacrifice (*vivāhahoma*), the bride’s kinsmen shall, at an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*) designated by an astrologer, lead the bride and the groom from the father’s house to the groom’s house or the village by means of a chariot or other vehicle.

If, while a husband and wife are traveling toward a village, the sacrificial vessel or the cart should break on the way, then, while the bride maintains physical contact [with her husband], he should offer seven oblations according to either the *Āpūrvika* procedure or the *Āghāra* procedure, reciting: "Oṃ yadṛte cidabhiśriṣaḥ... iḍāmagne pu... imaṃ me varuṇa... tattvā yāmi... tvaṃ no agne... sa tvaṃ no agne... tvamagne ayāsi. The deity of the first [verse] is Indra Maghavān; the deity of the second is Agni; the deities of the others are well-known.

Then, having joined it together and tied a knot with a cord or similar material, one should mutter the *mantras* containing the word "svasti. The *mantra* for joining is stated by Śāṅkhāyana as: "Oṃ, manifest the essence of the khadira tree"; for tying the knot: "Oṃ, like a swift horse that turns back. He has also prescribed the muttering of the five-verse hymn beginning with "May they measure out prosperity for us. Having placed the entire wedding fire into a single vessel along with its ashes, they carry it behind the bride and groom.

And this fire is to be maintained for as long as one lives, beginning from the marriage *homa*. Although maintaining it for life is already established by the use of the word "perpetual" (*nitya*) in the Sūtra, the explicit statement "it is to be maintained" is intended to show that in cases other than when departing on a journey—if the fire must be moved to another location for some reason—it should be carried directly in its physical form and not merely deposited (*samāropa*). This is also the view of the Āpastambas.

If one should depart on a journey, according to the sūtra stating that "the mounting [of the fire] onto oneself, onto the two kindling woods (araṇis), or onto a fuel-stick (samit) is unexplained," there is only the mounting [of the fire], but not its physical carrying. In the ritual alternative involving the insertion of a fragment, either the physical carrying by means of a cart or other vehicle must be performed, or else the mounting [of the fire] itself; however, in this case, there is simply no mounting onto a fuel-stick. As for the maintenance [of the fire], it should be carried out with sacrificial wood or balls of cow-dung, but never with husks.
As it is said in the Saṃgraha:
"The fire should be maintained with balls made of clay or with firm, sacrificial pieces of wood."
"In no way should it be held by those with husks," so it has been declared by the wise.

In the *Pārijāta*: "One should not maintain the fire with chaff. If that [fire] has gone out, then it must be churned immediately thereafter. Or, it may be brought from the house of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). If it was previously churned, then it should be churned from the embers (*avakṣāṇa*). An ember is a piece of wood that has been partially burnt while situated in that fire. If the embers are incapable [of producing fire], then one should touch the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) with those ashes and churn. If it has been brought [from elsewhere], then it should be brought [to the site].

In the *Prāyaścitta-sūtra*, the plural form "embers" (*avakṣāṇāni*) indicates that if fire is not produced from one ember, then it should be churned from another; if it is still not produced from that, then from yet another. It does not mean that one must churn from all the embers available. Rather, it means that churning with the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) is performed only when fire is not produced from any of the embers; it does not mean that churning with the kindling sticks follows immediately after failure to produce fire from a single ember.

Although this is not stated in the Gṛhyasūtra, it should nevertheless be accepted because it is not contradictory. The attainment of those required Śrauta injunctions that are not in conflict [with the Gṛhya] is obtained through the force of the Gṛhya tradition situated within the Śrautasūtras: "If [the fire] has gone out, it should be churned, or brought from the house of a Śrotriya; and there is fasting for the wife or the husband when it has gone out."

Thus ends the Sūtra on the expiation for following [the fire]. The word "and" (ca) serves to combine the fast with both churning and fetching [of the fire]. Regarding the section on "following," the repetition of the term "following" is for the purpose of indicating that this expiation should take place both before and after the completion of the marriage ceremony. Therefore, in every case of the fire being followed, one must perform the fast after producing the fire either by churning or by fetching it. This is not correct, because the matter is already established by the inclusion of the word "constant" (nitya).

In that case, this is the purpose [of the following statement]: "This very expiation (prāyaścitta) shall apply, and no other. From this, it is understood that there is indeed another expiation elsewhere. What is that? Āpastamba has stated: "Or rather, one should offer with the subsequent verse and should not fast. The subsequent verse is "ā yāścāgne" (VS 3.11). Regarding this, Mātṛdatta has explained that the modification consists only of the words "anabhiśastīśca" (and [grant] freedom from accusations).

Based on the natural sense of this commentary (*bhāṣya*), when the fire is extinguished due to loss, theft, or other causes, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consists solely of fasting and oblations; it is not merely fasting alone, nor oblations alone. In this commentary, by demonstrating the expiation consisting of fasting and oblations for cases other than following the fire in death (*anugamana*), it is shown that this serves as a supplement (*kṣepaka*) for other expiations consisting of eighteen oblations and so forth; otherwise, even those [other expiations] would have been demonstrated here.

However, that not every portion other than the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is a supplement (*kṣepaka*) is understood from the observation of the introductory heading (*pratīka*) of this section: "In that [fire], the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarmāṇi*) are performed; the fire beginning with the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) is called the *aupāsana*. Yet, according to the natural implication of the author of the *Vaijayantī*, that the entire section is a supplement is known from the statement of a certain teacher who will say: "By means of that *aupāsana*, one possesses the status of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), and by means of the *pārvaṇa* oblation of rice-porridge (*caru*), one becomes a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsayājī*)."

Furthermore, according to the text of the Bhāṣyakāra, it is only the rule for reconnection (*punaḥsaṃdhāna*) that is an insertion (*kṣepaka*), and not any other; however, according to the text of the Vaijayantīkāra, every section (*khaṇḍa*) is an insertion. Yet, based on both texts, it is the rule for reconnection alone that possesses the status of an insertion. Therefore, scholars should examine this more thoroughly and accept whatever is logically sound.

Then, having established one of the fires on a consecrated site smeared with cow-dung, either the husband or the wife should observe a fast; if the husband has gone abroad, the wife observes the fast. If the fire is extinguished during the day, the fast lasts until evening; if it is extinguished at night, the fast lasts until morning. In the event of an inability to fast, one must perform the expiation consisting of the *ayāścāgna* oblation as described in the section on initiation (*upanayana*), as well as the *sarvaprāyaścitta* homa. If the fire is extinguished while fasting during the day, the omitted homa must be performed specifically in the evening.

If the fast occurs at night, it should be performed early in the morning; however, this refers only to the fast itself and not to the *homa* (fire sacrifice). If, however, the *āhuti* (oblation) is part of the rite, it must be performed immediately after the expiatory *homa*. If the husband is away on a journey or if she herself is unable to observe the fast, she should appoint a priest (*ṛtvij*) for the sake of the *homa* and have him offer the oblation with the mantra "āyāścāgne" (RV 10.128.1). In the absence of a priest, she should offer the oblation herself.

Then, having reached the door of his own house, the groom instructs his wife: "Place your right foot first; do not step upon the threshold. She, placing her right foot first and without stepping upon the threshold, enters.

Then, having entered the house and prepared a fire-altar (*agnyāyatana*) in the eastern half of that hall, he should sit down behind it with his wife, facing the east. Having sipped water (*ācamya*) and performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (*Śrī Parameśvara*), by means of generating the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*) for my marriage, I shall perform the rite called 'Entering the House' (*gṛhapraveśa*). Alternatively, there may be no such resolve.
Then, having worshipped Gaṇeśa, he should silently establish the marriage fire (*vivāhāgni*) upon the altar purified by the rites of digging out the earth and so forth, and cause it to blaze.
Then, to the west of the fire, having spread out a red bull's hide with its neck facing east and the hair side up, [he recites]:
"Om! Here let the cows settle; here the horses, here the men;
here let Pūṣan also settle, he who bestows a thousand sacrificial fees."

Thus, the husband and wife sit down facing either the east or the north; in the case of facing east, the wife sits to the right of the husband, and in the case of facing north, she sits behind him or on his left side. The mantra belongs to both. From this point until the rising of the stars, they remain silent. In the absence of a bull's hide, a bed of grass is to be used. Accordingly, the *Āśvalāyana Smṛti* states: "At the entry into the home, the spreading of a bull's hide is prescribed."

"But in its absence, there should be a covering for a bed made of grass. Here, "bed" (*talpa*) refers to a seat. When the stars have risen, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction together with his bride, facing either east or north along with her, he worships the directions with the half-verse beginning "O Goddesses, you six wide ones... This belongs to the *Ṛgveda* hymn "Agni, the Directions," and is in the *Triṣṭubh* meter; its application is in the act of worship (*upasthāna*). He worships the directions with: "Om! O Goddesses, you six wide ones, make us spacious; O All-Gods, display your heroism here! Because of the plural marker in the mantra, it is recited once.

For the verse beginning with "mā hāsma hi," the deity is Agni, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and its application is for the ritual worship (upasthāna). Reciting the mantra once—"Oṃ mā hāsma hi prajayā mā tanūbhiḥ"—one performs the worship of the constellations. Since it is impossible to worship all the constellations, one worships as many as come within the range of vision; because this is impracticable [to do otherwise], the mantra is recited only once.

For this mantra consisting of a single quarter, *māradhāma*, Agni, Candramas (the Moon), and the Triṣṭubh metre are the deities; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the rite of worship (*upasthāna*). One worships the Moon with: *oṃ māradhāma dviṣate somarājan*. And [one worships] with:
*oṃ saptarṣayaḥ prathamāṃ kṛttikānāmarundhatīṃ ye dhruvatā ha ninyuḥ | ṣaṭkṛttikāmukhyayogaṃ vahantīyamasmākaṃ bhrājatvaṣṭamī* ||1||* *Note: The final verse is from the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.85.13.*
Thus he worships the Seven Sages together with Arundhatī. Because of the plural marker in the mantra, the recitation is performed once:
"Oṃ! You are of firm abode, of firm origin; you are firm, established in firmness.
You are the pillar of the stars; protect me from those who attack."

Homage to Brahman, the firm and the unshakable; homage to Prajāpati, the son of Brahman; homage to the thirty-three gods, the sons of Brahman; homage to the Aṅgirases, the grandsons of Brahman. He who knows you, the firm and unshakable Brahman, along with your sons and grandsons—his sons and grandsons become firm in this world, as do his servants, pupils, clothing, woolen blankets, gold, women, kings, food, fearlessness, long life, renown, splendor, fame, and strength.

May these—brahmic luster, food, and sustenance—all these be firm and unshakable within me. I know you as the firm Brahman; may I be firm in this world and in this community. I know you as the unshakable Brahman; may I not be shaken from this world and from this community. May my hateful rival be shaken from this world and from this community. I know you as the motionless Brahman; may I not be moved from this world and from this community. May my hateful rival be moved from this world and from this community.

"May my rival be driven away from this world and from this district; I know you as the unshakable Brahman—may I not be shaken from this world and from this district, and may my hateful rival be shaken from this world and from this district. I know you as the nave of all—may I become the nave of this district. I know you as the center of all—may I become the center of this district. I know you as the cord of all—may I become the cord of this district."

"I would become the central pillar; I know you as the central pillar of all. May I become the central pillar of this country. I know you as the navel; I know you as the navel of all. May I become the navel of this country. Just as the navel is the center of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), so am I the center. Let that evil, numbering one hundred and one, fall upon him who hates us and whom we hate. May a hundred and one blessings come to me. With these words, he worships the *dhruva* star.

Even if the stars and other celestial bodies are not visible due to being obscured by clouds and the like, one should perform the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation) directed toward that specific object of worship in each respective direction.

Then, having conversed with his wife in a voice pleasing to the mind at the very place where the *upasthāna* was performed, he re-enters the hall, sprinkles the spread ox-hide, discards it, touches water, and sits down to the west of the fire facing eastward together with his wife.
Now follows the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) for entering the house.

The bridegroom, together with his wife, having sipped water (*ācamya*), restrained his breath (*prāṇāyāmya*), kindled the fire, meditated upon it, and taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), performed the rites beginning with "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) and ending with the breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*). He then declares: "In this ritual of the *Āgneya-sthālīpāka* sacrifice, which is an ancillary part of entering the house, I shall encompass those deities who are to be worshipped. I shall worship Agni with one offering of cooked rice (*caru*). I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with one offering of the remainder of the cooked rice."

Having said, "I shall sacrifice to these deities immediately," he should place fuel-sticks into the fire with the *vyāhṛtis*, spread grass around the fire, and strew *darbha* grass to the north of the fire. Upon that, he should set out the winnowing basket, the black antelope skin, the mortar and pestle, the cooking pot for the *caru*, the stirring-spoon, a vessel for catching the scattering of rice grains, the wooden ladle, the pot for clarified butter, the vessel for the *prokṣaṇī* water, *darbha* grass for placing the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the *upaveṣa* stick, *darbha* grass for wiping, *darbha* grass for kindling, clarified butter, and a fuel-stick. He should arrange all these in their proper places.

In the event of the absolute absence of rice grains—which are prescribed as substitutes for *vrīhi*—and of husked medicinal herbs, the wife, upon taking the prepared rice, should mentally visualize the entire sequence of rites starting from the touching of the rice at the time of threshing up to the end of the three-fold husking (*triṣphalīkaraṇa*), in order to fulfill the requirement of their being constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice. Alternatively, all external physical actions may also be performed.

In the former alternative, there is no placing (*āsādana*) of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), mortar, and pestle; however, in the second alternative, the placing of the black antelope skin and the other implements does indeed take place.

Then, having prepared the two strainers (*pavitra*), having placed the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) to the west of the fire and having placed the two strainers inside it, he silently pours out four handfuls [of grain]. Having poured in enough *vrīhi* rice for the feeding of one Brāhmaṇa, he places the winnowing basket containing the poured-out rice to the north of the fire. Having consecrated the sprinkling-water (*prokṣaṇī*), having sprinkled the rice situated in the winnowing basket, and having turned the vessels face upwards, he sprinkles them.

(And the bull is the price in the payment of the price. Then, to the north of the wife of the fire, having thrice shaken out a black antelope skin used for the slaughter outside, having spread it with the neck pointing westward and the hair on the upper side, having placed the hindquarters of the animal there, having set the mortar upon that, having poured the rice-grains into it, having pounded them while seated with the pestle, having placed a winnowing basket to the east of the mortar, and having poured the grains from the mortar into the basket, he should thrice winnow them to the north of the black antelope skin.
Having destroyed the husks, he scatters those husks under the black antelope skin with his right hand, without looking at them.

Then, having squeezed the husks deposited by the right hand itself, and having touched water, and having separated [the grain], he pours it into the vessel prepared for the scattering; taking that [grain], he throws it into the mortar, threshes it three times, and having thrown the thrice-threshed fragments to the north of the black antelope skin, he washes the rice grains and pours them down behind the fire.

Then the bridegroom, having washed the rice grains and poured them into the vessel for the *caru* oblation, should stir them with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) and cook them over the fire. Having cleansed the large ladle (*darvī*) and the stirring-spoon, he should perform the rites beginning with the melting of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and ending with the laying down of the sacrificial strainers (*pavitra*). In that process, the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) should be performed for the *caru* together with the clarified butter; or alternatively, the rites from the cleansing of the ladle up to the laying down of the strainers may be performed even before the pouring of the rice grains into the *caru* vessel. If there is the practice of spreading *darbha* grass behind the fire, he should perform those rites and then place the clarified butter upon the *darbha* grass.

In this interpretation—that the use of the root *yaj* is for the purpose of merely obtaining the formal invitation (*āgūraṇa*) in the form "I shall sacrifice" (*yakṣye*)—one takes rice sufficient for the oblation, the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas, and the serving of food; having had these grains pounded by the wife, one places the resulting rice-grains into a pot containing water and cooks them over the fire. In this case, the Vedic ritual requirements (*śrautadharma*) such as the pouring out [of grain] (*nirvāpa*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and the shaking of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) do not apply. The laying down of the black antelope skin is optional (*kṛtākṛta*). In the absence of a spreading [of grass], there is also no placing [of the vessels] upon the vessels.

The *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) must indeed be performed. Then, having spread the darbha grass that was brought forward behind the fire and placed the clarified butter (*ājya*) thereon, he pours the cooked *caru* over it with the ladle (*darvī*) and the butter, carries it out toward the north, and places it upon the strewn grass behind the fire to the north of the butter. Having sprinkled water around the fire and silently placed the fuel-stick (*samidh*) that was set aside, he takes a portion with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) and offers it into the blazing fire, while his wife holds onto him: "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni! [Offered] while his wife holds onto him, he says: "This is for Agni, not for me."

Having offered again, while his wife maintains contact with him, he offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation—unconnected with the previous offering—into the eastern half of the northern half [of the fire], saying: "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. "This is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, not mine. Although the word *atha* (then) does not occur here, nevertheless, because of the suffix *ktvā*, the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation is performed with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Thereafter, he should throw the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) into the fire; or else, there is no throwing of the spoon.

Then, having removed the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa), and having offered four expiatory oblations (prāyaścittāhuti) with the Vyāhṛtis both individually and collectively, and having performed the final sprinkling (uttara-pariṣeka), he should worship the fire while reciting the *saṃsthājapa* mantra; then, having honored it and applied the sacred ash (vibhūti) to his forehead, he should feed a learned Brāhmaṇa with the remnants of the sacrificial offering (haviḥ-śeṣa). In the event of the loss of the sacrificial remnants, there shall be no feeding of the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, for the sake of ensuring the completeness of the performed rite, one should give a bull or its equivalent value to the preceptor (*ācārya*), give even more to others, feed the Brahmins according to one's means, and meditate upon Viṣṇu for the perfection of the ritual.

According to the view that the wife alone is the primary performer, the wife should procure a bull or its value for the purpose of giving it as a gift to the officiant and request him, saying: "Please perform the sacrifice for me with the *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to Agni."

Then the bridegroom should perform the rites from the *anvādhāna* (placing of the fire) up to the sprinkling of the sacrificial vessels (*pātraprokṣaṇa*). Then the wife performs the rites from the shaking of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) up to the washing of the rice grains (*taṇḍulakṣālana*).

Thereafter, the bridegroom should perform the rites from the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) up to the conclusion, excluding the formal renunciation (*tyāga*) and the giving away (*dāna*). The wife shall perform the renunciation and the giving away.
This is the procedure according to the view that the wife is the primary performer.

Alternatively, after the placing of the vessels, having spread out a black antelope skin—or not spreading it—the wife performs the threshing; having husked the grain three times, she should discard the husks to the north.

Then the husband, having performed the rites from the wiping of the ladle up to the placing of the two strainers (or, if following the procedure of spreading darbha grass, up to that point), should pour clarified butter over the cooked sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the ladle, carry it out toward the north, and place it upon darbha grass behind the fire (or, if there is no spreading of darbha grass, directly on the ground). The subsequent rites, beginning with the sprinkling of water, are the same.

Then, having had the lustration (*nīrājana*) performed for them by married women whose husbands and sons are living, the couple, having received blessings from the twice-born (*dvija*), should remain there joyful.
Thereafter, whatever rites are prescribed by custom, such as the worship of Mahālakṣmī and so forth, all of that should be performed by the matrons (*purandhrī*).
Thus concludes the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* at the entry into the house.
Now, this sūtra concerning that subject is explained.
Therein, the sūtra is as follows:

"Then he causes her to sacrifice with a sthālīpāka offering dedicated to Agni; the wife husks [the grain], and having cooked it, having sprinkled it with ghee, having removed it from the fire, and having offered an oblation to Agni, he offers to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; with that [remnant], he [feeds] a Brāhmaṇa."
"He gives a bull to that learned man who is honored by him.

The word "atha" (then) is used to indicate that the rite should take place immediately after the [bride's] entry, specifically during the first part of the night, so that it does not occur after midnight; and it is also for the purpose of showing that where one performs the sacrifice with the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni following the worship of the quarters and other deities, it is only there that he causes the wife to sacrifice, offering while she maintains contact, and not in other *sthālīpāka* rites. After the word "yājayati" (he causes to sacrifice), the word "varaḥ" (the bridegroom) is to be supplied as the subject.

Alternatively, from the very statement "he causes her to sacrifice," it is understood that the wife alone is the sacrificer (*yaṣṭrī*), while the husband has become the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Therefore, the acts of relinquishment (*tyāga*) and giving (*dāna*) have the woman as their sole agent. For this very reason, the use of the pronoun *asya* (of him) is consistent. Nor should it be asked: "How can this be, since she lacks the authority to give away her husband's property? For it is established in all schools of thought (*sarvatantra-siddha*) that she does possess authority even in giving with his permission.

One might argue that it should simply have been stated, "he causes this [offering] to be sacrificed," because its being dedicated to Agni is established by the subsequent injunction, "having offered to Agni," and its being a *sthālīpāka* is established by the injunctions, "he threshes" and "he cooks"; therefore, for what purpose is this redundant phrase, "with a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni," introduced? It is said in reply: it is for the purpose of making known that here Agni alone is the principal deity, and not Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

Therefore, it is established that after the oblation to the first deity, even if there is a defect in the sacrificial material (*havis*), no new material is produced for the sake of the second deity in the form of *Sviṣṭakṛt*; rather, the oblation is performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) alone. Furthermore, the following ritual rules are thereby established: one offers [the butter] in the eastern half of the northern half, without allowing it to touch the other oblations, and the portion taken for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* must be larger than the portions taken for the principal offerings. The explicit mention of "with the *sthālīpāka*" is intended to prevent the application of what is stated in another Sūtra—that in this *sthālīpāka* sacrifice dedicated to the deity Agni, the oblation may also be performed with clarified butter.

Alternatively, "with the *sthālīpāka*" is the prescriptive rule, while "having cooked" is a restatement intended to ensure there is no interval between the cooking and the pouring of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*). By this, it is established that the ritual procedure ending with the casting of the strainers (*pavitrapraharaṇa*) must be completed prior to the state where the food is perfectly cooked.

Since the requirement is already established by the word "caru" alone, the mention of "sthālīpākena" (with the *sthālīpāka*) is for the purpose of indicating that the *āpūrvika* ritual procedure applies only where the injunction is made using the term *sthālīpāka*. Consequently, in other cases, the ritual procedure is established by implication as being like that of the *āghāra* offering. However, in the case of the *caru-homa* which serves as the substitute for the *prāyaścitta-iṣṭi*, the *āpūrvika* procedure alone applies. This is because even in another scripture it is stated: "Those *puroḍāśas* which belong to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), those are the *sthālīpākas* for one who has not maintained them (*anāhitāgni*)," thus establishing the term *sthālīpāka* as the basis for the injunction.

Alternatively, this is for the purpose of making it known that the *āpūrvika* ritual procedure applies only where the oblation is performed with the *sthālīpāka* itself and not with any other substance. Consequently, even in the case of a simple *caru*-oblation prescribed by the term *caru*, the *āpūrvika* ritual procedure alone is to be followed. The use of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) instead of the root *hu* (to offer) is intended to ensure the application of all the Śrauta characteristics as required. By this, the attainment of the rites beginning with the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), such as the shaking over the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and the rules for threshing, is established.
Alternatively, the employment of the root *yaj* is for the purpose of obtaining merely the incitement (*āgūraṇa*) in the form "I shall sacrifice" (*yakṣye*).

The wife threshes the rice grains intended for the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking). Although it would have been sufficient to say "she threshes," the specific formulation "the wife threshes" is used for this purpose: that the wife alone performs the rites starting from the shaking of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) up to the pouring out of the rinsing water of the rice, but not the triple-threshing (*triṣphalīkaraṇa*) as is done in the *śrauta* ritual. However, the cooking and subsequent steps are performed by the husband alone, not by the wife. It is precisely for this reason that the verbal suffix *-lyap* was abandoned and the construction "the wife threshes" (*patnyavahanti*) was employed instead.

Alternatively, the statement "the wife threshes" is intended to mean that she alone is the "wife" who has been accepted through the procedure just described—beginning with the *dhruva* and ending with the *upasthāna*—and no one else. By this, it is established that a woman married through the *āsura* or other such forms of marriage does not possess the status of being "associated with the sacrifice.
There is also a traditional legal text (*smṛti*) on this point: "A woman who has been purchased by means of a price is not designated as a 'wife'."

"She is neither for the rites of the gods nor for the rites of the ancestors; the wise know her to be a slave-woman. And: "But that woman who has been married in an unrighteous manner is not called a wife;
she is unfit for the rites of the gods and the ancestors; the wise know her to be like a slave-woman."

"Adharmyoḍhā" means one who has been married by an unrighteous form of marriage. Regarding the statement "he offers to Sviṣṭakṛt," because of the specific injunction "he offers to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," the oblation here is performed by name alone, and not by the formula "that which belongs to him. Therefore, with the remainder of the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooked rice), he "serves"—meaning he feeds—a *brāhmaṇa* who is learned, that is, endowed with sacred knowledge and Vedic study. The mention of the *brāhmaṇa* is for the purpose of excluding the *kṣatriya* and the *vaiśya*.
By the force of the word "serves," the *caru* must be prepared in a quantity sufficient for both the oblation and the feeding of the *brāhmaṇa*.

Alternatively, the statement "he causes her to sacrifice" is for the purpose of establishing her participation (*anvārambha*). In this view, the bridegroom alone is the agent of the renunciation and the gift. In this ritual procedure, the Sūtra—"He gives a bull to one who is honored by him"—should be explained in this way: he gives the bull to that person who is honored by the performer of this *sthālīpāka* sacrifice; it does not mean he gives it to the performer of other *sthālīpāka* sacrifices.

Alternatively, the genitive case in the word *asya* (of him) is changed to the nominative *ayam* (this one). Thus, "this person"—whoever is honored in the world by virtue of learning (*vidyā*) and noble lineage (*abhijana*)—"this one," as the performer of this *sthālīpāka*, gives a bull (*ṛṣabha*).

However, some take the portion of the sūtra beginning with "to that Brāhmaṇa" and ending with "he gives a bull to him who is honored by him" as a single unit; according to their view, only the honored person is to be fed, and the bull is to be given to that very person.

But when, due to an extremely pressing situation or by the authority of another scripture, the marriage takes place at night—even then, if it is before midnight, one should sit upon a bull's hide and perform the entire ritual, from the worship of the directions and so forth up to the *sthālīpāka*, immediately thereafter. If it is after midnight, however, it should be understood that one must first sit down and perform the worship of the directions and so forth, and then the *sthālīpāka* is to be performed only on the following day.
Thus says Āśvalāyana: "But when midnight has passed, indeed on the following morning..."

"Those who know the Vedas understand that [the rite] should be performed upon entering the house. If the bride's house is in another village, then one should go to that village; if there is one's own house there, the pavilion and other preparations should be made right there. In its absence, it may be done in another house after first establishing ownership. Furthermore, this *sthālīpāka* (offering of cooked rice) must be performed in one's own home, preceded by the rules for departure and so forth, and not in the father-in-law's house or another house. However, nowadays the learned perform it even in these two locations.

The rekindling of the sacred fires (samāropa) must not be performed prior to the first performance of the *sthālīpāka* for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), following the *sthālīpāka* at the time of entering the house. Regarding the nature of the *caru*, the *Sārasaṃgraha* states: "The *caru* is that which has lost its heat, is well-cooked, not burnt, and not hard."
"It should not be cooked too loosely, nor should it be devoid of flavor.

This alone is the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all *sthālīpāka* offerings; however, the *sthālīpākas* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are indeed its modifications (*vikṛti*). Thus concludes the procedure for entering the house.
Now, the worship and gift of the *airiṇī* (bamboo):

On the fourth day from the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) or from the day of the marriage ceremony, at night, or on a day when the *bhadrā* muhūrta occurs, the gift of the bamboo vessel known as the *airiṇī* must be performed by the givers of the bride for the sake of the bridegroom alone—or, in his absence, for one equal to him—in accordance with the practice of the learned.
[The verse states: "Accompanied by cloth, fruit, and betel, it increases the lineage of the couple."
A bamboo vessel called an airiṇī, completely filled with cooked foods.
"With eleven karas, accompanied by gold, the form of Airiṇī should indeed be fashioned by the wise"— here, "rudrasaṃkhyaiḥ" means with eleven in number.

Having performed these acts, having sipped water (ācamana) together with his wife, and having restrained his breath (prāṇāyāma), he should perform the worship of the bridegroom, his father, mother, and other members of that party, with perfumes, flowers, garments, and so forth, according to his means, for the sake of attaining the full fruit of the marriage. In this regard as well, they perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).

Having worshipped Gaṇeśa and, according to one's means, having offered perfumes and flowers to the paternal and maternal relatives of the bridegroom and having given silk cloths, fine fabrics, *dukūla* garments, and so forth, one should perform the worship of Airiṇī for the sake of attaining the full fruit of the gift of the daughter, for the increase of the lineage, and for the pleasure of Umā-Maheśvara. One should also give the gift of the lineage-vessel called Vairiṇī to the mother of the bridegroom or to a woman of equal status. It is as follows:
"O Airiṇī, you are the goddess Umā; Maheśa is the Lord of Girijā.
Therefore, I shall worship you, Airiṇī, the granter of all desires."
"Together with clothing and a lamp, and accompanied by sixteen winnowing baskets,
I shall give this to the bridegroom’s mother for the successful completion of the gift of the daughter."
Having spoken thus and having worshipped Umā and Maheśvara within that bamboo vessel, one should give that bamboo vessel to the bride's mother or to her equal.
The mantras for this are:
"The bamboo is the progenitor of the lineage, the most excellent; the bamboo is the source from which the lineage arises."
May he, pleased by this gift of bamboo, grant me prosperity.
This meritorious bamboo vessel is produced from the bamboo species.
Since the gift of bamboo is the most excellent, grant me peace from this.
All these bamboo vessels have indeed been prepared by me and given to the beloved of Umā for the sake of the increase of my lineage.
This gift, which causes the lineage to flourish and is endowed with good fortune and other virtues,
is covered with a cloth, filled [with grain], and accompanied by fruit and gold.
"This [gift], which causes the destruction of all sins and is filled with various substances, is the supreme among all gifts; therefore, grant me peace.

Then, he himself should hold a bamboo vessel containing a lamp upon the heads of his excellent father, mother, and others, reciting the two mantras: "May Svasti measure out for us," and "Svasti na indra."
Then the giver himself, having taken the girl and seated her separately on the laps of the bridegroom’s father and the others, should pray:
"This girl, seven years of age, has been nurtured by me like a son;
she is now given to your son—may she be protected with affection."

In the case of a six-year-old girl, however, the modification is: "This girl is six years old. For those aged eight years and so forth, it should be adjusted accordingly: "This girl is eight years old," "This girl is nine years old," or "This girl is ten years old. Similarly, in the phrase "to the son," one should substitute "to the grandson," "to the brother," "to the kinsman," or "to the friend.
Then, having seated the bride in the same manner on the lap of the bridegroom’s mother or others, she should offer her prayers.

Then, according to custom, the bride’s maternal uncle and mother, along with other well-dressed women of that family, should cause the bride to give away small bamboo poles, winnowing baskets, and sieves covered with cloth. In this manner, whatever else is required by local custom should be performed. Then, for the successful completion of the rite, the giver should remember Viṣṇu. All of this must be done before eating with one’s wife.
To emphasize that there is a fault in failing to perform this, they recite the following verse: "If one performs the dismantling of the pavilion without giving the bamboo pole..."
"Out of ignorance, the fool brings about the destruction of the lifespan of the couple."
In reality, however, this is baseless because it is not seen in the great treatises (*mahānibandha*). Furthermore, in the *Śākalakārikā*:
"Having given garments to the couple, one should then worship the goddess Airiṇī."
Likewise, one should present a bamboo vessel and a maiden to the bridegroom alone.
The gift of the bamboo staff (vaṃśadāna) is intended as an ancillary part of the gift of the bride on the fourth day;
one should perform it during the third watch of the night, and it does not incur any fault even if performed under an unfavorable astrological conjunction (kuyoga).
"If there should be either a *pāta* or a *vaidhṛti* on the fourth day,
then the worship of Airiṇī and so forth should take place specifically during the latter part of that same night.
The intended meaning is that even if the *pāta* and *vaidhṛti* should occur on the very fourth day, the rite must be performed then and not at any other time.
In reality, however, because this is not seen in either ancient or modern texts, it is to be disregarded.
Thus ends the worship and gift for Airiṇī.
Now follows the rite of the fourth day.

In this regard, the Gṛhya-sūtra states: "On the fourth day, during the latter part of the night, having established the sacred fire and performed the rites up to the expiations, he offers nine expiatory oblations; having thus performed everything up to the expiations and recited 'sa tvaṃ no agne' up to its end, he offers these nine expiatory oblations with the mantra 'agne prāyaścitta'."

Mātṛdatta states: The statement "having performed up to the expiation" (*prāyaścittiparyantaṃ kṛtvā*) is for the purpose of indicating that the entire set of *vyāhṛtis* constitutes an unordained expiation (*anādiṣṭaprāyaścitta*). By this, it is established that when no specific expiation is mentioned, the oblation is to be made with the entire set of *vyāhṛtis*. For this very reason, it bears the designation "universal expiation" (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Therefore, having performed everything up to the entire set of *vyāhṛtis*, one should offer the nine principal oblations (*pradhānībhūtā āhutīḥ*) as the expiations.

In this context, the indication that the *caturthī-karman* is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been made because it is appropriate to designate the name "expiation" specifically within the midst of expiatory rites, given that the *caturthī-karman* is itself an expiatory rite. Furthermore, the fact that the *caturthī-karman* is an expiatory rite is to be understood from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras beginning with "O Agni, expiation."

In the previous explanation, there are the following defects: the abandonment of the immediate succession to the well-known *vyāhṛti* oblations; the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamaka*) for why only these four [verses], beginning with "imaṃ me," should bear the designation of expiation (*prāyaścitta*); and the postulation of the performance of the principal rite in the middle of the subsidiary oblation (*aṅgahoma*), which is not prescribed by scripture. However, in our own explanation, these defects do not apply. On the contrary, it should be observed that our view is superior, as it establishes—based on what is well-known in other scriptures and among ritual practitioners—that the complete *vyāhṛti* oblation in one's own scripture is designated as the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). This appears to be the correct position.

Now, the procedure (*prayoga*). Beginning from the day of taking the hand in marriage, on the fourth night—when one-third of it remains—the bridegroom, together with his wife, shall bathe, sit facing east, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Having announced the place and time, he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "For the propitiation of the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of removing the blemish of this wife having been enjoyed by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni, I shall perform the *caturthī-homa*. This resolve is intended according to the view that the marriage ceremony does not conclude with the rites of the fourth night.

Then, having worshipped Gaṇeśa and meditating on this fire as being named Śikhin, he kindles the fire; having meditated on the four [verses] beginning with "catvāri," and having taken up three fuel-sticks, he performs the rites from "śraddha ehi" up to the end of the breath-control (prāṇāyāma). Then, having recited the section beginning with "yā yakṣyamāṇā" up to the end of the *vyāhṛtis*, he says: "In this rite of the fourth oblation, I shall sacrifice with a single oblation of clarified butter to Agni Prāyaścitti, to Vāyu Prāyaścitti, to Āditya Prāyaścitti, to Āditya Prāyaścitti, to Vāyu Prāyaścitti, to Agni Prāyaścitti, to Agni Prāyaścitti, to Vāyu Prāyaścitti, and to Āditya Prāyaścitti."
In the *aṅgahoma*, one should perform the rites ending with the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samidabhyādhāna*), beginning with "Varuṇa with two [verses]" or "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," and so forth.
Regarding the *saṃsrāvahoma* on the head, some say that one should recite: "Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati, with the clarified butter from the residue (*saṃsrāva*)."

And this [sequence] should be understood as occurring either before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, or before the performance of the subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*), depending on the chosen option. Having set out the vessels for the pouring of the remnants—namely, a vessel, a water-pot, a wooden ladle (*darvī*), a butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for carrying forward the *praṇītā* waters, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *upaveṣa*, the *saṃmārga* grass-blades, the fuel (*idhma*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the grass-blades for kindling, and the clarified butter—and having performed the rites from the selection of the *brahmán* priest up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he should offer nine principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*).

"Oṃ, O Agni, you are the expiation; you are the expiation. I, a Brāhmaṇa desiring protection, approach you. Whatever terrible form she has, destroy that from here, Svāhā! To Agni Prāyaścitti, this [is offered], not mine. "Oṃ, O Vāyu, you are the expiation; you are the expiation. I, a Brāhmaṇa desiring protection, approach you. Whatever censurable form she has, destroy that from here, Svāhā! To Vāyu Prāyaścitti, this [is offered], not mine.
"Oṃ, O Āditya, you are the expiation; you are the expiation. I, a Brāhmaṇa desiring protection..."
"I approach [thee]; that body of hers which is husband-slaying, destroy it from here, svāhā!"—this is for Āditya as the expiation.
These same [mantras] again in reverse order: "Oṃ, Āditya, prāyaścitti; Vāyu, prāyaścitti; Agni, prāyaścitti."
Again, in the previous order:
"Oṃ agne prā0, vāyo prā0, āditya prā0.

At the conclusion of the oblations of the nine principal offerings, one should pour drops of clarified butter into the vessel previously prepared for the purpose of collecting the remnants (*saṃpātāvanaya*). After the nine oblations, one offers that residual clarified butter from the ladle onto the head of the wife.

"Oṃ bhūr, I offer glory (*bhaga*) unto you, svāhā!"—to Agni this [is offered]. "Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I offer fame (*yaśas*) unto you, svāhā!"—to Vāyu this [is offered]. "Oṃ suvaḥ, I offer prosperity (*śrī*) unto you, svāhā!"—to Sūrya this [is offered]. "Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I offer splendor (*tviṣi*) unto you, svāhā!"—to Prajāpati this [is offered]. Having thus offered these four oblations upon the head, the procedure from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, beginning with the verse "imaṃ me," up to the concluding recitation (*saṃsthājapa*), is the same. There is no offering of the three-fold food (*trivṛdannahoma*) here.

Then, having placed a jar filled with water near the fire and having circumambulated that [fire] together with the water-jar, he should prepare a place for the bed to the west of the fire, enclose it, and have his wife lie down there with her head toward the east or toward the north; in this case, the scriptural injunction specifies that she should lie with her head toward the north. Then:
"Oṃ, with the auspicious five-branched [wood], which possesses hostility against enemies, with a thousandfold glory..."
"We touch you with our hand for the sake of good progeny. With his right hand, he touches her vulva, saying:
"Oṃ, may our names be united, may our hearts be united, may our navels be united, may our skins be united; may you be united with desire."

With the words, "I bind you with a cord for non-release," he effects the union. He says: "Oṃ! Be devoted to me; be my companion. That form of yours which is husband-slaying, I make that one a slayer of paramours; be auspicious to me; be sharp-edged against paramours."
Thus he embraces her:
"O honey, this is indeed honey; my tongue is a speaker of honey. In my mouth is the honey of the bees; in my teeth, the act of chewing has been performed."
"That enchantment of the Cakravākas which is drawn from the rivers—
if even the gods and Gandharvas are joined by it, then we two shall be united by that very same bond."
Thus, with these two verses, he joins his mouth to her mouth. This act of approaching is necessary because it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the woman.
Then, having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor and a more abundant one to others, he should remember Viṣṇu for the sake of ensuring the excellence of the ritual performance.

According to the ancient method of practice, however, the following distinction is to be observed: after the *vyāhṛti* offerings during the *anvādhāna*, one says, "I shall sacrifice to Varuṇa with two oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*); I shall sacrifice to Agni and Varuṇa with one oblation of clarified butter; I shall sacrifice to Agni and Varuṇa with one oblation of clarified butter," and then follows the mention of the principal deities. After that, [the formula] begins with "Agni who is free from bonds" (*ayāsasam agnim*) and so forth. The fire-oblation (*homa*) proceeds according to this. All else is the same.
This concludes the fourth-day rite (*caturthī-karma*). Now follows the removal of the deity-pavilion (*devakamaṇḍapodāsana*).
Regarding that, the time for the raising of the deity's pedestal is as follows:
"A wise person should perform the raising of the deity's pedestal on an even day;
the sixth [day] is uneven and not desired, except for the fifth and seventh."
The meaning is that among even days, the sixth day is not desired, and among odd days, the fifth and seventh days—along with any others—are not desired.
Regarding the number of days, it is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"Starting from the day of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), up until the sixteenth day..."
"The construction of a temple should be performed at marriage and at a vow; [these are] ten."

The meaning is that the period for marriage is sixteen days, and for the investiture with the sacred thread (*mauñjībandha*) it is ten days. During these days, one should perform the dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the deities installed and the recitation of the *puṇyāha* and other formulas on any remaining day—avoiding odd-numbered days other than the fifth and seventh, and, among even days, avoiding the sixth—just as in the case of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

The dismissal of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-visarjana*) should be performed on a day other than those nine, three, or sixty days starting from the wedding day. At the conclusion of the *puṇyāha-vācana* and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the officiating priest (*purohita*) shall place the [sacrificial] branch and other items into a bamboo vessel and pour a little of the consecrated water sprinkled upon them onto the head of the performer and his family members. At the time of pouring, he should recite: "Oṃ pretya ca... ityāgacchati. This is repeated twice. This is according to established custom (*ācāra*).

Then the performer, with palms joined in reverence upon his head, should say to the twice-born: "May auspicious things befall our lineage every six months; may you so declare. They, in turn, should reply: "May auspicious things befall your lineage every six months.

Then, having honored the twice-born with perfumes, flowers, fruits, betel, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should receive their blessings. In this same manner, the father of the bridegroom should also perform the ritual for the dismissal of the deities.

As for the statement in the *Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa-ṭīkā* that the dismantling (*udvāsana*) [of the pavilion] should not be performed on the ninth, third, or sixth day starting from the wedding day—that should be understood to apply to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and not to the deity and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the dismantling of the pavilion. Now, the things to be avoided on account of the wedding.
In that regard, from the placement of the *mātṛkā* until the dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the *mātṛkā*, there are certain things to be avoided, as well as others to be avoided even thereafter.
Regarding the former, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), the utterance of *svadhā*, traveling, and bathing with cold water."
"The sapindas shall not perform [the rites] until the dismissal of the mother."

In this context, by the terms *apasavya* and *svadhā*, the corresponding ritual action is indicated. Although the meaning is already established by the word *apasavya* alone, the inclusion of the word *svadhā* is for the purpose of excluding the *vaiśvadeva* offering that is associated with the *pitṛyajña* (the sacrifice to the ancestors), as in the formula: "Svadhā to the ancestors, svāhā! This is because it accords with established custom: "The cremation of the deceased, bathing with curd, bathing with cold water, the *vaiśvadeva*, the performance of the *svadhā* rite, the *brahmayajña*, and fasting [are prohibited]."
The study of the Veda and likewise the teaching of the Veda,
as well as the crossing of boundaries, shall not cease until the erection of a temple.

And because of the statement in the *Dharmapradīpa*: "Even though [the word *svadhā*] occurs in rites for the ancestors, such as the *iṣṭi*, just like the word *svadhā* in the mantra 'Svadhā to the ancestors, may there be nourishment (*ūrj*)', nevertheless, the prohibition does not apply there, because the Vedic (śrauta) [text] possesses greater authority. The same applies to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña performed by one who has maintained the sacred fires."

Although there is no occasion for this prohibition because the raising of the deity occurs before the new moon day—since it is only prohibited that the ritual duties be included within the period ending with the raising of the deity—nevertheless, this should be understood as applying when the raising of the deity itself does not take place due to some obstacle.
As stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"The daily *śrāddha*, Vedic study, and bathing with cold water..."
"When an auspicious rite has commenced, there is no [impurity] until the dismantling of the pavilion."
The *nitya-śrāddha* is the daily *śrāddha*. Gārgya states:
"Once the *nāndī-śrāddha* has been performed, [it remains valid] until the dismissal of the mothers."
The Darśa-śrāddha, the Kṣaya-śrāddha, and bathing with cold water.
The offering with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), the utterance of "svadhā," the daily ancestral rite (nityaśrāddha),
as well as the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), Vedic study, and crossing the boundary of a river [are forbidden].
"The sapindas shall not perform fasting, religious vows, or even the eating of funeral feasts (śrāddha) until the dismantling of the pavilion."
(In the *Saṃskāradarpaṇa*, another Smṛti states:
"The sapindas shall not perform an earthen tilaka, an ash tilaka, or a bath with cold water until the conclusion of the removal of the sacrificial pavilion.")
Even the learned avoid such acts as listening to the Vedānta or reciting the Gītā.
In another Smṛti it is said: "During marriage, the tying of the girdle, for one year, half a year, or half of that [quarter]."
"A wise person should always avoid both the beginning of building a house and its entry."
Some maintain that there is no correspondence here according to the numerical order.
Bṛhaspati states:
"At a sacred ford, at a wedding, on a journey, in battle, or during a national upheaval..."
"And in the event of a fire in a city or village, there is no fault in touching what has been touched."
(Saṃgraha:
"In matters of auspiciousness such as marriage, in consecrations, and during great festivals,
one must not depart until their completion, even in the event of birth-impurity or death-impurity.")
Now, following that, are the things to be avoided.
Yogayājñavalkya states:
"One should not bathe once a festival has passed, nor until an auspicious rite has been performed."
"Having followed after his friends and kinsmen, and having honored his chosen deity."

Kārṣṇājini states: "At marriage, the initiation of vows, and the tonsure ceremony, one should not perform the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), bathing with earth, or the libation of sesame seeds for a year, half a year, or half of that [respectively]."
The vow refers to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
In the *Hemādri*, Jyotiṣparāśara states:
"In the case of marriage, one should indeed avoid twelve months that have been prescribed [as inauspicious]."
"For the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍanirvāpa) and for the tying of the girdle (mauñjībandha), the sapindas are indeed only six."
In some places, that same author states an exception:
"In the case of the Mahālaya, at a Śrāddha for Gayā, on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father,
and likewise at the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for any mortal whatsoever..."

"Even one who has performed a marriage should always perform the offering of the *piṇḍas*. Here, the term "Gayā-śrāddha" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for śrāddhas at all sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrthas*). The mention of the "anniversary of death" (*kṣayāha*) is an elliptical expression for the obligatory śrāddhas such as the *Aṣṭakās* and others. Now, it might be argued: "If the offering of *piṇḍas* is thus established even in the case of the *Mahālaya*, then the specific mention of the *Mahālaya* would be redundant. Therefore, it is impossible to say that the mention of the 'anniversary of death' is merely an elliptical expression [intended to include other occasions]. To this, we reply: No.

Since the prohibition of offering *piṇḍas* during the *Mahālaya* implies the existence of another time [for that rite], the performance of the *Mahālaya* at that other time would otherwise occur; however, this must not be so. Rather, the *Mahālaya* with *sapiṇḍana* must be performed at its own proper time, for only thus can its purposefulness be maintained. The mention of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *navaśrāddhas* and the sixteen *śrāddhas*. The phrase "of the mother and father" is a qualification of the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*), and like the term "oblation for both," it is not intended to be restrictive; therefore, the offering of *piṇḍas* must indeed be performed even for the annual rites of brothers, paternal uncles, and others. Baudhāyana also says:

"At marriage, at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and at the tonsure (*caula*), one should perform the *tila-tarpaṇa* (libation with sesame) respectively for a year, half a year, and half of that; however, some say it is not required.
An exception to this rule will be stated in the section on libations (*tarpaṇa*).
In the *Madanaratna*, another *Smṛti* states: "In this case, those who are *sapiṇḍas* should not offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*), except for the *preta-piṇḍa*;
however, at the *pitṛ-yajña*, at other sacrifices, and at Gayā, they should indeed offer them."
In the *pitṛyajña*, that is, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*; in the sacrifice for the ancestors (*pitryeṣṭi*); and in the Soma sacrifice (*saumika makha*)—these are the *sapiṇḍas*. Satyavrata states:
"On the anniversary of the death of one's parents, at Gayā, and during the *mahālaya* [festival]..."
"Even though he has already performed the marriage ceremony, the son should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍanirvapaṇa).
In the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"During an oil-bath, during impurity (sūtaka), at a marriage, and upon the birth of a son..."
"And among all auspicious occasions, Gopicandana should not be worn.
And this lasts until the end of the month:
"At weddings and other such events, Gopicandana should not be worn for one month."

Thus, from the statement in the *Jyotirnibandha*: "Having performed marriage and the investiture of the sacred thread (*vratabandhana*), one should not undertake a pilgrimage for a year or half a year.
And in another *Smṛti*:
"Having performed marriage and the investiture of the sacred thread, [one should wait] a year or half a year before undertaking a pilgrimage."
"Furthermore, those who are *sapiṇḍas* (agnates) should not perform the shaving of the head, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), nor rites involving sesame seeds.
In the *Jyotiṣpradīpa*:
"Bathing with one's clothes on, rites involving sesame seeds, following the deceased, and the offering of the water-vessel (*kalaśa*)."
One should avoid visiting new holy places (tīrthas) or seeing deities for one year from the auspicious occasion [of a marriage];
likewise, for six months following a marriage or the commencement of a vow, one should not undertake a new vow,
nor should one perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) of a vow, nor observe a fast.

"One should not discard worn-out vessels and the like, nor should one sweep the house; likewise, after the marriage of a son and after the investiture of the sacred thread (vratibandhana), one must never shave one's head for a full year or even for half a year."

By the mention of "son" here, the daughter is also included. "Muṇḍana" means shaving. However, cutting (of the hair) certainly takes place, for it is said: "But when shaving is forbidden, cutting is indeed prescribed."
Thus, from the statement of another Smṛti:
(In the *Smṛtiratnākara-saṃgraha*— "But after marriage and initiation, for one year or even half a year...")
One should not perform the commencement of a vow, nor likewise the conclusion of a vow;
one should not offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas), nor should one give water-pots (karakas). Having performed a festival for the deity for a year or even half a year, [one should then undertake the vow].
"One should avoid covering the house immediately after the auspicious ceremony.
Regarding the year of marriage, it is stated in another Smṛti that if the wife of the father or other relative who performs the marriage of a son or daughter is pregnant, then a defect occurs:
"If one's own wife is pregnant in the year of the wedding, there is loss, death, destruction of the fetus, and delusion."
"For the sake of pacifying that [evil], one should fashion an image of Death with three gold *niṣkas*, worship it, and give it away.

Regarding the word "pūjya" (having worshipped), although there is no compound here, the substitution of *lyap* for *ktvā* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Regarding the word "dadyāt" (should give), the words "to a Brāhmaṇa" are to be supplied as the object. Thus end the things to be avoided.
Now, regarding remarriage by way of a further discussion:

if, after the marriage has been performed, it is subsequently discovered that the auspicious moment (lagna) was defective due to the absence of purity in the five-fold astrological factors (pañcāṅga-śuddhi) and so forth, then one should perform a remarriage at a specific time prescribed in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra).
Nṛsiṃha states in the Śrīdharīya:
I shall now describe the remarriage of a couple, which bestows auspicious prosperity,
when defects arise in the ascendant or the moon-ascendant due to unfavorable planets, lunar mansions, and so forth.
On other inauspicious occasions, when malefic planetary configurations and the like occur,
or during the marriage of a couple when impurity (āśauca) and such arise.

In this context, the term "impurity" (*āśauca*) should be understood as including marriage; for even there, impurity exists. This [interpretation] is due to a misconception. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), portents (*utpāta*) are included, or it refers to the period of impurity following the death of a preceptor (*guru*). For the sake of pacifying that defect, a second marriage is desired. Furthermore, the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) is excellent, and [the merit] increases especially during it.
The two months of Āṣāḍha and Mārgaśīrṣa are to be avoided; the remaining months bring auspiciousness.
The asterisms, lunar days, divisions, zodiac signs, days of the week, and other factors mentioned for marriage [are likewise required].
The Karaṇas known as Yogas, along with the planetary positions, aspects, and conjunctions,
likewise bestow auspiciousness at that time of marriage.
"A marriage performed in the forenoon or during the first part of the night shall be auspicious. Thus concludes the section concerning remarriage. Now, the causes for a second or subsequent marriage:

In this regard, the Dharmasūtra states: "When one has a wife endowed with both virtue and offspring, one should not take another; in the absence of either, another may be taken before the establishment of the sacred fires. Once the fires have been established, she who is already present becomes connected with the ritual acts which have this [establishment] as their constituent part."

In rites pertaining to the Śruti, the Gṛhya-sūtras, and the Smṛtis, there is the perfection of dharma consisting of faith and capability, as well as the perfection of progeny, which is the state of having a son. When such a wife exists, one should not take another; that is, one should not marry another woman. By the use of the feminine gender in the word "anyām" (another), the term "wife" (*bhāryām*) is to be supplied. In the absence of either dharma or progeny, another may be taken in marriage. Even in that case, it must be before the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), and not after the installation. This statement is made for this very purpose.

When it is stated that [the rite] should not be performed when both [conditions] are fulfilled, the portion stating that it *should* be performed in the absence of either one follows as a logical consequence. And when it must be performed in the absence of either one, what doubt could there be regarding its performance in the absence of both? Regarding the point that it should be performed even in the absence of both, the reason is provided by the phrase "prior to the establishment of the fires" (*prāg-agnyādheyāt*). This refers to the passage beginning with "when the establishment exists" (*ādhāne sati*). When the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) exists—that is, when it is present—one becomes qualified for and is connected to the ritual acts. By which acts? By those of which this establishment of the fires is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) or a contributing factor (*upakāraka*), such as the Agnihotra and others.

In this context, because of the statement "while the wife is living," even if a son has been obtained, the taking of another wife must certainly be performed for the sake of fulfilling religious duties (*dharma*), whether that [first] husband has died before or after the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*).
And so Manu says:
"Having given the fires to his wife who dies first at her funeral rites..."
"One may perform the act of taking a wife again, and likewise the re-establishment of the sacred fires."

Yājñavalkya also says: "One should take a wife and the sacred fires according to the rules, without delay. Now, an objection may be raised: since one is already connected with domestic (*gārhya*) and traditional (*smārta*) rites prior to the formal establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*), why is it said that one becomes connected with rites only when the *ādhāna* has taken place? This is true; however, from this very statement of the reason, it is inferred that even though the requirements for dharma and progeny may exist before the *agnyādhāna*, there is no great fault in a person blinded by passion occasionally taking a wife [at that time].

The author of the *Ujjvalā* has explained that if the wife of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is either lacking in faith for the ritual duties or lacks the capacity for them, and if his sons are deceased or unborn, then a remarriage must indeed be performed.
Regarding a further marriage for the sake of pleasure (*ratyartha*), there is this distinction: "He who, having passed over one wife, desires to marry another for the sake of pleasure..."
"One who is capable, having gratified his previously married wife with wealth, may marry another."
Yājñavalkya states:

"If he abandons a wife who obeys his commands, is skillful, bears him heroic sons, and speaks kindly, he shall be made to pay her a third part of his estate; if he has no property, he must provide maintenance for her."
The meaning is that a man with wealth must provide a third part of his fortune, while one without wealth must provide maintenance consisting of food and clothing.
Regarding a woman who, dissatisfied with such maintenance, leaves the house, Manu says: "But a superseded wife who, being provoked, goes out from the house..."
"She must be restrained immediately; she must not be abandoned in the presence of the family."

Yājñavalkya has stated those [wives] for whom supersession is permissible: "A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, a rogue, one who is barren, one who wastes wealth, one who speaks unpleasantly,
one who bears only daughters, and likewise one who hates her husband may be superseded."

"Even one who has been superseded must be maintained; otherwise, there would be a great sin. Here, *adhivedana* means the taking of another wife. Regarding a woman who drinks liquor (*surāpī*), which means a drinker of intoxicants: in the case of drinking liquor, it is not merely supersession, but even abandonment; for its mention in the *Smṛti* as a cause for abandonment occurs in the context of "likewise in the case of a great sin.
This is also supported by the statement: "Half the body of him whose wife drinks liquor falls away."
For this very reason, Manu says:
"A woman who drinks liquor, is untruthful in conduct, or is antagonistic;
one who is diseased, or who always acts for the sake of injury and destroys wealth—such a wife may be superseded by taking another."
"Afflicted" means one who is chronically ill. The word division is *asatyavṛttā* (one of unchaste conduct).
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"A wife who creates obstacles to dharma, who is unchaste, and excessively wrathful..."
"One should abandon [a wife] for the sake of protecting dharma, and likewise one who speaks unpleasantly.

Mādhava explains that "one should abandon" means one should take another [wife], but not that one should renounce [the enjoyment of] her. Regarding the time to wait before taking another wife (*adhivedana*), Manu says:
"A barren wife should be superseded in the eighth year, but one whose children have died in the tenth."
"In the eleventh [month], she gives birth to a daughter who speaks unpleasantly immediately."
In the *Saṃgraha*, however, it is said:
"One should abandon a childless wife in the tenth year, one whose children are all female in the twelfth,
one whose children have died in the fifteenth, but one who speaks unpleasantly immediately."

Kātyāyana states: "If a man who possesses a wife and maintains the sacred fires should, for some other reason, desire to marry another wife, where is his fire-sacrifice (homa) ordained to be performed?"
"The oblation should be performed only in one's own sacred fire (svāgni), never in a common (laukika) fire. Maṇḍana also says:
"If one should marry a second wife while the first is still living..."
"At that time, one who maintains the sacred fire should perform the marriage rite in his own dwelling."

In the *Sudarśanabhāṣya*, however, it is stated that the second marriage oblation (*vivāhahoma*) is performed with the common fire (*laukika*). This applies when [the sacred domestic fire] is unavailable; for instance, in the case of a marriage in another village, since the *gṛhya* fire is not present there, the marriage oblation is indeed performed in the common fire.

Regarding the specific time for a second or subsequent marriage for one whose wife has died, it is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*: "The rite for remarriage of a bridegroom begins from the day of the death of his wife."
"In an odd year it is auspicious, but even in a pair [of years], it bestows death."
The word *ca* has the sense of *tu*; the word *api* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*. The prohibition of the third marriage to a human woman is stated in the *Saṃgraha*:
"He who would marry a third [woman] who is a human woman, or even a fourth..."
"There will be the loss of wealth, grain, and so forth, or she may become a widow."
In the *Mātsya*: "A man who is a householder, endowed with sons, grandsons, and so forth, and maintains the sacred fires,
should never marry a third wife for the sake of accomplishing his desires."
"If one should go to a human woman either out of delusion or ignorance, he is surely destroyed;
there is no doubt, according to the word of Garga."

Only after performing the third *arka-vivāha* (marriage to the sun) should the marriage to a human woman (*mānuṣī-vivāha*) be performed for the fourth and subsequent marriages—according to the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "For the sake of the fourth and subsequent marriages, one should marry the sun in the third. (From the *Brāhma Purāṇa*: "One should perform the *arka-vivāha* on a Sunday, or under the asterism *Hasta*, or on a Saturday, or on an auspicious day during the forenoon.")

Having carefully examined a place to the east or north of the village that is endowed with fine flowers and fruits, one should prepare the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) and so forth beneath it according to the prescribed rule.
First, one should appoint a preceptor for the purpose of giving the daughter of the Arka tree in marriage;
having approached the vicinity of the Arka tree, one should there recite the *svasti* and other benedictory verses.
One should perform the Nāndī-śrāddha with gold and worship the eight groups [of deities];
the giver of the bride, moreover, should worship the groom with madhuparka according to his capacity.

"One should worship [the guest] with the sacred thread, a garment, and ornaments for the hands, ears, and so forth, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic school, using the honey-mixture (madhuparka)."
[The rite is] according to what is stated in one's own branch [of the Veda] or that stated in the donor's branch:
"The pavilion, the Mātṛkās, the three gods, likewise the groups of ancestors,
Gaṇeśa, Durgā, the lords of the field, the family deities, and the eight classes."
Thus are the eight groups described in the *Smṛtidarpaṇa*. Now follows its ritual application (*prayoga*).

On a Sunday, on the day of the *Hasta* asterism, on a Saturday, or on any auspicious day, during the forenoon, the performer—having bathed, adorned himself, dressed in new garments, and decorated with red perfumes and the like—should examine a single *arka* tree possessing excellent characteristics, rich in flowers, fruits, and branches, located in the eastern or northern direction from his village. Having approached the vicinity of that *arka*, having bathed it, wrapped it in cloth, and decorated it with red perfumes and the like, he should [select] one Brahmin as the preceptor (*ācārya*) for the purpose of giving the *arka*-maiden in marriage.

Having imagined [the Sun] to be very near, he should sit down in such a way that He does not come within the range of his vision; then, having performed the *ācamana* (sipping of water), the *prāṇāyāma* (breath control), and having announced the place and time, he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "For the propitiation of the venerable Supreme Lord, through the accomplishment of my eligibility for the third marriage with a human woman—preceded by the removal of defects indicated by that third marriage with a human woman—I shall perform my own third marriage with the Sun. Then, as part of that rite, he should perform the worship of Gaṇapati, the recitation of the *puṇyāha* (declaration of auspiciousness), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjana*), and [the offering] with gold.
Having performed the *nāndī-śrāddha*, he should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) to the north of the sun for the purpose of the *homa* offering.

Then the donor shall honor the recipient of the sun with the materials for the *madhuparka* provided by the bridegroom, as well as with turbans and other ornaments such as those for the hands and ears. The *madhuparka* may be offered according to the ritual branch (*śākhā*) of the recipient or according to his own branch.
Thereafter, the recipient—
O Sun, who dwells in the three worlds and possesses seven horses, together with your shadow (Saptāśvacchāyā),
ward off the defect born of the third marriage and grant us happiness.

Standing thus before the Sun and having offered prayers to him, he should wrap him with a white cloth and cotton threads. For the verse beginning with *ā satyena*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Savitṛ, and the meter is Triṣṭubh; its application is in worship: "Oṃ, ā satyena rajasā... vipaśyan. Having invoked the Sun together with his shadow there with this very mantra, and having offered the services beginning with the seat and ending with the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) using this same mantra—for the verse *ā satyena*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Savitṛ, and the meter is Triṣṭubh—[he completes the rite].

For the three mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the deities are Agni or the Viśvedevas, the metre is Gāyatrī, and their application (*viniyoga*) is for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). [The mantras are]:

"Oṃ ā satyena rajasā... vipaśyan" and "Oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā... At the conclusion of all [the rites], having sprinkled [the deity] with this very mantra, "ā satyena," one should worship with clothing, the sacred thread (*upavīta*), garlands, perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps; then, having offered rice cooked with jaggery (*guḍaudana*), one should present betel leaves and other offerings.
"This ancient one who brings me joy, whom I have touched,
