and who was touched by Brahmā— may she, the daughter of the Sun, protect us!
Having recited this while circumambulating the sun, he said:
"Salutations to you, O auspicious goddess; salutations to the self of Savitṛ.
Protect me with compassion, O goddess; you have come here as my wife. You, O Arka, were created by Brahmā for the welfare of all living beings."
You are the primordial source of trees and the increaser of the gods' delight;
swiftly destroy the sin born of my third marriage and death itself.
Grant me long life, grant me fame, grant me progeny, and even grant me cattle.
"O Sun, grant me splendor and nourishment; O Sun, remain firm in your own place.

Thus he should perform another circumambulation. Then follows the choosing of the Sun’s daughter. Those on the side of the groom should say: "We choose this daughter of the Sun, the great-granddaughter of Āditya, the granddaughter of Savitṛ, and the daughter of Arka—she who belongs to the Kāśyapa gotra and is born of the [so-and-so] gotra, possessing the [so-and-so] pravara, the great-granddaughter of so-and-so, the granddaughter of so-and-so, and the daughter of so-and-so. The Preceptor (Ācārya) should reply, "Choose her! This should be repeated twice.
Then, at an auspicious moment, the groom, reciting the two mantras, "Oṃ svasti na indro vṛddhaśravāḥ... and "Oṃ aṣṭau devāḥ kṣavāḥ somyāsaḥ...", should gaze at the sun.

Thereafter, accompanied by twice-born men led by the preceptor who utter blessings, he should summon the preceptor—who has been appointed for the purpose of giving the Sun’s daughter—to his side; having seated him, he should accept her from him according to the prescribed rule. That rule is as follows:

The preceptor, preceded by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), shall recite the name, lineage (*gotra*), and other details as before, and give [the girl] with the words: "I give this girl named so-and-so to you for the purpose of establishing the eligibility for the third marriage to a human being, preceded by the removal of the defects indicated for the third marriage to a human being.
The recipient should accept her, saying, "I accept. This should be repeated a second time. Then the preceptor should entreat the recipient:
"O Brahmin, accept this daughter of the Sun, adorned according to my ability,
given to you, O Brahmin, of such-and-such lineage and named such-and-such Śarman."

Then the recipient, remaining silent, should perform the rite of placing unbroken grains (*akṣata*) into the joined palms preceded by the binding of the marriage-thread (*kaṅkaṇa*), just as in a wedding ceremony. He should wrap the sun with a five-fold cord using the mantra "By Truth... (*yāvat satyena...*) or with the *Gāyatrī*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details for this are as before. The specific distinction regarding the application (*viniyoga*) is that it is for the purpose of wrapping. The seer and other details for the *Gāyatrī* have been stated in the section on the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*). The statement of the application is: "The application is for the purpose of wrapping."

Or, one may recite while simply wrapping it silently. In this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), the specific modification lies in the statement of application (*viniyoga-vākya*): "The application is for the recitation (*japa*).

Then, having divided that thread again into five parts, one should bind it to the left shoulder of the *Arka* tree—recalling that the mantra "bṛhatsāma... has the Viśvedevas as its deity, Indra as its seer, and the Jagatī as its meter; its application is for binding the thread upon the *Arka* shoulder and for scattering ashes over it—and having bound it with "Oṃ bṛhatsāma... protect," one should scatter ashes on that thread using this very [mantra].
Then, having performed the *nīrājana* ceremony for her, one should adorn her with ornaments according to one's means.

Then, in the directions starting from the east, one should touch the ground while reciting "The earth, the sky," make heaps of rice while reciting "The medicinal herbs," and place the water-pots while reciting "Smell [this]," and likewise install them in the directions starting from the southeast.

Then, having wrapped each of the eight established water-pots (kalaśas) with cloth and thread, and having filled them with cool water mixed with turmeric and fragrance while reciting the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge," he places fragrant substances and other offerings into each of them with their respective mantras and covers them with full vessels (pūrṇapātra); in all cases, there is a repetition of the mantras.
Then, having invoked Mahāviṣṇu into those pots by means of the name-mantra alone, he should worship Him with the ritual services (upacāras) beginning with the seat (āsana).

Then, having sat down behind the prepared sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) to the north of the *arka* tree while touching the *arka*, and having performed the consecration of the mound according to the procedure of digging out, scratching lines, and so forth; having established the common fire named Yojaka there, kindled it, and fanned it; having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), performed the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) ending with "Śraddhā, come hither" and so on; and having recited from "In this *arka*-wedding-homa-rite, those who are to be sacrificed to... up to the end of the *vyāhṛtis* or up to the goddess Prasādhanī, [he proceeds] to the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*).

Having said, "I shall sacrifice to Bṛhaspati, Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati with one oblation of clarified butter for each," he should perform the *aṅgahoma* (limb-offerings), saying "to Varuṇa with two [verses]," and so forth; or, up to the *vyāhṛti-homa*, or up to the *prasādhanī-devī-homa*, according to the alternative specified during the *anvādhāna*. Then follows the principal offering (*pradhānahoma*). For the verse beginning with "saṃ gobhiḥ" (RV 10.70.10), Aṅgiras is the seer, Bṛhaspati is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal *ājya-homa* of the *arka-vivāha*.

"Oṃ! Like Bhaga, the descendant of Aṅgiras, approaching with cattle, has led away Aryaman; like Mitra among the people, he anoints the husband and wife. O Bṛhaspati, [drive] the swift horses toward the prize as in battle, svāhā!
This is for Bṛhaspati.

For the verse beginning with *yasmai tvā*, Vāmadeva is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the Triṣṭubh is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal *ājya* oblation of the Arka marriage rite: "Oṃ, O Sovereign, for whatever desire we sacrifice to you, having granted that desire to us, now drink this clarified butter, Svāhā! [To Agni, this...].

The seers (*ṛṣis*) of the *vyāhṛtis* taken individually and collectively are, in order: Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, and Bhṛgu. The deities (*devatās*) are, in order: Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati. The meters (*chandas*) are, in order: Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, and Bṛhatī. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the primary *ājya* oblation at the wedding of Arka: "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā"—to Agni this [oblation]. "Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā"—to Vāyu this [oblation]. "Oṃ svaḥ svāhā"—to Sūrya this [oblation]. "Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā"—to Prajāpati this [oblation].

Then, according to the specific fortnight (pakṣa) mentioned during the *anvādhāna*, one should complete the entire remainder of the oblation, beginning with the *aṅga-homa* or the *sviṣṭakṛt* offerings. There is no *trivṛd-annahoma* in this rite.
Then, having circumambulated the *arka* tree from left to right, [one recites]:
"This rite performed by me among the stationary beings, with its membrane..."
"Grant us the offspring of Arka; you ought to forgive all of that."

Having thus made this prayer and recited the peace-mantra "śaṃ no vātaḥ," he should give a pair of cows to the preceptor (ācārya) and offer sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to his capacity to the other Brahmins as well.
Then the preceptor shall sprinkle the recipient along with the sun using the waters contained in the established pitcher.

Then the recipient, having discarded those garments, should wear others; the discarded garments belong to the teacher. Then, on the fifth day, having worshipped the Arka tree as before, having dismissed it, having worshipped the fire, having caused the *puṇyāha* and other auspicious declarations to be recited, having fed the Brahmins, having given a generous gift, and having given ornaments, garments, and so forth to the Brahmin for the sake of the ritual’s perfection, he should remember Viṣṇu. Thereafter, he should marry a human woman according to the prescribed rite. And this procedure for the fire-offering (*homa*) according to the *Bāhvṛca* (Ṛgveda) has been stated here because the fire-offering procedure taught by Baudhāyana is currently unavailable.

Some maintain that this *arka-vivāha* (marriage by purchase) does not apply to one belonging to the Kāśyapa lineage because of the identity of the lineage (*gotraikyāt*). Others hold that here, the identity of lineage is not a defect. A bridegroom of the Kāśyapa lineage, having appointed a preceptor (*ācārya*) whose lineage is not incompatible with his own, should receive the *arka* from him.

The preceptor, however, having visualized [the bride] as given by Sūrya during the formal acceptance (*varaṇa*) and other rites, should—in place of the *Kāśyapa* lineage—proclaim his own lineage as a qualification of the girl; and in place of the words Āditya, Savitṛ, and Arka, he should proclaim the names of his own grandfather, father, and himself respectively. If it is deemed appropriate, scholars should accept that the marriage of the bridegroom of the *Kāśyapa* lineage to the Sun (*arka*) is thus accomplished.
This concludes the *Arkavivāha*.
Now follows the procedure for the conjunction of the two fires (*agnidvayasamsarga*).

In this regard, the Baudhāyana-sūtra states: "Now, if a householder who has a wife should take a second wife, how should he act in that case? [The rule is: the *vivāha-homa* (marriage oblation) for the elder wife—if it was performed far away—is to be done in the common (*laukika*) fire. At whatever time he takes [the second wife], from then on both wives shall maintain the sacred fires for twelve or thirteen days. Having established the secondary fire (*apara-agni*), strewn grass around it, melted the clarified butter (*ājya*), purified it, and taken four portions into the offering-ladle (*sruva*), he offers while the second wife holds onto him, with the mantra: *namasta ṛṣe gadā...*."

Having recited "evā brahmantavedastu svāhā," he should then place that fuel-stick upon the fire with the verse, "This is your seasonal womb. Having kindled the eastern fire and placed the fuel-stick upon it with the two verses beginning "ājuhvāna" and "udbudhyasva," and having strewn grass around it, he takes four portions of clarified butter in the offering-spoon. While his two wives hold on to him, he touches that [butter] and offers it with this hymn beginning "yo brahmā brahmaṇaḥ. Then, having performed the rites up to the "mouth of the fire" (the introductory oblations), he makes an offering from the cooked food with the verse, "samita saṃkalpethām."

Having recited the *puronuvākyā* verse, he offers with the *yājyā* verse, "O Agni Purīṣya... Then he offers oblations with the formulas beginning with "Thou art Purīṣya," up to the end of the section. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is established as standard until the granting of the boon of the milch cow. Then, to the east of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon a clump of *darbha* grass with the two verses, "The Brahman was born first" and "The Father [beheld] the Virāj. Thus, the venerable Baudhāyana says that the performance of the ritual procedure is thereby completed. Now follows the practical application (*prayoga*).

At the time of the second marriage *homa*, the performer, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on the altar and performed the purificatory rites such as drawing lines (*ullekhana*), should install the *gṛhya* fire of his former wife—reciting, "I establish this fire named Yojaka"—and there the second marriage *homa* should be performed. When the bride has been accepted, the formula of dedication (*ullekha*) is simply: "for the sake of establishing her status as a wife. However, when the rite is performed in a common fire (*laukikāgni*) due to the absence of the *gṛhya* fire, even this dedication is not required.
From the time when both fires are present together, one should attend to both fires separately with oblations and other rites for twelve or thirteen days.

Then, on the following day, after the two morning oblations, one should perform the union (*saṃsarga*) of the two fires. This period of attendance should be understood to last for twelve or thirteen days, provided that the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) has not yet been performed. However, if the *anvārambhaṇa-sthālīpāka* is to be performed, it must be done immediately after completing that rite.

Then, facing east and sitting together with his two wives, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and restrained his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), he should announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the propitiation of the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of accomplishing the performance of the rites to be carried out with the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) in a single ritual sequence (*tantra*), I shall perform the union of the two domestic fires. As a part of that, he should perform the worship of Gaṇapati, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*), and the *Nāndī-śrāddha*. The specific difference there is that one should say, "May Indra and the other gods be pleased."

Then, having prepared two sacrificial mounds (sthaṇḍila) oriented toward the north, and having separately placed the respective fires brought by the two wives to the north of the mounds, he performs the purificatory rites for the southern mound beginning with the scraping; having established and kindled the second marriage fire there, strewn it around, and spread *darbha* grass to the north, he places the *sruva* ladle, the *darvī* spoon, the clarified butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*), the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling vessel, the *upaveṣa* fire-stirring stick, the *saṃmārga* cleansing *darbhas*, the *avajvalana* flaming *darbhas*, the clarified butter, and the fuel sticks (*samidh*) within reach.

Having performed the rites beginning with the purification of the *pavitra* and ending with the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya-saṃskāra*), and having placed the prepared fuel-stick (*samidh*) into the fire, he takes four portions of butter into the *darvī* ladle with the *sruva* spoon. While his second wife maintains physical contact with him, he offers the oblation with the verse "Obeisance to thee, O Seer" (*namas ta ṛṣe*). Soma and Indra are the deities; the meter is *Bṛhatī*. Its application is in the fire-offering (*homa*). He offers it, saying: "Oṃ namas ta ṛṣe... [the rest of the mantra] ...vedastu svāhā. [The dedication is: "To Indra, this... [the rest].

Then, having sprinkled a fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *khadira* or any other suitable wood with pure water, while his second wife holds on to that fuel-stick, he should consign the fire into it with the mantra "This is your womb" (*ayaṃ te yoniḥ*). The deity is Agni; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; the application is for the act of consignment (*samāropaṇa*). Reciting "Oṃ, this is your [womb]... [granting] wealth" (*ayaṃ te... rayim*), he should consign the fire.

Then, having placed that fuel-stick (*samidh*) into the hand of his second wife and having performed the sweeping (*uddhanana*) and other rites for the northern sacrificial mound (*uttara-sthaṇḍila*), he establishes there the fire from the first marriage and kindles it. For the verse beginning with *ājuhvānaḥ*, Agni is the deity, Agni is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. For the verse beginning with *udbudhyasva agne*, Agni is the deity, Agni is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the placing of the fuel-stick (*samidh*) upon which fire has been mounted: having placed the fuel-stick upon which fire is mounted with the verses "Oṃ ājuhvānaḥ supratīka" and "Oṃ udbudhyasva agne," and having strewn grass around the altar (*paristīrya*), sprinkled water around it (*pariṣicya*), and adorned it, one takes four portions of clarified butter (*ājya*)—either from another clarified butter consecrated separately or from the previously consecrated clarified butter—using the *sruva* and *darvī* ladles. Then, while being assisted by his two wives, he touches that clarified butter while reciting the eight-verse *Ghṛtasūkta* beginning with "yo brahmā brahmaṇaḥ," as prescribed in the *Āyuṣyakalpa*.

Oṃ! May he who is Brahmā, who brought forth the Veda from Brahmā, the Lord of Prāṇa, clad in animal skin, the wielder of the Pināka bow—the God Īśāna—grant us long life; to him I offer this oblation of clarified butter. || 1 ||
Shining forth from the midst of the waters, radiant and lovely in his splendor, may that God come hither;
having cast us off from the terrible noose of death, may he consume our clarified butter for the sake of our long life. 2.

We cause to increase with clarified butter for the sake of long life that embryo which Brahmā placed within the wives of Brahmā—him who is multiform, victorious, possessing golden pillars, and who honors the domestic ritual. 3.

We satiate with clarified butter for the sake of long life here that Vidyā— who is Śrī, Lakṣmī, Ambikā, Aupalāṅgī, and Ṣaṣṭhī, whom they call Indrasenā— who has Brahman as her source and is identical in form with Him.

The daughters of Dakṣa, belonging to all wombs, sharing a common womb, thousands in number, of universal forms and diverse forms—may they, together with their sons, their husbands, and their herds, graciously accept this clarified butter for our long life. || 5 ||
May the divine hosts, many-formed and ancient, who cut short our lifespan, destroy our heroes!
To them I offer oblations in many ways with clarified butter; do not harm our progeny, nor our heroes. 6.

He who alone existed here in the beginning, from whom the guardian of the world arose—he to whom the world returns at the time of its dissolution; may that God consume our oblation of clarified butter here for the sake of long life.

"Having offered oblations of clarified butter to the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, Sādhyas, Ṛbhus, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Viśvedevas, Bhṛgus, Sarpas, and all the Aṅgirases, we constantly invoke them for our own long life. || 8 ||

Having touched [the vessel] with this very hymn, he offers that clarified butter (ājya) verse by verse at the end of each *svāhā*: "To Brahman, this [offering]" (1); "To the Devas, this" (2); "To Jyotis, this" (3); "To Vidyā, this" (4); "To the Dākṣāyaṇīs, this" (5); "To the divine hosts, this" (6); "To the Deva, this" (7). The renunciation (*tyāga*) is performed in sequence as follows: "To the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, Sādhyas, Ṛbhus, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Bhṛgus, Sarpas, and Aṅgirases, this."

In the previous case, the sprinkling was performed with mantras; here, the subsequent sprinkling should be performed. Then, having meditated upon [Agni] with the verse beginning "Four are the horns," and having taken up three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should perform the rites from "O Faith, come! up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Having stated, "Those deities who are to be worshipped in this rite of the *saṃsarga-homa* for the merging of the two domestic fires," and so forth, up to the end of the *vyāhṛti*s, or up to the goddess *Prasādhanī*, [one proceeds to] the principal oblation: "I shall worship Agni with one oblation of ground rice (*caru*) accompanied by both the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) and the offering verse (*yājyā*)."

I shall worship Agni Jātavedas, Agni Vaiśvānara, and the [deities] beginning with Pṛthivī, each with one oblation of clarified butter (ājyāhuti). I shall worship Nirṛti with five oblations of clarified butter. [Touching water. I shall worship Indra with one oblation of clarified butter. I shall worship Agni in the form of the ploughman of the earth with six oblations of clarified butter.

Having said, "I shall sacrifice to Kāmadugha and Sītā with one oblation of clarified butter for each," and having performed the *aṅgahoma* according to the specific fortnight (*pakṣa*) mentioned during the *anvādhāna*—such as "Varuṇa with two [verses]" and so forth—or alternatively, saying "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the remaining oblation of cooked rice (*caru*)" and so forth; and having performed everything up to the internal taking of the fires (*ātmany-agnigrahaṇa*), he spreads darbha grass to the north of the fire. Upon that, he places the *sruva* ladle, the *darvī* spoon, the vessel for clarified butter, the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, the vessel for the *prokṣaṇī* water, the vessel for the *caru*, the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), the winnowing-basket (*śūrpa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), and the mortar (*ulūkhala*).

One should place the pestle, the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), the *saṃmārga* (cleansing) *darbha* grasses, the fuel (*idhma*), the enclosing *barhis* grass, the *darbha* for kindling by fire, and the clarified butter (*ājya*) within reach. Then follows the selection of the *brahmā* priest and other rites. Having cooked the sacrificial rice-porridge (*caru*) according to the ritual rules for *caru*, one should cleanse the *sruva* and *darvī* spoons and perform the consecration of the clarified butter. At that time, during the rite of carrying fire around the oblation (*paryagnikaraṇa*), one should carry fire around both the clarified butter and the *caru* together.

Then, having laid the enclosing sticks (paridhis), having poured clarified butter over the cooked sacrificial porridge (caru), having removed it from the fire towards the north and placed it on the sacrificial grass (barhis), he should perform the rites up to the sprinkling of water (pariṣeka) or up to the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī, according to the specific mention in the *anvādhāna* ritual; thereafter, he should perform the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*). Having spread a base of ghee in the offering-spoon (*darvī*), he should take a portion of the size of a finger’s joint from the middle and the eastern half of the porridge using the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*); if he is one who performs five-fold portions (*pañcāvattin*), he should take a third portion from the western half. Having poured clarified butter over the portion with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and having moved the remainder back toward himself, he should be joined by his two wives in taking hold of him.

For these two [verses] beginning with *samitam*, Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Agni is the deity. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the oblation of cooked rice (*caru-homa*) primarily for the union of the two domestic fires (*gṛhyāgni*). One offers with the *puronuvākyā* and *yājyā*: "Oṃ *samita saṃkalpe*... *nyākaram*" and "Oṃ *agne pu*... *dhehi svāhā*. [The dedication is: "To Agni, this...

Alternatively, having recited the first verse in monotone (*ekaśrutya*), one joins it with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) consisting of three morae (*trimātra*); then, having recited the second verse together with that in monotone and protracted the final vowel, one should offer with the utterance *svāhā*.

For example: "Oṃ *samita saṃka*syamānau | *iṣamūrjamabhisaṃ*ttānyākaro3magne purī*tvaṃ naḥ | *iṣamūrjaṃ yajamānāya dhehī3 svāhā*" (Oṃ, being kindled together; for food and strength, having brought them together... O Agni, you who are our fortress, bestow food and strength upon the sacrificer, Svāhā!).
But for those who perform the five-fold division (*pañcāvattin*), such as the Jāmadagnyas, Vatsas, Bidas, and likewise the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas: [the procedure is as follows].
"The Bhārgavas, Cyāvanas, and Aurvas are declared to be those who perform the five-fold division (pañcāvattin)."

For the eighteen mantras beginning with "purīṣyas tvam," Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*). The deity of the first is Agni; of the second, Jātavedas; of the third, Pṛthivī and others; of the fourth, Agni Vaiśvānara; of the five beginning with the fifth, Nirṛti; of the tenth, Indra; of the six beginning with the eleventh, Agni in the form of the ploughman and the earth-drawer; of the seventeenth, Kāmadhuk; and of the eighteenth, Sītā. The meter of the first is *anuṣṭubh*; that of the second is a five-footed *paṅkti*.

The third [verse] is in *triṣṭubh* meter; the fourth is in *anuṣṭubh*; the six beginning with the fifth are in *triṣṭubh*; the twelfth and thirteenth are in *gāyatrī*; the fourteenth is in *triṣṭubh*; the fifteenth is a five-footed *paṅkti*; the sixteenth is in *triṣṭubh*; the seventeenth is a *virāḍ-anuṣṭubh*; and the eighteenth is in *triṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal *ājya-homa* for the conjunction of the two domestic fires (*gṛhyāgni*): "Oṃ purīṣyas-tva... sadaḥ svāhā"—to Agni, this [is offered]. "Oṃ bhava taṃ naḥ... madya naḥ svāhā"—to the two Jātavedases, this [is offered].

"Oṃ māteva putraṃ... muñcantu svāhā. To Earth and the others, this [offering]. "Oṃ yadasya pāre... vaiśvānara svāhā. To Agni Vaiśvānara, this [offering]. "Oṃ namaḥ sute ni... rohayema svāhā. To Nirṛti, this [offering].
"Oṃ yatte devī... pramuktaḥ svāhā"—to Nirṛti, this [is offered]. "Oṃ yasyāste asyāḥ krūra... viśvataḥ svāhā"—to Nirṛti, this [is offered].
"Oṃ asunvantama... tubhyamastu svāhā"—to Nirṛti, this [is offered].
"Oṃ devīma0 vicaṣṭe svāhā. This is for Nirṛti; [it is] not mine. Touching water five times. "Oṃ niveśanaḥ saṃgamano0 pathīnāṃ svāhā. This is for Indra.

"Oṃ saṃvaratrā dadhātana... makṣita svāhā. To Agni in the form of the ploughman, this [offering]. "Oṃ niṣkṛtāhāvama vaṭa akṣita svāhā. To Agni in the form of the ploughman, this [offering]. "Oṃ sīrā yuñjanti... sumnayā svāhā. To Agni in the form of the ploughman, this [offering].
"Oṃ yunakta sīrā0 māyātsvāhā"—to Agni in the form of the plougher of the earth, this [offering].
"Oṃ lāṅgalaṃ pavīrava vāhana svāhā"—to Agni in the form of the plougher of the earth, this [offering].
"Oṃ śunaṃ naḥ phālā0 masmāsu dhatta svāhā"—to Agni in the form of the plougher of the earth, this [offering].
"Oṃ, O wish-granting cow, yield [milk] at will for all creatures, svāhā!"—this is for Kāmaduh. "Oṃ, may the furrow be anointed with ghee and honey; turn toward us, svāhā!"—this is for Sītā.

Then, having spread a base of ghee on the ladle (*darvī*), he cuts a portion from the northern half of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), making a portion larger than the joint of a thumb; if he is one who performs five-fold portions, he cuts twice and pours ghee over it twice, but does not pour ghee back over the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). He offers it in the northeast with the mantra: "Oṃ, whatever of this rite was left over, to the fulfiller, svāhā!"—this is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, not for me. Then, having thrown the stirring-spoon into the fire, he makes an offering with the residual drops (*saṃsrāva*). Or, there may be no throwing of the stirring-spoon at all.

And this *avadāna* ritual is intended by the author of the commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*), but not according to the opinion of others. In the absence of the *avadāna* ritual, there is no offering of fine garments (*suvāsas*).

Thereafter, the procedure beginning with the casting of the ritual cord (*śulba*) is the same. Here, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a cow. After giving the fee, one should place a bunch of *darbha* grass in front of the fire. With the two mantras, "The Brahman was born first" (*brahma jajñānaṃ*) and "The father of the Virājs" (*pitā virājām*), the Viśvedevas are the deities and Triṣṭubh is the meter; their application (*viniyoga*) is for the depositing of the remnants of the oblation. One should deposit the remnants of the oblation there with these two: "Oṃ brahma jajñānaṃ prathamaṃ... and "Oṃ pitā virājāṃ... etc., ending with "...vardhayantaḥ."
Then, having worshipped the fire, applied the ashes, and given abundant gifts according to his means, he should feed the Brahmins and meditate upon Viṣṇu for the perfection of the rite.

Regarding this, some say that this rule applies to one who is unable to maintain the *aupāsana* fire separately and perform the *homa* and other rites, whereas for one who is capable, the maintenance and so forth must be performed separately. This is not correct; for in matters concerning transcendental effects (*adṛṣṭa-kārya*), it is improper to adopt an alternative position by mere whim without the authority of scripture. At such a time, there exists no scripture that enjoins *homa* and other rites preceded by the separate maintenance [of the fire]. Furthermore, it is observed as a fault to resort to a position contrary to scripture even in the absence of a specific scriptural injunction.
Thus, it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*: "The procedure proclaimed by Baudhāyana and others for the determination of Dharma..."
Acting otherwise than that by means of arguments regarding causes, one goes to a downward state.
"And one's life-span may be diminished through the fault of reviling one's guru.

Accordingly, having completed the vow, for twelve or thirteen days one should maintain the sacred fire separately and perform oblations therein. However, in the event of the death of either spouse, one should divide the *aupāsana* fire, and perceiving one portion as "this is his very fire," one should perform the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*) with that portion. One should continue the *aupāsana* and other rites using only the portion belonging to the surviving wife. According to the view that one maintains a single portion of the *aupāsana* fire for one's own sake, the *aupāsana* oblations and so forth should likewise be performed there in that same manner.
Thus ends the procedure for the marriage of a second husband and the combination of two fires in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.

Thus concludes the twelfth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā* composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita— who was himself the performer of the Agnicit, Vājapeya, Pauṇḍarīka, and Sarvatomukha sacrifices, and who bore the surname Oko.
Now follows the domestic fire-oblation (*aupāsanahoma*).

Regarding this, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* states: "Every day, in the evening and in the morning, one offers these two oblations with the hand, using either rice or barley, saying: 'To Agni, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! Some authorities prescribe that the first [oblation] in the morning be dedicated to Sūrya."

Every day, always, morning and evening, he offers two oblations with his own hand using either rice or barley, as will be described. Which are they? "To Agni, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! Regarding the morning offering, some teachers say that the first oblation, which has the Sun as its deity, takes the form "To Sūrya, svāhā," and that this replaces the [second] oblation "To Agni, svāhā" in that position.

The inclusion of the word "nitya" (constant) is for the purpose of preventing the subsequent recurrence of the two words "parvan" (festival day). By this, it is established that the *homa* may take place even prior to the *gṛhapraveśanīya* rite, and its status as a daily (*prātyahika*) constant obligation is also secured. Otherwise, because [the rule] were introduced after the *gṛhapraveśanīya*, the performance would necessarily occur only after the *gṛhapraveśanīya* and only on festival days (*parvasu*).

Alternatively, the inclusion of the term *nitya* (constant) is for the purpose of indicating that it lasts as long as one lives (*yāvajjīvika*). Since the *agnihotra* is observed, there might otherwise be the notion that one may cease [the practice] either in the evening and morning sacrifices or upon reaching old age; this [term] is used so that such a thing may not occur. By this, it is also understood that the time for the *agnihotra* is also its time. Its preparation of the materials is like the preparation of materials for the *agnihotra*. The commencement is in the evening, not in the morning. And its time for taking out the fire (*uddharaṇa*) is the time for making the fire manifest (*prāduṣkaraṇa*).
And it has been stated by the Bahvṛcas: "Its times for making the fire manifest and for the oblation are explained by those of the *agnihotra*."

In this view, because of the governing rule "from here onwards," there is no *homa* prior to the rite of entering the house (*gṛhapraveśanīya*). The very same reason that constitutes the non-completion of the marriage—which serves as the ground for the absence of the *sthālīpāka*—also applies to the absence of the morning and evening *homas*. By this it is understood that the marriage concludes with the *gṛhapraveśanīya*, and the *caturthī-homa* is for the purpose of sexual union. The mention of "taking the hand" (*hastagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding the *darvī* (ladle). The expression "these two" is for the sake of restriction regarding the oblations; therefore, since there is no restriction on the substance, one may use any one of the ten substances prescribed for the *agnihotra*.

This has been stated by the Bahvṛcas: "The offering substance (haumya), however, excluding meat, may at will consist of rice, barley, and sesame. Since the status of these as oblations (āhuti) is already established by their very suitability [for the rite], the explicit mention of them as "oblations" is for the purpose of restriction; that is, they should be *only* oblations and not part of any other ritual procedure (*tantra*). In this ritual alternative (*kalpa*), there is also an exclusion of the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*) and the sprinkling of water (*pariṣeka*). Furthermore, it is to indicate that the oblation should never be performed with the fingertips alone, but rather that the oblation is restricted to being made with the upper side of the hand, just like the *juhū* ladle. The time for taking out the fire for the Agnihotra is given in the Śrautasūtra:
"When the sun is behind the trees, [one should perform] the evening Agnihotra; at dawn, the morning Agnihotra."

The term "removes" (*uddharati*) is drawn over from the preceding sūtra. This refers to two names based on their connection with two different times. The meaning is that the removal [of the fire] must take place at a time prior to the time of the principal rite along with its subsidiaries—specifically, when the sun has not yet risen and before it has set. Regarding trees, the time when the sun stands over them, neither below nor above, is called *adhivṛkṣasūrya*; therein, the removal is for the sake of the evening *agnihotra*. Likewise, at dawn, it is for the sake of the morning *agnihotra*. By the word "sun" (*sūrya*), the rays are indicated through figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*).

Even in the case of the option to perform the *homa* after sunrise, the drawing out [of the fire] should be done at dawn; likewise, even in the case of the option to perform the *homa* after sunset in the evening, it should be understood that it occurs when the sun is behind the trees.
Vaikhānasa, however, says: "In the evening, when the sun is behind the trees or half-set; in the morning, at dawn or before sunrise."

Kātyāyana, however, states: "But [the time] when neither has set nor risen. Even that should be accepted in the event of impossibility. And this sūtra is intended to override the general rule (paribhāṣā): "The time of the principal [rite] is the time for its subsidiaries.

Regarding the time for the *homā* as well, the Śrautasūtra says: "One performs the evening *agnihotra* after the first [star] has set, or having seen the stars, or at nightfall; one performs the morning *agnihotra* before sunrise, or after it has risen, or according to some, it should be offered at the moment when speech begins to flow."

The time for extraction was stated in the preceding sūtra; by this [sūtra], another time for the *homa* is shown. From this it is understood that there is no fault even if one performs the *saṃdhyopāsana* during the interval [between the two]. That which is called "the first setting" (*prathamāstamaya*) is the period immediately following the disappearance of the sun; therein, one offers the evening *agnihotra* either when the stars appear, or at *pradoṣa*, which consists of the beginning of the night comprising two *ghaṭikās*. All three [of these] are indeed the evening time.

Likewise, the morning time (*prātaḥkāla*) is threefold: two *ghaṭikās* prior to sunrise, the period immediately preceding sunrise, or after sunrise. Among these, the morning *agnihotra* is performed. Regarding this, the author of the *Vaijayantī* has explained that according to some recensional traditions (*śākhins*), "the morning *agnihotra* should be offered when the speech of birds becomes manifest. (In the *Ācāraratna*, Pṛthvīcandra states: "For those who offer the oblation before sunrise, one should give the *arghya* water, offer the oblation before the sun rises, and then mutter the *gāyatrī*; however, for those who offer the oblation after sunrise, one should first mutter the *gāyatrī* and then offer the oblation.")
Kātyāyana has also stated that the daughter and the daughter-in-law may act as the performers of the *uddharaṇa* (the lifting up):
"The removal [of the fire] by either the daughter or the daughter-in-law is not prohibited.
This should be understood to apply when the performer of the *homa* is unable to perform the *uddharaṇa*. *Vihāra*, *viharaṇa*, and *uddharaṇa* are synonymous.

Manu states regarding the oblation (homa) at times such as sunrise and so forth: "The oblation is performed in every way—at sunrise, before sunrise, and likewise during the twilight; such is the Vedic revelation."
The nature of these [times] has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"When the sun is seen as a mere line by its rays, one should know that it has risen; there, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa)."
When the night has reached its sixteenth part and is adorned with planets and constellations,
having recognized that it is the time before sunrise, one should perform the fire-oblation there.
Likewise, at the time of dawn, when the circle of stars has vanished but the sun is not yet visible, that is the period known as *samayādhyuṣita*.

The upper limit for one who offers oblations after sunrise is stated by Kātyāyana in the *Candrikā*: "As long as the sun, having risen from the Hasta [asterism], has not yet passed over the mountain, so long is the rite of offering in the morning meritorious; for those who offer at sunrise, there is no other [time]."

Its nature at sunset has also been stated by that same [author]: "As long as the stars are not clearly perceived all around in the sky, and as long as the redness does not depart, so long is the evening oblation offered."

Vaikhānasa and Āśvalāyana state the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*): "The time for the evening *homa* ends at *pradoṣa*; that for the morning [ends] at *saṃgava*. *Pradoṣa* is the fourth part of the night; it is that which has [the fourth part] as its end. According to some, the fifth and sixth *nāḍikās* (twenty-four-minute periods) are designated by the word *pradoṣa*, and the time for the *homa* ends with that. *Saṃgava* is the second part of the day divided into five parts. Devatrāta’s statement that it is the second watch (*yāma*) of the day is intended in terms of parts. And this *sūtra* is aimed at prescribing the secondary time.

This expiation does not apply to the secondary times of *pradoṣa* and *saṃgava* for the *homa*, even in cases other than an emergency; however, the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) certainly applies.
This is also stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "The time for the evening *homa* ends at *pradoṣa*; [the morning *homa* ends] at *saṃgava*."
"Morning is not intended here as [the time for] the tantra. Regarding the specific nature of *pradoṣa* (evening) and *saṅgava* (forenoon), Āśvalāyana says:
"The period of three muhūrtas that occurs after sunset..."

"That which is the time for the evening *homa* is declared to end at *pradoṣa*. But that period of six *nāḍikās* which follows after the sun has risen is known as the *saṃgava-anta*, the time for the *homa* of Brahmins."

The same author states the expiation for the transgression of this secondary time: "Having passed that [time], one should offer four portions of clarified butter with the mantra: 'If in the evening, obeisance to the Evening; svāhā! If in the morning, obeisance to the Morning; svāhā!'"

As for that which is stated in the *Māvilagr̥hya*: "Now, if one should not find an oblation or an offerer for the morning and evening homas in the domestic fire, what should he do? The morning offering does not pass beyond the time of the evening offering, nor does the evening offering pass beyond the time of the morning offering. And as for the statement of Baudhāyana:

"The morning offering for the evening rite should not be missed until the morning, nor the evening offering for the morning rite until the evening; the *pārvaṇa* [offering] should not be missed until the next *pārvaṇa*.
And as for the *Nidāna-sūtra*:
"The entire day is the time for the morning offering, the entire night is the time for the evening offering, and the full fortnight is the time for the *darśa* [new moon] offering."
"The dark fortnight [of the month] of Pūrṇamāsa.
This refers to occasions of great calamity, such as the loss of one's kingdom.
Regarding the first *aupāsana* oblation, Śaunaka states the following distinction:

"If the marriage fire should be produced at night, then, having commenced [the rites], one should attend upon that fire in the evening of the following day. However, in the *Sudarśanabhāṣya*, it is stated: "If the production of the fire occurs during the night within the first nine nāḍīs, then the commencement of the *homa* takes place at that very time; if it occurs after that, the commencement takes place in the evening of the next day."
Now, regarding the materials for the *homa*:

therein, rice (*vrīhi*) or barley (*yava*) are the primary substances. This is because it is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "Every day, in the evening and morning, one offers two oblations with rice or barley using the hand. Furthermore, in the *Candrikā*, another *Smṛti* states:
The sacrificial oblation (havis) is said to be of three kinds: prepared (kṛta), both prepared and unprepared (kṛtākṛta), and unprepared (akṛta).
Their characteristics are correctly stated in due order:
rice, flour, and the like are "prepared"; rice grains and the like are "both prepared and unprepared."
"And *vrīhi* and the like are declared to be *akṛta*; thus the sacrificial oblation (*havya*) is said by the wise to be of three kinds.
*Akṛta* [grain] should be offered after being washed. Accordingly, the *Chāndogya-gṛhya* states: "If it is *akṛta*, one should wash it and then offer it. In another *Smṛti*:
"Rice, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, *vrīhi*, wheat, and barley..."
"The grains to be offered in the oblation for these are wild rice (*taṇḍula*), bamboo millet (*yāvanāla*), and *priyaṅgu*.
In another Smṛti:
"Wild rice (*nīvāra*), *śāli* rice, wheat, *vrīhi* rice, and barley (*yava*)."

"They should be offered as oblations in their own form; those sesame seeds [should be offered] in their own form. In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "Milk, curd, clarified butter, gruel, boiled rice, rice grains, soma, oil, water, *vrīhi* rice, barley, and sesame seeds are the substances to be offered in oblation" (*taṇḍula* refers to *nīvāra*, *śyāmāka*, and *yāvanāla*; *vrīhi*, barley, wheat, and *priyaṅgu* are to be offered in their own form; sesame seeds are to be offered in their own form; and oil is that derived from sesame, wild sesame, *atasī*, and safflower). Hemādri identifies *yāvanāla* as "joṃdhalā. In the *Smṛtibhāskara*:
In the absence of barley, however, one should use wheat, or then bamboo-seeds (*veṇuyava*) and so forth;
and according to the statement of the Chandogas, one should offer oblations even when the sacrificial materials are exhausted.

"It is either the fruit of the sacrifice-tree, or its leaf, or even its water. With the exception of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), all other substances are secondary alternatives (*anukalpa*). Among these, whichever substance was first employed between rice and barley at the initial performance must be used in all subsequent performances. This is because it has been stated by the learned in the section on substitutes (*pratinidhi-prakaraṇa*) that, "in the absence of that [primary substance], only a substitute is to be taken, and not another prescribed substance. The authoritative proof for this is the sūtra: "In the case of what has been selected, however, the rule is fixed by the commencement [of the action]."
The statement cited by the learned authorities is also as follows:
"Form, time, the subsequent offering, the deity, and likewise the cooking—
those positions which were established at the outset shall indeed always remain so."

"Form" (*rūpa*) means a substance possessing form; in some places, the reading is simply "substance" (*dravya*). Some maintain that examples of form include such [Vedic] prescriptions as "at the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, there is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth, or else clarified butter," or "the milk is for Vāyu, or the gruel," and so forth. Others hold that "form" refers to the essential nature of the Dākṣāyaṇa Darśapūrṇamāsa and similar rites. Still others say that "form" is the form of the action itself, citing such rules as "at the Agniṣṭoma, he touches [the victim] with water once or thrice," and so on. According to the first view, the examples are those from the Smṛtis, such as "with rice or with barley," and so forth.

According to the second view—[the time is determined by] being *āpūrvika* (performed on the same day as the primary sacrifice) or having the *āghāra* libation, and so forth. According to the third view, however, there are many such examples. Examples from the Śruti regarding time include: "in the animal sacrifice," "in the year," "in the rainy season," "at the beginning of the return [of the sun]," and so on. Examples from Smṛti include: "both times," "every evening," and so on. Examples of both types include: "the Full Moon sacrifice is to be performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*)," "it is to be performed over two days (*dvyahakālā*)," or "one offers the oblation either after sunrise or before sunrise. An example of the *anunirvāpa* (subsequent offering), however, is exclusively from the Śruti.

If the position that the Vaimṛdha sacrifice is to be performed as an *anunirvāpya* (subsequent offering) immediately after the *Paurṇamāsa* is accepted, then it must indeed be performed. Regarding the deities of the *Upāṃśuyāja*, the examples from the Śruti are Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, or Agni-Soma; for the *Sāṃnāyya*, Indra or Mahendra; and for the *Nirūḍhapaśu*, Indra-Agni, Sūrya, Prajāpati, and so forth. Examples from the Smṛti include "To Agni, Svāhā! and "To Sūrya, Svāhā! and so forth. As for the *Āgrayaṇa*, both Indra-Agni and Agni-Indra serve as examples.

The illustration regarding cooking (*śrapaṇa*), however, is strictly from the Śruti: "The cooking of the oblation (*havis*) is to be done either in the Āhavanīya or in the Gārhapatya fire. The meaning is that in cases of such alternatives (*vikalpa*), whichever position was initially accepted must be maintained until the very end.

On this point, some say: "This is merely an illustration; therefore, the rule is established for all instances of alternative options, such as 'or he adds fuel with the Vyāhṛtis,' and so forth. In this view, the Smārta illustrations to be understood are the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings, as well as the secondary offerings (*upahoma*).

Others, however, considering it improper for the [text] to have the character of a mere indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), maintain that this restriction applies only to those [acts] already enumerated and not elsewhere. The morning oblation (*prātarhoma*) is performed with the very same substance as the evening oblation (*sāyaṃhoma*), because they share a single result.

Maṇḍana also says: "Whatever substance is used in the evening oblation, that alone is desired for the morning. Likewise, there is a restriction regarding the performer; in cases where it is absolutely impossible otherwise, [the act] cannot be performed without the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
And so it is stated in the Gadādharabhāṣya:
"A twice-born man should offer oblations either into the Vedic fire or the Smārta fire, morning and evening;
if there is only one [fire], many may offer together, but [if they do so] in a worldly fire, it would be [an invalid act]."

In the *Madanaratna*: "The best of the twice-born should offer oblations into a single fire both evening and morning; if one offers in the evening and another in the morning, he becomes a mere worldly fire."
In the *Smṛtisāra*:
"One should offer oblations into the fire alone both in the evening and in the morning;
if another person were to offer the morning oblation, that fire would certainly become useless."
"One should offer four oblations both in the evening and in the morning;
this applies specifically to the Agnihotra and the Smārta fire," as stated in the Gadādharabhāṣya on the Smṛtisaṃgraha.
"No one other than the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) shall offer the morning oblation.
Upon the transgression of this rule, an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) must be offered with all the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*:
"Also in the case of the destruction of the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*), and in the event of an exchange of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or the ritual materials (*dravya*)."
Upon the destruction of the purifier (pavitra), upon the Veda, and upon any breakage of the sacrificial vessel;
"And an oblation of clarified butter should be offered with the Vyāhṛtis and with the Praṇava."

Regarding the rule "and there is a reversal of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)," if one accepts the two readings as *vyāhṛtyā praṇavena ca*, then in the event of a reversal of the substance (*dravya*), there is merely an oblation of all the *vyāhṛtis*. Even if one accepts the reading *vyāhṛtyā praṇavena vā*, an oblation of all the *vyāhṛtis* alone is fixed here. "And this restriction regarding the substance and the agent applies only to the view that involves a collective intention (*samudāya-saṃkalpa*)," according to the *Prayogārṇava*. Some maintain that this restriction does not apply when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the performer of the morning oblation (*prātar-homa*).
The purification of the oblation substance is stated in the *Baudhāyana-gṛhya*:
"Having illuminated the sacrificial substance, having thrown [a portion] onto the tip of a *darbha* blade, and having carried fire around it, one should place it on a grass mat behind the fire."

The placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) must necessarily be performed prior to the oblation (*homa*). This is because a fault is heard [in scripture] in the Śruti: "One should not offer into a fire that lacks fuel-sticks; if one were to offer into a fire that lacks fuel-sticks, that becomes as if unoffered," and in the Baudhāyana Gṛhya-sūtra: "One should not offer into a fire that lacks fuel-sticks; if one were to offer into a fire that lacks fuel-sticks, it would be just as if one were to give food to one who has no tongue. Therefore, one should offer only when there are fuel-sticks. Furthermore, the placing of fuel-sticks after [the oblation] is mentioned as optional in the Chandoga-pariśiṣṭa: "Some [authorities] say there is fueling even afterwards. The status of being optional follows from the expression "some [authorities]" (*eka*).
The measure for the *avadāna* (cutting-off portion) is stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: "A prastha of grain is declared to be the amount for sixty-four oblations;
half of that for sesame seeds, while rice grains and paddy are equal [in measure]."
The meaning is that it is the sixty-fourth part of a measure of grain amounting to one *prastha*.
Regarding the definition of a *prastha*, it is stated in the *Saṃgraha*: "A *pala*, a *kuḍava*, a *prastha*, an *āḍhaka*, and a *droṇa*..."
"In the measures of grain, these should be understood as increasing fourfold in successive order."
The definition of a *pala* is also given in that same work: "Two *palas* are a *prasṛta*, while one *pala* is known as a *muṣṭi*.
Baudhāyana, however, states:
"One hundred [grains] of rice or barley is prescribed as one oblation," he says;
the meaning is that one oblation consists of a hundred grains of grain.
However, the subsequent oblation should be made with slightly more, because this [rite] follows the pattern of the Śrauta rituals. Agastya states:
"The measure of a liquid substance shall be a stream as long as a cow's ear.
And in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: "An oblation of grain shall fill twelve finger-joints; if it is with ghee or other liquids, it shall fill the mouth of the *sruva* ladle."
"And the oblation is offered into that fire by means of the divine sacred channel, into the fire which possesses bright embers and a clear flame."
Regarding the impossibility of obtaining the substances required to complete the twelve parvan offerings, Śaṅkha states in the *Ṭoḍarānanda*:
"In the lunar vow (*induvrata*), [the materials] are prescribed to be the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit;
likewise for the oblations in the fire, and for the clay used for purification."
In the *Saṃgraha*, there is a specific rule regarding the home: "One should not offer oblations with the tips of the fingers without having separated them;
rather, according to the Smṛti, one should offer oblations with the upper side of the fingers."
Baudhāyana also states:
"One should perform the pouring out [of the oblation], the pouring of remnants, the offering of parched grains, and the daily offerings with the *kāya* tīrtha.
The daily offering (*nityahoma*) refers to the *aupāsana* and other such rites.
There is a specific rule in the Gobhila [Gṛhyasūtra]:
"One should not offer while having disheveled hair, nor with the knees not pressed down;
for if one offers with the knees not pressed down, the sacrificial oblation (havis) is carried off by Rākṣasas."
And this applies to the subject of all *homa* offerings.
Yājñavalkya states in the *Ācāraratna*:
"Having offered oblations to the deities Agni and Sūrya, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras."
In the *Smṛtipradīpa*, however, worship (*upasthāna*) is stated as follows: "One should worship Agni and Sūrya with their respective mantras, being composed in mind."

Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*). At the evening oblation (*sāyaṃ-homa*), either the silent recitation (*japa*) of a mantra dedicated to Agni or the ritual worship (*upasthāna*) with mantras dedicated to Agni must be performed. At the morning oblation (*prātar-homa*), however, either the silent recitation of a mantra dedicated to Sūrya or the ritual worship with mantras dedicated to Sūrya must be performed. In this oblation, the performer (*kartṛ*) is himself alone; for no other [performer] has been prescribed by the Teacher (*ācārya*), and Āśvalāyana has explicitly stated that he alone is the primary performer. In cases of incapacity, absence, or being preoccupied with other duties, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others may act. Thus says Dakṣa:
"The officiating priest, the son, the preceptor, the servant, the sister's son, and the husband of a female friend—
whatever is offered by these very persons is indeed as if offered by oneself."

There is also a reading, "the wife in the place of the son," which is favorable to the Āśvalāyanas, based on their sūtra: "Either [the sacrificer] himself, or the wife, or the son, or a maiden, or a resident pupil. However, this is not favorable to those who follow the Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra, because of the prohibition in the Dharmasūtra: "A woman shall not offer oblations, nor one who has not been initiated. For this very reason, there is also no oblation performed by a maiden. Commentators explain that this prohibition is intended as a restrictive rule for the twice-born (dvija). *Viṭpati* means a son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*). In the *Mādhavīya*, the relative merit of various officiating priests is stated:
"One oblation offered by a disciple is better than a hundred oblations offered by others."
"For it is better that one be killed by oneself than by a hundred sons through the performance of oblations."
Kātyāyana states:
"The *hotṛ* priest should not be excessively old, nor lacking in learning, nor foolish; he should not be afflicted by illness, nor uninitiated, in the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra*."
"For these fall into hell, as does he for whom they sacrifice; therefore, the officiating priest (hotṛ) should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas."
The term *vaitāna* (pertaining to the three sacred fires) is an elliptical expression for *smārta-karman* (acts prescribed by the Smṛtis).
As Gopāla states: "Whether the oblation is offered by those of little learning or by the unlearned, or even by the wife."
And one should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice in the common fire, except in times of distress.
"Having spread them out with strainers, one should perform the full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) in the rite of the hearth."

The commentator explains that here there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both the *pūrṇāhuti* and the *iṣṭi*. The *iṣṭi* here is the *Tantumatī*, according to the statement of Baudhāyana. However, in the Smārta tradition, a *caru* takes the place of the *iṣṭi*. This [latter rule] applies to cases other than times of distress (*anāpad*). But in times of distress, when a Brāhmaṇa alone is chosen for the office of officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), one should offer oblations from the *ājyasthālī* with the *sruva* ladle during the unprescribed expiations (*anādiṣṭaprāyaścitta*) with the formulas: "To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Hiraṇyagarbha, svāhā! To the Lord of the Bhṛgus, svāhā! To the Lord of the Aṅgirases, svāhā! as well as the *sarvaprāyaścitta*.

There is also a reading: "To the Lord of the Bhṛgus, svāhā! To the austerity of the Aṅgirases, svāhā! Even when one is occupied with other duties, on the *parvan* day, however, one must perform it oneself; for there is a rule regarding the *parvan* that "on the *parvan* day, the sacrificer himself offers the Agnihotra. Although this is a Śrauta rite, nevertheless, due to the force of the Smārta injunctions found within the Śrauta texts, it is understood to apply to the Smārta rite as well. Nor should it be argued that, by this logic, the shaving of the head (*vapanam*) would also apply to the *parvan* day.

In the statement, "The sacrificer shall have his hair shaved on the two *parvan* days," the inclusion of the term "sacrificer" (*yajvan*) indicates that shaving on the *parvan* day applies only to one who maintains the *āhitāgni* fires, and not to one who possesses only the *smārta* (domestic) fires; such is the meaning conveyed. If, however, there is incapacity or absence [of the fire], then another person should indeed perform the oblation, for there can be no total omission because the rite is obligatory. Bṛhaspati states the expiation for one who, despite being capable and present, does not himself offer the oblation on the *parvan*: "If an *āhitāgni* fails to perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) on the *parvan*..."
Or if he does not approach his wife during her season, he too shall perform half of a *kṛcchra* penance."

Here, the mention of *upasthāna* (attendance) is an elliptical indication for the *homa* (fire-oblation). This *homa* must be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others only when both husband and wife are present; it may be done in their absence only if one of them is present. If neither is present, even what has been offered is as if unoffered.
As it is stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:
"The *homa* should not be performed by the officiating priests and others in the absence of both husband and wife."
"If it should occur out of sight of both parties, the offering is rendered useless."
In another Smṛti: "In his presence, the sacrificer shall be the one who performs the dedication and the renunciation;
in his absence, however, the wife shall be the one who performs the dedication and the renunciation."
"But in his absence, the son shall be the one who performs the formal dedication and renunciation.
When the sacrificer is insane, or when the wife is in her fertile period, or has given birth, there is no authorization for the wife.
However, in the absence of the wife, the Adhvaryu priest may act with her authorization.
"In cases of insanity, childbirth, or during the menstrual period, one should perform [the rite] without permission."

Thus it is stated in the *Madanapārijāta*. From this very statement, it is understood that officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others require permission for the purpose of performing the *homa* oblation. Furthermore, there is a clear statement in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The officiating priest, the son, or the wife, or even the pupil or a uterine brother..."
"Having obtained permission, one should especially perform the oblation according to the prescribed rule."
The expression "especially" (*viśeṣeṇa*) is used for the purpose of seeking specific permission, such as: "I have some necessary business; I am in some difficulty; you must perform the *homa* for me.
Furthermore, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:
"One who is observing a fast should not be away on a journey; his wife shall maintain the vow."
"In every way, the sacrificer, being pure, should indeed renounce [the offering] while facing that direction."
"Facing that direction" means facing the direction in which the fires are located.
Āśvalāyana states the definition of an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*):
"He chooses the priests as those who are neither deficient nor redundant in their limbs, both on the mother's and the father's side."
As was stated previously: "Some say one should choose young men as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Lāṭyāyana and Drāhmāyaṇa also state:

"An officiating priest should be a descendant of seers (*ārṣeya*), learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*), of virtuous conduct (*sādhucaraṇa*), eloquent (*vāgmin*), neither deficient in limbs nor having superfluous limbs."
"He is *dvayasata*, neither too dark nor too fair.
Regarding the term *dvayasata*, Agnisvāmin and Dhanvin have explained it as: "He for whom the two [parents] are equal in both [lineage and qualities] is *dvayasata*.
Vādhūla also states: "One chooses a lineage (*ārṣeya*) who knows his own ancestors."
By this, the exclusion of those whose kinship is unknown is established.

Baudhāyana also states: "Now, the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is prescribed: the *ṛtvij*s shall be Brāhmaṇas endowed with [proper] birth, lineage, Vedic learning, and conduct; they should have the qualities of fire as their limbs, be free from triple sores, not have crossed a moat, not be outcasts, not born of an outcast mother, not unlearned in the Vedas, and not [the sons of] a plowman, a wool-carder, a daughter’s son, a son by another’s field, a son by a pregnant bride, a son by a remarried woman, or one who has a younger brother born after him, nor those who have two ancestral lineages (*dvipravara*)."

Likewise: "Some say that those who possess [proper] origin, conduct, and learning are authoritative; if one chooses them, let him choose only those whose limbs are unimpaired. *Yoni* means a pure origin. *Gotra* means a noble lineage. *Śruta* means study. *Vṛtta* means conduct. Those endowed with these are "possessed of them. *Aviguṇāṅgāḥ* means those whose limbs are unimpaired (*avyāpannāṅgāḥ*). Regarding *atrikiṇinaḥ*: those who have three scars (*kiṇa*) are *trikiṇinaḥ*. *Kiṇas* are marks on the body resulting from blows and the like. Here, by the word *trikiṇa*, what is intended are the scars produced by wrestling, donning armor, striking with the hands, the snapping of bowstrings, carrying heavy loads, and so forth.

The meaning is that they should not possess even one of these three types of scars. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood that they must not bear marks produced by the repeated practice of forbidden acts. "Not having crossed the *parigha*" means they should not be seafarers who have transgressed the *parigha*, which is the boundary or the tide-line of the ocean. "Not those who go to the ends" (*nāntagāḥ*): "the end" (*anta*) refers to a border region, a frontier region, or, in other words, a land of barbarians (*mleccha*).

Those who go to the "end" (anta) would not [be eligible]; that is, those who go to the low castes (*antavarṇa*), meaning those who go to a Śūdra woman, they would not [be eligible], according to others. "The end" (*anta*) is an elliptical expression; it should be understood that those who go to a woman who is forbidden to be approached (*agamyā*) would also not [be eligible]. They are not "born of the end" (*antaja*); those born of the aforementioned regions would not [be eligible]. According to others, those born of a Śūdra woman would not [be eligible]. They are not "those who have not studied" (*ananūcāna*); those who have not studied—that is, those who are not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*)—are not to be chosen.

Those who live by performing agriculture with a plough are *hāleyas*. Those who live by selling wool, hair-felt, combs, and so forth, are *vāleyas*. At the time of giving a daughter in marriage, [the father says]:
"The son who is born of her shall be my son."

The meaning is that one should not choose these—the *hāleya* and others—as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). A *putrikā-putra* (son of an appointed daughter) is one born from a daughter who was given away with the specific intention [that her son would be the heir]. A *parakṣetra* (born on another's field) is one produced by a paramour in the wife of another. A *sahoḍha* (born together) is one who was already in the womb at the time of marriage and was given away along with his mother. A *kānīna* (maiden-born) is one born while the girl was still unmarried. An *anujāvara* is an elder brother who is subordinate to a younger brother. A *dvipravara* is one born into one lineage but given away into another lineage. One should not appoint such persons as officiating priests.

The meaning is that some teachers say that lineage (*yoni*), conduct (*vṛtta*), and learning (*vidyā*)—specifically Vedic learning—are the criteria that motivate the selection [of a priest]. The author of the *Bhāṣya* explains this to mean that if one should select those who are endowed with such lineage, conduct, and learning, then one selects only those whose limbs are unimpaired.
This is also stated in the *Dharma-sūtra*: "One does not select a priest who has not studied the Vedas, nor one who is bargaining."

One who has studied and can expound the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*) is called *anūcāna*. One who is not such is *ananūcāna*. [The text] does not prescribe that one should choose such a non-*anūcāna* as a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*), nor does it define him by saying "this much should be given. This was explained by Ujjvalākṛt. The statement in the *Dharmasūtra* is intended to demonstrate that, as an alternative, the performance of the *aupāsana-homa*, *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, *vaiśvadeva*, and other rites may also be carried out by a priest.
Āpastamba also says:
"He chooses Brahmins as priests who are not [of the same lineage as his own] *ārṣeya*, who are either young or old, who are *anūcāna*, whose speech is clear, and who are not deficient in limb."

Since this is already established by the rule "the officiating of priests belongs to Brāhmaṇas," the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" again is for the sake of emphasis. Alternatively, the possibility that even a Kṣatriya who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice might be eligible is raised and refuted here, based on the Vedic text: "Therefore, the officiating of priests belongs to one who has performed the Vājapeya. The inclusion of the terms "young" and "old" is because, generally, there may be a lack of proficiency in ritual acts among those who are too young or too old. Rudradatta states that "those with upraised voices" means those whose vocal organs and articulations are clear.
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is intended to exclude Kṣatriyas and others even in times of distress (*āpad*).
"The office of officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) belongs to the best of the twice-born, but not to Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas;
for the rule regarding Brāhmaṇas as officiating priests is recorded even for the sake of the sacrifice itself," so say the Miśras.
Also in the Rāmāyaṇa:
"He whose officiating priest (yājaka) is a Kṣatriya, and especially one who is a Caṇḍāla—how could the celestial sages partake of his sacrificial oblation (havis) in the assembly?

By this, the moderns maintain that those who subsist on the livelihoods of Kṣatriyas and others are also excluded. Furthermore, one should not choose a husband who is pregnant or menstruating. Thus, it is stated in the Smṛti in the *Prāyaścittadarpaṇa*:
"When a woman is menstruating or pregnant, she is not fit for the selection [of priests] in a sacrifice; thus spoke the sage Gālava.
By the word "sacrifice" (yajña), rites such as the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) and others are included. This, moreover, is an illustration for all Smārta (tradition-based) rituals.
In the Rudraskandha-bhāṣya:
"When his wife is menstruating,
her husband should always avoid officiating as a priest, eating at a śrāddha feast, traveling on a journey, and bathing in the ocean."
Garga says: Shaving, officiating as a priest, traveling, anointing the body,
worshipping deities in another's house, and bathing in the ocean— these [should be avoided].

And the consumption of a *śrāddha* meal should be avoided if the wife is in her menses. Śāṭyāyani says: "A husband whose wife is in her menses [should avoid] a journey, officiating at a sacrifice, and eating at a *śrāddha*."
"One should avoid bathing in rivers, as well as oil massage and shaving.

In that regard, there are three kinds of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*): those who are like gods, those who are like ancestors, and those who are like men. Among them, those who are appointed for each specific rite by the patron himself are 'god-like. Those who proceed with the rites having been appointed by ancestors are 'ancestor-like. And those who are appointed once and for all by the patron himself for the sake of all the rites are 'man-like.'"

In this context, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are indeed human beings. However, it should be understood that the ritual impurity (*āśauca*) applies only to those priests who have become *pitṛs* (ancestors) or *devas* (gods), and not to those who remain human. Furthermore, the presence of the wife is required at the *homa*; for according to Pāṇini’s rule, "The [suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied to *pati* when joined with *yajña*" (*patyur no yajñasaṃyoge*), the word *patnī* is derived specifically in connection with sacrifice. This is also supported by the scriptural injunction: "The *hotṛ* and other priests must perform the *homa* even in the absence of the couple."

In her absence, the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) must be offered. If she is in her courses (*anālambhukā*), there is no fault. When the sacrificer is away on a journey and she is in her courses, the commentators explain in the section on the expiation for the *agnihotra* offering that she should not remain within the house separated by another room, but rather outside, near the house of the *aupāsana* fire.
Regarding the sequence of the *śrauta* and *smārta* offerings, Bharadvāja states two views:
"Having performed the *vaitānika* (śrauta) offering, the wise man should perform the *smārta* one."
"Because the Smṛtis have their root in the Veda, some have known that which is based on the Smṛti as ancient.
Regarding the praise of the *aupāsana* (domestic fire) in the Bharadvāja-sūtra:

"Just as lords, by the power of their sovereignty, leave their own bodies, enter the bodies of others, and then return again to their own bodies, yet this is not difficult for them to perceive; and just as the fires established in the *aupāsana* (domestic fire) reside within the sacrificer, therefore one must not neglect the *aupāsana*. Just as a bull produces a calf from its mate, even so the *agnihotra* that has failed is produced anew in the *aupāsana*; for the *agnihotra* is indeed the continuity of the *aupāsana*, and it is not otherwise."
One should not make a distinction between the *aupāsana* and the *agnihotra*; one should offer both the *aupāsana* and the *agnihotra*. Furthermore, it is known from scripture:
"There are seven forms of *pākayajña* sacrifices in the *aupāsana*, and fourteen in the *agnihotra*.
Aṅgiras praises the *aupāsana-homa*:
"If one were to give away Mount Meru of gold and the entire earth with its oceans,
that would perhaps be equal to the morning and evening fire-oblations, or perhaps it would not.
Regarding the sin incurred by failing to perform them, Garga says:
One who has taken a wife must not remain even for a moment without the sacred fire;
if a twice-born man remains so, he becomes a *vrātya* and likewise fallen.
Just as [the rules for] bathing, the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), and the study of the Veda [are mandatory], [so too is the maintenance of the fire].

In that very same way, the *aupāsana* fire must be maintained; there is no standing [as a householder] apart from it. For he who considers himself a householder while having abandoned the marriage fire—his food must not be eaten, for he is declared to be one who cooks in vain (*vṛthāpāka*).

Where the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the guests do not eat, that is to be known as "vain cooking" (vṛthāpāka); one should never eat from such a meal. One who eats from a vain cooking must perform an expiation (prāyaścitta).

"Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and consumed clarified butter (ghṛta), one becomes purified. He himself states an exception: "One who lives on the food of his father, and one who lives on the food of his brother..."
"Or one who is devoted to knowledge and study does not incur fault even without the sacred fire.
Baudhāyana has stated a means for a widower (*vidhura*) to avoid the fault of being without an *āśrama* when he is unable to marry:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhi*) for one whose wife has died and who is unable to perform a marriage. Having encircled the common fire (*laukikāgni*) with the *praṇava*, having brought it forward with the verse, "Agni has looked upon the forefront of the dawns," and having established it with the verse, "He who is asked about heaven," he should place four fuel-sticks (*samidh*) upon it with the four verses beginning, "That of Savitṛ," "Those [powers] of Savitṛ," "Today, O God Savitṛ," and "All things, O God Savitṛ. Having adorned the fire, he should offer oblations into the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). He should perform this daily at the proper time, from the beginning of the *praṇava* until the end of the oblation, until his marriage or until his renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

"Bhagavān Baudhāyana states that there is no fault of not having a place of residence (anāśrama) after death. However, Śākala has prescribed the performance of both the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* and the *āgrayaṇa* rites as well, saying:
"One should perform two *sthālīpākas*, and likewise the *āgrayaṇa*;
so say the teachers, in that very same sacrificial fire."

Also in the Bhāradvājīya Pitṛmedhasūtra: "If one is unable to perform the rite of marriage, one may establish the sacred fires for one's own sake; however, the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Āgrayaṇa sacrifices are required, while the remaining rites do not take place."

Some maintain that even for one who maintains only half of the sacred fires, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *sthālīpāka*, and the *aupāsana* oblations are not to be performed; others hold that they are to be performed.
Now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*).

The evening fire-oblation (*sāyaṃ-homa*) takes place either at the primary time—any one of the following: the period after taking the bride's hand, immediately before entering the house, or as long as life lasts, at the time when the stars have set (*pradoṣa*)—or at the secondary time, consisting of the first division of the night divided into four parts. The morning fire-oblation (*prātar-homa*), however, takes place either at the primary time—any one of the following: the time before dawn, at sunrise, or at the time when birds begin to call—or at the secondary time, consisting of the first two divisions of the day divided into five parts.

Some maintain that the first commencement must take place at the primary time (*mukhyakāla*) alone; others hold that it may also be performed during the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*). In reality, however, only that secondary time which is specifically prescribed should be accepted. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to perform the first *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* on the third and subsequent days. For here, there is no specific prescription for a secondary time; rather, there is a general rule stating that the secondary time is that which follows its own [primary] time. In the case of the *aupāsana-homa* and similar rites, however, there is a specific prescription for the secondary time: "The time for the evening *homa* ends at nightfall, and that for the morning [ends] at the *saṃgava* [period]."

Therefore, the first *aupāsana* oblation takes place even during the secondary period (*gauṇakāla*) consisting of evening (*pradoṣa*) and the time of the sun's rising (*saṃgava*). Sudarśana, intending this very point, has stated: "If nine *nāḍīs* have not yet elapsed, then the commencement of the first *aupāsana* occurs. The commencement is indeed in the evening. In both the evening and morning rites, there is the same substance and the same performer. On the day of the full moon (*parvan*), one should offer the oblation oneself.

The performer, accompanied by his wife, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma), shall announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord, as long as I have the capacity and for as long as I live, I shall perform the evening and morning *aupāsana* oblations.

However, if one is certain that—following the commencement of the *agnihotra*—the *aupāsana* oblation is not to be performed even by one who maintains only half of the sacred fires (*ardhādhānin*), then the specific modification in the resolve is: "Until the time prior to the commencement of the *agnihotra*, I shall perform the evening and morning *aupāsana* oblations. In reality, however, the position of performing them is indeed the more appropriate one.
