Then, having worshipped Gaṇeśa and caused the declaration of the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) and so forth to be recited, one should say: "May Agni, Sūrya, and Prajāpati be pleased. Even in the morning, if the position is taken that Agni is the deity, the modification (*ūha*) should be: "May Agni and Prajāpati be pleased. This [sequence] is to be performed only at the first performance, not at every subsequent performance.

Then, having again performed the sipping of water (*ācamana*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and the formal recitation of the place and time (*deśakālasaṃkīrtana*), one should make the following resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*), I shall perform the evening and morning domestic fire-offerings (*aupāsanahoma*). Now, I shall perform the evening domestic fire-offering with rice (*vrīhi*). If using barley (*yava*), one should say "with barley. Alternatively, there may be two separate resolves: "I shall perform the evening domestic fire-offering with rice or barley, and I shall perform the morning domestic fire-offering with rice or barley."
In this view, there is no rule requiring identity of substance or identity of agent. Furthermore, in either case, the mention of the substance need not be included in the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).

Then, having meditated on the fire as "having four horns" (*tataścatvāri śṛṅga*), and having strewn grass around it, he places the sacrificial materials to the north of the fire. Upon them, he places either one fuel-stick (*samidh*) with its tip pointing east and measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length, or two such fuel-sticks with their tips pointing east. Then, with his right hand, he causes the fire of the domestic hearth (*aupāsana-agni*) to blaze upward by means of *darbha* blades whose flames are directed downward; having taken those blazing *darbhas* in his left hand, he places the tips of the *darbhas* into the fire with his right hand at a distance of one joint of the thumb.

Having cast away the blazing *darbha* grass with his right hand, touched water, and taken other *darbha* blades, he performs the *paryagni-karaṇa* (circumambulation with fire) around the *aupāsana* fire with those blazing blades; having cast those *darbhas* away as well and touched water, he places the sacrificial materials upon a *kūrca* (grass mat) behind the fire. Alternatively, there may be no casting away of the tips of the *darbhas*, because that is prescribed in another *sūtra*. In this view, there is no grasping [of the fire] with the left hand after the upward flaming; however, the *paryagni-karaṇa* certainly takes place, as it is a derivative of the *śrauta* ritual.

In this manner, the depositing in the *kūrca* is performed. Then, one should perform the preliminary sprinkling (*pūrvapariṣeka*). Thereafter, during the wedding oblation (*vivāhahoma*), having wiped the right hand according to the prescribed method and having worshipped the fire with the mantra "yastvā hṛdā," one silently places a fuel-stick (*samit*) with its tip pointing eastward upon the oblation materials. Having taken the oblation material—measured by twelve finger-joints—with the palm of the right hand whose fingers are touching it, one offers it into the blazing fuel-stick, omitting a space of two finger-breadths from the base, on the northern side, while reciting "agnaye svāhā. [The dedication is: "To Agni, not mine."

Then, taking all the remaining sacrificial materials left over from the first oblation and meditating on Prajāpati in his mind, he mentally utters the mantra "To Prajāpati, svāhā! and, leaving a space of two finger-breadths beyond the site of the first oblation, he offers the sacrifice along the northern side. "This is for Prajāpati, not for me. In the case of an oblation of liquid substances, however, the offering is made with either a *darvī* ladle or a *sruva* spoon. Then he should place a second fuel-stick (*samidh*) on the fire; or rather, there may be no placing of a second fuel-stick at all. In this latter case, there is only one fuel-stick at the time of the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).

Then, having discarded the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa) to the north of the fire, one should perform the final sprinkling (uttarapariṣeka). Alternatively, there may be no spreading of grass, no initial sprinkling, no discarding of the grass, and no final sprinkling. Then, for the three mantras beginning with "Agnirmūrdhā," Agni is the seer (ṛṣi), Agni is the deity, and the Gāyatrī is the meter. For the mantra "Prajāpate," the Viśvedevas are the seers, Prajāpati is the deity, and the Triṣṭubh is the meter; their application (viniyoga) is in the rite of worship (upasthāna).

Having worshipped Agni with the three mantras: "Oṃ agnirmūrdhā divaḥ...", "tvāmagne...", and "ayamagniḥ...", he worships Prajāpati with the mantra: "Oṃ prajāpate na... (or he may simply perform the silent recitation).

In this alternative, the specific modification lies in the statement of application (*viniyoga-vākya*), which should read: "This is the application for the recitation (*japa*). Then, having performed the concluding recitation (*saṃsthājapa*), worshipped the fire, applied the sacred ash (*bhasma*), and prayed with the mantra "Faith (*śraddhā*) and Intelligence (*medhā*)," one should pay obeisance and dedicate the rite to the Lord of Karma with the formula: "May the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*) be pleased by this evening *aupāsana* oblation. Regarding the morning *aupāsana* oblation, however, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "I shall offer the morning *aupāsana* oblation with rice (*vrīhi*). In the case of using barley (*yava*), the resolve is: "with barley."

Regarding the first oblation, there is an option between the deities: "To Agni, Svāhā! or "To Sūrya, Svāhā! In the case where Agni is the deity, the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) is exactly as in the evening *homa*. However, in the case where Sūrya is the deity—the three mantras beginning with *ud vayam*, *ud tyam*, and *citram*—Soma is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sūrya is the deity; the meter of the first is *anuṣṭubh*, of the second is *gāyatrī*, and of the third is *triṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for the ritual attendance.

Having performed the worship of the Sun with the three mantras, "oṃ udvayaṃ," "udu tyaṃ," and "citraṃ," the procedure for the worship of Prajāpati and so forth is the same. In that regard, the specific difference lies in the formula for the dedication to the Lord (*īśvarārpaṇavākya*), which should be: "May the venerable Supreme Lord be pleased by this morning *aupāsana* oblation. However, in the case of an oblation of milk, one must first remove some embers from the exterior fire to heat the milk-pot, place it upon them, and then pour back into it water measured by a *sruva* ladle; this must indeed be done because it is prescribed in one's own *sūtra*. Its application here is due to its being a part of the *Śrauta* ritual.

However, there is no placing upon the embers (*adhiśrayaṇa*) nor sprinkling (*pratiṣeka*) for the curd (*dadhi*), the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), and the *soma*, because of the scriptural statement: "Whatever [action] other than placing upon the embers and sprinkling is performed, that is done for the curd, the rice-grains, and the *soma*. Here, the curd is worldly (non-Vedic); the rice-grains, however, are those of *vrīhi* rice, as this is universally established in that very context. For *soma*, it is the juice itself and not the creeper; whereas the *pūtīka* plants are a scripturally enjoined substitute specifically for the purpose of sacrifice, not for all [uses].

Regarding these [substances], there is an option concerning the placement of two tips of *darbha* grass, as in the case of rice and barley. However, in the case of *yavāgū* (gruel), sprinkling comes first and inspection later, according to the statement by the author of the *Vaijayantī* during his commentary on the Sūtra: "One cooks the *yavāgū* while sprinkling it. The same applies to boiled rice (*odana*). By the word *yavāgū*, loose rice is meant. Regarding barley, wheat, *priyaṅgu*, rice, and sesame, [the rule is as stated]. In the case of oil, there is an option regarding the placement of two tips of *darbha* grass.

In the case of clarified butter (*ājya*), however, it should be understood that the placing of two tips of *darbha* grass [into the ladle] is mandatory. If one is unable to perform this *aupāsana-homa* oneself, one should appoint a priest for the purpose of the oblation, saying, "I choose you as my priest," and have it performed by him. The formal renunciation (*tyāga*) must, however, be made by oneself or by the wife. If the wife lacks the authority to act, it should be understood that the renunciation may even be made by the priest in her absence. If an expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) falls due in the middle of this rite, then, instead of performing the actual oblation, one should simply mutter the oblation-mantra (*homamantra*).

In a rite that does not involve clarified butter (*ājya*), there is recitation (*japa*); in a rite that involves clarified butter, there is an oblation (*homa*)—so it has been stated by the commentators. Since there is a prohibition stating "one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) does not offer oblations" once the consecration has been performed, no *homa* takes place until the completion of the sacrifice.
This concludes the domestic fire offering (*aupāsana-homa*). Now, as an incidental topic, the combined offering (*samasya-homa*) is described.
In that regard, Prajāpati says: "One who is in distress may combine both the evening and morning oblations into the evening [offering] and perform them there;
in that case, there should be either one or two fuel-sticks."
Because the evening *homa* is primary, its ritual procedure (*tantra*) is prescribed;
one should perform four oblations therein, two of which are the evening oblations.
If there is one fuel-stick for the morning oblation and another for the evening homa,
and that second stick has been prepared, it shall serve for the morning oblation.
One should wipe the ladle twice as in the evening oblation and twice as in the morning oblation;
the ritual attendance (upasthāna) should be performed once, and the remainder should be according to the archetype (prakṛti).
Having offered two oblations, some indeed lie down or close their eyes;
having thus interrupted those two offerings, he should then perform two further oblations.
Sometimes all [the fires] are combined at dawn when there is an emergency regarding the Guru;
however many are combined here, they all commence again in the evening.
"And they conclude at dawn, but do not begin at dawn.
Now follows the rule for the fortnightly oblations (*pakṣahoma*).
Regarding this, Maṇḍana and Smṛtyarthasāra state:
Whether one is afflicted by disease, beset by distress, fallen into calamity, or even traveling on a journey;
whether during the ruin of a kingdom, in the absence of wealth, or even while living in the house of a teacher.
When other such signs have appeared,
one should perform the Agnihotra sacrifices equally, as far as possible.
Whatever is stated here after pointing out one among these signs,
one should understand that it has been established for all such signs.
"Either all the fortnightly oblations (*pakṣahoma*) or even just the remaining oblations.
By the phrase "of the *agnihotra*s," the domestic oblations (*aupāsana-homa*) are also included, because they are equal to the *agnihotra* oblations; for it is said:

"Whatever is the rule for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), that shall be for the one who maintains the domestic fire (*aupāsanika*). "All" refers to those beginning from the first day of the fortnight up to the end of the fortnight. "Remaining" refers to some other portion beginning from a previous limit.
As for that which was said:
"On the third, the fourth, or the fifth, and on subsequent days,
the oblations beginning with those [mantras] and ending with those [mantras] are designated as the 'remnant' (śeṣa)."

To claim, on the basis of this statement from the *Trikāṇḍī*, that only the third case (instrumental) functions as the starting point (*pūrvāvadhi*) and not the second case (accusative), is merely a deception of the ignorant; for this statement is not found in the *Trikāṇḍī*. Marīci states:
"Where a bodily affliction occurs and one becomes distressed by fear..."
Just as the offering to the wings (pakṣahoma) is prescribed even in other calamities.
"When the fortnightly oblations have been offered, one should desist from that [rite] in the middle;
if one performs the oblation again, it shall not be a cause of fault."

By the word *ced* (if), an alternative (*vikalpa*) is indicated. In the *Ācāraratna*, it is stated that the mention of the *pakṣahoma* (fortnightly oblation) is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the remaining oblations.

Baudhāyana also says: "Now, the consolidation (*samāsa*) of the Agnihotra rites occurs in times of calamity—during national upheaval, affliction by disease, the necessity of traveling on a journey, when there is a need to reside at the teacher’s house, upon the death of mother, father, wife, son, or others, due to the restraint of a powerful person, or when place, time, and materials are unavailable—that is, in extreme emergencies."

*Agrihotrāṇām* refers to the oblations connected with the *agnihotra*. *Rāṣṭravibhramaḥ* is the upheaval or disturbance of the kingdom. *Vyādhiḥ* is a specific mental affliction or mental suffering; *pīḍā* is external suffering. *Atyayaḥ* is destruction. *Balavato nirodhaḥ* is restraint caused by a powerful agent. In the reading *balavati nirodhādau*, the qualification "powerful" (*balavat*) should be understood as applying to the restraint and the other [consequences]. Maṇḍana also says: "In that case, the limit is the calamity itself, not the counting of days. Gopāla states the fault in performing the *homa* irregularly due to laziness and so forth: [The passage continues with the citation from Gopāla.]
"This should not be done out of kinship, nor out of passion, nor out of greed;
rather, one who possesses the power and is faithful should act thus in times of distress."

"If one performs [the rites] when there is no occasion for it, he should sacrifice with the *tantumatī* offering. *Jāmitā* means laziness. One who is capable should not fail to perform this rule for the daily oblations (*samasyahoma*) out of laziness, passion, or greed. However, he should certainly perform them in times of distress. If he should perform them when there is no distress, then the meaning is that he must sacrifice with the *tantumatī* offering. In this context, in place of the *tantumatī* sacrifice, there is the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) for the *tāntumata*.

"Those which are *puroḍāśas* (sacrificial cakes) for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), those are *carus* (boiled rice offerings) for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)."
Thus from another scripture. But in the *Yajñapārśva*:
"One who is not afflicted by illness, not away from home, free from anxiety, and free from calamity..."
"But he who should offer the fortnightly oblation (pakṣahoma) must perform the penance for an outcaste."

The rule is that the previously mentioned expiation (*prāyaścitta*) pertains to cases of non-repetition, whereas that stated by Yajñapārśva pertains to cases of repetition. Some maintain that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) [of both]. Thus, one should not perform these three options continuously.
And so says Maṇḍana: "In the third immediate alternative, one should not practice the combination."
Likewise:
"Having performed the oblations there day after day even with great difficulty,
one may again perform the Pakṣahoma and other rites at will at the end of a fortnight."
Since this is impossible in every respect, he himself has said: "If it should continue even in times of distress, in any way whatsoever for as long as one lives;
one should perform the Pakṣahoma offerings uninterruptedly for as long as one lives."

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*— "If one should pass three fortnights by means of fortnightly oblations, there must be a re-establishment of the fires"— that is intended to refer to a case where [the neglect] has not occurred.
A specific detail is given in the *Smṛtibhāskara*:
"On the day of the fast (aupavasathya), the evening oblation (sāyaṃ-homa) shall be performed separately;
likewise, on the day of sacrifice (yajaniya), the morning oblation (prātar-homa) shall be performed separately."
Maṇḍana states: "If, due to some cause, the fast on the lunar festival day is omitted,
then even the evening oblation for that day is combined with the previous ones."
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*):

"For the sake of the occasion of misfortune (*āpad*), beginning from the evening of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the evening of the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), I shall perform so-and-so many evening *aupāsana* oblations; and for the sake of the same occasion, beginning from the morning of the second lunar day until the morning of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), I shall perform so-and-so many morning *aupāsana* oblations, drawing them forward and offering them by way of a single performance (*tantra*)."

In this regard, for the *āpannimitta* (occasional rite) performed in the evening, one should resolve in the evening: "Starting from tonight’s *aupāsana* oblation until the evening of the fourteenth day, I shall offer so-and-so many evening *aupāsana* oblations in a single ritual sequence (*tantra*), using either rice or barley. For the morning rite, one should resolve in the morning: "Starting from tomorrow morning until the morning of such-and-such a festival day, I shall offer so-and-so many morning *aupāsana* oblations in a single ritual sequence, using either rice or barley. In the case of separate resolutions (*bhinnasaṃkalpa*), the phrase ending with "in this regard" (*tatredānīm*) is not used.

In the procedure for the remaining oblations (*śeṣahoma*), however, one should recite at evening: "Beginning from the evening of such-and-such a day until the evening of the fourteenth day, I shall offer so many evening *aupāsana* oblations by way of a single ritual performance (*tantra*) with either rice or barley. And at dawn: "Beginning from the morning of such-and-such a day until the morning of such-and-such a festival day, I shall offer so many morning *aupāsana* oblations by way of a single ritual performance with either rice or barley. Alternatively, one need not say anything up to the word "beginning" (*ārabhya*) in either case.

However, when due to some cause it is certain that the *anvādhāna* will not take place on the upcoming festival day (*parvan*), then some authorities maintain that even the evening *homa* of that day should be combined with the previous ones. Even so, if the occasion (*āpatti*) does not arise, one should act in the same manner during the other half of the month as well. In the third case, even if the occasion arises, there is no combination of the fortnightly *homas* (*pakṣahoma-samāsa*); rather, there is only a combination of the remaining *homas* (*śeṣahoma-samāsa*). This applies likewise to the combinations of the remaining [offerings].

If, at some point after two daily *homas* of a *pakṣahoma*, there arises the necessity of traveling due to an urgent matter, then some authorities maintain that one should perform the combined *dvayahika* and *tryahika homas* on the first day (*pratipad*), go to another village, and then perform the remaining *homas*.

If, immediately after the evening *pakṣahoma* or even after the *śeṣahoma*, a major calamity (*mahadāpatti*) occurs on that very night before the morning time, then at that very moment, by means of "closing" (*nimīlana*), one should conceive of an interval of a day having passed; having then re-established the fires (*vihṛtya*) as if it were morning, the morning *homās* should be performed combined (*samasya*). If a major calamity occurs in the evening, one should perform the *homās* for both times in the evening itself.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "Starting from the evening of such-and-such a day until the evening of the fourteenth day, I shall perform so many evening oblations (*sāyaṃ-homa*); and starting from the morning of such-and-such a day until the morning of such-and-such a festival, I shall perform so many morning oblations (*prātar-homa*); all these, however, I shall offer in brief at the evening time itself with such-and-such materials," one should first offer the two evening oblations according to the prescribed rule, pause for a short while, and then, immediately after closing one's eyes—

The two morning oblations are to be offered. Even though, under the view that Agni is the deity, there is identity of the deity, the two oblations are nevertheless distinct due to the intervention of the rule of closing [the eyes].

In the event of a major transgression at dawn, one should make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), thinking: "Until such-and-such time in the morning, I shall offer so many morning oblations (*prātar-homa*) as the cause for this major transgression; and starting from such-and-such evening until the evening of the fourteenth day, I shall offer so many evening oblations (*sāyaṃ-homa*) all at once in the morning with such-and-such materials. Having made this resolve, one should first offer the two morning oblations according to the prescribed ritual, pause for some time, and then offer the two evening oblations.

Here too, because they are separated by an interval, the two morning oblations are indeed distinct. However, when there is a possibility of a very long period of a major calamity (*āpatti*), one should perform the fortnightly oblations (*pakṣahoma*) continuously for as long as one lives. In all cases, the limit is strictly the end of the calamity, not the completion of a count of fortnights. Whether the fortnightly oblation or the supplementary oblation (*śeṣahoma*) has been performed, if the calamity ceases during the interval, then the performance of those previously offered oblations becomes optional.

The elders maintain that when the fortnightly oblation (*pakṣahoma*) and so forth have been performed, there is no expiation even if the fire is not made manifest at sunrise and sunset, because that [manifestation] is intended solely for the purpose of the oblation.
Thus ends the procedure for the daily domestic oblation (*aupāsana-homa*), the fortnightly oblation, and the supplementary oblation in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.

This concludes the work composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was himself the son of Śrīmat Sāgnicit Vājapeyayājī Pauṇḍarīkayājī Sarvatomukhayājī Okopāhva—of the lineage of the venerable Agnicits.
The thirteenth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now, in order to explain the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, the determination of the *parvan* (lunar phase) is stated first.
Regarding that, the sequence of the two is given in the *Śrautasūtra*: "The earlier is the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), the later is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)."

In all instances, the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices are prescribed, with the Darśa mentioned first. Since it might follow that both should be performed according to the order of the textual recitation (pāṭhakrama), this sūtra is commenced. Although the word "Darśa" is placed first according to the rule "alpāctaram" [Pāṇini 2.2.34], the meaning is that the Pūrṇamāsī sacrifice itself comes first.

Even in the Śruti, within the section on the Ārambhaṇīyā [introductory rite], in the explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning the Sārasvata-homas, the nature of the *anuloma* (direct) and *pratiloma* (inverse) orders is first demonstrated by the passage beginning with "He who [performs] these in direct order... and ending with "...that is the inverse order. Then, after stating the fault in performing the Full Moon sacrifice first—beginning with "If one were to perform the Full Moon first, one would perform them in the inverse order"—the injunction for the Sārasvata-homas is established as the remedy for that fault. Thus, the sequence is indeed: the Full Moon sacrifice first, followed by the New Moon sacrifice.

This has been demonstrated; here, there are also many indicative marks (*liṅga*), such as the *anumantraṇa*, the *sūktavāka*, the deity-invoking verses (*devatā-yājyā*), and so forth. The same applies to the two *pārvaṇa-sthālīpākas*.
As it was stated by Śaunaka and Baudhāyana:
"When the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) arrives immediately after the marriage..."
"Therefore, one should begin by performing the *sthālīpāka* on the festival days (*parvan*).
Even if the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) should fall immediately after the marriage,
nevertheless, the performance of the *sthālīpāka* for the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and other such occasions is prescribed."
Another Smṛti text also states: "If the full moon day is reached prior to the fourth oblation,
the sacrifice must be performed on that very day, preceded by the anvādhāna."
In that regard, it is stated in the *Saṃgraha* that even if an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) or similar period occurs between the *vivāha-homa* and the commencement of the *sthālīpāka*,
the rites must still be performed: "The *pārvaṇeṣṭi*, the *āgrayaṇa*, the ritual of twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*),
the *agnihotra*, the *pākayajñas*, and other such rites [are to be performed] even during an intercalary month."
"One should perform the obligatory rites, but not the inaugural rite (*prārambha*); such is the settled rule.
Also, in another *Smṛti*:
"In the intercalary month (*malimluca*) and in the month of Pauṣa, the *anvārambhaṇa* is not desired."
"In the case of the stupor (mauḍhya) of Jupiter and Venus, as well as during lunar and solar eclipses.

These two statements refer to the commencement of rites such as the *sthālīpāka* when one has failed to begin them at their proper time due to laziness or other causes. There is no fault in commencing what has reached its proper time.
Thus says Garga:

"One should perform the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*) and the New Moon sacrifice (*darśeṣṭi*) at their proper times; if there is a delay in these two, they should be performed in an auspicious month under a favorable asterism. Regarding this, the *Prayogapārijāta*, *Hemādri*, and others maintain that the mention of the naming ceremony is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and traditional (*smārta*) rites, while the mention of the New Moon sacrifice is an elliptical indication of all obligatory and occasional Vedic (*śrauta*) rites.
Maṇḍana, however, says: "If the full moon following the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) falls within an intercalary month (malamāsa),
one should never perform the Ārambhaṇīyā and other rites on that day."

By the sūtra, "Henceforth, one should always sacrifice on the *parvan* days with an *āgneya* *sthālīpāka*," the performance of the *āgneya-sthālīpāka* on the *parvan* days consisting of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is prescribed. Regarding the nature of those two—the full moon and the new moon—Gobhila says:
"That which is the greatest distance between the sun and the moon is the *paurṇamāsī*; that which is the closest proximity is the *amāvāsyā*."

The word *darśa* denotes the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) either through the etymology "that wherein the moon is seen only by yogis," or through a figurative inversion (lit. contrary indication) meaning "that wherein the moon is not seen by humans. This is supported by the lexicon: "Darśa is the conjunction of the sun and the moon. Thus, the meaning is "that wherein there is a meeting of the sun and the moon. Regarding the definition of the full moon (*pūrṇimā*), the *Matsya Purāṇa* and the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* state:
"When the waning of the digits has passed and [the moon] is full day and night, [it meets] with the other [the sun] mutually..."
Because the moon and the sun are full during the afternoon, it is known as Pūrṇimā (the Full Moon).

In the afternoon, at the time of sunset, just as the sun sets with its orb fully complete, so too in the subsequent moment the moon rises with its orb fully complete; the mention of the moon and the sun is intended to illustrate the relationship between the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) and the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika). The etymological definition of *amāvāsyā* is given in the Matsya, Vāyu, and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas: "When the moon and the sun dwell together (*amā vasetām*) among the stars (*ṛkṣeṣu*), this fifteenth night is therefore called *amāvāsyā*."
"Amā" means "together.
However, another etymological explanation is given in the Śruti:
"'Amā' indeed means 'let us dwell together today in wealth,' for Indra is the foremost among the gods."
"That which bestows wealth (vasu) on the new moon day is the reason for the name *amāvāsyā*.
Furthermore, each of these two—the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)—is of two kinds: namely, *Anumati* and *Rākā*, and *Sinīvālī* and *Kuhū*.
The nature of these is described in the Kaṭha recension and the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.
"That which is the earlier full moon is Anumati; that which is the later is Rākā.
That which is the earlier new moon is Sinīvālī; that which is the later is Kuhū.
The definition of these has been stated by Bṛhad-Vasiṣṭha:
*Rākā* is the full moon; *Anumati* is remembered as the moon when slightly diminished.
When the moon is seen during the day on the full-moon night, it is remembered as *Anumati*.
If that [new moon] is seen at night, it is celebrated as Rākā;
they call the new moon on which the moon is visible Sinīvālī.
"The great seers call this very new moon night 'kuhū', because the moon has disappeared."

In this context, the time required for the pronunciation of three short syllables (*laghu-akṣara*) is called the *saṃdhi* (junction) for those [tithis] excluding *kuhū*. For *kuhū*, however, it is measured by two syllables.
Thus, the *Bhagavatī-purāṇa* states in the *Hemādri*:
"Of Anumati, Rākā, and Sinīvālī—excluding *kuhū*..."
"The time for these [breaths] is two lavas; that which is merely a kuhū is known as kuhū."
The nature of a *lava* is stated in the *Mādhavīya*, based on another Smṛti: "A fourth part of a short syllable is called a *truṭi*;
two *truṭis* are declared to be a *lava*, and two *lavas* are a *nimeṣa*."

Thus, two *lava*s constitute a short syllable (*laghvakṣara*). A single portion of the full moon day (*parvan*) and a second portion of the first lunar day (*pratipad*), measured by the duration required to pronounce a short syllable, combined together form the conjunction (*saṃdhi*). However, the conjunction between the new moon day (*kuhū*) and the first lunar day is measured by the duration of the two syllables "ku-hū. Accordingly, the *Matsya Purāṇa* and the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* state: "When the cuckoo utters the sound 'ku-hū,' for as long as that time lasts, this new moon day is known by that duration and is remembered as *kuhū*."

Thus, when the nature of the *saṃdhi* (the junction) is understood, the injunction "one should sacrifice at the *saṃdhi*" implies that the sacrifice is to be performed at the junction; however, because the junction is so extremely subtle that it is unfit for the performance of ritual action, the word *saṃdhi* indicates the two sides of the junction. Accordingly, the scriptural injunction "one should sacrifice at the *saṃdhi*" prescribes the sacrifice with respect to both sides of the junction. For this very reason, another scripture states: "One should sacrifice on both sides of the *saṃdhi*. Hemādri, citing Baudhāyana, also says:
"Because the time of the *saṃdhi* is so subtle, the term *saṃdhi* is used to refer to its vicinity."
"They say that proximity is the object, whether by means of what precedes or what follows."

Here, by the words *pūrva* (prior) and *para* (subsequent), the day of the full moon (*parvadina*) preceding the conjunction and the day of the first lunar day (*pratipaddina*) following it are respectively designated. Since there might otherwise be a tendency to include the entirety of the full moon day and the first lunar day, Vṛddha-Śātātapa provides this restriction:
"The fourth part of the full moon day and the first three parts of the first lunar day..."
"That is to be known as the time for sacrifice, declared as 'morning' by the wise."
Gobhila states the distinction regarding the time for sacrifice:

"If the junction of the new moon day and the first day of the lunar fortnight occurs at the *āvartana* (the sun's turning point), the sacrifice is desired on that very day; if it occurs later than that, it is on the following day."

Likewise: "If the junction of the full moon or new moon day occurs before the turning back [of the sun], one should sacrifice on that very day; its commencement, however, takes place on the preceding day."
Laukāxi says: "If the parvan ends in the forenoon or at midday, one should fast on the preceding day;
the sacrifice is prescribed for that very day."
In another Smṛti as well:
"If the junction [of the new moon] occurs at the time of the sun's turning back (āvartana), or even before it, the sacrifice should be performed on that day;
if it occurs after, then on the following day."
"If the junction occurs after the turning point [of the sun] and the commencement takes place on that day, the sacrifice is to be performed on the following day;
such is the determination regarding the two lunar phases."
Likewise:
"If the festival day (parvan) concludes in the afternoon or at night, one should fast on that day;
the sacrifice is prescribed for the following morning."

If the conjunction [of day and night] occurs during the forenoon or at the turning point (*āvartana*), the sacrifice takes place on that very same day, while the preparatory rites (*anvādhāna*) and so forth are performed on the preceding day. However, if the conjunction occurs after the turning point, the preparatory rites and so forth are performed on that day, and the sacrifice on the following day; this is the distilled meaning. By the word *āvartana*, the time consisting of the midday junction between the two parts of the day is denoted: "The forenoon is indeed before the turning point, and the afternoon is after it; the junction between those two, which is called the turning point, is midday."
Thus, from the statement cited in the *Madanaratna*:

"Of those two, the forenoon and the afternoon. Some maintain that this junction (*saṃdhi*) is measured at one *muhūrta*. Their intention is based on the principle of the midnight [junction]. The determination of the *parvan* is also stated in the *Śrautasūtra*:
"One should observe the fast on the previous full moon, or on the complete previous new moon, or on the day when [the moon] is not visible."

Now, the meaning of this sūtra is described in accordance with the determination of the section on Smṛti: "If one should fast on the fourteenth day joined with the previous [day], provided it is incomplete on the following day"—this is established by implication through a consideration of the subsequent sūtra. Or, "if it is complete. This means it would be joined with the first lunar day (pratipad) in such a way that they are equal. The meaning is that it remains pervading the first half of the day divided into two parts. And thus, if it is incomplete, the other [day] is taken.

Otherwise, it is understood by implication that it refers to the preceding day. Here too, it should be known that there is an internal distinction regarding the *sadyaskāla* (immediate) rite. The same applies to the phrase "the preceding new moon. Regarding the statement "on the day when [the moon] is not seen," this should also be applied here as before, drawing in the phrase "the full [duration of] the new moon" on the day when the new moon is not visible, according to the previous reasoning. Here, the word "fasting" (*upavāsa*) does not mean the absence of eating, because that would contradict the statement "the couple eat.
Rather, by the word "fasting," the single meal of the husband and wife is intended, since this will be explained later in the section on Dharma. Or else—
"But he who has turned away from evils and dwells together with virtues—
that is to be known as *upavāsa* (fasting)."
The author of the *Vaijayantī* has explained that the meaning of the term "fasting" (*upavāsa*) as established by the *Smṛti* texts should be accepted.

In this regard, by the statement "the fourth part of the *parvan*," the fourth part of the *parvan* and the three parts of the *pratipad* are prescribed as the time for the sacrifice. Among these, if the conjunction (*saṃdhi*) occurs at the turning of the sun (*āvartana*) or before it, then the fourth part of the *parvan* is the time for the sacrifice. If the conjunction occurs at dawn (*uṣaḥkāla*), the first part of the *pratipad* is the time for the sacrifice; if at midnight (*niśītha*), the second part; and if at the beginning of the night, the third part.

[Objection: But by this same logic, the fourth part of the *pratipad* [tithi] occurring at the junction in the afternoon would also constitute a time for sacrifice. [Reply: This is not so, for it is said:
"One should never perform sacrifices during the fourth part of the *pratipad*; the Rākṣasas destroy that [offering]. This is the eternal Vedic injunction."

Because, as stated above, sacrifice is prohibited during the fourth part [of the day], one might argue that in such a case the sacrifice itself should be omitted; but this is not so, because Vṛddha-Śātātapa provides an exception: "Where the junction [of the day] occurs in the afternoon, the sacrifice should be performed on the following morning."
"One who performs [it] during the first part [of the day] does not incur fault even in the fourth."

If it is argued that, in that case, the prohibition would be without a subject matter (*nirviṣaya*), it is not so; for it has its application within the scope of the *saghaskāla* [period]. Kātyāyana indicates that subject matter as follows:
"If the junction [of day and night] occurs after the *saṅgava* period and before the sun's turning back..."
"That full-moon day is to be understood as the lunar date (tithi) for the rule regarding the immediate performance (sadyaskāla)."

When the conjunction (*saṃdhi*) occurs between the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) and the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) within the interval between the *saṃgava* and *āvartana* periods, the previously cited scriptural statements establish that the preliminary rites such as the *anvādhāna* should take place on the day prior to the conjunction day. However, by the rule concerning the *sadyaskāla* (immediate-performance) sacrifice, these rites are deferred to the day of the conjunction itself. This is also supported by the sūtra: "Or he performs everything immediately in the case of the *sadyaskālā* [sacrifice]. One should understand this to be consistent with the commentary provided by the authors of the *Vaijayantī*, for there the injunction regarding the *sadyaskāla* is presented as a positive application (*anvaya*).

The prohibition regarding the fourth part of the day is expressed in the form of a negative (vyatireka). This being the case, the prohibitive statement becomes meaningful. This same principle applies to the new moon (amāvāsyā) as well; however, there is no requirement for it to be performed on the very same day (*sadyaskālatā*) in that instance, because in the sentence "if the junction [of day and night] occurs," only the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) is mentioned. Furthermore, the prohibition of the sacrifice on a day when the moon is visible should be understood to apply when the junction occurs either before the turning of the sun (*āvartana*) or at that very time.

This should be understood as it is stated in the *Ādhava* text and the *Vaijayantī* commentary. Hemādri, however, says: "Even when the junction [of the lunar day] occurs in the afternoon, if the moonrise falls within the fourth quarter of the *pratipad* on the following day, and if there is extreme waning of the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) and so forth, the sacrifice is to be performed on the preceding day. If, due to confusion, the sacrifice was not performed at the time of the sun's turning back (*āvartana*) or before the junction, but was instead performed on the white *pratipad*, then Kātyāyana states the expiation:
"If the moon is visible in the western quarter (*vāruṇī*) on the day of sacrifice..."
"In that case, having offered oblations with the Vyāhṛtis, one should give a staff to a twice-born man."
The method for calculating the junction (*saṃdhi*) has been stated by Mādhava: "Whatever *vṛddhi* exists on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), one should add half of that to the *parvan*;
likewise, having added half of the *kṣaya*, the junction should always be determined."
Kātyāyana also says: "Whatever ghaṭikās are deficient or likewise excessive on the following day, having halved them, one should apply that decrease or increase to the preceding day."

When the new moon (amāvāsyā) lasts for a certain number of ghaṭikās on the previous day and the first lunar day (pratipad) likewise lasts for that same number of ghaṭikās on the following day, the junction (saṃdhi) should be understood as it naturally stands. However, when there is a decrease (kṣaya) of the pratipad and an increase (vṛddhi) of the parvan [the new moon], then half of that increase should be added to the pratipad, and the junction should be understood [there]. But when there is a decrease of the parvan and an increase of the pratipad, then half of that increase should be added to the parvan, and one should determine the junction [there].

In that case, if the *saṃdhi* (the junction between two lunar phases) occurs either during the turning back [of the moon] by means of equalizing its decrease and increase, or prior thereto, then the sacrifice (*yāga*) takes place on that very day. If the *saṃdhi* occurs later, the sacrifice takes place on the following day.
Regarding the prohibition of completing the *iṣṭi* within the middle of the *parvan*, it was stated by Manu:
"If the *iṣṭi* is completed when the first day of the lunar phase (*pratipad*) has already begun..."
"Having performed the *punarādheya* again, the entire *iṣṭi* must be carried out by those most skilled in sacrifice."

The specific detail regarding this is stated by Gobhila in the *Nirṇayapradīpa*: "If the festival day (*parvan*) is completed either at the time of the sun's turning back (*āvartana*) or before it, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) should take place in the forenoon alone; the feeding of the twice-born occurs after the junction (*saṃdhi*)."

From this statement it is known that this [prohibition] does not apply at the junction [of the day] after the *āvartana* (the sun's turning point). Thus, the eating by the twice-born occurs as before. In the *Madanapārijāta*, it is stated that this rule does not apply to the *gṛhya* fire.
Now, regarding the *sthālīpāka*, the *Gṛhyasūtra* says: "From this point forward, one should always perform the sacrifice on the *parvan* days with a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni."

Therefore, immediately after the *sthālīpāka* performed upon entering the house, he constantly performs the sacrifice with an *āgneya-sthālīpāka* on the festival days (*parvan*). The expression "after this" is stated because the journey is long; otherwise, even if a festival day should arrive earlier [before the completion of the journey], the *sthālīpāka* might not take place. By this, it is also understood that even before the fourth oblation (*caturthī-homa*), if a festival day arrives, the rite must indeed be performed.

Even though permanence (*nityatva*) is established by implication, the explicit statement "permanently" (*nityam*) is intended to mean "for as long as one lives," so that there might not be a relinquishment after thirty-two years. If it is asked, "What occasion is there for such a relinquishment?"—one might suspect that because this [rite] is a constituent part of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, its duration of thirty-two years could optionally alternate with a lifelong performance. This [text], however, makes it known that one should fast on the new-moon day (*parvan*), perform the ritual action on the first day (*pratipad*), and commence the sacrifice on the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).
Thus it is stated by the followers of the Ṛgveda:
"For that [sacrifice], there is fasting together with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and the binding of the fuel and the sacrificial grass."
Regarding the ritual duties (*dharma*), this very point will be stated:

having introduced the topic with "on both [full and new moon] festival days (*parvan*) there is fasting," it continues, "on the following day, the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) [is performed]. Since it is established that from this point forward on festival days one should always act in this manner, the specific statement "one sacrifices with the *āgneya-sthālīpāka*" is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that one must indeed sacrifice with the *āgneya-sthālīpāka* and not otherwise.
Now, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is found in the *Dharmasūtra*:
"On the *parvan* days of both [fortnights], there is fasting (*aupavasta*), which means eating at another time and being satisfied with food;

whatever may be dear to these two, that they should eat on this day, and they should sleep on the ground and abstain from sexual intercourse. On the following day, there is the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering). Here, *parvan* refers to the junction of the fortnights (*pakṣasaṃdhi*); in this context, the day connected with that is intended. On those *parvan* days, there is fasting for both husband and wife, meaning the omission of eating. The phrase "eating at [other] times" is taken from the preceding sūtra.

Regarding the statement from the Śruti, "Eating in the evening and in the morning is enjoined for the twice-born," which establishes that eating at both times applies without distinction, he says: "aupavastam" (it is indeed fasting). Eating at one time during another period is also *aupavasta*—that is, it is indeed a fast (*upavāsa*). That too is by day, not at night, because it is seen so in the Śruti: "He does not eat this night. The word "ca" (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned: on the festival days (*parvan*), when they eat at one time, they should eat as much food as is necessary for satiety.

On this day, which is a festival day (*parva*), the couple should eat whatever is pleasing to their minds from among grains, condiments, and so forth—excluding meat, salt, and the like—and they should eat on the ground, not on a bed or similar furniture. They should also observe abstinence from sexual intercourse on this day. Regarding the second day, when the next morning has dawned, it has been explained by Ujjvalākāra that the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) should be performed, beginning with the placing of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*).

By the phrase "beginning with the placing of the vessels," it is understood that the rites preceding the placement of the vessels must be performed on the previous day. A specific detail is found in the *Chāndogya-gṛhya* and *Gobhila-gṛhya*:
"They say that one who is traveling abroad should not observe a fast; rather, the vow belongs to his wife. Therefore, he should act according to his own inclination.
This too should be accepted when [the full observance] is impossible. Regarding the items to be avoided on the *parvan* day, Bharadvāja says:
"One intending to perform a sacrifice should avoid women, oil, meat, and anything produced from trees."
Quarreling, selling, excessive laughter, and talking too much;
"The three-fold arts (song, dance, and instrumental music), sleeping at improper times, food from others, and likewise falsehood."

"Āmiṣa" refers to meat, black gram (*māṣa*), and so forth. "Tree-born resin" (*vṛkṣaja-niryāsa*) is also prohibited here even if it is white. As for the Vedic text stating, "Whether it be red or that which exudes from a cut, one must not eat that; however, one may eat another at will," this is intended to permit the consumption of white resin in cases other than during a vow (*vrata*). "The triple symphony" (*tauryatrika*) refers to instrumental music. Since the general prohibition of speaking untruth is already established, its repetition here is for the purpose of making it an integral part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*); therefore, the Vedic expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed in this case. Jābāli says: "Vegetables, meat, lentils (*masūra*), chickpeas (*caṇaka*), and likewise *kodrava* [grain]..."
"One should avoid black gram, honey, and the food of others on the day of fasting."
Here, by the word *madhu*, honey (*kṣaudra*) is intended;
for regarding liquor (*madya*), its prohibition is already established by the rule: "A Brāhmaṇa shall not drink liquor. *Aupavastaka* refers to the day of the festival (*parva*). Kātyāyana also says:
"One observing a fast should not consume salt, honey, meat, alkaline substances, or anything with which an oblation is offered; nor should one eat any grain whatsoever at night."

By the word *kṣāra* (alkaline/acidic), that substance is meant which causes saliva to flow upon being eaten. By the phrase "that by which one offers," it is stated that even a substance accepted as a means for sacrifice (*yāgasādhana*) is not to be consumed.
Vādhūla, Baudhāyana, and Vaikhānasa state: "On this entire day, one should avoid all leguminous grains (*kośīdhānya*), except for sesame."

Kātyāyana has also stated that mung beans are acceptable, just like sesame seeds: "Except for sesame and mung beans, [the following are not to be accepted]: śaibya, wheat and kodrava among grains, chickpeas, divine-grain (devoidha), all leafy vegetables, and likewise sugarcane products."
"One observing a vow should always avoid sarjikṣāra, yavakṣāra, ṭaṅkaṇakṣāra, and likewise sea salt."

In this context, by the mention of *sāmudra* (sea salt), the non-prohibition of *saindhava* (rock salt) and *mānasa* (lake salt) is understood, because they are fit for sacrificial offerings (*haviṣya*).
Thus it has been said:
"The foods of the sages (*munyanna*), milk, soma, and meat that is not seasoned..."
"That which is not pungent and is salty is, by its very nature, called sacrificial oblation (havis)."
"All [types of] salt except for *akṣāra* are *saindhava*, according to all the authors of the legal digests (*nibandha*).
It is also stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
'Salt that is *saindhava* and that which originates from Lake Mānasa...'"
"For these two are indeed the supreme purifiers, even as they are visibly [anointed] with clarified butter."
Kātyāyana states in the Chandogapariśiṣṭa:
"Sleeping on the ground is prescribed on the full moon and the new moon days;
this is prescribed even for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, following after the [domestic] fire."
Baudhāyana says: "One should not study on the parvan days, nor should one approach a woman on the parvan days; for on the parvan days, Rākṣasas and Piśācas become intent upon sorcery."

In the Sūtra: "On the full moon day, at the morning meal, the husband and wife should eat mixed with clarified butter, provided they do not eat anything else besides beans; they may eat as much as they desire before the driving away of the calves on the new moon day."

"Suhitau" means satisfied. While it might be thought that the distinction—that they should not be satisfied on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) but may be satisfied on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*)—applies to the *sthālīpāka* (cooked grain offering), it does not; for satisfaction with food has been stated without such qualification. One who is unable to consume the meal mixed with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) may instead eat it mixed with curd (*dadhi*), according to the statement of Āpastamba: "With curd or with milk. Furthermore, this rule regarding clarified butter and so forth for the obligatory daily meal, which is already established by natural inclination (*rāga-prāpta*), is prescribed here as being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).

Eating, however, serves solely the purpose of the person. Therefore, Pitṛbhūti maintains that if one is unable to eat due to incapacity or other such reasons, then one should not eat in order to maintain the integrity of the observance (*niyama*).
Bhartṛsvāmin also says:
"Eating is for the sake of warding off hunger; the restriction regarding it applies at this specific time, provided there is a desire [to eat]."
"It does not recur when there are many *iṣṭis*.

If among many wives the one who is not the principal (*amukhyā*) is in her courses (*anālambhukā*), then the sacrifice must indeed be performed. But if the eldest (*jyeṣṭhā*) is in her courses, then the sacrifice must not be performed.
This has been stated by Gautama in the Hemādri:
"When the day for sacrifice has arrived, if his wife is in her menses, he should nevertheless perform the sacrifice; and the eldest wife should act in this same manner."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"Even among many wives, if the eldest is possessed of menses,
a wise man should not perform a sacrifice by excluding her."
It follows by implication that the sacrifice must be performed excluding the youngest [wife].
And there is a statement in the *Pādma-purāṇa*:
"Among many wives who share one husband, if the youngest is possessed of menses..."
"Even while being excluded, one may perform a sacrifice according to the prescribed rules."
All others besides the eldest are to be understood by the term "younger" (*kaniṣṭhā*), and not only the very last one.
For this very reason it is said:
"Even among many wives, she who is not the principal [eldest] and is joined with menses..."
Even while being excluded, one may perform a sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.
Thus it is stated in another Smṛti that she is not the primary [wife].
However, the primacy of the eldest wife is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"The eldest wife shall indeed be the primary one in sacrifice, in giving, in worship, and in the home."
"Likewise, by performing actions in this manner, one shall become a partaker of the results as described."
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa* as well:
"O lord of men, whatever is performed without the eldest wife,
all that becomes fruitless, like a wood-apple eaten by an elephant."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"O King, one should perform rituals with great effort together with the eldest [wife];
an action performed together with her becomes fruitful for men."

The defect that was stated regarding the performance of a ritual in the absence of the eldest wife is to be understood as applying when she is present. When the eldest has died, whichever woman is the eldest among those remaining should be regarded as the primary one. Thus, it is established that the sacrifice must be performed even by excluding wives other than the one who is the eldest and currently present. By this, the view that if even one among many wives is in her menses, the sacrifice should not be performed, is refuted. And this applies to all instances except the first performance:
"A rite such as the Agnihotra, once commenced and enjoined by the Śruti..."

This is because it is heard in the statement of Kātyāyana that [the practice] was commenced with the words: "If a twice-born man, having abandoned a woman who is flooded with her menses, performs [the rite]...
and: "Whether she be the eldest or the youngest wife, if she is menstruating..."
This is because another Smṛti states: "If it were [permissible] during the first performance, then no obstruction would be recognized.

Commentators explain *prakrānta* as that which has been commenced, begun, or performed once. However, according to those who say that *prakrānta* means that which has been undertaken through a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth, it should be understood that in their view, an obstruction occurs even during the first performance after such a resolve.
Now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*).

On the morning of the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, after the *aupāsana* oblation, the performer, together with his wife, shall sit behind the *aupāsana* fire. Having sipped water (*ācamya*) and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he shall announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "As long as I have the capacity, for the duration of my life, I shall sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa-sthālīpākas*."

Once it is determined that the view—that after the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Pārvaṇa Sthālīpākas are not performed—is indeed followed by the woman, then, provided she possesses the requisite qualification, there is this distinction in the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): until the time prior to the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, she resolves, "I shall sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa Sthālīpākas."

Then one should perform the rites beginning with the worship of Gaṇapati and ending with the *nāndī-śrāddha*. In this case, the specific modification is that "May Agni be pleased" is used. Alternatively, prior even to the primary formal resolve (*pradhāna-saṃkalpa*), one should perform the worship of Gaṇapati, the recitation of the *puṇyāha* and other verses, the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjana*), and the *nāndī-śrāddha*; immediately thereafter, the primary formal resolve should be performed.

Then, for the sake of commencing [the rite], one should perform the Caturhotṛ-homa, the Sārasvata-homa, and the Anvārambhaṇīya sthālīpāka. Although the Caturhotṛ-homa and the others are not mentioned in the Gṛhya-sūtra, nevertheless—because of the similarity in principle between the Darśapūrṇamāsa-sthālīpākas and the Darśapūrṇamāsa-iṣṭis—and because Mātṛdatta has stated that certain characteristics of the Darśapūrṇamāsa apply here, these [elements] are also obtained here by way of such implication. Furthermore, there is also the practice of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) in this regard.

Having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), having announced the place and time, and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "Intending to perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa Sthālīpākas, I shall offer the Caturhotṛ oblation together with its Grahas," he should spread Darbha grass to the north of the fire. Upon that grass, he should set down the *sruc* or *darvī* ladle, the *sruva* spoon, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the *upaveṣa* fire-stirring stick, the *saṃmārga* Darbha blades, the *avajvalana* Darbha blades, the clarified butter, and the fuel sticks (*samidh*). Having performed the rites beginning with the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers and ending with "having placed the *pavitra* strainers in the fire," he should strew grass around the fire and sprinkle water around it silently;
or else, there may be neither the strewing nor the sprinkling.

Then, having adorned the fire and having taken [ghee] once with the *sruc* or the *darvī*, he places the prepared fuel-stick (*samidh*) upon it. For the *Caturhotṛ-mantra* beginning with "Pṛthivī hotā" (Earth is the Hotṛ), together with the mantra known as the *Graha* beginning with "Vācaspate vāco vīryeṇa," Prajāpati Vācaspati Brahmā is the seer; the Yajus is the meter. Its application is in the oblation (*homa*). Having mentally recited: "Oṃ Pṛthivī hotā... Bṛhaspatir upavaktā," he stands to the south of the fire and offers the oblation with: "Oṃ Vācaspate vāco... svāhā. [The dedication is: "This is for Vācaspati Brahmā, not for me."

Then, if there is a covering of grass (paristaraṇa), one should discard those [grass-blades] to the north. Regarding the recollection of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, there is an option. Then, one who is about to begin the *Sārasvata* oblations and the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* *sthālīpāka*, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), "I shall offer the two *Sārasvata* oblations," and having strewn *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, he should place upon it the *sruk* or *darvī* ladle, the *sruva* spoon, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the *upaveṣa* stick, the *darbha* blades for wiping, the *darbha* blades for kindling, two fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and the clarified butter. [The procedure continues with] the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers and so forth.

Having performed the rites up to the point of "placing [the fuel] in the fire," he should strew grass around the fire and silently sprinkle water around it; or alternatively, there may be neither the strewing nor the sprinkling. Then, having adorned the fire, he takes eight times—or twice—with the *sruva* ladle into the *sruc* or the *darvī* spoon. Having placed the two pieces of fuel that were set aside into the fire, he offers with half of the clarified butter while standing to the south of the fire, reciting: "Oṃ pūrṇā pa... mādayantā svāhā. [The formula] "pūrṇā paścāt" has Soma Pūrṇamāsa as its deity, Triṣṭubh as its meter, and its application is in the oblation (*homa*). [The dedication is: "This is for Pūrṇamāsa, not for me."

For the verse "yatte devā adadhuḥ," Soma is the seer, Amāvāsyā is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application is in the oblation (*homa*). With the remaining clarified butter, he offers in the same manner: "Oṃ yatte devā adadhuḥ... suvīra svāhā. [The dedication is: "This is for Amāvāsyā, not for me. Regarding the recollection of the seer and other details, there is an option. If the surrounding grass (*paristaraṇa*) is present, he should discard them to the north.
Now follows the procedure for the *Anvārambhaṇa-sthālīpāka* (the first-fruits offering at the commencement of the rainy season).

One who is about to begin the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *sthālīpāka* offerings should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the *anvārambhaṇa-sthālīpāka*. Having kindled the fire and meditated upon it, and having taken three fuel sticks (*samidh*), he should perform the rites from "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) up to the end of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then he says: "In this *anvārambhaṇa-sthālīpāka* rite, I shall encompass all those deities who are to be worshipped. I shall worship Agni and Viṣṇu with one oblation of cooked rice (*caru*); I shall worship Sarasvatī with one oblation of cooked rice; I shall worship Sarasvant with one oblation of cooked rice."

"I shall worship Agni Bhagin with one oblation of cooked rice (*caru*). Having stated, "In the supplementary *jaya-upahoma*: 'I shall worship Citta, Citti,' and so forth, ending with 'and Prajāpati with one oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*)," and having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* homa—beginning with "I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the remnants of the offering"—and having completed everything up to the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samid-abhyādhāna*), he should strew grass around the fire, spread *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, and upon them place the *sruva* spoon, the *darvī* ladle, the vessel for clarified butter, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, and the *upaveṣa*.

One should set out the darbha grass for placing the oblation, a winnowing basket, a black antelope skin, a mortar and pestle, four caru-pots, four stirring-spoons, darbha blades for cleansing, darbha blades for kindling, clarified butter, and fuel sticks.

According to the Āśvalāyana Sūtra—"Having mixed [the grains], one should offer the extracted portion"—and because the cooking of the three carus in milk is seen in a single location in the text "having cooked the sthālīpāka in milk" for the Śūlagava sacrifice, there may be only one caru-pot, only one stirring-spoon, and either four vessels for the purpose of extracting the portions or one large vessel; this is the distinction regarding the setting out of the vessels.

Then, having placed a winnowing basket (śūrpa) behind the fire and in front of himself, and having set the two strainers (pavitra) upon it, he should, with his right hand, silently pour out four handfuls for each deity while meditating upon that respective deity; having performed the pouring-in of the remaining grain (anvāvāpa), he places the oblation (havis) to the north of the fire, prepares the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī), sprinkles the oblation three times with the hand holding the strainers, turns the vessels face upwards, and sprinkles them all three times with all the water.

Then the wife, to the north of the fire, should perform the rites beginning with the shaking of the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) and ending with the husking of the grain (phalīkaraṇa), just as in the case of the Āgneya sthālīpāka.

Then the performer of the *homa* divides the prepared oblation into four equal portions, touches them in sequence saying, "This for Agni and Viṣṇu; this for Sarasvatī; this for Sarasvant; this for Agni Bhagina," and having poured water into four pots, he places the four portions therein in order and sets the pots upon the fire. If only one pot has been prepared, then having poured into that very pot enough water for the cooking, he places the entire oblation in it and sets it upon the fire.

Alternatively, there is no offering (nirvāpa) and so forth; rather, only the threshing by the wife must be performed. However, the carrying of fire around the oblation (paryagnikaraṇa) must certainly be done—this is another view.

Then, having cleansed the *sruva* ladle, the *darvī* spoon, and the *mekṣaṇa* stirring-stick, one should perform the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*). In that regard, the distinction is that the carrying of fire around the clarified butter is performed together with the sacrificial food (*havis*).

Then, having spread the darbha grass obtained there upon the ground behind the fire and having placed the clarified butter (ājya) upon it, he pours ghee over the cooked sacrificial porridges (carus) in sequence, removes them to the north, and places them on the sacrificial grass (barhis) behind the fire, arranged from south to north. In the case where they are cooked together, since there is only one caru, he pours ghee over it only once; then, having spread a base layer of ghee in each of the four vessels for taking out portions, he takes equal portions from it into them, saying: "This for Agni and Viṣṇu; this for Sarasvatī; this for Sarasvant."

"This [portion] is for Agni Bhagina"—thus one should now designate the deities in order, moving toward the south. However, when only a single vessel for drawing out the oblation has been set down, then both the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the drawing out (*uddharaṇa*) take place in that same single vessel, distinguished by location. Then, having sprinkled water around with the formulas beginning "O Aditi, give permission," and having silently placed a fuel-stick (*samidh*) on the fire, he should perform the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*). Having taken a portion from the first *caru* with the first *dhṛṣṭi*-shaped spoon, he offers it with the formula, "Svāhā to Agni and Viṣṇu. [The dedication is: "This is for Agni and Viṣṇu, not mine."

Then, having taken a portion of the second caru with a second stirring-spoon, he offers it before the first oblation, saying: "To Sarasvatī, svāhā!"—this is for Sarasvatī, not for me. Then, having taken a portion of the third caru with a third stirring-spoon, he offers it before the second oblation, saying: "To Sarasvant, svāhā!"—this is for Sarasvant, not for me.

Then, having taken a portion of the fourth *caru* with the fourth stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), he offers it before the third oblation, saying: "To Agni Bhagin, svāhā!"—[the formula being] "This is for Agni Bhagin, not mine. In the case of using a single vessel, since only one stirring-spoon has been set out, the taking [of the portion] is done with that very same spoon.

Then, with the *darvī* ladle, one should perform the supplementary oblation (*upahoma*) for the victory of the Vaiśeṣika. Regarding that, the specific rule is as follows: having taken twelve portions into the *darvī* with the *sruva* spoon, one offers the twelve *jaya* oblations. These have been described in the general ritual procedure. Again, having taken [the ghee] once, one offers it with the mantra: "Oṃ, Prajāpati conquered... bhūva svāhā. [The dedication is: "This is for Prajāpati, not for me."

Then, having once taken a portion from the northern half of each respective *caru* with its corresponding stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), he offers it into the northeast—without allowing it to touch the other oblations—with the formula: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!"—"This is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, not mine. If there is only one stirring-spoon, the taking of the portions is done with that same spoon. Thereafter, the throwing away of the stirring-spoon is optional.

Then, having removed the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa), performed the expiatory oblation (prāyaścitta-homa) with all the vyāhṛtis, and performed the final sprinkling (uttara-pariṣeka), he should worship the fire after approaching it with the *saṃsthā-japa*, apply the sacred ash (bhasma), give a pair of cattle as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya), give more to others, feed the Brahmins, and for the perfection of the rite, remember Viṣṇu.
These—the Caturhotṛ-homa, Sārasvata-homa, and Anvārambhaṇa-sthālīpāka—are optional (kṛtākṛta), because they are not mentioned in the Sūtra.
Thus ends the procedure for the Anvārambhaṇa-sthālīpāka.
Now follows the procedure for the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* (the full-moon and new-moon domestic offerings).

On the day of the preliminary preparation (*anvādhāna*), after the *aupāsana-homa*, one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) and one who has maintained them (*āhitāgni*)—accompanied by his wife, having sipped water (*ācamya*) and performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*)—should announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī, as long as I have the capacity and for as long as I live, I shall sacrifice with the *darśa-pūrṇamāsa-sthālīpākas*."

When it is determined that one accepts this very view—that after commencing the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* offerings are not to be performed—then there is a specific modification in the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa-sthālīpākas*, namely: "Until the time prior to the commencement of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, I shall perform the *darśapūrṇamāsa-sthālīpākas*. In reality, however, the position of performing them is indeed more appropriate.

Then, having worshipped Gaṇeśa and caused the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and so forth to be recited, one should say, "May Agni be pleased. This much is to be done only at the first performance, and not at every subsequent performance.

Then, having again performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and the formal proclamation of the place and time, one should make the resolve: "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*), I shall sacrifice with the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* *sthālīpāka* offerings. Therein, for the full-moon rite, one should make the resolve: "I shall sacrifice tomorrow with the *pūrṇamāsa-sthālīpāka*. In the case of an immediate performance, one says: "I shall sacrifice today. For the new-moon rite, however, the resolve is simply: "I shall sacrifice tomorrow with the *darśa-sthālīpāka*. Furthermore, the *darśa-sthālīpāka* itself may take two days' time. Alternatively, there may be two separate resolves: "I shall sacrifice tomorrow with the *pūrṇamāsa-sthālīpāka*" and "I shall sacrifice tomorrow with the *darśa-sthālīpāka*."

Having thus resolved, having kindled the fire, and having meditated upon it, he takes three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and performs the rites from "O Faith, come! up to the end of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). He declares: "In this ritual of the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice for the full moon, those deities who are to be sacrificed to, I shall encompass them. I shall sacrifice to Agni with one oblation of cooked rice (*caru*); I shall sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with one oblation of the remains of the offering. Having said, "These two deities I shall sacrifice to tomorrow," he should place the fuel-sticks for the preparatory rite (*anvādhāna*) with the *vyāhṛtis*. In the case of an immediate performance, he says, "I shall sacrifice today."
The same applies for the *darśa* (new moon sacrifice). The distinction there is that it is the ritual of the *darśa-sthālīpāka-yajña*.

Then, having strewn grass around the fire (*paristīrya*), he cuts darbha grass for the purpose of placing the vessels and so forth, ties it into a handful, and places it above the *aupāsana* fire in such a way that it does not fall [into the fire]. Because it is seen in the *śrauta* rites, the strewing may also take place after the evening oblation (*sāyaṃ-homa*). On this day, the husband and wife eat food mixed with clarified butter—excluding beans, meat, salt, alkaline substances, and the like—or, if they are unable [to obtain such], mixed with curd or milk; and they avoid whatever grain they intend to offer in the sacrifice. If they are unable [to do even this], they may eat [ordinary food].

Then, when the next day has dawned, after the morning *aupāsana* oblation, if he maintains the *śrauta* fires, he performs the sacrifice following the *iṣṭi*. To the north of the fire, having spread *darbha* grass, he places upon it the wooden ladle (*darvī*), the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the vessel for catching the grains that fall, the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the mortar (*ulūkhala*), the pestle (*musala*), the pot for the sacrificial porridge (*carusthālī*), the stirring spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), *darbha* grass for placing the oblation, *darbha* grass for cleansing, *darbha* grass for kindling, clarified butter, and fuel sticks. Having prepared the two strainers (*pavitra*), he places the winnowing basket to the west of the fire.

Having placed the two strainers upon it, having silently poured out four handfuls [of grain], and having placed a winnowing basket filled with rice to the north of the fire, he prepares the sprinkling water, sprinkles the rice in the winnowing basket, turns the vessels face upwards, and sprinkles them.

Then, to the north of the wife of the fire, having thrice shaken out a black antelope skin with its neck pointing westward and its hair on the upper side so as to serve as a place for cutting, and having spread it out, he places the hindquarters of the animal upon it; having established the mortar there, he pours rice-grains into it and, while remaining seated, threshes them with a pestle. Having placed a winnowing basket to the east of the mortar and poured the rice-grains from the mortar into the basket, he winnows them three times to the north of the black antelope skin, thereby scattering away the husks.

Without looking at them, he pours those husks beneath the black antelope skin with his right hand. Then, having pressed down the husks poured out with his very same right hand, touched water, and separated the rice grains, he causes them to fall into a vessel set out for that purpose; taking them, he places them in the mortar, threshes them three times, and having thrown the chaff to the north of the black antelope skin, he washes the rice grains and pours the washing water behind the fire.

Then the performer, having poured the washed rice grains into the vessel for the *caru* and stirred them with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), should cook them; then, having cleansed both the ladle (*darvī*) and the stirring-spoon, he should perform the rites beginning with the melting of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and ending with the placing of the two strainers (*pavitra*). In this process, the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) is performed for the *caru* together with the clarified butter.

Then, having spread the darbha grass obtained thereupon to the west of the fire and having placed the clarified butter (ājya) upon it, he should pour the cooked caru over with the clarified butter using a ladle, remove it from the fire towards the north, and place it on the strewn grass to the north of the clarified butter; then he should sprinkle water around the fire. Alternatively, at the conclusion of the placement of the vessels, having either spread a black antelope skin or not, and having had the wife perform only the threshing, he should husk the grain three times and discard the husks to the north.

Then, having performed the rites beginning with the wiping of the ladle (*darvī*) and ending with the placing of the purifiers (*pavitra*), and if the option of spreading *darbha* grass is chosen, having done that as well; one should sprinkle the cooked sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with clarified butter using the ladle, remove it from the fire toward the north, and place it on *darbha* grass behind the fire. If the option of not spreading *darbha* grass is taken, one should place it directly on the ground and then sprinkle the fire. These two methods of procedure are to be understood as applicable to all *sthālīpāka* offerings.

Then, having silently placed the seated fuel-stick on the fire and having taken a portion with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), he offers it into the blazing fire while his wife holds onto him: "Oṃ agnaye svāhā. [He thinks: "This is for Agni, not for me. Having again taken a portion, while his wife holds onto him, he offers it without letting it touch the previous offering, in the eastern half of the northern half [of the fire], saying: "Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā. [He thinks: "This is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, not for me. There may or may not be the holding-on-to (by the wife). Then he should throw the stirring-spoon into the fire; or there may be no throwing.

Then, having removed the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa), having offered four expiatory oblations (prāyaścittāhuti) with the Vyāhṛtis both individually and collectively, having performed the final sprinkling (uttara-pariṣeka), having worshipped the fire while standing near it with the Saṃsthājapa, having applied the sacred ash (vibhūti) to his forehead, and having given abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins and fed them, he should remember Viṣṇu. There is no gift of a bull (ṛṣabha-dāna) here. The ritual procedure beginning with the placing of fuel-sticks (samid-abhyādhāna) is the same in both of the methods of performance shown above.

This is because of the indicative force of the repeated statement, "He sacrifices with a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni," and because of the injunction of Āpastamba: "From this point forward, on the *parvan* days, the rite should be performed by the two [husband and wife] who have fasted, excluding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The same applies to the new moon (*darśa*) sacrifice.
