In this regard, if the wife is in her menses prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), then on the second day or any other day after the prohibited period—specifically from the fifth day onwards—one should perform the *sthālīpāka* for the full moon sacrifice either over a period of two days or immediately (*sadyaskāla*), provided the intervening period has passed.

In the case of impurity (*āśauca*), the commencement of the first *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *sthālīpāka* sacrifices does not take place. Nor should it be said that these two must be performed by one who is not of the same lineage (*asagotra*). For, just as there is non-commencement due to the unavailability of the primary material in the first performance, non-commencement is more appropriate here as well, owing to the absence of entitlement for the primary performer. However, even if interrupted, the *darśasthālīpāka* should be performed within the two-day period itself.

Among the wives of a man who has many wives, if the eldest wife becomes menstruating prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), then the *sthālīpāka* must be performed on the fifth day or subsequent days. If she becomes menstruating after the resolve, then having placed her within the house, the *sthālīpāka* should be performed at its own proper time.

Regarding the first performance, some hold that if menstrual blood appears for all or even any of the wives after the resolve, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) do not take place at all; others hold that they do take place.

If, after marriage, the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *sthālīpāka* sacrifices has not been undertaken and the sacred fires have subsequently been extinguished, then when they are rekindled after a long period of time, there arises the possibility of the impurity of menstruation (*rajas-doṣa*) at the time of their commencement. Or, when a bride is obtained after ten years or more, even at the time of the wedding itself, there is the possibility of the impurity of menstruation; in such cases, the first commencement [of the rites] does not take place. The same applies to the *āgrayaṇa-sthālīpāka* and other such rituals.

If the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the Sthālīpākas have not been commenced at their proper time, then one should cook Sthālīpākas dedicated to the deities of the *vibhraṣṭeṣṭi*. At the time of cooking, one should take the scum (*maṇḍa*) that has formed on top of the first and third potsherds and pour it into the oblation for Indra.

Then, having performed the rites from the preparation of the clarified butter (*ājya-saṃskāra*) up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) according to the *āpūrvika* ritual procedure, he should silently place a fuel-stick (*samidh*) on the fire and offer three oblations with the formulas: "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni; Oṃ, svāhā to Indra; Oṃ, svāhā to Soma. Having offered these, he should perform the subsequent ritual sequence beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering according to the *āpūrvika* rules. Regarding the first *darśa-sthālīpāka* that has been omitted: some say that when the next new moon arrives, one should perform the *vibhraṣṭa-sthālīpāka* and then perform the *sthālīpāka* at its own proper time.
Others say that after performing the *vibhraṣṭa-sthālīpāka*, one may perform the first *darśa-sthālīpāka* even during a secondary period (*gauṇakāla*).
Others maintain that one should perform only the *pathikṛt* and *vaiśvānara* offerings, but not the *vibhraṣṭa-sthālīpāka*.

However, it seems more appropriate to me that because the *darśa-sthālīpāka* has already been commenced by the commencement of the *paurṇamāsa-sthālīpāka*, there is no *vibhraṣṭa-sthālīpāka*. Otherwise, even the *anvārambhaṇīya-sthālīpāka* would have to be performed as a separate rite occasioned by a new commencement. According to the commentary on the *Śatapathabrāhmaṇa*, if the wife becomes menstruating before the commencement of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, then the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* should be commenced after offering the *saptahotṛ* oblation at the next *darśa*. The same applies in the case of ritual impurity (*āśauca*).

Thus concludes the procedure for the *darśapūrṇamāsa-sthālīpāka*. Now follows the *āgrayaṇa*. Although this is not mentioned in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, it must nevertheless be performed according to the general *sthālīpāka* rite prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* by following the alternative method (*anukalpa*) stated in the *Śrauta-sūtra*: "Having cooked four *śarāva*-measures of rice, one offers oblations to the deities of the *āgrayaṇa*, with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fourth, and then feeds [the guests] that side-dish. This is because of established custom (*ācāra*). Since it was not explicitly mentioned by the author of the *Sūtra*, its performance is optional (*kṛtākṛtaḥ*).

Regarding the option of performing [the sacrifice]: it must be performed every year until the commencement of the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, but not thereafter. Regarding the option of not performing it: there is no fault even in eating new grain, because there is no injunction [to the contrary]. Nevertheless, performance is preferable in accordance with established custom (*ācāra*). Its time is stated in the *Śrautasūtra*:
"Whether one sacrifices with an *iṣṭi*, or with an animal sacrifice (*paśu*), or with Soma, one should sacrifice on either the new-moon day or the full-moon day."

Regarding this, the author of the *Vaijayantī* states that by the terms *amāvāsyā* (new moon) and *paurṇamāsī* (full moon), the first days (*pratipad*) following them are also included. Rāmāṇḍāra, commenting on the *Āpastamba-sūtra* which has the same meaning, says: "By the terms *amāvāsyā* and *paurṇamāsī*, the final moment [of those nights] is grasped; therefore, it occurs during the day-and-night (*ahorātra*) containing that moment. Mādhava also states: "The conclusion is that all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), such as the *iṣṭi*, take place only on the *parvan* [day].
Regarding this, Baudhāyana mentions the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) of the gods and Revatī.
"Or rather, one should perform the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice under a lunar mansion belonging to the gods, or under Revatī.

Regarding the performance of the rite under a lunar mansion belonging to the gods, there is also a Śruti text: "Whatever one might do under those very lunar mansions belonging to the gods, he performs it on an auspicious day. Regarding the performance of the rite under the Revatī lunar mansion, there is likewise a Śruti text:
"Therefore, one should perform [the rite] for cattle under the Revatī asterism; whatever is performed subsequent to the Soma sacrifice truly comes to pass.
In response to the inquiry as to which are the divine asterisms (*devanakṣatra*), it is stated in that very same place:
"Kṛttikā is the first; Viśākhā is the last. These are the divine asterisms."

These lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) must be understood as occurring only within the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*), and not even those occurring within the waning fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Consequently, the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) takes place only on the lunar mansions situated within the bright fortnight. In that case, whether the full-moon day (*parvan*) occurs at the conclusion of the day or at the junction of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), one should perform the modified sacrifice on that very day and then commence the primary sacrifice (*prakṛti*), because the time prescribed by the scriptural injunction "if one should desire" (*yadi iṣṭyā*) has been obtained. This is a point of complete agreement between the Mīmāṃsakas and the ritualists (*yājñikas*).

Regarding the junction of the morning (*pūrvāhṇasaṃdhi*), the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that since the time of the junction is prescribed for the primary sacrifice (*prakṛti*) on the preceding lunar day (*parvan*), it is proper to perform the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) on that very same day, overriding the morning time obtained through extension (*atideśa*)—just as the two-day period is overridden—because the morning time is already occupied by the primary sacrifice.

However, the ritualists (*yājñikas*), as stated in the *Kālatattvavivecana*, say that after performing the primary sacrifice at either the *āvartana* (midday) or the preceding junction, the performance of the modified sacrifice must take place on the very day of the junction itself.
Regarding the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, a specific rule is stated in the Śruti concerning the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*: [text follows].

"At whatever time the new moon (amāvāsyā) should occur, having sacrificed with that [new moon], one should then sacrifice with this [Āgrayaṇa]; if it should be the full moon (paurṇamāsī), having sacrificed with that [full moon], one should then sacrifice with the full moon [offering]. The remainder [of the sentence] is "before the turning point" (āvartanāt). "Should occur" means it should arrive. "With that" refers to the new moon; "with this" refers to the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice. If the full moon should arrive before the time of the turning point, then having sacrificed with that Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, one should sacrifice with the full moon offering.
Maṇḍana also states:
"If the junction of the lunar phases (parvasaṃdhi) occurs before the turning [of the sun], one should perform the primary rite (prakṛti) at that time and the modified rite (vikṛti) afterwards;
if it should occur after, then the modified rite is performed at that time and the primary rite on the following day."

The meaning of this is as follows: if the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasaṃdhi*) occurs before the sun’s turning point (*āvartana*), one should first perform the *prakṛti* (archetypal rite) on that day of conjunction and subsequently perform the *vikṛti* (modified rite). However, when the junction occurs after the turning point, then on the day of conjunction only the *vikṛti* takes place, while the *prakṛti* is performed on the following day. Dhūrtasvāmin, Kapardisvāmin, and others have also stated this. In that regard, the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice is of three kinds: the *Āgrayaṇa* of rice (*vrīhi*), the *Āgrayaṇa* of barley (*yava*), and the *Āgrayaṇa* of *śyāmāka* millet.
Regarding these, the Sūtra states: "One sacrifices with the first-fruits of the rice, and likewise with the *śyāmāka* grains."
"He sacrifices with the first-fruits of barley.
"First-fruits" (agrapāka) means that which is harvested at that specific time. The times for these are stated by Vaikhānasa, Āpastamba, and Bharadvāja:
"In autumn with rice, in spring with barley, and in the rainy season with *śyāmāka* grain."

In that regard, the *yavāgrayaṇa* (the first-fruits offering of barley) is both performed and not performed. This is stated in the *Vaijayantī* on the *Bāhvṛcya*: "The *yavāgrayaṇa* is both performed and not performed. And this is for the purpose of authorizing the eating of new grain.
Accordingly, the Sūtra says: "We shall explain the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*; having performed it, one does not eat the fruits of new herbs, whether cultivated or wild."
The meaning is that, having not performed that Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, one does not eat the fruits of new cultivated or wild plants.
Maṇḍana has clearly stated all of this:
"Śyāmāka, bamboo seeds, rice, or barley—before the Āgrayaṇa..."
"One should not eat"—this has been clearly set forth in the *Yajñapārśva*.
One may eat at will these things— grains in pods, leafy vegetables, and the fruits of trees— even without having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice.
Among grains stored in granaries, nothing is understood to be unfit for consumption;
even mung beans, black gram, and sesame seeds are so according to the established doctrines of Bharadvāja and others.
One should not eat new grains in the new [autumn] months before the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.
One should avoid rice, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, barley, bamboo-grain, as well as *śāli* rice, mung beans, wheat, and *kaṅgu*.
"One may eat other things at will," so it was said by Garga.
Some do not eat the fruits of the harimantha and kalāya,
nor any other edible foods that have been mentioned immediately after.
A wise person may eat even those at will while they are in an unripe state;
"green barley" is an illustration for all types of unripe grain.
The commentator on the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* has described it thus:
"The author of the Bhāradvājīya-bhāṣya stated that the other grain resembling barley is the green barley (*haritayava*),
and not some other kind of barley."

"Therefore, one should not eat other fruits as well, with the exception of those [specific ones]. Green *manthā* beans are *caṇaka* (chickpeas), and *kalāya* are *satīna* (a type of pea). The meaning is that some teachers do not eat the fruit of these plants in the form of *caṇaka* and *kalāya*. The prohibition against eating new grain before the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice is the same for both.
And likewise Maṇḍana says:
"This prohibition against eating new [grain] applies equally to both husband and wife.
He has also stated the nature of what is considered "new":
Since novelty depends upon a limit, that limit is now stated:
at what distance does antiquity lie, and how near is novelty?
The full moon day of Jyeṣṭha is well known as the lower limit for grains,
while the full moon day of Āśvina shall be the upper limit in this case.
Whatever grain may arise between those two such full-moon days, they call that "new" (nava) in relation to the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice performed at that time.
And that very [grain] would be considered "old" after the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice;
for according to the rules regarding the Āgrayaṇa, it is regarded as "new" only in relation to that [sacrifice].
Those times which are present to his mind are considered to have their own mutual limits:
after the rainy season, [the grain] ripens, and in autumn, by means of the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.
That which is produced after spring is [offered] with the *prāvṛṭ-āgrayaṇa*;
in whichever season one performs the *āgrayaṇa*, it is called "produced in that season."
"They say that grain which is [freshly] harvested is new, while that which has ripened underground is old.
And this [offering] does not apply even to an *āhitāgni* who maintains the *ardhādhāna* (half-fuel) rite, because it is already accomplished by the *śrauta* ritual alone. Maṇḍana also says:
Thus, by those who uphold the Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa, it has been stated on the grounds of logical parity: "When the half-consecration (ardhādheya) has been performed, for him only the Vedic Āgrayaṇa occurs;
the Smārta Āgrayaṇa does not take place."
If one is unable to perform it oneself, it should be performed by a priest who has already performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.
As Maṇḍana says:
"One who has not performed the *Āgrayaṇa* shall not serve as his priest for the *Āgrayaṇa*."

"It has been established in the *Dharmaśāstra* by Śaṅkha that [one is] 'possessed of fire' (*agnimān*). Even when one does not eat new grain, this rite must certainly be performed according to the view that it should be done. "The Soma sacrifice is to be performed every year, as is the animal sacrifice at each solstice."
For it is stated by Yājñavalkya: "The Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsyas must indeed be performed;
in the absence of these, a twice-born man should perform the Vaiśvānareṣṭi.
Among these, the first Āgrayaṇa must take place on the full-moon day (parvan) itself, whereas for the second and subsequent ones, there is no such restriction.
Now, the procedure:

At the prescribed time, having performed the morning *aupāsana* oblation, the sacrificer, together with his wife, should sit behind the fire. Having sipped water (*ācamana*) and performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "For the propitiation of the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of accomplishing my entitlement to consume the nine types of grains such as rice (*vrīhi*) and others, together with my wife, I shall perform the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice for the first-fruits (*āgrayaṇa*) of rice."

If, however, for some reason one does not perform the *navānna-prāśana* (the first feeding of new grain), then the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) should be made thus: "For the sake of pleasing the illustrious Supreme Lord, I shall perform the *sthālīpāka* offering of the *vrīhyāgrayaṇa*. If, however, in a given year a particular type of grain is not produced, then the *āgrayaṇa* for that grain is omitted in that year. The first *āgrayaṇa* is not performed during the heliacal setting of Jupiter or Venus, during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), and so forth. Even in subsequent performances, if a pure time is available, it should not be done during such periods as the setting [of Jupiter or Venus].

Then, having worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should perform the recitation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*), and the *nāndīśrāddha*. In this regard, the specific detail for the first performance is that one should say, "May Indra, Agni, and the others be pleased."

Then, having kindled the fire and meditated upon it, and having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), he performs the rites up to the end of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the formula beginning "O Faith, come here" (*śraddha ehi*). He then declares: "In this *Āgrayaṇa* *sthālīpāka* rite, I shall encompass all those deities who are to be sacrificed to. I shall sacrifice to Indra and Agni, to the Viśvedevas, and to Heaven and Earth, each with one offering of cooked rice (*caru*) made from fresh *vrīhi* grain. In the *Sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, I shall sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an offering of the remaining cooked rice."

Having said, "I shall sacrifice immediately to these deities," one should perform the placing of the fuel-sticks (*anvādhāna*) and the adding of the kindling wood (*samid-abhyādhāna*) with the *vyāhṛti* formulas. According to the view that the *ājyānī* oblation is to be offered before the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the mention of the deities of the *ājyānī* oblation must be made immediately after the mention of the principal deities during the *anvādhāna*. It is as follows: regarding the *ājyānī* oblation—one shall sacrifice to Indra with an oblation of clarified butter; one shall sacrifice to Heaven and Earth with an oblation of clarified butter; and one shall sacrifice to Summer, Winter, Spring, Autumn, and the Rainy season with an oblation of clarified butter.

Having said, "I shall worship Idāvatsara, Parivatsara, and Saṃvatsara with an oblation of clarified butter; I shall worship the Devas and Pitṛs with an oblation of clarified butter," he should perform the rites from the offering of the remnant of the cooked rice (caru) to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt up to the placing of the fuel-sticks (samid-abhyādhāna).

Then, "having strewn grass around the fire," and so forth. During the placement of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*), one should set down: a wooden ladle (*darvī*), a vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), a vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), a fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), a cooking pot (*carusthālī*) sufficient for boiling the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) measured by four *śarāva* units, a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), one *śarāva* for the purpose of pouring out the grain (*nirvāpa*), *darbha* grass for wiping (*saṃmārga*), *darbha* grass for kindling (*avajvalana*), clarified butter, and fuel sticks (*samidh*). According to the view that the stirring-spoon is discarded [at the end], the placing of the stirring-spoon occurs after the placing of the *śarāva*.

Then, having prepared the two strainers (*pavitra*), he places a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) behind the fire; having placed the two strainers upon it with their tips pointing eastward, he takes the prepared shallow bowl (*śarāva*), fills it with rice grains, and pours them out into the winnowing basket while meditating upon all the deities. He does this in this manner three times.

Then, to the north of the fire, having placed a winnowing basket containing the poured-out rice, one should perform the *ājyānī* oblation. It is as follows: Having spread *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, and having placed upon it the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the *upaveṣa*, the *darbha* blades for wiping, the *darbha* blades for kindling, the clarified butter sufficient for the oblation, and five fuel-sticks; then, taking the two strainers already prepared, having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters, and having turned the vessels intended for the *ājyānī* oblation face upwards and sprinkled them with water.

Having performed the heating of the *sruva* and *sruk* spoons and so forth, up to the point of pouring out the clarified butter (*ājya*) three times and setting it aside, one should place the two *pavitra* strainers in their designated positions. In the alternative procedure where other rites are performed, there is indeed the disposal [of the strainers], but there is no surrounding-strewing (*paristaraṇa*) of the fire, since that is already accomplished by the strewing previously performed.

Then, having silently sprinkled water around [the fire], and having taken five portions [of clarified butter] with the *sruva* ladle into the *sruc* offering-ladle, he places five fuel-sticks upon the fire. For the five mantras beginning with "To the one armed with a hundred weapons" (*śatāyudhāya*), Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Indra is the deity of the first; Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivyau*) of the second; Summer, Winter, Spring, Autumn, and the Rainy season of the third; the *iduvatsara*, *parivatsara*, and *saṃvatsara* years of the fourth; and the Gods and the Father (*pitṛ*) of the fifth. The meter (*chandas*) for all is the Jagatī. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the oblation (*homa*).

Thus one should remember the Ṛṣis and so forth; there is no remembering of the deities (*varṣi*) and so forth here. "Oṃ śatāyudhāya... viśvā svāhā. To Indra, this, not to me. "Oṃ ye catvāraḥ... sarve svāhā. To Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), this, not to me. "Oṃ grīṣmo hemanta... syāma svāhā. To Grīṣma, Hemanta, Vasanta, Śarad, and Varṣā, this, not to me. "Oṃ iduvatsarāya... hatāḥ syāma svāhā. To Iduvatsara, Parivatsara, and Saṃvatsara, this, not to me.

"Oṃ bhadrān naḥ śreyaḥ syonaḥ svāhā. [Reciting] "This is for the gods and the ancestors, not mine," he should offer the five *ājyānī* oblations while standing to the south of the fire. Then, taking the *prokṣaṇī* vessel from the *sthālīpāka* vessel, he should prepare the *prokṣaṇī* water and perform the rites beginning with the sprinkling of the sacrificial food (*havis*) up to the cooking of the *caru* measured in four *śarāva* portions.

Next, having performed the rites beginning with the pouring of clarified butter over the *caru* up to its placement upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he should sprinkle water around the fire with the mantras beginning with "adite" and place one of the prepared fuel-sticks (*samidh*) upon it.
Then, having taken a portion from the caru with the stirring-spoon, he offers it with the mantra: "Oṃ, svāhā to Indra and Agni! [Thinking: "This is for Indra and Agni, not mine."

Then, having again taken a portion in the same manner, he offers it with: "Oṃ, svāhā to the Viśvedevas. [He says: "This is for the Viśvedevas, not mine. Having again taken a portion in the same manner, he offers it with: "Oṃ, svāhā to Heaven and Earth. [He says: "This is for Heaven and Earth, not mine. At this point, there may be an offering of clarified butter (ājyānī-homa). In this alternative, there is no preparation of the clarified butter, because prepared butter is already present. However, the placing of a fuel-stick (samit) upon the fire must indeed occur after each oblation, since there is no sacrificial wood (idhma) available. Or else, the ājyānī-homa may simply be omitted.

Then, having taken a further portion from the northern half with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), he offers it toward the northeast with the formula, "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," so that it does not touch the other oblations. [The dedication is: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, this, not mine. Then he should throw the stirring-spoon into the fire, or he may not throw it.

Then, having discarded the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa), he should offer four expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittāhuti*) with the *darvī* ladle using the *Vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively; having performed the subsequent sprinkling (*uttarapariṣeka*) with the mantras beginning with "O Aditi, you have assented," he should worship the fire with the *saṃsthājapa*, apply ashes to his body, give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*), and for the perfection of the rite, he should call Viṣṇu to mind.
Then, having fed the Brahmins with fresh rice mixed with side dishes and the remnants of the oblation, he himself [should eat] prior to the *prāṇāhuti* offerings.

For the mantra *bhadrān naḥ*, the deities are the Viśvedevas, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the consumption of fresh rice. Having recited the mantra, "Oṃ bhadrān naḥ śreyaḥ syonaḥ," one should eat the new grain according to the procedure for the *prāṇāhuti* offerings, accompanied by beloved kinsmen and others. If there is vomiting after eating food mixed with the remnants of the oblation (*hutaśeṣa*), one must perform the very same expiation as for vomiting the *iḍābhāga*.
This is stated in the *Ādhānadīpikā*: "If, indeed, vomiting should occur when the *iḍābhāga* has been consumed..."
Then, one should recite this mantra ten times with these verses.
"Having performed a bath and the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), for the pacification of that fault."

Having first performed a bath for the sake of purification silently, one should then perform another bath and the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the mantra beginning "ābhir gīrbhiḥ," followed by the recitation (*japa*) of that same mantra ten times. However, according to the reading, "Having performed the sprinkling with this [mantra] for the pacification of its defects," the procedure should be understood as follows: having performed the sprinkling with the mantra "ābhir," one should then perform the recitation of this very mantra ten times. The initial bath, however, is established by the sense of the context. This reading alone is appropriate.
Thus concludes the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice for the first-fruits of rice (*vrīhy-āgrayaṇa*).

Now follows the *Yavāgrayaṇa*. That takes place in the spring. Therein, the formula for the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "I shall perform the *sthālīpāka* of the first-fruits of barley. The sacrificial oblation (*caru*) consists of fresh barley. The specific distinction is that the mantra "etamu tyaṃ madhunā saṃyutaṃ yavam" (this barley joined with honey) is used in place of the mantra "bhadrān naḥ śreyaḥ". Everything else is the same. Regarding the mantra "etamu tyam": the seers are the Viśvedevas; the deity is barley-food; the meter is *jagatī*; and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the consumption of fresh barley-food—thus should the seer and other details be known. This *Yavāgrayaṇa* may be performed or omitted at will.
Now follows the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice with *śyāmāka* grain.

The formula for the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "I shall perform the *sthālīpāka* offering of *śyāmāka*. The sacrificial oblation (*caru*) consists of fresh *śyāmāka* grain; Soma is the deity. Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second [deity], and Agni is the first.

For the mantra beginning with "May Agni eat first," the deities are the Viśve Devās, the substance is the *śyāmāka* food, and the meter is *Anuṣṭubh*. There is a separation [of the ritual] at the consumption of the fresh *śyāmāka* food. The specific detail is that the mantra for consuming the fresh *śyāmāka* food is: "Oṃ, may Agni eat first, the protector of the people... The rest is the same.

Alternatively, for the sake of accomplishing the *śyāmākāgrayaṇa*, one should prepare sacrificial grass (*barhis*) made of *śyāmāka* stalks for the *pārvaṇasthālīpāka*. Or else, having given fresh *śyāmāka* grains to a cow, the morning and evening *aupāsana* oblations should be offered with her milk; by that alone, its accomplishment is achieved. If one is unable to perform the *vrīhyāgrayaṇasthālīpāka*, the two *pārvaṇasthālīpākas* should be performed using only new *vrīhi* rice. Or else, having given the new *vrīhi* rice to a cow, the morning and evening *aupāsana* oblations should be offered with her milk.
Maṇḍana also states another alternative method:
"In the Gṛhya-sūtra, Baudhāyana has stated: 'If the New Moon sacrifice (naveṣṭi) cannot be performed, one should provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas or perform the Vaiśvadeva rite.'"

This should be understood to apply when the secondary alternatives (*anukalpa*) prescribed in the Sūtras are impossible. Furthermore, this *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice does not take place during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), an *asta*, and so forth, because the pure time (*śuddhakāla*) is available. However, in the absence of old grain, it may indeed take place even then. If, due to divine or human obstacles, the *Āgrayaṇa* is not performed during the autumn season, then one should perform the overdue *Āgrayaṇa* during the winter or the cool season.
This concludes the *Āgrayaṇa-sthālīpāka*.
Now follows the *Garbhādhāna* (conception rite).
In this regard, first the results of the month, fortnight, and so forth at the onset of the first menstruation are stated.
Among these, the result for the month is given in the *Vidhānamālā* according to the *Vārāha*:
"At her first menses, a woman will certainly become a widow if it occurs in the month of Caitra."
In Vaiśākha she shall have many sons; in Jyeṣṭha she shall become afflicted by disease.
In Āṣāḍha she shall be childless; in Śrāvaṇa she will be wealthy;
in Bhādrapada she will be unfortunate; and in Āśvina she will be a mere ascetic woman.
A young woman who becomes a widow in Kārttika will have many children in Mārgaśīrṣa;
she will be unchaste in Pauṣa, but endowed with the happiness of sons in Māgha.
"In Phālguna she is endowed with happiness; this is recorded as the fruit for the first season.
Regarding the fruit of the lunar fortnight, the *Smṛticandrikā* states: "In the bright fortnight she will be of virtuous character; in the dark fortnight she will become unchaste."
Up until the tenth [tithi] of the dark fortnight, one should designate the fruit as middling.

"On the Ekādaśī and other such days, the fruit is proclaimed to be inferior. Regarding the fruit of the lunar days (*tithi*) as well, it is stated in that very same place: "The first day (*pratipad*) indeed bestows widowhood, while the second day increases one's sons."
The third lunar day bestows good fortune, while the fourth destroys happiness.
The fifth [lunar day] indeed bestows happiness, while the sixth destroys one's progeny;
the seventh leads to the loss of wealth, and the eighth grants sons and good fortune.
The ninth day brings affliction to women, while the tenth bestows happiness;
the eleventh leads to the destruction of wealth, and the twelfth increases pleasure.
"The thirteenth day, however, bestows auspiciousness, while the fourteenth is ill-fated;
the full moon and the new moon days increase suffering and disease."

In another Jyotiḥ-grantha, however, it is said: "A fortunate woman who begins her menses on the first lunar day (pratipad) becomes menstruating [on that very day]"; likewise, "the seventh [day] increases wealth"; likewise, "on the eighth [day], she is a demoness-like woman"; likewise, "on the eleventh [day] she is endowed with happiness; on the twelfth [day], she is an unfortunate woman"; and likewise, "on the full moon day (pūrṇamāsī), she has excellent sons. Thus, contrary results are stated for the lunar days beginning from the first and ending with the twelfth.

In this context, the *pratipad* (first lunar day) situated near the full moon (*pūrṇimā*) is to be accepted. However, in the statement "the *pratipad* bestows widowhood," the *pratipad* situated near the new moon (*amā*) is to be accepted, because that [lunar day] is equal to the non-self (the soul-less) due to its lack of the moon's waning. When there is a prohibition regarding the seventh lunar day, the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa*) is to be accepted; the same should be understood for the eighth, eleventh, and twelfth lunar days. The prohibition regarding the full moon refers to the first half of the full moon, because that possesses the nature of *bhadrā*; the injunction, however, should be understood to refer to the other portion. Regarding the fruit of the weekday, the *Vārāha-saṃhitā* states in the *Vidhānamālā*: "On Sunday, a woman becomes a widow; on Monday, she has dead offspring."
If Mars is so placed, she becomes a destroyer of her own self; if Mercury, she will give birth to a daughter.
"If Jupiter [is in the seventh house], a woman will have sons; if Venus, she will give birth to both daughters and sons;
if Saturn, she will be unchaste and die before her husband."
She is Rajovatī. However, in the Nāradīya it is said:

"One who is sickly, devoted to her husband, miserable, possessed of sons, an enjoyer of pleasures, beloved by her husband, or a partaker of suffering [is born] on Sundays and the other days respectively."

The term *mṛtaprajā* (one whose children have died) refers to a Monday during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), while *pativratā* (a devoted wife) refers to a Monday during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*); therefore, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the results of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), it is stated in the *Vārāha*:
"Aśvinī brings happiness to women; Bharaṇī increases their desire."

Kṛttikā should be known as bestowing wretchedness; Rohiṇī shall be the giver of happiness. Mṛgaśiras leads to the enjoyment of desires, while the asterism presided over by Rudra (Ārdrā) bestows happiness.
The constellation of Aditi (Punarvasu) would grant happiness, and the asterism of Bṛhaspati (Puṣya) increases happiness.
Āśleṣā is known to cause the destruction of happiness; Maghā is remembered as bestowing widowhood; Pūrvaphalgunī increases the joy of sons and daughters;
Uttaraphalgunī indeed leads to the loss of wealth; and Hasta promotes the increase of sons.
Citrā makes a woman beautiful of form; of this there is no doubt.
Svātī is for the welfare of women, while Viśākhā is the destroyer of happiness. Anurādhā leads to wealth and enjoyment, whereas Jyeṣṭhā bestows separation from one's husband.
"The root asterism Śravaṇā, as well as Pūrvāṣāḍhā, causes the destruction of wealth;
Uttarāṣāḍhā bestows happiness, and Śravaṇa increases happiness.
The five asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā grant happiness to women during their first menses."

In the *Ratnamālā*, however, it is said: "The first lunar day (*pratipad*) occurring on the signs of the hands (Aries), the five subsequent ones (Taurus–Virgo), the root (Capricorn), the sun (Leo), Viṣṇu (Sagittarius), the triad of horses (Gemini, Libra, Aquarius), Jupiter (Pisces), and the moon (Cancer) brings women fortune, longevity accompanied by happiness, wealth, and an increase in good luck."

It is said: "If [the moon] is in the three eastern asterisms (Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Pūrvabhādrapadā) or in the asterisms of Yama (Bharaṇī) and the Serpent (Āśleṣā), it will surely bring widowhood to her.
In Maghā and Īśa (Ārdrā) there is grief; likewise, in Aditi (Punarvasu) she is barren, and in Indra (Jyeṣṭhā) and Anala (Kṛttikā) she is poor.

The group of five beginning with Hasta consists of the asterisms Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā. By the word "uttara" (northern), the three Uttaras (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Uttarabhādrapadā) are meant. Īśa is Ārdrā. Aindra is Jyeṣṭhā. Anala is Kṛttikā.
In another treatise, there is this distinction:

"If she is menstruating during the first portion of the asterisms of Aśvinī, Maghā, Mūla, Āśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Revatī, she becomes an unchaste woman; if during the last portion, she becomes barren or one whose children have died."

Dasra refers to the Aśvinī constellation; Sarpa refers to Āśleṣā; Śakra refers to Jyeṣṭhā; and Pauṣṇa refers to Revatī. Regarding these, there is a mutual contradiction in the results of certain constellations; this is to be resolved by their inclusion within the bright (śukla) or dark (kṛṣṇa) lunar fortnights. Auspicious results pertain to constellations occurring within the bright fortnight, while prohibited results pertain to constellations occurring within the dark fortnight. Thus concludes the results of the constellations. Now, the results of the *yogas*. Vasiṣṭha states in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
If a woman is menstruating during the first period on the Viṣkambha yoga, she will be unfortunate;
on Atigaṇḍa, she will be barren; on Śūla, she will suffer from colic;
on Gaṇḍa, she will become unchaste; and on Vyāghāta, she will be a suicide.
"In Vajra, she is said to be wanton; in Pāta, a killer of her husband;
in Parigha, a barren woman whose children die; and in Vaidhṛti, a slayer of her husband.
The remaining yogas bring auspiciousness, yielding results according to their names."
In another text, there is this specific detail:
"On the new moon, at the solar transits, during the *viṣṭi* and other such [inauspicious] times, as well as during the *vyatīpāta* and *vaidhṛti* yogas;
in the first half of the *parigha* yoga, and in the six *gaṇḍa*, *atigaṇḍa*, and [other] *gaṇḍa* periods."
"In Vyāghāta and Śūla there are nine [inauspicious] nāḍīs, and five in the appearance of the Ṛtu";
the word "to be avoided" is to be supplied as the remainder.
The results of these are stated in that very same work:
"In these [lunar days], a woman in her menses experiences, in sequence: widowhood, loss of wealth, loss of sons, great fear, widowhood,
increase of enemies, poverty, a diminished life-span,
loss of luster, and misfortune."
Thus ends the fruit of Yoga.
Now, the fruit of Karaṇa:
"If [the Moon is] in Bava, a woman will be either menstruating, barren, or a widow."
In Bālava, a woman becomes possessed of sons; in Kaulava, she becomes a young woman; in Taitila, she becomes highly esteemed; in Gara, a woman perishes;
in Vaṇija, she has lost her offspring; and in Viṣṭi, she is destitute of wealth.
"In Śakuni and Catuṣpāda, a woman shall attain widowhood;
in Nāga, a woman finds no pleasure; in Kiṃstughna, she becomes a widow. Thus ends the fruit of the Karaṇas.
Now, the results of the ascendant (*lagna*).
Vasiṣṭha, in the *Jyotirnibandha*, states: "In Aries, she is unchaste; in Taurus, she belongs to another."
In Gemini, she is rich in wealth and enjoyments; in Cancer, she is unchaste.
In the sign of Leo she will be rich in sons; likewise, in Virgo she will be illustrious;
in Libra she will be wise; and in Scorpio she will be devoted to her husband.
In the sign of Dhanus, she is of ill conduct; in the next (Makara), she is devoted to her husband;
in Makara, she is devoid of pride; and in Kumbha, there is poverty and barrenness.
"In the case of the unusual sign of Pisces as the ascendant, the placement of the planets is like that for marriage."

The meaning is that she is of ill conduct in the first part of the bow [sign] and devoted to her husband in the latter part. The placement of the planets and the worship of the planets are like those for marriage. The meaning is that it becomes two or three times according to one's capacity.
However, in the *Vārāha* [section] of the *Jyotirnibandha*: "In Aries, she is a killer of herself or a destroyer of the embryo; in Taurus, she shall have sons."
In Gemini, there is a woman who gives birth to twins; in Cancer, a woman whose children have died.

If [the conception occurs] under Siṃha, she attains widowhood; if under Kanyā, she will give birth to daughters; if under Tulā, she will be blessed with many sons; and if under Vṛścika (Alini), she will be devoted to wicked deeds.

"It has been said: 'In Sagittarius (Cāpa), she will be rich in sons and wealth; in Capricorn (Mṛga), she will be of wicked conduct; in Aquarius (Kumbha), she will have offspring once; and in Pisces (Mīna), she will have few children.'"

*Ali* means a scorpion; *alinī* is an archaic (Vedic) usage. Here too, the determination should be understood as before, based on whether [the Moon] falls within the bright or dark fortnight. Thus ends the results of the ascendant.
Now, the results of the planets situated in the seventh house at the time of the first appearance of menses (*ṛtudarśana-lagna*), according to the *Nārasiṃhīya*:
The Sun situated in the seventh house from the ascendant causes widowhood;
the Moon should be known as the giver of virtuous sons, and one will certainly obtain good fortune.
Mars causes the loss of sons, while Mercury bestows virtuous sons;
Jupiter brings wealth and longevity, and Venus causes rivalry with co-wives.

"If Saturn [is there], she will be barren; if Rāhu, death is certain. Thus end the results for planets situated in the seventh house at the time of the onset of menstruation. Now, the results of the *velā* (time).
In that very same [text]:
"The first appearance of menses for women at the time of dawn increases sorrow;
at the hour of Saṃgava it leads to a succession of happiness; at midday, to a succession of wealth."
In the afternoon there is the acquisition of wealth; in the evening, middling results;
in the first part of the night, it is sufficient for happiness; and at midnight, there is the loss of wealth.
"The loss of wealth at the end of the night is recorded as the result for the first menses;
likewise, there will be great fear during the two twilights, as well as the loss of wealth."
But elsewhere it is said:
"In the forenoon there is indeed gain; at midday, middling results;
in the afternoon, widowhood; and in the first part of the night, there shall be auspiciousness."
It is said: "At midnight, the middling [period] occurs; in the latter part of the night, the auspicious ones occur."
Auspicious [acts] during the auspicious [period], and inauspicious during the inauspicious. Thus ends the result of the time-periods.
Now, the results of planetary eclipses. Bhārgava says:
If birth should occur during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or at the very beginning of the appearance of the menses—
whosoever is born in such a manner, his death will surely come; of this there is no doubt.
"There shall be disease, suffering, poverty, grief, and strife."

The meaning is: it belongs to him from whom the birth occurs, and to that woman who experiences the appearance of the menses (*ṛtudarsana*). The pacification (*śānti*) for these causes will be explained in the *Śāntiratnamālā*. Thus ends the result for the planet itself.
Now, the result for the observer:
"The menstrual blood (*rajas*) which is seen by a mature woman (*puraṃdhrī*) leads to the happiness of women."
But whatever is seen by a woman who has been dismembered is remembered as bringing widowhood.
"If a maiden or a man sees the dust, it will result in happiness;
likewise, if women see it themselves, it leads to their own destruction."

A *puraṃdhrī* is a woman endowed with good fortune; a *viśastā* is a widow. These are the results for the observer (*draṣṭṛ*). Now, the results for the querent (*praṣṭṛ*): "If the mother asks, it is fruitless; if the father asks, there is happiness."
The brother-in-law incurs poverty, while the sister attains the happiness of long life.
"The sister-in-law obtains wealth; the uterine sister obtains abundant wealth;
and the brother-in-law [obtains] a reduction in his lifespan—thus does the woman receive [her lot]."

If the brother-in-law asks, then the meaning is that Rajovatī incurs poverty. If the father’s sister (pitṛṣvasā), the father’s sister-in-law, asks, then wealth goes [to her], meaning she obtains wealth.
Now, the fruit of the garment worn:
"She who wears white garments shall be fortunate; she who wears new garments shall be devoted to her husband."
She would be unfortunate with worn-out clothes, but fortunate when wearing linen garments.
"If the menstrual blood be red, she will be barren; if it be variegated in color, she will have sons;
but if it be black, the woman will become a widow—such is the characteristic sign of the menses."
Thus ends the fruit of wearing the garment.
Now, the fruit of the menses:
"The fruit of the menses for women in their first period is now being declared."
She becomes fortunate and endowed with sons when her menstrual flow is of a white color.
If it resembles the blood of a hare or is like lac, there will be the birth of a son and a daughter; but if it is blue, one will have offspring who die.
If the menstrual flow is white like camphor, a woman dies immediately; if it is tawny, her children die;
and if it is black, the woman becomes a widow—one should thus predict the outcome according to the color of the menses.

If there is only a single drop of blood, she is a wanton woman; if the blood is scanty, she is independent; if it flows moderately, she is excellent; but if the blood is profuse, she will be unfortunate.
If it is red, there will be a son; if black, a daughter who dies;
if it has a slimy appearance, she will be barren; and if pale, she will be a "crow-barren" woman (one whose children die in infancy).
"If it is yellow, she is said to be a wanton woman; if the color of the *guñjā* berry, she is fortunate;
if it has the luster of vermilion, she is a maiden—such are the characteristics of the menstrual flow."

"In *rakte*, *lohite*, and *rakte* means when [the blood] is red, that is, when it is of a red color; such is the fruit of *rajas*. Now, the fruit of portents: 'If the first menstruation occurs during the twilights, under an eclipse, or on the *viṣṭi* yoga, it is inauspicious.'"
Thus ends the result of the portents.
Now, the result of the number of dots (*bindu*):
"A menstruating woman obtains good fortune by means of even a single dot."
With two dots there is enjoyment; with three dots there is disease.
"Poorness occurs when [the moon] is in the higher signs; this is the characteristic of [the influence of] Rajas.
Thus ends the fruit of the Bindus.
Now follows the fruit of the time of activity and instrumentality.
Devarāta says:

"A woman holding a broom, wood, grass, fire, or a winnowing basket in her hand would then be an unchaste woman; however, if she is engaged in ascetic practice while using a bed, and menstrual blood is seen, she would then be fortunate."
In another text:
"Just as a winnowing basket filled with dry wood, husks, brooms, and other such inauspicious things appears in an auspicious place, so it would be during the first menses."
In matters of eating, bedding, travel,
and virtuous pursuits involving refined gold, one prospers when endowed with auspicious implements and when the ascendant and planets are favorable.
"It shall be auspicious when the asterism is favorable, and it shall be so when the zodiacal sign is joined by a planet."
Thus ends the fruit of the time of action and its instruments.
Now, the fruit of the place.
In the *Jyotirnibandha*:
The attainment of happiness in the center of the house, separation at the door of the house;
rising from the bed shall bring happiness, as well as wealth and a lineage of offspring.
Dust in the father's house brings wretchedness to the father's family;
it is likewise inauspicious in the temple of the deity, in the father’s own abode, in a place of reproach, or in another's dwelling.

"On the road, there is separation from one's husband; in a prison, one's offspring die. *Devasthāna* means a temple. *Pitṛsthāna* means a cremation ground. *Nindyasthāna* means a despicable place. *Anyaveśma* means a house other than that of one's husband. This concludes the results pertaining to the places. Regarding the results of the lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth, Devarāta states the increasing degrees of importance as follows:
"The lunar day is said to have one quality, while the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) has four qualities."
A week is known to be sixfold, and a month is traditionally said to be eightfold.
One should know that a cloth [stained by it] is ten times more inauspicious, and the sight [of such a woman] is even more so;
for if the inauspicious menses of women are seen during their first period.

"In that case, a ritual procedure must be performed, specifically one that destroys misfortune (*ariṣṭaghna*). Here, "procedure" (*vidhāna*) refers to a propitiatory rite (*śānti*). That propitiatory rite will be explained in the *Śāntiratnamālā*. Now, the rules for all seasons:
In this regard, the Gṛhya-sūtra states: "For three nights, she who has menstrual flow observes the vows as explained for a Brāhmaṇa."

The meaning is that she performs the vow together with a garment that has stains. Alternatively, in the phrase *malavadvāsasā*, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the nominative; thus, *malavadvāsā* (she who has a stained garment) is the correct reading. The meaning is that she performs the vows prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa texts, such as, "Therefore, one should not converse with a woman who has a stained garment. That which possesses *mala*—that is, *rajas* (menstrual blood)—is called *malavat*. By this very fact, it is understood that a menstruating woman should remain with only a single garment until her ritual bath (*snāna*).

Since the Śruti prohibits drinking from a leaf, it is understood that there is no prohibition against eating from a leaf. The basis for this will be demonstrated later. Furthermore, that [prohibition] should be understood from custom as applying to leaves other than those of sacrificial trees such as the *palāśa*.
(In the *Smṛtimañjarī*: "Therefore, one should not lie down in the same house as a woman in her courses...")
One should avoid accepting gifts from her, conversing with her, and eating her food.
If a husband approaches his wife while she is menstruating, the son born will be a Caṇḍāla;
if he approaches her in the forest, the son born will then be a thief.
If he should approach her while she has her back turned, she would have a face flushed with shame;
and the son born of a woman who turns her back during her courses is likewise a coward.
If she bathes during her menstrual period, the child born will die in water;
if she applies oil as an ointment, the offspring is born with leprosy.
If one scratches the ground during menstruation, one becomes short-lived and wicked;
if one applies collyrium to the eyes, one is born either one-eyed or blind.
If one cleanses the teeth, the son will have black teeth;
if one clips the nails, the son will be born with deformed nails.
If he should cut a rope or the like, he is born as a eunuch;
if he weaves a rope with threads, he will die by hanging.
"If one eats food from a vessel during the menstrual period, a son born insane will be produced;
if one eats from a broken bowl, he is born as a dwarf."
"In the Ṛtu-vessel she should drink water; [then] a son born insane (unmādī) is produced.
In the Kharva-vessel she should drink water; such a one is born as a dwarf (vāmana).
This reading is also found in some places. This very reading is appropriate because it accords with the Śruti.

From this statement of the Brāhmaṇa, the following duties—namely bathing, smearing [the body], cleaning the teeth, clipping the nails, cutting grass and the like, the casting away of cords, and drinking from vessels made of leaves or hollow gourds—are prohibited specifically for a married woman (saubhāgyavatī) who is menstruating. This is because, in the case of a widow, there is no possibility of procreation, and thus defects pertaining to offspring cannot arise. Although it might follow that even anointing the body and similar acts are prohibited solely by virtue of being a widow, nevertheless, it is stated:
"For a widow, even if she is menstruating, bathing and the other rites are indeed not [permitted]."

Thus, from the statement of Gālava found in the *Smṛtidarpaṇa*, it should be understood that for her as well, religious duties such as ritual bathing (*snāna*) and so forth are indeed prohibited. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), scraping the body (*pralekhana*) and other acts are included.
In the *Bhāvaprakāśa*’s *Bhojanakutūhala*:
"From the day of the onset of the menstrual flow, she shall remain a celibate student (*brahmacāriṇī*)."
She should sleep on a bed of *darbha* grass and must not even look at her husband;
for three days she should subsist on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) taken in her hand, in a shallow bowl, or on a leaf.
She must avoid shedding tears, cutting her nails, anointing herself with oil, or applying cosmetics.

"One should avoid applying collyrium to the eyes, bathing, sleeping during the day, running, listening to very loud sounds, laughing, speaking excessively, physical exertion, digging the earth, and traveling abroad."
Vasiṣṭha also states:

"For three nights a woman in her menses remains impure; she should not apply collyrium, nor anoint herself, nor bathe in water, nor sleep on the ground, nor sleep during the day, nor touch fire, nor handle a rope, nor clean her teeth, nor eat meat, nor look at the planets, nor laugh, nor engage in any vulgar conduct. She should drink from a vessel that is not broken, or she may drink from her cupped hands, or from a vessel of iron or bronze; so it is known."

The word division is *aśuciḥ* (impure). One should not bathe in water. When an occasional (*naimittika*) bath is required, one should certainly not perform a bath consisting of immersion (*nimajjana*).
For this very reason, Parāśara says: "If a woman is in her menses when an occasional bath is required..."

"Having performed the bath with water poured from another vessel, one should observe the vow"—thus he speaks of bathing with water that has been drawn out. "Not small" means large. "Of metal" means of copper.
Dakṣa says:

A woman who is menstruating should not apply collyrium or ointments, bathe, travel abroad, clean her teeth, or gaze upon the planets; likewise, she should avoid sleeping during the day, using betel leaf, and hanging up fans or similar items.
"In this manner described, one should observe the vow for three nights. (In this context, daily bathing is prohibited.
Garga says:

"She should avoid food consisting of cow's milk products, wearing flowers and ornaments, applying collyrium, using a comb, using perfumes, sitting upon a seat or a bed, and touching fire for three days."

*Kaṅkata* is a hair-comb. *Pīṭhaśayye* is a compound analyzed as *pīṭham ca śayyā ca*, meaning a stool and a bed; the phrase refers to the act of climbing upon those two. Since only the stool and the bed are mentioned here, there is no prohibition against climbing a staircase. She is a woman in her menses. In another Smṛti it is said:
"On the ground, on a vessel of black iron, in the hand, in a clay bowl, or indeed on something burnt..."
"A woman in her menses, however, may eat [from any vessel], but she should drink water from a copper one.
Atri says: "She should avoid honey and meat, as well as eating from a shallow bowl."

"One should eat perfumes, garlands, betel for cleansing the mouth, and so forth from a fired clay bowl, and one should drink liquids using the hollowed palms as a vessel. Here, "akharva" means not small; "āsyaśodhana" means cleansing the mouth.

"Perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, betel-leaf, and vessels of bell-metal"—this is the reading of Devarāta's statement. By the prohibition of vessels made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), the permission for those made of gold, silver, and so forth is understood. In the *Viśvaprakāśa*:
Day-sleep, ornaments, play, manual crafts, household chores,
betel, travel, eating at night,
looking at celestial bodies, touching them, and looking at other men.
"A woman in her menses should avoid laughing and talking.
Here, "talking" (jalpana) refers to speaking at length.
Now, the specific ritual application of the rules for a woman in her menses, as composed by the author of the *Prayogapārijāta*, is presented.

She refrained from anointing herself with oil, cleaning her teeth, clipping her nails, applying collyrium to her eyes, making ropes and the like with thread, cutting them, binding fans and such objects, stringing pearls and gems into garlands, drawing on the ground, eating from small bowls or leaf-plates, consuming honey, ghee, alkaline substances, curd, or sandalwood paste, using perfumes, flowers, ornaments, or wearing washed garments, chewing betel, looking at herself in a mirror, sleeping during the day, and [neglecting] purification through cleansing and other rites.

Avoiding bathing, touching fire, or touching another woman in her menses, a Śūdra, an outcaste, a dog, a cock, and so forth; eating food—excluding milk, curd, and ghee—in a vessel of bell-metal or a large earthenware vessel; wearing wooden sandals or leather shoes at the time of going out or returning; drinking water from an iron or bronze vessel, or with the hollowed palms of the hands; and on the day of her bath, performing purification with sixty applications of clay, brushing her teeth, and bathing during the *saṃgava* period (the third of the five divisions of the day), she should look upon the face of her husband or her chosen deity. Thus it is said.

The word *alpa* (small) is construed with both *śarāva* (earthenware vessel) and *parṇa* (leaf). Therefore, there is a prohibition against using a small leaf, but not against large leaves such as those of the plantain tree (*kadalī*).
Regarding the specific rule for the first menses, it is stated in the *Prayogapārijāta* and the *Smṛticandrikā*: "And for a married woman, [the rite is performed] after her first menstrual period."
Having prepared a seat with unbroken grains, one should cause her to sit upon it.
They should offer turmeric, fragrant flowers, and the like, as well as betel-leaf and a garland;
they should cause her to recite blessings, saying: "May you be possessed of a husband and sons."
One should perform the lustration ceremony with lamps and cause the deity to dwell in a house provided with lamps;
likewise, one should offer cakes, savory foods, and sacrificial oblations mixed with mung beans and molasses.

"One should give [gifts] to the daughters of Brahmins, and one should provide them with food. Now, regarding the limit for the period of menstrual impurity (*rajo-doṣa*), Marīci states in the *Madanapārijāta*:
"A woman who has reached her menses becomes pure for her husband on the fourth day by bathing;
however, for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, she becomes pure on the fifth day."

The first half [of the verse] means that she becomes fit for approach (*upagamana*). This should be understood as referring to the cessation of the menstrual flow (*rajonivṛtti*), according to the statement of Āpastamba: "She is to be approached when the menses have ceased, by no means while they have not ceased. The second half, however, establishes her lack of qualification for ritual acts (*karmānadhikāra*). Although the statement of Marīci establishes that there is unfitness for all Śrauta and Smārta rites—whether pertaining to the gods or the ancestors—even when the menses have ceased on the fourth day, [the present text follows the rule]:
"A virtuous woman who has become menstruating becomes pure through bathing once the menses have stopped."

Thus, in the statement of Manu, the *Madanapārijāta*—by employing such phrases as "a virtuous woman is fit for the prescribed rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*"—demonstrates that even in the case of a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) performed for the sake of fulfilling her eligibility in accordance with the primary rite, her eligibility is established; likewise, there is purification on the fourth day for the *śrauta* sacrifices such as the *darśa*.
It is said: "On the fourth day, having bathed with water mixed with cow’s urine, she should again wear those same garments, the yoke-strap, and the net, purified by mantras."

Thus, because of the statement of Baudhāyana in the section on Soma, and because of the statement "when [it is] by means of a three-night [rite]," as well as the observation of the Commentator that Śrauta rites must indeed be performed even on the day of bathing for a menstruating woman—and not only on the fifth day—there is no such restriction; rather, according to the *Prāyaścittacandrikā*, eligibility occurs precisely upon the cessation of the flow, on the fourth day.

Thus, the opening statement of the *Madanapārijāta* text is intended to include the *upanayana* and other rites as well, because even in those cases, eligibility arises on the fourth day through the consecration preceded by the *śrīsūkta* oblation which will be described later. This applies when other days are unfavorable; however, it should be understood that if other days are favorable, this [rite] occurs on the fifth day itself, preceded by propitiatory rites (*śānti*).
Thus ends the section on the duration of the impurity caused by menstruation.
Now follows the procedure for the ritual bath (*snānavidhi*).
In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:

"A Brāhmaṇa woman in her menses should perform purification on the fourth day with sixty palas of clay; women of the Kṣatriya and other castes should use a quarter less of clay; a widow should use double the amount of clay. Then, having washed away the impurity and performed the cleansing of the teeth, she should bathe with her clothes on at the time of *saṅgava*."
Atri states: "On the fourth day, a woman in her courses, having performed purification according to the rule with sixty separate applications of clay,
as well as the cleansing of her teeth,"
But having missed the *saṅgava* period, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on,
using ashes, cow dung, earth, or any one of these.
Having bathed and put on a garment, adorned with perfumes and flowers,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), she should worship the Sun with flowers as is appropriate.
"O Lord, you ought to grant me this boon from Indra now.
Having spoken thus, she should then pray to her own husband with the disposition of Indra.
"A woman who, having bathed after her menses, looks upon a man out of affection, shall give birth to a son resembling him; therefore, she should look only at her husband."
Kātyāyana states:
"Bathing with women in their courses, wearing garlands, and applying ointments are not to be practiced;
likewise, one should eat light food only during the day, using either the hand or an earthen vessel."
She should eat sacrificial food that is sweet and free from pungent or bitter flavors;
she should sleep on the ground covered with a mat in a secluded place, with her head toward the east.
On the fourth day, the patient should bathe with lukewarm water;
having bathed on the fourth day, she should gaze upon the Sun with devotion.
"She should not look upon anyone other than her husband, her brother-in-law, or her father-in-law.
However, in another Smṛti it is said:
"On the fourth day, she should perform a bath when the sun has risen."

Thus, bathing is prescribed immediately after sunrise; therefore, there is an option [regarding the time]. However, performing the practice of bathing before sunrise is indeed a violation of proper conduct (*durācāra*).
Vyāsa describes the method for occasional bathing (*naimittika-snāna*) for a woman in her menses: "If a woman is in her menses when the occasion for occasional bathing has arrived..."
Having performed his bath with water filtered through a vessel, he should observe the vow.
"One's limbs, including the major and minor parts of the body, should somehow be sprinkled with water;
one should not wring out the garment, nor should one put on another cloth."
The author Uśanas describes the method of purification for a menstruating woman afflicted by fever and other ailments:
"If a woman is overcome by fever and drenched with menstrual flow, how may her cleansing be accomplished? By what ritual act may she become pure?"
When the fourth day has arrived, another woman should touch her;
having immersed herself in water with her clothes on, she should bathe again and again, and then touch her once more.
She should sip water ten or twelve times again and again;
at the end, she should discard her garments, and then she shall become pure.
"Thereafter, one should give gifts according to one's capacity; by means of a *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) rite, one is purified.
For all those who are afflicted by illness, purification is prescribed in this very manner."
Thus concludes the procedure for bathing.
Now, as an incidental discussion, follows the consideration regarding the occurrence of the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) during menstruation.
On this point, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
"Even when menstruation has commenced, the Dvādaśī vow must not be abandoned.
The phrase "Dvādaśī vow" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa). [As it is said: "If menstruation should occur for women who have begun a long-term penance..."
"There shall never be an obstruction of the vow even in that case," according to the statement of Satyavrata.

The meaning of Satyavrata’s words is as follows: if a woman who is observing a long-term optional vow (kāmyavrata) to be accomplished over a period such as nine nights or a month sees her menses in the middle of it, she should certainly continue the fast and other observances; however, she should perform the worship and other rites to be completed on that specific day on the fifth day [of the flow].
As it is said: "On the fifth day she becomes pure for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors."
According to this statement, and because Mādhava says that one should perform the worship, giving, and so forth that were omitted on the fifth day; Hemādri, however, states:
"Whether she be pregnant, in her postpartum state (*sūtakī*), a maiden, or even menstruating (*rohiṇī*)."

He explained the *Padma Purāṇa* passage—"When she is impure, being purified herself, she should have it performed by another"—as follows: since the gender of the subject is not intended to be significant, whether it be a man or a woman, when a vow involving fasting, worship, and so forth is prescribed for a specific time such as a lunar day (*tithi*), one who is impure should fast and perform the worship herself, while having other rites performed by another. However, this applies to such cases; in other vows, such as the *kokilā-vrata*, the rule is "on the fifth day," and so on. Furthermore, in the case of Ekādaśī and similar observances, if impurity (*āśauca*) lasting five or six days were to occur, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to break the fast (*pāraṇā*) at the end of the month; and if impurity lasting five or six days were to occur at the end of a month-long fast, survival itself would become impossible.
As for that which was said—
"When a woman established in her religious observances perceives menstrual flow in the interval [of her vow],
she should fast for four nights, bathe, and then perform the remainder of the vow"—
this is the statement of Aṅgiras. And as for the statement of Hārīta:

Some maintain that the statement, "If a woman established in her religious observances (*niyama*) should somehow see her menses, she should fast for three nights and thereafter complete the remainder of her vow," refers specifically to the case of widows fasting, because for them there is a prohibition against eating during that period.

Others, however, maintain that because the qualification "of those who have performed long austerities" (*dīrghatapasaḥ*) is employed in the statement of Satyavrata, this prohibition concerns all single-day fasts (*ekāhopavāsa*) other than the Dvādaśī vow. They say that in the case of long-term vows such as the three-night or nine-night fasts, the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) must occur only during the period when the menstrual flow has ceased. Still others, however, hold that the term "long austerity" includes even the single-day fast, since it is "long" in comparison to a fast consisting only of a single meal at night (*nakta*) and so forth; therefore, they say that for the single-day fast as well, the *pāraṇā* must take place only after the cessation of the flow. In the midst of a period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), however, the *pāraṇā* may occur at any time.

"For when a voluntary fast has begun, if a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interval, one should perform that voluntary vow there, omitting the gift and the worship," according to the statement in the *Mādhavīya* based on the *Kaurma Purāṇa*.

And because of the statement of Viṣṇu: "In the case of vows, sacrifices, marriages, ancestral rites (śrāddha), fire-offerings (homa), worship, and recitation (japa), there shall be no birth-impurity (sūtaka) once they have commenced; however, there is birth-impurity if they have not commenced."
In the Rudrayāmala:
"During the period of impurity (sūtaka), one should perform the breaking of the fast on the ninth day, preceded by a fire sacrifice (homa);
at its conclusion, one should feed the Brahmins and give gifts according to one's capacity."

The phrase "on the ninth day" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the conclusion of the vow. "At its end" means at the end of the period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*). The commencement [of the vow], however, has been stated in the section on marriage by the rule: "In a sacrifice, the commencement is the formal invitation (*varaṇa*).
This concludes the deliberation on the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*).
Now follows the deliberation on purification in the event of menstrual flow occurring even after the ritual bath.
Bṛhaspati states in the *Prayogapārijāta*:
"That which arises from passion (*rāga*), from disease (*roga*), from substances (*dravya*), and likewise from time (*kāla*)—
Bhārgava has declared that blood [is classified] according to its origin from passion, disease, or substances."
"But that which arises at the [proper] time is called *rajas*; therefore, she is impure only during that [period].
The word division is *aśuciḥ* (she is impure). The meaning is: "In that very period, [namely] during the *rajas* arising at the [proper] time, that woman remains impure for three nights.
He himself stated the definitions of these:
That fat which is produced in barren women even before giving birth is said to arise from passion; it originates from the differentiation of the marrow.

That which occurs repeatedly due to an imbalance of the humors, such as bile (pitta) and the rest, is designated as disease-born (rogaja); now, that which arises from substances (dravyaja) is described.
That which arises from the consumption of substances that cause an imbalance of the bodily elements (dhātus) is designated as being born of substance; now, that which is born of time is described.
Starting from the day of the onset of menstruation, on the twenty-first day, or after one month has passed, whatever menstrual flow occurs is declared to be "seasonal" (kālaja).
"When a woman who has become menstruating becomes menstruating again,
she shall be impure for three nights after the twentieth day."

A specific distinction is stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: "If menstruation occurs again within seventeen days, there is merely a bath; on the eighteenth day, one night; on the nineteenth, two days; and from the twentieth onwards, three nights.
This refers to the case of a woman whose menstruation generally occurs only after the twentieth day.
Kaśyapa states: "When a woman who has already experienced her menses becomes menstruating again,
she remains impure for three nights, even if it occurs before eighteen days have passed."
"On the eleventh day, however, it is one day and night; on the twelfth day, two nights; beyond that, it should be known as three nights—so it was spoken by Kauṇḍinya."
And this statement refers to those women for whom menstruation occurs predominantly even before sixteen days due to the particular stage of their youth.
In the *Smṛtyarthasāra* as well:
"For women who generally experience menstruation after the thirteenth day, there is no impurity prior to the eleventh day."
"On the eleventh day, one night; on the twelfth, two nights; beyond that, three nights.

This is also stated in the *Prayogapārijāta*. Furthermore, this should be understood as occurring after the days of ritual bathing (snāna), based on the scriptural statement: "Women have sixteen nights of the season (*ṛtu*).
Regarding menstrual flow caused by disease, Bṛhaspati says: "There is no impurity in [menstrual blood] born of disease."
"For the menstrual flow that issues daily from women due to disease does not make them impure, because it is considered a natural bodily transformation."

*Vaikārika* means that which arises from a physical disorder (*vikāra*). The mention of "by disease" (*rogeṇa*) is an elliptical expression intended to include [menstruation] caused by passion (*rāga*) or substances (*dravya*). Because of the hearing of the word "daily" (*anvaham*), if there is an interval in between, and if she generally becomes menstruating only after twenty days or more, then the previously stated rule should be understood here as follows: for twenty days and onwards it is three nights; on the nineteenth day it is two days; on the eighteenth day it is one night; and until the seventeenth day, it is merely bathing.

However, if she becomes menstruating in abundance even before the sixteenth day, then the rule is as follows: for eleven days there is one night of impurity, on the twelfth day two nights, and from the thirteenth day onwards three nights. Even if, by some chance, the menstrual flow continues every single day starting from the very first appearance of the menses, this same procedure applies.
Furthermore, regarding menses arising from disease, the eligibility for ritual acts occurs only upon the cessation of the flow:
"A woman who is menstruating does not become pure merely by bathing; she remains impure until her flow has ceased."
For as long as the dust continues to arise, it will certainly not cease.
Thus, according to the statement of Śaṅkha in the *Śrāddhahemādri*.
Prajāpati states a specific rule regarding the appearance of menses in a woman who has recently given birth:
"A woman who has recently given birth, however, after twenty days have passed since her bath..."
The menstrual flow is called *ārta-vī*, whereas the preceding flow is termed *naimittika-rajas*.
"But the wise say that in the case of occasional rites, there shall be no impurity."
Bṛhaspati says:
"Prajāpati has declared that when the menstrual flow is known with certainty, it is a cause for impurity; but when there is merely doubt, there shall be purity."
In the previous [verse], the word division is *aśuddhiḥ* (impurity).
(Yama states:
"Due to addiction, failure to perform duties, sleep, and even forgetfulness...")
Not realizing she was discharging menstrual blood, she remained pure regarding her previous ritual acts.
"In the event of faults known or unknown, or of unspoken inauspicious occurrences,
one should perform the *puṇyāhavācana* according to the instruction of the Brahmins.
Now follows the determination of the days regarding the appearance of the menses (*rajas*).
Regarding this, Kaśyapa states: "From midnight to midnight shall be the day for impurity (*sūtaka*) and so forth.
The term *ārdharātram* means up to and including midnight. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the period of menstruation (*ṛtu*) is included.
Yājñavalkya, however, says:
"One should divide the night into three parts; two parts belong to the preceding day, while the final portion is joined with the morning in the case of the menstrual period and birth-impurity."

In this context, the absence of the *saṃdhi* (twilight) period is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). Regarding menstruation occurring at night or during childbirth and other such events, one should divide the night into three parts; if it occurs within the first two parts, the preceding day is to be taken, whereas if it occurs thereafter, the following day is to be taken—this is the meaning. However, in another *Smṛti*, it is stated:
"If birth, death, menstruation, or impurity due to childbirth occurs precisely at night, the preceding day alone is to be taken, as long as the sun has not yet risen."

The day is defined in three ways: from the latter half of the first watch of the night until the first half of the second watch of the night; from the third part of the night—when it is divided into three parts—until the end of the first two parts of the second watch of the night; and from sunrise until sunrise. Thus, these three positions are established. Furthermore, this should be understood as being determined by location, according to the statement in the *Saṃgraha*: "The arrangement of all three positions depends on the difference of country."
Thus concludes the determination of the days following the appearance of menses.
Now, as a related topic, the method of purification upon mutual contact or upon touching a dog, a Śūdra, and so forth, is described.
Regarding this, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states in the *Smṛtimañjarī*:

"If two women who have reached their menses have come into contact with each other—provided they are of the same caste and share the same husband—they must bathe upon touching one another; thereafter, she should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)."

When there is mutual contact between two women who are menstruating— whether they are of the same caste, related by birth, or of the same *gotra*— they both become pure simply by bathing, provided it was unintentional.
If, however, through ignorance, one eats [the food] of these two, there shall be a fast for one day followed by the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
This applies when two women who are menstruating are unrelated to each other and of the same caste.
If one touches [an impure object] unintentionally, one becomes pure by bathing and then eating;
however, if it is intentional, one should not eat until purification is achieved. But if one has already eaten, one must fast for a day and night.
"Some say that the fast should last for as many days as [the number of] those days;
if one is unable to fast, one should perform an equivalent act of giving."

Śūlapāṇi states that the gift of a silver māṣa is the substitute for the fast (*upavāsa*). One should neither eat nor consume [solid food]. Regarding this, Kaśyapa has also mentioned the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*):
"If a Brāhmaṇa woman who is menstruating is touched by another Brāhmaṇa woman..."
"One who has fasted for one night is purified by the five products of the cow."
And this applies when it is unintentional:
"If two Brahmin women who are menstruating touch one another, the Brahmin woman shall remain without food for that duration; she is purified by three nights [of fasting]."
This rule stated by Parāśara applies when the contact is intentional.

Regarding the touch between two co-wives (sapatnī) who belong to the same gotra and have the same husband, Vasiṣṭha says: "When two women in their menses, belonging to the same gotra and having one husband, touch each other..."
"Whether out of desire or even without desire, one is purified immediately by bathing."

In the phrase *rajasvale'nyonyam*, the absence of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
