Regarding contact with one another when both are menstruating and of different castes, Parāśara states: "If a Brāhmaṇī and a Kṣatriyā likewise touch each other while both are menstruating..."
Purification shall occur in three nights, according to the word of Vyāghra.
If a Brahmin woman who is menstruating is touched by a Vaiśya woman,
she shall remain without food for five nights and is purified by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a menstruating woman is touched by a Śūdra woman and a Brāhmaṇa woman,
the purification for the Brāhmaṇa woman shall occur after six nights, even if it was done intentionally.
"A Brāhmaṇa woman shall undergo half [of the penance] for all castes when acting out of ignorance."

In this regard, just as for a Brāhmaṇī woman and one who is menstruating there is fasting and the consumption of *pañcagavya* upon touching each other, so too is that same penance for others when they touch a menstruating woman of their own caste (*savarṇa*). Just as for a Brāhmaṇī woman there is a three-night fast upon touching a Kṣatriya woman, so it is for a Kṣatriya woman upon touching a Vaiśya woman, and for a Vaiśya woman upon touching a Śūdra woman.
And thus, in the *Smṛti* cited in Bhavadeva’s *Nibandha*: "If a woman who is menstruating should touch another [menstruating] woman..."
"One of the same caste [is purified] by the five products of the cow for three nights; one of a different caste [is purified] in the same manner."
Bhavadeva states that [this applies] when accompanied by the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and fasting.
Likewise, Śātātapa says:
"If two women who are both in their menses touch one another..."
"But if [the offender] has eaten with one of the same caste while fasting, then he must consume the five products of the cow."
As for that which Vṛddhavasiṣṭha stated: "If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former shall perform an Ardhakṛcchra penance, while the latter shall perform a Pādakṛcchra."

If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman who are immediate neighbors touch each other while in their menses, the Brāhmaṇa woman shall perform a quarter-less penance (three-quarters), while the Kṣatriya woman, being the next lower caste, shall perform a quarter-Kṛcchra. If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman who are immediate neighbors likewise touch each other while in their menses,
the former shall perform a quarter-less penance, while the latter shall perform a quarter-Kṛcchra.
"The Brāhmaṇa woman is first, and the Vaiśya woman is next.
If a menstruating Brāhmaṇa woman and a Śūdra-born woman touch each other,
the former shall perform one Kṛcchra penance, while the Śūdra woman is purified by giving a gift."
Giving a gift equal to the value of a foot is the expiation.
If two menstruating women— one of Kṣatriya birth and one of Śūdra birth— touch each other,
the former is purified by three fasts, while the latter is purified by a single day and night.
The Kṣatriya woman is the first (the senior), and the Śūdra woman is the last (the junior). When a menstruating Kṣatriya woman and a Vaiśya woman touch each other,
the former is purified after three nights, while the latter is purified in one day and night.
The former is a Kṣatriya woman and the latter is a Vaiśya woman: "If two women who have become menstruating— namely a Vaiśya and a Śūdra— touch each other,
the former is purified after three nights, while the latter is purified in one day and night."
The Vaiśya woman is to the east; the Śūdra woman is to the north.
And this applies to touching out of desire:
"This is the eternal rule regarding the touching of the castes when done intentionally."
This is because of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).
Regarding the penance for touching an outcast (*patita*), a *caṇḍāla*, and so forth, Bṛhaspati and Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha state:
"If a woman in her menses is touched by an outcast, an untouchable (*antya*), or one who cooks with dogs..."
Having passed those days, one should perform the penance:
on the first day it shall be three nights; on the second, two days;
on the third day, one day and night; and on the fourth, merely a night-meal.

"Having passed those days characterized by the observances of a menstruating woman, [one should perform penance] by fasting"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Bhavadeva maintains that in all such cases, the consumption of *pañcagavya* must also be performed.
As for the statement of Baudhāyana: "A menstruating woman who has been touched by a Caṇḍāla, an outcaste, a dog, or a crow..."
She should remain without food for as long as it takes to become pure."
Thus, [this applies] when she is either unable or unwilling. As for that which Śātātapa says:
"If a woman in her courses or a woman who has recently given birth should touch a corpse or one of the lowest castes, she becomes pure in three nights; so said the sage Vārṣyāyaṇi."
Likewise, another Smṛti states: "If one touches a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapaca, or even an Ātreyī woman,
having fasted for three nights, one becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
Likewise, Kātyāyana states:
"If a woman in her menses is ever touched by a Caṇḍāla,
she should perform the penance after those days have passed."
"There shall be a fast for three nights and purification by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)"— this refers to the first day. Regarding one who is unable to fast, Aṅgiras says:
"If even a Caṇḍāla or a Śvapaca should touch an Ātreyī woman,
he should subsist on [food] not prepared at the proper time and is purified by the five products of the cow."
The drinking of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) should be understood as occurring immediately after bathing.
Regarding climbing a single tree together with a *caṇḍāla*, Parāśara states:
"A woman in her courses who has climbed a single tree together with a *caṇḍāla*..."
"Having fasted for a day and night, one becomes purified by means of the five products of the cow."
Regarding the specific rule for contact with a dog and other such animals, Yama says:
"If a woman in her menses is touched by a dog, a jackal, or a crow,
she shall remain without food until she becomes pure according to the prescribed time."
This applies when it is unintentional.

However, regarding intentional contact with a menstruating woman, Bṛhaspati states: "If a non-Śūdra woman who is impure due to menstruation is touched by a dog, she should observe [the penance] for two days."
"On the third day, one should observe [the vow] for a full day and night; thereafter, one should practice eating only at night."

The meaning is that if one is touched by a dog or similar animal on the first or second day, the penance lasts for two days; on the third day, it is for a full day and night (ahorātra); and thereafter, on the fourth day, it is for a single night (nakta). In this case as well, the phrase "having passed those days" should be applied.
Baudhāyana states: "But a menstruating woman who is touched by domestic cocks or pigs..."
Having bathed with dogs, one should drink [the water] as long as the moon is visible.

The meaning is that seeing the moon at night [renders her pure]; or, for one unable to do this, it refers to the fourth day. Regarding contact with a washerman and others, Śūlapāṇi maintains that it is exactly equal to contact with a dog, because those two cases are identical.
As for what Pracetas says: "A woman in her menses who is touched by a dog, a Caṇḍāla, or a donkey..."
"By fasting for five nights, one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
Thus, [this applies] to habitual practice out of desire. However, regarding the touch of a dog, an outcaste (antyaja), or others while eating, Baudhāyana states:
"If a menstruating woman, while eating, should touch a dog, an outcaste, or the like, she becomes pure after six nights by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel."
"In case of inability, one should give gold to the Brahmins, or else provide them with food."
In another Smṛti:
"If she touches a menstruating woman, or out of delusion an impure man, she shall not eat until after her bath; having eaten, she should perform the Kṛcchra penance."
"Having touched a woman in her courses, or five-toed animals, or cloven-hoofed or single-hoofed beasts, or any birds, one should not eat until the day of bathing has passed."

Regarding the mutual contact of two persons who are both impure from food remnants, Atri states: "If a menstruating woman is ever touched by one who is impure from food remnants, she is purified by the Kṛcchra penance; the former [the toucher] is purified by giving gifts, provided he is a Śūdra."

Giving a gift equal to the penance for a foot-wound [is the purification]. Here, by the word "preceding" (*pūrva*), Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and women are denoted. Therefore, when two menstruating women of the same caste—Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya—touch one another, the penance is a *Prājāpatya*. However, when they are of different castes, an increase of one [penance] for each successive caste should be inferred. But when two such Śūdra women touch one another, purification is achieved by performing a *Prājāpatya* along with fasting and the giving of a gift as prescribed. And this applies to intentional contact; in the case of unintentional contact, it is half of that. As for Śūlapāṇi:
"If a woman in her courses should ever be touched by one who is impure from food remnants, she is purified by a Kṛcchra penance; a Śūdra woman is purified by a gift."

Thus he recited. "By one who is *ucchiṣṭa*" means by a Caṇḍāla or similar person. Here too, the gift [of food] is equal to a *pādakṛcchra* penance. In these cases, the state of being a menstruating woman (*rajasvalā*) alone is the cause. Therefore, Śūlapāṇi maintains that there is no distinction between Kṣatriya or Vaiśya women and Brāhmaṇa women (Brāhmaṇīs) regarding this.
However, concerning contact with a twice-born man who is *ucchiṣṭa*, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"If a menstruating woman should somehow touch twice-born men who are *ucchiṣṭa*..."
"But if [the food] is merely touched by the leavings, one should fast for a day and night; if it is above the leavings, one should spend three days [fasting]."

In the phrase *adhocchiṣṭa*, the sandhi is archaic (*ārṣa*). If a Brāhmaṇa woman touches the leavings of a Kṣatriya or others, a greater penance must be prescribed for her. Likewise, if she touches the leavings of a person of lower status, the penance is lessened.
Regarding the case of seeing another woman in her menses while eating, Āpastamba states: [text follows]

"If one eats while seeing either a woman in her courses or another woman who is menstruating, he shall not eat until the time for bathing has passed; thereafter, he should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
And Śūlapāṇi says that this [penance] applies when it is done intentionally.
Regarding the sight of a Caṇḍāla at the time of eating, Atri states: "If a menstruating woman, while eating, sees a Caṇḍāla..."
"One should perform three fasts, however, if the act was committed intentionally, one should perform a Prājāpatya penance."

Regarding the touch of a woman in her menses by one who is impure due to death or birth, Śātātapa states: "If a woman drenched in menstrual blood should touch a corpse or one born after a birth-impurity,
she shall fast for three nights after bathing once the three days [of her own period] have passed."
Atri states:

"If a woman who is flooded with menstrual flow should touch one who has touched a corpse or a birth-impurity, she should perform a *kṛcchra* penance without eating; but if she has already eaten, she must do so for three days."
Regarding touching one who is impure due to death or birth, Mārkaṇḍeya states concerning the sight of a menstrual period:
"If one touches a person in a state of death-impurity or birth-impurity upon seeing her menses, how should it be?
One should not eat until the time for bathing has passed; having eaten, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
"Until the time of bathing" means until the end of the fourth day.
In the *Madanaratna*, another *Smṛti* states: "If, when a state of impurity has arisen, she is wearing soiled garments..."
"Liberation shall come through the consecration; one should abstain from food for three days."

Liberation is attained through consecration (abhiṣeka), and nourishment through immediate bathing; this refers to one who is incapable or to the case of a woman with young children. For one who is capable, however, there is a fast for three nights.
Regarding hearing of the death of a kinsman and similar occasions, Vyāsa states:
"If there should be impurity for a woman wearing soiled garments..."
"Purity shall come through consecration, and there shall be no enjoyment for three days."

In this case as well, the arrangement is as before. The phrase "three days" is an indication for the remaining period [of impurity]. Impurity (*aprāyatya*) arises from such things as the death of a relative. Regarding the touching of animals and the like, Kaśyapa states:
"Having touched a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), five-nailed animals, even-toed or single-hoofed animals, and all birds, one remains impure until the day of bathing."
*Anaśa* means fasting.
Regarding a bite by a dog or similar animal, Pulastya states: "When a woman in her menses is bitten by a dog, a jackal, or an ass..."
By fasting for five nights, one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
"Above the navel it is double [the length], at the mouth likewise triple, and at the head it is recorded as quadruple; elsewhere than on a bite, one becomes impure."

The phrase "except during the state of menstruation" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. In whatever instance bathing is prescribed within the three-day period, it should be performed according to the previously mentioned method for occasional (naimittika) bathing.
Thus concludes the consideration of purification for a menstruating woman.
Now, incidentally, follows the method of purification for sentient and insentient objects touched by a menstruating woman.

In that regard, for sentient beings, there shall be a bath with one's clothes on; for insentient objects such as seats and the like, there shall be washing. Upon touching a sentient being touched by a woman in her menses, there shall be sipping of water (ācamana).
As it is said: "A man touched by a woman in her menses should perform a bath with his clothes on."
One should wash with pure water those inanimate objects that have been touched by her.
Indeed, upon touching one who has touched a woman in her courses, purification is achieved by sipping water (ācamana).

This is because it is stated in another Smṛti: "A *udakyā* is a woman in her menses. And this [refers] to unintentional contact; however, for intentional contact: "A *divākīrti*, a *udakyā*, an outcast (*patita*), and likewise a woman who has recently given birth..."
"Having touched a corpse or one who has touched it, one becomes pure by bathing."
Thus, for him as well, bathing alone is prescribed according to the statement of Manu.
Regarding the third person, Saṃvarta states:
"If one should touch someone who has touched that [corpse], bathing is ordained for him."
"Sipping water [with the mouth] facing upwards is prescribed, as is the sprinkling of ritual substances."
This also applies when done unintentionally; however, if done intentionally, bathing alone is required. And so says Gautama:
"Regarding those who have touched a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse, [one must bathe] upon touching someone who has touched them."
"One becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on.
Thus it is for the fourth as well:
"A man who has touched one who has been touched by an impure person, and even a third person..."
"One becomes pure by washing both hands and feet with water and performing the ritual sipping (ācamana)," according to the statement of Devala.
By the use of the word "also" (api), those who have passed five days [of impurity] and so forth are also included.
Regarding the touch of an impure woman in her courses (udakyā) and others, he says the same:
"If one who is himself impure should touch these [impure things],
he becomes pure again by means of a fast or likewise by means of a *kṛcchra* penance."
In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:

"If dust is seen while food is being served, the food touched by it must be discarded. If the vessel containing the food is touched by a Caṇḍāla, a woman recently delivered, a menstruating woman, or the like, or if it is touched by a washerman or the like, one should cast it into water and then touch either fire or the sun."
Thus ends the method of purification for animate and inanimate objects touched by a woman in her menses. Now, as an incidental topic, the duties of women are briefly stated.
Regarding this, Manu says:
Neither by a woman who is in her youth nor even by one who is old should any action be undertaken independently, even within the home.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, husband, or even her son;
for through such separation, she becomes censured in both families.
"A wife should always be steadfast, skillful in domestic affairs, attentive to the refinement of household utensils, and not wasteful in her expenditures."
Manu says:
"The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; at no time is there independence for a woman."
"Women must be guarded especially against even the slightest lapses of heedfulness;
for if they are not protected, they will bring grief upon two families."
In the *Bhārata*: "Traveling, association with wicked people, separation from her husband,
wandering about, sleeping, and residing in another's house— these are indeed the six vices of women."
They do not seek beauty, nor do they have regard for age;
whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Manu assigned to women the use of beds and seats, ornaments, desire, anger, as well as straightforwardness, a malicious disposition, and evil deeds.
"No one is able to protect a woman by force. Thus the faults of women have been stated in the Purāṇa:
"Untruthfulness, recklessness, deceit, folly, and excessive greed..."
"Impurity and cruelty are the innate defects of women."
Yājñavalkya states:
"With her household utensils well-kept, skillful, modest, and averse to wasteful expenditure,
she should attend upon the feet of her parents-in-law, being entirely devoted to her husband."
"Wives must carry out the word of their husbands; this is the supreme duty of a woman.
For even one defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) must be awaited until purification."

The essential meaning is this: as long as a husband defiled by a *mahāpātaka* (grave sin) or other such offenses has not been purified, she should not accept his word even when summoned by him for sexual union, nor likewise for the sake of a meal.
Manu says:
"Whether he be devoid of character, or acting according to his lusts, or abandoned by [good] qualities..."
A husband should always be served by a virtuous wife with ritual attentions as if he were a god.
The word "to be honored" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by serving her husband, she is exalted in heaven.
"A woman who, while her husband is living, observes fasts and practices vows,
takes away her husband's lifespan and goes to hell."

The authors of the *Nibandhas* maintain that this prohibition against fasting refers specifically to the fasts associated with vows such as the month-long fast (*māsa-upavāsa*), the *dhāraṇā*, and the *pāraṇā*, but not to the fasts associated with family customs (*kuladharma*) or vows such as the *Gaurī-vrata*. This is reasonable; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of the practice of family-custom fasts and other auspiciousness-inducing vows, such as the *Haritālikā-vrata*. Yājñavalkya states:
"A woman in her courses shall not show her own face for three nights."
She should not even let her own voice be heard until she has bathed and become pure.
Having bathed well, she should look at the face of her husband and that of no one else;
or else, having meditated upon her husband in her mind, she may look at the sun.
Turmeric, saffron, vermilion, and collyrium,
as well as a bodice, betel-leaf, and auspicious, beautiful ornaments.
A bodice, a palm-leaf fan, and so forth; likewise,
ornaments for the hair, the braided coiffure, and jewelry for the hands and ears—
a virtuous woman, desiring long life for her husband, should never defile these.
One should never converse with a woman who hates her husband;
she should never be alone anywhere, nor should she ever bathe naked.
That woman should never sit anywhere upon a mortar, nor on a pestle, nor on a wooden mallet, nor even on a grinding stone; nor on a mechanical device, nor on the threshold.
A woman who, filled with anger, gives a retort when spoken to,
is born as a dog in a village or as a jackal in a desolate forest.
One should not engage in excessive speech; one should abandon quarreling from afar.
In the presence of gurus, one should never speak nor indeed laugh.
If a tigress that bites men, when struck, desires to strike back— that woman who abandons her husband and eats only what is sweet— she is such a tigress.
"In the village she might be a sow, or a tigress devouring excrement. The Yogin said:
"The refinement of the body for play, the witnessing of social gatherings and festivals,"
"A woman whose husband is away from home should avoid laughter and traveling to the houses of others."
Devala says: "Devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband, well-conducted, and having conquered her senses,
she attains fame in this world and the highest state after death."
In another Smṛti:
"A woman desiring to bathe at a sacred ford (tīrtha) should drink the water from her husband’s feet;
for a woman, her husband alone is superior even to Śiva or Viṣṇu."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "That woman who offers the arghya water to Vivasvat at the time of dawn shall never experience widowhood for seven births."
Having drawn a mandala on the outside, one should constantly worship the sun there with unbroken rice grains and other offerings; indeed, the deities become pleased with her who does so.
A woman who, having become pure and composed, worships the doorway at the time of dawn,
attains all her desires.
When a woman does not daily offer a portion of her food to her elder sister according to her ability, she shall go to hell after death.
"Women who desire sons, grandsons, and wealth must certainly perform the daily propitiation of the elder sister by means of an offering."
"In Bhārata,
in the Kali age, the marketplaces will have meat as their primary commodity, the crossroads will be dominated by phallic emblems of Śiva, and women will have hair as their chief ornament."
Paraśurāma states its meaning:
"The eighth is food, Śiva is the Veda, the trident is indeed sale, and the hair they call the vulva— so say those who perceive the true meaning of the Vedas."
By the phrase "they will exist in the Kali age," the intention is to demonstrate their censurable nature.
Thus, the relevant meaning is that women must avoid sexual misconduct.
"The husband is a god, the husband is a guru; he is dharma, sacred fords, and vows."

Therefore, having renounced everything, she should worship her husband alone. She who eats only when he eats, sits only when he sits, and sleeps only when he sleeps— that woman is to be known as a devoted wife (pativratā).

"When her husband is distressed she is distressed, when he is joyful she is joyful, when he is away she is dejected and emaciated, and when he is present she bows low in spirit— such a woman is to be known as devoted to her husband."

Śaṅkha states: "She should not walk quickly out of affection; she should not converse with a stranger; she should not engage in laughter; she should dress herself in a garment reaching down to the ankles; she should not leave her breasts uncovered; she should not harbor hatred toward her husband or his relatives; and she should not stay in the company of courtesans, rogues, and the like."
"Unobstructed and uncovered.
In another Smṛti: "She eats when her husband has eaten; while he stands, she stands."
And when [others] are asleep, he remains awake; he is the first to awaken.
She should never show herself unadorned to her husband;
when her husband has gone abroad on business, she should remain devoid of ornaments.
One should not utter that person's name for the sake of increasing one's own longevity;
even when reviled, one should not revile in return, and even when struck, one should remain serene.
The meaning is this: she who, when told by her husband, "Do this," says, "O Master, consider it done";
and who, when summoned, comes quickly leaving her household chores behind—she is a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
The word division is "āgacchati" (he comes).
One should personally purify all the articles for worship in water;
one should personally collect the water, leaves, flowers, and so forth, for the purpose of worship.
"She should consume the remnants of her husband's food, such as flour, cooked rice, fruits, and so forth;
having said, 'This is a great favor,' she accepts what is given by her husband."
Women, Śūdras, and the degraded twice-born have no entitlement to hear the Vedas.
Accordingly, the Purāṇa states:
"The threefold Veda is not within the range of hearing for women, Śūdras, and the degraded twice-born."
Thus has the Bhārata been narrated, composed out of compassion by the Sage."

One born to a Śūdra woman from a twice-born man is a *dvijabandhu* (a kinsman of the twice-born). If he lacks the qualification even for listening [to the scriptures], what need is there to mention his lack of qualification for reciting them?
As stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"And others, O Viṣṇu, such as Brāhmaṇas and likewise kings..."
And Vaiśyas are qualified for the practice of knowledge according to their respective degrees of excellence.
O great sage, even the wives of the twice-born have the right to practice the knowledge of the Śruti;
so too do the Śūdras who are dispassionate, as well as women.
"The hearing of the established doctrine (siddhānta) is declared by the wise to be the hearing of the Purāṇas."
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the meaning of the *smṛti*.
Also in the *Rāmāyaṇa*:
"A twice-born man reciting it shall attain the status of a preeminent speaker; a well-born Kṣatriya shall attain the state of a sovereign king."
"A merchant shall attain the fruit of merit, and even a Śūdra who listens shall attain greatness."
This too is solely through the agency of the Brahmins.
As it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya*:
"O best of kings, having placed the image of the deity and the Brahmins in front [of oneself]..."
"It must certainly be heard by the Śūdra as well as by the other twice-born castes."
In another Smṛti as well:
"One should cause the four castes to hear [the Purāṇas], having placed a Brāhmaṇa at the forefront.
Precisely because of this injunction for hearing the Purāṇas, there is no fault even in hearing the Vedic mantras contained therein.

This has been stated in the Vārttika: "Setting aside those very Vedic mantras that have been incorporated into the Mahābhārata and other works, people employ them according to worldly convention, disregarding the rules governing mantras."

Although the status of being Vedic cannot exist without having an unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa-hetutva*), and therefore the existence of hymns (*stotra*) and the like within the Veda is inferred, nevertheless, there is an absence of fault due to the explicit scriptural statement. Thus, for a Śūdra, knowledge arises through hearing the Purāṇas by means of a Brāhmaṇa. If it be objected: "In this way, according to the injunction for hearing, since it is stated that 'one should cause the four castes to hear,' even for the twice-born (*dvija*), there would be only the hearing of the mantras and not their recitation," we reply:
"It should be studied by the Brāhmaṇa, the Vaiśya, and the Kṣatriya."
"From conception until the funeral pyre."
From such statements as these, it follows that study alone is a constituent part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*),
whereas listening (*śravaṇa*) is for the sake of a specific result:
"He who would listen to this constantly, and he who would recite it..."
That man shall not encounter anything inauspicious, neither in this world nor in the next.

This is because the fruits [of such recitation] are declared in passages such as those concerning the recitation of the Caṇḍī, and because of the statement by Yājñavalkya: "The learned man who causes this to be heard by the twice-born on every festival day—his reward is that of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; may you grant your approval of this."

Although there are injunctions for both the study and the hearing of the Purāṇas, study serves a visible purpose because it leads to knowledge which is for the sake of ritual action (*karma*); hearing, however, has only an invisible purpose. For Śūdras, the situation is reversed: hearing has a visible purpose because it leads to knowledge for the sake of ritual action, and it also has an invisible purpose because it is for the sake of its own fruit; study, however, does not exist for them at all, according to the statement: "A Śūdra must only hear [the scriptures], he must never study them."
And because of the statement in the *Harivaṃśa*: "But by hearing [it], one of the Śūdra caste attains a good rebirth.
By this, the eligibility for reciting the *Viṣṇusahasranāma*, the *Caṇḍīstotra*, and other Purāṇic texts is also refuted.
As for that which is found in the hymn expounding the *Sahasranāma*—
"A Brāhmaṇa shall become a master of the Vedānta; a Kṣatriya shall be victorious;
a Vaiśya shall be enriched with wealth; and a Śūdra shall attain happiness."
This statement also refers exclusively to the act of hearing. And the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya said in his commentary on this:
"In the phrase 'the Śūdra shall attain happiness,' the Śūdra [attains it] by means of hearing alone.
However, in the hymn that sets forth the Thousand Names of Gaṇapati:
"Perfectly accomplished by a single recitation, this mantra of a thousand names should be chanted even by women, Śūdras, and outcasts for the attainment of auspiciousness."

From this statement, it follows that [the twice-born] possess the qualification [for recitation]. The same applies elsewhere as well. To say more: in rites such as bathing, giving gifts, and *śrāddha* performed by a Śūdra, only the twice-born may recite the Puranic mantras; for the Śūdra, however, there is only the hearing [of them]. Women and uninitiated Śūdras have no qualification for the installation [of deities]:
"O Lord of Men, women, those who are uninitiated, and Śūdras have no qualification for the installation of Viṣṇu or Śaṅkara."
Some say this is because of such scriptural statements.

Others hold that for a Śūdra, there is an option (vikalpa) regarding the installation of Viṣṇu and other deities. Furthermore, worship should be performed without physical contact. Mantras such as the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva are to be understood as ending with *namaḥ*. The source of this should be sought in works such as the *Kamalākara* which elucidate the status of Śūdras.
In this context, those statements intended for Śūdras should also be understood as applicable to women.
"Women and Śūdras share the same duties," according to this scriptural statement.
Thus, the duties of women have been briefly described.
Now follows the time for the *garbhādhāna* (conception) rite.

In this regard, the Dharmasūtra states: "And during the *ṛtu*, one should have union with one's wife according to the vow. The *ṛtu* consists of sixteen days and nights beginning from the day of the appearance of the menses. In that period, "union" (*saṃnipāta*), meaning sexual intercourse, must be performed with one's wife. The singular number is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), for the word *dāra* (wife) is actually plural in form. "According to the vow" (*anu-vrata*) means in accordance with the restriction prescribed by the scriptures.
Manu states the number of days in the fertile period (*ṛtu*): "The natural fertile period of women is recorded as sixteen nights,
together with four other days that are censured."
"Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on an even night."
In this context, by the mention of "night," the prohibition of daytime is implied.
Accordingly, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One should not go [to her] during the menses, even by day."
Yājñavalkya states:

"Women have sixteen nights [of fertility] during their season; one should approach them during those that are even-numbered. Furthermore, one should observe celibacy and avoid the sacred festival days (parvan) as well as the first four nights."

For women, the *ṛtu*—the period suitable for conception—consists of sixteen nights. Among these, intercourse is mandatory on all even-numbered nights, as indicated by the use of the plural in the word *yugmāsu*. Even in cases where celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is prescribed, such as during *śrāddha* ceremonies and the like, there is no fault of violating celibacy for one who engages in intercourse during the *ṛtu*. Vijñāneśvara maintains that because the term *parvāṇi* is used in the plural, it includes both the eighth and fourteenth days. As for the passage in the *Śivarahasya* cited in the *Hemādri*:
"One observing a vow should not engage in sexual intercourse during the day, nor on the anniversary of his birth."
And having given or eaten at a śrāddha on the parvan days, one who seeks spiritual welfare should not [do so].

Thus, the prohibition against sexual intercourse on the day of performing a *śrāddha*, giving gifts, or eating at such an occasion refers specifically to times other than the fertile period (*anṛtu*). However, it does not apply during the new moon (*darśa*) and similar occasions, because these are excluded from the category of forbidden days (*parvan*). "A woman should bathe after her menses on the fourth day;
the fertile period is thus declared to last for up to sixteen days."
"In that case, on an odd day she shall be female, and on an even day he shall be male."

Regarding this, Vyaṅkaṭadīkṣita states in the course of his commentary on the passage from the *Śivagītā* contained in the *Padmapurāṇa*: "As for the doubt—arising when both a general rule and a specific rule, which have obtained their respective scopes by mutually excluding one another (such as the rule 'one must certainly approach [one's wife] during her season' and the injunction for celibacy at śrāddhas and the like), might apply simultaneously—what is to be sublated? It is with the intention that even for one who approaches [his wife], there is no violation of celibacy, that he speaks of 'celibacy' (*brahmacarya*)..."

Vijñāneśvara has explained that "and" (ca) implies the root [text], but this is to be reconsidered; for it contradicts the statement of Vṛddha-Manu found in the section on Śrāddha: "Even when enjoined during the period following menstruation, one should never approach a woman at any time. Therefore, [one should not approach her] even during the menstrual period by day.

They say: "The statements regarding *brahmacarya* (celibacy/abstinence) found even in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*—just like the passage from the *Ātharvaṇa-śruti*, 'Life-breath indeed departs from those who engage in sexual union by day; that which is done at night is truly *brahmacarya*'—which is cited as the foundational source for the *Śaṅkha-Likhita-smṛti* rule 'one should go [to one's wife]'—are merely *arthavāda* (laudatory or explanatory statements)," according to the works of Mādhavācārya and others. This is what they maintain.

The term *ṣoḍaśadināvadhi* means "having a limit of sixteen days," that is, extending up to that limit. Thus, the period of menstruation (*ṛtukāla*) is specified by the authors of the scriptures as consisting of sixteen days, beginning from the day the menses appear. This being the case, on the fourth day a woman becomes purified after her menstrual bath (*ṛtusnātā*). Consequently, following the fourth day, during that fertile period (*ṛtu*), if she engages in intercourse on an odd-numbered day such as the fifth, a female child will be born; if on an even-numbered day such as the sixth, a male child will be born.

Although an abundance of *rajas* (the female reproductive element) and so forth is stated to be the cause for [the birth of] a female and the like, nevertheless, there is no contradiction when there is an abundance of *rajas* in an odd-numbered day and an abundance of *śukra* (the male reproductive element) in an even-numbered day. However, when there is an abundance of *śukra* in an odd-numbered day, then a male is indeed born, though with a female form; this is because the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), *rajas*, prevails over the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) consisting of time and form—so say Vijñāneśvara and others.

In this way, it should also be understood that even when there is an excess of *rajas* (ovum) during the even nights, it is the female who takes on the male form. Here, by specifying the menstrual period (*ṛtu*) as consisting of sixteen days and stating that the birth of a son or other offspring occurs only after the fourth day, it is indicated that the first four days must be avoided.
Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"The menstrual period of women consists of sixteen nights; during that time, one should approach her on the even nights."
"And in practicing celibacy, one should avoid the [specific] parvan days and the first four nights."
Even among the even-numbered days, he should approach only those that are not otherwise prohibited;
and these have been stated by Manu: "Of those [days], the first four are censurable, as is the eleventh."
"The thirteenth day and the remaining ten nights are to be known as the auspicious ones."
Regarding the prohibition against sexual intercourse on the eleventh and thirteenth lunar days, the *Madanapārijāta* states: "It is not [permitted] during the fortnight.

As for the practice of approaching one's wife at night on the fourth day, which is mentioned in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*: "Having bathed, wearing clean clothes and ornaments, and having conversed with a Brahmin, he sips water and invites her"; and that which is stated by Āpastamba: [the same].

"They teach that from the fourth day until the sixteenth, one should approach one's wife during the even nights for the sake of progeny and spiritual excellence"; and as it is stated by Hārīta: "When she has bathed on the fourth day and during the even nights, the depositing of the seed is performed; thus, he establishes a Brahma-embryo."
Thus, this should be understood as referring to the cessation of her menses.
For Āpastamba has stated: "Bathing for a woman in her courses is recommended on the fourth day; she may be approached once the menses have ceased, but by no means while they have not ceased."

And because of the statement of Manu: "When her menses have ceased, a virtuous woman who has been menstruating [becomes fit] by bathing. However, in reality, it is utterly improper to restrict the practice of approaching on the fourth day—which is explicitly stated in one's own *sūtra*—by means of a *smṛti*. Thus, this very alternative—that approaching indeed takes place on the fourth day even if the menses have not yet ceased—is the more sound one. Mādhava explains that in the verse of Manu, the word "virtuous" (*sādhvī*) implies she is fit for approaching. Consequently, the prohibition of the fourth day in the aforementioned verse of Manu refers to the actual presence of menstrual flow.

It should be understood that although the fourth day is already included by the phrase "on even nights" (*yugmāsu*) in the immediately preceding statement of Hārīta, its separate mention is intended to highlight its primary importance. This [practice] also applies only when menstruation has ceased.

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya stated: "One should avoid the *parvan* days. When the question arises as to which those days are, the *Brahmapurāṇa* says: "The fourteenth, the eighth, the new moon, and the full moon..."
O Indra among kings, these are the sacred festival days (parvan), as is the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti).
"And the man who indulges in oil, women, and meat among all these [forbidden things],
O King, goes to the hell named Viṇmūtrabhojana."
By the use of the word "and" (ca), the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is included. On these festival days (parvan), Manu also says:
"The new moon (amāvāsyā), the eighth (aṣṭamī), the full moon (paurṇamāsī), and the fourteenth (caturdaśī)."
"A twice-born man who has completed his studies (a snātaka) should always remain a celibate student (brahmacārī), even during the period favorable for conception."
The Śruti also says:
"One should not approach a woman on the new moon day or the full moon day; if one were to approach her, he would become devoid of virility.
Yājñavalkya says:
"Proceeding in this manner, one should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the asterisms Maghā and Mūla.
When the Moon is in a favorable state, a man shall once again procreate a son endowed with auspicious marks."

"Kṣāmā" means emaciated. And this state of emaciation occurs precisely through the observance of the *rajasvalā* (menstruating woman) vows; otherwise, it may be achieved by eating little, avoiding oily foods, and so forth, for the purpose of diminishing the menstrual flow.
Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"If the female seed (*śukra*) is in excess, a girl shall be born; if the male seed is in excess, a boy shall be born."
Therefore, for the sake of increasing semen, one should provide unctuous food.
"One should make the woman eat light food; thus one shall procreate a son.
Manu says:
"A male is born when the male seed is in excess, and a female when the female seed is in excess."
"If [the semen] is equal, it results in a male; if both male and female [semen are equal], it results in twins; and if it is diminished or scanty, the opposite occurs."
One who is neither male nor female is a *napuṃsaka*. If there is a division of the seed between male and female, then Yama says:
"If, at the time of union, the man is deluded by passion..."
"If one should emit the semen in two ways, twins are born therein."

When the moon is waning, devoid of essence (*niḥsāra*), or small, the opposite occurs, resulting in non-conception. The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "Maghā and Mūla" is intended to include other asterisms prohibited by other treatises. When the moon (*indu*) is well-situated, meaning positioned in an auspicious place; the sense is that it should occur once in a single night, not twice or thrice.
Nārada says: "Wearing the sacred thread (*upavītī*) on an even lunar day, and not naked, one should desire a woman."
"A man desiring a son, having abandoned the paternal roots and origins," so it is said.
The meaning is that a man desiring a son should avoid these asterisms and travel on an even lunar day (*yugmatithi*). *Ahir* refers to Āśleṣā; *paitṛka* refers to Maghā.
The lunar days suitable for travel have been stated by Śrīdhara:
"Having avoided the sixth, eighth, fifteenth, fourth, and fourteenth days on both [fortnights]..."
"The remaining lunar days (tithis) shall be auspicious for the impregnation ceremony (niṣeka), as shall the days of the week (vāra) belonging to the Moon, Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury."

"In both cases," that is, in both [of the two] positions; "conception" (*niṣeka*) is the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*); "Śaśāṅka" is the Moon; "Ārya" is Jupiter (*guru*); "Sita" is Venus (*śukra*); "Induja" is Mercury (*budha*). Regarding the asterisms, it is said in the *Ratnamālā*:
"The asterisms of Viṣṇu (Śravaṇā), Prajeśa (Rohiṇī), Ravi (Hasta), Mitra (Anurādhā), Samīra (Svātī), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Mūla, the three Uttarās, and Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) are for the rite of conception."
"Puṣya, Vasu, Śītakarman, Citrā, and Āditya are to be honored; they yield middling results, while others are fruitless."

Viṣṇu is Śravaṇa; Prajeśa is Rohiṇī; Ravi is Hasta; Mitra is Anurādhā; Samīra is Svātī; Pauṣṇa is Revatī; Mūla is well known; by the word "Uttarā," the three Uttarās are meant; Varuṇabha is the constellation Śatabhiṣaj. In the rite of *niṣeka* (the ceremony of conception), these [asterisms] are to be honored. Puṣya is well known; Vasava is Āśraviṣṭhā (Śraviṣṭhā); Śītakara is Mṛgaśīrṣa; Aśvinau is the constellation Aśvinī.

Citrā, the two well-known Ādityas (Punarvasū)—these yield middling results. The meaning is that the remaining stars are fruitless. Some maintain that because Mūla is both prescribed and prohibited, there is an option (*vikalpa*); however, in reality, the worshipability of Mūla must be considered with caution.
As stated in the *Vṛddhavasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:
"In the two [asterisms] of Pūṣan (Revatī), in those of the Pitṛs (Maghā), Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī), Sārpa (Āśleṣā), the two of Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), and in one's own birth asterism..."
"The establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) should not be performed during times afflicted by portents or malefic planets, nor at an unfavorable lagna."

The inauspicious *lagna*s are those known as Aries, Scorpio, Capricorn, and Aquarius. Regarding Śravaṇa and Revatī, there is an option (*vikalpa*) because they are both prescribed and prohibited. In this context, all three types of birth [days] should be avoided.
Thus, Bṛhaspati states in the *Prayogapārijāta*:
"One should avoid ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), medical treatment, sexual intercourse, and anointing with oil."
"One should avoid the caulakarma, upanayana, and other such rites during the three [specific] births."

The three births [refer to] the birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*), the tenth, and the nineteenth. Some say that the birth asterism refers to the asterisms preceding and following it. Jyotir-Vasiṣṭha states: "During an eclipse, during the *vaidhṛti* and *pāta* yogas, at the beginning of the *viṣṭi* karana, in the first part of the *pārigha* yoga, during the twilights, on festival days (*parvan*), and on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father, approaching one's wife must be avoided."
In Jyotiṣa:
"On even days, one desiring a son should approach his virtuous wife during the conjunctions (yogas) to be described hereafter;
on odd days, one desiring a daughter should do so, avoiding the Gaṇḍa [periods] consisting of the portions of the lunar day (tithi) and the ascendant (lagna)."

It is stated in the *Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa* that even the day preceding the anniversary of a parent's death (*śrāddha*) should be avoided. Furthermore, this [rite] should be performed even during the heliacal setting of Jupiter or Venus, as it is said: "During all festivals, at the *sīmantonnayana*, and at the birth of a child following the *ṛtu* period..."
"And for Jupiter and Venus, the fault of debilitation does not exist."

Thus it is stated by Bhṛgu in the *Jyotirnibandha*. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), there is the inclusion of *aticāra* (excessive motion) and other such phenomena. This also applies during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). [As it is said: "One should not perform [the rite] even when the proper time has arrived, if it falls on the new moon, a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), an inauspicious lunar day (*viṣṭi*), or similar occasions."

"One should not avoid the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* during an intercalary month," according to the statement of Garga. Regarding the sequence of approaching [the husband] when there are multiple wives and their fertile periods (*ṛtu*) coincide, Devala says:
"When the fertile periods coincide, one should approach them in the order of Brahmin and the other castes."
"Or for the sake of protection, or for one who has no son, or even according to the order of seizure."

The *tīrtha* is the fertile season (*ṛtu*). When there is simultaneity [of multiple wives], one should approach the childless wife first. This means that whether all the wives are childless or already have children, he should proceed according to the order of their castes (*varṇa*) or the order of their marriage (*grahaṇa*). The order of marriage refers to the sequence of taking the hand in marriage (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). Thus says Kaśyapa: "In the case of simultaneity regarding the fertile season, however, one should approach them according to the order of marriage. Approaching the wife during the fertile season is prescribed in the Śruti: "One should approach one's wife during her season."

Bṛhaspati states the expiation for failing to approach one's wife during her season: "He who has established the sacred fires but does not perform the ritual attendance on the festival days, and he who does not approach his wife during her season, shall also perform half a *kṛcchra* penance."
In this context, the *ṛtu* (season) consists of thirteen days starting from the day of menstruation, or twelve days starting from the fifth day.
As for what Saṃvarta says:
"He who does not approach his wife when she is in her season, being restrained and observing her vow..."
"One hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are prescribed for one who has transgressed a rule unintentionally. This refers to cases where the act was not done deliberately.

And this refers to the case where the place and the object are identical, according to the statement of Parāśara: "He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him, is joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo; there is no doubt in this matter."
By the statement "in the presence," it is implied that there is no fault in the case of one who is not present.
Devala says:
"He who, being healthy, does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses..."
"One incurs the sin of killing an embryo, and the offspring that has been obtained perishes."

By the statement "one who is healthy," it is implied that there is no fault for one who is unwell. Thus, there is no fault for one who approaches his wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*) while in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or similar conditions.
And so says Manu:
"During a period of birth-impurity or captivity, a Brahmin is exempt from [the prohibition against] offerings to the gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*)."
"Likewise, one is not smeared by sin even from failing to observe the Ṛtu [periods]. Here, *enasā* means by sin.
Vyāsa says: "Whether afflicted by disease, imprisoned, on journeys, or during the sacred festival days (*parvan*)."
"But for women during their fertile period, the sin of destroying an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā) does not apply."

Regarding the phrase "during the fertile period," the word "not approaching" is to be understood as the ellipsis. This rule concerning approaching one's wife during the fertile period applies only to one who has not yet fathered a son. This is because its validity is established on the basis of the Vedic scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born with three debts: to the sages through celibacy, to the gods through sacrifice, and to the ancestors through progeny. Since this [rule] is thus justified, it is improper to assume another scriptural authority.
Accordingly, Manu says: "By the mere birth of an eldest son, a man becomes a father of sons."
"And because he is indeed free from debt to his ancestors, he therefore deserves everything."
The Kūrma Purāṇa also states: "He should approach his wife during her fertile period until a son is born."

Thus, since the purpose of the scripture has been fulfilled by the birth of a single son and one has become free from debt (*anṛṇya*), the procreation of further sons is not mandatory; so say some. Others, however, maintain that because the fertile period (*ṛtu*) is the occasioning cause, a repetition of the occasional rite is appropriate for each occasion, and they cite the traditional law: "Many sons are to be desired, so that even if only one should go to Gayā."
It is obligatory for a wife also to approach her husband during the fertile period (*ṛtu*); otherwise, there is a fault.
As it is said in the *Saṃgraha*:
"A woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not consent to her husband..."
"That woman, having died, shall become a sow again and again."
Yama also states:
"A woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not approach her husband,
shall be proclaimed in the midst of the village as a killer of the embryo (bhrūṇahā) and banished."

The meaning of the second half of the verse is that, having publicly proclaimed and exposed that woman as a "feticide" (*bhrūṇaghnī*) in the midst of the village, one should cause her to dwell separately. Here too, it should be understood that the condition of "proximity" (*saṃnidhau*) applies. As for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), it should be known to be exactly as previously stated. Furthermore, there is no fault in a husband not approaching his wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*) if she is afflicted by disease or other such conditions; this is because, in the verse of Vyāsa cited immediately above, the masculine gender was not intended to be restrictive. The Śruti also speaks of approaching her even outside the fertile period: "They said, 'Let us choose a boon: let us obtain offspring at any time, and let us have sexual union according to our desire.'"

"Let us unite," [he says]; therefore, women obtain offspring from that seasonal union. They unite according to their desire until the birth, for they have been chosen at the proper time. Regarding "from the seasonal union" (*ṛtviyāt*), this means from the connection with a man during the fertile period. "Until the birth" (*āvijanitoḥ*) means up to the point of delivery. "They unite" (*saṃbhavanti*) means they engage in sexual intercourse. Also, in the *Dharmasūtra*: "Even in the interval [between periods], cohabitation is permitted only with one's wife, on account of the word of the Brāhmaṇas."
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Or he may act according to his desire, keeping in mind the boon granted to women;
yet he should remain devoted to his own wife, for women are declared to be worthy of protection."
This is the boon granted by Indra.
Bṛhaspati also said:
"Men should diligently engage in intercourse during the fertile period."
Or rather, it may always be performed except on festival days, for that is indeed pleasing to women."
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well:
"Thinking thus, a man should approach his own wives when they are in their fertile season, provided they are free from the aforementioned defects and are desirous; even outside the fertile season."
But as for the one who says:
"He who does not approach his wife during her season, and he who approaches her outside her season— they are said to be equal in sin, as is he who sheds seed in a non-vaginal opening."
Thus, the prohibition against approaching one's wife outside of her fertile period (*ṛtu*) stated by Baudhāyana should be understood to apply when the woman lacks desire.
Vyāsa states the prohibition regarding certain women: "One should not approach a woman who has not bathed, nor one who is ill, nor one who is menstruating."
Neither one who is undesirable, nor one who is angry, nor one who is disapproved of, nor one who is pregnant.
"One should avoid approaching an elderly woman, a barren woman, one of immoral conduct, one whose children have died, one who has not yet reached puberty, or one who already has many sons."

One who is free from defects such as hypocrisy and the like is praiseworthy; one who is not praiseworthy is unpraiseworthy—the meaning is that one should avoid her. An elderly woman, even if she has menses, is one incapable of conception. A *puṣpiṇī* is one who is in her fertile period (*ṛtumatī*); other than that is the *apuṣpiṇī*. By this, intercourse with one who has not yet reached puberty or whose menses have ceased is forbidden. In the phrase "one who has many sons," by the word "many sons," a number starting from eleven is to be understood, based on the scriptural indication:
"Place ten sons in her. Regarding the regulation of sexual union according to specific periods, it is stated in the *Kāmaśāstra*:
"For one who desires a woman, no loss of strength occurs if he does so daily during the summer and winter, or every third day during other seasons."

As for that which is stated in the Vāgbhaṭṭīya: "In spring and autumn, one may indulge in desire at will after three days; in the rainy season and summer, after a fortnight; but during the cold season and the dewy season, one who is strong may indulge as he pleases."
Thus it has been stated; therein, by the designation "the strong one," it is said that the purpose is visible, and thus the arrangement is according to one's strength.
Paiṭhīnasi states the extension of the rule:
"In an enclosed place, he should call her for sexual intercourse. "Enclosed" means surrounded [by a curtain].
The prohibition regarding specific locations is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "One should not engage in sexual intercourse within a hermitage, nor near a deity, a twice-born, or a guru;
nor indeed at a sacred tree, a crossroads, a field boundary, or at a four-way junction."

The syntactical connection is as follows: one should not engage in sexual intercourse (*vyavāya*) within the hermitage (*āśrama*) of gods, twice-born men (*dvija*), or gurus. *Vyavāya* means sexual union; one who possesses that is called a *vyavāyin*.
Regarding the proximity of a lamp at the time of lovemaking, it is stated in the *Ratiprakāśa*: "One should perform the act of love near a lamp.
And in the *Jyotirnibandha*: [text omitted].
"If a person forms an attachment to a lamp that is not yet lit, he shall suffer poverty for as long as his life lasts; of this there is no doubt."
And this lamp must be lit by the wife alone.
As it is said in that very same place:
"The wife alone, following the will of her husband, having lit the lamp..."
"Having paid homage to her husband, she should take delight together with him."
Having lit a small wick in a lamp, one should perform the lighting of the [main] lamp by means of that [wick], but not directly from the lamp itself.
For it is stated as a fault in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "By lighting a lamp with a lamp, one becomes poor and afflicted by disease."
Extinguishing a lamp is forbidden for a man,

according to the scriptural statement: "The extinguishing of a lamp by men and the cutting down of a *kūśmāṇḍa* tree by women will certainly result in the extinction of the lineage within a very short time."

And this should be understood as universally applicable. In the *Jyotirnibandha* (in the *Ācāraprakāśa*, a compendium of *smṛti*): "One should not extinguish a lamp with the wind arising from one's bodice, nor with the wind from one's mouth, nor with the wind produced by the hands."
Having uttered "visṛja," one should extinguish the lamp with the corner of the garment;
and one should remain silent until the remainder [of the flame] is extinguished.
In this context, the word *visṛja* (release) refers to the lamp. "O lamp, release your light"—this is the meaning of *visṛja*.
*Añcalāt* means from the hem of the garment. *Śeṣaḥ* means the remainder of the lamp.
"A woman who, at the time of dusk, engages in union with her husband..."
That woman who takes away the life-span of her husband shall go to hell.

One who has touched her foot, one whose body is clinging [to her], as well as one who is impure, one who strikes her, and one who displays anger, wrath, or reproach— there is no fault in sexual union with such a person.
A woman should enjoy the company of her husband together with his bodice;
otherwise, she will certainly become a widow within three years or in the middle [of that period].
If a girl whose ears are covered by palm-leaf ornaments should engage in sexual intercourse,
she will become a widow in this world in her fifth or seventh year.
If a woman refuses her husband when he, overcome by passion, makes a request for union, she shall always be considered a "child-widow."
"He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him sinks,
along with his ancestors, into the terrible sin of killing an embryo.
Saffron, collyrium, betel, and likewise vermilion—
A washed garment and a flower are auspicious when joined together.
Having paid homage at the feet of her husband, she should afterwards lie down upon the bed;
thus the woman attains happiness and does not become a partaker of suffering.
One should avoid union with a woman whose mouth is stained by betel, who is naked, who cries out or weeps, who has a foul face, or who is afflicted by hunger.
A householder should always eat food and betel that have been left over by his elders;
however, he should not eat what has been left over by anyone other than his wife.
"If she should cast her own shadow or that of her husband upon the lamp,
those two spouses will certainly fall into poverty."
Regarding the bath and what follows it, a specific rule is stated in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*:
"One should bathe with lukewarm water; having bathed, one should first look at the sun.
Then the husband should be looked upon, and one should engage in conversation with him alone."

Regarding the specific procedure for approaching one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), the *Gṛhyasūtra* states: "Having sipped water, he invites [his wife] who has bathed, is wearing clean garments, is adorned, and has conversed with a Brāhmaṇa.

The term *snātām* means "one who has performed her bath. *Prayatavastrām* means "wearing pure garments. *Alaṃkṛtām* means "adorned with perfumes and ornaments. *Brāhmaṇasaṃbhāṣām* refers to a woman whose conversation (*saṃbhāṣā*) has been properly conducted (*samyag-bhāṣaṇa*) with a Brāhmaṇa who is not crooked (*akauṭila*). The meaning is that, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he calls such a woman to his side.
(In the *Jyotirgrantha*: "Having first chewed betel, one should engage in union with one's wife.
In the *Śaunakīya*: "One areca nut is always best; two areca nuts would be fruitless.")
The triad is most excellent; nothing superior to it is ever seen.
One should give a document with thirty-two leaf-marks to every sovereign king;
that with twenty-four leaf-marks is declared for vassal lords.
It should be known that a leaf of eighteen petals is especially for sons-in-law;
one of twelve petals is for the learned, and one of ten petals is for kinsmen.
Among all [leaves], the eight-petaled one is common to all; the four-petaled one is also [permissible]. However, the three-petaled leaf must not be given, nor likewise the single-petaled one.
Six betel leaves should be offered, especially to enemies;
the fruit [of the offering] is obtained in sequence by means of one, two, three, four, five, or six areca nuts.
A disease arises from the base of a leaf, and the occurrence of sin from the tip of a leaf;
a powdered leaf takes away one's lifespan, and a vein destroys the intellect.
One should likewise hold a single leaf that is upward-pointing and wide;
when smeared with the powder of the thumb and anointed, it bestows wealth.
The man who eats betel nut without placing a leaf in his mouth shall always be poor from birth and will not remember Hari at the end.
Taking the betel powder with the index finger, one should not eat the betel;
if a fool should eat it, he will go to the Raurava hell.
From the joining of the little finger, ring finger, middle finger, index finger, and thumb, there arise, in sequence:
sorrow, loss, death, lack of sovereignty, and short life.
By applying an ointment with one's thumb, it bestows all accomplishments;
the attainment of victory, women, clothing, and so forth will come to pass—of this there is no doubt.
One should not eat with the left hand, nor likewise with the hand of a woman;
if a fool should cause one to eat [in such a manner], his fortune perishes.
Betel leaf beautifully adorned with the essence of *khadira* wood by day,
but with the essence of *khadira* at night, would take away even the splendor of Indra himself.
One should eat with an abundance of fruit in the morning, an abundance of powder at midday, and an abundance of leaves at night; for one who does so, prosperity increases.
"A wise man should always extract the essence of the *kramuka* tree three times, the essence of the leaf (*parṇasāra*) twice, and once together with that of the *khadira* tree.
At the time of sexual union, one should perform the act after having made the woman remove her bodice (*akañcuka*).

For it is heard in the *Ratiprakāśa* regarding penance that one should perform a bath with clothes on after having engaged in sexual pleasure while wearing a bodice: "If there is silver on the index finger at the time of sexual intercourse, that must be discarded and the topknot (*śikhā*) must be released.
[One should avoid] the index finger joined with silver and the topknot provided with the *brahmagranthi*."
For it is heard in the *Saṃgraha* regarding penance: "One who has engaged in eating, sexual intercourse, or urination becomes pure through a *kṛcchra* penance.
Regarding the duty following sexual union, the *Dharmasūtra* states: "Contact with water [is required]."
Bathing (*snāna*) consists of touching water (*udakopasparśana*). This has been explained by Ujjvalākṛt as referring to the period of the menstrual cycle (*ṛtukāla*).
Parāśara also states: "Because of the suspicion of pregnancy during the fertile period, bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.
And this bathing is without the head. With reference to the bathing occasioned by approaching one's wife during her fertile period, [it is said]:
"One should perform the immersion without the head," according to the statement of Bṛhad-Vasiṣṭha.
Regarding the non-seasonal period (anṛtu), however, the Dharmasūtra states:
"Having washed off the stains and both feet, and having sipped water (ācamana), there is the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the limbs."
Parāśara also states: "But when one approaches [his wife] outside the prescribed period, the purification is like that for urine and feces.
However, for women, there is no requirement for bathing or washing the feet, because they lack such impurity. And so says Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"Even Umā and her husband would both become impure when they have gone to bed;
upon rising from bed, the woman becomes pure, while the man remains impure. Regarding the birth of a child, Atri says:
"A mortal man may indeed desire a pregnant woman for six months, but only after the eruption of her teeth;
in this way, dharma is not lost."

The particle *eva* connects with the phrase "for six months" immediately following. Nor should it be argued that this [text] contradicts the Vedic injunction, "They may go at will until the birth of a child," because that passage permits intercourse up to the point of childbirth; for there, by the word *vijanana*—which is synonymous with *prasava* (birth)—only the technical sense of birth as defined in the rule "From then on, there shall be procreation" (*ata ūrdhvaṃ prasūtiḥ syāt*) is intended, and thus there is no contradiction. The meaning is: once a boy has been born, one may approach him after the eruption of his teeth, but not before then.
Regarding Mātsyaka and Kaśyapa, it is stated that even if the menses have not arrived after twelve years, sexual union may take place: "If, after twelve years, the flower does not appear externally,
the flower certainly exists internally, as in the case of the jackfruit, the udumbara fig, and so forth."
Therefore, a wise man should engage in sexual union with a woman there."

From the statement "after twelve years," it should be understood that going [to one's wife] before that time is prohibited by implication. However, going for the sake of the *caturthī-karma* (the fourth-day rite) certainly does take place, because that is prescribed by sacred law (*vaidha*).
Āśvalāyana says:
"A twice-born man who has been initiated for a great sacrifice may go to his parents' home before the year [is up]."
"A wise man, even when requested by his wife during her fertile period, should strive to approach her with restraint."

One should not go [to her]. "Solicited" means requested; the remainder is that it is for the sake of enjoyment by the wife. "Before the appearance of the menses, one should not approach his wife; having gone, he falls low. By rendering the semen futile, he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin."

Thus, the prohibition stated by Dakṣa and Āśvalāyana pertains to the followers of the Ṛgveda and others. However, Sudarśana maintains that for those of the Taittirīya school, sexual intercourse should indeed be performed when prompted by natural desire.

Regarding the approach of a woman in her menses during the period of three nights, Yājñavalkya states the expiation: "Having approached a woman in her courses, one becomes pure after consuming clarified butter at the end of the three nights."
"At the end of three nights" means at the conclusion of three days of fasting;
for Marīci has stated: "He who approaches a woman in her menses should perform three days of fasting; he should consume cow's ghee, and thereby he is released from that sin."
He is one who approaches a woman during her menses; and this [refers to] unintentional action. But regarding intentional action, Saṃvarta says:
"If one should approach a woman during her menses, or likewise one who is pregnant or fallen (patita), the atikṛcchra penance is the purification for the sake of cleansing his sin."
Furthermore, this prohibition against approaching a pregnant woman takes effect only from the seventh month onwards, in accordance with the three statements cited immediately above.
Regarding the performance of expiation for the non-performance of the *garbhādhāna* rite, Āśvalāyana says:
"Due to the non-performance of the *garbhādhāna*, the son born of her becomes defiled."
"Without having given a cow to a twice-born man, the husband should perform the *puṃsavana* rite."
The word "api" (even) should be supplied immediately after "akṛtvā" (without having performed). [As it is said:
"Some teachers maintain that once the expiation has been performed, even a past deed must be performed; however, other wise ones say 'no'."

This is because of the agreement with the scriptural statement. The meaning of the second half of the verse is that, having given a cow to a twice-born man, the husband should perform the *puṃsavana* rite even without having performed the *garbhādhāna*. Furthermore, this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies when the *garbhādhāna* alone is performed together with the *puṃsavana* after its primary time has passed; however, when the *puṃsavana* alone is performed after its primary time has passed, it should be understood that the previously mentioned penance consisting of *kṛcchra* [is required]. Alternatively, both may be combined in either case.

Furthermore, this *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) must certainly be performed at an auspicious moment after first performing a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) when the defects are slight, having deliberated upon the auspicious and inauspicious results of the month and other factors; it does not depend on waiting for a naturally auspicious time. However, if the defects are numerous, one should perform only the propitiatory rite during the first menstrual period, and then perform it when a subsequent auspicious period arrives.
Thus says Jyotir-Vasiṣṭha:
"If that flower [the menstrual flow] is seen to have many defects, then the rite of propitiation (*śāntika-karma*) must be performed."
"And likewise, one should avoid sharing a bed with her until the appearance of menses on the final day."

In this context, "abundance of defects" (*prabhūtadoṣatva*) should be understood as having multiple defects or having very great defects. The "great defects," moreover, take the form of bestowing widowhood, crookedness, the destruction of progeny, and so forth.
Jyotiṣkaśyapa also says: "If a flower is seen on lunar days, weekdays, or asterisms that are defective..."
"One should avoid traveling there, because of the sight [of them] even in auspicious places."

In this context, because the performance [of the rite] is prescribed with regard to the expectation of an auspicious time when defects are abundant, it is thereby authorized that the performance of *garbhādhāna* (conception) may follow the *śāntika* rite during that very same season when defects are not abundant. That *śāntika* rite is to be found in the *Śāntiratnamālā*.
Now follows the procedure for *garbhādhāna*:
therein, upon the appearance of menses, a woman is considered *rajasvalā* (in her courses) for three nights.

[One should avoid] the habitual use of collyrium and ointments, daily bathing, sleeping during the day, contact with fire and the like, the letting go of the rope [of the body], going outside, scraping [the teeth], cutting [nails], cleaning the teeth, eating meat, looking at planets, looking at deities, engaging in vulgar conduct, chewing betel, holding fans and the like, wearing another’s garment, ascending a seat or a bed, wearing turmeric, perfumes, garlands, and the like, eating from a bronze vessel, cleansing the mouth, playing, performing artistic crafts, domestic chores, traveling on a road, eating at night, rubbing the head, tearing the nails, and entering another’s house.

She should avoid looking at the sun, laughing, speaking much, eating much, and so forth. She should remain impure for three nights. She should eat from a burnt earthen bowl. She should drink liquids with her cupped hands, or from a large earthen vessel, or from a copper one. However, there is this distinction: during the first menstrual period, there is no fault in wearing fragrant substances, garlands, and the like, nor in chewing betel. Everything else is the same. Regarding the rites of the Smṛtis and the Gṛhya-sūtras, she becomes eligible [to perform them] after bathing on the fifth day;
however, regarding the Śrauta rites, she becomes eligible even after bathing on the fourth day.

The agent, when the *rajas* has ceased, during any night among those from the fourth to the thirteenth excluding the eleventh and the thirteenth; otherwise, during any night among those from the fifth onwards, on any lunar day (*tithi*) other than the sixth, eighth, fourth, fourteenth, eleventh, full moon, or new moon, provided it is free from the *viṣṭi* yoga and similar obstacles, and unconnected with a funeral anniversary (*kṣayāha*) or other such *śrāddha* rites, and on any day of the week other than Sunday, Tuesday, or Saturday.

One should perform the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) under any lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) other than Śravaṇa, Rohiṇī, Hasta, Anurādhā, Svātī, Revatī, and the three Uttarās, as well as the one known as Śatabhiṣaj—provided it is not defiled by portents or malefic planets—or else under any of the following: Puṣya, Śraviṣṭhā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Aśvinī, Citrā, or Punarvasu, when the Moon is situated in a favorable position and the ascendant (*lagna*) is other than Aries, Scorpio, Capricorn, or Aquarius. In this regard, for one desiring a son, the rite should be performed on even nights; for one desiring a daughter, on odd nights. Herein, there is no prohibition regarding the setting of Jupiter or Venus, the intercalary month (*malamāsa*), and so forth.

At an auspicious moment prescribed by an astrologer, the performer, having performed his daily obligatory rites in the morning, together with his wife, shall perform *ācamana* (sipping water), restrain his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), and proclaim the place and time. Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord, for the purpose of accomplishing the purification of the womb (*kṣetrasaṃskāra*)—which serves as the means for destroying the impurities arising from the seed and the womb, and for the attainment of the excellence of all purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to every embryo to be conceived based on this wife—I shall perform the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) in her," he should then perform its constituent parts: the worship of Gaṇapati, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), and the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*).

One should perform the *nāndī-śrāddha* according to the method previously described; the specific modification here is that one should say, "May Brahmā be pleased. Then, at night, having prepared a bed according to the method stated in the *Ācāraratnamālā*—a bed provided with new cloth, scented ointments, and a mouth fragrant with betel-leaf and the like, adorned with flowers, garlands, and ornaments, fragrant itself, and made slender by the three-night vow or by eating little—one should first converse with a learned, straightforward Brāhmaṇa of pure disposition, and then ascend the bed oneself.

Having done so, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), adopt the *nivīta* posture, remove the silver ring from his index finger if one is worn, and loosen his topknot (*śikhā*). Then, with the mantra, "Oṃ, may Viṣṇu prepare the womb... become a cow for [the sake of] milk," he should call her near for the purpose of sexual union. Next, having laid her on the bed to his left side near the lamp, he performs the sexual act with the mantra:
"Oṃ, may our names be united, our hearts be united, our navels be united, our skins be united;
I unite you with the bond of desire so that there shall be no release."

"Oṃ! That which is called the *saṃvanana* (the rite of enchantment) of the cakravāka birds, brought forth from the rivers—since the gods and Gandharvas are united by it, may you two be united in your own [affection]. Thus he says while seeking her face.
"Oṃ bhūḥ! With Prajāpati as the bull, I cause [you] to flow; receive a hero, O [Name]!"
Oṃ bhuvaḥ! By means of Prajāpati, the supreme bull, I cause [the seed] to flow; bestow a hero, O [Name]!

With each of these mantras—"Oṃ suvaḥ, by Prajāpati, the supreme bull, I cause [the seed] to fall; bestow a hero, O so-and-so"—one should cause the semen to fall. If there is an excess, it should be caused to fall silently. In these mantras, having removed the word "asau," the wife's name should be inserted in the vocative case ending in *-danta*, such as "amukadā. The various types of sexual union should be observed from treatises on love (kāmaśāstra), such as the *Pañcasāyaka*.

If one should desire [offspring], based on the statement "having made the fingers female" (*svīḥ kṛtvāṅgulīḥ*), then some say that there is an absence of the mantra because of the contradiction with the gender [of the word *pumān*] and the contradiction with the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).

Others, however, say that there is no absence of the mantra because the masculine gender is not intended to be significant due to its being a generic reference (*jātinirdeśa*), or because the birth of male offspring such as sons and daughters exists, and thus there is no contradiction between the gender and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
