Then, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and having performed a bath without the head, he should take out the silver [amulet] held between the forefinger, hold it again on that same finger, tie his topknot (*śikhā*), perform the traditional sipping of water (*ācamana*) and breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and meditate upon Viṣṇu. However, if the intercourse occurs at a time other than the prescribed season (*ṛtu*), there is only the washing of the feet and sprinkling of the limbs, but no full bath. Nevertheless, the washing of any residual stains (*lepa*) must still be done even in this case. Thereafter, the two should sleep separately. As for the wife, however, there is no impurity (*aśucitā*) in either of these two instances.
One should not approach her at will during times other than the proper season; however, one who approaches her by her own desire incurs no fault whatsoever.

Then, when the next day has dawned, after the completion of the daily rites, one should give more abundant gifts to the Brahmins, dismiss the deities, and feed the Brahmins. Whatever else is required by family custom should also be performed. Alternatively, the dismissal of the deities may take place after the *nāndī-śrāddha*, while the feeding of the Brahmins, the giving of abundant gifts, and so forth, should occur on the second day itself. This is because performing these before the principal rite is extremely contradictory, as it is observed everywhere that these constitute subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) following the principal rite (*pradhāna*).

The sage Ātreya maintains that all acts of approaching [the wife] for sexual intercourse must be accompanied by mantras; his intention is that the performance of a subsidiary act (guṇa) repeats with each principal act (pradhāna). Bādarāyaṇa, however, holds that only the approach on the fourth night following marriage and the approach on the fourth day and so forth after the appearance of menses are to be accompanied by mantras, and no others; his intention is that the former is for the purpose of consecrating the woman (*strī-saṃskāra*), while the latter is for the purpose of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*).

If, by chance, the *caturthī-karma* has not been performed and the fertile period (*ṛtu*) arrives, then one should perform the *caturthī-karma* preceded by the expiation consisting of a *kṛcchra* penance, and immediately thereafter perform the *garbhādhāna* sacrament. Regarding the first appearance of menstruation during an inauspicious month or similar occasion, some say that one should not perform auspicious customs such as chewing betel; however, from the second instance onward, one may perform them following an auspicious propitiatory rite (*śānti*). In the case of an inauspicious first appearance of menstruation, one should wait for the second.

Others maintain that even when that [second] unfavorable [aspect] is extensive, one should perform a pacification (*śānti*). Still others hold that one should perform the pacification according to one's capacity during the first [aspect] alone; and even if the second and subsequent aspects are unfavorable, after performing an extensive pacification, one should perform the auspicious rites (*maṅgalācāra*) and the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). Furthermore, many say that even if the third aspect is defective, one should perform the impregnation after performing an extremely extensive pacification, but not even after performing a pacification for the first and second [aspects]. Among these views, one should adopt what is logical.

In this regard, even when there is a single significant inauspicious defect, the pacification (*śānti*) to be described hereafter must be performed. However, when two, three, or more inauspicious factors coincide, it should be performed by increasing the number of oblations (*āhuti*) to be described later for the purpose of dispelling the many inauspicious results indicated by them; this should be understood according to one's capacity and so forth. Thus concludes the procedure for the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*).

Even when the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) has been performed in this manner, if a fetus is still not conceived, then the *Nārāyaṇabali* and the *Nāgabali* must be performed for the purpose of removing obstructing spirits (*preta*). Although the *Baudhāyana-sūtra* alone is to be adopted by followers of the Yajurveda due to its superior authority, nevertheless, because the *sūtra* for the *Nāgabali* is currently unavailable here, the procedure for the *Nāgabali* according to the Ṛgveda (*Bāhvṛca*) is now demonstrated.

Although the procedure for the Nārāyaṇabali is stated by Baudhāyana, it is prescribed specifically for the Bāhvṛca (Ṛgvedin) because of its being taught as a mandatory adjunct [to his specific ritual context]. (If it were performed according to the method stated in the Baudhāyana-sūtra, however, the fallacy of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) would ensue.
Now follows the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* on the Nārāyaṇabali:
"Now, the Nārāyaṇabali [should be performed] within a year; at a pure time, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, having bathed and being pure..."
Having duly worshipped Viṣṇu and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, in that place, [he should offer] oblations mixed with sesame seeds and soaked in honey and ghee before them.

Meditating on the deceased as the form of Viṣṇu, and with his sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), facing south, he should offer those ten rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing southward, using his left hand, saying: "O [Name], of the Kāśyapa lineage, this rice-ball is for you, whose deity is Viṣṇu. Having honored the rice-balls with water-offerings (*arghya*) and other rites, and having performed the ceremonies up to the dismissal (*pravāhaṇa*), he should cast them into a river. Then, having invited an odd number of Brāhmaṇas at night and remained fasting, he should, on the following day at midday, worship Viṣṇu and feed the Brāhmaṇas according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, intending it for the deceased.

When the Brahmins are satisfied, having silently performed the rites up to the pouring of water according to the *piṇḍa* procedure near them, he should offer four *piṇḍas* made from the remnants of the food, proceeding from left to right (toward the south), saying: "To Viṣṇu, to Brahmā, to Śiva with his retinue, and to Yama; O Viṣṇu, this *piṇḍa* is for you. Then, meditating upon the deceased as Devadatta of the Kāśyapa lineage, he should offer a fifth *piṇḍa*, saying: "O Viṣṇu, this is for you," [visualizing him] in that form. Then, having gratified those who have sipped water with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he should especially honor one among them who is virtuous.

Then, with the thought that they are the deceased, one should satisfy them with garments, ornaments, cattle, and gold. With those [materials] in hand, holding sacred grass (*pavitra*), one should cause the offering of water and sesame seeds to be given, saying: "This handful of water and sesame seeds is for the deceased of the Kāśyapa lineage. Having caused this *Nārāyaṇa-bali* rite to be recited—"May the Blessed Viṣṇu, by means of this *Nārāyaṇa-bali*, make this Devadatta pure, free from sin, and worthy"—one should dismiss [the deities]. This is the ritual procedure for the *Nārāyaṇa-bali*. In the same way, having worshipped another deity of one's own choice on the Yamadvitīyā day, one should perform this rite; he too shall make him free from sin.

"One should perform it; however, even one who performs meritorious deeds should not fail to offer this *bali*. If it is not performed, the merit does not reach the other world; it perishes in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Therefore, one should perform it according to one's ability. On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, the performer, having bathed and completed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*) in a pure place such as a riverbank, should sip water (*ācamana*), perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and announce the place and time. He should then make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of removing the state of being a *preta* from the deceased who obstructs the prosperity of my family, I shall perform the Nārāyaṇabali. Having invoked Viṣṇu and Vaivasvata Yama respectively into two jars established according to the ritual for placing jars (*kalaśasthāpanavidhi*)—using two images fashioned of gold—he should [worship] with the Puruṣasūkta for Yama.

Having worshipped [the deity] with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) in due order while reciting "O Soma," one should, on a line to the east of that, after spreading *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south, pour water in ten places from right to left, saying, "May Viṣṇu, in the form of the deceased (preta), be purified. Then, facing south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), and bending the left knee, one should offer ten rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) soaked in honey and ghee and mixed with sesame seeds upon the *kuśa* grass with tips pointing south, using the left hand turned away, while meditating on the deceased in the form of Viṣṇu, saying: "O deceased of the Kāśyapa lineage, named so-and-so, whose deity is Viṣṇu, this rice-ball is for you."

Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings and performed the rites ending with the *pravāhaṇa*, he should cast [the vessel] into a river or similar body of water. On that very night, he should invite an odd number of Brahmins—five, three, or one—with the intent for the Śrāddha to be performed on the following day, saying, "May a moment be granted," and then observe a fast.

On the following day at midday, having worshipped Viṣṇu and intended the deceased as being in the form of Viṣṇu, one should perform the rites according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure, beginning with the washing of the feet and ending with the inquiry regarding satisfaction (*tṛptipraśna*). Then, in the presence of the Brāhmaṇas, having silently performed the rites from the drawing of lines (*ullekhana*) up to the pouring of water (*udakaninayana*) as in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, one should offer four *piṇḍas* using the name-mantras for Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śiva with his retinue, and Yama. Finally, meditating on the deceased in the form of Viṣṇu, one should offer the fifth *piṇḍa* with the formula: "O Viṣṇu, this *piṇḍa* is for you."

Having performed the rites from the offering of worship up to the dismissal (*pravāhaṇa*), and having silently provided the *ācamana* water, he should satisfy the Brahmins with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). To one among them who possesses good qualities, he should give clothing, ornaments, a cow, gold, and so forth, regarding him as the deceased; or, if they belong to the same lineage (*pakṣa*), he may give it to that one alone. Then he should say: "May you all offer handfuls of sesame-water for the deceased. They, with *pavitra* grass in hand, should offer a handful of water containing *kuśa* grass and *tulasī* leaves, saying: "This is a handful of sesame-water for the deceased, belonging to the *Kāśyapa* gotra, named [Name], who is of the form of Viṣṇu."

Then he should cause the Brahmins to recite: "By this Nārāyaṇa-bali rite, may the Blessed Viṣṇu make this deceased person pure, sinless, and worthy. Then the Brahmins respond, "So be it" (*tathāstu*). Thereafter, the performer, having bathed, should eat. Thus concludes the procedure for the Nārāyaṇa-bali.
Now follows the Nāga-bali. Regarding this, Śaunaka says:
Now I shall describe the supreme procedure for the consecration of everything;
one should then perform it according to the rules on the day of Sinīvālī or the full moon.
Or he may perform it on the fifth lunar day, or under the asterism Āśleṣā, or on that very day,
provided the Brahmin was a slayer of serpents in a previous birth.
Having bathed and returned from there, one should give a "brahmin's staff" (a gift) to a twice-born man,
proclaim one's own execution, and perform fourteen *kṛcchra* penances.
If this killing has been committed in this very life, one should give an iron staff to a learned Brahmin who maintains a family, for the sake of purifying the sin.
Or, in the absence of [the offender], one should cause the price of the staff to be paid to the Brahmin;
indeed, this very same [penalty] should be caused to be paid to the perpetrator of the act in lieu of actual execution.
Three *niṣkas*, two *niṣkas*, or one *niṣka* is the lowest [fee] for those who perform the *anumati* and other rites; half a *niṣka* or half of that [again] is [the fee].
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; one should give according to one's means.
Having obtained the permission of the guru, one should perform the consecration immediately thereafter.

Having fashioned the form of a serpent from the flour of *priyaṅgu*, rice, wheat, or sesame— meaning it may be made from the flour of any one of these— or having placed that [image] upon a new winnowing basket (*śūrpa*);
With this mantra, which is about to be recited, one should pray to the serpent.
"Come, O serpent who died previously, enter into this flour;
for the sake of the funeral rites, I pray with devotion and a concentrated mind."
Having offered a handful of flowers along with garments, sacred threads, perfumes, unbroken rice grains, blossoms, and so forth,
the performer should prostrate and lead [the deity] outside.
Having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should sit upon the ground;
preceded by the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), he should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the purificatory rite.
The rite of consecration for a serpent must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread;
having established a common fire, one should perform the offering of fuel sticks.
Then, having sprinkled the ground in the south-eastern direction of the fire with water,
one should prepare a funeral pyre and strew it with *kuśa* grass whose tips point toward the southeast.
Having sprinkled water around the fire, spread the sacrificial grass around it, and poured water around it, one should worship it;
having performed everything up to the placing of the fuel, including the setting out of the six vessels and so forth.
Having offered the two Āghāra oblations with clarified butter into the eyes according to the prescribed rule,
the wise man, having carefully taken hold of the serpent, should place it upon the funeral pyre.
Having touched water, he should touch his ears and go near the fire;
with the sruva-ladle, he should offer clarified butter into the fire with the three Vyāhṛtis.
One should offer clarified butter into the mouth of the serpent with the combined Vyāhṛtis;
then, one should pour the remainder of the clarified butter from the *sruva* ladle onto the body of the serpent.
Having sprinkled him with all the Vyāhṛtis, with water from his hand and from the cups, he should consign the fire into the funeral pyre, saying, "O Agni, protect him."
Having placed the *sruva* ladle there along with the sacrificial vessels upon the sacred grass (*barhis*),
and having circumambulated the funeral pyre clockwise, one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness;
then one should worship the burning fire with the mantra "Salutation to the Serpent" (*namo'stu sarpa*).
Whether done knowingly or unknowingly, this killing of a serpent was committed by me;
O serpent, forgive all of that in me, whether it occurred in this life or in a previous birth.
Having thus prayed to the lord of the nāgas and having returned after bathing again and again,
he should then sprinkle the fire with milk and clarified butter while reciting the three vyāhṛtis.
Once the serpent has been offered as an oblation, one should thereafter sprinkle water upon the fire;
one should not perform the collection of bones, but having bathed and sipped water (ācamana), should return home.
The duties beginning with celibacy (brahmacarya) must be performed; purification is desired after three nights.
When the fourth day arrives, one should perform a bath along with one's clothes.
One should feed eight twice-born men with offerings of ghee, milk-rice, and various foods;
the performer should honor the Brahmins with the names and titles that are about to be described.
The serpent Ananta, as well as Śeṣa, Kapila, and the Nāga himself, along with Kālika,
Śaṅkhapāla, and Bhūdhara, are proclaimed [as the world-supporters].
One should perform the washing of the feet with these individual names;
one should honor the twice-born with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, lamps, and other offerings.
When this rite has been performed, including all the preparatory ceremonies, one is liberated from the sin caused by harming snakes; of this there is no doubt.
"Freed from diseases such as leprosy and the like, this indeed is a medicine in every respect;
having attained long life, health, and sovereignty, one shall obtain all desires."
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*):

One should perform it at a time free from the heliacal setting of Jupiter and Venus and so forth, during either of the two solstices (*ayana*), on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*), or on a day conjoined with the asterism Āśleṣā. For that purpose, one should first perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of fourteen *kṛcchra* penances to obtain the requisite qualification.

The procedure for this is as follows: on the day before the aforementioned date, or on that very day, having circumambulated and bowed to the assembly (*parṣad*) with the thought "all is auspicious," one should place three *niṣkas*, two *niṣkas*, one *niṣka*, or a single *niṣka* before the assembly according to the degree of the offense. If acting as the presiding authority (*anumantṛ*) or similar role, one should place half a *niṣka* or half of that again, according to one's capacity. Then, [one should recite]: "Of the fault produced by the killing of a snake—whether committed knowingly or unknowingly—in this birth or in another birth, by me, [named] Amukaśarman..."
He should request them, saying: "Having granted me favor for the sake of my exoneration, may you prescribe the penance. They should reply, "We shall prescribe it.
Then the performer [should say]:
"All of you are discerners of dharma and protectors, O twice-born ones."
O best of the twice-born, may you perform the complete purification of my body.
I have committed a most terrible sin, whether consciously or unconsciously;
through your grace, please grant me favor and bestow upon me the permission for auspiciousness.
"May I become purified by the worshipful ones, the best of the twice-born.
Having recited these verses, he should bow to the assembly, saying, "May you all favor me.

Thereafter, the performer (kartā) should perform the worship of the legal digest (nibandha), the worship of the assembly, and the worship of the reciter (anuvādaka). To the reciter, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in the form of a salary according to his capacity.

Then the reciter shall give instruction three times: "O [Name] Śarman, for the sake of removing the fault produced by the killing of a snake—whether done by you in this life or in another birth, whether knowingly or unknowingly—you shall become pure and free from affliction after performing the funeral rites for the snake according to the rules, preceded by the performance of fourteen *kṛcchra* penances as instructed by this assembly.
Then the performer, having accepted with "Om" and having bowed to the assembly, shall dismiss both the assembly and the reciter.

Then, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), having announced the place and time, and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the sake of removing the fault produced by the killing of a snake—whether done knowingly or unknowingly by me, [named] Amukaśarman, in this life or in another—I shall perform the expiation consisting of fourteen *kṛcchra* penances as instructed by the assembly, through the substitution of [specific] offerings," he should recite:
"Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the murder of a Brahmin, they reside in the hair; therefore, I shave my hair."
Having thus had his hair, beard, nails, and body hair shaved— excluding the tuft on the crown, the armpits, and the pubic region— he recites:
"O Lord of the Forest, grant us long life, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence."
Having thus petitioned the lord of the forest, he should take from it a piece of wood one span (prādeśa) in length and say:
"For the destruction of foul breath, for the purification of the teeth, for spitting,
and for the [cleansing of] my limbs, I perform the brushing of my teeth."

Having thus cleansed his teeth with that wooden stick and performed twelve mouthfuls of rinsing, he should perform the baths with ashes, cow-dung, and clay according to the procedure for the *utsarjana* rite to be described below. Then, having bathed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and water from *kuśa* grass using their respective mantras, and having bathed with pure water using the three mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he should perform the bath according to the bathing procedure to be described below. (If the performer has a living father or other elders, then for the sake of preserving his hair, he should perform the previously mentioned expiation twice.)

The procedure there is as follows: having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), "I shall perform a penance consisting of fourteen *kṛcchra*s along with a penance for the preservation of my hair, equal in number to the primary penance," one should perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) and other rites.

Then, one should perform the worship of Viṣṇu, the *viṣṇuśrāddha*, the gift of a cow (*godāna*), the *vyāhṛti-homa*, and the *pañcagavya-homa*. Regarding these, the worship of Viṣṇu is performed with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ"; for the sake of accomplishing the *viṣṇuśrāddha*, one should invite Brahmins, worship them, and give them four portions of cooked rice (*āmānna*).
The primary procedure for the Viṣṇu-śrāddha will be explained in the section on Śrāddha rites.
Some authorities maintain, however, that one whose father is still living should not perform the Viṣṇu-śrāddha.
Then, having worshipped a Brahmin and a cow, he should give the cow to him along with accessories prepared according to his means; or, in the absence of a cow, its value.

Then follows the *vyāhṛti-homa*: the performer, having sipped water (*ācamya*) and purified the sacrificial ground through rites such as *ullekhana*, installs the common fire with the mantra, "I establish the fire named Viṣṇu," and having kindled it and meditated upon it, he takes three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), performs the *prāṇāyāma* ending with "O Faith, come here" (*śraddha ehi*), and declares: "In this ritual of *homa*, which is an ancillary part of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the purpose of the consecration of the serpents (*sarpa-saṃskāra*), I shall encompass all those deities who are about to be worshipped."

I shall sacrifice to Agni with seven oblations of clarified butter using the first *vyāhṛti*; to Vāyu with seven oblations of clarified butter using the second *vyāhṛti*; to Sūrya with seven oblations of clarified butter using the third *vyāhṛti*; and to Prajāpati with seven oblations of clarified butter using all the *vyāhṛtis* together. In the *pañcagavya* homa: I shall sacrifice to Agni with one oblation of *pañcagavya*, to Soma with one oblation of *pañcagavya*, to Viṣṇu with three oblations of *pañcagavya*, and to Rudra with one oblation of *pañcagavya*.

Here follows the touching of water. With one oblation of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) I shall worship Savitṛ; with one oblation of the five products of the cow I shall worship Brahmā; and with the fourth part, the *praṇava*, I shall worship either the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or Agni. I shall perform as many oblations as there are [total] oblations.

Having said, "I shall sacrifice immediately to these deities," he places fuel-sticks on the fire, spreads grass around the fire, and spreads *darbha* grass to the north of the fire. Upon that grass, he places a wooden ladle (*darvī*), green *kuśa* blades consisting of seven parts each, a vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), a copper vessel for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), a vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), a fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), *darbha* blades for wiping, *darbha* blades for kindling, sacrificial grass (*barhis*), one fuel-stick, clarified butter, and the five products of the cow. Having prepared the two strainers (*pavitra*) and consecrated the sprinkling water, he sprinkles the vessels and the five products of the cow.

Having cleansed the ladle and the seven-leafed *kuśa* grass with their respective mantras, one should combine the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in a copper vessel covered by a purifier. Then, having poured water into it while reciting the mantra "devasya tvā" over the seven-fold *kuśa* grass, one should stir it with the three mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."

Then follows the anointing with clarified butter (*ājya*) and other rites. At the time of the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) of the clarified butter, there is also the circumambulation of the *pañcagavya*. At the conclusion of the placing of the two purifiers (*pavitra*), having spread sacrificial grass (*barhis*) behind the fire, one places the vessel for the clarified butter and the vessel for the *pañcagavya* there; then, to the north of that, one places the ladle (*darvī*) and the seven-leaved *kuśa* grass. Having sprinkled water around the fire starting from the east, and having silently placed the prepared fuel-stick (*samidh*) upon it, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the ladle using the *vyāhṛtis*—both individually and collectively—repeated seven times.

Then, taking seven-bladed *kuśa* grass, he offers oblations by repeatedly lifting [the ladle] with them: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! For these two, Vāmadeva or the Viśvedevas are the seer (*ṛṣi*); Agni and Soma are the deities (*devatā*) respectively; the metre is *yajus*. For the verse beginning with "Irāvatī," Soma and Viṣṇu are the deities and *triṣṭubh* is the metre. For "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," Soma and Viṣṇu are the deities and *gāyatrī* is the metre. For "Viṣṇornukaṃ," Soma and Viṣṇu are the deities and *triṣṭubh* is the metre. For "Mā naḥ toke," Agni, the Viśvedevas, or Rudra are the deities and *triṣṭubh* is the metre.

For the Gāyatrī verse beginning with *tat savituḥ*, Viśvāmitra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Agni is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter. For the verse beginning with *brahma jajñānam*, Agni is the seer, Brahman is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. For the Praṇava, Agni is the seer, the Supreme Brahman or the Supreme Self is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter. The application (*viniyoga*) of all these is in the oblation of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

‘Oṃ agnaye svāhā’—to Agni, this [offering]. ‘Oṃ somāya svāhā’—to Soma, this [offering]. ‘Oṃ irāvatī... mayūkhaiḥ svāhā’—to Viṣṇu, this [offering]. ‘Oṃ viṣṇornukaṃ vīryāṇi... gāya svāhā’—to Viṣṇu, this [offering]. ‘Oṃ mā nastoke... vidhema te svāhā’—to Rudra, this [offering]. Having touched water: ‘Oṃ tatsavitur... yāt svāhā’—to Savitṛ, this [offering]. ‘Oṃ brahma jajñānaṃ... vaḥ svāhā’—to Brahmā, this [offering].

With the syllable *oṃ svāhā*, one should offer as many oblations with those very *kuśa* blades as are required for the fourth-part oblation (*caturthabhāga-homa*) performed with the *praṇava*. [The dedication is] "To the Supreme Self, this... or "To Agni, this...". Then, having stirred the remaining *pañcagavya* with the *praṇava* and consecrated it with the *praṇava*, he should ask the twice-born, "I shall undertake the vow," and being permitted by them with the words, "Do so," he should sit outside his seat and drink everything with the *praṇava*.

Then, having washed his face, hands, and feet, and having sipped water twice, he should sit upon his seat; (thereafter, having completed the remainder of the oblation beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt*), he should perform the expiation consisting of fourteen *kṛcchra* penances as instructed by the assembly.

In the case where the gift of material wealth (*dravyadāna*) serves as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*), one should first place the wealth intended as the ransom for the cows corresponding to the number of *kṛcchra* penances, worship it, and then worship the Brahmins. One should then give the wealth representing the ransom for the fourteen *kṛcchra* penances prescribed by the assembly, saying: "I give this to you, O Brahmins of various names and lineages; I relinquish it for the purpose of giving," or simply give it. Thereafter, as before, one should perform the *vyāhṛti-homa*, the worship of Viṣṇu, the *viṣṇu-śrāddha*, and the gift of a cow. In this instance, there is no offering of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Then, having given a morsel of food to a cow, and being capable, one should give the ten gifts consisting of a cow, land, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, clothing, grain, molasses, silver, and salt—preceded by worship and accompanied by ritual fees—to the Brahmins. One should then request the Brahmins, saying: "May the expiation performed by me be rendered flawless; so please say. When they have replied, "May it be flawless," one should meditate upon Viṣṇu for the perfection of the rite.

If, in this very life, one has directly committed the killing of a Brahmin, one should give an iron staff (*lohadaṇḍa*). The procedure for this is as follows: Having announced the place and time, and saying, "For the sake of removing the fault arising from the killing of a snake committed by me in this birth, I give this iron staff or its monetary equivalent to you, the Brahmin named So-and-so Śarman; it is not mine," one should place it along with water into the hand of the Brahmin. Then, for the sake of achieving the completion of the gift of the iron staff, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), saying, "I give this sacrificial fee."
Having given [the gift], he should say: "By this gift of an iron staff, may Ananta be pleased, not I.
Now follow the mantras for the ten gifts:
"In the limbs of cows reside the fourteen worlds."
"Therefore, may there be auspiciousness for me in this world and in the next"—thus [it is said] regarding the cow.
"The earth, the support of all crops, was raised up by the Boar;
may she, who bestows infinite harvests and fruits, grant me peace. Thus for the Earth.
"Sesame seeds are eternally destroyers of sin, having originated from the body of Viṣṇu;
O Keśava, by the gift of sesame seeds, destroy all my sin"—thus [is the mantra] for sesame seeds.
"The seed of gold, residing within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha and belonging to the Fire-god, bestows the fruit of infinite merit; therefore, may it grant peace. Thus [is the mantra] for gold.

"May the clarified butter (ājya), produced from the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu), the supreme oblation for the gods, which increases the lifespan—may it always protect me. Thus [is the mantra] for the clarified butter.
"O garment, you who are the refuge of all worlds, the supreme protector of modesty, and the wearer of beautiful attire—grant me eternal peace. Thus [is the prayer] for the garment.
"It makes the donor fortunate in this world and in the next;
therefore, grain is given. Hence, grant me peace. This is for grain.
Just as the *praṇava* is among all mantras and Pārvatī is among women,
so too is sugarcane juice always considered the most excellent of all juices.
"Therefore, O jaggery, grant me supreme peace at all times"—thus for jaggery.
"Silver, born from the eye of Śiva, is exceedingly dear to the ancestors;
by the gift of that silver to me, may there indeed always be peace. Thus [is the mantra] for silver.
"Since all flavors of food are not superior without salt, therefore, by the offering of this, may there always be peace for me. Thus [is the mantra] for salt.
Thus are the mantras for the gift:
"A milch cow with her calf, accompanied by household utensils, should be given;
or land measured by a nivartana, or even half of that."

Or half of that, or half of a *nivartana*. Alternatively, a quantity sufficient for a house should be given, provided it possesses auspicious characteristics; it may measure three *droṇas* of black [grain], or it may be measured by *āḍhakas*.
Alternatively, auspicious sesame seeds measuring two *prasthas* should be given as a gift;
a *niṣka*’s worth should be offered, or even half a *niṣka*.
Alternatively, half of that amount, or even half of that again, should be given as gold;
there should be one *prastha* or one *āḍhaka* measure of clarified butter, or it may be measured by a single *prastha*.
Pure and stainless ghee, measuring either two jars of one span each or a single jar, should be given as a gift.
One should give three garments, or even a single garment;
it should be sufficient for wearing, unwashed, very firm, soft,
and made of linen or cotton— such cloth is prescribed for the gift.
Grain twice the amount of sesame seeds, and molasses measured at three prasthas.
"In the giving of gold, silver should be weighed by its own standard; the measurement of salt is like that of molasses; such is declared to be the measurement of substances."

A *nivartana* consists of thirty *daṇḍas*, each *daṇḍa* being ten *hastas* long. It should be endowed with auspicious marks such as the *uparava* and free from defects. The definitions of the *droṇa*, *āḍhaka*, and *prastha* are to be understood from the statement, "The *pala*, the *kuḍava*, and the *prastha* [are the measures]. The definition of a *niṣka* is "four *suvarṇas* constitute a *niṣka*. [The weight] is according to its own measure, that is, by the measure of a silver *māṣa*.

Having performed the preceding rites in this manner, one should carry out the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the serpent on the day specified. The performer, having performed his daily obligatory duties in the morning and gathered the necessary materials, should go to a praiseworthy place such as a sacred bathing site (*puṇyatīrtha*). Accompanied by his wife, wearing clean washed garments, and having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should receive the permission of his Guru. Then, having fashioned the form of a serpent from a mixture of the flours of *priyaṅgu*, *vrīhi* rice, wheat, and sesame—or from the flour of any one of these—he should place it upon a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) and pray to the serpent:
"Come, O serpent who died previously; enter into this flour!"
"For the sake of spiritual refinement, I pray with devotion in brief."
Then:
"Oṃ, let us know the Lord of Serpents; let us meditate upon the King of Snakes;
may that Nāga inspire us."

Thus, having performed the worship with the sixteen services beginning with the invocation using the *Bhujaṅga-gāyatrī*, having offered a handful of flowers and prostrated, one should present the offering, saying: "O Serpent, accept this *bali* and grant me prosperity," and then, having washed the hands and feet, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Then, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of removing the fault produced by the killing of a snake—whether committed in this life or in another birth, whether knowingly or unknowingly—I shall perform the rite of consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the snake. Having thus resolved, and having established and kindled a common fire (*laukikāgni*) on a ground purified by scraping and other rites, he should take three fuel-sticks (*samidh*). Then, having performed the rites beginning with "O Faith, come" (*śraddha ehi*) up to the end of breath control, he should proceed with the formula: "In the rite of the oblation for the consecration of the snake, those who are to be sacrificed," and so forth.

Having recited [the mantras] ending with *prasādhanī* or ending with the *vyāhṛtis* during the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*), one says: "I shall worship Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya each with a single oblation of clarified butter; I shall worship Prajāpati with a single oblation of clarified butter using all the *vyāhṛtis* at the mouth of the serpent. Having said this, one places fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the fire, sprinkles water upon the ground in the south-eastern direction of the fire, constructs a funeral pyre (*citi*) there, and silently sprinkles water around both the fire and the pyre with *darbha* grass blades whose tips point toward the south-east.

Having strewn [grass] around the fire as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, and having spread Darbha grass to the north of the fire, he should place the vessels there: the wooden spoon (darvī), the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), the vessel for sprinkling water (prokṣaṇīpātra), the fire-stirring stick (upaveṣa), the fuel (idhma), the sacrificial grass (barhis), the Darbha blades for cleansing (saṃmārgadarbha), the Darbha blades for kindling (avajvalanadarbha), and the clarified butter (ājya). Having prepared the two strainers (pavitre) and consecrated the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇīḥ), and having sprinkled the vessels, cleansed the spoon, and consecrated the clarified butter, and having laid the enclosing sticks (paridhīn), he should sprinkle water around the fire with the formula "Adite" and then place the fuel.

Having added fuel with the mantra, one should perform the rites from the *āghāra* oblations through the recitation of the *anvādhāna*, up to the oblation for the goddess Prasādhanī, or ending with the *vyāhṛti* oblations. Then, having taken hold of the serpent, placed it upon the funeral pyre, touched water, touched his ears, and sipped water, he should approach the fire and perform the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*): "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā"—to Agni this [belongs], not to me; "Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā"—to Vāyu this [belongs], not to me; "Oṃ suvaḥ svāhā"—to Sūrya this [belongs], not to me.

Thus, one should offer three oblations of clarified butter into the fire with the *vyāhṛtis* using the wooden ladle (*darvī*), saying: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā. With this, one should offer the fourth oblation into the mouth of the serpent, saying: "To Prajāpati, this [is the offering]. The recollection of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details is as before. The application (*viniyoga*) formula states: "The application of the individual *vyāhṛtis* is for the oblation; the application of the collective *vyāhṛtis* is for the oblation of clarified butter into the mouth of the serpent. There is no [recitation of] the *varṣyā* and so forth. One should pour the remainder of the clarified butter onto the body of the serpent using the very same ladle.

Then, for the *abhyukṣaṇa* (sprinkling), there is the application (*viniyoga*) of all the *vyāhṛtis*; the deity is Prajāpati, the metre is Bṛhatī. [The verses beginning with] "na varṣyādayaḥ" are not used here. Having sprinkled with water held in the hand from the *camasa* vessels while reciting all the *vyāhṛtis*, one should then cast the fire situated in its hearth onto the *citi* (the sacrificial pile) with the verse "agne rakṣāṇaḥ," whose deities are the Viśvedevas, the Ṛṣi is Rakṣohāgni, and the metre is Gāyatrī. The application is for the casting of the fire into the *citi*: "Oṃ agne rakṣāṇo... rodaha. One should thus cast the entire fire located in its place onto the *citi*. The [verses] beginning with "na varṣyādayaḥ" are not used here.

Then, having cast the ladle, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the vessels, and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into the fire, and having circumambulated that fire from left to right, he should pay homage to the serpent, ask for forgiveness with the words "O serpent, forgive me," and perform the ritual worship (*upasthāna*). For the three mantras beginning with "Homage be to the serpents" (*namo astu sarpebhyaḥ*), Agni, the serpents, and the *gāyatrī* meter are the deities; their application is in the worship of the serpent. He worships with these three mantras beginning with "Homage be to the serpents. [The mantras] beginning with "the rain-clouds" (*varṣyādayaḥ*) are not used. [He recites:
"Whether knowingly or unknowingly, the killing of a serpent has been committed by me."
"O serpent, whether [the offense occurred] in a previous birth, may you forgive all of that from me"—thus one should pray.
Then one should pray with ancient mantras as follows:
"O Karkoṭaka, salutations to you; O Śaṅkhapāla, salutations to you.
O Great God, King of Nāgas, salutations to your forms."
To those serpents who are hoodless and those who possess hoods, to those who are venomous and those who are venomless—
to all these snakes dwelling in the banyan tree, O you of meritorious form, salutations be unto you!
O Lord, this world is held by you upon a single portion of the circle of your own hoods like a minute atom; salutations be to you!
O best of serpents, you have offered a poisonless couch to the Blessed One, the illustrious Vāsudeva,
using your own body as a pillow.
Save me, save me, O possessor of great wealth, from all calamities and suffering!
Grant me a virtuous lineage, free from blemish and long-lived.
Protect me, who have sought refuge through devotion, O compassionate one, O lover of the distressed!
Whether knowingly or unknowingly, the killing of a serpent was committed by me.
"O Lord, whether in another birth, in this one, or by my ancestors, quickly destroy that sin; forgive my transgression. Thus one should pray.

"Those snakes which are hoodless and those which have hoods, those with venom and those without venom, and those that dwell in banyan trees—all these snakes are Your forms, O King of Nagas; salutations unto You"—this is the meaning.

Then, having performed a bath with one's clothes on and approached the fire, [one recites] the *vyāhṛtis* in their entirety; Prajāpati is the seer, Prajāpati is the deity, and the *bṛhatī* is the meter. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sprinkling of the funeral pyre (*cityagni*). [The rule] regarding rain and so forth does not apply. Having sprinkled that fire with milk and clarified butter while reciting "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," and having extinguished it with water once the serpent has been offered as an oblation, one should cause it to flow away into the water. There is no collection of bones (*asthisaṃcayana*).

Then, having bathed and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should go home. There is impurity for three nights, along with the observance of celibacy and other rules; however, according to the opinion of Baudhāyana, the impurity lasts for one day—so says the author of the text. In this matter, the impurity applies only to the performer [of the rite], because of the scriptural statement: "The giver of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) shall undergo the impurity, but not his relatives or those born of the same lineage. In this ritual, the sacred thread is not worn over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta).
When the fourth day arrives, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
then, one should feed eight twice-born men with offerings of ghee and milk-rice.

"The performer, being well-composed, should worship the Brahmins with name-designations," it is said. "On the fourth day" is an elliptical expression; the meaning is that in the case of a one-day period of impurity (*ekāhāśauca*), it should take place on the second day.

On the following morning, having bathed with his clothes on, having performed his daily obligatory rites, and having invited eight well-bathed Brahmins, [he should say]: "May a moment be granted for the sake of the Serpent. [The Brahmins reply]: "Om, so be it. May you receive it; may I receive it. The same applies hereafter.

Having offered a moment [of meditation] at the site of Ananta, the site of Śeṣa, the site of Kapila, the site of Nāga, the site of Kālika, the site of Śaṅkhapāla, and the site of Bhūdhara, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) upon the square maṇḍala with water mixed with scents and unbroken rice (akṣata), using these very names: "O Serpent, this is the water for the feet," and so forth.

Then, when they have sipped water, he himself sips water and, having seated them facing east in a row from south to north in due order, says: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; O Serpent, sit upon this seat," and so forth. Having provided a seat consisting of two blades of *darbha* grass in every case, he pours water into eight vessels placed upon those two blades of *darbha*, consecrates it all at once with the *Gāyatrī* mantra, and silently adds barley, perfume, and flowers. Having announced, "Svāhā! This is for the Arghya," he offers the Arghya water with the *devatīrtha* part of his hand, saying, "O Serpent, this is your Arghya."

One should offer [the following]: "O Ananta, this is for you; this is the *arghya*," and so forth. "O Serpent, this is your fragrance; O Ananta, this is your fragrance," and so forth. "O Serpent, these are flowers," and so forth. "O Serpent, this is incense," and so forth. "O Serpent, this is a lamp," and so forth. "O Serpent, this is a garment," and so forth.

Then, having served food and other items into the vessels, or having had them served, one should sprinkle them with water while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra. Taking water with Kuśa grass and barley, one should offer it, saying: "May this food—already served and yet to be served, and that which will be given until satiety—to the Serpent [Sarpa] become *svāhā*, not mine. In the same manner, [one offers] to Ananta and the others. Reciting "Brahmārpaṇam... (The offering is to Brahman...), one should say: "May there be inexhaustible satisfaction for those to whom this food has been assigned; by this feeding of the Brāhmaṇas, may the Serpents and others be pleased, not me. Thus, one should discard the water with Kuśa grass and barley. Then the Brāhmaṇas should eat. There is no prohibition against the offering of *bali* oblations in this context.

Then, after the Brahmins have sipped water (ācamana), the performer, having spread Darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward upon them, should offer this oblation (bali) to the serpent with rice mixed with milk, saying, "I offer this oblation to Sarpa," "I offer this oblation to Ananta," and so forth. Then he should worship the offerings with perfumes, flowers, garments, and other articles.
Next, he should give betel leaves, gold, and other sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
Then, having asked them for forgiveness and bowed down, and having followed them for some distance before returning, he should perform the gift of a golden serpent.
"Having thus performed the consecration of the serpent and offered the *nāgabali* thereafter, one is liberated from the offense by means of a golden serpent"— according to this statement.
Having worshipped the preceptor (*ācārya*) and having worshipped the golden serpent with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), one should offer a prayer.
In this regard, the mantras are as follows:
"And those serpents in the world of Brahmā, headed by the Naga Śeṣa—homage be to them!
May they always be well-pleased and gracious toward me. (1) And those serpents in the world of Viṣṇu..."
And those headed by Vāsuki—to them be homage, O Subhūti! || 2 || And likewise those serpents in the world of Rudra, headed by Takṣaka—to them be homage, O Subhūti! || 3 ||

Salutations to those who were present at the burning of Khāṇḍava and who took refuge in heaven; su0 || 4 || Salutations to those serpents who were protected by Āstīka during the snake-sacrifice; su0 || 5 || And salutations to those serpents on Mount Malaya, headed by Karkoṭaka; su0 || 6 || Salutations to them.

And to those serpents who are in the world of Dharma and are gathered in the Vaitaraṇī river—homage be to them! Su0 || 7 || And to those serpents who dwell in the ocean and in the netherworld (pātāla)—homage be to them! Su0 || 8 || To those serpents who are on the mountain peaks and in the crevices of caves...

They are established there. Homage be to them, O Subhūti! || 9 || Whether in the village or in the forest, those serpents who indeed roam about—homage be to them, O Subhūti! || 10 || And those serpents upon the earth, and those serpents present at the sacrificial offering (bali)—homage be to them, O Subhūti! || 11 || And those serpents in the nether world (rasātala), Ananta and the others, possessed of great venom—homage be to them, O Subhūti! || 12 ||

Having praised the Lord of Nagas in this manner, one should present it to the preceptor: "Having proclaimed the place and time, for the sake of accomplishing the integrity of the rite of consecration (*saṃskāra*) performed for the serpent, I give this golden Naga, together with a water-pot (*kalaśa*), cloth, and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), to you; it is not mine. Having given it thus, one should say: "By this gift of the golden Naga, may Ananta and the other Nagas be pleased."

Then, a gift of a cow should be given to the preceptor (*ācārya*). Having honored the preceptor, he should give him this black cow with her calf—having horns tipped with gold, hooves with silver, a copper-colored back, a bronze milking vessel, accompanied by clothing and a ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and joined by a bull—with the words: "I give this to you. He should say: "By this, may Ananta and the other [deities] be pleased. In the absence of a cow, its price should be paid. Then the preceptor should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the patron (*yajamāna*) and his family with pure water.

Then the performer should request: "May whatever rite has been performed by me be entirely flawless (*acchidra*); may you all say so. When they have replied, "May it be flawless," he should arrange for the feeding of Brahmins and the distribution of abundant gifts to ensure the successful completion of the rite. Then, having recollected Viṣṇu with the verses beginning "By whose remembrance... and "Through negligence... (*pramādāt...*), he should say: "May Ananta, the Lord of Serpents, be pleased by this rite known as the *sarpa-saṃskāra*.
Thereafter, accompanied by friends, he should partake of a meal.
For one whose father is living, the Nārāyaṇabali and the Nāgabali do not take place.
This concludes the procedure for the Nāgabali.
Even if the desired result is not achieved in this manner, the rite described in the Mahārṇava should be performed.
And that is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"The fourfold barren woman is she who becomes so through the loss of her offspring;
she who has no children at all is known as 'barren,' while another is remembered as one whose children die."
Likewise, another woman may suffer from miscarriages, while yet another may be a "crow-barren" woman (one who bears only one child).
I shall describe the remedy for that; understand its true nature.
One should have a sturdy cow made of gold according to one's means, along with its calf; the Teacher has stated that the cow should be made from a *pala* of gold and the calf from a *pāda*.
"With gold according to one's ability," [it says]: "either with a pala, or with half of that, or even with half of that again."

The meaning is that one should act according to the manner described in the technical rules (paribhāṣā). The statement "the cow with a pala [of gold] and the calf with a quarter-pala" is intended to show the primary ritual procedure.
One should provide the cow with silver hooves and attach a jewel to its tail.
Facing the east, the wise man should tie a bell around the neck of the cow together with her calf.

With sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, fragrant garlands, and other most beautiful offerings, one should present the sixteen types of service, and the food offering (naivedya) should consist of milk-rice (pāyasa).
And likewise, modakas, cakes, molasses, salt,
and cumin were placed upon a very spacious, sturdy winnowing basket made of bamboo.
Indeed, one cow should be given to Brāhmaṇa women;
immediately thereafter, one should give six, eight, or ten.

Regarding the phrase "with sixteen services," the word "should worship" (*pūjayet*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The *Mahārṇava* states that the meaning is: having placed a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) filled with sweetmeats (*modaka*) and other offerings before the cow, one should give baskets filled with the aforementioned substances—either eighteen or sixteen—to Brahmin women accompanied by their husbands.
[One should honor] a Brahmin who is skilled in the meaning of all scriptures, who knows all the Vedas, who is endowed with learning and humility, peaceful, and has conquered his senses.
Having summoned one who is free from greed, beloved by all people, and devoid of blemish, and having honored him with devotion through garments, perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
With that very [substance], one should first perform the worship of the cow and the calf;
and there, one should cause a fire-oblation (homa) to be performed, abounding in sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice (caru).

Having recited the mantra "somo dhenum," this same mantra is also used for the worship. Regarding this, the *Mahārṇava* states that, according to the principle of distinctness of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*), the cow itself is also the deity. Here, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) of one thousand and eight offerings for each of the sacrificial fuels (*samidh*) and so forth; the author also notes that this is because it is prescribed that one should cause the rite to be performed in an intense manner.
Facing east, standing while the recipient is seated facing north, one should present the cow.
And having placed its tail in his hand according to the rule with the mantra, he said:
She who entered the sacrificial session of the Aṅgirases, she who is the daughter of Surabhi,
and she who is the daughter of Bhānu, Agni, and Varuṇa— [that cow].
May those cows who roam in the forests and groves be pleased with me; may they, the bestowers of sons and grandsons, grant me happiness.
"May they grant [this] without interruption, day and night, as well as to my lineage.
Having thus given that gift, one should prostrate and dismiss [the recipients].
Thus concludes the gift of a golden cow (*suvarṇadhenu*) which removes barrenness.
There is also another means, beginning with: "And by the misappropriation of a deposit, one who is childless indeed gives birth [to offspring]."
Aruṇa said:
"House, wealth, and grain are in vain; a birth without a son is fruitless.
Having taken pity on me, please tell me an expiation."
Sūrya said:
"A pilgrimage to the confluence where the Revā and Tāpī rivers meet must be undertaken;
there, the husband and wife should perform the most excellent bath while wearing but a single garment."
O bird, one should listen to the Harivaṃśa and perform the marriage ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa;
furthermore, one should satisfy one hundred and eight Brāhmaṇas with sweet food.
One should perform a thousand recitations of the mantra beginning with "īśāvāsyā," followed by a fire sacrifice (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number, according to the prescribed rules.
Having diligently worshipped Śiva with one hundred thousand lotuses, one should proceed.
In the Kali age, because the worship of the earthen linga generates great merit, the worship of a lotus for Śiva in that form is exceedingly praiseworthy.
O Vainateya, one should likewise give a golden cow with her calf, as well as a Surabhi cow;
one should present a jar of ghee to a Brāhmaṇa.
"When this is done, O Vainateya, offspring is born in the Kali age."
Now follows the procedure for listening to the *Harivaṃśa*.

The performer, having performed the propitiation of Vināyaka (*vināyaka-śānti*) or the worship of Vināyaka according to his capacity at a moment prescribed by an astrologer, and having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*)—by means of a substitute such as the gift of cows or gold, a pilgrimage to a sacred ford (*tīrtha-yātrā*), or other such acts according to his ability—at an auspicious month such as Vaiśākha or Kārttika (during either the northern or southern solstice) and at an auspicious moment prescribed by an astrologer, shall first announce the place and time.

The couple should make the following resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Desiring to first eliminate the defect of childlessness caused by sins accumulated in previous births, and subsequently to obtain a long-lived, healthy, and imperishably virtuous son, we two, husband and wife, shall listen to the *Harivaṃśa*. Alternatively, the resolve may be: "I shall listen to the *Harivaṃśa* together with this wife.

However, if one wife has a son while the other does not, then the resolve should be made as follows: "For the sake of obtaining for this wife of mine a long-lived, healthy, and imperishably virtuous son, I shall listen to the *Harivaṃśa* together with this wife."

Then, having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*), and so forth, with hands holding gold, betel leaves, and areca nuts, one should choose [the reciter] by saying: "I choose you, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, to be the reciter of the *Harivaṃśa*. When he replies, "I am chosen," one should honor him with the washing of his feet, the water-offering (*arghya*), two garments, two sacred threads (*upavīta*), a ring, earrings and other ornaments, sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, and so on; then, at the base of his right hand, one should perform the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*) while reciting the *Bṛhatsāman*.

Then, the officiant himself should perform the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*) on the hands of the couple in this same manner; however, for the woman, the binding of the protective thread is on the left hand.

Then, every day, having performed ritual sipping (*ācamana*), the well-bathed and well-adorned couple [should recite] Vedic mantras such as *trāyantām* and *āpo hi ṣṭha*, as well as Puranic mantras such as *surāstu*.
[The officiant should address them: "Salutations to you, O Blessed Vyāsa, expert in the meaning of all scriptures!"
O son of Satyavatī, you are the embodiment of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.

Having thus paid homage to Vyāsa, they should sit facing east upon two seats in a clean place; meditating on the Supreme Lord with one-pointed minds, they should listen while observing the restraints such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*).

The reciter, too, having performed his daily rites according to the rules and having recited the auspicious verses beginning with "Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa," should offer salutations—saying "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa, salutation to Narottama, salutation to the Goddess Sarasvatī, salutation to Vyāsa, salutation to Gaṇapati, salutation to Brahmā, salutation to Viṣṇu, salutation to Śiva, salutation to the Gurus"—and then cause [the text] to be read. The husband and wife should worship the reciter and the book every day.

Upon the completion of the book, one should give gold, linen cloth, and a cow that is well-adorned, provided with its implements and bedding, accompanied by her calf, and yielding milk—according to the procedure prescribed for the gift of a cow—to the reciter.
Then, the listener should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) of eight hundred and eight sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter, while reciting the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī.
The procedure for this is as follows:

Having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the rites beginning with the smearing of the fire-altar and ending with the installation of the fire. In this rite, the fire is named Balavardhana. Then follows the preparatory offering (anvādhāna). Taking three fuel-sticks (samidh), and having performed the rites from "O Faith, come here" (śraddha ehi) up to breath control, one should recite from "In the rite of oblation which is an auxiliary to the hearing of the Harivaṃśa, those deities who are to be worshipped... up to the end of the Vyāhṛtis, or up to the goddess Prasādhanī. In the primary oblation (pradhānahoma), [one worships] Viṣṇu with the mantra: "We know Nārāyaṇa... (viṣṇuṃ nārāyaṇāya vidmaha iti).

Having said, "I shall sacrifice with one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds smeared with ghee, using the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī," [he proceeds]. In the *aṅga-homa*, he says, "Varuṇa with two oblations of clarified butter," and so forth; or alternatively, "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an oblation of sesame seeds smeared with the remaining clarified butter," and so forth. At the setting out of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*), the sesame seeds are set out together with the clarified butter. At the time of the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) of the clarified butter, there is also the circumambulation of the sesame seeds smeared with ghee.

Then, having performed the rites beginning with the removal of the clarified butter (*ājyodvāsana*) and ending with the *vyāhṛti* oblations—or ending with the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī, according to the specific enumeration of the *anvādhāna*—one should perform the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*). Recalling the seers and other details for the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra "Nārāyaṇāya," as follows: "The deities are the sacrificial ones; the Upaniṣads; Viṣṇu; the metre is Anuṣṭubh; its application is in the oblation"—one should perform the oblation with sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter according to the stated number.
Then, according to the specific enumeration of the *anvādhāna*, one should complete the remainder of the oblation, including the subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*) and the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation.

Then, having fed one couple who has recited [the text], the patron should say to the reciter, "May what was deficient become complete. The reciter should reply, "So be it. Then the husband and wife, having loosened their protective cords (*rakṣābandhana*) and soaked them in milk, should cast them into pure water. The reciter also, having loosened his protective cord and soaked it in milk, should cast it into pure water.
Thereafter, the husband and wife should eat together with the reciter and his friends. Then everyone should depart as they please. This is the procedure for listening to the *Harivaṃśa*.
Now, the procedure for the worship of the earthen *liṅga* in brief.
Regarding this, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, in the *Tithitattva*, states:
"It may be made of clay, ash, a lump of cow dung, or likewise of copper or bell-metal."
"Having fashioned a linga and worshipped it even once, one shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas."
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"He who worships the earthen *liṅga* shall be long-lived, strong, illustrious, possessed of sons, wealthy, and happy; he obtains his desired boon."
"Therefore, the earthen *liṅga* should be known as the accomplisher of all goals. Thus it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*: "One should have *liṅgas* made of sand and also those made of earth."
By performing a thousandfold worship, even he obtains his desired fruit."
In that very *Kālakaumudī*:
"A man should never, under any circumstances, fashion a *liṅga* smaller than an *akṣa* nor shorter than a thumb; he should never perform it in such a manner."

An *akṣa* consists of eighty *raktikās*, according to Amara’s statement: “Sixteen of those [make] an *akṣa*. By the word *aṅguṣṭha*, the knot of the large joint of the thumb is meant, as stated in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: “Wherever the measurement of a thumb or finger is prescribed, one should always measure there by means of the knots of the large joints.”
The meaning is that [the image] should be the size of a thumb or a finger.
Regarding this very point, Gautama says:
"One should always perform the rites for the gods at night, facing north."
"One who is pure should always perform the worship of Śiva facing the north."
The meaning is: always, both by day and by night.
Regarding that very point, the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* states:
"Without the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) of ashes, and without a rosary of Rudrākṣa beads..."
Even if worshipped, Mahādeva would not be the bestower of fruit for him.
"Therefore, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should indeed be made on the forehead even with clay."
It is also stated in that very same work that one should consecrate each rudrākṣa bead individually with the mantra "oṃ hūṃ namaḥ" and then wear the rosary.
For the sake of qualification therein, the five-syllable mantra is taught in that very same work:
"Whether impure or pure, or even having reached any state whatsoever..."
Or even one who is burdened with great sins, by constantly reciting this mantra, [is purified].
"Śiva, the Lord, declared that everyone shall be qualified [for this].
The procedure for taking the clay is stated in the Śiva Purāṇa:
"Then, one should fetch clay produced from a pure location."
Having taken earth with effort using this mantra, "Salutation to the illustrious Aṣṭamūrti," and having purified the clay there, a person should establish it according to the prescribed rule.
Alternatively, one should bring it together on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
"And again, in just one month, he should indeed bring forth that very same amount. Thus it is stated.
The procedure for worship is described in the Devīpurāṇa: "The fetching of clay, the kneading, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and the invocation..."
The bathing, the worship, and after that, the dismissal.
"Hara, Maheśvara, Śūlapāṇi, Pinākadhṛk, Paśupati, Śiva, and Mahādeva— thus in order."

The meaning is that the rites mentioned immediately above should be performed according to the sequence of their names. Although only the names are assigned here, it is nevertheless stated: "Having meditated [on them] preceded by the *praṇava*, one who is composed should then offer flowers and so forth individually with a salutation (*namaskāra*)."
Thus, from this general statement, it should be understood that [the offerings] end with the word *namaḥ*.
In the Nandipurāṇa:
"In the offering of oblations consisting of cows, land, gold, garments, and so forth, as well as flowers..."
The mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" should be known as the accomplisher of all aims.
"And this six-syllabled mantra, beginning with Oṃ, is superior to all mantras.
By the word "garments and so forth," other articles of worship (upacāras) are included.
Prior to the dismissal [of the deity], the worship of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) by means of counter-clockwise circumambulation is described in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:

"These eight [forms] of Hara are to be worshipped in order from the east onwards; they should be worshipped ending with the southeast. One should worship Śiva on the pedestal (vedī) and in the liṅga."

The meaning is that one should worship these on the altar and Śiva on the *liṅga*. In this context, the east is indeed well-established, because of the prohibition in the *Rudrayāmala*: "One should not [face] the east in front of Śambhu.
(Then one should perform *japa*; and that has been described in the *Śivapurāṇa*—)
"Having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) consisting of a tenth part of that,
and likewise the sprinkling (*mārjana*) consisting of a tenth part, desiring the welfare of Śiva."
In general, it is said that if libation (*tarpaṇa*) and purification (*mārjana*) are impossible, the recitation (*japa*) should be fourfold or twofold.
In the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*: "One should worship two liṅgas every day with jasmine flowers."
The wise one should thus offer an oblation of jaggery for the duration of a year.
"One should perform the worship of the *liṅga*, and an auspicious son will be born."
Now follows the method of this worship:

having proclaimed the place and time, and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"For the sake of pleasing Śrī Sāmbasadāśiva, I shall perform the worship of two earthen liṅgas"—and having placed the materials for worship near oneself, performed the wearing of sacred ash (*vibhūti*) and rudrākṣa beads, and carried out the ritual of the seat (*āsanavidhi*) and so forth; then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with either the five-syllabled mantra *namaḥ śivāya* or the six-syllabled mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*, [one recites]:
"O Goddess Earth, support of all, this clay is of your very form."
"I indeed take hold of you for the sake of the Linga; may you be auspicious at all times."

Having thus prayed to the earth, and having taken from there the purified clay situated in a clean place with "Oṃ, salutation to Hara," and having poured water upon it, he should stir it with "Oṃ, salutation to Maheśvara. Then, having fashioned a *liṅga* with the root mantra, he should quickly place unbroken rice (*akṣata*) upon its head. Having installed it with "Oṃ, salutation to Śūlapāṇi" and performed the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), he should meditate on Śiva according to the method described by Śāradā: "One should constantly meditate on Maheśa. [Then recite: "Oṃ, salutation to Pinākadhṛṣ."

One should invoke [the deity] with: "O Śrī Sāmbasadāśiva, come here; be present here. In all cases, there is the addition of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Having offered the seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) using the root mantra alone, one should offer the water for bathing with "Oṃ, obeisance to Paśupati," and then offer the services beginning with clothing and ending with perfumes with "Obeisance to Śiva."

Having offered *mallikā* flowers, having presented *bilva* leaves, having offered incense and lamps, having presented various offerings and molasses (*guḍa*), and having offered fruit, betel, and a priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) and offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Salutation to Śarva, whose form is earth; salutation to Bhava, whose form is water; salutation to Rudra, whose form is fire; salutation to Ugra, whose form is air; salutation to Bhīma, whose form is ether; salutation to Paśupati, whose form is the sacrificer.

"Salutation to Mahādeva, whose form is Soma; salutation to Īśāna, whose form is Sūrya. Having thus worshipped the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) on the altar of the *liṅga* in the well-known directions starting from the east, moving counter-clockwise, one should mutter the root mantra according to one's capacity. One should then perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and purification (*mārjana*) consisting of a tenth part of that [mantra-repetition]. In the event of impossibility, the repetition may be fourfold or twofold in that place, or even mere repetition alone.
Then, having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the hands as before, and having meditated as before with the thought "I shall meditate eternally," one should contemplate.
"You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Lord of Gods, may accomplishment become firmly established in me through your grace."
Having thus offered the recitation and praised [the deity] with hymns:
"O Mṛḍa, I am always yours, my life is centered in you, and my mind is fixed on you;
O Treasure of Compassion, knowing this, O Lord of Beings, be gracious to me."
Whether performed out of ignorance or knowledge, may whatever recitation, worship, and so forth has been done by me become fruitful through your grace, O Śaṅkara.
"I am a great sinner, O Lord, and you are a great purifier;
having understood this, O Lord of Gods, do as you wish."
Having thus prayed, one should recite the following "Eight Verses of Aspiration" for the sake of obtaining a son, and perform circumambulations and prostrations.
Then:
"Just as you have now come here, O Lord of Gods, for the sake of compassion..."
Furthermore, O Lord, you must certainly come together with me once again.

Having dismissed [the deity] with the mantra, "Oṃ, salutation to Mahādeva," one should dedicate the ritual action to the Lord of Karma (Karmeśvara). This should be performed daily without interruption for the duration of one year by the husband, joined in celibacy (*brahmacarya*), or likewise by the wife; first, having performed the worship of the earthen Gaṇapati and the worship of the earthen Skanda. At the conclusion of the worship, the recitation of the *Abhilāṣāṣṭaka* should be carried out for the duration of the year.
That recitation is as follows: "Viśvānara said: Brahman alone is one and without a second; all is real, truly real; there is no diversity here whatsoever."
The one God exists, not a second; therefore, I take refuge in You alone, the Great Lord. || 1 ||
O Śambhu, you alone are indeed the creator of all; though possessing manifold forms, you are also of a single form, yet formless.
Just as the sun, though one, appears as many in the various waters, I seek refuge in no other lord than you. || 2 ||

Just as a snake [is imagined] in a rope, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, a city in a mirage, and water in a desert, so too is this manifold universe; I take refuge in that Great Lord who, when known, [reveals this). 3.

Coldness in water, burning power in fire, heat in the sun, clarity in the moon, fragrance in a flower, and ghee within milk—that which exists in these, O Śambhu, is You; therefore, I take refuge in You.

You perceive sound though you have no ears; indeed, you taste though you have no tongue; you smell though you have no nose; you come from afar though you have no feet; you see though you have no eyes; and you know flavors though you have no tongue—who can truly know you? Therefore, I take refuge in you.
Neither the Veda itself, O Lord, has known You directly, nor Viṣṇu, nor the Creator of all;
neither the lords of yogis nor the gods headed by Indra have known You. Only Your devotee knows You; therefore, I take refuge in You.
I do not know your lineage, nor your birth, nor your name, nor your form, nor your character, nor your land;
yet, being such as you are, you fulfill all the desires of the three worlds—I worship you! || 7 ||
Everything comes from you; indeed, you are everything, O enemy of Smara! You are the Lord of Gaurī, and you are the naked one, supremely peaceful.
You are the old man, you are the youth, and you are the child; whatever exists, you are that. Since there is nothing that is not you, I bow to you.
Having thus offered praise, the brahmin, exceedingly joyful, prostrated himself upon the ground like a staff;
at that moment, that boy, the eldest of all elders, spoke: "O god on earth, choose a boon."
Then, rising up with a joyful heart, the virtuous sage Viśvānara replied:
"O Lord, what is unknown to you, who are all-knowing? (10)
O Blessed One, you are the inner self of all, the All, and the bestower of everything;
why do you direct me, who am subject to begging and a cause of wretchedness, toward a request? (11)
Having heard these words of Viśvānara, the pure god,
smiling with a pure smile, then spoke to the pure one of pure vows.
The boy said:
"The desire that you formed in your heart for Śuciṣmatī, O Śuci,
will undoubtedly be fulfilled in no long time."
O high-minded one, you shall become the son of Śuciṣmatī,
renowned by the name Gṛhapati, pure and beloved by all the immortals.
This meritorious hymn, the *Abhilāṣāṣṭaka*, which you have uttered, grants all desires when recited three times a day for one year in the presence of Śiva. (15)
The recitation of this hymn bestows sons, grandsons, and wealth;
it brings about all forms of peace and destroys all calamities.
It brings about the attainment of heaven and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having risen early in the morning and bathed well, one should worship the Śāmbhava Liṅga.
Chanting this hymn for a year, one who is childless shall obtain a son,
especially if one is joined with specific observances during the months of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha.
Whoever recites this at the time of bathing obtains the entire fruit [of the vow] through the grace of the month of Kārttika; I am the imperishable one [who grants it]. (19)
I shall become your son; whoever else recites this "Eightfold Prayer of Desires" (Abhilāṣāṣṭaka), it must not be given to just anyone.
This must be guarded with great effort; it brings about the birth of even those who have long been barren.
By both woman and man, according to the rule, it should be placed near the linga. (21)
"This hymn, when recited for one year, bestows a son; there is no doubt about this.
Having said this, the boy vanished, and that Brahmin also returned home.
Thus ends the hymn to Vīreśvara in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the Saṃtānagopāla mantra.
Regarding that, first, the characteristics of a Guru are briefly stated in the Nārada-pañcarātra:
A Brāhmaṇa who knows all times should bestow grace upon everyone;
in his absence, the best of the twice-born—tranquil in soul and absorbed in the Blessed One—should do so.
"One whose self is cultivated, who is omniscient, who knows the scriptures, who is devoted to right action,
and who is endowed with the three accomplishments, is consecrated for the office of an Ācārya."
In the *Tattvasāra* and the *Rudrayāmala*:
"A husband should not initiate his wife; a father should not initiate his daughter;
likewise, a son should not [initiate his father], nor should a brother initiate his brother."
And furthermore, in that same context:
"One who eats excessively, is dilatory, and is greedy for sense-objects;
one who delights in sophistry, is wicked, a mere talker, and a reviler of virtues."
Aroma, Bahuroma, Nindita, Āśramasevaka, Kāladanta, Asitoṣṭha, and Durgandhiśvāsavāhaka.
"Even if he is himself a lord, a teacher who is endowed with wicked characteristics and is addicted to accepting many gifts brings about the destruction of prosperity."
In the *Tantrarāja*: "One who is handsome, pleasant-faced, pure, easy to approach, and a knower of many tantras;
one who is free from doubt, a cutter of doubts, and independent—such a person is considered a Guru."
Beauty is faultlessness; furthermore, in physical form it is a pleasant countenance;
in speech, it is addressing others with a smile; and in character, it is clarity and straightforward conduct.
Accessibility, freedom from pride, contentment,
lack of dependence, absence of doubt, and the awakening to reality— these result from the exposition of that [treatise].
"Indifference to gain, non-interruption [of instruction], gravity, and knowledge of what is beneficial—one who is such as this is to be known as a guru; any other brings suffering to the disciple."
The word *ajihmavṛttitā* (straightforwardness of conduct) is the division [of the compound]. *Bahutantratā* means the knowledge of many systems (*tantra*).
Likewise:
"Endowed with the first four [qualities], possessed of faith, and of firm resolve..."
Free from greed, with steady limbs, acting after due reflection, and having conquered his senses.
"There should be faith in the higher reality and firm devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity;
such a one shall be a disciple, while any other causes suffering to the guru."
"By the first four" refers to [the qualities] such as beauty and so forth.
