Regarding the time for examining the disciple, it is stated in that very same [text]:
"Having observed the fitness [of the candidate] for one, two, three, four, or five years..."
And also the qualities associated with devotion, according to the sequence of the castes and their intermixture.
"One should recite the Vidyā with undistracted mind according to the very sequence stated previously.

This refers to the "mixed" (saṃkara) castes, including those born in the natural order (anuloma). The meaning is: among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa; that is to say, the examination of the Brāhmaṇa's fitness lasts for one year, whereas for the Kṣatriyas and others, the examination lasts for two years and so forth. Now, the duties of the disciple:

Primarily, one should contemplate the self as self-luminous; one should not turn one's back toward those worthy of worship. One should maintain one’s body, wealth, and life for the sake of the guru. One should do what he says. One should not deliberate upon whether his words are appropriate or inappropriate. One should harbor no longing for the wealth of others. One should not engage in self-praise, disparagement of others, speech that strikes at the vitals, derisive joking, reviling, cursing, or causing fear.

When the Guru and the Paramaguru arrive at the same time, one should first prostrate to the Paramaguru. Then, with the permission of the Guru, one should perform a salutation to him (or, with his permission, perform a salutation to the Guru). One should observe these and other such minor rules. Thus, in brief, are the duties of a disciple.
Regarding the imparting of knowledge:
"Having set aside the mantra of one's father as well as that of one's maternal grandfather..."
Of a younger brother and of one who has taken the side of an enemy.
"If, through negligence or ignorance, one should perform the initiation for a father,
then, having performed an expiation, one should undergo initiation once again."

The mention of the "father" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) that includes the maternal grandfather and others as well. Regarding the expiation, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, since such is seen to be the rule in all cases. However, this prohibition does not apply to the reception of a mantra that is already perfected (*siddha*).
Thus it is stated in the *Siddhayāmala*:
"O Dear One, if by the power of fortune one should obtain a perfected lore (*siddhavidyā*),"
"At that very moment, one should undergo initiation, having abandoned all deliberation regarding a guru."

Furthermore, because of an internal scriptural statement to the effect that "one does not incur fault regarding a mantra already mastered," when there is an eclipse at a sacred pilgrimage site (*puṇyatīrtha*), a desired mantra may certainly be received even from one's father or other elders. Likewise, in the *Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā*, Vyāsa says to Śaunaka:
"My father, a treasure-house of compassion, is gracious-hearted and composed."
"At the great sacred site of Kurukṣetra, on the occasion of the solar festival, he gave [it]."
From the context, it is connected with the word "mantra. Regarding "the youngest," this refers to anyone who is younger than oneself. Likewise, in the Śaiva Āgama:
"O Maheśvarī, [it is given] to mendicants, to forest-dwellers, and to those belonging to the [four] castes."
A householder who seeks worldly enjoyment rather than liberation should not undergo initiation into the mantra.
"For those who have abandoned the sacred fires, who are devoid of ritual action, who are ascetics without possessions,
and who dwell in the forest— even such as these are [excluded], since the student (brahmacārī) belongs to a lower stage of life.
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, they have no entitlement to the imparting of mantras."

One who has entered a lower stage of life (*nyūnāśramī*) [is not qualified], because the householder’s stage (*gārhasthya*) is the second stage of life in relation to it. By this, it is understood that even ascetics (*yatins*) such as householders should not undertake the reception of mantras.
For this very reason, the *Sārasaṃgraha* states the definition of a guru: "A practitioner of austerity (*tapasvī*), a speaker of truth, and a householder with a composed mind."

Even in the Śivasadbhāva it is said: "O Dear One, one who seeks enjoyment and liberation should not, during initiation, choose ascetics (yatins) or forest-dwellers (vaikhānasas) as his guru; likewise, a householder should not choose one who belongs to a [celibate] stage of life (varnin)."
The *vaikhānasas* are forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*). The *varṇin* is a student (*brahmacārī*).
In this matter, women also have the right [to practice].
"Whether purely Vedic or mixed, it is prescribed for the Brahmins and the other castes."
A Tantrika is proclaimed to be acceptable even for a Śūdra who is devoted to a Brāhmaṇa.
Women and Śūdras should also perform the worship of Viṣṇu with faith according to the path taught in their own scriptures, keeping their husband in their hearts.

"Women also have the right to perform the worship of Viṣṇu and other such rites, provided they are devoted to the pleasure of their husbands; this is the eternal Śruti," according to the statement in the Padma Purāṇa.
[However: "A Śūdra and women shall never recite the Vedic mantras."
For it is stated in the words of Yājñavalkya: "The wise prescribe either a Śiva-mantra ending in *namaḥ* or a Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Also: "Laghuśyāmā, Kālarātri, Gopāla, and Jānakīpati..."
Chinnamastā, Mātaṅgī, Tripurā, Kālikā, and Śiva.

"Ugratārā and Bhairava are to be bestowed upon the four castes; these mantras especially grant excellent accomplishment to those with deer-like eyes. This is also because of such statements from the *Mantraprakāśa* and other texts.
Now, in this context, the mantras that bestow accomplishment during childhood, youth, and old age are shown in sequence: [The mantras follow here.]
Mantras are of three kinds: seed-mantras (bījamantra), mantras, and garland-mantras (mālāmantra).
Seed-mantras consist of up to ten syllables; thereafter, mantras consist of up to twenty syllables.
"Those *mālā-mantras* are traditionally held to consist of more than twenty syllables."
These very [mantras] are also perfected through double the number of recitations even during other states.
Now, as an incidental matter, the specific distinction of the genders of mantras is stated: "Mantras ending in *vaṣaṭ* and those ending in *phaṭ* are known to be masculine."
"The feminine [mantras] end in *vauṣaṭ* and *svāhā*, while the neuter ones end in *huṃ* and *namaḥ*."
The application of these is as follows:
"In the rites of subjugation, eradication, and obstruction, male mantras bestow success;
for the destruction of minor acts and diseases, female mantras grant swift success."
"In the case of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), those who are impotent (*klība*) are prescribed; such is the application of the mantra.
Now, regarding the method for receiving a mantra in the absence of a guru, as stated in the *Śāradātilaka* and other texts:
"The procedure for receiving mantras in the absence of a guru is now described."
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Having written that mantra either on a silver plate or on a palm leaf,
one should place it upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and worship Maheśvara.
Having offered milk-rice and other oblations, and having prostrated before him,
one should recite the mantra a hundred times in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
"And for all mantras indeed, such a method of reception is desired."
Alternatively:
"On the northern bank of a river that flows toward the ocean,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in a pure place on an auspicious day."
Then, having written the mantra on a palm leaf and placed it there,
one should invoke the Sun-god and worship him according to the prescribed rite.
"In his presence, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times as instructed by the preceptor;
thus the wise man should receive it—this is remembered as the preliminary rite."
Now, regarding the time:
"The commencement of the mantra should take place in Caitra, as it bestows all human goals;
in Vaiśākha, one will have a desire for jewels, and in Jyeṣṭha, death would occur."
In Āṣāḍha there will be the loss of kinsmen; in Śrāvaṇa, one's purpose will be fulfilled;
in Bhādrapada, there will be the destruction of offspring; and in Āśvina, there will be an accumulation of jewels.
In Kārtika there shall be perfection of mantras, and it shall be the same in Mārgaśīrṣa;
in Pauṣa there shall be affliction from enemies, while Māgha increases intelligence.
"In Phālguna, all desires shall be fulfilled; one should avoid the intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
The mention of the *malamāsa* is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the *kṣayamāsa*. "On the first day, the second, and the third, being pure..."
On the fourth day there will be loss of wealth; on the fifth day there is an increase of intelligence.
On the sixth day, there is the destruction of knowledge; on the seventh day, one obtains happiness;
on the eighth day, there will be the loss of intellect; and on the ninth day, the decay of the body.
On the tenth day there is royal fortune; on the eleventh, one becomes pure;
on the twelfth, all success shall be attained; and on the thirteenth, poverty occurs.
On the fourteenth day, there is birth as an animal; at the end of the month, there is decline.
The "end of the month" refers to the new moon (amāvāsyā).
On the full moon, the increase of dharma is traditionally taught for the retention of mantras.

By the word "full moon" (pūrṇimā), only the latter half of the full moon day is to be understood, and not the first half; for that [first half] is generally prohibited for all rites due to its being designated as *bhadrā*. It is said: "On Sunday there shall be wealth; on Monday there shall be peace;
Mars destroys longevity; and on Wednesday [there is loss of] beauty."
Knowledge is attained on Thursday, good fortune is said to occur on Friday, and the loss of fame occurs on Saturday; thus the days of the week are proclaimed.
One attains happiness under Aśvinī; under Bharaṇī, death occurs;
under Kṛttikā, one becomes miserable; and under Rohiṇī, one becomes a master of speech.
In Mṛgaśīrṣa there is the attainment of happiness; in Ārdrā, the loss of kinsmen;
under the two Punarvasus, one becomes wealthy; and in Puṣya, the destruction of enemies.
Under Āśleṣā there may be death; under Maghā, liberation from suffering;
and under the two Pūrvaphalgunīs, one attains beauty—of this there is no doubt.
One will possess knowledge under the stars Uttaraphalgunī and Hasta, and become wealthy under Citrā; there shall be attainment of knowledge under Svātī, and the destruction of enemies.
In Viśākhā there is happiness, and in Anurādhā there is an increase in what is desired;
in Jyeṣṭhā there may be loss of sons, while in Mūla there is an increase in fame.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā bestows fame, and Uttarāṣāḍhā likewise bestows fame;
under Śravaṇa one becomes miserable, and under Dhaniṣṭhā there is poverty.
If the moon is in Śatabhiṣaj, there will be intelligence; in Pūrvabhādrapadā, one will be happy;
in Uttarābhādrapadā, there will be happiness; and in Revatī, there is an increase in fame.
Śubha, Siddhi, and likewise Āyuṣmān; after that, Dhruva-yoga;
then Prīti, Saubhāgya-yoga, Vṛddhi-yoga, and Harṣaṇa.
Sukarman, Dhṛti, Siddha, Brahmā, Aindra,
Śobhana, Varyāṇa, and Śiva are auspicious for the reception of mantras.
Regarding the acquisition of mantras, the remaining [karaṇas] are proclaimed to be inauspicious:
namely, Bava, Bālava, Taitila, Kaulava, and Vaṇija.
"O beautiful lady, the instruments in all tantras are exclusively auspicious."
In the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā:
"The commencement of mantras and other rites in Aries bestows wealth and grain;
in Cancer, there shall be the attainment of all perfections; and Virgo grants prosperity to men."
In Libra, there shall be all accomplishments; in Scorpio, all gains;
they say Capricorn bestows sons, and Aquarius grants the abundance of wealth.
Indeed, other *lagna*s would result in undesirable fruits;
initiation is auspicious during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), and even during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) up until the fifth day.
"By those desiring prosperity during the bright fortnight, and by those desiring liberation during the other [dark] fortnight.
In this regard, one must examine the debilitation of Jupiter and Venus, the favorability of the moon and the stars, and the strength of the planets in the ascendant (*lagna*).
As for the strength of the planets:

"Malign planets situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, and benefic planets situated in the quadrants and trines, are auspicious for initiation; however, all [planets] situated in the eighth house cause total destruction."

The eleventh house is the *āya*. The malefics (*pāpa*) are the evil planets: the Sun, Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, and the waning Moon, as well as those [other planets] conjoined with them; the benefics (*śubha*) are the auspicious planets: Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus, provided they are not waning and are free from conjunction with malefics. The quadrants (*kendrāṇi*) are the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth houses. The trines (*trikoṇe*) are the ninth and fifth houses. All planets, whether malefic or benefic, situated in the aforementioned places, are indeed auspicious for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
For this very reason, the construction [of the sentence] is that if all [planets] are situated in the eighth house (*randhra*), they are destroyers.

Furthermore, according to another Tantra, there are times suitable for initiation even apart from the aforementioned periods: "Initiation should be performed at the equinoxes, at the two solstices, at the solar transits, during the Damanaka festival, even at an improper time, as well as during the Pavitra rite and on the festivals of the Guru."

At the equinoxes (viṣuva), namely during the transits of the sun into Libra and Aries; at the two solstices (ayana-dvaṃdva), namely during the transits into Cancer and Capricorn; at the [other] transits (saṃkrānti) other than those; on the festival of Damanaka (damanotsava), that is, on the day of worship using *damanaka* flowers on the full moon of Caitra and so forth; on the occasion of the sacred thread (pavitre), namely on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa; on the festivals of the Guru (guruparvan), namely on the days of the Guru’s birth and his passing;
and elsewhere as well: "at a great holy site, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, and in sacred forests and groves."
"One performing the initiation of mantra (mantradīkṣā) need not purify the month, the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), and so forth."
And another method:
"On whichever day the Guru is pleased, all days, all planets, all lunar mansions, and all zodiac signs bring about auspiciousness."
"When the Guru is satisfied, all the deities are satisfied for him;
one should satisfy the Guru with devotion, and then two things will come to pass."

The "pair" refers to enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). The particle *eva* (only) has the sense of "also. Regarding time according to the distinction of qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), it is said:
"For those seeking liberation, [all] time is [appropriate]; for women, however, all time is [appropriate]."
Now, the Wheel of Debt and Wealth: "Starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra,
one should count according to the sequence of the *mātṛkā* letters and multiply by three."
When divided by seven, the remainder is declared to be the "heap of names" (nāmarāśi).
In this manner, one proceeds starting from the syllables of the mantra up to the first letter of the name.
Having counted [the syllables] and multiplied by three, the wise one should divide by seven;
the remainder is known as the *mantrarāśi*, while the subtractions and additions are performed as before.
Alternatively, having separated the syllables of the mantra here according to their vowels and consonants,
one should double them and join them with the syllables of the practitioner.
The aggregate of mantras is declared to be divided by such eight [factors];
likewise, the collection of syllables of the name is also doubled and applied.
The wise state that the name-total is to be divided by eight using the syllables of the mantra;
here, the states of being in debt or having wealth are proclaimed as before.
"Debt or wealth is to be cleared according to either of the aforementioned methods.
(Now, as an incidental topic, the method for clearing the Siddha and Ari [Siddhāri] is described:
"By five vertical and five horizontal lines... )
Having fashioned a sixteen-compartment grid, one should fill it with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
As it is said: "In the sequence of one,
three, eleven, nine, seven, eighteen, twelve, six, eight, fourteen, twenty-eight, five, five, fifteen, one, one, and three,
let the wise man inscribe the sixteen letters beginning with 'a', 'ka', 'tha', and 'ha' [in the respective squares]."

The meaning of this is as follows: *Rudra* is the eleventh square; *Dṛk* is the second; *Nigamas* is the fourth; *Arkas* is the twelfth; *Paṅkti* is the tenth; *Nāga* is the eighth; *Bhūpās* is the sixteenth; and *Kāma* is the thirteenth. Having written the vowels beginning with *a* in order in the squares from the first to the thirteenth, then the consonants from *ka* to *ta*, and then the consonants from *tha* to *sa*, one should then write the letters *ha* and *kṣa* in the first, third, and eleventh squares. "In the four groups of four squares located here in the intermediate directions, that square where the first letter of the practitioner's name appears is designated as 'Siddhi' (accomplished)."

Following the sequence of circumambulation from this [central point], the next triad of four squares is designated as the *sādhya* (the one to be accomplished), the *susiddha* (the well-accomplished), and the *śatru* (the enemy).

In each of the four squares as well, the determination of [the states] such as Siddha, Sādhya, and so forth, for whichever syllable is in whichever square, is made according to the sequence already stated.

"In this way, starting from the fourfold set of the *sādhya* [sign] and so forth, the names *sādhyasiddha*, *sādhyasādhya*, and so on, are considered in sequence according to the corresponding positions in the grid."
The clear meaning is that from Siddha and Siddha onwards, among these sixteen [classes], whichever mantra has which as its first syllable, it is designated by that same name.
Now, their results:
"The *Siddha* [mantra] is accomplished in time; the *Sādhya* is accomplished or it may not be."
"Once well-accomplished, at that very moment, it cuts off the enemy's root."
In the *Tantrarāja*: "The *siddhasiddha* is accomplished through recitation (*japa*); the *siddhasādhya* is accomplished through double that amount;
the *siddhasusiddha* is accomplished upon attainment; the *siddhāri* destroys those born of one's own lineage."
One who is difficult to cure causes extreme affliction; one who is both difficult and impossible to cure causes extreme suffering.
Through worship, the *sādhya* becomes well-accomplished (*susiddha*); the enemy of the *sādhya* (*sādhyāri*) seizes one's own wife.
Through half the recitation, the well-accomplished-siddha (*susiddhasiddha*) bestows the fruit as desired.

A *susiddha* becomes a *sādhya* through recitation and other means for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise, it is the reverse. And a *susiddha* becomes a *susiddha* when effort was exerted in a previous birth.
Therefore, one should employ that mantra for the accomplishment of all siddhis;
otherwise, it will certainly destroy one's own family entirely, along with its enemies.

"One conquered by an enemy (arisiddha) kills one's son; one to be conquered by an enemy (arisādhya) kills one's daughter; one well-conquered by an enemy (tatsusiddha) kills one's wife; and an enemy of the enemy (aryari) destroys the practitioner."

"From attainment" means from the mere act of attaining. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "by recitation and so forth," the offerings of oblations (*homa*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), and the feeding of Brahmins are included.
Now, the clearing of debts and assets by another method:
"Having doubled the circle of vowels and consonants residing within the *sādhya* [mantra]..."
Having combined that with the one called the sādhana, one should divide by eight.

The remainder shall be the quantity to be proven (sādhya); otherwise, the practitioner (sādhaka) should apply it. However, if the remainder is greater than the divisor, the one being proven (sādhya) is a debtor, which brings auspiciousness.
"The remainder after subtraction shall be purified and become auspicious through one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra.

Here, "the mantra to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) refers to the collection of vowels and consonants [of that mantra]. "Otherwise" means: having doubled the aggregate of vowels and consonants contained in the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), one should add the mass of vowels and consonants contained in the mantra to be accomplished and divide by eight; the meaning is that one should know the remainder to be the "practitioner's heap" (*sādhakarāśi*).

The meaning is as follows: when it is said that [the mantra] has been "purified" according to the established sequence, if the favorable mantra is deficient in relation to the practitioner, then one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) and so forth after first clearing away the deficiency by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for each missing syllable. That mantra whose numerical total (*mantrarāśi*) is greater is to be known as "indebted" (*ṛṇin*); this one is indeed to be accepted. That mantra whose numerical total is less is "wealthy" (*dhanin*); this one is to be rejected. Other methods should be understood from other sources.

Now, an exception to this [rule], consisting of non-redundant statements found in the *Sīmasiddhāntaratna*, *Aṅgasāra*, *Rudrayāmala*, *Agastisaṃhitā*, *Siddhāntaśekhara*, and other works, is collected here: "In the case of a single-syllable mantra, a *kūṭa* (cryptic) mantra, a *traipura* mantra, one offered by a woman, one obtained in a dream, or even among the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha..."
Likewise, in the Prāsāda mantra, the Praṇava, the Sapindākṣara mantra,
the Mṛtyuñjaya, the Pāśādi, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Caṇḍanāyaka;
In the *vyomavyāpin*, in *māyā*, in the *mālā-mantras*, and in *aghora*;
in those consisting of one, three, five, six, seven, eight, nine, eleven, and eleven syllables; in the neuter, in that with thirty-two syllables, and in the *kālikā* and *śyāmalā* mantras.
In the mantras of Siddhakālī and Caṇḍikā, as well as in the Rāma-mantras, [the same applies].
In the Gopālamātṛkā-mantra, together with Haravallabhā,
are Śrīvidyā, Siddhavidyā, Mātaṅgī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Padmāvatī, Madhumatī, Dattātreya, and Pārvatī;
likewise Mitreśa, Uḍḍīśa, Ṣaṣṭhīśa, Caryānanda, and Manu.
For the seven Praṇava-mantras, as well as for Haridrā and Ucchiṣṭa,
the goddesses are Āsurī, Sumukhī, Reṇukā, and Sarasvatī.
Also [the mantras] of Kumbhodbhava, Arṇava, and Mataṅga-gaṇika,
as well as the Śābara mantras, even when recited by elderly men.
One should not purify mantras inherited through family lineage, nor those that have already been mastered,
nor those belonging to the Bahurūpa class, nor even those of the Jaina or Buddhist traditions.
"One should not clear a debt or credit resulting from [the status of] a Siddha, an enemy, and so forth.
Regarding "kūṭe," it means in a mantra consisting of secret syllables (*kūṭākṣara*). "Strīsamarpite" means offered by a specific woman.
And likewise, in another Tantra:
Virtuous, of good conduct, devoted to her guru, with senses subdued,
knowing the true essence of the meaning of all mantras, well-behaved, and intent on worship—
she indeed becomes fit for the guru, provided she is free from widowhood.
"The initiation for women is declared auspicious, and it is remembered as being eightfold greater than that of a mother."
The specific procedure regarding what must be done with that which is obtained in a dream is as follows:

"Having deposited the life-force (*prāṇa*) of the Guru into the jar obtained in a dream, one should contemplate the life-force of the Guru as being deposited in the jar; that is to say, one should perform the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the Guru within the jar."
Having written [the mantra] on a banyan leaf with saffron during an auspicious planetary conjunction (grahaṇa), one then attains purity; otherwise, it shall be fruitless.

This, however, applies in the absence of a true guru; but when one is available, one should receive it from him alone. In the *Prāsāda* [mantra], which is enriched with the seed-syllable of the temple (*prāsāda-bīja*). The *pāśa*-seed is [the syllable *pha*]. In the *Vyomavyāpin*, beginning with the letter *ha*. In *Māyā*, that is, in *Hṛllekhā*. In the *Aṅka*, the nine-syllabled [mantra]. In the *Dantārṇa*, the thirty-two-syllabled [mantra]. Regarding *Haridra* and *Ucchiṣṭa*, these are their respective *Gaṇapati* mantras. The term *aṇu* refers to a *mantra*. It is stated in the *Vātulāgama* that certain mantras are free from curses:
"In ancient times, there existed a pentad of mantras that were devoid of curses."
"The Śrīvidyāsāluva mantra, the Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha [mantras]."
In that regard,
however: "Having inserted the *hṛllekhā* (hrīṃ), the *kāmabīja* (klīm), or the *śrībīja* (śrīṃ) into all mantras and the like, one should recite them for the sake of the mantra's accomplishment."
"Even a wicked mantra is perfected when encapsulated by the *tāra* (the syllable Om)," and in the *Hiraṇyagarbha-saṃhitā*:
"Those who remember the mantra having encapsulated it with the initial letters of their own names or with the letters of their own friends."
The ellipsis implies that "that mantra is accomplished for them. *Anusmaraṇa* (recollection) means *japa* (repetition).
The consecration (*saṃskāra*) and other rites for mantras, however, should be consulted in works such as the *Śāradātilaka* and the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*.
At the outset, for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*), the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) must necessarily be performed. And so says Vaiśampāyana:
"A mantra that is perfected through *puraścaraṇa* indeed bestows its fruit;
for what purpose are fire-offerings (*homa*), what purpose are recitations (*japa*), and what purpose are the elaborate ritual placements of mantras (*mantranyāsa*)?"
For if there were no preliminary service (puraskriyā) for secret mantras, [they would be ineffective];
indeed, the preliminary service of mantras is said to be the primary seed.
"O Goddess, just as one devoid of vigor is incapable of all actions,
so too is a mantra proclaimed to be ineffective when it lacks *puraścaraṇa*."
The etymology of the term *puraścaraṇa* is given in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"The practice of the root mantra is called *puraścaraṇa*,
because it must be performed prior to the rites known as *viniyoga*."
"Or it is stated thus because of the application [of the mantra] at the beginning.

As for the definition of *viniyoga* (application), it is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "The application, according to the path of the scriptures, of [the means to] dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa..."
The application of a perfected mantra has been thus proclaimed by the wise.
This application, preceded by the *puraścaraṇa* rite, has been prescribed for the sake of attaining results— just as the service of a mantra is like the service of a king.
"Because it precedes the performance [of the rite], it is called *puraścaraṇa*.

By this it is stated that *puraścaraṇa* is the ritual action that generates the efficacy for the rite known as *viniyoga*, or the action that serves as the cause for the purification of the self through the mantra in this world and the next.

Now, the extraction of the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), the assignment of the seer and other factors (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*) of the mantra, the meditation (*dhyāna*), the number of recitations (*japasaṃkhyā*), and the procedure for worship (*pūjāvidhi*) are described.
Now I shall declare the Anuṣṭubh mantra of Kṛṣṇa, which bestows sons:
at the end of the syllables of the name "Devakī-suta," one should utter the word "Govinda."
Having uttered the word "Vāsudeva" ending in the vocative case,
and having said "O Kṛṣṇa, give me a son," he should address the Lord of the Universe.
The mantra ending with "I have gone for refuge" consists of thirty-two syllables; Nārada is said to be its sage (ṛṣi), and the Anuṣṭubh is declared to be its meter (chandas).

The Lord Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of the pressed soma, accompanied by Vijaya, stood upon his chariot; having brought [the vessel] from the midst of the ocean, he touched it with his feet and with his entire body.
The son of Vasudeva, who is worthy of being remembered, gave his daughters to the twice-born;
[the result is] a hundred thousand recitations and ten thousand oblations with sesame seeds soaked in sweetened milk.
"The worship previously described is thus the mantra that bestows sons upon men. Thus it is said.

In the *Mantrakaumudī*, the application of the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire) is stated at the beginning; in other [texts], however, it is also stated at the end. In this context, the libations (*tarpaṇa*), the ritual purification (*mārjana*), and the feeding of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇabhojana*) are also to be performed.
"Japa, homa, tarpaṇa, mārjana, and feeding Brahmins—
this five-limbed *puraścaraṇa* is declared by those who know the mantras," according to the statement in the *Mantrakaumudī* and other texts.
The specific number for these [limbs] is also stated in that very same work:
"A person [should perform] the *tarpaṇa* with a tenth part of that [japa],
the *mārjana* with a tenth part of that, and the feeding [of Brahmins] with a tenth part of that."

The ritual of limb-assignment (*aṅganyāsa*), the wheel-diagrams (*cakra*), and so forth, are to be performed according to the procedure for the ten-syllable mantra of Gopāla. It is as follows: "To the *ācakra* is declared the heart; to the *vicakra* the head;
to the *sucakra* the crest-lock (*śikhā*); and thereafter, the protection of the three worlds."
"The armor for the Discus is declared from the word 'Asurāntaka';
one should fashion this weapon for the Discus; thus is the pentad of limbs for the mantra."

But in another Tantra it is said: "To the discus that is the end-maker of the asuras, [offer] two eyes; to the Sudarśana discus, the weapon. Thus the six limbs have been described. Now, for the discus:
"Having worshipped the four limbs beginning with the heart in the corners starting from the southeast..."
One should worship the weapon in the cardinal directions and the eight queens on the petals.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, the daughter of Nagnajit (Nāgnajiti),
Arkajā, Mitravindā, Lakṣmaṇā, Jāmbavatī, and Suśīlikā.

The eight queens, golden-hued and adorned with various ornaments and garlands, [are placed] at the tips of the petals; and Vasudeva, the husband of Devakī and lord of the cowherds, [is placed at the center].
Immediately thereafter, one should worship Yaśodā, Balabhadra, Subhadrā, the cowherds and cowherdesses, as well as Indra and the other gods, along with their weapons such as the thunderbolt.
"And one should perform the ritual applications (prayoga) declared for these ten-syllable mantras."
Regarding the system of the six limbs (*aṅga-ṣaṭka*), the arrangement is stated in another tantra:
"Having worshipped the four limbs beginning with the Heart in the corners starting from the southeast,
one should worship the Eye in the cardinal directions and worship the Weapon in all directions."
Now, briefly, the duties of the performer of the *puraścaraṇa*:
in the *Tantrasāra*— "Sleeping on the ground, eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), observing silence, and having his senses subdued."
Free from envy and pride, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
Vyāsa says: "Subsisting on milk, or eating fruits, or eating vegetables, or consuming sacrificial ghee,
or subsisting on alms, one should perform *japa* [recitation], as well as *japa* such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
Salt, alkaline substances, and sour things; the *gṛñjana* radish, eating from bell-metal vessels, betel, eating twice a day, living with those difficult to dwell with, and heedlessness.
"One should also avoid recitation at night that is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti.
"Dusamvāsa" means dwelling together with the wicked.
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
Sleeping on the ground, practicing celibacy, observing silence,
being free from envy, bathing daily at the three periods of the day, and avoiding trivial activities.
Daily worship, daily charity, the praise and glorification of the deity,
occasional rites of adoration, and faith in the guru and the deity.
"These twelve qualities rooted in Japan (the land of the rising sun) shall grant the accomplishment of mantras.
Thus, one who performs the *puraścaraṇa* should observe these and other such rules.
Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the cessation of the eightfold sexual intercourse.
As it was stated by Dakṣa:
"Remembering, praising, playing, looking, secret conversation,
intention, determination, and the completion of the act."
"The wise declare this to be the eightfold sexual union;
celibacy is the opposite of this, and it likewise possesses these same eight characteristics."

Recollection, verbal praise, and looking [at the object of desire] preceded by longing (*abhilāṣa*) are forbidden. *Keli* refers to external activities such as jesting and the like. *Guhyabhāṣaṇa* is secret consultation for the purpose of sexual union. *Saṃkalpa* is mental action. *Adhyavasāya* is the determination to engage in sexual union. *Kriyānivṛtti* is the completion of the act.
As for bathing three times a day (*triṣavaṇa-snāna*), that is intended for those who are capable;
for it is stated in the words of Vaiśampāyana: "Bathing three times a day is prescribed; in case of incapacity, one should perform it twice or once."
As for the minor rites (*kṣudrakarma*),
it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Deceit, hatred, as well as destruction, driving away, delusion, killing, and disease— these are remembered as the minor [rites]."

Daily worship consists precisely of that preceded by the procedure for recitation (*japa*). Occasional worship (*naimittikārcana*) refers to special worship performed on occasions such as the anniversary of [the deity's] birth and so forth.
That has been described in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"Having performed the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) with devotion one thousand and eight times..."
That which one should mutter every day is known as the daily (nitya) recitation.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), and on the full moon— on these occasions, there is the occasional (naimittika) recitation.
"Then, from that constant [recitation], it becomes tripled, as does the worship of Hari.

The term "of Hari" (harer) is an indicative mark for one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā). It has been stated by Viṣṇu that when the *puraścaraṇa* has commenced, there is no obstruction to the recitation (*japa*) even during the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*):
"In the case of vows, sacrifices, marriages, ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), fire-offerings (*homa*), worship, and recitation..."
"There is no birth-impurity (sūtaka) regarding what has already begun, but there is birth-impurity regarding what has not yet begun."

The meaning of the word *prārambha* (commencement) was stated by Viṣṇu: "In a sacrifice, *prārambha* is the choosing [of priests]; in a vow (*vrata*) or a sacrificial session (*satra*), it is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*); in marriage and similar rites, it is the *nāndīmukha*; and in a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), it is the preparation of the cooked food."
In the *Mantramahodadhi*:
"First, in order to bring the deity under control, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite;
in a secluded place such as a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), preceded by the formal acquisition of the ground."
Having divided that ground into nine parts, one should draw [the diagram] starting from the east;
within the squares, one should place the seven consonant groups, with the *lakṣa* (the letter *kṣa*) in the center, as well as the vowels.
The first letter of the name of the field (kṣetra) is located in whichever square (koṣṭha).
Having sat down, one should perform the recitation (japa) in no other place that causes distress;
one should perform the recitation until midday, either in a whisper or mentally.
One should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) at night, having bathed three times and remaining steady;
one should avoid agitation, laziness, spitting, anger, and stretching out the legs.
During the time of recitation (japa), the wise man should avoid speaking another language and looking at an outcaste (antyaja).

"Speaking another language" (anyabhāṣā) and "an outcaste" (antyaja)—the latter being a *cāṇḍāla*—refer to "speaking another language and looking at an outcaste" (*anyabhāṣāntyajekṣe*). The meaning is that one should avoid conversing with others and gazing upon an outcaste.
[He should also avoid] conversing with women or *śūdras*, [engaging in] censure, chewing betel, and sleeping during the day.
One should always avoid accepting gifts, dancing, singing, and crookedness.
One should take refuge in sleeping on the ground, celibacy, worshiping the deity three times a day,
occasional worship, and the praise of the Lord with full confidence.
"Day by day, it is exactly thus; there is never any deficiency or excess."

Having made a square of nine compartments, one should write the seven groups of consonants beginning with *ka* starting from the eastern direction, and at the end, *laṃ* and *kṣaṃ*. Likewise, having made nine compartments in the central [section], one should write pairs of vowels starting from the east. The mouth is to be known as being in whichever compartment the first letter of the name of the field (*kṣetra*) occurs; below that, in sequence, are the hands, sides, feet, tail, and so forth. One should perform the recitation (*japa*) sitting there at the mouth, and not elsewhere on the hands, sides, or other parts. Regarding this: "One who has desires should face north, but one free of desires should recite facing east."
"Abhicāra and so forth [should be performed] in the night-watch (yāma), while killing is prescribed for the south-west (nairṛtya)"—
according to this statement, it may be done according to one's desire.
Now, the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra) by another method:

On a levelled ground, having drawn four lines each extending east-west and four extending north-south, one should form nine compartments. Therein, proceeding clockwise starting from the east, one should write the eight groups of consonants known as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *la* in the eight corners in sequence, and the two vowels beginning with *a* [namely *a* and *ā*] in the remaining spaces; then, one should write the syllable *Śrī* in the central compartment. Alternatively, the vowels may be written in the central compartment in order starting from the east. This Kūrma-cakra is of three types, distinguished by the field (*kṣetra*), the village (*grāma*), and the house (*gṛha*).

In that regard, for a field or a village, the square containing the first syllable of its respective name is the mouth of the tortoise; this very location is called the place of the lamp (*dīpasthāna*). In the case of a house, however, the square containing the first syllable of the householder’s name is the mouth. The two squares situated on either side of it are the hands; those situated below them are the belly; those situated below those are the feet; the square situated in the middle of the belly is the back; and the square situated in the middle of the feet is the tail—such is the distinction.

For one who has meditated upon the tortoise in the manner described above—visualized within the sacred field (*kṣetra*) and so forth—there is the accomplishment of all aims through recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) performed at its mouth or back. The breasts are located on the two hands; the interior cavities are not employed [for this purpose]. Thus, the non-essentiality of the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*) in certain instances has been stated.
For example: "At Kurukṣetra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean..."
"One should not contemplate a lamp-stand at Mahākāla or in Kāśī."
Because it is characterized by the location of the lamp (*dīpasthāna*), the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*) is also called the "lamp-location.
In this diagram, one should contemplate the positions of the enemies among the aforementioned squares; having first abandoned those, the remaining positions of friends are to be adopted.
The consideration of enemies and friends is as follows:
By the letter *tha*, [the seed-syllable] of *advaya* is [indicated], and by that same [letter], also that of *ṭha*;
by the letter *pa*, [the seed-syllable] of the two *lṛ*s is [indicated], and by that same [letter], also that of *pa*.
The letter *au* is [substituted] for *dvaya* by means of *ṣa*; *ṣa* is [substituted] by means of *au* and *yu*;
*ja* is [substituted] by means of *ṭa*; and *jña* is [substituted] by means of *kha*.
The letter *u* [is joined] with *la*, the letter *pha* with *dha*,
the letter *bha* with *ra*, and the letter *ya* with *sa*.
"One should cultivate a sense of friendship toward these other castes [and] enmity toward these [others].
Prior to beginning the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), for the sake of attaining success in the mantra, one should perform three hundred thousand recitations of the *gāyatrī*.
This is stated in the *Mantrakaumudī*:
"For the sake of the accomplishment of all mantras, one should recite the Gāyatrī thirty thousand times.
The necessity of the rule regarding the seat is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* and other texts:
"Having consecrated and worshipped the seat, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) there."
Regarding that, on that seat;
Nārada describes the seat: "It should be provided with kuśa grass, deerskin, and cloth, and four finger-breadths in height."
It should be four-cornered, two cubits in size, very firm, soft, and stainless.
"Having prepared a seat, one should commence the rite of recitation.
Regarding skins, Vaiśampāyana says: "A tiger skin is for all accomplishments; a deer skin is for the accomplishment of knowledge."
A seat made of cloth removes disease, while one made of cane increases prosperity.
"Silk is said to be nourishing, and woolen cloth (kambala) is the liberator from suffering.
Here, the garment is made of wool (*āvika*), not of cotton (*kārpāsa*).
For it is said: "Recitation performed upon a cotton seat becomes fruitless."
Thus, because a fault is heard in the *Brahmayāmala* regarding a seat made of cotton cloth (*kārpāsamaya*),
the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) must also necessarily be performed.
"A worship performed by one devoid of the purification of the elements is like a malevolent spell (*abhicāra*)."
Just as worship performed without devotion would yield a contrary result.
Thus, because the fault of not performing it has been stated by the Pot-born (Agastya),

the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana*) is also mentioned in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Having thus performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), one should then indeed establish the vital breaths."
The vital breaths (*asūn prāṇān*).

Regarding the internal (*antarmātṛkā*) and external (*bahirmātṛkā*) nyāsas as well, it is stated in that very same place: "Having performed the internal *mātṛkā* nyāsa, one should then perform the external nyāsa."
The external placement (*bahirnyāsa*) is the placement of the external *mātṛkā*.
The necessity of this placement is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
"Meditation, recitation, worship, and fire-offerings—even when performed by one who has mastered the mantra—"
"Lacking the proper arrangement of their limbs, these will not yield fruits."
In the *Kapilapañcarātra*:
"When recitation is performed without the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), and deities (*devatā*), even if it is accomplished, its fruit will be insignificant."
Now, regarding the mudrās: therein, concerning the external placement (bahirnyāsa) mudrās, the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā states:
"One should place the [mantric] syllables (aṇu) with flowers, or with the ring finger, or even mentally."

In this regard, the established rule is as follows: with flowers, one performs the rite upon the form of the deity; with the hand (anāmaya), upon one's own body; and mentally, within the cakras beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, since physical contact with the hands is impossible there.

It is performed with the hand including the thumb—according to the statement in the *Padyavāhinī*: "The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) everywhere is agreed upon to be done with the thumb and the ring finger."

Regarding the mudrās for the placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), it is stated in the *Tantrarāja* and other texts: "The four fingers beginning with the index finger, with the thumb extended, [are placed] at the heart; and at the head; while a fist devoid of the thumb is [placed] at the surface of the crest-lock (*śikhā*)."
By the force of the word "ca" (and), [the remaining fingers] are placed on the heart and the head.
Starting from the shoulder and extending to the navel, the ten fingers constitute the armor (*varman*).
The three fingers beginning with the index finger are for the three eyes; two are for each of the two eyes.
The wise practitioner, having performed three claps with his outstretched hands,
should brandish the tips of his index fingers and thumbs while binding the directions.

"This is declared to be the weapon-mudrā (astramudrā) of Viṣṇu; these have been proclaimed. Regarding the mudrās for the ritual placement of the seer and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa), it is stated in that same work: "The fingers are prescribed for the ritual placement of the seer, the meter, and the deity."
"The four fingers, excluding the thumb," so it has been declared by the learned.
Now, the mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana):
"Having formed the añjali with both hands, one should place the two thumbs upon the root joints of the ring fingers; this is considered the āvāhana-mudrā."

If this [mudrā] is with the palms facing downward, it is called *sthāpanī* (the establishing mudrā). The meaning is that if this *āvāhanī* mudrā is with the palms facing downward, it becomes the *sthāpanī* mudrā. By this very [statement], it is understood that the *āvāhanī* mudrā has the hands turned upward (*uttāna*).
From the joining of two fists with the thumbs raised, however, arises the *saṃnidhāpanī* (the mudrā for bringing into presence).
With the thumb inserted inside, that very same [mudrā] is considered to be the Saṃrodhinī.
The meaning of *saṃrodhinī* is two fists with the thumbs tucked inside.
*Sammukhīkaraṇī* consists of a pair of upward-facing fists;
that is to say, the *sammukhīkaraṇī* mudrā consists of two upward-facing fists.
The placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the body of the deity is the act of "making complete" (*sakalīkṛti*).
This refers to the *mudrā* known as *sakalīkaraṇī*.
When, by means of the *saṃnirōdha-mudrā*, the two index fingers (*tarjanī*) are straightened, [it constitutes this].
This is considered the Avaguṇṭhana-mudrā when rotated all around.
O Dear One, this Mahāmudrā, in which the thumbs are interlaced and the other fingers are extended, is declared to be that which brings about supreme union.
The meaning of *mahāmudrā* is as follows: one should interlace the two thumbs of both hands and extend the other fingers.
This very [mudrā] is called *paramīkaraṇī*.
Then, one should place the right fingers into the middle of the left fingers.
Having joined the right index finger with the middle finger of the left hand, likewise.
One should join the left index finger with the middle finger of the right hand;
one should join the right little finger with the ring finger of the left hand.
One should join the right ring finger with the left little finger;
this mudrā, when positioned facing downwards, is proclaimed as the Dhenu-mudrā.

This very [mudrā] is called the *amṛtīkaraṇī*. With the little finger and ring finger on their backs, the thumb upon the index finger, and the middle finger curved while the [other] is straight— this mudrā is named the *aṅkuśā*.
The meaning is that one should make the middle finger straight and join the index finger at the middle joint of the middle finger, then bend it.
Having grasped the left thumb with the right fist,
and having likewise turned the fist upward, one should extend the thumb.
"The fingers of the left hand thus embraced, joined, and well extended,
with the tips touching the right thumb— this is the conch mudrā, which bestows prosperity."
"One should join the tips of the ring finger, the thumb, and the middle finger of the right hand; the remaining two fingers should be raised—this is declared to be the mṛgamudrā."

The meaning of the word *mudrā* is given in the *Tantrasāra*: "Those which effortlessly bestow joy (*mudam*) upon the Self for the sake of attaining its true nature (*svarūpalābha*) through the gateway of the body are considered to be *mudrās*, that is, powers (*śaktis*)."
"They liberate one from planetary afflictions and the like, and they cause the flood of sins to melt away;
because they effect liberation and melting, they are described as 'mudrās' in the scriptures."
Regarding the place for recitation (*japadeśa*), the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* states:
"Recitation is praised when performed in the presence of the sun, fire, the guru, the moon, or a burning lamp; or likewise in the presence of Brahmins or cows."
Alternatively, one should dwell wherever the mind finds serenity.
Recitation performed at home is said to be equal [in merit], while that performed in a cow-pen is ten times more effective.
And likewise in a grove or a forest, it is said to be a thousandfold.
"It is ten thousandfold on a meritorious mountain, but a hundred-thousandfold by a river;
they say it is ten millionfold in a temple of the gods, and infinite in the presence of Śiva."
The mention of Śiva is an indication for one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva).
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"One should recite [the mantra] in a fire-sanctuary, at the edge of water, or even in a temple."
"At a sacred bathing place, in a cow-pen, in a field of the twice-born, or in one's own home."
Śaṅkha also says: "Recitation performed at home is said to have one-fold merit; at a river and the like, it is twice as effective;
in a cow-pen, ten-fold; and in a fire-sanctuary, more than a hundred-fold."
"At the perfected tirthas, in sacred fields, and in the presence of a deity, [the merit is] hundreds of thousands of crores; in the presence of Viṣṇu, it is infinite."
The term "Viṣṇu" is an illustration representing one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*).
It is also stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Because the Guhyakas, Rākṣasas, and Siddhas carry [the body] away by force..."
"Therefore, one should always perform the recitation in a solitary and auspicious place."
Now, concerning the rosary (*japamālā*):
it is of three kinds—consisting of the letters of the *mātṛkā*, consisting of beads such as *rudrākṣa*, and consisting of the joints of the right hand.
Regarding these, the author of the *Sārasaṃgraha* states the first:
By means of a garland of letters fashioned from the syllables of the Mātṛkā, beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', accompanied by the bindu, and arranged in both direct and reverse order.
"Mantras consisting of individual syllables, when recited, grant swift accomplishment;
this is true even for hostile mantras of men—how much more so for those that are well-accomplished and the like?"
Its method is stated in the *Tantraprakāśa*: "Having visualized the phonemes from 'a' to 'kṣa' situated within the *brahmanāḍī*,
and having joined each phoneme with the *bindu*, the wise one should mutter his own chosen mantra."
O Goddess of the Universe, having joined [the letters] in sequence starting with 'a' and likewise starting with 'ka', one should then conceive of the letter 'kṣa' as Meru therein.
Then the script shall consist of a rosary numbering fifty;
by means of this, the recitation of all mantras accomplishes every purpose.
"The syllable *kṣa* is at the junction of Meru; from *la* onwards in reverse order, one should recite the mantras with each one separated by an interval; thus it bestows the fruit."
When the daily recitation (*japa*) of one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight [mantras] is to be performed, then the method should be understood as follows:
"By means of the division into the eight groups (*varga*), there shall be one hundred and eight. In this context, the term *akṣamālā* (rosary) is used in its primary sense.
And it is said in the Śāradātilaka:
"Because it is joined with the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa', it is celebrated as the 'garland of letters' (akṣamālā).
Also in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Goddess, the letter 'a' is the first, and the letter 'kṣa' is the last;
this is renowned as the 'Akṣamālā' (the Garland of Letters), which takes the form of the phonemes of Mātṛkā."

The recitation of the eight groups (*varga-aṣṭaka*) should be performed at the conclusion of the prescribed number of repetitions, such as one hundred and so forth. As it is said in the *Mātṛkārṇava*: "Beginning first with the letter *A*, one should mentally recite the Mātṛkā up to its end."
"Having held that [mantra] at its conclusion, one should recite it again until the very end during the descent (āvaroha).

Then one should mutter the eight classes of consonants ending in 'la' (lānta), and subsequently again at the conclusion, up to the letter 'ha' (ānta); this is declared as the withdrawal (saṃhāra) in the *Yāmala*, this being the *Mālā* taught by Paśupati."

Having placed [the final bead] in the position of Meru; the letter *kṣa* is the end (*avasāna*). [The beads] ending in *la*—namely those designated as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *la*. After that, following the completion of the number indicated; at the end, meaning at the conclusion of the indicated number such as one hundred. The particle *eva* is used for emphasis. However, in the *Sārasaṃgraha*, the second [type of rosary] is described:
"Now I shall explain the procedure for the rosary for one desiring the fruit of mantra:
it is said to consist of twenty-five beads and bestows liberation."
With thirty [syllables] she is the giver of wealth, and with twenty-seven syllables she is always present;
however, when fashioned with fifteen syllables, she is the performer of malevolent rites.
With fifty-four syllables, she bestows success in rites performed for specific desires;
when arranged with one hundred and eight syllables, she is considered the granter of all desired objects.
Jewels originating from conch shells are said to bestow prosperity;
those made of crystal grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation, while lotus-seed beads increase nourishment.
Rudrākṣas are said to bestow enjoyment and liberation, granting all spiritual perfections;
those originating from the *putrajīva* tree grant abundance of sons, cattle, and grain.
Gems originating from coral bestow wealth, good fortune, and subjugation;
pearls are said to grant liberation and provide the abundance of all prosperity.
"Those made of *kuśa* grass remove sin, while those made of gold and silver grant desires.
Hārīta says:
"A garland made of conch or silver, or one made of gold with wild lotuses..."
And with lotus seeds, rudrākṣas, corals, gems, and pearls.
"A rosary made of silver, indrākṣa seeds, or likewise the joints of the fingers,
as well as a rosary made of putrajīva seeds, is indeed recommended for the practice of recitation."
Gautama also says: "Counting with the fingers is declared to be one-fold;
with a line it is eightfold; and with *putrajīva* beads it is ten times more."
With conch gems and coral, it would be a hundred; with crystal, a thousand;
with crystal, ten thousand; and with pearls, it is said to be a hundred thousand.

"With lotus seeds, ten lakhs [of recitations] are performed; with golden beads, it is said to be ten million (koṭi); and with knots of kuśa grass or rudrākṣa beads, infinite fruit is said to be obtained."

"For Gopāla, however, a rosary of lotus seeds is highly recommended," according to the statement of Gautama: "Silent, peaceful, pure, and self-controlled, one should always recite the mantra of Gopāla with a concentrated mind, using a rosary of lotus seeds."
In the *Uttara-tantra*, there is a prohibition against mixing [beads]:
"If one performs recitation with *indrākṣa* beads, or likewise with *rudrākṣa* or crystal beads,
nothing else— such as *putrajīva* and so forth— should be inserted in between."
If one should employ anything else in the act of recitation upon a rosary,
O beloved one, it will grant neither his desire nor liberation.
"In another birth he is born as one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
thereafter, he enters into association with Caṇḍālas of sinful deeds."
Prajāpati states the number of beads:
"One should make [a rosary] of one hundred and eight, or likewise fifty-four;
it should be made of twenty-seven; beyond that, more is not beneficial."
A rosary of one hundred and eight beads is proclaimed as the best;
that of fifty-four, O child, is proclaimed as the middling.
"The lowest [bead] is always said to be the twenty-seventh in number.
Regarding recitation (*japa*) numbering ten thousand (*ayuta*) and so forth, it is stated: "A person should not allow the rosary to be broken during the rite of recitation.

Since there is a prohibition against breaking the rosary, and because these [other types of] rosaries cannot possibly serve as instruments for *japa*, and since there is no specific injunction for a rosary composed of one hundred beads, one must nevertheless conceive of a rosary composed of exactly one hundred beads here due to the necessity of the situation (*anāyatyā*).
Some say this is because of the statement: "For a recitation of ten thousand (*ayuta*) or more, the rosary is said to consist of beads numbering one hundred.

Others, however, maintain that for a recitation of ten thousand or more, only a rosary of letters (*varṇamālā*) numbering one hundred should be used, and not one made of gems; for an unbroken rosary of such [gems] is impossible here, and because the statement prescribing a rosary of one hundred gem-beads lacks a scriptural basis. But for a recitation of one thousand and eight, the rosary may be either made of letters or made of the hands; this will be explained further on. Gautama says:
In the Śaiva Āgama:
"One should not touch the thread with the index finger, nor shake it, nor rub it;
one should not touch it with the left hand, nor allow it to fall from the hand."
When moving the beads with the thumb, one should not touch another bead;
at the time of recitation, the wise practitioner should never cross over the *meru* bead.
And at the time of turning it over, one must not cause any clashing;
for when it creaks with a *khaṭakhaṭ* sound while swinging, the mind becomes restless due to the strife.
"If it moves, there is enmity; if it breaks, the occurrence of disease;
if it falls from the hand, a great obstacle; and if the thread snaps, one perishes."
When the middle finger moves inward between the other fingers, when the jewel (maṇi) breaks, and when the thread is cut—this also includes the breaking of the cord.
Likewise:
"In the case of spitting, sneezing, or yawning, one should abandon one round of recitation."
If, through negligence, there should be contact with the index finger, one should abandon the turning back.
"The repetition of the mantra [is required]. If an improper touch occurs during the recitation, one should wash [the hands] and recite it again.
And furthermore:
"If the Meru [the central bead] is thus bypassed or the rosary falls,
one becomes pure by performing three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consuming clarified butter."
(Furthermore:
"If the rosary should fall from the hand, or become broken,
or touched [by something impure], one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then consecrate it."
"One should perform one hundred and eight recitations of the root mantra.
Now, regarding the time for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of this rosary,
it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"On the twelfth lunar day, the Vaiṣṇava rosary should be prepared with great care during the divine period by the best of practitioners, those who know the mantras and are devoted to Viṣṇu."
The forenoon is the portion pertaining to the gods.
The Sūtra also states regarding that very time: "A Vaiṣṇava garland should be made of cotton or else of silk threads."

Regarding the cotton thread, the specific detail is given in that very same [text]: "Then, having carefully washed the thread— made by a meritorious woman of the best of the twice-born, devoid of knots, and tripled [in strands]— and having folded it three times over."
(In another Tantra: "By a Brahmin woman or a married woman; in her absence, by one of another caste.
A thread made of cotton, tripled and then tripled again [to form nine strands]...")
"Having washed them there, one should join the beads to the garland according to the prescribed method."
And furthermore: "In other [types of] threads, however, there is indeed no fixed rule regarding thickness and length. This refers to threads other than cotton.
Now follows the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of this garland.
The method for constructing the rosary is described in the *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"Having fashioned the rosary with beads shaped like the segments of a cow's tail,
one should attach a single bead called the *meru* to the thread at its root and tip."
"One should make a knot with its tip; thus is the rosary (akṣamālikā) described."
In the Vārāhasaṃhitā:
"Having gathered various dice as described, free from defects,
and having washed them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) by means of the knowledge of the five Vedāntas..."
The meaning is: with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*.
One should fasten [the image] onto a gold thread that has been doubled or tripled, or onto a silver, linen, or hemp thread, provided it is free from hair and other such impurities.
Or on cotton, as available, once it has been washed and thoroughly purified;
with the back against the back part and the mouth against the mouth itself.
"But the auspicious, similar jewels, strung together with a golden thread, should have intervals between them."
In the *Tantracintāmaṇi*: "The wise one should wash the rosary with water infused with *kuśa* grass and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*);
thereafter, he should place the rosary upon nine leaves of the *aśvattha* tree."
Having placed the *mātṛkās* there with the five [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta,
one should then consecrate the rosary with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and with water.
One should wash that garland again with the first mantra,
and rub it with fragrant sandalwood using the second mantra.
One should well-incense the garland with guggulu and agaru using the third [mantra],
and anoint it with musk, sandalwood, and so forth using the fourth.
One should consecrate all the gems with the fifth mantra;
then, one should indeed consecrate Mount Meru with the third mantra one hundred times.
"Thereupon, one should properly worship the rosary with those five mantras.
Also elsewhere:
"Taking each individual bead, one should fix it there upon the thread."
Having joined face to face, one should join back to back.
One should place the single-syllable mantra, according to the stated number, in front as the Meru;
then, one should fashion a knot-binding within each individual jewel.

Having placed the *mātṛkās* there with a concentrated mind, [he should purify them] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using the Gāyatrī, the root mantra, and likewise with the Sadyojāta and other mantras.
"Having washed [it] and consecrated it with those very same mantras, one should fumigate it thoroughly."
In another work, however, a further distinction is stated regarding the consecration of the rosary (*mālā-saṃskāra*):
"One should perform the stabilization of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) therein, having invoked one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
[The term] 'chosen deity' refers to that whose mantra is to be recited."
Having worshipped and consecrated [the rosary] with the root mantra, and likewise with the letters of the Mātṛkā and the root mantra—
meaning that one consecrates the rosary with the letters of the Mātṛkā and the root mantra—
one should then offer eight hundred oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
One should, however, pour the ghee from the *saṃpāta* back into the garland for every oblation.
"But in the event of an inability to perform the fire-oblation (homa), the practitioner should perform the consecration of the rosary with the root-mantra,
repeating it twice the number of oblations prescribed.
Thus it is stated in another Tantra.
"A wise person should always employ [the rosary] according to the rules during the time of recitation.
A rosary that has come under the gaze of another is fruitless for the rite of recitation.
During the time of recitation, one should not show the rosary even to one's guru."
"Holding [the beads] with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, one should perform the recitation."
In the *Uttaratantra*:
"At the beginning of recitation and other rites, one should carefully worship the rosary after sprinkling it with water;
having placed it within the mandala, either held in the left hand or otherwise."
The sprinkling of the rosary with the chosen mantra is thus proclaimed.
Oṃ, O Mālā, O Great Illusion, you whose nature is all powers!
The fourfold aims of life have been entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me.
Having performed worship, one should then take the garland in the right hand,
first uttering the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati, and immediately thereafter [the mantra].
The twice-born should pray to the garland, saying, "O Mālā, grant me freedom from obstacles," while holding the garland with his right hand near his own heart.
Meditating upon the Goddess, one should perform the recitation; one should not touch it with the left hand.
At the conclusion of the recitation, having paid homage to her, one should then place it upon the head.
O Mālā, you who grant joy and bestow auspiciousness upon all the gods, O blessed one,
always bring me welfare, glory, and valor.
The Puṣkara [syllable *ha*] situated upon the seed of Śikhin [*ra*], conjoined with the subtle-subtle [*u*],
and joined with Ākāśa [*ī*] and the Moon [*i*], becomes the Heart-mantra for the sake of accomplishment.
"This five-syllabled mantra is proclaimed for the rosary;
one should employ it in its taking up, its installation, and its worship."

*Puṣkara* is the letter *ha*; *Śikhī* is the letter *ra*; *Sūkṣmasūkṣmā* is the vowel *ī*. It is joined with the dot (*bindu*) and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) from *Ākāśa* and *Śaśin*. This is its own form for the sake of accomplishment. The heart-mantra is *namaḥ*. (At the end of the recitation, one should not keep that rosary [with oneself].
As it is said in that very same place: "One should not keep the prayer rosary on the hand, on the head, or on the neck.")
"Having performed the recitation at the time of recitation, one should always cast [the beads] in a pure place."
Furthermore, there is another distinction in another tantra: "The rosary that has been consecrated for the purpose of reciting a particular mantra—
one should perform the recitation of that very mantra with it, and not that of any other."
There is also another distinction in another tantra:
"Having strung together the Śakti-mantra with the Śiva-mantra, one should recite it;
having strung together the Śiva-mantra with the Śakti-mantra, O Śivā, one should recite it."
"If the beads are strung together with the *dhruva* or with the *mātṛkās*, then all the *mantras* should be consecrated with that rosary. Here, *dhruva* refers to the *praṇava*. [It is said:
"If the rosary should fall from the hand through negligence, or if it should become broken..."
"Or if she has been touched by one who is prohibited, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Now follows the third, the *karamālā* (finger-garland):
"O Goddess of the lords of the thirty-three, [the first bead] is on the middle joint of the middle finger."
Having made Meru, one should perform the recitation (japa) up to the base of the index finger.
"Starting from the middle joint of the ring finger, indeed in a clockwise sequence.
Regarding the hand rosary used for counts such as one hundred and eight or one thousand and eight, the *Bhairavītantra* states:
"Beginning from the middle of the ring finger, however, in the order ending with the little finger..."
"The rosary of the hand is proclaimed to extend from the middle finger to the root [the thumb]."

Gautama also said: "One should always perform the recitation (*japa*) with the little finger, the ring finger, the thumb, and the middle finger. When the counting is performed over the nine joints—starting from the base of the ring finger, the base of the middle finger, the base of the little finger, the middle of the middle finger, the tip of the middle finger, the tip of the ring finger, the middle of the ring finger, the base of the ring finger, and ending at the base of the middle finger—the mantra is recited nine times. In this manner, by repeating it twelve times, one hundred and eight recitations are completed. By repeating it one hundred and twelve times, one thousand and eight recitations are completed. In this way, the calculation for ten thousand (*ayuta*) and other higher numbers should be inferred accordingly. Now, the procedure for *japa*:
In the *Kapilapañcarātra*: "With a one-pointed mind, his self serene, holding a rosary, pure,
with neck slightly bent and held high, tranquil, and free from scratching or blinking."
"A wise person should recite the mantra in sequence— clearly, with the visarga, with the mātrās, with the bindu, and with the syllables— not too fast and not with excessive pauses."
Vyāsa says:
"Neither walking, nor laughing, nor looking to the side;
neither leaning against anything, nor talking, nor likewise with the head covered."
"One should not recite while stepping with one foot upon the other, nor likewise with the hands;
nor with an unconcentrated mind, nor while making others hear."
Baudhāyana also says: "One engaged in ritual action should indeed avoid touching anything below the navel.
Vyāsa also says: "One should not speak at the time of recitation, nor during vows, fire-offerings, and the like."
But if that best of the twice-born remains attached to these very things while traveling, [he will fall].
"Then, having saluted the Brahmin, one should inquire after his yoga and kṣema.
Gautama also says:
"Anger, delusion, sneezing, sleep, spitting, and yawning..."
"And one should avoid the sight of dogs and low-caste persons during the practice of recitation."
In the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"The sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is threefold; learn its divisions.
It is traditionally held to be threefold: vocal, whispered (*upāṃśu*), and mental."
"Among the three types of recitation-sacrifices (*japayajña*), each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
The characteristics of the vocal (*vācika*) and whispered (*upāṃśu*) forms are stated in the Purāṇa:
"That which is performed with words in high, low, and circumflex tones, with distinct syllables and clear words..."
One should recite the mantra with the voice; this is known as vocal japa.
"One should recite the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly;
when it is not heard by others even a little, that is remembered as *upāṃśu-japa*."
Viśvāmitra has stated the definition of mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*):
"The repeated contemplation of the meaning of words, proceeding from letter to letter and from word to word by means of the intellect through a series of syllables, is called mental recitation."
And the gradation among these three was stated by him [the author] himself:
"The mental recitation is said to be the best, the whispered is remembered as middling,
and the vocal is declared to be the lowest among all mantras, O twice-born ones."
"One [recitation] is said to be for the verbal, a hundred for the whispered,
and a thousand for the mental— thus it was declared by Manu, Atri, Bhṛgu, and Nārada."
Agastya (Kumbhasambhava) states the characteristic of *japa*:
"The constant repetition of the mantra received from the guru,
preceded by the internal placement (*nyāsa*) of its constituent syllables, is known as *japa*."
"O friend" (*aṅga*) is an extremely sharp form of address. The connection is that *japa* (recitation) is the internal revolving of the syllables.
As stated in the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā*: "In this manner, according to the prescribed rule, [it should be done] without being slow or hurried."
One should perform the recitation for the stated number of times for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*.
Contemplating with his intellect the unity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra,
he should recite it with one-pointed mind from the morning until midday.
"That which was commenced according to a specific number must be performed day after day;
if one performs it less or more than that, the person becomes fallen from his vow."
And this recitation (japa) should be performed only during the day.

For the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra* states, "One should perform the recitation during the day; such is the rule for the purificatory rite (puraścaraṇa)," by mentioning the word "day. Furthermore, the son of the jar (Agastya) prohibits recitation at night, saying, "One should avoid recitation at night."

This rule does not apply when there is the possibility of disturbances caused by place, time, and so forth; for another tantra states: "One should perform the recitation practice every day with the same number [of repetitions] with which it was commenced; indeed, there is no fixed rule in the event of an affliction."
In that case as well, the recitation (japta) should be performed only up to the fourth part, and not during the fifth part:
"That time is called Rākṣasī; it is censured for all ritual acts."
Thus it is because [this practice] is censured in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
Vaiśampāyana says:
"The rule of continuity has been declared; one should not skip a day."
Indeed, if a day passes by, a man shall not achieve success in mantra.
"One should recite on the following day exactly as many times as one recited on the previous day; otherwise, it will cause an obstruction to success."
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
"When the one most skilled in mantras perceives something impure at the time of recitation,
he should then perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and complete the remainder of the recitation."
"And when the practitioner should likewise become impure himself,
he should bathe, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) as before, recite the mantra once again."

The *nyāsa* (ritual placement) is that which establishes one's qualification [for the rite]. By this it is understood that, if impurity should arise during urination or similar acts, one should bathe; otherwise, having performed *prāṇāyāma*, the six-limbed *nyāsa*, and so forth, one should complete the remainder of the rite.
As stated in the *Kapila-pañcarātra*:
"If there is an interruption in the recitation (*japa*), fire-offering (*homa*), or worship (*arcana*) due to distraction or laziness..."
"When he rises, he should then again perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa)."
Gautama says: "For meditation, worship, and recitation, three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) each are prescribed at the beginning and the end, moving through the nostrils."
Yogayājñavalkya states: "If, at any time during the recitation of mantras and other such practices, there should be a lapse in the restraint of speech,
one should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu."
The Vaiṣṇava mantra is "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ". Saṃvarta also says:
"Having heard worldly gossip and having heard the speech of men..."
"And that which is recited without counting shall all be fruitless."
(Gautama also says:
"Whether walking or standing, or performing actions according to one's own will,
or being impure— even without a specific count— all that shall become fruitless.")

Nārada said: "Upon completing the count, one should, with a concentrated mind, offer oblations into the fire-pit as prescribed, according to the rules, using one's own substances in the tenth part of the number of recitations."

Alternatively, having recited [the mantra] every day, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with a tenth part [of that number]. (In another Tantra it is also stated: "At the end of each hundred thousand [recitations], there should be a fire-oblation and so forth. In the event of an inability to perform the fire-oblation, the primary rule is that for Brahmins, the recitation for the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) should be double the number prescribed for the recitation itself. The secondary rule is that the recitation should be double the number of the fire-oblations. For Kṣatriyas and others, the recitation should be triple and so forth. The same applies to the libation (*tarpaṇa*). For a Śūdra who is devoted to the twice-born, and for the wives of the twice-born, there is only recitation as a substitute for the fire-oblation; they have no entitlement to perform the fire-oblation itself.

However, it should be observed in the *Kalpasūtra* that there is no substitute whatsoever for the feeding of Brahmins. After the fire-oblation (*homa*), the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites must be performed.
As it is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"Having thus completed the fire-oblation, one should then offer libations to the deity in water."
Having invoked [the deity], one should perform the libation and the consecration with a tenth part of that [number].

The meaning is that one should offer libations with the words "I satisfy, obeisance" (*tarpayāmi namaḥ*), preceded by the name of the desired deity in the accusative case; that is, having taken the name of the deity intended for the current rite in the accusative, one should satisfy them with "I satisfy, obeisance.
However, at the end of the root mantra, the word "I sprinkle" (*siñcāmi*) should be added during the ritual sprinkling.
Then, one should satisfy the best of the twice-born with various kinds of food.
Having gratified those of pleasing appearance, one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
through the propitiation of Brahmins, the deficiencies of men reach completion.
"The deities become propitious and one's heart's desires are fulfilled.
