(All mantras must be recited only after learning them from the mouth of a guru, and not otherwise.
"He who recites mantras written in a book... )
"While still alive he is a *cāṇḍāla*, and when dead he will indeed become a dog"—
for thus is the recitation (*japa*) prohibited in the *Sāṃkhyāyana-tantra* unless it is received from the mouth of a Guru.
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*).

The performer, together with his wife, having bathed well and performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), should first perform a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) for the sake of purifying the body according to the gravity or lightness of the sin. Then, having performed the propitiation of Vināyaka (*vināyakaśānti*) for the attainment of freedom from obstacles, the sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajña*) for the favor of the planets, and the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra thirty thousand times (*ayutatraya*) for the perfection of the mantras; and having invited on an auspicious day pure Brahmins who are conversant with the mantras, being authorized by them, he should proclaim the place and the time.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in one of the following ways—"For the sake of attaining perfection in the mantra through devotion to Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of progeny, I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa*," or "By means of the attainment of the mantra of the deity Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of progeny, for the sake of pleasing the deity Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of progeny, I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa*"—one should perform, according to the prescribed method, the worship of Gaṇapati, the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*), and the *nāndīśrāddha*, all for the sake of ensuring freedom from obstacles.

Then, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), and having made that ground pure according to the procedure beginning with "having made that earth free from obstacles," one should spread, in order from bottom to top, *kuśa* grass, an antelope skin (*ajina*), and a cloth for the sake of a seat upon the prepared spot. Having sprinkled them with water using the *Gāyatrī* and the root mantra, [one recites]: "The seer of the mantra 'O Earth' (*pṛthvi*) is Merupṛṣṭha; the deity is Kūrmapṛṣṭha; the meter is Sutala; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the act of sitting upon the seat. "Oṃ, O Earth, by you the worlds are supported... [and so on], ending with "the seat. Homage to Anantāsana (the Infinite Seat).

Salutation to Vimalāsana; salutation to Padmāsana; salutation to Kūrmāsana; salutation to Yogāsana; salutation to Ādhāraśaktikamalāsana; in the center, salutation to Paramasukhāsana. Having thus sat upon the seat facing east, one should assume either the Svastika or Padma posture. Regarding their characteristics, the *Gautamītantra* states:
"Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs..."
The yogi should dwell with the body straight; that is declared to be the svastika posture.
"Having placed both soles of the feet upon the thighs,
this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is dear to the hearts of yogins."
Then:
"O you with upward-pointing hair, O three-eyed one, O eater of flesh and blood!
Stay, O Goddess, in the binding of the topknot, O Cāmuṇḍā, O unconquered one!"

Having thus prayed to Cāmuṇḍā, one should offer salutations as follows: on one’s own head—*guṃ* to the Gurus, *namaḥ*; on the right shoulder—*gaṃ* to Gaṇapati, *namaḥ*; on the left (shoulder)—*duṃ* to Durgā, *namaḥ*; on the right knee—*kṣaṃ* to Kṣetrapāla, *namaḥ*; on the left knee—*saṃ* to Sarasvatī, *namaḥ*. Having thus paid homage, [one should recite]: *am*, *ātmane namaḥ*; *saṃ*, *sattvātmane namaḥ*; *raṃ*, *rajaātmane namaḥ*; *taṃ*, *tamaātmane namaḥ*. "Salutation be to Ananta; salutation be to the Creator; salutation to Vasiṣṭha; salutation be to Śakti."

Salutations to Parāśara, the eternal; salutations to you, the son of Satyavatī. Salutations to the gurus and to the sandals of the gurus; salutations to those who are beyond and to the sandals of those who are beyond. Salutations to the sandals of the Siddheśvara-ācārya; salutations to the sandals of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
"Salutation to the great ones, salutation to the small ones, salutation to the young, and salutation to the aged!
Let us worship the gods if we are able; O gods, may I not incur the censure of my elders. Thus one should pay homage.
"May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth."
May those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.

Having dispelled the terrestrial obstacles by striking the ground with the heels of the left foot three times while reciting, "May the spirits and *piśācas* depart in all directions; without causing offense to anyone, I shall commence the Brahma-rite," having dispelled the atmospheric obstacles by clapping the hands three times, and the celestial obstacles by gazing with a divine vision, one should perform the binding of the quarters (*digbandha*) with the mantra, "For the warding off of all beings, to the one with the arrow, to the one with the *śārṅga* bow, to the Sudarśana, the king of weapons, *huṃ phaṭ*," and having visualized a rampart of fire all around, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

It is as follows: having meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī—situated at the Mūlādhāra, resembling a lotus fiber, possessing the luster of lightning, shaped like a sleeping serpent, encircling the self-manifested Liṅga (Svayaṃbhū-liṅga) with three and a half coils—one should, by means of the Praṇava, raise her from the Mūlādhāra like a female serpent. Then, having caused the heart-lotus to open upward by the Praṇava, one should lead the individual soul (jīvātman) residing there through the sequence of piercing the six cakras to the Brahma-randhra. Having united it with the Supreme Self in the form of the Bindu located within the thousand-petaled lotus, one should bring about the state of oneness with the Supreme Self by means of the mantra "Haṃsaḥ So’ham" (I am He).

One should meditate on the earth-mandala, extending from the feet to the knees, as square, golden-colored, marked with thunderbolts, associated with the *nivṛtti-kalā*, having Brahmā as its deity, and joined with the seed-syllable *laṃ*.

For this mantra beginning with *syonā*, the deities are the ritualists (*yājñikya*), the secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*), the earth (*bhūmi*), and the meter is *gāyatrī*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the salutation to the earth. *Oṃ syonā pṛthivi bhavā nṛkṣarā niveśanī | yacchā naḥ śarma saprathāḥ.* One should offer salutation with: *laṃ bhūmyai namaḥ*. However, for the followers of the Ṛgveda, [the seer] is Medhātithi, the deity is the Earth, and the meter is *gāyatrī*. Its application is in the salutation to the Earth. *Oṃ syonā pṛthivi bhavā nṛkṣarā niveśanī | yacchā naḥ śarma saprathaḥ.* *Laṃ bhūmyai namaḥ.*

One should meditate upon the water-maṇḍala, extending from the knees to the navel, shaped like a half-moon, white in color, marked with two lotuses, belonging to the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā, having Viṣṇu as its presiding deity, and joined with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*. For the mantra "apsu me," the seers are the Viśvedevas, the deity is Water, the meter is Anuṣṭubh; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the salutation to Water: "Oṃ apsu me somo... bheṣajī. *Vaṃ*, obeisance to Water. However, for the followers of the Ṛgveda: Medhātithi is the seer, Water is the deity, the meter is Anuṣṭubh;
its application is in the salutation to Water: "Oṃ apsu me somo... bheṣajīḥ. *Vaṃ*, obeisance to Water.

One should meditate upon a triangular circle of light, red in color and marked with the *svastika*, extending from the navel to the heart; it belongs to the *vidyā-kalā*, has Śiva as its presiding deity, and is joined with the seed-syllable *raṃ*. For the verse beginning with "Agniṃ dūtam," Prajāpati is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is in the salutation to light. "Oṃ agniṃ dūtaṃ vṛṇīmahe... yajñasya sukratum. *Raṃ*—salutation to light. However, for the followers of the Ṛgveda: "Agniṃ dūtam"; Kaṇva Medhātithi is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is in the salutation to light.

"Oṃ agniṃ dūtaṃ vṛṇīmahe... sukratum. "Raṃ, obeisance to Tejas. One should meditate upon the circular wind-maṇḍala, smoke-colored, marked with six dots, having the syllable *śaṃ* as its digit (*kalā*), Īśāna as its presiding deity, and joined with the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, extending from the heart to the middle of the eyebrows. For the mantra "Oṃ vāyo śata..."—the Viśvedevas are the seers, Vāyu is the deity, Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application is in the salutation to Vāyu. "Oṃ vāyo śata... pājasā. "Yaṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. However, for the followers of the Ṛgveda: "Tava vāyo vyaśva..."—Āṅgirasa Vyaśva is the seer, Vāyu is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is in the salutation to Vāyu.

"Oṃ tava vāyavṛ0 vṛṇīmahe. [With the mantra] "Yaṃ vāyave namaḥ," one should meditate upon the sphere of space (*ākāśamaṇḍala*), which extends from the center of the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), is circular, white in color, marked by the moon, belonging to the *śāntyatīta-kalā*, having Sadāśiva as its presiding deity, and joined with the seed-syllable *haṃ*. For the mantra "Ghṛtaṃ ghṛtapāvānaḥ," Soma is the seer, Ākāśa is the deity, and Yajus is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the salutation to Ākāśa. "Oṃ ghṛtaṃ ghṛtapāvā0 tvā'ntarikṣāya. [With the mantra] "Haṃ, ākāśāya namaḥ. For the followers of the Ṛgveda, however, the primordial calf is Ākāśa, and Gāyatrī is the meter.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the salutation to space: "Oṃ, from the ancient... [thee] by day. *Haṃ*, salutation to space (*ākāśa*). I perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands, feet, anus, genitals, and speech upon the earth and the other elements in sequence; likewise, of movement, grasping, excretion, pleasure, and speech in sequence; likewise, of the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears in sequence; likewise, of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound in sequence; and likewise, of the *samāna*, *udāna*, *vyāna*, *apāna*, and *prāṇa* breaths in sequence. Having thus performed the placement, I dissolve the five-fold earth (*pṛthivī*) into water by means of the practice of six *udghātas*, reciting *laṃ* six times.

I dissolve water, which possesses four qualities, into fire by means of five upward breath-exhalations (*udghāta*), with the syllable *vaṃ* (five times). I dissolve fire, which possesses three qualities, into air by means of four upward breath-exhalations, with the syllable *raṃ* (four times). I dissolve air, which possesses two qualities, into space by means of three upward breath-exhalations, with the syllable *yaṃ* (three times). I dissolve space, which possesses one quality, into the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*) by means of two upward breath-exhalations, with the syllable *haṃ* (twice). I dissolve that ego-principle into the Great Principle (*mahattattva*). I dissolve that Great Principle into primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
"I dissolve that primordial nature (prakṛti) into the Supreme Brahman. Thus one should dissolve it.
Then:
"Brahmin-slaughter as its head, and theft of gold as its two arms..."
The two thighs are joined with the drinking of liquor, and the two hips with violating the teacher’s bed.
The pair of words associated with that [name] were his major and minor limbs;
his body hairs were secondary sins, and his beard and eyes were red.
"One should visualize [him] with his face turned downward, black in color, the size of a thumb, holding a sword and a shield, and wrathful, in the left side of the belly."

Then, having dried the personified sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) by repeating the wind-seed syllable *yam* sixteen times, and having incinerated it by repeating the fire-seed syllable *ram* sixty-four times, one should expel those ashes through the right nostril by repeating the wind-seed syllable *yam* thirty-two times. Then, having drenched those ashes with nectar by repeating the nectar-seed syllable *vam* sixteen times, and having visualized the body becoming solid by repeating the earth-seed syllable *lam* sixteen times, [one should do so] with the space-seed syllable *ham*.

Having contemplated one's fitness for propitiating the deity by repeating [the mantra] sixteen times, one should contemplate the sequence of creation as follows: from Brahman comes Prakṛti; from Prakṛti, Mahat; from Mahat-tattva, Ahaṃkāra; from Ahaṃkāra, Ākāśa; from Ākāśa, Vāyu; from Vāyu, Agni; from Agni, Āpaḥ; from Āpaḥ, Pṛthivī; from Pṛthivī, Oṣadhayaḥ; from Oṣadhayaḥ, Anna; from Anna, Retas; and from Retas, Puruṣa. Then, contemplating that "this very Puruṣa consists of the essence of food" (*anna-rasa-maya*), one should, with the *praṇava*, visualize the heart-lotus facing upwards and recite: "Haṃsaḥ So 'ham" (I am He).

Having visualized the individual soul (jīvātman) as having arrived at the heart-lotus by means of the mantra, one should visualize the Kuṇḍalinī as having returned to its own place. Now follows the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā (the ritual installation of the vital breaths).

Of this Śrī Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the seers (ṛṣis); the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are the meters (chandas); the deity is the vital power (prāṇa-śakti) whose form is consciousness; *āṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja); *hrīṃ* is the power (śakti); *kroṃ* is the pin (kīlaka); and its application (viniyoga) is for the installation of the vital breaths. *Oṃ*, salutation to the seers Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—on the head. *Oṃ*, salutation to the meters Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma—on the face. *Oṃ*, salutation to the deity, the vital power whose form is consciousness—on the heart. *Oṃ*, salutation to the seed-syllable *āṃ*—on the private parts.

*Hrīṃ*, salutation to Śakti at the feet; *Kroṃ*, salutation to Kīlaka at the navel; *Namaḥ*, salutation to the application (*viniyoga*) for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana*) on all limbs. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ*. To the self consisting of ether, air, fire, water, and earth: *Āṃ*, salutation to the heart. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ*. To the self consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell: *Īṃ*, *svāhā* to the head.

Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ, to the self consisting of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose; ūṃ, to the crest-lock (śikhā), vaṣaṭ! Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ, to the self consisting of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; aiṃ, to the armor (kavaca), huṃ! Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ, to the self consisting of speaking, grasping, excretion, locomotion, and sexual pleasure; auṃ, to the three eyes (netratraya), vauṣaṭ!

Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ, to the Self consisting of mind, intellect, ego, consciousness, and bliss; aḥ astrāya phaṭ. Having thus performed the placement upon the six limbs with their respective mudrās, [one places] "āṃ namaḥ" from the navel down to the tips of both feet; "hrīṃ namaḥ" from the throat up to the navel; and "kroṃ namaḥ" from the crown of the head down to the throat.

Then, [placing them] in the heart itself: Yaṃ, obeisance to the self of the skin; Raṃ, obeisance to the self of the blood; Māṃ, obeisance to the self of the flesh; Vaṃ, obeisance to the self of the fat; Śaṃ, obeisance to the self of the bone; Paṃ, obeisance to the self of the marrow; Saṃ, obeisance to the self of the semen; Haṃ, obeisance to the self of the vital essence (*ojas*); Laṃ, obeisance to the individual self (*jīvātman*); Kṣaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self (*paramātman*).

Then, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: *yaṃ* namaḥ in the heart-lotus; *raṃ* namaḥ in the southeast; *laṃ* namaḥ in the east; *vaṃ* namaḥ in the west; *śaṃ* namaḥ in the northeast; *ṣaṃ* namaḥ in the southwest; *saṃ* namaḥ in the north; *haṃ* namaḥ in the south; and *kṣaṃ* namaḥ in the pericarp.

Thereafter, having performed the all-pervading placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) from the head down to the feet using the entire Mātṛkā alphabet, [one should meditate on the Goddess] seated upon a lotus as red as the sun rising over the ocean of blood, holding a noose, a goad, a bow of sugarcane, and arrows.
One should meditate thus: "I bow to the Goddess, who is red in color, three-eyed, and holding a trident and a skull at the tips of her hands.

As for the arrangement of the weapons: the first two are held in the upper left and right hands; the next two are held in the hands below those; and the final two are held in the hands below those. *Śarāsa* means a bow.

Then, placing the palm of the right hand upon the heart, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) as follows: reciting "Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ saḥ, hrīṃ oṃ haṃsaḥ, my vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are here; my vital breaths are here," and having again recited from "Oṃ" up to the end of the *ajapā*, saying: "my life-force (*jīva*) is situated here"; and having again recited in the same manner: "all my senses (*sarvendriyāṇi*"); and having again recited in the same manner: "my speech, mind, eyes, ears, skin, nose, and vital breaths—having come here, may they remain happily for a long time, svāhā! Thus one should perform the consecration of the vital breaths.

The mantra for the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana*) is either: "All my senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, touch, smell, and life-breath—are but one," or "Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Vaṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ Hoṃ Haṃsaḥ So’ham.
One should then recite: "Oṃ Asunīte, bring back [the life] to us; have mercy on us, grant us well-being."

In the *Jñānārṇava*, however, it is stated that the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) is accomplished by merely saying "Āṃ So'ham. One should recite the *praṇava* (Om) fifteen times for the sake of accomplishing the fifteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*). This concludes the consecration of the vital breath.
Now follows the internal deposition of the *mātṛkās* (*antarmātṛkānyāsa*).

Therein, having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the *mātṛkā* [syllables], one should perform the *mātṛkā*-installation (*nyāsa*). Regarding that, the sequence of breath-control is as follows: inhalation (*pūraka*) with the vowels, retention (*kumbhaka*) with the letters beginning with *ka*, and exhalation (*recaka*) with the letters beginning with *ya*. Having thus performed the three breath-controls, [one should assign]: "Obeisance to the Seer Brahmā" on the head; "Obeisance to the Gāyatrī metre" on the mouth; "Obeisance to the Deity Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī" on the heart; and "Obeisance to the seed-syllables which are the consonants" on the private parts.

Salutation to the Vowels and the Śaktis at the feet; salutation to Vyakti and Kīlaka at the navel; salutation to the application (viniyoga) of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa on all limbs. Oṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, salutation to both thumbs. Oṃ iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, salutation to both index fingers. Oṃ uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ, vaṣaṭ to both middle fingers. Oṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ, huṃ to both ring fingers.

Oṃ oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ, to the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ. Oṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ, to the palms and backs of the hands, phaṭ. Oṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, to the heart, namaḥ. Oṃ iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, to the head, svāhā. Oṃ uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ, to the crest-lock (śikhā), vaṣaṭ. Oṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ, to the armor (kavaca), huṃ.

Oṃ oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. Oṃ aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ phaṭ to the weapon. [Perform] the pervasive [protection] three times with all the *mātṛkās*.
Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):

"Her face, arms, feet, heart, belly, and chest are fashioned from the distinctions of the fifty letters; she possesses a radiant matted hair adorned with a digit of the moon, and is as white as the moon or jasmine."

"I bow to that Bhāratī, who holds a rosary, a water-pot, and a book written with excellent characters in her hands; who has three eyes; who is seated upon a lotus; who is pure and radiant; and who bears the weight of full breasts and hips."

The placement of the weapons begins from the upper right hand and extends to the lower right hand. [The goddess holds] a book written with the *cintāmaṇi* jewel. Having meditated thus, one should perform the internal placement (*nyāsa*) of the vowels (*mātṛkā*). Therein, first, at the sixteen-petaled *viśuddhi*-cakra located in the throat, one should place [the mantras] starting from the east and proceeding clockwise: *Oṃ aṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ āṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ aḥ namaḥ*. Then, at the twelve-petaled *anāhata*-cakra located in the heart, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise: *Oṃ kaṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ khaṃ namaḥ*.

Oṃ gaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ghaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṅaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ caṃ namaḥ | Oṃ chaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ jaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ jhaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ñaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṭaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṭhaṃ namaḥ | Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), [one places them] in the ten-petalled *maṇipūra-cakra* located in the navel region, proceeding clockwise starting from the east: Oṃ ḍaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ḍhaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṇaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ taṃ namaḥ | Oṃ thaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ daṃ namaḥ | Oṃ dhaṃ namaḥ.

Oṃ naṃ namaḥ | Oṃ paṃ namaḥ | Oṃ phaṃ namaḥ | Having thus performed the placement (vinyāsa) in the six-petalled Svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra located at the base of the *liṅga*, proceeding clockwise starting from the east: Oṃ baṃ namaḥ | Oṃ bhaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ maṃ namaḥ | Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ raṃ namaḥ | Oṃ laṃ namaḥ | Having thus performed the placement in the four-petalled Mūlādhāra-cakra located at the Mūlādhāra, proceeding clockwise starting from the east: Oṃ vaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ śaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṣaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ saṃ namaḥ |

Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) at the *ājñā-cakra* located between the eyebrows, which has two petals, in the sequence from right to left: *oṃ haṃ namaḥ*; *oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ*. Having thus performed the placement, one should perform the external *mātṛkā-nyāsa*:
"Her face, arms, shoulders, waist, and chest are divided by the fifty letters; she wears a radiant crown bound with the crescent moon, and her full, lofty breasts..."
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who possesses three eyes and radiant white luster, holding in her lotus-like hands a mudrā, a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and a sacred lore.

Having meditated thus: *Oṃ namaḥ* on the head (the syllable *tāra* is at the beginning of each). *Āṃ namaḥ* on the face; *Iṃ namaḥ* on the right eye; *Īṃ namaḥ* on the left eye; *Uṃ namaḥ* on the right ear; *Ūṃ namaḥ* on the left ear; *Ṛṃ namaḥ* on the right nostril; *Ṝṃ namaḥ* on the left nostril; *Ḷṃ namaḥ* on the right cheek; *Ḹṃ namaḥ* on the left cheek; *Eṃ namaḥ* on the upper lip; *Aiṃ namaḥ* on the lower lip.

Oṃ namaḥ, to the upper row of teeth. Auṃ namaḥ, to the lower row of teeth. Aṃ namaḥ, to the head. Aḥ namaḥ, to the neck. Kaṃ namaḥ, to the root of the right arm. Khaṃ namaḥ, to the right elbow. Gaṃ namaḥ, to the right wrist. Ghaṃ namaḥ, to the roots of the fingers of the right hand. Ṅaṃ namaḥ, to the tips of the fingers of the right hand. Caṃ namaḥ, to the root of the left arm. Chaṃ namaḥ, to the left elbow. Jaṃ namaḥ, to the left wrist.

*Jhaṃ namaḥ*, at the bases of the fingers of the left hand; *ñaṃ namaḥ*, at the tips of the fingers of the left hand; *ṭaṃ namaḥ*, at the base of the right foot; *ṭhaṃ namaḥ*, at the right knee; *ḍaṃ namaḥ*, at the right ankle; *ḍhaṃ namaḥ*, at the bases of the toes of the right foot; *ṇaṃ namaḥ*, at the tips of the toes of the right foot; *taṃ namaḥ*, at the base of the left foot; *thaṃ namaḥ*, at the left knee; *daṃ namaḥ*, at the left ankle; *dhaṃ namaḥ*, at the bases of the toes of the left foot.

*Naṃ namaḥ*, on the tips of the toes of the left foot; *paṃ namaḥ*, on the right side; *phaṃ namaḥ*, on the left side; *baṃ namaḥ*, on the back; *bhaṃ namaḥ*, at the navel; *maṃ namaḥ*, at the abdomen; *yaṃ namaḥ*, at the heart; *raṃ namaḥ*, on the right shoulder; *laṃ namaḥ*, at the crown of the head; *vaṃ namaḥ*, on the left shoulder; *śaṃ namaḥ*, from the heart to the tip of the right hand; *ṣaṃ namaḥ*, from the heart to the tip of the left hand; *saṃ namaḥ*, from the heart to the tip of the right foot.

*Haṃ namaḥ*, from the heart to the tips of the left feet; *laṃ namaḥ*, from the heart to the private parts; *kṣaṃ namaḥ*, from the heart to the top of the head. This is the placement (*nyāsa*) performed with the thumb and ring finger. *Ācakrāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*. *Vicakrāya śirase svāhā*. *Sucakrāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*. *Trailokyarakṣaṇacakrāya kavacāya huṃ*. *Āsurāntakacakrāyāstrāya phaṭ*. In the case of the six limbs (*aṅga-ṣaṭka*), [the sequence is]: *Āsurāntakacakrāya netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*; *Sudarśanacakrāyāstrāya phaṭ*. Such is the application. Now follows the placement of the root mantra (*mūlamantra-nyāsa*).
"Oṃ klīṃ! O son of Devakī, Govinda, Vāsudeva, Lord of the Universe!
Grant me a son, O Kṛṣṇa; I have come to you for refuge."

Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with this root mantra, [one should know]: for this Śrī Sutapradagopālakṛṣṇa mantra, Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi); Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); the deity (devatā) is Gopālakṛṣṇa, the bestower of sons; its application (viniyoga) is in worship, recitation, and other rites. Oṃ klīṃ, O Devakī’s son Govinda, salutation to the two thumbs. Oṃ Vāsudeva, Lord of the world, salutation to the two index fingers. Oṃ, grant me a son, Kṛṣṇa, salutation to the two middle fingers. Oṃ, I have come to you for refuge, salutation to the two ring fingers.

Oṃ klīṃ, O son of Devakī, Govinda, Vāsudeva, Lord of the Universe! Grant me a son, O Kṛṣṇa; I have come to you for refuge. [Salutation] to the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhikā). Oṃ klīṃ, O son of Devakī, Govinda, salutation to the heart (hṛdayāya namaḥ). Oṃ, Vāsudeva, Lord of the Universe, svāhā to the head (śirase svāhā). Oṃ, grant me a son, Kṛṣṇa, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhāyai vaṣaṭ). Oṃ, I have come to you for refuge, huṃ to the armor (kavacāya huṃ). Oṃ klīṃ, O son of Devakī, Govinda, Vāsudeva, Lord of the Universe!
Grant me a son, Kṛṣṇa; I have come to you for refuge. [Salutation] to the weapon (astrāya phaṭ).

For this mantra of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of sons: *Namaḥ* to Nārada, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; *namaḥ* to the *anuṣṭubh* meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; *namaḥ* to Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the deity who bestows sons (*devatā*), on the heart; *namaḥ* to the application (*viniyoga*) for worship, recitation, and so forth, on all limbs. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the respective mudrās and having performed the three-fold pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, one should meditate [on Him] thus:
"Accompanied by Vijaya, seated upon His chariot, having brought [the children] from the midst of the ocean, He gave them to the twice-born; may that son of Vasudeva be remembered!"

In another tantra, however, meditation is described in a different manner: "I bow to Mukunda, who rests upon the lap of Yaśodā, drinking from his mother’s lotus-face while gazing with a gentle smile at his radiant body, and touching her other breast with his fingers."

One should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, who is dark-complexioned, four-armed, and clad in yellow garments; he is the infallible one who holds the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
"I meditate upon Him who, having recovered lost children, restores them to a Brahmin,
whose head is adorned with peacock feathers, and who resembles a flash of lightning"— thus it is said elsewhere as well.

Having meditated upon any one of these according to one's desire and having worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the worship of the water-pot (*kalaśa*). Having placed the water-pot filled with pure water on one's left side, one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrthas*) into that jar using the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* while reciting the mantra beginning with "Viṣṇur mūrdhni... (Viṣṇu is at the head). Having worshipped the water-pot with scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣatas*), one should place a washed conch shell to its right in a supporting vessel. Having filled the conch with the water from the pot and displayed the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, one should recite:
"Oṃ, we know Pāñcajanya; we meditate upon the Purifier."

Having worshipped that [conch] with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains using the Śaṅkha-gāyatrī mantra, "tannaḥ śaṅkhaḥ pracodayāt," he should pour a little of that water into the pitcher. Then, taking a little water from the conch into another vessel, he should sprinkle the articles of worship, the ground, and himself with that water. Having worshipped the bell with the mantra "jagaddhvani mantramātaḥ svāhā," [he should ring it] for the arrival of the gods and the departure of the Rākṣasas.
"O Ghaṇṭā, produce the auspicious sound that is the mark for summoning the deities"—thus one should play [the bell].

Then, having established the water-pot (kalaśa) according to the ritual procedure beginning with "The earth, the sky," and having performed the rites from filling it with pure water up to the placement of the full-vessel (pūrṇapātra), one should invoke Varuṇa therein and worship him.

Then, having spread a yellow cloth over that [seat], one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp using either the "eight-fragrance" (aṣṭagandha) consisting of uśīra, bālaka, candana, keśara, kuṣṭha, aguru, mustā, and jaṭāmāṃsī, or the "eight-fragrance" consisting of kastūrī, candana, keśara, aguru, māṃsī, muktā, karpūra, and kuṣṭha; and therein one should invoke the deities. The method of invocation is as follows: below the lotus (in the directions starting from the east): *namaḥ* to the Power in the form of the Support (*ādhārarūpiṇī śakti*); *namaḥ* to Kūrma; *namaḥ* to Śeṣa.

Salutation to Varāha. Salutation to Maṇḍūka. Salutation to Kālāgnirudra. Salutation to Dharaṇī. Salutation to Vṛndāvana. Thus at the bottom of the lotus. Now, on the couch—in the four directions beginning with the southeast: salutation to Dharma; salutation to Jñāna; salutation to Vairāgya; salutation to Aiśvarya. Then, in the four directions beginning with the east: salutation to Adharma; salutation to Ajñāna; salutation to Avairāgya; salutation to Anaiśvarya.
Above that are the deities of the lotus: *namaḥ* to the bulb (*kanda*), *namaḥ* to the stalk (*nāla*), *namaḥ* to the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and *namaḥ* to the petals (*patra*).

Then, within the pericarp: *namaḥ* to the Sun, *namaḥ* to the Moon, and between the two, *namaḥ* to Fire. Upon the petals, in order starting from the east: *namaḥ* to Vimalā, *namaḥ* to Utkarṣiṇī, *namaḥ* to Jñānā, *namaḥ* to Kriyā, *namaḥ* to Yogā, *namaḥ* to Prahvī, *namaḥ* to Satyā, and *namaḥ* to Īśānā.

In front of the deity—[reciting] "Salutation to Anugrahā"—one should invoke the deities of the pedestal (*pīṭhadevatā*) and then invoke Śrī Gopālakṛṣṇa in the center of the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*). This is as follows: having fashioned an image of Gopālakṛṣṇa made of gold or other metals according to one's capacity and endowed with the characteristics described in the meditation (*dhyāna*), one should perform the *agnyuttāraṇa* (the rite of removing the [consecrated] fire) from the image according to the specific tradition by means of continuous streams of milk and water. Then, having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the ritual installation of the vital breaths) according to the previously mentioned method, one should stand at the right side of the image [facing] the deity.

Having arranged various offerings and oblations (upahāra-bali) in front, and having poured cow's ghee into a vessel made of metal, one should open the eyes of the deity with two golden needles while reciting either "taccakṣur deva hitam" or "citram devānām. Then, reciting "oṃ añjanti tvāmadhvare... upasthe," one should simultaneously anoint both eyes with honey using the two middle fingers. After bathing the image with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and pure water, [one should place] the image facing oneself within the fire-mandala.

Having fixed the heart-lotus with its face downward, one should contemplate it as turned upward by the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*) and blossomed by the sun of knowledge (*jñānārka*). Then, reciting "Haṃsaḥ so 'ham," one should visualize Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who resides in the heart-lotus as the Self, entering through the path of the nostrils and arriving at the flower held in one's own joined palms. Having uttered the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should cast that flower into the image. [Then follow: the rites of invocation (*āvāhanī*), installation (*sthāpanī*), bringing near (*saṃnidhāpanī*), confinement (*saṃnirodhinī*), facing toward [the deity] (*saṃmukhīkaraṇī*), unification (*saṃkalīkaraṇī*), and veiling (*avaguṇṭhanī*).
One should display the nine mudrās known as *paramīkaraṇī* and *amṛtīkaraṇī*. Then, having established [the deity] with the mantra "narya prajām," one should offer salutation.

Next, the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*)—in the corners starting from the southeast (Āgneya) and proceeding clockwise: "Salutation to Ācakra; I invoke Ācakra. Salutation to Vicakra; I invoke Vicakra. Salutation to Sucakra; I invoke Sucakra. Salutation to Trailokyarakṣaṇacakra; I invoke Trailokyarakṣaṇacakra."

Then, in the four directions starting from the east, proceeding clockwise: "Obeisance to the Asurāntaka-cakra; I invoke the Asurāntaka-cakra. In the six-petaled [arrangement], after the Asurāntaka-cakra, one says "Obeisance to the Sudarśana-cakra; the Sudarśana-cakra," with the distinction that this applies to all directions.

Then, upon the leaves, proceeding clockwise starting from the east: "Obeisance to Rukmiṇī; I invoke Rukmiṇī. Obeisance to Satyabhāmā; I invoke Satyabhāmā. Obeisance to Nāgnajitī; I invoke Nāgnajitī. Obeisance to Arkajā; I invoke Arkajā. Obeisance to Mitravindā; I invoke Mitravindā. Obeisance to Lakṣmaṇā; I invoke Lakṣmaṇā. Obeisance to Jāmbavatī; I invoke Jāmbavatī. Obeisance to Suśīlā; I invoke Suśīlā."

Then, on the tips of the petals, proceeding clockwise starting from the east: "Obeisance to Vasudeva; I invoke Vasudeva. Obeisance to Devakī; I invoke Devakī. Obeisance to Nandagopa; I invoke Nandagopa. Obeisance to Yaśodā; I invoke Yaśodā. Obeisance to Balabhadra; I invoke Balabhadra. Obeisance to Subhadrā; I invoke Subhadrā. Obeisance to the cowherds; I invoke the cowherds. Obeisance to the cowherdesses; I invoke the cowherdesses."

Then, in the order beginning with the east, one should invoke the eight world-protectors, Indra and the others, in their respective directions: "Salutation to Indra, I invoke Indra; salutation to Agni, I invoke Agni; salutation to Yama, I invoke Yama; salutation to Nirṛti, I invoke Nirṛti; salutation to Varuṇa, I invoke Varuṇa; salutation to Vāyu, I invoke Vāyu; salutation to Kubera, I invoke Kubera; salutation to Īśāna, I invoke Īśāna. Thus one should invoke the eight world-protectors, starting with Indra.

Then, in the presence of each respective [deity], [one should say]: "Obeisance to the Vajra; I invoke the Vajra. Obeisance to the Śakti; I invoke the Śakti. Obeisance to the Daṇḍa; I invoke the Daṇḍa. Obeisance to the Khaḍga; I invoke the Khaḍga. Obeisance to the Pāśa; I invoke the Pāśa. Obeisance to the Aṅkuśa; I invoke the Aṅkuśa. Obeisance to the Gadā; I invoke the Gadā. Obeisance to the Triśūla; I invoke the Triśūla. Thus are the weapons, beginning with the Vajra.

Having thus invoked the deities of the enclosure and established [the deity] with the mantra *narya prajām*, one should worship the Lord—along with the deities of the seat and the enclosure—with devotion using the root mantra and the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), and then perform the consecration of the rosary (*mālā-saṃskāra*).

He should proceed as follows: having washed the rosary with *kuśa* grass water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), using the *gāyatrī*, the five mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, and the root mantra; having placed the rosary upon nine *aśvattha* leaves arranged in the shape of a lotus; having applied the *mātṛkā* vowels beginning with *aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ*; and having again washed it with the *gāyatrī*, the five mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, the root mantra, and the *pañcagavya*, and consecrated it with these very same [mantras]; [he should then wash it] with the *pañcagavya* and pure water while reciting the mantra "sadyojātam... and so forth.

Having washed them again with the repetition of the mantra, having rubbed them with fragrant sandalwood while reciting "To Vāmadeva," having incensed them with black agallochum, guggulu, and other substances while reciting "To Aghora," and having anointed them with musk, saffron, and other unguents while reciting "To Tatpuruṣa," one should consecrate all the gems while reciting "To Īśāna. The mantra is to be repeated for each individual gem.

Then, having consecrated Mount Meru one hundred times with the mantra "aghorebhyaḥ," and having uttered the sequence beginning with "oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ" and ending with "so 'haṃ," he should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) by adapting the formula "the vital breaths of the rosary" (*mālāyāḥ prāṇāḥ*) and so forth. Having invoked the deity of the mantra, Gopāla, therein and worshipped him with the root mantra alone, he should consecrate [the rosary] with the root mantra and the *mātṛkās*. Now follows the ritual procedure for the fire-offering (*homa*) of the rosary-consecration.

Having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), having prepared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) and so forth, having established the worldly fire named Balavardhana upon the ground, having kindled it and meditated upon it, and having taken three fuel-sticks (samidh), one should perform the rites from "Śraddhā, come! up to the end of breath control. Then one should declare: "In this rite of consecrating the rosary (mālā-saṃskāra-homa), I shall encompass those deities who are to be worshipped; with the root mantra, I shall worship the deity of the mantra with one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (ājya)."

Having said, "I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an oblation of the remaining clarified butter," one should perform the rites prior to the principal oblation (pradhānahoma) according to the *āpūrvika* procedure, beginning with the placing of the fire and the adding of the fuel-sticks (*samid*).
Then:
"Oṃ klīṃ, O son of Devakī, Govinda, Vāsudeva, Lord of the Universe!"
"Give me my son, O Kṛṣṇa; I have come to you for refuge. Svāhā!"

Thus, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra. After each oblation, one should pour the residual drops of the butter into the rosary. Having offered one oblation of the remaining butter with the mantra "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā," one should perform the subsequent rites, such as the sprinkling of water, according to the *Āpūrvika-tantra*. If one is unable to perform the fire sacrifice, the rosary should be consecrated by reciting the root mantra twice the number of times prescribed for the sacrifice. Then, one should worship the rosary while contemplating it as the deity, using the mantra "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Siddhi. This is the consecration of the rosary. Then—
Oṃ, O Māṃ, O garland, O great illusion, whose nature is all powers!
The fourfold aims of life have been entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me. Hrīṃ, obeisance to Siddhi.

Having thus paid homage to the rosary with the mantra "Hrīṃ Siddhyai Namaḥ," and having taken it in the right hand while reciting the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati, one should pray, "O Rosary, grant me freedom from obstacles. Then, holding the rosary—covered with cloth or the like—near one's heart, and turning the beads with the thumb and middle finger, one who observes the prescribed rules such as celibacy, with an erect body, should perform the recitation (japa) according to one's ability until midday, either mentally or in a whisper.

On the day of commencement, one should perform the recitation (japa) every day for exactly the same number of times as was performed on that initial day. In the event of anticipated obstacles, the recitation should be continued even until the fourth part of the day has passed; there is no fault of exceeding the prescribed number in such a case. Upon the completion of the recitation, one should pay homage to the rosary with the mantra: *hrīṃ siddhyai namaḥ*, and then recite:
"O Rosary, you who grant pleasure to all the gods and bestow auspiciousness upon me, O Blessed One, always grant me welfare, fame, and valor! *hrīṃ siddhyai namaḥ*."
Having thus placed the rosary upon his head, he should deposit it in a well-concealed place.

Then, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, having performed the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) and the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) as before, and having meditated upon the Deity as before, he should worship the Deity with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*).
[He should pray: "O You, the protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation (*japa*) performed by us."
"O Lord of Gods, may accomplishment be firmly established in me through your grace."

Thus, with a stream of water, one should offer the *japa* into the right hand of the Deity. If one performs the *japa* on behalf of another, then in the place of the word "mayi" (in me), the modification "yajamāne" (in the patron) should be made. In this manner, until the completion of the *puraścaraṇa*, one should worship the Deity every day and perform the ritual actions—beginning from the rules for the seat (*āsana-vidhi*) up to the offering of the *japa*—excluding the consecration of the image (*mūrti-saṃskāra*) and the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the consecration of the rosary (*mālā-saṃskāra*). Upon the completion of the *puraścaraṇa*, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*).

It proceeds as follows: having sipped water (ācamana), restrained the breaths (prāṇāyāma), and worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should invite Brahmā and the other deities and worship them. Here, some also perform the recitation for an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana).

Then, having performed the worship of the deity, one should carry out the rites from the preparation and smearing of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) up to the installation of the fire. In this context, the fire is named Balavardhana.

Then follows the *anvādhāna* (the formal preparation). Having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and performed the rites from "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) up to the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should recite the mantra of Kṛṣṇa the Cowherd who bestows sons, followed by the statement regarding the *homa* rite consisting of a tenth part of the recitation (*japa*), beginning with "In this [rite]... (*yā ityādi*) and ending either with the goddess Prasādhanī or with the *vyāhṛtis*. For the principal *homa*: "I shall sacrifice to Kṛṣṇa the Cowherd who bestows sons, using oblations of sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter, milk, and honey, in a number equal to a tenth part of the recitation, by means of the root mantra."

"I shall worship the deities of the *pīṭha* and the deities of the enclosure with one oblation each of sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter, milk, and honey, or with an oblation of clarified butter alone. "I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an oblation of the remaining substance of what has been offered," and so forth. Or, in the *aṅga-homa*, "Varuṇa with two [verses]," and so on. At the setting out of the vessels, one should set out milk, honey, and sesame seeds together with the clarified butter. Then follows the seating of the Brahman priest and the subsequent rites.

At the time of the circumambulation (*paryagnikaraṇa*) of the clarified butter, having smeared the sesame seeds with clarified butter, milk, and honey, one should perform the circumambulation of those as well along with the clarified butter.

Then, having performed the rites up to the *prasādhanī-homa* or up to the *vyāhṛti-homa*, following the sequence beginning with the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the formal announcement (*anvādhāna*), he should have the principal oblation (*pradhāna-homa*) performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

The priests, having sipped water twice (*dvir-ācamya*), placed their right knees on the ground, and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the ritual of seating (*āsana-vidhi*), and the purifications of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) along with the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, should perform the oblation with attentive minds in the *mṛgī-mudrā*, facing either east or north. The sesame seeds should be measured by handfuls (*culaka*) or in a number of one hundred. The clarified butter (*ājya*) should be the measure of one *karṣa*. A *karṣa* is the measure of sixteen *māṣas*, each *māṣa* being ten *guñjās*. The food (*anna*) should be the measure of a mouthful (*grāsa*).

If the *homa* is to be accomplished over many days, one should conclude it on an auspicious day with a certain number of offerings each day, preceded by the protection of the fire (*vahnirakṣaṇa*). Every day, at the beginning and end of the *homa*, one should worship the principal deity and the subsidiary deities (*aṅgadevatāḥ*). On the day of commencement and the day of completion, one should worship the fire with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), accompanied by *svāhā* and *svadhā*.

When the principal *homa* is completed, one should personally offer to the deities of the *pīṭha* and the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*) a single oblation of sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter, milk, and honey, or a single oblation of clarified butter, according to whichever option was specified during the *anvādhāna*. Then, using the remnants of the offering, one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other subsidiary *homas*, following the specifications stated during the *anvādhāna*. If the *prāyaścitta-homa* was not performed, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* at the conclusion of the *sviṣṭakṛt*; if it was performed, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* at its conclusion. Having completed the remainder of the *homa*, one should perform the subsequent worship (*uttarapūjā*) of the Deity.
Then the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should sprinkle the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), together with his wife, with water from the jar while reciting the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā.

Thereafter, the sacrificer, having given to the officiating priests a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of gold or its equivalent according to his means, and having presented the image along with its pedestal to the preceptor (*guru*), should dedicate the act of the fire-oblation (*homakarman*) to the Lord (*Īśvara*).

Then, having recited the root mantra, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with milk or water amounting to one-tenth of the oblations (*homa*), saying: "I satisfy Gopālakṛṣṇa, the bestower of sons; *namaḥ*. Having performed the sprinkling (*mārjana*) at the end of the root mantra with one-tenth of the libations, saying: "I sprinkle Gopālakṛṣṇa, the bestower of sons; *namaḥ*," one should feed the Brahmins with one-tenth of the sprinklings. If one is unable to perform this preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) oneself, one should have it performed by a preceptor (*ācārya*) who is skilled in this practice. One should give the image to that very preceptor.

In those specific ritual applications where the *homa* itself is the primary element because it bestows the fruit—and not merely as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of a recitation (*japa*)—the number of Brahmin feedings, being unmentioned in the *tantra*, should be taken as that prescribed in the *smṛtis*. In that regard, for a *lakṣahoma*, nine hundred and sixty is the principal option; five hundred and twenty is the middling; and three hundred and ten is the lowest.

Where, because there is no contradiction between the rules prescribed in the Smṛtis and the Tantras as being ancillary to the principal deity, one adopts the position of their combined performance (*samuccaya*) such that the *grahas* are also worshipped, there the feeding of Brāhmaṇas as an ancillary rite must also be performed. In that regard, according to the best option, seven hundred and twenty Brāhmaṇas should be fed; according to the middling option, three hundred and forty; and according to the lowest option, one hundred and ten.

According to the statement, "In the Kali age, it is said to be fourfold," one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* consisting of four hundred thousand repetitions and then undertake the ritual for a specific desire (*kāmyaprayoga*). In that regard, the specific modification in the *saṃkalpa* formula is as follows: "For the sake of pleasing Gopālakṛṣṇa, the bestower of sons, by means of the removal of all defects obstructing the birth of offspring and through the attainment of a secure lineage and a virtuous son, I shall perform the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra of Gopālakṛṣṇa, the bestower of sons, four hundred thousand times. In the case of employing a preceptor (*ācārya*), one should modify the *saṃkalpa* to read, "I shall have [it] performed through the preceptor."

In the case where the recitation (*japa*) is performed by a woman, the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites must be carried out through the medium of a preceptor (*ācārya*) or similar authority. Here, one should feed one hundred and eight Brahmins. The rest is the same as in the *puraścaraṇa* rite. The procedure for the Tantric fire-oblation should be consulted in my work on the "General Procedure for Fire Oblations" (*Sāmānyahomavidhi*).

(Now, those things prescribed for the time of *puraścaraṇa*: stability of mind, purity, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra, freedom from despondency, faith, enthusiasm, contentment, restraint of the senses, celibacy, prostration before the guru, worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day, special worship on specific festival days and occasions, praise of the deity, trust in the deity, and trust in the guru; eating from a row of *palāśa* leaves excluding the middle leaf, eating only once a day in measured portions, eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), eating at night, sleeping on washed *darbha* grass spread over a clean cloth, bathing three times a day, and so forth.
In case of inability, however, merely the morning bath suffices. Now, the prohibited things:)

Speaking unpleasantness or untruth, deceit, intoxication, instability, agitation, indolence, spitting, anger, stretching out the feet, chewing betel, sleeping during the day, walking in the shade of the *karanja*, *vibhītaka*, *arka*, or *snuhi* trees, crookedness, dancing, singing, receiving gifts, conversing with women who have been initiated for a sacrifice, with *śūdras*, with outcasts, or with atheists and the like, looking at *caṇḍālas* and others, wearing many or a single soiled garment, performing optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), performing prohibited acts, eating from a bell-metal vessel, associating with the wicked, bathing in hot water, wearing a tunic (*kañcuka*) and a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), and injury to living beings, as well as the use of sandals, vehicles, and beds.

[The prohibitions include] climbing trees, being naked, having hands devoid of calluses, and overeating. *Vibhītaka* means *behaḍā*; *snuhī* means *niga* or *vaḍuṅga*. From the prohibition against eating from a bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), it is understood that the use of gold vessels and others that have not been used by anyone else is permitted.

As for foods and edibles, they consist of white varieties of grain, winter *nīvāra* rice, *kaṅgu* millet, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, barley, and sugar-cane products other than jaggery, all unhusked by Śūdras; as well as black sesame, mung beans, peas, various tubers, coconut, plantain, *lavalī*, jackfruit, mango, emblic myrobalan, fresh ginger, sea salt, cow's products from which the essence has not been extracted, long pepper, cumin, oranges, and so forth.

But those things forbidden are: jaggery, artificial salt, stale food, food lacking oiliness, sour gruel (*kāñjika*) defiled by insects and the like, *gṛñjana*, eggplant (*vṛntāka*), *śigru*, *bilva*, *karañja*, garlic, onion, radish, and so forth; as well as sesame-oil-fried items, black gram (*māṣa*), lentils (*masūra*), chickpeas (*caṇaka*), wheat, and *devadhānya* grains.

Thus concludes the section on the rite for removing childlessness, the rite for listening to the *Harivaṃśa*, the rite for the worship of the Earth (*Pārthiva-pūjana*), and the rites concerning the mantras of Saṃtānagopāla and Kṛṣṇa, from the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.

Thus ends the fifteenth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā* composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita— who was himself the performer of the Agnicit, Vājapeya, Pauṇḍarīka, and Sarvatomukha sacrifices, and bore the surname Okopāhva Śrīmat Sāgnicit.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Vyāsa has also described medicinal means:
"One should grind the root-paste of *Aṅkola* and mix it with jaggery."
One should eat only as much as fits in a crow's egg; thus, one will suddenly become possessed of sons.
Having taken a sprout from a milky tree and ground it, one should drink the milk;
the affliction caused by Devodara will perish, and one shall obtain auspiciousness.
Having ground the root of the *karṇikā* plant, she should drink milk;
she should not eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and she will quickly become possessed of sons.
The "milk-tree sprout" (kṣīravṛkṣāṅkura) is the banyan sprout (vaṭāṅkura). The "karṇikā" is the *gokarṇī* plant.
[As it is said: "A woman who for three days drinks cumin combined with *nāgakeśara* and cow's ghee will certainly conceive."

Parāśara describes the means in the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha): "Desiring the happiness of a son, she should perform her bath with palāśa leaves at a great sacred ford, during a great conjunction, or at the confluence of a great river."
And Devarāta says:
"On the eleventh lunar day, a woman desiring offspring should bathe [the image] leaf by leaf with a thousand palāśa leaves, using the Sāvitra mantra and accompanied by a pavitra."

(Also in the Baudhāyana Gṛhya-sūtra: "Now follows the oblation for the sake of offspring: during the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, on the new moon day, at the equinox, or at the solstice, having prepared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide either on a riverbank or in the shade of an *aśvattha* tree..."

Having served food to the Brahmins and having caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", he should establish Brahmā in the eastern direction, Dhātṛ on his two sides, Vidhātṛ to the south, and [the other] to the north; then he should worship them, first invoking: "I invoke Brahmā; I invoke Prajāpati; I invoke Parameṣṭhin; I invoke Hiraṇyagarbha. Having thus invoked them, he offers water for the feet with the Sāvitrī verse, using the Sāvitrī.

He should offer white food to Brahmā with those very names, mung-bean food to Dhātṛ, and yellow food to Vidhātṛ. Then, having caused [the deity] to sip water for purification with the Sāvitrī mantra, and having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Praṇava, he worships Brahmā with the mantra:

"Obeisance to Speech, obeisance to the Lord of Speech. He worships Agni with the mantra: "Obeisance to Brahman; the seven-knowing, the seven-tongued, and the sevenfold fire is established. Indeed, the seven universal beings are established in Agni—who else is established?"

"‘Thou art the Reality, thou art the Universe, thou art the Source’—having thus addressed [the husband], he should then summon a woman, bathe her with eight thousand Palāśa leaves while reciting the Sāvitrī, and offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta. With the remnants of those oblations, he should offer on her head while reciting the Praṇava and pay homage to the Adhvaryu priest.
He then adorns both the Adhvaryu and the woman with garments and earrings. Thereupon she becomes pregnant; so says the venerable Baudhāyana."

On the two sides [of Brahmā] are Brahma-dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ. Regarding those—Brahma, Dhātṛ, and Vidhātṛ—the invocation and so forth for Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ is performed with the mantra, "I invoke Dhātṛ," and so on. *Nivedana* refers to the offering of food (*naivedya*). "Eight thousand" means eight thousand plus eight. The rest has a clear meaning.
The method for aphrodisiac treatment (*vājīkaraṇa*) for one with diminished virility has been stated by the Teacher Vaḍava:
"That by which one becomes like a stallion, exceedingly strong and moving without obstruction..."
"That which is called vājīkaraṇa is the supreme vitalizer of the body's vigor."
And its application was stated by that very same author:
"Mustard oil, prepared with a paste of *bhallātaka*, *bṛhatī* fruit, and pomegranate,
when used according to the prescribed method for massaging the penis, makes it resemble the member of a stallion."
In a medical treatise:
"One should cook ghee with sugar, *aśvagandhā*, rock salt, and goat's milk;
from its application as an ointment or through massage, supreme enlargement of the penis is produced."

*Sitā* is sugar. *Aśvagandhā* is *āskanda*. *Sindhūttha* is rock salt (*saindhava*). Other such remedies are to be found in medical treatises such as the *Pañcasāyaka* and others. Even if the desired result is not obtained by these means, one should adopt an appointed son (*dattaka-putra*).
Now follows the procedure for the appointed son.
That procedure is set forth in the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*:

We shall now explain the ritual for the adoption of a son. A son is produced from semen and blood, having the mother and father as its cause; therefore, the mother and father have authority over his giving, abandoning, or selling. However, one should not give away or adopt an only son, for he is for the sake of the continuity of the ancestors. A woman may neither give nor adopt a son without the permission of her husband. One who intends to adopt shall prepare two garments, two earrings, a finger-ring, and a teacher who has mastered the Vedas, as well as sacrificial grass made of *kuśa*.

Having prepared a sacrificial fuel of *parṇa* leaves, he then summons his kinsmen, announces the matter to the king and the assembly, and, having served food to the Brahmins within the house and caused them to pronounce "Auspicious day!", "Welfare!", and "Prosperity!", he performs the rites from the tracing of the altar for the sacrifice to the gods up to the pouring of the *praṇītā* water. Then, going before the giver, he should beg, saying, "Grant me a son," to which the other replies, "I grant. He then takes hold of him, saying, "I take you for Dharma."

"May I take you for the sake of continuity," he says. Then, having adorned him with two garments, two earrings, and a ring, and having performed the rites from the putting on of the garment up to the "mouth of the fire" (the oblation to Agni), he offers the cooked food. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), "He who [thinks] of you with a humble heart," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "For the sake of that well-doer, O Jātavedas. Then, having offered the *vyāhṛtis*, the rite is completed from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards up to the granting of the boon of the cows; he gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of these two garments, these two earrings, and this ring.
"If this is done, a legitimate son (aurasa) is born who has authority over a fourth part," so said the venerable Baudhāyana.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "originating from the semen and blood, caused by the mother and father. By the phrase "caused by the mother and father," there is an exclusion of those born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and others. And this is a qualification of "origination. After the words "originating from the semen and blood," the word "of whom" (*yasya*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. By this, it is indicated that only the legitimate son (*aurasa*) may be given away, abandoned, or sold, and not others such as the adopted son (*dattaka*) and so forth. Regarding the statement "the mother and father have authority": the intention is that the authority for giving belongs to the mother and father alone. For he [the son] exists for the sake of the lineage of his ancestors.

For since that son alone serves for the continuation of the lineage of his ancestors, the meaning is that one should not give away an only son. In the phrase "and the ring," the word *ca* (and) is intended to include items such as an umbrella and so forth. The mention of "grass made of *kuśa*" is for the purpose of making it known that no substitute is permitted here. The same applies to the phrase "the fuel consisting of *parṇa* wood. Regarding the word "in the midst": the intention is that the announcement to the King should be made in the presence of the kinsmen.

By the word *dadāti* ("he gives"), which follows immediately after the mention of the *aṅgulīyaka* ("ring"), the giving of two garments, earrings, and a ring belonging to the son is enjoined. However, a woman may accept [these gifts] only with the permission of her husband; and that [permission] applies only to one who is married, because it serves a visible purpose. For a widow, however, acceptance occurs even without that [husband's permission], by the command of her father, or in his absence, by the command of her kinsmen.
Precisely for this reason, it is said: "The father shall protect the maiden; once she is married, the husband and sons [shall protect her], or [the father] in old age."
In their absence, their kinsmen [shall take charge]; a woman has no independence anywhere.

Thus, Yājñavalkya has stated that dependence upon the husband exists specifically during particular stages of life; in his absence, or when he is incapacitated due to old age or other causes, such dependence likewise applies to sons and others. Kātyāyana also says:
"A woman who is indeed not authorized by her father, husband, or son..."
Therefore, whatever one performs for the sake of the afterlife would be fruitless.

Thus, the permission of the father, husband, and others is stated as referring specifically to a particular stage of life (*avasthā-viśeṣa*). The term *aurdhvadehika* refers to rites pertaining to the next world. That very stage in which the husband’s permission was previously obtained is here reiterated; it is not an unprecedented injunction. Therefore, the moderns (*navīna*) maintain that a widow possesses the right [to perform these rites] even without her husband’s permission. Furthermore, according to the *Dvaitanirṇaya*, one who has been married and has begotten a son may also become an adopted son (*dattaka*). As for the statement by Vṛddha-Gautama cited in the *Dattakamīmāṃsā* and other works—"If an adopted son is born, and at some point a biological son (*aurasa*) should be born..."—[the context remains as follows:]
They shall both be equal sharers of all their father's wealth.

This statement is to be understood as referring to a case where the adopted son (*dattaka*) possesses good qualities while the biological son (*aurasa*) lacks them, because of the qualifying term *yathājāta*. The meaning of *yathājāta* is "one who has a collection of qualities as they are born" (*yathā-guṇānāṃ jātaṃ samūho yasmin*), that is, one who possesses a multitude of virtues; for the word *yathā* has the power to denote similarity when connected with qualities.
For this very reason, Manu says:
"But he whose adopted son is endowed with all virtues..."

"He shall indeed inherit that property, even if he has come from another lineage"—thus [the author] stated that in the absence of a legitimate son (aurasa), the adopted son takes the entire inheritance. That is indeed appropriate when a legitimate son exists, [in which case] he takes a half-share.
Regarding the specific case where the formal rite of adoption (parigraha-vidhi) is absent, the same author says:
"He who adopts a son without performing the formal rite should make him a sharer in the marriage ceremony,
but not a sharer in the wealth."

The meaning is that for one who has been taken [as a son] without the formal rite of adoption (*parigraha-vidhi*), only the marriage ceremony is to be performed, not the giving of wealth; however, in that case, only the wife and others are the sharers of the wealth, because without the rite, sonship is not produced for him. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Gautama says:
"Those sons who may be among one's own gotras, such as the *datta* (given) or *krīta* (bought) and so forth..."
"By means of the prescribed rite they attain the status of the lineage; however, sapinda relationship is not ordained."

The rule is that they attain the status of a lineage only through the prescribed ritual; for the rituals of giving and so forth, by being included within the definitions of the *dattaka* (adopted son) and others, serve to establish their very nature.

As it has been said: "One may take a son by means of water in times of distress. The mention of "distress" (*āpad*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the entire procedure of giving; by this, the procedure of receiving [the child] is also implied. This is because of the *Mānava* [Smṛti]: "Even when obtained from another lineage... which means "obtained according to the correct rite. It was with this very intention that Vasiṣṭha also, having begun by stating, "In the cases of giving, selling, or abandoning him, the mother and father have authority," set forth the procedure for formal acceptance (*parigraha*).

In the statement of Manu, "those begotten [on women] and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the *kṛtrima* (artificially made), *apaviddha* (cast off), and *svayaṃdatta* (self-given) sons. Therefore, the status of these five types of sons as sons occurs only through their acceptance according to the rules prescribed by Baudhāyana and others, and not otherwise. The detailed exposition, however, should be sought elsewhere.

In that regard, one who is five years old, or younger than that, whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not yet been performed according to his paternal lineage (*pitṛgotra*), is to be accepted; but not one who is older, nor one whose tonsure has already been performed. Among these, the son of a brother is to be accepted. In his absence, anyone who is of the same lineage (*sagotra*) or even a sapinda relative. In his absence, however, a sapinda who is not of the same lineage. In his absence, a non-sapinda who is of the same lineage. In his absence, however, even one who is neither a sapinda nor of the same lineage.

Even therein, one must exclude the sister’s son, the daughter’s son, the mother’s sister’s son, and the father’s sister’s son; and likewise, one must exclude those who are unworthy of the notion of being a "son," such as brothers, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles. For the three castes, [the bridegroom] must be of the same caste as oneself. Even therein, he must be of the same sub-caste (*jāti*) as defined by regional distinctions, such as being a Gujarati. Furthermore, he must have brothers and must be other than the eldest brother. The authorities for this should be sought in ancient and modern treatises; they are not shown here for fear of prolixity.
(Regarding this, the [astrological] constellations and so forth are stated in the *Vyavahārasāra*—)

"This acceptance of what has been given occurs when the five [asterisms] beginning with Hasta, the asterisms Abhijit, Vasu, and Puṣya are present; on the days of the Sun, Moon, Jupiter, and Venus; on lunar dates (tithis) excluding the Riktās; and indeed when the signs of Pisces, Aquarius, Leo, and Taurus are rising."
The "five beginning with Hasta" are the constellations Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā. Bhiṣaj is the constellation Aśvinī. Vasu is Śraviṣṭhā. Kṣamāja is Mars (Bhauma). The rest is clear.
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*).

Having fasted on the preceding day, and having prepared two garments, earrings, a ring, an umbrella, a turban, sacrificial grass made of *kuśa*, fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, and other materials for the oblation; having summoned his learned and beloved kinsmen and relatives, honored them, and announced his intention before them, the king—and likewise the members of the assembly—being permitted by them, shall, with sacred grass in hand, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), restrain his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), and proclaim the place and the time.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Lord Śrī Parameśvara, by means of the accomplishment of the discharge of my father's debt resulting from my childlessness, and by means of the accomplishment of protection from the *punannāma* hell, I shall perform the formal adoption of a son," he should worship Gaṇapati as a constituent part of that rite; then, having given food to his circle of kinsmen and to the Brāhmaṇas, he should perform the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*), the *nāndīśrāddha*, the selection of the officiating priest (*ācāryavaraṇa*), and the offering of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).

(However, in the case of acceptance by a woman, there is a distinction in the formula of resolve (*saṃkalpa*), which should be: "This is for my husband and for me. One should have the rites from the worship of Gaṇapati up to the selection of the preceptor (*ācārya-varaṇa*) performed through a Brāhmaṇa. In the formula for selecting the preceptor for the purpose of the *homa* that is an ancillary part of the acceptance of a son, the distinction is as follows: "I choose you as the preceptor for the sake of the *homa* ancillary to the acceptance of a son.")

Then the teacher, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma), having carried out the purification of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) beginning with the scraping, having established there the worldly fire named Balavardhana, having kindled it and meditated upon it, and having taken three fuel-sticks (samidh), he performs the rites from "Śraddhā, come! up to the end of the breath-control. Then, regarding the fire-sacrifice (homa) which is a constituent part of the formal adoption of a son, he recites "Those deities who are to be worshipped" and so forth, ending either with the goddess Prasādhanī or with the Vyāhṛtis. Then, for the specific principal oblation: "I shall worship Agni with an oblation of parched grain (caru)."

"I shall worship Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati with one oblation of clarified butter for each; I shall worship Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an oblation of the remnant of the *caru*, and so forth. Or, in the case of the *aṅgahoma*, "Varuṇa with two [verses]," and so on.

At the setting out of the vessels, he should set down together: the *sruva* ladle, the *darvī* spoon, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling vessel, the vessel for the *caru* oblation, the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), the winnowing-basket (*śūrpa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the mortar and pestle, the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*), two garments, two earrings, a ring, an umbrella, a turban, the *saṃmārjana* (cleansing) *darbha* grasses, the *avajvalana* (igniting) *darbha* grasses, fuel consisting exclusively of *parṇa* wood, sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consisting exclusively of *kuśa* grass, and the clarified butter. Then, having performed the rites beginning with the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers and ending with the bringing forward of the *praṇītā* water, he concludes.
Then the recipient, having gone into the presence of the donor along with the Brahmins and his circle of kinsmen, should stand near him and beg, saying, "Give me a son."

Then the giver, having said "I give," having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), having proclaimed the place and time, and having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), I shall perform the gift of my son," he should worship Gaṇapati and, according to his means, worship the recipient with garments, perfumes, and other offerings. He should then say: "This son, for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord, I bestow upon you—through the accomplishment of the fulfillment of my father's debt, the attainment of the name 'Punnāman' (one who has a son), and protection from the hell called Put, and for my own sake; accept him, he is not mine. The recipient should accept him.

At the end of the words "You [are] my son," he should pour water containing unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and *tulasī* leaves into the hand of the recipient—some say this should be done three times. (In the case of giving to a woman, however, the modification "this son of your husband and of you" must be made in the formula of giving. Then the recipient, having accepted him with both hands while reciting: "Om, at the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I accept you for Dharma; I accept you for the sake of continuity," should seat him on his own lap and smell his head.

Then, for the verse beginning with *yuvaṃ vastrāṇi*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and the Vasus; the meter is Triṣṭubh; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the donning of garments. Reciting: "Oṃ, you two wear garments of fatness... you are united," he should cause [the bridegroom] to put on one of the two garments already placed there. Having caused him to wear the second as an upper garment (*uttarīya*) with this same mantra, having silently tied a turban, applied a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) with saffron and other substances, adorned him with earrings and a ring, and, if possible, decorated him further with other ornaments—

Having brought the child, who is covered by an umbrella and accompanied by dancing, singing, and instrumental music, to his own home while reciting the two verses beginning with "May Indra Vṛddhaśravas grant us well-being" and "The eight divine Vasus, the Soma-loving ones," he should wash the child's hands and feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and seat him on his mother's lap behind the sacred fire.

Then the teacher, having measured out four handfuls of grain with a winnowing basket and having cooked the *caru* according to the ritual procedure for *caru*, having sprinkled it with clarified butter and removed it from the fire, he should perform the rites up to the oblation to the goddess Prasādhanī—or up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations—following the sequence beginning with the sprinkling of water and the kindling of the fires; then he should perform the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*). Having spread a base of clarified butter with the *darvī* ladle, he should take two portions of the *caru* with the *mekṣaṇa* spoon according to the rule for taking portions, sprinkle the taken portion with clarified butter, and offer the remainder of the oblation after pouring it back [into the vessel]. For the two verses beginning with "He who [injured] thee with his heart," the deities are the Viśvedevas and Agni, and the metre is Triṣṭubh.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the principal *caru* oblation in the ritual of adopting a son (*putrapratigraha*). Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "Oṃ, you whom with a longing heart... may we attain," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*): "Oṃ, to whomsoever you, O Jātavedas, [grant] well-being, svāhā. [The dedication is: "To Agni, this... Alternatively, the oblation is performed according to the rules for the invitatory and offering verses as stated in the section on the conjunction of two fires.

Then, one should offer four oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *vyasta* and *samasta* *vyāhṛtis*. The seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details for these [mantras] have already been stated previously. The specific difference in the statement of application (*viniyoga-vākya*) is: "The application is in the principal *ājya*-oblation specifically for the formal adoption of a son.

Then, having completed the remainder of the sacrifice—beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering or the subsidiary oblations (*aṅga-homa*)—one should give a cow to the preceptor (*ācārya*). One should also give those same two garments, earrings, and a ring. The gift of the cow may or may not be performed. Thereafter, one should feed ten or three Brahmins.
Then, having worshipped the fire and caused the declaration of the completion of the rite to be recited, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu for the perfection of the ritual.

In this same manner, the adoption of a daughter given away (dattakaputrī) should also be performed according to the prescribed rule; for in the rules regarding giving and receiving [in adoption], the masculine gender of the person designated is not intended to be significant, and because the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* state that Kuntī was a daughter given away (*dattaka*).

Thus, some maintain that even a woman, with her husband’s permission, must perform the formal acceptance of the gift accompanied by mantras, just as the chariot-maker does. Others, however, argue that since the husband’s permission serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) that establishes the woman’s primary entitlement (*pradhānādhikāra*), the mantras for the oblation and so forth are obtained through the principle of "entitlement based on one already entitled" (*adhikṛtādhikāra*). Consequently, because the exclusion of mantras for women and Śūdras is established by the rule "women and Śūdras [act] without mantras," the acceptance of the gift is likewise accomplished without mantras, just like the acceptance of other types of objects.

Although Medhātithi stated that *dattakatva* (the status of being an adopted son) is an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) form like marriage and is accomplished through a *homa* sacrifice—and since a *homa* is impossible for a woman—nevertheless, Harinātha and others maintain that she should have the *homa* and other rites performed through a Brahmin, just as she performs vows and other observances herself. Furthermore, according to the Kaustubha, even a widow may adopt after obtaining the permission of her living husband or by ascertaining his intention.

In the *Dattakamīmāṃsā*, citing the *Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra*—"Now, [the rules apply] to the son born of a remarried woman (*uḍhaka*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the adopted son (*kṛtrima*), the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the son born of a woman through a female intermediary (*strīdvāraja*), the son born of an Āsura marriage and others, the son born of a woman remarried (*ūḍhaja*), and the son born of a gift (*dakṣiṇāja*), as well as [the lineage] of the two parents"—it is stated that the son born of a woman through a female intermediary is connected to both lineages by the sūtra: "The mother's [lineage] follows, the father's [lineage] precedes.
