Furthermore, the connection to the father’s lineage occurs by virtue of being a son; and sonship arises solely through the father’s authorization, not through formal adoption, because in this case the vow is performed by the woman herself. *Ūḍha* refers to one born of a woman who was remarried (*sahoḍha*).

The *strīdvāraja* is born from a woman, requested by a woman, and exists through a woman. The *dakṣiṇāja* is one born when a maiden has been obtained as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at a sacrifice. The others are well known; thus says Śabarasvāmin.

If it is argued that the adoption of a *dattaka* son is untenable because the author of the *Sūtras* rejected the substitution of a son in the passage, "There is no substitute for ownership, a wife, a son, a country, time, fire, a deity, a ritual act, or a word," we say no. For that [passage] is intended to preclude the pronouncing of blessings and the performance of recitation in cases such as the invocation of the *Subrahmaṇyā* in the *Pitāputrīya* rite, where one must perform the substitution of a son by saying, "I pray for that radiant blessing for the sake of progeny."

Otherwise, there would result a contradiction with many Smṛti texts, such as: "They speak of substitutes for a son. Furthermore, the Śruti passage—"One should say, 'I pray for that luminous blessing for the sake of progeny'; for one who has a son born, a son endowed with splendor and Vedic luster is born"—should be understood as evidence that the pronouncement of such a blessing must not be performed by treating the substitute as the son. Thus ends the procedure for the adoption of a son. Now follows the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punaḥsaṃdhāna*).
Regarding this, the *Gṛhyasūtra* states: "If [the fire] has been interrupted for twelve days, it must be re-established; or, having calculated [the number], one should offer all the *homa*s.

In the phrase "interrupted for twelve days," the word "if there is a *homa*" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, the meaning is that if the *homa* is interrupted for twelve days, the fire must be re-established. Alternatively, the meaning is that one should calculate—that is, count—the evening and morning *homa*s for that same number of days and offer them according to the rule of combination (*samasyavidhi*). In this case, the fire is not to be re-established. And this option applies in times of distress.
Other occasions for performing the rite have also been stated:

"If the *pārvaṇa* [offering] is interrupted, one should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the *pāthikṛta* [rite]; if two [are interrupted], with the *vaiśvānara-pāthikṛta*; if many, there is a re-establishment (*punarādheya*) of the fires; and in the event of loss, destruction, or when the fire has become mixed with other fires, there is a re-establishment.

Here, *pārvaṇa* refers to the *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) performed on the *parvan* days. The word "in that" (*tasmin*) is a locative of occasion, meaning "on account of that. In the phrase "loss," the word "of the fire" (*agneḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

It is indicated that the conditions prescribed by such scriptural statements as, "If the sun rises or sets while his wife is away, for him there shall be a *punarādheya* (re-establishment of the fires)," are to be understood by the word *viśeṣa* (particularity). That which constitutes its destruction even while the fire is present is expressed by the word *vināśa* (destruction). In reality, however, this [work] is indeed superior, because it has been upheld in the *Prayogavaijayantī*.
In the *Śatadvayī*:

"If, during the time of recreation, the wife should go beyond the boundary due to some fault in her actions, the fire will undoubtedly meet its destruction; here, the 'boundary' intended is that of the house."
Maṇḍana [states]:
"If one who has maintained the sacred fires should travel a path of a hundred yojanas without performing the Agnihotra,
his Agnihotra is destroyed."

In some manuscripts, the reading "together with the Agnihotra" is also seen. Likewise: "He who, for a year, does not offer oblations himself but causes them to be offered by a priest or others, for him there shall be either a re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) or the Pavitreṣṭi."
Likewise:
"If one has mounted [the fire] in the araṇis or within oneself without the mantra,
there will be an extinction of the flame, like the extinction of that which was never mounted."
"Even if one has ascended according to the scriptures, if one descends from the scriptural path,
then when the third time for the oblation arrives, there is a re-establishment of the fires."

The mention of "taking [the fire] to the forest" (*araṇy-ātmagrahaṇa*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) which serves as the locus for the ritual transfer (*samārohaṇa*) prescribed for householders. "Jvalana" means fire (*agni*).
Likewise:
"If the sun rises or sets while his wife is away..."
For him, there should be a re-establishment of the fires; however, others say here that it is otherwise.
If the eldest wife is united with the fire, the others may go according to their desire—
either together with the sacrificer or by themselves alone.

Baudhāyana, however, says that if there is only one wife present near the fire, he should remain away from home, sleep on the ground, abstain from sexual intercourse with her, and yet maintain his vow.
"He permits the others to go abroad as they please";
this is stated in the Bhavabhāṣya, and it is also declared in the verses concerning the deceased (preta-ślokas).
If even one [wife] does not remain near the *agnihotra* fire while her husband is present,
some have declared that there is no destruction of the fires.
If the husband and wife go elsewhere at any time— even other than at twilight—
having left the fires either at the edge of the village or at the boundary, some authorities consider the fires to have followed them there.
Others say that [the debt] is lost by going to another village, but not merely by passing [the boundary];
however, they declare that it is lost solely by crossing the boundary itself.
When both have crossed beyond and returned again within the boundary before sunrise or sunset, some maintain that there is no loss [of the ritual] in this case.
If the time for the fire-oblation (*homa*) prescribed in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* has passed,
the fire perishes for those who have crossed the boundary, until sunrise and sunset.
"When the wife crosses a river flowing toward the ocean without the sacred fires, then there shall be the destruction of the fires; such is the Vedic revelation."

Regarding the *Chandogapariśiṣ�*ṭa and the *Karmapradīpa*, it is stated that if the time for the *homa*—which consists of nine *nāḍikās*—is exceeded, the fire (*anala*) would perish. This is not so, however, due to the cause of sunrise and sunset; this is another alternative view. Likewise: "Or, when there is another wife, or when the husband is near the sacrificial fire, then the wife may pass by [the fire] at will, even across a river."

Some say [this refers to] a river that does not flow to the ocean; and this applies when she does not arrive at the time of the *homa* sacrifice. Regarding the section on departure, Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana states:
"If the eldest wife of a man with many wives goes astray..."
"In this matter, those skilled in logic maintain that there should be a re-establishment of the sacred fires."
Regarding transgression by a wife who goes beyond the boundary without her husband or the fires,
that same author states in the section on re-consecration (*punarādheya*):
"If a wife should cross the boundary without her husband and the fires..."
In that regard, others, however, say that destruction [of life] occurs; yet one does not incur fault when traveling out of fear.
If one who has maintained the sacred fires, together with his wife, crosses the boundary and departs,
it is prescribed that he must perform the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) once the time for the fire-oblation has elapsed.
When fire is extinguished by water as its cause,
the re-establishment of the sacred fires (punarādheya) must be performed once the fire has been lost.
If the owner crosses the boundary without having made a formal agreement,
"not making" (asamādhāna) refers to the failure to produce [the agreement] by means of the prescribed rite for following [the rules].
[The boundary is not crossed if it is marked by] pigs, donkeys, crows, jackals, dogs, cocks, monkeys, or Śūdras.
Nor by outcastes, sinners, or corpse-carriers, nor by one in a state of birth-impurity or a woman in her menses.
Or with feces, urine, and excrement; or with pus, tears, phlegm, and blood; or with stool, bones, flesh, and marrow; or even with other loathsome things.

If one touches the fire-drills when they have been set up, or even touches the fire itself, or bathes while the fires are kindled within him, or speaks with those who are outcastes and the like; [these are grounds for loss of caste].
Alternatively, if one, deluded by lust, should approach a woman outside her season,
some declare that on these occasions there is the destruction of the sacred fire.
In that case, if the fire contained in the kindling wood (araṇi) becomes defiled, there should be a re-establishment of the sacred fires;
however, in the case of other such occasions, they prescribe the formal laying of the fires (agnyādheya).
Or rather, "in all cases of injury, there is again the kindling with the words 'punastvā'."

Furthermore, since there is no re-establishment (*punarādheya*) for domestic rites (*gārhyakarman*), there is only a re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃdhāna*). Regarding the matter of touching one who is menstruating (*rajasvalā*), Gobhila also states:
"If a menstruating woman should touch the Agnihotra fire..."
A sacrifice with an eight-potherd cake should be performed for Agni Tantumat.

"Even through contact with Caṇḍālas, outcasts, women in their courses, women who have recently given birth, corpses, and the like, there would be destruction [of the fire]; therefore, one should establish it again," so say some.

Vyaṅkaṭeśa maintains that the mere touching of any fire necessitates the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*). Others hold that the determination depends on whether the act was committed intentionally or unintentionally.
And it is said in the Mahābhārata: "If a woman in her menses should touch the Śrauta fire through ignorance..."
"A sacrifice with an eight-potherd cake is to be performed for Agni Śuci."

In this context, because the term *śrauta* (Vedic) is used as a qualification for the fire, even if there is contact [with an impurity] through ignorance regarding the Smārta fire, there must simply be a re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃdhāna*). Many authorities hold that the distinction based on whether the act was performed directly or indirectly is indeed appropriate. Keśava, Varadarāja, and others maintain that in the case of contact with a Caṇḍāla or a person who has fallen from his caste (*patita*), there must be a fresh installation of the fires (*ādhāna*). Some say the same applies to touching one in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or a corpse. The author of the *Prāyaścittasāra* and others state that upon touching human bone, there must be a re-installation of the fires, whereas upon touching other bones, there is merely the performance of the *Śucīṣṭi* sacrifice.
Maṇḍana says: "When the defect of menstrual flow has arisen, as well as in cases of birth-impurity or death-impurity..."
A learned Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires while traveling abroad deserves to perform the rite of re-establishing the fires (punarādheya).
"And even among many women, one should not approach a single woman who is menstruating;
he should carry the fires in a winnowing basket and deserves to perform the re-establishment of the sacred fires."
"When a wife goes alone taking the fire with her, others say there is a destruction of the sacred fire; however, she incurs no fault if she does so out of fear while traveling."
A wife who does not desire it should not travel alone with the sacred fires;
such a journey is prescribed only when misfortune, such as the loss of the kingdom, has occurred.
Some say that there is no undertaking of any rite whatsoever based on the works of Laugākṣi and others,
even if the wife should become menstruating or be in childbirth.
According to that opinion, there is no re-pledging because it is an alternative to the act of touching;
among those with many wives, the eldest wife touches [the debtor], not the others.
If, while the fires are blazing, no oblation is offered for half a month, then at the end of that fortnight,
one must perform all the omitted homas as if they were a single fortnightly homa.
After performing the *samasya* oblation, the *iṣṭi* becomes *tantumatī*;
there is no need for a re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) there—so says the Kauṣītaki Śruti.
"If there is an omission of the fire-oblation for a year or half a year, there is another opinion [regarding the penance]:
'In times of distress, they are not destroyed, provided the sacrificial fires continue to blaze.'"
In the *Prāyaścittakutūhala*:
"Whether it be a woman or a man who mounts a donkey, a camel, or a bull,
for every *yojana* [traveled], a *kṛcchra* penance must be performed, and even the sacred fire is destroyed."
In the *Yajñapārśva*:
"If a man or a woman mounts an elephant, a camel, or a bull,
for every *yojana* traveled, a *kṛcchra* penance is required and even the sacrificial fire is destroyed."
Furthermore, this prohibition against riding elephants refers to those other than kings, since the riding of elephants by kings is seen in many Purāṇas:
"He whose umbrella and horse [are present], and who possesses the prosperity of riding an elephant, shall occupy the station of Indra; therefore, one should not question him."

This is also from the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), there is a conjunction of [penances] such as the *taptakṛcchra* and re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). The prohibition against riding donkeys, camels, and bulls applies even to one who maintains no sacred fire (*niragni*). As it is said: "If a twice-born man should go about having mounted a camel, a donkey, or a bull..."
Furthermore, his rites must be performed again, including the shaving of the topknot.

For there exists an independent prohibition stating: "At the outset, however, one should perform the penance for three years according to the prescribed rule. But such a prohibition does not apply to the mounting of an elephant, as there is no such specific prohibition against it. Thus, it is established that after the *samāvartana* (return home) and before the production of the *aupāsana* fire, there is no prohibition even for a Brāhmaṇa regarding the mounting of an elephant. Furthermore, in the case of mounting an elephant, there is no combination (*samuccaya*) of the *taptakṛcchra* penance, the re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), and other such rites.

For if a twice-born man should go [on a journey], then according to the immediately preceding cited statement, since the performance of the *taptakṛcchra* penance, re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), and so forth is prescribed specifically for mounting a donkey, a camel, or a bull;
as stated by Yajñapārśva:
"One should not travel during the time for the fire-ritual, nor on a festival day (*parvan*)."
And one should not go for the sake of play or other such pursuits without a valid reason.
"But he who, being an Āhitāgni, out of greed goes on a journey during the junctions of the Parvan festivals,
must perform the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) as an expiation at every menstrual period."
Likewise:
"If one who has maintained the sacred fires should, out of delusion, follow a corpse, then the destruction of those fires would occur; so say the wise."
This refers to another lineage:

"If one who has maintained the sacred fires (agnihotrin) should follow a deceased person out of negligence, one should understand that it results in the destruction of the fires; however, if it concerns a sapiṇḍa relative, it does not constitute a fault."
Thus it is stated in the *Prāyaścittakeśavīkāra*:

"If one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should, through negligence, follow after a corpse, one should understand that his fires are destroyed; however, there is no fault if this occurs among those of the same lineage (*sagotra*)."
Thus, it is stated in the *Prayogadarpaṇa* and in the words of the *Smṛti*:
"In the case of following the corpse of one who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, and upon touching a corpse, there is a re-establishment of the fires (*punarādhāna*).

Some maintain that the mention of the "one who has maintained the sacred fires" (*āhitāgni*) is an elliptical designation for anyone possessing the fires. Other such occasions [for re-establishment] should likewise be examined in that very same source.
The ground for the application of the word "river" is also stated in that very same place:
"The space between the two banks is not what is denoted by the word 'river';
rather, it is the mass of water situated in that location which constitutes the river."
The wise do not accept that water which does not flow for eight thousand bow-lengths deserves to be designated by the term "river."
Others have declared that water which travels a hundred yojanas by a single name is to be designated by the term "river."
Thus, in brief, are the occasions for re-establishing the sacred fires. Now follow the expiations for the abandonment of the fires.
Regarding this, the Smṛti states:
"If the fire is extinguished by atheism, negligence, or laziness in any way whatsoever, an expiation must be performed; it is as follows."
Manu says:
"A Brāhmaṇa who, out of his own will, neglects the sacred fire becomes an Agnihotrī who has abandoned the fire;
he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month, for that is equal to the killing of a hero."
"Apavidhya" means having abandoned or discarded; the construction is "having abandoned [the fire] for a month.
As for what Hārīta says:

"If the Agnihotra has been neglected for one year, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and then re-establish the fires; if it has been neglected for two years, one should perform the Somāyana and Cāndrāyaṇa; if it has been neglected for three years, [one should perform] a year..."
"One should perform the *kṛcchra* penance and then re-establish the fires"—this should be understood as applying when the act is unintentional.

Śaṅkha, however, states: "One who has extinguished the sacred fires shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance for one year and give a cow as a gift. Thus, he prescribes the gift of a cow as an additional requirement for an extinction lasting three years. Viṣṇu also says:
"One who has extinguished the Vedas and the fires shall subsist on alms for one year, bathing at the three periods of the day and sleeping on the ground."
Vyāghra says: "One should avoid fire for two months regarding those two; one should practice in this manner.
However, out of atheism, one should perform one *kṛcchra* penance and offer the materials for the *homa*."

Regarding those two, negligence and laziness: *homadravya* refers to that amount of substance sufficient for the oblation for as long as the oblation has not been performed. Thus it is stated in the *Bharadvāja-gṛhya*:
"For as long a time as one remains without performing the oblation, all that substance [is required];
the gift to the Brahmins is exactly like that oblation."
Jātūkarṇya also says:
"One should offer the oblation into the fire after the time has passed, or one should give it to a Brahmin oneself;
having properly performed the *ādhāna* again, the twice-born man [should do so] for one who knows the Veda."

In this context, the term "oblation" (*homa*) is an elliptical expression for the *sthālīpāka* (cooked sacrificial rice). Although, when the sacred fire has been extinguished, there is no obligation to perform oblations and the like—and thus no fault incurred by their omission—making the offering of oblation-material for the purpose of expiating the loss of the oblation technically unrequired; nevertheless, because the statement of Vyāghra contains the phrase "due to atheism" (*nāstikyāt*), it should be understood that the offering of oblation-material for the sake of expiating the loss of the oblation is to be performed only when the fire is extinguished out of atheism, and not in the case of the other two [causes of extinction]. Mādhava maintains that this offering of oblation-material does not apply when the Śrauta fire is abandoned.
The moderns, however, hold that it is appropriate even when both types of fires are abandoned.
Regarding the abandonment [of food] for four months, Vyāghra himself says:
"But when the four months are fully completed, having abandoned the fire-offering, one should perform the Atikṛcchra penance; thereby one is liberated from the sin."
In another Smṛti as well:
"A twice-born man who abandons the sacred fire out of atheism should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
likewise, he should perform the Atikṛcchra for two months, and for four months."

The meaning is that for the abandonment [of the preceptor] during four months, it is an *atikṛcchra* penance; for six months, a *parāka*; and from beyond that until one year, a milk-vow (*payovrata*). Thus Uśanas says: "He who indeed abandons [the preceptor] after six months should perform a *parāka*."
Thereafter, with a concentrated mind, one should observe the milk-vow for one month.
"The sages of celebrated vows have declared that it lasts for exactly one year."

After six months and up until one year, the general penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) prescribed by Yājñavalkya should be applied in consideration of the caste, capacity, qualities, and other factors of the offender. However, after one year, Manu states: "He who abandons the sacred fire (*agni*) after a year should perform the milk-vow (*payovrata*) for two months, or even for three months."

In this regard, there is an option between the two-month and three-month periods depending on whether the duration of time is short or long. And all these penances apply when one abandons the sacred fire out of atheism (*nāstikya*). However, when one abandons it through negligence (*pramāda*), there is a specific rule in the *Bhāradvāja-gṛhya*: "Up to three nights, there should be a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*); up to twenty nights, a fast; from there upwards until sixty nights, one should fast for three nights; and from there upwards until a year, one should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance."
"With the passage of much time, there is a great accumulation of faults"—
this very point is stated by Aparārka regarding the unintentional abandonment of the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*).
On this same subject, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"But that Brahmin who, O Lord, through negligence abandons the sacrificial fire,
should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) or likewise observe a fast."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "O Lord, listen to me: if one neglects the sacred fire for sixty nights through negligence, one should then observe a fast and thereafter perform a Prājāpatya penance."

By the word "then" (*tataḥ*), a period of three nights is indicated. For abandoning the sacred fire for two months, there is a fast of three nights; for abandoning it for a year, a *prājāpatya* penance is prescribed. However, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, it is stated that if twelve days have passed, there is a fast of three days; if a month has passed, a fast of twelve days; and if a year has passed, a month-long fast or subsisting on milk, or a *kuśmāṇḍī* oblation, or both in succession. This applies when the act is intentional (*kāmataḥ*). In the case of inability to fast, one should subsist on milk for a month. According to the *Madanapārijāta*, after a year, if the lapse of time is even longer, both [the month-long fast and the milk diet] should be performed.
Regarding the abandonment of the fire due to laziness, another Smṛti states:
"When, due to laziness, one abandons the fire after twelve days, then one should perform three days of fasting; likewise, if it is after a month."
There shall be a fast for twelve days when six months have elapsed;
likewise, one should observe the milk-vow for a month when a year has elapsed.
One should perform a month-long fast, or likewise subsist on milk;
one should perform the *kūśmāṇḍa* oblation, or both in succession.
The milk-vow (payovrata) may last for two months or three months, depending on whether the duration is short or long; beyond that, it should be observed when a much longer period has elapsed.
In this manner, there may be a multiplicity of expiations up to three years;
however, for each of those three years, one should perform the Prājāpatya vow for one year.
"In the same way, it may also be performed when the time has passed, and even longer than that.
Now, as an incidental matter, the definitions of the *kṛcchra* and other penances are given briefly.
Among them, the definition of *kṛcchra* is stated in the *Dharmasūtra*:

"Let him eat at night for three days, let him eat during the day for [the next] three days, let him observe the vow of not asking for anything for three days, and for three days let him not eat anything at all.
This is the rule for the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance.
It has also been stated by Manu:

"A twice-born man performing the Prājāpatya penance should eat in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, eat food obtained unasked for three days, and for the final three days he should not eat at all."
Yājñavalkya has also said: "By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for, and by one fast, the *laghukṛcchra* (light penance) is declared."
"In whatever manner [it is performed], that which possesses three qualities (or three parts) is called a *prājāpatya*.

Regarding the phrase "the *laghukacchū* is exemplified," there is an alternative reading: "the *pādakṛcchra* is proclaimed. *Śiśukacchū* is another name for the *laghukacchū*. By the term "in whatever manner" (*yathākathaṃcit*), the four alternatives established in other *smṛtis* are included: [the penance] performed in direct order, in reverse order, like a staff-repetition (*daṇḍakalita*), or with intervals at its own places (*svasthānaviśrāma*). Regarding the measurement of the number of mouthfuls, Āpastamba says:
In the evening, twenty-two morsels are prescribed; in the morning, twenty-six are remembered.
Twenty-four are for the *āyācita* fast, and the three beyond that are for the *niraśana* (complete fasting).
"They should be the size of a hen's egg, or such that they may easily enter the mouth.

Regarding these two views, the distinction is based on whether one is capable or incapable [of fasting]. In the *Pārāśara-smṛti*, however, the first half-verse is recited as follows: "In the evening, twelve morsels are prescribed; in the morning, fifteen are recorded."
But in the Caturviṃśatimata it is said:
"In the morning there are twelve morsels, and in the evening exactly fifteen;
in the ayācita [fast] there are two, and in the next [stage], one eats only air."
The classification of these enumerations is established according to the capacity or incapacity [of the practitioner].
The definition of the *kṛcchra-saṃvatsara* is stated in the Dharmasūtra:
"One should practice in this very manner for a year; that is the *kṛcchra-saṃvatsara*."

Since the twelve-night *kṛcchra* was prescribed in the preceding sūtra, it is that very one which is referred to by the word "thus" (*evam*). This [penance] applies to the repeated consumption of food that is unfit to be eaten.
Yājñavalkya states the definition of the *atikṛcchra*:
"This same [rite] shall be the *atikṛcchra*, [provided there is] eating with a handful of food."

In this context, regarding those nine days during which food is obtained, eating only what fills the palm is prescribed. A "pāṇipūra" is an amount of food equal to a single mouthful. This is according to the statement of Manu: "A twice-born person performing the Atikṛcchra penance should eat one mouthful each day for three days as before, and fast for the final three days."
The definition of *kṛcchra* has also been stated by that same author: "The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of [subsisting on] milk for twenty-one days.
Having determined the size of a mouthful using a leaf-cup or similar vessel, one should consume an amount of milk sufficient for a single mouthful over twenty-one days.

According to the *Madanapārijāta*, one may perform it either according to the number of twenty-two or other counts prescribed by Prajāpati, or for as long as it takes to sustain life. In this context, "payas" (milk) means water, because the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states: "In the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance, however, one should drink cold water.
And Bhavadeva cites the statement of Gautama: "The Kṛcchrātikṛcchra consists of fasting (*abhakṣa*)."
Yājñavalkya states the definition of the *parāka* penance:
"The *parāka* is proclaimed [to consist] in fasting for twelve days.
Jābāli describes the *māsopavāsa-kṛcchra*:
"By fasting for one month, however, there is the destruction of even great sins (mahāpātaka).
Regarding the *yāvakakṛcchra*, Śaṅkha says: "Consuming barley mixed with cow-dung while remaining composed for one month,"
"One should observe the vow of eating only barley-gruel for the removal of all sins."

Manu describes the *taptakṛcchra* penance as follows: "A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air, each for one day, bathing once daily and remaining composed."
But in another Smṛti it is said: "One should drink each of these—boiled milk, ghee, and water—daily for one day each, followed by a fast for one night; this is declared to be the Taptakṛcchra."

The quantity of milk and the other substances has been stated by Parāśara: "One should drink six *palas* of water, three *palas* of milk, and one *pala* of clarified butter; this is prescribed as the *taptakṛcchra* penance."
Having described the *taptakṛcchra*, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "This same [practice], performed with cold [substances], is the *śītakṛcchra*.
Regarding the *sāṃtapana*, Śaṅkha says: "Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass."
"One fast for one night is known as the *sāṃtapana* penance.
He [the same author] describes the *yatisāṃtapana* as follows: "This very same [penance], practiced for three days, is known as the *yatisāṃtapana*."
"Yati-sāṃtapana" is merely a designation; therefore, the eligibility for it belongs not only to ascetics (*yati*), but to everyone. Yājñavalkya describes the *mahāsāṃtapana* as follows:
"One who observes a fast should consume each of the substances of the *sāṃtapana* separately over six days."
"But this Kṛcchra, completed in seven days, is known as the Mahāsāṃtapana."
Yama states: "These very same drinks, each for two days at a time, constitute what is called the *atisāṃtapana* penance; it purifies even a dog-eater. This [penance] lasts for twelve days.
"One should drink cow's urine for three days, and indeed drink cow dung for three days;
then curd for three days, milk for three days, and ghee for three days; thereafter one becomes pure."
(This is a fifteen-day [observance]. Jābāla says: "One should employ each one of these six for three nights.")
"One should fast for the final three days; this they know as the Mahāsāṃtapana."
This lasts for twenty-one days.
Śaṅkha describes the Tulāpuruṣa Kṛcchra:
"Of oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal, [one should consume] each day respectively."
"Through the repeated practice of fasting in between, it is called the tulāpuruṣa."
*Ācāma* refers to the liquid flowing from boiled rice, that is to say, *maṇḍa*.
Regarding the *vajra-kṛcchra*, Aṅgiras says: "One should consume barley-gruel mixed with cow urine."
This Kṛcchra penance, however, has been declared by Aṅgiras himself as being completed in a single day.
"The divine [penance] that removes all sins is known by the name Vajra.
This is an alternative (vikalpa) in relation to the previously mentioned curd and buttermilk.
Yama describes the Cāndrāyaṇa:
"One should increase the piṇḍa by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight;
this is proclaimed as the Cāndrāyaṇa known as 'Barley-Middle' (yavamadhyam)."
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and increase it during the dark fortnight;
this is declared to be the *cāndrāyaṇa* known as "ant-like" (*pipīlikāmadhya*).
Restrained in soul and firm in his vow, one should eat exactly three morsels for a month of sacrificial food (haviṣya);
this is known as the Ṛṣicāndrāyaṇa.
One should eat four morsels in the morning and likewise four in the evening;
this is indeed remembered as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa for children.
"One should eat eight morsels at midday when the sun is in the meridian for an entire month;
this is indeed the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa, which destroys all impurities."

"Śiśucāndrāyaṇa" is merely a designation; likewise, "Yaticāndrāyaṇa" is also a designation. In the cases of the "Barley-Middle" (yavamadhya) and "Ant-Queen-Middle" (pipīlikāmadhya), there is a decrease or increase in the number of morsels corresponding to the decrease or increase of the lunar days (tithis).
And so Viṣṇu says:
"One should eat those morsels without changing the size of the mouth, increasing them gradually as the digits of the moon increase."
"One should increase [the intake] at the full moon and decrease it at the new moon, and one should not eat on the day of the new moon.
Viṣṇu describes the general Cāndrāyaṇa: "In the general Cāndrāyaṇa, one should eat three times eighty morsels in whatever manner possible."

The meaning is that, by observing the rule regarding the number [of morsels] every day, one should eat two hundred and forty morsels in a month. In the various forms of *cāndrāyaṇa*—namely, the *pipīlikā-madhya*, the *yava-madhya*, and others—the commencement may take place on any day, not necessarily only on the first day (*pratipad*). Regarding the measure of a morsel, Yājñavalkya says:
"In the bright fortnight, one should consume morsels equal in size to a peacock's egg, increasing them according to the lunar days (*tithi*). *Śikhin* means a peacock.
Regarding the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, Parāśara states: "One should indeed determine the size of the morsel to be that of a hen's egg.
Śaṅkha, however, says: "In the lunar vow (induvrata), the morsels are prescribed to be the size of fresh āmalaka fruits."

The *induvrata* is the *cāndrāyaṇa*. The application of these various measures is determined by whether one is capable or incapable [of performing them]. The obligatory fast prescribed for the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) and other such occasions is superseded by the rule for the *cāndrāyaṇa*, because this latter is optional (*kāmya*), as stated in the verse: "One should perform this for the sake of dharma, [attaining] the same world as the Moon," and because it is occasional (*naimittika*), being prescribed for specific causes such as the consumption of garlic. However, the optional fast on the eleventh day and so forth may be accomplished through another means.

For it has been stated by Kātyāyana and others that the fruit is obtained even when the rite is performed through a representative (*pratinidhi*). Furthermore, this sublation of the fast on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and so forth does not apply to the general *cāndrāyaṇa*, because in that case there is no rule regarding the consumption of morsels (*grāsa*) every single day. Now, the substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*) in brief:
according to the Caturviṃśatimata—
A *kṛcchra* penance, ten thousand recitations of the Goddess’s mantra, two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
a thousand oblations of sesame seeds, and likewise the complete recitation of the Vedas.
"Twelve Brahmins should be fed, as well as the Pāvakeṣṭi sacrifice;
or else the Pāvamāneṣṭi—thus the wise have declared them to be equivalent."
Parāśara states: "A kṛcchra penance, ten thousand recitations of the Goddess's mantra, two hundred prāṇāyāmas,
and bathing twelve times at a sacred pilgrimage site with the head unwetted [by other water]."
The word division is *anārdra-śiraḥ-snānam* (not bathing with wet hair).
In another Smṛti cited by Aparārka: "Subsisting on air, one should [offer] fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial food, grain, or sesame seeds."
Having offered twelve thousand oblations with the Gāyatrī mantra, one shall attain purification from the kṛcchra penance.
"One who has fasted, observing silence according to the rules at the edge of water, should recite the Goddess twelve thousand times; this is called the Prājāpatya penance."
Some say that *dvādaśasāhasram* means twelve thousand, or a thousand plus twelve. *Jalānte* means near water. Yājñavalkya also says:
"In whatever place a person considers himself to be defiled..."
"In each of those cases, there shall be an oblation with sesame seeds and likewise a recitation with the Gāyatrī."
"Confused" means associated with evil.
Aparārka states:
"Having fasted with faith, one should, according to dharma, offer vessels of sesame seeds."
From twelve exponents of the Brahman, [one receives] an equal amount by means of the Prājāpatya rite.
He who, having fasted while carrying loads of grass upon his head, should personally offer them to a herd of cows for twelve days performs the Kṛcchra penance; of this there is no doubt.
One who subsists on air should satisfy twelve pure Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas with gifts of food and gold; this is called the Kṛcchra penance.

Having performed one hundred and thirty-two breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) during times of distress, one should remain standing facing the east for a day and night; this is called the Kṛcchra penance.
"One of firm vows should perform twelve thousand prostrations before cows, Brahmins, ancestors, and gods; this shall constitute three *kṛcchra* penances."
Regarding the vessels for sesame seeds, it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The sesame vessel is said to be of three kinds: inferior, superior, and middling.
A copper vessel weighing ten palas is proclaimed to be the lowest."
"The middle [penance] is declared to be double that, while the highest is remembered as triple.
A *bhāra* is measured at two thousand *palas*.
Vasiṣṭha says:
One should consume barley-gruel mixed with cow’s urine;
this is declared by Aṅgiras himself as the *aikāhika-kṛcchra* (the one-day penance).
Sitting at night and standing during the day, one should subsist on air for three nights.
"One should understand this as the Prājāpatya penance; one should offer clarified butter with the Kūśmāṇḍa mantras."
In the Mādhavīya, another Smṛti states:
"If a Brāhmaṇa performing the Prājāpatya penance is somehow unable [to do so],
he should properly feed five excellent Brāhmaṇas as desired."

Regarding this, some maintain that according to the *kapiñjalādhikaraṇa* principle, three Brahmins should be fed on each of the five days. Others hold that the number five applies to both [the days and the Brahmins] by way of the *dehalīdīpa* (threshold-lamp) maxim; thus, five Brahmins should be fed in total. In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:
"The *rudraikādaśinī*, the *kṛcchra*, and the *nivartana* consist of twelve parts."
"On the bank of the Sindhu river for one yojana, there are two hundred oblations of clarified butter."
As for the definition of a *nivartana*: "A *nivartana* consists of thirty *daṇḍas* [measured] by a staff of ten *hastas*.
The meaning is that a *kṛcchra* penance is incurred by the gift of land measuring one-twelfth of a *nivartana*.
This is stated in the *Mādhavīya*.
"If one is unable to perform the Prājāpatya rite, one should give a milch cow;
in the absence of a cow, its equivalent value must be given—of this there is no doubt."
In the *Madanaratna*, the *Brāhma* states: "In the absence of cows, there shall be one *niṣka*, or half of that, or even a quarter.
In the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "For a *prājāpatya* penance, however, one cow [is required]; likewise, two for an *atikṛcchra*."
In the Parāka and Taptātikṛcchra penances, it is traditionally taught that those [days] are three each.
"In the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, eight [periods] are to be known, or three, depending on one's capacity."

In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, however, it is stated: "Six fasts are the substitute for a *prājāpatya* penance; and the feeding of one Brahmin is the substitute for a single fast. Regarding the killing of a bird, Śūlapāṇi maintains that the gift of a silver *māṣaka* mentioned by Hārīta—"one should give a silver *māṣaka* or observe a *nakta* [fast]"—is a substitute for the *nakta*. Śūlapāṇi himself also states: "Those performing the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance should perform four *kṛcchras*."
Likewise:
"He who is unable to effect atonement through the Cāndrāyaṇa and Parāka penances should perform five Prājāpatyas for the sake of self-purification."

Bhavadeva states that for the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, four cows [are the substitute]. Here, the various heavy and light options are determined according to whether one is capable or incapable [of performing the primary rite]. These are the substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*).
Now, furthermore, regarding the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punaḥsaṃdhāna*), the following are the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) [suitable for it]:
“Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, the two Punarvasūs, the two Phalgunīs, Hasta, Citrā, Viśākhā,
Anūrādhā, Śroṇā, and the two Uttaraproṣṭhapadas are the lunar mansions for the establishment of the sacred fires.”

The constellation Kṛttikā is singular, despite being expressed with a plural ending. Anūrādhāḥ, Proṣṭhapadāḥ, and Punarvasū are masculine. Phalgunyau and Viśākhe are feminine. The others are clear. [As stated in the rule: "On the new moon day, on the full moon day, or under an auspicious constellation during the waxing fortnight. The waxing fortnight is the first half of the month. By the term "waxing fortnight," although the full moon day is already included, its mention again is for the sake of emphasis and to include the first day (pratipad) of that fortnight as well.

By the phrase "during the waxing fortnight," [the requirement] "under an auspicious lunar mansion" (puṇye nakṣatre) is conjoined; for the word "or" (vā) has no connection here. Furthermore, the re-establishment of the fires should not be performed in the month of Āṣāḍha.
This is because of the statement of Kātyāyana: "A Brahmin should never establish the fires in the month of Āṣāḍha; nor a Kṣatriya in the month of Bhādrapada, nor a Vaiśya in the month of Āśvina."

A Vaiśya is born from the thighs. The detailed account, however, should be known from the Śrauta texts. Since the re-establishment (*saṃdhāna*) of a fire that has been interrupted is occasional (*naimittika*), it is appropriate to perform it even during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) immediately after the occasion arises, provided it has not already lapsed, just like the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice.
With this very intention, it is stated in the *Dīpikā*:
"That which is occasional—such as the re-establishment of the fire following its loss, or [the re-consecration] of the images..."
"When the [rituals] such as the *saṃskāras* have been omitted, then again, the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth,

as well as the fire-offerings for cremation (*dāheṣṭi*) and the like, which were prescribed for their specific times, shall be performed according to the secondary rule (*gauṇa*) when that time has passed; furthermore,
any [ritual] that would otherwise be omitted due to an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) should be extended."

Alternatively, only those asterisms and other factors prescribed for marriage (*vivāha*) should be accepted. In this view, the six principal *ājya* oblations pertaining to the marriage *homa*, along with the three *lāja* oblations, should be understood as being combined either with the *āyāśca* oblation or with a fast (*upavāsa*). This is also logically sound. However, if there is an absolute absence of sons and so forth, then due to the contradiction with the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantra, the six *ājya* oblations are simply omitted; only the three *lāja* oblations are to be performed. Even here, the combination with either the aforementioned oblation or a fast remains applicable.

In reality, however, it should be understood that here the general lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) and so forth favorable for auspicious rites are intended. In this ritual manual (*kalpa*), there is no requirement for the six oblations pertaining to the marriage fire-sacrifice (*vivāha-homa*) nor the three oblations of parched grain (*lājā*). Because there is no confusion [of ritual elements], this alone is appropriate in all cases. It should be observed that in all views, when the rite is performed immediately following the specific occasion (*nimitta*), there is no dependence on the lunar mansions and the like. Now follows the procedure for rekindling the sacred fires (*punaḥsaṃdhāna*).

The performer should first prepare the materials for the oblation, such as the vessel for the *sthālīpāka* and other cooking pots; coverings for surrounding the fire-altar on all sides; branches of the *udumbara* or *plakṣa* trees; sand; saline earth (*ūṣāḥ*); a mound of earth dug up by a rat; a termite hill; earth from a pit; earth trampled by a boar; gravel; fragments of gold and silver; a lotus leaf; shoots of the horse-gram tree, *udumbara*, *palāśa*, *śamī*, and *vikaṅkata*; wood from a tree struck by lightning; and so forth. Sand is well known. Saline earth (*ūṣāḥ*) is alkaline soil.

*Ākhūtkara* is earth scattered by wild rats; *utkīrṇā* (scattered) refers to that which is devoid [of such]. *Utkīrṇā* [in the sense of] dug up refers to village [earth]. By the word *valmīka*, an anthill (*varola*) is meant; its *vapā* is earth having the form of an anthill. *Sūda* is lake-earth; in its absence, crab-earth. *Varāhavihata* is earth scattered by wild boars. *Śarkarāḥ* are small stones, well known in common parlance as *kāṅkara*. As for the nature of a *śakala*, it is stated in the Smṛti: "Half a barley-corn is called a *truṭi*; two *truṭis* are remembered as a *śakala*."

*Puṣkaraparṇa* is the leaf of the lotus (*kamalinī*). The four beginning with *aśvattha* are well known. *Vikaṅkata* is a thorny tree, commonly known in the vernacular as *sutavī*. One struck by lightning is one struck by a thunderbolt; in its absence, one struck by the wind [is used].

Having thus prepared the ritual materials and requisites, if the sign of the disappearance of the firewood occurs at night, then on the morning of the second day, upon its passing, on an auspicious day under one of the asterisms prescribed for the *ādhāna*—namely Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Punarvasu, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hasta, Citrā, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, or Uttaraproṣṭhapadā—or under any other general asterism favorable for auspicious rites, [the sacrifice is performed] together with his wife.

Having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) together with the proclamation of place and time, he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Due to my lack of faith, for this duration of time, I shall perform such-and-such an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord (*śrīparameśvara*), by way of removing the transgression (*pratyavāya*) born from the interruption of the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*). However, if the interruption was due to negligence (*pramāda*), he should say: "due to my negligence for this duration of time"; and if the interruption was due to laziness (*ālasya*), he should say: "due to my laziness for this duration."

Having thus resolved, the husband and wife together perform the penance according to the calculation of the duration for which the sacred fire was discontinued. In case of incapacity, this is done by means of substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*). In that regard, if due to atheism (*nāstikya*) the interruption lasts up to twelve days, the penance is a *parāka*. Thereafter, up to one year, it is a month-long vow of subsisting on milk (*payovrata*). When the year is complete, the vow is either two-monthly or three-monthly. Thenceforth, every year, there is a repetition of this very same [penance].

If the fire is extinguished through negligence for three nights, one must perform one hundred *prāṇāyāmas*. For a period up to twenty-two nights, there is a fast for one day. Up to two months, there is a fast for three nights. For a full year, the *prājāpatya* penance is required.

However, if the interruption is due to laziness, then for a twelve-day period there is a fast for three days. Upon the lapse of a month, there is a fast for twelve days. Upon the lapse of six months, there is a milk-vow (*payovrata*) for one month. Upon the lapse of a year, there is a month-long fast, subsisting on milk, or the *kūśmāṇḍa* oblation; or these may be performed in combination.

In the *Prayogapārijāta*, however, more is stated on this point: for a period up to twelve days, there is a three-day fast; for a period up to one month, a twelve-day fast; for a period up to one year, a month-long milk-vow (*payovrata*); for a period up to two years, a month-long milk-vow and a *cāndrāyaṇa*; for a period up to one year [from two years], a *cāndrāyaṇa* and a *somāyana*; and beyond that, a year-long *kṛcchra* penance, or, for those possessing wealth, the gift of a cow (*godāna*).

One should make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "This sufficient quantity of rice or another grain, or clarified butter (*ājya*), or the substance used for its purchase, intended for the evening and morning *homa*s that have been omitted due to the cessation of the sacred fires through atheism (*nāstikya*), and for the *sthālīpāka* offerings of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), I give to such-and-such Brahmins. Having thus resolved, one should give according to the calculation of the duration of the fire-cessation. If one follows the alternative of performing the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, the formula should be modified after the words "of the *sthālīpāka* offerings of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" by adding "and of the *sthālīpāka* of the *Āgrayaṇa*."

Furthermore, regarding this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) after an interruption, if there has been a delay and the sacrificer has not performed the conjunction of the two fires, then an expiation must also be performed for the interruption of the two fires, calculated according to the respective duration of time. If the interruption was due to atheism (*nāstikya*), there is the offering of the materials for the *homa* and the offering of the materials for the *sthālīpāka*. For a sacrificer who has not yet commenced the *sthālīpāka*, there is merely the performance of the *sthālīpāka* that had been omitted; there is no offering of the materials for the *sthālīpāka* that were lost, because those [materials] have not been commenced. Even the mention of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *āgrayaṇa*, and *sthālīpāka* is not included in the formula of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa-vākya*).

Then, together with his wife, having again performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and the formal proclamation of the place and time, and having made the resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"I shall perform the re-establishment of the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) which was interrupted due to such-and-such a cause"—he should worship Gaṇeśa. Having smeared the fire-altar (*agnyāyatana*) with ashes and cow-dung and enclosed it, he should mark it out as before with any one of the [five] fruits joined with a fragment of copper. Then, having performed the sprinkling, pouring, and placing of water, and having dug up the ground with a spade and sprinkled it, and having strewn sand and [covered it] with branches of the *udumbara* tree...

Having covered [the fire-places] with branches of the *plakṣa* tree, one should silently deposit the earthy materials—namely, sand, saline soil, molehills, ant-hills, fresh earth, earth dug up by a boar, and gravel—and the wooden materials—namely, fragments of gold and silver, a lotus leaf, and leaves of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *palāśa*, *śamī*, and *vikaṅkata* struck by lightning—in the fire-pits. If all the earthy materials are unavailable, one should take sand; if the wooden materials are unavailable, one should take *aśvattha*.

Having thus silently cast in the ritual materials and having brought fire produced from its own source, he should establish it in the fire-pit with the mantra *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om*, kindle it, and meditate upon it. Taking three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and performing the rites beginning with *śraddha ehi* up to the end of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should recite from "those who are to be sacrificed to" (*yā yakṣyamāṇāḥ*) up to the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, for the specific principal oblation (*vaiśeṣika-pradhāna-homa*), he says: "I shall sacrifice to Agni accompanied by the *Mindhā* verses with an oblation of clarified butter."

I shall worship Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and the two Aśvins with an oblation of clarified butter (ājyāhuti). I shall worship Tantumant Agni with three ājyāhutis; Abhyāvartin Agni; Aṅgirasa Agni; Agni with two [verses]; Agni; Vāyu; Sūrya; Prajāpati; Ayāsa Agni; Manasvant Agni; Prajāpati; Saptavant Agni; and Vācaspati Brahmā with an ājyāhuti.
Having performed the limb-offering (aṅgahoma) beginning with "Varuṇa with two [verses]" and ending with the vyāhṛti-homa, one should perform the special principal offering (vaiśeṣika-pradhānahoma).

Regarding the two mantras beginning with *yanma ātmanaḥ* and *punaragniḥ*, Soma is the seer (*ṛṣi*). For the first, the deity is Agni accompanied by *minda*; for the second, the deities are Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and the Aśvins. The meter (*chandas*) of the first is Gāyatrī; the meter of the second is Anuṣṭubh. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the special principal *ājya* oblation for the re-establishment of a domestic fire that has been interrupted. *Oṃ yanma ātmano mindābhūdvicarṣaṇiḥ svāhā.* To Agni accompanied by *minda, this [is offered].*

"Oṃ punaragniścakṣu0 makṣyoḥ svāhā. This [is for] Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and the two Aśvins—[this is] for them. For the three mantras beginning with "tantuṃ tanvannudbudhyasvāgne trayastriṃśattantavaḥ," Agni is the seer (ṛṣi). Agni Tantumat is the deity. The meter of the first is Jagatī; of the second, Triṣṭubh; of the third, Jagatī. Their application (viniyoga) is in the special principal *ājya* oblation for the re-establishment of the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) that has been interrupted. "Oṃ tantuṃ tanvanrajaso0 jana svāhā. This [is for] Agni Tantumat—[this is] for him.
"Oṃ udbudhyasvāgne... meta svāhā"—to Tantumant Agni, this [is offered]. "Oṃ trayastriṃśattanta... svāhā"—to Tantumant Agni, this [is offered].

For the four mantras beginning with *agne 'bhyāvartin*, Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*). The deity of the first is Agni Abhyāvartin; of the second, Agni Aṅgiras; and of the third and fourth, Agni. The meter of the first is Pañcapadōṣṇik; of the second, Pañcapadā Mahābṛhatī; and of the third and fourth, Gāyatrī. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal clarified-butter oblation (*ājya-homa*) specific to the re-establishment of a discontinued domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*): "Oṃ agne 'bhyāvartin... dhanena svāhā. [The dedication is: "This [is for] Agni Abhyāvartin."
"Oṃ agne aṅgiraḥ... mā kṛdhi svāhā"—to Agni Aṅgiras, this [is offered]. "Oṃ punarūrjā... viśvataḥ svāhā"—to Agni, this [is offered]. "Oṃ saha rayyā ni... spari svāhā"—to Agni, this [is offered].

For the *vyāhṛtis* taken individually and collectively, the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as before; the application formula (*viniyoga-vākya*) begins with "vicchinna," etc. "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā"—to Agni, this [is offered]. "Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā"—to Vāyu, this [is offered]. "Oṃ suvaḥ svāhā"—to Sūrya, this [is offered]. "Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā"—to Prajāpati, this [is offered]. Regarding the verse "ayāścāgne": Vāmadeva is the seer, *ayās* and Agni are the deities, and *paṅkti* is the meter. Its application is in the principal *ājya* oblation for the specific rite of one whose domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) has been interrupted.
"Oṃ ayāścāgne... bheṣaja svāhā"—to Ayās Agni, this [is offered].

For the mantra *manojyotir juṣatām*, Agni Manasvān is the deity, Agni is the Ṛṣi, and Triṣṭubh is the metre. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal clarified-butter offering (*ājya-homa*) specific to one whose domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) has been interrupted: "Oṃ manojyoti... ghṛtena svāhā. [The dedication is: "This is for Agni Manasvān."

For the verse beginning with *prajāpate*, the deities are the Viśvedevas and Prajāpati; the meter is Triṣṭubh. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal *ājya* oblation for one whose domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) has been interrupted. "Oṃ *prajāpate na tvad etāny anyaḥ... rayīṇām svāhā*. To Prajāpati, this [oblation]. For the verse beginning with *sapta te agne*, the deity is Agni Saptavān; the meter is Jagatī. Its application is in the principal *ājya* oblation for one whose domestic fire has been interrupted. "Oṃ *sapta te agne samidhaḥ sapta jihvāḥ... ghṛtena svāhā*. To Agni Saptavān, this [oblation].

With the mantra "Cittiḥ srug" (the Daśahotṛ formula), together with the portions known as the *graha* mantras beginning with "Vācaspataye vidhe nāman," Prajāpati is the deity, Vācaspati is the seer, and the Yajus is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the principal *ājya* oblation of the specific domestic fire when it has been interrupted. Having offered eighteen oblations with "Oṃ cittiḥ srug... nṛmṇaṃ dhāt svāhā; to Vācaspati Brahmā, this... and so forth, and having performed the concluding recitation (*saṃsthājapa*) beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa," he should perform the *trivṛdanna-homa* according to the prescribed method, then conduct the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the benediction (*svastyayana*), and the proclamation of prosperity (*ṛddhivācana*), and finally say, "May Agni be pleased."

Then, having immediately performed the *sthālīpāka* for Agni according to the procedure for the *parvan-sthālīpāka*, he should give a pair of garments, a cow, a bull, or the money equivalent thereof as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brāhmaṇa. Thereafter, having fed the Brāhmaṇas according to his means and given them further gifts, he should remember Viṣṇu for the perfection of the rite. "The morning oblation, being a subsidiary part, is prescribed even at an improper time."
Thus say some who are learned in the Gṛhya-sūtras; others, however, maintain that it is not an auxiliary part.

Regarding this, some authors of the Gṛhyasūtras state that because the morning *aupāsana* oblation is prescribed as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*), it must be performed even when the prescribed time has not arrived.

Others, however, maintain that since there is no authoritative evidence for the morning *aupāsana* oblation being a constituent part of the re-establishment, it should not be performed at an un-prescribed time. According to the view of those who hold it to be a constituent part, it must be performed prior to the *Āgneya-sthālīpāka*. According to the view of those for whom it is not a constituent part, the first oblation included within the re-establishment ceremony does not exist at all. Thus, there is an option regarding the performance of the obligatory morning oblation as it pertains to its specific time.
In this regard, there are two verses:
"The commencement [of the rite] occurs at evening, both at the initial installation and the re-installation;
the wise man should begin the *sthālīpāka* on the full moon day."
"On the day of the re-establishment of the fires, the two morning oblations are offered;
thereafter, beginning from evening, one should perform the oblations at their proper time."

Nowadays, the prevalent practice concerns only the commencement of the rite in the evening. If both fires have been extinguished prior to the rule for rekindling (*saṃsarga-vidhi*), then, having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the re-establishment (*punaḥ-saṃdhāna*) of my first domestic fire which has been extinguished," one should, after performing the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for that interruption, re-establish that fire together with the eldest wife; in the same manner, one should re-establish his fire together with the youngest wife.

In that context, where it says "of the first domestic fire," the distinction is that it refers to "the second domestic fire. In reality, however, an expiation consisting solely of fasting and oblations is appropriate, because it is so stated in the Sūtra. The section beginning with "from the taking of the hand" (*pāṇigrahaṇādi*) is an interpolation, as it has not been commented upon; this is indicated by the evidence found in the commentary on the Sūtra regarding the phrase "when [the fire] has gone out, whether of the wife or of the husband."

Regarding this, some teacher will state that by means of the *aupāsana* fire one possesses the status of an *āhitāgni*, and by means of the *pārvaṇa* *caru* offering, the status of one who performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; for this reason, the author of the *Vaijayantī* says in the section on the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), "some [teacher]... Furthermore, that fast (*upavāsa*) should be understood as lasting until evening because it is a daytime rite. As for the oblation, however, it is with the mantra "O Agni, come hither" (*ayāścāgne*). Thus ends the section on re-establishment (*punaḥsaṃdhāna*) in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was himself the son of Śrīmat Sāgnicit Vājapeyayājī Pauṇḍarīkayājī Sarvatomukhayājī Okopāhva.
The sixteenth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā*.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Now follows the procedure for departure. Regarding this, the Gṛhya-sūtra states as follows:

"If he should depart, the procedure for the internal consignment (*samāropaṇa*) has been explained; or he should consign [the fire] into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), or onto a fuel-stick (*samidh*).

According to the rule for the kindling woods, [the sticks] should be made of *khadira*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, or *aśvattha* wood. Having brought fire from the house of a *śrotriya* to the place where he intends to stay, he establishes the fire on that same stick upon which it was consigned, using the two verses beginning with "Being invoked, awaken! (*ājuhvāna udbudhyasva*). The ritual procedure for the oblation (*homakalpa*) has been explained."

The meaning of this is as follows: if he should depart—that is, if he should go on a journey—then it has been explained by the portion of the sūtra beginning with "We shall explain departure other than from the house" and ending with "having brought the common fire (laukika-agni), he causes [the fires] to descend into it. The sense is that he should perform the internal depositing (samāropaṇa) either within himself or into the two kindling woods (araṇī).

If it were merely stated, "If he should go on a journey, the rule for him has been explained," then both the *vāstoṣpati-homa* and the *avasita-homa* would also apply; it is for the purpose of excluding those that the Sūtra is composed in this manner. "Going forth" (*prayāṇa*) means traveling with one's fire and wife; "sojourning" (*pravāsa*) means staying elsewhere than with them, such as in another village for one night or longer. "In oneself" (*ātman*) means in one's own person; the locative case ending is elided according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "Now they say: 'If one who has mounted the two kindling woods should perish,'" the Śruti praises the very superimposition of the Self; thus, the superimposition of the Self is what is meant. The meaning is: "by that same mental construction as [the construction] when [fire] is superimposed upon the two kindling woods."

*Kalpa* means *prakāra* (manner). It was stated that one should deposit [the fire] upon a fuel-stick (*samit*); regarding that, he states the rule for the fuel-stick: "made of *khadira* wood," etc., meaning from any one of the trees beginning with *khadira*. In whatever place one shall dwell—that is, make one's residence—one brings fire from the house of a *śrotriya*, i.e., from the home of one learned in the Vedas. Then, while reciting the two mantras, "Oblating" (*ājuhvāna*) and "Awake" (*udbudhyasva*), he places that very fuel-stick upon which the fire had been mounted back into that fire. This has already been explained.

The phrase "by means of the sūtra" is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]: "From this point onwards, it is constant; beginning with 'in the evening and in the morning,' some transmit the solar [oblation] first in the morning. Alternatively, the meaning is that the *homakalpa* explained in the Śruti refers to the ritual procedure for the *vāstoṣpatihoma*. In this view, the preceding heavy sūtra should be understood as intended to exclude the conclusion of the *homa* (i.e., the final disposal). If this [sūtra] were merely an insertion (*kṣepaka*), there would be no depositing of the fuel-stick (*samitsamāropa*) at all. Since the depositing upon oneself (*ātmasamāropa*) and the depositing upon the kindling-wood (*araṇisamāropa*) are required, they are obtained from the Śrautasūtra. This obtainment is established because the Smārta tradition is recited within the midst of the Śrauta rites.
Regarding one who has performed the self-ascension (*ātmasamāropaṇa*), Baudhāyana has stated the following rules:

"When [the fires] have been ascended into oneself, one should not eat, one should not drink, one should not sleep on high, one should not immerse oneself in water, and one should not engage in sexual intercourse;
however, one may eat at will, one may drink at will, and one may indeed sleep on high at will."

"One should not engage in sexual intercourse after immersing oneself in water. "Upari" means on a bed or similar surface. The phrase "one should not immerse oneself in water" prohibits immersion (*nimajjana*) specifically, but not bathing (*snāna*). For bathing is of two kinds: that consisting of immersion and that consisting of ablution (*āplavana*). Of these, immersion consists of submerging oneself within the water. Ablution, however, consists of the washing of the body, as prescribed in such passages as "having bathed with cold and warm waters, having sipped water, they perform the ablution.
Therefore, in the *Avabhṛtha* sacrifice—

The statement in the Sūtra—"The wife and the sacrificer, having bathed, run after each other on the back while immersing themselves"—is consistent with this, as it describes a mode of bathing distinct from mere immersion (*majjana*). However, if immersion (*majjana*) is performed, there must be a re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*).
Thus says Maṇḍana:
One might sink along with those who have ascended to the Self, or speak with outcasts and the like;
or else, deluded by passion, one might approach a woman outside her season.
Regarding these omens, some say there is the destruction of the fire;
or rather, in the event of all such calamities, there is the rekindling [of the fire] with the words "punastvā."

The phrase "in those cases where [the fire] has mounted onto oneself" (ātmarūḍheṣu) applies everywhere. In this statement, because the destruction of the fire is said to be only optional (*pākṣikatva*) due to conversing with outcasts and so forth, or approaching a woman during her menses, it is understood by implication that in other cases there is no destruction of the fire at all. Furthermore, according to the *Pradīpa*, when one transgresses any other rule—excluding sexual intercourse and bathing—the recitation of the *Manasvatī* mantra is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Here, the mention of sexual intercourse and bathing is intended to indicate conversing with outcasts and the like, in order to maintain consistency with the *Maṇḍana*. Āpastamba states in the *Ātmasamāropaṇakaumudī*:

"If one should immerse the fuel-stick (*samidh*) mounted on the fire in water, or if the fire mounted on oneself should immerse itself in water, one should immerse either the head or the right hand; some say this constitutes a cause for re-establishing the sacred fires (*punarādheya*).

This distinction should be understood as follows: in the case of the option of depositing [the fire] in the mouth, the immersion of the head is prohibited; in the case of the option of depositing it in the hand, the immersion of the hand is prohibited.
In the *Prāyaścittasāra*, concerning the imposition of the self [upon the deity], it is stated:
"Having immersed oneself in water, one should not bathe, nor should one approach a woman;
likewise, after voiding urine or feces, one should not remain impure for long."
Baudhāyana says:

"Now, if one should practice what is forbidden by the vow while the fires are mounted upon oneself, or if there should be the aforementioned defect regarding the destruction of the kindling woods—since the destruction [of the fires] has been stated to occur through the destruction of the kindling woods—one must perform the re-establishment of the fires (agnyādheya)."

The intended meaning here is as follows: when the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) are damaged, their abandonment alone has been prescribed; through that, the destruction of the fires occurs because they are "mounted" (*samārūḍha*) upon them. Likewise, by viewing the two hands as being equivalent to the kindling woods, it was stated that either the aforementioned fault regarding the destruction of the woods would apply, or else the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) would be required. However, no such fault is possible in the case of the inner self (*antarātman*). Nevertheless, if one were to intentionally perform an act contrary to one's vows (*avrata*), such as eating what is forbidden to eat, then a fault would accrue to the self, resulting in the necessity for rites such as re-initiation (*punarupanayana*).

In that case, because the fires have been mounted [upon the kindling woods], their destruction occurs at that very moment, and there must be a re-establishment (*punarādhāna*). However, since the body merely occupies the place of the *āyatana* (the locus), even if touched by a Śūdra or others, purification is achieved simply through bathing and so forth. Otherwise, even the *Gāyatrī* and other mantras would be destroyed. Although the Self (*ātman*) is all-pervading, when the fire has been mounted specifically upon a particular location, one may go about after wrapping the *araṇī* or the fuel-stick (*samit*) with seven, five, or three layers of cloth.
And this has been stated in the *Yajñapārśva*:
"Endowed with seven, or five, or even three layers of wrapping..."
"The two kindling woods (araṇī) are not defiled by contact with those who have fallen [from their caste] and the like."
The fuel-sticks should also be understood as being like the fire-drill (araṇī). Regarding the materials for wrapping, Śaunaka has stated:
"Deer skin, woolen blanket, darbha grass, cow hair, hemp, birch bark, and palm leaf—these are remembered as the sevenfold wrapping."

It should be understood that in the view of five materials, there is the exclusion of birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) and palm leaf (*tālapatra*); and in the view of three materials, there is the exclusion of cow-hair cloth (*gocarma*), hemp cloth (*śāṇa*), birch bark, and palm leaf.
Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*).

When about to depart, having first taken the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) that were accepted [by him], he performs the ritual with the verse "This is your womb... (*ayaṃ te yoni...*). Agni Jātavedas is the deity, Agni is the seer, and Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the act of consigning the fire (*samāropaṇa*). Reciting "Oṃ, this is your womb... wealth," while being assisted by his wife, he consigns the fire into those two [drills]. Then, having placed the two fire-drills in a pure spot at the place of residence and having prepared the fire-altar (*agnyāyatana*), he performs the descent [of the fire] with the verse "Descend" (*upāvaroha*). The Viśvedevas are the deities, Jātavedas is the seer, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter; its application is for the act of descending the fire (*upāvarohaṇa*).

Reciting, "Oṃ, descend, O Jātavedas, into the dwelling," the sacrificer, while the wife maintains contact with him, descends [the fire] by churning before sunset; having made it well-kindled and performed the consecration of the site, he should establish that fire. At the time of churning, while another person performs the churning, he remains touching the two kindling woods (araṇī) for as long as it takes for the fire to be born. If the effort of production is fruitless, then the mantra should be recited again and the effort renewed. The mantra belongs to the sacrificer alone.

Regarding the self-ascension (*ātmasamāropa*): for the verse "O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice" (*yā te agne yajñiyā*), the deities are the All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*), the meter is the *triṣṭubh*, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the self-ascension. With the words, "Oṃ, O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice... come to your dwelling," he ascends [the fire] into himself.

Then, at the place of residence, having established the *araṇis* in a pure spot before sunset, he descends [the fire] with the mantra, "O Jātavedas, descend. Regarding this "internalizing of the fire" (*ātmasamāropa*), some say it is the heating of the right hand over the fire; others say it is the heating of both hands. Having heated them silently, one should take that heat into the mouth with the mantra; or, according to others, having heated them with the mantra, one should take it into the mouth silently.

The "descending" (*upāvarohaṇa*) consists of releasing the breath through the nose while superimposing the Self [upon the fire]. This is according to the view that the heat is to be grasped in the mouth; however, if one follows the view that it is merely the warming of the hands, it should be understood as touching [the fire] with the mantra. If the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) have not been formally accepted, then one should fetch a common worldly fire from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), establish it in a consecrated place, and perform the descending of the fire superimposed upon oneself into that [new fire] using that same mantra.

Regarding the transfer of the fire (*samitsamāropa*), however, one should take a fuel-stick (*samit*) from any of the *khadira*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, or *aśvattha* trees, and having placed it upon that [fire] with the mantra "This is yours" (*ayaṃ te*), one should establish the common fire (*laukikāgni*)—brought from the house of a *śrotriya*—in a purified location where one dwells, within a consecrated place; having kindled it and placed the fuel-stick upon which the fire was transferred into it with the two verses beginning "Oblating... (*ā juhvāna*) and "Awake! (*udbudhyasva*), one should perform the daily oblation (*nityahoma*).

If the sacrificer is ill or away on a journey, he should appoint a priest for the purpose of the *samāropa* (the internalizing of the fires), and the rite should be performed by him. In the absence of such a person, it may even be performed by his wife; for it has been established that a substitute is indeed permissible for the sacrificer in rites other than those constituting his own personal consecration (*saṃskāra*). If she too is unfit, it should be performed by a son or another relative. However, the *ātmasamāropa* must be performed by the sacrificer himself or by his wife, and not by the priest, a son, or others.

In times of distress or when it is time for departure, if the sacrificer is absent, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) must perform the *araṇī-samāropa* (the consigning of the fire into the two kindling woods). It should be understood that the wife may likewise perform the *ātma-samāropa* (the consigning of the fire into herself), and so forth. Regarding the consigning of the fire into the *araṇīs* and the fuel-stick (*samit*): if the mantra "This is your womb" (*ayaṃ te yoniḥ*) is not recited due to error, or is recited incorrectly, then the consigning is not accomplished. If the fire is lost because it was neglected due to an error regarding the consigning, the fire must be produced according to the rule for expiation for loss (*anugata-prāyaścitta*), and not by means of the rule for deconsigning (*avaropa*).

Furthermore, "re-linking" (*punaḥsaṃdhāna*) refers specifically to the re-establishment [of the fires]. When the sacrificer has gone abroad, the wife must have the fire re-linked by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) before twelve days have passed, on account of the cause of following the fire. However, after that period, once the sacrificer has returned, there is only "re-linking. In that case, the wife alone must perform the renunciation of her vows (*saṃkalpa*). Likewise, the re-linking of the fire on account of causes such as the loss of the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) occurs only after the sacrificer’s return.

When the sacrificer has gone abroad and his wife has reached her menstrual period, even if the fires have been extinguished, the officiating priest must indeed perform the expiatory rites beginning with the re-establishment of the fires for the purpose of atoning for the extinction of the fires. It should not be argued that the formal consigning (*samāropa*) and deconsigning (*avaropa*) of the fires do not take place during a period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) because of one's impurity, nor that these two acts should be performed by the priest; for this is contradicted by the indicative power of the mantras, and because the agency of the sacrificer himself is established by his own and other sūtras as well as their commentaries.

If, however, impurity (āśauca) should occur on the day of the full moon (parvan) for one who has established the sacred fires, then there must be a re-establishment of the fires (punar-saṃdhāna). If, through error, one performs the subsidiary oblations (saṃskārāṅga-homa) and so forth without first performing that re-establishment of the fire, then upon remembering the omission, one should offer the universal expiation (sarva-prāyaścitta), but not perform the primary ritual action again. At the time of crossing the village boundary and at the time of crossing a river, the husband and wife perform the "taking hold of the fire-drills" (araṇy-anvārambha); if this is not done, the fire becomes common (laukika).
Some say that even when crossing various boundaries, this applies only to the first and the last.

In times of distress, when the sacrificer is absent, the wife alone takes hold [of the fire].
