When there are multiple wives, it is mandatory that the eldest alone takes hold, according to the statement in the *Saṃgraha*: "The eldest wife of one who has many wives takes hold of the fire, not the others. There is no taking hold by the wife during the self-transference (*ātmasamāropa*). It should be understood that even when the sacrificer has not departed, if the wife goes to another village or crosses a river at the time of the oblation, the fire becomes merely worldly (*laukika*).

Thus ends the procedure for departure. Now follows the procedure for living abroad. Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "We shall explain living abroad excepting [the case of] the house; 'Prepare the fires,' etc., ending with 'he looks at his wife. Here, the commentary is presented only for that portion of the Sūtra which is relevant. Having recited the two mantras beginning with "May we not go astray," he comes to the place of the sacrificial fire-altar (*vihāra*). He restrains his speech in the presence or near the fires. In their absence, having gone to a place where the roofs (*chadīṃṣi*) over the fires are no longer visible, he releases his speech.

He states that the performance of the vow must be carried out at the time of the vow: "he performs the vow during the times of the vow. The vow consists of such rules as "one should not eat from the time of the *prāduṣkaraṇa* until the *homa*," and so forth. He further states that this must be done at every season (*ṛtu*): "he attends [the fire] at each season. This means that in the event of a delay due to travel, one should perform the attendance upon departure for each season—that is, every two months.

If he should encounter a journey while away from home when the fires have not been formally established (*anupasthita*), he should, while still at that very spot, turn toward the sacrificial fire-enclosure (*vihāra*) and proceed after having performed the *upasthāna* rite there. Having returned from his journey, while standing at the place from which the first roof-tiles of the fires become visible in the next area, he should restrain his speech, approach the fires, and then release his speech.

It is a worldly maxim that "what man would wake a superior, great, and venerable man who is fast asleep—that is, sleeping deeply? Therefore, who could possibly be the awakener of Agni? According to the opinion of some teachers, the worship (*upasthāna*) is to be performed for Agni precisely when he has not been made manifest—that is, while he is covered with ashes—and that [worship] is to be done with the two [mantras] beginning with *abhayaṃkara*. Since the worship of the unmanifested [Agni] has already been prescribed in its proper context, it is the rule for the minor worship (*alpopasthāna*) alone that applies here, not the former one.

Because that [rite] pertains to many fires, the plural form in the phrase "of those not made manifest" (*aprāduṣkṛtānām*) is employed according to the Śruti, since there are many fires in that case. One who is about to go on a journey should perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) with the mantra: "O Giver of Fearlessness, grant me fearlessness; may it be well with me as I depart. But having returned from his journey, he should say: "O Giver of Fearlessness, you have granted me fearlessness; may it be well with me as I have returned. Then he should perform the rites beginning with "O houses, do not fear" and ending with "he looks at his wife. Regarding the matter of silence, two views have been stated by Maṇḍana:
Beginning from the vicinity of the fire, he remains silent until the sacrificial grass is seen at the dwelling place of the bearer of oblations.
"The intention of the Sāṃkhyāyanas is that one should maintain silence for exactly as long as it takes for the fires to come within the range of vision."
When the fire has been established in the *araṇi* wood and one has departed on a journey, that very same [text] states:
"Even the fire established in the *araṇi* must be attended to with fear-dispelling mantras,
because it cannot be led away, like a fire covered by ashes."
Regarding this matter, another view has also been stated by that same author:
"Or else, whether one should depart while the fire is in the kindling-wood or return [after it has been established],
in both cases there is no ritual attendance (upasthāna), according to the Kauṣītaki Śruti."
If, after performing the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), one does not go on a journey, then the attendance upon [the fire] that has arrived must certainly be performed.
And thus, that same [text] states:
"If, having performed the attendance with the thought 'I shall go on a journey,' one does not actually go on the journey..."
And regarding this, the Kauṣītaki Śruti also speaks of attendance upon those who have arrived.
Having formed the intention, "I shall go abroad on account of a journey," if one does not actually depart, the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) must nevertheless be performed.
Regarding this, the same author says: "If, after intending the ritual attendance prior to departure, one turns back..."
Those who follow the logic of established procedure know that one must indeed attend upon [the preceptor].
"In that case as well, the arrival and attendance are desired, according to the Kauṣītaki Śruti.
If the attendants of the king and others do not grant an opportunity for attendance, then one should depart after performing the attendance right here.
And thus, that very [text] says:
If powerful men such as kings forcibly lead away the sacrificer,
those of cruel disposition do not grant him the opportunity to perform his ritual attendance.

"At that time, being situated in that very place, one should perform the attendance (upasthāna) for all the fires according to the ritual procedure (tantra), using the mantra beginning with 'ihaiva' and so forth."

In the Gṛhyasūtra, however, one should employ only this mantra: "Being here, [I call] you who are there" (*ihaiva santas tatra santam tvā*); not the one beginning with "O Agnis, being here, [I call] you who are there" (*ihaiva santas tatra sato vo agnayaḥ*), because fire is singular.
Even if one should encounter the necessity of traveling abroad while staying anywhere at all, this same rule applies.
And so says Maṇḍana:
"I shall come this very day," having said this, he departs without attending [to the ritual];
if by chance he remains there, some say he should perform this very rite.
However, if one who was staying anywhere else, upon arriving in exile, has forgotten and failed to perform the rite, even in that case this same rite must be performed.

And likewise Maṇḍana says: "Even when [the time] has been forgotten, this same rule should apply even then. Regarding departing without having performed the attendance out of pride and intentionally, he himself says:
"When one has departed intentionally out of pride without performing the attendance..."
"Having performed the recitation for what has not yet been mastered, this same procedure shall apply there as well."
This refers to what was just mentioned: the form of worship (*upasthāna*) performed right here.

Regarding this, the commentators on the *Bharadvāja-sūtra* have also stated that there is an oblation with the *manasvatī* verse: "If one departs on a journey without having performed the worship, then one offers the *manasvatī*."

Even in the case of failing to perform the attendance (*upasthiti*) for one who has arrived, this same expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is to be understood. In the view that the attendance is performed with the word "here" (*iha*), the phrase "may we not go away" (*mā pragāma*) is omitted. Furthermore, Maṇḍana has stated that the restriction of silence (*vāgyama*) is optional:
"In the view that the attendance is performed with the word 'here', the phrase 'may we not go away' is dropped."
The author of the Bhāṣya has shown that there is no violation of the vow of silence in this case.
But others say that the omission of the mantra is an indicative mark for the omission of silence;
[in the view] that "here" [is the mantra], there is nothing else—thus Narayana declared.

Some maintain that the worship performed with the mantra "ihaiva" (right here) must be done only with the "abhayaṃkara" (fear-dispelling) formula, as it is a worship performed on the occasion of [the guest] having departed. Others hold that by the word "ihaiva," the worship is performed with that very [mantra]. The worship performed upon [the guest's] arrival is not done with "ihaiva. Thus says Maṇḍana:
"The worship with 'ihaiva' is intended for one who has departed, not for one who has arrived.
In this regard, however, the worship performed upon returning is indeed done with the "abhayaṃkara" formula alone.
The *Manasvatī* oblation is prescribed in the Sūtra for an absence exceeding ten nights:
"If he travels away for more than ten days, the Adhvaryu offers an oblation with the mantra, 'May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]'.
Maṇḍana also states: "Āśvalāyana says that having traveled abroad, one should offer the oblation after more than ten nights have passed."

The act of returning home and so forth should be performed only after the *manasvatī* oblation. Thus says Maṇḍana: "When the *manasvatī* oblation has been offered, [one performs] the returning home and so forth.

The Commentator [Śabara] maintains that this *manasvatī* oblation is included within the *prāduṣkṛta-upasthāna* (the ritual attendance upon the fires made manifest), and thus it is neither the *abhaya-kara-upasthāna* nor the *iha-upasthāna*. Others, however, desire the *manasvatī* to be performed on the fire that has been drawn out for the purpose of the oblation; the sequence of the Sūtra is likewise such. But in the case of staying away for more than a year, there is the *pavitreṣṭi*.
And likewise Maṇḍana [states]:
"Having been away for more than a year, one should sacrifice with the Pavitreṣṭi";
thus Baudhāyana and others have declared, while others do not accept the sacrifice.
Wherever one might perform the *iṣṭi*-portion, having offered the *manasvatī* oblation there,
one should again spread the fires, perform the *iṣṭi*, and proceed with the rites such as returning to the house.
"If the time sufficient for the *iṣṭi* is not obtained on that day,
then everything should be performed at that very time, and only the *iṣṭi* itself [completed] on the following day."

In the domestic ritual (*gṛhya*), however, at the place where the *iṣṭi* would occur, there is a *caru* offering (based on the scriptural injunction: "Those *puroḍāśa* cakes which belong to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) are, for one who has not maintained them, *caru* offerings"). Regarding absence during a season, the *vrātabhṛtī* sacrifice is mentioned by some; here too, there is a combination with the *manasvatī* offering. For absence during a season, the *vrātabhṛtī* is performed; for absence exceeding a year, the *pavitreṣṭi*. This is stated in another *sūtra*: "If he should remain absent for a season, he should sacrifice with the *vrātabhṛtī*; if he should remain absent for a year, [he should sacrifice] with the *pavitreṣṭi*."

In another Sūtra, however, it is said: "If he should dwell abroad for a year, he should perform the Pavitreṣṭi or the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice. Thus, the Vaiśvānarī is also mentioned as an alternative. Commentators explain that in all cases, the mantra *mano jyotiḥ* is to be combined [with the other offerings]. In the *Candrikā*, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"For one whose dharma has been stumbled upon and who is being oppressed by his powers..."
"There is a two-month period of exile beyond which one does not [return], like one who has maintained the sacred fires."

The meaning is that for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there is no prohibition against traveling abroad after two months have passed, as there is for one who has maintained the fires (*āhitāgni*).
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* that one may travel abroad after appointing a twice-born man for the sake of the fire-oblations:
"Having deposited the fire in his own wife and likewise having appointed a priest..."
"A Brahmin who has business should travel abroad; he should not dwell there for long without purpose."
In this context, "one who has business" refers to one seeking wealth, not one seeking sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and the like.
And so Maṇḍana says:
"For a maintainer of the *agnihotra* fire, it is indeed proper to go abroad in order to acquire wealth."
"For with wealth one may perform sacrifices, but one would not go to sacred fords and such places."
He himself states the reason for not visiting sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*) and the like:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, cows, Brahmins, the ancestors, and the deities—
the sacred sites and ascetic powers reside in the house of one who maintains the *agnihotra*."
Upon reaching a sacred ford (tīrtha) en route, one must certainly perform a ritual bath;

as it is said: "If one traveling for the sake of wealth or other purposes should happen to reach a sacred ford along the way, a modest person may bathe there, but he should not travel separately for that purpose."

The specific rule is that during the journey, upon reaching the point of boarding a boat, they should place a winnowing basket filled with earth there, or having placed the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) therein, or while holding onto the *Tapatī* river, they should proceed to the opposite shore.
Now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*).

Intending to go on a journey, having sipped water (ācamana) and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) for the purpose of departing," he attends upon the fire while it is covered with ashes, saying: "O Giver of Fearlessness, grant me fearlessness; may it be well with me as I am about to depart. Then he departs from that place, reciting: "May we not stray from the path, nor from the sacrifice, O Indra, we who possess Soma; may our enemies not stand against us. Lead us upward, O Agni, you who are invoked with clarified butter; unite us with abundance of wealth and with many offspring. Thus he goes.
From this point onward, he restrains his speech until the roof-shingles become visible, or until the fire becomes visible; immediately thereafter, he releases his speech.

If there is a lapse in the restraint of speech during the interval, he performs the recitation of the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" (the Vaiṣṇava ṛc) and the recitation of all the Vyāhṛtis, and then restrains his speech again. Upon returning to the house, he restrains his speech as long as the roof-shingles remain visible, or until the fire becomes visible.

Then, having returned home, washed his hands and feet, sipped water (ācamana), and released his speech, he worships the fire while it is still covered with ashes, saying: "O you who grant fearlessness, do not cause me fear; may there be well-being for me; I have returned from my journey. This must be performed by one staying abroad at every change of season. In this case, even if there has been no departure from that place, one must simply perform the worship and observe the vow at the prescribed time.

If, however, while staying anywhere, one should fall into exile, then remaining right there and facing his own fire, he should perform the worship (*upasthāna*) with the verse "ihaiva santatra santam tvā... (VS 3.18). For this verse, the Viśvedevas are the deities, Agni is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter; its application is for the purpose of worship. Having performed the worship with the mantra: "Oṃ, remaining here, I worship you, O Agni, who are there, with my mind and thought," he may depart. If men such as kings lead him away by force and do not grant him the opportunity for worship, then he should perform the worship while still in that place.

Upon returning from a journey, immediately after performing the *upasthāna* (homage), one should perform the rites beginning with "Do not fear the house," and so forth. This will be explained later, following the examination for the pacification of the site (*vāstuśamana*). If one who has performed the *upasthāna* and departed returns on that very same day, the *upasthāna* must indeed be performed again. Even if the knowledge of impurity (*āśauca*) arises after the returner has already entered the house, the *upasthāna* for the one who has returned still takes place.
As Maṇḍana says in a Śrauta text:
"When the impurity of dust has arisen, as well as during birth-impurity or death-impurity,
one should perform obligatory and occasional rites, but no rite performed for a specific desire."
By this very [rule], there is no fault even when traveling to a place from which one cannot return.
As for that which was said:
"When the impurity of menstruation has arisen, or during birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka)..."
"A learned Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires while traveling abroad deserves to perform the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya)."

Thus, this [verse] prohibits travel for one who has consecrated the sacred fires (*agniyukta*); otherwise, the term "one possessing the fires" (*agnimat*) would be rendered meaningless. As for those prohibitions against traveling during periods of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) and so forth, they pertain to the domain of *smārta* (domestic) rites, according to the *Prāyaścittakutūhala*. Some, however, say that it prohibits travel for one who has personally enkindled the fires (*ātmasamārūḍhāgnika*). In reality, however, in this statement beginning with "when the defect of menstrual flow has arisen," the word "also" (*api*) should be construed after the word "one possessing the fires."

And likewise, just as there is a prohibition against the movement of one who is joined with fire—that is, one upon whom fire has been formally mounted—so too is there a prohibition for one who is devoid of fire. In this way, the practice of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is also upheld. Regarding this, some hold that during a period of impurity (āśauca), the attendance upon the domestic fire (gṛhyāgni) does not take place; others hold that it certainly does take place because this [attendance] is also based on Śruti.

In the case of the *araṇi* (the fire-drill), even for the fire that has ascended into the *araṇis*, there is worship with a non-terrifying mantra, just as one approaches a fire covered by ashes. Likewise, if one goes out without performing the mental worship of the fire that has ascended into the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), then upon returning, there is the *manasvatī-homa* and the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). If one goes out unintentionally, there is the recitation of the three *anājñāta* verses and the universal expiation. Even if one fails to perform the worship upon returning, this same expiation applies.

If one is away from home for more than ten nights, the *manasvatī* offering must be made. If the absence exceeds a season (*ṛtu*), a *caru* oblation is to be offered to Agni Vratapati. If the absence exceeds a year, one should offer oblations to the deities of the *pavitreṣṭi*: therein, a *caru* to Agni Pavamāna; clarified butter (*ājya*) to Sarasvatī Priyā; a *caru* to Agni Pāvaka; clarified butter to Savitṛ Satyaprasava; a *caru* to Agni Śuci; clarified butter to Vāyu Niyutvat; and a *caru* to Agni Vratapati; and clarified butter to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.

A *caru* offering is for Agni Vaiśvānara; clarified butter is for Dadhikrāvan. The oblation is performed in due order according to the procedure involving the *āghāra* libations, following the method prescribed for the *sthālīpāka*. Alternatively, only the *sthālīpāka* for Vaiśvānara need be performed. In both cases, however, there is a combination with the *manasvatī* verse. Standing facing the direction in which the fire is located, one should perform the propitiation (*upasthāna*) connected with the oblation.

When the husband is away on a journey, the wife must have the *aupāsana-homa*, the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, and occasional expiatory rites (*naimittika-prāyaścitta*) performed through a priest. Only the formal renunciation of ownership (*uddeśa-tyāga*) is to be performed by herself. If she herself is menstruating or has recently given birth, then even that renunciation must be performed by the priest alone. As for the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, however, it may be performed according to the secondary rule: "Having caused the *agnihotrī* cow to be milked elsewhere, one should offer the oblation with her milk."

Furthermore, the *sthālīpāka* offerings performed on account of events such as the rekindling of the sacred fire or the burning of a house should not be performed until the husband’s return. When the occasion for a *sthālīpāka* arises for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is required. Regarding the cause of travel, it is wealth and knowledge, but not pilgrimage sites and the like. If the husband is unable to go abroad for the sake of acquiring wealth, the wife must also undertake the journey for that purpose even without performing the ritual invocation (*upasthāna*). However, she is not required to perform the invocation associated with the fire-oblation (*homa*).

The performance of the vows, however, certainly takes place. Regarding the entire procedure for travel (*pravāsa*) prescribed in the *Gṛhya* texts, it should be understood that whether performed or not performed, there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in its omission; yet, if performed, there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*). Nevertheless, according to the view favoring its performance, it must by all means be carried out. Thus ends the procedure for travel. Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) for the *sthālīpāka* that has been omitted.

The performer, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—“I shall sacrifice with the *sthālīpāka* for the traveler together with the *sthālīpāka* for [the deceased] so-and-so”—and having kindled the fire, meditated upon it, taken three pieces of fuel (*samidh*), and performed the rites beginning with “O Faith, come! up to the end of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), says: “In this rite of the *sthālīpāka* for [the deceased] so-and-so, which is interspersed with that for the traveler, I shall encompass all those deities who are to be sacrificed to; I shall sacrifice to Agni Pathikṛt with an oblation of cooked rice (*caru*); I shall sacrifice to Agni with an oblation of cooked rice; I shall sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with an oblation of the remainder of the cooked rice. These...

Having said, "I shall sacrifice to the deities immediately," he should place the fuel-sticks for the *anvādhāna* into the fire, surround the fire with grass, and then, having spread *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, he should set down upon it the wooden ladle (*darvī*), the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), two pots for the sacrificial porridge (*carusthālī*), two stirring-spoons (*mekṣaṇa*), a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), a mortar (*ulūkhala*), a pestle (*musala*), *darbha* blades for sweeping, *darbha* blades for kindling, clarified butter, and fuel-sticks.

If one accepts the alternative view stated by Āśvalāyana—that "one should offer this oblation after having separated it [from the main portion] by means of impossibility"—then the distinction is that there is only one *caru*-pot, only one stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), and either two vessels for the separation or just one.

From that point, the procedure from the preparation of the strainers (*pavitra*) up to the removal of the *caru* is the same. In this latter view—where one offers after having separated it—the designation is: "This is for Agni Pathikṛt; this is for Agni."

Then, having sprinkled water around the fire and silently placed the prepared fuel-stick upon it, he takes a portion from the first *caru* with the first *caru*-ladle that was set out and offers it with: "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Pathikṛt. [The formula for the disposal is: "This is for Agni Pathikṛt.
Then, taking a portion from the second *caru* with the second *caru*-ladle, he offers it with: "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni. [The formula for the disposal is: "This is for Agni."

Then, taking portions from the northern halves of both sacrificial oblations (*caru*) one by one with that *mekṣaṇa* spoon into the *darvī* ladle, he offers them into the northeast, not touching the previous two offerings, with the mantra: "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. [The dedication is: "This to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

In the case where both oblations are cooked in a single vessel, since there is only one *mekṣaṇa*, the offering should be made by skillfully scooping from both oblations with that very *mekṣaṇa*. However, in a rite involving many deities, because such a method is impossible, one should take the portions into the *darvī* ladle with the *mekṣaṇa* and perform the offering with that ladle.

Then, having performed or not performed the removal of the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*), one should perform the dismissal of the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*), the *vyāhṛti* oblations, the subsequent sprinkling (*uttarapariṣeka*), the worship of the fire, the concluding recitation (*saṃsthājapa*), the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), the feeding of the Brahmins, the giving of further gifts, the remembrance of Viṣṇu, and the dedication to the Lord (*īśvarārpaṇa*). Alternatively, only the *pāthikṛta* rite need be performed; however, even the ordinary (*prākṛta*) rite must not be omitted once its time has passed.

If this *sthālīpāka* has not been performed even at the subsequent festival (*parvan*), then, preceded by the penance (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of a quarter-*kṛcchra*, one should perform the *vaiśvānara-sthālīpāka*—either alone or with a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) using the standard *sthālīpāka*—and immediately thereafter the *pāthikṛta-sthālīpāka*. This latter should be performed either with a common ritual procedure together with the second *sthālīpāka* that was omitted, or as a standalone rite. Alternatively, the *vaiśvānara* and *pāthikṛta* rites themselves may be performed without a common ritual procedure.

If, however, the second [offering] was not performed at the subsequent parvan, then, having performed half a *kṛcchra* penance on the first day (*pratipad*) and so forth, one should perform these two very same *sthālīpāka* offerings—either independently or as part of a combined ritual (*samānatantra*)—together with the *vaiśvānara* and *pāthikṛt* offerings using the standard *sthālīpākas*.
If the third [offering] was also not performed at the subsequent parvan, then there is simply a re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punaḥsaṃdhāna*).

The period up until the *uttara-sthālīpāka* (the subsequent rice-pot offering) constitutes the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) for the preceding [rite]. It is only upon the transgression of this [secondary] time that expiations such as the *pāthikṛt* are required, not upon the transgression of the primary time (*mukhyakāla*). This is the first position. The second position holds that this expiation is required even upon the transgression of the primary time. Furthermore, if the *sthālīpāka* has been interrupted due to the wife being in a state of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) or being in her menses (*rajasvalā*), it must not be performed on the second, fourth, fifth, eighth, ninth, fourteenth, or fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight.
This has been stated by Āśvalāyana in the *Prayogapārijāta*:

"One should not perform the ancestral sacrifice on the fourteenth day, nor on the fourth day, nor during the middle five days, nor on the ninth or the second day; likewise, the oblations should not be offered."

Regarding the term *madhyapañcake*: "in the middle" (*madhye*) means within the fortnight (*pakṣa*), specifically on the eighth day; "in the pentad" (*pañcake*) means on the fifth day, specifically on the fifth lunar day. Some maintain that one should not say, "The *madhyapañcaka* is that which is both the middle and a pentad," because such an interpretation would result in the prohibition of the days from the sixth through the tenth, thereby rendering the mention of the ninth day redundant.

Since the mention of the ninth day (*navamī*) serves the purpose of demonstrating the extreme gravity of the fault [of omission], it is possible that there is no fault in performing the rite on any of the other lunar days—the sixth, seventh, eighth, or tenth—if [the rite] cannot be performed on the ninth; however, others maintain that on the ninth day, the rite must not be performed under any circumstances. The term *āhutayaḥ* means the oblations of the *sthālīpāka*.
In the *Sāyaṇīya*, Prajāpati states: "The New Moon and the Full Moon sacrifices are omitted, or perhaps both of them."
"For one [offense], there shall be a pādakṛcchra; for two, half is proclaimed."
Thus concludes the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* performed in a concealed manner.
Now, the construction of a house by a householder, which follows as a matter of course, is described.
Regarding this, the following is the *Gṛhyasūtra*:
"One intending to have a hall built [should do so] during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under the asterism Rohiṇī, or under the three Uttaras," and so forth.
Regarding this, the restriction of months has been stated by Nārada:
"Mārgaśīrṣa, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, Māgha, Śrāvaṇa, and Kārttika..."
"The months for the construction of a house are those that bestow sons, health, and wealth. *Saumya* refers to Mārgaśīrṣa.
The days of the week and so forth are also mentioned in that same source: "All days of the week, with the exception of Sunday and Tuesday, bring auspiciousness."
Having obtained the strength of the moon and the sun, when the ascendant is aspected by benefics.
"The raising of pillars and so forth should be performed; however, one should avoid other [inauspicious] times.
Regarding the asterisms, Garga has stated: "The three Uttaras, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Anurādhā, and the three Karas (Hasta, Citrā, and Svātī)..."
"The pair of Dhaniṣṭhās and Revatī are commended for the commencement of building a house."
The three *karas* are Hasta, Citrā, and Svāti. The two *dhaniṣṭhās* are the constellations Dhaniṣṭhā and Śatatārakā. *Pauṣṇa* is Revatī. The detailed account is to be found in the *Śāntiratnamālā*.
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*).

During the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, under any one of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) such as Rohiṇī, Uttarā-phalgunī, Uttarā-āṣāḍhā, or Uttarā-proṣṭhapadā—or, if these are unavailable, under any other mansion prescribed by the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra)—at a moment (muhūrta) indicated by an astrologer; having performed his daily obligatory rites, sipped water (ācamana), and restrained his breath (prāṇāyāma); having announced the place and time and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "Intending to have a hall constructed, I shall perform the fire-oblation (homa)"; he should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa and so forth, ending with the Nāndī-śrāddha.

In this context, the specific variation occurs in the sentences such as "O venerable sirs, declare an auspicious day for the rite of laying the foundation," and in the sentence designating the deity of the auspicious day, which should be: "May Vāstoṣpati be pleased."

Then, having kindled the *aupāsana* fire and meditated upon it, and having taken three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), he should perform the rites from "O Faith, come! (*śraddha ehi*) up to the end of the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Having recited from "Those deities which are to be sacrificed to" (*yā yakṣyamāṇāḥ*) up to the end of the *vyāhṛti*s, and having performed the subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*) starting with "Varuṇa by two [verses]" up to the end of the *vyāhṛti* oblations, and having completed the subsidiary oblations, the *jaya* and other minor offerings, and ending with the recitation of the *saṃsthājapa*, he should perform the triple-oblation of food (*trivṛd-anna-homa*) and the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*).

In that regard, there is a specific modification in the formula for the *anvādhāna* (the preliminary rite of adding fuel) concerning the two acts of preparing the *śalākā* (wooden splinters) and the *homa* (oblation). Here too, [the formula] is simply "May Vāstoṣpati be pleased. There is no special *vaiśeṣika-homa* (distinctive oblation) here; and the *jaya* and other [oblations] are optional in this case.

Then, having put on a new (unwashed) garment and sipped water twice, [he performs the rite]. For the mantra "devasya tvā" (*devasya tvā savituḥ...*), Soma, Agni, or the Viśvedevas are the deities; Savitṛ is the deity; the *abhri* (wooden spade) is the object; the *yajus* is the meter. Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the taking up of the *abhri*. Having taken the *abhri* with: "Oṃ, by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I take thee; thou art the *abhri*, thou art the female helper (*nārī*)," [he proceeds]. For the mantra "parilikhitam" (*parilikhitam rakṣaḥ...*), Soma is the deity; the pit (*avaṭa*) is the object; the *yajus* is the meter. Its application is in the tracing around [the pit].

"Oṃ, O Parilikhita, I cut thee around. With this mantra, he traces the pit three times clockwise—once with the mantra and twice silently. In this manner, having dug as many pits as required, he scatters the earth from the pits inside the hall. The sequence for raising [the posts] follows the sequence of the pits. "Oṃ, right here I fix the firm hall; may it stand in safety, sprinkling ghee."

"O house, may we follow you, possessing good heroes, all heroes, and unharmed heroes. With these words, he raises the southern pillar of the doorway; the meaning is that having raised it, he places it in its hole.

Then, having placed before him the best of the twice-born and a full water-pot adorned with curds, unbroken rice, copper leaves, flowers, and fruits, and having given gold and garments to the twice-born, he should enter his own home, which is the abode of auspiciousness and peace.
Likewise:
"He who enters a new house without performing the worship of the site (vāstupūjā) experiences various diseases, afflictions, and all manner of calamities."
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*):
"O houses, do not fear; do not tremble. Bearing strength, we come to you. Bearing strength, a seeker of wealth and wise, I come to the houses, rejoicing in my mind."
To those whose homes become radiant with joy when one departs on a journey or returns from it—we invoke those houses; may they recognize us as we recognize them.
Invoked here are the cows; invoked are the goats and sheep.
And so, the sweet essence of food is invoked within our homes.
Invoked are the friends who have many companions and share in mutual joy;
may all our men be unharmed, and may our homes be secure at all times.
Full of vigor, full of milk, full of refreshment, indeed from the ocean; never perishing, never thirsting—O houses, do not fear us!

Thus, preceded by a married woman (*suvāsinī*) carrying a full water-pot, accompanied by his chosen deity and his family, he proceeds toward the house. At the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) indicated by the astrologer and others, he enters the house, reciting: "Oṃ! For your well-being and for peace I enter; O Auspicious One, O Beneficent One, may there be well-being, may there be well-being. Immediately after entering, on this day, he does not engage in any quarrel.

"Oṃ! I enter these houses with a well-disposed mind—houses that do not destroy heroes, but are full of heroes and very gracious; carrying abundance and being well-intentioned, may I dwell within them with a well-disposed mind."
Thus he sits down in the middle of the house.

With the words, “Oṃ, may we indeed cross over all enemies with you, as one crosses flowing waters,” he gazes at his wife. If there are two wives, the word *tvayā* (with you) is modified to *yuvābhyām* (with you two); if there are many wives, it is modified to *yuṣmābhiḥ* (with you all). Regarding the phrase “he has not come on this day,” the inclusion of the word *āgataḥ* (come) is intended to indicate that this rule for entering applies even to one who has not yet established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) but has returned from another village. Therefore, this rule applies both to the entry into a new house and to the arrival from another village.

Some maintain that this [rite] is intended only for the entry into a new house; that is not correct, because the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*—in the passage stating, "Even one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) should look upon his house"—shows that the entry is prescribed even for one who has not established the fires when returning from another village. Others, however, maintain that it applies only to the arrival from another village; that too is not correct, because it contradicts the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra* which speaks of "entering the house" (*gṛhaprapadana*). Therefore, it should be understood that it is appropriate for both purposes. This rule applies even to the entry into a house that has already been prepared.
However, if preparing one or two halls is required, one should enter that very place after pacifying it according to the prescribed procedure.
Thereafter, the worship of Gaṇapati and the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) should be performed. Whatever else is obtained through family tradition should also be done.
Thus ends the ritual manual for the preparation of the site, the pacification of the site, and the entry into the site, from the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*.

Thus ends the seventeenth section in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Smārta-Saṃskāra-Ratnamālā* composed by Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita— who was himself the performer of the Agnicit, Vājapeya, Pauṇḍarīka, and Sarvatomukha sacrifices, and bore the surname Okopāhva Śrīmatsāgnicid.
This first book of the Gṛhyasūtra is completed. || 1 ||
Thus, the first half of this *Saṃskāraratnamālā* has reached its conclusion here.
